docs.title: React Hooks and Effects
docs.text: Hooks are functions that let function components use React features such as state and context. Effects synchronize a component with systems outside React, such as subscriptions or browser APIs.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Hooks support reusable stateful logic without class components. Effects are useful when rendering must connect to an external system, but using them for ordinary calculations can make code harder to follow.

docs.title: How effects work
docs.text: useEffect runs after React commits a render. Its dependency list tells React which reactive values the effect uses. A cleanup function can unsubscribe or release resources before the effect runs again or the component is removed. Development Strict Mode may run setup and cleanup an extra time to reveal unsafe effects.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function OnlineStatus() {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    const update = () => setOnline(navigator.onLine);
    update();
    window.addEventListener("online", update);
    window.addEventListener("offline", update);
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener("online", update);
      window.removeEventListener("offline", update);
    };
  }, []);

  return <p>{online ? "Online" : "Offline"}</p>;
}

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Follow the Rules of Hooks: call hooks at the top level of a component or custom hook, not conditionally or inside loops. Dependency array lists reactive values used by an effect; cleanup reverses external setup; custom hook reuses stateful logic between components.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• An effect is not the normal place to derive one value from another; compute derived values during rendering when possible.
  • An empty dependency array does not mean “run once in every environment”; development behavior and component remounts matter.
  • Effects do not run during server rendering.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Synchronizing with Effects
  • React reference: useEffect

docs.title: React Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review React's component model, state, rendering, and common application patterns.

docs.title: 1. What is React?
docs.text: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components. It describes UI based on data and updates the rendered interface when relevant state changes.

docs.title: 2. What is a React component?
docs.text: A component is a reusable unit of UI, commonly a JavaScript function that returns React elements. Components can receive props and use state and other React features.

docs.title: 3. What are props?
docs.text: Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child. A component should treat its props as read-only and ask the owner to change data through callbacks or shared state.

docs.title: 4. What is state?
docs.text: State is data managed by a component or React store that can change over time. Updating state requests a render; it does not directly mutate the already-rendered UI.

docs.title: 5. Why should state not be mutated directly?
docs.text: React relies on update patterns and identity to reason about changes. Mutating existing state can make updates hard to detect and reason about. Create updated arrays or objects and pass them through the state setter.

docs.title: 6. What are Hooks?
docs.text: Hooks are functions such as useState and useEffect that let function components use React features. Call Hooks at the top level of a component or custom Hook, not conditionally or inside loops.

docs.title: 7. What is useEffect for?
docs.text: useEffect synchronizes a component with an external system after rendering, such as a subscription or browser API. It is not needed for every calculation or for deriving values that can be computed during render.

docs.title: 8. Why do list items need keys?
docs.text: Keys help React match items between renders so it can update the correct elements. Use a stable identifier from the data; array indexes can cause incorrect state association when items are inserted, removed, or reordered.

docs.title: 9. What is reconciliation?
docs.text: Reconciliation is React's process for comparing the new element description with the previous one and determining updates to apply. It is an implementation concept, not a guarantee that every update has a particular performance cost.

docs.title: 10. What is a controlled input?
docs.text: A controlled input gets its current value from React state and updates that state through an event handler. An uncontrolled input keeps its current value in the DOM and can be read with a ref or form APIs.

docs.title: 11. What is Context used for?
docs.text: Context makes a value available to descendants without passing it through every intermediate component's props. It is useful for shared values such as theme or locale, but frequent broad updates may cause unnecessary rendering.

docs.title: 12. What is a ref?
docs.text: A ref stores a mutable value that persists between renders without itself triggering a render. Refs can also reference DOM elements for focus or measurement when appropriate.

docs.title: 13. What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
docs.text: useMemo caches a computed value between renders when dependencies are unchanged. useCallback caches a function identity. They are performance tools, not correctness fixes, and should be used when measurement or component behavior justifies them.

docs.title: 14. What is an Error Boundary?
docs.text: An Error Boundary catches certain rendering errors in its descendant component tree and displays fallback UI. It does not catch every error, such as most event-handler errors or arbitrary asynchronous failures.

docs.title: 15. What is Suspense used for?
docs.text: Suspense displays a fallback while a supported child operation is pending, such as certain code-loading or data integrations. It only handles work integrated with Suspense; it does not automatically track every Promise.

docs.title: 16. How should a React component be tested?
docs.text: Test observable behavior: render the component, interact as a user would, and assert visible results or accessible state. Keep tests focused and avoid depending unnecessarily on private implementation details.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React overview
  • React documentation
  • React: Rules of Hooks

docs.title: 17. A component shows stale search results when a slower earlier request finishes last. How do you prevent it?
docs.text: Treat each query as a distinct request and prevent obsolete results from replacing the latest state. With an effect, abort the previous fetch using AbortController during cleanup, or track a request identifier and ignore responses that are no longer current. Also represent loading and error states explicitly. Do not rely on response order matching request order.

docs.title: 18. A list of editable rows loses typed values after items are reordered. What is likely wrong?
docs.text: The list may use array indexes as keys. React uses keys to match sibling elements between renders, so an index can cause component state to follow a position instead of the item. Use a stable unique identifier from the data. If the underlying item identity truly changes, choose a new key intentionally so React resets that component's local state.

docs.title: 19. A component renders in a loop after adding an effect. What do you inspect?
docs.text: Check whether the effect updates state that appears in its dependency list, causing another effect run, and whether dependencies are recreated on every render. Determine whether the effect is actually synchronizing with an external system; derived values usually belong in render or a memoized calculation, not an effect. If synchronization is needed, make the effect idempotent and provide correct cleanup.

docs.title: 20. A child wrapped in memo still renders every time its parent renders. Why?
docs.text: memo can skip rendering only when props compare equal by its comparison behavior. New object and function literals have new identities on each parent render, so they can invalidate the comparison. First measure whether the render is costly. Then reduce unnecessary prop changes or use memoization where it provides a measured benefit; memo, useMemo, and useCallback are not guarantees against all renders.

docs.title: 21. A subscription keeps firing after a component disappears. What should the effect do?
docs.text: The effect should return a cleanup function that unsubscribes using the same subscription handle or callback identity. Cleanup also runs before an effect re-synchronizes when dependencies change. Test mount, dependency changes, and unmount; development Strict Mode may intentionally run an extra setup/cleanup cycle to reveal effects that are not safe to repeat.

docs.title: 22. Two distant components need the same data, and updating Context makes a large part of the app render. What options do you consider?
docs.text: First confirm the cost with the Profiler. Keep state near the components that own it when possible; split Context values by update frequency or responsibility, or use a state store with selectors when the application needs fine-grained subscriptions. Context is a propagation mechanism, not automatically a performance problem, and premature global state can make ownership harder to follow.

docs.title: React Lists, Forms, and UI States
docs.text: Lists, forms, and request states are common building blocks in React applications. Model them explicitly so the interface remains understandable for loading, empty, success, and error situations.

docs.title: Rendering lists and keys
docs.text:
Use map() to return UI for each item. A key helps React match items between renders and should come from stable data such as a database ID.

function TaskList({ tasks }) {
  if (tasks.length === 0) return <p>No tasks yet.</p>;

  return (
    <ul>
      {tasks.map((task) => (
        <li key={task.id}>{task.title}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

Keys are only required among siblings and are not passed to the component as a normal prop. Array indexes can cause incorrect associations when items are inserted, deleted, or reordered; use them only when the list is static and never changes order.

docs.title: Controlled form fields
docs.text:
A controlled input gets its value from React state. Its onChange handler updates that state:

import { useState } from "react";

function SearchForm() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");

  function submit(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    console.log("Search:", query);
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={submit}>
      <label htmlFor="query">Search</label>
      <input
        id="query"
        value={query}
        onChange={(event) => setQuery(event.target.value)}
      />
      <button type="submit">Search</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Controlled fields are useful when the UI must respond to each edit, validate as the user types, or coordinate multiple fields.

docs.title: Uncontrolled form fields
docs.text: An uncontrolled input keeps its current value in the DOM. Use defaultValue for its initial value, and read the submitted data through FormData or a ref. This can be simpler for a basic form. Do not mix value and defaultValue for the same field.

docs.title: Request and form states
docs.text:
Represent state explicitly:

type RequestState<T> =
  | { status: "idle" }
  | { status: "loading" }
  | { status: "success"; data: T }
  | { status: "error"; message: string };

A discriminated union prevents impossible combinations such as loading and error being true at the same time. Show validation errors next to fields, announce status changes appropriately, and prevent accidental duplicate submissions when needed.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use semantic labels and native form controls. A controlled input's state should update synchronously in its change handler. Controlled input gets its value from React; uncontrolled input holds its value in the DOM; discriminated union represents mutually exclusive state cases.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A key is used by React for matching and is not automatically a component prop.
  • An array index is not always a safe key.
  • Client-side validation improves UX but does not replace server validation.
  • A disabled button alone may not explain why submission is unavailable.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Rendering lists
  • React Learn: Reacting to input with state
  • React Learn: Sharing state between components

docs.title: React Refs and Performance
docs.text: A ref stores a value that persists between renders without causing a render when it changes. Refs can also provide access to a DOM node for tasks such as focusing an input.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { useRef } from "react";

function SearchBox() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);

  return (
    <>
      <input ref={inputRef} aria-label="Search" />
      <button onClick={() => inputRef.current?.focus()}>Focus search</button>
    </>
  );
}

Ref values are mutable and are not reactive state. If a changed value must be shown in the UI, use state instead.

docs.title: Measuring performance
docs.text:
Start by identifying a real user-visible problem. Use browser Performance tools and React profiling tools where available. Avoid adding memoization (memo, useMemo, useCallback) without evidence that repeated rendering or calculation is a bottleneck.

Ref is a mutable container associated with a component; memoization caches a result or component work under specified conditions; profiling measures where time is spent.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Do not use refs as a second state system or to bypass React for routine UI updates. Direct DOM manipulation may conflict with React's own updates. A component re-render is not automatically a performance problem; optimize measured expensive work.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Referencing values with refs
  • React Learn: Manipulating the DOM with refs
  • React Developer Tools

docs.title: React Rendering and Reconciliation
docs.text: Rendering is React calling components to calculate the UI for current props and state. Reconciliation is how React compares the new description with the previous one and decides what changes are needed in the host environment.

docs.title: What triggers a render?
docs.text: A component may render when its state changes, its parent renders and passes new props, or a context value it reads changes. Rendering calculates a description; it does not mean React replaces the whole DOM tree.

docs.title: Render and commit
docs.text: React's render work calculates the next UI. The commit phase applies required changes to the DOM and runs relevant effects. React may skip work or render again before committing; components should therefore remain pure and avoid side effects during render.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Keep rendering deterministic: the same props and state should describe the same UI. Give list items stable keys so React can match them across updates. Reconciliation compares element trees; commit applies changes; pure component render avoids changing external state while calculating UI.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Every render does not mean every DOM node is recreated.
  • A component function may run more than once in development.
  • Do not perform network requests or mutate global values during render.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Render and commit
  • React Learn: Keeping components pure

docs.title: React State and Events
docs.text: State is data that changes over time and affects what a component displays. Event handlers connect user actions—such as clicks and form input—to updates.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Interactive interfaces need a reliable source of truth. React state lets a component describe the UI for the current data rather than manually editing DOM nodes after every action.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: useState returns a current value and a setter. Calling the setter schedules a render using the updated value. When a new value depends on the previous one, use the functional update form to avoid stale values.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount((current) => current + 1)}>
      Count: {count}
    </button>
  );
}

The state setter requests a render; it does not directly edit the DOM.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Keep state as close as practical to the components that need it. State is component data that can change; event handler is a function run in response to an event; render calculates the UI for current props and state.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Do not mutate arrays or objects stored in state; create updated values.
  • A state update may be batched and is not an immediate variable assignment.
  • Props and state have different owners: a component receives props and owns its local state.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: State — a component's memory
  • React Learn: Responding to events

docs.title: React Suspense and Error Boundaries
docs.text: Suspense lets a part of a React tree display a fallback while a supported child is not ready. Error boundaries display fallback UI when descendant rendering throws an error.

docs.title: Suspense
docs.text:
import { Suspense, lazy } from "react";

const HelpPanel = lazy(() => import("./HelpPanel"));

function Page() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading help…</p>}>
      <HelpPanel />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

lazy defers loading a component's code until it is rendered. Suspense behavior for data sources depends on the library or framework providing that integration; wrapping an arbitrary Promise does not automatically make it Suspense-enabled.

docs.title: Error boundaries
docs.text: An error boundary catches errors thrown while rendering descendants and shows fallback UI. In React's core API, error boundaries are traditionally implemented with a class component or supplied by a framework/library. They do not automatically catch errors in event handlers, arbitrary asynchronous callbacks, or server requests; handle those at their proper boundary.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Place boundaries around areas that can fail or load independently. A useful fallback should preserve context, explain what happened, and offer a next step when possible. Log unexpected failures without exposing sensitive details.

Fallback is temporary or recovery UI; code splitting loads code in separate chunks; error boundary catches descendant render/lifecycle errors within its supported scope.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Suspense does not automatically fetch data from any Promise.
  • A React error boundary does not catch every JavaScript error.
  • A loading fallback should not be the only feedback for a failed operation.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React reference: Suspense
  • React reference: lazy
  • React: Error Boundary

docs.title: Testing React Interfaces
docs.text: React interface tests verify behavior a user or another component depends on. They help catch regressions when props, state, forms, and async UI change.

docs.title: What to test
docs.text:
• A component shows the expected content for its inputs.
  • User actions produce visible, correct results.
  • Loading, success, empty, and error states are understandable.
  • Important keyboard and form behavior works.

Prefer queries based on accessible roles and labels where possible. Tests should check observable behavior rather than private implementation details such as internal hook call counts.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: With a testing library installed and configured, a test might render a button and assert that activating it changes the visible count. Keep setup specific to the project's chosen test runner; React itself does not prescribe one universal test stack.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use unit tests for small logic, component tests for UI behavior, and end-to-end tests for important user journeys across the app. Assertion checks an expected result; mock replaces a dependency for a test; test double is a controlled substitute such as a fake or stub.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A test that passes does not prove every real-world browser case works.
  • Snapshot output alone may not explain whether behavior is correct.
  • Tests tied to implementation details can break during harmless refactoring.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Testing Library
  • Vitest documentation

docs.title: Advanced and Utility Types
docs.text: TypeScript includes features for deriving, combining, and transforming types. These tools help model real application data without duplicating every definition.

docs.title: Unions and intersections
docs.text: A union such as A | B represents a value that may be either type. An intersection such as A & B combines requirements from both types. Use discriminated unions for variants that need different fields or behavior.

docs.title: Useful built-in utility types
docs.text:
• Partial<T> makes properties optional.
  • Pick<T, K> selects a subset of properties.
  • Omit<T, K> removes selected properties.
  • Record<K, V> describes an object keyed by K with values of type V.
  • Readonly<T> prevents reassignment of properties in checked code.
  • ReturnType<F> derives a function's return type.
type Account = { id: string; name: string; active: boolean };
type AccountUpdate = Partial<Pick<Account, "name" | "active">>;
type AccountById = Record<string, Account>;

These are compile-time descriptions. Readonly does not freeze an object at runtime, and Partial does not validate incoming JSON.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Prefer types that make valid states clear and remain easy to understand. Mapped type transforms properties of another type; conditional type selects a type based on a type relationship; utility type is a reusable built-in type transformation.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A complex type is not automatically more precise or safer.
  • Readonly<T> is generally shallow unless nested values are also readonly.
  • Utility types do not change runtime objects.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook: Utility Types
  • TypeScript Handbook: Creating types from types

docs.title: TypeScript Compiler and Project Configuration
docs.text: The TypeScript compiler (tsc) checks TypeScript source and can emit JavaScript. A project configuration describes which files and language features the compiler should use.

docs.title: tsconfig.json
docs.text: tsconfig.json marks a TypeScript project and configures compiler behavior. Options such as strict, target, module, and moduleResolution affect checking or output. Frontend frameworks often provide recommended defaults; understand and extend those defaults instead of copying an unrelated setup.

docs.title: Type checking and emitting
docs.text: Some tools transpile TypeScript without performing full type checking. Therefore a project may need a separate tsc --noEmit check in addition to its bundler or framework build.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext"
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

This illustrates options only; actual projects should use compatible settings for their runtime, module system, and build tool.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Keep the compiler version and configuration under version control so local and CI checks agree. Type checking analyzes type compatibility; emit writes output files; module resolution determines how imports map to files or packages.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Successful transpilation does not necessarily mean type checking passed.
  • strict affects multiple checks and may reveal existing issues when enabled.
  • A tsconfig option copied from another framework may conflict with the project's build system.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook: TSConfig
  • TypeScript: Compiler options

docs.title: TypeScript Functions, Objects, and Generics
docs.text: TypeScript describes function inputs and outputs, object shapes, and relationships between reusable values. These types help callers understand contracts and help the checker catch mismatches.

docs.title: Object types
docs.text:
type User = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  nickname?: string;
  readonly createdAt: Date;
};
  • ? marks a property optional; reading it may produce undefined.
  • readonly prevents reassignment through that type in checked code; it does not freeze the object at runtime.
  • Types are generally structural: compatible property shapes can be assignable even when type names differ.

interface and type can both describe object shapes. Interfaces can be declaration-merged and extended; type aliases can represent unions, tuples, and other type expressions. Choose a consistent project convention.

docs.title: Function types and overloads
docs.text:
type Formatter = (value: number, currency?: string) => string;

const formatPrice: Formatter = (value, currency = "USD") =>
  new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency }).format(value);

Function types can describe parameters, optional/rest parameters, and return values. Use overload signatures only when callers truly get different type-level behavior from different argument shapes; avoid overloads that obscure a simple union.

docs.title: Generics
docs.text:
A generic type parameter preserves a relationship between types:

function first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}

const firstName = first(["Ari", "Sam"]); // string | undefined

Constraints narrow which types are accepted:

function getId<T extends { id: string }>(value: T): string {
  return value.id;
}

Generic defaults and multiple type parameters can model more complex relationships, but use the simplest type that communicates the contract.

docs.title: keyof, indexed access, and typeof
docs.text:
type Product = { id: string; price: number; title: string };
type ProductKey = keyof Product; // "id" | "price" | "title"
type ProductPrice = Product["price"]; // number

const defaults = { pageSize: 20, compact: false };
type Defaults = typeof defaults;

These operators derive types from existing structures and reduce duplication.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
type ApiResult<T> =
  | { ok: true; data: T }
  | { ok: false; error: string };

function first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}

type Book = { id: string; title: string };
const result: ApiResult<Book[]> = {
  ok: true,
  data: [{ id: "b1", title: "Web Basics" }],
};

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text:
Use generics when the input/output relationship matters, not simply to make a function look reusable. Use readonly arrays and properties when mutation should be discouraged. Types do not validate runtime API data; validate external boundaries.

  • Structural typing checks compatible members, not just declared names.
  • readonly is a compile-time restriction and is often shallow.
  • T extends U constrains T; it does not mean T is exactly U.
  • Avoid defaulting to any for convenience.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook: Object types
  • TypeScript Handbook: Functions
  • TypeScript Handbook: Generics
  • TypeScript Handbook: keyof

docs.title: TypeScript Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: Review these questions after learning the TypeScript lessons. TypeScript checks source code before runtime; it does not replace runtime validation.

docs.title: 1. What is TypeScript?
docs.text: TypeScript is a programming language that builds on JavaScript with a static type system. It is typically checked and transformed into JavaScript for execution; browsers do not execute TypeScript types.

docs.title: 2. What is type inference?
docs.text: Type inference is the compiler deriving a type from a value or context, so developers do not need to annotate every variable.

docs.title: 3. What is the difference between any and unknown?
docs.text: any disables many type checks for a value. unknown can hold any value, but code must narrow or validate it before using it as a specific type. Prefer unknown at untrusted boundaries.

docs.title: 4. What is never used for?
docs.text: never represents a value that cannot occur, such as a function that always throws or an impossible branch after exhaustive narrowing.

docs.title: 5. What are union types?
docs.text: A union such as string | number says a value can be one of several types. The program must narrow the value before using operations that only apply to one member.

docs.title: 6. What is type narrowing?
docs.text:
Narrowing uses control flow or type guards to refine a broader type into a more specific one:

function show(value: string | number) {
  if (typeof value === "string") return value.toUpperCase();
  return value.toFixed(2);
}

docs.title: 7. What is the difference between interface and type?
docs.text: Both can describe object shapes. Interfaces can be extended and declaration-merged; type aliases can express unions, intersections, and other type expressions. Choose the form that best communicates the model and follow project conventions.

docs.title: 8. What are generics?
docs.text:
Generics let code express relationships between input and output types without choosing one concrete type in advance:

function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}

docs.title: 9. What is a type assertion?
docs.text: A type assertion tells the compiler how the programmer wants a value treated. It is removed at runtime and does not check or convert the value. Use it only when the program has information the compiler cannot infer.

docs.title: 10. What are utility types?
docs.text: Utility types transform existing types. Examples include Partial<T>, Pick<T, K>, Omit<T, K>, and Readonly<T>. They affect compile-time checking and do not enforce runtime behavior.

docs.title: 11. What is a discriminated union?
docs.text: A discriminated union is a union of object types that share a property whose literal value identifies the variant. Checking that property lets TypeScript narrow the object safely.

docs.title: 12. What is the difference between optional and nullable properties?
docs.text: An optional property may be absent. A nullable property is present with a value that may be null. These states are distinct and should be modeled according to the data contract.

docs.title: 13. Do TypeScript types validate API responses at runtime?
docs.text: No. Type annotations and assertions are erased from emitted JavaScript. Validate untrusted responses at runtime with checks or a schema-validation library before relying on them.

docs.title: 14. What does strict do in tsconfig.json?
docs.text: The strict option enables a family of stronger type-checking options. It helps catch issues such as implicit any and possible null access. Individual flags and project settings can further change the checks.

docs.title: 15. What is the difference between tsc and a runtime?
docs.text: tsc type-checks and can emit JavaScript. A JavaScript runtime such as a browser or Node.js executes JavaScript. Build tools may combine or replace these steps, but type checking and execution remain different concerns.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript overview
  • TypeScript Handbook
  • TypeScript: tsconfig.json

docs.title: 16. An API response is typed as User, but a missing field crashes the page. Why did TypeScript not catch it?
docs.text: A type annotation does not validate JSON at runtime. If the response was asserted as User or trusted through an unchecked cast, the compiler accepted the claim without inspecting the payload. Treat external data as unknown, validate its shape at the boundary with explicit checks or a schema library, and only then expose a trusted domain type to the rest of the application.

docs.title: 17. A function accepts a union but callers repeatedly pass the wrong object shape. How can the type model help?
docs.text: Model valid variants as a discriminated union with a literal tag, such as { kind: "email"; address: string } | { kind: "sms"; phone: string }. The tag makes narrowing explicit and lets the compiler reject combinations that do not belong to either variant. Avoid a bag of many optional fields when only certain combinations are valid.

docs.title: 18. A switch over a union silently misses a new variant after the type changes. How can you make it exhaustive?
docs.text: After handling each known discriminant, assign the remaining value to never in a default branch. If a new union member is added, the remaining value is no longer never, producing a compile-time error. This is a compile-time safeguard; still decide how unknown values from external data should be handled at runtime.

docs.title: 19. A generic helper returns any despite having a type parameter. What should you check?
docs.text: Look for an any input, an overly broad constraint, an unsafe assertion, or a library declaration that leaks any. any can flow through generic code and disable checking. Prefer unknown for untrusted values, constrain type parameters only as needed, and preserve the relationship between inputs and outputs rather than asserting a desired result.

docs.title: 20. A value can be missing, null, or a concrete value. How should the type express it?
docs.text: Model the states explicitly, for example value?: string | null when the property may be absent, explicitly null, or a string. Then handle each state intentionally; optional chaining can avoid an exception but may collapse meaningful states. Match the API contract and compiler options such as strictNullChecks, and normalize the value at the boundary if downstream code needs fewer states.

docs.title: 21. A developer adds as SomeType to silence a compile error. When is that appropriate?
docs.text: An assertion changes the compiler's view but does not convert or validate the runtime value. Use one only when a fact is established by surrounding logic that TypeScript cannot express, and keep the assertion close to that proof. Prefer a type guard, parser, or improved type model when possible; broad or chained assertions can hide real defects.

docs.title: Runtime Validation of Data
docs.text: TypeScript checks code during development and build time, but external data arrives while an application is running. Runtime validation checks that data actually has the expected shape before code relies on it.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Network responses, browser storage, user input, and environment values are not made trustworthy by adding a TypeScript annotation. A malformed response can still cause a runtime failure or an incorrect decision.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Treat data from outside the typed program as unknown. Check its structure and values, then convert it to a trusted application representation. Larger projects often use a schema-validation library; small boundaries can use careful explicit checks.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
type Profile = { id: string; displayName: string };

function parseProfile(value: unknown): Profile {
  if (
    typeof value === "object" &&
    value !== null &&
    "id" in value &&
    "displayName" in value &&
    typeof value.id === "string" &&
    typeof value.displayName === "string"
  ) {
    return { id: value.id, displayName: value.displayName };
  }
  throw new Error("Invalid profile response");
}

This is a small example; production schemas may need limits, nested checks, and useful error reporting.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Validate at trust boundaries, especially before using values for access control, database writes, or rendering. Trust boundary is where data enters from a source not controlled by the current code. Parsing turns input into a structured representation; validation verifies constraints.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• const profile: Profile = await response.json() does not inspect the JSON.
  • A successful HTTP status does not guarantee a response has the expected content.
  • Validation improves correctness but does not replace authorization or output encoding.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook: unknown
  • MDN: Working with JSON

docs.title: TypeScript Types and Narrowing
docs.text: TypeScript's type system describes the values a program expects. Type narrowing uses checks and control flow to refine a broad type to a more specific one.

docs.title: Everyday type forms
docs.text: Type form Example Meaning Primitive string, number, boolean Common basic values Array string[], Array<number> Ordered values of one element type Object { id: string; active: boolean } Named properties with declared types Optional property { nickname?: string } Property can be absent or undefined Union string \| number Value can be one of several types Literal "idle" \| "loading" Value must match listed values Tuple [string, number] Ordered positions with known types unknown unknown Must be checked before being used as a specific type never never No possible value; useful for exhaustive branches

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Types help editors explain how code is used and help catch mismatches before execution. Narrowing is especially useful when a value may be absent or may have one of several shapes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: TypeScript infers many types from assigned values. An annotation can make a public contract clearer. Union types represent alternatives; checks such as typeof, in, and equality comparisons can narrow those alternatives inside a branch.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
type Result =
  | { ok: true; value: string }
  | { ok: false; message: string };

function showResult(result: Result): string {
  if (result.ok) {
    return result.value;
  }
  return result.message;
}

Checking the discriminant ok allows TypeScript to know which properties exist in each branch.

docs.title: Common narrowing checks
docs.text:
function describe(value: string | number | null): string {
  if (value === null) return "No value";
  if (typeof value === "number") return value.toFixed(2);
  return value.toUpperCase();
}

Other narrowing tools include in for object properties, instanceof for class instances, equality checks, and user-defined type guards. Prefer checks that prove the value's shape rather than assertions that merely tell the compiler to trust you.

docs.title: Exhaustiveness checks
docs.text:
When handling a union, a never assignment can help identify a new case that was not handled:

type Theme = "light" | "dark";

function labelTheme(theme: Theme): string {
  switch (theme) {
    case "light": return "Light";
    case "dark": return "Dark";
    default: {
      const exhaustive: never = theme;
      return exhaustive;
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Prefer precise types over any, which disables many useful checks. Use unknown for data whose shape has not yet been verified. A union allows one of several types; a discriminated union shares a property whose value identifies each case; narrowing reduces possible types after a check.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Type annotations are removed from emitted JavaScript and do not validate data at runtime.
  • A type assertion changes the checker's view; it does not convert or verify the value.
  • any can hide errors rather than solve them.
  • An optional property may be missing; reading it can produce undefined.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook: Everyday types
  • TypeScript Handbook: Narrowing

docs.title: TypeScript with React
docs.text: TypeScript can describe React component props, event handlers, state, and children. It helps document component contracts and catch incompatible values while editing.

docs.title: Typing component props
docs.text:
type GreetingProps = {
  name: string;
  formal?: boolean;
};

function Greeting({ name, formal = false }: GreetingProps) {
  return <p>{formal ? `Good day, ${name}` : `Hi, ${name}`}</p>;
}

TypeScript can infer many event types from JSX context. Add annotations when they clarify an API or when inference cannot identify the intended type.

docs.title: State and events
docs.text: Use useState with a clear initial value when inference is sufficient. When state may have multiple forms, use a union type. Prefer native DOM event types provided by React's type definitions rather than broad any.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Avoid typing every component as a generic React component type unless a real API requires it. Type the data the component accepts and returns, and keep runtime validation at external boundaries.

Props type describes a component's input contract; event type describes the event value provided to a handler; inference derives types from the surrounding JSX and values.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• TypeScript does not validate props received from arbitrary runtime JavaScript automatically.
  • React.FC is not required for every function component.
  • A type assertion cannot repair an incorrectly shaped response.

docs.title: Backend Development
docs.text:
Backend development is the work of building the server side of an application: the code that receives requests, applies business rules, stores and reads data, talks to other services, and returns reliable responses. Users rarely see the backend directly, but every login, payment, search, upload, and notification depends on it.

A backend is more than "an API". It decides who a caller is and what they may do, validates every input it receives, keeps data consistent when many requests arrive at once, survives slow or failing dependencies, and records enough information for developers to understand what happened when something goes wrong.

docs.title: What this section teaches
docs.text:
You will learn how to:

  • Explain what a backend is responsible for and trace one request from the browser to the database and back.
  • Use the HTTP protocol precisely: methods, every important status code, headers, caching, and CORS.
  • Run JavaScript on the server with Node.js and understand its runtime, event loop, modules, streams, and processes.
  • Build APIs with Express: routing, middleware, validation, error handling, authentication, uploads, security, testing, and production setup.
  • Design APIs that are consistent, versioned, documented, and safe to retry.
  • Apply the concepts every backend needs: authentication and authorization, sessions and tokens, OAuth, rate limiting, logging, background jobs, real-time communication, file storage, and configuration.

docs.title: How a backend handles a request
docs.text:
1. A client sends an HTTP request, such as POST /api/orders, to a server.
  2. Infrastructure in front of the application (a CDN, load balancer, or reverse proxy) forwards the request to an application instance.
  3. Middleware runs shared steps: parsing the body, logging, checking the caller's identity, and applying rate limits.
  4. The router matches the method and path to a handler.
  5. The handler validates the input and calls the business logic.
  6. The business logic reads or writes data in a database, cache, queue, or external service.
  7. The server returns a status code, headers, and a body that describe the result, and errors are turned into consistent error responses.

Node.js and Express do not replace these ideas. They are one practical way to implement them, and the same concepts apply to backends written in other languages and frameworks.

docs.title: Learning path
docs.text:
The navigation is organized into three subject groups:

  1. Node.js: the JavaScript runtime that executes server code.
  2. Express: a minimal web framework built on Node.js for routing and middleware.
  3. Important Backend Concepts: protocol, API, security, and reliability knowledge that applies to any backend stack.

A useful order for a first pass is:

  1. Read Backend Fundamentals and Client-Server Model and Request Lifecycle.
  2. Learn the HTTP vocabulary: HTTP Methods, HTTP Status Codes, and HTTP Headers.
  3. Work through Node.js from the runtime to streams and processes.
  4. Build APIs with Express.
  5. Return to the remaining backend concepts, such as CORS, authentication, rate limiting, and background jobs, and apply each one in your Express project.

Every lesson includes an explanation of how the concept works, practical examples, best practices, important terminology, common mistakes, revision questions, and official learning resources. Each subject ends with interview questions and answers.

docs.title: Related sections
docs.text:
Some backend topics have their own sections in these notes:

  • Networking and Protocols for DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP versions, and WebSockets at the protocol level.
  • Databases for data modeling, queries, indexes, and transactions.
  • Application Architecture for caching, Redis, message queues, and scalability.
  • Servers and Infrastructure for Nginx, reverse proxies, and load balancing.
  • DevOps and Deployment for Docker, CI/CD, environment variables, and monitoring.
  • Security and Testing for OWASP, API security, and testing strategy.

docs.title: A first practical exercise
docs.text:
Build a small task API with Node.js and Express:

  1. GET /tasks returns a list, and POST /tasks creates a task.
  2. Return 201 Created for a new task, 400 Bad Request for invalid input, and 404 Not Found for a missing task.
  3. Add a logging middleware and a central error handler.
  4. Call the API from a page on a different port and fix the CORS error you see in the browser console.

Then use curl -i to inspect the status line and headers of each response.

docs.title: Before moving on
docs.text:
• What responsibilities belong to a backend rather than a frontend?
  • Which steps does a request pass through before reaching a route handler?
  • Why should every input from a client be validated on the server, even when the frontend already validates it?
  • Why are Node.js and Express tools for applying backend concepts rather than the concepts themselves?

docs.title: Important Backend Concepts
docs.text: Frameworks change, but the problems a backend solves stay the same. This subject covers the knowledge every backend developer needs, whatever language or framework they use: how HTTP works in detail, how to design APIs, how to identify and authorize callers, and how to keep a service correct and available when traffic grows and dependencies fail.

docs.title: What this subject covers
docs.text:
• HTTP in depth: methods, every important status code, headers, caching, and CORS. These are the vocabulary of every web API.
  • API design: REST, consistent naming, pagination, versioning, error formats, alternative styles such as GraphQL and gRPC, and webhooks.
  • Security: authentication and authorization, sessions, cookies, JWT, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, and input validation.
  • Reliability: error handling, logging and monitoring, rate limiting, timeouts and retries, idempotency, and race conditions.
  • Architecture patterns: background jobs, real-time communication, file storage, and configuration and secrets.

docs.title: How the concepts fit together
docs.text:
Follow one request, POST /api/orders, through a production backend:

  1. Request lifecycle: DNS, TCP, and TLS connect the client to a load balancer, which forwards the request to an application instance.
  2. CORS: if the request came from a browser on another origin, the browser first checks that the API allows that origin.
  3. Rate limiting: the API checks that this caller has not exceeded its allowed request rate, or responds with 429 Too Many Requests.
  4. Authentication and authorization: a session cookie or token identifies the user, and the API checks that they may create orders.
  5. Validation: the body is checked against a schema, or the API responds with 400 Bad Request.
  6. Idempotency and concurrency: an idempotency key stops a retried request from creating a second order, and an atomic update stops two requests from selling the last item twice.
  7. Background jobs: sending the confirmation email is queued instead of making the client wait.
  8. Response: the API returns 201 Created with a Location header, or a consistent error response if something failed.
  9. Observability: logs, metrics, and traces with a shared request ID record what happened.

Each step is one lesson in this subject.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
The status code, headers, and body together describe the result of a request. Use curl -i to see all three:

$ curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/orders \
    -H "content-type: application/json" \
    -d '{"productId": "p_123", "quantity": 1}'

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /api/orders/o_789
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"id":"o_789","productId":"p_123","quantity":1,"status":"pending"}

201 Created says a new resource exists, Location says where to find it, and the JSON body describes it. A real Express server also sends headers such as Content-Length, ETag, Date, and Connection; they are left out here to keep the example short.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Learn these concepts alongside Node.js and Express rather than after them: each Express lesson applies one or more of these ideas. When a framework does something for you, such as setting a header or choosing a status code, check that it matches what the concept requires.

  • A 200 OK status with {"error": "..."} in the body is not error handling; the status code should describe the result.
  • CORS does not protect your server; it tells browsers which other origins may read your responses.
  • Authentication (who are you?) and authorization (what may you do?) are separate checks, and both run on the server for every request.
  • Frontend validation improves the user experience, but only server-side validation protects data.
  • A single-threaded runtime such as Node.js can still have race conditions, because requests interleave at every await and production runs many instances.

docs.title: Express
docs.text: Express is a minimal web framework for Node.js. It adds routing, middleware, and convenient request and response helpers on top of the built-in node:http module, so you can build APIs and web servers without handling every low-level HTTP detail yourself.

docs.title: What Express provides
docs.text:
• Routing: match an HTTP method and path, such as GET /users/:id, to the code that handles it.
  • Middleware: functions that run in order for each request to parse bodies, log, authenticate, or reject a request early.
  • Request helpers: req.params, req.query, req.body, req.get(), and more for reading what the client sent.
  • Response helpers: res.status(), res.json(), res.redirect(), res.cookie(), and res.sendFile() for building replies.
  • Routers: express.Router() groups related routes and middleware into modules that can be mounted under a path.
  • Error handling: a dedicated error-handling middleware signature for turning failures into consistent responses.

Express is deliberately unopinionated. It does not choose a database, validation library, authentication system, or folder structure for you. You add these yourself, which keeps Express flexible but means you must make and document those decisions.

Express 5 is the current major version. The most visible changes from Express 4 are that errors from async handlers reach the error handler automatically, and that route path syntax for wildcards and optional segments has changed. The lessons show Express 5 and point out Express 4 differences where you are likely to meet them in older code.

docs.title: How Express handles a request
docs.text:
1. Node.js receives the HTTP request and passes it to the Express app.
  2. Express runs registered middleware in the order it was added, for example express.json(), a logger, and an authentication check.
  3. Each middleware either ends the response or calls next() to continue.
  4. The router finds the first route whose method and path match.
  5. The route handler validates input, calls the business logic, and sends a response.
  6. If anything fails, the error is passed to error-handling middleware, which sends an error response.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json()); // Parse JSON request bodies into req.body.

const tasks = [{ id: 1, title: "Learn Express" }];

app.get("/tasks", (req, res) => {
  res.json(tasks);
});

app.post("/tasks", (req, res) => {
  const title = req.body?.title;
  if (typeof title !== "string" || title.trim() === "") {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "title is required" });
  }
  const task = { id: tasks.length + 1, title };
  tasks.push(task);
  res.status(201).json(task);
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("API listening on http://localhost:3000");
});

GET /tasks returns the list, and POST /tasks validates the input, then returns 201 Created with the new task or 400 Bad Request with an error.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Learn Node.js and the HTTP basics in Important Backend Concepts first, especially HTTP methods and status codes. Register middleware in a deliberate order, keep route handlers thin by moving business logic into services, validate every input, and handle errors in one place.

  • Express is not part of Node.js; it is a separate npm package.
  • Registering a route does not validate its input; you must add validation.
  • Middleware order changes behavior: a body parser registered after a route does not run for that route.
  • res.json() does not stop your function; code after it still runs unless you return.
  • Express does not make an API secure by default; headers, rate limits, CORS, and authentication are added deliberately.

docs.title: Node.js
docs.text: Node.js is an open-source JavaScript runtime that runs outside the browser. It executes server programs, command-line tools, build tooling, and automation, and it provides APIs for files, networking, processes, and binary data that a browser deliberately does not expose.

docs.title: What Node.js provides
docs.text:
• A JavaScript engine: V8 compiles and runs your JavaScript.
  • An event loop: libuv schedules timers, I/O callbacks, and other queued work so one JavaScript thread can serve many connections.
  • Non-blocking I/O: file, network, and DNS operations start and report back later instead of making the program wait.
  • Core modules: built-in APIs such as node:fs, node:path, node:http, node:events, node:stream, node:crypto, and node:worker_threads.
  • A module system: CommonJS and ES modules for splitting code into files and reusing packages.
  • A package ecosystem: npm, the registry and client used to install and publish packages.

Node.js does not include a web framework, a database, or an application structure. Frameworks such as Express add routing and middleware on top of the built-in node:http module.

docs.title: How Node.js runs a server
docs.text:
1. Node.js starts, loads your entry file, and runs its top-level code.
  2. The code registers work for later, such as a server that listens on a port.
  3. When a request arrives, libuv notices the network event and queues a callback.
  4. The event loop runs that callback on the single JavaScript thread.
  5. While the handler waits for a database or file, the thread is free to run other callbacks.
  6. When the result arrives, its callback or promise continuation runs and the response is sent.

This model handles many concurrent I/O-bound requests efficiently. Long synchronous work, such as hashing a large file in a loop, blocks every other request until it finishes, which is why CPU-heavy work is moved to worker threads or separate services.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const server = createServer((request, response) => {
  // Runs on the event loop for every incoming request.
  response.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/json" });
  response.end(JSON.stringify({ message: "Hello from Node.js" }));
});

server.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Listening on http://localhost:3000");
});

Save this as server.mjs and run node server.mjs. A real service also needs configuration, input validation, logging, graceful shutdown, and error handling, which the following lessons cover.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Learn JavaScript first, especially functions, promises, and async/await. Use asynchronous APIs in request handlers, keep secrets in environment variables instead of source code, and choose dependencies carefully because each one is code you run.

  • Node.js is a runtime, not a language and not a framework.
  • Node.js is not "single-threaded" in every sense: your JavaScript runs on one main thread, but libuv uses a thread pool and the operating system for I/O.
  • Asynchronous I/O does not make CPU-bound work fast; it only stops waiting from blocking other work.
  • Node.js is not a browser, so window, document, and the DOM do not exist.
  • Node.js can serve HTTP without Express; frameworks add structure, not capability.
