docs.text: A set of small command-line tools that expose how Node.js really works: a log analyzer that processes a multi-gigabyte file with streams in little memory, an event-loop lag monitor, a file hasher that compares the main thread with worker threads, and a plain node:http server that shuts down gracefully on SIGTERM. Practices the Node.js lessons. Follow the full step-by-step guide.

docs.title: TaskFlow API
docs.text: A task-manager REST API built with Express that gains one feature per lesson: CRUD routes, validation, consistent error responses, JWT login with refresh tokens and roles, pagination, CORS, automated tests, and production setup with logs, health checks, and graceful shutdown. Practices the Express lessons.

docs.title: ShopLite Checkout
docs.text: A small shop backend that forces you to solve real backend problems: a payment endpoint that is safe to retry, a stock update that can never oversell, a signed webhook from a payment provider, a rate-limited login, emails sent by background jobs, image uploads through signed URLs, and live order status. Practices the Important Backend Concepts lessons.

docs.title: API Design Best Practices
docs.text: An API is a product whose users are developers. Once clients depend on it, every name, field, and status code becomes hard to change. Good API design makes endpoints predictable, consistent, safe to evolve, and pleasant to use. This page collects the conventions that well-run APIs follow.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• APIs outlive their first client. A mobile app version in users' pockets may call your API for years; a breaking change can crash it.
  • Consistency reduces mistakes. If every list paginates the same way and every error has the same shape, client code can be written once.
  • Good design prevents performance problems. Unpaginated lists and unbounded filters are how one request takes down a database.
  • Clear contracts enable parallel work. With an agreed OpenAPI document, frontend and backend teams can build at the same time.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe uses cursor pagination. Stripe's list endpoints accept limit, starting_after, and ending_before, where the cursors are object IDs, and the response includes has_more. Stripe describes this as cursor-based pagination.
  • GitHub paginates with the Link header. GitHub's REST API returns a subset of results and a link header pointing to other pages; endpoints that support per_page let clients change the page size. GitHub's best practices tell clients to follow the links rather than build pagination URLs by hand.
  • Stripe and GitHub version by date. Stripe requests use the account's default API version unless the Stripe-Version header overrides it. GitHub uses the X-GitHub-Api-Version header and says a previous version is supported for at least 24 months after a new one is released.
  • Stripe makes POST safe to retry. Stripe accepts idempotency keys on all POST requests, so a client can retry a payment request without charging twice.
  • Zalando publishes its API rules. The Zalando RESTful API guidelines include rules such as "MUST support problem JSON", "SHOULD prefer cursor-based pagination, avoid offset-based pagination", and "MUST not break backward compatibility". They are a good example of turning the practices on this page into a company-wide standard.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
Element Convention Example Path segments Lowercase nouns, hyphens between words, plural collections /api/shipping-addresses/12 Query parameters One casing style used everywhere (camelCase is common in JSON APIs) ?pageSize=20&sortBy=createdAt JSON fields One casing style used everywhere; camelCase is most common for JavaScript clients, snake_case is also popular "createdAt" or "created_at" Booleans Read as a yes/no question "isActive", "hasAttachments" Enumerations Lowercase strings, documented "status": "paid" Actions A noun sub-resource or a verb sub-path, used consistently POST /orders/9/cancellation or POST /orders/9/cancel

The specific choice matters less than applying it everywhere. Mixed casing (created_at in one response, updatedAt in another) is a sign of an API designed one endpoint at a time.

docs.title: Resource modelling
docs.text:
• Model what clients care about, not your tables. A "checkout" resource may touch carts, payments, and inventory internally.
  • Hide implementation details: internal flags, database column names, and join tables do not belong in responses.
  • Keep representations stable and reasonably complete, so clients do not need five requests to render one screen.
  • Use sub-resources for owned data (/orders/9/items) and top-level resources for things that stand alone.
  • Embed or link related data deliberately. Offer an expand or include parameter (?include=customer) instead of always nesting everything.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text: Every collection endpoint needs pagination before the data grows. There are two main styles.

docs.title: Offset/limit pagination
docs.text:
GET /api/orders?limit=20&offset=40      (or ?page=3&pageSize=20)

The database skips offset rows and returns limit rows.

  • Pros: simple, supports "jump to page 7", easy to show total pages.
  • Cons: gets slower as the offset grows (the database still walks past the skipped rows), and results shift when rows are inserted or deleted between requests, so users see duplicates or miss items.

docs.title: Cursor (keyset) pagination
docs.text:
GET /api/orders?limit=20
GET /api/orders?limit=20&cursor=eyJjcmVhdGVkQXQiOiIyMDI2LTExLTAzVDEwOjE1OjAwWiIsImlkIjo5MDF9

The cursor encodes the position of the last item returned (for example its createdAt and id). The next query asks for items after that position:

SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)   -- position from the cursor
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 21;                            -- one extra row tells us if there is more
  • Pros: fast at any depth with an index on the sort columns; stable when data changes; ideal for infinite scroll and feeds.
  • Cons: no jumping to an arbitrary page; total counts are a separate, potentially expensive query.
Offset/limit Cursor Performance on deep pages Degrades Constant Consistency during inserts/deletes Duplicates or gaps Stable Jump to page N Yes No Typical use Admin tables, small datasets Feeds, large or fast-changing collections, public APIs

Make cursors opaque (base64-encoded JSON is common) so clients cannot depend on their contents, and always include a tie-breaker such as id in the sort so the order is unique.

docs.title: Pagination metadata
docs.text:
Return paging information with the data:

{
  "data": [ { "id": "ord_901" }, { "id": "ord_900" } ],
  "pagination": {
    "limit": 20,
    "nextCursor": "eyJpZCI6Im9yZF85MDAifQ",
    "hasMore": true
  }
}

Or use the standard Link header (RFC 8288), as GitHub's API does:

Link: <https://api.example.com/orders?cursor=abc&limit=20>; rel="next",
      <https://api.example.com/orders?limit=20>; rel="first"

Always enforce a maximum limit (for example 100) on the server, and use a sensible default when the client sends none.

docs.title: Filtering, sorting, field selection, and search
docs.text:
Feature Common convention Example Exact filter Field name as parameter ?status=paid&customerId=cus_7 Multiple values Comma list or repeated parameter ?status=paid,shipped Ranges Suffixes or bracket syntax ?createdAfter=2026-11-01 or ?total[gte]=1000 Sorting sort with - for descending, comma for secondary ?sort=-createdAt,id Field selection fields listing what to return ?fields=id,status,total Expanding relations include or expand ?include=customer,items Full-text search q parameter or a search endpoint ?q=desk+lamp

Rules:

  • Allowlist filterable and sortable fields. Never pass client input straight into a database query; that invites injection and unindexed queries.
  • Index what you allow clients to filter and sort by.
  • Validate types: query strings are always strings, so convert and check them.

docs.title: Versioning strategies
docs.text:
You will eventually need a breaking change. Versioning lets old clients keep working while new ones move on.

Strategy Example Pros Cons URI path /api/v1/orders, /api/v2/orders Obvious, easy to route, cache, and test in a browser Version is part of the resource identity; tends to version everything at once Custom header Api-Version: 2026-11-01 Clean URLs; date-based versions allow fine-grained changes Less visible; easy to forget; caches must Vary on it Media type Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json Most aligned with HTTP content negotiation Awkward for clients and tooling Query parameter /api/orders?version=2 Simple Mixes versioning with filtering; easy to drop by accident

URI versioning is the most common and the easiest to operate. Whatever you choose, version rarely: most changes can be made compatibly.

docs.title: Backward-compatible vs breaking changes
docs.text:
Usually safe (additive) Breaking Adding a new endpoint Removing or renaming an endpoint Adding an optional request field with a default Making an optional field required Adding a field to a response Removing or renaming a response field Adding a new enum value (if clients were told to expect unknown values) Changing a field's type or meaning (string to number, cents to dollars) Adding a new optional query parameter Changing default behavior, sorting, or pagination Relaxing validation Tightening validation on existing inputs Adding a new error code (documented) Changing status codes clients rely on

Two rules make additive changes safe: servers ignore unknown request fields (or reject them consistently from day one), and clients ignore unknown response fields. Tell client developers to tolerate unknown fields and enum values.

docs.title: A consistent error format: RFC 9457 problem details
docs.text:
Pick one error shape and use it for every error. RFC 9457 defines a standard one with the media type application/problem+json:

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/validation-error",
  "title": "Your request is not valid.",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "2 fields failed validation.",
  "instance": "/api/orders",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "quantity", "message": "must be at least 1" },
    { "field": "email", "message": "must be a valid email address" }
  ],
  "requestId": "7f3c9a2e"
}
Member Meaning type A URI identifying the problem type; ideally a page documenting it. Defaults to about:blank title A short, human-readable summary of the problem type; stays the same for every occurrence status The HTTP status code, repeated for convenience detail A human-readable explanation of this occurrence instance A URI identifying this specific occurrence (often the request path or an error ID) extensions Any extra members you define, such as errors or requestId

Clients should branch on type (stable) rather than parsing detail (human text that may change).

docs.title: Dates, times, and IDs
docs.text:
• Dates and times: ISO 8601 strings in UTC with a Z suffix: "2026-11-03T10:15:00Z". Avoid Unix timestamps in JSON (ambiguous units) and local times without an offset. Use date-only strings ("2026-11-03") for calendar dates like birthdays.
  • Money: integers in the smallest unit plus a currency ({"amount": 4999, "currency": "USD"}), never floating point.
  • IDs: treat them as opaque strings, even if they look numeric. Prefer non-guessable IDs (UUIDs, or prefixed random IDs like ord_8Fh2...) for public resources; sequential integers leak business volume and invite enumeration attacks. Prefixes make logs and support tickets clearer.

docs.title: Bulk operations
docs.text:
Many small requests are slow; one giant request is fragile. For bulk work:

  • Offer a batch endpoint such as POST /api/contacts/batch with a capped array size.
  • Decide whether the batch is all-or-nothing (a transaction) or partial. For partial success, return 200 (or 207 Multi-Status if you follow WebDAV conventions) with a per-item result:
{
  "results": [
    { "index": 0, "status": 201, "id": "con_1" },
    { "index": 1, "status": 422, "error": { "title": "email is not valid" } }
  ]
}
  • For very large imports, accept a file and process it in the background.

docs.title: Long-running operations
docs.text:
Do not keep an HTTP request open for minutes. Instead:

Clients poll the status resource, or the server notifies them through a webhook or a real-time channel when the job finishes. See background jobs and webhooks.

docs.title: Documentation with OpenAPI
docs.text:
The OpenAPI Specification describes an HTTP API in a YAML or JSON document: paths, parameters, request and response schemas, auth schemes, and examples.

openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: Orders API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /api/orders/{id}:
    get:
      summary: Get an order
      parameters:
        - name: id
          in: path
          required: true
          schema: { type: string }
      responses:
        "200":
          description: The order
          content:
            application/json:
              schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Order" }
        "404":
          description: Order not found
          content:
            application/problem+json:
              schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Problem" }
components:
  schemas:
    Order:
      type: object
      required: [id, status]
      properties:
        id: { type: string }
        status: { type: string, enum: [pending, paid, shipped] }
    Problem:
      type: object
      properties:
        type: { type: string }
        title: { type: string }
        status: { type: integer }

From one document you can generate interactive docs (Swagger UI, Redoc), client SDKs, mock servers, and contract tests. Keep it in the repository and update it in the same change as the code.

docs.title: Deprecation
docs.text:
When you plan to remove something, warn clients early and in a machine-readable way:

Deprecation: @1780272000                  (RFC 9745: deprecated since 2026-06-01, as a Unix time)
Sunset: Fri, 01 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT     (RFC 8594: will stop working at this time)
Link: <https://api.example.com/docs/migrate-v2>; rel="deprecation"

Also announce it in the changelog, email API consumers, monitor who still calls the old endpoint, and only remove it after the sunset date. After removal, 410 Gone is clearer than 404.

docs.title: Idempotency keys
docs.text: For non-idempotent operations such as payments, let clients send a unique Idempotency-Key header. If a retry arrives with the same key, the server returns the original result instead of charging twice. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Decision Use When Avoid when Pagination style Cursor (keyset) Feeds, large or fast-changing collections, public APIs Users must jump to page N or see exact totals Offset/limit Small datasets, admin tables with page numbers Deep pages on large tables; data changing between requests New version URI or header version A breaking change you cannot avoid Additive changes; add fields or endpoints instead Error format RFC 9457 problem details Any API that returns errors to programs Never; at most, extend it with your own members Bulk endpoint POST .../batch with a size cap Clients regularly create or update many items Rare bulk needs; per-item requests are simpler Long-running work 202 + status resource Work that can outlive a proxy timeout Fast operations; a direct response is simpler Idempotency keys Idempotency-Key header Payments, orders, anything costly to duplicate Naturally idempotent methods (GET, PUT, DELETE)

The practices on this page matter most for APIs other teams or companies depend on. For a small internal API used by one frontend you also own, the same ideas apply, but you can keep the ceremony light: you can change both sides together, so formal versioning and deprecation headers are often unnecessary.

docs.title: Cursor pagination in Express
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
const MAX_LIMIT = 100;

const encodeCursor = (obj) => Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(obj)).toString("base64url");
const decodeCursor = (str) => JSON.parse(Buffer.from(str, "base64url").toString("utf8"));

app.get("/api/orders", async (req, res) => {
  const limit = Math.min(Number(req.query.limit) || 20, MAX_LIMIT);

  let after = null;
  if (typeof req.query.cursor === "string") {
    try {
      after = decodeCursor(req.query.cursor); // { createdAt, id }
    } catch {
      return res.status(400).type("application/problem+json")
        .json({ title: "Invalid cursor", status: 400 });
    }
  }

  // Fetch one extra row to know whether another page exists
  const rows = await db.findOrders({ after, limit: limit + 1 }); // keyset query
  const page = rows.slice(0, limit);
  const last = page.at(-1);

  res.json({
    data: page,
    pagination: {
      limit,
      hasMore: rows.length > limit,
      nextCursor: rows.length > limit ? encodeCursor({ createdAt: last.createdAt, id: last.id }) : null,
    },
  });
});

db.findOrders stands for a query like the SQL keyset example above.

docs.title: A problem-details error helper
docs.text:
import { STATUS_CODES } from "node:http";

export function sendProblem(res, status, { type, title, ...extras } = {}) {
  res.status(status).type("application/problem+json").json({
    type: type ?? "about:blank",
    // RFC 9457: with "about:blank", the title should be the standard
    // status phrase ("Not Found"); custom titles belong to custom types
    title: type ? title : STATUS_CODES[status],
    status,
    ...extras,
  });
}

// Usage inside handlers
// sendProblem(res, 409, {
//   type: "https://api.example.com/problems/email-taken",
//   title: "Email already registered",
//   detail: "Try signing in instead.",
// });
// sendProblem(res, 404, { detail: "No order with id ord_901." }); // title "Not Found"

Clients branch on type, so give every problem they must handle differently its own documented type URI, and use about:blank only for errors that mean nothing beyond the status code.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Design the contract first (OpenAPI), review it, then implement.
  • Be consistent in casing, pagination, errors, dates, and IDs across the whole API.
  • Paginate every list and cap page sizes.
  • Allowlist and index filter and sort fields.
  • Prefer additive changes; version only for unavoidable breaking changes.
  • Use one error format (RFC 9457) with stable type identifiers.
  • Use UTC ISO 8601 dates, integer money, and opaque IDs.
  • Return 202 plus a status resource for slow work.
  • Announce deprecations with headers and a sunset date.
  • Treat the API docs as part of the code.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Deep pages get slower and slower. Detect: slow-query logs show queries with large OFFSET values, and latency rises with the page number. Cause: offset pagination on a large table. Fix: switch to keyset pagination with an index on the sort columns plus a unique tie-breaker.
  • Users see duplicates or miss items while scrolling. Detect: support reports of repeated items in feeds; it happens more during busy periods. Cause: rows inserted or deleted between offset-based page requests. Fix: cursor pagination.
  • One request exhausts memory. Detect: a memory spike or out-of-memory restart right after a request with ?limit=100000. Cause: no maximum page size. Fix: clamp limit on the server and return the applied value in the response.
  • A new enum value breaks clients. Detect: client errors such as "unknown status" or deserialization failures right after you add a value like "refunded". Cause: clients that treat enums as closed lists. Fix: document that new values can appear, have clients handle unknown values, and announce additions.
  • Dates shift by hours. Detect: records created near midnight show on the wrong day for some users. Cause: local times without an offset in the API. Fix: send UTC ISO 8601 timestamps and convert only in the client's display layer.
  • An endpoint is removed while someone still uses it. Detect: a burst of 404s from one API key or user agent right after a release. Cause: removal without measuring usage. Fix: log usage per client after announcing deprecation, contact remaining callers, and return 410 Gone after the sunset date.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• API contract: the agreed description of endpoints, inputs, outputs, and errors.
  • Offset pagination: paging by skipping a number of rows.
  • Cursor (keyset) pagination: paging from the position of the last item seen.
  • Opaque cursor/ID: a value clients must pass back unchanged and not interpret.
  • Breaking change: a change that makes existing correct clients fail.
  • Problem details: the RFC 9457 standard JSON error format.
  • OpenAPI: a specification for describing HTTP APIs in YAML or JSON.
  • Deprecation / sunset: marking a feature as discouraged / announcing when it will stop working.
  • Idempotency key: a client-chosen unique value that makes retries of a request safe.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Returning unbounded lists ("we only have 50 users") that later grow to millions.
  • Offset pagination on large, fast-changing data, causing slow queries and duplicate items.
  • Letting clients sort or filter by any field, producing slow unindexed queries.
  • Renaming a field "because it reads better" and breaking every client.
  • Different error shapes per endpoint, forcing clients to special-case each one.
  • Local times without offsets and floats for money.
  • Sequential IDs on public resources, which leak volume and enable scraping.
  • Holding a request open for a long job until a proxy times it out with 504.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Compare offset and cursor pagination. When would you choose each?
  2. List three backward-compatible changes and three breaking changes.
  3. What are the standard members of an RFC 9457 problem details object, and which one should clients branch on?
  4. Why should dates be sent as UTC ISO 8601 strings and money as integers?
  5. How should an API handle a report that takes five minutes to generate?
  6. Which headers announce that an endpoint is deprecated and when it will be removed?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs.
  • RFC 8288: Web Linking defines the Link header used for pagination.
  • RFC 8594: The Sunset HTTP Header Field.
  • RFC 9745: The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field.
  • OpenAPI: OpenAPI Specification (latest).
  • OWASP: REST Security Cheat Sheet.

docs.title: API Styles: REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and RPC
docs.text: REST is the most common way to build web APIs, but not the only one. GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the data they need, gRPC offers fast, strongly typed calls between services, and RPC styles such as JSON-RPC and tRPC model an API as a set of functions. Each style makes different trade-offs, and many companies use more than one.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Choosing the wrong style creates years of friction: a public API in gRPC that browsers struggle to call, or a chatty internal REST API that wastes bandwidth between services.
  • You will meet all of these in real systems: GraphQL from GitHub and Shopify, gRPC inside microservice platforms, JSON-RPC in blockchain nodes and editor tooling, SOAP in banks and government systems.
  • Understanding the trade-offs helps you design a REST API better, too: many REST practices exist to solve problems GraphQL and gRPC solve differently.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub offers GraphQL next to REST. GitHub's GraphQL API overview says GraphQL lets you "replace multiple REST requests with a single call to fetch the data you specify", and describes defining precisely the data you want as a powerful advantage over traditional REST endpoints.
  • Shopify made GraphQL the default for its Admin API. Shopify's docs state the REST Admin API is a legacy API as of October 1, 2024, and that starting April 1, 2025, all new public apps must be built exclusively with the GraphQL Admin API.
  • etcd defines its whole API in gRPC. The etcd documentation says all etcd APIs are defined in gRPC services, which categorize the remote procedure calls the server understands, including streaming APIs such as watch streams.
  • Slack's Web API is RPC over HTTP. Slack calls its Web API a collection of HTTP RPC-style methods, with URLs like https://slack.com/api/METHOD_FAMILY.method, and says it is not a REST API.
  • JSON-RPC powers Ethereum nodes and AI tool protocols. Every Ethereum client implements a JSON-RPC specification so applications get a uniform set of methods, and the Model Context Protocol requires that all messages follow JSON-RPC 2.0.

docs.title: REST recap
docs.text:
• Many URLs, one per resource; standard HTTP methods; status codes carry the outcome.
  • Works with every HTTP client, proxy, CDN, and browser; responses to GET are cacheable by standard HTTP caches.
  • Weaknesses: the server decides the response shape, so clients may get too much data (over-fetching) or need several requests to build one screen (under-fetching).

See REST APIs.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text: GraphQL is a query language and runtime for APIs, created at Facebook and now governed by the GraphQL Foundation. The server publishes a typed schema; clients send queries naming exactly the fields they want, usually to a single endpoint (POST /graphql).

docs.title: Schema and types
docs.text:
type Author {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
  books: [Book!]!
}

type Book {
  id: ID!
  title: String!
  publishedYear: Int
  author: Author!
}

input NewBook {
  title: String!
  authorId: ID!
}

type Query {
  books(limit: Int = 20): [Book!]!
  book(id: ID!): Book
}

type Mutation {
  addBook(input: NewBook!): Book!
}

type Subscription {
  bookAdded: Book!
}
  • Scalars: Int, Float, String, Boolean, ID (plus custom scalars such as DateTime).
  • Object types have fields; input types describe arguments.
  • ! means non-null; [Book!]! is a non-null list of non-null books.
  • Query type: read operations. Mutation type: writes. Subscription type: a stream of events, usually over WebSockets.

docs.title: Queries, mutations, and subscriptions
docs.text:
The client asks for exactly the shape it needs, including nested data, in one request:

query BookPage($id: ID!) {
  book(id: $id) {
    title
    author {
      name
      books { title }
    }
  }
}

{
  "data": {
    "book": {
      "title": "Understanding REST",
      "author": { "name": "Ana Li", "books": [{ "title": "Understanding REST" }, { "title": "HTTP basics" }] }
    }
  }
}

A mutation changes data and returns the fields you ask for:

mutation {
  addBook(input: { title: "GraphQL in depth", authorId: "a1" }) {
    id
    title
  }
}

A subscription keeps a connection open and pushes results when events occur:

subscription { bookAdded { id title } }

docs.title: Resolvers
docs.text: Each field in the schema is backed by a resolver function. The GraphQL engine walks the query and calls the resolver for every requested field. A resolver receives the parent object, the field's arguments, a shared context (per request: the current user, data loaders), and query info.

docs.title: Over-fetching and under-fetching solved
docs.text: The mobile app asks for three fields, the desktop app for twenty, and neither needs a custom endpoint. A screen that needed five REST calls can be one GraphQL query.

docs.title: The N+1 problem and DataLoader
docs.text:
Resolvers run per field, so a naive implementation of the query above runs one query for the list of books plus one query per book to load its author: N+1 database round trips.

DataLoader fixes this by collecting all load(id) calls made during one tick of the event loop and resolving them with a single batched query, plus per-request caching of results.

import DataLoader from "dataloader";

// Create a new loader per request (in the GraphQL context) so caches never
// leak data between users
function createLoaders(db) {
  return {
    author: new DataLoader(async (ids) => {
      const rows = await db.authors.findByIds(ids); // ONE query: WHERE id IN (...)
      const byId = new Map(rows.map((a) => [a.id, a]));
      return ids.map((id) => byId.get(id) ?? null); // same order as ids
    }),
  };
}

const resolvers = {
  Book: {
    author: (book, _args, ctx) => ctx.loaders.author.load(book.authorId),
  },
};

docs.title: Caching difficulties
docs.text:
• Queries usually go as POST to one URL, so standard HTTP caches and CDNs cannot cache them by URL.
  • Every client can request a different shape, so responses vary endlessly.
  • Common answers: client-side normalized caches (Apollo Client, urql, Relay) that cache objects by type and ID, persisted queries (the client sends a hash of a pre-registered query, which can be a cacheable GET), and server-side caching in resolvers.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A GraphQL response has data and/or an errors array. Partial success is normal: one field can fail while others succeed.

{
  "data": { "book": { "title": "Understanding REST", "author": null } },
  "errors": [
    {
      "message": "Author service unavailable",
      "path": ["book", "author"],
      "extensions": { "code": "SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE" }
    }
  ]
}

Traditionally, servers return HTTP 200 even when errors is present, because the request itself was processed. That means HTTP-level monitoring and status-code-based retries do not see these failures; you must inspect the errors array and track error codes in extensions. (The GraphQL-over-HTTP specification work refines this, for example using 4xx for requests that fail before execution, such as unparseable queries. Apollo Server already answers a query that fails validation, such as one asking for a field that does not exist, with 400 and the code GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED.)

docs.title: Security and performance limits
docs.text:
Because clients write arbitrary queries, one request can be enormously expensive:

{ authors { books { author { books { author { books { title } } } } } } }

Protect the server with:

  • Depth limits (reject queries nested deeper than, say, 8 levels).
  • Complexity or cost analysis (assign costs to fields and reject queries above a budget); rate limit by cost, not by request count.
  • Pagination arguments with maximums on every list field.
  • Persisted queries / allowlists for first-party clients.
  • Authorization in resolvers or the business layer, per field where needed; the single endpoint means you cannot authorize by URL.
  • Considering disabling introspection in production for private APIs.

docs.title: Evolution without versions
docs.text: GraphQL APIs typically evolve one schema instead of versioning: add new fields freely, mark old ones with @deprecated(reason: "..."), and remove them once usage drops to zero.

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text:
gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework originally developed at Google. You define services and messages in Protocol Buffers (protobuf), generate client and server code in many languages, and call remote methods as if they were local functions.

syntax = "proto3";

package orders.v1;

service OrderService {
  rpc GetOrder (GetOrderRequest) returns (Order);                   // unary
  rpc ListOrders (ListOrdersRequest) returns (stream Order);        // server streaming
  rpc UploadEvents (stream OrderEvent) returns (UploadSummary);     // client streaming
  rpc Chat (stream ChatMessage) returns (stream ChatMessage);       // bidirectional
}

message GetOrderRequest {
  string id = 1;
}

message Order {
  string id = 1;
  string status = 2;
  int64 total_cents = 3;
}

The numbers (= 1, = 2) are field tags used in the binary encoding. Never change or reuse a tag; that is how protobuf stays backward compatible.

How it works:

  • Binary protobuf encoding: much smaller and faster to parse than JSON.
  • HTTP/2 transport: multiplexed streams over one connection, header compression, and long-lived streams.
  • Four call types: unary (one request, one response), server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming.
  • Code generation: protoc (or the Buf tool) generates typed stubs, so the contract is enforced at compile time.
  • Deadlines: every call should carry a deadline; it propagates to downstream calls.
  • Its own status codes (OK, INVALID_ARGUMENT, NOT_FOUND, PERMISSION_DENIED, UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, and others) sent in HTTP/2 trailers, not HTTP status codes.

Browser limits: browsers do not give JavaScript the low-level HTTP/2 control gRPC needs, so web apps use gRPC-Web (through a proxy such as Envoy, or a server that speaks it natively) or a compatible protocol such as Connect. That is why gRPC shines between backend services and less for public, browser-facing APIs. See gRPC.

docs.title: JSON-RPC
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0 is a tiny, transport-agnostic RPC protocol. You send a method name and parameters; you get a result or an error.

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "orders.get", "params": { "id": "ord_901" }, "id": 1 }

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "result": { "id": "ord_901", "status": "paid" }, "id": 1 }

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "error": { "code": -32601, "message": "Method not found" }, "id": 1 }
  • A request without an id is a notification (no response expected).
  • Several requests can be sent as a batch array.
  • Reserved error codes include -32700 (parse error), -32600 (invalid request), -32601 (method not found), -32602 (invalid params), and -32603 (internal error).
  • Used by Ethereum nodes, the Language Server Protocol (editor tooling), and the Model Context Protocol (AI tool integrations). It runs over HTTP, WebSockets, or standard input/output.

docs.title: tRPC
docs.text:
tRPC is a TypeScript library for building type-safe APIs without a schema language or code generation. The server defines procedures; the client imports the router's type and gets full autocompletion and compile-time checking of inputs and outputs.

// server
const appRouter = router({
  orderById: publicProcedure
    .input(z.object({ id: z.string() }))
    .query(({ input }) => db.orders.findById(input.id)),
});
export type AppRouter = typeof appRouter;

// client (type-only import; no generated code)
const order = await trpc.orderById.query({ id: "ord_901" }); // fully typed

It is excellent when one team owns a TypeScript frontend and backend (often a monorepo, often with Next.js). It is a poor fit for public APIs or clients in other languages, because the contract lives in TypeScript types.

docs.title: SOAP
docs.text:
SOAP (originally Simple Object Access Protocol) is an older, XML-based messaging protocol, widely used in enterprise systems in the 2000s.

<soap:Envelope xmlns:soap="http://www.w3.org/2003/05/soap-envelope">
  <soap:Body>
    <GetOrder xmlns="http://example.com/orders">
      <Id>ord_901</Id>
    </GetOrder>
  </soap:Body>
</soap:Envelope>
  • Messages are XML envelopes, usually sent with POST to one endpoint.
  • A WSDL document describes the operations and types; tools generate clients from it.
  • A family of WS-* standards adds security, transactions, and reliable messaging.
  • Verbose and heavyweight, but still common in banking, insurance, healthcare, payments, and government integrations. You are more likely to consume a SOAP service than to build a new one.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: REST GraphQL gRPC JSON-RPC tRPC SOAP Model Resources + HTTP methods Typed graph, client-chosen fields Typed remote procedures Remote procedures Typed TypeScript procedures XML operations Contract OpenAPI (optional) Schema (required) .proto files (required) Informal / docs TypeScript types WSDL Payload Usually JSON JSON Binary protobuf JSON JSON XML Transport HTTP/1.1, 2, 3 HTTP (+ WebSockets for subscriptions) HTTP/2 Any (HTTP, WebSocket, stdio) HTTP (+ WebSockets) HTTP (others possible) Browser support Native Native Needs gRPC-Web or a proxy Native Native Possible but awkward HTTP caching Excellent for GET Hard (needs persisted queries or client caches) No No Limited No Streaming SSE or WebSockets alongside Subscriptions Built-in, four modes Via transport Subscriptions No Performance Good Good; depends on resolvers Excellent Good Good Heavier Learning curve Low Medium Medium to high Low Low (for TS developers) High Best for Public APIs, CRUD, web and mobile apps Many clients with different data needs, complex nested UIs Internal service-to-service calls, low latency, streaming Simple command-style APIs, tooling protocols Full-stack TypeScript apps owned by one team Legacy enterprise integrations

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
Choosing a style
docs.text:
• Public API for third parties: REST (with OpenAPI). Everyone can call it with anything.
  • Product with web and mobile clients needing different data from a rich domain: GraphQL, often as a gateway in front of other services.
  • Internal microservices with high throughput or streaming: gRPC.
  • One team, TypeScript end to end: tRPC.
  • Integrating with a bank or government system: whatever they offer, often SOAP.
  • Mixing is normal: gRPC between services, a GraphQL or REST layer facing clients, webhooks for events.

docs.title: When not to use each
docs.text:
• GraphQL: not for simple CRUD APIs with one client, file downloads, or APIs that depend on HTTP caching and CDNs; not without the capacity to build query limits, DataLoader batching, and error monitoring.
  • gRPC: not for public, browser-facing APIs where callers cannot easily generate stubs or use HTTP/2 directly; not when humans need to debug calls with curl and a browser.
  • tRPC: not for public APIs, mobile apps in other languages, or teams that do not share one TypeScript codebase.
  • JSON-RPC: not when you want HTTP semantics (caching, status codes, resource URLs) to do part of the work.
  • SOAP: not for new APIs, unless a partner requires it.
  • REST: less suited when one screen needs data from many resources with many client variants (GraphQL), or for chatty internal streaming (gRPC).
If your main constraint is... Prefer Then add Unknown third-party clients REST OpenAPI, webhooks for events Many client shapes over one data graph GraphQL DataLoader, depth/cost limits, persisted queries Latency and throughput between services gRPC Deadlines, protobuf linting, a gateway for browsers One team, one TypeScript monorepo tRPC Zod validation on inputs A tool or agent protocol JSON-RPC A clear method catalog and error codes

docs.title: A small GraphQL server in Node.js
docs.text:
import { ApolloServer } from "@apollo/server";
import { startStandaloneServer } from "@apollo/server/standalone";

const authors = [{ id: "a1", name: "Ana Li" }];
const books = [{ id: "b1", title: "Understanding REST", authorId: "a1" }];

const typeDefs = `#graphql
  type Author { id: ID!, name: String! }
  type Book { id: ID!, title: String!, author: Author! }
  type Query { books: [Book!]!, book(id: ID!): Book }
  type Mutation { addBook(title: String!, authorId: ID!): Book! }
`;

const resolvers = {
  Query: {
    books: () => books,
    book: (_parent, { id }) => books.find((b) => b.id === id) ?? null,
  },
  Mutation: {
    addBook: (_parent, { title, authorId }) => {
      const book = { id: `b${books.length + 1}`, title, authorId };
      books.push(book);
      return book;
    },
  },
  // Field resolver: runs for every Book whose author is requested
  Book: {
    author: (book) => authors.find((a) => a.id === book.authorId),
  },
};

const server = new ApolloServer({ typeDefs, resolvers });
const { url } = await startStandaloneServer(server, { listen: { port: 4000 } });
console.log(`GraphQL ready at ${url}`);

Query it:

curl -s http://localhost:4000/ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query":"{ books { title author { name } } }"}'

docs.title: The same read in each style
docs.text:
REST:     GET /api/books/b1?include=author
GraphQL:  POST /graphql   {"query":"{ book(id:\"b1\") { title author { name } } }"}
gRPC:     bookService.GetBook({ id: "b1" })            (generated client, binary over HTTP/2)
JSON-RPC: POST /rpc       {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"books.get","params":{"id":"b1"},"id":1}
tRPC:     trpc.bookById.query({ id: "b1" })

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Pick the style for the consumer, not for fashion: public and browser clients favor REST or GraphQL; internal hot paths favor gRPC.
  • GraphQL: use DataLoader, enforce depth and cost limits, paginate every list, authorize in the business layer, and monitor errors separately from HTTP status codes.
  • gRPC: set deadlines on every call, never reuse protobuf field numbers, version packages (orders.v1), and keep .proto files in a shared repository.
  • RPC styles: keep method names consistent and document error codes.
  • Whatever the style: a clear contract, consistent errors, authentication, rate limiting, and observability still apply.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• GraphQL database load explodes on one screen. Detect: traces show hundreds of nearly identical database queries for a single GraphQL request. Cause: the N+1 problem in field resolvers. Fix: batch with a per-request DataLoader, and alert on queries per request.
  • One client's query pins the CPU. Detect: CPU spikes that line up with one deeply nested or very wide query in the logs. Cause: no depth or cost limits. Fix: enforce depth and complexity limits, cap list sizes, and use persisted queries for your own clients.
  • Errors invisible to monitoring. Detect: the HTTP error rate is near zero while users report failures; responses are 200 with an errors array. Cause: monitoring only counts HTTP status codes. Fix: log and count GraphQL errors by extensions.code and operation name.
  • Stack traces in GraphQL error responses. Detect: production responses contain extensions.stacktrace. Cause: Apollo Server's includeStacktraceInErrorResponses defaults to true unless NODE_ENV is production or test. Fix: set NODE_ENV=production in production, or set the option to false explicitly.
  • gRPC calls pile up during an incident. Detect: in-flight calls and memory grow while a downstream service is slow, and few calls end with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED. Cause: calls without deadlines wait indefinitely. Fix: set a deadline on every call and propagate it downstream.
  • Corrupted data after a protobuf change. Detect: values appear in the wrong fields during a rolling deploy when old and new services talk to each other. Cause: a deleted field's number was reused. Fix: never reuse field numbers; the protobuf language guide says you must reserve deleted field numbers with reserved.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Over-fetching / under-fetching: receiving more data than needed / needing several requests to get enough data.
  • GraphQL schema: the typed description of everything a GraphQL API can return.
  • Resolver: the function that produces the value of one GraphQL field.
  • N+1 problem: one query for a list plus one query per item.
  • DataLoader: a utility that batches and caches loads within a request.
  • Persisted query: a pre-registered query referenced by an ID or hash.
  • Protocol Buffers: Google's language-neutral binary serialization format and schema language.
  • Unary / streaming RPC: a call with one request and one response / with a stream of messages in one or both directions.
  • RPC: remote procedure call; invoking a function on another machine.
  • WSDL: the XML document describing a SOAP service.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "GraphQL replaces databases or REST everywhere." It is an API layer; resolvers still call databases and services, often REST or gRPC ones.
  • Ignoring N+1 in GraphQL, turning one query into hundreds of database calls.
  • Leaving GraphQL queries unbounded, so one malicious query exhausts the server.
  • Treating a GraphQL 200 as success without checking errors.
  • Exposing gRPC directly to browsers without gRPC-Web or a gateway.
  • Reusing protobuf field numbers, silently corrupting data between old and new services.
  • Choosing tRPC for a public API consumed by other languages.
  • Calling a level-0 "POST everything" API REST. That is RPC over HTTP.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What problem do over-fetching and under-fetching describe, and how does GraphQL address them?
  2. Explain the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how DataLoader solves it.
  3. Why is HTTP caching harder with GraphQL than with REST?
  4. What are the four gRPC call types, and why is gRPC uncommon for public browser APIs?
  5. When is tRPC a good choice, and when is it a poor one?
  6. Which style would you choose for internal, high-throughput service calls, and why?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• GraphQL: Introduction to GraphQL and the GraphQL specification.
  • gRPC: Introduction to gRPC and core concepts.
  • Protocol Buffers: protobuf.dev.
  • JSON-RPC: JSON-RPC 2.0 Specification.
  • tRPC: tRPC documentation.
  • OWASP: GraphQL Cheat Sheet.

docs.title: Authentication and Authorization
docs.text: Authentication asks, "Who are you?" Authorization asks, "What are you allowed to do?" A backend must answer both questions on every protected request: first establish the identity behind the request, then decide whether that identity may perform the requested action on the requested resource.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Many serious web application breaches are not exotic attacks; they are missing or incorrect access checks. Broken access control is ranked first in the OWASP Top 10 (2021), which found some form of it in 94% of the applications tested. A signed-in user changes an ID in a URL and reads someone else's invoice. An API accepts a role from the request body. A password database leaks and the passwords were stored in a form that can be reversed. Each of these is an authentication or authorization failure.

Getting this right protects users' data, keeps the application compliant with privacy and security obligations, and makes the rest of the system simpler: when identity and permission are established in one well-tested place, individual route handlers do not each invent their own rules.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Mandatory MFA at GitHub. Since March 2023, GitHub has required users who contribute code on GitHub.com to enable two-factor authentication, to protect developers and the wider software supply chain (GitHub Docs: mandatory 2FA).
  • Passkeys at Google. Google's developer guidance explains that with passkeys a site stores only a public key, and a passkey works only on the site it was registered for, so users cannot be tricked into signing in to a look-alike site (Google for Developers: Passkeys).
  • Least-privilege tokens at GitHub. Fine-grained personal access tokens can be limited to specific repositories and specific permissions; GitHub recommends them over classic tokens, which can access every repository the user can (GitHub Docs: personal access tokens).
  • Attribute-based access control in AWS IAM. IAM policies can grant permissions based on attributes — AWS calls them tags — attached to users, roles, and resources, so one policy covers many resources (AWS IAM: ABAC).
  • Authorization as a shared service at Google. Zanzibar stores and evaluates access control lists for hundreds of Google services, including Calendar, Cloud, Drive, Maps, Photos, and YouTube (Google Research: Zanzibar).

Popular tools and providers: identity providers such as Auth0, Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Amazon Cognito, Firebase Authentication, and Keycloak (open source); policy engines such as Open Policy Agent and OpenFGA.

docs.title: Authentication versus authorization
docs.text:
Question Authentication (AuthN) Authorization (AuthZ) What it decides Who is making the request Whether that identity may do this action Typical inputs Password, passkey, one-time code, token, session cookie Identity, roles, attributes, resource ownership, policy Failure status 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated) 403 Forbidden (authenticated, but not allowed) When it runs At sign-in, then on each request (verify session or token) On every request that reads or changes protected data

The two are separate steps. A valid login proves identity; it does not grant access to everything.

docs.title: Authentication factors
docs.text:
An authentication factor is a category of evidence:

  • Something you know (knowledge): a password or PIN.
  • Something you have (possession): a phone with an authenticator app, a hardware security key, or a device that holds a passkey.
  • Something you are (inherence): a fingerprint or face, usually used to unlock a local device or key rather than sent to the server.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires evidence from at least two different categories. Two passwords are still a single factor.

docs.title: Storing passwords
docs.text:
A backend should never be able to recover a user's password. It stores a password hash produced by a slow, salted algorithm designed for passwords:

  • Argon2id — the current first choice in OWASP guidance.
  • scrypt — memory-hard, a good alternative.
  • bcrypt — widely available and acceptable; note that it only uses the first 72 bytes of input.

General-purpose hashes such as SHA-256 or MD5 are the wrong tool: they are designed to be fast, which lets an attacker test billions of guesses per second against a leaked database.

  • Salt: a unique random value per password, stored alongside the hash. It makes identical passwords produce different hashes and defeats precomputed tables. Modern password-hashing libraries generate and embed the salt for you.
  • Pepper: an optional secret value applied to every password and stored outside the database (for example, in a secret manager). A database leak alone is then not enough to start cracking.
  • Work factor: the cost parameters (iterations, memory) that make each hash deliberately slow. Increase them as hardware improves and rehash on the user's next successful login.

Encryption is also wrong for passwords: anything encrypted can be decrypted by whoever obtains the key.

docs.title: Multi-factor authentication options
docs.text:
Method How it works Notes TOTP (authenticator app) Server and app share a secret; both derive a 6-digit code from the current time (RFC 6238) Good baseline; phishable if a user types the code into a fake site SMS or voice codes Server sends a code to a phone number Weakest option: SIM swapping, number porting, interception Email codes or links Code or link sent to the user's mailbox Only as strong as the email account Push approval App on a registered device approves a sign-in Watch for "MFA fatigue" — users approving repeated prompts Passkeys / WebAuthn Device holds a private key bound to the site's origin; server stores the public key Phishing-resistant, no shared secret on the server; the strongest common option

Passkeys use public-key cryptography: the server sends a challenge, the authenticator signs it with a private key that is never sent to the server, and the server verifies the signature with the stored public key. (The private key stays on the device, or is end-to-end encrypted when a password manager syncs it between the user's devices.) Because the key is bound to the site's origin, a look-alike phishing domain cannot use it.

docs.title: Keeping a user signed in
docs.text:
After authentication, the server needs proof on later requests that this client already signed in. The two main approaches are:

  • Session-based: the server stores session data and gives the browser an opaque session ID in a cookie.
  • Token-based: the server issues a signed token (often a JWT) that the client presents on each request.

Both are covered in depth in sessions, cookies, and JWT. Signing in with an external identity provider ("Sign in with Google") uses OpenID Connect, covered in OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, and SSO.

docs.title: Authorization models
docs.text:
Model Decision based on Example Good for ACL (access control list) A list of who may do what on each resource Document shared with specific users File sharing, per-object grants RBAC (role-based) The roles assigned to a user admin can delete users; editor can publish Most business applications ABAC (attribute-based) Attributes of user, resource, action, and environment Doctors may read records of patients in their own clinic during working hours Fine-grained, policy-driven rules ReBAC (relationship-based) Relationships in a graph You may edit a document if you are a member of the team that owns its folder Collaboration apps, nested sharing

Real systems often combine them: RBAC for broad capabilities ("can manage billing") plus an ownership or relationship check for specific records.

docs.title: Least privilege and deny by default
docs.text: Least privilege means every user, service, and token gets only the permissions it needs, for only as long as it needs them. Deny by default means that if no rule explicitly allows an action, it is refused. A new route without a permission check should fail closed, not open.

docs.title: Object-level authorization and IDOR
docs.text:
Broken object level authorization (BOLA), also called IDOR (insecure direct object reference), is ranked first in the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023). It happens when a handler loads a record by the ID in the request without checking that the current user may access that record:

GET /api/invoices/1001   ← my invoice, fine
GET /api/invoices/1002   ← someone else's invoice; server returns it anyway

A role check is not enough here: both users have the role customer. The server must check the relationship between this user and this specific record, on every read, update, and delete.

docs.title: Enforce on the server, on every request
docs.text: The frontend can hide buttons for convenience, but it is not a security boundary. Anyone can call the API directly with curl or a modified client. Every protected endpoint must authenticate the caller and authorize the action, and it must take identity and roles from the verified session or token, never from the request body or query string.

docs.title: 401 versus 403
docs.text:
• 401 Unauthorized: the request has no valid credentials (missing, expired, or invalid). Despite the name, it means "unauthenticated." RFC 9110 requires a 401 response to include a WWW-Authenticate header naming the expected scheme, for example WWW-Authenticate: Bearer.
  • 403 Forbidden: the server knows who the caller is, and the caller is not allowed to do this. Signing in again will not help.
  • 404 Not Found instead of 403: acceptable when revealing that a resource exists would itself leak information (for example, another user's private document).

See HTTP status codes for the full list.

docs.title: Account security
docs.text:
• Rate limiting and lockout: limit sign-in attempts per account and per IP. Prefer progressive delays or temporary lockouts over permanent lockouts, which let an attacker lock legitimate users out. See rate limiting and throttling.
  • Generic errors: respond "Invalid email or password" for both unknown emails and wrong passwords, and keep response times similar, to avoid user enumeration. Apply the same idea to registration and password reset ("If an account exists, we sent an email").
  • Password reset tokens: generate long random tokens with a cryptographically secure generator, store only a hash of the token, make them single-use and short-lived (minutes, not days), and invalidate existing sessions after a reset.
  • Breached-password checks: reject passwords known from public breaches instead of enforcing complicated composition rules.
  • Re-authentication: require the password or MFA again before sensitive actions such as changing email, password, or MFA settings.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Every backend with private data needs authentication and authorization; the real decisions are how to authenticate and which authorization model to use.

Run your own password sign-in when:

  • The product is small, users are your own customers, and you can follow the password storage, rate limiting, and reset guidance on this page.

Use an external identity provider (OpenID Connect) instead when:

  • Users already have company or social accounts (workforce apps, B2B SaaS with single sign-on).
  • You need MFA, passkeys, breached-password checks, and account recovery without building them yourself.
  • Compliance requires centralized audit and account lifecycle management.

Avoid:

  • Inventing your own token or password scheme.
  • Relying on the frontend, API gateway, or "hidden" URLs as the only check.
Need Good fit Not a good fit Broad capabilities ("can manage billing") RBAC Per-record rules — roles alone cannot say "only your own invoices" Rules on context (department, region, time) ABAC Tiny apps where two roles are enough Sharing and nested ownership (docs, folders, teams) ReBAC Simple single-owner records — an ownerId check is enough Strongest sign-in for consumers Passkeys, with a fallback Kiosk or shared devices without a recovery plan Second factor where passkeys are not yet possible TOTP authenticator apps SMS as the only factor for high-value accounts

docs.title: Hashing and verifying a password with Argon2id
docs.text:
import argon2 from "argon2";

// At registration: store only the hash (it embeds the salt and parameters)
export async function hashPassword(plainPassword) {
  return argon2.hash(plainPassword, { type: argon2.argon2id });
}

// At sign-in: compare a candidate password with the stored hash
export async function verifyPassword(storedHash, candidatePassword) {
  return argon2.verify(storedHash, candidatePassword);
}

docs.title: Sign-in that avoids user enumeration
docs.text:
// Hash of a throwaway password, computed once at startup, so unknown emails
// still pay the cost of a hash comparison and take a similar time.
const dummyHash = await hashPassword("not-a-real-password");

export async function signIn(email, password) {
  const user = await users.findByEmail(email.toLowerCase());
  const hashToCheck = user ? user.passwordHash : dummyHash;
  const valid = await verifyPassword(hashToCheck, password);

  if (!user || !valid) {
    // Same message whether the email exists or not
    throw new UnauthorizedError("Invalid email or password");
  }
  return user;
}

docs.title: Role check middleware (RBAC)
docs.text:
// Runs after authentication middleware has set request.user
export function requireRole(...allowedRoles) {
  return (request, response, next) => {
    if (!request.user) {
      return response.status(401).json({ error: "Sign in required" });
    }
    if (!allowedRoles.includes(request.user.role)) {
      return response.status(403).json({ error: "Not allowed" });
    }
    next();
  };
}

app.delete("/api/users/:id", authenticate, requireRole("admin"), deleteUser);

docs.title: Ownership check (preventing IDOR)
docs.text:
Always scope the query by the current user rather than loading first and hoping to remember the check:

SELECT id, title, amount FROM invoices WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?;

app.get("/api/invoices/:id", authenticate, async (request, response) => {
  const invoice = await db.invoices.findOne({
    _id: request.params.id,
    ownerId: request.user.id, // identity from the verified session, not input
  });
  if (!invoice) {
    return response.status(404).json({ error: "Invoice not found" });
  }
  response.json(invoice);
});

The Express side of this — wiring sessions, JWT middleware, and Passport — is covered in authentication in Express. REST APIs should also avoid leaking private details in their error responses.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use established libraries and protocols (Argon2/bcrypt libraries, WebAuthn libraries, OpenID Connect providers) instead of inventing schemes.
  • Centralize authentication in middleware and keep authorization rules in a small, testable policy layer.
  • Deny by default; require an explicit permission for every protected route.
  • Check object ownership or relationship for every record-level operation.
  • Offer MFA, and prefer passkeys or authenticator apps over SMS.
  • Expire sessions and tokens, and support revocation (sign out everywhere).
  • Log authentication events (sign-ins, failures, MFA changes, password resets) without logging passwords, codes, or tokens.
  • Write tests for "user A cannot access user B's data" for every resource.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Credential stuffing. Symptom: failed sign-ins jump across many different accounts from many IP addresses. Detect: a dashboard of failed sign-ins per minute and the ratio of failures to successes; auth logs with the same password failing against many emails. Cause: attackers replaying passwords leaked from other sites. Fix: rate limit per account and per IP, check new passwords against breached-password lists, add MFA, and add bot detection or a challenge after repeated failures.
  • Sign-in becomes slow under load. Symptom: p95 latency of POST /login climbs from about 100 ms to seconds during peak traffic. Detect: latency histogram for the sign-in route, CPU and memory on the auth instances. Cause: password hashing is deliberately expensive, and async hashing libraries such as bcrypt run on libuv's fixed-size thread pool (four threads unless UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE changes it), so hashes queue up. Fix: benchmark hash parameters on production hardware, scale sign-in capacity separately, and raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE only after measuring.
  • An IDOR reaches production. Symptom: a bug report or security report says a user saw another customer's data. Detect: audit logs show reads where the record's owner differs from the requesting user. Cause: a handler loads a record by ID without an ownership condition. Fix: scope every query by owner or tenant, add "user A cannot read user B's record" tests for each resource, and review new routes for the check.
  • Lockouts used as an attack. Symptom: a wave of support tickets from users who cannot sign in. Detect: the count of locked accounts rises sharply without matching user activity. Cause: permanent lockout after N failures lets anyone lock out any account. Fix: use progressive delays or temporary locks, challenge suspicious attempts, and let users unlock through a verified email.
  • Permission changes do not take effect. Symptom: a user who lost the admin role can still perform admin actions. Detect: audit log entries for admin actions by users whose current role is not admin. Cause: roles were copied into a long-lived token or cached session. Fix: keep access tokens short-lived, re-check roles on the server for sensitive actions, and revoke sessions when roles change.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Identity: the person or service represented by a request.
  • Principal: the authenticated identity a request runs as.
  • Credential: evidence used to authenticate, such as a password, key, or token.
  • Authentication (AuthN): establishing or verifying identity.
  • Authorization (AuthZ): deciding whether an identity may perform an action on a resource.
  • MFA: multi-factor authentication; evidence from two or more factor categories.
  • Passkey: a WebAuthn credential — a key pair bound to the site's origin, where the private key is never sent to the server.
  • Password hash: the output of a slow, salted one-way function used to verify passwords without storing them.
  • Salt / pepper: a per-password random value / a global secret applied to all passwords and stored outside the database.
  • RBAC / ABAC / ReBAC: role-, attribute-, and relationship-based access control.
  • Least privilege: granting only the minimum access needed.
  • IDOR / BOLA: accessing an object by changing its identifier because the server does not check ownership.
  • User enumeration: discovering which accounts exist from differences in responses or timing.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Signed in means allowed." Authentication does not grant access to every action or record.
  • Hiding UI is not access control. Every API call must be checked on the server.
  • Trusting identity or role from the request body. Read them only from the verified session or token.
  • Hashing passwords with SHA-256 or MD5. Fast hashes are easy to brute force; use a password-hashing algorithm.
  • Encrypting passwords. Encryption is reversible; hashing is not.
  • Treating encoding as security. Base64 or a JWT payload is readable by anyone; encoding is not encryption.
  • Different errors for "no such user" and "wrong password." This reveals which accounts exist.
  • Long-lived or reusable reset tokens. Make them random, hashed, single-use, and short-lived.
  • Returning 403 when 401 is correct, or vice versa. 401 means "who are you?"; 403 means "I know who you are, and no."

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and which status code does each failure usually produce?
  2. Why are Argon2id, scrypt, and bcrypt suitable for passwords while SHA-256 is not?
  3. What makes passkeys resistant to phishing when TOTP codes are not?
  4. Describe an IDOR vulnerability and the server-side check that prevents it.
  5. How do RBAC and ABAC differ? Give an example rule that RBAC alone cannot express.
  6. How should a sign-in endpoint respond to avoid user enumeration?
