docs.title: Backend Fundamentals
docs.text: Backend development builds the server-side parts of an application. A backend receives requests, applies business rules, reads and writes data, talks to other services, and returns responses. Users never see it directly, but every login, search, payment, and saved form depends on it.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Some responsibilities cannot safely live in a browser or mobile app:

  • Trust: code running on a user's device can be read and changed by that user. Access rules, prices, and permission checks must be enforced where the user cannot tamper with them.
  • Shared data: many users and devices need to see the same orders, messages, and accounts. A central service coordinates that data.
  • Secrets: database passwords, payment-provider keys, and signing keys must never be shipped to a client.
  • Heavy or slow work: sending email, generating reports, and processing video should not depend on a user keeping a browser tab open.
  • Many clients, one set of rules: a web app, a mobile app, and partner integrations can all use the same backend, so the rules live in one place.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe keeps secret keys on the server. Stripe's API keys documentation states that only publishable keys are safe to expose outside your application's back end. A checkout page can use a publishable key in the browser, but creating charges or refunds needs a key that must stay in your backend. This is the "secrets" responsibility above in practice.
  • Shopify chose a modular monolith over microservices. Shopify Engineering describes, in Deconstructing the Monolith, how one of the largest Ruby on Rails codebases evolved into a modular monolith: all code in one codebase, with boundaries defined and respected between components. They judged that microservices would bring their own set of challenges.
  • Slack moves slow work to a job queue. In Scaling Slack's Job Queue, Slack explains that its job queue runs business logic that is too time-consuming to run inside a web request, and that it is used for every message post, push notification, URL unfurl, and calendar reminder. That is asynchronous processing at very large scale.

docs.title: What a backend does
docs.text: Responsibility What it means Example Expose an API Accept requests in an agreed format and return responses GET /api/orders/42 returns order 42 as JSON Business logic Apply the rules of the product An order total includes tax and cannot be negative Data persistence Store data so it survives restarts and is shared Save the order in a database Authentication Establish who is calling Check a session cookie or access token Authorization Decide what that caller may do A customer may read only their own orders Validation Reject malformed or dangerous input A quantity must be a positive integer Integrations Call other systems Charge a card through a payment provider Background work Run work outside the request Email a receipt after the order is placed Observability Record what happened Log errors, measure latency, trace slow requests

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
A small backend can be a single process and a database. As an application grows, more specialized parts appear:

  • Application server: the program you write. It routes requests, runs business logic, and coordinates everything else. In this section that is Node.js with Express.
  • Database: the durable source of truth, such as PostgreSQL or MongoDB. See database fundamentals.
  • Cache: a fast store, such as Redis, that keeps copies of data that is expensive to compute or fetch. See caching.
  • Message queue: a buffer that lets one part of the system hand work to another without waiting. See message queues.
  • Background workers: processes that take jobs from the queue. See background jobs and scheduling.
  • Object storage: a store for files such as uploads and generated PDFs. See file storage and uploads.
  • Load balancer or reverse proxy: spreads traffic across servers, terminates TLS, and shields the application. See reverse proxy.

docs.title: Stateless and stateful servers
docs.text:
A stateless server keeps no memory of a client between requests. Every request carries what the server needs (a token or session ID), and any shared state lives in a database or cache.

A stateful server keeps client-specific data in its own memory, such as an in-memory session map or an open game room.

Stateless Stateful Scaling out Add servers freely; any server can handle any request Requests must return to the server holding the state (sticky sessions) Restart or crash Nothing is lost beyond in-flight requests In-memory state is lost Where state lives Database, cache, or the client (token) Process memory Typical use REST APIs, most web backends WebSocket rooms, multiplayer games, some streaming

Prefer stateless application servers. When you need state, put it in a shared store such as Redis so any instance can read it. See scalability.

docs.title: Synchronous and asynchronous processing
docs.text:
Synchronous processing means the client waits while the server finishes the work and returns the result in the same response. It is right for fast operations whose result the client needs now, such as reading a profile.

Asynchronous processing means the server accepts the work, returns quickly (often 202 Accepted), and finishes the work later in a background worker. It is right for slow or unreliable work such as video encoding, bulk imports, or calls to flaky third-party services.

Do not confuse this with asynchronous code. Node.js uses non-blocking I/O inside a single request, but the client still waits for that request's response. See the event loop.

docs.title: Monoliths and microservices
docs.text:
A monolith is one deployable application that contains all features. A microservice architecture splits features into separately deployed services that talk over the network.

Most teams should start with a well-structured monolith. Microservices add network failures, distributed data, and operational overhead; they pay off when many teams need to deploy independently or parts of the system have very different scaling needs. See software architecture.

docs.title: Common backend languages and frameworks
docs.text:
Language Popular frameworks Typical strengths JavaScript / TypeScript (Node.js) Express, Fastify, NestJS, Hono One language with the frontend; strong for I/O-heavy APIs Python Django, FastAPI, Flask Fast development; strong data and machine-learning ecosystem Java / Kotlin Spring Boot, Ktor Mature enterprise tooling; strong performance Go net/http, Gin, Echo Simple concurrency; small, fast binaries C# ASP.NET Core High performance; strong tooling on Windows and Linux Ruby Ruby on Rails Convention-driven, very productive for CRUD apps PHP Laravel, Symfony Huge hosting ecosystem; mature web frameworks Rust Axum, Actix Web Memory safety and very high performance

The concepts in this section (HTTP, APIs, authentication, errors, queues) apply to every stack. Only the syntax changes.

docs.title: How a frontend talks to a backend
docs.text:
1. The frontend sends an HTTP request, usually with fetch(), to an API URL.
  2. The request carries a method, path, headers (such as Authorization or a cookie), and sometimes a JSON body.
  3. The backend authenticates the caller, validates the input, runs the logic, and talks to the database.
  4. The backend returns a status code, headers, and usually a JSON body.
  5. The frontend checks the status and updates the interface.

See the client-server model and request lifecycle for the full journey, and JSON and fetch for the frontend side.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
You need your own backend when:

  • Data must be shared between users or devices and kept consistent.
  • Rules must be enforced where users cannot tamper with them: prices, permissions, quotas, payments.
  • You hold secrets: database credentials, payment keys, signing keys.
  • Work must continue without the user's browser: emails, reports, imports, scheduled jobs.
  • Several clients (web, mobile, partners) must share one set of rules.

You may not need a custom backend when:

  • The site is static content (documentation, a portfolio, a landing page): a static host or CDN is enough.
  • A managed service already covers the need (authentication, a hosted database with row-level rules, a payment provider's hosted checkout) and you have little custom logic.
  • The logic is a few small, event-driven functions; serverless functions can be simpler than running servers.
Situation Static hosting Managed backend service Serverless functions Your own backend server Content only, no user data Best fit Overkill Overkill Overkill Simple app, standard auth and CRUD No Good fit Good fit Works, more effort Custom business rules, integrations No Limited Good for small pieces Best fit Long-running work, WebSockets, steady high traffic No Limited Awkward (time limits, cold starts) Best fit Full control of data and infrastructure No No Partial Yes

docs.title: A task API, conceptually
docs.text:
For a task-list product, the backend might expose:

Request What the backend does Response GET /api/tasks Authenticates the user, loads only their tasks 200 with a JSON array POST /api/tasks Validates the title, saves the task with the user's ID 201 with the new task PATCH /api/tasks/42 Checks task 42 belongs to the user, applies the change 200 with the updated task DELETE /api/tasks/42 Checks ownership, deletes 204 with no body

docs.title: A minimal backend in Express
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json()); // parse JSON request bodies

const tasks = []; // in-memory only: lost on restart, not shared between servers

app.get("/api/tasks", (req, res) => {
  res.json(tasks);
});

app.post("/api/tasks", (req, res) => {
  const title = req.body?.title;
  if (typeof title !== "string" || title.trim() === "") {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "title is required" });
  }
  const task = { id: tasks.length + 1, title: title.trim(), done: false };
  tasks.push(task);
  res.status(201).json(task);
});

app.listen(3000, () => console.log("API on http://localhost:3000"));

This shows routing, validation, and status codes. A real backend replaces the array with a database, adds authentication, and handles errors centrally. The rest of this section builds each of those pieces.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Separate concerns. Routes receive requests, services hold business rules, and data-access code talks to the database. Each layer is easier to test and change. See project structure.
  • Never trust the client. Validate every input and enforce every permission on the server, even if the UI already hides the button.
  • Keep servers stateless so you can run several copies behind a load balancer.
  • Return predictable responses: correct status codes and one consistent error format. See HTTP status codes.
  • Move slow work off the request path with queues and workers.
  • Keep secrets out of code and load configuration from the environment. See configuration and secrets.
  • Make failures visible with structured logs, metrics, and alerts. See logging and monitoring.

docs.title: Backend developer responsibilities checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] The API contract is documented (paths, inputs, outputs, errors).
  • [ ] Every endpoint authenticates the caller and checks permissions.
  • [ ] All input is validated; unknown fields are rejected or stripped.
  • [ ] Errors return the right status code and do not leak internals.
  • [ ] Database queries are indexed and paginated.
  • [ ] Slow and unreliable work runs in the background with retries.
  • [ ] Timeouts are set on every outgoing call.
  • [ ] Secrets come from configuration, never from source control.
  • [ ] Logs, metrics, and health checks exist before production.
  • [ ] Changes stay backward compatible for clients already in use.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Random logouts after adding a second server. Symptom: users are signed out or get 401 at random. Detect: the 401 rate jumps when the instance count goes from one to two, and logs show "session not found" on instances that did not create the session. Cause: sessions kept in process memory. Fix: store sessions in a shared store such as Redis, or use tokens, so any instance can serve any request.
  • Slow requests killed by the platform. Symptom: report or export endpoints fail for large accounts only. Detect: p99 latency near the proxy's limit, and 504 responses or platform timeout errors. On Heroku, the router ends requests that take longer than 30 seconds and logs an H12 error. Cause: slow work done inside the request. Fix: return 202 Accepted, queue the work, and let the client poll or get notified.
  • A secret shipped to the client. Symptom: unexpected charges or data access with your credentials. Detect: a secret-scanning alert on the repository or bundle, or a provider notice about an exposed key. Cause: a server-side key placed in frontend code or a VITE_/NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable. Fix: rotate the key immediately and move every call that needs it to the backend.
  • An endpoint that was fine in testing times out with real data. Symptom: GET /api/orders gets slower every month. Detect: slow-query logs and response sizes growing with table size. Cause: an unpaginated, unindexed list. Fix: paginate, cap the page size, and index the filter and sort columns.
  • Invalid input shows up as 500 errors. Symptom: the error-rate alert fires, but nothing is broken. Detect: 5xx logs full of database constraint or type errors caused by bad input. Cause: missing validation. Fix: validate at the edge and return 400 or 422, keeping 5xx for real server faults.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Client: a program that initiates a request, such as a browser, mobile app, or another server.
  • Server: a program that listens for requests and responds to them.
  • API (Application Programming Interface): the contract that defines how clients talk to a backend.
  • Endpoint: one operation in an API, usually a method plus a path.
  • Business logic: the rules that describe what the product does.
  • Persistence: keeping data beyond a single request or process lifetime.
  • Stateless server: a server that keeps no per-client memory between requests.
  • Synchronous processing: the client waits for the work to finish.
  • Asynchronous processing: the work is accepted now and finished later.
  • Monolith: one deployable application containing all features.
  • Microservice: a small, independently deployed service owning one capability.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Backend code is secure because it runs on a server." A server is only as secure as its validation, authorization, and dependency hygiene.
  • "The database is the backend." The database stores data; the backend also enforces rules, validates input, and coordinates services.
  • "If the UI hides it, users can't do it." Anyone can send requests directly with curl or a script. The server must check everything.
  • "A 200 response means the operation was correct." It means the server reports success; the result can still be wrong if the logic is.
  • "We need microservices from day one." Most products are better served by a modular monolith until there is a concrete reason to split.
  • Storing session data in process memory and then adding a second server, which breaks logins at random.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Name four responsibilities that must live on the server rather than in the browser, and explain why for each.
  2. What is the difference between a stateless and a stateful server, and why does it matter when you add a second server?
  3. When would you choose asynchronous processing with 202 Accepted over a normal synchronous response?
  4. What does each building block do: cache, message queue, object storage, load balancer?
  5. Why should a team usually start with a monolith?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Introduction to the server side explains server-side responsibilities and request processing.
  • MDN: Client-server overview walks through how clients and servers communicate over HTTP.
  • Next: Client-server model and request lifecycle.

docs.title: Background Jobs and Scheduling
docs.text: Not every piece of work should happen while the user waits for an HTTP response. Sending emails, generating PDFs, resizing images, calling slow third-party APIs, and nightly cleanups are better done in the background by separate workers, either right away (a job queue) or at set times (scheduling). This keeps responses fast and makes slow or unreliable work retryable.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
If a sign-up handler sends a welcome email inline and the email provider takes 8 seconds or is down, the user waits 8 seconds or sees an error — even though their account was created fine. Doing heavy work inside requests also:

  • Ties up server capacity, so fewer requests can be served.
  • Hits proxy and client timeouts for long tasks (reports, exports, imports).
  • Loses work when the process restarts mid-request.
  • Makes retries hard: the user would have to resubmit.

Background jobs move that work off the request path. The request records what needs to happen and returns quickly; workers do the work, retry failures, and report progress.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub webhooks. GitHub asks receivers to respond within 10 seconds and suggests setting up a queue so the server can acknowledge the webhook immediately and process the payload in the background (GitHub Docs: webhook best practices).
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues. A redrive policy's maxReceiveCount sets how many times a consumer can receive a message before SQS moves it to a dead-letter queue for inspection (Amazon SQS: dead-letter queues).
  • Kubernetes CronJobs. A CronJob creates a Job approximately once per scheduled time; in some circumstances two Jobs, or none, may be created, so Kubernetes says those Jobs should be idempotent (Kubernetes: CronJob).
  • BullMQ job IDs for deduplication. BullMQ ignores a job added with an ID that already exists, which is how producers avoid enqueueing the same work twice (BullMQ: job IDs).

Popular tools and providers: BullMQ (Node.js on Redis), Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ, Google Cloud Tasks, Celery (Python), Sidekiq (Ruby), Temporal for long-running workflows, and schedulers such as Kubernetes CronJobs and Amazon EventBridge Scheduler.

docs.title: What belongs in the background
docs.text: Good candidates Keep in the request Sending emails, SMS, push notifications Validating input and saving the core record Generating PDFs, reports, exports Anything the response depends on Image and video processing Fast reads Calling slow or unreliable third-party APIs Checks that must block the action (payment authorization, permission) Webhook processing and fan-out Search indexing, cache warming, analytics events Scheduled cleanups, reminders, billing runs

docs.title: The job queue model
docs.text:
• Producer: the code that creates a job — usually your API, after saving the main record.
  • Job: a small message describing the work: a type and the data needed (IDs, not huge payloads), plus an ID.
  • Broker / queue: stores jobs durably until a worker takes them.
  • Worker: a separate process (often the same codebase started with a different entry point) that takes jobs, performs them, and acknowledges success or reports failure.

Workers scale independently of the API: add more workers when the queue grows.

docs.title: Common tools
docs.text:
Tool Notes BullMQ (Node.js, on Redis) Popular in Node; retries, backoff, delayed and repeatable jobs, priorities, rate limits, concurrency, job progress RabbitMQ General-purpose message broker; acknowledgments, routing, dead-letter exchanges Amazon SQS Managed queue; visibility timeouts, dead-letter queues, FIFO queues Kafka Event streaming log; great for high-volume event pipelines, less for simple task queues Database-backed queues (e.g. pg-boss, Agenda on MongoDB) No extra infrastructure; fine for moderate volume

The broader trade-offs between brokers are covered in message queues.

docs.title: Retries and backoff
docs.text:
Jobs fail for transient reasons (network errors, rate limits, a dependency restarting). Configure:

  • A maximum number of attempts (for example, 5).
  • Exponential backoff between attempts (for example, 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s) so a struggling dependency gets breathing room.
  • Which errors are retryable: do not retry a job whose input is invalid; fail it immediately.

See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

docs.title: Dead-letter queues
docs.text: A job that fails all its attempts should not disappear. It moves to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) or a "failed" state, where engineers can inspect it, fix the cause, and replay it. Alert when the DLQ grows.

docs.title: Idempotent jobs
docs.text:
Most queues deliver at least once: if a worker crashes after doing the work but before acknowledging, the job runs again. Therefore jobs must be idempotent — running them twice must not double the effect:

  • Send the "order confirmation" email only if order.confirmationSentAt is empty, and set it atomically.
  • Use the job ID or a business key as an idempotency key when calling payment or messaging APIs.
  • Use unique constraints to prevent duplicate inserts.

Also keep job payloads small: store IDs and load fresh data in the worker, so the job works on current state rather than a stale snapshot.

docs.title: Delayed and repeatable jobs
docs.text:
• Delayed job: run once, after a delay — "send a reminder 24 hours after sign-up if the profile is incomplete."
  • Repeatable job: run on a schedule — every 5 minutes, or with a cron expression.

docs.title: Cron syntax
docs.text:
Cron expressions describe schedules with five fields (some libraries add a sixth, leading field for seconds):

┌───────────── minute (0–59)
│ ┌─────────── hour (0–23)
│ │ ┌───────── day of month (1–31)
│ │ │ ┌─────── month (1–12 or JAN–DEC)
│ │ │ │ ┌───── day of week (0–7 or SUN–SAT; 0 and 7 are both Sunday)
│ │ │ │ │
* * * * *
Symbol Meaning * Every value , List: 1,15 = 1st and 15th - Range: 9-17 = 9 through 17 / Step: */5 = every 5 units Expression Runs * * * * * Every minute */15 * * * * Every 15 minutes 0 * * * * At minute 0 of every hour 0 2 * * * Every day at 02:00 30 9 * * 1-5 09:30 Monday to Friday 0 0 1 * * Midnight on the first day of each month 0 6 * * 0 06:00 every Sunday

Time zones matter. A job at 0 2 * * * runs at 02:00 in the scheduler's time zone. Set the time zone explicitly (often UTC), and be careful around daylight-saving changes, when 02:00 may happen twice or not at all in local time.

Watch the day-of-month and day-of-week combination: in standard cron, if both are restricted (not *), the job runs when either matches.

docs.title: node-cron and in-process schedulers
docs.text:
Libraries such as node-cron run a function on a schedule inside your Node process. They are simple, but:

  • If the app runs on three instances, the job runs three times.
  • If the process is down at the scheduled time, the run is missed.
  • Long jobs compete with request handling for the event loop.

docs.title: Running scheduled jobs exactly once across instances
docs.text:
Options, from simplest to most robust:

  1. A dedicated scheduler process: run exactly one scheduler instance (separate from the scaled API), which enqueues jobs for workers.
  2. Queue-based repeatable jobs: BullMQ repeatable jobs (job schedulers) are stored in Redis and produced once per interval regardless of how many workers exist.
  3. Distributed lock: each instance tries to acquire a lock (for example, Redis SET NX with expiry) before running; only the winner runs. Make the job idempotent anyway.
  4. Platform schedulers: Kubernetes CronJobs, AWS EventBridge Scheduler, cloud scheduler services that call an endpoint or start a task.

docs.title: Reporting progress to clients
docs.text:
For long tasks the user is waiting on (exports, imports):

POST /api/exports              → 202 Accepted
                                 Location: /api/exports/exp_91
                                 { "id": "exp_91", "status": "queued" }

GET  /api/exports/exp_91       → 200 { "status": "processing", "progress": 40 }
GET  /api/exports/exp_91       → 200 { "status": "completed",
                                      "downloadUrl": "https://..." }

The client polls the status URL, or receives updates over SSE, WebSockets, or a notification (see real-time communication). Status is stored in the database or the job system.

docs.title: Monitoring queues
docs.text:
Track and alert on:

  • Queue depth (waiting jobs) and its trend — a growing backlog means workers cannot keep up.
  • Job age / latency — how long the oldest job has been waiting.
  • Failure rate and DLQ size.
  • Processing duration per job type.
  • Stalled jobs — jobs whose worker died mid-processing.

Dashboards such as Bull Board show BullMQ queues; cloud queues expose metrics in their consoles.

docs.title: Graceful shutdown for workers
docs.text: When a worker receives SIGTERM (during deploys), it should stop taking new jobs, let current jobs finish (within a time limit), then exit. Jobs that cannot finish should be returned to the queue, not lost.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a background job when:

  • The work takes more than a few hundred milliseconds and the response does not depend on its result (emails, PDFs, image processing).
  • The work calls an unreliable third party and should be retried.
  • A webhook or event must be acknowledged quickly and processed later.
  • Work must happen on a schedule (cleanups, reminders, billing runs).

Keep the work in the request when:

  • The response needs the result (a price, a permission decision, a payment authorization).
  • It is fast and reliable — a queue adds infrastructure and failure modes.
Need Good fit Avoid Send an email after sign-up Job queue with retries Inline call in the request Process a webhook Acknowledge with 2xx, then queue Doing the work before responding Nightly cleanup on one server node-cron node-cron on a scaled app Nightly cleanup on a scaled app Queue job scheduler or platform cron One schedule per instance Long multi-step workflow (days, human steps) Workflow engine such as Temporal A chain of ad hoc jobs Strict per-customer order Partitioned queue or single-concurrency group Many parallel workers on one queue

docs.title: A BullMQ queue, producer, and worker
docs.text:
// queue.js — shared connection settings
import { Queue } from "bullmq";
import IORedis from "ioredis";

// BullMQ workers require maxRetriesPerRequest: null on their connection
export const connection = new IORedis(process.env.REDIS_URL, {
  maxRetriesPerRequest: null,
});

export const emailQueue = new Queue("emails", {
  connection,
  defaultJobOptions: {
    attempts: 5,
    backoff: { type: "exponential", delay: 1000 }, // 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, ...
    removeOnComplete: 1000, // keep the last 1000 completed jobs
    removeOnFail: false,    // keep failed jobs for inspection
  },
});

// api.js — producer: respond fast, enqueue the slow work
import { emailQueue } from "./queue.js";

app.post("/api/users", async (request, response) => {
  const user = await createUser(request.validated.body);

  // jobId makes the enqueue idempotent: a job with an existing ID is ignored.
  // BullMQ rejects custom IDs containing ":", so use another separator.
  await emailQueue.add(
    "welcome-email",
    { userId: user.id },
    { jobId: `welcome-email-${user.id}` }
  );

  response.status(201).json({ id: user.id });
});

// worker.js — a separate process: node worker.js
import { Worker, UnrecoverableError } from "bullmq";
import { connection } from "./queue.js";

const worker = new Worker(
  "emails",
  async (job) => {
    const user = await users.findById(job.data.userId); // load fresh data
    if (!user) {
      // Retrying will not help; fail permanently
      throw new UnrecoverableError("User no longer exists");
    }
    if (user.welcomeEmailSentAt) return; // idempotent: already done

    await emailProvider.send({ to: user.email, template: "welcome" });
    await users.markWelcomeEmailSent(user.id);
  },
  { connection, concurrency: 10 }
);

worker.on("failed", (job, error) => {
  logger.error({ jobId: job?.id, err: error }, "email job failed");
});

process.on("SIGTERM", async () => {
  await worker.close(); // waits for active jobs to finish
  process.exit(0);
});

docs.title: A repeatable job instead of in-process cron
docs.text:
import { Queue } from "bullmq";
import { connection } from "./queue.js";

const maintenanceQueue = new Queue("maintenance", { connection });

// Upsert a scheduler: runs daily at 02:00 UTC no matter how many workers exist
await maintenanceQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
  "cleanup-expired-sessions",
  { pattern: "0 2 * * *", tz: "UTC" },
  { name: "cleanup-expired-sessions", data: {} }
);

docs.title: node-cron for a single-instance app
docs.text:
import cron from "node-cron";

// Fine for one instance; runs once per instance if you scale out
cron.schedule(
  "*/15 * * * *",
  async () => {
    await refreshExchangeRates();
  },
  { timezone: "UTC" }
);

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep requests fast: save the core data, enqueue the rest, respond.
  • Put only IDs and small parameters in job payloads; load fresh data in the worker.
  • Make every job idempotent; assume it may run more than once.
  • Configure attempts, exponential backoff, and a dead-letter destination.
  • Fail immediately on non-retryable errors.
  • Run workers as separate processes that scale independently.
  • Ensure scheduled jobs run once across instances (dedicated scheduler, queue schedulers, or locks).
  • Set time zones explicitly for schedules.
  • Monitor queue depth, job age, failures, and DLQ size; alert on growth.
  • Shut workers down gracefully.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The backlog keeps growing. Symptom: emails arrive hours late. Detect: queue depth and the age of the oldest waiting job rise steadily. Cause: jobs arrive faster than workers finish them — too few workers, low concurrency, or a slow dependency. Fix: scale workers, raise concurrency where the dependency allows, and alert on job age rather than depth alone.
  • Enqueueing fails after "making it idempotent". Symptom: sign-ups return 500 after a custom job ID is added. Detect: the error message Custom Id cannot contain : from BullMQ. Cause: BullMQ rejects most custom job IDs that contain a colon. Fix: use another separator, such as welcome-email-42.
  • Workers stop processing after a Redis blip. Symptom: the queue grows while workers are running. Detect: worker logs show Redis connection errors and BullMQ warns that maxRetriesPerRequest must be null. Cause: the ioredis connection gives up on commands instead of waiting for Redis. Fix: create worker connections with maxRetriesPerRequest: null.
  • The nightly job runs three times. Symptom: customers get three copies of a report. Detect: logs show the job starting on every instance at the same minute. Cause: node-cron runs inside each scaled instance. Fix: use a queue job scheduler, a single scheduler process, or a platform cron, and make the job idempotent.
  • Jobs run twice after a deploy. Symptom: duplicate side effects around release time. Detect: the same job ID appears as processed twice, or as stalled and then retried. Cause: workers were killed mid-job, so the job was redelivered. Fix: close workers gracefully on SIGTERM, give them enough shutdown time, and keep jobs idempotent.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Background job: work performed outside the request-response cycle.
  • Producer / consumer (worker): creates jobs / processes jobs.
  • Broker: the system that stores and delivers jobs.
  • Acknowledgment: a worker's confirmation that a job completed.
  • Dead-letter queue: where jobs go after exhausting retries.
  • At-least-once delivery: jobs may be processed more than once.
  • Idempotent job: a job safe to run repeatedly.
  • Delayed job: a job scheduled to run after a delay.
  • Repeatable job / job scheduler: a job produced on a recurring schedule.
  • Cron expression: a five- (or six-) field schedule format.
  • Concurrency: how many jobs a worker processes at once.
  • Stalled job: a job whose worker stopped responding mid-processing.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Doing slow work inside the request, causing timeouts and poor throughput.
  • Fire-and-forget promises (sendEmail() without awaiting or queueing): the work is lost on restart and errors go unnoticed.
  • Non-idempotent jobs that send duplicate emails or charges on retry.
  • Large payloads in jobs, holding stale copies of data.
  • In-process cron on a scaled app, running the job once per instance.
  • Ignoring time zones and daylight saving in schedules.
  • No dead-letter handling, so failed jobs vanish silently.
  • Retrying jobs that can never succeed, wasting resources.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which kinds of work should move to background jobs, and why?
  2. Describe the roles of the producer, broker, and worker.
  3. Why must background jobs be idempotent, and how can you make an email job idempotent?
  4. Explain each field of the cron expression 30 9 * * 1-5.
  5. What goes wrong when node-cron runs in an app scaled to three instances, and how do you fix it?
  6. How should an API report progress for a long-running export?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• BullMQ documentation
  • node-cron on npm
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
  • RabbitMQ: Dead letter exchanges
  • Kubernetes: CronJob
  • Related notes: Message queues, Redis, Timeouts, retries, and idempotency

docs.title: Client-Server Model and Request Lifecycle
docs.text: In the client-server model, a client asks for something and a server answers. A single click in a browser sets off a chain of steps: name lookup, network connections, encryption, proxies, your application code, and the database. This page follows one request through every hop and back.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
When a request is slow or fails, the cause can sit at any hop: DNS, TLS, a load balancer, your code, or the database. Knowing the full path lets you:

  • Read an error and know which layer produced it (a 502 from a proxy is not the same problem as a 500 from your code).
  • Find where latency comes from instead of guessing.
  • Decide where a concern belongs: TLS at the proxy, authentication in middleware, business rules in a service.
  • Understand why HTTP is called stateless and how logins still work.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
Every hop in this page has a timeout or limit set by the platform in front of your app. Three well-documented examples:

  • AWS Application Load Balancer. The load balancer attributes list a default idle timeout of 60 seconds, and AWS recommends configuring your application's idle (keep-alive) timeout to be larger than the load balancer's. Otherwise, the app can close a connection the load balancer is about to reuse, which is the source of the classic intermittent 502.
  • Cloudflare. When Cloudflare connects to your origin but gets no HTTP response within its default 125-second proxy read timeout, it returns its own Error 524. The status code comes from the CDN, not from your application.
  • Heroku. The Heroku router terminates a request after 30 seconds, returns an error page, and logs an H12 error, even if your app is still working on it. The countdown starts after the router has sent the whole request to the app.

docs.title: The client-server model
docs.text:
• A client initiates communication: a browser, a mobile app, a CLI, or another server calling your API.
  • A server listens on an address and port and responds to requests.
  • The roles describe who starts the conversation, not the hardware. Your backend is a server to the browser and a client to the payment provider it calls.

HTTP follows a request-response pattern: the client sends one request, the server sends one response. The server does not push data on its own over plain HTTP; for that, see real-time communication.

docs.title: The full journey of one request
docs.text: Suppose a user opens https://shop.example/orders and the page calls GET https://api.shop.example/api/orders?page=1.

docs.title: Each hop in detail
docs.text:
1. URL parsing. The browser splits the URL into scheme, host, port (default 443 for HTTPS), path, and query string.
  2. DNS resolution. The host name is turned into an IP address. Results are cached by the browser, the operating system, and resolvers, so this is often instant on repeat visits. See DNS.
  3. TCP connection. For HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, the client opens a TCP connection with a three-way handshake. That costs one network round trip before any data flows. See TCP and UDP.
  4. TLS handshake. For HTTPS, client and server agree on encryption keys and the client verifies the server's certificate. TLS 1.3 needs one more round trip on a new connection. See TLS and SSL.
  5. HTTP request. The client sends the method, target, headers, and an optional body. See HTTP methods and HTTP headers.
  6. CDN or edge cache. If a CDN sits in front and holds a fresh cached copy, it answers without touching your servers. API responses are often not cached, but static files and public data can be. See CDN.
  7. Load balancer or reverse proxy. It usually terminates TLS, chooses a healthy backend instance, enforces limits (body size, timeouts), and forwards the request over the internal network. It adds headers such as X-Forwarded-For so the app knows the real client IP. See load balancing.
  8. Application middleware. Code that runs for many routes: assigning a request ID, logging, parsing the body, CORS, rate limiting, and checking the session or token. See middleware.
  9. Routing. The framework matches the method and path to a handler.
  10. Controller. Reads parameters, validates input, and calls a service.
  11. Service. Applies business rules and decides what data is needed.
  12. Cache and database. The service checks a cache, and on a miss queries the database. This is very often the slowest step.
  13. Response. The app sets a status code, headers, and a body. It travels back through the proxy and CDN to the client.
  14. Client handling. The browser checks the status, parses the body, and updates the page. For a document, it may then request more resources.

docs.title: Where latency comes from
docs.text:
Hop What adds time How to reduce it DNS Uncached lookups, slow resolvers DNS caching, sensible TTLs TCP + TLS Round trips on each new connection, distance to server Connection reuse (keep-alive), HTTP/2, TLS 1.3, servers or CDN near users Proxy / load balancer Extra hop, queueing under load Keep it close to the app; scale it Middleware Expensive work on every request Keep middleware cheap; scope it to routes that need it Business logic CPU-heavy work blocking the event loop Move heavy work to workers or queues Database Missing indexes, too many queries, large results Indexes, pagination, caching, fewer round trips External APIs Slow third parties Timeouts, caching, asynchronous processing Response size Large JSON bodies Pagination, field selection, compression

A useful habit: measure each step (with logs, timing headers, or tracing) before optimizing. See logging and monitoring.

docs.title: HTTP versions in brief
docs.text:
Version Transport What changes for you HTTP/1.1 TCP One request at a time per connection; browsers open several connections HTTP/2 TCP Many requests multiplexed over one connection; compressed headers HTTP/3 QUIC over UDP Faster connection setup; one lost packet does not stall every stream

Your application code uses the same methods, headers, and status codes in every version. The proxy or CDN often speaks HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to browsers and HTTP/1.1 to your app. See HTTP and HTTPS and QUIC and HTTP/3.

docs.title: Keep-alive and connection reuse
docs.text:
Opening a TCP and TLS connection is expensive. HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default (persistent connections) so later requests skip the handshakes. HTTP/2 goes further and sends many requests over one connection at the same time.

On the server side, keep-alive has a timeout: an idle connection is closed after a while. A classic bug happens when the app server's keep-alive timeout is shorter than the load balancer's: the balancer reuses a connection the app just closed, and some requests fail with 502. Node.js closes idle keep-alive connections after 5 seconds by default (responses carry Keep-Alive: timeout=5), while load balancers often wait much longer; AWS Application Load Balancers default to 60 seconds. Set the app's keep-alive timeout longer than the proxy's idle timeout. See running Express in production.

Your backend is also a client. Reuse connections when it calls databases (connection pools) and other APIs (HTTP agents with keep-alive).

docs.title: Where failures surface
docs.text:
What you see Usually produced by Typical cause Browser network error, no status Client, DNS, or network DNS failure, TLS error, server unreachable, CORS block 500 Internal Server Error Your application Unhandled exception, bug, failed dependency not mapped to another code 502 Bad Gateway Proxy or load balancer App crashed, closed the connection, or returned an invalid response 503 Service Unavailable Proxy or the app itself No healthy instances, overload, maintenance 504 Gateway Timeout Proxy or load balancer App took longer than the proxy's timeout 4xx codes Your application (sometimes the proxy) Bad input, missing auth, not found, rate limited

The first question when debugging is "which layer returned this?" Response headers (such as Server or a request-ID header) and proxy logs usually tell you. See HTTP status codes.

docs.title: Statelessness and how state is carried
docs.text:
HTTP is stateless: each request is understood on its own, and the protocol does not remember earlier requests. Applications still need to know who is logged in and what is in a cart, so state travels in one of these ways:

  • Cookies. The server sets a cookie (often a session ID); the browser sends it back automatically on later requests to that site.
  • Tokens. The client stores a token (for example a JWT) and sends it in the Authorization header.
  • Server-side storage. The session ID or token points to data held in a database or cache such as Redis.
  • The URL. Query parameters carry non-sensitive state such as the page number or filters.

See sessions, cookies, and JWT.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
The lifecycle is always there; the choices are which layers to put in front of your app and where each concern lives.

Put a CDN in front when:

  • You serve static assets or public, cacheable responses to users far from your servers.
  • You want edge protection (TLS, DDoS filtering) without running it yourself.

Do not rely on a CDN for personalized API responses; they must not be cached publicly, so the CDN only adds a hop for them.

Put a reverse proxy or load balancer in front when:

  • You run more than one app instance, or want zero-downtime deploys.
  • You want TLS termination, request size limits, and timeouts in one place.

Talking directly to a single app process is fine for local development and internal tools, but it leaves TLS, health checks, and failover to you.

Concern Best place Why not elsewhere TLS termination Load balancer or proxy One place to manage certificates; apps stay simple Static files CDN or proxy Node.js processes are better spent on dynamic work Authentication and authorization App middleware Needs your user data and business rules Rate limiting Gateway or app (shared store) Proxy limits are coarse; app limits know the user Business rules Service layer Must be tested and reused independently of HTTP Request IDs Edge, propagated by every layer One ID must follow the request end to end

docs.title: Watch a request with curl
docs.text:
curl -v https://api.example.com/health

-v prints the steps: the resolved IP, the TCP connection, the TLS handshake, the request headers sent (> lines), and the response headers received (< lines). Use an endpoint you are allowed to call.

Time each phase:

curl -o /dev/null -s -w "dns=%{time_namelookup} connect=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} first_byte=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total}\n" https://api.example.com/health

If first_byte is much larger than tls, the time is being spent on the server, not on the network.

docs.title: The raw request and response
docs.text:
GET /api/orders?page=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.shop.example
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
X-Request-Id: 7f3c9a2e

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Cache-Control: private, no-cache
X-Request-Id: 7f3c9a2e

{"data":[{"id":"ord_1","total":4999}],"page":1,"hasMore":false}

docs.title: Tracing the request through Express
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const app = express();

// Middleware: give every request an ID and time it
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  req.id = req.get("X-Request-Id") ?? randomUUID();
  res.set("X-Request-Id", req.id);
  const start = performance.now();
  res.on("finish", () => {
    const ms = (performance.now() - start).toFixed(1);
    console.log(`${req.id} ${req.method} ${req.originalUrl} ${res.statusCode} ${ms}ms`);
  });
  next();
});

// Router + controller
app.get("/api/orders", async (req, res) => {
  const page = Number(req.query.page ?? 1);
  const orders = await findOrdersForPage(page); // service + data access
  res.json({ data: orders, page });
});

async function findOrdersForPage(page) {
  return [{ id: "ord_1", total: 4999 }]; // stands in for a database query
}

app.listen(3000);

The finish event fires once the response is sent, so the log line shows the final status and the total time spent inside the app.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Propagate a request ID from the edge through every service and log line so one request can be traced end to end.
  • Set timeouts at every layer, and make each inner timeout shorter than the outer one (database < app < proxy < client).
  • Reuse connections with keep-alive and connection pools.
  • Configure trust in proxy headers correctly so the app sees the real client IP and protocol. See the request object.
  • Cache where it is safe: static assets at the CDN, expensive reads in a cache, and HTTP caching headers for public data.
  • Keep middleware cheap and run expensive checks only on routes that need them.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Intermittent 502 errors with no app errors. Symptom: about one request in a few thousand fails with 502, often the first request after an idle period. Detect: the load balancer's logs show it generated the 502, while the app logged no error for that request. Cause: the app's keep-alive timeout (5 seconds by default in Node.js) is shorter than the load balancer's idle timeout. Fix: raise server.keepAliveTimeout above the load balancer's idle timeout, as AWS recommends for its load balancers.
  • 504, 524, or H12 on slow endpoints. Symptom: large exports or reports fail, small ones work. Detect: the error is produced by the proxy or platform (Cloudflare 524, Heroku H12, a load balancer 504) at a fixed duration. Cause: the request outlives the proxy's timeout. Fix: make the work asynchronous (202 plus a status URL), or speed it up; raising timeouts only hides the problem.
  • Every request appears to come from one IP. Symptom: rate limiting blocks all users at once, and logs show the same client IP for everyone. Detect: the logged IP is the load balancer's private address. Cause: the app reads the socket address, not the forwarded header. Fix: configure trusted proxies (Express trust proxy) for exactly the proxies you run.
  • High latency on backend-to-backend calls. Symptom: a call that takes 20 ms inside the data center takes 100 ms or more from your app. Detect: tracing shows time in connection setup and TLS handshakes on every call. Cause: a new connection per request. Fix: reuse one HTTP client or agent with keep-alive, and use database connection pools.
  • Timeouts that do not nest. Symptom: clients retry while the server is still working, multiplying load during an incident. Detect: duplicate request IDs or repeated identical requests in logs during slowdowns. Cause: the client's timeout is shorter than the server's work, or inner timeouts are longer than outer ones. Fix: order timeouts database < app < proxy < client, and make retried operations idempotent.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Client: the side that initiates a request.
  • Server: the side that listens and responds.
  • Round trip (RTT): the time for a message to reach the other side and a reply to come back.
  • DNS resolution: converting a host name to an IP address.
  • TLS termination: decrypting HTTPS at a proxy and forwarding plain HTTP internally.
  • Reverse proxy: a server that sits in front of application servers and forwards requests to them.
  • Upstream: the server a proxy forwards to (your app, from the proxy's point of view).
  • Keep-alive: reusing an open connection for more than one request.
  • Stateless protocol: each request is interpreted without memory of earlier ones.
  • Latency: the delay before a response arrives.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "HTTP keeps me logged in." HTTP is stateless; cookies or tokens carry the login on every request.
  • Treating every 5xx as an app bug. 502 and 504 usually come from a proxy that could not get a good, timely answer from the app.
  • Ignoring connection setup cost. Opening a new TLS connection for every backend-to-backend call adds round trips; use keep-alive agents and pools.
  • App keep-alive shorter than the load balancer's idle timeout, causing intermittent 502 errors.
  • Trusting X-Forwarded-For from anyone. Only trust it when it is set by your own proxy.
  • Optimizing code first when the time is actually spent in a missing database index or a slow external call.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. List the steps between typing a URL and your Express handler running.
  2. Which hops add round trips on a brand-new HTTPS connection, and how does keep-alive help?
  3. A user sees 504 Gateway Timeout. Which component produced it, and what are the likely causes?
  4. If HTTP is stateless, how does a server know which user sent a request?
  5. Why should the app's keep-alive timeout be longer than the load balancer's idle timeout?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: An overview of HTTP covers the client-server model, requests, and responses.
  • MDN: Client-server overview explains what happens when a browser talks to a web server.
  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics defines the request-response semantics shared by every HTTP version.

docs.title: Concurrency and Race Conditions
docs.text: A backend handles many requests at the same time. When two of them read and change the same data concurrently, the result can depend on the exact timing of their steps — a race condition. Race conditions cause lost updates, double bookings, and money appearing or disappearing, and they are hard to find because they only happen under specific timing.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Race conditions rarely show up in local testing, where one developer clicks one button at a time. In production, they appear as:

  • A product with 1 unit in stock sold to two customers.
  • A seat or appointment slot booked twice.
  • A balance withdrawn twice, or a coupon redeemed more than its limit.
  • A counter (likes, views) that ends up lower than the real number.
  • One user's edit silently overwriting another's.

These bugs damage trust and money, and they are often exploited deliberately: attackers send many requests in parallel to redeem a gift card several times. Knowing the standard defenses lets you design them out from the start.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Kubernetes. Every object has a resourceVersion. When a client updates an object using a stale version, the API server detects the lost update and returns 409 Conflict — optimistic concurrency built into the platform (Kubernetes: API concepts).
  • Amazon DynamoDB. Writes are unconditional by default, but conditional writes succeed only if the item's attributes still meet the expected conditions, checked against the most recent version of the item (DynamoDB: working with items).
  • Elasticsearch. Because replication requests can arrive out of order, Elasticsearch uses optimistic concurrency control (if_seq_no and if_primary_term) so an older version of a document never overwrites a newer one (Elasticsearch: optimistic concurrency control).
  • Database defaults differ. PostgreSQL's default isolation level is Read Committed, and its Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed (PostgreSQL: transaction isolation); MySQL's InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read (MySQL: InnoDB isolation levels). The same code can therefore behave differently on the two databases.

Popular tools: database features (unique indexes, conditional updates, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, serializable isolation), Redis SET NX for locks, and partitioned queues (for example, Kafka partitions keyed by entity) for per-entity ordering.

docs.title: What a race condition is
docs.text:
A race condition happens when the correctness of an operation depends on the relative timing of concurrent operations on shared state. Classic shapes:

  • Lost update: two requests read the same value, each computes a new value, and the second write overwrites the first.
  • Check-then-act: a request checks a condition ("seat is free"), then acts on it ("book seat"), but another request changes the condition in between.
  • Double spend: two requests both verify a balance is sufficient, then both deduct.

docs.title: Lost update, step by step
docs.text: Each request is correct on its own; together they are wrong.

docs.title: Why single-threaded Node.js still has races
docs.text:
Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, so two lines of JavaScript never run at literally the same instant. Races still happen because:

  1. Interleaving at await: while one request awaits a database read, the event loop runs other requests. Everything between a read and a write that spans an await can interleave with other requests.
  2. Multiple processes: production runs several Node processes or containers behind a load balancer. They share the database, not memory.
  3. The database is concurrent: it processes queries from many connections at once.
// Race: the await between read and write lets other requests interleave
app.post("/api/products/:id/buy", async (request, response) => {
  const product = await db.products.findOne({ _id: request.params.id });
  if (product.stock < 1) {
    return response.status(409).json({ error: "Out of stock" });
  }
  // Another request may have bought the last item while we awaited
  await db.products.updateOne(
    { _id: product._id },
    { $set: { stock: product.stock - 1 } }
  );
  response.status(201).json({ ok: true });
});

In-process locks (a JavaScript Map of "busy" flags) only protect one process; they do not help across instances.

docs.title: Defense 1: atomic database operations
docs.text:
Let the database perform the check and the change as a single atomic operation, so no other request can slip in between.

// MongoDB: conditional update — only decrements if stock is still >= 1
const result = await db.products.updateOne(
  { _id: productId, stock: { $gte: 1 } },
  { $inc: { stock: -1 } }
);
if (result.modifiedCount === 0) {
  // Either the product does not exist or it is out of stock
}

-- SQL: the condition and the change happen in one statement
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND stock >= 1;
-- check the affected row count: 0 means out of stock

Note the difference between SET stock = stock - 1 (computed by the database from the current value) and SET stock = 0 computed in application code from a stale read. Prefer operators like $inc, $push, $addToSet, and findOneAndUpdate that work on the current value.

docs.title: Defense 2: unique constraints
docs.text:
Many "only one" rules can be enforced by a unique index, which the database guarantees even under concurrency:

  • One account per email: unique index on email.
  • One booking per seat per show: unique index on (showId, seatId).
  • One vote per user per poll: unique index on (pollId, userId).
  • One processing of each webhook event: unique index on eventId.

Insert, and treat the duplicate-key error (MongoDB 11000, PostgreSQL 23505) as "already exists" — usually a 409 Conflict. Checking first with a find and then inserting is a check-then-act race; the constraint is the real guarantee.

docs.title: Defense 3: optimistic concurrency control
docs.text:
Assume conflicts are rare. Each record carries a version number (or a last-modified timestamp). An update succeeds only if the version is unchanged since it was read, and increments it.

On conflict, return 409 Conflict (or reload and retry if the change can be reapplied automatically).

Over HTTP, the same idea uses ETags and conditional requests:

GET /api/documents/7
→ 200 OK, ETag: "v3"

PUT /api/documents/7
If-Match: "v3"
→ 200 OK, ETag: "v4"                (version still matched)
→ 412 Precondition Failed           (someone changed it; reload first)

This prevents the "last write wins" problem when two people edit the same document. See HTTP headers and HTTP status codes.

docs.title: Defense 4: pessimistic locking
docs.text:
Assume conflicts are likely, and lock the row while working on it:

BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE;  -- locks the row
-- other transactions trying to lock this row wait here
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $2 WHERE id = $1;
COMMIT;                                                  -- releases the lock
  • Simple to reason about: only one transaction works on the row at a time.
  • Costs throughput (others wait), and can cause deadlocks if transactions lock rows in different orders. Databases detect deadlocks and abort one transaction, which you should retry.
  • Keep locked sections short; never hold a lock while calling an external API.

MongoDB has no SELECT ... FOR UPDATE; use atomic conditional updates, optimistic versioning, or multi-document transactions.

docs.title: Defense 5: transactions and isolation levels
docs.text:
A transaction groups operations so they all succeed or all fail (atomicity) and controls how concurrent transactions see each other's changes (isolation). Isolation levels trade safety for concurrency:

Isolation level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom read Notes Read uncommitted Possible Possible Possible Rarely used; PostgreSQL treats it as read committed Read committed Prevented Possible Possible Default in PostgreSQL and many databases Repeatable read Prevented Prevented Possible (standard); prevented in PostgreSQL's implementation MySQL InnoDB default Serializable Prevented Prevented Prevented Behaves as if transactions ran one at a time; may abort with serialization errors you must retry
  • Dirty read: reading another transaction's uncommitted change.
  • Non-repeatable read: reading the same row twice in a transaction and getting different values because another transaction committed in between.
  • Phantom read: re-running a query and getting new rows that another transaction inserted.
  • Lost update and write skew (two transactions each read an overlapping set, then write different rows, together violating a rule like "at least one doctor on call") can still occur below serializable in some databases.

A transaction at the default level does not automatically prevent the lost-update example above. Combine transactions with atomic updates, FOR UPDATE, version checks, or the serializable level. See MongoDB transactions and database fundamentals.

docs.title: Defense 6: distributed locks
docs.text:
Sometimes the shared resource is not a single database row — for example, "only one instance should regenerate this report" or "only one sync job per account." A distributed lock in Redis can coordinate instances:

SET lock:report:42 <unique-token> NX PX 30000
  NX  → only set if the key does not exist (acquire)
  PX  → expire after 30 s so a crashed holder does not block forever
Release: delete the key only if it still holds your token (atomic Lua script)

Caveats:

  • If the holder pauses (GC, slow network) longer than the expiry, the lock expires and a second holder starts — two holders at once. Locks with expiry are best for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work), not as the only protection for correctness.
  • For correctness, use fencing tokens: a number that increases with each lock acquisition, which the protected resource checks and rejects if it is older than one already seen.
  • Prefer database constraints and atomic operations when the data lives in a database.

docs.title: Defense 7: serialize work through a queue
docs.text: If operations on one entity must happen one at a time, send them through a queue partitioned by that entity (for example, all events for account 42 go to the same partition or a single-concurrency job group). One consumer processes them in order, so there is nothing to race. This is common for ledgers, inventory, and per-user sync jobs. See background jobs and scheduling.

docs.title: Choosing a defense
docs.text: Situation Usual choice Increment, decrement, conditional change of one record Atomic update with a condition "Only one of X may exist" Unique constraint Users editing the same document Optimistic concurrency (version / ETag + If-Match) Money transfer between rows, high contention Transaction with FOR UPDATE (lock in a consistent order) Multi-row invariant (write skew) Serializable transaction with retry, or redesign Duplicate job runs across instances Distributed lock (plus idempotent job) Strict ordering per entity Partitioned queue Retried client requests Idempotency keys

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a concurrency defense whenever:

  • Two requests can change the same record — stock, balances, seats, quotas, counters, documents.
  • A rule depends on "check, then act" (unique email, one vote per user, coupon limits).

You may not need one when:

  • Data is append-only (logs, events) and never updated in place.
  • Each record has a single writer, such as a user editing a private draft that nothing else changes.

Optimistic or pessimistic?

Optimistic (version check) Pessimistic (FOR UPDATE) Best when Conflicts are rare Conflicts are frequent on the same rows Cost without conflicts Almost none Every transaction takes a lock On conflict Reject (409 / 412) and retry or reload Wait for the lock Good for Users editing documents, settings, profiles Balances, inventory under heavy contention Risk Many retries under high contention Deadlocks and lock waits

Avoid distributed locks when the data lives in one database — a constraint or conditional update is simpler and correct.

docs.title: Booking a seat safely with a unique index (MongoDB)
docs.text:
// One-time setup: the database enforces one booking per seat per show
await db.bookings.createIndex({ showId: 1, seatId: 1 }, { unique: true });

app.post("/api/shows/:showId/seats/:seatId/book", async (request, response) => {
  try {
    await db.bookings.insertOne({
      showId: request.params.showId,
      seatId: request.params.seatId,
      userId: request.user.id,
      createdAt: new Date(),
    });
    response.status(201).json({ booked: true });
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.code === 11000) {
      return response.status(409).json({ error: "Seat already booked" });
    }
    throw error;
  }
});

docs.title: Optimistic update with a version field
docs.text:
export async function renameDocument(id, expectedVersion, title) {
  const result = await db.documents.updateOne(
    { _id: id, version: expectedVersion },
    { $set: { title }, $inc: { version: 1 } }
  );
  if (result.matchedCount === 0) {
    throw new ConflictError("The document was changed by someone else. Reload and try again.");
  }
}

docs.title: Transfer with row locks in PostgreSQL (node-postgres)
docs.text:
export async function transfer(pool, fromId, toId, amount) {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");
    // Lock both rows in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks
    const [firstId, secondId] = fromId < toId ? [fromId, toId] : [toId, fromId];
    await client.query("SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id IN ($1, $2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE", [firstId, secondId]);

    const debit = await client.query(
      "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1",
      [amount, fromId]
    );
    if (debit.rowCount === 0) throw new ConflictError("Insufficient funds");

    await client.query("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2", [amount, toId]);
    await client.query("COMMIT");
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw error;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

docs.title: Testing for races
docs.text:
Fire concurrent requests in a test to prove the defense works:

// 20 parallel purchases of a product with stock = 1 → exactly one success
const results = await Promise.all(
  Array.from({ length: 20 }, () => request(app).post("/api/products/p1/buy"))
);
const successes = results.filter((r) => r.status === 201).length;
assert.equal(successes, 1);

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Assume every read-modify-write that spans an await can race.
  • Push checks and changes into one atomic database operation where possible.
  • Enforce uniqueness with database constraints, not prior lookups.
  • Use version fields or ETags with If-Match for user-edited resources.
  • Keep transactions and locks short; lock rows in a consistent order; retry deadlocks and serialization failures.
  • Do not call external services while holding locks or open transactions.
  • Treat distributed locks as an efficiency tool; add fencing or idempotency for correctness.
  • Write concurrency tests for critical flows (stock, bookings, payments).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A flash sale oversells. Symptom: more orders than units, or stock below zero. Detect: a reconciliation check comparing orders with inventory, or an alert on negative stock. Cause: read-then-write in application code under parallel requests. Fix: a conditional atomic update (stock >= 1), plus a database CHECK (stock >= 0) as a final guard.
  • Intermittent "deadlock detected" errors. Symptom: a small share of transfers fail with a 500. Detect: PostgreSQL error code 40P01 (deadlock_detected) in logs. Cause: two code paths lock the same rows in different orders. Fix: always lock in a consistent order (for example, by ID), keep transactions short, and retry the aborted transaction.
  • Serialization failures after raising isolation. Symptom: errors rise after switching a flow to Serializable. Detect: error code 40001 (serialization_failure). Cause: expected behavior — the database aborts transactions that would break serializability. Fix: wrap the transaction in a retry loop with backoff, and keep the transaction's reads and writes small.
  • A scheduled job runs twice. Symptom: customers receive two copies of a report. Detect: logs show two instances holding the same lock. Cause: the job ran longer than the lock's expiry, so a second instance acquired it. Fix: extend the lock while working, use fencing tokens, and make the job idempotent.
  • One hot row slows everything. Symptom: p99 latency spikes on endpoints that update a shared counter. Detect: pg_stat_activity shows many sessions waiting with wait_event_type = 'Lock'. Cause: every request updates the same row. Fix: shard the counter across several rows, batch increments, or aggregate asynchronously.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Concurrency: multiple operations in progress during overlapping time.
  • Race condition: a bug where the outcome depends on timing.
  • Critical section: code that must not run concurrently on the same data.
  • Lost update: one write overwriting another based on stale data.
  • Check-then-act: acting on a condition that may have changed since it was checked.
  • Atomic operation: an operation that happens completely or not at all, with no visible intermediate state.
  • Optimistic concurrency control: detect conflicts at write time with a version check.
  • Pessimistic locking: lock data before changing it so others wait.
  • Isolation level: how much concurrent transactions are shielded from each other.
  • Deadlock: two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds.
  • Write skew: concurrent transactions each making a valid change that together break an invariant.
  • Distributed lock: a lock coordinated across processes, often in Redis.
  • Fencing token: an increasing number used to reject stale lock holders.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Node is single-threaded, so there are no race conditions." Interleaving at await and multiple instances still cause them.
  • Read, compute in JavaScript, then write the result, instead of using atomic operators.
  • Checking for duplicates with find before insert without a unique index.
  • "Wrapping it in a transaction fixes it." Default isolation levels still allow lost updates and write skew.
  • In-memory locks in a multi-instance deployment.
  • Trusting a Redis lock with expiry for strict correctness.
  • Long transactions that hold locks while waiting on network calls.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Show, step by step, how two concurrent purchases can sell the last item twice.
  2. Why can races occur in Node.js even though JavaScript runs on one thread?
  3. How do a conditional atomic update and a unique index each prevent a race?
  4. Explain optimistic concurrency with a version field, and how ETags and If-Match apply it over HTTP.
  5. Which anomalies does each isolation level prevent?
  6. What is the risk of using a Redis lock with an expiry, and how do fencing tokens help?

docs.text:
• PostgreSQL: Transaction isolation
  • PostgreSQL: Explicit locking
  • MongoDB: Atomicity and transactions
