docs.title: Configuration, Environments, and Secrets
docs.text: The same backend code runs on a developer's laptop, in automated tests, on a staging server, and in production — but it talks to different databases, uses different API keys, and logs at different levels in each place. Configuration is everything that changes between those environments. Secrets are the sensitive part of configuration: passwords, keys, and tokens. Handling both well keeps deployments predictable and credentials safe.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Configuration mistakes are a common cause of outages and breaches:

  • A database password committed to a public repository can be found quickly by automated scanners — and it stays in the Git history after the file is deleted.
  • Staging accidentally points at the production database and test data corrupts real records.
  • A missing environment variable is only discovered when the first payment is attempted — hours after the deploy.
  • A shared "admin" key used by every environment cannot be rotated without downtime.

A clear approach — config separate from code, validated at startup, secrets in a proper store — prevents these and makes it safe to promote the same build from staging to production.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The Twelve-Factor App stores config in environment variables and gives a litmus test: could the codebase be made open source at any moment without compromising any credentials? (The Twelve-Factor App: Config).
  • GitHub secret scanning scans the entire Git history on all branches of a repository for hardcoded credentials such as API keys, passwords, and tokens (GitHub Docs: about secret scanning).
  • AWS Secrets Manager rotation periodically updates a secret in both the secret store and the database or service that uses it, and can do so automatically (AWS Secrets Manager: rotation).
  • Dynamic secrets in HashiCorp Vault. Vault's database secrets engine generates database credentials on demand, so services no longer need hard-coded credentials and keys are easier to roll (Vault: database secrets engine).
  • Kubernetes Secrets are, by default, stored unencrypted in the API server's data store (etcd), so clusters must enable encryption at rest and restrict access (Kubernetes: Secrets).

Popular tools and providers: AWS Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, Doppler, and 1Password Secrets Automation; secret scanners such as GitHub secret scanning, Gitleaks, and TruffleHog.

docs.title: Configuration versus code
docs.text:
Belongs in configuration Belongs in code Database URLs, hostnames, ports Business rules and algorithms API keys and credentials Route definitions Log level, feature toggles Validation schemas Third-party endpoints that differ by environment Fixed product constants (e.g. maximum name length) Timeouts and pool sizes you tune per environment Defaults that are the same everywhere

A useful test from the twelve-factor methodology: could you make the codebase open source right now without exposing any credentials? If not, some configuration is in the code.

docs.title: Twelve-factor configuration
docs.text:
The Twelve-Factor App methodology recommends storing config in the environment:

  • Config varies between deploys; code does not. The same build artifact (container image) is deployed to every environment with different config.
  • Environment variables are language- and OS-agnostic and are not checked into the repository by accident as easily as config files.
  • Config is granular: independent variables per setting rather than named bundles like config.production.js that multiply with every new environment.

In practice, many teams combine environment variables with a secret manager and small non-secret config files; the principle — config outside the build, supplied per deploy — is what matters.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
Environment Purpose Data Development Local work on a developer machine Fake or seed data; local or dev services Test / CI Automated tests Disposable databases created per run Staging Production-like rehearsal for releases Realistic but non-production (or anonymized) data Production Real users Real data; strictest access

Environment parity (dev/prod parity) means keeping environments as similar as possible — same database engine and major versions, same deployment process, same kind of infrastructure — so problems appear before production. Using SQLite locally but PostgreSQL in production, for example, hides bugs.

Never let lower environments use production credentials or data stores.

docs.title: Configuration sources and precedence
docs.text:
Common sources, typically overriding each other in this order (later wins):

  1. Defaults in code — safe values that apply everywhere (PORT=3000 for local development, a request timeout).
  2. Config files — non-secret settings checked into the repository, if you use them.
  3. Environment variables — set by the platform, container, or process manager for each deploy.
  4. Secret manager — sensitive values fetched at startup or injected by the platform.
  5. Command-line flags — occasional overrides for scripts and tools.

Document the order your app uses, and log (non-secret) effective configuration at startup to make debugging easier.

Locally, a .env file loaded by Node's --env-file flag or the dotenv package is convenient. It must be listed in .gitignore; commit a .env.example with variable names and placeholder values instead. See process, environment variables, and configuration for the Node.js mechanics.

docs.title: Validate configuration at startup and fail fast
docs.text:
Environment variables are always strings (or missing). Parse and validate them once, at startup, into a typed configuration object, and refuse to start if anything is wrong:

  • Required values are present.
  • Types are correct (PORT is a number, URLs are valid URLs).
  • Values are allowed (LOG_LEVEL is one of the known levels).
  • Combinations make sense (if EMAIL_PROVIDER=ses, AWS settings exist).

The rest of the code imports the validated config object and never reads process.env directly. A misconfigured deploy then fails in seconds with a clear message, instead of serving errors for hours.

docs.title: NODE_ENV and environment names
docs.text: NODE_ENV=production is a widely used convention that many libraries read to enable optimizations and disable development features (for example, Express caching view templates and hiding detailed errors). Use it for that purpose only. For "which deployment is this?" use a separate variable such as APP_ENV=staging, so staging can run with NODE_ENV=production behavior while still being identifiable.

docs.title: Feature flags
docs.text:
Feature flags are configuration that turns behavior on or off without a deploy:

  • Release a feature to internal users, then a percentage of users, then everyone.
  • Kill switches to disable a misbehaving feature instantly.
  • Separating deploy (code is shipped) from release (feature is enabled).

Simple flags can be environment variables; dynamic, per-user flags need a flag service or a database-backed system. Remove old flags once a feature is fully released — stale flags become confusing technical debt.

docs.title: What counts as a secret
docs.text:
• Database usernames and passwords, connection strings with credentials.
  • API keys and tokens for third-party services (payments, email, SMS, AI).
  • Signing keys: JWT secrets or private keys, cookie/session secrets, webhook signing secrets.
  • Encryption keys.
  • OAuth client secrets.
  • TLS private keys and certificates' private parts.
  • Cloud access keys.

Public identifiers (a public Stripe key, an OAuth client ID, a public URL) are configuration, not secrets. Anything bundled into frontend code or a mobile app is public, no matter what the variable is called.

docs.title: Secret managers
docs.text:
A secret manager stores secrets encrypted, controls who and what can read each one, records access in audit logs, and supports rotation:

Service Notes AWS Secrets Manager Encrypted secrets, IAM access control, built-in rotation for some databases AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Hierarchical parameters, SecureString encrypted values; simpler and cheaper for basic needs HashiCorp Vault Self-hosted or managed; dynamic secrets (short-lived credentials generated on demand), leasing, many backends Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault Cloud equivalents Kubernetes Secrets Platform-level injection into pods; enable encryption at rest and tight RBAC

The app fetches secrets at startup (or the platform injects them as environment variables or files), using an identity granted by the platform — such as an IAM role — rather than another hard-coded credential.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
Rotation means replacing a secret with a new one periodically and immediately after any suspected leak. Design for it:

  • Support two valid values during a transition (old and new signing keys; JWKS with multiple keys identified by kid).
  • Avoid secrets that are copied into many places manually.
  • Prefer short-lived, automatically issued credentials (dynamic database credentials, cloud roles) over long-lived static keys.
  • Restarting or reloading should pick up new values without code changes.

docs.title: Keeping secrets out of git and logs
docs.text:
• Add .env and other local secret files to .gitignore before the first commit.
  • Enable secret scanning (pre-commit hooks, repository scanning in your Git host) to catch committed keys.
  • If a secret is committed, rotate it immediately. Deleting the file or rewriting history does not help — the secret may already be copied, cached, or cloned.
  • Never log secrets. Redact known fields (authorization, password, apiKey), and never log the whole process.env or full configuration objects. See logging, monitoring, and tracing.
  • Do not put secrets in URLs (they end up in logs and browser history) or in error messages.
  • Do not bake secrets into container images; supply them at runtime.

docs.title: Least privilege per environment
docs.text:
• Each environment has its own credentials; a staging key must not work in production.
  • Each service gets credentials scoped to what it needs (read-only database user for a reporting service; an API key limited to sending email).
  • Developers do not need production secrets on their machines; production access is limited, audited, and ideally temporary.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use environment variables when:

  • Values differ per deploy (URLs, ports, log level, feature flags) and the platform can set them (containers, PaaS, process managers).

Use a secret manager when:

  • Values grant access (database passwords, API keys, signing keys) in staging or production.
  • You need rotation, audit logs of who read a secret, or per-service access.

Use a config file when:

  • Settings are non-secret, structured, and the same in every environment — for example, a list of supported currencies. Keep it in the repository.

Do not:

  • Commit .env files, or bake secrets into container images.
  • Put secrets in frontend environment variables — they ship to every user.
Value Where it belongs PORT, LOG_LEVEL, APP_ENV Environment variable DATABASE_URL without a password, timeouts Environment variable Database password, Stripe secret key, JWT signing key Secret manager, injected at runtime Local development secrets .env file, git-ignored Feature flag toggled without a deploy Flag service or database Fixed product constants Code

docs.title: Validated configuration module with Zod
docs.text:
// config.js — the only place that reads process.env
import { z } from "zod";

const schema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(["development", "test", "production"]).default("development"),
  APP_ENV: z.enum(["local", "test", "staging", "production"]).default("local"),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65535).default(3000),
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(),
  REDIS_URL: z.string().url(),
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32, "JWT_SECRET must be at least 32 characters"),
  LOG_LEVEL: z.enum(["trace", "debug", "info", "warn", "error", "fatal"]).default("info"),
  FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT: z
    .enum(["true", "false"])
    .default("false")
    .transform((value) => value === "true"), // "false" must not be truthy
});

const parsed = schema.safeParse(process.env);

if (!parsed.success) {
  // Print variable names and problems only — never the values
  console.error("Invalid configuration:");
  for (const issue of parsed.error.issues) {
    console.error(`  ${issue.path.join(".")}: ${issue.message}`);
  }
  process.exit(1); // fail fast: do not start with bad config
}

export const config = Object.freeze(parsed.data);

// server.js
import { config } from "./config.js";

app.listen(config.PORT, () => {
  logger.info({ port: config.PORT, appEnv: config.APP_ENV }, "server started");
});

docs.title: .env.example committed to the repository
docs.text:
# Copy to .env and fill in real values. Never commit .env.
NODE_ENV=development
APP_ENV=local
PORT=3000
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/app_dev
REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379
JWT_SECRET=replace-with-at-least-32-random-characters
LOG_LEVEL=debug
FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=false

# Run locally with Node's built-in .env loader
node --env-file=.env server.js

docs.title: Loading a secret from AWS Secrets Manager at startup
docs.text:
import {
  SecretsManagerClient,
  GetSecretValueCommand,
} from "@aws-sdk/client-secrets-manager";

const client = new SecretsManagerClient({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION });

export async function loadDatabaseCredentials() {
  // The service's IAM role grants read access to this one secret
  const result = await client.send(
    new GetSecretValueCommand({ SecretId: process.env.DB_SECRET_ID })
  );
  return JSON.parse(result.SecretString); // { username, password, host, ... }
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep configuration out of code; deploy the same build to every environment.
  • Read process.env in one module; validate, coerce, and freeze it at startup; fail fast on errors.
  • Commit .env.example with names only; never commit .env files.
  • Store production secrets in a secret manager; grant access by platform identity.
  • Use separate credentials per environment and per service, with least privilege.
  • Design for rotation; rotate immediately after any leak.
  • Enable secret scanning and redact secrets in logs.
  • Treat anything in frontend bundles as public.
  • Use NODE_ENV for runtime mode and a separate variable for the deployment name.
  • Clean up feature flags after release.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A deploy starts but fails on the first real request. Symptom: the health check passes, then payments fail with "invalid API key." Detect: errors begin exactly at the deploy time; the new variable is missing in the production environment. Cause: configuration is read lazily, deep in the code. Fix: validate all configuration at startup and exit non-zero, so the deploy fails before taking traffic.
  • A feature turns on everywhere by accident. Symptom: a flag set to "false" behaves as enabled. Detect: the code checks if (process.env.FEATURE_X). Cause: environment variables are strings, and "false" is truthy. Fix: parse flags into booleans in one config module.
  • A secret is pushed to the repository. Symptom: a secret scanning alert, or unexpected usage on the key's account. Detect: the alert names the commit and file. Cause: a .env file or hard-coded key was committed. Fix: revoke and rotate the secret immediately — deleting the file does not remove it from Git history — then review the key's usage logs.
  • Staging changes production data. Symptom: test orders appear in the production database. Detect: writes to production from staging hosts in database audit logs. Cause: staging was configured with a production connection string. Fix: separate credentials per environment, and network rules that stop staging from reaching production.
  • Rotation causes an outage. Symptom: every instance fails to reach the database right after a scheduled rotation. Detect: authentication errors begin at the rotation time. Cause: apps cached the old password and never reloaded it, or the old credential was revoked immediately. Fix: support two valid credentials during rotation, and reload secrets on failure or on a schedule.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Configuration: values that vary between deployments of the same code.
  • Secret: configuration that grants access and must be kept confidential.
  • Environment variable: a named value in a process's environment.
  • Twelve-factor app: a methodology for building deployable services, including storing config in the environment.
  • Environment parity: keeping development, staging, and production similar.
  • Fail fast: stopping immediately when configuration is invalid.
  • Feature flag: a configuration switch that enables or disables behavior without a deploy.
  • Secret manager: a service that stores, controls, and audits access to secrets.
  • Rotation: replacing a secret with a new value.
  • Dynamic secret: a short-lived credential generated on demand.
  • Secret scanning: automated detection of credentials in code.
  • Least privilege: granting only the access required.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Hard-coding credentials or URLs "just for now."
  • Committing .env files or pasting secrets into issues and chats.
  • Thinking deleting a committed secret fixes the leak. Rotate it.
  • Reading process.env all over the codebase without validation, so typos and missing values fail late.
  • Treating "false" as false — environment variables are strings.
  • Sharing one set of credentials across all environments.
  • Putting secrets in frontend environment variables, which ship to every user.
  • Logging the whole configuration or process.env for debugging.
  • Using NODE_ENV values like staging, which libraries do not recognize.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between configuration and secrets? Give three examples of each.
  2. Why does the twelve-factor methodology store config in the environment, and what does "same build for every environment" mean?
  3. Why validate configuration at startup, and what should happen if it is invalid?
  4. What should you do immediately if a secret is committed to a repository?
  5. How do secret managers improve on plain environment variables?
  6. Why should staging and production never share credentials?

  • Node.js: How to read environment variables
  • AWS Secrets Manager documentation
  • HashiCorp Vault documentation
  • Related notes: Environment variables, Process, environment variables, and configuration

docs.title: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)
docs.text: CORS is the mechanism that lets a server tell browsers which other websites may read its responses. Browsers block a page's JavaScript from reading responses from a different origin unless the server explicitly allows it with Access-Control-* headers. Almost every frontend-backend setup runs into CORS at some point, so it pays to understand exactly how it works.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• If your frontend at https://app.example.com calls an API at https://api.example.com, the browser enforces CORS. Without the right headers, every request fails with a "blocked by CORS policy" error, even though the server handled it.
  • A misconfigured CORS policy can let a malicious site read your users' private data using their logged-in session.
  • CORS errors are among the most confusing errors in web development because the browser hides the real response. Knowing the rules turns hours of guessing into a two-minute fix.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub's REST API allows any origin. GitHub's docs state that the REST API supports CORS for AJAX requests from any origin. Its sample response shows Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and an Access-Control-Expose-Headers list (ETag, Link, x-ratelimit-*, and others) so browser code can read pagination and rate-limit headers.
  • Amazon S3 buckets carry their own CORS configuration. The S3 user guide describes configuring a bucket so JavaScript on a website can make cross-origin requests to it, and hosting web fonts in a bucket, because browsers require a CORS check before loading web fonts from another origin.
  • Amazon API Gateway makes proxy backends responsible for CORS. For Lambda proxy and HTTP proxy integrations, your backend is responsible for returning Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Allow-Methods, and -Allow-Headers, because a proxy integration does not return an integration response. Forgetting this in the Lambda function is a common cause of CORS errors.

docs.title: The same-origin policy
docs.text:
An origin is the combination of scheme + host + port. Two URLs have the same origin only if all three match. The path does not matter.

Compared with https://app.example.com (port 443 implied):

URL Same origin? Why https://app.example.com/orders Yes Only the path differs https://app.example.com:443/ Yes 443 is the default HTTPS port http://app.example.com/ No Different scheme https://api.example.com/ No Different host (subdomains count) https://example.com/ No Different host https://app.example.com:8443/ No Different port http://localhost:5173 vs http://localhost:3000 No Different ports

The same-origin policy is the browser rule that a page's scripts may only read responses from their own origin. It does not stop everything cross-origin:

Allowed across origins by default Blocked by default Loading images, scripts, stylesheets, fonts (fonts need CORS), iframes Reading the response of fetch() or XMLHttpRequest Submitting an HTML form to another site Reading pixels of a cross-origin image drawn on a canvas Following links and redirects Reading another origin's DOM, cookies, or storage

docs.title: Why the policy exists
docs.text:
Browsers attach cookies to requests automatically. Without the same-origin policy, any site you visit could run:

// On https://evil.example, while you are logged in to your bank
const res = await fetch("https://bank.example/api/accounts", { credentials: "include" });
const data = await res.json(); // your balances, sent to the attacker

The request would carry your bank session cookie, and the attacker's script could read the answer. The same-origin policy blocks the read. CORS is the controlled way to relax it for origins the server trusts.

docs.title: What CORS is
docs.text:
• The browser adds an Origin header to cross-origin requests.
  • The server decides whether that origin is allowed and answers with Access-Control-Allow-* headers.
  • The browser compares the headers with the request. If they allow it, the page's JavaScript gets the response; if not, the browser throws a network error and hides the response.

Two consequences surprise most people:

  1. The server still receives and processes simple requests. CORS blocks the page from reading the response, not the request from arriving.
  2. CORS is enforced only by browsers. curl, Postman, mobile apps, and server-to-server calls ignore it completely. CORS is not an access control system for your API.

docs.title: Simple requests
docs.text:
A request is "simple" (the specification says it needs no preflight) when all of these are true:

  • The method is GET, HEAD, or POST.
  • The only headers set by the page are CORS-safelisted ones: Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Language, Content-Type, and a simple single-range Range.
  • Content-Type, if present, is one of application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain.
  • There is no streaming request body and no upload progress listener.

The browser sends the request directly with an Origin header and checks the response:

Browser (page on https://app.example.com)          Server (api.example.com)
   |                                                     |
   |--- GET /api/products ------------------------------>|
   |    Origin: https://app.example.com                   |
   |                                                     | handles request
   |<-- 200 OK ------------------------------------------|
   |    Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
   |    Content-Type: application/json                    |
   |                                                     |
   | Allow-Origin matches -> JavaScript can read the body |

If Access-Control-Allow-Origin is missing or does not match, the response still arrived, but the browser refuses to give it to JavaScript.

docs.title: Preflighted requests
docs.text:
Anything that is not simple needs permission first. That includes:

  • PUT, PATCH, DELETE, or any other method.
  • Content-Type: application/json (yes, almost every JSON API call).
  • An Authorization header or any custom header such as X-Request-Id.

The browser first sends an OPTIONS request, the preflight, describing what it intends to do. Only if the server approves does it send the real request.

Points to note:

  • The preflight carries no cookies or Authorization header. Your authentication middleware must not reject OPTIONS requests, or every preflight fails.
  • The preflight response must have an OK status (200-299). 204 is conventional.
  • The actual response also needs Access-Control-Allow-Origin; passing the preflight is not enough.
  • Preflights must not be redirected. A 301 from http:// to https:// or from /orders to /orders/ breaks them.

docs.title: Request headers (set by the browser, never by your code)
docs.text: Header Sent on Meaning Origin Every CORS request (cross-origin fetch() or XHR, including preflights), WebSocket handshakes, and any request whose method is not GET or HEAD. Not on plain cross-origin image, script, or stylesheet loads The origin of the page making the request Access-Control-Request-Method Preflight The method the real request will use Access-Control-Request-Headers Preflight The non-safelisted headers the real request will send, lowercase, comma-separated

docs.title: Response headers (set by your server)
docs.text:
Header Sent on Meaning Access-Control-Allow-Origin Preflight and actual response The single origin allowed to read the response, or * for any origin (not with credentials) Access-Control-Allow-Methods Preflight Methods allowed for the actual request Access-Control-Allow-Headers Preflight Request headers the actual request may include Access-Control-Allow-Credentials Preflight and actual response true lets the browser send cookies and expose the response for credentialed requests Access-Control-Expose-Headers Actual response Response headers that JavaScript may read beyond the safelisted ones Access-Control-Max-Age Preflight Seconds the browser may cache this preflight result

Details for each:

  • Access-Control-Allow-Origin holds exactly one value: one origin or *. A comma-separated list is invalid. To allow several origins, check the request's Origin against an allowlist and echo back the matching one.
  • Access-Control-Allow-Methods lists methods such as GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE. Simple methods are always allowed. * works only for requests without credentials.
  • Access-Control-Allow-Headers must include every header named in Access-Control-Request-Headers, such as Authorization, Content-Type. The * wildcard works only without credentials, and it never covers Authorization, which must be listed by name.
  • Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is required when the frontend sends cookies (credentials: "include"). Without it, the browser hides the response.
  • Access-Control-Expose-Headers: by default JavaScript can read only the safelisted response headers: Cache-Control, Content-Language, Content-Length, Content-Type, Expires, Last-Modified, and Pragma. To read X-Request-Id, Location, or a rate-limit header, list it here.
  • Access-Control-Max-Age avoids a preflight before every request. If absent, browsers cache the result for about 5 seconds. Browsers also cap it (Chromium at 2 hours, Firefox at 24 hours), so very large values are pointless.

docs.title: Credentials: cookies and CORS
docs.text:
By default, cross-origin fetch() does not send cookies. To send them:

await fetch("https://api.example.com/api/me", { credentials: "include" });
// XMLHttpRequest equivalent: xhr.withCredentials = true;

For a credentialed request, the server must respond with:

  • Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to the exact requesting origin, never *.
  • Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
  • No * in Allow-Methods, Allow-Headers, or Expose-Headers (it is treated literally, not as a wildcard).

The cookies themselves must also be allowed to travel. That depends on site, not origin. A site is the scheme plus the registrable domain: app.example.com and api.example.com are different origins but the same site (example.com).

Frontend API Relationship Cookie needs https://app.example.com https://api.example.com Cross-origin, same-site SameSite=Lax (or Strict) works https://myshop.dev https://api.example.com Cross-site SameSite=None; Secure, and browsers increasingly block such third-party cookies

The practical advice: host the frontend and API on the same site (or behind one domain with a reverse proxy) when you use cookie authentication. See sessions, cookies, and JWT.

docs.title: Vary: Origin and caches
docs.text: If your server returns a different Access-Control-Allow-Origin depending on the request's Origin, add Vary: Origin. Otherwise a CDN or browser cache may store the response for https://a.example.com and serve it, with the wrong header, to https://b.example.com, which then gets a CORS error seemingly at random.

docs.title: Dynamic allowlists and their dangers
docs.text:
Most real APIs keep a list of allowed origins and echo back the matching one. Implement the comparison carefully:

Approach Problem Echo back any Origin with Allow-Credentials: true Any website can read your users' data. This is the worst CORS misconfiguration origin.endsWith("example.com") Matches https://evilexample.com origin.includes("example.com") Matches https://example.com.attacker.net Unanchored regex /example\.com/ Same as includes Allowing the null origin Sandboxed iframes, file:// pages, and some redirects send Origin: null; an attacker can produce it on purpose Exact match against a Set of full origins Correct Anchored regex /^https:\/\/[a-z0-9-]+\.example\.com$/ Correct for "any subdomain over HTTPS", if you trust all subdomains

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * without credentials is safe for genuinely public, non-personalized data (a public product catalog, open data APIs), because no cookies are involved.

docs.title: CORS and error responses
docs.text: When your app throws and an error handler (or a proxy error page) returns 500 without CORS headers, the browser reports a CORS error instead of the 500. Register CORS middleware before your routes so every response, including errors and 404s, carries the headers. Then the frontend sees the real status.

docs.title: CORS vs CSRF
docs.text:
They are often confused but solve different problems:

  • CORS controls whether a page can read a cross-origin response.
  • CSRF (cross-site request forgery) abuses the fact that browsers send cookies with cross-site requests, even when the attacker cannot read the response. A hidden form on an evil site can still submit POST /api/transfer with the victim's cookie.

CORS does not prevent CSRF, because simple requests are sent and processed before any CORS check. Protect cookie-authenticated, state-changing endpoints with SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, or Origin header checks. A permissive CORS policy makes things worse: it lets an attacker read responses too. See web security fundamentals.

docs.title: Where CORS does not apply
docs.text:
• curl, Postman, Insomnia, and other HTTP tools.
  • Mobile and desktop apps making native HTTP calls.
  • Your backend calling another backend.
  • Same-origin requests.

That is why "it works in Postman but not in the browser" is the classic CORS symptom. It also means CORS is no substitute for authentication and authorization.

docs.title: Avoiding CORS with a proxy
docs.text:
If the browser only ever talks to one origin, there is no cross-origin request and no CORS:

  • In development: the frontend dev server (Vite, Next.js) proxies /api to the backend on another port.
  • In production: a reverse proxy serves the frontend and forwards /api to the backend under the same domain. See reverse proxy.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Configure CORS with an allowlist when:

  • A browser app on one origin must call an API on another origin that you control, such as app.example.com calling api.example.com.
  • Several known frontends (web app, admin app, partner portal) share one API.

Use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * only when:

  • The data is public and not personalized, and requests carry no cookies.
  • You want any website to be able to read it, like a public open-data API.

Do not use CORS (avoid the cross-origin request instead) when:

  • You control both frontend and backend and can serve them from one origin behind a reverse proxy, especially with cookie authentication.
  • The caller is not a browser: servers, mobile apps, and CLIs ignore CORS, so it adds nothing for them.
Option Cookie auth works easily Preflight cost Risk if misconfigured Best for Same origin via reverse proxy Yes None Low Your own frontend and API CORS with exact-origin allowlist Yes (same-site), with credentials Yes, cacheable with Max-Age Data leaks if origins are matched loosely Separate frontend and API origins Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * No (credentials not allowed) Yes Low for public data Public, non-personalized APIs Reflect any origin with credentials Yes Yes Any site can read user data Never

docs.title: Express with the cors package
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import cors from "cors";

const app = express();

const allowedOrigins = new Set([
  "https://app.example.com",
  "http://localhost:5173", // Vite dev server
]);

app.use(
  cors({
    origin(origin, callback) {
      // No Origin header: same-origin or non-browser client (curl, server-to-server)
      if (!origin || allowedOrigins.has(origin)) return callback(null, true);
      return callback(null, false); // no CORS headers -> browser blocks the read
    },
    credentials: true, // allow cookies; sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
    methods: ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"],
    allowedHeaders: ["Content-Type", "Authorization"],
    exposedHeaders: ["X-Request-Id", "Location"],
    maxAge: 600, // cache preflight for 10 minutes
  }),
);

app.use(express.json());
// ...routes, then error handlers (they inherit the CORS headers set above)

app.listen(3000);

Registered first, this middleware also answers preflight OPTIONS requests from allowed origins with 204, before authentication runs. Requests from other origins get no CORS headers, so the browser blocks them. More options are covered in configuring CORS in Express.

docs.title: The same thing by hand
docs.text:
const allowedOrigins = new Set(["https://app.example.com"]);

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const origin = req.get("Origin");
  res.vary("Origin"); // the response depends on Origin

  if (origin && allowedOrigins.has(origin)) {
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", origin);
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials", "true");
    res.set("Access-Control-Expose-Headers", "X-Request-Id");
  }

  // A preflight is an OPTIONS request carrying Access-Control-Request-Method
  if (req.method === "OPTIONS" && req.get("Access-Control-Request-Method")) {
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Methods", "GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE");
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Headers", "Content-Type, Authorization");
    res.set("Access-Control-Max-Age", "600");
    return res.sendStatus(204);
  }
  next();
});

docs.title: The frontend side
docs.text:
// Token in a header: triggers a preflight because of Authorization + JSON
await fetch("https://api.example.com/api/orders", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  body: JSON.stringify({ productId: "p-42", quantity: 1 }),
});

// Cookie session: must opt in to sending credentials
const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/api/me", { credentials: "include" });
console.log(res.headers.get("X-Request-Id")); // null unless exposed by the server

docs.title: Simulating a preflight with curl
docs.text:
curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3000/api/orders \
  -H "Origin: https://app.example.com" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: POST" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization"

Check that the response is 2xx and that the Access-Control-Allow-* headers cover the method and headers you asked for. Repeat with -H "Origin: https://evil.example" and confirm no Allow-Origin comes back.

docs.title: A Vite dev proxy instead of CORS
docs.text:
// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  server: {
    proxy: {
      // Browser calls http://localhost:5173/api/... (same origin);
      // Vite forwards it to the backend
      "/api": { target: "http://localhost:3000", changeOrigin: true },
    },
  },
});

docs.title: Troubleshooting common browser errors
docs.text: Console message (Chromium wording, shortened) Cause Fix No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource The response had no CORS headers: origin not allowed, CORS middleware not applied to this route, or the request failed with an error page that skipped CORS Register CORS middleware first; check the allowlist; check server and proxy logs for the real error Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check: It does not have HTTP ok status The OPTIONS request got 401, 403, 404, or 405, usually because auth middleware or routing ran before CORS Answer preflights before authentication; let the CORS middleware handle OPTIONS The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include' Credentials with * Echo the exact origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials' header is '' which must be 'true' Credentials requested but not allowed Send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true Request header field authorization is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Headers in preflight response Header missing from the allowed list Add it to Access-Control-Allow-Headers Method PATCH is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Methods in preflight response Method missing from the allowed list Add it to Access-Control-Allow-Methods The 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header contains multiple values, but only one is allowed Both the proxy (Nginx) and the app add the header, or a comma-separated list was sent Set CORS headers in exactly one place; send one origin The 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header has a value that is not equal to the supplied origin Wrong origin configured (scheme, port, trailing slash), or a cache served another origin's response Fix the allowlist entry; add Vary: Origin Redirect is not allowed for a preflight request The preflight was redirected (HTTP to HTTPS, missing trailing slash) Call the final URL directly No error, but response.headers.get("X-Custom") is null The header is not exposed Add it to Access-Control-Expose-Headers

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use an explicit allowlist of full origins and compare exactly.
  • Never reflect arbitrary origins with credentials, and never allow the null origin.
  • Use * only for public, non-credentialed data.
  • Register CORS before authentication, routes, and error handlers, so preflights succeed and errors stay readable.
  • Send Vary: Origin whenever the allowed origin is dynamic.
  • Set Access-Control-Max-Age to reduce preflight traffic.
  • Configure CORS in one layer only (app or proxy, not both).
  • Prefer same-site deployments or a proxy for cookie-based auth, which removes most CORS and third-party-cookie problems.
  • Remember CORS is not security for your API. Authenticate and authorize every request regardless.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every preflight fails after adding authentication. Detect: the browser reports "It does not have HTTP ok status", and server logs show OPTIONS requests answered 401. Cause: auth middleware runs before CORS and rejects the preflight, which never carries credentials. Fix: register CORS first so it answers OPTIONS.
  • "Multiple values" error after putting the API behind Nginx or a gateway. Detect: the response contains two Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. Cause: both the proxy and the app add CORS headers. Fix: configure CORS in exactly one layer.
  • CORS errors that hide real 5xx errors. Detect: the browser shows a CORS error while server or proxy logs show a 500, 502, or 504 at the same moment. Cause: error pages produced by a crashed handler or by the proxy carry no CORS headers. Fix: register CORS before error handlers, and add CORS headers to proxy error responses if browsers need to read them.
  • Random failures for one frontend after another one called the API. Detect: a cached response's Access-Control-Allow-Origin names a different origin than the failing page. Cause: a CDN cached a per-origin response without Vary: Origin. Fix: send Vary: Origin and purge the cache.
  • CORS works locally but fails on API Gateway with Lambda. Detect: the preflight succeeds, but the actual response has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Cause: with proxy integrations the function itself must return the CORS headers, as AWS documents. Fix: add the headers to every response the function returns, including errors.
  • Cookie login works on the same site but not cross-site. Detect: the request goes out without the cookie, even with credentials: "include" and correct CORS headers. Cause: the cookie's SameSite setting, or the browser's third-party cookie blocking. Fix: host the frontend and API on the same site, or switch to token-based auth for truly cross-site clients.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Origin: scheme + host + port of a URL.
  • Site: scheme + registrable domain; used for SameSite cookie rules.
  • Same-origin policy: the browser rule that scripts may only read responses from their own origin.
  • CORS: a protocol of headers through which a server allows other origins to read its responses.
  • Simple request: a cross-origin request that is sent without a preflight.
  • Preflight: an OPTIONS request the browser sends to ask permission before a non-simple request.
  • Credentialed request: a cross-origin request that includes cookies or HTTP authentication.
  • Safelisted header: a request or response header CORS allows without extra permission.
  • CSRF: an attack that makes a victim's browser send an authenticated request the victim did not intend.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "CORS protects my API." It only restricts browsers reading responses; any other client can call your API freely.
  • "The request never reached my server." Simple requests always reach it; only the response is hidden from the page.
  • Using mode: "no-cors" to "fix" CORS. It returns an opaque response that JavaScript cannot read at all.
  • Requiring authentication on OPTIONS requests, which breaks every preflight.
  • Fixing CORS on the frontend. CORS is configured on the server (or avoided with a proxy); frontend code cannot grant itself permission.
  • Putting a list of origins in Access-Control-Allow-Origin. It accepts exactly one.
  • Disabling CORS checks in the browser for development and then shipping a broken configuration.
  • Thinking subdomains are the same origin. api.example.com and app.example.com are different origins (but the same site).

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which three parts of a URL make up its origin? Are http://localhost:3000 and http://localhost:5173 the same origin?
  2. List three things that turn a simple request into a preflighted one.
  3. Why must a server not combine Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials, and what should it send instead?
  4. Why do API calls work in Postman but fail in the browser?
  5. Explain why CORS does not protect against CSRF.
  6. Your error handler returns 500, but the browser shows a CORS error. Why, and how do you fix it?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is the most complete practical guide.
  • MDN: Same-origin policy.
  • Fetch Standard: CORS protocol is the normative specification browsers implement.
  • OWASP: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet.
  • Related: Origins, CORS, and browser security covers the browser side, and configuring CORS in Express covers every option of the cors package.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: Error handling is how a backend detects failures and responds in a controlled way. A backend will meet invalid input, missing records, conflicting updates, slow or unavailable dependencies, and plain programming mistakes. Good error handling turns each of these into a predictable response for the client and useful diagnostics for the people running the system.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Failures are normal in networked systems: databases restart, third-party APIs time out, users send bad data, and code has bugs. Without a deliberate strategy, an application may crash on the first unexpected value, return 200 OK with an error message buried in the body, expose stack traces and connection strings, or silently lose data.

With a clear strategy:

  • Clients get consistent, correct status codes and machine-readable errors.
  • Users see helpful messages, not internal details.
  • Operators get logs and alerts with enough context to fix the problem.
  • Transient failures are retried, and real bugs are surfaced instead of hidden.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe returns structured errors with a type (such as invalid_request_error), a human-readable message, and a param naming the field at fault (Stripe API: errors). Every request also gets an identifier in the Request-Id response header, which Stripe asks you to quote when contacting support (Stripe API: request IDs).
  • Google APIs follow AIP-193: services must return a google.rpc.Status message with canonical error codes when an API error occurs, so clients can share one error-handling path (AIP-193: Errors).
  • Zalando makes RFC 9457 mandatory in its public RESTful API guidelines: APIs "MUST support problem JSON" using application/problem+json (Zalando RESTful API Guidelines).

Popular tools: error trackers such as Sentry, Rollbar, Bugsnag, and the error-tracking features of Datadog and New Relic; libraries such as http-errors for typed HTTP errors in Node.js.

docs.title: Categories of errors
docs.text:
Operational errors are expected failure conditions in a correct program:

  • Invalid input or validation failure.
  • Record not found.
  • Permission denied.
  • Conflict (duplicate email, outdated version).
  • Dependency failure: database unreachable, upstream timeout, rate limited.

Programmer errors are bugs:

  • Reading a property of undefined.
  • Passing the wrong type to a function.
  • Forgetting to await a promise.
  • A broken assumption ("this list is never empty").

Operational errors are handled: map them to a response and continue. Programmer errors are fixed: log them loudly, return a generic 500, and, if the process may be in an inconsistent state, restart it.

A second useful split:

Transient Permanent Meaning Might succeed if tried again Will fail the same way every time Examples Network timeout, 503, connection reset, deadlock, 429 Validation error, 404, 403, malformed request Action Retry with backoff (if the operation is idempotent) Do not retry; return the error

See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

docs.title: Fail fast versus graceful degradation
docs.text:
• Fail fast: detect problems as early as possible and stop. Validate configuration at startup and refuse to boot if a required value is missing. Reject invalid requests before doing any work. A loud early failure is far cheaper than a quiet late one.
  • Graceful degradation: when a non-essential dependency fails, keep the core feature working. If the recommendations service is down, the product page still loads without recommendations. If the cache is unavailable, read from the database (watching for overload).

Decide per dependency: is it essential to this request (fail) or optional (degrade)?

docs.title: How errors propagate through layers
docs.text:
A layered backend lets each layer handle what it understands and pass the rest upward:

  • The data layer catches driver-specific errors only to translate them (for example, MongoDB duplicate key 11000 or PostgreSQL unique violation 23505 → ConflictError). Unknown errors are rethrown unchanged.
  • The service layer throws domain errors that describe business problems (NotFoundError, InsufficientStockError) and knows nothing about HTTP.
  • The controller usually does not catch at all; errors flow to the framework.
  • The error middleware is the single place that maps errors to HTTP responses and logs them.

Catch an error only where you can do something useful: translate it, add context, retry it, or degrade gracefully. Otherwise let it propagate.

docs.title: Mapping errors to status codes
docs.text:
Error type Status Example Validation error 400 (or 422) Missing required field Not authenticated 401 Missing or expired token Not authorized 403 User lacks permission Not found 404 No order with that ID Conflict 409 Email already registered; version mismatch Precondition failed 412 If-Match ETag does not match Too large 413 Upload exceeds the limit Rate limited 429 Too many requests Unexpected bug 500 Unhandled exception Upstream bad response 502 Payment provider returned garbage Dependency unavailable 503 Database down, maintenance Upstream timeout 504 Upstream did not respond in time

Full details: HTTP status codes.

docs.title: Consistent error responses: problem details
docs.text:
Clients handle errors much more easily when every endpoint uses the same shape. RFC 9457 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs) defines a standard JSON format with media type application/problem+json:

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/insufficient-stock",
  "title": "Insufficient stock",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Only 2 units of this product are available.",
  "instance": "/api/orders",
  "requestId": "req_7f3a9c"
}
Member Meaning type A URI identifying the problem type (stable; clients can switch on it) title Short, human-readable summary of the problem type status The HTTP status code detail Human-readable explanation of this occurrence instance A URI identifying this occurrence extensions Any extra members, such as errors (field list) or requestId

Even if you do not adopt RFC 9457 exactly, include a stable error code the client can program against, a safe message, and a request ID.

docs.title: User-facing versus internal messages
docs.text:
• User-facing: what went wrong and what to do — "This email is already registered. Try signing in instead."
  • Internal: stack trace, SQL, file paths, upstream response, user ID — goes to logs only.

For 500 errors, the client should see something generic ("Something went wrong. Please try again. Reference: req_7f3a9c") while the full error is logged with the same request ID. Never expose stack traces, database errors, or secrets in production responses.

docs.title: Logging with context
docs.text:
A log line that says only Error: connection refused is hard to act on. Include:

  • A request or correlation ID that also appears in the response, so a support ticket can be traced to the exact log entries.
  • The route, method, and status code.
  • Relevant identifiers (user ID, order ID) — not passwords, tokens, or sensitive personal data.
  • The error name, message, stack, and cause chain.

Log each error once, at the place it is handled (usually the error middleware). Logging and rethrowing at every layer creates duplicate noise. See logging, monitoring, and tracing.

docs.title: Never swallow errors
docs.text:
// Swallowed: the failure disappears and the caller thinks it worked
try {
  await sendInvoiceEmail(order);
} catch (error) {}

Every catch must do at least one of: handle it (fallback, retry), translate and rethrow, or log it and deliberately continue with a documented reason. An empty catch hides bugs and data loss.

docs.title: Preserving the cause
docs.text:
When translating an error, keep the original with the standard cause option so the root cause is not lost:

try {
  await paymentClient.charge(order);
} catch (error) {
  throw new PaymentFailedError("Card charge failed", { cause: error });
}

docs.title: Error tracking tools
docs.text: Error tracking services (such as Sentry, Rollbar, or the error features of APM tools) capture exceptions with stack traces, group duplicates, show how many users are affected, link to releases, and alert the team. Logs tell you what happened; error trackers tell you which bugs matter most.

docs.title: Crash and restart
docs.text:
For programmer errors that escape all handlers — an uncaught exception or an unhandled promise rejection — Node's process may be in an unknown state (half-finished operations, leaked resources). The robust approach:

  1. Log the error with full detail.
  2. Stop accepting new requests and let in-flight ones finish if possible.
  3. Exit with a non-zero code.
  4. Let a supervisor (container orchestrator, systemd, PM2) start a fresh process, while other instances behind the load balancer keep serving.

Trying to keep a corrupted process alive usually produces stranger failures later. See errors, debugging, and performance in Node.js.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Every backend needs error handling; these are the choices to make for each failure.

Fail fast when:

  • Configuration is missing or invalid at startup.
  • Input is invalid — reject it before doing any work.
  • A dependency that the request cannot work without is down.

Degrade gracefully when:

  • An optional dependency fails (recommendations, avatars, analytics) and the core feature can still work.

Retry when:

  • The failure is transient and the operation is idempotent or protected by an idempotency key.

Do not:

  • Retry validation errors, authorization failures, or bugs.
  • Catch errors only to log and rethrow them at every layer.
  • Keep running after an uncaught exception.
Failure Response to the client What the server does Invalid input 400 or 422 with field errors Nothing else; no retry Missing record 404 Nothing else Duplicate or version conflict 409 or 412 Nothing else Optional dependency down 200 with partial data Log a warning, alert if sustained Required dependency down 503 (or 502 / 504) Retry with backoff if idempotent; alert Unexpected bug Generic 500 with request ID Log with stack, report to error tracker Uncaught exception Connection may drop Log, exit, let the supervisor restart

docs.title: Domain error classes
docs.text:
// errors.js
export class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, { status = 500, code = "INTERNAL_ERROR", cause } = {}) {
    super(message, { cause });
    this.name = this.constructor.name;
    this.status = status;
    this.code = code;
    this.expose = status < 500; // client-caused: safe to show the message
  }
}

export class ValidationError extends AppError {
  constructor(message, errors = []) {
    super(message, { status: 400, code: "VALIDATION_ERROR" });
    this.errors = errors;
  }
}

export class NotFoundError extends AppError {
  constructor(message = "Resource not found") {
    super(message, { status: 404, code: "NOT_FOUND" });
  }
}

export class ConflictError extends AppError {
  constructor(message, options) {
    super(message, { status: 409, code: "CONFLICT", ...options });
  }
}

docs.title: A worked example across layers
docs.text:
// Data layer: translate driver errors, rethrow the rest
export async function insertUser(user) {
  try {
    return await db.collection("users").insertOne(user);
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.code === 11000) {
      throw new ConflictError("Email already registered", { cause: error });
    }
    throw error; // unknown: let it propagate unchanged
  }
}

// Service layer: business rules, no HTTP knowledge
export async function registerUser(input) {
  if (await isDisposableEmail(input.email)) {
    throw new ValidationError("Disposable email addresses are not allowed");
  }
  const passwordHash = await hashPassword(input.password);
  return insertUser({ email: input.email, passwordHash });
}

// Controller: no try/catch; Express 5 forwards rejected promises
app.post("/api/users", async (request, response) => {
  const user = await registerUser(request.validated.body);
  response.status(201).json({ id: user.insertedId });
});

// Error middleware: the single place that maps and logs
app.use((error, request, response, next) => {
  if (response.headersSent) {
    return next(error); // let Express close the connection
  }

  const known = error instanceof AppError;
  const status = known ? error.status : 500;
  // Only our own codes reach the client; driver errors may carry numeric codes
  const code = known ? error.code : "INTERNAL_ERROR";

  request.log.error({ err: error, requestId: request.id, status }, "request failed");

  response
    .status(status)
    .type("application/problem+json")
    .json({
      type: `https://api.example.com/problems/${code.toLowerCase()}`,
      title: known && error.expose ? error.message : "Internal server error",
      status,
      requestId: request.id,
      ...(error.errors ? { errors: error.errors } : {}),
    });
});

In this example, duplicate registrations become a clean 409, disposable emails become 400, and any unexpected bug becomes a generic 500 whose full details are only in the logs. Express-specific details — async errors in Express 4 versus 5, the four-argument signature, 404 handlers — are in error handling in Express, and middleware ordering is covered in middleware.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Separate operational errors (handle) from programmer errors (fix, restart).
  • Translate low-level errors into domain errors at the layer boundary.
  • Handle and log errors in one central place; log each error once.
  • Use correct status codes and a consistent error format (RFC 9457 or similar).
  • Include a request ID in every error response and log line.
  • Keep internal details out of responses; keep secrets out of logs.
  • Never write empty catch blocks; preserve cause when rethrowing.
  • Retry only transient failures, only for idempotent operations, with backoff.
  • Validate configuration at startup and fail fast.
  • Crash and restart on unknown errors; run multiple instances so a restart is invisible.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Error responses suddenly turn into HTML. Symptom: clients fail with Unexpected token '<' while parsing a 500 response. Detect: 5xx responses with Content-Type: text/html. Cause: the error handler itself threw (for example, calling a string method on a driver error whose code is a number), or it was registered before the routes, so Express's built-in handler answered. Fix: keep the error handler defensive, register it last, and test it with unexpected error types.
  • Work silently disappears. Symptom: customers report missing confirmation emails, but no errors were logged. Detect: a business metric gap, such as orders placed versus confirmations sent. Cause: an empty catch, or a promise that was never awaited. Fix: log and alert in every catch, move side effects to a job queue with retries, and enable lint rules against empty blocks and floating promises.
  • The service is stuck in a crash loop. Symptom: the load balancer returns 502 and Kubernetes reports CrashLoopBackOff. Detect: restart count rises, and the same uncaught exception appears in each instance's last log lines. Cause: a bug or bad configuration hit on every start. Fix: validate configuration at startup with clear messages, alert on restart rate, and roll back the release.
  • Log volume and cost explode. Symptom: the logging bill jumps and real errors are hard to find. Detect: log volume per message shows the same error repeated, or client 4xx responses logged at error level. Cause: each layer logs and rethrows; expected client errors are logged as errors. Fix: log once in the error middleware, log 4xx at info or warn, and sample noisy messages.
  • Stack traces reach users. Symptom: a security scan finds stack frames or SQL in error responses. Detect: search response bodies for stack-frame lines. Cause: NODE_ENV is not production, and Express's built-in error handler includes the stack trace outside production; or a custom handler sends error.message for every error. Fix: set NODE_ENV=production and expose messages only for known client errors.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Operational error: an expected failure condition, such as a missing record or timeout.
  • Programmer error: a defect in the code.
  • Transient error: a failure that may succeed on retry.
  • Domain error: an error expressed in business terms, independent of HTTP.
  • Error middleware: framework code dedicated to handling errors centrally.
  • Problem details: the RFC 9457 standard JSON error format.
  • Correlation ID / request ID: an identifier linking a response to its log entries.
  • Error cause: the original error attached to a new, higher-level error.
  • Graceful degradation: continuing with reduced functionality when a non-essential part fails.
  • Fail fast: detecting and stopping on problems as early as possible.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Returning 200 with { "error": ... }. Clients, proxies, and monitoring treat it as success.
  • Returning 500 for client mistakes. Bad input is a 4xx.
  • Exposing stack traces or database messages to clients in production.
  • Swallowing errors with empty catch blocks.
  • Logging the same error at every layer, producing duplicate noise.
  • Assuming try/catch catches everything. It does not catch errors from callbacks or promises that are not awaited inside it.
  • Retrying non-idempotent operations blindly, causing duplicate charges.
  • Keeping a process alive after an uncaught exception.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between operational and programmer errors, and how should each be handled?
  2. Why should the service layer throw domain errors rather than HTTP errors?
  3. What are the members of an RFC 9457 problem details response?
  4. Why should each error be logged once, and where?
  5. Which errors are safe to retry, and what else must be true about the operation?
  6. Why is restarting the process the recommended response to an uncaught exception in Node.js?
