docs.title: File Storage and Uploads
docs.text: Many applications accept files — profile photos, documents, invoices, videos, CSV imports — and serve them back later. Doing this well involves choosing where files live, how they get there, how to validate them, who may download them, and how they are processed and eventually deleted. This page covers the backend design; the Express mechanics of receiving uploads are in file uploads with Multer.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Files are large, binary, and untrusted. Handled carelessly, they cause real problems:

  • A server's disk fills up, or files vanish when a container is replaced.
  • Uploads through the API exhaust memory and block other requests.
  • A "profile photo" is actually an HTML file with JavaScript, served from your domain (stored XSS), or malware passed on to other users.
  • Private documents are accessible to anyone who guesses the URL.
  • Old files accumulate forever, costing money and creating privacy risk.

A deliberate storage design solves these and scales from a hobby project to millions of files.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Amazon S3 presigned URLs use the creator's credentials to grant time-limited permission to download or upload a specific object; with the AWS CLI the longest expiry is 7 days (Amazon S3: presigned URLs). New S3 buckets, access points, and objects do not allow public access by default, and S3 Block Public Access settings override policies that try to open them (Amazon S3: Block Public Access).
  • Google Cloud Storage signed URLs give anyone holding the URL time-limited read, write, or delete access to one resource, with a maximum expiry of 604,800 seconds (7 days) (Google Cloud: signed URLs).
  • Resumable uploads at Cloudflare Stream. Videos over 200 MB must be uploaded with the tus protocol, and Cloudflare recommends tus for smaller files too on unreliable connections, because an interrupted upload can resume (Cloudflare Stream: resumable uploads).

Popular tools and providers: Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, Cloudflare R2, and MinIO (self-hosted, S3-compatible); Multer and Busboy for receiving uploads in Node.js; tus clients and servers for resumable uploads; ClamAV for malware scanning.

docs.title: Storage options
docs.text:
Option How it works Pros Cons Local disk Write files to the server's filesystem Simple; fast for one server Lost when containers are replaced; not shared across instances; manual backups; disk fills up Database (BLOB / GridFS) Store bytes in the database (MongoDB GridFS splits files into chunks) Transactions and backups together with data Bloats the database; expensive storage; database becomes a file server Object storage (S3 and compatibles) Store objects in buckets via an HTTP API Practically unlimited, durable, cheap; scales independently; signed URLs; lifecycle rules; CDN integration Network latency; some bucket configuration changes are eventually consistent (S3 object reads after writes are strongly consistent); new concepts to learn Network file system (EFS, NFS) Shared filesystem mounted on several servers Works with code expecting files Costlier; performance and locking subtleties

Object storage — Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, or S3-compatible services like Cloudflare R2 and MinIO — is the standard choice for production applications. Your database stores metadata (owner, name, size, type, storage key); the object store holds the bytes.

GridFS can be reasonable when files are modest in size and you want them in the same backup as your MongoDB data — see GridFS.

docs.title: Object storage concepts
docs.text:
• Bucket: a container for objects, with its own access policy and region.
  • Object key: the object's name within the bucket, such as users/42/avatars/7f3a9c.webp. The "folders" are just key prefixes.
  • Metadata: content type, cache headers, custom key-value metadata.
  • Access control: buckets should be private by default; access is granted through IAM policies or temporary signed URLs. Accidentally public buckets are a common cause of data leaks.
  • Storage classes and lifecycle rules: move old objects to cheaper tiers or delete them automatically after a period.

docs.title: Upload pattern 1: through your server
docs.text:
The client sends the file to your API as multipart/form-data; the server validates it and forwards it to storage.

Client ──(multipart upload)──► API server ──(stream)──► Object storage
                                   │
                                   └─► save metadata in database
  • Full control: validation, scanning, processing before storing.
  • Uses your bandwidth and server resources; long uploads hold connections.
  • Stream the file to storage instead of buffering it entirely in memory — a few concurrent 500 MB uploads held in memory can crash the process.
  • Enforce size limits while streaming, not after.

Good for small files (avatars, documents up to a few MB) and when you must inspect content before accepting it.

docs.title: Upload pattern 2: direct to storage with presigned URLs
docs.text:
The server authorizes the upload and gives the client a short-lived signed URL; the client uploads directly to object storage.

  • Your servers never handle the bytes — great for large files and high volume.
  • The signed URL limits what can be uploaded: one specific key, an expiry time, and (with presigned POST policies) content type and size ranges.
  • You must verify after upload, because the client controlled the bytes: check the object's actual size and type, scan it, then mark it usable.
  • Storage event notifications (for example, S3 events to a queue) can trigger processing instead of relying on the client to call "complete."
  • The bucket needs CORS configured to allow browser uploads from your origin.

docs.title: Large files: multipart and resumable uploads
docs.text:
For files of hundreds of megabytes or more:

  • Multipart upload (S3 and others) splits a file into parts uploaded separately (in parallel), then combined. Failed parts are retried individually instead of restarting the whole upload. Each part can have its own presigned URL.
  • Resumable upload protocols such as tus let clients resume after a network drop from the last confirmed byte.
  • Clean up incomplete multipart uploads with a lifecycle rule; abandoned parts still cost money.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Never trust the file name, extension, or the Content-Type sent by the client — all are client-controlled.

  • Size: enforce a maximum per file and per request; reject early (413 Content Too Large).
  • Count: maximum number of files per request.
  • Type by content: inspect the magic bytes (file signature) at the start of the file. PNG starts with 89 50 4E 47, PDF with %PDF, JPEG with FF D8 FF. Libraries such as file-type detect this.
  • Allowlist types your feature actually needs (for example, JPEG, PNG, WebP for avatars), rather than blocking dangerous ones.
  • Content checks: re-encode images (which strips embedded payloads and metadata like GPS location), and limit image dimensions to defend against decompression bombs.
  • Archives: be careful extracting ZIP files — check total extracted size ("zip bombs") and reject entries with ../ paths ("zip slip").

docs.title: Malware scanning
docs.text: If users share files with other users, scan uploads before making them available — for example, with ClamAV or a cloud malware-scanning service. A common flow: upload to a quarantine location or mark the record pending, scan asynchronously in a background job, then move the file to the clean location and mark it available, or delete it and notify the user.

docs.title: Key naming
docs.text:
• Generate keys on the server; never use the user's file name as the key (path traversal, collisions, overwrite, odd characters).
  • Use random or unique IDs: uploads/{userId}/{uuid}.pdf.
  • Keep the original file name only as metadata for display and the Content-Disposition download name (sanitized).
  • Prefix by tenant or owner to simplify access policies and deletion.

docs.title: Private and public files
docs.text:
• Public files (product images, public avatars) can be served from a public bucket path or, better, through a CDN.
  • Private files (invoices, medical documents, exports) stay in a private bucket. To serve them:
  • Signed download URLs: after an authorization check, the API returns a short-lived presigned GET URL (for example, valid for 5 minutes).
  • Proxy through the API: the API checks permissions and streams the file. More control, more server load.
  • Set Content-Disposition: attachment for user-uploaded files that should download rather than render, and set an accurate Content-Type with X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Ideally serve user content from a separate domain so a malicious file cannot run scripts on your main site's origin.

docs.title: Serving through a CDN
docs.text: A CDN caches files at edge locations close to users, reducing latency and storage egress costs. For public assets, use long cache lifetimes with versioned keys (a new key for a new version). For private files, CDNs support signed URLs or signed cookies. See CDN.

docs.title: Processing pipelines
docs.text:
Image resizing, thumbnail generation, PDF previews, video transcoding, and text extraction are slow — do them in background jobs, not in the upload request (see background jobs and scheduling):

upload complete ─► queue "process-image" ─► worker: scan, resize to
                                             3 sizes, convert to WebP,
                                             strip metadata ─► store
                                             variants ─► mark record ready

Video often uses dedicated managed services because transcoding is CPU- and time-intensive.

docs.title: Metadata in the database
docs.text:
A typical record:

{
  "_id": "file_7f3a9c",
  "ownerId": "user_42",
  "storageKey": "uploads/user_42/7f3a9c.pdf",
  "originalName": "Invoice March.pdf",
  "contentType": "application/pdf",
  "size": 248113,
  "checksum": "sha256:9b74c9897bac770ffc029102a200c5de...",
  "status": "available",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-07T14:32:10Z"
}

Authorization checks use this record (is the requester the owner?), and listings never have to touch object storage.

docs.title: Lifecycle and deletion
docs.text:
• When a record is deleted, delete the object too — or mark it and let a cleanup job remove orphans. Keep the two in sync.
  • Use lifecycle rules to expire temporary uploads, abandoned multipart parts, and old exports.
  • Consider versioning on buckets holding important data, to recover from accidental overwrites or deletes.
  • Respect data-retention and privacy obligations: when a user deletes their account, their files must go too (including variants, thumbnails, and backups within your policy).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use object storage with presigned URLs when:

  • Files are larger than a few megabytes, or there are many of them.
  • You run more than one app instance, or containers that are replaced.
  • Files are private and must be served only after an authorization check.

Upload through your server (streaming) when:

  • Files are small and you must inspect or transform them before they are stored.
  • Clients cannot reach the storage service directly.

Avoid:

  • The container's local disk for anything that must survive a redeploy.
  • Storing large files in the main database "to keep things simple" — it bloats backups and makes the database a file server.
Situation Approach Avatars and small documents Through the server (streamed), or presigned upload Videos and large archives Direct-to-storage multipart or resumable (tus) upload Private invoices and medical files Private bucket + short-lived signed download URL Public product images Public path behind a CDN with versioned keys Files that must share a MongoDB backup GridFS, for modest sizes Temporary exports Object storage with a lifecycle rule to delete them

docs.title: Creating a presigned upload URL (AWS SDK v3)
docs.text:
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { getSignedUrl } from "@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const s3 = new S3Client({
  region: process.env.AWS_REGION,
  // Recent SDK versions otherwise add a checksum of the (empty) request body
  // to presigned upload URLs, and the real upload then fails to match it
  requestChecksumCalculation: "WHEN_REQUIRED",
});
const ALLOWED_TYPES = new Map([
  ["image/jpeg", "jpg"],
  ["image/png", "png"],
  ["application/pdf", "pdf"],
]);
const MAX_SIZE = 10 * 1024 * 1024; // 10 MB

app.post("/api/uploads", authenticate, async (request, response) => {
  const { contentType, size, fileName } = request.body;
  const extension = ALLOWED_TYPES.get(contentType);

  if (!extension || !Number.isInteger(size) || size <= 0 || size > MAX_SIZE) {
    return response.status(400).json({ error: "Unsupported file type or size" });
  }

  const key = `uploads/${request.user.id}/${randomUUID()}.${extension}`;
  await db.files.insertOne({
    ownerId: request.user.id,
    storageKey: key,
    originalName: String(fileName ?? "file").slice(0, 200),
    contentType,
    size,
    status: "pending",
    createdAt: new Date(),
  });

  const uploadUrl = await getSignedUrl(
    s3,
    new PutObjectCommand({
      Bucket: process.env.UPLOADS_BUCKET,
      Key: key,
      ContentType: contentType,
    }),
    {
      expiresIn: 300, // seconds
      // Sign Content-Type so the client must upload with exactly this type
      // (by default only the host header is signed)
      signableHeaders: new Set(["content-type"]),
    }
  );

  response.status(201).json({ key, uploadUrl });
});

After the client uploads, a "complete" endpoint (or a storage event) should check the object with a HeadObjectCommand, compare its size, inspect its magic bytes, enqueue scanning, and only then mark it available.

docs.title: Short-lived download URL after an ownership check
docs.text:
import { GetObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";

app.get("/api/files/:id/download", authenticate, async (request, response) => {
  const file = await db.files.findOne({
    _id: request.params.id,
    ownerId: request.user.id,
    status: "available",
  });
  if (!file) {
    return response.status(404).json({ error: "File not found" });
  }

  // filename* carries a UTF-8, percent-encoded name (RFC 6266 / RFC 8187).
  // encodeURIComponent leaves ' ( ) * unescaped, which that syntax forbids.
  const encodedName = encodeURIComponent(file.originalName).replace(
    /['()*]/g,
    (char) => `%${char.charCodeAt(0).toString(16).toUpperCase()}`
  );

  const url = await getSignedUrl(
    s3,
    new GetObjectCommand({
      Bucket: process.env.UPLOADS_BUCKET,
      Key: file.storageKey,
      // Download with the original name instead of rendering in the browser
      ResponseContentDisposition: `attachment; filename*=UTF-8''${encodedName}`,
    }),
    { expiresIn: 300 }
  );

  response.json({ url });
});

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Store bytes in object storage and metadata in the database.
  • Keep buckets private; grant access with short-lived signed URLs after authorization checks.
  • Prefer direct-to-storage uploads for large files; stream when proxying.
  • Enforce size and count limits early; validate type by magic bytes against an allowlist.
  • Generate storage keys on the server; keep original names only as metadata.
  • Scan files that will be shared; quarantine until clean.
  • Process files asynchronously in background jobs.
  • Serve user-uploaded content with safe headers, ideally from a separate domain; use a CDN for public assets.
  • Use lifecycle rules for temporary data and incomplete uploads; delete objects when records are deleted.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Browser uploads fail with a CORS error. Symptom: the presigned PUT works from curl but fails in the browser. Detect: the browser console shows a CORS error on the storage domain's preflight. Cause: the bucket has no CORS rule allowing your origin and the PUT method. Fix: add a bucket CORS rule for your app's origin, the methods used, and the headers the client sends (such as Content-Type).
  • Presigned uploads are rejected after an SDK upgrade. Symptom: uploads that worked before now fail with a checksum mismatch. Detect: the upload URL contains x-amz-checksum-crc32 and x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm query parameters. Cause: recent AWS SDK versions calculate request checksums by default (WHEN_SUPPORTED), and for a presigned URL that is the checksum of an empty body. Fix: create the S3 client with requestChecksumCalculation: "WHEN_REQUIRED" (AWS SDKs: data integrity protections).
  • Users can upload any file type through a presigned URL. Symptom: HTML or executable files appear in a bucket meant for images. Detect: stored objects whose Content-Type or magic bytes do not match the allowlist. Cause: only the host header was signed, so the client chose its own Content-Type; nothing checked the bytes afterwards. Fix: sign content-type (signableHeaders), and verify the object (size, magic bytes) before marking it available.
  • Storage costs keep rising. Symptom: the bucket grows every month even though users delete files. Detect: the object count is far larger than the number of file records; incomplete multipart uploads appear in storage reports. Cause: orphaned objects and abandoned uploads. Fix: delete objects with their records, run an orphan-cleanup job, and add lifecycle rules for temporary prefixes and incomplete multipart uploads.
  • Download links leak. Symptom: a private file is reachable from a link posted elsewhere. Detect: access logs show downloads long after the link was issued. Cause: signed URLs with long expiries, or files in a public path. Fix: keep expiries to minutes, issue URLs only after an ownership check, and keep private files in private buckets.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Object storage: a service storing files as objects in buckets via an HTTP API.
  • Bucket: a top-level container in object storage.
  • Object key: the unique name of an object within a bucket.
  • Presigned URL: a temporary URL that grants permission for one specific operation on one object.
  • Multipart upload: uploading a large file in independently retried parts.
  • Resumable upload: an upload that can continue after interruption.
  • Magic bytes: the signature at the start of a file identifying its format.
  • multipart/form-data: the request encoding browsers use for file uploads.
  • Content-Disposition: a header controlling whether a response is shown inline or downloaded, and its file name.
  • Lifecycle rule: an automatic policy to transition or delete objects.
  • Quarantine: holding an upload separately until it is scanned.
  • CDN: a content delivery network caching content near users.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Storing uploads on a container's local disk, then losing them on redeploy.
  • Buffering whole uploads in memory.
  • Trusting the extension or Content-Type sent by the client.
  • Using the user's file name as the storage path.
  • Public buckets for private documents, or long-lived signed URLs.
  • Skipping post-upload verification for presigned uploads.
  • Serving user uploads from the main domain with a renderable type, enabling stored XSS.
  • Never deleting anything, leaving orphaned and outdated files.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is object storage preferred over local disk for production uploads?
  2. Walk through the presigned URL upload flow. What must the server verify after the client uploads?
  3. Why should file type be checked using magic bytes rather than the extension or Content-Type?
  4. How would you let a user download a private invoice securely?
  5. Why should image processing and malware scanning happen in background jobs?
  6. What lifecycle rules would you set for an uploads bucket?

docs.text:

docs.title: HTTP Headers and Content Negotiation
docs.text: Headers are the metadata of an HTTP message. They tell the other side what format the body is in, who the caller is, whether a response may be cached, which security rules the browser must enforce, and much more. A backend developer reads request headers on every request and sets response headers on every response.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Correct parsing: without the right Content-Type, a server cannot parse a body and a browser cannot render a response.
  • Authentication: credentials travel in Authorization or Cookie.
  • Performance: Cache-Control, ETag, and Content-Encoding decide whether a response is downloaded again, served from cache, or compressed.
  • Security: headers such as Strict-Transport-Security and Content-Security-Policy switch on browser protections against downgrade, clickjacking, and script injection.
  • Cross-origin access: CORS is implemented entirely with headers. See CORS.
  • Real client information behind proxies: X-Forwarded-For and Forwarded carry the original client IP and protocol.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub reports rate limits in response headers. Every REST API response carries x-ratelimit-limit, x-ratelimit-remaining, x-ratelimit-used, x-ratelimit-reset, and x-ratelimit-resource, so clients can pace themselves without a separate "how much quota is left?" call.
  • GitHub rewards conditional requests. Most GitHub endpoints return an etag header, and many return last-modified. GitHub's best practices explain that a conditional GET answered with 304 Not Modified is fast and does not use your rate limit, which makes polling much cheaper.
  • GitHub and Stripe select API versions with a header. GitHub reads X-GitHub-Api-Version (a date such as 2022-11-28); Stripe reads Stripe-Version and otherwise uses the account's default version. URLs stay the same across versions.
  • GitHub exposes custom headers to browsers. A cross-origin request to the GitHub API gets Access-Control-Expose-Headers listing ETag, Link, and the x-ratelimit-* headers, so browser code can read pagination links and rate-limit state.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
A header is a case-insensitive name, a colon, and a value. Headers come after the request or status line and end with a blank line, after which the body starts.

POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1          <- request line
Host: api.shop.example             <- headers
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 34
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...
                                    <- blank line ends the headers
{"productId":"p-42","quantity":1}  <- body

Rules worth knowing:

  • Names are case-insensitive. content-type and Content-Type are the same. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send them in lowercase. Node.js exposes request headers in lowercase (req.headers["content-type"]).
  • Some headers hold lists, separated by commas (Accept-Encoding: gzip, br). A list header may also be repeated, and the values are combined.
  • Set-Cookie is special: it is sent once per cookie and must not be combined with commas.
  • Parameters follow a semicolon: Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8.
  • The official term is "field"; "header" is the everyday name.

docs.title: Kinds of headers
docs.text: Kind Describes Examples Request headers The request, the client, or its preferences Host, User-Agent, Accept, Authorization, Cookie Response headers The response or the server Location, Set-Cookie, Retry-After, WWW-Authenticate, Allow Representation headers The body (in either direction) Content-Type, Content-Length, Content-Encoding, Content-Language Caching headers Storing and revalidating responses Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified, Vary, Expires Conditional headers Preconditions the server checks If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Match, If-Unmodified-Since Security headers Browser protections Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options CORS headers Cross-origin permissions Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and the other Access-Control-* headers

docs.title: Common request headers
docs.text:
Header Purpose Example Host Which site the request is for. Required in HTTP/1.1; lets one IP serve many domains Host: api.shop.example User-Agent Identifies the client software. Easy to fake; use only for analytics and debugging User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 ... Accept Response formats the client can handle, with optional preferences Accept: application/json Accept-Encoding Compression formats the client supports Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd Accept-Language Preferred human languages Accept-Language: en-US, en;q=0.9, fr;q=0.5 Authorization Credentials for the request Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci... or Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz Content-Type Format of the request body Content-Type: application/json Content-Length Size of the request body in bytes Content-Length: 348 Cookie Cookies the browser stored for this site Cookie: sid=abc123; theme=dark Origin Scheme, host, and port of the page that made a cross-origin or state-changing request Origin: https://app.shop.example Referer URL (or origin) of the page that linked here. Note the historical misspelling Referer: https://shop.example/cart If-None-Match "Send the body only if the ETag differs from these" If-None-Match: "a1b2c3" If-Modified-Since "Send the body only if it changed after this date" If-Modified-Since: Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:00:00 GMT If-Match "Only apply this change if the ETag still matches" (prevents lost updates) If-Match: "v7" Range Request part of a resource Range: bytes=0-1023 X-Forwarded-For Original client IP, appended by each proxy X-Forwarded-For: 198.51.100.7, 10.0.0.2 X-Forwarded-Proto Original protocol before the proxy terminated TLS X-Forwarded-Proto: https X-Forwarded-Host Original Host before the proxy rewrote it X-Forwarded-Host: shop.example Forwarded The standard (RFC 7239) version of the three above Forwarded: for=198.51.100.7;proto=https;host=shop.example

Forwarded headers can be forged

Anyone can send X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4. Trust these headers only when they were set by your own proxy, and configure your framework to know how many proxies sit in front of it. In Express that is the trust proxy setting. See the request object.

docs.title: Common response headers
docs.text:
Header Purpose Example Content-Type Format of the response body Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 Content-Length Body size in bytes Content-Length: 1532 Content-Encoding Compression applied to the body Content-Encoding: gzip Content-Disposition Show inline or download as a file, and the filename Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="invoice-42.pdf" Set-Cookie Store a cookie in the browser Set-Cookie: sid=abc; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/ Location The new resource (201) or redirect target (3xx) Location: /api/orders/901 Cache-Control Caching rules Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 ETag An identifier for this version of the resource ETag: "33a64df5" Last-Modified When the resource last changed Last-Modified: Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:00:00 GMT Vary Which request headers change the response (affects cache keys) Vary: Accept-Encoding, Origin Retry-After How long to wait before retrying (429, 503, redirects) Retry-After: 120 WWW-Authenticate How to authenticate; required with 401 WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="api" Allow Methods supported; required with 405 Allow: GET, POST Accept-Ranges The server supports range requests Accept-Ranges: bytes Content-Range Which part of the resource this response holds (206) Content-Range: bytes 0-1023/52000

Set-Cookie attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Max-Age, Domain, Path) are covered in sessions, cookies, and JWT.

docs.title: Security headers
docs.text:
These response headers turn on browser protections. They matter most for responses that render in a browser (HTML pages), but are cheap to send from APIs too. In Express, the helmet middleware sets sensible defaults; see Express security best practices.

Header Protects against Typical value Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) Downgrade to plain HTTP and cookie theft on insecure networks. The browser uses HTTPS only for this host for max-age seconds max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains Content-Security-Policy (CSP) Cross-site scripting and data injection. Lists which sources may load scripts, styles, images, frames, and so on default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none' X-Content-Type-Options MIME sniffing, where a browser guesses a type and runs an uploaded "image" as script nosniff X-Frame-Options Clickjacking (your page embedded invisibly in an attacker's frame). Legacy; superseded by CSP frame-ancestors DENY or SAMEORIGIN Referrer-Policy Leaking full URLs (which may contain IDs or tokens) to other sites strict-origin-when-cross-origin (the modern browser default) or no-referrer Permissions-Policy Pages or embedded frames using powerful features camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()

X-Frame-Options vs frame-ancestors: both control who may frame your page. CSP frame-ancestors is the modern standard and supports lists of allowed origins; X-Frame-Options only understands DENY and SAMEORIGIN. Send frame-ancestors, and add X-Frame-Options for old browsers if needed.

HSTS needs care: once a browser has seen it, the site cannot fall back to HTTP until max-age expires. Test with a short max-age first.

docs.title: CORS headers
docs.text: Browsers send Origin on cross-origin requests and only let the page read the response if the server replies with matching Access-Control-Allow-* headers. Every CORS header is explained in CORS.

docs.title: Content negotiation
docs.text:
Content negotiation lets one URL serve different representations: JSON or XML, English or French, gzip or Brotli.

The client states preferences with Accept, Accept-Language, and Accept-Encoding. A quality value (q, from 0 to 1, default 1) ranks alternatives:

Accept: application/json, text/csv;q=0.8, */*;q=0.1

This means "JSON is best, CSV is fine, anything else as a last resort".

The server picks a representation, labels it with Content-Type (and Content-Language/Content-Encoding), and adds Vary naming the headers it used, so caches keep separate copies.

Situation Status The server cannot produce anything in the client's Accept list 406 Not Acceptable (or ignore Accept and return the default format) The client sent a body in a format the server does not accept 415 Unsupported Media Type

Accept describes what the client wants back; Content-Type describes what is being sent. Mixing them up is a common bug.

Common media types for APIs:

Media type Used for application/json JSON bodies application/problem+json Error responses in RFC 9457 format application/x-www-form-urlencoded Classic HTML form posts multipart/form-data Forms with file uploads text/plain, text/html, text/csv Text formats application/octet-stream Arbitrary binary data text/event-stream Server-Sent Events

docs.title: HTTP caching in depth
docs.text:
Caching lets browsers, CDNs, and proxies reuse a response instead of asking the server again. Two questions drive it: may this be stored, and for how long is it fresh? and when it is stale, how do we check it cheaply?

Private caches belong to one user (the browser cache). Shared caches serve many users (CDNs, proxies).

docs.title: Cache-Control directives
docs.text:
Directive Meaning max-age=N The response is fresh for N seconds; caches may reuse it without asking s-maxage=N Like max-age, but only for shared caches (overrides max-age there) public Any cache, including shared ones, may store it (even if the request had Authorization) private Only the user's own browser may store it; CDNs must not no-cache May be stored, but must be revalidated with the server before every reuse no-store Must not be stored anywhere, ever. For sensitive data must-revalidate Once stale, the cache must not serve it without successful revalidation immutable The response will never change while fresh; the browser need not revalidate on reload stale-while-revalidate=N After going stale, the cache may serve the old copy for up to N seconds while it refreshes in the background

no-cache does not mean do not cache

no-cache means "always check with me first". no-store means "never keep a copy". For bank statements and personal data, use no-store.

Typical policies:

# Fingerprinted static asset (app.3f9a1c.js): cache for a year
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# Public, changes occasionally (product list): short freshness, CDN longer
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=30

# Per-user API data: browser only, always revalidate
Cache-Control: private, no-cache

# Sensitive data: never store
Cache-Control: no-store

docs.title: Validation with ETag and Last-Modified
docs.text:
When a cached response goes stale, the client can ask "has it changed?" instead of downloading it again:

1) First request
GET /api/products/42
                         200 OK
                         ETag: "a1b2c3"
                         Cache-Control: no-cache
                         { ...full body... }

2) Later request, revalidating
GET /api/products/42
If-None-Match: "a1b2c3"
                         304 Not Modified      <- no body; reuse the cached copy
                         ETag: "a1b2c3"
  • ETag is an opaque version identifier, often a hash of the body. A weak ETag (W/"a1b2c3") means "semantically equivalent"; a strong one means "byte for byte identical". Express generates weak ETags for res.send()/res.json() and answers 304 automatically when they match.
  • Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since works the same way using a date, with only one-second precision.
  • ETags also prevent lost updates: the client sends If-Match: "v7" with a PUT, and the server returns 412 Precondition Failed if the resource has changed.

docs.title: Vary and cache keys
docs.text:
A cache normally keys a response by method and URL. If the response depends on a request header, list it in Vary so the cache stores separate copies:

  • Vary: Accept-Encoding because gzip and Brotli bodies differ.
  • Vary: Origin when Access-Control-Allow-Origin changes per origin.
  • Vary: Accept-Language when you serve translated content.

Avoid Vary: Cookie or Vary: User-Agent on public content; they split the cache into near-useless fragments.

See caching for application and database caching.

docs.title: Custom headers and request IDs
docs.text:
You can define your own headers for metadata that has no standard header, such as a request ID or an API version. The old convention of prefixing custom headers with X- is deprecated (RFC 6648), because "experimental" headers often become standard and the prefix then becomes permanent baggage. Many widely used headers still carry it (X-Request-Id), and that is fine.

A request ID (also called a correlation ID) ties together every log line for one request across services:

  1. The edge proxy or the first service generates an ID if none was sent.
  2. Every service logs it and forwards it on outgoing calls.
  3. The response includes it so users can quote it to support.

Browsers can only read custom response headers cross-origin if the server lists them in Access-Control-Expose-Headers. See CORS.

docs.title: Header size limits
docs.text: Servers limit header size to protect memory. Node.js rejects requests whose headers exceed 16 KB by default with 431 Request Header Fields Too Large; proxies such as Nginx have their own limits. The usual culprits are too many or too large cookies and oversized tokens. Keep cookies small and avoid stuffing data into JWTs.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Caching headers:

  • Use public, max-age (and immutable for fingerprinted files) for assets and public data that many users share.
  • Use private, no-cache (or a short max-age) for per-user data that may live in the browser but must be revalidated.
  • Use no-store for sensitive data: account pages, tokens, financial or health records.
  • Do not rely on caches for data that must be correct immediately after a write, unless you invalidate them.

Custom headers versus the body:

  • Use a header for metadata about the message: request IDs, rate-limit state, API version, idempotency keys. Proxies and tools can read headers without parsing the body.
  • Use the body for the data itself and for anything large or structured.
  • Do not put secrets or personal data in custom headers that proxies log.
Response type Cache-Control Validator Notes Fingerprinted static asset public, max-age=31536000, immutable Not needed Change the file name to change the content Public, slowly changing data public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300 ETag Add stale-while-revalidate for smoother refreshes Per-user data private, no-cache ETag Revalidation saves bandwidth with 304 Sensitive data no-store None Never stored by browsers or CDNs

docs.title: Reading and setting headers in Express
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();

app.get("/api/report", (req, res) => {
  // Reading: req.get() is case-insensitive
  const lang = req.get("Accept-Language");
  const ua = req.get("User-Agent");

  // Setting
  res.set({
    "Cache-Control": "private, no-cache",
    "Content-Language": "en",
    "X-Request-Id": "7f3c9a2e",
  });
  res.json({ lang, ua });
});

app.listen(3000);

docs.title: Content negotiation with res.format
docs.text:
app.get("/api/users", (req, res) => {
  const users = [{ id: 1, name: "Ana" }];
  // res.format picks a handler from Accept and adds "Vary: Accept" itself
  res.format({
    "application/json": () => res.json(users),
    "text/csv": () => res.type("text/csv").send("id,name\n1,Ana\n"),
    default: () => res.status(406).send("Not Acceptable"),
  });
});

curl -H "Accept: text/csv" http://localhost:3000/api/users
curl -H "Accept: application/xml" -i http://localhost:3000/api/users  # 406

docs.title: Caching a public resource with ETag
docs.text:
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

app.get("/api/products/:id", (req, res) => {
  const product = { id: req.params.id, name: "Desk lamp", price: 3999 };
  const body = JSON.stringify(product);
  const etag = `"${createHash("sha1").update(body).digest("base64url")}"`;

  res.set({ ETag: etag, "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=60" });
  if (req.get("If-None-Match") === etag) {
    return res.status(304).end(); // client copy is current
  }
  res.type("application/json").send(body);
});

Express would generate and compare an ETag for you; doing it by hand shows the mechanism.

docs.title: Inspecting headers with curl
docs.text:
curl -I https://example.com/       # HEAD: response headers only
# GET, print response headers, discard the body; look for Content-Encoding
curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" https://example.com/

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Always send an accurate Content-Type, including charset=utf-8 for text.
  • Set an explicit Cache-Control on every response, especially on personalized data, so a CDN never serves one user's data to another.
  • Use no-store for sensitive data and immutable with long max-age for fingerprinted static files.
  • Add Vary whenever a response depends on a request header.
  • Send security headers (helmet in Express) and test CSP in report-only mode first.
  • Trust forwarded headers only from your own proxies.
  • Never put secrets in custom headers that get logged, and never in URLs.
  • Keep cookies and tokens small to stay under header limits.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• One user sees another user's data. Detect: CDN logs show cache hits on personalized endpoints such as /api/me, and the leaked response has Cache-Control: public or no Cache-Control at all. Cause: a shared cache was allowed to store a personalized response. Fix: send private or no-store on every personalized response, purge the CDN, and add a test that checks the header.
  • CORS errors that come and go. Detect: the same request fails for one origin only after another origin has called it, and the cached response's Access-Control-Allow-Origin names the other origin. Cause: per-origin CORS headers without Vary: Origin. Fix: add Vary: Origin and purge the cache.
  • Rate limits or audit logs keyed on the wrong IP. Detect: all traffic appears to come from the load balancer's address, or attackers bypass IP limits by sending their own X-Forwarded-For. Cause: forwarded headers not configured, or trusted from anyone. Fix: trust forwarded headers only from your own proxies, with the exact number of hops.
  • 431 errors for some users only. Detect: 431 Request Header Fields Too Large in logs, concentrated on users with many cookies. Cause: cookie bloat across subdomains, or very large tokens. Fix: audit and shrink cookies; scope them to the right domain and path.
  • A subdomain becomes unreachable over HTTP. Detect: browsers refuse to load http:// pages on a subdomain right after HSTS with includeSubDomains was deployed. Cause: a subdomain that still only serves plain HTTP. Fix: enable HTTPS everywhere before using includeSubDomains, and roll out HSTS with a short max-age first.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Header (field): a name-value pair of metadata on a request or response.
  • Representation header: a header that describes the body, such as Content-Type.
  • Media type (MIME type): a label for a data format, such as application/json.
  • Quality value (q): a weight from 0 to 1 that ranks alternatives in Accept* headers.
  • Content negotiation: choosing a representation based on the client's preferences.
  • Fresh / stale: whether a cached response is still within its allowed lifetime.
  • Revalidation: asking the server whether a stale cached copy is still valid.
  • ETag: an opaque identifier for a specific version of a resource.
  • Conditional request: a request whose effect depends on If-* headers.
  • Shared cache: a cache serving many users, such as a CDN.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Confusing Accept with Content-Type. Accept is what you want back; Content-Type is what you are sending.
  • "no-cache disables caching." It forces revalidation; no-store disables storage.
  • Caching personalized responses publicly, which can show one user's data to another through a CDN.
  • Forgetting Vary: Origin with per-origin CORS headers, so a CDN serves the wrong Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  • Reading req.headers["Content-Type"] in Node.js; the keys are lowercase. Use req.get("Content-Type") in Express.
  • Trusting User-Agent or X-Forwarded-For for security decisions.
  • Setting HSTS with a long max-age before HTTPS works everywhere on the domain and its subdomains.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between no-cache, no-store, and private?
  2. Walk through how ETag and If-None-Match produce a 304 response.
  3. When should a response include Vary, and what goes wrong without it?
  4. Why is X-Forwarded-For dangerous to trust, and how do you use it safely?
  5. Which security header replaces X-Frame-Options, and why is it better?
  6. When does a server return 406 and when 415?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: HTTP headers documents every standard header.
  • MDN: HTTP caching explains freshness, validation, and cache directives.
  • MDN: Content negotiation.
  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics defines fields, conditional requests, and content negotiation.
  • RFC 9111: HTTP Caching defines Cache-Control and cache behavior.
  • OWASP: HTTP Security Response Headers Cheat Sheet.

docs.title: HTTP Methods
docs.text: An HTTP method (sometimes called a verb) tells the server what the client wants to do with the target resource: read it, create something, replace it, change part of it, or delete it. Each method has defined properties, such as whether it is safe to repeat, that browsers, caches, proxies, and client libraries rely on.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Methods are a contract, not a naming convention. Infrastructure makes real decisions based on them:

  • Caches routinely store GET and HEAD responses. A POST response is cacheable only with explicit freshness information and a matching Content-Location, so in practice it is almost never cached.
  • Browsers and HTTP clients may automatically retry idempotent requests after a dropped connection, but should not retry a POST.
  • Crawlers and link prefetchers follow links with GET. If GET deletes data, a crawler can wipe your database.
  • CORS sends a preflight for methods other than GET, HEAD, and POST (and for some headers and content types). See CORS.

Using the right method makes your API predictable and safe to use.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub uses PUT for "make it so" operations and PATCH for updates. Starring a repository is PUT /user/starred/{owner}/{repo}: the client names the exact resource, repeating it is harmless, and GitHub's docs note you must send Content-Length: 0 because there is no body. Changing a repository's settings is PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}, which returns 422 if validation fails.
  • Stripe uses POST for both create and update. Updating a customer is POST /v1/customers/:id, and "any parameters not provided are left unchanged", which is partial-update (PATCH-like) behavior on POST. To make those non-idempotent requests safe to retry, Stripe accepts idempotency keys on all POST requests and says not to send them with GET and DELETE, which are already idempotent.
  • Kubernetes supports several PATCH formats. kubectl patch takes a --type of json (JSON Patch, RFC 6902), merge (JSON Merge Patch), or strategic (a Kubernetes-specific strategic merge patch), which is a real example of the patch-format choice described below.

docs.title: Properties every method has
docs.text:
• Safe: the method is read-only in intent. The client does not request any change to server state. Logging or counting views is fine; changing data the client asked about is not.
  • Idempotent: sending the same request once or ten times leaves the server in the same intended state. The responses can differ (a second DELETE may return 404), but the end state is the same. Every safe method is also idempotent.
  • Cacheable: a response to this method may be stored and reused for later requests.
Method Purpose Safe Idempotent Cacheable Request body Response body GET Read a representation Yes Yes Yes No defined meaning; avoid Yes HEAD Same as GET but headers only Yes Yes Yes No defined meaning; avoid No POST Process data / create a subordinate resource / trigger an action No No Only with explicit freshness info; rare in practice Yes Yes PUT Create or fully replace the resource at this URL No Yes No Yes Optional PATCH Partially modify a resource No Not by definition No Yes Optional DELETE Remove the resource No Yes No No defined meaning; avoid Optional OPTIONS Ask which methods/features the target supports; CORS preflight Yes Yes No Rare Optional TRACE Echo the request back for debugging Yes Yes No No Yes (the echoed request) CONNECT Open a tunnel through a proxy (e.g. for HTTPS) No No No No n/a

docs.title: GET
docs.text:
Retrieves a representation of a resource. It must not change server state in a way the client is responsible for.

  • Typical responses: 200 OK with the resource, 304 Not Modified for a conditional request, 404 Not Found.
  • Parameters go in the path (/orders/42) and query string (/orders?status=paid&page=2), never in a body.
  • Responses can be cached by browsers, CDNs, and proxies.
GET /api/orders/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.shop.example
Accept: application/json

docs.title: HEAD
docs.text: Identical to GET, except the server returns only the status line and headers, no body. Clients use it to check whether a resource exists, read its size (Content-Length), or check ETag/Last-Modified without downloading it. Express answers HEAD automatically for routes defined with app.get().

docs.title: POST
docs.text:
Asks the server to process the enclosed data according to the resource's own rules. It is the most general method:

  • Create a new resource in a collection: POST /api/orders.
  • Trigger an action that does not map to a resource: POST /api/orders/42/refund.
  • Submit a form, upload a file, run a search with a large query.

Typical responses: 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource, 200 OK with a result, 202 Accepted if processing continues in the background, 400/422 for invalid input.

POST is not idempotent: sending it twice can create two orders or charge a card twice. Protect important POST endpoints with idempotency keys. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

docs.title: PUT
docs.text:
Creates the resource at the given URL, or replaces it entirely with the request body. The body is the full new representation; any field you leave out is gone (or reset to its default).

  • Typical responses: 201 Created if it did not exist, 200 OK (with body) or 204 No Content if it was replaced.
  • Idempotent: putting the same document ten times leaves the same result.
  • The client chooses the URL, so PUT suits resources whose ID the client knows, such as PUT /api/users/42/avatar or PUT /api/settings/theme.

docs.title: PATCH
docs.text:
Applies a partial modification. Defined in RFC 5789, not in the core HTTP specification. The body is a set of changes, and its format is given by the Content-Type.

  • Typical responses: 200 OK with the updated resource, 204 No Content, 409 Conflict, 415 Unsupported Media Type for an unknown patch format, 422 if the patch cannot be applied.
  • Not idempotent by definition, because some patch operations are not (for example "append to this array" or "increment by 1"). A patch that only sets fields to fixed values is idempotent in practice.
  • Servers can advertise accepted patch formats with the Accept-Patch response header.

docs.title: DELETE
docs.text:
Removes the resource at the URL.

  • Typical responses: 204 No Content (most common), 200 OK with a status body, 202 Accepted if deletion is queued, 404 Not Found.
  • Idempotent: after the first successful delete the resource is gone; later deletes leave it gone. Whether the second call returns 204 or 404 is an API design choice; document it.
  • A request body has no defined meaning; some servers and proxies drop it. Put identifiers in the URL.

docs.title: OPTIONS
docs.text: Asks what communication options the target supports. The server can reply with an Allow header listing the methods. Browsers send OPTIONS as a CORS preflight before many cross-origin requests; see CORS. Express answers OPTIONS automatically with an Allow header if you do not define a handler.

docs.title: TRACE
docs.text: Asks the server to echo back the request it received, so a client can see what proxies changed. It can expose sensitive headers (the old cross-site tracing attack), so most servers disable it. You will rarely use it.

docs.title: CONNECT
docs.text: Asks a proxy to open a raw TCP tunnel to another host, which is how HTTPS traffic passes through a forward proxy (CONNECT api.example.com:443). Application APIs do not implement it.

docs.title: PUT vs PATCH vs POST
docs.text:
Take a user resource:

{ "id": 42, "name": "Ana", "email": "ana@example.com", "role": "editor" }
Request Body Result PUT /users/42 {"name": "Ana Li", "email": "ana@example.com", "role": "editor"} Whole resource replaced; any field not sent is removed or reset PUT /users/42 {"name": "Ana Li"} Email and role are now missing or defaulted (a common bug) PATCH /users/42 {"name": "Ana Li"} Only the name changes POST /users {"name": "Ben", "email": "ben@example.com"} New user created; server picks the ID POST /users/42/promote (empty) An action; not a plain field update

Rules of thumb:

  • Use POST to create when the server assigns the ID, and for actions.
  • Use PUT when the client sends the complete resource, or creates it at a URL it chooses.
  • Use PATCH for partial updates (the most common kind of update in real APIs).

docs.title: JSON Merge Patch vs JSON Patch
docs.text:
Two standard formats describe the changes in a PATCH body.

JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396, Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json) sends an object that looks like the resource. Present fields are set, fields set to null are removed, and missing fields are untouched.

{ "name": "Ana Li", "nickname": null }

It is simple and readable, but it cannot set a field to null (null means "remove"), and arrays are replaced wholesale, not edited.

JSON Patch (RFC 6902, Content-Type: application/json-patch+json) sends an ordered list of operations: add, remove, replace, move, copy, and test.

[
  { "op": "test", "path": "/version", "value": 7 },
  { "op": "replace", "path": "/name", "value": "Ana Li" },
  { "op": "add", "path": "/tags/-", "value": "vip" },
  { "op": "remove", "path": "/nickname" }
]

It can edit arrays precisely and test makes the patch fail if the document changed, but it is more verbose and harder to validate. The patch is applied atomically: if one operation fails, none apply.

Many APIs simply accept application/json with merge-style semantics. That is fine as long as the behavior for null and arrays is documented.

docs.title: Why GET must never change state
docs.text: GET requests are made by things you do not control: browser prefetching, link previews in chat apps, search crawlers, antivirus link scanners, and caches replaying responses. If GET /api/emails/9/delete deletes an email, a link preview can delete it. Change state only with POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE.

docs.title: GET with a body: don't
docs.text: RFC 9110 says content in a GET request has no generally defined meaning. Many proxies, CDNs, and client libraries (including browser fetch()) drop the body or reject the request. If a search query is too large for a URL, use POST /search (an action) instead.

docs.title: Mapping CRUD to methods
docs.text: Operation Method and path Success status List GET /api/articles 200 Read one GET /api/articles/:id 200 Create POST /api/articles 201 + Location Replace PUT /api/articles/:id 200 or 204 (or 201 if created) Update part PATCH /api/articles/:id 200 or 204 Delete DELETE /api/articles/:id 204

docs.title: Idempotency in practice
docs.text:
Request Repeat 3 times Idempotent? GET /accounts/7 Same read three times Yes PUT /accounts/7/email with {"email":"a@b.com"} Email is a@b.com Yes DELETE /carts/7/items/3 Item 3 is gone Yes PATCH /accounts/7 with {"email":"a@b.com"} Same state Yes, in practice PATCH /accounts/7 with {"op":"increment","field":"credits"} Credits +3 No POST /payments with {"amount":50} Three payments No (use an idempotency key)

Idempotency matters because networks fail mid-request. If a client does not know whether a request arrived, it can safely retry an idempotent one.

docs.title: 405 Method Not Allowed and the Allow header
docs.text:
If the resource exists but does not support the method, return 405 Method Not Allowed. RFC 9110 requires the response to include an Allow header listing the supported methods.

HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Allow: GET, HEAD, PATCH
Content-Type: application/problem+json

Compare with 501 Not Implemented, which means the server does not recognize or support the method for any resource.

docs.title: Method override, and why to avoid it
docs.text:
Old HTML forms can only send GET and POST, and some old proxies blocked other methods. The workaround was to send POST with a hidden field or a header such as X-HTTP-Method-Override: DELETE. Avoid it in new APIs:

  • It hides the real operation from caches, logs, and security tools.
  • It can let an attacker turn a POST into a DELETE past a filter that checks only the method.
  • fetch() and every modern client support all methods directly.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• GET: use for every read, including searches that fit in a URL. Do not use it for anything that changes state, or for data that must not end up in logs and browser history (passwords, tokens).
  • POST: use to create when the server picks the ID, for actions that are not plain field updates, and for searches too large for a URL. Avoid it for plain reads (you lose caching) and protect it with idempotency keys when duplicates would hurt.
  • PUT: use when the client sends the complete resource or creates it at a URL it chooses, and when you want retries to be safe. Avoid it for partial updates; missing fields get wiped.
  • PATCH: use for partial updates, which most edit forms are. Avoid it when clients cannot agree on a documented patch format, and remember it is not idempotent by definition.
  • DELETE: use to remove the resource at the URL. Avoid request bodies; put identifiers in the path.
You need to... Use Instead of Why Read data GET POST /getX Cacheable, safe to retry, bookmarkable Create with a server-generated ID POST /items PUT /items The client does not know the new URL Create or replace at a known URL PUT /items/42 POST Idempotent; retries are harmless Change a few fields PATCH /items/42 PUT with a partial body PUT replaces the whole resource Trigger an action (refund, publish) POST /items/42/refund PATCH with an action field Actions have side effects beyond the fields Remove DELETE /items/42 POST /items/42/delete or GET .../delete Idempotent, and GET can be triggered by crawlers

docs.title: A full set of routes in Express
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const articles = new Map(); // stand-in for a database
let nextId = 1;

app.get("/api/articles", (req, res) => {
  res.json([...articles.values()]);
});

app.get("/api/articles/:id", (req, res) => {
  const article = articles.get(req.params.id);
  if (!article) return res.sendStatus(404);
  res.json(article);
});

app.post("/api/articles", (req, res) => {
  const id = String(nextId++);
  const article = { id, title: req.body.title, body: req.body.body ?? "" };
  articles.set(id, article);
  res.status(201).location(`/api/articles/${id}`).json(article);
});

// PUT: full replacement; fields not sent are reset
app.put("/api/articles/:id", (req, res) => {
  const existed = articles.has(req.params.id);
  const article = { id: req.params.id, title: req.body.title, body: req.body.body ?? "" };
  articles.set(req.params.id, article);
  res.status(existed ? 200 : 201).json(article);
});

// PATCH: only the fields sent change
app.patch("/api/articles/:id", (req, res) => {
  const article = articles.get(req.params.id);
  if (!article) return res.sendStatus(404);
  const { title, body } = req.body;
  if (title !== undefined) article.title = title;
  if (body !== undefined) article.body = body;
  res.json(article);
});

app.delete("/api/articles/:id", (req, res) => {
  articles.delete(req.params.id); // deleting twice is harmless
  res.sendStatus(204);
});

// Registered after the real routes, so it only sees other methods.
// HEAD is already answered by the GET route above.
app.all("/api/articles", (req, res) => {
  res.set("Allow", "GET, HEAD, POST, OPTIONS");
  if (req.method === "OPTIONS") return res.sendStatus(204);
  res.sendStatus(405); // PUT, PATCH, DELETE on the collection
});

app.listen(3000);

Validation is left out to keep the method behavior visible. See request validation.

docs.title: Try them with curl
docs.text:
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/articles \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Hello"}'

curl -i -X PATCH http://localhost:3000/api/articles/1 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"body":"First post"}'

curl -I http://localhost:3000/api/articles/1     # HEAD: headers only
curl -i -X DELETE http://localhost:3000/api/articles/1
curl -i -X PUT http://localhost:3000/api/articles  # 405 with Allow

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Choose methods by their semantics, not by convenience.
  • Keep GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS free of side effects.
  • Return 201 Created with a Location header when POST creates something.
  • Prefer PATCH for partial updates; document how null and arrays behave.
  • Protect non-idempotent operations (payments, orders) with idempotency keys.
  • Return 405 with an Allow header for unsupported methods on a known resource.
  • Put identifiers in the path, filters in the query string, and data in the body.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Data disappears with nobody clicking "delete". Detect: access logs show GET requests to an action URL (such as /unsubscribe/... or /items/9/delete) from crawler or link-preview user agents just before the change. Cause: a state-changing GET. Fix: make the action a POST (a confirmation page can link to a form that posts).
  • Duplicate orders or charges after network blips. Detect: pairs of identical POSTs seconds apart from the same client, often after a timeout in the client logs. Cause: the client or a library retried a non-idempotent POST. Fix: require an Idempotency-Key and return the stored result for repeats, as Stripe does.
  • Fields wiped by an "update". Detect: audit logs show fields set to null or defaults right after a PUT from a client that only edits some fields. Cause: partial bodies sent with PUT. Fix: switch the client to PATCH, or reject PUT bodies that are missing required fields with 400/422.
  • A DELETE or GET body arrives empty in production only. Detect: the same request works locally but fails behind the CDN or proxy. Cause: some intermediaries drop bodies on methods where the body has no defined meaning. Fix: move the data into the path or query string, or use POST for a bulk action.
  • Clients get 404 and give up on a URL that exists. Detect: 404s for known paths with an unusual method in access logs. Cause: unsupported methods fall through to the "not found" handler. Fix: return 405 with an Allow header so clients see what is supported.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Method (verb): the action requested on a resource.
  • Safe method: a method that does not request a change to server state.
  • Idempotent method: repeating the request has the same intended effect as sending it once.
  • Cacheable: responses may be stored and reused.
  • Representation: the data sent for a resource, such as a JSON document.
  • Preflight: a browser's OPTIONS request that checks CORS permission before the real request.
  • JSON Merge Patch: a patch format that looks like a partial resource.
  • JSON Patch: a patch format made of ordered operations.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using GET for actions such as /logout or /delete, which crawlers and prefetchers can trigger.
  • Treating PUT as a partial update and accidentally wiping fields the client did not send.
  • "Idempotent means the same response every time." It means the same server state; the status code can differ.
  • Using POST for everything and losing caching, safe retries, and clarity.
  • Sending a body with GET or DELETE and having proxies silently drop it.
  • Returning 404 for a wrong method instead of 405 with Allow.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Define safe, idempotent, and cacheable, and give one method that is each.
  2. Why is DELETE idempotent even though the second call may return 404?
  3. A client sends PUT /users/42 with only {"name": "Ana"}. What should happen to the other fields, and why is that a common bug?
  4. When would you choose JSON Patch over JSON Merge Patch?
  5. Why is it dangerous for a GET endpoint to delete data?
  6. What must a 405 response include?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: HTTP request methods documents every method with examples.
  • RFC 9110: Section 9, Methods defines method semantics, safety, and idempotency.
  • RFC 5789: PATCH Method for HTTP.
  • RFC 7396: JSON Merge Patch.
  • RFC 6902: JSON Patch.

docs.title: HTTP Status Codes
docs.text: Every HTTP response starts with a three-digit status code that summarizes the outcome: success, redirect, client mistake, or server failure. Clients, browsers, caches, monitoring tools, and retry logic all make decisions based on this number, so choosing the right code is part of designing an API.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Clients branch on it. Frontend code, mobile apps, and SDKs decide whether to show data, ask the user to log in, retry, or display an error based on the status code.
  • Infrastructure acts on it. Browsers follow 3xx redirects, caches store 200 and revalidate with 304, load balancers mark instances unhealthy on 5xx, and retry libraries retry 503 but not 400.
  • Monitoring depends on it. Error-rate dashboards and alerts count 5xx responses. Returning 200 for failures hides outages.
  • It is the first debugging clue. 401 points to authentication, 403 to permissions, 502 to a proxy that could not reach your app.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub returns 404 instead of 403 for private resources. Its REST API troubleshooting guide says an unauthenticated request for a private resource gets 404 Not Found "instead of a 403 Forbidden response to avoid confirming the existence of private repositories". The same guide says requests that cannot be processed may get 422 Unprocessable Entity with a "Validation Failed" message and an errors property.
  • GitHub signals rate limits with 403 or 429. When you exceed the primary rate limit, you receive a 403 or 429 response and x-ratelimit-remaining is 0; clients should wait until the time in x-ratelimit-reset.
  • Stripe documents a status code summary and gives 402 a meaning. Stripe's error reference uses 402 Request Failed for "the parameters were valid but the request failed", 409 Conflict for a request that conflicts with another (such as reusing an idempotency key), 424 for a failure in a dependency outside Stripe, and 429 with a recommendation to use exponential backoff. It lists a failed charge or a declined card among its 4xx errors.
  • Proxies and CDNs add their own codes. Cloudflare returns non-standard 52x codes such as 521 (web server is down) and 524 (a timeout occurred). Seeing one tells you the CDN, not your application, produced the response.

docs.title: The five classes
docs.text:
The first digit defines the class. The other two digits refine it.

Class Meaning Who is "at fault" Typical client reaction 1xx Informational Interim response; the final response follows Nobody Keep waiting 2xx Successful The request was received, understood, and accepted Nobody Use the response 3xx Redirection The client must take another step, usually follow a new URL Nobody Follow Location or use the cache 4xx Client error The request is wrong or not allowed The client Fix the request; usually do not retry as-is 5xx Server error The server failed to handle a valid request The server Maybe retry later

A client that receives a code it does not recognize treats it as the x00 code of its class. An unknown 479 is handled like 400, and an unknown 531 like 500. That rule is why inventing private codes is pointless: clients will not know what they mean.

The text after the number (the reason phrase, such as Not Found) is only for humans. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 do not even send it. Clients must rely on the number.

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
^^^^^^^^ ^^^ ^^^^^^^^^
version  code reason phrase (informational only)

In Express you set the code with res.status(code) before sending, or send it alone with res.sendStatus(code), which uses the reason phrase as the body. See the response object.

docs.title: 1xx: Informational
docs.text: Interim responses sent before the final one. Application code rarely sends them directly; servers and proxies handle them.

docs.title: 100 Continue
docs.text:
• Meaning: "Your headers look fine; go ahead and send the body."
  • When: a client about to upload a large body sends Expect: 100-continue and waits. The server answers 100 to proceed, or a final error (such as 401 or 413) so the client does not waste bandwidth uploading.
  • Example: a 2 GB upload is rejected with 413 before any of it is sent.
  • Related headers: Expect (request).

docs.title: 101 Switching Protocols
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server agrees to switch to the protocol named in the client's Upgrade header.
  • When: opening a WebSocket. The client sends Upgrade: websocket, and the server replies 101; after that the connection speaks WebSocket, not HTTP. See real-time communication.
  • Related headers: Upgrade, Connection: Upgrade.

docs.title: 103 Early Hints
docs.text:
• Meaning: "While I prepare the real response, start loading these."
  • When: a server or CDN sends Link headers for critical CSS or fonts early, so the browser can preload them while the page is still being generated.
  • Related headers: Link: </app.css>; rel=preload; as=style.

docs.title: 200 OK
docs.text:
• Meaning: the request succeeded. The body depends on the method: the resource for GET, the result of the action for POST, the updated resource for PATCH/PUT.
  • When: the default for a successful read or an update that returns data.
  • Example: GET /api/orders/42 returns the order as JSON.
  • Express: res.json(order) (200 is the default).

docs.title: 201 Created
docs.text:
• Meaning: a new resource was created.
  • When: after POST to a collection, or PUT to a URL that did not exist yet.
  • Example: POST /api/orders creates order ord_901.
  • Related headers: Location should point to the new resource. The body usually contains it so the client does not need another request.
  • Express: res.status(201).location(/api/orders/${order.id}).json(order)

docs.title: 202 Accepted
docs.text:
• Meaning: the request was accepted for processing, but the work is not finished (and might still fail).
  • When: long-running or queued work: video encoding, report generation, bulk imports, sending a large email campaign.
  • Example: POST /api/reports returns 202 with a link to check status.
  • Related headers: Location (or a body field) pointing to a status resource such as /api/reports/jobs/77.
  • Express: res.status(202).location(/api/jobs/${job.id}).json({ jobId: job.id, status: "queued" })

docs.title: 203 Non-Authoritative Information
docs.text: • Meaning: the request succeeded, but a transforming proxy modified the content from what the origin sent. Rarely used; your API should not send it.

docs.title: 204 No Content
docs.text:
• Meaning: success, and there is intentionally no body.
  • When: DELETE succeeded; PUT/PATCH succeeded and you choose not to return the resource; a "fire and forget" action such as marking a notification as read.
  • Rules: a 204 response cannot have a body. Do not send JSON with it.
  • Express: res.sendStatus(204) or res.status(204).end().

docs.title: 206 Partial Content
docs.text:
• Meaning: the response contains only the byte range(s) the client asked for.
  • When: resuming a download, video players seeking within a file, parallel downloads.
  • Related headers: request Range: bytes=0-1048575; response Content-Range: bytes 0-1048575/52428800 and Accept-Ranges: bytes.
  • Express: res.sendFile() and express.static handle range requests for you.

docs.title: 3xx: Redirection
docs.text:
The key differences between redirect codes are permanent vs temporary and whether the method and body are preserved.

Code Permanent? Method preserved? Typical use 301 Yes Not guaranteed (clients may change POST to GET) Old URL moved forever (pages, GET) 302 No Not guaranteed Temporary redirect, mostly for GET 303 No No: becomes GET (or HEAD) After a form POST, send the user to a result page 307 No Yes Temporary redirect that must keep POST and body 308 Yes Yes Permanent move of an API endpoint that receives POST

docs.title: 300 Multiple Choices
docs.text: • Meaning: several representations are available and the client may choose. Rarely used in practice.

docs.title: 301 Moved Permanently
docs.text:
• Meaning: the resource has a new permanent URL.
  • When: a page or domain moved for good (http:// to https://, /blog/old-slug to /blog/new-slug). Search engines transfer ranking to the new URL, and browsers cache the redirect.
  • Related headers: Location.
  • Caution: for historical reasons clients may change a POST into a GET when following it. Use 308 when the method must be kept. Because browsers cache 301 aggressively, a mistaken 301 is hard to undo.
  • Express: res.redirect(301, "https://new.example.com/path")

docs.title: 302 Found
docs.text:
• Meaning: the resource is temporarily at another URL; keep using the original URL in future.
  • When: temporary redirects of GET requests, such as sending a logged-out user to /login.
  • Related headers: Location.
  • Caution: like 301, clients may switch POST to GET. Use 303 or 307 to be explicit.
  • Express: res.redirect("/login") sends 302 by default.

docs.title: 303 See Other
docs.text:
• Meaning: "The result is at another URL; fetch it with GET."
  • When: the Post/Redirect/Get pattern: after a form POST creates an order, redirect to /orders/901 so refreshing the page does not resubmit the form.
  • Related headers: Location.
  • Express: res.redirect(303,/orders/${order.id})

docs.title: 304 Not Modified
docs.text:
• Meaning: "The copy you already have is still current; use it."
  • When: answering a conditional GET whose If-None-Match matches the current ETag, or whose If-Modified-Since is not older than the last change.
  • Rules: no body. The client reuses its cached copy, which saves bandwidth and time.
  • Related headers: request If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since; response ETag, Cache-Control, Last-Modified.
  • Express: sends 304 automatically for res.send()/res.json() when the generated ETag matches. See HTTP headers.

docs.title: 307 Temporary Redirect
docs.text:
• Meaning: temporary redirect that must keep the original method and body.
  • When: temporarily routing a POST /api/upload to another server during maintenance; HSTS upgrades in browsers appear as an internal 307.
  • Related headers: Location.
  • Express: res.redirect(307, "https://backup.example.com/api/upload")

docs.title: 308 Permanent Redirect
docs.text:
• Meaning: permanent redirect that must keep the method and body.
  • When: an API endpoint moved permanently and clients still POST or PUT to the old URL.
  • Related headers: Location.
  • Express: res.redirect(308, "/api/v2/orders")

docs.title: 4xx: Client errors
docs.text: The request has a problem the client must fix. Retrying the same request unchanged will normally fail again (exceptions: 408, 425, 429). Include a body that explains what went wrong, ideally in one consistent format such as RFC 9457 problem details.

docs.title: 400 Bad Request
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server cannot or will not process the request because of a client error: malformed syntax, invalid framing, or invalid input.
  • When: malformed JSON, a missing required field, a wrong type ("quantity": "lots"), an invalid query parameter. Many APIs use 400 for all validation errors.
  • Example: POST /api/orders with body {"quantity": -3}.
  • Express: res.status(400).json({ title: "Invalid request", errors: [{ field: "quantity", message: "must be at least 1" }] })
  • Note: Express's JSON parser produces a 400 automatically for malformed JSON. See body parsing.

docs.title: 401 Unauthorized
docs.text:
• Meaning: despite the name, it means unauthenticated: no valid credentials were provided. "Who are you?"
  • When: missing token, expired token, invalid signature, no session cookie.
  • Related headers: the response must include WWW-Authenticate describing how to authenticate, for example WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="api", error="invalid_token".
  • Client reaction: refresh the token or send the user to log in.
  • Express: res.status(401).set("WWW-Authenticate", 'Bearer realm="api"').json({ title: "Authentication required" })

docs.title: 402 Payment Required
docs.text:
• Meaning: reserved by the HTTP specification for future use, with no standard semantics.
  • When: some APIs use it when a subscription has lapsed or a quota needs payment. If you use it, document it clearly.

docs.title: 403 Forbidden
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server understood the request and knows who the caller is (or does not need to), but refuses it. "I know who you are; you can't do this."
  • When: a regular user calls an admin endpoint; a user tries to edit another user's document; an IP is blocked; a CSRF token check fails.
  • Client reaction: do not retry with the same credentials; logging in again will not help.
  • Express: res.status(403).json({ title: "You do not have permission to delete this project" })

docs.title: 404 Not Found
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server has no current representation for the target URL, or will not reveal that one exists.
  • When: unknown route, or GET /api/orders/999 where order 999 does not exist.
  • Also used: instead of 403 to avoid revealing that a private resource exists (see "403 vs 404" below).
  • Express: return res.status(404).json({ title: "Order not found" }), and a final catch-all handler for unknown routes.

docs.title: 405 Method Not Allowed
docs.text:
• Meaning: the resource exists but does not support this method.
  • When: DELETE /api/orders on a collection that cannot be deleted.
  • Related headers: the response must include Allow, for example Allow: GET, POST.
  • Express: res.set("Allow", "GET, POST").sendStatus(405)

docs.title: 406 Not Acceptable
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server cannot produce a representation matching the client's Accept headers.
  • When: the client sends Accept: application/xml to a JSON-only API. Many APIs ignore Accept and return JSON anyway, which is allowed.
  • Express: res.format() sends 406 when nothing matches. See HTTP headers.

docs.title: 407 Proxy Authentication Required
docs.text: • Meaning: like 401, but the client must authenticate with a proxy between it and the server. Comes with Proxy-Authenticate. Your API will not send it.

docs.title: 408 Request Timeout
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server gave up waiting for the client to finish sending the request.
  • When: a client opened a connection but sent headers or the body too slowly. Usually sent by the server or proxy, not application code.
  • Related headers: typically Connection: close. Clients may retry.
  • Node.js: controlled by server.requestTimeout and server.headersTimeout. See the http module.

docs.title: 409 Conflict
docs.text:
• Meaning: the request conflicts with the current state of the resource.
  • When: creating a user whose email already exists; updating a record that someone else changed (version mismatch); trying to cancel an order that has already shipped.
  • Body: explain the conflict so the client can resolve it.
  • Express: res.status(409).json({ title: "Email already registered" })

docs.title: 410 Gone
docs.text:
• Meaning: the resource existed but has been removed permanently, and no forwarding address is known.
  • When: a deleted promotion page, a retired API version, a deliberately expired share link. Unlike 404, it tells clients and search engines to stop asking.
  • Express: res.status(410).json({ title: "API v1 was retired. Use /api/v2." })

docs.title: 411 Length Required
docs.text: • Meaning: the server refuses a request body without a Content-Length header. Rare with modern clients and chunked transfer.

docs.title: 412 Precondition Failed
docs.text:
• Meaning: a condition in the request headers evaluated to false.
  • When: optimistic concurrency. The client sends If-Match: "v7" with a PUT, but the resource is now at "v8" because someone else edited it. The update is rejected instead of silently overwriting their change.
  • Related headers: If-Match, If-Unmodified-Since, ETag.
