  • Express: if (req.get("If-Match") !== currentEtag) return res.sendStatus(412);
  • See concurrency and race conditions.

docs.title: 413 Content Too Large
docs.text:
• Meaning: the request body is larger than the server will accept. (Older name: Payload Too Large.)
  • When: an upload over the size limit, a JSON body over the parser limit.
  • Related headers: Retry-After if the condition is temporary.
  • Express: express.json({ limit: "100kb" }) produces 413 for larger bodies automatically.

docs.title: 414 URI Too Long
docs.text:
• Meaning: the URL is longer than the server will process.
  • When: a client stuffs huge filters or data into the query string. The fix is usually to move the data into a POST body.

docs.title: 415 Unsupported Media Type
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server will not accept the body's format.
  • When: the client sends Content-Type: text/xml to a JSON endpoint, or sends a PATCH in a patch format you do not support.
  • Related headers: Accept-Patch (for PATCH) or a description of accepted types in the body; Accept-Encoding if the problem is the content encoding.
  • Express: if (!req.is("application/json")) return res.sendStatus(415);

docs.title: 416 Range Not Satisfiable
docs.text:
• Meaning: the requested byte range is outside the resource.
  • When: Range: bytes=900000- on a 500 KB file.
  • Related headers: Content-Range: bytes */512000 tells the client the real size.

docs.title: 417 Expectation Failed
docs.text: • Meaning: the server cannot meet the request's Expect header (for example an unsupported Expect value). Rare.

docs.title: 418 I'm a teapot
docs.text: • Meaning: an April Fools' joke from RFC 2324 (the "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol"). RFC 9110 lists it as "(Unused)" and reserves it in the IANA registry, so it cannot currently be assigned to anything else. Some sites return it for fun or to brush off bots. Never use it in a real API.

docs.title: 421 Misdirected Request
docs.text: • Meaning: the request reached a server that is not configured to answer for that host. Happens with HTTP/2 connection reuse across host names sharing a certificate. Infrastructure-level; clients retry on a new connection.

docs.title: 422 Unprocessable Content
docs.text:
• Meaning: the body is syntactically correct (valid JSON, correct content type) but semantically invalid, so the server cannot process it. (Older name: Unprocessable Entity.)
  • When: valid JSON whose values break business rules: an end date before the start date, a referenced product that does not exist, a password that fails the policy.
  • Express: res.status(422).json({ title: "Validation failed", errors: [{ field: "endDate", message: "must be after startDate" }] })
  • See "400 vs 422" below.

docs.title: 423 Locked
docs.text:
• Meaning: the resource is locked. From WebDAV.
  • When: a document is checked out by another user in a collaborative editor that uses explicit locks.

docs.title: 424 Failed Dependency
docs.text: • Meaning: the request failed because a previous request it depended on failed. From WebDAV; uncommon in general APIs.

docs.title: 425 Too Early
docs.text: • Meaning: the server will not risk processing a request sent as TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT), because early data can be replayed. The client retries after the handshake completes. Infrastructure-level.

docs.title: 426 Upgrade Required
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server refuses the request with the current protocol, but would accept it after the client upgrades.
  • Related headers: Upgrade lists the required protocol(s).

docs.title: 428 Precondition Required
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server requires the request to be conditional.
  • When: an API that refuses PUT/PATCH/DELETE without If-Match, to prevent "lost update" problems where two clients overwrite each other.
  • Express: if (!req.get("If-Match")) return res.sendStatus(428);

docs.title: 429 Too Many Requests
docs.text:
• Meaning: the client sent too many requests in a given time (rate limiting).
  • When: a user exceeds 100 requests per minute; too many login attempts.
  • Related headers: Retry-After tells the client how long to wait (in seconds or as a date). Many APIs also send rate-limit headers showing the limit, remaining requests, and reset time.
  • Client reaction: wait and retry with backoff.
  • Express: res.status(429).set("Retry-After", "30").json({ title: "Too many requests" })
  • See rate limiting and throttling.

docs.title: 431 Request Header Fields Too Large
docs.text:
• Meaning: the headers (all together, or one of them) are too large.
  • When: a client sends a huge cookie jar or a giant token. Node.js rejects headers over its limit (16 KB by default) with 431.
  • Fix: shrink cookies and tokens rather than raising the limit.

docs.title: 451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server is legally required to deny access, for example because of a court order or sanctions.
  • Related headers: a Link header with rel="blocked-by" can identify who requires the block. The number refers to the novel Fahrenheit 451.

docs.title: 5xx: Server errors
docs.text: The server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request. These count against your error rate and should trigger investigation. Never put stack traces or internal details in the response body.

docs.title: 500 Internal Server Error
docs.text:
• Meaning: a generic, unexpected failure on the server.
  • When: an unhandled exception, a bug, a failed dependency you did not map to a more specific code.
  • Body: a generic message plus a request ID for support, never the stack trace.
  • Express: the default error handler sends 500 for errors without a status. See error handling in Express.

docs.title: 501 Not Implemented
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server does not support the functionality needed, such as a method it does not recognize at all.
  • When: a client sends a method your server does not implement for any resource. Some APIs use it for planned endpoints that do not exist yet.
  • Compare: 405 means the method is known but not allowed on this resource.

docs.title: 502 Bad Gateway
docs.text:
• Meaning: a server acting as a gateway or proxy received an invalid response from the upstream server.
  • When: Nginx or a load balancer forwards to your app, and your app has crashed, closed the connection, or returned garbage. Also when your own backend calls another service that fails, and you choose to report it.
  • Debugging: check whether the app process is running and whether keep-alive timeouts are mismatched. See the request lifecycle.

docs.title: 503 Service Unavailable
docs.text:
• Meaning: the server is temporarily unable to handle the request: overloaded, in maintenance, or has no healthy instances.
  • When: planned maintenance, shedding load during a spike, a readiness check failing during startup or shutdown, a required dependency (the database) being down.
  • Related headers: Retry-After with seconds or a date.
  • Express: res.status(503).set("Retry-After", "120").json({ title: "Down for maintenance" })

docs.title: 504 Gateway Timeout
docs.text:
• Meaning: a gateway or proxy did not get a response from the upstream server in time.
  • When: your handler takes 90 seconds and the load balancer's timeout is
  • Or your app calls a payment API that does not answer within your timeout.
  • Fix: speed up the slow work, move it to a background job (202), or adjust timeouts consistently.

docs.title: 505 HTTP Version Not Supported
docs.text: • Meaning: the server does not support the HTTP version used in the request. Rare.

docs.title: 507 Insufficient Storage
docs.text: • Meaning: the server cannot store what is needed to complete the request. From WebDAV. Some storage APIs use it when a disk or quota is full.

docs.title: 508 Loop Detected
docs.text: • Meaning: the server detected an infinite loop while processing the request. From WebDAV; rare elsewhere.

docs.title: 511 Network Authentication Required
docs.text: • Meaning: the client must authenticate to gain network access. Sent by captive portals (hotel or airport Wi-Fi login pages), not by origin servers.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a specific standard code when:

  • Clients need to react differently: 401 (log in again) versus 403 (show "access denied") versus 429 (wait and retry).
  • A companion header carries the details: Location with 201, Allow with 405, Retry-After with 429 and 503.
  • Monitoring must separate client mistakes (4xx) from server faults (5xx).

Fall back to the class's general code (400, 500) when no specific code fits; clients already treat unknown codes that way.

Do not:

  • Return 200 with an error in the body (except where the protocol defines it, such as GraphQL execution errors).
  • Invent private codes such as 299 or 461; clients cannot know them.
  • Use WebDAV or infrastructure codes (423, 425, 508) in a JSON API without a strong reason and clear documentation.
Approach Clients can branch on it Monitoring sees failures Caches and proxies behave correctly Verdict Precise standard code + error body Yes Yes Yes Use this Generic 400/500 for everything Partly Partly Yes Acceptable fallback 200 + {"success": false} Only by parsing the body No No (errors may be cached) Avoid Private non-standard codes No (treated as x00) Partly Unpredictable Avoid

docs.title: Choosing codes in one Express resource
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json({ limit: "100kb" })); // larger bodies -> 413 automatically

const users = new Map([["1", { id: "1", email: "ana@example.com", version: 1 }]]);

app.post("/api/users", (req, res) => {
  const { email } = req.body ?? {};
  if (typeof email !== "string") {
    return res.status(400).json({ title: "email is required" }); // malformed input
  }
  if (!email.includes("@")) {
    return res.status(422).json({ title: "email is not valid" }); // semantic problem
  }
  if ([...users.values()].some((u) => u.email === email)) {
    return res.status(409).json({ title: "email already registered" }); // state conflict
  }
  const user = { id: String(users.size + 1), email, version: 1 };
  users.set(user.id, user);
  res.status(201).location(`/api/users/${user.id}`).json(user);
});

app.get("/api/users/:id", (req, res) => {
  const user = users.get(req.params.id);
  if (!user) return res.status(404).json({ title: "user not found" });
  res.set("ETag", `"${user.version}"`).json(user); // clients send this back in If-Match
});

app.put("/api/users/:id", (req, res) => {
  const user = users.get(req.params.id);
  if (!user) return res.status(404).json({ title: "user not found" });
  const ifMatch = req.get("If-Match");
  if (!ifMatch) return res.sendStatus(428); // require conditional updates
  if (ifMatch !== `"${user.version}"`) return res.sendStatus(412); // stale version
  Object.assign(user, { email: req.body.email, version: user.version + 1 });
  res.set("ETag", `"${user.version}"`).json(user);
});

app.delete("/api/users/:id", (req, res) => {
  users.delete(req.params.id);
  res.sendStatus(204);
});

// Unknown routes
app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ title: "route not found" }));

// Unexpected errors
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  console.error(err);
  res.status(err.status ?? 500).json({ title: "Something went wrong" });
});

app.listen(3000);

docs.title: Checking codes with curl
docs.text:
curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/users/99            # 404
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{bad json'  # 400 from the parser
curl -i -X PUT http://localhost:3000/api/users/1 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"email":"x@y.z"}'   # 428

docs.title: Decision guide: which code should my endpoint return?
docs.text: Situation Code Read succeeded 200 Created a resource 201 + Location Accepted work that will finish later 202 + status URL Succeeded, nothing to return (delete, update without body) 204 Client's cached copy is still valid 304 Resource moved permanently (GET pages) 301 Resource moved permanently, method must be kept 308 Redirect after a form POST to a result page 303 Temporary redirect, method must be kept 307 Malformed JSON, missing or wrongly typed field 400 Valid JSON that breaks business rules (if you separate it) 422 No credentials, or invalid/expired credentials 401 + WWW-Authenticate Authenticated but not allowed 403 (or 404 to hide existence) Resource or route does not exist 404 Resource removed permanently 410 Method not supported on this resource 405 + Allow Duplicate, or the resource's state forbids the action 409 If-Match / If-Unmodified-Since did not match 412 Conditional request required but missing 428 Body too large 413 Wrong Content-Type 415 Rate limit exceeded 429 + Retry-After Unexpected exception 500 Upstream service returned an invalid response 502 Overloaded, maintenance, dependency down 503 + Retry-After Upstream service timed out 504

docs.title: General rules
docs.text:
• Use the most specific code that is correct, and fall back to the class's x00 code when nothing fits.
  • Always send a useful body for errors in one consistent format (see API design best practices), but never leak stack traces, SQL, or internal hostnames.
  • Pair codes with their headers: 201 with Location, 401 with WWW-Authenticate, 405 with Allow, 429/503 with Retry-After.
  • Document every code each endpoint can return in your API reference.
  • Keep 5xx for real server faults. A user's invalid input is a 4xx; if it shows up as 500, your monitoring will cry wolf.

docs.title: 401 vs 403
docs.text:
• 401: "I don't know who you are" (missing, invalid, or expired credentials). Logging in or refreshing a token can fix it.
  • 403: "I know who you are, and the answer is no." Logging in again does not help.

A frontend typically redirects to login on 401 and shows "access denied" on 403.

docs.title: 400 vs 422
docs.text:
• 400: the request itself is broken: malformed JSON, wrong types, missing required fields.
  • 422: the request is well formed, but the values make no sense for the business rules.

Both are acceptable for validation errors. Many APIs use 400 for all of them; others use 422 for semantic validation. Pick one convention and apply it everywhere.

docs.title: 404 vs 410
docs.text:
• 404: not found, with no statement about the future. It may exist later.
  • 410: it existed and is gone for good. Caches and search engines can stop asking.

docs.title: 403 vs 404 for hiding resources
docs.text: If a user requests /api/projects/secret-merger and is not a member, returning 403 confirms the project exists. When existence itself is sensitive, return 404, the same response as for a project that truly does not exist. GitHub does this for private repositories.

docs.title: 301 vs 308
docs.text: Both are permanent. 301 allows clients to change POST to GET; 308 forbids it. Use 301 for web pages and 308 for API endpoints that receive POST, PUT, or PATCH.

docs.title: 302 vs 303 vs 307
docs.text: All are temporary. 302 is ambiguous about the method (browsers turn POST into GET). 303 says "use GET on the new URL" (perfect after form submissions). 307 says "repeat the same method and body at the new URL".

docs.title: 500 vs 502 vs 503 vs 504
docs.text: Code Produced by Means 500 Your application Your code failed unexpectedly 502 A proxy or gateway The upstream answered badly or hung up 503 A proxy or the app Temporarily unable to serve (overload, maintenance, no healthy instances) 504 A proxy or gateway The upstream did not answer in time

docs.title: The 200-with-error-body anti-pattern
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"success": false, "error": "User not found"}

This breaks caching (the error may be cached as a success), monitoring (no errors appear on dashboards), retry logic, and every client that checks response.ok. Return the real status code with the error body instead. (A documented exception is GraphQL, covered in API styles.)

docs.title: 204 vs 200 with an empty body
docs.text: 204 explicitly says "there is no body". 200 with an empty body is legal but confuses clients that try to parse JSON from every 200. If there is nothing to return, use 204; if the client needs data, return 200 with the data.

docs.title: Quick reference table
docs.text: Code Name One-line meaning 100 Continue Send the body 101 Switching Protocols Upgrading (e.g. to WebSocket) 103 Early Hints Preload these while you wait 200 OK Success 201 Created New resource created (Location) 202 Accepted Queued; will finish later 203 Non-Authoritative Information Modified by a proxy 204 No Content Success, no body 206 Partial Content Requested byte range 300 Multiple Choices Several options available 301 Moved Permanently New permanent URL (method may change) 302 Found Temporary URL (method may change) 303 See Other Go GET the result elsewhere 304 Not Modified Your cached copy is fine 307 Temporary Redirect Temporary, same method and body 308 Permanent Redirect Permanent, same method and body 400 Bad Request Malformed or invalid request 401 Unauthorized Not authenticated (WWW-Authenticate) 402 Payment Required Reserved; sometimes billing 403 Forbidden Authenticated but not allowed 404 Not Found No such resource 405 Method Not Allowed Wrong method (Allow) 406 Not Acceptable Cannot satisfy Accept 407 Proxy Authentication Required Authenticate with the proxy 408 Request Timeout Client too slow to send 409 Conflict Conflicts with current state 410 Gone Permanently removed 411 Length Required Content-Length needed 412 Precondition Failed If-Match etc. failed 413 Content Too Large Body too big 414 URI Too Long URL too long 415 Unsupported Media Type Wrong Content-Type 416 Range Not Satisfiable Bad byte range 417 Expectation Failed Cannot meet Expect 418 I'm a teapot Joke code; reserved 421 Misdirected Request Wrong server for this host 422 Unprocessable Content Well formed but semantically invalid 423 Locked Resource locked 424 Failed Dependency A required earlier request failed 425 Too Early Won't process replayable early data 426 Upgrade Required Switch protocols first 428 Precondition Required Send a conditional request 429 Too Many Requests Rate limited (Retry-After) 431 Request Header Fields Too Large Headers too big 451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons Blocked for legal reasons 500 Internal Server Error Unexpected server failure 501 Not Implemented Functionality not supported 502 Bad Gateway Upstream gave an invalid response 503 Service Unavailable Temporarily unavailable (Retry-After) 504 Gateway Timeout Upstream did not answer in time 505 HTTP Version Not Supported Unsupported HTTP version 507 Insufficient Storage No space to complete 508 Loop Detected Infinite loop detected 511 Network Authentication Required Captive portal login

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• An outage that dashboards do not show. Symptom: users report failures, but the 5xx rate is flat. Detect: sample response bodies or client error reports show {"success": false} with status 200. Cause: the 200-with-error anti-pattern. Fix: return real 4xx/5xx codes and alert on them.
  • Alerts firing for bad input. Symptom: the 5xx alert fires every day, nobody can find an outage. Detect: 500 responses whose logged errors are validation, parse, or "not found" errors. Cause: unmapped client errors fall through to the default 500. Fix: map validation to 400/422, missing records to 404, conflicts to 409, and keep 5xx for real faults.
  • Clients hammering the API after a 4xx. Symptom: traffic spikes made of identical failing requests. Detect: access logs show one client repeating a request that gets 400 or 401 many times per second. Cause: retry logic that retries every error. Fix: retry only transient failures such as 408, 429, 502, 503, and 504 (honoring Retry-After), with exponential backoff, as Stripe recommends for its 429 responses.
  • A redirect you cannot take back. Symptom: after reverting a 301, some users still land on the new URL. Detect: traffic keeps arriving at the redirect target from browsers that never request the old URL again. Cause: browsers cached the permanent redirect. Fix: test with 302 or 307 first, and only switch to 301/308 once the move is final.
  • Some users cannot load anything: 431. Symptom: only certain users get errors, often long-time users. Detect: 431 Request Header Fields Too Large in server or proxy logs for those users. Cause: oversized cookies or tokens. Fix: remove stale cookies, keep tokens small, and set cookies on the narrowest domain and path.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Status code: the three-digit number summarizing a response.
  • Reason phrase: the human-readable text after the code; ignored by clients and absent in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
  • Status class: the group given by the first digit (1xx to 5xx).
  • Redirect: a 3xx response telling the client to look elsewhere, via Location.
  • Conditional request: a request with If-* headers that the server evaluates before acting (304, 412).
  • Upstream: the server a proxy forwards to; the source of 502/504.
  • Rate limiting: restricting how many requests a client may send in a time window (429).

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Returning 200 for errors with {"success": false} in the body.
  • Using 401 for permission problems. 401 is about identity; use 403 for permissions.
  • Returning 500 for invalid input, which pollutes error dashboards and hides real outages.
  • Sending a body with 204 or 304. Both must not have one.
  • Forgetting the companion header: Location on 201, Allow on 405, WWW-Authenticate on 401, Retry-After on 429/503.
  • Using 301 for an API endpoint that receives POST, which some clients turn into a GET. Use 308.
  • Inventing custom codes such as 299 or 499 in a public API. Clients treat them as 200 and 400. (499 appears in Nginx logs when the client closed the connection, but it is not a standard code and is never sent to clients.)
  • Leaking stack traces in 500 responses.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What does a client do with an unknown status code such as 437?
  2. Explain the difference between 401 and 403 with an example of each.
  3. A user submits a form with POST. Which redirect code should send them to the result page, and why not 302?
  4. When would you return 404 instead of 403 for a resource the user is not allowed to see?
  5. Which component usually produces 502 and 504, and what does each one tell you?
  6. Which headers belong with 201, 401, 405, and 429?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: HTTP response status codes has a page for every code with examples.
  • RFC 9110: Section 15, Status Codes is the authoritative definition of the standard codes.
  • RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes defines 428, 429, 431, and 511.
  • RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs defines a standard error body format.

docs.title: Backend Concepts Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review the core backend concepts: HTTP, APIs, security, reliability, and the building blocks behind production services. Try to answer each one aloud before reading the answer.

docs.title: Backend fundamentals and the request lifecycle
1. What are the main responsibilities of a backend?
docs.text: A backend receives requests, authenticates and authorizes them, validates input, runs business logic, reads and writes persistent data, integrates with other services, and returns responses. It also handles cross-cutting concerns such as logging, error handling, security, and performance.

docs.title: 2. What does it mean for a server to be stateless, and why is it useful?
docs.text: A stateless server keeps no per-client data in its own memory between requests; any state lives in the request (a token) or in a shared store (database, Redis). Any instance can then handle any request, which makes horizontal scaling, load balancing, and restarts simple.

docs.title: 3. Describe what happens when a browser requests https://api.example.com/orders.
docs.text: The browser resolves the domain with DNS, opens a TCP connection (or QUIC for HTTP/3), performs a TLS handshake, and sends the HTTP request. It may pass through a CDN, load balancer, and reverse proxy before reaching an app server, where middleware, routing, controllers, services, and the database produce a response that travels back the same way.

docs.title: 4. Why might a request fail with 502 or 504 even though the app code is fine?
docs.text: These come from a proxy or gateway in front of the app. 502 Bad Gateway means the upstream returned an invalid response or the connection failed (for example, the app crashed). 504 Gateway Timeout means the upstream did not respond within the proxy's timeout, often because of a slow query or dependency.

docs.title: HTTP methods, status codes, and headers
5. What is the difference between safe and idempotent methods?
docs.text: A safe method does not request a state change (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE). An idempotent method has the same intended effect whether performed once or repeatedly (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE). POST is neither by definition, so retries need application-level idempotency protection when duplicate effects matter.

docs.title: 6. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
docs.text: PUT replaces the whole resource with the representation sent, and is idempotent. PATCH applies a partial modification; it is idempotent only if the patch is (setting a field is, incrementing a counter is not). JSON Merge Patch and JSON Patch are standard patch formats.

docs.title: 7. When should you return 201, 202, and 204?
docs.text: 201 Created after creating a resource, ideally with a Location header pointing to it. 202 Accepted when the request was accepted for later processing (a background job). 204 No Content when the request succeeded and there is no body to return, such as a successful delete.

docs.title: 8. What is the difference between 401 and 403?
docs.text: 401 Unauthorized means the request lacks valid authentication — the server does not know who you are, or your credentials are invalid or expired. 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are and you are not allowed to do this; signing in again will not help.

docs.title: 9. What is the difference between 400 and 422?
docs.text: 400 Bad Request means the request is malformed or invalid in general. 422 Unprocessable Content means the request is well-formed (for example, valid JSON) but its content fails validation rules. Many APIs use 400 for all validation errors; the important thing is consistency.

docs.title: 10. What is the difference between 301, 302, 307, and 308?
docs.text: 301 and 308 are permanent redirects; 302 and 307 are temporary. 307 and 308 require the client to repeat the same method and body, while clients historically changed POST to GET on 301 and 302. 303 See Other explicitly tells the client to fetch another URL with GET.

docs.title: 11. How do ETags and conditional requests work?
docs.text: The server sends an ETag identifying a version of a resource. A client can send If-None-Match with that value on a GET; if unchanged, the server returns 304 Not Modified without a body, saving bandwidth. With If-Match on a PUT, the server returns 412 Precondition Failed if someone else changed it, preventing lost updates.

docs.title: 12. What do Cache-Control: no-cache and no-store mean?
docs.text: no-cache allows storage but requires successful validation before reuse. no-store tells caches not to store the response, but is not a complete privacy guarantee. max-age sets freshness lifetime; private allows private caches such as a user agent to store the response while prohibiting shared caches from storing it.

docs.title: 13. What is the same-origin policy, and what is CORS?
docs.text: The same-origin policy stops scripts on one origin (scheme, host, and port) from reading responses from another origin. CORS is a mechanism that lets a server opt in, using response headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin, to allow specific other origins to read its responses. The browser enforces it.

docs.title: 14. What is a preflight request?
docs.text: For requests that are not "simple" — for example, PUT or DELETE, a JSON Content-Type, or custom headers like Authorization — the browser first sends an OPTIONS request with Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers. The server must answer with matching allow headers before the browser sends the real request.

docs.title: 15. Why can't you use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with cookies?
docs.text: When a request includes credentials (cookies, HTTP authentication), the browser requires the server to echo a specific origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; a wildcard is rejected. This prevents any website from reading authenticated responses. Servers that reflect origins must use an allowlist and send Vary: Origin.

docs.title: REST, API design, and API styles
16. What are the key constraints of REST?
docs.text: Client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, a uniform interface (resources identified by URIs, manipulated through representations, self-descriptive messages, and hypermedia), a layered system, and optional code on demand. Most "REST APIs" follow some of these, especially resources and HTTP semantics.

docs.title: 17. How would you design endpoints for a blog's posts and comments?
docs.text: GET /posts, POST /posts, GET /posts/{id}, PATCH /posts/{id}, DELETE /posts/{id}, and nested GET /posts/{id}/comments and POST /posts/{id}/comments. Use plural nouns, let HTTP methods express the action, return appropriate status codes, and support pagination on lists.

docs.title: 18. Compare offset and cursor pagination.
docs.text: Offset pagination (?page=3&limit=20) is simple and allows jumping to a page, but gets slow on large offsets and can skip or repeat items when data changes. Cursor (keyset) pagination (?after=<last-id>) uses an indexed position, stays fast, and is stable under inserts, but cannot jump to an arbitrary page.

docs.title: 19. What are common API versioning strategies?
docs.text: A version in the URI (/v1/orders), in a custom header, or in the media type (Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json). URI versioning is the most visible and easiest to route. Whatever the strategy, prefer backward compatible, additive changes so new versions are rarely needed.

docs.title: 20. Why use a standard error format such as RFC 9457 problem details?
docs.text: A consistent format (type, title, status, detail, instance, plus extensions like field errors) lets clients handle errors generically and programmatically. It avoids each endpoint inventing its own shape, and separates stable error types from human-readable messages.

docs.title: 21. When would you choose GraphQL over REST?
docs.text: When clients need flexible queries across related data and you want to avoid over-fetching and many round trips — for example, several frontends with different data needs. Trade-offs include harder HTTP caching, the N+1 query problem (solved with batching such as DataLoader), query cost limiting, and errors that are often returned inside a 200 response.

docs.title: 22. When is gRPC a good choice?
docs.text: For internal service-to-service communication that needs high performance, strict contracts, and streaming. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, generates typed clients, and supports bidirectional streaming. It is less convenient for browsers and public APIs, which usually use REST or GraphQL.

docs.title: 23. What is a webhook, and how does it differ from polling?
docs.text: A webhook is an HTTP callback: when an event happens, the provider sends a POST to a URL the consumer registered. Polling means the consumer repeatedly asks whether anything changed. Webhooks deliver events promptly without wasted requests, but the consumer must expose a reliable, secure endpoint.

docs.title: 24. How do you receive webhooks securely and reliably?
docs.text: Verify the signature (usually an HMAC over the raw body with a shared secret, compared in constant time), check a timestamp to reject replays, respond with 2xx quickly, process the event asynchronously via a queue, and deduplicate by event ID because providers retry and may deliver events more than once or out of order.

docs.title: 25. What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
docs.text: Authentication establishes who is making the request. Authorization decides whether that identity may perform a specific action on a specific resource. Both must happen on the server for every protected request.

docs.title: 26. How should passwords be stored?
docs.text: As hashes from a slow, salted password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt — never plain text, never reversible encryption, and never a fast hash like SHA-256 alone. Each password gets a unique salt; an optional pepper stored outside the database adds protection if the database leaks.

docs.title: 27. What is IDOR (broken object-level authorization)?
docs.text: It is when an API loads an object by an ID supplied in the request without checking that the caller may access it, so changing /invoices/1001 to /invoices/1002 returns someone else's invoice. Prevent it by scoping queries to the current user or checking ownership/relationship on every access.

docs.title: 28. Compare RBAC and ABAC.
docs.text: RBAC grants permissions based on roles (admin, editor). ABAC evaluates policies over attributes of the user, resource, action, and environment ("doctors can read records for patients in their clinic"). RBAC is simpler; ABAC is more expressive. Many systems combine roles with ownership checks.

docs.title: 29. How do you prevent user enumeration on a login endpoint?
docs.text: Return the same message ("Invalid email or password") and similar response times whether the account exists or not, and apply the same approach to registration and password reset flows. Add rate limiting so attackers cannot probe many accounts quickly.

docs.title: 30. What do the HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite cookie attributes do?
docs.text: HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript, limiting theft through XSS. Secure sends it only over HTTPS. SameSite controls whether it is sent on cross-site requests: Strict limits sending to same-site contexts; Lax also permits some top-level cross-site navigations using safe methods; None permits cross-site use when Secure is set. Browser privacy settings may still block cross-site cookies.

docs.title: 31. What is a JWT, and is its payload secret?
docs.text: A JSON Web Token is a compact token of three base64url parts — header, payload (claims), and signature. A signed JWT is not encrypted: anyone can decode and read the payload. The signature only proves it was issued by a key holder and not modified, so never put secrets in it.

docs.title: 32. What must a server check when verifying a JWT?
docs.text: The signature using an explicitly allowed algorithm and the right key, the expiry (exp) and not-before (nbf) with small clock tolerance, the issuer (iss), and the audience (aud). Accepting the algorithm from the token header enables alg: none and algorithm-confusion attacks.

docs.title: 33. Sessions or JWTs — which would you choose?
docs.text: For a browser app talking to its own backend, server-side sessions in HttpOnly cookies are simple, secure, and instantly revocable. JWTs suit distributed APIs, mobile clients, and service-to-service calls where avoiding a lookup matters, but need short expiry and refresh tokens because revocation is hard.

docs.title: 34. How do refresh token rotation and reuse detection work?
docs.text: Each time a refresh token is used, the server issues a new one and invalidates the old one. If an old, already-used refresh token is presented again, the server assumes theft and revokes the whole token family, forcing the user to sign in again. This limits the damage from a stolen refresh token.

docs.title: 35. What is CSRF, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: Cross-site request forgery tricks a user's browser into sending an authenticated request (with cookies) to your site from another site. Defenses include SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens required on state-changing requests, checking the Origin header, and never changing state with GET.

docs.title: 36. Explain the OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE, and what OIDC adds.
docs.text: The client redirects the user to the authorization server with a state and a code challenge (hash of a secret verifier). After sign-in and consent, the server redirects back with a short-lived code, which the client exchanges along with the verifier for tokens. OpenID Connect adds an ID token and a standard UserInfo endpoint to OAuth 2.0. Provider discovery is defined by a related specification and is an optional deployment feature.

docs.title: 37. What is the difference between validation and output encoding?
docs.text: Validation checks input against rules and rejects what does not conform, at the trust boundary. Output encoding transforms data for the context it is placed in (HTML, JavaScript, CSS, or URLs) so it is treated as data rather than code. For SQL use parameterized queries; for shells, avoid constructing command strings and use safe argument APIs. You need both; there is no single input sanitization that is safe for every output.

docs.title: 38. How does NoSQL injection work in a MongoDB login query?
docs.text: If the API passes JSON input straight into a query, an attacker can send an operator object such as {"password": {"$ne": null}}, which matches any value. Validate that fields are the expected primitive types (strings) before building queries, and use schemas that reject unexpected shapes.

docs.title: 39. What is mass assignment?
docs.text: Copying request fields directly into a database update or model, which lets clients set fields they should not control, such as role or balance. Prevent it by validating with a strict schema that allows only specific fields and by building update objects explicitly.

docs.title: 40. What is the difference between operational and programmer errors?
docs.text: Operational errors are expected failures in correct code — invalid input, not found, timeouts — and are handled and mapped to responses. Programmer errors are bugs, such as reading a property of undefined; they should be logged, return a generic 500, and be fixed. Unknown errors that escape all handlers usually warrant a process restart.

docs.title: 41. Why should errors be handled in one central place?
docs.text: A central error handler maps every error to a correct status code and a consistent response, logs it once with context and a request ID, and keeps internal details out of client responses. Handlers stay simple because they can let errors propagate instead of repeating try/catch logic.

docs.title: 42. What is the difference between logs, metrics, and traces?
docs.text: Logs are detailed records of individual events. Metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time, ideal for dashboards and alerts. Traces follow a single request across services as timed spans, showing where time is spent. They answer different questions and work best together.

docs.title: 43. Why monitor p95 and p99 latency rather than the average?
docs.text: Averages hide slow outliers: a few very slow requests barely move the mean. Percentiles show what the slowest 5% or 1% of requests experience, which often includes your most active users. Teams track percentiles such as p95 and p99; a latency SLO can also state the fraction of requests that must meet a specific threshold.

docs.title: 44. Explain the token bucket rate limiting algorithm.
docs.text: A bucket holds up to a fixed number of tokens and refills at a steady rate. Each request consumes a token; when the bucket is empty, requests are rejected with 429. It enforces an average rate while allowing short bursts up to the bucket's capacity.

docs.title: 45. What problems arise when rate limiting a scaled-out app?
docs.text: Per-instance memory counters allow the limit multiplied by the number of instances, so counters must live in a shared store like Redis and be updated atomically. The app must also identify the real client IP correctly behind proxies (trust proxy), without trusting forged X-Forwarded-For headers.

docs.title: 46. Why should every outbound call have a timeout?
docs.text: Without a timeout, a slow or hung dependency holds connections, memory, and waiting users indefinitely, and can exhaust the service's capacity, causing a cascading failure. A timeout bounds the damage; note that a timeout means the outcome is unknown, not that the operation failed.

docs.title: 47. What is exponential backoff with jitter?
docs.text: Retry delays grow exponentially (for example, 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms) up to a maximum, and random jitter spreads them out so many clients do not retry in synchronized waves. Combined with a maximum number of attempts, it gives transient failures time to clear without overwhelming the dependency.

docs.title: 48. How do idempotency keys work?
docs.text: The client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it with every attempt (for example, in an Idempotency-Key header). The server atomically records the key, performs the operation once, stores the response, and returns the stored response for repeats — so retrying a payment cannot charge twice.

docs.title: 49. What is a circuit breaker?
docs.text: A component that monitors calls to a dependency. When failures exceed a threshold it opens and fails calls immediately, giving the dependency time to recover. After a cooldown it half-opens to allow trial calls, closing again on success or reopening on failure.

docs.title: 50. How can a race condition happen in single-threaded Node.js, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: Requests interleave at every await, and production runs multiple processes, so a read-check-write sequence can interleave with another request's (two buyers both see stock 1). Prevent it with atomic conditional updates ($inc with a condition, UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= 1), unique constraints, optimistic version checks, or row locks in transactions.

docs.title: 51. Why use background jobs, and why must they be idempotent?
docs.text: Slow or unreliable work (emails, reports, image processing, third-party calls) is moved off the request path so responses stay fast and failures can be retried. Queues usually deliver at least once, so a job may run twice after a crash; idempotent jobs ensure duplicates cause no extra effects.

docs.title: 52. How do you run a scheduled job once when the app has several instances?
docs.text: In-process schedulers like node-cron run once per instance. Use a single dedicated scheduler process, queue-based repeatable jobs (such as BullMQ job schedulers), a distributed lock so only one instance runs each occurrence, or a platform scheduler such as a Kubernetes CronJob.

docs.title: 53. When would you use SSE instead of WebSockets?
docs.text: When updates flow only from server to client — notifications, progress, live feeds, streaming AI output. SSE works over plain HTTP, reconnects automatically with Last-Event-ID, and is simpler to operate. WebSockets are better when both sides send frequent messages, such as chat or multiplayer games.

docs.title: 54. How would you implement large file uploads?
docs.text: Have the API authorize the upload and return a short-lived presigned URL so the client uploads directly to object storage, using multipart or resumable uploads for very large files. Afterwards, verify the object's size and real type (magic bytes), scan it, process it in a background job, store metadata in the database, and serve private files through short-lived signed URLs.

docs.title: 55. How should configuration and secrets be managed?
docs.text: Keep configuration out of code and deploy the same build to every environment, supplying config through environment variables and secrets through a secret manager. Validate config at startup and fail fast, use separate least-privilege credentials per environment, never commit or log secrets, and rotate any secret that leaks.

docs.title: 56. A payment webhook was processed twice and the customer was credited twice — what happened, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: What to check first: whether both runs had the same provider event ID, and how long your endpoint took to answer the first delivery. How to confirm: logs or the provider's dashboard show two deliveries of one event, often a retry after a slow or failed response. Stripe, for example, retries for up to three days and tells you to track event IDs to spot duplicates. Likely causes and fixes: delivery is at least once, and the handler is not idempotent. Record processed event IDs under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the side effect, respond 2xx quickly, and do the work from a queue. See webhooks and timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

docs.title: 57. The browser shows a CORS error only for requests that carry an Authorization header. Why?
docs.text: What to check first: the OPTIONS preflight in the browser's network panel — Authorization is not a CORS-safelisted header, so it always triggers a preflight. How to confirm: the preflight returns 401 or 404, or its Access-Control-Allow-Headers does not list authorization. Likely causes and fixes: authentication middleware runs before CORS and rejects the credential-less preflight, or the allowed headers omit Authorization — which a * wildcard does not cover. Answer preflights before authentication and list Authorization explicitly. See CORS and CORS in Express.

docs.title: 58. After adding a second app instance, users are signed out at random. What do you look at?
docs.text: What to check first: where sessions are stored. How to confirm: requests that fail are served by a different instance from the one that created the session; logs show "session not found". Likely causes and fixes: sessions live in process memory, such as express-session's default MemoryStore. Move them to a shared store like Redis, or use tokens that any instance can verify. See sessions, cookies, and JWT.

docs.title: 59. Right after putting the API behind a load balancer, every user starts getting 429. What happened?
docs.text: What to check first: the IP address the rate limiter uses as its key. How to confirm: the limiter's keys in logs are all the load balancer's IP; express-rate-limit logs ERR_ERL_UNEXPECTED_X_FORWARDED_FOR when it sees X-Forwarded-For while trust proxy is off. Likely causes and fixes: trust proxy is unset, so every client shares one key. Set it to the exact number of proxies in front of the app — not true, which would let clients forge their IP. See rate limiting and throttling.

docs.title: 60. p99 latency on every endpoint jumps from 200 ms to 8 seconds, but CPU is low. How do you investigate?
docs.text: What to check first: traces for slow requests and the latency of each downstream dependency. How to confirm: spans show requests waiting on one dependency or on a connection pool; many sockets are open to a single host. Likely causes and fixes: a slow dependency with no timeout holds connections, and because they are shared, unrelated endpoints wait too. Undici, behind Node's fetch, waits up to 300 seconds for headers by default. Set timeouts on every call, add a bulkhead per dependency, and consider a circuit breaker. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency and logging, monitoring, and tracing.

docs.title: 61. During a flash sale, stock went negative and more orders were accepted than units existed. What went wrong?
docs.text: What to check first: how the purchase handler checks and updates stock. How to confirm: a concurrency test with 20 parallel purchases of an item with stock 1 produces more than one success. Likely causes and fixes: read-then-write in application code, so requests interleave at each await. Use one atomic conditional update (UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock >= 1, or $inc with a stock: { $gte: 1 } filter), add a CHECK (stock >= 0) constraint, and keep the concurrency test in CI. See concurrency and race conditions.

docs.title: 62. After "Sign in with Google", some users land back on the sign-in page with "Invalid sign-in state". Why?
docs.text: What to check first: whether the pre-login session cookie that stores state is sent on the callback request. How to confirm: the callback request has no session cookie, or reaches an instance that cannot find the session. Likely causes and fixes: the cookie is SameSite=Strict, so it is not sent on the cross-site redirect back from Google, or sessions are not shared across instances. Use SameSite=Lax for that cookie and a shared session store. See OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, and SSO.

docs.title: 63. After rotating the JWT signing key, every user is signed out at once. What went wrong?
docs.text: What to check first: which keys the verifiers accept and when the old key was removed. How to confirm: a spike of signature verification failures starts exactly at the deploy; failing tokens carry the old kid. Likely causes and fixes: the old key was removed while tokens signed with it were still valid. Publish both keys in the JWKS with different kid values, sign new tokens with the new key, and retire the old key only after the longest token lifetime has passed. See sessions, cookies, and JWT.

docs.title: 64. Welcome emails are arriving hours after sign-up. Where do you look?
docs.text: What to check first: queue depth and the age of the oldest waiting job. How to confirm: the backlog grows steadily, and per-job processing time or the email provider's latency has risen. Likely causes and fixes: too few workers, low worker concurrency, or a slow or rate-limited provider. Scale workers, raise concurrency within the provider's limits, and alert on job age rather than queue depth alone. See background jobs and scheduling.

docs.title: 65. The nightly report was emailed three times. How do you find and fix the cause?
docs.text: What to check first: how the job is scheduled and how many instances run. How to confirm: logs show the job starting on every instance at the same minute, or a second instance starting after the first one's lock expired. Likely causes and fixes: node-cron runs once per instance, or a distributed lock expired while a slow job was still running. Use a queue job scheduler or a single scheduler process, extend locks while working, and make the job idempotent. See background jobs and scheduling and concurrency and race conditions.

docs.title: 66. Clients receive an HTML error page instead of JSON for some 500 errors. Why?
docs.text: What to check first: the response Content-Type and the server log for the same request ID. How to confirm: the logs show an error thrown inside the error-handling middleware, or the handler is registered before the routes. Likely causes and fixes: the error handler itself crashed — for example, calling .toLowerCase() on a driver error whose code is a number — so Express's built-in handler answered with HTML. Register the handler last, expose only your own error codes, and test it with unexpected error types. See error handling.

docs.title: 67. An SSE progress bar jumps straight from 0% to 100%. What is happening?
docs.text: What to check first: whether events reach the client as they are written. How to confirm: curl -N directly against the app streams events, but through the proxy they arrive all at once at the end. Likely causes and fixes: a reverse proxy buffers the response, or compression middleware holds data back. Send X-Accel-Buffering: no (or turn off proxy_buffering in Nginx) and exclude text/event-stream from compression. See real-time communication.

docs.title: 68. Direct uploads to S3 with presigned URLs started failing after an AWS SDK upgrade. What changed?
docs.text: What to check first: the query parameters of a newly generated upload URL. How to confirm: the URL now contains x-amz-checksum-crc32 and x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm. Likely causes and fixes: recent SDK versions calculate request checksums by default (WHEN_SUPPORTED), and on a presigned URL that is the checksum of an empty body, so the real upload does not match. Create the client with requestChecksumCalculation: "WHEN_REQUIRED". See file storage and uploads.

docs.title: 69. A security review found bearer tokens in your log platform. What do you do?
docs.text: What to check first: which code path logs the tokens, and how long the logs are retained and who can read them. How to confirm: search the logs for Bearer and authorization; find the logger or middleware that writes whole request headers. Likely causes and fixes: request logging without redaction. Treat the tokens as leaked: revoke or expire them, add redaction paths such as req.headers.authorization, add a test that checks redaction, and delete the affected logs within your retention policy. See logging, monitoring, and tracing and configuration and secrets.

docs.title: 70. A deploy passed its health checks, but every payment now fails with "invalid API key". How do you prevent this next time?
docs.text: What to check first: the environment variables present in the new release compared with the previous one. How to confirm: the payment key variable is missing or empty in the new environment, and errors start exactly at the deploy time. Likely causes and fixes: configuration is read lazily, so the app started without it. Validate all configuration at startup and exit non-zero, so the deploy fails before taking traffic; keep secrets in a secret manager per environment. See configuration and secrets.

docs.text:
• Backend concepts overview
  • HTTP status codes
  • Authentication and authorization
  • Timeouts, retries, and idempotency
  • OWASP Cheat Sheet Series
  • MDN: HTTP

docs.title: Logging, Monitoring, and Tracing
docs.text: Once a backend runs in production, you can no longer attach a debugger and watch it. Logs, metrics, and traces are how you see what it is doing: logs record individual events, metrics summarize behavior as numbers over time, and traces follow a single request across services. Together they are called observability — the ability to understand a system's internal state from the data it emits.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Questions you will need to answer in production:

  • A customer says checkout failed at 14:32. What happened to their request?
  • Is the API slower today than last week? For everyone, or one endpoint?
  • Error rates doubled after the last deploy. Which change caused it?
  • The database is at 95% CPU. Which service is sending the load?
  • Are we meeting the reliability we promised customers?

Without good logs, metrics, and traces, every incident becomes guesswork. With them, you find problems before users report them, fix them faster, and make capacity and performance decisions from data.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google SRE's four golden signals. Google's Site Reliability Engineering book says that if you can only measure four metrics of a user-facing system, measure latency, traffic, errors, and saturation (Google SRE book: Monitoring distributed systems).
  • Prometheus at SoundCloud. The Prometheus monitoring and alerting toolkit was originally built at SoundCloud in 2012 and is now an independent open-source project (Prometheus: overview).
  • Distributed tracing at Uber. Jaeger was released as open source by Uber Technologies in 2016 to monitor distributed workflows and find performance bottlenecks, and was later donated to the CNCF (Jaeger documentation).
  • Cheaper logs at Grafana Labs. Grafana Loki does not index the contents of log lines; it indexes only labels for each log stream, which is what keeps it cost-effective at scale (Grafana Loki: overview).

Popular tools and providers: Prometheus and Grafana, Grafana Loki and Tempo, Jaeger, the ELK / OpenSearch stack, OpenTelemetry, and hosted platforms such as Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb, and AWS CloudWatch.

docs.title: The three pillars
docs.text:
Signal What it is Good for Example Logs Timestamped records of discrete events Details of what happened in a specific case order 812 failed: card declined Metrics Numeric measurements aggregated over time Trends, dashboards, alerts http_requests_total{status="500"} = 42/min Traces The path of one request through services, as timed spans Finding where time is spent across services Checkout 1.8 s: payment call 1.5 s

They complement each other: a metric alert tells you error rates are up; a trace shows which service is failing; logs show the exact error.

docs.title: Log levels
docs.text:
Level Use it for Production default trace Extremely detailed step-by-step flow Off debug Diagnostic detail useful while developing or investigating Usually off; enable temporarily info Normal significant events: server started, job completed, user signed up On warn Something unexpected that the system handled: retry succeeded, deprecated API used, slow query On error An operation failed and needs attention: request failed with 500, job failed after retries On, alertable fatal The process cannot continue and is about to exit On, alert

Choose levels deliberately. If everything is error, nothing is; if routine validation failures are logged as error, real problems get lost.

docs.title: Structured logging
docs.text:
Plain text logs are hard to search and parse:

2026-11-07 14:32:10 Order 812 failed for user 42 after 3 attempts

Structured logs are JSON objects with consistent fields that log systems can index and filter:

{"level":"error","time":"2026-11-07T14:32:10.512Z","msg":"order failed",
 "orderId":"812","userId":"42","attempts":3,"requestId":"req_7f3a9c",
 "err":{"type":"CardDeclinedError","message":"Card declined"}}

Now you can query "all errors for orderId 812" or "count of CardDeclinedError per hour" without regular expressions.

In Node.js, pino is a fast, widely used structured logger. It writes JSON to standard output; the platform (container runtime, log agent) ships it to a central system. Apps should not manage log files themselves in containerized environments — write to stdout and let the infrastructure collect it.

docs.title: What to log
docs.text:
• Requests: method, route, status, duration, request ID (often one line per request).
  • Significant business events: sign-up, order placed, payment failed.
  • Errors with stack traces and cause chains.
  • Calls to external services that fail or are slow.
  • Security events: sign-ins, failed sign-ins, permission denials, password and MFA changes.
  • Startup configuration (non-secret values) and shutdown.

docs.title: What never to log
docs.text:
• Passwords, password reset tokens, MFA codes.
  • Access tokens, refresh tokens, session IDs, API keys, cookies, Authorization headers.
  • Secrets, connection strings, private keys.
  • Full payment card numbers and similar regulated data.
  • Unnecessary personal or health data — log an ID, not the record.

Use your logger's redaction feature to remove known sensitive fields automatically, and review what request/response logging captures. Logs are often kept for months and accessed by many people; treat them as sensitive.

docs.title: Correlation and request IDs
docs.text:
A request ID (correlation ID) is generated when a request enters the system (or taken from an incoming header such as X-Request-Id set by the load balancer), attached to every log line for that request, returned to the client in a response header, and forwarded to downstream services. You can then search one ID and see every log line from every service involved.

Client ─► API gateway ──(X-Request-Id: req_7f3a9c)──► Orders ──► Payments
             │                                         │           │
             └──────── all log lines carry requestId=req_7f3a9c ───┘

In modern systems, the W3C traceparent header (from distributed tracing) often serves the same purpose.

docs.title: Log aggregation
docs.text:
With many instances, logs must be collected centrally:

  • ELK / OpenSearch stack: agents (Beats, Fluent Bit) ship logs to Elasticsearch or OpenSearch; Kibana or OpenSearch Dashboards search them.
  • Grafana Loki: indexes labels rather than full text; cheaper at scale; queried with LogQL in Grafana.
  • Cloud services: AWS CloudWatch Logs, Google Cloud Logging, Azure Monitor.
  • Commercial platforms: Datadog, New Relic, Splunk, and others.

Set retention periods deliberately — logs cost money to store and may be subject to data-protection rules.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Metric types:

  • Counter: only goes up (resets on restart). Requests served, errors, jobs processed. You usually look at its rate.
  • Gauge: goes up and down. Memory in use, queue length, active connections.
  • Histogram: counts observations in buckets. Request durations; lets you compute percentiles.

Two standard methods for choosing what to measure:

  • RED (for services): Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests per second), Duration (latency distribution).
  • USE (for resources like CPU, disks, pools): Utilization, Saturation (queued work), Errors.

docs.title: Percentiles
docs.text:
Averages hide pain. If 99 requests take 50 ms and one takes 5 seconds, the average is about 100 ms, which looks fine. Percentiles describe the distribution:

  • p50 (median): half of requests are faster than this.
  • p95: 95% are faster; 1 in 20 is slower.
  • p99: 1 in 100 is slower — often your most active users, since they make the most requests.

Track p50, p95, and p99 latency per endpoint, and alert on tail latency, not the average.

Prometheus (with Grafana for dashboards) is a widely used open-source metrics stack; cloud providers and APM tools offer managed equivalents.

docs.title: Dashboards and alerting
docs.text:
• Dashboards show the RED metrics per service, resource usage, dependency health, and business metrics (orders per minute).
  • Alerts should fire on symptoms users feel — error rate, latency, availability — rather than every internal cause. Each alert should be actionable, have a clear owner, and link to a runbook.
  • Avoid alert fatigue: noisy alerts that fire constantly get ignored, including the important one.

docs.title: Distributed tracing
docs.text:
In a system with many services, one user request may touch ten of them. A trace records that whole journey:

  • A trace is the full tree of work for one request, identified by a trace ID.
  • A span is one timed operation within it (an HTTP handler, a database query, an outbound call), with a start time, duration, attributes, and a parent span.
  • Context propagation passes the trace ID and parent span ID to downstream services, usually in the W3C traceparent header.

OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for producing traces, metrics, and logs. Its Node.js SDK can auto-instrument common libraries (HTTP, Express, database drivers) and export to many backends (Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Zipkin, cloud and commercial APMs).

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
Health endpoints let load balancers and orchestrators route traffic only to healthy instances:

  • Liveness (/livez): is the process running and not stuck? If it fails, the orchestrator restarts the instance. Keep it simple — do not check dependencies here, or a database blip restarts every instance.
  • Readiness (/readyz): can this instance serve traffic right now (started, connected to required dependencies, not shutting down)? If it fails, traffic is routed elsewhere but the instance is not killed.

docs.title: SLI, SLO, SLA, and error budgets
docs.text:
• SLI (service level indicator): a measured quantity of service quality, such as "percentage of requests that succeed in under 300 ms."
  • SLO (service level objective): the target for an SLI, such as "99.9% of requests succeed in under 300 ms over 30 days."
  • SLA (service level agreement): a contract with customers, with consequences (credits, refunds) if missed. SLAs are usually looser than internal SLOs.
  • Error budget: the allowed unreliability implied by the SLO. A 99.9% monthly SLO allows about 43 minutes of failure in 30 days. If the budget is spent, the team prioritizes reliability over new features.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Every production service needs logs and metrics. Tracing and SLOs depend on the system's size.

Use each signal for its job:

  • Logs for the details of one event: what failed for this request, with which IDs.
  • Metrics for trends and alerts: rates, error ratios, latency percentiles, saturation.
  • Traces when a request crosses several services, queues, or databases and you need to know where the time went.

You may not need yet:

  • Distributed tracing for a single service with one database — request logs with durations are often enough.
  • Formal SLOs and error budgets before you have real users and a clear idea of what "good" means.

Avoid:

  • debug logging permanently on in production.
  • Alerts on internal causes (CPU at 80%) that do not affect users.
Question Best signal Why did this specific checkout fail? Logs, found by request ID Is the error rate higher than last week? Metrics Which downstream call made checkout slow? Traces Should someone be woken up now? Alerts on symptom metrics or SLO burn rate Are we keeping our reliability promise? SLIs measured against an SLO

docs.title: Structured request logging with pino in Express
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import pino from "pino";
import pinoHttp from "pino-http";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const logger = pino({
  level: process.env.LOG_LEVEL ?? "info",
  // Remove sensitive values wherever they appear in logged objects
  redact: ["req.headers.authorization", "req.headers.cookie", "*.password"],
});

const app = express();

app.use(
  pinoHttp({
    logger,
    // Reuse the incoming request ID or create one
    genReqId: (request, response) => {
      const id = request.get("x-request-id") ?? randomUUID();
      response.setHeader("x-request-id", id);
      return id;
    },
  })
);

app.get("/api/orders/:id", async (request, response) => {
  // request.log is a child logger that already includes the request ID
  request.log.info({ orderId: request.params.id }, "fetching order");
  response.json({ id: request.params.id });
});

app.listen(3000, () => logger.info({ port: 3000 }, "server started"));

docs.title: Recording RED metrics with prom-client
docs.text:
import client from "prom-client";

const httpDuration = new client.Histogram({
  name: "http_request_duration_seconds",
  help: "HTTP request duration in seconds",
  labelNames: ["method", "route", "status"],
  buckets: [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 2, 5],
});

app.use((request, response, next) => {
  const stopTimer = httpDuration.startTimer();
  response.on("finish", () => {
    stopTimer({
      method: request.method,
      // Use the route pattern, not the raw URL, to keep label values bounded
      route: request.route?.path ?? "unmatched",
      status: response.statusCode,
    });
  });
  next();
});

// Prometheus scrapes this endpoint (protect or expose it internally only)
app.get("/metrics", async (request, response) => {
  response.type(client.register.contentType);
  response.send(await client.register.metrics());
});

docs.title: Liveness and readiness endpoints
docs.text:
let shuttingDown = false;

app.get("/livez", (request, response) => response.sendStatus(200));

app.get("/readyz", async (request, response) => {
  if (shuttingDown) return response.sendStatus(503);
  try {
    await db.command({ ping: 1 }); // required dependency
    response.sendStatus(200);
  } catch {
    response.sendStatus(503);
  }
});

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  shuttingDown = true; // stop receiving new traffic before closing
});

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Log structured JSON to stdout; let the platform collect and ship it.
  • Use log levels consistently; keep debug off in production by default.
  • Attach a request/trace ID to every log line and propagate it downstream.
  • Redact secrets and sensitive data automatically; review request logging.
  • Measure RED for every service and USE for key resources.
  • Alert on user-visible symptoms using percentiles, with runbooks attached.
  • Keep metric label values bounded (route patterns, not raw URLs or user IDs) to avoid high-cardinality explosions.
  • Instrument with OpenTelemetry to avoid vendor lock-in.
  • Separate liveness from readiness.
  • Define SLOs and use error budgets to balance reliability and features.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The metrics system runs out of memory. Symptom: Prometheus becomes slow or crashes, and dashboards time out. Detect: the number of active time series climbs steadily after a deploy. Cause: a label with unbounded values — the raw URL (/api/orders/8123) instead of the route pattern, or a user ID. Fix: label by route pattern and status class, and drop the bad label at scrape time while the code is fixed.
  • A database blip restarts every pod. Symptom: a short database outage becomes a full outage. Detect: Kubernetes events show "Liveness probe failed" on all pods at once. Cause: the liveness probe checks the database, so every instance is killed together. Fix: liveness checks only that the process responds; dependency checks go in the readiness probe.
  • Secrets end up in the log store. Symptom: a security review finds bearer tokens or passwords in log search. Detect: search the logs for Bearer or "password". Cause: whole request headers or bodies were logged without redaction. Fix: configure redaction paths, add a test that checks them, and rotate every credential that leaked.
  • Traces stop at the first service. Symptom: the trace view shows the API's spans, but downstream work appears as separate, unconnected traces. Detect: child services have spans with no parent. Cause: traceparent is not propagated — a custom HTTP client, or a message queue that does not carry trace context. Fix: use OpenTelemetry instrumentation for HTTP clients and inject trace context into message headers.
  • The on-call engineer ignores pages. Symptom: a real incident is noticed late. Detect: many alerts per week that needed no action. Cause: alerts on causes (CPU, memory) rather than user-visible symptoms. Fix: alert on error rate, latency percentiles, or SLO burn rate, and attach a runbook to every alert.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Observability: understanding a system's internal state from its outputs.
  • Structured log: a log entry with machine-readable fields, usually JSON.
  • Log level: the severity of a log entry.
  • Correlation ID: an ID linking all events of one request.
  • Counter / gauge / histogram: metric types for increasing totals, current values, and distributions.
  • RED / USE: rate-errors-duration and utilization-saturation-errors methods.
  • Percentile (p95, p99): the value below which that percentage of observations fall.
  • Trace / span: a request's full journey / one timed operation in it.
  • Context propagation: passing trace identifiers between services.
  • OpenTelemetry: an open standard and toolkit for traces, metrics, and logs.
  • Liveness / readiness probe: checks for "restart me" versus "send me traffic."
  • SLI / SLO / SLA: indicator, objective, and agreement for service quality.
  • Error budget: the amount of failure an SLO allows.
  • Cardinality: the number of unique label combinations in a metric.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Logging secrets or tokens, especially by logging whole request headers or bodies.
  • Unstructured, inconsistent log messages that cannot be queried.
  • Everything at error level, which hides real errors.
  • Monitoring averages instead of percentiles.
  • Alerting on causes (CPU 80%) instead of symptoms (latency, errors).
  • Liveness probes that check the database, causing mass restarts when it blips.
  • Using user IDs or full URLs as metric labels, creating millions of time series.
  • "We have logs, so we have observability." Without metrics and traces, trends and cross-service latency are hard to see.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What different questions do logs, metrics, and traces answer?
  2. Why is structured logging preferred over plain-text log lines?
  3. List five things that should never appear in logs.
  4. Explain the RED method and why p99 latency matters more than the average.
  5. What is the difference between a trace and a span, and how does context propagation work?
  6. How do liveness and readiness checks differ, and why should liveness not check dependencies?
