docs.title: OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, and SSO
docs.text: OAuth 2.0 is a framework that lets an application get limited access to a user's resources on another service without ever seeing the user's password. OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a thin identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that also tells the application who the user is. Together they power "Sign in with Google," third-party API access, and single sign-on across company apps.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Before OAuth, an app that wanted to read your calendar asked for your email password. That gave the app full, permanent access to your account, and the only way to revoke it was to change your password everywhere. OAuth replaces password sharing with scoped, revocable tokens issued by the service that owns the account.

Backend developers meet OAuth and OIDC constantly: adding social login, calling Google, GitHub, Microsoft, or Stripe APIs on a user's behalf, protecting their own APIs with an identity provider such as Auth0, Okta, Keycloak, Cognito, or Entra ID, and securing machine-to-machine calls. Misconfigured flows are a common source of account takeover bugs.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• "Sign in with Google". Google's sign-in is OpenID Connect: the app receives an ID token digitally signed by Google and must validate its signature (keys from the jwks_uri in Google's discovery document), iss, aud, and exp before trusting it (Google Identity: OpenID Connect). Google publishes its authorization and token endpoints, and the PKCE methods it supports, in that discovery document.
  • The device flow at GitHub. GitHub supports the device authorization flow for headless apps such as CLI tools and the Git Credential Manager, and marks PKCE as strongly recommended for its web flow (GitHub Docs: authorizing OAuth apps).
  • Microsoft identity platform. Microsoft documents the authorization code flow paired with PKCE and OpenID Connect for single-page apps and server-based web apps that sign users in with Microsoft Entra ID (Microsoft Learn: auth code flow).

Popular tools and providers: identity providers such as Google, Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Auth0, Amazon Cognito, and Keycloak; client libraries such as openid-client and Passport.js strategies.

docs.title: The problem OAuth solves
docs.text:
OAuth is about delegated authorization: the user (resource owner) authorizes an application (client) to do specific things (scopes) with their data on a service (resource server), and the authorization server issues an access token representing that grant.

OAuth by itself does not define how to log a user in. An access token says "the holder may call this API," not "this is Alice." Identity is what OpenID Connect adds.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Role Who it is Example Resource owner The user who owns the data You Client The application requesting access A scheduling app Authorization server Authenticates the user, asks for consent, issues tokens Google's accounts service Resource server The API holding the data; accepts access tokens Google Calendar API

docs.title: Confidential and public clients
docs.text:
• Confidential client: runs on a server and can keep a secret (a client_secret or a private key). Example: an Express backend.
  • Public client: cannot keep a secret because its code runs on the user's device. Examples: single-page apps, mobile apps, desktop apps. Anything shipped to users can be extracted.

Public clients must use PKCE and never embed a client secret. Confidential clients should also use PKCE: the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700) makes PKCE mandatory for public clients and recommended for confidential ones, and the OAuth 2.1 draft requires it for every client that uses the authorization code flow.

docs.title: Authorization code flow with PKCE
docs.text:
This is the recommended flow for user-facing apps. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, pronounced "pixie") stops an attacker who intercepts the authorization code from redeeming it.

Step by step:

  1. The client creates three values: a random state (CSRF protection for the redirect), a random code_verifier (43–128 characters), and the code_challenge, which is the base64url-encoded SHA-256 hash of the verifier.
  2. Redirect to the authorization endpoint with client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state, code_challenge, and code_challenge_method=S256.
  3. The user authenticates at the authorization server (never at the client) and approves the scopes on a consent screen.
  4. The authorization server redirects back to the registered redirect_uri with a short-lived, single-use code and the same state. The client rejects the response if state does not match what it stored.
  5. Token exchange: the client sends the code and the original code_verifier to the token endpoint over a back channel (server to server). The server hashes the verifier and compares it with the challenge from step 2. Confidential clients also authenticate here.
  6. Use the access token to call the resource server. Store the refresh token securely on the server.

An attacker who steals the code from the redirect cannot redeem it without the code_verifier, which never left the client.

docs.title: Client credentials flow
docs.text: For machine-to-machine calls with no user involved: a backend authenticates with its own credentials and receives an access token for its own permissions.

docs.title: Device authorization flow
docs.text:
For devices with no browser or awkward input (smart TVs, CLIs, consoles):

  1. The device asks the authorization server for a device_code and a short user_code.
  2. It shows: "Go to example.com/device and enter ABCD-EFGH."
  3. The user completes sign-in and consent on a phone or computer.
  4. Meanwhile the device polls the token endpoint until it receives tokens (or is told to slow down or that the code expired).

docs.title: Refresh tokens
docs.text: Access tokens are short-lived. A refresh token lets the client get a new access token without sending the user through the flow again (grant_type=refresh_token). Treat refresh tokens like passwords: keep them server-side for confidential clients, and expect rotation (a new refresh token on each use) from modern authorization servers. Some providers only issue a refresh token when you request a specific scope or parameter (for example, offline_access in OIDC).

docs.title: Deprecated grants
docs.text:
• Implicit grant: returned the access token directly in the redirect URL fragment. Tokens leaked through browser history, referrer headers, and logs, and there was no way to bind them to the client. Replaced by authorization code + PKCE for SPAs.
  • Resource owner password credentials grant: the client collected the user's username and password and sent them to the token endpoint. This defeats the purpose of OAuth, trains users to type passwords into third-party apps, and cannot support MFA or passkeys properly.

RFC 9700 says clients should not use the implicit grant (or any response type that returns access tokens in the authorization response) and that the password grant must not be used. The OAuth 2.1 draft leaves both grants out of the specification entirely.

docs.title: Scopes and consent
docs.text:
A scope is a named permission the client requests, such as calendar.readonly or repo. The authorization server shows them on the consent screen; the user can approve or refuse; the issued token carries only the approved scopes. Request the minimum scopes you need, and ask for additional scopes incrementally when the feature that needs them is used.

The resource server must check scopes on each request: a token with calendar.readonly must not be able to delete events.

docs.title: Access token formats
docs.text:
• Opaque tokens: random strings with no readable content. The resource server validates them by calling the authorization server's introspection endpoint (RFC 7662) or a shared store. Easy to revoke.
  • JWT access tokens: self-contained, signed tokens the resource server verifies locally with the issuer's public keys (JWKS). Validate signature, iss, aud, exp, and scopes. Harder to revoke before expiry. See sessions, cookies, and JWT.

The client should treat access tokens as opaque either way; only the resource server interprets them.

docs.title: OpenID Connect: adding identity
docs.text:
OIDC uses the same authorization code flow, with the openid scope, and the token response also includes an ID token — a JWT describing the authentication event and the user.

ID token claim Meaning iss The identity provider that issued the token sub A stable, unique identifier for the user at that provider — use this as the account key aud Your client ID; reject tokens issued for another client exp, iat Expiry and issue time nonce The random value you sent in the request; prevents replaying an old ID token auth_time, amr, acr When and how the user authenticated (for example, with MFA) email, email_verified, name, picture Profile claims, depending on requested scopes (email, profile)

Other OIDC pieces:

  • UserInfo endpoint: returns profile claims for an access token.
  • Discovery document: https://<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration lists the authorization, token, userinfo, and JWKS endpoints and supported features, so libraries can configure themselves.
  • ID token versus access token: the ID token is for your app to learn who signed in. The access token is for calling APIs. Do not send ID tokens to APIs as access tokens.

docs.title: Single sign-on (SSO) and SAML
docs.text:
Single sign-on lets a user authenticate once with an identity provider (IdP) and then access many applications without signing in again, because each app trusts the IdP's session. In companies, this centralizes MFA, password policy, and off-boarding: disable one account and access to every app stops.

  • OIDC is the modern choice for web, mobile, and API-based apps.
  • SAML 2.0 is an older XML-based standard still widely used for enterprise SSO into business software. The IdP sends a signed XML assertion to the app (the service provider) through the browser.

Many SaaS products support both; enterprise customers often ask for SAML.

docs.title: Walkthrough: "Sign in with Google"
docs.text:
1. Register your app in the provider's console: get a client_id (and a secret for a server app) and register exact redirect URIs.
  2. User clicks "Sign in with Google." Your backend creates state, nonce, and a PKCE verifier, stores them in the user's pre-login session, and redirects to Google with scope=openid email profile.
  3. The user signs in at Google and consents.
  4. Google redirects to your callback with code and state. You check state, then exchange the code (with the verifier) for tokens.
  5. You validate the ID token: signature with Google's JWKS, iss, aud equals your client ID, exp, and nonce.
  6. You look up the user by the provider and sub (not by email alone), creating an account on first sign-in. Only link to an existing account by email if email_verified is true and your linking rules allow it.
  7. You create your own session for the user (for example, a session cookie). You do not need to keep Google's tokens unless you will call Google APIs.

docs.title: Security pitfalls
docs.text:
• Missing or unchecked state: allows login CSRF — an attacker makes the victim's browser complete a flow that signs them into the attacker's account.
  • Loose redirect URI matching: if the server allows wildcards or prefix matches, attackers can redirect codes or tokens to their own site. Register exact URIs.
  • Open redirects in your app: an unvalidated ?next= parameter on the callback can leak codes or tokens.
  • Token leakage: tokens in URLs, logs, analytics, or Referer headers. Keep tokens out of query strings.
  • Not validating ID tokens: skipping aud, iss, exp, or nonce checks lets tokens for other apps or old tokens be accepted.
  • Using email as the identity key: emails can change or be unverified; use iss + sub.
  • Client secrets in frontend or mobile code: public clients cannot keep secrets; use PKCE.
  • Over-broad scopes: requesting more than needed increases damage if a token leaks.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect when:

  • Users should sign in with an account they already have (Google, Microsoft, a company identity provider).
  • Your app calls another service's API on a user's behalf.
  • Many of your own apps should share one sign-in (SSO).
  • Services call each other and need short-lived, scoped credentials.

Do not use it when:

  • You only need your own users to sign in to your own app with a password — a session is enough; OIDC adds value only with an external identity provider.
  • A partner integration is server-to-server and an API key with rotation is agreed — OAuth adds machinery without benefit.
  • You are tempted to use the implicit or password grants — use the authorization code flow with PKCE instead.
Situation Flow or standard Web, mobile, or SPA user sign-in Authorization code + PKCE, with OIDC Calling a third-party API for a user Authorization code + PKCE, minimal scopes Backend service calling another service Client credentials TV, console, or CLI without a browser Device authorization flow Enterprise customer requires SSO OIDC, or SAML 2.0 if their IdP needs it Simple partner integration API key (not OAuth)

docs.title: Generating PKCE values in Node.js
docs.text:
import { randomBytes, createHash } from "node:crypto";

export function createPkcePair() {
  // 32 random bytes → 43-character base64url string
  const codeVerifier = randomBytes(32).toString("base64url");
  const codeChallenge = createHash("sha256")
    .update(codeVerifier)
    .digest("base64url");
  return { codeVerifier, codeChallenge };
}

export function createState() {
  return randomBytes(16).toString("base64url");
}

docs.title: Starting the flow and handling the callback (Express sketch)
docs.text:
app.get("/auth/google", (request, response) => {
  const { codeVerifier, codeChallenge } = createPkcePair();
  const state = createState();
  const nonce = createState();

  // Remember them for the callback (server-side session)
  request.session.oauth = { state, nonce, codeVerifier };

  const url = new URL("https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth");
  url.search = new URLSearchParams({
    response_type: "code",
    client_id: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID,
    redirect_uri: process.env.GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI,
    scope: "openid email profile",
    state,
    nonce,
    code_challenge: codeChallenge,
    code_challenge_method: "S256",
  }).toString();

  response.redirect(url.toString());
});

app.get("/auth/google/callback", async (request, response, next) => {
  const saved = request.session.oauth;
  delete request.session.oauth; // single use

  if (!saved || request.query.state !== saved.state) {
    return response.status(400).send("Invalid sign-in state");
  }

  // Exchange the code for tokens (back channel, server to server)
  const tokenResponse = await fetch("https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "content-type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
    body: new URLSearchParams({
      grant_type: "authorization_code",
      code: String(request.query.code),
      redirect_uri: process.env.GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI,
      client_id: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID,
      client_secret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET,
      code_verifier: saved.codeVerifier,
    }),
  });
  if (!tokenResponse.ok) {
    return response.status(502).send("Could not complete sign-in");
  }
  const tokens = await tokenResponse.json();

  // Validate the ID token with a library (signature via JWKS, iss, aud,
  // exp, nonce), then find or create the user by iss + sub.
  const claims = await verifyGoogleIdToken(tokens.id_token, saved.nonce);
  const user = await users.findOrCreateByProvider("google", claims.sub, claims);

  // Create your own session; regenerate the ID to prevent fixation
  request.session.regenerate((error) => {
    if (error) return next(error);
    request.session.userId = user.id;
    response.redirect("/");
  });
});

In production, prefer a maintained OIDC client library (for example, openid-client) or your identity provider's SDK, which handles discovery, JWKS caching, and ID token validation for you.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use the authorization code flow with PKCE for every user-facing client.
  • Never use the implicit or password grants in new systems.
  • Register exact redirect URIs; never allow wildcards in production.
  • Always send and verify state; send and verify nonce with OIDC.
  • Validate ID tokens and JWT access tokens fully: signature, iss, aud, exp.
  • Request minimal scopes; ask for more only when needed.
  • Keep client secrets and refresh tokens on the server, encrypted at rest.
  • Identify users by iss + sub; link accounts by email only when verified.
  • Use your identity provider's discovery document and a maintained library.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Redirect URI mismatch. Symptom: the provider shows an error page instead of the consent screen, typically after a new deploy or domain. Detect: the provider names the error — Google, for example, reports redirect_uri_mismatch. Cause: the redirect URI you send differs from the registered one — http versus https behind a proxy, a trailing slash, a different port. Fix: build the redirect URI from configuration, not from the incoming request's host, and register the exact URI for every environment.
  • "Invalid sign-in state" on the callback. Symptom: some users bounce back to the sign-in page after consenting. Detect: the callback logs missing or mismatched state. Cause: the pre-login session cookie was not sent on the redirect back from the provider — it was SameSite=Strict (the return is a cross-site navigation), or the callback landed on another instance without a shared session store. Fix: use SameSite=Lax for that cookie and a shared session store.
  • invalid_grant when exchanging the code. Symptom: sign-in fails intermittently at the token step. Detect: the token endpoint returns invalid_grant. Cause: the code was used twice (a refreshed callback page or a retried request), it expired, or the code_verifier or redirect_uri did not match. Fix: exchange each code once, never retry the exchange automatically, and send the same redirect_uri as in the authorization request.
  • Stored refresh tokens stop working. Symptom: background syncs with a provider fail until the user reconnects. Detect: a rising rate of invalid_grant on refresh requests. Cause: the user revoked access, the provider expired the token, or — with rotation — two workers refreshed with the same token at once and the second use counted as reuse. Fix: refresh a given token from one place at a time, save the new refresh token atomically, and prompt the user to reconnect when refresh fails.
  • ID tokens fail validation after the provider rotates keys. Symptom: all sign-ins fail with "no matching key". Detect: the ID token's kid is not in your cached JWKS. Cause: the JWKS was cached forever. Fix: refetch the JWKS (rate-limited) when an unknown kid arrives, or use a library that does.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• OAuth 2.0: a framework for delegated authorization using access tokens.
  • OpenID Connect (OIDC): an identity layer on OAuth 2.0 that adds ID tokens and standard user claims.
  • Resource owner / client / authorization server / resource server: the four OAuth roles.
  • Grant type: a method for obtaining tokens, such as authorization_code or client_credentials.
  • Authorization code: a short-lived, single-use code exchanged for tokens.
  • PKCE: Proof Key for Code Exchange; binds the code to the client that started the flow.
  • Scope: a named permission requested by the client.
  • Access token / refresh token / ID token: credential for APIs / credential for new access tokens / statement of who signed in.
  • Redirect URI: where the authorization server sends the user back.
  • state / nonce: random values that protect the redirect and the ID token against CSRF and replay.
  • Discovery document: OIDC metadata at /.well-known/openid-configuration.
  • SSO: single sign-on; one authentication grants access to many apps.
  • SAML: an XML-based SSO standard common in enterprises.
  • IdP: identity provider.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "OAuth is a login protocol." OAuth is authorization; OIDC adds authentication.
  • Using an access token to identify the user in your own app instead of validating an ID token.
  • Sending ID tokens to APIs as if they were access tokens.
  • Putting a client secret in a SPA or mobile app. It will be extracted.
  • Skipping PKCE because the client is "confidential."
  • Not checking state, allowing login CSRF.
  • Matching users by email from an unverified provider.
  • Keeping the provider's tokens when you only needed sign-in. If you do not call the provider's APIs, discard them and use your own session.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What problem did OAuth solve compared with sharing passwords with third-party apps?
  2. Walk through the authorization code flow with PKCE. What does the code_verifier protect against?
  3. Why were the implicit and password grants deprecated?
  4. What is the difference between an access token and an ID token, and who is each intended for?
  5. When would you use the client credentials flow and the device authorization flow?
  6. List four checks your backend must perform on an ID token.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• OAuth 2.0 overview (oauth.net)
  • RFC 6749: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
  • RFC 7636: PKCE
  • RFC 8628: OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant
  • RFC 9700: OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice
  • OAuth 2.1 (oauth.net)
  • OpenID Connect Core 1.0
  • OWASP OAuth 2.0 Cheat Sheet
  • Related notes: Authentication and authorization, Sessions, cookies, and JWT

docs.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
docs.text: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client may make in a period of time, such as 100 requests per minute per API key. Requests over the limit are rejected, usually with 429 Too Many Requests, until the client's allowance recovers. Throttling is a close relative that slows or queues excess requests instead of rejecting them outright.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Without limits, a single client can consume all of your capacity:

  • Abuse and brute force: attackers try thousands of passwords, coupon codes, or OTPs per minute; scrapers download your whole catalog.
  • Overload protection: a buggy client stuck in a retry loop, or a traffic spike, can take the service down for everyone.
  • Fairness: one heavy tenant should not degrade service for others.
  • Cost control: each request may call paid APIs (SMS, AI models, maps).
  • Commercial plans: free tiers get lower limits than paid tiers.

Rate limiting is a standard part of API security (see API security) and of resilience in general.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub's REST API allows 5,000 requests per hour for authenticated users and 60 per hour for unauthenticated requests. Responses carry x-ratelimit-remaining and x-ratelimit-reset; over the limit, GitHub answers 403 or 429 and asks clients not to retry before the reset time (GitHub Docs: REST API rate limits).
  • Stripe applies a global limit per account — 100 requests per second in live mode — plus lower limits on some endpoints, and returns 429 Too Many Requests when they are exceeded (Stripe: rate limits).
  • Amazon API Gateway throttles requests with the token bucket algorithm, where a burst setting allows a short overrun of the steady rate (AWS: API Gateway throttling).
  • Nginx limits request rates with its limit_req module using the "leaky bucket" method (nginx: ngx_http_limit_req_module).

Popular tools and providers: express-rate-limit with rate-limit-redis, Nginx limit_req, API gateways such as Amazon API Gateway, Kong, and Envoy, and edge services such as Cloudflare rate limiting rules.

docs.title: Identifying the client
docs.text:
A limit needs a key — who is being counted:

Key Pros Pitfalls IP address Works for anonymous traffic Many users behind one NAT or corporate proxy share an IP; attackers rotate IPs; IPv6 gives each user huge ranges User ID Accurate per person Only after authentication API key / client ID Natural for public APIs and plans Keys can be shared or leaked Combination e.g. per account and per IP for sign-in More state to track

Behind a proxy or load balancer, the TCP connection comes from the proxy, so every request appears to have the proxy's IP. The real client IP is in a header such as X-Forwarded-For, but clients can forge that header. Only trust it from proxies you control: in Express, configure trust proxy to the exact number of proxy hops (or their addresses) rather than true. A wrong setting either rate-limits everyone as one client or lets attackers spoof any IP.

For IPv6, limit by a prefix (such as /64) rather than a single address, since one user can easily control many addresses in their prefix.

docs.title: Fixed window
docs.text:
Count requests in fixed time buckets (for example, each calendar minute). Reset the counter at the start of each window.

limit = 5 per minute
12:00:00 ─────────────── 12:01:00 ─────────────── 12:02:00
  ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✘ ✘            ✔ ✔ ...
            count resets ──┘
  • Simple: one counter per key per window (Redis INCR + EXPIRE).
  • Boundary burst problem: a client can send 5 requests at 12:00:59 and 5 more at 12:01:00 — 10 requests in two seconds, double the intended rate.

docs.title: Sliding window log
docs.text:
Store the timestamp of every request. On each request, discard timestamps older than the window and count what remains.

window = 60 s, limit = 5
now = 12:01:30 → keep timestamps after 12:00:30 → count them → allow if < 5
  • Exact; no boundary burst.
  • Memory grows with the limit (one entry per request per key); more expensive at high limits.

docs.title: Sliding window counter
docs.text:
Approximate a sliding window using the current and previous fixed-window counts, weighted by how far into the current window you are:

estimate = current_count + previous_count × (1 − elapsed_fraction_of_current_window)

previous minute: 8 requests, current minute: 3 requests, 25% into the minute
estimate = 3 + 8 × 0.75 = 9
  • Cheap (two counters) and smooths out boundary bursts.
  • Slightly approximate; good enough for most APIs.

docs.title: Token bucket
docs.text:
A bucket holds up to capacity tokens and refills at a steady rate. Each request takes one token; if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.

  • Allows bursts up to the capacity, while enforcing an average rate.
  • Very common in API gateways and cloud services.
  • State per key: token count and last refill time.

docs.title: Leaky bucket
docs.text:
Requests enter a queue (the bucket) and are processed ("leak out") at a constant rate. If the queue is full, new requests are dropped.

incoming (bursty) ──► [ queue, size N ] ──► processed at fixed rate ──►
                        full → reject
  • Produces a smooth, constant output rate — useful when protecting a downstream system that cannot handle bursts.
  • Adds latency (requests wait in the queue); this is throttling behavior.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Algorithm Bursts Accuracy Memory Typical use Fixed window Up to 2× at boundaries Low at edges Very low Simple limits, low stakes Sliding window log No Exact High Strict limits, low volume (e.g. sign-in) Sliding window counter Smoothed Approximate Low General API limits Token bucket Yes, up to capacity Good Low API gateways, public APIs Leaky bucket No (smoothed output) Good Queue size Protecting fragile downstreams

docs.title: Distributed rate limiting with Redis
docs.text:
With several app instances, an in-memory counter per instance is wrong: three instances each allowing 100 requests per minute allow 300 in total, and the count depends on which instance the load balancer picks. Keep the counters in a shared store, usually Redis.

The operations must be atomic, or two instances can read the same count and both allow a request. A fixed window needs INCR (atomic) followed by setting an expiry when the key is new:

INCR    ratelimit:user42:202611071432     → returns the new count
EXPIRE  ratelimit:user42:202611071432 60  → only when the count is 1

For token buckets and sliding windows, run the read-compute-write logic in a Lua script, which Redis executes atomically.

Decide what happens if Redis is unavailable: fail open (allow requests, risking overload) or fail closed (reject, risking an outage). Sign-in limits often fail closed; general API limits often fail open with an alert.

docs.title: Responding to limited requests
docs.text:
• Status 429 Too Many Requests.
  • Retry-After header: seconds to wait (or an HTTP date) before retrying.
  • Rate limit headers so clients can pace themselves. The IETF RateLimit header fields specification (a draft in progress) uses RateLimit-Policy and RateLimit fields describing the quota and what remains. Many APIs still use the older non-standard X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset.
  • A clear error body: which limit was hit and when to retry.
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type":"https://api.example.com/problems/rate-limited",
 "title":"Too many requests","status":429,
 "detail":"Limit of 100 requests per minute exceeded. Retry in 30 seconds."}

503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After is used when the server as a whole is overloaded, not a specific client over its quota.

docs.title: Rate limiting, throttling, and quotas
docs.text:
Term Meaning Example Rate limiting Reject requests above a rate 100 requests/min, extra get 429 Throttling Slow down or queue excess requests Add delay after 5 failed sign-ins; process jobs at 10/s Quota A total allowance over a long period, often tied to billing 10,000 API calls per month on the free plan Concurrency limit Maximum simultaneous in-flight requests At most 5 parallel exports per account

The terms are often used loosely; be precise in API documentation.

docs.title: Where to enforce
docs.text:
Client ─► CDN / WAF ─► API gateway / load balancer ─► reverse proxy ─► app
          (DDoS,        (per-key quotas,             (per-IP          (per-user,
           bot rules)    plan limits)                 limits)          per-action,
                                                                       business rules)
  • Edge (CDN, WAF): absorbs volumetric attacks before they reach you.
  • API gateway: per-API-key and per-plan limits; central configuration.
  • Reverse proxy (for example, Nginx limit_req): cheap per-IP limits — see Nginx.
  • Application: limits that need business context — per user, per account, per action (password attempts, SMS sends, exports).

Defense in depth: coarse limits at the edge, precise limits in the app.

docs.title: Client-side handling
docs.text:
Clients should treat 429 as a signal to slow down:

  • Honor Retry-After when present.
  • Otherwise retry with exponential backoff and jitter, with a maximum number of attempts (see timeouts, retries, and idempotency).
  • Pace requests proactively using the remaining-quota headers.
  • Never retry instantly in a tight loop — that makes overload worse.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use rate limiting when:

  • An endpoint is open to the internet, especially sign-in, sign-up, password reset, OTP, and search.
  • Requests cost money (SMS, email, AI calls) or are expensive (exports, reports).
  • Tenants or API keys must get a fair share, or plans have different limits.

Use something else when:

  • The problem is a sudden flood of traffic from many sources — that is a DDoS, absorbed at the network edge (CDN or WAF), not in the app.
  • The service is slow for everyone because it is under-provisioned — limiting hides the problem; scale or cache instead.
  • A downstream system needs a steady flow — queue the work and process it at a fixed rate (throttling) instead of rejecting requests.
Problem Tool Response to the client Brute force on sign-in Per-account and per-IP limit 429 with Retry-After One API key overusing a shared API Token bucket per key 429 with quota headers Free versus paid plan allowance Monthly quota 429 or 402, with plan details Too many parallel exports per account Concurrency limit 429 or 409 until one finishes Fragile downstream system Queue with a fixed processing rate (throttle) 202 Accepted, processed later Whole service overloaded Load shedding at the gateway 503 with Retry-After

docs.title: express-rate-limit with a shared Redis store
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import { rateLimit, ipKeyGenerator } from "express-rate-limit"; // v8
import { RedisStore } from "rate-limit-redis";
import { createClient } from "redis";

const redisClient = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
await redisClient.connect();

const app = express();

// Exactly one proxy (the load balancer) sits in front of the app
app.set("trust proxy", 1);

// General API limit: 100 requests per minute per client
const apiLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 60 * 1000,
  limit: 100,
  standardHeaders: "draft-8", // RateLimit-Policy and RateLimit headers
  legacyHeaders: false,       // no X-RateLimit-* headers
  store: new RedisStore({
    sendCommand: (...args) => redisClient.sendCommand(args),
  }),
});

// Strict limit for sign-in, keyed by email + IP
const signInLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  limit: 5,
  standardHeaders: "draft-8",
  legacyHeaders: false,
  // ipKeyGenerator groups IPv6 addresses by subnet so one user cannot
  // rotate through addresses in their own range
  keyGenerator: (request) =>
    `${String(request.body?.email ?? "").toLowerCase()}|${ipKeyGenerator(request.ip)}`,
  store: new RedisStore({
    prefix: "signin:",
    sendCommand: (...args) => redisClient.sendCommand(args),
  }),
});

app.use("/api", apiLimiter);
app.post("/api/sign-in", express.json(), signInLimiter, signInHandler);

The default key is the client IP (with IPv6 grouped by subnet). Option names and header formats have changed across major versions of express-rate-limit, so check the documentation for the version you install.

docs.title: A token bucket in plain JavaScript (single process)
docs.text:
// Illustrates the algorithm; use a shared store for multiple instances
const buckets = new Map();

function allowRequest(key, capacity = 10, refillPerSecond = 1) {
  const now = Date.now();
  const bucket = buckets.get(key) ?? { tokens: capacity, updatedAt: now };

  // Add tokens for the time elapsed since the last request
  const elapsedSeconds = (now - bucket.updatedAt) / 1000;
  bucket.tokens = Math.min(capacity, bucket.tokens + elapsedSeconds * refillPerSecond);
  bucket.updatedAt = now;

  const allowed = bucket.tokens >= 1;
  if (allowed) bucket.tokens -= 1;

  buckets.set(key, bucket);
  return allowed;
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Choose keys deliberately: per user or API key when authenticated, per IP (or IPv6 prefix) otherwise, and combinations for sign-in.
  • Configure trust proxy precisely so the client IP is correct and cannot be spoofed.
  • Use a shared store for limits when running more than one instance, with atomic operations.
  • Apply stricter limits to expensive or sensitive actions (sign-in, OTP, SMS, password reset, exports, AI calls).
  • Return 429 with Retry-After and quota headers; document your limits.
  • Layer limits: edge, gateway or proxy, and application.
  • Monitor how often limits trigger; tune them from real traffic.
  • Decide fail-open versus fail-closed behavior when the limiter's store is down.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every user is throttled at once. Symptom: 429s for everyone right after an infrastructure change, such as adding a load balancer. Detect: the limiter keys in logs all show the same IP — the proxy's; express-rate-limit also logs a validation error (ERR_ERL_UNEXPECTED_X_FORWARDED_FOR) when X-Forwarded-For arrives but trust proxy is off. Cause: trust proxy is unset or counts the wrong number of hops. Fix: set it to the exact number of proxies and check request.ip in a test request.
  • Clients exceed the documented limit several times over. Symptom: a client with a limit of 100 per minute makes about 300. Detect: request counts per key summed across instances. Cause: each instance keeps its own in-memory counter. Fix: use a shared store such as Redis.
  • A Redis outage takes the API down. Symptom: every request fails while Redis is unreachable. Detect: store connection errors from the limiter. Cause: the limiter blocks traffic when its store fails (the default in express-rate-limit). Fix: choose deliberately — set passOnStoreError: true to fail open for general limits, and keep failing closed for sign-in.
  • 429s keep climbing after the spike ends. Symptom: the rejected rate stays high even though real users have gone. Detect: the same clients retry within milliseconds of each 429. Cause: clients ignore Retry-After and retry without backoff. Fix: always send Retry-After, document it, and use backoff with jitter in your SDKs.
  • A whole office is locked out of sign-in. Symptom: support tickets from many users at one company. Detect: many accounts share one IP that hits the per-IP limit. Cause: sign-in limited by IP only. Fix: key by account and IP together, and give per-IP limits more headroom.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Rate limit: the maximum number of requests allowed per time window.
  • Throttling: slowing or queuing excess requests instead of rejecting.
  • Quota: a total allowance over a longer billing period.
  • Window: the time period over which requests are counted.
  • Token bucket: a bucket of tokens refilled at a fixed rate; requests spend tokens.
  • Leaky bucket: a queue drained at a constant rate.
  • Burst: a short spike of requests above the average rate.
  • Fail open / fail closed: allow or deny traffic when the limiter cannot decide.
  • Retry-After: a response header telling the client when to retry.
  • X-Forwarded-For: a header carrying the original client IP through proxies.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Per-instance in-memory limits in a multi-instance deployment.
  • Trusting X-Forwarded-For from anyone, letting attackers pick their IP.
  • Not configuring trust proxy, so every client shares the proxy's IP and the whole site gets limited together.
  • Only limiting by IP for sign-in, which lets distributed attacks through and blocks offices behind one NAT.
  • Returning 500 or 403 instead of 429 for limited requests.
  • No Retry-After, leaving clients to guess and retry aggressively.
  • Non-atomic read-then-write counters in Redis, which miscount under concurrency.
  • "Rate limiting stops DDoS." It helps, but volumetric attacks must be absorbed at the network edge.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is the fixed window algorithm vulnerable to bursts at window boundaries?
  2. How does a token bucket allow bursts while enforcing an average rate?
  3. Why must distributed rate limiting use atomic operations in a shared store?
  4. What can go wrong when an app behind a load balancer reads the client IP incorrectly?
  5. Which headers should accompany a 429 response, and how should clients react?
  6. Where in the request path would you enforce per-IP, per-API-key, and per-action limits?

docs.text:
• MDN: 429 Too Many Requests
  • MDN: Retry-After
  • RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes (429)
  • Express: Behind proxies (trust proxy)
  • OWASP API Security Top 10

docs.title: Real-Time Communication: Polling, SSE, and WebSockets
docs.text: Plain HTTP is request-response: the client asks, the server answers, and the server cannot speak first. Real-time features — chat, live notifications, dashboards, collaborative editing, order tracking — need the server to push updates as they happen. There are four main techniques: short polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and WebSockets. Each fits different needs.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Choosing the wrong technique is expensive. Polling every second from 50,000 clients creates huge load for mostly empty responses. Using WebSockets for a simple one-way notification feed adds connection management, scaling, and proxy complexity you did not need. Understanding the trade-offs lets you pick the simplest approach that meets the latency and direction requirements, and plan for scaling stateful connections across multiple servers.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Slack Socket Mode. Slack apps can receive Events API payloads and interactive events over a WebSocket instead of exposing a public HTTP Request URL — useful for apps behind a firewall (Slack: Using Socket Mode).
  • Streaming AI responses with SSE. Anthropic's Messages API streams responses incrementally as server-sent events, so text appears as it is generated instead of after the whole answer is ready (Anthropic: streaming messages).
  • Mastodon's streaming API offers the same real-time updates either as server-sent events over a long-lived HTTP connection or over a WebSocket, letting each client pick (Mastodon: streaming API).

Popular tools and providers: the ws library and Socket.IO for Node.js, the browser EventSource API, Redis pub/sub for fan-out across instances, and hosted services such as Ably, Pusher, and AWS API Gateway WebSocket APIs.

docs.title: Short polling
docs.text:
The client asks for updates on a fixed interval.

Client                    Server
  │── GET /notifications ──►│  nothing new
  │◄──────── 200 [] ────────│
  │      (wait 5 s)          │
  │── GET /notifications ──►│  nothing new
  │◄──────── 200 [] ────────│
  │      (wait 5 s)          │
  │── GET /notifications ──►│  one new item
  │◄──── 200 [{...}] ───────│
  • Simple; works everywhere; stateless on the server; easy to cache and scale.
  • Latency is up to the interval; most requests return nothing; load grows with clients × frequency.
  • Fine for infrequent updates (every 30–60 seconds) or low client counts.
  • Use conditional requests (ETag/If-None-Match → 304) or a since cursor to keep responses small.

docs.title: Long polling
docs.text:
The client makes a request; the server holds it open until there is new data or a timeout (for example, 30 seconds), then responds. The client immediately sends the next request.

Client                    Server
  │── GET /updates?since=41 ─►│  hold...
  │                           │  (event happens at 12 s)
  │◄──── 200 [{id: 42}] ──────│
  │── GET /updates?since=42 ─►│  hold... (no event for 30 s)
  │◄──────── 204 ─────────────│  timeout: empty response
  │── GET /updates?since=42 ─►│  hold...
  • Near real-time with plain HTTP; works through almost any proxy.
  • Each waiting client holds a connection; there is overhead per message (a full request/response); ordering and missed events need a cursor.
  • Historically used as a fallback when WebSockets were not available.

docs.title: Server-Sent Events (SSE)
docs.text:
SSE is a standard for one-way server-to-client streaming over a normal HTTP response that stays open. The server sends a response with Content-Type: text/event-stream and writes events as text.

Event stream format — fields separated by newlines, events separated by a blank line:

retry: 5000

id: 42
event: order-status
data: {"orderId":"812","status":"shipped"}

id: 43
data: plain message on the default "message" event

: this line is a comment (often used as a keep-alive)
Field Meaning data: The event payload (multiple data: lines join with newlines) event: Event type; the browser dispatches it to listeners for that name id: Event ID; the browser remembers the last one retry: Reconnection delay in milliseconds : Comment, ignored by the client

Browser side, the EventSource API:

const source = new EventSource("/api/orders/812/events");
source.addEventListener("order-status", (event) => {
  const update = JSON.parse(event.data);
  console.log(update.status);
});
source.onerror = () => {
  // The browser reconnects automatically
};

Key properties:

  • Automatic reconnection: if the connection drops, the browser reconnects and sends a Last-Event-ID header with the last ID it saw, so the server can resend missed events.
  • One direction only: the client sends data through normal HTTP requests.
  • Text only (send JSON as text); works with normal HTTP infrastructure, cookies, and authentication.
  • Over HTTP/1.1, browsers limit connections per domain (about six), and each open EventSource uses one — which matters with many tabs. HTTP/2 multiplexing removes most of this limit.
  • EventSource cannot set custom headers such as Authorization; use cookies or a fetch-based SSE client if you need headers.

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
A WebSocket is a persistent, full-duplex connection: both client and server can send messages at any time over one TCP connection. It starts as an HTTP request that asks to upgrade the protocol:

GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
Origin: https://example.com

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

(now both sides exchange WebSocket frames: text, binary, ping, pong, close)

  • Low overhead per message after the handshake; true bidirectional, low-latency messaging.
  • Supports text and binary data.
  • Stateful: each server holds open connections, which affects scaling, deploys, and load balancing.
  • No built-in reconnection, message acknowledgments, rooms, or replay — you build them or use a library.
  • Use wss:// (WebSocket over TLS) in production.

Protocol-level details — framing, the accept-key calculation, close codes — are covered in WebSockets.

docs.title: The ws library and Socket.IO
docs.text:
• ws: a fast, minimal WebSocket implementation for Node.js. You get raw WebSocket connections and handle message formats, heartbeats, and reconnection yourself.
  • Socket.IO: a higher-level library with its own protocol on top of WebSocket (with HTTP long-polling fallback). It adds automatic reconnection, acknowledgments (callbacks when a message is received), rooms and namespaces for broadcasting to groups, and adapters for scaling. A Socket.IO client cannot talk to a plain WebSocket server, and vice versa.

docs.title: Authentication for WebSockets
docs.text:
The browser WebSocket API cannot set custom headers like Authorization on the handshake. Common approaches:

  • Cookies: if the WebSocket endpoint is on the same site, the session cookie is sent with the upgrade request. Validate it during the handshake, and check the Origin header, because cross-site pages can also open WebSockets to your server with the user's cookies (cross-site WebSocket hijacking).
  • Short-lived ticket: the client calls an authenticated HTTP endpoint to get a one-time token, then connects with it (for example, in the first message, or briefly in the query string — query strings may appear in logs, so keep the token single-use and short-lived).
  • First message auth: accept the connection, require an authentication message within a few seconds, and close it otherwise.

Authorize every message or subscription, not just the connection: a user allowed to connect is not necessarily allowed to join every room. Also handle tokens or sessions that expire while a connection stays open.

docs.title: Heartbeats
docs.text:
Idle connections can be silently dropped by proxies, load balancers, NAT devices, or mobile networks, and a server may not notice a vanished client for a long time. Heartbeats detect this:

  • The server sends a WebSocket ping frame periodically; the client replies with a pong automatically. If no pong arrives before the next check, terminate the connection.
  • For SSE, send a comment line (: ping) every 15–30 seconds to keep proxies from closing idle streams.
  • Set proxy timeouts (for example, Nginx proxy_read_timeout) longer than the heartbeat interval.

docs.title: Scaling real-time connections
docs.text:
With several server instances behind a load balancer, two problems appear:

  1. Connection affinity: Socket.IO's long-polling fallback sends several HTTP requests that must reach the same server, requiring sticky sessions. Pure WebSocket and SSE connections are single long-lived connections, so affinity matters less, but reconnects may land elsewhere.
  2. Cross-instance delivery: user A is connected to server 1, user B to server 2. A message for B must reach server 2. The standard solution is a pub/sub backbone: every instance publishes events to Redis (or another broker) and subscribes to receive events for its connected clients.

Socket.IO provides a Redis adapter for this. Also plan for:

  • Load balancer support for upgrades and long-lived connections (see load balancing).
  • Deploys: restarting a server drops its connections; clients must reconnect with backoff and jitter so they do not all reconnect at once.
  • Connection limits: file descriptors and memory per connection.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Short polling Long polling SSE WebSockets Direction Client pulls Client pulls (server delays reply) Server → client Both ways Latency Up to the interval Low Low Lowest Protocol Plain HTTP Plain HTTP HTTP (text/event-stream) Upgrade to WebSocket Reconnection N/A Client loops Built into EventSource You implement it (or library) Binary data Yes (HTTP) Yes No (text) Yes Server state Stateless Held requests Open connections Open connections Infrastructure Anything Anything Most HTTP infra; disable proxy buffering Needs upgrade support Good for Rare updates, simple needs Fallback, moderate needs Notifications, feeds, progress, AI token streaming Chat, games, collaboration, live trading

docs.title: How to choose
docs.text:
1. Updates are infrequent and seconds of delay are fine → short polling.
  2. The server pushes, the client rarely sends → SSE.
  3. Both sides send frequently with low latency → WebSockets (or Socket.IO if you want rooms, acknowledgments, and reconnection built in).
  4. Very restrictive networks with no streaming support → long polling.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use real-time push when:

  • Users act on updates within seconds: chat, live dashboards, order tracking, collaborative editing, streaming AI output.
  • Polling would mean many requests that mostly return nothing.

Do not use it when:

  • Data changes rarely (every few minutes or less) — short polling or a refresh button is simpler and cheaper.
  • The update can wait for the next page load or an email.
  • You have no plan for scaling connections, reconnecting, and resuming after missed events.
Need Choose Not Hourly weather widget Short polling WebSockets Deployment or export progress bar SSE WebSockets Notification feed SSE Polling every second Chat, multiplayer game, live cursors WebSockets (or Socket.IO) SSE plus many POSTs Proxies that break streaming Long polling SSE Streaming AI tokens to a browser SSE Long polling

docs.title: SSE endpoint in Express
docs.text:
import { EventEmitter } from "node:events";

const orderEvents = new EventEmitter(); // in production: Redis pub/sub

app.get("/api/orders/:id/events", authenticate, (request, response) => {
  response.set({
    "Content-Type": "text/event-stream",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
    Connection: "keep-alive",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": "no", // ask Nginx not to buffer the stream
  });
  response.flushHeaders();

  // Resend anything missed since the client's last event (if you store them)
  const lastEventId = request.get("last-event-id");
  // ...look up and write events after lastEventId...

  const send = (event) => {
    response.write(`id: ${event.id}\n`);
    response.write("event: order-status\n");
    response.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify(event.data)}\n\n`);
  };

  const listener = (event) => {
    if (event.data.orderId === request.params.id) send(event);
  };
  orderEvents.on("update", listener);

  // Keep-alive comment so proxies do not close an idle connection
  const heartbeat = setInterval(() => response.write(": ping\n\n"), 20000);

  // Clean up when the client disconnects
  request.on("close", () => {
    clearInterval(heartbeat);
    orderEvents.off("update", listener);
  });
});

docs.title: WebSocket server with ws, origin check, and heartbeats
docs.text:
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { WebSocketServer } from "ws";

const server = createServer(app); // share the port with Express
const wss = new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true });

server.on("upgrade", async (request, socket, head) => {
  // Reject cross-site connections and unauthenticated users
  if (request.headers.origin !== "https://app.example.com") {
    socket.write("HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden\r\n\r\n");
    return socket.destroy();
  }
  const user = await userFromSessionCookie(request.headers.cookie);
  if (!user) {
    socket.write("HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized\r\n\r\n");
    return socket.destroy();
  }
  wss.handleUpgrade(request, socket, head, (ws) => {
    wss.emit("connection", ws, request, user);
  });
});

wss.on("connection", (ws, request, user) => {
  ws.isAlive = true;
  ws.on("pong", () => { ws.isAlive = true; });

  ws.on("message", (raw) => {
    let message;
    try {
      message = JSON.parse(raw.toString());
    } catch {
      return ws.close(1008, "Invalid message"); // 1008 = policy violation
    }
    // Validate and authorize each message before acting on it
    handleMessage(user, message, ws);
  });
});

// Heartbeat: terminate connections that did not answer the last ping
const interval = setInterval(() => {
  for (const ws of wss.clients) {
    if (!ws.isAlive) {
      ws.terminate();
      continue;
    }
    ws.isAlive = false;
    ws.ping();
  }
}, 30000);

wss.on("close", () => clearInterval(interval));
server.listen(3000);

docs.title: Socket.IO with rooms and the Redis adapter (sketch)
docs.text:
import { Server } from "socket.io";
import { createAdapter } from "@socket.io/redis-adapter";
import { createClient } from "redis";

const pubClient = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
const subClient = pubClient.duplicate();
await Promise.all([pubClient.connect(), subClient.connect()]);

const io = new Server(server, { cors: { origin: "https://app.example.com" } });
io.adapter(createAdapter(pubClient, subClient)); // broadcast across instances

io.on("connection", (socket) => {
  socket.on("join-room", (roomId, ack) => {
    // Authorize before joining
    socket.join(roomId);
    ack({ ok: true });
  });
  socket.on("chat-message", ({ roomId, text }) => {
    io.to(roomId).emit("chat-message", { text, from: socket.id });
  });
});

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Choose the simplest technique that meets direction and latency needs.
  • Authenticate during the handshake, check Origin, and authorize every message or subscription.
  • Use heartbeats; tune proxy timeouts to exceed them.
  • Make clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter; resume from a cursor or Last-Event-ID.
  • Use a pub/sub backbone (such as Redis) when running multiple instances.
  • Validate and size-limit every incoming message.
  • Disable response buffering for SSE at proxies.
  • Use wss:// and HTTPS in production.
  • Clean up listeners and timers when connections close to avoid leaks.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• SSE events arrive in bursts or only at the end. Symptom: progress jumps from 0% to 100%. Detect: events reach the client together, much later than the server wrote them. Cause: a proxy (often Nginx) buffers the response, or compression middleware holds data back. Fix: send X-Accel-Buffering: no or turn off proxy_buffering for that location, and exclude text/event-stream from compression.
  • Connections drop every 60 seconds. Symptom: clients reconnect once a minute while idle. Detect: close events at a regular interval in server logs. Cause: a proxy or load balancer idle timeout (Nginx's proxy_read_timeout defaults to 60 seconds) is shorter than the time between messages. Fix: send heartbeats more often than the timeout, and raise the proxy timeout for streaming routes.
  • Memory grows until the process restarts. Symptom: heap usage climbs with the number of connections ever opened. Detect: heap snapshots show retained listeners or sockets; MaxListenersExceededWarning in logs. Cause: listeners and timers are not removed when clients disconnect, or dead connections are never detected. Fix: clean up on close, and terminate connections that miss a heartbeat.
  • Messages reach only some users. Symptom: a chat message is seen by users on one server but not another. Detect: the recipients that missed it are connected to a different instance. Cause: broadcasting only to local connections. Fix: add a pub/sub backbone such as the Socket.IO Redis adapter or Redis channels.
  • A deploy causes a thundering herd. Symptom: CPU and authentication load spike right after each release. Detect: thousands of reconnects in the same second. Cause: every client reconnects immediately when its server restarts. Fix: reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, and drain connections gradually during deploys.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Short polling: repeated requests on a fixed interval.
  • Long polling: a request held open until data is available or a timeout.
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE): one-way event streaming over HTTP using text/event-stream.
  • EventSource: the browser API for consuming SSE.
  • Last-Event-ID: header sent on SSE reconnection with the last event ID received.
  • WebSocket: a full-duplex protocol established through an HTTP upgrade.
  • 101 Switching Protocols: the response that completes a WebSocket upgrade.
  • Frame: a unit of WebSocket data (text, binary, ping, pong, close).
  • Heartbeat: periodic ping/pong or keep-alive messages to detect dead connections.
  • Sticky session: routing a client's requests to the same server.
  • Pub/sub: a messaging pattern where publishers send to channels and subscribers receive from them.
  • Room: a Socket.IO grouping for broadcasting to a subset of clients.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using WebSockets for one-way notifications where SSE would be simpler.
  • Polling too frequently, multiplying load for empty responses.
  • No Origin check on WebSocket handshakes, enabling cross-site WebSocket hijacking with cookies.
  • Authenticating only at connect time and never authorizing messages or rechecking expired sessions.
  • No heartbeats, leaving dead connections and leaking memory.
  • Broadcasting only within one instance in a multi-instance deployment.
  • Assuming Socket.IO is plain WebSocket. Its clients and servers only talk to each other.
  • Forgetting proxy buffering and timeouts, which break SSE streams.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Compare short polling and long polling in latency and server load.
  2. Describe the SSE event format and how Last-Event-ID helps after a reconnect.
  3. Walk through the WebSocket upgrade handshake. Which status code completes it?
  4. Why can't browsers send an Authorization header with a WebSocket, and what alternatives exist?
  5. How do you deliver a message to a user connected to a different server instance?
  6. Which technique would you choose for a chat app, a deployment progress bar, and a weather widget updated hourly? Why?
