docs.title: REST APIs
docs.text: An API (Application Programming Interface) defines how software systems talk to each other. REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for networked applications, described by Roy Fielding in 2000. In everyday web development, a "REST API" means an HTTP API where URLs identify resources and standard HTTP methods read or change them.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• REST is the most common style for web and mobile backends, and for public APIs from payment, messaging, and cloud providers.
  • It reuses what HTTP already provides (methods, status codes, caching, content negotiation), so clients, proxies, and tools understand it without custom software.
  • A consistent REST design means a developer who has learned one endpoint can guess how the rest work.
  • REST's constraints, especially statelessness, are what let an API scale horizontally behind a load balancer.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe. The Stripe API reference opens with: "The Stripe API is organized around REST. Our API has predictable resource-oriented URLs, accepts form-encoded request bodies, returns JSON-encoded responses, and uses standard HTTP response codes, authentication, and verbs." Note that request bodies are form-encoded, not JSON: REST does not require JSON.
  • GitHub. GitHub's REST API uses resource URLs such as /repos/{owner}/{repo}, standard methods, Link headers for pagination, and ETag-based conditional requests, which reuse HTTP features exactly as REST intends.
  • Shopify moved from REST to GraphQL for its Admin API. Shopify states that the REST Admin API is a legacy API as of October 1, 2024, and that from April 1, 2025, new public apps must be built exclusively with the GraphQL Admin API. REST is common, but not the only choice for large platforms.
  • Slack's Web API is deliberately not REST. Slack describes its Web API as a collection of HTTP RPC-style methods with URLs like https://slack.com/api/METHOD_FAMILY.method, and says it is not a REST API. It is a useful contrast to resource-oriented design.

docs.title: The six REST constraints
docs.text:
Fielding defined REST as a set of constraints. An API is RESTful to the degree that it follows them.

Constraint What it means What it buys you Client-server The user interface and the data storage are separate concerns Frontend and backend evolve independently; many clients share one API Stateless Each request contains everything needed to understand it; the server keeps no session context between requests Any server can handle any request; easy horizontal scaling and retries Cacheable Responses say whether they can be cached Fewer requests, lower latency, less server load Uniform interface Resources are identified by URIs and manipulated through representations using a standard set of methods; messages are self-descriptive Generic clients, proxies, and tools work with every API Layered system A client cannot tell whether it talks to the server directly or through proxies, gateways, and caches Load balancers, CDNs, and API gateways can be added transparently Code on demand (optional) Servers may send executable code, such as JavaScript, to extend the client Rarely used in APIs; the only optional constraint

The uniform interface is the heart of REST. It has four parts:

  1. Identification of resources: every resource has a URI.
  2. Manipulation through representations: clients change a resource by sending a representation of it (for example a JSON document), not by calling remote functions.
  3. Self-descriptive messages: each message carries enough metadata (method, Content-Type, cache headers, status code) to be understood on its own.
  4. Hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS): responses contain links that tell the client what it can do next.

docs.title: Resources and URIs
docs.text:
A resource is any concept the API exposes: a user, an order, a search result, the current weather. A URI names it. A representation is a particular format of its current state, usually JSON.

Naming rules most teams follow:

  • Use nouns, not verbs. The method is the verb. GET /api/orders, not GET /api/getOrders.
  • Use plural collection names. /api/orders for the collection, /api/orders/901 for one item.
  • Nest only for real ownership, and only one level deep. /api/orders/901/items is clear; /api/customers/7/orders/901/items/3/notes is fragile. Once an item has its own ID, give it a top-level path too.
  • Use lowercase and hyphens in paths: /api/shipping-addresses.
  • Keep filters, sorting, and paging in the query string: /api/orders?status=paid&sort=-createdAt&limit=20.
  • Model actions as sub-resources when they do not fit CRUD: POST /api/orders/901/cancellation or POST /api/orders/901/cancel.
/api/orders                      collection
/api/orders/901                  single resource
/api/orders/901/items            sub-collection owned by order 901
/api/orders?status=paid&page=2   filtered view of the collection

docs.title: Methods mapping
docs.text:
Method On a collection (/orders) On an item (/orders/901) GET List orders Read order 901 POST Create a new order Usually not used (or an action) PUT Rarely: replace the whole collection Replace order 901 entirely (or create it at this URI) PATCH Rarely: bulk partial update Update some fields of order 901 DELETE Rarely: delete the whole collection Delete order 901

See HTTP methods for safety and idempotency.

docs.title: Representations
docs.text:
The same resource can have several representations. JSON is the common choice for APIs, but the client can ask for another format with Accept, and the server labels its choice with Content-Type. See content negotiation.

{
  "id": "ord_901",
  "status": "paid",
  "total": { "amount": 4999, "currency": "USD" },
  "createdAt": "2026-11-03T10:15:00Z",
  "customerId": "cus_7"
}

A representation is not the database row. Expose what clients need, hide internal columns, and keep the shape stable even if storage changes.

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text: REST APIs communicate outcomes with HTTP status codes: 200 for reads, 201 with Location for creation, 204 for deletion, 400/422 for invalid input, 401/403 for auth problems, 404 for missing resources, 409 for conflicts. See HTTP status codes.

docs.title: HATEOAS
docs.text:
With hypermedia, a response tells the client which actions are available, the way links and forms do on a web page:

{
  "id": "ord_901",
  "status": "paid",
  "_links": {
    "self": { "href": "/api/orders/901" },
    "items": { "href": "/api/orders/901/items" },
    "cancel": { "href": "/api/orders/901/cancellation", "method": "POST" },
    "customer": { "href": "/api/customers/7" }
  }
}

If the order has shipped, the server simply leaves out the cancel link, and a hypermedia-aware client hides the button. Clients follow links instead of building URLs, so the server can change URLs without breaking them.

In practice, few APIs implement full HATEOAS; most document their URLs and expect clients to build them. Including at least self links and pagination links (next, prev) is common and useful.

docs.title: The Richardson Maturity Model
docs.text:
Leonard Richardson described levels of "REST-ness" for HTTP APIs:

Level Description Example 0: The swamp of POX One URL, one method; everything is a remote procedure call tunneled over HTTP POST /api with {"action": "getOrder", "id": 901} 1: Resources Separate URLs for resources, but still one method POST /api/orders/901 for everything 2: HTTP verbs Resources plus proper methods and status codes GET /api/orders/901 returns 200; DELETE returns 204 3: Hypermedia controls Level 2 plus HATEOAS links Responses include _links to next actions

Most well-designed public APIs sit at level 2, which is what people usually mean by "RESTful".

docs.title: Statelessness in practice
docs.text:
Stateless means the server does not remember anything about the client between requests. Every request must carry what the server needs:

  • Authentication in every request: a token in Authorization, or a session cookie the browser sends automatically.
  • Context in the URL or body: the page number, filters, the ID being edited.

Stateless does not mean the application has no state. Orders and users live in a database; that is resource state, and it is fine. What REST forbids is session state held in one server's memory that the next request depends on (for example "the server remembers you were on page 3"). A server session stored in Redis and looked up by a cookie on every request is a common, pragmatic compromise.

The payoff: any instance can serve any request, crashed instances lose nothing, and failed requests can be retried on another server.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use REST when:

  • The API is public or used by many third parties with different tools; every language has an HTTP client.
  • The domain maps naturally to resources (orders, users, invoices) with create, read, update, and delete operations.
  • You want HTTP caching, CDNs, and standard tooling (curl, OpenAPI, gateways) to work without extra effort.

Consider something else when:

  • Many clients need very different slices of a rich, nested data graph, and over-fetching or many round trips hurt: GraphQL may fit better.
  • Internal services need low-latency, high-throughput, or streaming calls with strict contracts: gRPC may fit better.
  • The API is a set of commands rather than resources (a chat or tooling protocol): an RPC style can be more honest than forcing actions into resources.
Need REST GraphQL gRPC RPC (JSON-RPC, tRPC) Public API for unknown clients Best Good Poor (browser limits, tooling) Fair HTTP caching and CDNs Best Hard No No Clients choose exactly the fields Limited (fields, include) Best No No Internal high-throughput calls Good Fair Best Good Streaming Via SSE or WebSockets Subscriptions Built in Depends on transport

See API styles for the details.

docs.title: A complete resource: articles
docs.text:
Method and path Purpose Request body Success response GET /api/articles?author=7&limit=20&cursor=abc List, filtered and paginated none 200 + list and paging info GET /api/articles/42 Read one none 200 + article POST /api/articles Create {"title": "...", "body": "..."} 201 + Location + article PUT /api/articles/42 Replace Full article 200 + article PATCH /api/articles/42 Update some fields {"title": "New title"} 200 + article DELETE /api/articles/42 Delete none 204 GET /api/articles/42/comments List an article's comments none 200 + list POST /api/articles/42/publication Action: publish none 200 + article

Create:

POST /api/articles HTTP/1.1
Host: api.blog.example
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...

{"title":"Understanding REST","body":"REST is an architectural style..."}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /api/articles/42
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":42,"title":"Understanding REST","body":"REST is an architectural style...",
 "status":"draft","authorId":7,"createdAt":"2026-11-03T10:15:00Z"}

List:

GET /api/articles?author=7&limit=2 HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: private, no-cache

{
  "data": [
    {"id": 42, "title": "Understanding REST", "status": "draft"},
    {"id": 41, "title": "HTTP basics", "status": "published"}
  ],
  "nextCursor": "eyJpZCI6NDF9"
}

Validation error:

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type":"https://api.blog.example/problems/validation","title":"Validation failed",
 "status":422,"errors":[{"field":"title","message":"must not be empty"}]}

docs.title: Implementing it in Express
docs.text:
This is a sketch of the routing layer. An in-memory articleService stands in for the real service, and the handlers not shown answer 501 until you write them.

import express from "express";

// Stand-in for a service layer backed by a database
const articles = new Map([["42", { id: "42", title: "Understanding REST", status: "draft" }]]);
const articleService = {
  list: async () => [...articles.values()],
  findById: async (id) => articles.get(id) ?? null,
};

// Handlers (controllers) call services that hold the business rules
async function listArticles(req, res) {
  res.json({ data: await articleService.list() });
}

async function getArticle(req, res) {
  const article = await articleService.findById(req.params.id);
  if (!article) return res.status(404).json({ title: "Article not found" });
  res.json(article);
}

// Placeholder for createArticle, updateArticle, deleteArticle, publishArticle
const notWrittenYet = (req, res) => res.sendStatus(501);

const router = express.Router();
router.get("/", listArticles);
router.post("/", notWrittenYet);
router.get("/:id", getArticle);
router.patch("/:id", notWrittenYet);
router.delete("/:id", notWrittenYet);
router.post("/:id/publication", notWrittenYet);

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.use("/api/articles", router);
app.listen(3000);

GET /api/articles/42 returns the article, GET /api/articles/7 returns 404, and the unwritten handlers return 501 Not Implemented.

See routing and routers and project structure for how to organize this, and authentication and authorization for protecting it.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Design resources around the client's needs, not your table layout.
  • Be consistent in naming, casing, pagination, and error format across every endpoint. See API design best practices.
  • Use methods and status codes by their HTTP meaning.
  • Keep the server stateless; store shared state in a database or cache.
  • Return the created or updated resource so clients avoid an extra request.
  • Paginate every collection from day one.
  • Version deliberately and never break existing clients silently.
  • Document the API with OpenAPI so clients and tests share one contract.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Mobile app crashes right after a backend deploy. Detect: the client crash reporter spikes with JSON parsing or "missing field" errors that match the deploy time. Cause: a renamed or removed response field, a breaking change. Fix: make only additive changes, version breaking ones, and run contract tests against the old clients' expectations.
  • Users can read other users' records. Detect: access logs show one account fetching many sequential IDs (/api/orders/1001, /1002, ...), or a security review finds it. Cause: the handler checks that the user is logged in but not that the resource belongs to them (an insecure direct object reference). Fix: check ownership on every request, ideally in the query (WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2).
  • Screens are slow because of many requests. Detect: traces show one page view making ten or more sequential API calls. Cause: resources shaped like tables instead of client needs. Fix: add include/expand options or a backend-for-frontend endpoint; run independent calls in parallel.
  • A list endpoint times out as data grows. Detect: latency and response size of GET /collection grow week over week; slow-query logs show full scans. Cause: no pagination, or no index on the sort column. Fix: paginate with a capped limit and index the sort and filter columns.
  • Requests fail on some instances only. Detect: errors correlate with the instance ID in logs. Cause: per-instance state (in-memory sessions, local uploaded files) that breaks statelessness. Fix: move shared state to a database, cache, or object storage.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• API: a contract that defines how programs interact.
  • REST: an architectural style defined by constraints such as statelessness and a uniform interface.
  • Resource: any named concept the API exposes.
  • URI: the identifier of a resource.
  • Representation: a specific format of a resource's state, such as JSON.
  • Endpoint: a method plus a path, such as GET /api/articles/:id.
  • Collection: a resource that contains other resources.
  • HATEOAS: responses include links describing available next actions.
  • Stateless: the server keeps no client session context between requests.
  • Idempotent: repeating a request leaves the same server state.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "REST means JSON." REST is an architectural style; JSON is just one representation format.
  • "REST means CRUD over HTTP." CRUD maps neatly to REST, but REST is about resources, representations, and constraints, not only database operations.
  • Verbs in URLs (/createUser, /getOrders) duplicate what methods already say.
  • Returning 200 for every outcome and putting the real result in the body.
  • Deep nesting that forces clients to know a whole ownership chain to reach an item.
  • Exposing database internals, such as column names and auto-increment IDs, as the public contract.
  • Calling an API RESTful because it uses HTTP. Level 0 APIs use HTTP but are RPC.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Name the six REST constraints and say which one is optional.
  2. What does "stateless" forbid, and what does it still allow?
  3. Design the endpoints for a "comments on a post" resource, with methods, paths, and success codes.
  4. What is HATEOAS, and why do most APIs only partially implement it?
  5. At which Richardson level is an API that uses proper URLs and methods but no links?
  6. How would you model the action "cancel an order" in a REST API?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Primary source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Chapter 5 defines REST and its constraints.
  • MDN: REST gives a concise overview.
  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics defines the methods, status codes, and headers REST APIs rely on.
  • OWASP: REST Security Cheat Sheet.
  • Next: API design best practices.

docs.title: Sessions, Cookies, and JWT
docs.text: HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone, and the server does not remember that the same browser signed in a minute ago. Sessions, cookies, and tokens are the mechanisms that carry "this client is already authenticated" from one request to the next. Choosing and configuring them correctly decides how secure, scalable, and revocable your sign-in system is.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: After a user signs in, every later request must prove who it comes from. If that proof is easy to steal, forge, or replay, an attacker becomes the user. If it cannot be revoked, a stolen credential stays valid until it expires. If it is configured loosely, cross-site attacks can make the browser send it on the attacker's behalf. Understanding cookie attributes, session stores, and JWT verification is therefore core backend knowledge, not an implementation detail.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google Sign-In ID tokens. Google documents the checks an app must run on every ID token: the signature against keys from the jwks_uri in its discovery document, then iss, aud (your client ID), and exp (Google Identity: OpenID Connect).
  • Firebase Authentication. Firebase ID tokens are RS256-signed JWTs. The Admin SDK's verifyIdToken() returns the decoded token when it has the correct format, is not expired, and is properly signed — and the docs note that this does not check whether the token was revoked, which is the classic JWT trade-off (Firebase: Verify ID tokens).
  • Refresh token rotation at Auth0. Each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the one that was used; if an already-used refresh token is presented again, Auth0 also invalidates the most recently issued token in that family (Auth0: refresh token rotation).
  • SameSite by default in Chrome. Chrome treats cookies that have no SameSite attribute as SameSite=Lax, which blocks most cross-site sends and therefore most CSRF (web.dev: SameSite cookies explained).

Popular tools and providers: express-session with a Redis store, the jose and jsonwebtoken libraries, Passport.js, and hosted token services such as Auth0, Okta, Amazon Cognito, and Firebase Authentication.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
A cookie is a small name-value pair the server asks the browser to store with the Set-Cookie response header. The browser then sends it back automatically in the Cookie request header on matching requests.

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: sid=3f9a1c...; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=3600

GET /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Cookie: sid=3f9a1c...

docs.title: Set-Cookie attributes
docs.text:
Attribute What it does Guidance Expires=<date> Absolute expiry time Without Expires or Max-Age, it is a session cookie removed when the browser session ends Max-Age=<seconds> Relative lifetime; takes precedence over Expires Max-Age=0 deletes the cookie Domain=<domain> Sends the cookie to that domain and its subdomains Omit it to restrict the cookie to the exact host that set it (safer) Path=<path> Sends the cookie only for URLs under this path Not a security boundary; usually Path=/ Secure Sends the cookie only over HTTPS Always set for authentication cookies HttpOnly Hides the cookie from JavaScript (document.cookie) Always set for session/refresh cookies; limits damage from XSS SameSite=Strict Never sent on cross-site requests, including clicking a link from another site Strongest CSRF protection; can feel like being "signed out" when arriving from links SameSite=Lax Sent on top-level navigations (GET links) but not on cross-site subrequests or form POSTs Good default; Chromium browsers treat cookies without SameSite as Lax, but other browsers differ — always set it explicitly SameSite=None Sent on all cross-site requests Requires Secure; only for genuine cross-site use (embedded widgets, separate API domain) Partitioned Stores the cookie separately per top-level site (CHIPS) For third-party embeds that need state without cross-site tracking

Cookie name prefixes let the browser enforce rules:

  • __Secure-name: must be set with Secure from an HTTPS page.
  • __Host-name: must be Secure, must have Path=/, and must not have a Domain attribute — so it is locked to one exact host. This is the best choice for a session cookie.

"Same-site" is not the same as "same-origin": app.example.com and api.example.com are different origins but the same site (same registrable domain). A request from the app to the API is therefore a same-site request, so cookies that api.example.com set with SameSite=Lax or Strict are still sent with it. (Each host still only receives its own cookies, unless a cookie was set with a shared Domain.)

docs.title: Session-based authentication
docs.text:
The server keeps the session state and gives the client only a random, unguessable session ID.

Browser                         Server                     Session store
   │  POST /login (email, pw)     │                            (Redis)
   │─────────────────────────────►│ verify password            │
   │                              │ create session ───────────►│ sid → { userId, roles,
   │  Set-Cookie: sid=abc; HttpOnly│                            │        createdAt }
   │◄─────────────────────────────│                            │
   │                              │                            │
   │  GET /api/orders             │                            │
   │  Cookie: sid=abc             │ look up sid ──────────────►│
   │─────────────────────────────►│◄─────────── { userId } ────│
   │  200 OK (user's orders)      │                            │
   │◄─────────────────────────────│                            │
   │  POST /logout                │ delete sid ───────────────►│

Key properties:

  • The cookie carries no user data, only a random identifier (at least 128 bits of entropy from a secure random generator).
  • All state lives on the server, so the server can revoke a session instantly by deleting it.
  • With several app instances, the store must be shared — usually Redis or a database — instead of process memory.
  • Regenerate the session ID on sign-in (and privilege changes) to prevent session fixation, where an attacker plants a known session ID before the victim signs in.
  • Use an idle timeout (expire after inactivity) and an absolute timeout (expire after a maximum lifetime regardless of activity).

docs.title: Token-based authentication
docs.text:
Instead of storing state, the server issues a signed token that contains the claims it needs. The client sends it on each request, commonly in the Authorization header:

GET /api/orders HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOi...

The server verifies the signature and expiry, then trusts the claims without a database lookup. This is convenient for APIs, mobile apps, and service-to-service calls, but it makes revocation harder.

docs.title: JWT structure
docs.text:
A JSON Web Token (RFC 7519) has three base64url-encoded parts separated by dots:

header.payload.signature

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9      ← header  {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}
.eyJzdWIiOiJ1XzQyIiwiZXhwIjoxNzk...      ← payload {"sub":"u_42","exp":1790000000}
.Qm9vZ3VzU2lnbmF0dXJlRXhhbXBsZQ          ← signature over header + "." + payload
  • Header: the algorithm (alg) and type, and sometimes a key ID (kid).
  • Payload: the claims.
  • Signature: proves the header and payload were produced by someone holding the key and have not been modified.

A signed JWT (JWS) is not encrypted. Anyone can base64url-decode the payload and read it, so never put passwords, secrets, or sensitive personal data in it. (Encrypted JWTs, JWE, exist but are less common.)

docs.title: Registered claims
docs.text: Claim Meaning What the server checks iss Issuer — who created the token Matches the expected issuer sub Subject — whom the token is about (user ID) Used as the identity aud Audience — who the token is intended for Includes this API; rejects tokens meant for another service exp Expiration time (seconds since epoch) Current time is before exp (allow a small clock skew) nbf Not before Current time is after nbf iat Issued at Useful for age checks and "revoke tokens issued before X" jti JWT ID — unique token identifier Used for denylists and replay detection

docs.title: Signing algorithms and JWKS
docs.text:
Algorithm Type Keys When to use HS256 HMAC with SHA-256 One shared secret signs and verifies A single service that both issues and verifies tokens RS256 RSA signature Private key signs; public key verifies Many services verify, only the issuer can sign ES256 ECDSA (P-256) signature Private/public key pair, smaller signatures than RSA Same as RS256, more compact

With asymmetric algorithms, the issuer publishes its public keys as a JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) at a URL. Verifiers fetch and cache it, pick the key by the token's kid, and can follow key rotation without redeploying.

docs.title: Verifying a JWT — every step
docs.text:
1. Parse the three parts; reject malformed tokens.
  2. Check the alg against an allowlist you configured (for example, only RS256). Never let the token choose the algorithm.
  3. Select the key (by kid from your JWKS, or your configured secret).
  4. Verify the signature.
  5. Validate exp and nbf (with a small clock tolerance), iss, and aud.
  6. Only then trust sub and the other claims; apply any revocation check.

docs.title: Attacks to know
docs.text:
• alg: none: an attacker sends an unsigned token with "alg":"none". A library that honors the header accepts it. Defense: an explicit algorithm allowlist.
  • Algorithm confusion: a server expects RS256 and verifies with an RSA public key. An attacker crafts an HS256 token signed using that public key as the HMAC secret. A naive library uses the public key as an HMAC secret and accepts it. Defense: fix the algorithm per key; never accept both symmetric and asymmetric algorithms with the same key.
  • Weak HMAC secrets: short or guessable secrets can be brute forced offline from any captured token. Use at least 256 bits of randomness.
  • Missing aud check: a token issued for one service is replayed against another that trusts the same issuer.

docs.title: Where to store tokens in the browser
docs.text:
Storage XSS exposure CSRF exposure Notes localStorage / sessionStorage Readable by any script on the page — XSS steals the token None (not sent automatically) Simple, but one XSS bug leaks long-lived credentials In-memory JavaScript variable Still usable by injected script while the page is open, but not persisted None Lost on reload; often paired with a refresh cookie HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookie Script cannot read it (XSS can still make requests while the page is open) Sent automatically — needs SameSite and/or CSRF tokens Generally the safer choice for browser apps

A common browser pattern: keep a short-lived access token in memory and the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie scoped to the refresh endpoint.

docs.title: Access tokens, refresh tokens, and rotation
docs.text:
• Access token: short-lived (for example, 5–15 minutes), sent with every API request.
  • Refresh token: longer-lived, sent only to the token endpoint to get a new access token. Store it server-side (or a hash of it) so it can be revoked.

Refresh token rotation: every refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. Reuse detection: if an already-used refresh token is presented again, someone has a stolen copy — revoke the whole token family and force a new sign-in.

docs.title: Revoking JWTs
docs.text:
A signed token stays valid until exp unless the server checks something else. Options:

  • Short expiry: limits the window; combine with revocable refresh tokens.
  • Denylist: store revoked jti values (in Redis, with TTL equal to the remaining lifetime) and check on each request.
  • Token version: store tokenVersion on the user; put it in the token; increment it to invalidate every existing token ("sign out everywhere").
  • Introspection: ask the authorization server whether a token is active (common with opaque tokens in OAuth).

Every option except short expiry reintroduces a lookup — the main "stateless" advantage of JWTs shrinks once revocation is required.

docs.title: Sessions versus JWT
docs.text:
Aspect Server-side sessions JWT access tokens State Stored on the server Carried in the token Revocation Immediate (delete session) Hard; needs short expiry, denylist, or versioning Lookup per request Yes (fast with Redis) No (signature check only) Size on the wire Small random ID Larger; grows with claims Cross-domain / mobile / service-to-service Awkward Natural fit Data freshness Always current (roles read from store) Claims stale until the token expires Typical fit Traditional web apps, same-site SPAs Distributed APIs, mobile clients, OAuth/OIDC

Neither is universally better. For a browser app talking to its own backend, an HttpOnly session cookie is often the simplest secure option.

docs.title: CSRF with cookie-based authentication
docs.text:
Because browsers attach cookies automatically, a malicious site can trigger a request to your API that carries the victim's cookie — cross-site request forgery (CSRF). Defenses:

  • SameSite=Lax or Strict on authentication cookies blocks most cross-site sends.
  • CSRF tokens: the server issues a random token (for example, in a readable cookie or page) and requires it in a header or form field on state-changing requests; a cross-site page cannot read it. The "double submit cookie" pattern compares a cookie value with a header value.
  • Check Origin (or Sec-Fetch-Site) on state-changing requests.
  • Never change state on GET.

Tokens sent in an Authorization header are not sent automatically, so they are not vulnerable to CSRF — but they are exposed to XSS if stored in JavaScript-readable storage.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text:
• Sessions: delete the server-side session and clear the cookie (Max-Age=0 with the same Path and Domain).
  • JWT: discard tokens on the client, revoke the refresh token on the server, and (if needed) denylist the current access token's jti.
  • Sign out everywhere: delete all sessions for the user or bump the token version.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a server-side session in an HttpOnly cookie when:

  • A browser app talks to its own backend on the same site.
  • You need instant revocation (sign out, ban, role change).
  • You want the simplest secure default with no token handling in JavaScript.

Use JWT access tokens when:

  • Many services must verify identity without calling a central store.
  • Clients are mobile apps, CLIs, or other services rather than browsers.
  • You are integrating with OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect providers that issue them.

Avoid:

  • Long-lived JWTs without refresh tokens or a revocation plan.
  • Putting tokens in localStorage for apps that handle sensitive data.
  • SameSite=None cookies unless the app truly needs cross-site requests.
Scenario Recommended Why Server-rendered site or same-site SPA Session ID in __Host- cookie Revocable, not readable by scripts SPA on a different site from its API Short access token in memory + refresh token in HttpOnly cookie Limits XSS exposure while working cross-site Mobile app Access + refresh tokens in the platform's secure storage No cookie jar; tokens sent in Authorization Service-to-service calls Short-lived JWT from OAuth client credentials Verified locally; no user session involved Need to kick a user out immediately Sessions, or JWT plus a denylist check Plain JWTs stay valid until exp

docs.title: Setting a secure session cookie in Express
docs.text:
response.cookie("__Host-sid", sessionId, {
  httpOnly: true,       // not readable by JavaScript
  secure: true,         // HTTPS only (required for the __Host- prefix)
  sameSite: "lax",      // blocks most cross-site sends
  path: "/",            // required for the __Host- prefix
  maxAge: 60 * 60 * 1000, // 1 hour in milliseconds (Express converts it)
});

docs.title: Issuing and verifying JWTs with the jose library
docs.text:
import { SignJWT, jwtVerify } from "jose";

// At least 256 bits of randomness, loaded from configuration
const secret = new TextEncoder().encode(process.env.JWT_SECRET);

export async function issueAccessToken(user) {
  return new SignJWT({ role: user.role })
    .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "HS256" })
    .setSubject(user.id)
    .setIssuer("https://auth.example.com")
    .setAudience("orders-api")
    .setIssuedAt()
    .setExpirationTime("15m")
    .sign(secret);
}

export async function verifyAccessToken(token) {
  const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, secret, {
    algorithms: ["HS256"],               // explicit allowlist
    issuer: "https://auth.example.com",
    audience: "orders-api",
    clockTolerance: 5,                   // seconds of clock skew
  });
  return payload; // { sub, role, iat, exp, iss, aud }
}

docs.title: Authentication middleware for Bearer tokens
docs.text:
export async function authenticate(request, response, next) {
  const header = request.get("authorization") ?? "";
  const [scheme, token] = header.split(" ");
  // RFC 9110: a 401 response must name the expected scheme
  response.set("WWW-Authenticate", "Bearer");
  if (scheme !== "Bearer" || !token) {
    return response.status(401).json({ error: "Sign in required" });
  }
  try {
    const claims = await verifyAccessToken(token);
    request.user = { id: claims.sub, role: claims.role };
    response.removeHeader("WWW-Authenticate");
    next();
  } catch {
    response.status(401).json({ error: "Invalid or expired token" });
  }
}

See authentication in Express and cookies and sessions in Express for full wiring with express-session and a Redis store.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite on every authentication cookie; prefer the __Host- prefix.
  • Generate session IDs and refresh tokens with a cryptographically secure random generator; store refresh tokens hashed.
  • Regenerate session IDs at sign-in; enforce idle and absolute timeouts.
  • Keep access tokens short-lived; rotate refresh tokens and detect reuse.
  • Pin JWT algorithms, and always validate exp, iss, and aud.
  • Keep JWT payloads small and free of sensitive data.
  • Use a shared store (Redis) for sessions when running more than one instance.
  • Protect cookie-authenticated, state-changing endpoints against CSRF.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Users are signed out at random after scaling out. Symptom: sign-in works, then some requests return 401. Detect: logs show "session not found" on one instance for a session created on another. Cause: sessions live in process memory (express-session's default MemoryStore, which its docs say is not for production). Fix: use a shared store such as Redis.
  • The session cookie is never set behind a proxy. Symptom: sign-in "succeeds" but the browser has no cookie. Detect: no Set-Cookie header in the sign-in response. Cause: the cookie is marked secure, TLS ends at the load balancer, and the app sees plain HTTP, so express-session will not send it. Fix: app.set("trust proxy", 1) (or the exact number of proxies) so the app trusts X-Forwarded-Proto.
  • A cross-site SPA cannot stay signed in. Symptom: sign-in works, the next API call returns 401. Detect: browser DevTools shows the cookie blocked because of its SameSite setting, or the request has no Cookie header. Cause: the API is on a different site, the cookie is Lax, or the client did not use credentials: "include". Fix: serve the API from the same site, or use SameSite=None; Secure with CORS credentials enabled.
  • Valid tokens are rejected on some servers. Symptom: intermittent 401s right after sign-in. Detect: errors such as "nbf" claim timestamp check failed or "exp" claim timestamp check failed from jose. Cause: server clocks drift apart. Fix: run NTP on every host and allow a few seconds of clockTolerance.
  • Every user is signed out after a key change. Symptom: a spike of 401s right after a deploy. Detect: signature verification failures in logs. Cause: the old signing key was removed while tokens signed with it were still valid. Fix: publish old and new keys in the JWKS with different kid values, sign with the new key, and remove the old key only after the longest token lifetime has passed.
  • Requests fail once tokens grow. Symptom: 431 Request Header Fields Too Large or a 400 from the proxy for some users. Detect: the failing users have large permission lists. Cause: every permission was put into the JWT or cookie. Fix: keep claims small and look up detailed permissions on the server.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Stateless protocol: each request is handled independently; the server keeps no built-in memory of earlier requests.
  • Cookie: a value the server asks the browser to store and send back.
  • Session: server-side state tied to a client by a session ID.
  • Session fixation: forcing a victim to use a session ID the attacker already knows.
  • JWT: JSON Web Token; a compact, signed set of claims.
  • Claim: a statement inside a token, such as sub or exp.
  • JWS / JWE: signed / encrypted JSON Web Token formats.
  • JWKS: JSON Web Key Set; published public keys for verifying tokens.
  • Bearer token: a token that grants access to whoever holds it.
  • Refresh token rotation: issuing a new refresh token on every use and invalidating the old one.
  • CSRF: cross-site request forgery; tricking a browser into sending an authenticated request.
  • SameSite: cookie attribute controlling whether cookies go on cross-site requests.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "JWTs are encrypted." Signed JWTs are only encoded; anyone can read the payload.
  • "JWTs are always better than sessions." They trade easy revocation for fewer lookups; many web apps are simpler and safer with sessions.
  • Trusting the token's alg header. Always verify with a fixed algorithm allowlist.
  • Skipping aud and iss checks. Tokens from the same issuer for another service will be accepted.
  • Long-lived access tokens (days or weeks) with no revocation strategy.
  • Storing long-lived tokens in localStorage. Any XSS bug leaks them.
  • Setting Domain unnecessarily, which shares the cookie with every subdomain.
  • Using SameSite=None without need, which reopens CSRF exposure.
  • Not regenerating the session ID on sign-in, enabling session fixation.
  • Logging out only on the client while the server still accepts the session or refresh token.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why does a backend need sessions or tokens at all if the user already signed in?
  2. Explain HttpOnly, Secure, and each SameSite value. Which threat does each address?
  3. What are the three parts of a JWT, and why is its payload not secret?
  4. Describe the alg: none and algorithm-confusion attacks and how to prevent them.
  5. How do refresh token rotation and reuse detection limit the damage of a stolen refresh token?
  6. Compare server-side sessions and JWTs for revocation, scalability, and freshness of user data.

docs.text:
• MDN: Using HTTP cookies
  • MDN: Set-Cookie header
  • RFC 6265: HTTP State Management Mechanism
  • RFC 7519: JSON Web Token
  • RFC 8725: JWT Best Current Practices
  • OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

docs.title: Timeouts, Retries, and Idempotency
docs.text: Every call a backend makes to another system — a database, a payment provider, another microservice — can be slow, fail, or fail halfway. Timeouts bound how long you wait, retries give transient failures a second chance, and idempotency makes it safe to repeat an operation without doing it twice. These three ideas, plus circuit breakers and bulkheads, are the core toolkit for building reliable distributed systems.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Consider a checkout request that calls a payment API. The call times out. Did the card get charged? You do not know: the request may have been lost on the way, or the charge succeeded and the response was lost on the way back.

  • If you do not retry, a temporary network glitch fails a customer's order.
  • If you retry blindly, you may charge the customer twice.
  • If you never time out, one slow dependency ties up your server's connections and threads until the whole service stops responding.

Getting this right is the difference between a system that rides out everyday failures and one where every small outage cascades.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe's Idempotency-Key header. Clients send a unique key (Stripe suggests V4 UUIDs, up to 255 characters) so retries of a request are recognized. Stripe compares the parameters of a repeated request with the original and returns an error if they differ, and may prune keys once they are at least 24 hours old (Stripe API: idempotent requests).
  • The IETF Idempotency-Key draft standardizes the header: a retry that arrives while the original is still processing should get 409, and reusing a key with a different payload should get 422 (IETF draft: The Idempotency-Key HTTP header field).
  • AWS SDKs. In standard retry mode the SDKs retry with exponential backoff and jitter and keep a "retry quota" — a token bucket that stops retries when too many requests are failing, which is a retry budget (AWS SDKs and Tools: retry behavior). Amazon explains the reasoning in Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter.
  • Circuit breakers at Netflix. Netflix's Hystrix library was built to isolate calls to remote systems and stop cascading failures. It is now in maintenance mode, and Netflix says it uses projects such as resilience4j for new internal work (Netflix Hystrix on GitHub).

Popular tools: resilience4j (Java), Polly (.NET), opossum and cockatiel (Node.js circuit breakers and retry policies), and service meshes such as Envoy and Istio, which add retries, timeouts, and outlier detection outside the application code.

docs.title: Why calls between services fail
docs.text:
• Network problems: packet loss, connection resets, DNS failures.
  • The remote service is overloaded, restarting, or being deployed.
  • Rate limits (429).
  • Slow queries or garbage collection pauses causing timeouts.
  • Bugs and bad data causing errors.

A remote call has three possible outcomes, not two: success, failure, and unknown (timeout or lost response). Reliable designs handle the unknown case explicitly.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
A timeout is the maximum time you are willing to wait. Without one, a request can hang indefinitely while holding resources (a socket, memory, a database connection, a user waiting).

Timeout type What it bounds Connect timeout Establishing the TCP (and TLS) connection Read / response timeout Waiting for data after the request is sent Idle timeout Time with no activity on an open connection Total (deadline) timeout The whole operation, including retries

Guidelines:

  • Always set timeouts on outbound HTTP calls, database queries, and queue operations. Many clients default to no timeout or a very long one.
  • Base values on the dependency's normal latency (for example, a little above its p99), not on a guess like 30 seconds.
  • Propagate deadlines: if the incoming request must finish within 2 seconds, downstream calls should not each be allowed 5 seconds. Pass the remaining time budget along.
  • A timeout means "outcome unknown," not "operation failed." The remote side may still complete the work.

In Node.js, the built-in fetch supports cancellation through an AbortSignal; AbortSignal.timeout(ms) creates one that aborts automatically.

docs.title: Which failures to retry
docs.text:
Retry Do not retry Network errors (connection reset, refused, DNS temporary failure) 400 Bad Request, 422 — the request is wrong Timeouts (if the operation is idempotent) 401, 403 — credentials or permissions will not change 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict (usually) 429 Too Many Requests — after the Retry-After delay 501 Not Implemented Database deadlocks and serialization failures Errors caused by bugs in your own code

500 is ambiguous: retry at most once or twice, because it often indicates a bug that will repeat.

Only retry operations that are safe to repeat — idempotent ones, or ones protected by an idempotency key (see below).

docs.title: Exponential backoff with jitter
docs.text:
Retrying immediately, at fixed intervals, hammers a struggling service at exactly the moment it needs relief. Exponential backoff increases the delay after each attempt:

delay = min(maxDelay, baseDelay × 2^attempt)

base = 100 ms → 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600 ms ... capped at maxDelay

If thousands of clients failed at the same moment, they would all retry at the same moments too, creating synchronized waves. Jitter adds randomness to spread them out. A common choice is "full jitter":

delay = random(0, min(maxDelay, baseDelay × 2^attempt))

Also limit the number of attempts (for example, 3–5) and the total time.

docs.title: Retry storms and retry budgets
docs.text:
Retries multiply load. If each of three layers retries 3 times, one failing request at the bottom can become 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 attempts. During an outage, retries can keep a recovering service down.

Defenses:

  • Retry at one layer only (usually closest to the failure, or at the edge), not at every layer.
  • Use a retry budget: allow retries only while they are a small fraction (for example, 10%) of total requests.
  • Combine retries with a circuit breaker that stops calling a dependency that is clearly down.
  • Honor Retry-After from the server.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
An operation is idempotent if doing it once or many times has the same effect on the server's state.

Method Safe (no state change) Idempotent GET, HEAD, OPTIONS Yes Yes PUT (replace resource with this) No Yes DELETE No Yes (second delete changes nothing; may return 404) POST (create, charge, send) No No PATCH No Depends on the patch (set x = 5 yes, x += 1 no)

See HTTP methods. Idempotency is about the effect, not the response: a repeated DELETE may return 404 instead of 204, and that is fine.

docs.title: Idempotency keys for POST
docs.text:
To make a non-idempotent operation safe to retry, the client generates a unique key (such as a UUID) for each logical operation and sends it with every attempt, commonly in an Idempotency-Key header (used by Stripe and others, and described in an IETF draft).

POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 6f1d4a2e-9b3c-4f8e-a1d7-2c5e8b0f9a13
{ "orderId": "812", "amount": 4999 }

Server behavior:

  1. Look up the key (scoped to the client or account).
  2. Not seen before: record the key as "in progress," perform the operation, store the response (status and body) with the key, return it.
  3. Seen and completed: return the stored response without performing the operation again.
  4. Seen and still in progress (a concurrent duplicate): return 409 Conflict (or wait), so the operation does not run twice in parallel.
  5. Same key, different request body: reject with an error (422), because the client is misusing the key.
  6. Expire keys after a reasonable period (for example, 24 hours).

The "record as in progress" step must be atomic — for example, an insert into a table with a unique constraint on the key, or Redis SET key value NX — so two concurrent attempts cannot both start. See concurrency and race conditions.

docs.title: Circuit breaker
docs.text:
A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and stops calling it when it is clearly failing, giving it time to recover and making your service fail fast instead of waiting on timeouts.

  • Closed: normal operation; failures are counted.
  • Open: after too many failures (for example, 50% of the last 20 calls), calls fail immediately without touching the dependency.
  • Half-open: after a cooldown, a few trial calls are allowed. Success closes the circuit; failure opens it again.

docs.title: Bulkheads
docs.text: Named after ship compartments that stop one leak from sinking the whole ship: isolate resources per dependency so one slow dependency cannot exhaust everything. Examples: a separate connection pool or concurrency limit for the reporting database, a maximum number of in-flight calls to the recommendations service, separate worker pools for slow and fast jobs.

docs.title: Fallbacks
docs.text: When a call fails or the circuit is open, a fallback may still give the user something useful: cached data, a default value, a simplified response, or a queued request to process later. Fallbacks must be honest — showing stale prices is fine for a product list, not for a payment amount.

docs.title: At-least-once delivery and deduplication
docs.text:
Message queues and webhook systems usually guarantee at-least-once delivery: a message may be delivered more than once (for example, if a consumer crashes after processing but before acknowledging). "Exactly once" across systems is achieved in practice as at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing:

  • Give each message or event a unique ID.
  • Record processed IDs (with a unique constraint) in the same transaction as the side effect, when possible.
  • Skip messages whose IDs were already processed.

See background jobs and scheduling and message queues.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Always set timeouts on outbound calls. The other tools depend on the operation and the dependency.

Retry when:

  • The failure is transient (network error, 502, 503, 504, 429).
  • The operation is idempotent, or protected by an idempotency key.
  • There is time left in the caller's deadline.

Do not retry when:

  • The error is a client error (400, 401, 403, 404, 422) or a bug.
  • A user is waiting and the retry would push past an acceptable response time — fail fast and let the client decide.
  • Another layer (a client SDK, a service mesh) already retries the same call.

Add a circuit breaker when a dependency is called often and can fail for minutes at a time. It adds little for rarely called dependencies, because there is not enough traffic to judge their health.

Situation Tool Any network call Timeout (per attempt plus an overall deadline) Occasional network blips on a GET Retries with backoff and jitter Charging a card or sending a message Idempotency key, then retries A dependency is down for minutes Circuit breaker plus a fallback One slow dependency starves the others Bulkhead (separate pool or concurrency limit) Queue or webhook consumers Deduplicate by message ID

docs.title: fetch with a timeout and retries with full jitter
docs.text:
const RETRYABLE_STATUS = new Set([429, 502, 503, 504]);

function sleep(ms) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}

function backoffDelay(attempt, baseMs = 200, maxMs = 5000) {
  const exponential = Math.min(maxMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt);
  return Math.random() * exponential; // full jitter
}

export async function fetchWithRetry(url, options = {}, maxAttempts = 4) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt += 1) {
    try {
      const response = await fetch(url, {
        ...options,
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000), // per-attempt timeout
      });

      if (!RETRYABLE_STATUS.has(response.status)) {
        return response; // success or a non-retryable error
      }
      if (attempt === maxAttempts - 1) {
        return response; // out of attempts: let the caller handle it
      }

      // Release the connection: Node's fetch needs unread bodies cancelled
      await response.body?.cancel();

      // Honor Retry-After (seconds) when the server provides it
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      await sleep(retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : backoffDelay(attempt));
    } catch (error) {
      // Network error or timeout (error.name === "TimeoutError")
      if (attempt === maxAttempts - 1) throw error;
      await sleep(backoffDelay(attempt));
    }
  }
}

Use this only for idempotent requests, or send an idempotency key with non-idempotent ones.

docs.title: Calling a payment API with an idempotency key
docs.text:
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

// One key per logical operation, reused for every retry of that operation
const idempotencyKey = randomUUID();

const response = await fetchWithRetry("https://payments.example.com/charges", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "content-type": "application/json",
    "idempotency-key": idempotencyKey,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ orderId: "812", amount: 4999 }),
});

docs.title: Server-side idempotency middleware (simplified)
docs.text:
// Assumes a collection with a unique index on { accountId, key }
export function idempotent() {
  return async (request, response, next) => {
    const key = request.get("idempotency-key");
    if (!key) return next(); // or require it for this endpoint

    const scope = { accountId: request.user.id, key };
    try {
      // Atomic claim: fails with a duplicate-key error if the key exists
      await db.idempotency.insertOne({ ...scope, status: "in_progress", createdAt: new Date() });
    } catch (error) {
      if (error.code !== 11000) throw error;
      const existing = await db.idempotency.findOne(scope);
      if (existing?.status === "completed") {
        return response.status(existing.statusCode).json(existing.body);
      }
      return response.status(409).json({ error: "Request already in progress" });
    }

    // Capture the response so repeats can replay it
    const originalJson = response.json.bind(response);
    response.json = (body) => {
      db.idempotency
        .updateOne(scope, { $set: { status: "completed", statusCode: response.statusCode, body } })
        .catch((error) => request.log.error({ err: error }, "idempotency save failed"));
      return originalJson(body);
    };
    next();
  };
}

A production version also compares a hash of the request body, deletes the "in progress" record if the handler fails before responding, and expires old keys with a TTL index.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Set explicit timeouts on every outbound call; propagate deadlines.
  • Treat timeouts as "unknown outcome," not as definite failure.
  • Retry only transient failures and only idempotent (or key-protected) operations.
  • Use exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum attempt count, and a total time limit.
  • Retry at one layer; use retry budgets to avoid retry storms.
  • Honor Retry-After.
  • Require idempotency keys for operations that move money or send messages.
  • Add circuit breakers and bulkheads around critical dependencies.
  • Design consumers of queues and webhooks to deduplicate by message ID.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A recovering dependency is knocked down again. Symptom: a service comes back after an outage and immediately falls over. Detect: requests to the dependency run at several times the incoming user traffic, and retry counters spike. Cause: retries at several layers, without jitter or a budget, all firing at once. Fix: retry at one layer, add jitter and a retry budget, and open a circuit breaker while the dependency is down.
  • Customers are charged twice. Symptom: support reports duplicate charges after a period of payment timeouts. Detect: two successful payments for one order ID. Cause: a POST was retried without an idempotency key, or a new key was generated for each attempt. Fix: generate one key per logical operation, store it with the order before the first attempt, and reuse it for every retry.
  • Everything slows down because one dependency hangs. Symptom: latency climbs on all endpoints, not just the ones that call the slow dependency. Detect: many open sockets to one host and connection-pool wait times rising. Cause: no timeout on outbound calls — undici, which powers Node's fetch, waits up to 300 seconds by default for response headers. Fix: set a timeout on every call, and use a bulkhead so one dependency cannot take all connections.
  • Work runs twice after the client gives up. Symptom: duplicate records appear even though the client saw a timeout. Detect: server logs show requests completing after the caller's deadline. Cause: the caller timed out and retried, but the server kept processing the first attempt. Fix: propagate deadlines and cancel downstream work with an AbortSignal, and make the operation idempotent.
  • An idempotency key is stuck "in progress". Symptom: retries of one operation keep getting 409 long after the first attempt. Detect: idempotency records in in_progress that are older than the longest request. Cause: the process crashed before marking the record completed. Fix: expire in-progress claims after a timeout, and clear the claim when the handler fails before responding.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Timeout: the maximum time to wait for an operation.
  • Deadline: an absolute time by which the whole operation must finish.
  • Transient failure: a failure likely to succeed on retry.
  • Exponential backoff: increasing delays between retries.
  • Jitter: randomness added to delays to avoid synchronized retries.
  • Retry storm: retries amplifying load during an outage.
  • Retry budget: a cap on retries as a fraction of total traffic.
  • Idempotent: having the same effect whether performed once or many times.
  • Idempotency key: a client-supplied unique key that lets the server recognize repeats of one operation.
  • Circuit breaker: a component that stops calls to a failing dependency.
  • Bulkhead: isolating resources so one failure cannot exhaust them all.
  • Fallback: an alternative response when the primary path fails.
  • At-least-once delivery: a guarantee that messages arrive, possibly more than once.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• No timeouts, or relying on very long defaults.
  • Assuming a timeout means the operation did not happen.
  • Retrying POST requests without an idempotency key, causing duplicate orders or charges.
  • Retrying 4xx errors that will never succeed.
  • Fixed-interval retries without jitter, causing thundering herds.
  • Retries at every layer, multiplying load.
  • Non-atomic idempotency checks that let two concurrent duplicates both run.
  • "Exactly-once delivery solves it." In practice, use at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why are there three possible outcomes of a remote call, and how does that affect retry design?
  2. Which HTTP status codes are generally retryable, and which are not?
  3. Write the formula for exponential backoff with full jitter and explain why jitter helps.
  4. How does an idempotency key make a POST safe to retry? What must the server do with concurrent duplicates?
  5. Describe the three states of a circuit breaker and the transitions between them.
  6. Why is "exactly once" usually implemented as at-least-once delivery plus deduplication?

  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics — idempotent methods

docs.title: Validation and Sanitization
docs.text: Validation checks that incoming data has the shape, type, and meaning your code expects, and rejects it otherwise. Sanitization and output encoding make data safe for the specific place it is used next — a database query, an HTML page, a shell command, or a log file. Together they are the main defense against injection attacks and a large class of data-corruption bugs.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A backend receives data from sources it does not control: browsers, mobile apps, partner systems, webhooks, uploaded files. Any of them can send something unexpected — by mistake or on purpose. Without validation, a string where a number was expected crashes a handler; a negative quantity creates a refund; an object where a string was expected turns a database query into "match everything"; a filename containing ../ reads files outside the upload folder.

Several of the most serious OWASP risks come down to trusting input: injection, which in the OWASP Top 10 (2021) includes cross-site scripting and SQL injection, and mass assignment, which the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) covers under broken object property level authorization. A clear, consistent validation layer is one of the highest-value things a backend can have.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub's REST API returns 422 Unprocessable Entity when a request omits required parameters or uses the wrong type — for example, an array where the endpoint expects a string — along with a "Validation Failed" error (GitHub Docs: troubleshooting the REST API).
  • Stripe reports bad input as an invalid_request_error and includes a param field naming the parameter at fault, so a client can show the message next to the right form field (Stripe API: errors, Stripe: error handling).
  • Ruby on Rails blocks mass assignment with Strong Parameters: request parameters cannot be used for a mass update until the controller explicitly permits them, to stop users from updating sensitive attributes (Rails Guides: Strong Parameters).

Popular tools: schema validators such as Zod, Joi, Yup, AJV (JSON Schema), and express-validator; DOMPurify for sanitizing user-supplied HTML.

docs.title: Trust boundaries
docs.text:
A trust boundary is any point where data moves from a less trusted place into your code. Validate at every boundary, as early as possible:

Data from another internal service is still input. It may be buggy, outdated, or compromised.

docs.title: What to validate
docs.text: Source Examples of checks Path parameters id matches the expected ID format (UUID, ObjectId, integer) Query string Pagination numbers in range; sort is one of allowed fields; repeated parameters handled Request body Required fields present; types correct; lengths and ranges; no unknown fields Headers Content-Type is what you accept; custom headers have the expected format Cookies Present and well-formed; signed values verify Files Size, count, actual type (not just the extension), safe names Webhooks Signature verifies; payload matches the documented schema Environment variables Required values present and valid at startup Data from other services Response shape matches what you depend on

docs.title: Syntactic and semantic validation
docs.text:
• Syntactic validation checks form: is email a string that looks like an email address, is age an integer, is date a valid ISO 8601 date?
  • Semantic validation checks meaning in context: is the start date before the end date, does the product exist, is the quantity within stock, is this coupon still valid for this user?

Syntactic checks belong at the edge (request validation). Semantic checks usually need data and belong in the service layer.

docs.title: Allowlist versus denylist
docs.text:
• Allowlist (positive validation): define exactly what is allowed and reject everything else. status must be one of "open", "closed"; username must match ^[a-z0-9_]{3,30}$.
  • Denylist: try to block known-bad patterns, such as <script> or '. Attackers find variants you did not list.

Prefer allowlists. Use denylists only as an extra layer, never as the main defense.

docs.title: Schema validation
docs.text:
Rather than scattering if statements across handlers, describe the expected input as a schema and validate against it in one place. Libraries such as Zod, Joi, Yup, AJV (JSON Schema), and express-validator do this. A schema gives you:

  • Type checks, required/optional fields, lengths, ranges, patterns, enums.
  • Stripping or rejecting unknown fields, which prevents mass assignment.
  • Coercion where appropriate (query strings are always strings).
  • A typed, cleaned result to pass to the rest of the code.
  • Consistent, field-level error messages.

The same schema can often be shared with the frontend for instant feedback — but server validation is the one that counts.

docs.title: Type coercion pitfalls
docs.text:
• Query strings and form fields arrive as strings: ?page=2 gives "2". Coerce deliberately and validate the result ("abc" must not become NaN and slip through).
  • Number("") is 0 and Number(" ") is 0; parseInt("12abc") is 12.
  • Query parsers turn ?tags=a&tags=b into an array, and the "extended" parser (qs, the default in Express 4) turns ?user[role]=x into an object. Express 5's default "simple" parser keeps user[role] as a plain key but still produces arrays for repeated keys. Code expecting a string can receive an array or object.
  • JSON bodies can carry null, nested objects, very large numbers, or "__proto__" keys. Validate types, do not assume them.
  • Booleans: "false" is a non-empty string and therefore truthy.

docs.title: Sanitization versus output encoding
docs.text:
• Validation decides accept or reject.
  • Sanitization changes input to remove or neutralize unwanted parts — for example, trimming whitespace, normalizing Unicode, or stripping disallowed HTML tags from rich text with a dedicated HTML sanitizer.
  • Output encoding (escaping) transforms data at the moment it is placed into another context so it is treated as data, not code.

Encoding is context-specific. The same value needs different treatment in different places:

Destination Correct technique SQL query Parameterized queries / prepared statements MongoDB query Ensure values are primitives (not objects); use the driver's query API HTML body HTML-entity encoding (template engines do this by default) HTML attribute Attribute encoding, and quote attributes JavaScript in a page Avoid; pass data via JSON in a data attribute or API URL encodeURIComponent for components Shell command Avoid the shell; pass arguments as an array Log line Remove or escape newline characters; structured (JSON) logging

General rule: validate on input, encode on output. Do not try to "sanitize once" on input so that the data is safe everywhere — there is no single representation safe for every context.

docs.title: Injection attacks and defenses
docs.text:
SQL injection — user input concatenated into SQL:

// Vulnerable: email = "' OR '1'='1"
db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`);

// Safe: the driver sends the value separately from the query text
db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1", [email]);

NoSQL operator injection — an object where a string was expected:

POST /login   {"email": "admin@example.com", "password": {"$ne": null}}

// Vulnerable: password becomes { $ne: null } → matches any password
const user = await db.users.findOne({ email, password });

// Safe: validate types first; only strings reach the query
if (typeof email !== "string" || typeof password !== "string") {
  throw new ValidationError("Invalid credentials format");
}

(And never store or compare plain passwords — see authentication and authorization.)

OS command injection — input passed to a shell:

import { exec, execFile } from "node:child_process";

// Vulnerable: filename = "report.pdf; rm -rf /"
exec(`convert ${filename} out.png`);

// Safer: no shell; arguments are passed as an array
execFile("convert", [filename, "out.png"]);

Path traversal — ../ sequences escaping a directory:

import path from "node:path";

const uploadsDir = path.resolve("uploads");

app.get("/files/:name", (request, response) => {
  const target = path.resolve(uploadsDir, request.params.name);

  // Reject anything that resolves outside the uploads directory
  if (!target.startsWith(uploadsDir + path.sep)) {
    return response.status(400).json({ error: "Invalid file name" });
  }
  response.sendFile(target);
});

A request for /files/..%2F..%2Fsecret.txt decodes to ../../secret.txt, resolves outside uploads, and gets 400.

Stored XSS — input saved, then rendered as HTML later:

A comment containing <script>stealCookies()</script> is saved and shown to every visitor. Defense: encode on output (templating engines and frameworks like React escape by default), sanitize rich text with an HTML sanitizer that uses an allowlist of tags and attributes, and add a Content Security Policy.

Header and log injection — input containing newline characters (\r\n) can split HTTP headers or forge log lines:

username = "alice\n2026-11-07 INFO admin login succeeded"

Defense: reject control characters in fields that should not contain them, let frameworks set headers (Node rejects invalid header characters), and use structured JSON logging where values are escaped.

docs.title: Mass assignment
docs.text:
Mass assignment happens when the server copies a whole request body into a database record:

// Vulnerable: body = { "name": "Ann", "role": "admin", "balance": 99999 }
await db.users.updateOne({ _id: userId }, { $set: request.body });

Defense: validate against a schema that lists only the fields this endpoint may change and strips or rejects the rest; build the update object explicitly.

docs.title: Size and count limits
docs.text:
Unbounded input is a denial-of-service risk. Set limits on:

  • Request body size (express.json({ limit: "100kb" })).
  • String lengths, array lengths, object nesting depth.
  • Number of query parameters and form fields.
  • File size and number of files.
  • Page size in pagination (limit max 100).

Return 413 Content Too Large for oversized bodies and 400 for values out of range.

docs.title: Unicode normalization
docs.text:
The same visible text can be encoded in different ways. é can be one code point (U+00E9) or e plus a combining accent (U+0065 U+0301). Usernames that look identical may compare as different. Normalize identifiers with String.prototype.normalize("NFKC") before comparing or storing, so both forms of é become the same string.

Normalization does not merge look-alike characters from different scripts: Cyrillic а and Latin a stay different after NFKC, which enables impersonation. Restrict identifiers to a limited character set, or check them against a list of confusable characters, to prevent that.

docs.title: ReDoS (regular expression denial of service)
docs.text: Some regular expressions take exponential time on crafted input because of catastrophic backtracking — for example, nested quantifiers like ^(a+)+$ against "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!". Because Node runs JavaScript on one thread, one such request can freeze the whole server. Defenses: avoid nested quantifiers, limit input length before running a regex, prefer well-tested validators from libraries, and test patterns with ReDoS checkers.

docs.title: Validation error responses
docs.text:
When validation fails, respond quickly with a clear, machine-readable error:

  • 400 Bad Request: the request is malformed or fails validation. Many APIs use 400 for all validation failures.
  • 422 Unprocessable Content: the syntax is valid (well-formed JSON) but the content fails semantic rules. Some APIs use 422 for field validation.

Pick one convention and use it consistently. Return field-level details:

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/validation-error",
  "title": "Request validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "errors": [
    { "field": "email", "message": "Must be a valid email address" },
    { "field": "quantity", "message": "Must be between 1 and 100" }
  ]
}

Do not echo raw input back into HTML error pages, and do not reveal internal details such as database errors.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Validation itself is never optional at a trust boundary. The choices are which technique to use where.

Use schema validation (Zod, Joi, JSON Schema) when:

  • An endpoint accepts a body, query, or params with known fields — that is, almost always.
  • You want typed, cleaned values and consistent field-level errors.

Use hand-written checks when:

  • The rule needs data or context, such as stock levels, ownership, or date ranges. Put these semantic checks in the service layer.

Do not:

  • Use sanitization as a substitute for parameterized queries or output encoding.
  • Strip HTML from every field "just in case" — it corrupts legitimate data (names with < or &) and does not make output safe.
Technique Use for Not a substitute for Schema validation (reject or strip) Shape, types, ranges, unknown fields Semantic and ownership checks Parameterized queries Every database query with input Validation (still check types) Output encoding HTML, URLs, headers, logs Input validation HTML sanitizer (allowlist) Rich text that must keep some markup Encoding plain-text fields Rejecting unknown fields New APIs, internal clients Public APIs with old clients — strip instead while migrating

docs.title: A Zod schema used as Express middleware
docs.text:
import { z } from "zod";

const createOrderSchema = z
  .object({
    productId: z.string().uuid(),
    quantity: z.number().int().min(1).max(100),
    note: z.string().trim().max(500).optional(),
  })
  .strict(); // reject unknown fields such as "price" or "status"

const listOrdersQuery = z.object({
  page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1),   // "2" → 2
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20),
  status: z.enum(["open", "shipped", "cancelled"]).optional(),
});

function validate(schema, source = "body") {
  return (request, response, next) => {
    const result = schema.safeParse(request[source]);
    if (!result.success) {
      return response.status(400).json({
        title: "Request validation failed",
        status: 400,
        errors: result.error.issues.map((issue) => ({
          field: issue.path.join("."),
          message: issue.message,
        })),
      });
    }
    // Store the cleaned, typed value instead of the raw input
    request.validated = { ...request.validated, [source]: result.data };
    next();
  };
}

app.post("/api/orders", validate(createOrderSchema), createOrder);
app.get("/api/orders", validate(listOrdersQuery, "query"), listOrders);

Handlers then read request.validated.body and request.validated.query, never the raw request.body. More Express-specific patterns are in request validation.

docs.title: Semantic validation in the service layer
docs.text:
export async function createBooking({ roomId, startDate, endDate }, user) {
  if (endDate <= startDate) {
    throw new ValidationError("End date must be after start date");
  }
  const room = await rooms.findById(roomId);
  if (!room) {
    throw new NotFoundError("Room not found");
  }
  // ...availability check, then create
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Validate every input at the trust boundary, on the server, before use.
  • Use schemas with allowlists; reject or strip unknown fields.
  • Coerce types deliberately; never assume a query value is a string.
  • Use parameterized queries and driver APIs; never build queries with string concatenation.
  • Encode output for its context; rely on template auto-escaping.
  • Avoid the shell; pass command arguments as arrays.
  • Resolve and check file paths against an allowed base directory.
  • Set limits on body size, lengths, counts, and page sizes.
  • Normalize Unicode for identifiers; restrict character sets where possible.
  • Keep error responses consistent, field-level, and free of internals.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Old clients break after validation is tightened. Symptom: a spike of 400 responses right after a deploy, mostly from older mobile app versions. Detect: 400 rate per endpoint and client version; error bodies such as Unrecognized key: "price". Cause: a schema was made strict, or a field became required. Fix: strip unknown fields instead of rejecting them while old clients exist, make new fields optional, and version breaking changes.
  • One request freezes the server. Symptom: every request times out and one CPU core sits at 100%. Detect: event loop delay jumps; a CPU profile shows time inside a regular expression. Cause: catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) on user input. Fix: cap input length before matching, rewrite the pattern without nested quantifiers, and use maintained validators.
  • Legitimate requests get 413. Symptom: users with large forms or bulk imports see failures. Detect: logs show body-parser errors with type entity.too.large. Cause: express.json() defaults to a 100 KB limit. Fix: raise the limit only on routes that need it, or switch large uploads to direct-to-storage uploads.
  • Crafted query strings cause 500s. Symptom: errors such as TypeError: email.toLowerCase is not a function. Detect: the failing requests repeat a parameter (?email=a&email=b) so it arrives as an array. Cause: the handler assumed a string. Fix: validate the query with a schema and return 400.
  • Stored XSS reaches users. Symptom: users report unexpected pop-ups or redirects on pages with user content. Detect: Content Security Policy violation reports, or script tags found in stored fields. Cause: user content rendered without encoding (innerHTML, unescaped template output). Fix: encode on output, sanitize rich text with an allowlist sanitizer, and enforce a CSP.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Validation: checking input against rules and rejecting what fails.
  • Sanitization: modifying input to remove or neutralize unwanted parts.
  • Output encoding / escaping: converting data so the destination treats it as data, not code.
  • Trust boundary: where data passes from a less trusted to a more trusted context.
  • Allowlist / denylist: permit only known-good / block known-bad.
  • Schema: a declarative description of valid data.
  • Coercion: converting a value from one type to another.
  • Injection: untrusted data interpreted as code or commands.
  • Parameterized query: a query where values are sent separately from the query text.
  • Mass assignment: binding request fields directly to a model, including fields the client should not control.
