  • Path traversal: using ../ or absolute paths to access files outside an intended directory.
  • ReDoS: denial of service through a slow regular expression.
  • Unicode normalization: converting equivalent character sequences to one canonical form.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Relying on frontend validation. Attackers bypass the browser entirely.
  • "Sanitize once on input and it's safe everywhere." Safety depends on the output context.
  • Escaping quotes instead of parameterizing. Hand-written escaping misses edge cases.
  • Assuming JSON fields have the right type — {"$ne": null} is valid JSON.
  • Copying request.body into updates. This is mass assignment.
  • Checking the file extension only. Extensions and Content-Type headers are client-controlled.
  • Unbounded regexes on long input, risking ReDoS.
  • Returning 500 for bad input. Client mistakes are 4xx responses.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is a trust boundary, and why is data from another internal service still untrusted?
  2. Explain the difference between validation, sanitization, and output encoding, with one example of each.
  3. How does NoSQL operator injection work, and how does type validation stop it?
  4. Why are allowlists preferred over denylists?
  5. What is mass assignment, and how does a strict schema prevent it?
  6. When would you choose 400 versus 422 for a validation error?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP Mass Assignment Cheat Sheet
  • MDN: String.prototype.normalize()
  • Related notes: OWASP, API security, Error handling

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text: A webhook is an HTTP request one server sends to another when an event happens: "a payment succeeded", "a pull request was opened", "an SMS was delivered". Instead of your backend repeatedly asking a provider "anything new?", the provider calls a URL you registered and pushes the event to you. Webhooks are how most third-party services (payments, Git hosting, messaging, e-commerce) notify your system.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Real-time integration without polling. You learn about events seconds after they happen, without wasting requests asking for nothing.
  • Many business flows depend on them. An order is often marked paid only when the payment provider's webhook arrives, not when the user returns from the checkout page.
  • They are an attack surface. A webhook endpoint is a public URL that changes your data. Without signature verification, anyone can forge "this invoice was paid".
  • They fail in specific ways. Duplicate deliveries, out-of-order events, and retries are normal, and code that ignores them double-ships orders or loses updates.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe. Stripe signs every event in a Stripe-Signature header and requires the raw request body for verification. Its libraries reject events whose timestamp is more than 5 minutes from the current time by default, and it recommends NTP so your clock stays accurate. In live mode, Stripe retries failed deliveries for up to three days with exponential backoff. It does not guarantee event order and tells you to track event IDs to detect duplicates. It also asks endpoints to return 2xx before any complex logic.
  • GitHub. GitHub sends an HMAC-SHA256 of the payload in the X-Hub-Signature-256 header (sha256=<hex>). Your server should respond with 2xx within 10 seconds or GitHub considers the delivery failed, and it suggests a queue for the real work. GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed deliveries; you redeliver them manually or with code. The X-GitHub-Delivery header helps detect replays.
  • Shopify. Each HTTPS webhook includes a base64-encoded HMAC in X-Shopify-Hmac-SHA256, computed with the app's client secret over the raw request body; Shopify's own Express sample uses express.raw() and crypto.timingSafeEqual.

The three providers disagree on header names, encodings (hex or base64), and retry behavior, which is why you always follow the provider's documentation.

docs.title: Webhooks vs polling
docs.text:
Polling: your server asks repeatedly
  you  --GET /payments?since=...-->  provider   "nothing"
  you  --GET /payments?since=...-->  provider   "nothing"
  you  --GET /payments?since=...-->  provider   "payment pi_1 succeeded"

Webhook: the provider tells you once
  provider --POST /webhooks/payments {"type":"payment.succeeded",...}--> you
  you      --200 OK-->                                                   provider
Polling Webhooks Latency Up to the polling interval Near real-time Wasted requests Many empty responses Only real events Needs a public endpoint No Yes Reliability You control retries You depend on the provider's retries, plus reconciliation Complexity Simple Signature verification, deduplication, ordering

Many systems use both: webhooks for speed and a periodic reconciliation job that polls the provider's API to catch anything missed.

docs.title: The provider side
docs.text:
A provider that offers webhooks:

  1. Lets customers register endpoints (a URL plus the event types they want) and gives each endpoint a signing secret.

  2. Builds an event payload when something happens, with a unique event ID, type, timestamp, and data:

    {
  "id": "evt_8f2c1a",
  "type": "payment.succeeded",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-03T10:15:00Z",
  "data": { "paymentId": "pay_501", "orderId": "ord_901", "amount": 4999, "currency": "USD" }
}

  3. Signs the payload with an HMAC of the timestamp and body using the endpoint's secret, and sends it in a header.

  4. Delivers it with POST, a short timeout, and treats any 2xx as success.
  5. Retries failures (timeouts, connection errors, non-2xx) with exponential backoff over hours or days, then marks the endpoint as failing and alerts the customer.
  6. Offers tools: a delivery log, manual re-send, and test events.

Providers deliver at least once, so duplicates are expected, and they generally do not guarantee ordering.

docs.title: The consumer side (your endpoint)
docs.text:
Your job when receiving a webhook, in order:

  1. Expose a public HTTPS endpoint, such as POST /webhooks/payments.
  2. Read the raw body. The signature is computed over the exact bytes sent. If a JSON parser re-serializes the body first, whitespace or key order may change and verification fails.
  3. Verify the signature by recomputing the HMAC with your secret and comparing it to the header using a constant-time comparison.
  4. Check the timestamp against your clock (for example within 5 minutes) to reject replayed old requests.
  5. Deduplicate by event ID. If you have already processed evt_8f2c1a, acknowledge and do nothing.
  6. Respond 2xx quickly, ideally within a few seconds. Providers time out slow endpoints and retry, causing more duplicates.
  7. Process asynchronously: put the event on a queue and let a worker do the slow work (database updates, emails, calls to other APIs).
  8. Handle ordering yourself. A payment.refunded event can arrive before payment.succeeded. Use timestamps or version numbers, or fetch the current state from the provider's API instead of trusting event order.

docs.title: How HMAC signatures work
docs.text:
HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) combines a secret key with the message and a hash function such as SHA-256. Only someone with the secret can produce the right value, and changing a single byte of the message changes the result completely.

signature = HMAC-SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + rawBody)
header    = "t=1762164900,v1=5257a869e7ecebeda32affa62cdca3fa51cad7e77a0e56ff536d0ce8e108d8bd"

Including the timestamp in the signed content prevents an attacker from re-sending an old captured request with a fresh timestamp.

Signature formats vary by provider (header names, encoding as hex or base64, what exactly is signed). Always follow the provider's documentation, and use their official SDK verification function when one exists. An open specification called Standard Webhooks defines a common format some providers follow: it sends webhook-id, webhook-timestamp, and webhook-signature headers, signs id.timestamp.body, and encodes the signature in base64 with a v1, prefix. The examples on this page use a simpler, illustrative format (t=<timestamp>,v1=<hex> over timestamp.body), not the Standard Webhooks wire format.

docs.title: Security checklist
docs.text:
• HTTPS only, so payloads and signatures cannot be read or altered in transit.
  • Verify every signature; reject unsigned or invalid requests with 400 or 401.
  • Use constant-time comparison (crypto.timingSafeEqual), never ===, to avoid timing attacks.
  • Enforce a timestamp tolerance against replays.
  • Keep secrets in configuration and support two active secrets during rotation.
  • Limit the body size and the route's rate.
  • Treat the payload as a hint for sensitive actions. For high-value events, re-fetch the object from the provider's API using your API key before acting.
  • Return generic errors; do not echo internal details.
  • IP allowlists (if the provider publishes its ranges) are an extra layer, never a replacement for signatures.
  • As a provider, guard against SSRF: customers supply URLs, so refuse to deliver to private, loopback, or cloud-metadata addresses.

docs.title: Testing locally
docs.text:
Providers cannot reach localhost. Options:

  • Tunnels such as ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel give your local server a temporary public HTTPS URL to register with the provider.
  • Provider CLIs forward events to your machine, for example stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/webhooks/stripe.
  • Replay saved payloads with curl, computing a valid signature in a small script, so tests do not depend on the provider.
  • Use the provider's "send test event" button from its dashboard.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use webhooks when:

  • Another system must learn about events soon after they happen (payments, repository pushes, delivery receipts).
  • Events are infrequent compared to how often you would have to poll.
  • The receiver can expose a public HTTPS endpoint.

Prefer something else when:

  • The receiver cannot accept inbound connections (a desktop app, a device behind a firewall): poll, or use a long-lived outbound connection.
  • You need guaranteed, ordered delivery between your own services: use a message queue.
  • A browser needs live updates: use SSE or WebSockets from your backend.
  • Missing an event would be costly: keep webhooks, but add periodic reconciliation by polling.
Option Latency Who opens the connection Delivery guarantees Typical use Webhooks Seconds Provider calls you At least once, unordered, provider-specific retries Third-party event notifications Polling Up to the interval You call the provider You control retries Reconciliation, receivers that cannot be reached Message queue Milliseconds to seconds Both connect to a broker Configurable, durable Events between your own services SSE / WebSockets Milliseconds Client connects to server While connected Live updates to browsers and apps

docs.title: A complete Express receiver
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";

const app = express();
const WEBHOOK_SECRET = process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET; // shared with the provider
const TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300; // reject events older than 5 minutes

// Register BEFORE any global express.json(), so this route gets raw bytes
app.post(
  "/webhooks/payments",
  express.raw({ type: "application/json", limit: "1mb" }), // req.body is a Buffer
  async (req, res) => {
    // Header format used in this example: "t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC>"
    const header = req.get("Webhook-Signature") ?? "";
    const parts = Object.fromEntries(header.split(",").map((part) => part.split("=", 2)));
    const timestamp = Number(parts.t);
    const received = parts.v1 ?? "";

    // 1. Replay protection: the timestamp must be recent
    const ageSeconds = Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - timestamp);
    if (!Number.isFinite(timestamp) || ageSeconds > TOLERANCE_SECONDS) {
      return res.status(400).send("stale or missing timestamp");
    }

    // 2. Recompute the signature over "<timestamp>.<raw body>"
    const expected = createHmac("sha256", WEBHOOK_SECRET)
      .update(`${timestamp}.`)
      .update(req.body)
      .digest("hex");

    // 3. Constant-time comparison; timingSafeEqual needs equal lengths
    const a = Buffer.from(received, "hex");
    const b = Buffer.from(expected, "hex");
    if (a.length !== b.length || !timingSafeEqual(a, b)) {
      return res.status(401).send("invalid signature");
    }

    // 4. Only now trust and parse the body
    const event = JSON.parse(req.body.toString("utf8"));

    // 5. Hand off and acknowledge fast; the worker deduplicates by event.id
    await jobQueue.add("payment-event", event);
    res.sendStatus(200);
  },
);

app.use(express.json()); // the rest of the API parses JSON normally
app.listen(3000);

jobQueue stands for a queue client such as BullMQ. See background jobs and scheduling.

docs.title: The worker: idempotent processing
docs.text:
async function handlePaymentEvent(event) {
  // A unique index on processed_events.event_id makes duplicates fail the insert.
  // Do the insert and the business change in ONE transaction so they succeed or fail together.
  await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const firstTime = await tx.processedEvents.insertIfAbsent({ eventId: event.id });
    if (!firstTime) return; // duplicate delivery: already handled

    if (event.type === "payment.succeeded") {
      // Guard against out-of-order events: only move forward in the state machine
      await tx.orders.markPaidIfPending(event.data.orderId);
    }
  });
}

docs.title: The provider side: signing and delivering
docs.text:
import { createHmac } from "node:crypto";

export async function deliverWebhook(endpoint, event) {
  const body = JSON.stringify(event);
  const timestamp = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  const signature = createHmac("sha256", endpoint.secret)
    .update(`${timestamp}.${body}`)
    .digest("hex");

  const res = await fetch(endpoint.url, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Webhook-Id": event.id,
      "Webhook-Signature": `t=${timestamp},v1=${signature}`,
    },
    body,
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000), // never wait forever on a customer's server
  });

  // Non-2xx: throw so the job queue retries with exponential backoff
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Webhook delivery failed with status ${res.status}`);
}

docs.title: Sending a signed test event with curl
docs.text:
BODY='{"id":"evt_test_1","type":"payment.succeeded","data":{"orderId":"ord_901"}}'
TS=$(date +%s)
SIG=$(printf '%s' "$TS.$BODY" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$WEBHOOK_SECRET" -hex | sed 's/^.* //')

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/webhooks/payments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Webhook-Signature: t=$TS,v1=$SIG" \
  --data "$BODY"

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Verify signatures over the raw body with a constant-time comparison.
  • Reject stale timestamps to stop replays.
  • Acknowledge fast, process later through a queue.
  • Make processing idempotent with a unique constraint on the event ID.
  • Never rely on ordering; use state machines, timestamps, or re-fetch current state.
  • Reconcile periodically by polling the provider's API for anything missed.
  • Log every delivery (event ID, type, result) without logging secrets or sensitive payload fields.
  • Monitor failures: a stream of 401s often means a rotated secret.
  • As a provider: sign payloads, retry with backoff, document the format, offer a delivery log and re-send, and block private network targets.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every webhook suddenly fails verification. Detect: a wall of 400/401 responses in the provider's delivery log and your logs, starting with a deploy. Cause: a global body parser now runs before the webhook route, so the raw bytes are gone; or the signing secret was rotated in one place only. Fix: give the webhook route its own raw-body parser and accept both the old and new secret during rotation.
  • Duplicate side effects such as emails sent twice. Detect: the same event ID appears several times in logs, usually after slow responses or redeliveries. Cause: the endpoint took too long, the provider recorded a failure and the event was delivered again (by an automatic retry, as with Stripe, or a redelivery), and the handler is not idempotent. Fix: acknowledge fast, queue the work, and deduplicate by event ID with a unique constraint.
  • Valid events rejected as stale. Detect: "stale timestamp" rejections on one server only. Cause: that server's clock drifted. Fix: run NTP, which Stripe explicitly recommends, and alert on clock skew.
  • Events lost during an outage. Detect: gaps between the provider's data and yours after your endpoint was down. Cause: retries exhausted, or a provider that does not retry automatically, such as GitHub. Fix: redeliver failed deliveries from the provider's log or API, and run a reconciliation job.
  • Newer state overwritten by an older event. Detect: an order shows "paid" although the provider says "refunded"; logs show the events processed out of order. Cause: trusting arrival order. Fix: only move forward in a state machine, compare event or object timestamps, or re-fetch the object from the provider's API.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Webhook: an HTTP callback a server sends when an event occurs.
  • Webhook endpoint: the URL a consumer registers to receive events.
  • Event payload: the JSON describing what happened.
  • HMAC: a keyed hash that proves a message came from someone holding the secret and was not changed.
  • Signing secret: the shared key used to compute and verify HMAC signatures.
  • Replay attack: re-sending a captured valid request.
  • At-least-once delivery: every event is delivered one or more times; duplicates are possible.
  • Idempotent consumer: a receiver that produces the same result no matter how many times an event arrives.
  • Reconciliation: periodically comparing your data with the source of truth to repair gaps.
  • Tunnel: a service exposing a local server at a public URL for testing.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Skipping signature verification because "nobody knows the URL". URLs leak through logs, screenshots, and guessing.
  • Verifying against parsed and re-serialized JSON instead of the raw bytes, so valid signatures fail (or developers disable the check).
  • Comparing signatures with ===, which can leak timing information.
  • Doing slow work before responding, causing timeouts and duplicate retries.
  • Assuming exactly-once, in-order delivery and double-processing payments or applying stale updates.
  • Returning 500 for events you don't handle. Acknowledge unknown event types with 200 so the provider stops retrying.
  • Global express.json() registered before the webhook route, consuming the raw body.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Compare webhooks and polling. Why do many systems use both?
  2. Why must the signature be verified against the raw body?
  3. What attack does the timestamp in the signed content prevent?
  4. Why should a webhook endpoint respond quickly and process the event asynchronously?
  5. How do you make a webhook consumer safe against duplicate deliveries?
  6. A refund event arrives before the payment.succeeded event for the same payment. How should your system handle it?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 2104: HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication.
  • Node.js: Crypto module documents createHmac and timingSafeEqual.
  • Express: express.raw() for receiving the raw request body.
  • MDN: POST method.
  • Related: timeouts, retries, and idempotency and message queues.

docs.title: Implementing Authentication in Express
docs.text: Authentication answers "who is making this request?" and authorization answers "are they allowed to do this?". Express has no built-in login system, so you assemble one from password hashing, a way to remember the user (a session or a token), and middleware that protects routes. This lesson builds both a session-based and a JWT-based login and shows how to add role and ownership checks.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Authentication code guards every private route in an application, and the mistakes are expensive: plain-text passwords leak in breaches, tokens that never expire stay usable after theft, and missing ownership checks let one user read another user's data. Building the flow yourself once, carefully, teaches you what libraries and identity providers do for you.

For the underlying concepts, see authentication and authorization and sessions, cookies, and JWT.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Dropbox layers its password storage. Its engineering blog, How Dropbox securely stores your passwords, describes hashing with bcrypt (cost 10, a unique per-user salt) and then encrypting the result with a separately stored key it calls a "pepper", so a stolen database alone is not enough to start cracking.
  • Auth0 offers refresh token rotation. Its documentation explains that every time an application exchanges a refresh token, Auth0 also returns a new refresh token, and that automatic reuse detection revokes the token family when an old refresh token is presented again: the rotation-plus-reuse-detection pattern shown below.
  • GitHub redesigned its access tokens to be easy to recognize when they leak. Its post Behind GitHub's new authentication token formats introduces prefixes such as ghp for personal access tokens and gho for OAuth access tokens, so its secret scanning can detect leaked tokens with far fewer false positives.

Popular tools and providers: argon2, bcrypt, jsonwebtoken, jose, Passport.js, express-rate-limit; hosted identity providers such as Auth0, Okta, Amazon Cognito, and Firebase Authentication.

docs.title: The overall flow
docs.text: Once a user is logged in, every protected request passes through the same checks, authentication first and authorization second:

docs.title: Password hashing
docs.text:
Passwords are hashed, never stored as plain text and never encrypted. Encryption is reversible: whoever holds the key can recover every password. A password hash is one-way.

Use an algorithm designed to be slow and memory-hard:

Algorithm Package Notes Argon2id argon2 Modern recommendation; tunable memory and time cost bcrypt bcrypt (or bcryptjs) Widely used; OWASP recommends a work factor of 10 or more; only the first 72 bytes count scrypt node:crypto Built in; memory-hard

These libraries generate a random salt for every password and store it inside the hash string, so identical passwords produce different hashes. Never use fast hashes such as MD5 or SHA-256 alone for passwords.

docs.title: Two ways to remember the user
docs.text:
Session-based Token-based (JWT) What the client holds A random session ID in a cookie A signed token Where user state lives Server-side store (Redis, DB) Inside the token's claims Logout / revocation Delete the session: immediate Hard until expiry; needs short lifetimes or a denylist Typical clients Browser apps on your own domain Mobile apps, third-party clients, service-to-service Main risk CSRF (mitigate with SameSite, tokens) Token theft (keep lifetimes short, avoid localStorage)

Browser apps on your own domain usually do best with sessions. JWTs suit clients that cannot rely on cookies.

docs.title: JWT access and refresh tokens
docs.text:
A JSON Web Token has three base64url parts: header, payload (claims), and signature. The server signs it with a secret (HS256) or a private key (RS256/ES256), and later verifies the signature and the exp claim.

Because a stolen JWT works until it expires, systems use two tokens:

  • Access token: short-lived (5–15 minutes), sent on each API request in Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  • Refresh token: long-lived, sent only to a refresh endpoint to get a new access token. Store it hashed in the database so it can be revoked, and rotate it: issue a new one on every refresh and invalidate the old one.

docs.title: Where to store tokens in a browser
docs.text:
• localStorage: readable by any script on the page, so an XSS bug exposes the token. Avoid for long-lived tokens.
  • Memory (a JavaScript variable): lost on reload; pair it with a refresh token in an httpOnly cookie.
  • httpOnly cookie: unreadable by scripts; needs SameSite and CSRF protection because the browser sends it automatically.

docs.title: 401 vs 403
docs.text:
• 401 Unauthorized: the request has no valid credentials. "Who are you?" Log in or refresh the token.
  • 403 Forbidden: credentials are valid, but this user may not do this. Logging in again will not help.

docs.title: Passport.js in brief
docs.text: Passport is authentication middleware built around strategies: plug-ins for a method of logging in, such as passport-local (username and password), passport-jwt (Bearer tokens), and strategies for OAuth providers such as Google or GitHub. Each strategy calls a "verify" function you write, and passport.authenticate("strategy-name") runs it as middleware. Passport saves boilerplate when you support many login methods. For one or two methods, plain middleware like the examples below is often clearer. In recent versions req.logout() takes a callback.

docs.title: Login with a provider
docs.text: "Sign in with Google" uses OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect: your server redirects the user to the provider, the provider redirects back with a code, and your server exchanges the code for tokens that identify the user. You then create your own session or tokens as above. The protocol details are covered in OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Build authentication yourself in Express when:

  • You need a simple email-and-password login for one application and can maintain it (hashing, rate limits, password reset, account recovery).
  • You are learning how authentication works, or have unusual requirements no provider supports.

Prefer a hosted identity provider or a framework-level library when:

  • You need MFA, passkeys, SSO for business customers (SAML, OIDC), or social login.
  • Several applications must share one login.
  • You lack the time to own security fixes, breach response, and compliance for credentials.
Option You own Good for Trade-off Hand-built (this lesson) Everything: hashing, sessions/tokens, reset flows One app, full control, learning Most security responsibility Passport.js strategies Glue code and user storage Several login methods in one Express app Still your user database and flows Hosted provider (Auth0, Okta, Cognito, Firebase Auth) Integration only MFA, SSO, social login, many apps Cost, vendor dependency, less control Session vs JWT — Sessions for same-site browser apps; JWT for mobile and service clients See the comparison table above

docs.title: Registration and password hashing
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import argon2 from "argon2";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

// In a real app this is a database collection with a unique index on email.
const users = new Map();

app.post("/auth/register", async (req, res) => {
  const { email, password } = req.body ?? {};
  if (typeof email !== "string" || typeof password !== "string") {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "Email and password are required" });
  }
  if (password.length < 12) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "Use at least 12 characters" });
  }

  const normalizedEmail = email.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (users.has(normalizedEmail)) {
    return res.status(409).json({ error: "Email already registered" });
  }

  const passwordHash = await argon2.hash(password); // argon2id by default
  const user = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), email: normalizedEmail,
    passwordHash, role: "user" };
  users.set(normalizedEmail, user);

  res.status(201).json({ id: user.id, email: user.email });
});

With bcrypt the calls are await bcrypt.hash(password, 12) and await bcrypt.compare(password, hash).

docs.title: Verifying credentials safely
docs.text:
// A real hash of a random value, created once at startup. Comparing against
// it when the user does not exist keeps response times similar.
const DUMMY_HASH = await argon2.hash(crypto.randomUUID());

async function verifyCredentials(email, password) {
  const user = users.get(String(email).trim().toLowerCase());
  const hash = user?.passwordHash ?? DUMMY_HASH;
  const valid = await argon2.verify(hash, String(password));
  return user && valid ? user : null;
}

Return the same message for "no such user" and "wrong password", so the endpoint does not reveal which emails are registered.

docs.title: Session-based login
docs.text:
import session from "express-session";

app.use(session({
  secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET,
  resave: false,
  saveUninitialized: false,
  cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax",
    maxAge: 8 * 60 * 60 * 1000 },
  // store: a Redis or MongoDB store in production
}));

app.post("/auth/login", async (req, res, next) => {
  const user = await verifyCredentials(req.body?.email, req.body?.password);
  if (!user) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Invalid email or password" });

  req.session.regenerate((err) => {          // prevent session fixation
    if (err) return next(err);
    req.session.user = { id: user.id, role: user.role };
    res.json({ id: user.id, email: user.email });
  });
});

function requireSession(req, res, next) {
  if (!req.session.user) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Login required" });
  req.user = req.session.user;
  next();
}

The full cookie and session setup is covered in cookies and sessions.

docs.title: JWT-based login and verify middleware
docs.text:
import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";

const ACCESS_SECRET = process.env.JWT_ACCESS_SECRET;

function issueAccessToken(user) {
  return jwt.sign(
    { sub: user.id, role: user.role },           // claims
    ACCESS_SECRET,
    { expiresIn: "15m", algorithm: "HS256", issuer: "my-api" }
  );
}

app.post("/auth/token", async (req, res) => {
  const user = await verifyCredentials(req.body?.email, req.body?.password);
  if (!user) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Invalid email or password" });
  res.json({ accessToken: issueAccessToken(user), tokenType: "Bearer",
    expiresIn: 900 });
});

function requireJwt(req, res, next) {
  const header = req.get("authorization") ?? "";
  const [scheme, token] = header.split(" ");
  // A 401 should tell the client which auth scheme to use.
  res.set("WWW-Authenticate", "Bearer");
  if (scheme !== "Bearer" || !token) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Missing bearer token" });
  }
  try {
    // Pin the algorithm so a forged header cannot switch it.
    const claims = jwt.verify(token, ACCESS_SECRET,
      { algorithms: ["HS256"], issuer: "my-api" });
    res.removeHeader("WWW-Authenticate"); // authenticated: not needed
    req.user = { id: claims.sub, role: claims.role };
    next();
  } catch (err) {
    const expired = err.name === "TokenExpiredError";
    res.status(401).json({ error: expired ? "Token expired" : "Invalid token" });
  }
}

Example request and response:

GET /orders HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
{"error":"Token expired"}

docs.title: Refresh-token rotation
docs.text:
import { createHash, randomBytes } from "node:crypto";

const refreshTokens = new Map(); // tokenHash -> { userId, expiresAt }
const sha256 = (value) => createHash("sha256").update(value).digest("hex");

function issueRefreshToken(res, userId) {
  const token = randomBytes(32).toString("base64url");
  refreshTokens.set(sha256(token), {
    userId, expiresAt: Date.now() + 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 });
  res.cookie("refresh", token, {
    httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "strict",
    // Sent only to /auth/* routes (refresh and logout), not to the rest of
    // the API. A narrower path such as "/auth/refresh" would stop the
    // browser sending it to /auth/logout, so logout could not revoke it.
    path: "/auth",
    maxAge: 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  });
}

app.post("/auth/refresh", (req, res) => {
  const token = req.cookies?.refresh;          // requires cookie-parser
  const record = token && refreshTokens.get(sha256(token));
  if (!record || record.expiresAt < Date.now()) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Please log in again" });
  }
  refreshTokens.delete(sha256(token));         // rotate: old token is dead
  const user = findUserById(record.userId);
  issueRefreshToken(res, user.id);
  res.json({ accessToken: issueAccessToken(user) });
});

Production systems also detect reuse: if an already-rotated refresh token is presented, someone copied it, so revoke all of that user's tokens.

docs.title: Authorization: roles and ownership
docs.text:
function requireRole(...allowed) {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    if (!req.user) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Login required" });
    if (!allowed.includes(req.user.role)) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: "Not allowed" });
    }
    next();
  };
}

app.delete("/admin/users/:id", requireJwt, requireRole("admin"),
  (req, res) => res.sendStatus(204));

// Ownership: a user may read only their own orders.
app.get("/orders/:id", requireJwt, async (req, res) => {
  const order = await findOrder(req.params.id);
  if (!order || order.userId !== req.user.id) {
    // 404 instead of 403 avoids confirming that the order exists.
    return res.status(404).json({ error: "Order not found" });
  }
  res.json(order);
});

Missing ownership checks are called broken object-level authorization, and the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) ranks them first (API1). Checking roles alone is not enough.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text:
app.post("/auth/logout", (req, res) => {
  const token = req.cookies?.refresh;
  if (token) refreshTokens.delete(sha256(token)); // revoke server-side
  res.clearCookie("refresh", { path: "/auth", httpOnly: true,
    secure: true, sameSite: "strict" });   // same path as when it was set
  res.sendStatus(204);
});

The short-lived access token remains valid until it expires, which is why its lifetime is kept short.

docs.title: Brute-force protection
docs.text:
import { rateLimit } from "express-rate-limit";

const loginLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,   // 15 minutes
  limit: 10,                  // 10 attempts per IP per window
  standardHeaders: "draft-8", // send the standard RateLimit headers
  legacyHeaders: false,       // drop the old X-RateLimit-* headers
  skipSuccessfulRequests: true,
});

app.post("/auth/login", loginLimiter /* , login handler */);

Per-IP limits do not stop attackers spread over many IPs. Add per-account measures too: temporary lockout or increasing delays after repeated failures for one email, plus alerts and optional CAPTCHA.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Hash passwords with Argon2id or bcrypt; never store or log plain passwords.
  • Use one generic error for any login failure.
  • Regenerate sessions on login; destroy them on logout.
  • Keep access tokens short-lived; rotate and store refresh tokens hashed.
  • Pin JWT algorithms in jwt.verify() and validate iss/aud when used.
  • Load secrets from environment variables and keep them long and random.
  • Check authorization on every request, including ownership of the record.
  • Rate-limit login, registration, and password-reset endpoints.
  • Use HTTPS everywhere; tokens and cookies are credentials.
  • Consider an identity provider when you need MFA, SSO, or social login.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Valid tokens fail on some servers. Detect: intermittent 401s and JsonWebTokenError: invalid signature in logs from only some instances. Cause: instances signing and verifying with different secrets (a missing environment variable, or a secret generated at startup). Fix: load one secret (or key pair) from your secret manager on every instance; for rotation, verify against the old and new keys during the switch.
  • Freshly issued tokens are rejected as expired or not yet valid. Detect: TokenExpiredError or NotBeforeError seconds after login, often only when the issuer and verifier are different machines. Cause: clock skew between servers. Fix: keep clocks synchronized with NTP and allow a few seconds with jwt.verify's clockTolerance option.
  • Login becomes slow and CPU spikes during an attack. Detect: rising p99 latency on the login route, high CPU, and many 401s from a small set of IPs. Cause: credential stuffing; password hashing is deliberately expensive, so each attempt costs real CPU and memory. Fix: rate-limit by IP and by account, add increasing delays or CAPTCHA after failures, and alert on failure-rate spikes.
  • Users stay signed in after a password change or "log out everywhere". Detect: support reports, or audit logs showing API calls with old tokens. Cause: JWT access tokens stay valid until exp, and refresh tokens were not revoked. Fix: delete all of the user's refresh tokens on password change, keep access tokens short, and optionally add a token-version claim checked against the user record.
  • Users are randomly logged out with several tabs open. Detect: refresh-endpoint 401s "Please log in again" shortly after successful refreshes for the same user. Cause: two tabs refresh at the same moment with the same refresh token; rotation invalidates it for the second one (and reuse detection may revoke the whole family). Fix: let only one refresh run at a time on the client and share its result across tabs.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Authentication: Proving who the user is.
  • Authorization: Deciding what an authenticated user may do.
  • Hash: A one-way transformation; the original cannot be recovered.
  • Salt: Random data mixed into each password hash.
  • JWT: A signed token carrying claims such as sub and exp.
  • Bearer token: A token that grants access to whoever presents it.
  • Refresh token: A long-lived credential used only to get new access tokens.
  • Token rotation: Replacing a refresh token every time it is used.
  • RBAC: Role-based access control.
  • Strategy (Passport): A plug-in that implements one login method.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "JWTs are encrypted." The payload is only base64url-encoded; anyone can read it. Never put secrets in it.
  • Long-lived JWTs with no revocation. A stolen token works until expiry.
  • Using jwt.decode() to authenticate. It does not verify the signature; use jwt.verify().
  • Returning 403 for missing credentials. Missing or invalid credentials are 401.
  • Checking only roles. A logged-in user changing an ID in the URL must still be blocked.
  • Different errors for unknown email and wrong password. This lets attackers enumerate accounts.
  • Storing tokens in localStorage "because it is easy." Any XSS bug can steal them.
  • Assuming authentication middleware also authorizes. They are separate steps.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why are passwords hashed rather than encrypted, and what does a salt add?
  2. Compare session-based and JWT-based login for a browser app.
  3. Why do access tokens expire quickly, and how does refresh-token rotation limit the damage of theft?
  4. When should an API return 401, and when 403?
  5. What is an ownership check, and why are role checks not enough?
  6. Why are per-IP rate limits insufficient against credential stuffing?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet
  • jsonwebtoken on npm
  • argon2 on npm
  • Passport.js documentation
  • express-rate-limit on npm
  • Authentication security

docs.title: Body Parsing and Content Types
docs.text: A request body arrives as a stream of raw bytes. Before your code can use it, something must read those bytes, decode them, and turn them into a JavaScript value. In Express that job belongs to body-parsing middleware, and the request's Content-Type header tells the parser which format to expect.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: If no parser runs, req.body is undefined and handlers fail. If the wrong parser runs, data is misread. If parsers accept unlimited input, a client can exhaust memory with one huge request. Webhook providers sign the exact raw bytes they send, so parsing too early can make signature verification impossible. Getting body parsing right is a correctness, reliability, and security concern.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
Webhook providers are the clearest real-world reason to understand body parsing: each one signs the exact bytes it sends.

  • Stripe requires "the exact UTF-8 string Stripe sent, without any modifications" for signature checks. Its docs warn that frameworks which reorder keys or strip whitespace break verification, and that the webhook route must come before app.use(express.json()) in Express (Stripe documentation). Stripe's own API also "accepts form-encoded request bodies", a reminder that application/x-www-form-urlencoded is not only for HTML forms (Stripe API reference).
  • GitHub sends an HMAC-SHA256 signature in the X-Hub-Signature-256 header. Its docs say never to compare signatures with a plain == and suggest crypto.timingSafeEqual for a constant-time comparison (GitHub documentation).
  • Slack signs requests in X-Slack-Signature and tells developers to "use the raw request body ... before it has been deserialized from JSON or other forms" (Slack documentation).
  • Shopify puts a base64-encoded HMAC in X-Shopify-Hmac-SHA256, generated from the app's client secret and the raw request body (Shopify documentation). Providers differ in header names and encodings (hex or base64), so always follow the provider's own instructions.

docs.title: The Content-Type header
docs.text:
The client declares the body's format with Content-Type:

Content-Type Body looks like Typical sender Express parser application/json {"name":"Asha","age":30} fetch, mobile apps, API clients express.json() application/x-www-form-urlencoded name=Asha&age=30 HTML <form> (default) express.urlencoded() multipart/form-data Parts separated by a boundary; files included HTML forms with files, FormData multer or busboy (not built in) text/plain hello Simple clients, logs express.text() application/octet-stream Arbitrary bytes File uploads, binary APIs express.raw()

A parser only runs when the request's Content-Type matches its type option. A JSON parser ignores a form body, and vice versa.

docs.title: express.json()
docs.text:
app.use(express.json({
  limit: "100kb",      // default; larger bodies get 413
  strict: true,        // default; only objects and arrays at the top level
  type: "application/json", // which Content-Types to parse
}));
Option Default Meaning limit "100kb" Maximum body size; exceeding it produces a 413 error strict true Accept only arrays and objects, not bare values like "hi" or 42 type "application/json" Media types to parse; can be a string, array, or function inflate true Decompress gzip, deflate, or Brotli (br, new in Express 5) request bodies; with false, compressed bodies are rejected with 415 reviver — Passed to JSON.parse verify — verify(req, res, buf, encoding) called with the raw bytes before parsing

To accept vendor types such as application/vnd.api+json, pass type: ["application/json", "application/*+json"].

docs.title: express.urlencoded()
docs.text:
Parses HTML form submissions.

app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false, limit: "50kb" }));
  • extended: false (the Express 5 default) uses Node.js's querystring: user[name]=Asha stays as the key "user[name]".
  • extended: true uses the qs package, which builds nested objects: { user: { name: "Asha" } }. Express 4 defaulted to true.
  • parameterLimit (default 1000) caps the number of fields; a body with more fields is rejected with 413 (error type parameters.too.many).

All values arrive as strings. A checkbox that is unchecked sends nothing at all, so its key is simply missing.

docs.title: express.text() and express.raw()
docs.text:
// Body as a string
app.post("/notes/plain", express.text({ type: "text/plain" }), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ length: req.body.length });
});

// Body as a Buffer of the exact bytes received
app.post("/upload/binary", express.raw({ type: "application/octet-stream", limit: "5mb" }),
  (req, res) => {
    res.json({ bytes: req.body.length });
  });

docs.title: Multipart bodies
docs.text: multipart/form-data is used for file uploads. Express has no built-in parser for it; use multer (built on busboy). See file uploads with Multer.

docs.title: req.body when nothing was parsed
docs.text: In Express 5, req.body is undefined when no parser handled the request: no parser registered, a different Content-Type, or no body at all. Express 4 setups often produced {}. Defensive code reads req.body?.field or validates the whole body with a schema.

docs.title: Size limits and 413
docs.text: Without a limit, a client could send gigabytes and exhaust memory. The parsers stop reading when the limit is reached and raise an error with status 413 Payload Too Large (also called Content Too Large). Choose limits per route: a login form needs a few kilobytes, while an import endpoint might need megabytes.

docs.title: Malformed JSON and 400
docs.text:
If the body is not valid JSON, express.json() raises an error with status 400. Without your own error handler, Express's default handler returns an HTML error page. Handle parser errors in your error middleware to return JSON:

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  if (err.type === "entity.parse.failed") {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "Request body is not valid JSON" });
  }
  if (err.type === "entity.too.large") {
    return res.status(413).json({ error: "Request body is too large" });
  }
  if (err.type === "charset.unsupported" || err.type === "encoding.unsupported") {
    return res.status(415).json({ error: "Unsupported body encoding" });
  }
  next(err); // anything else goes to the general error handler
});

The type values come from body-parser, which powers Express's parsers; the errors also carry an appropriate status.

docs.title: Character sets
docs.text: Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 declares the text encoding. JSON exchanged between systems must be UTF-8, and Express's JSON parser rejects other charsets, such as latin1, with a 415 error (charset.unsupported). For text bodies, express.text({ defaultCharset: "utf-8" }) sets the fallback used when the request names no charset.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Use Avoid A JSON API express.json({ limit }) Global parsers with large limits for every route HTML forms, or APIs that accept form encoding express.urlencoded({ extended: false }) extended: true unless you need nested fields Webhooks that must be signature-checked express.raw({ type: "application/json" }) on that route, or the verify option Parsing the body before the check Plain text bodies (logs, CSV snippets) express.text() Reading text through the JSON parser File uploads Multer (or busboy) on the upload route only express.json()/express.raw() with huge limits Forwarding a request to another service unchanged No parser; stream the request through Parsing and re-serializing, which costs CPU and changes bytes

Use route-level parsers when routes need different limits or formats. Use one global parser when the whole app is a small JSON API with the same limit everywhere. Do not parse at all for very large or streaming uploads: parsers buffer the whole body in memory before your handler runs.

docs.title: Parsers applied only where they are needed
docs.text:
Global parsers run for every request, including ones that never read a body. Route-level parsers keep limits tight and avoid surprises.

const smallJson = express.json({ limit: "10kb" });
const bigJson = express.json({ limit: "2mb" });

app.post("/auth/login", smallJson, login);
app.post("/imports/products", bigJson, importProducts);

docs.title: Webhook signature verification with the raw body
docs.text:
Webhook providers sign the exact bytes they send. If express.json() parses and re-serializes the body first, whitespace and key order can change and the signature no longer matches. Keep the raw Buffer for the webhook route, and register it before any global JSON parser.

import express from "express";
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";

const app = express();

// 1. Webhook route: raw bytes, registered before express.json()
app.post("/webhooks/payments", express.raw({ type: "application/json" }), (req, res) => {
  const received = Buffer.from(req.get("X-Signature") ?? "", "hex");
  const expected = createHmac("sha256", process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET)
    .update(req.body)           // req.body is a Buffer here
    .digest();

  // timingSafeEqual needs equal lengths and avoids timing attacks
  if (received.length !== expected.length || !timingSafeEqual(received, expected)) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Invalid signature" });
  }

  const event = JSON.parse(req.body.toString("utf8"));
  // ...queue the event for processing...
  res.sendStatus(204);
});

// 2. Everything else: parsed JSON
app.use(express.json());

An alternative is the verify option, which hands you the raw bytes while still parsing:

app.use(express.json({
  verify: (req, res, buf) => {
    if (req.originalUrl.startsWith("/webhooks/")) req.rawBody = buf;
  },
}));

The header name and signing scheme differ per provider; follow its documentation. See webhooks.

docs.title: Supporting both JSON and form submissions
docs.text:
app.use(express.json());
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false }));

app.post("/subscribe", (req, res) => {
  const email = req.body?.email;
  if (typeof email !== "string") {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "email is required" });
  }
  res.status(201).json({ subscribed: email });
});

curl -X POST localhost:3000/subscribe -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"a@example.com"}'
curl -X POST localhost:3000/subscribe -d "email=a@example.com"
# curl -d sends application/x-www-form-urlencoded by default

docs.title: Requiring a specific content type
docs.text:
function requireJson(req, res, next) {
  // req.is() returns null when there is no body (GET, most DELETEs), so
  // only a body with another Content-Type is rejected
  if (req.is("application/json") === false) {
    return res.status(415).json({ error: "Content-Type must be application/json" });
  }
  next();
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Set explicit limit values that match each route's real needs.
  • Register parsers only for routes that read bodies, especially large limits.
  • Handle parser errors (entity.parse.failed, entity.too.large) and return consistent JSON errors.
  • Keep the raw body for webhook routes and register them before global JSON parsing.
  • Validate req.body after parsing; parsing proves the syntax is valid, not that the data is correct. See request validation.
  • Prefer extended: false unless you truly need nested form fields.
  • Reject unexpected content types with 415 for endpoints that accept only one format.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Legitimate imports fail with 413. Symptom: larger uploads or imports are rejected. Detect: two different sources: Express logs PayloadTooLargeError: request entity too large, while a 413 HTML page from Nginx never reaches your app at all, because Nginx's client_max_body_size defaults to 1m. Cause: a limit lower than the route needs, at either layer. Fix: raise the limit for that route only, in both Express and the proxy.
  • Webhook deliveries start failing after a refactor. Symptom: the provider's dashboard shows failed deliveries and retries. Detect: a spike in 401 Invalid signature responses on the webhook route. Cause: a global express.json() was moved above the webhook route, so the raw bytes are gone. Fix: register the raw webhook route first, and test it with a real signed payload.
  • req.body is undefined for one client. Symptom: "field is required" errors from a client that is sending the field. Detect: the request log shows Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8. Cause: a browser fetch with a string body and no Content-Type header is sent as text/plain, which express.json() skips. Fix: the client sets Content-Type: application/json; optionally return 415 for other types.
  • The frontend cannot read error responses. Symptom: frontend logs show JSON parse errors such as Unexpected token '<'. Detect: the error responses have Content-Type: text/html. Cause: malformed JSON reaches Express's default handler, which answers with an HTML page. Fix: handle entity.parse.failed in your error middleware and answer with JSON.
  • Latency spikes during large uploads. Symptom: all endpoints slow down while a few clients send big JSON bodies. Detect: event-loop delay metrics rise together with request size. Cause: JSON.parse runs synchronously on the main thread. Fix: keep JSON limits small and move bulk imports to file uploads processed in the background.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Request body: The data sent after the request headers.
  • Content-Type: The header declaring the body's media type and, optionally, its charset.
  • Media type (MIME type): A label such as application/json describing a data format.
  • Body parser: Middleware that reads the body stream and fills req.body.
  • Multipart: A body format that combines several parts, including files, separated by a boundary string.
  • Raw body: The exact bytes received, before parsing.
  • 413 / 415: Status codes for "body too large" and "unsupported media type".

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Forgetting express.json() and reading undefined from req.body.
  • Sending JSON without Content-Type: application/json, so the parser skips the body.
  • Expecting express.json() or express.urlencoded() to handle file uploads; multipart needs a separate parser.
  • Leaving the default HTML error page for malformed JSON in an API.
  • Parsing webhook bodies with a global JSON parser and then failing signature checks.
  • Assuming form values are numbers or booleans; they are strings.
  • Thinking a successful parse means the data is valid.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. How does Express decide which body parser handles a request?
  2. What is the difference between extended: false and extended: true?
  3. Why should every parser have a size limit, and what status does exceeding it produce?
  4. Why does webhook signature verification need the raw body, and how can you keep it?
  5. What is req.body in Express 5 when no parser ran?
  6. Which parser do you need for multipart/form-data?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Express 5 API: express.json()
  • Express 5 API: express.urlencoded()
  • Express: body-parser middleware
  • MDN: Content-Type
  • MDN: POST and form encodings
  • Related: the request object, HTTP headers.

docs.title: Cookies and Sessions in Express
docs.text: HTTP is stateless: every request arrives on its own, with no memory of the previous one. Cookies let a server ask the browser to store a small value and send it back on later requests, and sessions build on cookies to remember who a user is between requests. This lesson shows how to set cookies safely in Express, how signed cookies work, and how to run server-side sessions with express-session.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Almost every logged-in web experience depends on cookies: staying signed in, remembering a cart, keeping a language preference. A cookie that is set carelessly can be read by injected JavaScript, sent over plain HTTP, or attached to requests from another site. Those mistakes turn into session theft, session fixation, and cross-site request forgery (CSRF). Knowing what each cookie option does lets you choose settings on purpose instead of copying them.

For the general theory of sessions, cookies, and tokens, see sessions, cookies, and JWT.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub signs users in with a session cookie: its cookie list describes user_session as the cookie "used to log you in" for two weeks, plus a separate __Host-user_session_same_site cookie that lets browsers supporting SameSite check whether a request originates from GitHub. This is the same pattern as this lesson: an opaque session cookie, with SameSite as a cross-site defense.
  • Google Chrome changed how cookies without a SameSite attribute behave. Google's web.dev guide explains that such a cookie is treated as if it were SameSite=Lax, so sites that need a cookie in cross-site contexts must now opt in with SameSite=None; Secure.
  • Shopify found that cookies do not work reliably for apps embedded in its admin, which run inside an iframe on another site. Its documentation requires embedded apps to authenticate with short-lived ID tokens "because third-party cookies aren't reliably available in that context". Cookie-based sessions are the right tool when the app and API are the same site; cross-site embedding is where they break down.

Popular tools: express-session, cookie-parser, connect-redis, connect-mongo, csrf-csrf, and csrf-sync; session data usually lives in Redis or MongoDB.

docs.title: Cookie recap
docs.text:
1. The server sends a Set-Cookie response header.
  2. The browser stores the cookie under the server's site.
  3. On later requests that match the cookie's domain and path, the browser sends it back in a Cookie request header.
Browser                                  Express server
   | POST /login                               |
   |------------------------------------------>|
   |       200 OK                               |
   |       Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; HttpOnly;    |
   |                   Secure; SameSite=Lax     |
   |<------------------------------------------|
   | GET /account                               |
   | Cookie: sid=abc123                         |
   |------------------------------------------>|

A cookie is only a name and a value plus attributes. It is not encrypted, and the user can read and edit it. Anything security-sensitive must either be an unguessable identifier (a session ID) or be signed so tampering is detected.

docs.title: Setting cookies with res.cookie()
docs.text:
res.cookie(name, value, options) adds a Set-Cookie header. If value is an object, Express serializes it as JSON (prefixed with j:).

Option What it does What it protects against httpOnly Hides the cookie from document.cookie Theft by injected JavaScript (XSS) secure Sends the cookie only over HTTPS Interception on plain HTTP networks sameSite "strict", "lax", or "none": controls cross-site sending CSRF and cross-site leaks maxAge Lifetime in milliseconds (Express converts it to Max-Age seconds) Cookies that live forever expires Absolute expiry as a Date Same as maxAge; prefer one of the two domain Which host(s) receive the cookie Leaving it unset limits the cookie to the exact host path URL path prefix that receives the cookie (default "/") Sending a cookie to routes that do not need it signed Signs the value with the cookie-parser secret Undetected tampering

Without maxAge or expires, the cookie is a session cookie: the browser deletes it when it decides the browsing session has ended.

docs.title: SameSite in detail
docs.text:
• Strict: never sent on cross-site requests, including clicking a link from another site. Safest, but users arriving from an email link appear logged out.
  • Lax: sent on top-level navigations that use safe methods (such as following a link with GET) but not on cross-site POSTs, images, or fetch() calls. Some browsers use Lax as the default when the attribute is missing, but not all do, so always set SameSite explicitly.
  • None: sent on all cross-site requests. Browsers require Secure with it. Use only when a different site genuinely needs the cookie, such as an embedded widget.

"Site" means the registrable domain: app.example.com and api.example.com are the same site but different origins.

docs.title: Reading cookies with cookie-parser
docs.text:
Express does not parse the Cookie header by itself. The cookie-parser middleware fills two objects:

  • req.cookies: plain cookies.
  • req.signedCookies: cookies whose signature verified. A tampered signed cookie appears as false.

docs.title: How signed cookies work
docs.text:
When you pass a secret to cookie-parser and set signed: true, the stored value becomes s:<value>.<signature>, where the signature is an HMAC of the value using the secret. On each request cookie-parser recomputes the signature. If someone changes the value, the signatures no longer match.

Signing proves the value came from your server; it does not hide the value. Never put secrets or personal data in a cookie because it is signed.

docs.title: Server-side sessions with express-session
docs.text:
With express-session, the cookie holds only a random session ID. The data lives on the server in a session store.

On each request the middleware reads the cookie, verifies its signature, loads the session from the store, and exposes it as req.session. When the response finishes, a changed session is saved back.

Important options:

Option Meaning Recommended value secret Signs the session ID cookie. An array allows rotation: the first signs, all verify A long random value from an environment variable name Cookie name (default connect.sid) A neutral name such as sid resave Save the session on every request even if unchanged false (set it explicitly) saveUninitialized Store brand-new sessions that were never modified false for login sessions; avoids storing empty sessions and setting cookies before consent rolling Reset the cookie expiry on every response true for sliding expiry if you want it cookie Cookie options (httpOnly defaults to true) httpOnly, secure, sameSite, maxAge store Where session data lives Redis or MongoDB store in production

MemoryStore is not for production

The default MemoryStore keeps sessions in the process's memory. It leaks memory over time, loses every session on restart, and does not work across multiple processes or servers. Use a shared store such as Redis (connect-redis) or MongoDB (connect-mongo).

docs.title: Session lifecycle
docs.text: Moment What to do Why Login succeeds req.session.regenerate(), then store the user ID Prevents session fixation: an attacker cannot plant a known session ID before login Privilege change Regenerate again Same reason Each request Read req.session.userId Identifies the user Logout req.session.destroy() and clear the cookie Removes the server-side session, not just the cookie

docs.title: Secure cookies behind a proxy
docs.text:
In production, TLS often ends at a load balancer or nginx, which forwards plain HTTP to Express. Express then thinks the request is insecure, and express-session refuses to send a secure cookie. Tell Express to trust the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto header:

app.set("trust proxy", 1); // trust the first proxy hop

Only trust proxies you actually run; see security best practices.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use cookie-based server sessions when:

  • A browser app and its API are served from the same site (for example app.example.com and api.example.com), so the cookie is first-party.
  • You need instant logout and revocation: destroying the stored session ends access immediately.
  • You want the browser to handle credentials automatically, with HttpOnly keeping them away from JavaScript.

Avoid them, or add something else, when:

  • The client is a mobile app, CLI, or another server: a bearer token in the Authorization header is simpler than managing a cookie jar.
  • The frontend is embedded on a different site (an iframe in a partner's page): third-party cookies are often blocked.
  • You cannot run a shared session store and have several instances; use signed, self-contained tokens or a stateless cookie instead.
Approach State lives Revocation Best for Server session (express-session + Redis) Server store; cookie holds an ID Immediate (destroy the session) Same-site browser apps Signed cookie holding the data (cookie-session) In the cookie (size-limited, readable) Hard until expiry Tiny, non-sensitive state; no store available JWT in Authorization header Token on the client Hard until expiry (needs a denylist or short expiry) Mobile apps, service-to-service, third-party API clients JWT in an HttpOnly cookie Token in the cookie Same as JWT Browser apps that want stateless servers

docs.title: Setting, reading, and clearing a cookie
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import cookieParser from "cookie-parser";

const app = express();
app.use(cookieParser(process.env.COOKIE_SECRET)); // secret enables signing

app.post("/preferences/theme", express.json(), (req, res) => {
  res.cookie("theme", req.body.theme, {
    maxAge: 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000, // one year, in milliseconds
    httpOnly: true,
    secure: true,
    sameSite: "lax",
  });
  res.sendStatus(204);
});

app.get("/preferences/theme", (req, res) => {
  res.json({ theme: req.cookies.theme ?? "light" });
});

app.delete("/preferences/theme", (req, res) => {
  // Options such as path and domain must match the ones used to set it.
  res.clearCookie("theme", { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax" });
  res.sendStatus(204);
});

app.listen(3000);

The response to the first request contains:

Set-Cookie: theme=dark; Max-Age=31536000; Path=/; Expires=...; HttpOnly;
            Secure; SameSite=Lax

docs.title: A signed cookie
docs.text:
app.get("/visit", (req, res) => {
  const visits = Number(req.signedCookies.visits ?? 0) + 1;
  res.cookie("visits", String(visits), { signed: true, httpOnly: true });
  res.json({ visits });
});

If a user edits the visits cookie, req.signedCookies.visits becomes false, and the count restarts.

docs.title: Sessions with a Redis store
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import session from "express-session";
import { createClient } from "redis";
import { RedisStore } from "connect-redis"; // named export in current versions

const redisClient = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
await redisClient.connect();

const app = express();
app.set("trust proxy", 1);
app.use(express.json());

app.use(
  session({
    store: new RedisStore({ client: redisClient, prefix: "sess:" }),
    name: "sid",
    secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET,
    resave: false,
    saveUninitialized: false,
    cookie: {
      httpOnly: true,
      secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
      sameSite: "lax",
      maxAge: 8 * 60 * 60 * 1000, // 8 hours
    },
  })
);

A MongoDB store is set up the same way:

import MongoStore from "connect-mongo";

app.use(
  session({
    store: MongoStore.create({ mongoUrl: process.env.MONGODB_URI }),
    secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET,
    resave: false,
    saveUninitialized: false,
  })
);

docs.title: Login and logout with regeneration
docs.text:
app.post("/login", async (req, res, next) => {
  const user = await verifyCredentials(req.body.email, req.body.password);
  if (!user) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Invalid email or password" });
  }

  // New session ID after login: defeats session fixation.
  req.session.regenerate((err) => {
    if (err) return next(err);
    req.session.userId = user.id;
    req.session.role = user.role;
    // Save before responding so the next request sees the session.
    req.session.save((saveErr) => {
      if (saveErr) return next(saveErr);
      res.json({ id: user.id, name: user.name });
    });
  });
});

app.post("/logout", (req, res, next) => {
  req.session.destroy((err) => {
    if (err) return next(err);
    res.clearCookie("sid", { httpOnly: true, sameSite: "lax", secure: true });
    res.sendStatus(204);
  });
});

function requireLogin(req, res, next) {
  if (!req.session.userId) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Login required" });
  }
  next();
}

app.get("/account", requireLogin, (req, res) => {
  res.json({ userId: req.session.userId });
});

docs.title: A simple CSRF defense: checking the Origin header
docs.text:
SameSite=Lax already blocks most cross-site POSTs. A cheap second layer is to reject state-changing requests whose Origin header is not yours:

const allowedOrigins = new Set([process.env.APP_ORIGIN]);

function checkOrigin(req, res, next) {
  const safe = ["GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"].includes(req.method);
  const origin = req.get("origin");
  if (safe || (origin && allowedOrigins.has(origin))) return next();
  res.status(403).json({ error: "Cross-site request blocked" });
}

app.use(checkOrigin);

This check also rejects state-changing requests that send no Origin header at all, such as curl or server-to-server calls. That is fine for a browser-only, cookie-authenticated app; mount it only on cookie-based routes if other clients use tokens instead.

For forms and older browsers, use a CSRF token pattern (synchronizer token or double-submit cookie). The old csurf package is deprecated; maintained alternatives include csrf-csrf and csrf-sync.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Set httpOnly, secure, and an explicit sameSite on every cookie that identifies a user.
  • Store only an opaque session ID in the cookie; keep user data server-side.
  • Set resave: false and saveUninitialized: false explicitly.
  • Use a shared store (Redis, MongoDB) in production, never MemoryStore.
  • Regenerate the session on login and privilege changes; destroy it on logout.
  • Keep secrets in environment variables and rotate them by passing an array to secret.
  • Give sessions both an idle limit and an absolute lifetime.
  • Make GET routes safe (no state changes) so SameSite=Lax actually helps.
  • Set trust proxy correctly when TLS ends at a proxy.
  • Rename the default connect.sid cookie to avoid advertising your stack.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Users are logged out after every deploy or at random. Detect: a jump in 401 "Login required" responses after restarts or when traffic shifts between instances; at startup the process logs Warning: connect.session() MemoryStore is not designed for a production environment. Cause: the default MemoryStore, so each instance has its own sessions and a restart wipes them. Fix: a shared store such as Redis through connect-redis.
  • Login "succeeds" but the next request is anonymous, only in production. Detect: the login response in the browser's Network panel has no Set-Cookie header. Cause: cookie.secure: true while TLS ends at a load balancer, so Express sees plain HTTP and express-session refuses to send a secure cookie. Fix: app.set("trust proxy", 1) (matching your real proxy hops) or the session's proxy option.
  • The frontend on another domain gets 401s although login worked. Detect: API requests in the Network panel carry no Cookie header, and the browser may flag the cookie as blocked. Cause: the cookie is SameSite=Lax (or third-party cookies are blocked) while the frontend is cross-site. Fix: serve app and API from the same site, or use SameSite=None; Secure with credentialed CORS, or switch to tokens.
  • Everyone is logged out right after a secret rotation. Detect: a sudden, site-wide spike in "Login required" right after a config change. Cause: the old secret was replaced, so existing signed session IDs no longer verify. Fix: pass an array [newSecret, oldSecret] so new cookies use the new secret while old ones still verify, and drop the old one later.
  • Redis memory keeps growing with session keys. Detect: the number of sess:* keys and used_memory in INFO grow with traffic, mostly from anonymous visitors and bots. Cause: saveUninitialized: true stores a session for every visitor. Fix: saveUninitialized: false and an explicit cookie.maxAge (connect-redis uses the cookie expiry as the key TTL).

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Cookie: A name-value pair the browser stores and sends back to a server.
  • Session cookie: A cookie without Max-Age/Expires; removed when the browser session ends.
  • Persistent cookie: A cookie with an explicit lifetime.
  • Signed cookie: A cookie with an HMAC signature that detects tampering; still readable.
  • Session store: Server-side storage that maps session IDs to data.
  • Session fixation: An attack where the victim is made to log in with a session ID the attacker already knows.
  • CSRF: Cross-site request forgery: another site makes the browser send an authenticated request.
  • Trust proxy: An Express setting that tells it to believe X-Forwarded-* headers from known proxies.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Signed means encrypted." Signing only detects changes; anyone can read the value.
  • Forgetting cookie-parser. req.cookies is undefined without it. (express-session reads its own cookie and does not need it.)
  • Clearing with different options. res.clearCookie() must use the same path and domain, or the browser keeps the old cookie.
  • maxAge in seconds. Express expects milliseconds; maxAge: 3600 is 3.6 seconds.
  • Using MemoryStore in production. Sessions disappear on restart and do not work with more than one instance.
  • secure: true while Express sees plain HTTP. express-session skips the Set-Cookie header when the request is not HTTPS, so behind a proxy that terminates TLS the session cookie silently never arrives; configure trust proxy.
  • Logging out by clearing only the cookie. The session stays valid on the server until it expires; destroy it.
  • Assuming SameSite removes all CSRF risk. Same-site subdomains and state-changing GET routes can still be abused.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What does each of httpOnly, secure, and sameSite protect against?
  2. How does cookie-parser detect that a signed cookie was modified?
  3. Why should a session be regenerated after a successful login?
  4. Why is MemoryStore unsuitable for production?
  5. What problem does app.set("trust proxy", 1) solve for secure cookies?
  6. How do SameSite=Lax and an Origin check work together against CSRF?
