docs.title: Configuring CORS in Express
docs.text: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how a server tells browsers which other websites may call it from JavaScript. In Express, CORS is usually configured with the cors middleware package. This lesson shows how to configure it correctly; the underlying browser rules are explained in CORS concepts.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A typical setup has a frontend at https://app.example.com calling an API at https://api.example.com. Those are different origins, so the browser blocks the frontend from reading API responses unless the API sends the right CORS headers. Misconfigured CORS either breaks the frontend with confusing console errors or, if opened too widely with credentials, lets malicious sites make authenticated requests on a user's behalf and read the results.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub's REST API "supports cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) for AJAX requests from any origin". Its documented responses use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, allow the Authorization header in preflights, cache preflights for a day (Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400), and expose headers such as ETag, Link, and the rate-limit headers to JavaScript (GitHub documentation). A wildcard origin cannot be combined with cookies, so browser callers authenticate with a token they send themselves.
  • Amazon S3 lets you attach a CORS configuration to a bucket. AWS's own example is a website hosted in a bucket whose JavaScript needs to make authenticated GET and PUT requests to the bucket's S3 API endpoint, which the browser would otherwise block (AWS documentation).
  • Amazon API Gateway documents that with a Lambda proxy or HTTP proxy integration, "your backend is responsible for returning the Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, and Access-Control-Allow-Headers headers". An Express app behind such a gateway therefore still needs its own CORS middleware (AWS documentation).
  • Google Cloud Storage recommends CORS when "you want your website to fetch files, images, or scripts directly from a Cloud Storage bucket using a browser-based request", configured on the bucket (Google Cloud documentation).

Popular tools and providers: the cors npm package, reverse proxies such as Nginx, API gateways, and CDN or storage settings for static assets.

docs.title: A quick recap
docs.text:
• An origin is scheme + host + port: https://app.example.com:443.
  • Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: a page's JavaScript cannot read responses from another origin unless that origin allows it.
  • The server allows it with response headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  • For "non-simple" requests (for example PUT, DELETE, JSON bodies, or an Authorization header), the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request to ask permission.

docs.title: The cors package defaults
docs.text:
npm install cors

import cors from "cors";

app.use(cors()); // allow every origin

With no options, cors() sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, allows the methods GET, HEAD, PUT, PATCH, POST, DELETE, reflects whatever request headers the preflight asks for, and answers preflight requests with 204. That is fine for a truly public, read-only API that uses no cookies, but too open for most applications.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Meaning origin Boolean, string, RegExp, array, or function Which origins are allowed (see below) methods String or array Value of Access-Control-Allow-Methods allowedHeaders String or array Request headers the browser may send; defaults to reflecting the preflight's Access-Control-Request-Headers exposedHeaders String or array Response headers JavaScript may read beyond the safe defaults (for example X-Total-Count) credentials Boolean Send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true so cookies and auth headers work maxAge Number (seconds) How long browsers may cache the preflight result preflightContinue Boolean false (default): cors ends preflight itself; true: pass it to your own OPTIONS handler optionsSuccessStatus Number Status for successful preflights; default 204 (some very old clients need 200)

docs.title: Forms of the origin option
docs.text:
Value Behavior "*" or omitted Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * for every request true Reflect the request's Origin back (allows anyone, including with credentials: dangerous) false Disable CORS headers "https://app.example.com" Always send that one origin ["https://a.example.com", "https://b.example.com"] Reflect the origin only if it is in the list /\.example\.com$/ Reflect the origin if it matches the RegExp (origin, callback) => { ... } Decide dynamically; call callback(null, true) to allow or callback(null, false) to deny

Whenever origin is anything other than "*", including a single fixed string, the package adds Vary: Origin so caches do not serve one origin's response to another.

docs.title: Credentials need an explicit origin
docs.text:
When the frontend sends cookies (fetch(url, { credentials: "include" })) or the API relies on cookies for sessions, browsers require:

  • Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, and
  • Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to the exact origin, not *.
app.use(cors({
  origin: "https://app.example.com",
  credentials: true,
}));

CORS and cookie rules are separate checks. app.example.com and api.example.com are different origins but the same site, so a cookie with SameSite=Lax is still sent. If the frontend and API are on different sites (for example app.example.com and api.example.net), the cookie also needs SameSite=None; Secure, and some browsers block or partition such third-party cookies regardless. See cookies and sessions.

docs.title: Preflight handling
docs.text:
Registered with app.use(), the cors middleware runs for every method, including OPTIONS, so it answers preflights for all routes before any route or authentication middleware sees them. That is the simplest and most reliable setup. The flowchart shows the whole decision cors() makes for each request.

If you only enable CORS on specific routes, the preflight for that path must also get CORS headers:

const partnerCors = cors({ origin: "https://partner.example.com" });

app.options("/api/partner/orders", partnerCors);   // preflight
app.post("/api/partner/orders", partnerCors, createPartnerOrder);

To answer preflights for every path explicitly in Express 5, use the new wildcard syntax, app.options("/{*splat}", cors(options)); Express 4 tutorials show app.options("*", ...), which Express 5 rejects.

docs.title: CORS protects browsers, not your server
docs.text: CORS is enforced by browsers. curl, Postman, mobile apps, and other servers ignore it completely and can call your API regardless of your CORS settings. CORS is therefore not authentication or access control. Protect data with authentication, authorization, and rate limiting; use CORS only to decide which browser-based frontends may read responses.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Enable CORS when browser JavaScript served from one origin must read responses from your API on another origin: a frontend on app.example.com calling api.example.com, a public browser-callable API, or a widget embedded on customers' sites.

Do not enable it when:

  • Only servers, mobile apps, or command-line tools call the API. They do not enforce CORS, so the headers add nothing.
  • You can serve the frontend and API from the same origin (for example example.com and example.com/api through a reverse proxy). Same-origin requests need no CORS at all.
  • You are trying to restrict who can call the API. That needs authentication and authorization, not CORS.
Approach Use when Watch out for cors package in Express The app decides allowed origins, possibly per route Register it before authentication and routes Manual middleware You need behavior the package lacks Remember Vary: Origin and preflight handling Reverse proxy or API gateway headers Several services share one CORS policy at the edge Do not also add headers in Express (duplicate values) Same-origin hosting via a proxy You control both frontend and API deployment Needs routing configuration in the proxy Dev-server proxy (for example Vite) Local development only Production still needs a real solution

docs.title: A dynamic allowlist from configuration
docs.text:
import cors from "cors";

// e.g. CORS_ORIGINS="https://app.example.com,https://admin.example.com"
const allowedOrigins = new Set(
  (process.env.CORS_ORIGINS ?? "").split(",").map((o) => o.trim()).filter(Boolean),
);

const corsOptions = {
  origin(origin, callback) {
    // No Origin header: same-origin requests, curl, server-to-server
    if (!origin) return callback(null, true);
    callback(null, allowedOrigins.has(origin)); // false -> no CORS headers sent
  },
  credentials: true,
  methods: ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"],
  allowedHeaders: ["Content-Type", "Authorization", "X-Request-Id"],
  exposedHeaders: ["X-Total-Count", "X-Request-Id"],
  maxAge: 600, // cache preflight results for 10 minutes
};

app.use(cors(corsOptions)); // before routes and before auth middleware

Denying with callback(null, false) omits the CORS headers, so the browser blocks the response. The cors middleware then calls next(), so the request, including a preflight OPTIONS, continues to your other middleware and routes; a denied preflight therefore gets whatever they answer (often 401 or 404). Passing an Error to the callback instead sends it to your error handler, which would turn a CORS mismatch into a 500.

Keep development origins such as http://localhost:5173 in the development configuration only.

docs.title: A manual CORS middleware
docs.text:
Writing it by hand shows what the package does:

const ALLOWED = new Set(["https://app.example.com"]);

function manualCors(req, res, next) {
  const origin = req.get("Origin");

  if (origin && ALLOWED.has(origin)) {
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", origin);
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials", "true");
  }
  // The response differs by Origin, so shared caches must key on it
  res.append("Vary", "Origin");

  if (req.method === "OPTIONS") {
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Methods", "GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE");
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Headers", "Content-Type,Authorization");
    res.set("Access-Control-Max-Age", "600");
    return res.sendStatus(204); // end the preflight here
  }

  next();
}

app.use(manualCors);

docs.title: Checking headers with curl
docs.text:
curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3000/api/orders \
  -H "Origin: https://app.example.com" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: POST" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type,authorization"
# HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
# Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
# Vary: Origin
# Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
# Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE
# Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type,Authorization,X-Request-Id
# Access-Control-Max-Age: 600
# Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Total-Count,X-Request-Id
# (other headers such as Date and Connection omitted)

docs.title: Common browser errors and fixes
docs.text:
Browser console message (paraphrased) Usual cause Fix No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is present cors not registered, registered after the route, origin not in the allowlist, or the request failed before cors ran (crash, proxy error page) Register cors first; check the allowlist; check server logs for errors Allow-Origin must not be * when credentials mode is "include" credentials: true with a wildcard origin Set an explicit origin or an allowlist Response to preflight does not have HTTP ok status OPTIONS hit a 404, or auth middleware returned 401 for the preflight Register cors before auth and routes; make sure OPTIONS reaches it Request header authorization is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Headers Header missing from allowedHeaders Add the header to allowedHeaders Method PUT is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Methods Method missing from methods Add the method Allow-Origin header contains multiple values Both the proxy (for example Nginx) and Express add CORS headers Configure CORS in one place only JavaScript cannot read a custom response header Header not exposed Add it to exposedHeaders Cookies are not sent or not saved Missing credentials: "include" on fetch, or (for a cross-site API only) the cookie lacks SameSite=None; Secure Fix the client option and cookie attributes

Tip

During local development, a frontend dev-server proxy (for example Vite's server.proxy) makes API calls same-origin and avoids CORS entirely. Production still needs correct CORS if the origins differ.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use an explicit allowlist of origins loaded from configuration.
  • Never combine origin: true (reflect any origin) with credentials: true.
  • Register cors early, before authentication middleware and routes.
  • Allow only the methods and headers your frontend actually uses.
  • Expose only the response headers the frontend needs to read.
  • Set maxAge to reduce repeated preflight requests.
  • Configure CORS in one layer (app or proxy), not both.
  • Remember that CORS does not secure the API; authentication does.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Preflights rejected by authentication. Symptom: every non-simple request from the frontend fails while curl works. Detect: access logs show OPTIONS requests answered with 401 or 404; the browser console says the preflight response does not have an HTTP ok status. Cause: cors registered after authentication or routes, or the origin is missing from the allowlist (a denied preflight falls through to the rest of the app). Fix: register cors first and check the origin list.
  • "Multiple values" in Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Symptom: CORS breaks right after a proxy change. Detect: the response carries the header twice, or with two comma-separated origins. Cause: both Nginx (or an API gateway) and Express add CORS headers. Fix: configure CORS in exactly one layer.
  • Intermittent CORS errors behind a CDN. Symptom: the API works for one frontend and fails for another, depending on which one hit the cache first. Detect: cached responses carry an Access-Control-Allow-Origin for the wrong origin. Cause: a hand-written CORS middleware that reflects the origin without Vary: Origin. Fix: always send Vary: Origin when the header varies, or exclude those responses from shared caches.
  • Server errors reported as CORS errors. Symptom: the browser shows "No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header" for one endpoint. Detect: server logs show a 500 or a crash, or the proxy returned its own 502 page, for the same request. Cause: the failing response never passed through the cors middleware. When cors is registered first, errors that Express handles keep its headers, so the usual culprits are crashes, timeouts, and proxy error pages. Fix: fix the underlying server or proxy error rather than the CORS configuration.
  • A new frontend domain is blocked after launch. Symptom: the new site cannot call the API on launch day. Detect: CORS errors only for requests whose Origin is the new domain. Cause: the allowlist in the environment configuration was not updated. Fix: add the origin to configuration (for example CORS_ORIGINS) and include it in the release checklist.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Origin: The combination of scheme, host, and port of a URL.
  • Same-origin policy: The browser rule that restricts reading responses from other origins.
  • Preflight request: An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends to ask whether a cross-origin request is allowed.
  • Simple request: A cross-origin request that meets conditions allowing it to be sent without a preflight.
  • Credentialed request: A request that includes cookies or HTTP authentication.
  • Allowlist: The explicit set of origins permitted to call the API.
  • Vary: Origin: A header telling caches that the response depends on the request's Origin.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing CORS stops attackers from calling the API; it only constrains browsers.
  • Using app.use(cors()) with cookie-based sessions; credentials require an explicit origin.
  • Putting authentication middleware before cors, so preflights get 401.
  • Using Express 4's app.options("*", ...) in Express 5.
  • Fixing a CORS error by disabling browser security instead of fixing the server headers.
  • Reading a "CORS error" in the console when the real problem is a 500 response that lacked CORS headers; check the server logs.
  • Adding CORS headers in both Nginx and Express.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why do https://app.example.com and https://api.example.com count as different origins?
  2. What does a preflight request ask, and which headers answer it?
  3. Why can't Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * be used with credentials?
  4. When should you use a function for the origin option?
  5. Why must cors run before authentication middleware?
  6. Why is CORS not a substitute for authentication?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Express: cors middleware
  • cors on npm
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • MDN: Same-origin policy
  • Related: CORS concepts, origins, CORS, and browser security, HTTP headers.

docs.title: Error Handling in Express
docs.text: Error handling in Express is about catching failures from any route or middleware and turning them into consistent, safe HTTP responses in one place. Express provides a default error handler, a way to forward errors (next(err)), and special four-argument middleware for handling them. Express 5 also catches errors from async handlers automatically.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Errors are inevitable: invalid input, missing records, expired tokens, database outages, and plain bugs. Without central handling, each route answers errors differently, some failures leak stack traces to attackers, and some unhandled async errors leave requests hanging. A single error handler gives clients a predictable error format, keeps internal details private, and makes sure every failure is logged. The general principles are in error handling concepts; this lesson covers the Express mechanics.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Zalando's public RESTful API guidelines say APIs "MUST support problem JSON", the RFC 9457 application/problem+json format used in this lesson, and "MUST not expose stack traces", because they "can leak sensitive information" and reveal vulnerabilities to attackers (Zalando RESTful API Guidelines).
  • Stripe returns a consistent error object with fields such as type, code, message, and param, and documents what each HTTP status means for its API: 2xx success, 4xx a problem with the request, 5xx a problem on Stripe's side (Stripe API errors).
  • GitHub documents its error responses by status, for example 400 Bad Request with "Problems parsing JSON" and 422 with "Validation Failed" plus an errors list (GitHub REST API troubleshooting).
  • Sentry's Express integration captures errors from routes and middleware automatically and, by default, skips errors with 3xx and 4xx status codes, "since they're usually expected redirects or client errors" (Sentry for Express). That is the operational-versus-programmer split this lesson describes.

Popular tools and providers: Sentry, Datadog, and OpenTelemetry-based tools for error tracking; http-errors for creating errors with a status.

docs.title: Synchronous errors
docs.text:
Errors thrown synchronously in a handler or middleware are caught by Express automatically:

app.get("/boom", (req, res) => {
  throw new Error("Something broke"); // Express catches this
});

docs.title: Asynchronous errors: Express 5 compared with Express 4
docs.text:
In Express 5, when a handler or middleware returns a promise that rejects, Express calls next(err) with the rejection reason. async functions return promises, so a failed await reaches the error handler:

// Express 5
app.get("/users/:id", async (req, res) => {
  const user = await db.users.findById(req.params.id); // if this rejects...
  res.json(user);                                       // ...the error handler runs
});

In Express 4, the same code produces an unhandled promise rejection and the error handler never runs. Since Node.js 15, an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default, so one failing request takes down every request on that instance; if an unhandledRejection listener keeps the process alive, the client instead waits until it times out. Express 4 code must catch and forward the error itself:

// Express 4
app.get("/users/:id", async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    const user = await db.users.findById(req.params.id);
    res.json(user);
  } catch (err) {
    next(err);
  }
});

// Or a small wrapper reused for every async handler
const asyncHandler = (fn) => (req, res, next) =>
  Promise.resolve(fn(req, res, next)).catch(next);

Warning

Neither version catches errors thrown inside callbacks that run later, such as setTimeout or old-style callback APIs. Those run outside the promise Express is watching. Pass such errors to next(err) yourself, or switch to promise-based APIs.

docs.title: Forwarding errors with next(err)
docs.text:
Calling next with any value other than "route" or "router" marks the request as failed:

app.get("/files/:name", (req, res, next) => {
  fs.readFile(`uploads/${req.params.name}`, (err, data) => {
    if (err) return next(err); // callback-style API: forward manually
    res.send(data);
  });
});

docs.title: Error-handling middleware
docs.text:
Error handlers take four arguments, (err, req, res, next). Express counts the function's declared parameters to tell an error handler from normal middleware, so all four must be present.

Register them after all routes and normal middleware. Express looks for error handlers further down the list from where the error happened; one registered earlier never sees errors from later routes.

docs.title: The 404 handler is not an error handler
docs.text:
A request that matches no route is not an error in Express's eyes: the chain simply ends. Add a normal middleware after all routes to answer 404, before the error handler:

app.use((req, res) => {
  res.status(404).json({ error: `No route for ${req.method} ${req.originalUrl}` });
});

docs.title: Express's default error handler
docs.text:
If no custom error handler responds, Express's built-in one does:

  • Status: err.status or err.statusCode if it is a 4xx or 5xx code, otherwise 500.
  • Body: the error stack in development; only the status text (for example "Internal Server Error") when NODE_ENV is production.
  • Headers listed in err.headers are added to the response.
  • If the response has already started (res.headersSent), it closes the connection, because a status and headers can no longer be changed.
  • It also prints the error to standard error (except when the Express environment is test), even in production.

The default handler returns HTML, which is why APIs add their own JSON error handler.

docs.title: Operational errors and programmer errors
docs.text:
Operational errors Programmer errors Meaning Expected failures in a correct program Bugs in the code Examples Invalid input, record not found, expired token, database timeout undefined is not a function, wrong variable name, failed assertion Response A specific 4xx or 503 with a helpful message A generic 500; details only in logs Action Handle and continue Log, alert, and fix the code

A custom error class marks operational errors so the handler can tell them apart.

docs.title: Mapping errors to status codes
docs.text:
Situation Status Malformed request, invalid JSON 400 Bad Request Valid JSON that fails validation 422 Unprocessable Content (or 400 by convention) Missing or invalid credentials 401 Unauthorized Authenticated but not permitted 403 Forbidden Resource does not exist 404 Not Found Duplicate or conflicting state 409 Conflict Body too large 413 Content Too Large Too many requests 429 Too Many Requests Unexpected bug 500 Internal Server Error Dependency unavailable 503 Service Unavailable

See HTTP status codes for every code.

docs.title: A consistent error shape: problem details
docs.text:
RFC 9457, "Problem Details for HTTP APIs", defines a standard JSON error format with the media type application/problem+json:

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/insufficient-stock",
  "title": "Insufficient stock",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Only 2 units of product p-9 are available.",
  "instance": "/api/v1/orders"
}
  • type: a URI identifying the kind of problem (about:blank when you have nothing more specific).
  • title: a short, human-readable summary of that problem type.
  • status: the HTTP status code.
  • detail: an explanation specific to this occurrence.
  • instance: identifies this occurrence, often the request path.

You can add extension fields such as requestId or issues. Even if you do not adopt the standard exactly, keep one shape for every error.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Throw or next(err) an error when the request cannot be completed: the record is missing, the user is not allowed, a dependency failed, or a bug occurred. One handler then turns it into a consistent response.

Do not use errors for normal outcomes a client can expect, such as an empty search result (return 200 with an empty list) or a successful delete (204). Do not catch an error just to log it and return 200.

Choice Use when Avoid when Custom error class (AppError) with status Expected failures you want to describe to clients Wrapping every bug; unexpected errors should stay generic 500s application/problem+json (RFC 9457) Public or multi-team APIs that benefit from a standard shape A small internal API with an existing shape that clients already rely on Your own error JSON shape Existing clients depend on it Starting a new public API with nothing to stay compatible with Crash and let the supervisor restart Programmer errors outside the request cycle (uncaughtException) Operational errors such as a missing record or a bad request

docs.title: A custom error class
docs.text:
// errors/AppError.js
export class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(status, title, detail, options = {}) {
    super(detail, { cause: options.cause });
    this.name = "AppError";
    this.status = status;          // HTTP status to send
    this.title = title;            // short, safe summary
    this.isOperational = true;     // expected failure, safe to describe
    this.extra = options.extra;    // e.g. validation issues
  }
}

export const notFound = (what) => new AppError(404, "Not found", `${what} was not found`);
export const conflict = (detail) => new AppError(409, "Conflict", detail);

docs.title: Throwing from routes and services
docs.text:
app.get("/api/v1/orders/:id", async (req, res) => {
  const order = await orders.findById(req.params.id);
  if (!order) throw notFound(`Order ${req.params.id}`); // Express 5 forwards it
  if (order.customerId !== req.user.id) {
    throw new AppError(403, "Forbidden", "You cannot view this order");
  }
  res.json(order);
});

docs.title: The central error handler
docs.text:
// middleware/errorHandler.js
import { AppError } from "../errors/AppError.js";

const isProduction = process.env.NODE_ENV === "production";

export function errorHandler(err, req, res, next) {
  // Response already started: let Express close the connection
  if (res.headersSent) return next(err);

  let status = 500;
  let title = "Internal Server Error";
  let detail = "An unexpected error occurred.";
  let extra;

  if (err instanceof AppError) {
    ({ status, title, extra } = err);
    detail = err.message;
  } else if (err.type === "entity.parse.failed") {
    // From express.json(): the body was not valid JSON
    status = 400;
    title = "Bad Request";
    detail = "Request body is not valid JSON.";
  } else if (err.type === "entity.too.large") {
    status = 413;
    title = "Content Too Large";
    detail = "Request body is too large.";
  } else if (err.code === 11000) {
    // MongoDB duplicate key
    status = 409;
    title = "Conflict";
    detail = "A record with this value already exists.";
  }

  // Log everything server-side, with context for debugging
  const logLevel = status >= 500 ? "error" : "warn";
  console[logLevel]({
    requestId: req.id,
    method: req.method,
    url: req.originalUrl,
    status,
    message: err.message,
    stack: status >= 500 ? err.stack : undefined,
  });

  res
    .status(status)
    .type("application/problem+json")
    .json({
      type: "about:blank",
      title,
      status,
      detail,
      instance: req.originalUrl,
      requestId: req.id,
      ...(extra && { issues: extra }),
      // Never expose stack traces to clients in production
      ...(!isProduction && status >= 500 && { stack: err.stack }),
    });
}

The handler checks the error in a fixed order, so known errors keep their meaning and anything else becomes a generic 500:

docs.title: Wiring it together
docs.text:
// app.js
import express from "express";
import { errorHandler } from "./middleware/errorHandler.js";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.use("/api/v1", apiRouter);

// 1. Nothing matched -> 404
app.use((req, res) => {
  res.status(404).type("application/problem+json").json({
    type: "about:blank",
    title: "Not Found",
    status: 404,
    detail: `No route for ${req.method} ${req.originalUrl}`,
  });
});

// 2. Errors -> one consistent response (always last)
app.use(errorHandler);

export default app;

curl -i localhost:3000/api/v1/orders/999
# HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
# Content-Type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8
#
# {"type":"about:blank","title":"Not found","status":404,
#  "detail":"Order 999 was not found","instance":"/api/v1/orders/999",...}

docs.title: Errors outside the request cycle
docs.text: Errors in timers, background jobs, or forgotten promises never reach Express. Node.js reports them through the process-level uncaughtException and unhandledRejection events. Log them and let the process restart, because the application may be in an unknown state. See errors, debugging, and performance.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Have exactly one central error handler, registered last, plus a 404 handler just before it.
  • Throw (or reject with) error objects, never strings, so stacks are kept.
  • Use a custom error class for expected failures with a status and a safe message.
  • Return a generic message for unexpected 500 errors; keep details in logs.
  • Never send stack traces, SQL, or internal paths in production.
  • Include a request ID in error responses and logs so they can be matched.
  • Delegate to next(err) when res.headersSent is true.
  • In Express 4, wrap async handlers or use try/catch with next(err).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Stack traces in API responses. Symptom: a penetration test or bug report shows file paths and stack frames in error responses. Detect: error responses with Content-Type: text/html containing at ... lines. Cause: NODE_ENV is not production, and errors reach Express's default handler, which then sends err.stack. Fix: set NODE_ENV=production and register your own JSON error handler.
  • The custom error handler never runs. Symptom: clients receive Express's HTML error page instead of your JSON. Detect: error responses lack your fields (title, requestId). Cause: the handler was declared with three parameters, or registered before the routes. Fix: use exactly (err, req, res, next) and register it last.
  • Crash loops. Symptom: instances restart repeatedly and in-flight requests fail. Detect: uncaughtException or unhandled-rejection stacks in the logs and rising restart counts in PM2 or Kubernetes. Cause: errors thrown in timers, event listeners, or (in Express 4) un-awaited async handlers. Fix: forward those errors with next(err), move to promise-based APIs, and keep a process-level handler that logs and exits so the supervisor can restart cleanly.
  • Alert fatigue. Symptom: the on-call team ignores error alerts. Detect: most alerting errors are 401, 404, or 422 responses. Cause: client errors are logged and alerted like server failures. Fix: log 4xx at a lower level and alert on 5xx rates, as Sentry's default for Express already does for 3xx and 4xx.
  • Empty or useless error bodies. Symptom: clients receive {} for 500 errors. Detect: error responses with an empty object. Cause: res.status(500).json(err): an Error's message and stack are not enumerable, so JSON.stringify drops them. Fix: build the response body explicitly from safe fields.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Error-handling middleware: A function with the signature (err, req, res, next) that turns errors into responses.
  • Default error handler: Express's built-in handler used when no custom handler responds.
  • Operational error: An expected failure in a correctly working program.
  • Programmer error: A bug that should be fixed rather than handled.
  • Problem details: The RFC 9457 standard JSON format for HTTP API errors.
  • Unhandled rejection: A rejected promise with no handler attached.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Declaring the error handler with three parameters, so Express treats it as normal middleware.
  • Registering the error handler before the routes.
  • Using async handlers in Express 4 without catching errors, which crashes the process on modern Node.js (or leaves requests hanging).
  • Expecting the error handler to catch errors thrown inside setTimeout or other callbacks.
  • Treating a missing route as an error instead of adding a 404 handler.
  • Sending res.status(500).json(err), which can leak internals (and often serializes to {}).
  • Catching errors in a route, logging nothing, and returning 200.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which kinds of errors does Express 5 catch automatically, and which does it not?
  2. How does Express recognize error-handling middleware, and where must it be registered?
  3. Why is a 404 handled by normal middleware rather than the error handler?
  4. What is the difference between operational and programmer errors, and how should each be answered?
  5. What are the standard fields of a problem details response?
  6. Why should the handler check res.headersSent?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Express: Error handling guide
  • Express: Migrating to Express 5 (promise rejections)
  • OWASP: Error Handling Cheat Sheet
  • MDN: HTTP response status codes
  • Node.js: --unhandled-rejections
  • Related: error handling concepts, middleware, logging and monitoring.

docs.title: File Uploads with Multer
docs.text: Browsers send files to a server as multipart/form-data requests, a format that express.json() and express.urlencoded() cannot read. Multer is the standard Express middleware for parsing these requests: it extracts the text fields into req.body and the files into req.file or req.files. This lesson covers Multer's storage engines, limits, filtering, error handling, and how to upload files safely to object storage.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
File uploads are one of the riskiest features in a web application. An unlimited upload can fill a disk or exhaust memory. A trusted filename can overwrite server files through path traversal. A file served back with the wrong content type can run scripts in users' browsers. Handling uploads well means controlling size, type, naming, and where files end up.

For the architecture side (object storage, presigned URLs, scanning pipelines), see file storage and uploads.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Amazon S3 supports uploads that never pass through your server. Its presigned URL guide explains that a presigned URL "will allow an upload without requiring another party to have AWS security credentials or permissions": the server signs, the client uploads directly. This is the pattern shown later in this lesson.
  • Slack moved its file-upload API to a two-step design. Its files.getUploadURLExternal method returns an upload URL and a file ID; the client sends the bytes to that URL and then calls files.completeUploadExternal to finalize the upload. Separating "send bytes" from "register the file" is the same idea as presigned uploads.
  • Shopify uses staged uploads for product images, videos, and 3D models. The stagedUploadsCreate mutation generates secure, temporary upload URLs; the app uploads files directly to them and then creates the assets that reference the uploaded files.

Popular tools and providers: Multer and busboy for parsing in Express, file-type for magic-byte checks; object storage such as Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and Cloudflare R2.

docs.title: What a multipart request looks like
docs.text:
POST /profile/avatar HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----X9f2

------X9f2
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="displayName"

Ada
------X9f2
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="avatar"; filename="me.png"
Content-Type: image/png

<binary bytes of the PNG>
------X9f2--

Each part is separated by a boundary string. A part has its own headers: name is the form field name, filename is the name on the user's computer, and Content-Type is what the browser claims the file is. Multer streams through these parts using the busboy parser.

A browser form needs enctype="multipart/form-data"; with fetch, pass a FormData object and let the browser set the Content-Type header, including the boundary.

docs.title: Setting up Multer
docs.text:
import multer from "multer";
const upload = multer({ storage, limits, fileFilter });

upload is a factory; you call one of its methods to get route-level middleware:

Method Accepts Result upload.single("avatar") One file in field avatar req.file upload.array("photos", 5) Up to 5 files in field photos req.files (array) upload.fields([{ name: "front", maxCount: 1 }, { name: "back", maxCount: 1 }]) Files in several named fields req.files (object of arrays) upload.none() Text fields only Error if any file is sent upload.any() Files in any field req.files (array); avoid in most apps

Text fields always land in req.body. Apply Multer only on the routes that accept uploads, never globally with app.use(): a global upload middleware lets any route receive files.

docs.title: The file object
docs.text: Property Meaning fieldname The form field name originalname Filename from the user's computer: untrusted mimetype Content type claimed by the client: untrusted size Size in bytes buffer File contents (memory storage only) destination, filename, path Where it was saved (disk storage only)

docs.title: Storage engines
docs.text:
Memory storage keeps each file as a Buffer in file.buffer. It is simple and good when you immediately send the file elsewhere (to S3, or an image processor), but every concurrent upload consumes RAM, so always pair it with a small fileSize limit.

Disk storage writes files to a folder. You control the folder and the filename:

const storage = multer.diskStorage({
  destination: (req, file, cb) => cb(null, "uploads/tmp"),
  filename: (req, file, cb) => cb(null, `${crypto.randomUUID()}.upload`),
});

If you pass only dest: "uploads/", Multer saves files with random names and no extension, which is a safe default.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
limits stops oversized or abusive requests while they stream:

Limit Meaning fileSize Maximum bytes per file files Maximum number of files fields Maximum number of text fields fieldSize Maximum bytes per text field value parts Maximum total parts (files + fields)

Apart from fieldSize (1 MB), these limits default to unlimited (Infinity), so a Multer instance without limits accepts files of any size and number.

When a limit is exceeded, Multer stops and passes a MulterError to next() with a code such as LIMIT_FILE_SIZE, LIMIT_FILE_COUNT, or LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE (a file in a field you did not declare).

docs.title: Filtering file types
docs.text:
fileFilter(req, file, cb) runs before a file is stored. Call cb(null, true) to accept, cb(null, false) to silently skip, or cb(error) to reject the request.

The MIME type is only a claim

file.mimetype comes from the client and can be anything. A filter on it blocks honest mistakes, not attackers. For real verification, inspect the file's first bytes (its magic bytes) after upload, for example with the file-type package, and reject files whose actual type is not allowed. Image files can also be re-encoded with an image library, which removes hidden payloads and metadata.

Note that fileFilter only sees req.body fields that appeared before the file in the form, because the request is streamed in order.

Putting the pieces together, each file part passes these checks in order:

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Upload through Express with Multer when:

  • Files are small (avatars, attachments of a few megabytes) and you want to validate, resize, or scan them before storing.
  • The upload is part of a form submission that also carries text fields.
  • You need full control over the bytes on the server (for example, to strip image metadata).

Prefer direct-to-storage uploads (presigned URLs) when:

  • Files are large (videos, archives) or users are on slow connections: the upload would occupy a server connection, and a slow upload can run into Node's 5-minute default request timeout.
  • Upload volume is high and you do not want app servers paying for the bandwidth twice (client → server → storage).
Approach Bytes pass through your server Good for Watch out for Multer memoryStorage Yes, held in RAM Small files you forward or process immediately Memory per concurrent upload; always set fileSize Multer diskStorage Yes, written to local disk Larger files processed on the same machine Disk filling up; files lost when instances are replaced Streaming to storage (custom engine or busboy) Yes, streamed Medium files without buffering More code; still uses server bandwidth Presigned URL to object storage No Large or numerous files Bucket CORS setup; validate the file after upload

docs.title: Single image upload with limits and a filter
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import multer from "multer";

const app = express();

const ALLOWED_TYPES = new Set(["image/png", "image/jpeg", "image/webp"]);

function imageFilter(req, file, cb) {
  if (ALLOWED_TYPES.has(file.mimetype)) return cb(null, true);
  const err = new Error("Only PNG, JPEG, or WebP images are allowed");
  err.status = 415;
  cb(err);
}

const upload = multer({
  storage: multer.memoryStorage(),
  limits: { fileSize: 2 * 1024 * 1024, files: 1 }, // 2 MB, one file
  fileFilter: imageFilter,
});

app.post("/profile/avatar", upload.single("avatar"), (req, res) => {
  if (!req.file) return res.status(400).json({ error: "No file uploaded" });
  res.status(201).json({
    displayName: req.body.displayName,
    size: req.file.size,
    type: req.file.mimetype,
  });
});

Test it with curl:

curl -F "displayName=Ada" -F "avatar=@me.png" http://localhost:3000/profile/avatar
{"displayName":"Ada","size":48213,"type":"image/png"}

docs.title: Several files and named fields
docs.text:
// The single-file instance above has `files: 1`, which would reject these
// routes with LIMIT_FILE_COUNT, so they get their own instance.
const multiUpload = multer({
  storage: multer.memoryStorage(),
  limits: { fileSize: 2 * 1024 * 1024, files: 10 },
  fileFilter: imageFilter,
});

app.post("/listings/:id/photos", multiUpload.array("photos", 10), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ count: req.files.length });
});

const idUpload = multiUpload.fields([
  { name: "front", maxCount: 1 },
  { name: "back", maxCount: 1 },
]);

app.post("/verify-id", idUpload, (req, res) => {
  const front = req.files.front?.[0];
  const back = req.files.back?.[0];
  if (!front || !back) return res.status(400).json({ error: "Both sides needed" });
  res.sendStatus(202);
});

docs.title: Handling Multer errors in the error handler
docs.text:
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  if (err instanceof multer.MulterError) {
    const status = err.code === "LIMIT_FILE_SIZE" ? 413 : 400;
    return res.status(status).json({ error: err.message, code: err.code });
  }
  if (err.status) return res.status(err.status).json({ error: err.message });
  next(err); // anything else goes to the default handler
});

413 Content Too Large tells the client the file was too big; 415 Unsupported Media Type tells it the type is not accepted. See error handling in Express for the full pattern.

docs.title: Verifying the real type with magic bytes
docs.text:
import { fileTypeFromBuffer } from "file-type";

// A separate instance: the image filter above would reject PDFs.
const pdfUpload = multer({
  storage: multer.memoryStorage(),
  limits: { fileSize: 10 * 1024 * 1024, files: 1 },
});

app.post("/documents", pdfUpload.single("document"), async (req, res) => {
  if (!req.file) return res.status(400).json({ error: "No file uploaded" });
  // Read the real type from the file's first bytes, not the client's claim
  const detected = await fileTypeFromBuffer(req.file.buffer);
  if (detected?.mime !== "application/pdf") {
    return res.status(415).json({ error: "File is not a PDF" });
  }
  res.sendStatus(201);
});

docs.title: Uploading to object storage (S3)
docs.text:
Servers usually should not keep uploads on their own disk: disks fill up and files are lost when instances are replaced. Send them to object storage:

import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";

const s3 = new S3Client({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION });

app.post("/profile/avatar", upload.single("avatar"), async (req, res) => {
  const key = `avatars/${crypto.randomUUID()}`; // never the original name
  await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
    Bucket: process.env.UPLOAD_BUCKET,
    Key: key,
    Body: req.file.buffer,
    ContentType: req.file.mimetype,
  }));
  res.status(201).json({ key });
});

For large files, a better pattern skips your server entirely: the server creates a short-lived presigned URL, and the browser uploads straight to storage.

import { getSignedUrl } from "@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner";

app.post("/uploads/presign", async (req, res) => {
  const key = `uploads/${crypto.randomUUID()}`;
  const url = await getSignedUrl(
    s3,
    new PutObjectCommand({ Bucket: process.env.UPLOAD_BUCKET, Key: key,
      ContentType: "application/pdf" }),
    { expiresIn: 300 } // seconds
  );
  res.json({ url, key });
});

docs.title: Serving uploaded files safely
docs.text:
import path from "node:path";

const UPLOAD_DIR = path.resolve("uploads");

app.get("/files/:id", requireLogin, async (req, res) => {
  const file = await findFileRecord(req.params.id); // metadata from the DB
  if (!file || file.ownerId !== req.user.id) return res.sendStatus(404);

  res.set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff");
  // Force download instead of rendering in the browser.
  res.download(file.storedName, file.displayName, { root: UPLOAD_DIR });
});

Look files up by an ID in your database, not by a path from the URL. The root option makes Express refuse paths that escape the folder.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Apply Multer per route, never globally.
  • Always set limits, especially fileSize and files.
  • Allow a short list of types and verify magic bytes for anything important.
  • Generate your own storage names (UUIDs); keep the original name only as display metadata in the database.
  • Store files outside the web root and outside the project folder, ideally in object storage.
  • Prefer presigned URLs for large files so uploads do not tie up your server.
  • Serve user files with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, ideally from a separate domain.
  • Scan uploads for malware when users share files with each other.
  • Clean up temporary files when a request fails.
  • Record metadata (owner, size, type, storage key) in the database.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The process crashes under upload traffic. Detect: memory graphs climbing during uploads, containers restarted for exceeding their memory limit, or JavaScript heap out of memory in logs. Cause: memoryStorage with no or very high fileSize limits, multiplied by concurrent uploads. Fix: set limits, stream to disk or storage, or move large files to presigned uploads.
  • Large uploads fail with 413 before Express sees them. Detect: the 413 response is an HTML page from the proxy, not your JSON error; Express logs show no request. Cause: a reverse proxy limit; Nginx's client_max_body_size defaults to 1m. Fix: raise it for upload routes only, and keep Multer's fileSize as the real application limit.
  • Disk full errors. Detect: ENOSPC: no space left on device in logs and failed writes across the app. Cause: diskStorage temporary files that are never deleted when a request fails or after processing. Fix: delete files in a finally block or error handler, run a cleanup job, or avoid local disk.
  • Files "disappear" after a deploy or exist only on one instance. Detect: 404s for files that were uploaded successfully, often only on some requests behind a load balancer. Cause: files saved to local disk on one server, which is replaced or not shared. Fix: store files in object storage and keep only the key in the database.
  • Browser uploads to presigned URLs fail. Detect: a CORS error in the browser console, or an S3 error response with code SignatureDoesNotMatch. Cause: the bucket has no CORS rule allowing PUT from your origin, or the client sent headers (such as Content-Type) that differ from what was signed. Fix: add a bucket CORS configuration and send exactly the signed headers.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• multipart/form-data: A request body format that carries text fields and files as separate parts.
  • Boundary: The delimiter string that separates parts.
  • Storage engine: Multer's strategy for where file data goes (memory or disk, or a custom engine).
  • Magic bytes: Signature bytes at the start of a file that identify its real format.
  • Path traversal: Using ../ in a path to reach files outside the intended folder.
  • Presigned URL: A time-limited URL that grants permission for one storage operation.
  • Object storage: A service such as Amazon S3 that stores files as objects addressed by keys.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Expecting express.json() to parse uploads. It ignores multipart bodies; req.file stays undefined without Multer.
  • Setting Content-Type manually with FormData. The browser must add the boundary; setting the header yourself breaks the request.
  • Trusting originalname. It can contain ../, odd characters, or a misleading extension.
  • Trusting mimetype. A script can be sent as image/png.
  • Using memory storage without a size limit. A few large uploads can crash the process.
  • Field name mismatch. upload.single("avatar") with a form field named file causes a LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE error.
  • Serving uploads with express.static from a public folder. Users can upload HTML or SVG that runs scripts on your domain.

docs.text:
1. Why can't express.json() read a file upload?
  2. When would you choose memory storage over disk storage?
  3. Why is checking file.mimetype not enough to verify a file's type?
  4. How should a server respond when a file exceeds fileSize, and why?
  5. What are the advantages of uploading directly to storage with a presigned URL?
  6. Name three precautions when serving user-uploaded files back to users.

docs.title: Getting Started with Express
docs.text: Express is a minimal web framework for Node.js. It sits on top of the built-in node:http module and adds two things that almost every server needs: routing (matching a method and URL to code) and middleware (reusable steps that run for each request). This lesson sets up a first Express 5 project and explains what happens when a request arrives.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
You can build a server with only the http module, but you then write the same plumbing by hand: parsing URLs, matching paths, reading request bodies, setting headers, and sending JSON. Express removes that repetition while staying small and unopinionated. It does not decide your folder structure, database, validation library, or authentication method, so it is a good framework for learning how backends really work.

Express is also one of the most widely used Node.js frameworks. Many tutorials, middleware packages, and production services assume it, and frameworks such as NestJS can run on top of it.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• PayPal's first Node.js attempts used Express for routing. In a 2013 engineering post the team wrote that it liked "the ubiquity of express" but found that Express's non-prescriptive style "didn't scale well in multiple development teams". It responded by building kraken.js, "a convention layer on top of express", so many teams could share one structure (PayPal Technology blog).
  • NestJS, a framework for large TypeScript back ends, uses Express as its default HTTP server under the hood and can be switched to Fastify (NestJS documentation). What you learn about Express explains what a NestJS app does underneath.
  • Auth0 publishes a quickstart for protecting Express.js API endpoints with JWT access tokens. Its express-oauth2-jwt-bearer SDK is configured as Express middleware (Auth0 documentation).
  • Stripe's webhook documentation includes Express-specific advice: the webhook route must be registered before app.use(express.json()) because "Express applies middleware in order" (Stripe documentation).

Popular tools and providers: Fastify, Koa, Hono, and NestJS are the frameworks most often compared with Express; error-tracking and identity providers such as Sentry and Auth0 ship Express integrations.

docs.title: What Express adds to Node.js
docs.text:
Concern Plain node:http Express Match GET /users/42 Parse req.url and compare strings yourself app.get("/users/:id", handler) Read route values Split the path manually req.params.id Read query strings Parse with URL req.query Parse a JSON body Collect chunks, JSON.parse, handle errors app.use(express.json()) then req.body Send JSON Set status, header, stringify, end() res.status(201).json(data) Shared steps (logging, auth) Call helpers in every handler Middleware with app.use() Errors Try/catch everywhere Central error-handling middleware

An Express application object (app) is itself a request handler function with the signature (req, res). app.listen() simply creates a node:http server with app as its handler and starts listening.

docs.title: The request-response cycle
docs.text: Every request must end in exactly one response: a handler sends it, a middleware sends it (for example, rejecting an unauthenticated request), or the error handler sends it. If nothing responds, the client waits until it times out.

docs.title: Express 5 compared with Express 4
docs.text:
Express 5 is the current major version and is what npm install express installs. Most Express 4 code still works, but several behaviors changed. You will meet both versions in tutorials and older projects.

Topic Express 4 Express 5 Node.js version Very old versions supported Node.js 18 or newer Rejected promise in an async handler Not caught; you must call next(err) Passed to the error handler automatically Wildcard paths "*" Named: "/*splat" (or "/{*splat}" to include /) Optional segments "/users/:id?" "/users{/:id}" req.body with no parser {} in many setups undefined express.urlencoded() extended default true false Default query parser "extended" (qs, nested objects) "simple" (node querystring) express.static dotfiles Served unless configured Ignored by default Removed APIs — app.del(), req.param(), res.sendfile(), res.json(obj, status), res.send(status), res.redirect("back") res.status(code) Accepted odd values Throws unless the code is a valid integer (100–999) app.listen errors Thrown Passed to the listen callback

The Express 5 migration guide lists every change.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use Express when:

  • You are building a JSON API, a backend-for-frontend, or a small server-rendered site in Node.js and want a small, well-known core.
  • You need a particular integration: most Node.js libraries and SaaS SDKs for authentication, error tracking, and logging ship an Express version.
  • The team is learning backend fundamentals. Express hides little, so routing, middleware, and error handling stay visible.
  • You want to start simple and add structure as the service grows.

Consider something else when:

  • Many teams share one codebase and need enforced conventions. An opinionated framework such as NestJS, or a convention layer of your own as PayPal built, stops every team inventing its own structure.
  • Validation and serialization speed are central to the service. Fastify builds a schema-based approach into its core.
  • The code must run on edge or serverless runtimes that use Web Standard Request and Response objects. Hono targets those runtimes.
  • The work is mostly CPU-bound, such as image processing. The bottleneck is Node.js's main thread, not the framework; see worker threads, child processes, and cluster.
Situation Good fit Why Small or medium JSON API, team knows JavaScript Express Minimal core, huge ecosystem Large organization, many teams, TypeScript NestJS (on Express or Fastify) Modules, dependency injection, enforced conventions Throughput-critical API with strict schemas Fastify Schema-based validation and serialization Edge functions or several JavaScript runtimes Hono Web Standards API; runs on many runtimes Minimal core built only from async middleware Koa No middleware bundled in the core

docs.title: Create a project
docs.text:
mkdir tasks-api
cd tasks-api
npm init -y
npm install express

Open package.json and set "type": "module" so Node.js treats .js files as ES modules (import/export). Add scripts for development and production:

{
  "name": "tasks-api",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "node --watch server.js",
    "start": "node server.js"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^5.1.0"
  }
}

node --watch restarts the process whenever a file it loaded changes. Older projects use the nodemon package for the same job (npx nodemon server.js). Both are development tools only; production uses a plain node server.js under a process manager or container.

docs.title: A first server
docs.text:
// server.js
import express from "express";

const app = express();

// Parse JSON request bodies into req.body
app.use(express.json());

// A route: method + path + handler
app.get("/health", (req, res) => {
  res.json({ status: "ok" });
});

app.post("/tasks", (req, res) => {
  const { title } = req.body ?? {};
  if (!title) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "title is required" });
  }
  res.status(201).json({ id: 1, title });
});

// PORT usually comes from the environment in hosted platforms
const PORT = Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000;

app.listen(PORT, (error) => {
  // Express 5 passes server errors (such as a busy port) to this callback
  if (error) {
    console.error("Server failed to start:", error.message);
    process.exit(1);
  }
  console.log(`Listening on http://localhost:${PORT}`);
});

Run it with npm run dev and try it:

curl http://localhost:3000/health
# {"status":"ok"}

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/tasks \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Write notes"}'
# {"id":1,"title":"Write notes"}

docs.title: app.listen returns a Node.js server
docs.text:
const server = app.listen(PORT);

server.on("error", (error) => {
  if (error.code === "EADDRINUSE") {
    console.error(`Port ${PORT} is already in use`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
  throw error;
});

// Later, for graceful shutdown: stop accepting new connections
process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  server.close(() => process.exit(0));
});

EADDRINUSE means another process already listens on that port, often an older copy of your own server. Because app is just a handler, you can also create the server yourself, which is useful when another library (such as a WebSocket server) needs the same http.Server:

import { createServer } from "node:http";

const server = createServer(app);
server.listen(PORT);

Tip

Keep the Express app (app.js) separate from the code that starts it (server.js). Tests can then import the app without opening a port. See project structure.

docs.title: Alternatives you will hear about
docs.text:
Framework Style Strengths Trade-offs Express Minimal, middleware-based Huge ecosystem, simple mental model You choose and assemble most pieces Fastify Plugin-based, schema-first High throughput, built-in JSON schema validation and serialization Different plugin and lifecycle model to learn Koa Minimal, async middleware Small core from the original Express authors No built-in router or body parser NestJS Opinionated, TypeScript, dependency injection Structure for large teams, modules, decorators More concepts and boilerplate; runs on Express or Fastify underneath Hono Web Standards Request/Response Very small; runs on Node.js, Bun, Deno, and edge runtimes Younger ecosystem than Express

Learning Express first makes the others easier: they all solve the same problems of routing, middleware, validation, and error handling.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Pin Express to a major version (^5.x) and read the migration guide before upgrading an Express 4 project.
  • Read configuration such as PORT from environment variables; see process, environment variables, and configuration.
  • Register body parsers and other global middleware before routes, and the error handler last.
  • Always send a response or pass control onward with next().
  • Split app.js (configuration) from server.js (listening) early.
  • Use node --watch or nodemon only in development.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Port already in use on deploy. Symptom: the new instance exits at once and the process manager restarts it in a loop. Detect: the log line listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000 (with the listen callback above: Server failed to start: listen EADDRINUSE...). Cause: an old copy of the server is still running, or two services got the same PORT. Fix: shut down gracefully on SIGTERM and take each instance's port from the environment.
  • Requests that never finish. Symptom: clients time out and the reverse proxy returns 504 Gateway Timeout. Detect: proxy logs report an upstream timeout, and your request logger records requests that start but never log a finish. Cause: a middleware or handler branch that neither responds nor calls next(). Fix: make every branch respond or call next(), and test each branch.
  • req.body is undefined after upgrading to Express 5. Symptom: 500 errors on POST routes. Detect: TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'title' of 'req.body' as it is undefined. Cause: Express 4 defaulted req.body to {}; Express 5 leaves it undefined when no parser ran. Fix: register the right parser before the route and read req.body ?? {}, or validate the whole body.
  • Crash at startup after the upgrade. Symptom: the app never starts. Detect: PathError: Missing parameter name at index 1: *; visit https://git.new/pathToRegexpError for info. Cause: Express 4 path syntax such as "*" or ":id?". Fix: use "/*splat", "/{*splat}", or "{/:id}"; the migration guide lists codemods that automate several of the changes.
  • The process dies on an error thrown in a timer or event callback. Symptom: every in-flight request on the instance fails at once and the instance restarts. Detect: an uncaughtException stack in the logs and rising restart counts in PM2 or Kubernetes. Cause: the error was thrown outside the promise chain Express watches. Fix: use promise-based APIs or pass the error to next(err); see error handling in Express.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Application (app): The object returned by express(); it holds settings, middleware, and routes, and acts as the request handler.
  • Route: A combination of an HTTP method, a path pattern, and one or more handler functions.
  • Handler: A function (req, res, next) that processes a request.
  • Middleware: A function that runs during the request-response cycle and either responds or calls next().
  • Request-response cycle: Everything that happens between Express receiving a request and the response being sent.
  • Port: The number a server listens on so the operating system can deliver network traffic to it.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Express is not part of Node.js; it is a separate npm package.
  • Forgetting "type": "module" and then using import causes a syntax error (or requires .mjs files).
  • Reading req.body without registering express.json() gives undefined in Express 5.
  • Copying Express 4 wildcard routes such as app.get("*", ...) into an Express 5 app throws a path syntax error at startup.
  • Running two copies of the server on the same port fails with EADDRINUSE; it is not a bug in Express.
  • Express does not validate input, authenticate users, or structure your project for you; those are deliberate choices you add.

1. What does Express add on top of the node:http module?
