docs.title: Express Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review Express fundamentals, routing, middleware, request handling, security, testing, and running Express in production. Answers describe Express 5 behavior and note where Express 4 differs. Each question is tagged Beginner (definitions and basic usage), Intermediate (how it works, trade-offs, debugging common issues), or Advanced (internals, scale, failure modes, design decisions).

docs.title: 1. What is Express?
docs.text: Express is a minimal, unopinionated web framework for Node.js. It adds routing, a middleware pipeline, and helpers on the request and response objects on top of Node's http module. It leaves choices such as project structure, validation, and database access to the developer.

docs.title: 2. How is Express related to Node's http module?
docs.text: An Express app is a request-handler function. app.listen() creates a Node http.Server with the app as its handler and returns that server. req and res are Node's IncomingMessage and ServerResponse objects extended with Express helpers such as req.params and res.json().

docs.title: 3. What are the main changes in Express 5 compared with Express 4?
docs.text: Rejected promises from async handlers and middleware are passed to the error handler automatically. Route paths use new syntax: wildcards must be named (/*splat) and optional segments use braces ({/:id}). req.body is undefined when no body parser ran, express.urlencoded() defaults to extended: false, the default query parser is "simple", and old APIs such as app.del(), req.param(), and res.sendfile() were removed.

docs.title: 4. Describe the request-response cycle in Express.
docs.text: A request enters the app and passes through middleware and route handlers in the order they were registered. Each function can modify req/res, end the response, or call next() to continue. Exactly one response must be sent; if nothing matches, a 404 handler responds, and errors jump to error-handling middleware.

docs.title: 5. How do Express alternatives such as Fastify, Koa, and NestJS differ?
docs.text: Fastify focuses on performance and built-in schema validation. Koa, from the original Express team, uses a smaller core built around async middleware. NestJS is an opinionated framework with modules, decorators, and dependency injection, and can use Express or Fastify underneath.

docs.title: 6. What is a route in Express?
docs.text: A route combines an HTTP method, a path, and one or more handler functions, for example app.get("/tasks/:id", handler). Express runs the first matching route in registration order unless a handler calls next().

docs.title: 7. What is the difference between route parameters and query strings?
docs.text: Route parameters are named segments in the path (/users/:id) and appear in req.params; they usually identify a resource. Query strings follow ? (/users?role=admin&page=2) and appear in req.query; they usually filter, sort, or paginate. Both arrive as strings and must be validated and converted.

docs.title: 8. What is express.Router used for?
docs.text: express.Router() creates a mini-application with its own routes and middleware. Routers are mounted on a path with app.use("/api/tasks", router), which keeps routes modular and lets middleware such as authentication apply to a group of routes. mergeParams: true lets a child router read parameters from its parent's path.

docs.title: 9. Why does route order matter?
docs.text: Express checks routes and middleware in the order they were added and stops at the first one that responds. A general route such as /users/:id registered before /users/me will capture me as an ID. Catch-all routes and the 404 handler must come after specific routes.

docs.title: 10. How do you write wildcard and optional routes in Express 5?
docs.text: Wildcards must be named: /files/*filepath matches everything after /files/ and exposes it as req.params.filepath, an array of path segments. /{*splat} matches every path including /. Optional segments use braces: /users{/:id} matches both /users and /users/42. Express 4's * and :id? forms no longer work.

docs.title: 11. What is the difference between req.params, req.query, and req.body?
docs.text: req.params holds route parameters from the path, req.query holds parsed query-string values, and req.body holds the parsed request body. The body is only populated when a body-parsing middleware such as express.json() has run; otherwise it is undefined in Express 5.

docs.title: 12. What is the difference between res.send(), res.json(), and res.end()?
docs.text: res.json() serializes a value to JSON and sets Content-Type: application/json. res.send() chooses the content type from its argument (string, Buffer, or object). res.end() is Node's low-level method that finishes the response without Express's content-type or ETag handling.

docs.title: 13. What causes "Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client"?
docs.text: The code tried to send a second response, or set a header, after the first response started. Common causes are a missing return before res.json() in an if block, calling next() after responding, or both a callback and a promise sending responses. Use return res... and check res.headersSent in error handlers.

docs.title: 14. How do redirects work, and which status code should you use?
docs.text: res.redirect(url) sends a 302 Found by default with a Location header. Use 301/308 for permanent moves (308 keeps the method and body), 303 after a form POST to send the browser to a GET page, and 307 for a temporary redirect that must keep the method.

docs.title: 15. What is res.locals?
docs.text: res.locals is an object scoped to a single request. Middleware can store values there (such as the current user) for later middleware, handlers, and templates. Unlike app.locals, it is reset for every request.

docs.title: 16. What is middleware in Express?
docs.text: Middleware is a function with the signature (req, res, next) that runs during the request-response cycle. It can read or modify the request and response, end the cycle by sending a response, or call next() to pass control on. Logging, authentication, parsing, and validation are typically middleware.

docs.title: 17. What are the types of middleware?
docs.text: Application-level middleware is registered with app.use() or route methods; router-level middleware with a router; built-in middleware includes express.json(), express.urlencoded(), express.static(), express.raw(), and express.text(); third-party middleware includes cors, helmet, and cookie-parser; error-handling middleware takes four arguments (err, req, res, next).

docs.title: 18. What happens if middleware neither calls next() nor sends a response?
docs.text: The request hangs until the client or a server timeout gives up, because nothing ends the cycle. Every middleware path must either respond, call next(), or call next(err).

docs.title: 19. What do next(), next("route"), and next(err) do?
docs.text: next() passes control to the next matching middleware or route. next("route") skips the remaining handlers of the current route and moves to the next matching route. next(err) (with any value other than "route" or "router") skips normal middleware and jumps to error-handling middleware.

docs.title: 20. How does Express parse JSON and form bodies?
docs.text: express.json() parses bodies whose Content-Type is application/json into req.body; express.urlencoded() parses HTML form submissions. Both accept a limit option (100 KB by default) and respond 413 when a body is too large. Malformed JSON produces a 400 error that reaches the error handler.

docs.title: 21. How are file uploads handled?
docs.text: File uploads use multipart/form-data, which the built-in parsers ignore. Middleware such as Multer parses them, placing files in req.file or req.files and text fields in req.body. Set explicit limits: common Multer defaults leave file size, file count, field count, and part count unlimited (while field size has a default limit). Do not trust the client's filename or MIME type.

docs.title: 22. Why might a webhook route need the raw body?
docs.text: Webhook providers sign the exact bytes they send. To verify the signature, the route must hash the raw body, not a re-serialized JSON object. Use express.raw({ type: "application/json" }) on that route, or the verify option of express.json() to keep a copy of the raw buffer.

docs.title: 23. Why and where should requests be validated?
docs.text: Clients, including attackers, can send any data, so every input (params, query, body, headers) must be checked for type, shape, length, and allowed values on the server. Validation usually runs as route-level middleware using a schema library such as Zod or Joi, and returns 400 (or 422) with field-level details.

docs.title: 24. What is mass assignment, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: Mass assignment happens when the server saves a request body directly, so a client can set fields it should not control, such as role or isAdmin. Prevent it by validating against a schema that strips or rejects unknown fields and by copying only allowed fields into the database update.

docs.title: 25. How do you handle errors in async route handlers?
docs.text: In Express 5, a rejected promise or an error thrown inside an async handler is forwarded to the error handler automatically. Express 4 does not do this, so the rejection is unhandled. Since Node.js 15, an unhandled rejection is raised as an uncaught exception by default, so the whole process crashes and every in-flight request on it fails (clients see the connection reset); only if an unhandledRejection listener keeps the process alive does the request hang instead. In Express 4, wrap the code in try/catch and call next(err), or use a wrapper function.

docs.title: 26. How does error-handling middleware work?
docs.text: It is middleware with four parameters (err, req, res, next), registered after all routes. Express calls it when any middleware calls next(err) or throws. It typically maps known error types to status codes, logs unexpected errors, and sends a consistent error response. If headers were already sent, it should delegate with next(err).

docs.title: 27. How do you implement a 404 handler?
docs.text: Add a normal middleware after all routes, for example app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: "Not found" })). It runs only when no earlier route sent a response. It must come before the error handler, which has four parameters.

docs.title: 28. Why should production error responses not include stack traces?
docs.text: Stack traces, SQL errors, and file paths reveal how the system is built and help attackers. Send a generic message for unexpected errors, log full details server-side with a request ID, and include that ID in the response for support.

docs.title: 29. What is CORS, and how do you enable it in Express?
docs.text: CORS is a browser mechanism that lets a server allow web pages from other origins to read its responses. In Express, the cors middleware sets the Access-Control-Allow-* headers and answers preflight OPTIONS requests. Configure an explicit list of allowed origins instead of allowing all.

docs.title: 30. Why can't you combine Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials?
docs.text: Browsers refuse credentialed requests (cookies or HTTP authentication) when the allowed origin is the wildcard. With credentials: true, the server must return the exact requesting origin, and the frontend must send credentials: "include".

docs.title: 31. What do the httpOnly, secure, and sameSite cookie options do?
docs.text: httpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript, reducing theft through XSS. secure sends it only over HTTPS. sameSite controls whether the cookie is sent on cross-site requests (Strict, Lax, None) and is a key defense against CSRF.

docs.title: 32. How does express-session work?
docs.text: It stores a signed, random session ID in a cookie and keeps the session data in a server-side store. On each request it loads the data into req.session and saves changes afterward. Production apps need a shared store such as Redis or MongoDB, because the default MemoryStore leaks memory and does not work across instances.

docs.title: 33. Why regenerate the session after login?
docs.text: Regenerating issues a new session ID once the user is authenticated. This prevents session fixation, where an attacker gets a victim to log in using a session ID the attacker already knows.

docs.title: 34. How do you store passwords securely?
docs.text: Hash them with a slow, salted password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt, and store only the hash. Never store plain text or use reversible encryption, and never use fast hashes like MD5 or plain SHA-256 for passwords.

docs.title: 35. How does JWT authentication work in an Express API?
docs.text: After login, the server signs a token containing claims such as the user ID and an expiry. The client sends it in Authorization: Bearer <token>. Middleware verifies the signature and expiry with jwt.verify() (pinning the allowed algorithms) and attaches the user to req.user.

docs.title: 36. Why use refresh tokens?
docs.text: Access tokens are kept short-lived to limit the damage of theft. A long-lived refresh token, stored securely and sent only to the auth endpoints, obtains new access tokens. Rotating it on each use and storing it hashed lets the server revoke it.

docs.title: 37. What is the difference between 401 and 403?
docs.text: 401 Unauthorized means the request lacks valid credentials: the client should log in or refresh its token. 403 Forbidden means the client is authenticated but not allowed to perform the action.

docs.title: 38. What is an ownership check?
docs.text: An ownership check verifies that the authenticated user may access the specific record requested, for example that an order's userId matches req.user.id. Without it, a user can change an ID in the URL and read someone else's data: broken object-level authorization, which the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) ranks first.

docs.title: 39. How does express.static work?
docs.text: It maps request paths to files in a folder and sends them with proper content types, ETags, and range support. If no file matches, it calls next(). Options such as maxAge and immutable control caching, and dotfiles are ignored by default.

docs.title: 40. How do template engines integrate with Express?
docs.text: You set the views folder and the engine with app.set("views", ...) and app.set("view engine", "ejs"), then call res.render("name", data). Templates receive data from app.locals, res.locals, and the render call. Escaped output syntax prevents XSS.

docs.title: 41. How would you structure a large Express application?
docs.text: Separate routes, controllers, services, and data-access layers so HTTP concerns, business logic, and persistence stay independent. Keep configuration, middleware, and error classes in shared modules, and export the app from app.js while server.js calls listen(). Large apps often group these layers by feature.

docs.title: 42. How do you test an Express API?
docs.text: Export the app without calling listen() and use supertest to send requests in tests: await request(app).get("/tasks").expect(200). Assert on status codes, bodies, and headers, cover error paths, and give each test a fresh database state.

docs.title: 43. How do you handle databases and external APIs in tests?
docs.text: Use an isolated database (an in-memory fake, mongodb-memory-server, Testcontainers, or a dedicated test database) and reset it between tests. Replace third-party APIs with injected fakes or HTTP interception tools such as nock or MSW, so tests are fast, free, and deterministic.

docs.title: 44. What does helmet do?
docs.text: Helmet sets security-related response headers, including Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, frame protection, and Referrer-Policy, and removes X-Powered-By. It hardens browser behavior but does not fix application bugs such as injection.

docs.title: 45. How do you prevent NoSQL injection in an Express and MongoDB app?
docs.text: Validate that each input has the expected type, so an object such as {"$ne": null} cannot reach a query where a string is expected. Never pass raw request objects into filters, and consider Mongoose's sanitizeFilter option. Express 5's simple query parser avoids nested query-string objects, but JSON bodies still need validation.

docs.title: 46. Why does the trust proxy setting matter?
docs.text: Behind a proxy, Express sees the proxy's IP and protocol. Setting trust proxy to the correct number of hops makes req.ip, req.protocol, and req.secure reflect the client. Setting it to true blindly lets clients spoof X-Forwarded-For and bypass IP-based rate limits.

docs.title: 47. How do you protect login endpoints from brute-force attacks?
docs.text: Rate-limit attempts per IP (for example with express-rate-limit) and per account, add temporary lockouts or increasing delays, return the same error for unknown users and wrong passwords, and monitor for credential stuffing. Use a shared store for limits when running several instances.

docs.title: 48. What does NODE_ENV=production change?
docs.text: Express caches view templates and its default error handler hides stack traces. Many libraries also disable development checks and verbose logging. It does not configure security or performance by itself.

docs.title: 49. How do you implement graceful shutdown?
docs.text: On SIGTERM, mark the instance as not ready and keep serving briefly so the load balancer stops routing to it. Then call server.close() to stop accepting connections and let in-flight requests finish, close keep-alive connections as they become idle (otherwise they hold the server open until keepAliveTimeout), close database and cache connections, and exit. A forced-exit timer prevents hanging forever.

docs.title: 50. How do you use all CPU cores with Express?
docs.text: A Node process runs JavaScript on one thread, so run multiple processes: PM2 cluster mode, the cluster module, or several containers behind a load balancer. The app must be stateless, with sessions and rate limits stored in shared services such as Redis.

docs.title: 51. Users are randomly logged out when the app runs behind a load balancer. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: which session store express-session uses, and whether more than one instance is running.

How to confirm: look for the startup warning connect.session() MemoryStore is not designed for a production environment, and correlate 401 "login required" responses with requests landing on a different instance or with restarts.

Likely causes and fixes: the default MemoryStore keeps sessions per process, so another instance or a restart loses them: use a shared store such as Redis. If logouts happen site-wide right after a config change, the session secret was replaced; pass [newSecret, oldSecret] to rotate. See cookies and sessions.

docs.title: 52. Login succeeds in production, but the next request is anonymous. Locally everything works. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the login response in the browser's Network panel: is there a Set-Cookie header?

How to confirm: if the header is missing and the session cookie is configured with secure: true, check whether TLS ends at a proxy and what app.get("trust proxy") returns.

Likely causes and fixes: Express sees plain HTTP from the proxy, so express-session refuses to send a secure cookie. Set trust proxy to the real number of proxy hops (or use the session's proxy option). If the cookie is set but not sent back, check SameSite and whether the frontend is on a different site. See cookies and sessions.

docs.title: 53. The rate limiter blocks all users at once after a launch. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: which IP the limiter is counting: log req.ip for a few requests.

How to confirm: every request shows the load balancer's IP, and express-rate-limit logs the validation error ERR_ERL_UNEXPECTED_X_FORWARDED_FOR.

Likely causes and fixes: trust proxy is not set behind a proxy, so all clients share one key and one limit. Set trust proxy to the correct hop count (never true, which lets clients spoof their IP), and use a shared store such as Redis when several instances run. See security best practices.

docs.title: 54. The load balancer reports occasional 502 errors, but the Express logs show no failed requests. How do you investigate?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the 502s cluster on connections that were idle for a few seconds, and the load balancer's idle timeout setting.

How to confirm: compare the balancer's idle timeout (for example 60 seconds on an AWS Application Load Balancer by default) with Node's server.keepAliveTimeout (5 seconds by default).

Likely causes and fixes: Node closes an idle keep-alive connection just as the balancer reuses it. Set server.keepAliveTimeout longer than the balancer's idle timeout, for example 65 seconds. See running Express in production.

docs.title: 55. Every deployment causes a short burst of failed requests. How do you make deploys clean?
docs.text:
What to check first: what the process does on SIGTERM, and how long the orchestrator waits before killing it.

How to confirm: 5xx or connection-reset errors line up with deploy times; logs show the process exiting immediately, or "shutting down" followed by a forced kill at the end of the grace period.

Likely causes and fixes: the app exits on SIGTERM without draining, or closes before the load balancer stops routing to it, or keep-alive sockets keep server.close() from finishing. Fail readiness, wait a short drain delay, call server.close(), close idle connections as they go idle, close clients, and exit before the grace period ends. See running Express in production.

docs.title: 56. An Express 4 app restarts several times an hour, and clients see "connection reset". Logs show an error from an async route just before each restart. What is going on?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Express version and whether async handlers catch their errors.

How to confirm: the logs show an uncaught exception or unhandled promise rejection followed by the process exiting; reproducing the failing request crashes the process locally.

Likely causes and fixes: Express 4 does not catch rejected promises from async handlers. Since Node.js 15 an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default, taking every in-flight request down with it. Wrap handlers with try/catch and next(err) or an async wrapper, or upgrade to Express 5, which forwards rejections to the error handler. See error handling in Express.

docs.title: 57. "Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client" appears in the logs for one endpoint. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the handler's early-exit branches, such as validation or "not found" checks.

How to confirm: the stack trace points to a second res.json(), res.send(), or next() call after a response was already sent.

Likely causes and fixes: a missing return before an early res.status(...).json(...), calling next() after responding, or a callback and a promise both responding. Add return to every early response, and have error handlers delegate with next(err) when res.headersSent is true. See the response object.

docs.title: 58. The browser console shows a CORS error, but the request appears in the server logs. Where is the real problem?
docs.text:
What to check first: the actual status code of the failing response in the Network panel or server logs.

How to confirm: if the status is 500 (or a proxy error page), the response was produced by an error path that did not include CORS headers, so the browser reports CORS instead of the real error. If it is a preflight OPTIONS returning 401 or 404, authentication or routing ran before cors.

Likely causes and fixes: fix the underlying error, register cors() before authentication and routes so preflights and error responses carry the headers, and check that the origin is in the allowlist. See configuring CORS in Express.

docs.title: 59. Clients get Unexpected token '<' when parsing JSON from your API. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the response's Content-Type and body for the failing request.

How to confirm: the API returned 200 with text/html, usually the single-page app's index.html, or an HTML error page.

Likely causes and fixes: a mistyped or missing API route fell through to the SPA catch-all, or a body-parser error reached Express's default HTML error handler. Register API routes and a JSON 404 for /api before the catch-all, and handle parser errors such as entity.parse.failed in your own JSON error handler. See static files and template engines and body parsing and content types.

docs.title: 60. Users report that uploads larger than about 1 MB fail with an HTML 413 page. Multer allows 10 MB. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the 413 response comes from Express or from the reverse proxy.

How to confirm: the 413 body is the proxy's HTML page, and the Express logs show no request at all.

Likely causes and fixes: Nginx's client_max_body_size defaults to 1m, so the proxy rejects the body before it reaches Multer. Raise it for the upload routes only and keep Multer's fileSize as the application limit, or move large files to presigned direct-to-storage uploads. See file uploads with Multer.

docs.title: 61. Memory usage spikes and the container is restarted during busy upload periods. What do you look at?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Multer storage engine and its limits.

How to confirm: memory graphs climb with concurrent uploads, the orchestrator reports out-of-memory restarts, or logs show JavaScript heap out of memory.

Likely causes and fixes: memoryStorage keeps every file in RAM, and without fileSize and files limits a few large uploads exhaust memory. Set limits, stream to disk or object storage, or switch large files to presigned URLs. See file uploads with Multer.

docs.title: 62. p99 latency jumps for every route whenever someone exports a large report. How do you find and fix the cause?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the slowdown affects unrelated routes on the same process at the same moment.

How to confirm: event-loop delay metrics (for example from perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()) spike during exports, and a CPU profile shows synchronous work such as a huge JSON.stringify, a sync file read, or a long loop in the export handler.

Likely causes and fixes: CPU-heavy synchronous work blocks the event loop, so every other request waits. Stream the export, process it in batches, or move it to worker threads or a background job that produces a download. See running Express in production and the event loop.

docs.title: 63. After adding helmet(), the React app served by Express shows a blank page. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the browser console.

How to confirm: errors such as "Refused to load the script … because it violates the following Content Security Policy directive".

Likely causes and fixes: helmet's default Content Security Policy (default-src 'self', script-src 'self') blocks inline scripts and third-party domains the app relies on. Configure CSP directives for the sources you actually use instead of disabling CSP. See security best practices.

docs.title: 64. API tests pass locally but fail randomly in CI. How do you make them reliable?
docs.text:
What to check first: which tests fail across reruns of the same commit, and whether they share a database, collection, or port.

How to confirm: running the files one at a time (node --test --test-concurrency=1) makes the failures disappear.

Likely causes and fixes: node --test runs test files in parallel processes by default, so files sharing one database interfere, or tests depend on each other's data. Give each file its own database or collection names, reset state in beforeEach, and close clients in after() so the run exits. See testing Express APIs.

docs.title: 65. A user changes their password after a suspected account takeover, but the attacker's API calls keep working. Why, and what do you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the API authenticates: JWT access tokens, refresh tokens, or server-side sessions.

How to confirm: audit logs show requests with tokens issued before the password change, still accepted because their exp has not passed.

Likely causes and fixes: JWT access tokens stay valid until they expire, and refresh tokens were not revoked on the password change. Delete all of the user's refresh tokens (or sessions) on password change, keep access tokens short-lived, and optionally add a token-version claim checked against the user record. See implementing authentication in Express.

docs.title: Middleware
docs.text: Middleware is reusable request-processing code that runs between receiving a request and sending a response. In Express, a middleware function can inspect or change the request, do a task such as logging, end the response itself, or pass control to the next function in line. Express applications are essentially chains of middleware with route handlers at the end.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Many routes need the same cross-cutting behavior: parsing request bodies, recording request details, checking authentication, setting security headers, or measuring response time. Middleware lets you write that behavior once and apply it to the whole app, one router, or a single route, instead of copying it into every handler. Understanding the order in which middleware runs is the key to understanding why an Express app behaves the way it does.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe warns Express users that the order of middleware decides whether webhook verification works. Its documentation says the webhook route must come before app.use(express.json()), because "Express applies middleware in order" and a JSON parser that runs first changes the body before the signature check (Stripe documentation).
  • Auth0 protects Express APIs with middleware: its express-oauth2-jwt-bearer SDK is configured as JWT middleware that validates access tokens before protected route handlers run (Auth0 Express API quickstart).
  • Sentry's Express integration "captures errors from your routes and middleware automatically" and skips errors with 3xx and 4xx status codes by default, treating them as expected client errors (Sentry for Express).
  • PayPal built kraken.js as "a convention layer on top of express" so that many teams configured their apps the same way, after finding that plain Express "didn't scale well in multiple development teams" (PayPal Technology blog).

Popular tools and providers: helmet, cors, morgan, pino-http, compression, and express-rate-limit from npm, plus vendor middleware from identity and monitoring providers such as Auth0 and Sentry.

docs.title: The signature
docs.text:
function middleware(req, res, next) {
  // 1. Do some work with req / res
  // 2. Then EITHER send a response OR call next()
  next();
}
  • req and res are the same objects for every function in the chain, so data attached by one middleware (req.user) is visible to later ones.
  • next passes control to the next matching middleware or route.
  • If a middleware neither responds nor calls next(), the request hangs until the client times out.

docs.title: The middleware chain
docs.text:
Express runs middleware in registration order. Each request walks down the list until something sends a response.

Because order matters, a middleware registered after a route never runs for requests that route answers.

docs.title: Ways to call next
docs.text:
Call Effect next() Continue to the next matching middleware or route next("route") Skip the remaining handlers of the current route (route handlers only) next("router") Leave the current router and continue after it next(err) Skip normal middleware and jump to error-handling middleware

Any value other than "route" or "router" passed to next() is treated as an error.

docs.title: Types of middleware
docs.text:
Application-level middleware is registered on app:

app.use(requestLogger);                // every request
app.use("/admin", requireAdmin);       // paths starting with /admin
app.get("/profile", authenticate, getProfile); // one route

app.use("/admin", fn) matches /admin, /admin/users, and so on, but not /administrator. Inside fn, req.url has the mount path removed.

Router-level middleware is registered on an express.Router() and runs only for requests that reach that router:

const router = express.Router();
router.use(authenticate);              // every route in this router
router.get("/orders", listOrders);
app.use("/api", router);

Built-in middleware ships with Express:

Middleware Purpose express.json() Parse JSON bodies into req.body express.urlencoded() Parse HTML form bodies express.raw() Keep the body as a Buffer express.text() Parse plain-text bodies into a string express.static(dir) Serve files from a folder

Third-party middleware is installed from npm:

Package Purpose cors Send CORS headers; see configuring CORS helmet Set security headers; see security best practices morgan HTTP request logging cookie-parser Parse cookies into req.cookies compression Compress response bodies express-rate-limit Limit repeated requests multer Parse multipart/form-data uploads

Error-handling middleware has four parameters. Express recognizes it by the number of arguments, so all four must be declared even if next is unused:

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  console.error(err);
  res.status(err.status ?? 500).json({ error: "Something went wrong" });
});

It runs only when an error is passed with next(err) or thrown, and it must be registered after the routes. See error handling in Express.

docs.title: A typical registration order
docs.text:
app.disable("x-powered-by");
app.use(helmet());                 // 1. security headers on every response
app.use(cors(corsOptions));        // 2. CORS (also answers preflight)
app.use(requestId);                // 3. tag the request for logs
app.use(requestLogger);            // 4. log it
app.use(express.json({ limit: "100kb" })); // 5. parse bodies
app.use("/api/v1", apiRouter);     // 6. routes (with their own auth)
app.use(notFoundHandler);          // 7. nothing matched -> 404
app.use(errorHandler);             // 8. errors -> one consistent response

docs.title: Configurable middleware: the factory pattern
docs.text:
When middleware needs options, write a function that returns a middleware. Most packages (cors(options), express.json(options)) work this way.

function requireRole(...allowedRoles) {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    if (!req.user) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Sign in first" });
    if (!allowedRoles.includes(req.user.role)) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: "Not allowed" });
    }
    next();
  };
}

app.delete("/users/:id", authenticate, requireRole("admin"), deleteUser);

docs.title: Async middleware in Express 5
docs.text:
Express 5 handles middleware and handlers that return promises. If the promise rejects (for example an await throws), Express passes the error to the error handler for you.

app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  req.settings = await loadSettings(); // a rejection reaches the error handler
  next();
});

In Express 4 the same code produces an unhandled promise rejection that Express never sees. Since Node.js 15, an unhandled rejection crashes the whole process by default, taking every in-flight request with it; with an unhandledRejection listener that keeps the process alive, the request hangs instead. Express 4 code therefore wraps async functions in try/catch and calls next(err), or uses a helper wrapper.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Write it as middleware when:

  • The same step applies to many routes: authentication, logging, request IDs, security headers, rate limiting, body parsing.
  • The step must run before the handler and may end the request early, such as rejecting an invalid token with 401.
  • The step prepares shared data for later handlers, such as loading req.user.

Keep it out of middleware when:

  • It is business logic for one feature, such as calculating an order total. Put it in a service the handler calls, so it can be tested without HTTP.
  • It is expensive and most requests do not need it. A database lookup in global middleware also runs for health checks and static files.
  • It depends on the result of the handler. Use the finish event or the handler itself instead.
Scope Register with Use for Whole application app.use(fn) Security headers, CORS, request IDs, logging Path prefix app.use("/admin", fn) Rules for one area of the app One router router.use(fn) Authentication for a group of related routes One route app.get(path, fn, handler) Validation or permission checks for that route only Errors app.use((err, req, res, next) => ...) last Turning failures into one response format

docs.title: Request ID
docs.text:
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

export function requestId(req, res, next) {
  // Reuse an ID set by a trusted proxy, or create one
  req.id = req.get("X-Request-Id") ?? randomUUID();
  res.set("X-Request-Id", req.id); // lets clients quote it in bug reports
  next();
}

docs.title: Request logger with response time
docs.text:
The response has not been sent when the middleware runs, so it listens for the finish event, which fires after the response is handed to the operating system.

export function requestLogger(req, res, next) {
  const start = performance.now();

  res.on("finish", () => {
    const ms = (performance.now() - start).toFixed(1);
    console.log(`${req.id} ${req.method} ${req.originalUrl} ${res.statusCode} ${ms}ms`);
  });

  next();
}

Output:
3f1c... GET /api/v1/tasks 200 4.2ms
9a7b... POST /api/v1/tasks 400 1.1ms

A production logger should use a structured logging library and avoid recording passwords, tokens, or other sensitive values. See logging and monitoring.

docs.title: Authentication guard
docs.text:
import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";

export function authenticate(req, res, next) {
  const header = req.get("Authorization") ?? "";
  const [scheme, token] = header.split(" ");

  if (scheme !== "Bearer" || !token) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Missing bearer token" });
  }

  try {
    req.user = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET);
    next();
  } catch {
    res.status(401).json({ error: "Invalid or expired token" });
  }
}

Authentication middleware answers "who is this?". Authorization (what that user may do) is a separate check, such as requireRole above. See implementing authentication in Express.

docs.title: Applying middleware to only some routes
docs.text:
const router = express.Router();

router.get("/products", listProducts);              // public

router.use(authenticate);                           // everything below is protected
router.post("/products", requireRole("admin"), createProduct);
router.get("/orders", listMyOrders);

Middleware registered with router.use() applies to routes registered after it in that router.

docs.title: Leaving a router early with next("router")
docs.text:
const betaRouter = express.Router();

betaRouter.use((req, res, next) => {
  if (!req.user?.betaTester) return next("router"); // skip the whole router
  next();
});

betaRouter.get("/dashboard", sendBetaDashboard);

app.use(betaRouter);
app.get("/dashboard", sendStableDashboard); // non-beta users end up here

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep each middleware focused on one job and give it a descriptive name.
  • Register in a deliberate order: security headers and CORS early, body parsers before routes that read bodies, 404 and error handlers last.
  • Apply expensive middleware (body parsing, database lookups) only where it is needed, not globally.
  • Use the factory pattern for configurable middleware.
  • Always return after sending a response so next() is not also called.
  • Never log secrets or full request bodies by default.
  • Let errors flow to one error handler with next(err) (or a rejected promise in Express 5) instead of answering errors in many places.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Requests hang until the proxy gives up. Symptom: clients receive 504 Gateway Timeout from the load balancer. Detect: proxy logs show upstream timeouts, and the request logger has entries that start but never reach finish. Cause: a middleware branch that neither responds nor calls next(), often an if without an else. Fix: make every branch respond or continue, and test each branch.
  • Health checks fail and instances are removed. Symptom: the load balancer marks healthy instances unhealthy and traffic drops. Detect: the health endpoint returns 401 in the access logs. Cause: authentication middleware was registered globally before the health route. Fix: register /health before authentication, or apply authentication only to the routers that need it.
  • Browsers report CORS errors after a refactor. Symptom: the frontend breaks while curl works. Detect: OPTIONS requests answered with 401 or 404 in the access logs. Cause: CORS middleware moved below authentication or routes, so preflight requests never reach it. Fix: register CORS before authentication; see configuring CORS in Express.
  • Latency rises for every endpoint. Symptom: p95 latency climbs even for trivial routes. Detect: tracing or timing logs show the same middleware taking most of the time on every request. Cause: global middleware doing slow work, such as a database lookup or a large body parse, for requests that do not need it. Fix: scope it to the routes that use it, or cache the result.
  • Logs polluted by client-supplied IDs. Symptom: log lines with enormous or strange request IDs. Detect: log ingestion warnings about oversized fields. Cause: a request-ID middleware that trusts any incoming X-Request-Id. Fix: accept the header only from your own proxy, or check its length and format before using it.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Middleware function: Code invoked during the request-response cycle with (req, res, next).
  • next(): The callback that passes control to the next handler.
  • Application-level middleware: Middleware registered with app.use() or app.METHOD().
  • Router-level middleware: Middleware registered on an express.Router().
  • Error-handling middleware: A four-argument function (err, req, res, next) that processes errors.
  • Mount path: The path prefix given to app.use().
  • Middleware factory: A function that takes options and returns a middleware function.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Forgetting to call next() or respond, which leaves the request hanging.
  • Calling next() after sending a response, which leads to "Cannot set headers after they are sent".
  • Registering a logger or CORS middleware after the routes and wondering why it never runs.
  • Declaring an error handler with three parameters; Express then treats it as normal middleware.
  • Thinking middleware must modify the request; it can also log, check, or respond.
  • Assuming calling next() means a response was sent; it only continues the chain.
  • Confusing authentication middleware (identity) with authorization policy (permissions).
  • Doing heavy work, such as a database query, in global middleware that runs even for health checks and static files.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What three things can a middleware function do with a request?
  2. Why does registration order change application behavior?
  3. What is the difference between next(), next("route"), next("router"), and next(err)?
  4. How does Express recognize error-handling middleware?
  5. How does Express 5 treat a rejected promise in async middleware, and how did Express 4 differ?
  6. Why would you write a middleware factory instead of a plain function?

docs.title: Running Express in Production
docs.text: An Express app that works on a laptop is not yet ready for real users. Production adds process supervision, multiple instances, a reverse proxy, graceful restarts, health checks, logging, and monitoring. This lesson covers how to run Express reliably and quickly once it is deployed.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: In production, processes crash, servers are replaced, deployments happen during traffic, and load varies by the hour. An app that drops in-flight requests on every deploy, cannot be health-checked by a load balancer, or logs nothing useful will cause outages that are hard to diagnose. Most performance problems in Express apps also come from a few avoidable patterns: synchronous work, missing connection pooling, and uncached responses.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Kubernetes defines how most containerized apps are stopped. Its pod lifecycle documentation explains that deleting a pod sends SIGTERM to the main process with a grace period that defaults to 30 seconds, after which the container runtime sends SIGKILL to anything still running; a failed readiness probe removes the pod from its Services' endpoints. This is why the shutdown code below handles SIGTERM, fails readiness, and exits well within 30 seconds.
  • AWS Elastic Load Balancing keeps idle connections to your app open. Its Application Load Balancer documentation states that the idle timeout is 60 seconds by default and recommends configuring the application's idle timeout to be larger than the load balancer's: the reason for keepAliveTimeout = 65_000.
  • PM2 is a common way to run Node on virtual machines. Its cluster mode documentation describes scaling networked Node.js apps across all available CPUs without code changes, and a reload that, unlike restart, achieves a 0-second-downtime reload.

Popular tools and providers: PM2, systemd, Docker, Kubernetes, Amazon ECS; Nginx and cloud load balancers; pino and pino-http for logs; OpenTelemetry and APM services for tracing and metrics.

docs.title: A typical production layout
docs.text: Every instance must be stateless: sessions, rate-limit counters, and uploaded files live in shared services, so any instance can serve any request and instances can be added or removed freely.

docs.title: NODE_ENV=production
docs.text:
Setting NODE_ENV=production changes behavior in Express and many libraries:

  • Express caches compiled view templates.
  • The default error handler stops sending stack traces to clients.
  • Many libraries skip development-only checks and verbose logging.

It is a convention, not a magic switch: you still need to configure logging, security, and performance yourself. Never rely on NODE_ENV=development features being off unless you set the variable.

docs.title: Process managers vs containers
docs.text:
A single Node process stops if it crashes. Something must restart it.

Option How it works Good for PM2 Node-focused process manager: restarts on crash, cluster mode, log files, zero-downtime reload Virtual machines running Node directly systemd The Linux service manager restarts the process and starts it at boot Linux servers; minimal extra tooling Containers (Docker, Kubernetes, ECS) The orchestrator restarts containers and runs replicas Most modern deployments

With containers, run one Node process per container and scale by running more containers; the orchestrator already handles restarts, so PM2 is usually unnecessary inside them. See Docker.

docs.title: Using every CPU core
docs.text: JavaScript in one Node process runs on one thread, so one process uses about one CPU core. To use more cores, run several processes: PM2 cluster mode, Node's cluster module, or multiple container replicas behind a load balancer. See worker threads, child processes, and cluster and scalability.

docs.title: Behind a reverse proxy
docs.text: A reverse proxy such as nginx or a cloud load balancer usually terminates TLS, serves static files, compresses responses, buffers slow clients, and spreads load. Express then sees every request as coming from the proxy over HTTP. Set trust proxy to the number of proxies so req.ip, req.protocol, and req.secure reflect the real client. See reverse proxy.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text: Gzip or Brotli compression shrinks JSON and HTML responses dramatically. It costs CPU, so compress at the proxy (nginx, CDN) when possible. If Express must do it, use the compression middleware.

docs.title: Caching headers and ETags
docs.text:
• Express adds a weak ETag to responses sent with res.send()/res.json(). When a client repeats a request with If-None-Match, Express can answer 304 Not Modified with no body. The response is still computed, so ETags save bandwidth, not server work.
  • Cache-Control decides whether browsers, CDNs, and proxies may reuse a response. Public, rarely changing data can be cached by a CDN; per-user data needs private or no-store.

See caching for application-level caching with Redis.

docs.title: Keep-alive and server timeouts
docs.text:
HTTP keep-alive reuses one TCP connection for many requests. Node's HTTP server has several timeouts:

Setting Meaning server.keepAliveTimeout How long an idle keep-alive connection stays open (default 5 seconds) server.headersTimeout Maximum time to receive the request headers (default: the smaller of 60 seconds and requestTimeout) server.requestTimeout Maximum time to receive the whole request (default 5 minutes since Node 18)

If a load balancer keeps idle connections open longer than Node does, Node may close a connection just as the balancer sends a request on it, causing intermittent 502 errors. Set keepAliveTimeout longer than the load balancer's idle timeout: AWS, for example, sets an Application Load Balancer's idle timeout to 60 seconds by default and recommends configuring the application's idle timeout to be larger, so 65 seconds is a common choice.

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
Deployments and scaling send SIGTERM to the process. A graceful shutdown:

  1. Marks the instance as not ready, then keeps serving for a few seconds so the load balancer's health checks notice and stop sending new traffic.
  2. Calls server.close(), which stops accepting connections and waits for in-flight requests to finish. Idle keep-alive connections must also be closed, or they keep the server open until keepAliveTimeout expires.
  3. Closes database pools, Redis clients, and queue connections.
  4. Exits, with a forced-exit timer in case something hangs.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
Endpoint Question it answers Typical check If it fails Liveness (/livez) Is the process alive and not stuck? Return 200 if the event loop responds Orchestrator restarts the instance Readiness (/readyz) Can it serve traffic right now? Database and critical dependencies reachable; not shutting down Load balancer stops routing to it

Keep liveness checks simple: if liveness depends on the database, a database outage restarts every instance in a loop.

docs.title: Logging and request IDs
docs.text: Production logs should be structured (JSON), go to standard output, and be collected by the platform. pino is a fast JSON logger; pino-http logs each request with method, URL, status, and response time. Give every request an ID (reuse an incoming X-Request-Id from the proxy or generate one) and include it in every log line and in error responses, so one request can be traced across logs. See monitoring and logging.

docs.title: Monitoring and APM
docs.text: Track the request rate, error rate, and latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) for each route, plus process metrics: memory, CPU, and event-loop delay. Application performance monitoring (APM) tools and OpenTelemetry tracing show where time is spent inside a request, including database and external calls.

docs.title: Avoid blocking the event loop
docs.text: Any synchronous work in a handler pauses every request on that process: fs.readFileSync, crypto.pbkdf2Sync, JSON.parse of huge payloads, complex regular expressions, or large loops. Use asynchronous APIs, stream big data, and move CPU-heavy work to worker threads or a background job.

docs.title: Database connection pooling
docs.text: Opening a database connection is slow. Create one client or pool when the app starts and reuse it for every request; never connect inside a handler. Size the pool for your workload, and remember that the total connections equal the pool size times the number of instances, which must stay within the database's limit.

docs.title: Configuration via environment
docs.text: Read configuration (ports, URLs, secrets, feature flags) from environment variables validated at startup, so the same build runs in every environment. See process, environment variables, and configuration.

docs.title: Zero-downtime deployments
docs.text:
• Rolling deployment: replace instances a few at a time; readiness checks keep traffic away from instances that are starting or stopping.
  • PM2 reload: restarts cluster workers one by one.
  • Blue-green: start a full new version beside the old one and switch traffic at once.

All of these depend on graceful shutdown and readiness checks working.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Choose how to run Express in production by environment:

  • Containers with an orchestrator (Kubernetes, ECS, Cloud Run): one Node process per container, the platform handles restarts and scaling. Do not add PM2 inside the container.
  • Virtual machines without containers: PM2 or systemd supervises the process; PM2 cluster mode uses every core.
  • Very spiky or low traffic: a serverless platform may be cheaper, but long-lived connections, in-process state, and startup time behave differently from a normal server.

Do work in Express only when it belongs there: compress, serve static files, and terminate TLS at the proxy or CDN when you have one; keep Express for application logic.

Option Restarts on crash Uses all cores Zero-downtime deploys Best for node server.js in a shell No No No Never in production systemd Yes One process per unit Needs extra setup Simple Linux servers PM2 Yes Cluster mode pm2 reload VMs running Node directly Containers + orchestrator Yes Run more replicas Rolling deployments Most modern deployments Serverless Managed Managed Managed Spiky traffic, small APIs

docs.title: A production-ready server entry point
docs.text:
// src/server.js
import { createApp } from "./app.js";
import { db } from "./db.js";        // a pool created once at startup
import { logger } from "./logger.js";

const app = createApp();
let shuttingDown = false;

app.get("/livez", (req, res) => res.sendStatus(200));
app.get("/readyz", async (req, res) => {
  if (shuttingDown) return res.sendStatus(503);
  try {
    await db.ping();
    res.sendStatus(200);
  } catch {
    res.sendStatus(503);
  }
});

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const server = app.listen(port, () => logger.info({ port }, "listening"));

server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;  // longer than a 60s load-balancer idle timeout

// How long to keep serving after readiness fails, so the load balancer's
// health checks notice and stop routing here. Tune to your check interval.
const DRAIN_DELAY_MS = Number(process.env.DRAIN_DELAY_MS ?? 5_000);

async function shutdown(signal) {
  if (shuttingDown) return;         // ignore a second signal
  logger.info({ signal }, "shutting down");
  shuttingDown = true;              // 1. readiness now fails

  const forceExit = setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 30_000);
  forceExit.unref();                // don't keep the process alive just for this

  // 2. Keep serving briefly while the load balancer takes us out of rotation
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, DRAIN_DELAY_MS));

  server.close(async () => {        // 3. stop accepting; wait for in-flight
    await db.close();               // 4. release resources
    process.exit(0);
  });
  // close() drops connections that are idle right now, but a keep-alive
  // socket that finishes its last request afterwards would stay open until
  // keepAliveTimeout (65 s). Close such sockets as soon as they go idle.
  setInterval(() => server.closeIdleConnections(), 1_000).unref();
}

process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM"));
process.on("SIGINT", () => shutdown("SIGINT"));

(In a real app, register the health routes inside createApp() before the 404 handler; they are shown here to keep the example in one file.)

docs.title: Structured logging with request IDs
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import pino from "pino";
import pinoHttp from "pino-http";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

export const logger = pino({
  level: process.env.LOG_LEVEL ?? "info",
  redact: ["req.headers.authorization", "req.headers.cookie"],
});

const app = express();

app.use(pinoHttp({
  logger,
  genReqId: (req, res) => {
    // Reuse the proxy's ID if present (only trust it if your proxy sets it)
    const id = req.headers["x-request-id"] ?? randomUUID();
    res.setHeader("X-Request-Id", id);   // client can quote it in bug reports
    return id;
  },
}));

app.get("/tasks", (req, res) => {
  req.log.info("listing tasks");         // includes the request ID
  res.json([]);
});

A log line looks like this (trimmed: the real line also includes pid, hostname, and the request and response headers, with authorization and cookie shown as [Redacted]):

{"level":30,"time":1730900000000,"req":{"id":"6f1c...","method":"GET",
"url":"/tasks"},"res":{"statusCode":200},"responseTime":4,
"msg":"request completed"}

docs.title: Compression and cache headers
docs.text:
import compression from "compression";

app.use(compression());                  // only if the proxy does not compress

app.get("/api/countries", (req, res) => {
  res.set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=86400"); // safe for CDNs: same for all users
  res.json(countries);
});

app.get("/api/me", requireAuth, (req, res) => {
  res.set("Cache-Control", "private, no-store");     // never cache per-user data
  res.json(req.user);
});

docs.title: PM2 cluster mode
docs.text:
pm2 start src/server.js -i max --name api   # one process per CPU core
pm2 reload api                              # zero-downtime restart
pm2 logs api

docs.title: A systemd service
docs.text:
[Unit]
Description=Tasks API
After=network.target

[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/srv/tasks-api
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node src/server.js
Environment=NODE_ENV=production
EnvironmentFile=/etc/tasks-api.env
Restart=always
User=tasksapi

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text: Area Check Environment NODE_ENV=production; config validated at startup Processes Supervised (PM2, systemd, or orchestrator); restart on crash Scaling Stateless instances; shared session and rate-limit stores Proxy TLS at the proxy; trust proxy set correctly; compression at proxy or app Timeouts keepAliveTimeout above the load balancer's idle timeout Shutdown SIGTERM handled; readiness flips; drain delay; server.close() plus idle keep-alive sockets closed; resources closed; forced-exit timer Health Separate liveness and readiness endpoints Logging JSON logs to stdout; request IDs; secrets redacted Monitoring Error rate, latency percentiles, memory, event-loop delay; alerts Performance No sync calls in handlers; pooled DB connections; caching headers Deploys Rolling or blue-green; tested rollback

docs.title: General habits
docs.text:
• Measure before optimizing: find slow routes from real latency data.
  • Keep handlers asynchronous and small; offload heavy work.
  • Load-test before major launches; see performance testing.
  • Practice deployments and rollbacks so they are routine.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Intermittent 502 errors that do not match any app error. Detect: load balancer logs show 502s while the app logs no failed request; they cluster on connections that were idle. Cause: Node closes an idle keep-alive connection (default 5 s) just as the load balancer reuses it. Fix: set server.keepAliveTimeout longer than the balancer's idle timeout.
  • Every deploy causes a burst of failed requests. Detect: 5xx or connection-reset spikes exactly at deploy times. Cause: the process exits immediately on SIGTERM, or closes before the load balancer has stopped routing to it. Fix: fail readiness, wait a short drain delay, then server.close(), as in the example above.
  • Shutdown always takes the full grace period and ends in a forced kill. Detect: logs show "shutting down" but never a clean exit, and the orchestrator reports the container was killed. Cause: keep-alive connections stay open after server.close(), or database and Redis clients keep the event loop alive. Fix: close idle connections as they become idle (server.closeIdleConnections()) and close every client.
  • Latency climbs for all routes while CPU is high. Detect: event-loop delay metrics (for example from perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()) spike together with p99 latency across unrelated routes. Cause: synchronous or CPU-heavy work in a handler blocks the event loop. Fix: find it with a CPU profile, then make it asynchronous, stream it, or move it to worker threads or a job queue.
  • "Too many connections" from the database after scaling out. Detect: database errors refusing connections right after adding instances. Cause: total connections equal pool size times instances. Fix: lower per-instance pool sizes, cap autoscaling, or add a connection pooler in front of the database.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Process manager: A tool that starts, supervises, and restarts processes.
  • Stateless instance: A server that keeps no client state in its own memory between requests.
  • Graceful shutdown: Stopping new work, finishing in-flight work, then exiting.
  • Liveness probe: A check that the process is alive.
  • Readiness probe: A check that the instance can serve traffic now.
  • Keep-alive: Reusing one TCP connection for multiple HTTP requests.
  • Connection pool: A set of reusable open database connections.
  • APM: Application performance monitoring.
  • Rolling deployment: Replacing instances gradually during a release.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Running node server.js in a terminal session on the server. It stops when the session ends or the process crashes.
  • Storing sessions in memory with several instances. Users appear logged out when routed to another instance.
  • Exiting immediately on SIGTERM. In-flight requests fail on every deploy.
  • Liveness checks that test the database. A database blip restarts every instance.
  • Connecting to the database per request. Slow, and quickly exhausts database connections.
  • Default keep-alive behind a load balancer. Causes sporadic 502s.
  • "ETags make my API faster." They save bandwidth; the handler still runs.
  • Logging with console.log strings. Hard to search, filter, and correlate; use structured logs.

docs.text:

  2. Why must production instances be stateless, and what moves out of process memory?
  3. Describe the steps of a graceful shutdown and why each one matters.
  4. What is the difference between liveness and readiness checks?
  5. Why should keepAliveTimeout exceed the load balancer's idle timeout?
  6. Why does synchronous code in one handler slow down every other request?
