docs.title: Structuring an Express Project
docs.text: Express is unopinionated: it does not decide where routes, business logic, or database code should live. A single index.js works for a tutorial, but a real API needs a structure that keeps responsibilities separate, so code is easy to find, test, and change. This lesson presents a layered structure, compares it with feature-based organization, and walks one feature through every layer.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Without structure, route handlers grow into hundreds of lines that parse requests, run business rules, query the database, and format responses all at once. That code is hard to test (you need a running server and database), hard to reuse (a cron job cannot call a route handler), and risky to change. A clear structure gives every piece of code one obvious home.

For broader architecture choices (monoliths, services, clean architecture), see software architecture.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix used a hexagonal (ports and adapters) structure for a studio application so it could change where data came from. Its post Ready for changes with Hexagonal Architecture explains the goal: "the ability to swap data sources without impacting business logic", and notes that most tests could verify business logic without relying on protocols that easily change. That is the same reason this lesson keeps services free of HTTP and database details.
  • Shopify kept one large codebase but organized it by business domain. In Deconstructing the Monolith it describes evolving into a modular monolith: all code in one codebase, but with boundaries "defined and respected between different components", and dependencies isolated by decoupling business domains: feature-based structure at a very large scale.
  • NestJS, a Node.js framework that can run on Express, builds this structure in: its modules documentation recommends modules as "the recommended way to organize your components" and groups closely related controllers and services into feature modules.

Popular tools: express-generator (a starter skeleton), NestJS for an opinionated module structure, and eslint-plugin-import (its no-cycle rule catches circular imports between layers).

docs.title: The layers
docs.text:
Layer Responsibility Must not Routes Map method + path to controller functions; attach middleware (auth, validation) Contain logic Controllers Translate HTTP into function calls: read params/body, call a service, choose the status code Query the database or hold business rules Services Business logic: rules, calculations, coordinating repositories and external APIs Touch req/res or status codes Repositories / models Read and write data; hide query details Know about HTTP or business rules

The key rule: dependencies point downward. A service never imports a controller, and a repository never imports a service. Because services do not know about HTTP, the same service can be called from a route, a background job, a CLI script, or a test.

docs.title: A layer-based folder tree
docs.text:
my-api/
├── package.json
├── .env.example            # documents required variables, no real values
├── src/
│   ├── server.js           # starts listening; handles shutdown
│   ├── app.js              # builds and exports the Express app
│   ├── config/
│   │   └── index.js        # reads and validates environment variables
│   ├── routes/
│   │   ├── index.js        # mounts all routers under /api
│   │   └── tasks.routes.js
│   ├── controllers/
│   │   └── tasks.controller.js
│   ├── services/
│   │   └── tasks.service.js
│   ├── repositories/
│   │   └── tasks.repository.js
│   ├── middleware/
│   │   ├── auth.js
│   │   ├── validate.js
│   │   └── error-handler.js
│   ├── validation/
│   │   └── tasks.schemas.js
│   ├── errors/
│   │   └── app-error.js
│   └── utils/
└── test/
    └── tasks.test.js

docs.title: Splitting app.js and server.js
docs.text: app.js creates and configures the app and exports it without calling listen(). server.js imports the app, starts the HTTP server, and handles shutdown. Tests can then import the app and send requests to it in memory, with no port and no running server. See testing Express APIs.

docs.title: A configuration module
docs.text: Read environment variables in one place, validate them at startup, and export a typed, frozen object. The rest of the code imports config instead of reading process.env everywhere. If a required variable is missing, the process fails immediately at boot instead of later in a random request. See process, environment variables, and configuration.

docs.title: Light dependency injection
docs.text:
Instead of each module importing its dependencies directly, a factory function receives them:

export function createTasksService({ tasksRepository, clock = Date }) {
  /* ...uses tasksRepository and clock instead of importing them... */
}

This makes swapping dependencies trivial: tests pass an in-memory repository, production passes a database one. You do not need a dependency-injection framework; factory functions and one place that wires everything together (often app.js) are enough.

docs.title: Layer-based vs feature-based structure
docs.text:
A feature-based (modular) structure groups files by business feature:

src/
├── modules/
│   ├── tasks/
│   │   ├── tasks.routes.js
│   │   ├── tasks.controller.js
│   │   ├── tasks.service.js
│   │   ├── tasks.repository.js
│   │   └── tasks.schemas.js
│   └── users/
│       └── ...
└── shared/
    ├── middleware/
    ├── errors/
    └── config/
Layer-based Feature-based Finding code By technical role By business feature Changing one feature Touches many folders Touches one folder Small apps Simple and familiar Slightly more ceremony Large apps / teams Folders become very long Scales well; features can be owned by teams Extracting a service later Harder Easier: the module is already self-contained

Both use the same layers inside. Many teams start layer-based and move to feature-based as the app grows.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
• Use one style consistently, such as tasks.service.js or taskService.js.
  • Name routers by resource (tasks.routes.js mounted at /tasks).
  • Name controller functions after actions: list, getById, create, update, remove.
  • Put custom error classes in one place so the error handler can recognize them.

docs.title: npm scripts
docs.text:
{
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "node --watch --env-file=.env src/server.js",
    "start": "node src/server.js",
    "test": "node --test",
    "lint": "eslint ."
  }
}

docs.title: TypeScript note
docs.text: The same structure works in TypeScript. Common setups are compiling with tsc to a dist/ folder for production and using a runner such as tsx for development. Install @types/express for type definitions. Recent Node versions can also run TypeScript files directly by stripping type annotations (only syntax that can be erased); check the Node.js documentation for your version before relying on it.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a layered structure (routes, controllers, services, repositories) when:

  • The API has more than a handful of endpoints or more than one developer.
  • Business logic must be reused outside HTTP: background jobs, CLI scripts, message consumers.
  • You want fast unit tests of business rules without a server or database.

Keep it simpler when:

  • The service is tiny (a webhook receiver, a proxy with two routes): one file with clear functions is easier to read than ten folders.
  • You are prototyping and expect to throw the code away.
Structure Best for Trade-off Single file Prototypes, tiny services Becomes unmanageable quickly Layer-based folders Small to medium APIs, one team One feature is spread across many folders Feature-based modules Larger APIs, several teams More upfront organization Opinionated framework (NestJS) Teams wanting enforced conventions and dependency injection More concepts and boilerplate Separate services Independent scaling or deployment needs Distributed-system complexity; see software architecture

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text: The following implements "create and list tasks" through every layer. It runs as-is with an in-memory repository.

docs.title: src/errors/app-error.js
docs.text:
export class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, status = 500, code = "INTERNAL_ERROR") {
    super(message);
    this.status = status;
    this.code = code;
  }
}
export class NotFoundError extends AppError {
  constructor(message = "Not found") { super(message, 404, "NOT_FOUND"); }
}
export class ValidationError extends AppError {
  constructor(message, details) {
    super(message, 400, "VALIDATION_ERROR");
    this.details = details;
  }
}

docs.title: src/repositories/tasks.repository.js
docs.text:
// The only module that knows how tasks are stored.
export function createInMemoryTasksRepository() {
  const tasks = new Map();
  return {
    async insert(task) { tasks.set(task.id, task); return task; },
    async findById(id) { return tasks.get(id) ?? null; },
    async findByOwner(ownerId) {
      return [...tasks.values()].filter((t) => t.ownerId === ownerId);
    },
  };
}

A MongoDB or PostgreSQL version would expose the same three functions.

docs.title: src/services/tasks.service.js
docs.text:
import { NotFoundError, ValidationError } from "../errors/app-error.js";

// Business rules only: no req, no res, no status codes chosen here.
export function createTasksService({ tasksRepository }) {
  return {
    async create(ownerId, { title, dueDate }) {
      if (dueDate && new Date(dueDate) < new Date()) {
        throw new ValidationError("Due date must be in the future");
      }
      return tasksRepository.insert({
        id: crypto.randomUUID(), ownerId, title, dueDate: dueDate ?? null,
        done: false, createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
      });
    },
    async list(ownerId) {
      return tasksRepository.findByOwner(ownerId);
    },
    async get(ownerId, id) {
      const task = await tasksRepository.findById(id);
      if (!task || task.ownerId !== ownerId) throw new NotFoundError("Task not found");
      return task;
    },
  };
}

docs.title: src/controllers/tasks.controller.js
docs.text:
// Translates HTTP to service calls and back.
export function createTasksController({ tasksService }) {
  return {
    async list(req, res) {
      res.json(await tasksService.list(req.user.id));
    },
    async getById(req, res) {
      res.json(await tasksService.get(req.user.id, req.params.id));
    },
    async create(req, res) {
      const task = await tasksService.create(req.user.id, req.body);
      res.status(201).location(`/api/tasks/${task.id}`).json(task);
    },
  };
}

In Express 5, a rejected promise from these async handlers is passed to the error handler automatically, so no try/catch is needed here.

docs.title: src/routes/tasks.routes.js
docs.text:
import { Router } from "express";

export function createTasksRouter({ tasksController, requireAuth, validate,
  createTaskSchema }) {
  const router = Router();
  router.use(requireAuth);
  router.get("/", tasksController.list);
  router.get("/:id", tasksController.getById);
  router.post("/", validate(createTaskSchema), tasksController.create);
  return router;
}

docs.title: src/middleware/error-handler.js
docs.text:
import { AppError } from "../errors/app-error.js";

export function errorHandler(err, req, res, next) {
  if (res.headersSent) return next(err);
  if (err instanceof AppError) {
    return res.status(err.status).json({ error: { code: err.code,
      message: err.message, details: err.details } });
  }
  console.error(err); // replace with your logger
  res.status(500).json({ error: { code: "INTERNAL_ERROR",
    message: "Something went wrong" } });
}

docs.title: src/app.js: wiring everything together
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import { createInMemoryTasksRepository } from "./repositories/tasks.repository.js";
import { createTasksService } from "./services/tasks.service.js";
import { createTasksController } from "./controllers/tasks.controller.js";
import { createTasksRouter } from "./routes/tasks.routes.js";
import { errorHandler } from "./middleware/error-handler.js";
import { ValidationError } from "./errors/app-error.js";

// Minimal stand-ins; real versions live in middleware/ and validation/.
const requireAuth = (req, res, next) => { req.user = { id: "u1" }; next(); };
const createTaskSchema = (body) =>
  typeof body?.title === "string" && body.title.trim() !== "";
const validate = (schema) => (req, res, next) =>
  schema(req.body) ? next() : next(new ValidationError("Title is required"));

export function createApp({ tasksRepository = createInMemoryTasksRepository() } = {}) {
  const tasksService = createTasksService({ tasksRepository });
  const tasksController = createTasksController({ tasksService });

  const app = express();
  app.use(express.json({ limit: "100kb" }));
  app.get("/health", (req, res) => res.json({ status: "ok" }));
  app.use("/api/tasks", createTasksRouter({ tasksController, requireAuth,
    validate, createTaskSchema }));
  app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: { code: "NOT_FOUND",
    message: "Route not found" } }));
  app.use(errorHandler);
  return app;
}

docs.title: src/server.js
docs.text:
import { createApp } from "./app.js";

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const server = createApp().listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`API listening on port ${port}`);
});

process.on("SIGTERM", () => server.close(() => process.exit(0)));

A request now flows: route → auth and validation middleware → controller → service → repository, and errors from any layer end up in one handler.

POST /api/tasks  {"title":"Write notes"}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /api/tasks/5c2f...
{"id":"5c2f...","ownerId":"u1","title":"Write notes","dueDate":null,
 "done":false,"createdAt":"..."}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep req and res out of services; keep database calls out of controllers.
  • Export the app from app.js; call listen() only in server.js.
  • Validate configuration once at startup in a config module.
  • Wire dependencies in one place with factory functions.
  • Throw typed errors from services and map them to HTTP in one error handler.
  • Choose layer-based or feature-based structure deliberately, and apply it consistently.
  • Keep shared code (errors, middleware, config) separate from feature code.
  • Commit an .env.example listing variable names, never real values.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A crash hours after deploy on one rarely used path. Detect: an error such as TypeError: Invalid URL or a connection error mentioning undefined, only on one feature. Cause: a missing environment variable read directly from process.env deep in the code. Fix: validate all configuration in the config module at startup so the process refuses to boot without it.
  • Tests hang or fail with EADDRINUSE in CI. Detect: the test runner never exits, or reports the port is already in use when files run in parallel. Cause: the module tests import also calls listen(). Fix: export the app from app.js and call listen() only in server.js.
  • ReferenceError: Cannot access 'X' before initialization at startup. Detect: the error appears immediately on boot after a refactor. Cause: a circular import, often a lower layer importing a higher one. Fix: restore one-way dependencies and add a lint rule such as import/no-cycle.
  • Scripts and tests connect to the real database unexpectedly. Detect: connection logs or open handles when running a one-off script or unit test. Cause: a module opens connections at import time. Fix: create connections in the composition root (server.js or createApp) and pass them in.
  • A background job and the API disagree on business rules. Detect: data created by the job violates rules the API enforces. Cause: the rules live inside route handlers, so the job reimplemented them. Fix: move the rules into a service and call it from both.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Layered architecture: Code organized into layers with one-way dependencies.
  • Controller: Code that turns an HTTP request into a service call and the result into a response.
  • Service: Code that implements business rules independently of HTTP.
  • Repository: Code that hides how data is stored and queried.
  • Dependency injection: Passing a module its dependencies instead of having it import them directly.
  • Composition root: The single place where the application's objects are created and wired together.
  • Feature-based structure: Organizing files by business feature rather than technical role.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Fat route handlers. Business logic inside routes cannot be reused or unit-tested easily.
  • Passing req into services. It ties business logic to HTTP and to Express.
  • Reading process.env everywhere. Missing variables are discovered late and scattered.
  • Calling listen() in the file that tests import. Tests then fight over ports and leave servers running.
  • "More folders means better architecture." Structure should match the app's size; a tiny service does not need ten layers.
  • Circular imports between layers. If a repository imports a service, the layering is broken.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is each layer (routes, controllers, services, repositories) responsible for?
  2. Why should services not use req or res?
  3. What does splitting app.js and server.js make easier?
  4. How does a factory function provide dependency injection without a framework?
  5. When would you move from a layer-based to a feature-based structure?
  6. Why validate configuration at startup?

docs.title: The Request Object
docs.text: Every Express handler receives req, an object describing the incoming HTTP request. It extends Node.js's http.IncomingMessage with convenient properties such as req.params, req.query, and req.body. Knowing where each piece of client data lives, and what type it has, is the first step to handling it safely.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: All client input arrives through req: path segments, query strings, headers, cookies, and the body. Reading the wrong property, assuming a value is a number when it is a string, or trusting a header that a proxy or attacker could set are frequent causes of bugs and security holes. Understanding req also explains how features such as proxies, mounted routers, and content negotiation affect what your code sees.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
Almost every production Express app sits behind infrastructure that rewrites what req sees. The platforms document the headers they add, which is exactly what the trust proxy setting reads:

  • AWS Application Load Balancer stores the client's IP address in X-Forwarded-For and, by default, appends it to any value the client already sent. AWS warns that the header's entries "can only be considered trustworthy if added by systems that are properly secured within the network" (AWS documentation).
  • Heroku's router sets X-Forwarded-For, appending the client IP to the right of any existing list, plus X-Forwarded-Proto (for example https) and an X-Request-Id for each request (Heroku Dev Center).
  • Cloudflare sends CF-Connecting-IP, the IP address of the client that connected to Cloudflare, on traffic from its edge to your origin server (Cloudflare documentation).

Because each layer appends to X-Forwarded-For, the number of trusted hops must match your real setup: one for a single load balancer, two for a CDN in front of a load balancer.

docs.title: Anatomy of a request
docs.text: req.originalUrl keeps the whole URL, /api/v1/orders/77/items?notify=true, no matter which router handles the request.

docs.title: req.params
docs.text:
Values captured by route parameters such as /users/:id. They are always strings and are already URL-decoded (/users/a%20b gives "a b").

app.get("/users/:id", (req, res) => {
  const id = Number(req.params.id);
  if (!Number.isInteger(id)) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "id must be an integer" });
  }
  res.json({ id });
});

docs.title: req.query
docs.text:
The parsed query string. Express 5 uses the simple parser by default (Node.js's querystring module). Express 4 used the extended parser (the qs package), which builds nested objects.

Query string Simple parser (Express 5 default) Extended parser ?page=2 { page: "2" } { page: "2" } ?tag=a&tag=b { tag: ["a", "b"] } { tag: ["a", "b"] } ?user[name]=Asha { "user[name]": "Asha" } { user: { name: "Asha" } } ?active { active: "" } { active: "" }

Switch parsers with app.set("query parser", "extended"). Nested query objects are convenient but make validation harder, so many APIs stay with the simple parser.

Two rules follow from this table:

  1. Every value is a string or an array of strings. ?page=2 gives "2", and ?active=false gives the truthy string "false". Convert and validate explicitly.
  2. A key can unexpectedly be an array. ?page=1&page=2 gives ["1", "2"]. Code that calls req.query.page.trim() would crash.

In Express 5, req.query is a getter: you cannot replace it with a validated copy. Assigning to it throws a TypeError in ES modules, and changing one of its properties does not stick, because each read parses the query string again. Store parsed values in another property instead (see request validation).

docs.title: req.body
docs.text:
The parsed request body. It exists only after a body-parsing middleware such as express.json() has run for a matching Content-Type. In Express 5, req.body is undefined when no parser handled the request, so guard against it.

app.use(express.json());

app.post("/notes", (req, res) => {
  const text = req.body?.text;
  if (typeof text !== "string" || text.length === 0) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "text is required" });
  }
  res.status(201).json({ text });
});

See body parsing and content types for JSON, form, raw, and multipart bodies.

docs.title: Headers: req.headers and req.get()
docs.text:
req.headers is a plain object with lowercase header names. req.get() (alias req.header()) looks up a header case-insensitively.

req.headers["content-type"];   // "application/json"
req.get("Content-Type");       // "application/json"
req.get("Referrer");           // checks both Referrer and Referer

Headers are client-controlled. Never trust a header such as X-User-Role to make authorization decisions.

docs.title: Cookies: req.cookies and req.signedCookies
docs.text:
Express does not parse cookies itself. The cookie-parser middleware fills req.cookies and, when given a secret, verifies signed cookies into req.signedCookies.

import cookieParser from "cookie-parser";

app.use(cookieParser(process.env.COOKIE_SECRET));

app.get("/preferences", (req, res) => {
  res.json({
    theme: req.cookies.theme ?? "light",        // ordinary cookie
    cartId: req.signedCookies.cartId ?? null,   // false if tampered with
  });
});

See cookies and sessions.

docs.title: URL properties
docs.text:
Property Example value (router mounted at /api/users, request GET /api/users/42?x=1) Meaning req.originalUrl /api/users/42?x=1 The full URL as received; never rewritten req.baseUrl /api/users The mount path of the current router req.url /42?x=1 URL relative to the mount path (Express rewrites it) req.path /42 Path part of req.url, without the query string req.method GET HTTP method in uppercase

Use req.originalUrl for logging, because req.url changes inside mounted routers.

docs.title: Client and connection details
docs.text: Property Meaning req.ip Client IP address (respects the trust proxy setting) req.ips Chain of IPs from X-Forwarded-For when trust proxy is enabled req.hostname Host name from the Host header (or X-Forwarded-Host when trusted) req.protocol "http" or "https" (or X-Forwarded-Proto when trusted) req.secure true when req.protocol === "https"

docs.title: Behind a proxy: the trust proxy setting
docs.text:
In production, Express usually runs behind a load balancer or a reverse proxy such as Nginx. The proxy terminates HTTPS and forwards the request over plain HTTP, adding headers such as X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto.

// Trust exactly one proxy hop in front of the app
app.set("trust proxy", 1);

Only enable it when a proxy you control really sits in front of the app. If the app is directly exposed, a client could send a fake X-Forwarded-For header and spoof its IP, which breaks rate limiting and audit logs. See reverse proxy.

docs.title: Content checks: req.is() and req.accepts()
docs.text:
• req.is(type) checks the request's Content-Type. It returns the matching type, false if it does not match, or null if the request has no body. "No body" means no Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header, so a POST sent with Content-Length: 0 returns false, not null.
  • req.accepts(types) checks the Accept header and returns the best match the client accepts, or false.
app.post("/import", (req, res) => {
  if (!req.is("application/json")) {
    return res.status(415).json({ error: "Send application/json" });
  }
  res.json({ imported: true });
});

app.get("/report", (req, res) => {
  const type = req.accepts(["json", "csv"]);
  if (type === "csv") return res.type("csv").send("id,total\n1,20\n");
  if (type === "json") return res.json([{ id: 1, total: 20 }]);
  res.status(406).send("Not Acceptable");
});

docs.title: req.route
docs.text:
The route that matched, including its path pattern. Useful for logging metrics per route (/users/:id) rather than per URL (/users/42), which would create a separate metric for every id.

app.get("/users/:id", (req, res) => {
  console.log(req.route.path); // "/users/:id"
  res.end();
});

docs.title: Attaching your own data
docs.text:
Middleware commonly attaches data for later handlers, such as the authenticated user:

function authenticate(req, res, next) {
  req.user = { id: "u1", role: "admin" }; // normally from a verified token
  next();
}

res.locals is an alternative place for per-request data. In TypeScript, add custom properties through declaration merging so they are typed:

// types/express.d.ts
declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request {
      user?: { id: string; role: "admin" | "member" };
    }
  }
}
export {};

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Each part of req suits a different kind of data:

Data Read it from Do not use it for Which resource (/orders/77) req.params Optional filters Filters, sorting, pagination req.query Secrets or tokens (URLs end up in logs and browser history) Data being created or changed req.body GET requests (a GET body has no defined meaning in HTTP, and some servers and proxies reject it) Credentials, content type, versions, idempotency keys Headers via req.get() Authorization decisions based on headers the client can set freely, such as X-User-Role Browser session identifiers req.cookies / req.signedCookies Non-browser API clients, which usually send Authorization instead Client IP for logs and rate limits req.ip with trust proxy set correctly Anything security-critical when trust proxy is wrong

Choosing the trust proxy value:

Deployment Setting Why App reachable directly from the internet false (default) No proxy headers can be trusted One load balancer or reverse proxy (Nginx, AWS ALB, Heroku router) 1 Trust exactly one hop CDN in front of a load balancer 2, or the proxies' address ranges Two layers each append to X-Forwarded-For Proxy on the same machine "loopback" Trust only 127.0.0.1/8 and ::1 Known proxy addresses A list such as ["10.0.0.2", "10.0.0.3"] Most precise; nothing else is trusted

Avoid true unless every request is guaranteed to pass through your own proxies: it trusts the left-most X-Forwarded-For entry, which the client controls.

docs.title: A search endpoint that handles query strings safely
docs.text:
app.get("/products", (req, res) => {
  // Normalize: take the first value if an array was sent
  const first = (value) => (Array.isArray(value) ? value[0] : value);

  const page = Number.parseInt(first(req.query.page) ?? "1", 10);
  const limit = Math.min(Number.parseInt(first(req.query.limit) ?? "20", 10), 100);
  const inStock = first(req.query.inStock) === "true"; // "false" -> false

  if (!Number.isInteger(page) || page < 1 || !Number.isInteger(limit) || limit < 1) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "page and limit must be positive integers" });
  }

  res.json({ page, limit, inStock });
});

curl "http://localhost:3000/products?page=2&limit=500&inStock=false"
# {"page":2,"limit":100,"inStock":false}

docs.title: Logging request details
docs.text:
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    method: req.method,
    url: req.originalUrl,
    ip: req.ip,
    userAgent: req.get("User-Agent"),
  }));
  next();
});

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Treat every part of req as untrusted input and validate it.
  • Convert query and parameter strings to the types you need, and reject invalid values with a 400-range status.
  • Handle the case where a query key is an array.
  • Use req.get() for headers so case does not matter.
  • Set trust proxy to match your real infrastructure, never blindly to true on an exposed server.
  • Log req.originalUrl and req.route.path, not req.url.
  • Avoid logging bodies, cookies, or Authorization headers, which may contain secrets or personal data.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every user hits the rate limit at once. Symptom: many unrelated users get 429 Too Many Requests. Detect: access logs show the same private address (the load balancer's) as req.ip for every request; express-rate-limit also reports the validation error ERR_ERL_UNEXPECTED_X_FORWARDED_FOR when it sees that header while trust proxy is off. Cause: trust proxy is not set behind a proxy, so all clients share one IP. Fix: set trust proxy to the real number of proxy hops.
  • An abusive client is never rate-limited. Symptom: one client makes thousands of requests without being blocked. Detect: the proxy's logs show one connecting address while your app logs a different "client IP" on every request. Cause: trust proxy is true or trusts too many hops, so the client's own X-Forwarded-For value is believed. Fix: trust the exact hop count or the proxies' addresses.
  • HTTPS redirect loops and missing secure cookies. Symptom: browsers show ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS, or session cookies marked secure are never set. Detect: logs show req.protocol as http for traffic that arrived over HTTPS. Cause: TLS ends at the proxy and trust proxy is off, so Express ignores X-Forwarded-Proto. Fix: set trust proxy.
  • 500 errors from repeated query keys. Symptom: a search endpoint fails for a few clients. Detect: TypeError: req.query.q.trim is not a function in the error logs. Cause: ?q=a&q=b makes the value an array. Fix: normalize or validate query values before using them.
  • Secrets appear in logs. Symptom: API keys or tokens turn up in log search or a log export. Detect: secret scanning on the log store. Cause: logging whole req.headers objects, or accepting API keys in the query string, which proxies also log. Fix: redact Authorization and Cookie, and accept credentials only in headers.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Route parameter: A value captured from the path, in req.params.
  • Query string: The ?key=value part of a URL, parsed into req.query.
  • Request body: Data sent after the headers, parsed into req.body.
  • Request header: Metadata sent with the request, such as Content-Type or Authorization.
  • Mount path: The prefix where a router is attached; shown in req.baseUrl.
  • Trust proxy: The setting that tells Express to believe X-Forwarded-* headers from proxies.
  • Content negotiation: Choosing a response format based on the client's Accept header.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Comparing req.query.active === true; query values are strings.
  • Assuming req.body always exists; it is undefined without a matching parser in Express 5.
  • Reading req.ip behind a proxy without trust proxy and getting the proxy's address for every user.
  • Enabling trust proxy on a server reachable directly from the internet, letting clients spoof their IP.
  • Using req.url for logging inside a router and losing the mount prefix.
  • Trusting client headers for authorization decisions.
  • Trying to assign req.query = validated in Express 5; req.query is a getter.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between req.params, req.query, and req.body?
  2. Why is ?active=false a common source of bugs?
  3. How do req.originalUrl, req.baseUrl, req.url, and req.path differ inside a mounted router?
  4. What does the trust proxy setting change, and what is the risk of misconfiguring it?
  5. What do req.is() and req.accepts() check?
  6. How do you add a typed req.user property in TypeScript?

docs.title: Request Validation
docs.text: Request validation checks that incoming data has the shape, types, and values your code expects before any business logic runs. Express parses requests but does not validate them, so every API must add validation deliberately, usually as middleware built on a schema library.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Clients can send anything: missing fields, wrong types, huge strings, extra properties, or deliberately malicious values. Without validation, bad input reaches your database and business logic, causing crashes, corrupted data, and security problems such as injection or privilege escalation through extra fields. Good validation also gives clients clear, field-level error messages, which makes an API easier to use. The general principles are covered in validation and sanitization; this lesson shows how to apply them in Express.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
Large public APIs document their validation behavior, and they show both status-code conventions this lesson discusses:

  • GitHub answers invalid JSON with 400 Bad Request and the message "Problems parsing JSON". A well-formed request that fails validation gets 422 Unprocessable Entity with "Validation Failed" and an errors property whose code values (such as missing_field and invalid) tell the client what to fix (GitHub REST API troubleshooting).
  • Stripe uses 400 Bad Request when "the request was unacceptable, often due to missing a required parameter". Its error object includes a param field naming the parameter at fault, which Stripe suggests using "to display a message near the correct form field" (Stripe API errors).
  • Fastify builds validation into the framework with "a schema-based approach" and recommends JSON Schema for validating routes, instead of leaving it to add-on middleware (Fastify documentation).

Popular tools and providers: zod, joi, express-validator, and JSON Schema validators such as Ajv.

docs.title: Never trust the client
docs.text: Browser-side validation improves user experience, but anyone can bypass it with curl, a script, or modified frontend code. The server is the only place where validation actually protects your system.

docs.title: What to validate
docs.text:
Source Examples Notes req.params /users/:id Check format (integer, UUID, ObjectId) req.query ?page=2&sort=name Always strings; coerce, set defaults, cap limits req.body JSON or form fields Required fields, types, lengths, enums, formats Headers Idempotency-Key, X-Api-Version Validate any header your logic depends on Files Uploads Size, type, count; see file uploads

Validate syntax (is quantity an integer?) and semantics (is the quantity between 1 and 99, and does the product exist?). Schema libraries handle syntax and simple rules; checks that need the database, such as "email already registered", happen in the service layer.

docs.title: Validation compared with sanitization
docs.text:
• Validation decides whether input is acceptable and rejects it if not: "age must be an integer from 0 to 150".
  • Sanitization transforms input into a safe or normalized form: trimming whitespace, lowercasing an email, removing unknown keys.
  • Output encoding (escaping HTML when rendering) is a separate defense against XSS and happens when data is displayed, not when it is stored.

Prefer rejecting bad input over silently "fixing" it, except for harmless normalization such as trimming.

docs.title: Manual checks versus schema libraries
docs.text:
Manual checks work for one field but grow quickly:

const { email, password } = req.body ?? {};
if (typeof email !== "string" || !email.includes("@")) { /* ... */ }
if (typeof password !== "string" || password.length < 12) { /* ... */ }

Schema libraries describe the whole shape once, produce typed results, and report every problem at once:

Library Style Notes zod Schema objects in TypeScript-first style Infers TypeScript types from schemas; widely used joi Chainable schema builder Mature; popular in older Express codebases express-validator Express middleware chains per field Built on validator.js; validates req directly

docs.title: Choosing 400 or 422
docs.text:
• 400 Bad Request means the server could not process the request because it is malformed.
  • 422 Unprocessable Content means the request is well-formed (valid JSON, correct content type) but its content fails validation rules.

Both are used in real APIs. This guide uses a common convention:

  • Unparseable bodies (invalid JSON) → 400.
  • Well-formed requests that fail schema rules → 422.

Many APIs use 400 for both, which is also fine. What matters is choosing one convention, documenting it, and applying it everywhere. See HTTP status codes.

docs.title: A useful error format
docs.text:
Return every problem at once, with the location and field, so clients can highlight form fields:

{
  "error": "Validation failed",
  "issues": [
    { "location": "body", "path": "email", "message": "Invalid email address" },
    { "location": "body", "path": "items.0.quantity", "message": "Must be at least 1" }
  ]
}

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Validate in middleware when the rule depends only on the request itself: types, required fields, lengths, formats, enums, and pagination caps.

Do not validate in middleware when the rule needs your data, such as "this email is already registered" or "this product exists". Those checks belong in the service layer, which returns 409 or 404, because they can change between validation and the write.

Option Choose it when Trade-offs Manual checks One or two simple fields Grows messy fast; easy to miss a case zod You want one schema that also produces TypeScript types, possibly shared with the frontend Default error messages differ between major versions joi An existing codebase already uses it, or the team prefers its chainable style A second way of describing data if the rest of the stack uses another schema library express-validator You prefer per-field middleware chains built on validator.js Results include submitted values, so filter them before responding JSON Schema (Ajv, Fastify schemas, OpenAPI validators) The same schema must document the API and validate it Verbose; separate from your TypeScript types unless generated

docs.title: A reusable zod validation middleware
docs.text:
// middleware/validate.js
export function validate(schemas) {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    const validated = {};
    const issues = [];

    for (const location of ["params", "query", "body"]) {
      const schema = schemas[location];
      if (!schema) continue;

      const result = schema.safeParse(req[location] ?? {});
      if (result.success) {
        validated[location] = result.data;
      } else {
        for (const issue of result.error.issues) {
          issues.push({ location, path: issue.path.join("."), message: issue.message });
        }
      }
    }

    if (issues.length > 0) {
      return res.status(422).json({ error: "Validation failed", issues });
    }

    // Express 5: req.query is a read-only getter, so store results separately
    req.validated = validated;
    next();
  };
}

docs.title: Schemas for a create-order endpoint
docs.text:
// schemas/orders.js
import { z } from "zod";

export const orderParams = z.object({
  customerId: z.string().regex(/^\d+$/, "customerId must be numeric"),
});

export const createOrderBody = z.object({
  items: z.array(z.object({
    productId: z.string().min(1),
    quantity: z.number().int().min(1).max(99),
  })).min(1, "At least one item is required"),
  note: z.string().trim().max(500).optional(),
  // A client-sent "status" or "totalPrice" is not in the schema,
  // so z.object() strips it from the result
});

// routes/orders.js
import { Router } from "express";
import { validate } from "../middleware/validate.js";
import { orderParams, createOrderBody } from "../schemas/orders.js";

const router = Router({ mergeParams: true });

router.post("/", validate({ params: orderParams, body: createOrderBody }), (req, res) => {
  const { customerId } = req.validated.params;
  const { items, note } = req.validated.body;  // only known, typed fields
  res.status(201).json({ customerId, items, note });
});

export default router;

curl -X POST localhost:3000/customers/12/orders \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"items":[{"productId":"p1","quantity":0}],"status":"paid"}'
# 422
# {"error":"Validation failed","issues":[{"location":"body",
#   "path":"items.0.quantity","message":"Too small: expected number to be >=1"}]}

The exact message text depends on the zod version; you can pass custom messages to each rule.

docs.title: Coercing query strings
docs.text:
Query values are strings, so convert them as part of validation:

export const listProductsQuery = z.object({
  page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1),
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20),
  sort: z.enum(["name", "price", "createdAt"]).default("createdAt"),
  // Don't use z.coerce.boolean(): Boolean("false") is true
  inStock: z.enum(["true", "false"]).transform((v) => v === "true").optional(),
});

router.get("/products", validate({ query: listProductsQuery }), (req, res) => {
  const { page, limit, sort, inStock } = req.validated.query;
  res.json({ page, limit, sort, inStock });
});

GET /products?limit=500 is rejected, GET /products gets the defaults, and ?inStock=false correctly becomes false.

docs.title: Stripping unknown fields and mass assignment
docs.text:
Mass assignment happens when code copies the whole request body into a database update:

// Dangerous: a client can send {"role":"admin"} and promote itself
await User.updateOne({ _id: req.user.id }, req.body);

Validate against an explicit allowlist instead. z.object() removes keys that are not in the schema; z.strictObject() rejects requests that contain them, which helps clients notice typos.

const updateProfileBody = z.strictObject({
  displayName: z.string().trim().min(1).max(60).optional(),
  bio: z.string().max(280).optional(),
});

docs.title: The same idea with express-validator
docs.text:
import { body, validationResult } from "express-validator";

router.post(
  "/signup",
  body("email").isEmail().normalizeEmail(),
  body("password").isLength({ min: 12 }),
  (req, res) => {
    const result = validationResult(req);
    if (!result.isEmpty()) {
      // result.array() also contains each submitted value (here, the
      // password), so return only what the client needs
      const issues = result.array().map(({ location, path, msg }) => ({ location, path, message: msg }));
      return res.status(422).json({ error: "Validation failed", issues });
    }
    res.status(201).json({ email: req.body.email });
  },
);

normalizeEmail() does more than lowercase: for Gmail addresses it also removes dots, so Bob.Smith@GMAIL.com becomes bobsmith@gmail.com. Use it only if you want that canonical form stored.

docs.title: Validate configuration too
docs.text:
Environment variables are input as well. Validate them once at startup so a missing value fails immediately instead of during a request.

// config.js
import { z } from "zod";

const envSchema = z.object({
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().default(3000),
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().min(1),
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32),
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(["development", "test", "production"]).default("development"),
});

export const config = envSchema.parse(process.env); // throws with a clear list of problems

See configuration and secrets.

docs.title: Sharing schemas with the frontend
docs.text: Because zod schemas are plain JavaScript or TypeScript modules, a monorepo can put them in a shared package used by both the React form and the Express route. The frontend uses them for instant feedback; the backend still validates, because it cannot trust the client.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Validate every input source: params, query, body, relevant headers, and files.
  • Validate as early as possible, in middleware before the handler.
  • Use allowlists (known fields and values) rather than denylists.
  • Coerce and default query parameters, and cap pagination limits.
  • Return all validation issues at once with field paths.
  • Pick one status-code convention (400 or 422) and document it.
  • Keep database-dependent checks (uniqueness, existence) in the service layer and return 409 or 404 as appropriate.
  • Never pass req.body directly into a database update.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A user promotes themselves to admin. Symptom: accounts with roles nobody granted. Detect: audit logs show role changing through a profile-update endpoint. Cause: mass assignment: the endpoint copied req.body into the update. Fix: validate against an allowlist schema and update only named fields; backfill and review affected accounts.
  • A wave of 422s right after a frontend release. Symptom: forms fail for every user. Detect: a spike in 422 responses on one route, all with the same unrecognized_keys or missing-field issue. Cause: the frontend started sending or renaming a field that a strict schema rejects. Fix: deploy schema changes before client changes, and accept new optional fields first.
  • Slow queries from huge page sizes. Symptom: database CPU spikes and timeouts on list endpoints. Detect: slow-query logs with very large LIMIT values. Cause: ?limit=100000 was accepted. Fix: cap limit in the schema (for example .max(100)).
  • Filters silently ignore "false". Symptom: users filtering for out-of-stock items still see in-stock ones. Detect: logs show inStock: true for requests sent with ?inStock=false. Cause: Boolean("false") or z.coerce.boolean(), which treat any non-empty string as true. Fix: parse "true"/"false" explicitly.
  • Passwords appear in error responses and logs. Symptom: a security review finds submitted secrets in logs. Detect: log searches for password fields inside validation errors. Cause: returning or logging raw validator output, such as express-validator's result.array(), which includes each submitted value. Fix: map issues to location, path, and message only.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Validation: Checking input against rules and rejecting it if it fails.
  • Sanitization: Transforming input into a normalized or safe form.
  • Schema: A declarative description of valid data.
  • Coercion: Converting a value from one type to another, such as the string "2" to the number 2.
  • Allowlist: An explicit list of permitted fields or values.
  • Mass assignment: Accidentally letting clients set fields they should not control by copying request data wholesale.
  • 422 Unprocessable Content: A status for well-formed requests whose content is invalid.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Relying on frontend validation alone.
  • Using z.coerce.boolean() or Boolean(value) on query strings, which turns "false" into true.
  • Validating the body but forgetting params and query.
  • Returning only the first error, forcing clients to fix problems one at a time.
  • Trying to overwrite req.query with validated data in Express 5.
  • Thinking validation prevents every injection; queries must still be parameterized and output must still be encoded.
  • Leaking internal details (stack traces, SQL) in validation responses.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why must validation happen on the server even when the frontend validates?
  2. What is the difference between validation and sanitization?
  3. How would you validate and coerce ?page=2&limit=50?
  4. What is mass assignment, and how does a schema prevent it?
  5. When would you return 400, and when 422, under the convention in this lesson?
  6. Why is validating environment variables at startup useful?

docs.title: The Response Object
docs.text: Every Express handler receives res, the object used to build and send the HTTP response. It extends Node.js's http.ServerResponse with helpers such as res.status(), res.json(), res.redirect(), and res.cookie(). A response is a status code, headers, and an optional body, and each request gets exactly one.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Clients depend on the response contract: the status code tells them what happened, the headers tell them how to interpret the body, and the body carries the data. Sending the wrong status, the wrong Content-Type, or two responses for one request produces confusing bugs. Some helpers also carry security risks, such as serving files from a path the user controls.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe "uses conventional HTTP response codes to indicate the success or failure of an API request": 2xx for success, 4xx for errors caused by the request (such as a missing required parameter or a declined card), and 5xx for problems on Stripe's side. Its reference lists what each code means for its API, for example 401 when no valid API key was provided and 409 for conflicts (Stripe API errors).
  • GitHub paginates large REST API results with a link response header that carries rel="prev", rel="next", rel="first", and rel="last" URLs, the same kind of header res.append("Link", ...) builds (GitHub pagination docs).
  • GitHub also returns an etag header on most endpoints. A client that repeats the request with that value receives 304 Not Modified when nothing changed, and GitHub recommends authenticated conditional requests so that unchanged data does not count against the primary rate limit (GitHub REST API best practices).
  • Zalando's public RESTful API guidelines make "MUST use most specific HTTP status codes" a rule for its teams, so clients can react to the status alone (Zalando RESTful API Guidelines).

docs.title: The parts of a response
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created                         <- status line: res.status(201)
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 <- set by res.json()
Location: /api/v1/tasks/9                    <- res.location() / res.set()
Set-Cookie: seen=1; Path=/; HttpOnly          <- res.cookie()
ETag: W/"1b-..."                             <- generated by res.send()

{"id":9,"title":"Write notes"}               <- body: res.json(...)

Headers must be set before the body starts. Once the first byte of the body has been sent, the status and headers are fixed.

docs.title: Methods at a glance
docs.text: Method Purpose Ends the response? res.status(code) Set the status code; returns res for chaining No res.set(name, value) / res.header() Set a header (or several with an object) No res.append(name, value) Add another value to a header (for example Link) No res.get(name) Read a header already set on the response No res.type(type) Set Content-Type from a short name such as "json" No res.location(url) Set the Location header No res.cookie() / res.clearCookie() Set or clear a cookie No res.attachment(filename) Mark the body as a download No res.send(body) Send a string, Buffer, object, or array Yes res.json(value) Send JSON Yes res.sendStatus(code) Send a status with its standard text as the body Yes res.redirect([status,] url) Send a redirect Yes res.sendFile(path, options) Stream a file Yes res.download(path, filename) Stream a file as an attachment Yes res.render(view, locals) Render a template and send HTML Yes res.end() End the response, optionally with raw data Yes res.write(chunk) Send part of the body (Node.js method) No

docs.title: res.status() and chaining
docs.text:
res.status(404).json({ error: "Task not found" });

res.status() only sets the code. Without a sending method, nothing is sent. In Express 5 it throws if the value is not a valid integer status code, which catches bugs such as res.status("404") or res.status(undefined). For choosing codes, see HTTP status codes.

docs.title: res.send()
docs.text:
res.send() adapts to the type of its argument:

Argument Content-Type (if not already set) Notes String text/html; charset=utf-8 Set res.type("text") for plain text Buffer application/octet-stream Binary data Object or array application/json Delegates to res.json()

It also sets Content-Length, generates an ETag header for the body, and, when the request's If-None-Match matches that ETag, automatically answers 304 Not Modified without a body. In Express 5, res.send(404) no longer sets the status: it sends a 200 response whose body is 404. Use res.sendStatus(404) or res.status(404).send(...).

docs.title: res.json()
docs.text:
Serializes a value with JSON.stringify and sets Content-Type: application/json unless you set a type first. Values that JSON cannot represent are dropped or converted: undefined properties disappear, Date objects become ISO strings, and a BigInt throws.

res.json({ id: 1, createdAt: new Date() });
// {"id":1,"createdAt":"2026-11-07T10:00:00.000Z"}

app.set("json spaces", 2) pretty-prints during development.

docs.title: res.sendStatus() and res.end()
docs.text:
res.sendStatus(204);  // 204 with no body
res.sendStatus(403);  // 403 with body "Forbidden"
res.status(204).end(); // same as the first line

docs.title: Headers: res.set(), res.append(), res.type()
docs.text:
res.set("Cache-Control", "no-store");
res.set({ "X-Request-Id": requestId, "X-Total-Count": "250" });
res.append("Link", '</api/v1/tasks?page=3>; rel="next"');
res.type("csv"); // Content-Type: text/csv; charset=utf-8

docs.title: res.redirect()
docs.text:
Redirects send a Location header and a 3xx status. The default is 302 Found.

Status Meaning Method on the follow-up request 301 Moved Permanently Resource moved for good; clients may cache it Browsers may change POST to GET 302 Found Temporary redirect (Express default) Browsers usually change POST to GET 303 See Other "See the result at this URL" Always GET; used after a form POST 307 Temporary Redirect Temporary; repeat the same request elsewhere Method and body preserved 308 Permanent Redirect Permanent; repeat the same request elsewhere Method and body preserved 

app.post("/login-form", (req, res) => {
  // After a successful form POST, send the browser to a page with GET
  res.redirect(303, "/dashboard");
});

Express 5 removed res.redirect("back"); use res.redirect(req.get("Referrer") || "/"). Never redirect to a URL taken directly from user input, such as ?next=https://evil.example, without checking it against an allowlist: that is an open redirect.

docs.title: res.cookie() and res.clearCookie()
docs.text:
res.cookie("sessionId", id, {
  httpOnly: true,                 // not readable from JavaScript
  secure: true,                   // only sent over HTTPS
  sameSite: "lax",                // limits cross-site sending
  maxAge: 1000 * 60 * 60 * 8,     // milliseconds (8 hours)
  path: "/",
});

res.clearCookie("sessionId", { path: "/" }); // path/domain must match

maxAge is in milliseconds in Express. To clear a cookie, the path and domain must match how it was set. Express 5 ignores maxAge and expires passed to clearCookie(). Cookie security is covered in cookies and sessions.

docs.title: Files: res.sendFile(), res.download(), res.attachment()
docs.text:
import path from "node:path";

const reportsDir = path.resolve("storage/reports");

app.get("/reports/:name", (req, res, next) => {
  // root restricts the file to reportsDir; ".." segments are rejected
  res.sendFile(req.params.name, { root: reportsDir }, (error) => {
    if (error) next(error);
  });
});

app.get("/invoices/:id/download", (req, res) => {
  const file = path.join(reportsDir, `invoice-${Number(req.params.id)}.pdf`);
  res.download(file, "invoice.pdf"); // Content-Disposition: attachment
});
  • res.sendFile() needs an absolute path, or a relative path plus the root option.
  • Building a path from user input without root can let a request such as ../../etc/passwd escape the intended folder: a path traversal attack. Prefer looking up files by id in your database.
  • res.download() adds Content-Disposition: attachment so the browser saves the file. res.attachment("name.csv") sets that header without sending.

docs.title: res.locals and res.render()
docs.text:
res.locals holds data for the current request only. Template engines can read it, and middleware can use it to pass values to later handlers.

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.locals.currentYear = new Date().getFullYear();
  next();
});

res.render("view", data) renders a template; see static files and template engines.

docs.title: res.format() for content negotiation
docs.text:
app.get("/tasks/:id", (req, res) => {
  const task = { id: 1, title: "Write notes" };
  res.format({
    "application/json": () => res.json(task),
    // escapeHtml: your helper that escapes <, >, &, " and ' (prevents XSS)
    "text/html": () => res.send(`<h1>${escapeHtml(task.title)}</h1>`),
    default: () => res.status(406).send("Not Acceptable"),
  });
});

Express picks the handler that best matches the Accept header and sets Vary: Accept.

docs.title: One response per request
docs.text:
A response moves through three states, and only the first one allows changes to the status and headers:

Calling two sending methods for the same request throws Error [ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT]: Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client. The usual cause is a missing return:

app.get("/tasks/:id", (req, res) => {
  const task = tasks.get(req.params.id);
  if (!task) {
    res.status(404).json({ error: "Not found" }); // missing return!
  }
  res.json({ data: task }); // runs too -> ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT
});

Fix it with return res.status(404).json(...). The bug can also hide: if the second call were res.json(task) with task undefined, Express would send nothing and raise no error, so the missing return goes unnoticed. res.headersSent tells you whether headers have already gone out, which error handlers use to decide whether they can still send an error body.

docs.title: Streaming responses
docs.text:
For large or generated data, send the body in pieces instead of building it all in memory:

import { createReadStream } from "node:fs";
import { once } from "node:events";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";

app.get("/exports/orders.csv", async (req, res) => {
  const file = createReadStream("exports/orders.csv");
  // Wait until the file is open: a missing file rejects here, before any
  // header is sent, so the error handler can still answer normally
  await once(file, "open");
  res.type("csv").attachment("orders.csv");
  // pipeline handles backpressure and destroys both streams on error
  await pipeline(file, res);
});

app.get("/progress", (req, res) => {
  res.type("text");
  res.write("step 1 done\n");   // first chunk sent immediately
  res.write("step 2 done\n");
  res.end("finished\n");        // last chunk and end of response
});

Because pipeline destroys res when the source fails, a stream error after the response has started cannot become an error response: the client sees an aborted download instead. Checking that the source opens first, as above, turns the common "file not found" case into a normal error response. See buffers and streams.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
You need to send Use Avoid JSON data res.status(code).json(value) res.send(JSON.stringify(value)), which is labeled text/html Success with nothing to return res.sendStatus(204) or res.status(204).end() 200 with an empty object, which hides the meaning A file to display in the browser res.sendFile(name, { root }) Paths built from raw user input without root A file to download res.download() or res.attachment() Reading the whole file into memory first Large or generated data A stream piped with pipeline res.send() with a huge string or Buffer A rendered HTML page res.render(view, data) Building HTML strings by hand (escaping mistakes cause XSS) The same data in several formats res.format() Guessing the format from the URL or a query flag A different URL res.redirect(status, url) with a deliberate status Redirecting to unchecked URLs from the request

Use res.json() when the client is a program (frontend, mobile app, another service). Do not use res.send() with a number, or two sending methods in one request: both are Express 4 habits that now send the wrong thing or throw.

docs.title: A create endpoint with the right status and headers
docs.text:
app.post("/api/v1/tasks", (req, res) => {
  const task = { id: nextId++, title: req.body.title, done: false };
  tasks.set(String(task.id), task);

  res
    .status(201)                              // Created
    .location(`/api/v1/tasks/${task.id}`)     // where the new resource lives
    .json(task);
});

app.delete("/api/v1/tasks/:id", (req, res) => {
  const removed = tasks.delete(req.params.id);
  if (!removed) return res.status(404).json({ error: "Task not found" });
  res.sendStatus(204);                        // success, no body
});

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Ship"}'
# HTTP/1.1 201 Created
# Location: /api/v1/tasks/1
# Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
#
# {"id":1,"title":"Ship","done":false}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Always return when sending a response early.
  • Choose status codes deliberately: 201 with Location for creation, 204 for success with no body, 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors.
  • Keep one JSON shape for errors across the API; see error handling in Express.
  • Set cache headers intentionally (Cache-Control: no-store for private data).
  • Use root with res.sendFile() and never build file paths from raw user input.
  • Validate redirect targets to avoid open redirects.
  • Stream large files instead of reading them fully into memory.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT in the error logs. Symptom: clients get the first (often wrong) response, such as a 404 for an item that exists. Detect: Error [ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT]: Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client in the logs, pointing at the second res.json. Cause: a missing return, or a callback and a promise both responding. Fix: return on every early response; add a test for the early-exit branch.
  • Downloads cut off with no error response. Symptom: users report truncated files or "network error" in the browser. Detect: client errors such as ECONNRESET or "socket hang up", while server logs show the stream error (ENOENT, a database cursor failure). Cause: pipeline destroyed res after the source failed, so no error response could be sent. Fix: open or validate the source before sending headers, and log stream failures with the request ID.
  • One user sees another user's data. Symptom: support tickets about wrong account details. Detect: CDN or proxy logs show cache hits on per-user endpoints such as /api/me. Cause: private responses sent without Cache-Control: private or no-store, so a shared cache stored them. Fix: set explicit cache headers on every per-user response.
  • Open redirect reported by a security scan. Symptom: a scanner or bug-bounty report shows ?next=https://evil.example redirecting off site. Detect: access logs with absolute URLs in redirect parameters. Cause: res.redirect() with an unchecked value from the request. Fix: allow only relative paths or an allowlist of hosts.
  • Latency spikes on large list endpoints. Symptom: p99 latency and memory jump when a client asks for a big export. Detect: event-loop delay metrics rise while one request runs. Cause: res.json() on tens of thousands of rows runs JSON.stringify synchronously on the main thread. Fix: paginate, cap page sizes, or stream the export.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Status code: A three-digit number summarizing the result of the request.
  • Response header: Metadata about the response, such as Content-Type or Location.
  • Response body: The data sent after the headers.
  • ETag: An identifier for a version of a response body, used for caching and 304 Not Modified.
  • Content negotiation: Choosing a response format from the Accept header.
  • Open redirect: A redirect to an attacker-controlled URL taken from user input.
  • Path traversal: Using .. segments to read files outside an intended directory.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• res.status(404) alone does not send anything.
  • Forgetting return and triggering ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT.
  • Sending 200 with { "error": "..." }; clients and monitoring tools then treat failures as successes.
  • Thinking res.json() and res.send(object) differ in output; both send JSON.
  • Passing seconds to maxAge in res.cookie(); Express expects milliseconds.
  • Clearing a cookie with a different path than it was set with, so the browser keeps it.
  • Using res.send(404) from Express 4 tutorials in Express 5.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which res methods end the response, and which only configure it?
  2. What does res.send() do differently for a string, a Buffer, and an object?
  3. When would you use 303 instead of 302, and 308 instead of 301?
  4. What causes "Cannot set headers after they are sent", and how do you prevent it?
  5. Why is the root option important for res.sendFile()?
  6. When should you stream a response instead of using res.send()?

docs.text:

  • MDN: HTTP response status codes
  • MDN: Redirections in HTTP
