docs.title: Routing and Routers
docs.text: Routing decides which code runs for a request. In Express, a route is an HTTP method plus a path pattern plus one or more handler functions. Routers let you group related routes into modules and mount them under a common prefix such as /api/v1/users.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: An API is a set of routes. Clear routing makes the API predictable for clients and the code easy to navigate for developers. Mistakes in routing are common sources of bugs: a route registered in the wrong order can swallow requests meant for another, a missing 404 handler leaves clients with confusing responses, and an unexpected path syntax error can stop the server from starting.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
Public APIs show the routing decisions this lesson covers: resource paths, nesting, and where the version lives.

  • Stripe describes its API as having "predictable resource-oriented URLs", all under a /v1 prefix such as https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges. The exact behavior version is chosen separately with a Stripe-Version request header, so the URL prefix rarely changes (Stripe API reference, Stripe versioning).
  • GitHub keeps versions out of the URL entirely. Clients send an X-GitHub-Api-Version header with a date-based version, and requests without it default to the 2022-11-28 version (GitHub REST API versions).
  • Twilio puts a date-based version in the path and nests resources under their owner, for example POST https://api.twilio.com/2010-04-01/Accounts/{AccountSid}/Messages.json: the same shape as a nested router that reads a parent parameter (Twilio Message resource).

Popular tools and providers: express.Router, NestJS controllers, Fastify's router, and API gateways such as Amazon API Gateway.

docs.title: Route methods
docs.text:
Express provides a method for each HTTP verb. The path is matched against req.path (the URL without the query string).

Express method HTTP method Typical use app.get(path, ...handlers) GET (and HEAD automatically) Read a resource or list app.post(path, ...) POST Create a resource or trigger an action app.put(path, ...) PUT Replace a resource app.patch(path, ...) PATCH Partially update a resource app.delete(path, ...) DELETE Remove a resource app.options(path, ...) OPTIONS Custom preflight handling (rare) app.all(path, ...) Every method Shared logic for one path

When a GET route exists, Express also answers HEAD requests for it without a body. For method semantics, see HTTP methods.

docs.title: Path patterns in Express 5
docs.text:
Express 5 uses a stricter path syntax than Express 4. Characters such as ?, +, *, ( and ) are no longer special regex-like operators in string paths.

Pattern Matches req.params "/about" /about (and /about/ unless strict routing is on) {} "/users/:id" /users/42 { id: "42" } "/users/:userId/posts/:postId" /users/7/posts/99 { userId: "7", postId: "99" } "/files/:name.:ext" /files/report.pdf { name: "report", ext: "pdf" } "/users{/:id}" /users and /users/42 {} or { id: "42" } "/files/*splat" /files/a/b/c.txt { splat: ["a", "b", "c.txt"] } "/{*splat}" Every path, including / { splat: ["x", "y"] } for /x/y; {} for /
  • Route parameters (:id) capture one path segment. Their values are always strings.
  • Optional segments use braces: {/:id} means "this part may be missing". Express 4 used :id? instead.
  • Wildcards must be named in Express 5. *splat matches one or more segments and gives an array of the matched segments. Express 4 used a bare *.

docs.title: Regular expression routes
docs.text:
For patterns a string cannot express, pass a RegExp. Capture groups appear in req.params by index.

// Only numeric ids: /orders/123 matches, /orders/abc does not
app.get(/^\/orders\/(\d+)$/, (req, res) => {
  res.json({ orderId: req.params[0] });
});

Most APIs do not need regex routes. Matching any segment and then validating it (see request validation) usually gives clearer errors.

docs.title: First match wins
docs.text:
Express keeps routes and middleware in a list, in the order you register them. For each request it walks the list and runs the first route whose method and path match. A handler that sends a response ends the search.

Request: GET /users/me

1. app.get("/users/:id", ...)   <- matches first, id = "me"   (wrong!)
2. app.get("/users/me", ...)    <- never reached

Register specific routes before general ones:

app.get("/users/me", getCurrentUser);   // specific first
app.get("/users/:id", getUserById);     // general second

docs.title: Multiple handlers and next("route")
docs.text:
A route can have several handlers. Each must call next() to pass control to the next one, or send a response.

function loadUser(req, res, next) {
  const user = users.get(req.params.id);
  if (!user) return res.status(404).json({ error: "User not found" });
  req.user = user;          // share data with later handlers
  next();
}

function hideSensitiveFields(req, res) {
  const { passwordHash, ...safe } = req.user;
  res.json(safe);
}

app.get("/users/:id", loadUser, hideSensitiveFields);
// Arrays work too: app.get("/users/:id", [loadUser, hideSensitiveFields]);

next("route") skips the remaining handlers of the current route and continues matching later routes. It only works inside route handlers (app.get, router.post, and so on); in app.use middleware it behaves like a plain next().

app.get("/reports/:id", (req, res, next) => {
  if (req.query.format === "legacy") return next("route");
  next();
}, sendModernReport);

app.get("/reports/:id", sendLegacyReport); // reached by next("route")

docs.title: app.route() chaining
docs.text:
When several methods share a path, app.route() avoids repeating it:

app.route("/books")
  .get(listBooks)
  .post(createBook);

app.route("/books/:id")
  .get(getBook)
  .patch(updateBook)
  .delete(deleteBook);

docs.title: express.Router
docs.text:
A router is a mini application with its own middleware and routes. You mount it at a path prefix with app.use(). Inside the router, paths are written relative to that prefix.

app.use("/api/users", usersRouter)

GET /api/users        -> usersRouter handles  "/"
GET /api/users/42     -> usersRouter handles  "/:id"
POST /api/users/42/avatar -> usersRouter handles "/:id/avatar"

Router options:

Option Default Meaning mergeParams false Give the router access to parameters from the parent path, such as :userId in /users/:userId/posts caseSensitive false Treat /Users and /users as different paths strict false Treat /users and /users/ as different paths

The same caseSensitive and strict behaviors can be enabled for the whole application with app.set("case sensitive routing", true) and app.set("strict routing", true).

docs.title: Parameter preprocessing with router.param
docs.text:
router.param(name, callback) runs once per request whenever a route containing that parameter matches, before the route handlers. It is useful for loading a record by id in one place.

router.param("id", (req, res, next, id) => {
  const book = books.get(id);
  if (!book) return res.status(404).json({ error: "Book not found" });
  req.book = book;
  next();
});

router.get("/:id", (req, res) => res.json(req.book));
router.delete("/:id", (req, res) => { /* req.book is loaded */ });

app.param works the same way for application-level routes.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use express.Router modules when:

  • The API has more than a couple of resources; one router file per resource keeps each file small and easy to find.
  • A group of routes shares middleware, such as authentication for everything under /admin.
  • Resources are nested (/users/:userId/posts) and the child router needs the parent's parameters (mergeParams: true).

Avoid or keep it simple when:

  • The service has two or three routes. A single file is clearer than a folder of one-line routers.
  • You reach for a regular-expression route to validate a parameter. A plain :id plus validation gives clients a clear 400 instead of a confusing 404.
  • You need router.param logic that depends on other parameters or the body. A normal middleware is easier to follow.

Where to put the API version:

Approach Example Strengths Weaknesses URL prefix /api/v1/users (Stripe's /v1) Visible in logs and browsers; easy to route to separate code Every client URL changes on a major version Request header X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28 URLs stay stable; versions can be fine-grained Easy to forget; harder to test in a browser Date in the path /2010-04-01/Accounts/... (Twilio) Explicit and immutable Long URLs; same migration cost as a prefix No versioning /users Simplest Any breaking change breaks clients

docs.title: A modular users router
docs.text:
// routes/users.js
import { Router } from "express";

const router = Router();
const users = new Map([["1", { id: "1", name: "Asha" }]]);

// Router-level middleware: runs only for requests that reach this router
router.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.set("X-Resource", "users");
  next();
});

router.get("/", (req, res) => {
  res.json([...users.values()]);
});

router.get("/:id", (req, res) => {
  const user = users.get(req.params.id);
  if (!user) return res.status(404).json({ error: "User not found" });
  res.json(user);
});

router.post("/", (req, res) => {
  const id = String(users.size + 1);
  const user = { id, name: req.body.name };
  users.set(id, user);
  res.status(201).location(`/api/v1/users/${id}`).json(user);
});

export default router;

docs.title: Nested routers with mergeParams
docs.text:
// routes/posts.js
import { Router } from "express";

// Without mergeParams, req.params.userId would be undefined here
const router = Router({ mergeParams: true });

router.get("/", (req, res) => {
  res.json({ userId: req.params.userId, posts: [] });
});

export default router;

docs.title: Mounting, versioning, and the 404 handler
docs.text:
// app.js
import express from "express";
import usersRouter from "./routes/users.js";
import postsRouter from "./routes/posts.js";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const v1 = express.Router();
v1.use("/users", usersRouter);
v1.use("/users/:userId/posts", postsRouter);

app.use("/api/v1", v1);   // every v1 route lives under /api/v1

// 404: no earlier route matched. Must be registered after all routes.
app.use((req, res) => {
  res.status(404).json({ error: `No route for ${req.method} ${req.path}` });
});

export default app;

curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/users/1
# {"id":"1","name":"Asha"}

curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/users/1/posts
# {"userId":"1","posts":[]}

curl http://localhost:3000/api/v2/users
# {"error":"No route for GET /api/v2/users"}

The second request passes through both mounts. Each mount moves part of the path from req.path into req.baseUrl:

Versioning by URL prefix lets you run /api/v2 alongside /api/v1 while older clients migrate. See API design best practices for other versioning strategies.

docs.title: Query strings are not part of the route
docs.text:
// GET /products?category=books&page=2
app.get("/products", (req, res) => {
  const { category, page = "1" } = req.query;  // strings, not numbers
  res.json({ category, page: Number(page) });
});

The path pattern never includes ?category=.... Query values are read from req.query; see the request object.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Group routes by resource in separate router files and mount them in one place.
  • Use nouns for resources (/users, /orders/:id) and HTTP methods for actions; see REST APIs.
  • Register specific paths before parameterized ones.
  • Put the 404 handler after every route and the error handler after that.
  • Validate route parameters (for example, that :id is a valid id format) instead of trusting them.
  • Prefer router.param or a small loader middleware over repeating "find record or 404" in every handler.
  • Version public APIs from the start (/api/v1).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A specific route is shadowed. Symptom: GET /users/me returns 404 User not found or 400 id must be an integer. Detect: per-route metrics show /users/:id receiving traffic meant for /users/me, and request logs show id = "me". Cause: the parameterized route was registered first. Fix: register specific paths first and add a test for each specific path.
  • The app crashes at startup after an Express upgrade. Symptom: deploys fail and the old version keeps serving. Detect: PathError: Missing parameter name at index 1: *; visit https://git.new/pathToRegexpError for info in the startup logs. Cause: Express 4 syntax such as "*" or ":id?". Fix: rename wildcards ("/*splat", "/{*splat}") and optional segments ("{/:id}"), and run the app's tests against Express 5 before deploying.
  • Nested routes receive undefined parent IDs. Symptom: a child router returns empty lists or 404s for every parent. Detect: logs or queries contain userId: undefined. Cause: the child router was created without mergeParams: true. Fix: add the option and a test that asserts the parent ID arrives.
  • Metrics storage explodes. Symptom: the metrics backend slows down or its bill jumps. Detect: thousands of time series named after individual URLs (/users/1, /users/2, ...). Cause: labeling metrics with req.path or req.originalUrl. Fix: label with the matched route pattern (req.route.path, such as /:id) plus a fixed name for the router. req.baseUrl is not enough on its own: when a mount path has parameters it holds real values, such as /api/v1/users/1/posts.
  • Everything returns 404 after a refactor. Symptom: a sudden spike in 404 responses across all endpoints. Detect: the 404 rate on the dashboard jumps right after a deploy. Cause: the 404 handler, or a router mount, moved above the routes. Fix: keep mounting and handler order in one file, with the 404 and error handlers last.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Route path: The pattern a request path is matched against.
  • Route parameter: A named segment such as :id whose value is placed in req.params.
  • Wildcard: A pattern such as *splat that matches one or more segments.
  • Router: An isolated group of middleware and routes that can be mounted at a path.
  • Mount path: The prefix passed to app.use() when mounting a router.
  • Route handler chain: The list of functions attached to one route.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Registering /:id before /me makes me treated as an id.
  • Using Express 4 syntax ("*", ":id?") in Express 5 throws an error when the route is registered.
  • Expecting req.params.id to be a number; it is always a string.
  • Forgetting mergeParams: true on a nested router and getting undefined for the parent's parameters.
  • Placing the 404 handler before routes, so every request returns 404.
  • Calling next("route") from app.use middleware and expecting it to skip anything; there it simply continues like next().
  • Including the query string in a route path; query strings are parsed separately.

docs.text:

  3. What problem does mergeParams solve?
  4. What is the difference between next() and next("route")?
  5. Why must the 404 handler be registered after all routes?
  6. When would you choose router.param over a normal middleware?

docs.title: Express Security Best Practices
docs.text: Express gives you routing and middleware, not security. Headers, rate limits, input validation, injection protection, and safe error handling are your responsibility. This lesson goes through the protections every production Express app needs, what each one defends against, and how to configure it.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
An API is reachable by anyone on the internet, including automated scanners that probe for well-known weaknesses within minutes of deployment. Most breaches come from ordinary gaps (an injection, a missing ownership check, a leaked stack trace, an outdated dependency) rather than exotic attacks. Security is a set of habits applied consistently.

For the attack catalogue behind these practices, see OWASP and API security.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe protects its API with several kinds of limits. In Scaling your API with rate limiters it explains that it operates four types of limiters in production, including a request rate limiter ("N requests per second" per user) and a concurrent requests limiter that caps how many requests a user can have in progress at once, alongside load shedders that protect the whole system.
  • GitHub publishes its API limits and how clients learn about them. Its REST API rate limit documentation describes a personal limit of 5,000 requests per hour and says that exceeding it returns a 403 or 429 response with the x-ratelimit-remaining header at 0: limits that clients can read and respect.
  • GitHub Dependabot and npm automate dependency auditing. Dependabot alerts notify you about vulnerable dependencies so you can upgrade, and npm audit submits a description of your project's dependencies to the registry and asks for a report of known vulnerabilities.

Popular tools: helmet, express-rate-limit (with rate-limit-redis for several instances), cors, zod or joi for validation, pino with redaction, Dependabot or Renovate for updates, and a web application firewall at the edge.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Security is layered: each control covers gaps in the others.

docs.title: Security headers with helmet
docs.text:
helmet() sets a group of HTTP response headers that tell browsers to apply extra protections. The most important ones:

Header What it does Attack it reduces Content-Security-Policy Lists which sources of scripts, styles, images, and frames the page may load XSS, data injection Strict-Transport-Security Tells browsers to use HTTPS only for this site for a period Downgrade to HTTP, cookie theft on insecure networks X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff Stops browsers from guessing a different content type than declared Uploaded files being run as scripts X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors Controls whether other sites may embed your pages in frames Clickjacking Referrer-Policy Limits how much of the URL is sent in the Referer header Leaking paths or tokens in URLs to other sites Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy / Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy Isolate your pages and resources from other origins Cross-origin leaks

Helmet also removes the X-Powered-By header. For a pure JSON API, CSP matters less (browsers do not render JSON as a page), but the defaults are harmless and protect any HTML you serve.

docs.title: X-Powered-By
docs.text: By default Express adds X-Powered-By: Express. Removing it is a small step: Helmet's own documentation notes it offers very limited security benefit, but it saves bandwidth and may thwart simplistic attackers who scan for a framework. Helmet removes it; without helmet, call app.disable("x-powered-by").

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a window. express-rate-limit stores counters per key (the client IP by default). Apply a general limit to the API and stricter limits to sensitive routes: login, registration, password reset, and expensive search endpoints. When the limit is hit, respond 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header. Running several instances requires a shared store such as Redis so all instances count together. See rate limiting and throttling.

docs.title: Body size limits
docs.text: express.json() accepts 100 KB by default. Set an explicit limit that fits your API. Large bodies cost memory and CPU to parse; an attacker can send many of them to exhaust the server. Oversized requests are rejected with 413. File uploads need their own limits in Multer; see file uploads.

docs.title: Input validation
docs.text: Validate the type, shape, length, and allowed values of every input: body, params, query, headers, cookies. Reject unknown fields to prevent mass assignment (a client sending "role": "admin" that gets saved). See request validation.

docs.title: Injection
docs.text:
NoSQL operator injection. With MongoDB, if a client sends an object where you expect a string, it can change the meaning of a query:

POST /login
{"email": "admin@example.com", "password": {"$ne": null}}

User.findOne({ email, password }) would then match any password. Defenses: validate that each value is a string, never pass raw request objects into queries, and enable Mongoose's sanitizeFilter option, which wraps operator-like values. Express 5's default "simple" query parser does not build nested objects from query strings, which removes the ?a[$ne]= form of this attack from req.query, but JSON bodies can still carry objects.

SQL injection. Never build SQL by concatenating strings. Use parameterized queries, where values travel separately from the SQL text:

// Unsafe: "1 OR 1=1" in id dumps the whole table.
// await pool.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);

// Safe: the driver sends the value as data, never as SQL.
await pool.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", [req.params.id]);

Command injection. child_process.exec() runs a shell, so input such as file.png; rm -rf / becomes a second command. Use execFile() or spawn() with an argument array, and validate the input.

docs.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
docs.text: XSS means attacker-controlled data runs as script in another user's browser. APIs contribute when they store unsanitized HTML that a frontend later renders. Escape output in templates, set Content-Type correctly (JSON as application/json), use CSP, and sanitize rich text with a dedicated library if you must accept HTML.

docs.title: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
docs.text: If you authenticate with cookies, another site can make the browser send authenticated requests. Use SameSite=Lax or Strict cookies, keep GET requests free of side effects, check the Origin header on state-changing requests, and use CSRF tokens for traditional forms. APIs authenticated with Authorization: Bearer headers are not exposed to CSRF in the same way, because browsers do not attach those headers automatically. See cookies and sessions.

docs.title: CORS done correctly
docs.text: CORS relaxes the browser's same-origin policy; it never protects your server. Allow only the origins you trust, never reflect any Origin back while also allowing credentials, and remember that requests from scripts, curl, or other servers ignore CORS entirely. See configuring CORS in Express.

docs.title: "Trust proxy" done correctly
docs.text: Behind a load balancer, req.ip is the proxy's address unless you set trust proxy. Setting it to true trusts every X-Forwarded-For value, so a client can fake its IP and bypass IP-based rate limits. Trust a specific number of hops (1 for one proxy) or specific proxy addresses.

docs.title: Secrets management
docs.text: Keep secrets (database URLs, JWT secrets, API keys) in environment variables or a secrets manager, never in code or Git. Use different secrets per environment, rotate them, and never log them. See environment variables.

docs.title: Dependency auditing
docs.text: Most of an Express app's code comes from npm packages. Commit package-lock.json, install with npm ci in CI and production, run npm audit regularly, enable automated update pull requests (for example Dependabot), and be wary of new or unpopular packages with install scripts.

docs.title: HTTPS everywhere
docs.text: Serve all traffic over HTTPS, usually terminated at a reverse proxy or load balancer. Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, send HSTS, and mark cookies secure. See TLS and SSL.

docs.title: Errors that don't leak
docs.text: Stack traces, SQL errors, and file paths tell attackers how your system is built. Send generic messages for unexpected errors, log the details server-side, and run with NODE_ENV=production so Express's default handler hides stacks.

docs.title: HTTP parameter pollution
docs.text: ?role=user&role=admin makes req.query.role an array instead of a string. Code that expects a string may crash or behave unexpectedly, and a validator that checks only one value can be bypassed. Validate types explicitly in your validation layer. The older hpp middleware, which rewrites req.query to keep only the last value, was written for Express 4: in Express 5 req.query is a getter that re-parses the URL on every access, so rewriting it has no lasting effect.

docs.title: Regular expression denial of service (ReDoS)
docs.text: Some regular expressions take exponential time on crafted input, such as /^(a+)+$/ against a long string of as ending in !. Because Node runs JavaScript on one thread, one such request can freeze the whole server. Avoid nested quantifiers on user input, limit input length before matching, and prefer well-tested validation libraries. (Express 5's new path syntax removed regex features in route strings partly for this reason.)

docs.title: Logging without secrets
docs.text: Log enough to investigate incidents (request ID, user ID, route, status, timing) but redact passwords, tokens, cookies, Authorization headers, and personal data. Structured loggers such as pino support redaction paths.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Every internet-facing Express app needs the baseline: HTTPS, validation, parameterized queries, authorization checks, safe errors, and dependency updates. Some controls depend on how the app is used:

  • CSP and other browser headers matter most when you serve HTML. For a JSON-only API they are cheap insurance, not the main defense.
  • CSRF tokens are needed for cookie-authenticated browser apps; APIs that only accept Authorization: Bearer tokens do not need them.
  • App-level rate limiting may be unnecessary if an API gateway, load balancer, or WAF already enforces the same limits; avoid two layers that disagree.
  • trust proxy should be set only when a proxy you control sits in front of the app.
Control In the Express app At the edge (proxy, gateway, CDN, WAF) TLS / HTTPS Rarely Usually terminated here Security headers helmet() Possible, but keep one source of truth Rate limiting Per user or per route, business-aware Per IP, coarse, absorbs floods before they reach Node Input validation Always (only the app knows the schema) Generic rules only Authorization Always Not possible: needs business data Bot and DDoS protection Limited Best place

docs.title: A hardened app setup
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import helmet from "helmet";
import cors from "cors";
import { rateLimit } from "express-rate-limit";

const app = express();

app.set("trust proxy", 1);                 // exactly one proxy in front
app.use(helmet());                         // security headers, no X-Powered-By

app.use(cors({
  origin: ["https://app.example.com"],     // allowlist, not "*"
  credentials: true,
}));

app.use(rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  limit: 300,                              // per IP per 15 minutes
  standardHeaders: "draft-8",              // standard RateLimit headers
  legacyHeaders: false,
}));

app.use(express.json({ limit: "50kb" }));  // explicit body limit

const authLimiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, limit: 10,
  skipSuccessfulRequests: true });
app.use("/auth", authLimiter);

docs.title: Blocking NoSQL operator injection by validating types
docs.text:
import { z } from "zod";

const loginSchema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email().max(254),
  password: z.string().min(1).max(200),  // a string, never an object
}).strict();                              // unknown fields are rejected

app.post("/auth/login", async (req, res) => {
  const parsed = loginSchema.safeParse(req.body);
  if (!parsed.success) return res.status(400).json({ error: "Invalid input" });
  const user = await verifyCredentials(parsed.data.email, parsed.data.password);
  if (!user) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Invalid email or password" });
  res.json({ id: user.id });
});

docs.title: Safe command execution
docs.text:
import { execFile } from "node:child_process";
import { promisify } from "node:util";

const execFileAsync = promisify(execFile);

app.post("/thumbnails", async (req, res) => {
  const id = String(req.body?.id ?? "");
  if (!/^[a-f0-9-]{36}$/.test(id)) return res.status(400).json({ error: "Bad id" });
  // Arguments are passed as an array: no shell, no command injection.
  await execFileAsync("convert", [`/data/${id}.png`, "-resize", "200x200",
    `/data/${id}-thumb.png`]);
  res.sendStatus(202);
});

docs.title: An error handler that does not leak
docs.text:
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  if (res.headersSent) return next(err);
  const status = err.status ?? 500;
  req.log?.error({ err }, "request failed");   // full details in the logs
  res.status(status).json({
    error: status < 500 ? err.message : "Something went wrong",
  });
});

docs.title: Redacting secrets in logs
docs.text:
import pino from "pino";

export const logger = pino({
  redact: ["req.headers.authorization", "req.headers.cookie", "*.password"],
});

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text: Area Check Transport HTTPS only; HTTP redirects to HTTPS; HSTS enabled Headers helmet() applied; X-Powered-By removed Proxy trust proxy set to the real hop count or proxy IPs Limits Body size limits; upload limits; rate limits (shared store if multiple instances) Input Every route validates params, query, body; unknown fields rejected Queries Parameterized SQL; no raw objects in MongoDB filters Auth Passwords hashed; short-lived tokens; ownership checked on every record Cookies httpOnly, secure, sameSite set; CSRF protection for cookie auth CORS Explicit origin allowlist; credentials only when needed Errors Generic messages for 5xx; no stacks; NODE_ENV=production Secrets In env or a secrets manager; not in Git; rotated Dependencies Lockfile committed; npm ci; npm audit; automated updates Logging Request IDs; secrets and personal data redacted Processes No exec() with user input; no eval() or new Function() on input

docs.title: General habits
docs.text:
• Treat every input as hostile until validated.
  • Apply security middleware early in the chain, before routes.
  • Prefer allowlists (allowed origins, types, fields) over denylists.
  • Keep authorization checks in the server for every request, not only in the UI.
  • Fail closed: if a check errors, deny the request.
  • Automate dependency and secret scanning in CI.
  • Review security settings when adding a proxy, CDN, or new client.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Rate limits hit everyone at once, or never trigger. Detect: logs show the same client IP (the load balancer's) for all requests, and express-rate-limit logs the validation error ERR_ERL_UNEXPECTED_X_FORWARDED_FOR ("the 'X-Forwarded-For' header is set but the Express 'trust proxy' setting is false"). Cause: trust proxy not configured behind a proxy. Fix: set it to your real hop count; never true, which the library flags as ERR_ERL_PERMISSIVE_TRUST_PROXY.
  • The effective limit is several times higher than configured. Detect: a client makes limit × instances requests before seeing 429s. Cause: the default in-memory store counts per process. Fix: a shared store such as Redis (rate-limit-redis).
  • The frontend breaks right after adding helmet(). Detect: browser console errors such as "Refused to load the script … because it violates the following Content Security Policy directive". Cause: helmet's default CSP (default-src 'self', script-src 'self') blocks inline scripts and third-party domains. Fix: configure CSP directives for the sources you actually use, instead of disabling CSP.
  • An HTTP-only internal subdomain becomes unreachable. Detect: browsers refuse plain-HTTP connections to a subdomain after visiting the main site. Cause: helmet's default HSTS header is max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains, so browsers enforce HTTPS on every subdomain for a year. Fix: serve those subdomains over HTTPS, or disable includeSubDomains before rolling HSTS out.
  • Error responses expose stack traces or SQL. Detect: responses or scanner reports containing file paths or query text. Cause: NODE_ENV not set to production with the default handler, or a custom handler returning err.message for 5xx errors. Fix: a central handler with generic 5xx messages and NODE_ENV=production.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Security header: A response header that instructs the browser to apply a protection.
  • CSP: Content Security Policy; restricts where a page can load resources from.
  • HSTS: HTTP Strict Transport Security; forces HTTPS for a domain.
  • Clickjacking: Tricking users into clicking a hidden framed page.
  • Injection: Input interpreted as code or query syntax.
  • Mass assignment: Saving client-supplied fields the client should not control.
  • ReDoS: Denial of service caused by slow regular-expression matching.
  • Parameter pollution: Sending a parameter several times to confuse parsing or validation.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "CORS protects my API." It only controls which browser pages can read responses.
  • trust proxy: true everywhere. Clients can then spoof their IP.
  • Rate limiting in memory with several instances. Each instance counts separately, multiplying the real limit.
  • Validating only the frontend. Attackers call the API directly.
  • Returning err.message for every error. Internal messages can expose queries and paths.
  • "helmet makes the app secure." It hardens browser behavior; it does nothing for injection or authorization bugs.
  • Never updating dependencies. Known vulnerabilities accumulate.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Name four headers helmet sets and the attack each one reduces.
  2. How can a JSON body cause NoSQL injection, and how do you prevent it?
  3. Why is trust proxy: true dangerous for IP-based rate limiting?
  4. Why does an API using Bearer tokens face less CSRF risk than one using cookies?
  5. What is ReDoS, and why is it especially harmful in Node.js?
  6. What should an error response for an unexpected server error contain?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Express: Security best practices
  • helmet on GitHub
  • OWASP Node.js Security Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet
  • MDN: Content Security Policy
  • Web security fundamentals

docs.title: Static Files and Template Engines
docs.text: Not every response is JSON. Websites also need to deliver static files (images, stylesheets, scripts, fonts, a built single-page app) and sometimes server-rendered HTML built from templates. Express handles the first with the built-in express.static middleware and the second with template engines such as EJS, Pug, and Handlebars.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Serving files looks trivial until it goes wrong: a misconfigured static folder can expose .env files or source code, missing cache headers make every page load slow, and unescaped template output becomes a cross-site scripting (XSS) hole. Knowing what Express does here, and when to hand the job to nginx or a CDN, keeps both performance and security under control.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• PayPal moved web applications from Java to Node.js and described the stack in Node.js at PayPal: apps built on its kraken.js framework, which uses Express, rendered pages on the server with Dust templates. Server-side templates let the same JavaScript developers own both the page and the data orchestration.
  • Ghost, the publishing platform, builds every site's front end from templates: its theme documentation states that Ghost themes use the Handlebars templating language, which keeps templates (the HTML) separate from JavaScript logic through helpers.
  • Netflix rebuilt the netflix.com website on a Node.js architecture that renders on both the server and the client ("universal JavaScript"). In Making Netflix.com Faster the team reports a 70% reduction in startup time from this work, which shows why server rendering still matters for first-load performance.

Popular tools: express.static, template engines EJS, Pug, and Handlebars (express-handlebars); build tools such as Vite that emit hashed asset filenames; Nginx, object storage, and CDNs for serving files at scale.

docs.title: express.static
docs.text:
express.static(root, options) returns middleware that maps the request path to a file inside root. For app.use(express.static("public")), a request for /css/site.css serves public/css/site.css. If no file matches, it calls next() and the request continues to your routes.

It handles HEAD requests, Range requests (partial content for video), ETag and Last-Modified validation (returning 304 Not Modified), and refuses paths that try to escape the root with ../. With the default fallthrough: true, a refused path or denied dotfile is not answered with 403 directly: the middleware calls next(), so the request continues to your later routes and usually ends as a 404. Set fallthrough: false if you want the 403 error passed to your error handler instead.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default What it does maxAge 0 Sets Cache-Control: max-age (milliseconds, or a string such as "1d") immutable false Adds the immutable directive: the browser will not revalidate during maxAge etag true Sends an ETag so browsers can revalidate cheaply lastModified true Sends Last-Modified based on the file's modification time index "index.html" File served for a directory request; false disables it dotfiles "ignore" How to treat names starting with .: "ignore", "allow", or "deny" fallthrough true On a client error (missing file, denied dotfile, bad path), call next(); if false, call next(err) so the error handler answers (404, 403) extensions false Try extensions, e.g. ["html"] serves /about from about.html redirect true Redirect /docs to /docs/ when it is a directory setHeaders none Function to set extra headers per file

docs.title: Virtual path prefix
docs.text:
Mount the middleware on a path to give files a URL prefix that does not exist on disk:

app.use("/static", express.static("public"));
// GET /static/logo.png -> public/logo.png

docs.title: Multiple folders and order
docs.text:
Middleware runs in registration order, so the first folder that contains a matching file wins:

app.use(express.static("public"));      // checked first
app.use(express.static("uploads-cdn")); // checked only if public misses

Register static middleware early so file requests do not run through unrelated middleware such as authentication or body parsing, unless the files themselves need protection.

docs.title: Caching strategy
docs.text:
File type Strategy Fingerprinted build assets (app.3f9a1c.js) Long maxAge (one year) plus immutable: the name changes when content changes index.html of a single-page app no-cache: always revalidate so users get new deployments Images and fonts without fingerprints Moderate maxAge (hours to days) with ETag revalidation

no-cache does not mean "do not store"; it means "check with the server before reuse". See caching.

docs.title: Serving a single-page app
docs.text:
A React or Vue app built for production is a folder of static files plus index.html. Client-side routes like /settings/profile do not exist as files, so the server must return index.html for them and let the JavaScript router take over. In Express 5, a catch-all route uses a named wildcard:

  • "/*splat" matches any path below / (but not / itself).
  • "/{*splat}" matches every path, including /.

Express 4 used "*", which Express 5 no longer accepts.

docs.title: Never serve the project root
docs.text: express.static(".") or express.static(__dirname) publishes everything: package.json, source files, and possibly .env (if dotfile handling is changed). Always point it at a dedicated folder like public/ or dist/.

docs.title: Template engines
docs.text:
A template engine turns a template file plus data into HTML on the server.

views/profile.ejs  +  { user: { name: "Ada" } }  --render-->  <h1>Ada</h1>

Express integrates engines through two settings and one method:

  • app.set("views", dir): folder containing templates (default ./views).
  • app.set("view engine", "ejs"): default engine and file extension.
  • res.render("profile", data): render views/profile.ejs and send it.

Data available to templates comes from three places, merged in this order: app.locals (app-wide, such as the site name), res.locals (per request, often set by middleware, such as the current user), and the object passed to res.render().

In production (NODE_ENV=production), Express enables the view cache, so templates are compiled once instead of on every request.

docs.title: Popular engines and escaping
docs.text:
Engine Escaped output Raw output (dangerous) Style EJS <%= value %> <%- value %> HTML with embedded JavaScript Pug #{value} or p= value !{value} or p!= value Indentation-based, no closing tags Handlebars {{value}} {{{value}}} Logic-light HTML with helpers

Escaping converts characters such as < and " into entities like <, so user input displays as text instead of running as HTML. Use the raw form only for HTML you generated and trust, or for user content that has been sanitized with a dedicated library.

docs.title: Server-rendered pages vs API-only
docs.text:
Approach How it works Good for Server-rendered (templates) Express builds full HTML per request Content sites, admin tools, emails, simple apps without a frontend build API-only Express returns JSON; a separate frontend renders Single-page apps, mobile apps, multiple clients Framework SSR A frontend framework such as Next.js renders on the server Rich UIs that also need fast first loads and SEO

Many Express apps today are API-only, but templates remain useful for emails, PDFs, and small internal tools.

docs.title: When to let nginx or a CDN serve files
docs.text:
Node can serve files, but a reverse proxy or CDN does it more efficiently:

  • nginx serves files from disk with very little CPU and memory and handles many slow clients well.
  • A CDN caches files close to users worldwide and removes the load from your servers entirely.

A common setup: the frontend build is deployed to a CDN or object storage, and Express serves only the API.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Serve static files from Express when:

  • The app is small or internal and one process serving everything keeps deployment simple.
  • Files need application logic first (authentication, per-user access checks) and are not served often.
  • You are in development, or packaging a single-binary or single-container app.

Hand static files to Nginx, object storage, or a CDN when:

  • Traffic is high or global; each file request otherwise costs event-loop time in Node.
  • Files are large (video, downloads) or you want edge caching near users.

Use server-side templates when you render emails, PDFs, admin tools, or content pages that need no client-side app. Prefer an API plus a frontend framework when the UI is highly interactive or several clients share the API.

Option Serves Strength Weakness express.static Files from the app server Simple; can sit behind auth Uses Node resources; no edge caching Nginx / reverse proxy Files from disk next to the app Very efficient file serving Another component to configure Object storage + CDN Files from edge locations Global speed, offloads servers Deploy pipeline and cache invalidation Templates (EJS, Pug, Handlebars) HTML built per request No frontend build; good SEO Less interactive; server does rendering work SPA + JSON API HTML shell + client rendering Rich interactivity, many clients Slower first load without SSR

docs.title: Static assets with sensible caching
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import path from "node:path";

const app = express();
const publicDir = path.join(import.meta.dirname, "public");

app.use("/assets", express.static(path.join(publicDir, "assets"), {
  maxAge: "1y",
  immutable: true, // safe because build files are fingerprinted
}));

app.use(express.static(publicDir, {
  index: false,
  dotfiles: "deny", // never serve /.env and similar (falls through to 404)
  setHeaders: (res, filePath) => {
    if (filePath.endsWith(".html")) res.set("Cache-Control", "no-cache");
  },
}));

import.meta.dirname is available in ES modules on current Node versions; in CommonJS use __dirname.

docs.title: Single-page app with an API
docs.text:
const distDir = path.join(import.meta.dirname, "dist");

app.use("/api", apiRouter); // API routes first
// Unknown API paths get a JSON 404 instead of falling through to the HTML
app.use("/api", (req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: "Not found" }));

app.use(express.static(distDir, { index: false }));

// Any other GET returns index.html so the client router can handle it.
app.get("/{*splat}", (req, res) => {
  res.set("Cache-Control", "no-cache");
  res.sendFile("index.html", { root: distDir });
});

Order matters: if the catch-all came before /api, every API call would receive the HTML page.

docs.title: Rendering an EJS template
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.set("views", "views");
app.set("view engine", "ejs");
app.locals.siteName = "Task Tracker";

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.locals.currentUser = req.session?.user ?? null; // available to views
  next();
});

app.get("/tasks", async (req, res) => {
  const tasks = await listTasks();
  res.render("tasks", { tasks, title: "Your tasks" });
});

views/tasks.ejs:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head><title><%= title %> | <%= siteName %></title></head>
  <body>
    <% if (currentUser) { %>
      <p>Signed in as <%= currentUser.name %></p>
    <% } %>
    <ul>
      <% tasks.forEach((task) => { %>
        <li><%= task.title %></li>  <!-- escaped: safe for user input -->
      <% }) %>
    </ul>
  </body>
</html>

If a task title is <script>alert(1)</script>, <%= displays it as text. With <%- it would run as a script.

docs.title: Handlebars setup
docs.text:
import { engine } from "express-handlebars";

app.engine("handlebars", engine());
app.set("view engine", "handlebars");
app.set("views", "views");

app.get("/", (req, res) => res.render("home", { name: "Ada" }));

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Serve static files from a dedicated folder, never the project root.
  • Keep dotfiles ignored or denied.
  • Fingerprint build assets and cache them for a long time with immutable; revalidate HTML on every load.
  • Register API routes before a single-page app catch-all.
  • Use the escaped output syntax by default; treat raw output as a code-review red flag.
  • Put shared view data in res.locals through middleware rather than passing it to every res.render() call.
  • Run with NODE_ENV=production so the view cache is on.
  • Move heavy static traffic to nginx, object storage, or a CDN.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Users get a blank page or "failed to fetch module" errors after a deploy. Detect: frontend error monitoring shows chunk-loading errors and 404s for old hashed files right after a release. Cause: browsers still hold an old index.html (cached too long) that points to asset files the new deploy deleted. Fix: serve index.html with no-cache, and keep the previous release's hashed assets available for a while.
  • The frontend shows Unexpected token '<' when parsing JSON. Detect: an API call returns 200 with Content-Type: text/html. Cause: a mistyped or missing API route falls through to the SPA catch-all, which answers with index.html. Fix: register API routers first and add a JSON 404 handler for /api before the catch-all.
  • Secrets or source files are downloadable. Detect: access logs or a security scan show 200 responses for paths such as /.env, /.git/config, or /package.json. Cause: the static root points at the project folder, or dotfiles was set to "allow". Fix: serve only a build folder, keep dotfiles ignored or denied, and rotate any exposed secret.
  • Latency rises with traffic although API handlers are fast. Detect: most requests in the access log are for images, scripts, and fonts, and event-loop delay grows during peaks. Cause: Node is serving all static traffic. Fix: move assets to a CDN or Nginx and set long cache lifetimes for fingerprinted files.
  • A user's text runs as script in other users' browsers. Detect: an XSS report, or a code search finding raw output (<%-, !{}, {{{ }}}) with user data. Cause: unescaped template output. Fix: use the escaped syntax, sanitize the rare HTML you must allow, and add a Content Security Policy.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Static file: A file sent as-is, without per-request processing.
  • Virtual path prefix: A URL prefix that does not correspond to a folder on disk.
  • Fingerprinting: Adding a content hash to a filename so it changes when the content changes.
  • Template engine: A library that renders templates and data into HTML.
  • Locals: Data made available to templates (app.locals, res.locals).
  • Escaping: Encoding special characters so data is shown as text, not interpreted as markup.
  • View cache: Express's cache of compiled templates, on in production.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Serving express.static("."). This exposes the whole project.
  • Putting the SPA catch-all before API routes. API requests get HTML.
  • Using "*" as a wildcard in Express 5. Use a named wildcard such as "/*splat" or "/{*splat}".
  • Long-caching index.html. Users keep loading an old build after a deployment.
  • Using raw template output for user data. This creates XSS.
  • Relative paths that depend on where the process starts. Build paths from the module's directory with path.join().
  • Assuming Node must serve static files in production. A CDN or proxy is usually faster and cheaper.

docs.text:

  4. What is the difference between <%= %> and <%- %> in EJS?
  5. Where can data available to a template come from in Express?
  6. When would you serve static files from nginx or a CDN instead of Express?

docs.title: Testing Express APIs
docs.text: Automated tests prove that your API does what its contract promises: the right status codes, response bodies, headers, and side effects for each request. This lesson shows how to structure an Express app for testing, how to send requests with supertest, and how to handle databases, external services, and authentication in tests.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
APIs are used by frontends, mobile apps, and other services that break when a field is renamed or a status code changes. Manual testing with Postman does not scale and is not repeated on every change. A good automated suite runs in seconds on every commit and catches regressions before users do.

For general testing theory (test types, pyramids, test doubles), see testing fundamentals.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Spotify found the classic test pyramid a poor fit for microservices. In Testing of Microservices it describes a "Testing Honeycomb": focus on integration tests, have a few implementation-detail tests, and even fewer fully integrated tests (ideally none). That matches this lesson's advice to test APIs mainly through HTTP with supertest.
  • Google published a starting point for balancing test types. Its testing blog post Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests says Google often suggests a 70/20/10 split (70% unit, 20% integration, 10% end-to-end) as a first guess, because end-to-end tests are slow and flaky.
  • GitHub Actions documents the CI setup used at the end of this lesson: its Node.js guide installs Node with the setup-node action and runs the project's tests on every push.
  • Pact exists for teams whose APIs are consumed by other teams. Its documentation describes it as a code-first tool for testing HTTP and message integrations using contract tests, and notes that without contract testing the only way to check that applications work together is expensive and brittle integration tests.

Popular tools: node:test, Vitest, Jest, supertest, mongodb-memory-server, Testcontainers, nock, MSW, and Pact.

docs.title: What to test in an API
docs.text:
Level What it covers Example Speed Unit One function or service in isolation, dependencies faked tasksService.create() rejects a past due date Very fast Integration The HTTP layer plus real middleware, often a real test database POST /api/tasks returns 201 and stores the task Fast End-to-end The deployed system, as a client would use it Sign up, log in, create a task against a staging URL Slow

For APIs, integration tests through HTTP usually give the best value: they exercise routing, validation, middleware, error handling, and serialization together, while still running in milliseconds. Unit-test the complex business rules separately.

docs.title: Export the app without listening
docs.text: supertest needs the Express app, not a running server. If app.js exports the app and only server.js calls listen(), tests import app.js and supertest starts a temporary server on a random port for each request. See structuring an Express project.

docs.title: Choosing a test runner
docs.text:
Runner Notes node:test Built into Node; no dependency; node --test finds test files Vitest Fast, Jest-compatible API, native ES modules and TypeScript Jest Very popular; ES module support needs extra configuration

The examples use node:test with node:assert/strict. The supertest code is identical in all three.

docs.title: Test databases
docs.text:
Tests that write data need a database that is isolated and reset:

Option How it works Trade-off In-memory fake repository Inject a fake instead of the real repository Fastest; does not test real queries mongodb-memory-server Starts a real mongod process on a free port for the tests Real MongoDB behavior; downloads a MongoDB binary on install or first start Testcontainers Starts a real database in Docker for the test run Closest to production; needs Docker Dedicated test database A separate database on a shared server Simple; must never point at production data

Whatever you choose, give each test a known starting state: clear collections or tables before each test, or wrap each test in a transaction that is rolled back.

docs.title: External services
docs.text:
Tests must not call real third-party APIs: they are slow, flaky, may cost money, and can have side effects. Replace them by:

  • Injecting a fake client into the service (simplest with dependency injection).
  • Intercepting HTTP with nock or MSW (Mock Service Worker), so the code makes real-looking requests that are answered locally.

docs.title: Fixtures and factories
docs.text: A fixture is fixed test data; a factory is a function that builds valid test data with sensible defaults you can override. Factories keep tests short and make each test state only what it cares about.

docs.title: Coverage and CI
docs.text: Coverage tools report which lines your tests executed. Use coverage to find untested paths (especially error branches), not as a goal in itself. Run the suite in CI on every pull request so failures block merging; see CI/CD.

docs.title: Contract testing
docs.text: When other teams consume your API, contract tests check that responses still match an agreed contract: an OpenAPI schema that responses are validated against, or consumer-driven contracts with a tool such as Pact.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use each kind of test where it pays off:

  • Integration tests with supertest: for every route's status codes, validation errors, auth rules, and response shapes. This should be the bulk of an API suite.
  • Unit tests: for business rules with many cases (pricing, permissions, date logic), where going through HTTP would only add noise.
  • Real database in tests (mongodb-memory-server, Testcontainers): when queries, indexes, transactions, or unique constraints matter.
  • End-to-end tests: a few critical journeys (sign up, checkout) against a deployed environment.

Avoid:

  • Supertest for pure functions: call them directly.
  • Real third-party APIs in automated tests: use nock or MSW.
  • Large end-to-end suites as the main safety net: they are slow and flaky.
Approach Speed Confidence it gives Main cost Unit tests with fakes Fastest Logic is correct in isolation Misses wiring, queries, middleware Supertest + fake repository Fast HTTP contract, middleware, validation Misses real database behavior Supertest + real test database Medium Queries and constraints too Setup and cleanup per test End-to-end against staging Slow The whole system works together Flakiness, environment upkeep Contract tests (Pact, OpenAPI) Fast Consumers and provider still agree Agreeing on and maintaining contracts

docs.title: The app under test
docs.text:
// src/app.js
import express from "express";

export function createApp({ tasksRepository }) {
  const app = express();
  app.use(express.json());

  app.get("/health", (req, res) => res.json({ status: "ok" }));

  app.post("/tasks", async (req, res) => {
    if (typeof req.body?.title !== "string" || req.body.title.trim() === "") {
      return res.status(400).json({ error: "Title is required" });
    }
    const task = await tasksRepository.insert({ id: crypto.randomUUID(),
      title: req.body.title.trim(), done: false });
    res.status(201).location(`/tasks/${task.id}`).json(task);
  });

  app.get("/tasks/:id", async (req, res) => {
    const task = await tasksRepository.findById(req.params.id);
    if (!task) return res.status(404).json({ error: "Task not found" });
    res.json(task);
  });

  return app;
}

docs.title: Integration tests with node:test and supertest
docs.text:
// test/tasks.test.js
import { describe, it, beforeEach } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import request from "supertest";
import { createApp } from "../src/app.js";

function createFakeRepository() {
  const items = new Map();
  return {
    async insert(task) { items.set(task.id, task); return task; },
    async findById(id) { return items.get(id) ?? null; },
  };
}

describe("tasks API", () => {
  let app;

  beforeEach(() => {
    app = createApp({ tasksRepository: createFakeRepository() }); // fresh state
  });

  it("GET /health returns ok", async () => {
    const res = await request(app).get("/health").expect(200);
    assert.deepEqual(res.body, { status: "ok" });
  });

  it("POST /tasks creates a task", async () => {
    const res = await request(app)
      .post("/tasks")
      .send({ title: "  Write tests  " })      // sent as JSON
      .expect("Content-Type", /json/)
      .expect(201);

    assert.equal(res.body.title, "Write tests");
    assert.equal(res.headers.location, `/tasks/${res.body.id}`);
  });

  it("POST /tasks rejects a missing title", async () => {
    const res = await request(app).post("/tasks").send({}).expect(400);
    assert.match(res.body.error, /title/i);
  });

  it("GET /tasks/:id returns 404 for an unknown id", async () => {
    await request(app).get("/tasks/does-not-exist").expect(404);
  });

  it("created task can be read back", async () => {
    const created = await request(app).post("/tasks").send({ title: "A" });
    const res = await request(app).get(`/tasks/${created.body.id}`).expect(200);
    assert.equal(res.body.title, "A");
  });
});

Run with node --test. In a terminal, the default reporter prints (timings vary):

▶ tasks API
  ✔ GET /health returns ok (41.5ms)
  ✔ POST /tasks creates a task (27.8ms)
  ✔ POST /tasks rejects a missing title (8.2ms)
  ✔ GET /tasks/:id returns 404 for an unknown id (11.3ms)
  ✔ created task can be read back (12.0ms)
✔ tasks API (102.3ms)
ℹ tests 5
ℹ suites 1
ℹ pass 5
ℹ fail 0
...

When output is not a terminal (for example in CI logs), Node uses the TAP reporter instead; choose explicitly with --test-reporter=spec.

docs.title: The same test in Vitest or Jest
docs.text:
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest"; // Jest provides these globally
import request from "supertest";

it("GET /health returns ok", async () => {
  const res = await request(app).get("/health");
  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
  expect(res.body).toEqual({ status: "ok" });
});

docs.title: Testing authenticated routes
docs.text:
import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";

function authHeader(user = { id: "u1", role: "user" }) {
  const token = jwt.sign({ sub: user.id, role: user.role },
    process.env.JWT_ACCESS_SECRET, { expiresIn: "5m" });
  return { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` };
}

it("rejects requests without a token", async () => {
  await request(app).get("/orders").expect(401);
});

it("forbids non-admins", async () => {
  await request(app).delete("/admin/users/42").set(authHeader()).expect(403);
});

it("returns orders for a logged-in user", async () => {
  await request(app).get("/orders").set(authHeader()).expect(200);
});

For cookie-based sessions, request.agent(app) keeps cookies between requests, so you can log in once and then call protected routes:

const agent = request.agent(app);
await agent.post("/login").send({ email: "a@b.com", password: "secret" });
await agent.get("/account").expect(200); // session cookie sent automatically

docs.title: A real MongoDB with mongodb-memory-server
docs.text:
import { before, after, beforeEach } from "node:test";
import { MongoMemoryServer } from "mongodb-memory-server";
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";

let mongod, client, db;

before(async () => {
  mongod = await MongoMemoryServer.create();
  client = await MongoClient.connect(mongod.getUri());
  db = client.db("test");
});

beforeEach(async () => {
  await db.collection("tasks").deleteMany({}); // known starting state
});

after(async () => {
  await client.close();
  await mongod.stop();
});

docs.title: Mocking an external API with nock
docs.text:
import nock from "nock";

it("converts the price using the rates API", async () => {
  nock("https://rates.example.com")
    .get("/latest")
    .query({ base: "USD" })
    .reply(200, { EUR: 0.9 });

  const res = await request(app).get("/prices/100?currency=EUR").expect(200);
  assert.equal(res.body.amount, 90);
});

With MSW, the equivalent uses a request handler:

import { setupServer } from "msw/node";
// MSW 2 exports these from "msw"; MSW 3 imports them from "msw/http"
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";

const server = setupServer(
  http.get("https://rates.example.com/latest", () => HttpResponse.json({ EUR: 0.9 }))
);
server.listen(); // call server.close() after the tests

docs.title: A factory for test data
docs.text:
let counter = 0;
export function buildTask(overrides = {}) {
  counter += 1;
  return { title: `Task ${counter}`, done: false, ...overrides };
}

await request(app).post("/tasks").send(buildTask({ title: "Specific" }));

docs.title: Coverage and CI
docs.text:
node --test --experimental-test-coverage   # built-in coverage report
npx vitest run --coverage                   # Vitest with a coverage provider

A minimal GitHub Actions job:

name: test
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: lts/*
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Test behavior through HTTP: status, body, headers, and side effects.
  • Cover failure paths (400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 500), not only the happy path.
  • Give every test a fresh, known state; never depend on test order.
  • Never let tests touch production databases or real third-party APIs.
  • Keep secrets for tests in test-only environment variables.
  • Use factories so each test shows only the data that matters to it.
  • Run the suite in CI on every pull request.
  • Close database connections and servers after tests so the process exits.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
These problems show up in CI pipelines, where the suite runs on every change.

  • The CI job hangs until it times out although all tests passed. Detect: the test summary is printed but the step never finishes. Cause: open handles keep the event loop alive: a database client, a mongodb-memory-server instance, an interval, or a server started with listen(). Fix: close everything in after() hooks; as a last resort, Node's --test-force-exit flag exits once all tests have finished.
  • Tests pass locally but fail randomly in CI. Detect: different tests fail on reruns of the same commit. Cause: shared state; node --test runs test files in parallel processes by default, so files that share one database collection interfere. Fix: give each file its own database or collection names, reset state in beforeEach, or run with --test-concurrency=1.
  • Tests reach the internet. Detect: occasional timeouts or rate-limit errors from a third-party API in CI logs, or unexpected usage on a vendor account. Cause: a code path not covered by mocks. Fix: call nock.disableNetConnect() (allowing only localhost) so any unmocked request fails immediately and visibly.
  • A test run deletes real data. Detect: data loss in a shared or production database that coincides with a test run. Cause: the test database URL came from the wrong environment variable. Fix: refuse to start the suite unless the connection string points at a clearly named test database, and keep production credentials out of CI test jobs.
  • Database tests fail before running in CI. Detect: setup errors while mongodb-memory-server downloads its MongoDB binary, especially on locked-down runners. Cause: the binary download is blocked or slow. Fix: cache the downloaded binary between CI runs or use a database service container instead.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Integration test: A test of several parts working together, such as routing, middleware, and a database.
  • supertest: A library that sends HTTP requests to an Express app without a manually started server.
  • Test double: A stand-in for a real dependency (fake, stub, mock, spy).
  • Fixture: Fixed data or state prepared for a test.
  • Factory: A function that builds valid test data with overridable defaults.
  • HTTP interception: Catching outgoing requests in tests and answering them locally.
  • Contract test: A test that checks an API still matches the agreement its consumers depend on.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Calling app.listen() in the module tests import. Ports collide and the test process hangs.
  • Shared state between tests. A test passes alone but fails in the full suite.
  • Only testing success. Most production bugs live in error branches.
  • Asserting on whole bodies that contain IDs or timestamps. Assert on the stable fields instead.
  • Mocking everything. If the database, validation, and router are all mocked, the test proves little.
  • Forgetting await. The test finishes before the assertion runs and always passes.
  • "100% coverage means no bugs." Coverage shows what ran, not what was checked.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why does exporting the app separately from listen() make testing easier?
  2. What does an integration test through HTTP verify that a unit test does not?
  3. Compare an in-memory fake, mongodb-memory-server, and Testcontainers for database tests.
  4. How do you test a route that requires a session cookie?
  5. Why should tests intercept calls to third-party APIs?
  6. What is contract testing, and when is it worth adding?
