docs.title: Asynchronous Programming in Node.js
docs.text: Almost everything a backend does—reading files, querying databases, calling other services—takes time. Node.js handles that time without blocking by using asynchronous patterns: callbacks, promises, and async/await. This page covers each pattern, how errors flow through them, and how to run work in sequence, in parallel, and with timeouts.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Asynchronous code that is written badly causes the hardest backend bugs: requests that never respond, errors that disappear, operations that run one after another when they could run together, and crashes from unhandled rejections. Mastering these patterns is required for writing any reliable Node.js service. The browser-side basics are covered in async JavaScript; this page focuses on Node.js.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• MongoDB's Node.js driver removed callback support in version 5.0 and now offers a promise-only API. Code that still needs callbacks must use a separate mongodb-legacy package. Supporting two styles was holding the API back (MongoDB Node.js driver v5.0.0 release notes).
  • Stripe's Node.js library is used with await. Since v13 it automatically retries a failed request once when that is safe, retries more times with exponential backoff if you raise maxNetworkRetries, and adds idempotency keys so a retry cannot charge a customer twice (stripe-node README).
  • AWS's SDK for JavaScript v3 documentation shows a Lambda function that starts three DynamoDB calls and waits for all of them with Promise.all, which is the parallel pattern on this page (AWS SDK for JavaScript v3: Using promises).
  • Express 5 forwards a rejected promise from an async route handler or middleware to the error-handling middleware, which makes async handlers safe to write. With Express 4 you had to catch the error and call next(err) yourself (Express: Migrating to Express 5).

Popular tools and providers: built-in node:util (promisify), node:timers/promises, and AbortSignal; p-limit for capping concurrency; client libraries such as the AWS SDK v3 and the MongoDB driver that return promises.

docs.title: 1. Error-first callbacks
docs.text:
Node.js's original style passes a callback as the last argument. The callback receives an error first, then the result:

import { readFile } from "node:fs";

readFile("config.json", "utf8", (error, text) => {
  if (error) {
    console.error("Could not read config:", error.message);
    return; // stop: text is undefined
  }
  console.log("Config length:", text.length);
});

Rules of the convention:

  • The first argument is an Error or null.
  • On success, results follow the error argument.
  • The callback is called exactly once.
  • Errors are passed to the callback, not thrown, because the original call has already returned by the time the operation fails.

docs.title: Callback hell
docs.text:
Dependent steps nest deeper and deeper, and each level must handle errors:

getUser(id, (err, user) => {
  if (err) return handle(err);
  getOrders(user.id, (err, orders) => {
    if (err) return handle(err);
    getInvoice(orders[0].id, (err, invoice) => {
      if (err) return handle(err);
      send(invoice);
    });
  });
});

This "pyramid of doom" is hard to read, easy to get wrong (a missing return calls the next step with an error), and hard to run in parallel. Promises solve these problems.

docs.title: 2. Promises
docs.text:
A promise is an object representing a value that will be available later. It is always in one of three states:

Once fulfilled or rejected, a promise is settled and never changes.

const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => resolve("done"), 100);
});

promise
  .then((value) => value.toUpperCase()) // returns a new promise
  .then((upper) => console.log(upper))  // DONE
  .catch((error) => console.error(error))
  .finally(() => console.log("cleanup runs either way"));

Key behaviors:

  • .then() returns a new promise, so calls can be chained.
  • Returning a value from .then() fulfills the next promise with it; returning a promise makes the chain wait for it.
  • Throwing inside .then() rejects the next promise. The rejection skips later .then() handlers until a .catch() handles it.
  • .finally() runs on both outcomes and passes the original result through.

docs.title: Combining promises
docs.text: Method Resolves when Rejects when Typical use Promise.all(list) All fulfill → array of values in input order Any rejects (first rejection wins; others keep running but are ignored) Independent operations that must all succeed Promise.allSettled(list) All settle → array of { status, value } / { status, reason } Never Run everything, then report which failed Promise.race(list) First to settle fulfills First to settle rejects Timeouts, first response wins Promise.any(list) First to fulfill All reject → AggregateError Try several mirrors, use the first success

docs.title: 3. async and await
docs.text:
async/await is syntax built on promises that lets asynchronous code read like synchronous code:

  • An async function always returns a promise. Returning a value fulfills it; throwing rejects it.
  • await pauses the function until a promise settles, then gives the value or throws the rejection reason. Other code keeps running while it waits.
async function loadInvoice(userId) {
  try {
    const user = await getUser(userId);
    const orders = await getOrders(user.id);
    return await getInvoice(orders[0].id);
  } catch (error) {
    throw new Error(`Failed to load invoice for ${userId}`, { cause: error });
  }
}

docs.title: Sequential versus parallel
docs.text:
Each await waits before the next line starts. If operations do not depend on each other, start them together:

// Sequential: total time ≈ 300 + 200 = 500 ms
const profile = await fetchProfile(id);    // 300 ms
const settings = await fetchSettings(id);  // 200 ms

// Parallel: total time ≈ max(300, 200) = 300 ms
const [profile2, settings2] = await Promise.all([
  fetchProfile(id),
  fetchSettings(id),
]);

Use sequential code when a step needs the previous result, or when you must limit load on a downstream service.

docs.title: Converting callback APIs: util.promisify
docs.text:
util.promisify turns a function that follows the error-first convention into one that returns a promise:

import { promisify } from "node:util";
import { exec } from "node:child_process";

const execAsync = promisify(exec);
const { stdout } = await execAsync("node --version");
console.log(stdout.trim());

Most core modules also provide promise versions directly:

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";
import { lookup } from "node:dns/promises";

await sleep(500); // wait 500 ms without a callback

docs.title: Cancellation and timeouts: AbortController
docs.text:
An AbortController creates a signal that can cancel work. Many Node.js APIs—fetch, fs.readFile, timers/promises, events.once, child_process—accept a signal option.

const controller = new AbortController();
setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 2000); // cancel after 2 s

try {
  const response = await fetch("https://example.com/slow", {
    signal: controller.signal,
  });
  console.log(response.status);
} catch (error) {
  if (error.name === "AbortError") console.log("Request cancelled");
  else throw error;
}

AbortSignal.timeout(ms) is a shortcut that aborts automatically:

const response = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) });
// Rejects with a "TimeoutError" DOMException after 3 s.

AbortSignal.any([signalA, signalB]) combines signals, for example a user cancellation and a timeout.

docs.title: Async iteration: for await...of
docs.text:
Some sources produce values over time, such as streams, paginated APIs, and events. Async iterables let you loop over them:

import { createReadStream } from "node:fs";
import { createInterface } from "node:readline";

const lines = createInterface({ input: createReadStream("access.log") });

let count = 0;
for await (const line of lines) {
  if (line.includes(" 500 ")) count++;
}
console.log(`Server errors: ${count}`);

You can write your own with an async function* generator:

async function* fetchAllPages(url) {
  let next = url;
  while (next) {
    const response = await fetch(next);
    const body = await response.json();
    yield* body.items;
    next = body.nextPage;
  }
}

docs.title: Unhandled rejections
docs.text:
A promise that rejects with no .catch() and no await in a try block is an unhandled rejection. By default, Node.js treats it as a fatal error: it prints the error and the process exits with a non-zero code. This protects you from silently ignoring failures. Always handle rejections, and see errors, debugging, and performance for process-level handlers.

Measured on Node.js 22: Promise.reject(new Error("boom")) with no handler printed the error and ended the process with exit code 1, even though a timer was still pending.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Use async/await for almost all new application code: request handlers, services, and scripts.
  • Use Promise.all / allSettled when several independent operations can run at the same time, and the list is small or capped.
  • Use callbacks only when an API offers nothing else, and wrap them with util.promisify at the edge of your code.
  • Use for await...of for data that arrives over time: streams, paginated APIs, and lines of a file.
  • Use events or streams, not one promise, for something that produces many values or never "finishes", such as a socket.
  • Do not use Promise.all on unbounded lists (thousands of IDs from a request). Cap concurrency instead.
Need Best fit Why not the others One result, later async/await Callbacks nest and lose errors more easily Several independent results Promise.all Sequential await adds the waits together Many results over time Async iterator or stream A promise settles only once Repeated notifications EventEmitter Promises cannot fire twice A thousand jobs, gently Concurrency limit Promise.all starts all of them at once

docs.title: Retrying with a delay
docs.text:
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

async function withRetry(operation, attempts = 3, delayMs = 200) {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= attempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await operation(); // await inside try so failures are caught
    } catch (error) {
      if (attempt === attempts) throw error;
      await sleep(delayMs * attempt); // back off a little more each time
    }
  }
}

const data = await withRetry(() => fetch("https://example.com/api"));

docs.title: Limited concurrency
docs.text:
Promise.all on 10,000 items starts 10,000 operations at once, which can overwhelm a database. Process a fixed number at a time instead:

async function mapWithLimit(items, limit, worker) {
  const results = new Array(items.length);
  let nextIndex = 0;

  async function runner() {
    while (nextIndex < items.length) {
      const index = nextIndex++; // safe: JS runs on one thread
      results[index] = await worker(items[index]);
    }
  }

  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: limit }, runner));
  return results;
}

const users = await mapWithLimit(userIds, 5, (id) => fetchUser(id));

docs.title: Reporting partial failures
docs.text:
const results = await Promise.allSettled([
  sendEmail(user),
  sendSms(user),
  sendPush(user),
]);

for (const result of results) {
  if (result.status === "rejected") {
    console.error("Notification failed:", result.reason.message);
  }
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use async/await for new code; wrap old callback APIs with util.promisify or use the */promises modules.
  • Run independent operations in parallel with Promise.all, but cap concurrency for large lists.
  • Always set timeouts on network calls with AbortSignal.timeout.
  • Handle every rejection: await inside try/catch, or attach .catch().
  • Add context when rethrowing: new Error("message", { cause: error }).
  • Do not mix callbacks and promises for the same operation.
  • Return or await promises from functions; never start one and forget it unless you deliberately handle its errors.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Crash loops from unhandled rejections.
  • Symptom: the process exits with code 1, prints a stack trace, and the container restarts again and again.
  • Detect: restart counts climb, and the last log lines before each exit show the rejected error.
  • Cause: a "fire-and-forget" promise (an analytics call, a cache write) with no await or .catch().
  • Fix: await it or attach .catch() that logs the error. Keep a process-level unhandledRejection handler that logs and exits so the failure stays visible.
  • Requests that never finish.
  • Symptom: in-flight requests and memory keep rising; clients time out while the server never responds.
  • Detect: an "active requests" gauge grows, and traces show outbound calls with no end time.
  • Cause: outbound fetch calls without a timeout to a dependency that stopped answering.
  • Fix: add AbortSignal.timeout(ms) to every outbound call, shorter than your own request timeout.
  • A connection pool exhausted by Promise.all.
  • Symptom: a bulk endpoint triggers database errors about timing out while waiting for a pooled connection, and unrelated endpoints slow down too.
  • Detect: pool usage hits its maximum exactly when the bulk job runs.
  • Cause: Promise.all(ids.map(...)) started thousands of queries at once.
  • Fix: cap concurrency (mapWithLimit above or p-limit), or batch IDs into one query.
  • Retry storms.
  • Symptom: a dependency that slows down briefly gets overwhelmed and stays down.
  • Detect: requests to the dependency multiply exactly when its error rate rises.
  • Cause: every caller retries immediately, several times, without backoff.
  • Fix: use exponential backoff with jitter, a small attempt limit, and idempotency keys for writes. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.
  • Work silently skipped.
  • Symptom: a batch job reports success, but some records were never saved, and no error appears.
  • Detect: counts in the database do not match the input.
  • Cause: items.forEach(async ...) returned before the saves finished, and their errors were lost.
  • Fix: use for...of with await, or await Promise.all(...).

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Callback: A function passed to another function to be called later.
  • Error-first callback: A callback whose first argument is an error or null.
  • Promise: An object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous operation.
  • Settled: A promise that is fulfilled or rejected.
  • async function: A function that always returns a promise and can use await.
  • await: Pauses an async function until a promise settles.
  • Unhandled rejection: A rejected promise with no rejection handler.
  • AbortSignal: An object that signals that an operation should be cancelled.
  • Async iterable: An object that can be looped over with for await...of.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using async callbacks with forEach. forEach ignores the returned promises, so the loop "finishes" before the work does and errors are lost. Use for...of (sequential) or Promise.all(items.map(...)) (parallel).
// Wrong
ids.forEach(async (id) => await save(id));
// Right
for (const id of ids) await save(id);
await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => save(id)));
  • Forgetting await. const user = getUser(id) gives a pending promise, not the user, and errors become unhandled rejections.
  • return promise inside try. Returning a promise without await from inside a try block means its rejection is not caught there. Use return await promise when you want the local catch to run.
  • "await blocks the server." It pauses only the current function; other requests continue.
  • "Promise.all cancels the other operations when one fails." It stops waiting, but the other operations keep running.
  • Calling a callback twice or both calling it and throwing.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What are the rules of the error-first callback convention?
  2. What are the three states of a promise, and what does "settled" mean?
  3. Compare Promise.all, allSettled, race, and any when one input rejects.
  4. Why does ids.forEach(async (id) => ...) not wait for the work?
  5. How do you add a timeout to a fetch call in Node.js?
  6. What happens by default when a promise rejection is not handled?

docs.title: Buffers and Streams
docs.text: Servers constantly move bytes: request bodies, uploaded files, database results, compressed responses. A Buffer holds a fixed chunk of raw binary data in memory. A stream processes data piece by piece as it arrives, instead of waiting for all of it. Streams are how Node.js handles large or continuous data without running out of memory.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Reading a 1 GB file into memory for every download request will crash a server under load. Streaming the same file uses only a small, constant amount of memory per request and starts sending bytes immediately. HTTP requests and responses, sockets, files, compression, and hashing are all streams in Node.js, so understanding them—especially error handling and backpressure—is essential backend knowledge.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• AWS ships @aws-sdk/lib-storage, whose Upload class accepts buffers, blobs, or streams and sends them to S3 as concurrent multipart uploads. This makes it possible to upload large files, or streams of unknown size, without loading them into memory (AWS SDK for JavaScript v3: lib-storage).
  • node-postgres offers pg-query-stream, which delivers query result rows as a readable object-mode stream. A large export can then be piped to a CSV writer and the HTTP response, instead of materialising millions of rows (pg-query-stream).
  • MongoDB's Node.js driver makes query cursors async iterable, so for await (const doc of collection.find()) processes results one batch at a time (MongoDB docs: Access data from a cursor).
  • csv-parse from the CSV project is a Transform stream. Its docs recommend the stream API because it "ensures scalability by treating your data as a stream from the source to the destination" (csv-parse docs: Stream API).

Popular tools and providers: node:stream, node:zlib, and stream/promises; @aws-sdk/lib-storage for S3; busboy (used by Multer) for streaming multipart uploads; csv-parse and csv-stringify.

docs.title: Binary data and Buffers
docs.text:
Text is ultimately bytes. A Buffer is a fixed-length sequence of bytes (values 0–255). In Node.js, Buffer is a subclass of the standard Uint8Array, so it works with web APIs that accept typed arrays.

const fromText = Buffer.from("Héllo", "utf8"); // encode text to bytes
console.log(fromText);          // <Buffer 48 c3 a9 6c 6c 6f>
console.log(fromText.length);   // 6 bytes (é takes 2 bytes in UTF-8)
console.log(fromText.toString("utf8")); // "Héllo"

const zeroed = Buffer.alloc(10);        // 10 bytes, all zero
const fast = Buffer.allocUnsafe(10);    // 10 bytes, NOT cleared
const fromArray = Buffer.from([0x48, 0x69]); // "Hi"
Method Behavior Buffer.from(string, encoding) Encodes a string into bytes. Buffer.from(array or arrayBuffer) Creates bytes from numbers or wraps existing memory. Buffer.alloc(size) New zero-filled buffer. Safe default. Buffer.allocUnsafe(size) New buffer that may contain old memory contents. Faster, but you must overwrite every byte before exposing it. Buffer.concat(list) Joins buffers into one new buffer. buf.toString(encoding) Decodes bytes to a string. buf.subarray(start, end) A view of part of the buffer (shares memory). buf.equals(other) Byte-by-byte comparison.

docs.title: Encodings
docs.text:
Encoding Use utf8 Default for text. Characters take 1–4 bytes. base64 Binary as ASCII text (email attachments, data URLs, JSON payloads). base64url Base64 with URL-safe characters (- and _, no padding); used in JWTs. hex Two hexadecimal characters per byte (hashes, IDs). latin1 / ascii Legacy single-byte encodings. 
const secret = Buffer.from("api-key-123");
const b64 = secret.toString("base64");   // "YXBpLWtleS0xMjM="
Buffer.from(b64, "base64").toString();   // "api-key-123"

Base64 is not encryption

Base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse. Never use it to "hide" secrets.

docs.title: Slices share memory
docs.text:
const original = Buffer.from("hello");
const part = original.subarray(0, 2); // "he" — a view, not a copy
part[0] = 0x4a;                        // "J"
console.log(original.toString());      // "Jello" — original changed too

Use Buffer.from(part) when you need an independent copy. (buf.slice() on a Buffer also shares memory, unlike Uint8Array.prototype.slice, which copies. buf.slice() has been deprecated since Node.js 17.5; use subarray, which also makes the sharing obvious.)

docs.title: Why streams
docs.text: Streams give constant memory use and faster time-to-first-byte, and they let you chain processing steps: read → decompress → parse → write.

docs.title: The four stream types
docs.text: Type Direction Examples Readable A source you read from fs.createReadStream, an incoming HTTP request, process.stdin Writable A destination you write to fs.createWriteStream, an HTTP response, process.stdout Duplex Both readable and writable, independently TCP sockets (net.Socket) Transform A duplex whose output is computed from its input zlib.createGzip(), crypto.createHash() (as a stream), CSV parsers

docs.title: Reading modes and events
docs.text:
A readable stream starts in paused mode. It switches to flowing mode when you attach a data listener, call resume(), or pipe it somewhere. In flowing mode it pushes chunks as fast as they arrive.

Important events:

Stream Event Meaning Readable data A chunk is available. Readable end No more data will come. Writable finish All data has been flushed after end() was called. Writable drain The internal buffer emptied; safe to write more. Both error Something failed. Always handle it. Both close The underlying resource was closed.

docs.title: Backpressure
docs.text:
If a readable source is faster than a writable destination—for example, reading from a fast disk and sending to a slow mobile client—data piles up in memory. Backpressure is the mechanism that slows the source down.

  • Every stream has an internal buffer whose size limit is its highWaterMark (a byte count, or a number of objects in object mode).
  • writable.write(chunk) returns false when the buffer is at or above the limit. The producer should stop writing.
  • The writable emits drain when it can accept more data.

pipe() and pipeline() handle backpressure automatically. You only manage it yourself when calling write() manually.

docs.title: pipe() versus pipeline()
docs.text:
readable.pipe(writable) connects streams and handles backpressure, but it does not forward errors or clean up: if one stream fails, the others may stay open and leak resources.

stream.pipeline() connects any number of streams, handles backpressure, propagates errors, and destroys the streams when one of them fails (except those that have already ended or finished). Use the promise version from node:stream/promises:

import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";

await pipeline(source, transformA, transformB, destination);
// Resolves when everything finished; rejects if any step failed.

docs.title: Object mode
docs.text: By default streams carry Buffers or strings. In object mode (objectMode: true) each chunk can be any JavaScript value, which is useful for streams of records, such as rows from a database cursor.

docs.title: Creating streams from data
docs.text:
import { Readable } from "node:stream";

const numbers = Readable.from([1, 2, 3]);            // from an iterable
const lines = Readable.from(generateLinesAsync());    // from an async generator

docs.title: Async iteration
docs.text:
Readable streams are async iterables, the simplest way to consume them:

for await (const chunk of readable) {
  console.log("got", chunk.length, "bytes");
}

The loop respects backpressure, and errors are thrown inside the loop so a normal try/catch works.

docs.title: Web streams interoperability
docs.text:
Node.js also implements the web-standard ReadableStream, WritableStream, and TransformStream. For example, fetch() returns a web stream as response.body. Convert between the two families:

import { Readable } from "node:stream";

const response = await fetch("https://example.com/large.csv");
const nodeStream = Readable.fromWeb(response.body); // web → Node.js stream
const webStream = Readable.toWeb(nodeStream);        // Node.js → web stream

Readable.fromWeb() is marked stable from Node.js 22.17.0 and 24.0.0.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Use streams when the data is large, unbounded, or arrives over time: file downloads and uploads, exports, proxies, log processing, compression.
  • Use streams when you want the first bytes to reach the client before the whole result exists.
  • Use Buffers for small binary payloads you need in full: a hash, an image thumbnail, a signed token.
  • Do not stream small JSON responses or configuration files; a plain await readFile or res.json() is simpler and just as fast.
  • Do not hand-roll write() loops when pipeline() can connect the pieces; manual loops are where backpressure bugs come from.
Data size and shape Choose Why Small (KBs), needed whole Buffer / string Simplest code Large file to send or store pipeline(readStream, ...) Constant memory, backpressure handled Records from a database or CSV Object-mode stream or async iterator One record at a time Data from fetch() Web stream, or Readable.fromWeb response.body is a web stream

docs.title: Copying a large file
docs.text:
import { createReadStream, createWriteStream } from "node:fs";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";

await pipeline(
  createReadStream("video.mp4"),
  createWriteStream("video-copy.mp4"),
);
console.log("Copied with constant memory use");

docs.title: Compressing a file with gzip
docs.text:
import { createReadStream, createWriteStream } from "node:fs";
import { createGzip } from "node:zlib";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";

await pipeline(
  createReadStream("access.log"),
  createGzip(),                       // Transform: bytes in, compressed bytes out
  createWriteStream("access.log.gz"),
);

docs.title: Writing a Transform stream
docs.text:
import { Transform } from "node:stream";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";

const upperCase = new Transform({
  transform(chunk, encoding, callback) {
    callback(null, chunk.toString().toUpperCase()); // pass result on
  },
});

await pipeline(process.stdin, upperCase, process.stdout);
// echo "hello" | node upper.js   →   HELLO

Save it as upper.mjs, or as upper.js in a "type": "module" project, because it uses top-level await.

The transform function receives each chunk and calls callback(error, output) when done. Implement flush(callback) if you need to emit remaining data at the end.

docs.title: Streaming a file as an HTTP response
docs.text:
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { createReadStream } from "node:fs";
import { stat } from "node:fs/promises";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";

createServer(async (request, response) => {
  try {
    const file = "./reports/annual.pdf";
    const { size } = await stat(file);

    response.writeHead(200, {
      "Content-Type": "application/pdf",
      "Content-Length": size,
    });
    await pipeline(createReadStream(file), response); // response is Writable
  } catch (error) {
    if (!response.headersSent) {
      response.writeHead(error.code === "ENOENT" ? 404 : 500);
      response.end();
    } else {
      response.destroy(error); // headers already sent: abort the connection
    }
  }
}).listen(3000);

If the client disconnects mid-download, pipeline destroys the file stream so the file handle is not leaked.

docs.title: Respecting backpressure manually
docs.text:
import { createWriteStream } from "node:fs";
import { once } from "node:events";

const out = createWriteStream("numbers.txt");

for (let i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
  if (!out.write(`${i}\n`)) {
    await once(out, "drain"); // wait instead of filling memory
  }
}
out.end();
await once(out, "finish");

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Stream large or unbounded data (files, exports, proxies, uploads) instead of buffering it.
  • Use pipeline from node:stream/promises, not bare pipe().
  • Always handle error events, or let pipeline/for await surface them.
  • Respect write()'s return value when writing manually.
  • Limit the total size of data you accept from clients, even when streaming.
  • Prefer Buffer.alloc over Buffer.allocUnsafe unless you fill the buffer immediately.
  • Use subarray deliberately and copy when you need independent data.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Memory climbs during downloads or exports.
  • Symptom: RSS grows by roughly the file size per concurrent request, and the container is killed for exceeding its memory limit.
  • Detect: memory graphs line up with traffic to the export endpoint, and heap snapshots show large Buffers or strings.
  • Cause: reading the whole file or result set before sending it.
  • Fix: stream from the source with pipeline(), and set Content-Length only when the size is known.
  • File handles leak when clients disconnect.
  • Symptom: EMFILE: too many open files after a while, especially with mobile clients.
  • Detect: open file descriptor counts rise in step with aborted requests.
  • Cause: readable.pipe(res) without error handling; when the client disconnects, the file stream is never closed.
  • Fix: use pipeline(), which destroys the other streams when one fails.
  • Corrupted text in uploads or logs.
  • Symptom: accented characters or emoji appear as � at random places.
  • Detect: the corruption falls on chunk boundaries, and small inputs are fine.
  • Cause: converting each chunk to a string separately, which splits a multi-byte UTF-8 character.
  • Fix: collect Buffers with Buffer.concat, or call stream.setEncoding("utf8"), which handles split characters.
  • Slow clients exhaust memory.
  • Symptom: a few slow consumers (WebSockets, slow mobile downloads) make memory grow without limit.
  • Detect: writable.writableLength (bytes buffered) keeps rising for some connections.
  • Cause: code ignores write() returning false and keeps writing.
  • Fix: wait for drain, or close connections whose buffer exceeds a limit.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Buffer: A fixed-size chunk of binary data; a Uint8Array subclass.
  • Encoding: A scheme mapping bytes to text, such as UTF-8 or Base64.
  • Stream: An object that delivers or accepts data incrementally.
  • Readable / Writable / Duplex / Transform: The four stream types.
  • Chunk: One piece of data delivered by a stream.
  • Backpressure: Slowing a producer when the consumer cannot keep up.
  • highWaterMark: The buffer size at which a stream signals backpressure.
  • pipeline: A utility that connects streams with error propagation and cleanup.
  • Object mode: A stream mode where chunks are arbitrary JavaScript values.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using pipe() without error handling, leaking file handles and sockets when a step fails.
  • Ignoring write() returning false, letting memory grow without limit.
  • Converting binary data to strings (for example, concatenating chunks with +=), which corrupts multi-byte characters split across chunks. Use Buffer.concat or set an encoding on the stream.
  • Assuming one data event equals one message. Chunk boundaries are arbitrary; a JSON object or line may span several chunks.
  • "Base64 protects data." It is only an encoding.
  • Forgetting that subarray shares memory.

docs.text:

  3. What is backpressure, and which signals implement it?
  4. Why is pipeline preferred over pipe?
  5. What is the difference between Buffer.alloc and Buffer.allocUnsafe?
  6. Why can't you assume each data event contains a complete line?

docs.title: Errors, Debugging, and Performance
docs.text: Every backend fails sometimes: a file is missing, a database refuses a connection, a bug reads a property of undefined. This page covers how errors work in Node.js, how to tell expected failures from bugs, what to do with errors nobody caught, and how to debug, profile, and find memory leaks in a running Node.js process.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: How a service handles errors decides whether a failure becomes a clear 503 response and a useful log entry, or a silent hang, a crashed process, or corrupted data. When a server is slow or its memory keeps growing, profiling tools turn guesswork into evidence. These skills separate code that works on a laptop from code that survives production. HTTP-level error responses are covered in error handling in Express and the general concept in error handling.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix tracked down steadily rising latency on its Node.js website by recording CPU profiles and drawing them as flame graphs. The graphs showed most of the time inside Express's routing code, which led to the bug: a handler was registered over and over (Netflix Technology Blog: Node.js in Flames).
  • Sentry's Node.js SDK registers a handler, on by default, that captures uncaught exceptions which would make the process exit. It reports them and, by design, does not stop the process from exiting. This is the "log, report, exit" pattern on this page (Sentry docs: OnUncaughtException).
  • PM2 restarts an application automatically when it crashes or exits. It can back off between restarts with exponentially increasing delays, for example while a database is down, and can restart a process that passes a memory threshold such as --max-memory-restart 300M (PM2 docs: Restart strategies).

Popular tools and providers: Chrome DevTools and VS Code via --inspect; --cpu-prof and heap snapshots; Clinic.js; Sentry, Datadog, and New Relic for error tracking and APM; PM2, systemd, and Kubernetes for restarts.

docs.title: The Error object
docs.text:
const error = new Error("Order not found");
error.name;     // "Error"
error.message;  // "Order not found"
error.stack;    // "Error: Order not found\n    at findOrder (orders.js:12:11) ..."

Always throw Error objects (or subclasses), never strings: only Error objects carry a stack trace showing where the problem started.

docs.title: Built-in error types
docs.text: Type Thrown when Example TypeError A value is not the expected type undefined.toUpperCase() ReferenceError A variable does not exist console.log(usr) (typo) RangeError A number is outside an allowed range new Array(-1) SyntaxError Code or data cannot be parsed JSON.parse("{bad") AggregateError Several errors are grouped Promise.any when all reject

docs.title: System errors and error codes
docs.text:
Errors from the operating system and Node.js APIs carry a string code. Check error.code, not the message, because messages can change.

Code Meaning Typical cause ENOENT No such file or directory Wrong path, file deleted EACCES / EPERM Permission denied File permissions, privileged port EADDRINUSE Address already in use Another process uses the port ECONNREFUSED Connection refused Target service is down or the port is wrong ECONNRESET Connection reset by peer The other side closed the connection abruptly ETIMEDOUT Operation timed out Network problem, unresponsive host ENOTFOUND DNS lookup failed Wrong hostname EMFILE Too many open files File handles or sockets not closed

Node.js's own errors use codes beginning with ERR_, such as ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT or ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND.

docs.title: Adding context with cause
docs.text:
When you catch an error and throw a new one with more context, attach the original with the cause option so nothing is lost:

try {
  await db.query("SELECT ...");
} catch (error) {
  throw new Error("Failed to load customer report", { cause: error });
}

Logging the new error shows both messages and both stack traces.

docs.title: Custom error classes
docs.text:
Subclasses let code recognize error categories and carry extra data such as an HTTP status:

export class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, { statusCode = 500, code, cause } = {}) {
    super(message, { cause });
    this.name = this.constructor.name;
    this.statusCode = statusCode;
    this.code = code;
  }
}

export class NotFoundError extends AppError {
  constructor(resource) {
    super(`${resource} not found`, { statusCode: 404, code: "NOT_FOUND" });
  }
}

throw new NotFoundError("Order"); // error instanceof AppError === true

docs.title: Operational errors versus programmer errors
docs.text:
Operational errors Programmer errors (bugs) Expected failures in a correct program Mistakes in the code Invalid user input, missing file, database down, upstream timeout, duplicate key Reading a property of undefined, calling a function with wrong arguments, forgetting await Handle them: retry, return a 4xx/5xx response, use a fallback Fix the code. At runtime, log them and usually restart the process

A process that hit a bug may be in an unknown state (half-updated variables, leaked connections). Restarting is often safer than continuing.

docs.title: How errors propagate
docs.text:
• Synchronous code: a throw travels up the call stack until a try/catch handles it.
  • Promises and async functions: a throw becomes a rejection. It is handled by .catch() or by await inside try/catch.
  • Callbacks: errors arrive as the first callback argument; a throw inside a callback is not caught by a try around the original call, because that call returned long ago.
  • Event emitters and streams: errors arrive as error events.
try {
  setTimeout(() => {
    throw new Error("boom"); // NOT caught below: runs later, on a new stack
  }, 0);
} catch (error) {
  console.log("never runs");
}

docs.title: Uncaught exceptions and unhandled rejections
docs.text:
If an error escapes every handler:

  • An uncaught exception makes Node.js print the stack trace and exit with code 1.
  • An unhandled rejection (a rejected promise nobody handled) is, by default, treated the same way: it is raised as an uncaught exception and the process exits.

You can listen for both on process, but only to log and exit:

process.on("uncaughtException", (error) => {
  console.error("Uncaught exception:", error);
  process.exit(1); // state may be corrupt: let the process manager restart us
});

process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason) => {
  console.error("Unhandled rejection:", reason);
  process.exit(1);
});

Do not use these handlers to keep running as if nothing happened. Pair them with a process manager or orchestrator (PM2, systemd, Docker, Kubernetes) that restarts the process automatically, and send the error to your monitoring system.

docs.title: Debugging with the inspector
docs.text:
Node.js includes a debugger based on the Chrome DevTools protocol.

node --inspect server.js        # start normally, debugger listens on 127.0.0.1:9229
node --inspect-brk server.js    # pause on the first line, wait for the debugger
node --inspect --watch server.js

Then attach:

  • Chrome: open chrome://inspect and click "inspect" under your target.
  • VS Code: use the JavaScript Debug Terminal, or a launch configuration with "type": "node". Breakpoints, step-through, watch expressions, and the call stack all work.

You can also add a debugger; statement in code; execution pauses there when a debugger is attached.

Warning

Never expose the inspector port publicly. Anyone who can connect to it can run arbitrary code in your process. Keep it bound to 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: Console and util.inspect
docs.text:
Method Use console.log / console.error Output to stdout / stderr. console.table(rows) Print arrays of objects as a table. console.time(label) / console.timeEnd(label) Measure elapsed time. console.trace(message) Print a stack trace without throwing. console.dir(obj, { depth: null }) Print nested objects fully. util.inspect(obj, { depth: null, colors: true }) Format any value as a readable string.

For production logging, use a structured logger (see logging and monitoring).

docs.title: CPU profiling
docs.text:
When requests are slow and the event loop delay is high, find out which functions use the CPU:

node --cpu-prof server.js   # writes a .cpuprofile file when the process exits

Open the file in Chrome DevTools (Performance panel) or VS Code to see a flame chart. You can also record a profile live from the inspector's Performance tab. Community tools such as Clinic.js build on these capabilities.

docs.title: Memory: heap, garbage collection, and leaks
docs.text:
V8 stores objects on the heap and frees unreachable objects with the garbage collector (GC). A memory leak happens when objects stay reachable even though the program no longer needs them, so the GC cannot free them. Memory then grows until the process slows down from constant GC or crashes with FATAL ERROR: ... JavaScript heap out of memory.

Common causes in servers:

  • Global or module-level collections that only grow, such as a Map used as a cache with no size limit or expiry.
  • Event listeners added per request to long-lived emitters and never removed.
  • Timers and intervals that are never cleared and keep closures alive.
  • Closures capturing large objects longer than needed.
  • Unclosed resources: sockets, streams, database cursors.

Finding leaks:

  1. Watch process.memoryUsage().heapUsed (or your monitoring dashboards) over time. A sawtooth that keeps rising is suspicious.
  2. Take heap snapshots a few minutes apart—from the inspector's Memory tab, with v8.writeHeapSnapshot(), or by starting Node.js with --heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2 and sending that signal.
  3. Compare the snapshots in Chrome DevTools to see which object types keep growing, and follow their retainers to the code holding them.

The --max-old-space-size=<megabytes> flag changes the heap limit. Raise it when a workload legitimately needs more memory, but never as a fix for a leak; a leak eventually fills any limit.

docs.title: Measuring performance in code
docs.text:
import { performance } from "node:perf_hooks";

performance.mark("query-start");
await runQuery();
performance.mark("query-end");
performance.measure("query", "query-start", "query-end");

const [entry] = performance.getEntriesByName("query");
console.log(`query took ${entry.duration.toFixed(1)} ms`);

performance.now() gives a high-resolution timestamp for quick measurements. For event loop health, see monitorEventLoopDelay.

docs.title: Diagnostic reports
docs.text:
A diagnostic report is a JSON summary of a process's state: JavaScript and native stack traces, heap statistics, resource usage, environment, and loaded libraries. Generate one on a crash or on demand:

node --report-on-fatalerror --report-uncaught-exception server.js

process.report.writeReport(); // writes a report file now

Reports are useful when a process crashes in production and you cannot attach a debugger. On Node.js 22, process.report.writeReport() printed Writing Node.js report to file: report.<date>.<time>.<pid>.0.001.json and saved the file in the working directory.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Use the inspector (--inspect) locally and in staging to step through code. In production, use it only through a secure tunnel, briefly.
  • Use CPU profiles when latency or CPU is high and event loop delay rises; they show which functions burn time.
  • Use heap snapshots when memory grows steadily over hours; take two or three apart and compare them.
  • Use diagnostic reports for crashes you cannot reproduce, and for native or resource problems.
  • Use structured logs and error tracking for everything else; they are always on, unlike the tools above.
  • Do not profile blindly in production at full traffic. Writing a heap snapshot is synchronous and blocks the event loop, and it needs about twice the heap's size in memory, which can get the process OOM-killed. Profiling also slows the process. Take them from one instance that has been removed from the load balancer.
Problem First tool Then A bug you can reproduce Inspector + breakpoints A test that reproduces it Slow requests, high CPU --cpu-prof / flame graph Optimise the hottest frames Memory grows until crash Heap snapshots compared Fix the retainer, bound caches Crash with no clue Diagnostic report + error tracker Add logging around the failing path Errors in production Error tracker (with stack traces) Group, triage, fix

docs.title: Handling a specific system error
docs.text:
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const server = createServer((request, response) => response.end("ok\n"));

server.on("error", (error) => {
  if (error.code === "EADDRINUSE") {
    console.error(`Port ${port} is already in use. Stop the other process or set PORT.`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
  throw error; // anything else is unexpected
});

server.listen(port);

docs.title: A bounded cache that cannot leak
docs.text:
const MAX_ENTRIES = 1000;
const cache = new Map();

export function remember(key, value) {
  if (cache.size >= MAX_ENTRIES) {
    const oldestKey = cache.keys().next().value; // Maps keep insertion order
    cache.delete(oldestKey);
  }
  cache.set(key, value);
}

For anything beyond simple cases, use a library with expiry (an LRU cache) or an external cache such as Redis; see caching.

docs.title: Logging memory usage periodically
docs.text:
setInterval(() => {
  const { rss, heapUsed, heapTotal } = process.memoryUsage();
  const mb = (bytes) => (bytes / 1024 / 1024).toFixed(1);
  console.log(`rss=${mb(rss)}MB heap=${mb(heapUsed)}/${mb(heapTotal)}MB`);
}, 30_000).unref();

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Throw Error objects, never strings; use cause to keep context.
  • Check error.code for system errors instead of matching messages.
  • Separate operational errors (handle and respond) from bugs (log, fix, and restart).
  • Log and exit on uncaughtException and unhandledRejection; let a process manager restart the service.
  • Never leave --inspect open to the network.
  • Profile before optimizing; measure, change one thing, measure again.
  • Bound every in-memory cache and remove listeners and timers you add.
  • Monitor memory, CPU, and event loop delay in production.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Restart loops after a dependency outage.
  • Symptom: when the database goes down, the app restarts dozens of times a minute and floods the database with reconnects when it returns.
  • Detect: restart counts spike with the dependency's outage, and the crash logs show ECONNREFUSED at startup.
  • Cause: the app exits on a connection error, and the process manager restarts it immediately.
  • Fix: retry the connection with backoff at startup, and use the process manager's backoff option (PM2 --exp-backoff-restart-delay, or Kubernetes' built-in CrashLoopBackOff).
  • Silent failures.
  • Symptom: customers report missing data, but there are no errors in the logs.
  • Detect: search the code for empty catch {} blocks and .catch(() => {}); compare business counts with expectations.
  • Cause: errors swallowed without logging.
  • Fix: log with context and rethrow, or handle deliberately, never both nothing and continue.
  • Out-of-memory crashes every few days.
  • Symptom: the process dies with a line ending in JavaScript heap out of memory, or the container is OOMKilled, at regular intervals.
  • Detect: heap usage after each garbage collection keeps rising in metrics; comparing snapshots shows one object type growing.
  • Cause: an unbounded cache, listeners added per request, or timers never cleared.
  • Fix: bound or expire caches, remove listeners, and add a heap-usage alert well before the limit.
  • "Error: [object Object]" in logs.
  • Symptom: logs show useless error messages with no stack trace.
  • Detect: the logged values are strings or plain objects, not Error instances.
  • Cause: code that throws strings or objects, or logging String(error) instead of the error itself.
  • Fix: always throw Error (or a subclass) with cause, and log the whole error so the stack is kept.
  • An exposed debugger.
  • Symptom: a security scan finds port 9229 open.
  • Detect: the process was started with --inspect=0.0.0.0 in a production command.
  • Cause: a debugging flag left in a deployment manifest.
  • Fix: remove it. Anyone who can connect can run code in your process.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Stack trace: The list of function calls active when an error was created.
  • Error code: A stable string such as ENOENT identifying an error type.
  • Operational error: An expected failure in correct code.
  • Programmer error: A bug in the code.
  • Uncaught exception: An error that escaped every handler.
  • Unhandled rejection: A rejected promise with no rejection handler.
  • Inspector: Node.js's built-in debugging interface.
  • CPU profile: A recording of where processing time is spent.
  • Heap snapshot: A dump of all objects in memory at one moment.
  • Memory leak: Memory that stays allocated because unneeded objects remain reachable.
  • Garbage collector: The engine component that frees unreachable objects.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Empty catch blocks that swallow errors and hide failures.
  • Keeping the process alive after uncaughtException.
  • "try/catch catches errors in callbacks." Only errors thrown synchronously in the try block, or awaited rejections.
  • Comparing error messages instead of codes or classes.
  • Raising --max-old-space-size to "fix" a leak.
  • Leaving console.log debugging statements in hot paths, which slows servers and can leak sensitive data.
  • Optimizing without profiling, often in the wrong place.

docs.text:
1. Why should you throw Error objects instead of strings?
  2. What is the difference between an operational error and a programmer error, and how should each be handled?
  3. What should a process do in an uncaughtException handler, and why?
  4. How do you attach Chrome DevTools to a Node.js process?
  5. Name four common causes of memory leaks in Node.js servers.
  6. How would you find which code is responsible for growing memory?

docs.title: The Node.js Event Loop
docs.text: The event loop is the mechanism that lets a single JavaScript thread handle many operations at once. It repeatedly checks for completed work—expired timers, finished I/O, closed sockets—and runs the matching callbacks one at a time. Understanding its phases explains callback ordering and why blocking code hurts every request.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Every Node.js server depends on the event loop staying free. If one callback runs for 200 ms, every other request waits 200 ms. Knowing the loop's phases and queues lets you predict the order in which code runs, debug "why did this run first?" puzzles, and keep latency low under load. For how the loop works in browsers, see event loop and concurrency; Node.js uses the same idea with different phases.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix saw request latency on its Node.js website rise steadily, by about 10 ms every hour, along with CPU use. CPU flame graphs showed time spent in Express's router. Something was adding the same static-file handler to the route array 10 times an hour, and every request walked the whole array on the main thread, at about 1 ms of CPU per extra handler (Netflix Technology Blog: Node.js in Flames).
  • Cloudflare suffered a global outage when a web-application-firewall rule contained a regular expression that "backtracked enormously" and exhausted the CPU used to serve HTTP traffic. That proxy is not Node.js, but the failure is the one this page calls ReDoS: one pathological regex starves everything else on the CPU (Cloudflare blog: Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019).
  • Trello chose Node.js because instant updates required holding a lot of open connections. An event loop serving non-blocking I/O handles many idle connections on one thread (Atlassian blog: The Trello tech stack).

Popular tools and providers: perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay and performance.eventLoopUtilization() built into Node.js; Clinic.js; flame graphs from --cpu-prof or Linux perf; APM agents that chart event loop lag.

docs.title: The call stack and the loop
docs.text:
JavaScript executes on a call stack. When a function is called, a frame is pushed; when it returns, the frame is popped. Node.js can run a new callback only when the stack is empty. The event loop's job is to choose the next callback once the current one finishes.

When you run node app.js, Node.js:

  1. Runs your main module synchronously from top to bottom.
  2. Drains the microtask queues (explained below).
  3. Enters the event loop and keeps looping while there is pending work: active timers, open servers or sockets, pending file operations, and so on.
  4. Exits when nothing is left that could produce a callback.

docs.title: The phases
docs.text:
Each iteration of the loop (a "tick") goes through these phases in order. Every phase has a queue of callbacks to run.

Phase What runs there timers Callbacks from setTimeout and setInterval whose delay has passed. A delay is a minimum, not a guarantee. pending callbacks Some system callbacks deferred from the previous iteration, such as certain TCP error reports. idle, prepare Used internally by Node.js. poll Retrieves new I/O events and runs their callbacks (incoming requests, socket data, completed file operations). If there is nothing else to do, the loop waits here for I/O, up to the time of the next timer. check Callbacks scheduled with setImmediate. They run right after the poll phase. close callbacks close events, such as a socket that was destroyed.

docs.title: Microtasks: process.nextTick and promises
docs.text:
Two special queues are not phases. They are drained after the current callback finishes and before the next one starts, in any phase:

  1. The process.nextTick queue is drained first.
  2. Then the Promise microtask queue (.then, .catch, .finally, code after await, and queueMicrotask) is drained.
  3. If either queue gains new items while draining, those also run before the loop moves on.
 [callback finishes] → run ALL nextTick callbacks → run ALL promise
                       microtasks → (repeat if new ones were added)
                       → next callback / next phase

Because these queues are drained completely, code that keeps adding new nextTick callbacks can starve the event loop: I/O and timers never get a turn. Prefer queueMicrotask or promises for ordinary deferral, and setImmediate when you want I/O to get a chance to run first.

Top-level code in ES modules

Inside callbacks, process.nextTick callbacks run before promise callbacks. At the top level of an ES module, the module itself is evaluated as part of a promise job, so promise callbacks can run before nextTick callbacks there. Do not write code that depends on the relative order of these two queues.

docs.title: setTimeout(fn, 0) versus setImmediate(fn)
docs.text:
• setTimeout(fn, 0) schedules fn for the timers phase once at least 1 ms has passed (a delay of 0 is treated as 1 ms).
  • setImmediate(fn) schedules fn for the check phase of the current or next iteration.

From the main module, their order is not deterministic: it depends on whether 1 ms has already passed when the loop first reaches the timers phase. Inside an I/O callback (which runs in the poll phase), the order is always setImmediate first, because the check phase comes right after poll.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Keep work on the event loop when:

  • It is mostly waiting: database queries, HTTP calls, and file reads through async APIs.
  • Each callback finishes quickly (a few milliseconds at most).

Take work off the event loop when:

  • A single call computes for tens of milliseconds or more: hashing, image processing, large JSON, compression of big payloads.
  • The input size is controlled by users (a regex on user text, parsing an uploaded file).

Choosing a scheduling primitive:

Primitive Runs Use it for Avoid when process.nextTick(fn) Before any other queued work, right after the current operation Emitting an event after the caller has attached listeners Recursion or loops; it can starve I/O queueMicrotask(fn) / promise.then After the nextTick queue, before the next callback Ordinary "do this right after" deferral Long chains of CPU work; they also starve I/O setImmediate(fn) Check phase, after pending I/O callbacks Yielding inside long loops so I/O can run Precise timing setTimeout(fn, ms) Timers phase, at least ms later Delays and timeouts Yielding (adds at least 1 ms each time) Worker thread Another thread with its own loop CPU-heavy work Simple I/O; workers cost memory and startup time

docs.title: Predicting the order inside a callback
docs.text:
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("A: timer callback starts");

  setTimeout(() => console.log("F: timeout (next timers phase)"), 0);
  setImmediate(() => console.log("E: immediate (check phase)"));
  Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("D: promise microtask"));
  process.nextTick(() => console.log("C: nextTick"));

  console.log("B: timer callback ends");
}, 0);

Output:

A: timer callback starts
B: timer callback ends
C: nextTick
D: promise microtask
E: immediate (check phase)
F: timeout (next timers phase)
  1. A and B are synchronous.
  2. When the callback returns, the nextTick queue runs (C), then promise microtasks (D).
  3. The loop moves from timers to check and runs E.
  4. The new timer runs in the next iteration's timers phase (F).

docs.title: Deterministic setImmediate inside I/O
docs.text:
import { readFile } from "node:fs";

readFile(new URL(import.meta.url), () => {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("timeout"), 0);
  setImmediate(() => console.log("immediate"));
});

Always prints:

immediate
timeout

docs.title: Microtasks scheduled by microtasks
docs.text:
setTimeout(() => {
  Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("promise 1");
    process.nextTick(() => console.log("nextTick added by promise"));
  });
  Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("promise 2"));
}, 0);

promise 1
promise 2
nextTick added by promise

The promise queue finishes draining, then Node.js checks the nextTick queue again before moving on.

docs.title: Blocking the loop
docs.text:
Anything synchronous and slow blocks every other callback:

  • A long for or while loop over a large dataset.
  • Synchronous crypto such as crypto.pbkdf2Sync or bcrypt.hashSync.
  • JSON.parse or JSON.stringify on very large payloads (many megabytes).
  • Catastrophic regex backtracking, where a badly written pattern takes exponential time on certain inputs:
const evil = /^(a+)+$/;
const input = "a".repeat(24) + "!";
console.time("regex");
evil.test(input); // nested quantifiers backtrack: every extra "a" roughly doubles the time
console.timeEnd("regex");

On Node.js 22 this took about 1.5 seconds for 24 characters and about 8 seconds for 26. At 30 characters it would take minutes, and the whole process is frozen the entire time.

This is called ReDoS (regular expression denial of service) when an attacker controls the input. Avoid nested quantifiers on user input, limit input length, and test patterns.

docs.title: Splitting long work into chunks
docs.text:
If you must do CPU work on the main thread, process it in chunks and yield to the loop between them with setImmediate:

import { setImmediate as nextIteration } from "node:timers/promises";

async function sumLargeArray(numbers) {
  let total = 0;
  const chunkSize = 10_000;

  for (let i = 0; i < numbers.length; i += chunkSize) {
    for (let j = i; j < Math.min(i + chunkSize, numbers.length); j++) {
      total += numbers[j];
    }
    await nextIteration(); // let pending I/O and timers run
  }
  return total;
}

For truly heavy computation, use worker threads instead.

docs.title: Measuring event loop delay
docs.text:
perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay samples how late the loop is compared with when it should have run. High values mean something is blocking.

import { monitorEventLoopDelay } from "node:perf_hooks";

const histogram = monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 20 });
histogram.enable();

setInterval(() => {
  // Values are in nanoseconds; convert to milliseconds.
  const p99 = histogram.percentile(99) / 1e6;
  const max = histogram.max / 1e6;
  console.log(`loop delay p99=${p99.toFixed(1)}ms max=${max.toFixed(1)}ms`);
  histogram.reset();
}, 5000);

The numbers never drop to zero. The histogram is updated by a timer at the configured resolution (10 ms by default), so even an idle process reports a baseline near that interval, plus the operating system's timer granularity. On an idle Node.js 22 process on Windows, the default resolution gave a p50 of about 16 ms. Record your own baseline, and investigate with a CPU profile when values rise well above it and stay there (see errors, debugging, and performance). performance.eventLoopUtilization() is a complementary metric: the share of time the loop spent busy rather than idle.

docs.title: When the process exits
docs.text:
A process stays alive while it has referenced handles: a listening server, an active timer, an open socket. timer.unref() tells Node.js not to keep the process alive just for that timer:

const heartbeat = setInterval(() => console.log("still here"), 1000);
heartbeat.unref(); // process can exit even though the interval exists

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep each callback short. Aim for request handlers that spend most of their time awaiting I/O, not computing.
  • Never call synchronous file, crypto, or compression APIs inside request handlers.
  • Limit the size of request bodies and JSON payloads you parse.
  • Move CPU-heavy work to worker threads or a separate service.
  • Monitor event loop delay and alert on sustained increases.
  • Use setImmediate to yield during long-running loops; avoid recursive process.nextTick.
  • Treat timer delays as minimums; never rely on exact timing.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Latency grows slowly over hours.
  • Symptom: p50 and p99 latency rise steadily and reset after a restart, with CPU climbing in step.
  • Detect: a CPU flame graph shows time growing in one code path, such as a router or a cache loop, not in I/O waits.
  • Cause: a per-request loop over a structure that keeps growing, such as handlers or listeners added again and again (Netflix's case above).
  • Fix: find what keeps registering, register it once at startup, and add a test or a size metric for that structure.
  • One request freezes the server.
  • Symptom: every endpoint stalls for seconds at the same moment, and health checks fail.
  • Detect: event loop delay spikes in metrics. A CPU profile from that moment shows a regex, JSON.parse, or a *Sync call.
  • Cause: unbounded synchronous work on user input, such as a backtracking regex or a huge JSON body.
  • Fix: limit input sizes, rewrite the regex without nested quantifiers, and move parsing of large payloads to a worker thread.
  • Health checks fail under load although the app is "up".
  • Symptom: the orchestrator kills instances during traffic peaks, and restarts make it worse.
  • Detect: the liveness probe's timeout matches spikes in event loop delay or utilization near 1.
  • Cause: the probe handler waits in the same queue as slow callbacks.
  • Fix: remove the CPU-heavy work, scale out, and give liveness probes a realistic timeout. Shedding load (returning 503) is better than being restarted.
  • Timers fire late.
  • Symptom: scheduled jobs, timeouts, or rate-limit windows run late or drift.
  • Detect: log the expected and actual run time of each timer; compare with event loop delay.
  • Cause: timers run only when the loop reaches the timers phase; long callbacks delay them.
  • Fix: keep callbacks short, and never treat setTimeout as precise scheduling.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Event loop: The loop that picks the next callback to run when the call stack is empty.
  • Phase: One stage of a loop iteration with its own callback queue (timers, poll, check, and so on).
  • Call stack: The stack of currently executing function frames.
  • Microtask: A callback in the nextTick or Promise queue, run between every macrotask callback.
  • Macrotask: A callback run by a loop phase, such as a timer, I/O, or setImmediate callback.
  • Blocking: Synchronous work that prevents the loop from running other callbacks.
  • Starvation: When one queue keeps refilling so other work never runs.
  • Event loop delay (lag): How late callbacks run compared with when they were scheduled.
  • ReDoS: Denial of service caused by a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "setTimeout(fn, 0) runs immediately." It runs no sooner than about 1 ms later, and only after the current callback and all microtasks finish.
  • "setImmediate runs immediately." It runs in the check phase, after the poll phase; process.nextTick runs sooner despite its name.
  • "Async code can't block." An async function still blocks while it runs synchronous code between awaits.
  • "The event loop is a separate thread." The loop runs on the main thread; while your callback runs, the loop is not running.
  • Recursive process.nextTick for "async recursion". It starves I/O.
  • Relying on the order between nextTick and promise callbacks at the top level of a module.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. List the event loop phases in order and what runs in each.
  2. When are the nextTick and Promise microtask queues drained?
  3. Why is the order of setTimeout(fn, 0) and setImmediate(fn) unpredictable in the main module but predictable inside an I/O callback?
  4. Give three examples of code that blocks the event loop.
  5. How would you detect, in production, that the event loop is being blocked?
  6. What is starvation, and how can process.nextTick cause it?
