docs.title: Events and EventEmitter
docs.text: Many Node.js objects announce that something happened—a request arrived, a chunk of data is ready, a connection closed—by emitting named events. The EventEmitter class in node:events is the foundation for this. You register listener functions for an event name, and the emitter calls them when it emits that event.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Servers, streams, sockets, child processes, and the process object itself are all event emitters. Using them correctly means knowing when listeners run, how errors are reported, and how to avoid memory leaks from listeners that are never removed. You can also use EventEmitter to decouple parts of your own application.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• node-redis, the official Redis client, reports connection problems through an error event. Its README warns that you must listen to it: without a listener, the error is thrown and the Node.js process exits. A brief network blip can therefore crash an app that never added the listener (node-redis README).
  • Mongoose connections inherit from EventEmitter and emit connecting, connected, disconnected, and other events when connectivity to MongoDB changes. Applications listen to these to log outages and report health (Mongoose docs: Connection events).
  • BullMQ job workers emit completed, progress, and failed events. Applications attach listeners for logging and metrics without touching the job code (BullMQ docs: Workers).

Popular tools and providers: node:events itself; client libraries for Redis, MongoDB, and queues that expose connection and job events; ws and Socket.IO for event-based real-time messaging.

docs.title: The observer pattern
docs.text: EventEmitter implements the observer pattern (also called publish/subscribe within one process): one object emits events, and any number of listeners react to them without the emitter knowing who they are.

docs.title: Core methods
docs.text: Method What it does on(name, listener) / addListener Adds a listener that runs every time the event is emitted. once(name, listener) Adds a listener that runs once, then removes itself. off(name, listener) / removeListener Removes a specific listener (you need the same function reference). removeAllListeners([name]) Removes all listeners, optionally for one event. emit(name, ...args) Calls each listener with args; returns true if there were listeners. prependListener(name, listener) Adds a listener to the front of the list. prependOnceListener(name, listener) Like prependListener, but runs once. listenerCount(name) Number of listeners for an event. eventNames() Names of events that have listeners. setMaxListeners(n) Changes the leak-warning threshold for this emitter.

docs.title: Listeners run synchronously, in order
docs.text:
emit() calls every listener synchronously, in the order they were added, before emit() returns. It does not schedule them for later.

import { EventEmitter } from "node:events";

const emitter = new EventEmitter();
emitter.on("ping", () => console.log("listener 1"));
emitter.on("ping", () => console.log("listener 2"));

console.log("before emit");
emitter.emit("ping");
console.log("after emit");

before emit
listener 1
listener 2
after emit

If a listener throws, the exception propagates out of emit() and later listeners do not run. A listener that needs to do slow work should start asynchronous work rather than block.

Inside a regular function listener, this refers to the emitter. Arrow function listeners do not get their own this.

docs.title: The special error event
docs.text:
The event name "error" has special behavior. If an emitter emits "error" and no listener is registered, Node.js throws the error. In a server, that usually crashes the process.

const emitter = new EventEmitter();
emitter.emit("error", new Error("boom")); // throws the error itself

Run as a script, Node.js prints throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event, then Error: boom with its stack trace, and exits with code 1.

Always attach an error listener to emitters that can fail—streams, sockets, servers, and child processes:

emitter.on("error", (error) => {
  console.error("Emitter failed:", error.message);
});

docs.title: Memory leaks and the max-listeners warning
docs.text:
Every listener is a reference that keeps its function (and anything it closes over) in memory as long as the emitter exists. Adding a listener on every request to a long-lived emitter, and never removing it, is a classic memory leak.

To help catch this, Node.js prints a warning when more than 10 listeners are added for the same event on one emitter:

(node:24884) MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak
detected. 11 request listeners added to [EventEmitter]. MaxListeners is 10.
Use emitter.setMaxListeners() to increase limit

The number after node: is the process ID. Run with --trace-warnings to also print the stack trace of the line that added the eleventh listener.

The warning does not stop anything; it is a hint. If many listeners are legitimate, raise the limit with emitter.setMaxListeners(n). If not, find where listeners are added and remove them with off() or use once().

docs.title: Promise and async-iterator helpers
docs.text:
node:events provides helpers that connect events to async/await:

  • events.once(emitter, name) returns a promise that fulfills with an array of the event's arguments the next time it is emitted. It rejects if the emitter emits "error" first.
  • events.on(emitter, name) returns an async iterator that yields each emission's arguments.
import { once } from "node:events";
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const server = createServer((req, res) => res.end("ok"));
server.listen(3000);
await once(server, "listening"); // wait until the server is ready
console.log("Server is listening");

Both accept an AbortSignal so you can stop waiting.

docs.title: Extending EventEmitter
docs.text:
Your own classes can extend EventEmitter to emit domain events:

import { EventEmitter } from "node:events";

class Job extends EventEmitter {
  async run() {
    this.emit("start");
    try {
      for (let percent = 25; percent <= 100; percent += 25) {
        await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
        this.emit("progress", percent);
      }
      this.emit("done");
    } catch (error) {
      this.emit("error", error);
    }
  }
}

const job = new Job();
job.on("progress", (percent) => console.log(`${percent}%`));
job.once("done", () => console.log("Job finished"));
job.on("error", (error) => console.error(error));
job.run();

docs.title: EventTarget in Node.js
docs.text: Node.js also implements the web-standard EventTarget and Event classes used in browsers. APIs that follow web standards, such as AbortSignal, use EventTarget with addEventListener. The main differences: EventTarget listeners receive an Event object, there is no special "error" behavior, and adding the same listener twice has no effect. Node.js core modules mostly use EventEmitter.

docs.title: Where Node.js uses events
docs.text: Object Example events http.Server request, connection, listening, close, error http.IncomingMessage (request) data, end, close, error net.Socket connect, data, end, timeout, close, error Readable streams data, end, readable, close, error Writable streams drain, finish, close, error process exit, beforeExit, uncaughtException, unhandledRejection, SIGINT, SIGTERM, warning ChildProcess spawn, exit, close, error, message

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use EventEmitter when:

  • Something happens many times and several independent parts may want to react: connection state changes, progress updates, data arriving.
  • You want to keep a module free of knowledge about who reacts to it, such as audit logging or metrics on domain events within one process.
  • You build a low-level object (a client, a parser) that follows Node.js conventions.

Do not use it when:

  • There is exactly one result: return a promise instead.
  • The work must happen reliably or on another server: use a message queue or background job; in-memory events vanish on a crash.
  • You need ordered, flow-controlled data: use a stream, which adds backpressure on top of events.
  • Code must also run in browsers: prefer EventTarget.
Need Use Why One async result Promise / async function Settles once, works with await and try/catch Many notifications, same process EventEmitter Any number of listeners, synchronous delivery A flow of data with backpressure Stream Pauses the producer when the consumer is slow Work that must not be lost Message queue or job queue Survives restarts; other servers can consume it Browser-compatible events EventTarget Web standard; same API in browsers

docs.title: Decoupling side effects
docs.text:
import { EventEmitter } from "node:events";

export const appEvents = new EventEmitter();

// orders.js
export async function createOrder(data) {
  const order = await saveOrder(data);
  appEvents.emit("order:created", order); // the service doesn't know who listens
  return order;
}

// listeners.js
appEvents.on("order:created", (order) => {
  sendConfirmationEmail(order).catch((error) => {
    console.error("Email failed", error); // handle async errors inside the listener
  });
});

In-process events are not a message queue

Events emitted this way live only in memory. If the process crashes before a listener finishes, the work is lost, and other server instances never see the event. For work that must happen reliably, use a message queue or background jobs.

docs.title: Removing a listener correctly
docs.text:
function onData(chunk) {
  console.log("received", chunk.length);
}

socket.on("data", onData);
// later
socket.off("data", onData); // works: same function reference

socket.on("data", (chunk) => console.log(chunk.length));
socket.off("data", (chunk) => console.log(chunk.length)); // does nothing:
// a new arrow function is a different reference

docs.title: Waiting for an event with a timeout
docs.text:
import { once } from "node:events";

try {
  const [message] = await once(worker, "message", {
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000),
  });
  console.log("Worker replied:", message);
} catch (error) {
  console.error("No reply within 5 s or worker failed:", error.message);
}

On timeout, once() rejects with an AbortError ("The operation was aborted"), not the TimeoutError that fetch uses. The timer behind AbortSignal.timeout() does not keep the process alive by itself. Here the worker keeps it alive, but in a script with nothing else running, Node.js can exit before the timeout ever fires.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Always register an error listener on emitters that can fail.
  • Use once() for one-time events such as ready or listening.
  • Remove listeners you add for a temporary purpose, especially on long-lived emitters; keep a reference to the function so you can.
  • Handle errors inside async listeners; a rejected promise from a listener is not caught by emit().
  • Use clear, namespaced event names such as order:created.
  • Prefer events.once() with an AbortSignal over hand-written promise wrappers.
  • Use a queue, not in-memory events, for work that must survive restarts or span multiple servers.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A dependency hiccup crashes the process.
  • Symptom: a short Redis or database network blip is followed by every instance restarting.
  • Detect: crash logs show Unhandled 'error' event followed by an error from the client library, such as a connection reset.
  • Cause: no error listener on the client, socket, or stream.
  • Fix: attach an error listener to every client and stream you create, log the error, and let the library reconnect.
  • Memory grows with traffic.
  • Symptom: heap usage rises steadily, and MaxListenersExceededWarning appears in the logs.
  • Detect: emitter.listenerCount(name) reported in a metric keeps rising, and heap snapshots show many copies of the same closure.
  • Cause: a listener added to a long-lived emitter (the process, a database client) on every request and never removed.
  • Fix: use once(), or remove the listener with off() when the request ends. Never "fix" it with setMaxListeners(0).
  • One listener breaks a request.
  • Symptom: a request fails with an error from analytics code, unrelated to its own logic.
  • Detect: the stack trace shows the error thrown inside emit().
  • Cause: listeners run synchronously; a throw in one propagates to the code that called emit() and skips the remaining listeners.
  • Fix: wrap listener bodies in try/catch, and push slow or risky work to a queue.
  • Side effects lost on deploy.
  • Symptom: some customers never receive confirmation emails, usually around deploys.
  • Detect: the count of order:created events in logs is higher than the count of emails sent.
  • Cause: the email was triggered by an in-memory event, and the process was stopped before the listener finished.
  • Fix: write the work to a durable queue (or an outbox table) in the same flow that creates the order.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Event emitter: An object that emits named events and calls registered listeners.
  • Listener (handler): A function called when an event is emitted.
  • Emit: To trigger an event and call its listeners with arguments.
  • Observer pattern: A design where subscribers react to events from a subject without tight coupling.
  • error event: A special event that throws if no listener exists.
  • MaxListenersExceededWarning: A warning that suggests a possible listener leak.
  • EventTarget: The web-standard event interface, also available in Node.js.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "emit() is asynchronous." Listeners run synchronously before emit() returns.
  • Forgetting the error listener, causing a crash on the first failure.
  • Adding listeners inside request handlers to a shared emitter without removing them.
  • Trying to remove an anonymous function with off().
  • Silencing the max-listeners warning with setMaxListeners(0) instead of fixing the leak.
  • Using in-process events for durable work that must not be lost.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between on, once, and prependListener?
  2. Are listeners called synchronously or asynchronously? What happens if one throws?
  3. Why is the error event special?
  4. What does the max-listeners warning tell you, and how should you respond?
  5. How do events.once() and events.on() help with async code?
  6. Why are in-process events unsuitable for work that must not be lost?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Node.js API: Events
  • Node.js: The Node.js event emitter
  • MDN: EventTarget

docs.title: File System, Path, and OS Modules
docs.text: The node:fs module reads and writes files and folders, node:path builds and inspects file paths safely across operating systems, and node:os reports information about the machine. Together they let a backend load configuration, write logs and exports, process uploads, and inspect its environment.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: File access looks simple but hides real problems: blocking the event loop with synchronous calls, running out of memory by reading huge files at once, breaking on Windows because of hard-coded / separators, and—most seriously—path traversal vulnerabilities that let a user read any file on the server. Knowing the right API for each job prevents all of these.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Node.js itself shipped a security fix in July 2025 for CVE-2025-27210: on Windows, device names such as CON, PRN, and AUX could bypass path-traversal protection in path.normalize() and path.join(). It was an incomplete fix for an earlier CVE. Path handling is subtle enough that even the runtime gets it wrong, which is why you must keep Node.js patched and validate resolved paths yourself (Node.js blog: July 2025 security releases).
  • Heroku gives each dyno an ephemeral filesystem: files written are not visible to other dynos and are discarded when the dyno stops or restarts, including automatic restarts (Heroku Dev Center: Dynos).
  • Kubernetes documents that on-disk files in a container are ephemeral: when a container crashes or is stopped, every file it created or changed is lost (Kubernetes docs: Volumes).
  • AWS Lambda gives each execution environment a private /tmp directory of 512 MB to 10,240 MB. It is fine for scratch files during one invocation, not for data you need later (AWS Lambda docs: Configure ephemeral storage).

Popular tools and providers: node:fs, node:path, and node:os; chokidar for cross-platform file watching in dev tools; object storage such as Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage for durable files.

docs.title: Three API styles
docs.text:
node:fs offers the same operations in three styles:

Style Example Blocks the event loop? When to use Promise await fs.readFile(path) from node:fs/promises No Default choice in modern code Callback fs.readFile(path, callback) from node:fs No Older code and APIs Synchronous fs.readFileSync(path) Yes Startup scripts, CLIs, one-time configuration loading

Synchronous calls are acceptable before a server starts accepting requests (for example, reading a certificate at startup). Inside request handlers they block every other request while the disk responds. File operations in the promise and callback styles run on libuv's thread pool (see runtime and architecture).

docs.title: Reading and writing whole files
docs.text:
import fs from "node:fs/promises";

const text = await fs.readFile("notes.txt", "utf8");  // string
const bytes = await fs.readFile("logo.png");          // Buffer (no encoding)

await fs.writeFile("out.txt", "Hello\n");             // create or replace
await fs.appendFile("app.log", "started\n");          // add to the end
await fs.writeFile("data.json", JSON.stringify(data, null, 2));

writeFile replaces the file by default. The flag option changes this:

Flag Meaning "w" Write; create or truncate (default for writeFile). "a" Append; create if missing (default for appendFile). "wx" Write, but fail if the file exists (EEXIST). Useful to avoid overwriting. "r" Read; fail if missing (default for readFile). "r+" Read and write; fail if missing. 
await fs.writeFile("report.csv", csv, { flag: "wx" }); // never overwrite

docs.title: Working with folders
docs.text:
await fs.mkdir("exports/2026/11", { recursive: true }); // create parents too

const names = await fs.readdir("uploads");               // ["a.pdf", "img"]

const entries = await fs.readdir("uploads", { withFileTypes: true });
for (const entry of entries) {
  console.log(entry.name, entry.isDirectory() ? "dir" : "file");
}

await fs.rm("tmp", { recursive: true, force: true }); // delete a folder tree

{ recursive: true } on mkdir does not fail if the folder already exists. force: true on rm ignores a missing path.

docs.title: Metadata, moving, and copying
docs.text:
const info = await fs.stat("video.mp4");
console.log(info.size);          // bytes
console.log(info.isFile());      // true
console.log(info.mtime);         // last modified (Date)

await fs.rename("upload.tmp", "upload.pdf"); // move or rename (same volume)
await fs.copyFile("template.html", "page.html");
await fs.unlink("old.log");                  // delete a file

fs.lstat describes a symbolic link itself rather than the file it points to.

docs.title: Checking whether a file exists
docs.text:
A tempting pattern is "check, then act":

// Race-prone: the file can disappear between access() and readFile()
await fs.access(file);
const data = await fs.readFile(file);

Between the check and the action another process may delete or create the file. This is a TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) race. Instead, just perform the operation and handle the error:

try {
  const data = await fs.readFile(file, "utf8");
} catch (error) {
  if (error.code === "ENOENT") {
    // file does not exist
  } else {
    throw error;
  }
}

Common error codes: ENOENT (no such file or folder), EEXIST (already exists), EACCES/EPERM (permission denied), EISDIR (expected a file, got a folder), ENOTDIR, EMFILE (too many open files).

docs.title: File handles
docs.text:
fs.open() returns a FileHandle for repeated reads or writes on one file. Always close it, ideally in finally:

const handle = await fs.open("big.log", "r");
try {
  const buffer = Buffer.alloc(100);
  const { bytesRead } = await handle.read(buffer, 0, 100, 0); // first 100 bytes
  console.log(buffer.subarray(0, bytesRead).toString("utf8"));
} finally {
  await handle.close();
}

Forgetting to close handles eventually causes EMFILE errors.

docs.title: Watching files
docs.text: fs.watch() reports changes to a file or folder. It is useful for development tools, but its behavior varies by platform: events can be duplicated, file names may be missing, and recursive watching support depends on the OS and Node.js version. For production workflows, prefer explicit triggers (a queue message, an upload callback) over file watching.

docs.title: Large files: use streams
docs.text:
readFile loads the whole file into memory: a 1 GB file needs at least 1 GB of RAM for every request that reads it at the same time. Files larger than 2 GiB fail outright with ERR_FS_FILE_TOO_LARGE. For large files, stream them in chunks:

import { createReadStream } from "node:fs";
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

const hash = createHash("sha256");
for await (const chunk of createReadStream("backup.tar")) {
  hash.update(chunk); // one chunk at a time; memory use stays small
}
console.log(hash.digest("hex"));

See buffers and streams.

docs.title: The path module
docs.text:
Never build paths by joining strings with /. Windows uses \ and drive letters, and string joining mishandles extra or missing separators.

import path from "node:path";

path.join("uploads", "2026", "file.pdf");  // uploads/2026/file.pdf (\ on Windows)
path.join("/a/b", "../c");                 // /a/c   (normalizes ..)
path.resolve("uploads", "file.pdf");       // absolute: /current/dir/uploads/file.pdf
path.resolve("/srv", "/etc/passwd");       // /etc/passwd  (absolute segment resets)

path.basename("/srv/docs/report.pdf");          // report.pdf
path.basename("/srv/docs/report.pdf", ".pdf");  // report
path.extname("archive.tar.gz");                 // .gz
path.dirname("/srv/docs/report.pdf");           // /srv/docs
path.parse("/srv/docs/report.pdf");
// { root: "/", dir: "/srv/docs", base: "report.pdf", ext: ".pdf", name: "report" }
path.normalize("/srv//docs/./../logs");         // /srv/logs
path.sep;                                       // "/" or "\\"
path.isAbsolute("C:\\data");                    // true on Windows
Function Returns join(...parts) Parts joined with the OS separator and normalized; may stay relative. resolve(...parts) An absolute path, processed right to left until absolute; relative to the current working directory. basename(p, ext?) Last segment, optionally without the extension. dirname(p) Everything except the last segment. extname(p) Extension including the dot, from the last .. parse(p) / format(obj) Split a path into parts / build one from parts. relative(from, to) The relative path from one location to another.

path.posix and path.win32 give platform-specific behavior regardless of the current OS.

docs.title: Path traversal defense
docs.text:
If user input becomes part of a path, an attacker can send ../../etc/passwd to escape the intended folder. Defend by resolving the final path and checking that it stays inside the base folder:

import path from "node:path";
import fs from "node:fs/promises";

const UPLOAD_ROOT = path.resolve("uploads");

export async function readUpload(userSuppliedName) {
  const target = path.resolve(UPLOAD_ROOT, userSuppliedName);

  // Must be inside UPLOAD_ROOT (the separator prevents "uploads-evil/...")
  if (!target.startsWith(UPLOAD_ROOT + path.sep)) {
    throw new Error("Invalid file path");
  }
  return fs.readFile(target);
}

Better still, do not use user-supplied names at all: store files under generated IDs and keep the original name in a database. See file storage and uploads.

docs.title: The os module
docs.text:
import os from "node:os";

os.platform();        // "linux", "darwin", "win32"
os.cpus().length;     // logical CPU cores
os.availableParallelism(); // recommended degree of parallelism
os.totalmem();        // bytes of RAM
os.freemem();         // bytes currently free
os.tmpdir();          // OS temp folder
os.homedir();         // current user's home folder
os.hostname();
os.EOL;               // "\n" or "\r\n"
os.uptime();          // seconds since boot

Use os.tmpdir() for temporary files, os.EOL when writing text meant for the local OS, and the CPU count to size worker pools.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Use node:fs/promises for file work inside a running server: config reloads, exports, temporary files.
  • Use the sync API only at startup, in CLIs, and in build scripts.
  • Use streams (createReadStream) for anything large or of unknown size: uploads, backups, logs, CSV exports.
  • Use path.join / path.resolve for every path, and check resolved paths against an allowed root when any part comes from a user.
  • Do not use local disk as the only copy of user data on servers that can be replaced (containers, serverless, autoscaling groups). Use object storage or a database.
  • Do not use fs.watch as a production trigger; use a queue message or an upload callback.
Task Use Avoid Read a small config at startup readFileSync Async ceremony at module load (fine either way) Read a small file per request await fs.readFile readFileSync (blocks every request) Read a large file createReadStream readFile (memory; 2 GiB limit) Store user uploads Object storage (S3 and similar) Local disk on replaceable servers Temporary scratch file os.tmpdir() + generated name Fixed names that collide between requests

docs.title: Loading JSON configuration at startup
docs.text:
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

// Sync is fine here: this runs once, before the server accepts requests.
const configPath = path.join(import.meta.dirname, "..", "config.json");
export const config = JSON.parse(readFileSync(configPath, "utf8"));

docs.title: Writing a file atomically
docs.text:
A crash in the middle of writeFile can leave a half-written file. Write to a temporary file in the same folder, then rename it (a rename on the same volume replaces the target in one step):

import fs from "node:fs/promises";
import path from "node:path";

export async function writeJsonAtomic(file, data) {
  const temp = path.join(path.dirname(file), `.${path.basename(file)}.${process.pid}.tmp`);
  await fs.writeFile(temp, JSON.stringify(data));
  await fs.rename(temp, file);
}

docs.title: Finding all .log files recursively
docs.text:
import fs from "node:fs/promises";
import path from "node:path";

async function findLogs(dir) {
  const results = [];
  for (const entry of await fs.readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true })) {
    const full = path.join(dir, entry.name);
    if (entry.isDirectory()) results.push(...(await findLogs(full)));
    else if (path.extname(entry.name) === ".log") results.push(full);
  }
  return results;
}

console.log(await findLogs("/var/app"));

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use node:fs/promises in application code; use sync APIs only during startup or in scripts.
  • Stream large files instead of reading them whole.
  • Build paths with path.join/path.resolve, never string concatenation.
  • Never pass raw user input into file paths; if you must, resolve and verify the result stays inside an allowed folder.
  • Handle errors by error.code instead of checking existence first.
  • Close file handles in finally.
  • Don't rely on local disk for user data in scalable deployments: servers and containers are replaceable. Use object storage instead.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Uploaded files disappear.
  • Symptom: files that users uploaded return 404 hours later, or only on some requests.
  • Detect: the missing files were written by an instance that has since restarted, or the request hit a different instance.
  • Cause: files were saved to a container's or dyno's local disk, which is ephemeral and not shared.
  • Fix: write uploads to object storage and keep only metadata in the database.
  • EMFILE: too many open files.
  • Symptom: file and network operations start failing under load with EMFILE.
  • Detect: the count of open file descriptors for the process (/proc/<pid>/fd on Linux) climbs steadily.
  • Cause: FileHandles or streams that are never closed, often on error paths.
  • Fix: close handles in finally, use stream.pipeline() so streams are destroyed on error, and raise the OS limit only after fixing leaks.
  • Memory spikes on file endpoints.
  • Symptom: the process is killed for running out of memory, or crashes with JavaScript heap out of memory during exports or downloads.
  • Detect: memory graphs jump when that endpoint runs, and a large file triggers ERR_FS_FILE_TOO_LARGE.
  • Cause: readFile of large or user-controlled files, several requests at once.
  • Fix: stream the file to the response with pipeline().
  • Paths that work locally break on the server.
  • Symptom: ENOENT for files that clearly exist in the repository.
  • Detect: the error path is relative to a different folder than you expected; log process.cwd() at startup.
  • Cause: relative paths resolve against the process's working directory, which differs under a process manager or in a container.
  • Fix: anchor paths with path.join(import.meta.dirname, ...).
  • Path traversal in a download endpoint.
  • Symptom: a security scan or log shows requests such as ?file=../../etc/passwd returning 200.
  • Detect: access logs containing .., %2e%2e, or absolute paths in file parameters.
  • Cause: user input joined into a path without checking the result.
  • Fix: resolve and check against the allowed root (above), or better, map generated IDs to files. Keep Node.js patched for path-handling CVEs.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• File descriptor / FileHandle: A reference to an open file used for reads and writes.
  • Encoding: How bytes map to text, such as utf8.
  • Flag: A mode string such as "w", "a", or "wx" that controls how a file is opened.
  • Absolute path: A path from the file-system root.
  • Relative path: A path interpreted from the current working directory or another base.
  • Path traversal: An attack that uses .. segments to escape an allowed folder.
  • TOCTOU race: A bug where the state changes between checking and using a resource.
  • Atomic write: A write that either fully happens or not at all, often done with write-then-rename.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using readFileSync in request handlers.
  • Reading large files with readFile and running out of memory.
  • Hard-coding / in paths, breaking on Windows.
  • Assuming relative paths are relative to the source file. They are relative to process.cwd()—the folder where the process was started. Use import.meta.dirname to anchor paths to the file.
  • "path.join makes paths safe." It normalizes .. but does not stop a path from escaping a folder.
  • Using fs.exists-style checks before operations, creating races.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. When is a synchronous fs call acceptable in a server?
  2. What is the difference between path.join and path.resolve?
  3. How would you safely serve a file whose name comes from a URL parameter?
  4. Why is "check if the file exists, then read it" a race condition?
  5. What do the "wx" and "a" flags do?
  6. Why is relying on local disk a problem for horizontally scaled servers?

docs.title: Building HTTP Servers with the http Module
docs.text: Node.js can serve HTTP with no framework at all. The built-in node:http module creates a server, hands you each request and a response object, and leaves routing, body parsing, and error handling to you. Frameworks such as Express are built on top of this module.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Writing a server with node:http once shows exactly what a framework does for you: parsing URLs, collecting request bodies, setting headers and status codes, and handling errors. That knowledge makes framework behavior less magical and helps you debug problems—timeouts, half-sent responses, connection handling—that sit below any framework. For the protocol itself, see HTTP and HTTPS.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Next.js documents a custom server that is a plain createServer((req, res) => handle(req, res)) from Node.js's http module, wrapping Next.js's request handler. Teams use it when they need routing or hooks that the framework's built-in server does not offer (Next.js docs: Custom server).
  • AWS Application Load Balancers close idle connections after 60 seconds by default. AWS recommends that the application's idle timeout be larger than the load balancer's. Otherwise the app may close a connection just as the balancer sends a request on it, and the client gets 502 Bad Gateway. Node.js's default keepAliveTimeout is only 5 seconds, so this is a classic Node.js-behind-ALB bug (AWS docs: Application Load Balancer attributes).

Popular tools and providers: frameworks built on node:http such as Express, Fastify, Koa, and NestJS; Undici (behind fetch) and Axios for outbound calls; Nginx and cloud load balancers in front of Node.js.

docs.title: Creating a server
docs.text:
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const server = createServer((request, response) => {
  response.statusCode = 200;
  response.setHeader("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8");
  response.end("Hello from Node.js\n");
});

server.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Listening on http://localhost:3000");
});

createServer registers your function as the listener for the server's request event. It runs once per HTTP request. listen(port) binds the server to a TCP port.

docs.title: The request: http.IncomingMessage
docs.text:
The request object is a readable stream plus metadata:

Property Example Notes request.method "POST" Uppercase HTTP method. request.url "/orders/42?expand=items" Path and query string, not a full URL. request.headers { "content-type": "application/json" } Header names are lowercased. request.httpVersion "1.1" request.socket.remoteAddress "203.0.113.9" Client IP (or the proxy's IP behind a proxy).

The body is not available as a property. You must read it from the stream.

docs.title: The response: http.ServerResponse
docs.text:
The response object is a writable stream with helpers:

Method / property Purpose response.statusCode = 201 Sets the status code (default 200). response.setHeader(name, value) Sets a header before sending. response.writeHead(status, headers) Sets status and headers at once and sends them. response.write(chunk) Sends part of the body (headers are sent first if not already). response.end([chunk]) Finishes the response. Every request must end. response.headersSent true once headers have gone out; you can no longer change status or headers.

If you never call end(), the client waits until it times out.

docs.title: Parsing the URL
docs.text:
request.url is a relative path. Combine it with a base to use the URL class:

const url = new URL(request.url, `http://${request.headers.host}`);
url.pathname;                      // "/orders/42"
url.searchParams.get("expand");    // "items"

docs.title: Reading the request body
docs.text:
Body data arrives as chunks. Collect them, enforce a size limit, then decode:

const MAX_BODY_BYTES = 1_000_000; // 1 MB

async function readJsonBody(request) {
  const chunks = [];
  let size = 0;

  for await (const chunk of request) {
    size += chunk.length;
    if (size > MAX_BODY_BYTES) {
      const error = new Error("Payload too large");
      error.statusCode = 413;
      throw error;
    }
    chunks.push(chunk);
  }

  const text = Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8");
  try {
    return text ? JSON.parse(text) : {};
  } catch {
    const error = new Error("Invalid JSON");
    error.statusCode = 400;
    throw error;
  }
}

Without a limit, a client can send gigabytes and exhaust memory.

docs.title: Status codes and headers
docs.text: Choose the status code that describes the result—200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error, and so on. See HTTP status codes and HTTP headers for the full reference.

docs.title: Keep-alive and timeouts
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default: after one response, the same TCP connection can carry the next request. This avoids repeating the TCP (and TLS) handshake. The server closes idle connections after a timeout.

Setting Default Meaning server.keepAliveTimeout 5 s How long an idle keep-alive connection stays open. server.headersTimeout The smaller of 60 s and requestTimeout Maximum time to receive the complete request headers. server.requestTimeout 300 s Maximum time to receive the entire request; the server then answers 408. 
server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;
server.headersTimeout = 66_000;

Behind a load balancer

If a load balancer keeps idle connections open longer than your server does, the server may close a connection just as the load balancer sends a new request on it, producing intermittent 502 errors. Set keepAliveTimeout slightly longer than the load balancer's idle timeout (60 seconds by default on an AWS Application Load Balancer), and headersTimeout a little longer still, as in the example above.

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text:
node:https works like node:http but needs a TLS certificate and key:

import { createServer } from "node:https";
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

createServer(
  { key: readFileSync("key.pem"), cert: readFileSync("cert.pem") },
  (request, response) => response.end("secure\n"),
).listen(443);

In production, TLS is usually terminated at a reverse proxy or load balancer (Nginx, a cloud load balancer), which forwards plain HTTP to Node.js on a private network. See reverse proxy and TLS and SSL.

docs.title: Making HTTP requests from Node.js
docs.text:
Backends often call other services. Node.js includes a global fetch (implemented by the Undici library), the same API as in browsers:

const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/users/1", {
  headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000), // always set a timeout
});

if (!response.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Upstream responded ${response.status}`);
}
const user = await response.json();

fetch only rejects on network failures or aborts; a 404 or 500 is a fulfilled response, so check response.ok or response.status.

The lower-level http.request() gives full control over sockets and agents and is used by older libraries:

import { request } from "node:https";

const req = request("https://example.com", (res) => {
  console.log(res.statusCode);
  res.resume(); // consume the body so the socket can be reused
});
req.on("error", (error) => console.error(error));
req.end();

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
server.close() stops accepting new connections and calls its callback when existing ones have finished. Since Node.js 19 it also closes idle keep-alive connections right away; connections that are still serving a request stay open until their response ends. On older versions, call server.closeIdleConnections() yourself:

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  server.close(() => process.exit(0)); // finish in-flight requests first
  server.closeIdleConnections();        // needed only before Node.js 19
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10_000).unref(); // force exit if stuck
});

See process, environment variables, and configuration for a complete shutdown sequence.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Use node:http directly to learn how HTTP works in Node.js, for tiny internal services (a health check, a metrics endpoint), and when you need full control over sockets and streaming.
  • Use a framework (Express, Fastify, Koa) for anything with more than a handful of routes, request validation, or middleware. You would otherwise rewrite routing, body parsing, and error handling yourself.
  • Use fetch for outbound calls in new code; drop down to http.request() or an Undici Agent only for low-level control such as custom connection pooling.
  • Do not terminate TLS in Node.js in a typical cloud deployment; let the load balancer or Nginx do it.
Need Choose Why A REST API with many routes Express or Fastify Routing, middleware, error handling built in One health or metrics endpoint node:http No dependency needed Outbound JSON calls fetch + AbortSignal.timeout Built in; same API as browsers Streaming proxy with tight control node:http / Undici Direct access to streams and sockets

docs.title: A small JSON API without a framework
docs.text:
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const tasks = [{ id: 1, title: "Learn the http module", done: false }];

function sendJson(response, status, data) {
  const body = JSON.stringify(data);
  response.writeHead(status, {
    "Content-Type": "application/json; charset=utf-8",
    "Content-Length": Buffer.byteLength(body),
  });
  response.end(body);
}

const server = createServer(async (request, response) => {
  const url = new URL(request.url, `http://${request.headers.host}`);
  const match = url.pathname.match(/^\/tasks\/(\d+)$/);

  try {
    if (request.method === "GET" && url.pathname === "/tasks") {
      return sendJson(response, 200, tasks);
    }

    if (request.method === "POST" && url.pathname === "/tasks") {
      const body = await readJsonBody(request); // from the section above
      if (typeof body.title !== "string" || body.title.trim() === "") {
        return sendJson(response, 400, { error: "title is required" });
      }
      const task = { id: tasks.length + 1, title: body.title, done: false };
      tasks.push(task);
      response.setHeader("Location", `/tasks/${task.id}`);
      return sendJson(response, 201, task);
    }

    if (request.method === "GET" && match) {
      const task = tasks.find((t) => t.id === Number(match[1]));
      return task
        ? sendJson(response, 200, task)
        : sendJson(response, 404, { error: "Task not found" });
    }

    sendJson(response, 404, { error: "Route not found" });
  } catch (error) {
    sendJson(response, error.statusCode ?? 500, {
      error: error.statusCode ? error.message : "Internal server error",
    });
  }
});

server.listen(3000);

Try it:

curl -i localhost:3000/tasks
curl -i -X POST localhost:3000/tasks \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Ship it"}'
curl -i localhost:3000/tasks/99

Save it together with readJsonBody from the section above. Tested on Node.js 22, the requests return 200; 201 Created with Location: /tasks/2; and 404 with {"error":"Task not found"}. A missing title or broken JSON gives 400, and a body over 1 MB gives 413.

docs.title: What a framework adds
docs.text:
Compare the code above with what Express gives you:

Concern Plain node:http Express Routing Manual if checks and regexes app.get("/tasks/:id", ...) with parameters Body parsing Collect chunks, limit, parse express.json({ limit: "1mb" }) Sending JSON Set headers, stringify, end res.status(201).json(task) Shared logic Wrap handlers by hand Middleware chain Errors try/catch in every handler Central error-handling middleware Query strings URL and searchParams req.query

Frameworks exist to remove this repetitive code, not to replace the HTTP model. See getting started with Express.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• End every response exactly once, including on errors.
  • Limit request body size and reject oversize bodies with 413.
  • Set Content-Type (with charset for text) and Content-Length when known.
  • Always set timeouts on outgoing requests (AbortSignal.timeout).
  • Check response.ok after fetch; non-2xx responses do not reject.
  • Tune keepAliveTimeout to be longer than your load balancer's idle timeout.
  • Terminate TLS at a proxy or load balancer unless you have a reason not to.
  • Implement graceful shutdown so deploys do not cut off in-flight requests.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Intermittent 502 Bad Gateway behind a load balancer.
  • Symptom: a small fraction of requests fail with 502 at random, more often after quiet periods; your app logs show no error for them.
  • Detect: the load balancer's 502 metric rises while the app's own error rate stays flat.
  • Cause: Node.js closed an idle keep-alive connection (5 s by default) that the balancer still considered open (60 s by default on AWS ALB).
  • Fix: set server.keepAliveTimeout above the balancer's idle timeout (for example 65 s) and headersTimeout slightly above that.
  • Requests that hang until the client gives up.
  • Symptom: some requests never get a response; clients see timeouts.
  • Detect: access logs show requests with no matching response line, and the server answers 408 after requestTimeout for slow uploads.
  • Cause: a code path that never calls response.end(), often an early return or an unhandled error inside an async handler.
  • Fix: end the response on every branch, and wrap the handler in one try/catch that always sends an error response.
  • Memory exhaustion from request bodies.
  • Symptom: memory spikes and the process is killed during large or malicious uploads.
  • Detect: memory graphs jump with request size, not request count.
  • Cause: reading the whole body without a size limit.
  • Fix: enforce a limit while reading and answer 413, as readJsonBody does; set the same limit at the proxy.
  • Deploys drop in-flight requests.
  • Symptom: every deploy causes a burst of ECONNRESET or 502 errors for clients.
  • Detect: error spikes line up exactly with deploy times.
  • Cause: the process exits on SIGTERM without letting current requests finish.
  • Fix: handle SIGTERM with server.close() and a forced-exit timer, and keep the orchestrator's grace period longer than that timer.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• IncomingMessage: The request object; a readable stream with method, URL, and headers.
  • ServerResponse: The response object; a writable stream with status and header helpers.
  • Keep-alive (persistent connection): Reusing one TCP connection for multiple HTTP requests.
  • TLS termination: Decrypting HTTPS at a proxy before traffic reaches the application.
  • Undici: The HTTP client library that powers Node.js's built-in fetch.
  • Graceful shutdown: Stopping new work and finishing current work before exiting.
  • Headers sent: The point after which status and headers can no longer change.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Forgetting response.end(), leaving clients hanging.
  • Setting headers after the body started, causing ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT.
  • Reading bodies without a size limit.
  • Treating request.url as a full URL. It is only the path and query.
  • Assuming fetch throws on HTTP errors.
  • "Node.js needs Express to serve HTTP." Express is a convenience layer over node:http.
  • Ignoring idle keep-alive connections during shutdown on Node.js versions before 19, so server.close() never finishes.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What do IncomingMessage and ServerResponse represent, and which kind of stream is each?
  2. How do you read and limit a JSON request body with node:http?
  3. Why can a mismatch between keepAliveTimeout and a load balancer's idle timeout cause 502 errors?
  4. Why does fetch resolve for a 500 response, and how do you detect it?
  5. What does server.close() do and not do?
  6. List four things Express does that you must write yourself with node:http.

docs.title: Installing Node.js and Managing Versions
docs.text: Before writing a backend in Node.js you need the runtime installed, and you need to know which version to use. This page explains the Node.js release lines, the common ways to install and switch versions, and the everyday commands for running code.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Different projects often need different Node.js versions. A package may require a newer API, a deployment platform may support only certain lines, and an old project may break on a newer runtime. Pinning and switching versions deliberately avoids "works on my machine" problems and keeps production on a supported, security-patched release.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
Hosting platforms read the same version files you use locally, so pinning a version decides what runs in production:

  • Heroku chooses the Node.js version from the engines.node field in package.json (for example "26.x"). If the field is missing, it picks its current default major automatically, which can change under you (Heroku Dev Center: Node.js support).
  • Vercel lets engines.node in package.json override the Node.js major version selected in the project settings (Vercel docs: Node.js versions).
  • Netlify builds with the version in a NODE_VERSION environment variable, a .node-version file, or an .nvmrc file, any of which overrides the setting in its UI (Netlify docs: Manage build dependencies).
  • AWS Lambda deprecates a runtime when its language version reaches the end of community LTS. After that date it blocks first the creation and then the updating of functions on that runtime, which forces teams to plan upgrades (AWS Lambda docs: Runtimes).
  • GitHub Actions actions/setup-node can read the version for CI from .nvmrc, .node-version, or package.json through its node-version-file input, so CI uses the same version as development (actions/setup-node README).

Popular tools and providers: nvm, fnm, mise, and Volta (unmaintained) for switching versions; official node Docker images; Heroku, Vercel, Netlify, and AWS Lambda for hosting.

docs.title: Release lines
docs.text:
Each Node.js major version moves through phases:

Phase What it means Use it for Current The newest major version; receives new features and can change quickly. Trying new features, testing libraries ahead of time. Active LTS Long-Term Support: stable, receives bug and security fixes. Production applications. Maintenance LTS Only critical bug and security fixes. Existing production apps planning an upgrade. End-of-life (EOL) No more fixes, including security fixes. Nothing; upgrade.

Up to Node.js 26, a new major version came out roughly every six months. Even-numbered majors became LTS releases, while odd-numbered ones stayed in Current for six months and then reached end-of-life. The diagram above shows that model. An LTS line typically receives critical fixes for about 30 months in total.

The schedule changed with Node.js 27: majors now come out once a year, and every major becomes LTS after its six-month Current phase. Each one is preceded by a new Alpha phase for early testing. Always check the official release schedule before choosing a version, because the project sets the exact dates.

Rule of thumb

Use the latest Active LTS version for production and new projects unless a dependency or platform requires something else.

docs.title: Version numbers
docs.text: Node.js uses semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, for example 24.3.1. A major version can contain breaking changes; minor versions add features; patch versions fix bugs and security issues. Staying on the latest patch of your major line is important for security.

docs.title: Ways to install
docs.text:
Method How it works Good for Official installer (nodejs.org) Installs one version system-wide. Beginners, a single project. OS package manager (Homebrew, apt, winget) Installs from your OS's repository. Quick setup; versions may lag behind. nvm (Node Version Manager) Installs many versions in your home folder and switches between them per shell. Developers working on several projects (macOS/Linux; nvm-windows is a separate project for Windows). fnm (Fast Node Manager) A fast, cross-platform version manager; can switch automatically when you enter a folder. Same as nvm, including Windows. mise A general tool-version manager (Node.js, Python, and more) that switches per folder. Teams managing several languages. Volta Pins the Node.js and package-manager versions in package.json and switches automatically. Existing setups only: the project is unmaintained, and its authors recommend migrating to mise. Docker image node:<version> images contain the runtime. Consistent builds and deployments.

Version managers are preferred for development because they let each project use its own version without administrator rights.

docs.title: Pinning the version for a project
docs.text:
Two common files tell people and tools which version to use:

  • .nvmrc (read by nvm and fnm) contains just the version:
24
  • The engines field in package.json documents the supported range:
{
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=22"
  }
}

npm warns when the running Node.js does not satisfy engines. With engine-strict=true in .npmrc, installs fail instead.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a version manager (nvm, fnm, or mise) when:

  • You work on more than one project, or a project's .nvmrc differs from your system version.
  • You need to test a library against several Node.js majors.
  • You cannot or should not install software system-wide.

Use the official installer or an OS package manager when:

  • You need exactly one Node.js version on a machine, such as a student laptop or a single-purpose server.

Use a pinned Docker image (node:24-alpine, or an exact patch tag) when:

  • Development, CI, and production must run byte-for-byte the same runtime.

Avoid:

  • Odd-numbered Current releases up to Node.js 26, and any Current release, in production. They change faster and have short support windows.
  • Floating tags such as node:latest in production images, which can jump to a new major on the next rebuild.
Option Switch per project Needs admin rights Typical use Official installer No Yes One version per machine OS package manager No Usually Quick setup; versions may lag nvm / fnm / mise Yes No Developers with several projects Docker image Yes (per image) No (Docker needed) CI and production parity

docs.title: Checking what is installed
docs.text:
node --version    # e.g. v24.3.1
npm --version     # npm ships with Node.js
which node        # macOS/Linux: where the binary lives
where node        # Windows

docs.title: Using nvm
docs.text:
nvm install --lts      # install the latest LTS release
nvm install 22         # install the latest 22.x
nvm use 22             # switch this shell to 22.x
nvm ls                 # list installed versions
nvm alias default 22   # use 22.x in new shells
nvm use                # read .nvmrc in the current folder

docs.title: The REPL
docs.text:
Running node with no file opens the REPL (Read–Eval–Print Loop), an interactive prompt for experimenting:

$ node
> 2 + 3
5
> _ * 10          // _ holds the last result
50
> const os = await import("node:os")
> os.platform()
'linux'
> .help           // list REPL commands
> .exit           // or press Ctrl+D once, or Ctrl+C twice on a blank line

Useful REPL commands: .help, .exit, .clear, .editor (multi-line mode), .load file.js, and .save file.js.

docs.title: Running a file
docs.text:
// hello.js
const name = process.argv[2] ?? "world";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);

node hello.js            # Hello, world!
node hello.js Ada        # Hello, Ada!

docs.title: Restarting on file changes
docs.text:
node --watch server.js

--watch restarts the process whenever the entry file or a file it imports changes. It replaces the need for tools such as nodemon in many projects. Use --watch-path=./src to watch a specific folder instead; this turns off the automatic watching of imported files.

docs.title: Loading environment variables from a file
docs.text:
node --env-file=.env server.js

Node.js reads KEY=value lines from the file into process.env before your code runs. Never commit .env files that contain secrets. See process, environment variables, and configuration.

docs.title: Importing built-in modules with node:
docs.text:
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import path from "node:path";
import { createServer } from "node:http";

The node: prefix makes it clear the module is built in and cannot be shadowed by an npm package with the same name. Some newer modules, such as node:test and node:sqlite, are only available with the prefix.

docs.title: Running package binaries with npx
docs.text:
npx eslint .                  # run the project's local eslint
npx create-vite@latest my-app # download and run a package once

npx runs a binary from node_modules/.bin. If the package is not installed, it asks before downloading it into the npm cache (--yes skips the prompt). See npm and package management.

docs.title: Corepack and other package managers
docs.text:
Corepack is a tool that manages Yarn and pnpm versions declared in the packageManager field of package.json:

{ "packageManager": "pnpm@9.12.0" }

Corepack is bundled with Node.js from 14.19.0 up to, but not including, 25.0.0. If your Node.js does not include it, install it with npm install -g corepack, or install pnpm/Yarn directly.

docs.title: Running TypeScript files
docs.text:
Node.js can run .ts files directly by stripping type annotations before execution. This is on by default from Node.js 22.18.0 and 23.6.0, and stable from 24.12.0 and 25.2.0:

node app.ts

Type stripping removes types; it does not type-check your code, and it ignores tsconfig.json. It supports only syntax that can be erased: enum declarations, namespaces with runtime code, and parameter properties fail with an error. Keep running tsc --noEmit or your editor's checker for type errors, and use a tool such as tsx when you need full TypeScript.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use a version manager in development and commit .nvmrc so the whole team, and CI (actions/setup-node with node-version-file), uses the same major version.
  • Use the same major version locally, in CI, and in production. Pin the Docker base image to a major version, for example node:24-alpine.
  • Upgrade to the latest patch release regularly; patch releases often include security fixes.
  • Plan major upgrades before your line reaches end-of-life. Read the changelog for breaking changes and run your test suite on the new version.
  • Avoid installing Node.js with sudo package managers when you need multiple versions; it leads to permission problems with global packages.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The platform picked a different major.
  • Symptom: the app works locally but fails after deploy with TypeError: ... is not a function or a SyntaxError on newer syntax.
  • Detect: log process.version at startup and compare it with .nvmrc.
  • Cause: no engines.node field, so the platform used its own default.
  • Fix: set engines.node (for example "24.x") and .nvmrc to the same major.
  • A floating Docker tag jumped versions.
  • Symptom: an image rebuilt without code changes starts failing tests.
  • Detect: node --version in the build logs differs between the old and new image.
  • Cause: FROM node:latest or FROM node:lts now points to a newer major.
  • Fix: pin node:24-alpine or an exact patch tag, and upgrade on purpose.
  • Native add-ons break after an upgrade.
  • Symptom: the process fails at startup while loading a compiled .node file from a dependency.
  • Detect: the error stack points into that package's folder in node_modules.
  • Cause: add-ons written against the V8 or NAN APIs must be recompiled for each Node.js major. Add-ons built on the ABI-stable Node-API keep working across majors.
  • Fix: reinstall dependencies (npm ci) in the same image and Node.js version that runs in production; never copy node_modules from a developer machine.
  • A serverless runtime reached its deprecation date.
  • Symptom: deployments to AWS Lambda fail because function updates on the old runtime are blocked.
  • Detect: the platform's deprecation notices, or the runtime ID such as nodejs22.x in your infrastructure code.
  • Cause: the runtime's Node.js line reached end of LTS.
  • Fix: track Node.js end-of-life dates and upgrade a major well before the platform's deadline.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• LTS (Long-Term Support): A release line that receives fixes for an extended period and is recommended for production.
  • Current: The newest major release line, with the latest features.
  • End-of-life (EOL): A release line that no longer receives any fixes.
  • Version manager: A tool such as nvm, fnm, or mise that installs and switches between Node.js versions.
  • REPL: The interactive Read–Eval–Print Loop opened by running node.
  • engines: The package.json field that declares supported Node.js versions.
  • npx: A command that runs package binaries, installing them temporarily if needed.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Running a Current release in production. Up to Node.js 26, odd-numbered majors never became LTS and reached end-of-life after about six months.
  • Staying on an EOL version. It no longer receives security patches, even for serious vulnerabilities.
  • Assuming engines blocks installs. By default npm only warns.
  • Treating --watch as a production tool. It is for development; use a process manager or container orchestrator in production.
  • Believing type stripping type-checks code. It only removes types.
