docs.title: Node.js Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review the Node.js runtime, the event loop, asynchronous programming, modules, streams, configuration, scaling, and debugging. Try to answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is Node.js?
docs.text: Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser. It combines the V8 engine with libuv and built-in modules for files, networking, processes, and more, which makes it suitable for servers, command-line tools, and build tooling.

docs.title: 2. What roles do V8 and libuv play?
docs.text: V8 parses, compiles (with a just-in-time compiler), and executes JavaScript and manages memory with garbage collection. libuv provides the event loop, asynchronous I/O across operating systems, and a thread pool for work that cannot be done asynchronously by the OS.

docs.title: 3. Is Node.js single-threaded?
docs.text: Your JavaScript runs on a single main thread, so only one piece of your code executes at a time. Node.js itself uses additional threads—libuv's thread pool, garbage collection, and other internals—and you can create more with worker threads.

docs.title: 4. What does "non-blocking I/O" mean?
docs.text: When code starts an I/O operation such as a file read or database query, Node.js does not wait for it. It hands the work to the OS or thread pool, continues running other JavaScript, and runs a callback when the result is ready. This lets one thread serve many concurrent requests.

docs.title: 5. Which operations use the libuv thread pool?
docs.text: Most file system operations, dns.lookup(), CPU-heavy asynchronous crypto such as pbkdf2 and scrypt, and asynchronous zlib compression. Network sockets do not use the pool; they use OS mechanisms like epoll, kqueue, or IOCP. The pool has four threads by default, configurable with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE.

docs.title: 6. What kinds of applications is Node.js good and bad at?
docs.text: It is good at I/O-heavy work: APIs, real-time apps, streaming, proxies, backends-for-frontends, and tooling. It is poor at CPU-heavy work on the main thread, such as video encoding or large computations, unless that work moves to worker threads or separate services.

docs.title: 7. How does Node.js differ from JavaScript in the browser?
docs.text: Both run ECMAScript, but Node.js has no DOM, window, or document. It adds process, Buffer, file system, networking, and child process APIs, and supports CommonJS as well as ES modules. Many web APIs such as fetch, URL, and AbortController exist in both.

docs.title: 8. What is the event loop?
docs.text: The event loop is the mechanism that runs callbacks when the call stack is empty. It cycles through phases—timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, and close callbacks—running queued callbacks for each, and keeps the process alive while there is pending work.

docs.title: 9. What happens in the poll and check phases?
docs.text: The poll phase retrieves new I/O events and runs their callbacks; if nothing else is scheduled, the loop waits there for I/O. The check phase runs setImmediate callbacks immediately after poll.

docs.title: 10. What are microtasks in Node.js, and when do they run?
docs.text: Microtasks are callbacks in the process.nextTick queue and the Promise microtask queue. They run after the current callback finishes and before the next callback or phase: the nextTick queue is drained first, then promise callbacks, repeating until both are empty.

docs.title: 11. What is the difference between process.nextTick and setImmediate?
docs.text: process.nextTick runs its callback right after the current operation, before any I/O or timers. setImmediate runs in the check phase of the loop, after I/O callbacks. Despite the names, nextTick runs sooner. Recursive nextTick calls can starve the event loop.

docs.title: 12. Why is the order of setTimeout(fn, 0) and setImmediate(fn) sometimes unpredictable?
docs.text: From the main module, it depends on whether the minimum 1 ms timer delay has already passed when the loop reaches the timers phase. Inside an I/O callback the order is deterministic: setImmediate always runs first, because the check phase follows the poll phase.

docs.title: 13. What does "blocking the event loop" mean, and what causes it?
docs.text: It means a callback runs synchronously for so long that no other callback can run, so every request waits. Causes include long loops, synchronous crypto or file APIs, parsing very large JSON, and catastrophic regular expression backtracking.

docs.title: 14. How can you detect event loop blocking in production?
docs.text: Measure event loop delay with perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() and alert when percentiles rise. When delays appear, take a CPU profile with --cpu-prof or the inspector to find the responsible functions.

docs.title: 15. What is an error-first callback?
docs.text: A callback convention in which the first argument is an error (or null) and results follow. The callback is called exactly once, and errors are passed to it rather than thrown, because the original call has already returned.

docs.title: 16. What problems do promises solve compared with callbacks?
docs.text: Promises avoid deeply nested callbacks, provide a single error path with .catch(), can be chained and combined with Promise.all and similar methods, and guarantee that a result is delivered once. async/await builds on promises to make asynchronous code read sequentially.

docs.title: 17. Compare Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race, and Promise.any.
docs.text: all fulfills with all values or rejects on the first rejection. allSettled waits for every promise and reports each outcome. race settles like the first promise to settle. any fulfills with the first fulfillment and rejects with an AggregateError only if all reject.

docs.title: 18. Why doesn't array.forEach(async (item) => ...) wait for the work?
docs.text: forEach ignores the promises returned by the async callback, so it returns immediately and errors become unhandled rejections. Use for...of with await for sequential work or Promise.all(array.map(...)) for parallel work.

docs.title: 19. How do you run independent async operations in parallel?
docs.text: Start them without awaiting each one, then await them together with Promise.all. For large lists, limit concurrency (for example, with a small worker loop or a library) so you don't overwhelm downstream services.

docs.title: 20. How do you add a timeout or cancellation to an async operation?
docs.text: Use an AbortController and pass its signal to APIs that support it, such as fetch, fs.readFile, and timers/promises. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) creates a signal that aborts automatically after the given time.

docs.title: 21. What happens when a promise rejection is not handled?
docs.text: By default, Node.js treats an unhandled rejection like an uncaught exception: it prints the error and exits with a non-zero code. Every rejection should be handled with await in try/catch or with .catch().

docs.title: 22. What is an EventEmitter?
docs.text: EventEmitter from node:events lets objects emit named events and call registered listeners. Servers, streams, sockets, and process are emitters. Listeners are called synchronously in the order they were added.

docs.title: 23. Why is the error event special?
docs.text: If an emitter emits "error" and no listener is registered, Node.js throws the error, which usually crashes the process. Emitters that can fail, such as streams and sockets, should always have an error listener.

docs.title: 24. What does the MaxListenersExceededWarning mean?
docs.text: It warns that more than 10 listeners were added for one event on one emitter, which often indicates a memory leak from listeners added repeatedly and never removed. Fix the leak, or raise the limit with setMaxListeners if the listeners are legitimate.

docs.title: 25. What are the differences between CommonJS and ES modules?
docs.text: CommonJS uses require and module.exports, loads synchronously, and provides __dirname. ES modules use import and export, form a static dependency graph, support top-level await, use live bindings, require file extensions in relative imports, and use import.meta.dirname instead of __dirname.

docs.title: 26. How does Node.js decide whether a file is CommonJS or ESM?
docs.text: .mjs files are ESM and .cjs files are CommonJS. For .js files, the nearest package.json decides: "type": "module" means ESM and "type": "commonjs" means CommonJS. With no type field, the file is CommonJS unless it contains ES module syntax; since Node.js 22.7.0 such files are detected and run as ESM.

docs.title: 27. What is module caching?
docs.text: A module runs the first time it is loaded, and its exports are cached. Later imports or requires return the same object, which is why modules behave like singletons and why module-level state is shared across the application.

docs.title: 28. What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies?
docs.text: dependencies are needed at runtime in production. devDependencies are needed only for development, testing, and building, and can be omitted from production installs with npm ci --omit=dev.

docs.title: 29. What do ^ and ~ mean in version ranges, and why does the lockfile matter?
docs.text: ^1.2.3 allows any 1.x version from 1.2.3; ~1.2.3 allows 1.2.x versions from 1.2.3. Because ranges allow many versions, package-lock.json records the exact resolved tree so every install is identical. npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says.

docs.title: 30. When is it acceptable to use synchronous fs methods?
docs.text: During startup, in scripts, and in CLIs, where blocking does not affect other requests. Inside request handlers, synchronous calls block every concurrent request and should be avoided.

docs.title: 31. How do you prevent path traversal when building file paths from user input?
docs.text: Avoid user-supplied paths where possible and store files under generated IDs. If you must use input, resolve the full path with path.resolve and verify it still starts with the allowed base directory plus a separator before accessing it.

docs.title: 32. What is a Buffer?
docs.text: A Buffer is a fixed-length sequence of bytes used for binary data such as files, network packets, and images. It is a subclass of Uint8Array and converts to and from encodings such as UTF-8, Base64, and hex.

docs.title: 33. What are streams, and why are they useful?
docs.text: Streams process data in chunks as it arrives instead of loading it all into memory. They keep memory use constant, reduce time to first byte, and can be chained. Node.js has readable, writable, duplex, and transform streams.

docs.title: 34. What is backpressure?
docs.text: Backpressure is the mechanism that slows a fast producer when a consumer cannot keep up. write() returns false when a writable stream's buffer reaches its highWaterMark, and the stream emits drain when it can accept more. pipe and pipeline handle this automatically.

docs.title: 35. Why is stream.pipeline preferred over pipe?
docs.text: pipe handles backpressure but does not forward errors or clean up the other streams when one fails, which can leak file handles and sockets. pipeline propagates errors, destroys the streams when one fails (except those that already ended or finished), and offers a promise version.

docs.title: 36. How do you read a request body with the plain http module?
docs.text: The request is a readable stream, so collect its chunks (for example, with for await), enforce a maximum size, concatenate them with Buffer.concat, decode the result, and parse it. Frameworks like Express do this with body parsing middleware.

docs.title: 37. Why might a Node.js server behind a load balancer return intermittent 502 errors?
docs.text: A common cause is the server's keepAliveTimeout being shorter than the load balancer's idle timeout, so the server closes a connection just as the load balancer reuses it. Setting keepAliveTimeout slightly longer than the load balancer's timeout fixes it.

docs.title: 38. Does fetch in Node.js throw on a 404 or 500 response?
docs.text: No. fetch rejects only on network failures or aborts. HTTP error statuses produce a fulfilled response, so you must check response.ok or response.status.

docs.title: 39. How should a Node.js application handle configuration?
docs.text: Read environment-specific values from environment variables, convert and validate them once at startup in a single config module, and fail fast if anything is missing. Never hardcode secrets, and keep real secrets out of committed files.

docs.title: 40. What does NODE_ENV do?
docs.text: Node.js itself ignores it. It is a convention that libraries and frameworks read to change behavior. With NODE_ENV=production, for example, Express caches view templates and generates less verbose error messages. It describes the type of environment, not a specific deployment.

docs.title: 41. What is graceful shutdown, and how do you implement it?
docs.text: On SIGTERM or SIGINT, the process stops accepting new connections, finishes in-flight requests, stops background work, closes database and other connections, then exits. A forced-exit timeout prevents hanging past the platform's grace period.

docs.title: 42. How do you run CPU-intensive work without blocking the server?
docs.text: Move it to worker threads, ideally a pool sized near the number of CPU cores, or to a separate service or background job queue. The main thread then stays free to handle I/O and requests.

docs.title: 43. What is the difference between worker threads and child processes?
docs.text: Worker threads run JavaScript in extra threads within the same process, with cheap message passing and optional shared memory. Child processes are separate OS processes that can run any program, are fully isolated, and cost more to start. Use workers for CPU-heavy JavaScript and child processes for external programs.

docs.title: 44. Why is child_process.exec risky?
docs.text: exec runs a command string through a shell, so user-controlled input can inject extra commands. execFile and spawn with an arguments array do not invoke a shell and should be used when input is involved.

docs.title: 45. What does the cluster module do, and what are its limitations?
docs.text: It forks several worker processes from a primary process so they share one port and use multiple CPU cores. Workers do not share memory, so sessions, caches, and counters must live in an external store such as Redis. In container platforms, running more containers is often preferred.

docs.title: 46. What is the difference between operational errors and programmer errors?
docs.text: Operational errors are expected failures in correct code, such as invalid input or an unavailable database; they should be handled. Programmer errors are bugs, such as reading a property of undefined; they should be fixed, and at runtime the process is usually logged and restarted.

docs.title: 47. What should you do in an uncaughtException handler?
docs.text: Log the error and exit. After an unexpected exception the process may be in an inconsistent state, so continuing is unsafe. A process manager or orchestrator should restart the service automatically.

docs.title: 48. How do you find a memory leak in a Node.js service?
docs.text: Confirm memory keeps growing over time, take heap snapshots minutes apart with the inspector or v8.writeHeapSnapshot(), and compare them in Chrome DevTools to see which objects grow and what retains them. Common causes are unbounded caches, leaked listeners, uncleared timers, and closures.

docs.title: 49. How do you debug a Node.js application?
docs.text: Start it with --inspect (or --inspect-brk to pause at the first line) and attach Chrome DevTools via chrome://inspect or the VS Code debugger to use breakpoints, step through code, and inspect variables. Never expose the inspector port publicly.

docs.title: 50. How would you investigate a slow Node.js endpoint?
docs.text: Measure first: check response times, event loop delay, and downstream latency (database, external APIs). If the event loop is busy, capture a CPU profile to find hot functions; if time is spent waiting, examine queries, indexes, network calls, and missing parallelism or caching.

docs.title: 51. After a deploy, p99 latency doubled but CPU is flat. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether requests are now waiting rather than computing. Look at downstream latency (database, other APIs), connection pool usage, and the deploy diff for new sequential awaits.

How to confirm: traces show long spans for outbound calls while event loop delay stays at its usual baseline. If fs, crypto.scrypt, or DNS spans grew, suspect the four-thread libuv pool.

Likely causes and fixes: independent calls changed to sequential (use Promise.all), a slower query or missing index, a smaller connection pool, or thread-pool saturation (raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE at startup). See asynchronous patterns and runtime and architecture.

docs.title: 52. Every endpoint freezes for a few seconds at random moments. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: event loop delay (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()) at the moment of the freeze, and CPU on the process.

How to confirm: delay jumps far above its normal baseline while one core hits 100%. A CPU profile (--cpu-prof) taken during a freeze shows the synchronous function.

Likely causes and fixes: a backtracking regex on user input (ReDoS), JSON.parse of a huge body, or a *Sync call in a handler. Limit input sizes, fix the regex, and move heavy work to a worker thread. See the event loop.

docs.title: 53. The process crashes every two days with "JavaScript heap out of memory". How do you find the cause?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether heap usage after garbage collection keeps rising (a leak) or only spikes with certain requests (a large allocation).

How to confirm: take heap snapshots minutes apart under load and compare them; the growing object type and its retainers point to the code. Writing a snapshot blocks the loop and needs about twice the heap, so take it from an instance removed from the load balancer.

Likely causes and fixes: an unbounded Map cache, listeners added per request, uncleared timers. Bound the cache and remove listeners. Raising --max-old-space-size only delays the crash. See errors, debugging, and performance.

docs.title: 54. A Node.js API behind an AWS load balancer returns occasional 502s, but the app logs no errors. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the server's keepAliveTimeout (5 seconds by default) against the balancer's idle timeout (60 seconds by default on an Application Load Balancer).

How to confirm: the 502s appear only in the balancer's metrics, are rare, and often follow idle periods.

Likely causes and fixes: Node.js closes an idle connection that the balancer still reuses. Set server.keepAliveTimeout above the balancer's timeout (for example 65 s) and headersTimeout slightly higher. See the http module.

docs.title: 55. Every deploy causes a short burst of connection errors for clients. What do you fix?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the process logs that it received SIGTERM, and how the container starts it.

How to confirm: errors line up with instance terminations. If the container runs npm start, npm can swallow the signal; if the app ignores SIGTERM, it is killed mid-request.

Likely causes and fixes: start with CMD ["node", "server.js"], handle SIGTERM by calling server.close(), and force-exit before the platform's grace period (30 s by default on Kubernetes). See process and configuration.

docs.title: 56. Containers keep restarting with exit code 137. What does it mean?
docs.text:
What to check first: the orchestrator's termination reason for the container.

How to confirm: 137 is 128 + 9, meaning the process was killed with SIGKILL. A reason of OOMKilled points to memory; otherwise, check whether shutdown took longer than the grace period.

Likely causes and fixes: memory above the container limit (fix leaks, set --max-old-space-size below the limit) or a shutdown that never finishes (add a forced-exit timer). See process and configuration.

docs.title: 57. Logins became slow, and file uploads and outbound calls slowed with them, yet CPU has headroom. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how many thread-pool tasks run at once: password hashing with crypto.scrypt/pbkdf2, fs calls, and dns.lookup() share one pool of four threads by default.

How to confirm: timing around those calls grows together under load, while event loop delay stays normal.

Likely causes and fixes: hashing saturates the pool and everything else queues behind it. Set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE before the process starts (setting it from code is not guaranteed to work), cache DNS lookups, or move hashing to a worker pool. See runtime and architecture.

docs.title: 58. After npm update, the app crashes at startup with ERR_REQUIRE_ESM. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: which package the stack trace names, and the Node.js version in production.

How to confirm: the package's new major version is ESM-only, and the runtime is older than Node.js 22.12/20.19, which cannot require() ES modules.

Likely causes and fixes: upgrade Node.js, load the package with await import(), or pin the previous major until you migrate to ESM. See CommonJS and ES modules.

docs.title: 59. The app works locally but the production image fails with "Cannot find package". Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the missing package is in devDependencies.

How to confirm: the image is built with npm ci --omit=dev, so dev packages are absent, and the error names a module your runtime code imports.

Likely causes and fixes: move the package to dependencies, and run a smoke test against the built image in CI. See npm and package management.

docs.title: 60. CI fails at npm ci with "can only install packages when your package.json and package-lock.json ... are in sync". What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the line after the message, such as Missing: <package>@<version> from lock file.

How to confirm: package.json was changed without the lockfile, or the lockfile was not committed.

Likely causes and fixes: run npm install locally, commit both files together, and keep npm ci in CI. Do not switch CI to npm install, which would hide drift. See npm and package management.

docs.title: 61. After moving to PM2 cluster mode, users are randomly logged out and rate limits stop working. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: where sessions and rate-limit counters are stored.

How to confirm: logs show requests from the same user handled by different process IDs, and the problem disappears with one process.

Likely causes and fixes: each cluster worker is a separate process with its own memory, so in-memory sessions and counters are not shared. Store them in Redis or a database. See worker threads, child processes, and cluster and sessions, cookies, and JWT.

docs.title: 62. A one-second Redis network blip crashed every instance. How do you prevent it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the crash logs for Unhandled 'error' event.

How to confirm: the error comes from the Redis client, and no error listener was registered on it.

Likely causes and fixes: an EventEmitter that emits error with no listener throws and ends the process. The node-redis README says you must listen to error events. Add listeners to every client, socket, and stream, log the error, and let the client reconnect. See events and EventEmitter.

docs.title: 63. A bulk-import endpoint makes the database reject connections for the whole app. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: connection pool usage and the number of queries in flight while the import runs.

How to confirm: pool usage hits its maximum exactly during the import, and unrelated endpoints time out waiting for a connection.

Likely causes and fixes: Promise.all(rows.map(insert)) started thousands of queries at once. Cap concurrency (a small worker loop or p-limit), or batch rows into fewer queries. See asynchronous patterns.

docs.title: 64. Large report downloads crash the server or lead to EMFILE: too many open files. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the endpoint reads and sends the file.

How to confirm: memory jumps by about the file size per download (whole file read), or open file descriptors climb with aborted downloads (streams never closed).

Likely causes and fixes: readFile of large files (which also fails above 2 GiB) or pipe() without cleanup. Stream with await pipeline(createReadStream(file), response), which destroys the streams when the client disconnects. See buffers and streams.

docs.title: 65. Files users uploaded yesterday now return 404. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: where uploads are written.

How to confirm: they were saved to the container's or dyno's local disk, and the instance has restarted or the request reached another instance.

Likely causes and fixes: local disks on Heroku dynos, Kubernetes containers, and Lambda are ephemeral and not shared. Store uploads in object storage and keep only metadata in the database. See file system, path, and OS.

docs.title: Modules: CommonJS and ES Modules
docs.text: A module is a file whose variables and functions are private unless it explicitly exports them. Node.js supports two module systems: the older CommonJS (require and module.exports) and the standard ECMAScript modules (ESM, import and export). Most new code uses ESM, but backend developers meet both every day.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Modules let you split a backend into focused files—routes, services, database access—without polluting a shared global scope. Knowing both systems helps you read older code and libraries, configure package.json correctly, and fix common errors such as require is not defined in ES module scope or Cannot use import statement outside a module.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• node-fetch became ESM-only in version 3: you cannot load it with require(). Its README tells projects that cannot switch to ESM to stay on version 2, which still receives critical fixes. Many CommonJS projects hit this when they upgraded (node-fetch README).
  • Jest documents its ESM support as experimental: you enable it with extra configuration, and it relies on Node.js APIs that are themselves still experimental. That is why many test suites stay on CommonJS or use a transform (Jest docs: ECMAScript Modules).
  • Vite documents a common interop surprise: importing a CommonJS module's default export gives you the whole module.exports object, where you may expect module.exports.default. The result is errors such as foo is not a function (Vite docs: Troubleshooting).
  • TypeScript added the node16, node18, node20, and nodenext module settings to model Node.js's dual module system: how each file's format is decided and how the two formats may import each other (TypeScript handbook: Modules reference).

Popular tools and providers: TypeScript (module: "nodenext"), bundlers such as Vite, esbuild, and Rollup that convert between formats, and tsx for running mixed-format TypeScript.

docs.title: Why modules exist
docs.text: Without modules, every script shares one global scope, names collide, and the load order must be managed by hand. A module system gives each file its own scope, declares dependencies explicitly, and loads each file once.

docs.title: CommonJS
docs.text:
CommonJS was Node.js's original system.

// math.cjs
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
const PI = 3.14159;

module.exports = { add, PI }; // what require() will return

// app.cjs
const { add, PI } = require("./math.cjs");
const fs = require("node:fs");

console.log(add(2, 3), PI);

Characteristics:

  • require() is a normal function call. It loads synchronously and can appear anywhere, including inside if blocks.
  • It returns the value of the target module's module.exports.
  • Resolution can omit extensions: require("./math") tries ./math.js, ./math.json, ./math.node, then the folder ./math (its package.json main, or index.js) and so on.

docs.title: The module wrapper
docs.text:
Before running a CommonJS file, Node.js wraps it in a function:

(function (exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname) {
  // your module code
});

That is why require, module, exports, __filename (the file's absolute path), and __dirname (its folder) are available in every CommonJS file without being imported—and why top-level variables are local to the file.

docs.title: The exports pitfall
docs.text:
exports starts as a reference to module.exports. Adding properties works; reassigning exports breaks the link:

exports.add = add;            // works: adds to module.exports
module.exports = { add };     // works: replaces the exported value
exports = { add };            // does NOTHING: only rebinds the local variable

docs.title: Module caching
docs.text:
A module is executed the first time it is required. Its module.exports is cached by resolved filename, and later require() calls return the same object. This makes modules natural singletons:

// counter.cjs
let count = 0;
module.exports = { increment: () => ++count };

Every file that requires counter.cjs shares the same count.

docs.title: ECMAScript modules (ESM)
docs.text:
ESM is the JavaScript language standard, used by browsers and Node.js.

// math.js  (with "type": "module" in package.json)
export function add(a, b) {   // named export
  return a + b;
}
export const PI = 3.14159;

export default function multiply(a, b) { // one default export per module
  return a * b;
}

// app.js
import multiply, { add, PI } from "./math.js"; // default + named
import * as math from "./math.js";             // namespace object
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

console.log(add(2, 3), multiply(2, 3), math.PI);

Characteristics:

  • import and export are static declarations at the top level. Node.js parses them and builds the dependency graph before running code.
  • Imports are live bindings: if the exporting module changes an exported let, importers see the new value. Importers cannot reassign them.
  • Code runs in strict mode automatically.
  • Loading is asynchronous internally, which allows top-level await.

docs.title: How Node.js decides which system a file uses
__dirname in ES modules
docs.text:
ESM files do not have the CommonJS wrapper, so __dirname and __filename do not exist. Use import.meta:

import path from "node:path";

console.log(import.meta.url);      // file:///home/app/src/server.js
console.log(import.meta.filename); // /home/app/src/server.js
console.log(import.meta.dirname);  // /home/app/src

const viewsDir = path.join(import.meta.dirname, "views");

On older Node.js versions without import.meta.dirname, use path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)) from node:url.

docs.title: Top-level await
docs.text:
ESM files can use await outside any function:

// config.js
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

export const config = JSON.parse(await readFile("./config.json", "utf8"));

Modules that import config.js wait until it finishes. Use this for startup work, but remember it delays everything that depends on the module.

docs.title: Dynamic import()
docs.text:
import() is a function-like expression that loads a module on demand and returns a promise. It works in both ESM and CommonJS:

if (process.env.FEATURE_REPORTS === "on") {
  const { generateReport } = await import("./reports.js");
  await generateReport();
}

Use it to load optional or heavy modules lazily, or to load an ES module from CommonJS code.

docs.title: JSON modules
docs.text:
import pkg from "./package.json" with { type: "json" };
console.log(pkg.version);

The with { type: "json" } import attribute is required, and the JSON is available only as the default export (no named exports). JSON modules are stable from Node.js 22.12.0. In CommonJS, require("./data.json") works directly.

docs.title: Interoperability
docs.text:
• ESM importing CommonJS: works. The default import is the CommonJS module.exports value. Named imports often work too when Node.js can detect the export names statically.
import express from "express";           // CommonJS package, default import
import pkg from "some-cjs-lib";
const { helper } = pkg;                  // safe fallback for named values
  • CommonJS loading ESM: import() always works. Since Node.js 22.12.0 and 20.19.0, require() can also load an ES module synchronously, as long as its module graph has no top-level await. If it does, the call throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE. Version 22.12.0 still printed an experimental warning, and the feature is stable from 25.4.0. Older versions throw ERR_REQUIRE_ESM.
  • Dual packages can publish both formats using the exports field with import and require conditions.

docs.title: Resolution rules
Circular dependencies
docs.text:
When module A imports B and B imports A, one of them sees the other partially initialized.

  • In CommonJS, B receives A's module.exports as it is at that moment—often an incomplete object.
  • In ESM, live bindings help, but accessing an exported let, const, or class before it is initialized throws a ReferenceError.

Fix circular dependencies by moving shared code into a third module, or by passing dependencies as function parameters.

docs.title: The node: prefix
docs.text: Import built-in modules as node:fs, node:path, and so on. The prefix makes the source obvious and, in CommonJS, bypasses the require cache. Older built-ins load even without it: require("http") always returns the built-in module. Newer built-ins such as node:test and node:sqlite exist only with the prefix, so their short names stay free for npm packages.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Use ESM ("type": "module") for new applications and new libraries. It is the language standard, supports top-level await, and is what browsers, Deno, and Bun use.
  • Use CommonJS when you maintain an existing CommonJS codebase, or when a tool you depend on still handles CommonJS more reliably (for example Jest without extra configuration).
  • Use .mjs / .cjs for the odd file that must differ from the package's type, such as a CommonJS config file in an ESM project.
  • Use dynamic import() for optional features and heavy modules that are not needed at startup.
  • Avoid mixing both styles in one file, and avoid publishing a library as both formats unless you must support old Node.js versions. Two copies of the same library in one process (one CommonJS, one ESM) do not share state.
Situation Choose Reason New API or service ESM Standard syntax, top-level await, future-facing Existing large CommonJS app Stay CommonJS; migrate gradually Migration touches every import path Library for Node.js 22.12+ only ESM Those versions can require() it too Library that must support older Node.js Dual package via exports conditions CommonJS users there cannot require() ESM Test suite on Jest CommonJS or a transform Jest's native ESM support is experimental

docs.title: CommonJS and ESM compared
docs.text: Aspect CommonJS ES modules Syntax require(), module.exports import, export Standard Node.js convention ECMAScript language standard Loading Synchronous, at runtime Static graph, async loading Conditional loading require() anywhere import() (async) Top-level await No Yes __dirname / __filename Yes import.meta.dirname / import.meta.filename File extensions in imports Optional Required for relative paths Strict mode Opt-in Always Exports The module.exports object; destructured values do not update Live bindings

docs.title: A small ESM project layout
docs.text:
orders-api/
├── package.json        { "type": "module" }
└── src/
    ├── server.js       import { app } from "./app.js";
    ├── app.js          import { ordersRouter } from "./routes/orders.js";
    └── routes/
        └── orders.js   export const ordersRouter = ...

docs.title: Converting a CommonJS module to ESM
docs.text:
Before (CommonJS, total.cjs):

const path = require("node:path");
const { formatPrice } = require("./format");
module.exports = function renderTotal(items) { /* ... */ };

After (ESM, total.js in a "type": "module" package):

import path from "node:path";
import { formatPrice } from "./format.js"; // extension now required
export default function renderTotal(items) { /* ... */ }

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use ESM ("type": "module") for new projects.
  • Always include file extensions in relative ESM imports.
  • Import built-ins with the node: prefix.
  • Prefer named exports for utilities; they are easier to search for and refactor.
  • Keep modules focused; a module that exports everything becomes a hidden dependency hub.
  • Avoid circular dependencies; extract shared code instead.
  • Use dynamic import() for optional or heavy modules.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The app will not start after a dependency upgrade.
  • Symptom: startup crashes with Error [ERR_REQUIRE_ESM]: require() of ES Module ... not supported.
  • Detect: the stack trace names a package that recently released a new major version.
  • Cause: the dependency became ESM-only, and the app runs on a Node.js version older than 22.12/20.19 that cannot require() ESM.
  • Fix: upgrade Node.js, load the package with await import(), or pin the last CommonJS-compatible major until you migrate.
  • Builds pass but production crashes on imports.
  • Symptom: ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND: Cannot find module '/app/dist/utils'.
  • Detect: the missing path has no .js extension, while the compiled file is dist/utils.js.
  • Cause: TypeScript or a bundler emitted extensionless relative imports, which ESM does not resolve.
  • Fix: write ./utils.js in source imports and compile with module: "nodenext", or bundle the app.
  • A library upgrade breaks deep imports.
  • Symptom: ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED for an import such as some-lib/dist/internal/helpers.
  • Detect: the new version's package.json gained an exports field.
  • Cause: exports hides every file it does not list.
  • Fix: import only documented entry points, or ask the maintainers to export the subpath.
  • Shared state is not shared.
  • Symptom: a singleton (a config cache, a metrics registry) appears twice, or instanceof checks fail for objects from the same library.
  • Detect: log the resolved file path of the library from both places; one is the CommonJS build and one the ESM build.
  • Cause: some code require()s the library and other code imports it, so a dual package is loaded in both formats.
  • Fix: load it one way throughout the app, or keep state in a single format-neutral module.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Module: A file with its own scope that exports selected values.
  • CommonJS: Node.js's original module system using require and module.exports.
  • ES module (ESM): The standard JavaScript module system using import and export.
  • Named export: An export identified by its name.
  • Default export: The single main export of a module.
  • Live binding: An ESM import that reflects the exporter's current value.
  • Module cache: Storage that makes each module run once per process.
  • exports field: The package.json map of a package's public entry points.
  • Bare specifier: An import path such as express that refers to a package rather than a file.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Omitting .js in ESM imports, causing ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND.
  • Using require in an ES module, causing require is not defined in ES module scope. Use import, or createRequire from node:module if you truly need require.
  • Using import in a CommonJS file without "type": "module" or a .mjs extension.
  • Reassigning exports instead of module.exports.
  • Expecting __dirname in ESM.
  • "import and require are interchangeable." They differ in timing, bindings, and resolution rules.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. How does Node.js decide whether a .js file is CommonJS or ESM?
  2. Why does exports = {...} not export anything?
  3. What is module caching, and how does it make modules behave like singletons?
  4. How do you get the current file's folder in an ES module?
  5. When would you use dynamic import()?
  6. What does the exports field in package.json control?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Node.js API: ECMAScript modules
  • Node.js API: CommonJS modules
  • Node.js API: Packages (type and exports)
  • MDN: JavaScript modules
  • Modules and error handling in the browser

docs.title: npm and Package Management
docs.text: npm (originally "Node Package Manager") is the default tool for installing, updating, and publishing JavaScript packages, and the name of the public registry that hosts them. Every Node.js project describes itself and its dependencies in a package.json file, and npm uses that file to build the node_modules folder.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A typical backend depends on dozens of direct packages and hundreds of indirect ones. How you declare versions, lock them, install them in CI, and check them for vulnerabilities decides whether builds are reproducible and whether a compromised package can reach production. Package management is a daily skill, not a one-time setup.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• left-pad (2016): an author unpublished 273 packages from npm after a name dispute. One of them, the tiny left-pad, sat deep in the dependency trees of thousands of projects, including Babel. npm saw hundreds of install failures per minute and, in an unprecedented step, re-published the exact version (0.0.3) that dependents pinned, ending a 2.5-hour disruption (npm blog: kik, left-pad, and npm).
  • event-stream (2018): a new maintainer of the popular event-stream package added a dependency, flatmap-stream, that contained malicious code targeting one company's development environment. npm removed the malicious versions and took ownership of the package (npm blog: Details about the event-stream incident).
  • Shai-Hulud (2025): a self-replicating worm spread through compromised maintainer accounts by injecting malicious post-install scripts into popular packages, and stole secrets. GitHub responded by requiring 2FA for local publishing, limiting granular tokens to seven days, and pushing trusted publishing from CI (GitHub blog: Our plan for a more secure npm supply chain).
  • pnpm now refuses to run dependencies' build scripts unless they are listed in allowBuilds, because most compromised packages have used install scripts to run code (pnpm docs: Supply chain security).

Popular tools and providers: npm, pnpm, and Yarn as clients; the npm registry, GitHub Packages, and private registries such as Verdaccio or Artifactory; Dependabot and Renovate for update pull requests.

docs.title: package.json
docs.text:
{
  "name": "orders-api",
  "version": "1.4.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "main": "./src/server.js",
  "exports": "./src/server.js",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "node --watch --env-file=.env src/server.js",
    "start": "node src/server.js",
    "test": "node --test",
    "lint": "eslint ."
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^5.1.0",
    "zod": "^3.23.8"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "eslint": "^9.10.0",
    "supertest": "^7.0.0"
  },
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=22"
  }
}
Field Purpose name Package name. Lowercase, URL-safe; may be scoped like @acme/orders. version The package's own semantic version. private true prevents accidental npm publish. Use it for applications. type "module" makes .js files ES modules; "commonjs" (default) makes them CommonJS. main Entry point when someone imports the package (older field). exports Modern, stricter map of the package's public entry points. scripts Named commands run with npm run <name>. dependencies Packages needed at runtime in production. devDependencies Packages needed only for development, tests, and builds. peerDependencies Packages the consumer must install, typically for plugins (for example, a React component library declaring react). optionalDependencies Packages that may fail to install without failing the whole install. engines Supported Node.js (and npm) versions.

Create one with npm init (interactive) or npm init -y (defaults).

docs.title: Semantic versioning
docs.text:
Packages use semantic versioning (semver): MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.

  • MAJOR changes may break existing code.
  • MINOR adds features in a backward-compatible way.
  • PATCH fixes bugs in a backward-compatible way.
  • Pre-releases look like 2.0.0-beta.1.

Version ranges in package.json say which versions are acceptable:

Range Means Matches for 1.2.3 1.2.3 Exactly this version 1.2.3 only ^1.2.3 Compatible: same major >=1.2.3 <2.0.0 ~1.2.3 Approximately: same minor >=1.2.3 <1.3.0 >=1.2.3 <1.5.0 Explicit range As written 1.x / 1.* Any 1.x version >=1.0.0 <2.0.0 * / latest Anything Avoid

npm install express saves ^ ranges by default.

The 0.x special case

Before 1.0.0, any change may break things, so caret ranges are narrower: ^0.2.3 means >=0.2.3 <0.3.0, and ^0.0.3 means exactly 0.0.3.

docs.title: package-lock.json
docs.text:
Ranges allow many versions, so two installs on different days could produce different trees. package-lock.json records the exact version, download URL, and integrity hash of every installed package, including indirect (transitive) dependencies.

  • Commit it for applications so every developer, CI run, and server gets the identical tree.
  • The integrity hashes make npm reject tampered downloads.
  • Review lockfile changes in pull requests; unexpected new packages are a warning sign.

docs.title: npm install versus npm ci
docs.text: Command Behavior Use it npm install Installs from package.json, using the lockfile where it fits; may update the lockfile. Local development, adding packages. npm install <pkg> Adds a dependency and updates both files. Adding a runtime dependency. npm install -D <pkg> Adds a devDependency. Adding a tool. npm ci Requires a lockfile; deletes node_modules and installs exactly what the lockfile says; fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree; never writes package.json or the lockfile. CI pipelines and production builds. npm ci --omit=dev Same, without devDependencies. Production images.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
npm outdated            # shows Current, Wanted (max in range), Latest
npm update              # updates within your ranges and the lockfile
npm install express@6   # move to a new major deliberately

npm update never crosses a range boundary, so major upgrades are always a deliberate choice. Read changelogs before major upgrades.

docs.title: Scripts and lifecycle hooks
docs.text:
npm run dev       # runs scripts.dev
npm start         # shortcut for npm run start
npm test          # shortcut for npm run test
npm run lint -- --fix   # arguments after -- are passed to the script

npm adds node_modules/.bin to PATH while a script runs, so scripts can call locally installed tools by name (eslint, not ./node_modules/.bin/eslint).

If a script named prebuild or postbuild exists, npm runs it before or after build. Packages can also define install lifecycle scripts such as preinstall, install, postinstall, and prepare, which run automatically when the package is installed—this is important for security (see below).

docs.title: npx
docs.text:
npx <command> runs a package's binary from the local node_modules/.bin if it is installed. Otherwise npx asks for confirmation, then downloads the package into the npm cache and runs it (--yes skips the prompt).

npx prisma migrate dev
npx create-vite@latest my-app

docs.title: Global versus local installs
docs.text:
• Local (default): installed into the project's node_modules and recorded in package.json. Use this for everything the project needs, including tools.
  • Global (npm install -g): installed once for the machine. Use it only for standalone CLIs you run outside projects. Global tools are not recorded in any project, so teammates and CI do not get them.

docs.title: Security: the supply chain
docs.text:
Every dependency is code you run with full access to your machine and servers. Common risks:

  • Known vulnerabilities in a package version.
  • Typosquatting: malicious packages with names like expres or lodahs.
  • Malicious install scripts: postinstall runs arbitrary code during npm install.
  • Compromised maintainer accounts publishing a malicious new version of a popular package.
  • Dependency confusion: a public package shadowing an internal package name.

Defenses:

npm audit               # report known vulnerabilities
npm audit fix           # apply compatible fixes
npm ci --ignore-scripts # install without running lifecycle scripts
npm ls express          # see why a package is in the tree
  • Commit and review the lockfile; use npm ci in CI.
  • Check a package's maintainers, download history, and repository before adding it. Fewer dependencies mean a smaller attack surface.
  • Consider disabling install scripts (ignore-scripts=true in .npmrc) and allowing only the packages that genuinely need them.
  • Use scoped names (@your-org/...) and a private registry for internal packages.
  • Enable automated update tooling (such as Dependabot or Renovate) so fixes arrive as reviewable pull requests.

docs.title: Workspaces and monorepos
docs.text:
npm workspaces manage several packages in one repository with a single install and shared node_modules:

{
  "name": "acme",
  "private": true,
  "workspaces": ["packages/*", "services/*"]
}

npm install                         # installs all workspaces
npm run test --workspaces           # run test in every workspace
npm install zod -w services/orders  # add a dependency to one workspace

Workspaces can depend on each other by name, so a shared @acme/validation package can be used by several services without publishing it.

docs.title: pnpm and Yarn
docs.text:
Tool Key idea npm Default, ships with Node.js. pnpm Stores each package version once in a global content-addressable store and links it into projects; saves disk space, installs fast, and has a strict layout that prevents using undeclared dependencies. Does not run dependencies' build scripts unless they are listed in allowBuilds; by default the install fails when an unapproved one is found. Yarn Alternative client with workspaces and Plug'n'Play mode (no node_modules).

All use package.json; each has its own lockfile (pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock). Use one tool per project and commit its lockfile.

docs.title: Publishing basics
docs.text:
npm login
npm version patch          # bump version, create a git tag
npm publish --access public
  • Use the files field (or .npmignore) so you publish only built output, not tests or secrets.
  • Scoped packages are published with private visibility by default; --access public makes them public.
  • Prefer publishing from CI with provenance or trusted publishing, so users can verify where a package was built.

docs.title: .npmrc
docs.text:
.npmrc configures npm per project (./.npmrc) or per user (~/.npmrc):

save-exact=true
engine-strict=true
@acme:registry=https://npm.acme.example/
//npm.acme.example/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}

Reference tokens through environment variables as shown; never commit a real token. npm replaces ${VARIABLE_NAME} with the variable's value, and leaves the text unchanged if the variable is not defined.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Use npm install locally to add, remove, or update packages.
  • Use npm ci in CI and production builds, where the install must match the lockfile exactly and fail loudly if it cannot.
  • Use exact versions (save-exact=true) for applications that want every change to arrive through a reviewed pull request. Ranges plus a lockfile are also fine; the lockfile already pins what is installed.
  • Use local installs (devDependencies + npx) for project tools; reserve -g for personal CLIs.
  • Use workspaces when several packages or services in one repository share code.
  • Do not add a dependency for a few lines of code you can write and test yourself; each package is code you trust with your servers.
Client Strengths Trade-offs npm Ships with Node.js; no extra setup; workspaces Flat node_modules lets code import undeclared packages pnpm Fast, disk-efficient, strict layout, blocks unapproved build scripts Some old tools assume a flat node_modules Yarn Plug'n'Play (no node_modules), mature monorepo features PnP needs editor and tool support

docs.title: Adding and removing packages
docs.text:
npm install express            # runtime dependency
npm install -D vitest          # dev dependency
npm uninstall left-pad         # remove and update package.json
npm install express@5.1.0 -E   # exact version (-E = --save-exact)

docs.title: A production Docker install
docs.text:
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev            # exact, reproducible, no dev tools
COPY src ./src
USER node
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Commit package-lock.json for applications; use npm ci in CI and production builds.
  • Put build and test tools in devDependencies and install production images with --omit=dev.
  • Mark applications "private": true.
  • Keep dependencies few and up to date; remove unused ones.
  • Run npm audit in CI and act on high-severity findings.
  • Upgrade majors deliberately, one at a time, with tests.
  • Use the engines field and .nvmrc to declare the Node.js version.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• CI fails with a lockfile error.
  • Symptom: the pipeline stops at the install step.
  • Detect: the log shows npm error code EUSAGE and "npm ci can only install packages when your package.json and package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json are in sync", followed by a line such as Missing: is-number@7.0.0 from lock file.
  • Cause: someone edited package.json by hand, or committed it without the updated lockfile.
  • Fix: run npm install locally and commit both files together. Never switch CI to npm install to make the error go away.
  • "Works on my machine", crashes in the container.
  • Symptom: the production image fails at startup with Cannot find package 'zod' (ESM) or Cannot find module 'zod' (CommonJS).
  • Detect: the missing package is listed under devDependencies, and the image was built with npm ci --omit=dev.
  • Cause: a runtime import of a dev-only package.
  • Fix: move it to dependencies, and run a smoke test against the built image in CI.
  • An update breaks code that never imported the package.
  • Symptom: after npm update, a module that was always "there" is missing.
  • Detect: npm ls <package> shows it was only present as a dependency of another package.
  • Cause: the code relied on a phantom dependency that npm's flat node_modules happened to expose.
  • Fix: declare every package you import in your own package.json. pnpm's strict layout catches this early.
  • A compromised dependency.
  • Symptom: a security advisory, unexpected outbound network traffic from build machines, or new packages in a lockfile diff nobody requested.
  • Detect: npm audit in CI, dependency update tools, and review of package-lock.json changes in pull requests.
  • Cause: a malicious version published through a stolen maintainer account, often running code in postinstall.
  • Fix: pin to the last safe version, disable install scripts, rotate any secrets the build could reach, and prefer packages published with provenance.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Package: A folder or archive described by a package.json, usually published to a registry.
  • Registry: A server that stores packages, such as the public npm registry.
  • Dependency: A package your code needs.
  • Transitive dependency: A dependency of one of your dependencies.
  • Semantic versioning: The MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH versioning convention.
  • Lockfile: A file that pins the exact resolved dependency tree.
  • Lifecycle script: A script npm runs automatically, such as postinstall.
  • Workspace: A package inside a monorepo managed by one root install.
  • Supply-chain attack: An attack delivered through a dependency rather than your own code.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Not committing the lockfile, so different machines install different versions.
  • Using npm install in CI, which may change the tree instead of failing when files disagree.
  • Putting tools in dependencies, which bloats production images.
  • "^ means latest." It means the latest version within the same major.
  • Deleting the lockfile to "fix" install errors, which silently upgrades everything.
  • Trusting a package because it is popular. Popular packages are attractive targets.
  • Installing project tools globally, so teammates and CI lack them.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between dependencies, devDependencies, and peerDependencies?
  2. Which versions does ^1.4.2 allow? And ~1.4.2? And ^0.4.2?
  3. Why should package-lock.json be committed, and what does it contain?
  4. When should you use npm ci instead of npm install?
  5. Name three supply-chain risks and one defense for each.
  6. What problem do workspaces solve?
