docs.title: Process, Environment Variables, and Configuration
docs.text: Every running Node.js program is an operating-system process, and the global process object is its control panel: command-line arguments, environment variables, exit codes, signals, memory usage, and standard input and output. This page explains how a backend reads its configuration and shuts down cleanly.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: The same code runs on a laptop, in CI, in staging, and in production, with different database addresses, secrets, and ports. That difference must live in configuration, not code. Production platforms also stop and restart your process constantly—during deploys, scaling, and crashes—so handling signals and shutting down gracefully decides whether users see failed requests.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The Twelve-Factor App, a methodology its authors drew from their work on the Heroku platform, says an app should store config in environment variables. They are easy to change between deploys without code changes and are unlikely to be committed to the repository by accident (The Twelve-Factor App: Config).
  • Kubernetes gives a Pod a grace period to terminate gracefully, which defaults to 30 seconds. Your process receives SIGTERM at the start of that period (Kubernetes docs: Pod lifecycle).
  • Docker's docker stop sends SIGTERM to the container's main process, then SIGKILL after a grace period. The signal reaches only that main process (Docker docs: docker container stop).
  • The official Node.js Docker image's best-practices guide recommends CMD ["node","index.js"] instead of npm start, so SIGTERM and SIGINT reach Node.js "instead of npm swallowing them". It also recommends docker run --init (nodejs/docker-node: Best practices).

Popular tools and providers: --env-file and process.loadEnvFile() built into Node.js; dotenv; zod or envalid for validation; AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, and Doppler for secrets; PM2, systemd, Docker, and Kubernetes for process lifecycle.

docs.title: The process object
docs.text:
process is global; you can also import it with import process from "node:process".

Property / method Example value Use process.pid 48213 Process ID, useful in logs. process.platform "linux" OS family. process.cwd() "/srv/app" Current working directory (where the process was started). process.argv ["/usr/bin/node", "/srv/app/cli.js", "--force"] Command-line arguments. process.env { PORT: "3000", ... } Environment variables. process.exitCode 1 Exit code used when the process ends naturally. process.exit(code) — Ends the process immediately. process.memoryUsage() { rss, heapTotal, heapUsed, external, arrayBuffers } Memory in bytes. process.uptime() 523.4 Seconds since the process started. process.hrtime.bigint() 1234567890123n High-resolution monotonic time in nanoseconds, for measuring durations. process.version "v24.3.1" Node.js version. 
const start = process.hrtime.bigint();
await doWork();
const ms = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / 1e6;
console.log(`took ${ms.toFixed(1)} ms`);

Use process.hrtime.bigint() or performance.now() for durations; system clock time (Date.now()) can jump when the clock is adjusted.

docs.title: Command-line arguments
docs.text:
process.argv[0] is the Node.js executable and process.argv[1] is the script. Your arguments start at index 2. util.parseArgs parses flags without a library:

// cli.js — run: node cli.js --port 8080 --verbose report.csv
import { parseArgs } from "node:util";

const { values, positionals } = parseArgs({
  options: {
    port: { type: "string", short: "p", default: "3000" },
    verbose: { type: "boolean", short: "v", default: false },
  },
  allowPositionals: true,
});

console.log(values);       // [Object: null prototype] { port: '8080', verbose: true }
console.log(positionals);  // [ 'report.csv' ]

values is created without a prototype, so console.log labels it [Object: null prototype]. It behaves like a normal object for reading properties.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Environment variables are key–value strings that the operating system or a platform passes to a process. They are the standard way to configure a backend per environment.

PORT=8080 DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/app node server.js

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

Facts to remember:

  • Values are always strings. "false" is truthy and "10" is not a number until you convert it.
  • A missing variable is undefined.
  • Changing process.env affects only the current process and its children.

docs.title: Loading variables from a file
docs.text:
For local development, keep variables in a .env file and load them:

node --env-file=.env server.js

# .env (never commit real secrets)
PORT=3000
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/orders
JWT_SECRET=dev-only-secret-change-me

Node.js also provides process.loadEnvFile(path). The popular dotenv package does the same in older setups. In production, real values come from the platform: container settings, a secrets manager, or the deployment system—not a file committed to git. See environment variables and configuration and secrets.

docs.title: Validating configuration at startup
docs.text:
Read and validate all configuration once, at startup, in one module. If something required is missing or malformed, fail immediately with a clear message instead of failing on the first request hours later.

// config.js (zod 4)
import { z } from "zod";

const schema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(["development", "test", "production"]).default("development"),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(3000), // "8080" → 8080
  DATABASE_URL: z.url(),
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32),
  LOG_LEVEL: z.enum(["debug", "info", "warn", "error"]).default("info"),
});

const result = schema.safeParse(process.env);
if (!result.success) {
  console.error("Invalid configuration:", z.flattenError(result.error).fieldErrors);
  process.exit(1);
}

export const config = Object.freeze(result.data);

With an invalid DATABASE_URL and a short JWT_SECRET, this prints { DATABASE_URL: [ 'Invalid URL' ], JWT_SECRET: [ 'Too small: expected string to have >=32 characters' ] } and exits with code 1. (With zod 3, write z.string().url() and result.error.flatten().fieldErrors.)

The rest of the application imports config instead of reading process.env directly, which keeps types correct and makes it obvious what settings exist.

docs.title: What NODE_ENV does
docs.text: NODE_ENV is a convention, not a Node.js feature. Node.js itself ignores it. Libraries read it: with NODE_ENV=production, Express caches view templates and CSS generated by CSS extensions, and generates less verbose error messages. Many other tools skip development-only behavior. Use it to describe the kind of environment (development, test, production), not which deployment it is—staging should usually run with NODE_ENV=production and its own configuration values.

docs.title: Standard streams
docs.text:
Stream Use process.stdin Readable: input piped or typed into the process. process.stdout Writable: normal output (console.log). process.stderr Writable: errors and diagnostics (console.error).

Containers and platforms collect stdout and stderr as logs, so servers should log there rather than to local files.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
A process reports success or failure to whatever started it through its exit code.

Code Meaning 0 Success. 1 General failure; also used by Node.js for an uncaught exception. 13 Node.js: an ES module's top-level await never settled. 128 + N Terminated by a fatal signal N; Node.js follows the same convention (for example, 130 = SIGINT, 137 = SIGKILL, 143 = SIGTERM).

There are two ways to exit:

process.exitCode = 1;  // exit with 1 when the event loop is empty (preferred)
process.exit(1);       // exit NOW: pending writes, timers, and I/O are dropped

Prefer setting process.exitCode and letting work finish. Use process.exit() when you must stop immediately, such as after logging a fatal error.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
Operating systems send signals to processes:

Signal Sent when Default behavior SIGINT You press Ctrl+C in a terminal. Exit. SIGTERM A process manager, Docker, or Kubernetes asks the process to stop. Exit. SIGKILL Forced kill (for example, after a shutdown grace period). Exit immediately; cannot be caught. SIGHUP The terminal closed; some tools use it to reload config. Exit.

Orchestrators usually send SIGTERM, wait for a grace period (Kubernetes defaults to 30 seconds), then send SIGKILL. Your process should finish its work within that window.

On Windows, signal support is limited: Ctrl+C produces SIGINT, and you can listen for SIGTERM, but Windows does not send it the way Linux does. Production Linux containers are where signal handling matters most.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Use environment variables for anything that differs between environments: URLs, ports, credentials, feature switches.
  • Use a secrets manager (injected as environment variables or read at startup) for credentials in production; .env files are for local development.
  • Use one validated config module that every other file imports.
  • Use process.exitCode for normal failures, and process.exit() only when you must stop at once.
  • Do not put structured or large config (lists of rules, feature matrices) into dozens of environment variables; load a config file or a config service and validate it the same way.
  • Do not read process.env in hot paths; read it once at startup.
Config kind Where it belongs Example Per-environment values Environment variables DATABASE_URL, PORT Secrets Secrets manager → environment JWT_SECRET, API keys Defaults shared by all environments Code (in the config schema) LOG_LEVEL default info Large or structured settings Versioned config file or service Rate-limit rules per plan

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
A graceful shutdown follows this sequence:

Step 1 matters behind a load balancer: once the instance reports "not ready", the load balancer stops sending it new traffic.

docs.title: A complete shutdown handler
docs.text:
// server.js
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { config } from "./config.js";
import { app } from "./app.js";
import { db } from "./db.js";

const server = createServer(app);
server.listen(config.PORT, () => {
  console.log(`Listening on port ${config.PORT} (pid ${process.pid})`);
});

let shuttingDown = false;

async function shutdown(signal) {
  if (shuttingDown) return; // ignore repeated signals
  shuttingDown = true;
  console.log(`${signal} received: shutting down`);

  // Safety net: never hang longer than the platform's grace period.
  const forceExit = setTimeout(() => {
    console.error("Shutdown timed out; forcing exit");
    process.exit(1);
  }, 20_000);
  forceExit.unref();

  try {
    await new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      server.close((error) => (error ? reject(error) : resolve()));
      server.closeIdleConnections(); // idle keep-alive sockets (automatic since Node.js 19)
    });
    await db.close(); // after requests finish, close the pool
    console.log("Shutdown complete");
    process.exitCode = 0;
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Error during shutdown", error);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  }
}

process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM"));
process.on("SIGINT", () => shutdown("SIGINT"));

docs.title: Reading piped input
docs.text:
// count-lines.js — run: cat access.log | node count-lines.js
let lines = 0;
for await (const chunk of process.stdin) {
  lines += chunk.toString().split("\n").length - 1;
}
console.log(`${lines} lines`);

docs.title: Starting the process correctly in containers
docs.text:
# Run node directly so it receives SIGTERM.
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]

npm start adds a wrapper process. The official Node.js Docker best-practices guide warns that npm can swallow SIGTERM and SIGINT, so containers should start Node.js directly. When Node.js runs as process ID 1 in a container, also consider an init process (docker run --init) so signals and zombie processes are handled correctly.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Put every environment-specific value—URLs, ports, credentials, feature switches—in environment variables, not code.
  • Validate configuration once at startup and fail fast on errors.
  • Convert types explicitly; environment variables are strings.
  • Never commit .env files with real secrets; commit a .env.example with placeholder values instead.
  • Never log secrets or the whole process.env.
  • Handle SIGTERM and SIGINT with a graceful shutdown and a forced-exit timeout.
  • Prefer process.exitCode over process.exit().
  • Log to stdout/stderr and let the platform collect logs.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Deploys cause a burst of errors.
  • Symptom: clients see 502/503 or ECONNRESET for a few seconds on every deploy.
  • Detect: errors line up with pod or instance terminations, and the app never logs "SIGTERM received".
  • Cause: the process never sees SIGTERM (started via npm start, or a shell wrapper as PID 1), or it exits without draining requests.
  • Fix: CMD ["node", "server.js"], a SIGTERM handler that closes the server, and a forced exit shorter than the platform's grace period.
  • Exit code 137 in the logs.
  • Symptom: containers restart with exit code 137, and shutdown logs are cut off.
  • Detect: the orchestrator reports the container as killed, or OOMKilled for memory.
  • Cause: 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL): either the grace period ran out during shutdown, or the container exceeded its memory limit.
  • Fix: finish shutdown faster than the grace period (Kubernetes defaults to 30 s), or fix memory use and set --max-old-space-size below the container limit.
  • The app starts with wrong settings.
  • Symptom: production connects to a test database, or a feature flag behaves the opposite way.
  • Detect: log the non-secret config values (never secrets) at startup, and compare them with what you expected.
  • Cause: a missing variable silently fell back to a default, or "false" was treated as truthy.
  • Fix: validate with a schema, make production-critical values required (no defaults), and parse booleans explicitly.
  • Secrets leak into logs.
  • Symptom: API keys appear in log search or error trackers.
  • Detect: secret-scanning alerts, or searching logs for known key prefixes.
  • Cause: logging process.env or a whole config object on startup or in error handlers.
  • Fix: log an allowlist of safe keys, redact secrets in the logger, and rotate any leaked credential.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Process: A running instance of a program with its own memory and ID.
  • Environment variable: A named string value passed to a process by its environment.
  • process.argv: The array of command-line arguments.
  • Exit code: The number a process returns when it ends; 0 means success.
  • Signal: An OS notification sent to a process, such as SIGTERM.
  • Graceful shutdown: Finishing in-flight work and releasing resources before exiting.
  • Grace period: The time a platform waits after SIGTERM before sending SIGKILL.
  • Fail fast: Stopping immediately when a required precondition is not met.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating process.env.DEBUG === "false" as false, or using if (process.env.FLAG), which is true for "false".
  • Reading process.env all over the codebase instead of through one validated config module.
  • Hard-coding secrets "temporarily."
  • "NODE_ENV=production makes Node.js faster." Node.js ignores it; libraries decide what it changes.
  • Calling process.exit() right after console.log, which can cut off output that has not been flushed.
  • Not handling SIGTERM, so every deploy drops in-flight requests.
  • Starting containers with npm start, so signals never reach Node.js.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why are environment variables used for configuration, and what type are their values?
  2. What are the benefits of validating configuration at startup?
  3. What is the difference between process.exit(1) and process.exitCode = 1?
  4. What do SIGTERM and SIGKILL mean, and which one can you handle?
  5. List the steps of a graceful shutdown.
  6. What does NODE_ENV actually control?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Node.js API: Process
  • Node.js API: util.parseArgs
  • Node.js API: Command-line options (including --env-file)
  • Node.js: How to read environment variables
  • The Twelve-Factor App: Config

docs.title: Project: Node Internals Lab
docs.text: In this project you build four small command-line tools, each designed to make one part of the Node.js runtime visible: a log analyzer that processes a file larger than your memory budget with streams, an event-loop lag monitor that shows exactly what blocking code does to other requests, a file hasher that compares the main thread with worker threads, and an HTTP server that shuts down gracefully on SIGTERM. Reading about the event loop and streams is useful; measuring them on your own machine is what makes the ideas stick.

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
• Read and write large files with constant memory using streams and pipeline() (buffers and streams, file system, path, and OS).
  • Respect backpressure by checking write() and waiting for drain (buffers and streams).
  • Measure event-loop delay with monitorEventLoopDelay and see blocking code delay unrelated requests (the event loop).
  • Break long CPU work into slices with setImmediate (asynchronous programming).
  • Run CPU-bound work in parallel with a small worker pool, and learn when that does not help (worker threads, child processes, and cluster).
  • Handle SIGTERM and SIGINT, fail readiness, drain, and exit cleanly (process, environment variables, and configuration, the http module).
  • Measure memory and time instead of guessing (errors, debugging, and performance).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Node.js, Active LTS (22 or newer). The tools use fetch, node:timers/promises, os.availableParallelism(), and ES modules. Check with node --version; see installing Node.js and managing versions.
  • About 2 GB of free disk space for the generated log file.
  • A terminal with curl. In Windows PowerShell, type curl.exe, because plain curl is an alias for Invoke-WebRequest.
  • For the SIGTERM milestone: Linux, macOS, WSL, or Docker. Windows cannot deliver SIGTERM to another process; Ctrl+C (which sends SIGINT) works everywhere.
  • Read first: runtime and architecture, the event loop, and modules: CommonJS and ES modules.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The lab is four independent tools. Each one exercises a different part of the runtime:

The key mechanism of the stream tools is backpressure: data flows forward in chunks, and a slow consumer makes the producer pause instead of filling memory.

The graceful-shutdown server follows a fixed sequence when the platform asks it to stop:

docs.title: Starting structure
docs.text:
node-internals-lab/
├── package.json            "type": "module" and npm scripts
├── scripts/
│   ├── generate-log.js     writes a large access log (milestone 2)
│   └── generate-blobs.js   writes random binary files (milestone 7)
├── tools/
│   ├── log-analyzer.js     stream + readline analyzer (milestone 3)
│   ├── extract-errors.js   Transform + gzip pipeline (milestone 4)
│   ├── lag-monitor.js      HTTP server + loop-delay monitor (milestones 5–6)
│   ├── hash-file.js        hashes one file
│   ├── hash-worker.js      worker thread entry point
│   ├── hash-files.js       main thread vs worker pool (milestone 7)
│   └── graceful-server.js  SIGTERM handling (milestone 8)
└── data/                   generated files (add to .gitignore)

docs.title: Milestone 1: Set up the lab
docs.text:
Goal: an ES-module project with one npm script per tool.

Read first: modules: CommonJS and ES modules, npm and package management.

Steps

  1. Create the folder and run npm init -y.
  2. Add "type": "module" so .js files use import.
  3. Add scripts for each tool and a .gitignore containing data/ and node_modules/.
{
  "name": "node-internals-lab",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "gen:log": "node scripts/generate-log.js data/app.log 30000000",
    "analyze": "node tools/log-analyzer.js data/app.log",
    "errors": "node tools/extract-errors.js data/app.log data/errors.log.gz",
    "lag": "node tools/lag-monitor.js",
    "gen:blobs": "node scripts/generate-blobs.js data/blobs 8 64",
    "hash": "node tools/hash-files.js data/blobs",
    "hash:workers": "node tools/hash-files.js data/blobs --workers",
    "server": "node tools/graceful-server.js"
  }
}

The project needs no dependencies: everything comes from Node.js core modules.

Done when:

  • node --version prints v22. or later.
  • npm run lists the eight scripts.

docs.title: Milestone 2: Generate a multi-gigabyte log with backpressure
docs.text:
Goal: write tens of millions of lines without the writer's memory growing.

Read first: buffers and streams, file system, path, and OS.

Steps

  1. Open a write stream with createWriteStream(file).
  2. Build one line per iteration in the format 2026-11-07T10:00:00.000Z GET /api/cart 200 123ms.
  3. Call out.write(line). When it returns false, the stream's internal buffer is full: await once(out, "drain") before writing more.
  4. Call out.end() and wait for "finish".
// scripts/generate-log.js (core loop)
import { createWriteStream } from "node:fs";
import { once } from "node:events";

const out = createWriteStream(file);
for (let i = 0; i < total; i++) {
  const line = `${time} ${pick(methods)} ${pick(paths)} ${pick(statuses)} ${ms}ms\n`;
  // write() returns false when the buffer is full: wait for "drain"
  if (!out.write(line)) await once(out, "drain");
}
out.end();
await once(out, "finish");

Use a status list that includes 500 and 503 so later milestones have errors to find. Without the drain check the loop still works, but every line waits in memory until the disk catches up, and memory grows with the file size.

Done when:

  • node scripts/generate-log.js data/app.log 2000000 prints wrote 2,000,000 lines to data/app.log and the file is about 98 MB (about 49 bytes per line).
  • npm run gen:log (30 million lines) produces a file of about 1.5 GB. Expect it to take a few minutes; 12 million lines took 66 seconds on the test machine.

docs.title: Milestone 3: Analyze the log with constant memory
docs.text:
Goal: count lines by status and path for a file larger than you would ever load into memory.

Read first: buffers and streams, asynchronous programming (the for await section).

Steps

  1. First, see why the obvious approach fails. Try reading the whole file:

    import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
const text = await readFile("data/app.log", "utf8"); // whole file as one string

    On a file larger than about 512 MB this throws RangeError: Invalid string length: V8 caps strings at buffer.constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH characters (536,870,888 in Node.js 22). Smaller files load, but memory grows with the file.

  2. Read the file as a stream and split it into lines with node:readline, which also handles lines split across chunks.

  3. Update two Map counters per line.
  4. Sample process.memoryUsage().rss every 100 ms to record peak memory.
// tools/log-analyzer.js (core loop)
import { createReadStream } from "node:fs";
import { createInterface } from "node:readline";

const rl = createInterface({ input: createReadStream(file), crlfDelay: Infinity });
for await (const line of rl) {
  if (line === "") continue;
  const [, , path, status] = line.split(" ");
  byStatus.set(status, (byStatus.get(status) ?? 0) + 1);
  byPath.set(path, (byPath.get(path) ?? 0) + 1);
}
// TODO: print the line count, time, peak RSS, 5xx total, and top 3 paths

Done when: npm run analyze prints a report like this (counts are random; the shape and the flat memory are what matter):

lines:          12,000,000
time:           10.8 s
peak memory:    64 MB (RSS)
5xx responses:  2,001,694

Peak memory stays roughly the same (around 60–100 MB) whether the file is 100 MB or 1.5 GB. On the test machine a 98 MB file peaked at 67 MB and a 588 MB file at 64 MB.

docs.title: Milestone 4: A Transform and gzip pipeline
docs.text:
Goal: copy only server errors (5xx) into a compressed file, using a custom Transform stream inside pipeline().

Read first: buffers and streams (Transform streams, pipeline, backpressure).

Steps

  1. Open the input with { encoding: "utf8" } so chunks are strings that never split a multi-byte character.
  2. Write a Transform that splits each chunk on "\n", keeps the last, possibly incomplete piece in leftover for the next chunk, and pushes only lines whose status starts with 5.
  3. Handle leftover once more in flush(), which runs after the last chunk.
  4. Connect read → transform → createGzip() → write with pipeline() from node:stream/promises. It handles backpressure across all four streams and destroys all of them if one fails.
// tools/extract-errors.js (the tricky part)
function serverErrorsOnly() {
  let leftover = ""; // a chunk can end in the middle of a line
  return new Transform({
    transform(chunk, encoding, callback) {
      const lines = (leftover + chunk).split("\n");
      leftover = lines.pop();
      const errors = lines.filter((line) => line.split(" ")[3]?.startsWith("5"));
      if (errors.length > 0) this.push(errors.join("\n") + "\n");
      callback();
    },
    flush(callback) {
      if (leftover.split(" ")[3]?.startsWith("5")) this.push(leftover + "\n");
      callback();
    },
  });
}

await pipeline(
  createReadStream(input, { encoding: "utf8" }),
  serverErrorsOnly(),
  createGzip(),
  createWriteStream(output),
);

Done when:

  • npm run errors prints kept N lines and wrote data/errors.log.gz, where N equals the 5xx responses count from milestone 3.

  • This check prints the same count and true:

    node -e "const z=require('zlib'),fs=require('fs');const l=z.gunzipSync(fs.readFileSync('data/errors.log.gz')).toString().split('\n').filter(Boolean);console.log(l.length,l.every(x=>x.split(' ')[3].startsWith('5')))"

    For a 2,000,000-line file the test run kept 333,226 lines in a 2.3 MB gzip file.

docs.title: Milestone 5: Watch blocking code freeze the event loop
docs.text:
Goal: see, in numbers, that one synchronous request delays every other request.

Read first: the event loop, building HTTP servers with the http module.

Steps

  1. Create a node:http server with three routes: /fast answers immediately, /block?ms=800 runs a busy loop for 800 ms, and /chunked?ms=800 comes in milestone 6.
  2. Enable a loop-delay histogram and print it every second, then reset it.
// tools/lag-monitor.js (monitor and blocking route)
import { monitorEventLoopDelay } from "node:perf_hooks";

const histogram = monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 10 });
histogram.enable();
setInterval(() => {
  const ms = (ns) => (ns / 1e6).toFixed(1); // the histogram reports nanoseconds
  console.log(`loop delay p50=${ms(histogram.percentile(50))}ms ` +
    `p99=${ms(histogram.percentile(99))}ms max=${ms(histogram.max)}ms`);
  histogram.reset();
}, 1000);

function blockFor(ms) {
  const end = Date.now() + ms;
  while (Date.now() < end) {} // nothing else can run until this returns
}
  1. Start it with npm run lag. In a second terminal start a slow request, and in a third time a fast one while the slow one runs:
curl "http://localhost:3000/block?ms=800"
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{time_total}s\n" http://localhost:3000/fast

Done when:

  • The /fast request sent during /block takes about as long as the block (747 ms in the test run, instead of a few milliseconds).
  • The monitor prints a line such as loop delay p50=15.7ms p99=813.7ms max=813.7ms for that second.

At idle the numbers sit near the 10 ms sampling resolution (a little higher on Windows, whose timers tick about every 15.6 ms). The jump in p99 and max is the signal.

docs.title: Milestone 6: Keep the loop responsive by slicing work
docs.text:
Goal: do the same 800 ms of CPU work without freezing other requests.

Read first: the event loop (splitting long work into chunks), asynchronous programming.

Steps

  1. Add /chunked?ms=800, which does the work in 10 ms slices.
  2. After each slice, await setImmediate() from node:timers/promises so timers, I/O, and other requests can run.
import { setImmediate as yieldToLoop } from "node:timers/promises";

async function workInSlices(ms) {
  const end = Date.now() + ms;
  while (Date.now() < end) {
    blockFor(Math.min(10, end - Date.now()));
    await yieldToLoop(); // let other callbacks run between slices
  }
}

Done when:

  • A /fast request sent during /chunked?ms=800 returns in a few milliseconds (8 ms in the test run), while /chunked itself still takes about 800 ms.
  • The monitor's max stays near 20 ms during /chunked.

Slicing keeps the server responsive but does not make the work faster or use more cores. For that, use worker threads (next milestone).

docs.title: Milestone 7: Hash files with a worker pool
docs.text:
Goal: compare hashing on the main thread with a pool of worker threads, and find out when workers help.

Read first: worker threads, child processes, and cluster.

Steps

  1. Generate test data: npm run gen:blobs writes 8 files of 64 MB of random bytes.
  2. Write hashFile(file, algorithm): stream the file and call hash.update(chunk) for each chunk, then hash.digest("hex").
  3. Main-thread mode: hash the files one after another.
  4. Worker mode: start min(files, os.availableParallelism()) workers and send each one the next file path when it finishes the previous one.
  5. Print the first 16 hex characters of each digest and the total time.
// tools/hash-worker.js
import { parentPort, workerData } from "node:worker_threads";
import { hashFile } from "./hash-file.js";

parentPort.on("message", async (file) => {
  try {
    parentPort.postMessage({ file, digest: await hashFile(file, workerData.algorithm) });
  } catch (error) {
    parentPort.postMessage({ file, error: error.message });
  }
});

// tools/hash-files.js (pool skeleton)
const worker = new Worker(new URL("./hash-worker.js", import.meta.url), {
  workerData: { algorithm },
});
const giveNextFile = () => {
  const file = queue.shift();
  if (file) return worker.postMessage(file);
  worker.terminate();
  // TODO: resolve the promise when the last worker has finished
};
worker.on("message", (result) => { results.push(result); giveNextFile(); });
worker.on("error", reject);
giveNextFile();

Done when:

  • Both modes print identical digests.
  • You can explain these timings from the test machine (8 cores):
8 files, sha256,   main thread: 0.72 s
8 files, sha256,   8 workers:   0.67 s
8 files, sha3-512, main thread: 5.48 s
8 files, sha3-512, 8 workers:   1.36 s

SHA-256 is hardware-accelerated on most CPUs, so the job is limited by reading the files and workers barely help. SHA3-512 is much more CPU intensive, so spreading it across cores is about four times faster. Measure before adding workers.

docs.title: Milestone 8: Shut down gracefully on SIGTERM
docs.text:
Goal: when the platform stops the process (a deploy, docker stop, Kubernetes), finish in-flight requests instead of dropping them.

Read first: process, environment variables, and configuration (signals and graceful shutdown), building HTTP servers with the http module.

Steps

  1. Count in-flight requests: increment on each request, decrement on the response's "close" event.
  2. Add /readyz (200 normally, 503 while shutting down) and a /slow route that takes 3 seconds.
  3. On SIGTERM or SIGINT: fail readiness, keep serving for a short drain delay so the load balancer notices, then call server.close(), which stops new connections and waits for in-flight requests.
  4. Exit with code 0 when close() calls back. Start an unref'd timer that forces process.exit(1) if something hangs.
// tools/graceful-server.js (shutdown sequence)
async function shutdown(signal) {
  if (shuttingDown) return;
  shuttingDown = true; // /readyz now answers 503
  setTimeout(() => {
    server.closeAllConnections();
    process.exit(1); // safety net: never hang a deploy
  }, DRAIN_DELAY_MS + 10_000).unref();

  await sleep(DRAIN_DELAY_MS); // keep serving while the load balancer drains us
  // close() waits for in-flight requests; since Node.js 19 it also closes idle keep-alive sockets
  server.close((error) => process.exit(error ? 1 : 0));
}
process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM"));
process.on("SIGINT", () => shutdown("SIGINT"));

Done when (Linux, macOS, or WSL):

  1. Start the server: npm run server prints its process ID.
  2. In a second terminal start a slow request: curl http://localhost:3000/slow.
  3. Within a second, send kill -TERM <pid>.
  4. curl http://localhost:3000/readyz during the drain delay prints shutting down with status 503.
  5. The slow request still completes with slow request finished, and the server logs:
SIGTERM: readiness now fails, 1 request(s) in flight
closing server, 1 request(s) still running
all requests finished, exiting
  1. echo $? in the server's terminal prints 0, and new requests fail with "connection refused".

On Windows, press Ctrl+C in the server's terminal instead of kill; the same handler runs for SIGINT.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Process the log in parallel: split the file into byte ranges, give each range to a worker, and handle lines that cross range boundaries.
  • Expose the loop-delay histogram as a /metrics endpoint and graph it.
  • Profile /block with node --cpu-prof tools/lag-monitor.js and open the .cpuprofile file in Chrome DevTools.
  • Replace the hand-written pool with a library such as Piscina and compare the code.
  • Cancel the analyzer cleanly on Ctrl+C with an AbortController passed to createReadStream.
  • Run the graceful server in a container and stop it with docker stop, which sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL after a grace period; see Docker.

docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module package.json has no "type": "module" Add it, or rename the files to .mjs The generator's memory keeps growing write()'s return value is ignored, so lines pile up in the buffer if (!out.write(line)) await once(out, "drain") RangeError: Invalid string length The whole file was read into one string Stream it with createReadStream and readline Counts are slightly off or the last line is missing Lines split across chunks were dropped or counted twice Keep a leftover in the Transform and handle it in flush(), or use readline Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000 Another server (often an earlier run) holds the port Stop it, or run with PORT=3001 Workers are not faster The work is limited by I/O, not CPU (SHA-256 with hardware support) Measure first; workers help only CPU-bound work, such as --algorithm=sha3-512 Cannot find module .../hash-worker.js The worker path was resolved from the current directory Use new URL("./hash-worker.js", import.meta.url) kill -TERM or Stop-Process ends the server without the shutdown logs Windows terminates the process instead of delivering SIGTERM Use Ctrl+C (SIGINT) on Windows, or test in WSL or Docker

docs.title: Node.js Runtime and Architecture
docs.text: Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser. It combines Google's V8 engine with a C library called libuv and a set of built-in modules, so JavaScript programs can read files, open network connections, and run as long-lived servers.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Knowing how Node.js is built explains most of its behavior: why one process can serve thousands of concurrent connections, why a single slow loop can freeze an entire server, and why some "asynchronous" operations still use threads. Backend developers who understand the runtime write code that stays responsive under load and know when Node.js is the wrong tool.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix rebuilt the netflix.com website UI on Node.js and React so the same JavaScript could render pages on the server and update them in the browser. The old stack used different languages on the server and the client, which made markup logic hard to share. The rebuild was part of an effort that cut startup time by 70% (Netflix Technology Blog: Making Netflix.com Faster).
  • PayPal moved its web applications from Java to Node.js in 2013. In a side-by-side test of the same page, the Node.js version (built on Express) served double the requests per second, and its average response time was 35% lower (about 200 ms faster) (PayPal Tech Blog: Node.js at PayPal).
  • Trello built its server in Node.js because instant updates meant holding many open connections, which suits an event-driven, non-blocking server. The first prototype was a single Node.js process talking to the browser over a WebSocket (Atlassian blog: The Trello tech stack).
  • Visual Studio Code runs extensions in a separate Node.js "extension host" process, locally or on a remote machine. A slow extension therefore cannot freeze the editor's user interface (VS Code docs: Extension Host).

Popular tools and providers: Node.js, Deno, and Bun as runtimes; nvm and Volta for versions; PM2 for process management; Chrome DevTools and --cpu-prof for profiling.

docs.title: The main building blocks
docs.text:
• V8 is the JavaScript engine also used in Chrome. It parses your code, compiles it to machine code with a just-in-time (JIT) compiler, runs it, and manages memory with a garbage collector. V8 knows nothing about files or sockets; it only executes JavaScript.
  • libuv is a C library that provides the event loop and a uniform asynchronous I/O interface across Linux, macOS, and Windows. It also owns a small thread pool for work that the operating system cannot do asynchronously.
  • C++ bindings connect JavaScript functions such as fs.readFile() to the native code that performs the work.
  • Core modules such as node:fs, node:http, node:path, and node:crypto are the JavaScript APIs you import. They are written partly in JavaScript and partly in C++.

docs.title: Just-in-time compilation in V8
docs.text: V8 does not interpret your code line by line forever. It first compiles JavaScript to bytecode and runs it with an interpreter (Ignition). Functions that run often become "hot" and are recompiled by optimizing compilers into fast machine code based on the types they have seen. If those assumptions break—for example, a function that always received numbers suddenly gets a string—V8 can deoptimize and fall back to slower code. Consistent object shapes and argument types help V8 keep code optimized.

docs.title: Single-threaded JavaScript, non-blocking I/O
docs.text:
Your JavaScript runs on one main thread. At any moment, only one piece of your JavaScript is executing. Node.js stays fast because it does not wait for slow operations. When your code asks for a file or a network response, Node.js hands the work to libuv and immediately continues running other JavaScript. When the operation finishes, libuv queues a callback, and the event loop runs it when the main thread is free.

 Request A arrives ──► JS handler starts DB query ──► returns immediately
 Request B arrives ──► JS handler starts file read ──► returns immediately
        ...                    (main thread is free)
 DB result ready   ──► callback for A runs ──► response A sent
 File ready        ──► callback for B runs ──► response B sent

This model is called event-driven, non-blocking I/O. A thread-per-request server would need one thread (and its memory) per waiting request; Node.js needs one thread plus queued callbacks.

docs.title: Where the work really happens
docs.text:
Not every asynchronous operation is handled the same way:

Operation How libuv performs it TCP/UDP sockets, HTTP servers and clients OS async mechanisms (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows). No thread pool. Timers (setTimeout, setInterval) Tracked by the event loop itself. File system operations (fs.readFile, fs.stat, …) libuv thread pool, because most OSes lack portable async file APIs. dns.lookup() (used by http.get("example.com")) Thread pool (it calls the OS resolver getaddrinfo). dns.resolve*() Network-based via c-ares; no thread pool. CPU-heavy crypto: crypto.pbkdf2, crypto.scrypt, crypto.randomBytes (async) Thread pool. zlib async compression Thread pool.

The thread pool has 4 threads by default. You can change it with the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable, set before the process starts:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 node server.js

If an application performs many slow file reads or password hashes at once, requests can queue for a free pool thread even though the main thread is idle. For CPU-heavy pool work such as hashing or compression, a bigger pool helps only if the machine has spare CPU cores. Setting the variable from inside the program (process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE = ...) is not guaranteed to work, because the pool may already exist by then.

docs.title: Node.js compared with browser JavaScript
docs.text:
Both run ECMAScript, but the surrounding APIs differ.

Concern Browser Node.js Global object window (also globalThis) global (also globalThis) Page APIs document, DOM, localStorage None System access Sandboxed; no direct files fs, child_process, os, net Binary data ArrayBuffer, Blob Buffer (a Uint8Array subclass), plus web types Process info Not available process (env, argv, exit, signals) Modules ES modules ES modules and CommonJS Shared web APIs Native fetch, URL, AbortController, TextEncoder, structuredClone, Web Streams, WebSocket client

Use globalThis when code must run in both environments.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use Node.js for:

  • I/O-heavy APIs that mostly wait on databases, caches, and other services.
  • Real-time applications such as chat, notifications, and live dashboards over WebSockets, where one process holds many open connections.
  • Backend-for-frontend (BFF) layers that combine several APIs for a UI, especially when the team already writes JavaScript or TypeScript.
  • Server-side rendering of React, Vue, or Svelte apps, where the same code runs on the server and in the browser.
  • Streaming data such as file uploads, proxies, and log processing.
  • CLIs and tooling: npm, bundlers, linters, and test runners are mostly written for Node.js.

Avoid it, or add extra design, for:

  • CPU-bound work (video encoding, image processing, large calculations, machine-learning inference) on the main thread. Use worker threads, separate services, or a language better suited to the job.
  • Workloads needing strict real-time latency guarantees, since garbage collection pauses and a shared thread make timing less predictable.
  • Long, heavy number crunching inside a request, which blocks every other request on that process.
Workload Node.js Common alternative and why JSON API over a database Good fit Go or Java if the team already uses them; similar results for I/O-bound work Thousands of idle WebSocket connections Good fit Go or Elixir also handle many connections well Image or video processing Only with worker threads or a separate service Go, Rust, C++, or a managed media service Data science and ML Poor fit Python, with its numeric and ML libraries CLI tools for JavaScript projects Good fit (the ecosystem standard) Go or Rust for single-binary tools outside the JS ecosystem

docs.title: Node.js, Deno, and Bun
docs.text:
Runtime Engine Notes Node.js V8 Largest ecosystem and longest production track record. Deno V8 Secure by default (no file, network, or environment access until granted), runs TypeScript directly, built-in toolchain; works with npm packages and package.json projects. Bun JavaScriptCore Designed as a drop-in replacement for Node.js; ships a runtime, package manager, test runner, and bundler in one binary.

All three run modern JavaScript. Node.js remains the default choice for most production backends because of its ecosystem and stability.

docs.title: Seeing non-blocking I/O
docs.text:
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

console.log("1. Start reading");
const promise = readFile(new URL(import.meta.url)); // reads this file
console.log("2. Read requested; main thread continues");
const content = await promise;
console.log(`3. Read finished: ${content.length} bytes`);

Output:

1. Start reading
2. Read requested; main thread continues
3. Read finished: 300 bytes

The byte count is the size of your script file, so yours will differ. What matters is the order: line 2 prints before the read completes.

docs.title: Watching the thread pool fill up
docs.text:
crypto.pbkdf2 uses the thread pool. Starting six hashes with the default pool of four shows that the last two wait for a free thread:

import { pbkdf2 } from "node:crypto";

const start = Date.now();

for (let i = 1; i <= 6; i++) {
  pbkdf2("password", "salt", 200_000, 64, "sha512", () => {
    console.log(`hash ${i} done after ${Date.now() - start} ms`);
  });
}

Typical output (times vary by machine):

hash 1 done after 210 ms
hash 3 done after 212 ms
hash 2 done after 215 ms
hash 4 done after 218 ms
hash 5 done after 420 ms
hash 6 done after 423 ms

Run it again with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=6 and all six finish at roughly the same time on a machine with six or more cores.

docs.title: Blocking the main thread
docs.text:
import { createServer } from "node:http";

createServer((request, response) => {
  if (request.url === "/slow") {
    const end = Date.now() + 5000;
    while (Date.now() < end) {} // busy loop: blocks EVERY request for 5 s
  }
  response.end("ok\n");
}).listen(3000);

While /slow runs, a request to / cannot be answered, because the single JavaScript thread is busy. CPU work belongs in worker threads.

Measured on Node.js 22: with /slow running, a request to / waited about 4.9 seconds before it got ok.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep request handlers short and asynchronous; move CPU-heavy work off the main thread.
  • Prefer async APIs (node:fs/promises) over *Sync versions inside request paths; sync APIs are acceptable during startup.
  • Monitor event loop delay in production (see the event loop).
  • Tune UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE only when measurements show thread-pool queuing.
  • Keep object shapes and argument types consistent in hot code paths.
  • Run several processes (cluster, containers) to use all CPU cores; one Node.js process uses one core for JavaScript.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Thread pool saturation.
  • Symptom: file reads, password hashing, and outbound connections all slow down together, while CPU use and event loop delay look normal.
  • Detect: trace spans for fs, crypto.scrypt/pbkdf2, or the DNS step of outbound HTTP calls grow under load.
  • Cause: more than four slow pool tasks are running at once. dns.lookup(), which http.get() uses for host names, also runs in the pool.
  • Fix: set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE before the process starts, cache DNS results, and stream files instead of reading them whole.
  • A blocked event loop.
  • Symptom: every endpoint becomes slow at once, health checks time out, and the orchestrator restarts healthy-looking instances.
  • Detect: perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() p99 jumps, and one core sits at 100%.
  • Cause: synchronous CPU work in a handler, such as a huge JSON.parse, a *Sync call, or a slow regular expression.
  • Fix: take a CPU profile (node --cpu-prof), then move the hot code to a worker thread or make it incremental.
  • Idle cores.
  • Symptom: throughput stops rising at about one core's worth of work, although the host has more cores.
  • Detect: per-core CPU metrics show one core busy and the rest idle.
  • Cause: one Node.js process runs JavaScript on one thread.
  • Fix: run one process per core with cluster or PM2, or run several containers with about one CPU each.
  • Heap out of memory.
  • Symptom: the process crashes with a log line ending in JavaScript heap out of memory, often after hours of uptime.
  • Detect: restart counts rise, and process.memoryUsage().heapUsed grows steadily in metrics.
  • Cause: a leak, or loading a large dataset into memory at once.
  • Fix: compare heap snapshots to find the leak, stream large data, and set --max-old-space-size (in MiB) below the container's memory limit.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Runtime: The environment that executes a program and provides APIs to it.
  • V8: The JavaScript engine that compiles and runs JavaScript and collects garbage.
  • libuv: The C library that provides Node.js's event loop, thread pool, and cross-platform async I/O.
  • Event loop: The mechanism that runs queued callbacks when the main thread is free.
  • Thread pool: libuv's worker threads (4 by default) for file system, DNS lookup, some crypto, and zlib work.
  • Non-blocking I/O: Starting an input/output operation without waiting for it to complete.
  • JIT compilation: Compiling code to machine code while the program runs, based on observed behavior.
  • Core module: A module built into Node.js, imported with the node: prefix.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Node.js is single-threaded." Your JavaScript runs on one thread, but Node.js itself uses additional threads for the thread pool, garbage collection, and other internal work.
  • "Async means it runs in parallel." Network I/O is handled by the OS and file I/O by the thread pool, but your callbacks still run one at a time on the main thread.
  • "Node.js is fast at everything." It excels at waiting on I/O, not at CPU-heavy computation.
  • Using *Sync APIs in request handlers. Each call blocks every other request until it finishes.
  • Assuming browser APIs exist. document and window are not available in Node.js.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What do V8 and libuv each contribute to Node.js?
  2. Which operations use the libuv thread pool, and which use OS-level asynchronous mechanisms?
  3. Why can a single while loop make an entire Node.js server unresponsive?
  4. What does UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE change, and when would increasing it help?
  5. Name three workloads Node.js handles well and one it handles poorly.
  6. How does globalThis help code run in both browsers and Node.js?

docs.title: Worker Threads, Child Processes, and Cluster
docs.text: A Node.js process runs your JavaScript on one main thread, which uses one CPU core. To run CPU-heavy work without freezing the server, or to use every core on a machine, Node.js offers three tools: worker threads (more threads in the same process), child processes (separate programs), and the cluster module (several copies of your server sharing a port).

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A single image resize, PDF render, or large calculation on the main thread blocks every other request (see the event loop). And a server on an 8-core machine that runs one Node.js process leaves seven cores idle. Choosing the right tool—and knowing when to scale with more containers instead—is a core backend skill. For the operating-system background, see processes and threads.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Heroku explains that Node.js is single-threaded, so it "can't automatically take advantage of additional CPU cores". Apps must fork multiple processes with the Cluster API, and Heroku recommends that all Node.js apps support clustering, tuned through the WEB_CONCURRENCY variable (Heroku Dev Center: Optimizing Node.js application concurrency).
  • PM2's cluster mode scales a networked Node.js app across all CPUs "without any code modifications", using the Node.js cluster module underneath. pm2 reload restarts the processes one at a time for a zero-downtime reload (PM2 docs: Cluster mode).
  • Piscina is a widely used worker-thread pool for Node.js. Services use it to run CPU-heavy tasks such as image or document processing in a fixed set of reusable workers instead of on the main thread (Piscina on GitHub).

Popular tools and providers: node:worker_threads, node:child_process, and node:cluster; Piscina for worker pools; PM2 and systemd for process management; Kubernetes and ECS for running one process per container.

docs.title: The CPU-bound problem
docs.text: Work is I/O-bound when it mostly waits (database queries, HTTP calls) and CPU-bound when it keeps the processor busy (hashing, compression, image processing, parsing huge files). Node.js handles I/O-bound work well on one thread. CPU-bound work must move somewhere else.

docs.title: Worker threads
docs.text:
The node:worker_threads module runs JavaScript in additional threads inside the same process. Each worker has its own V8 instance, event loop, and memory heap, so a worker's long computation does not block the main thread.

Key pieces:

API Purpose new Worker(file, { workerData }) Starts a worker running file, passing initial data. workerData (in the worker) The data passed at creation. parentPort.postMessage(value) (in the worker) Sends a message to the main thread. worker.postMessage(value) / worker.on("message") Two-way messaging from the main thread. worker.on("error"), worker.on("exit") Failure and termination events. isMainThread true in the main thread.

How data moves: messages are copied with the structured clone algorithm (similar to a deep copy). Large buffers can be transferred instead—ownership moves to the receiver with no copy—by listing them in the transferList. A transferred ArrayBuffer becomes unusable in the sender.

Shared memory: a SharedArrayBuffer can be read and written by several threads at once. Coordinating that safely requires Atomics operations. Shared memory is powerful but rarely needed in typical backends.

Costs: starting a worker takes time and memory, so creating one per request is wasteful. Keep a pool of long-lived workers instead.

docs.title: Worker pools
docs.text:
A pool starts a fixed number of workers (often equal to the number of CPU cores) and queues tasks for them. Libraries such as Piscina implement this:

import Piscina from "piscina";

const pool = new Piscina({
  filename: new URL("./resize-worker.js", import.meta.url).href,
});

const thumbnail = await pool.run({ path: "photo.jpg", width: 200 });

The worker file exports a function that receives each task.

docs.title: Child processes
docs.text:
The node:child_process module starts separate operating-system processes. They can be any program: a shell command, Python, ImageMagick, ffmpeg, or another Node.js script.

Function Shell? Output Typical use spawn(cmd, args) No (by default) Streams (stdout, stderr) Long-running commands or large output. execFile(file, args) No Buffered into a string Running a program with arguments and getting its output. exec(commandString) Yes Buffered (default maxBuffer is about 1 MB) Quick shell one-liners with trusted input only. fork(modulePath) No Streams + an IPC message channel Running another Node.js script and exchanging messages.

Shell injection

exec runs its string through a shell. If any part comes from a user, an input such as photo.jpg; rm -rf / runs a second command. Use execFile or spawn with an arguments array, which never invokes a shell:

// Dangerous
exec(`convert ${userFile} out.png`);
// Safe: arguments are passed directly, not parsed by a shell
execFile("convert", [userFile, "out.png"]);

Child processes are heavier than worker threads (separate memory, startup cost), but they isolate crashes completely and can run non-JavaScript tools.

docs.title: The cluster module
docs.text:
The node:cluster module starts several copies of your server—workers— from one primary process. All workers share the same port, and incoming connections are distributed among them. The default is round-robin by the primary on every platform except Windows, where the operating system decides. In a quick test on Windows, four requests in a row all went to the same worker.

Each worker is a full Node.js process with its own memory. They do not share state: an in-memory cache, session store, or rate-limit counter in one worker is invisible to the others. Shared state must live in an external store such as Redis or a database.

docs.title: PM2 cluster mode
docs.text:
The PM2 process manager wraps the cluster module so you don't write the primary logic yourself:

pm2 start src/server.js -i max   # one process per CPU core
pm2 reload all                   # zero-downtime restart, one worker at a time
pm2 logs

docs.title: Scaling with containers instead
docs.text: In containerized deployments, the common pattern is to run one Node.js process per container and run several containers behind a load balancer. The orchestrator (Kubernetes, ECS, and so on) handles restarts, health checks, and scaling. Using cluster inside each container is possible but usually unnecessary.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Do not reach for these tools when:

  • The work is I/O-bound (database calls, HTTP requests): one Node.js thread already handles it well, and workers add overhead.
  • The task runs for a few milliseconds: starting a worker or a process costs more than the work.
  • You already scale with several containers behind a load balancer: running cluster inside each container usually adds nothing.
  • The heavy job does not need to finish during the request: put it on a job queue instead.
Need Use Why CPU-heavy JavaScript (hashing, parsing, image work in JS) without blocking requests Worker threads (with a pool) Same process, cheap messaging, main thread stays free. Run an external program (ffmpeg, git, a Python script) Child process (spawn/execFile) Only option for non-Node programs; isolated. Run another Node.js script with message passing and full isolation fork Separate process with an IPC channel. Use all CPU cores for HTTP traffic on one machine or VM Cluster or PM2 cluster mode Several server processes on one port. Scale across machines, survive machine failure More containers/instances behind a load balancer Horizontal scaling; see scalability. Long or heavy jobs that need not finish during the request Background job queue Retries and durability; see background jobs.

docs.title: Offloading a calculation to a worker
docs.text:
// fib-worker.js
import { parentPort, workerData } from "node:worker_threads";

function fibonacci(n) {
  return n < 2 ? n : fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2); // deliberately slow
}

parentPort.postMessage(fibonacci(workerData));

// server.js
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { Worker } from "node:worker_threads";

function runFibonacci(n) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const worker = new Worker(new URL("./fib-worker.js", import.meta.url), {
      workerData: n,
    });
    worker.once("message", resolve);
    worker.once("error", reject);
    worker.once("exit", (code) => {
      if (code !== 0) reject(new Error(`Worker exited with code ${code}`));
    });
  });
}

createServer(async (request, response) => {
  if (request.url === "/fib") {
    const result = await runFibonacci(42); // main thread stays free meanwhile
    return response.end(`fib(42) = ${result}\n`);
  }
  response.end("fast route still responds instantly\n");
}).listen(3000);

(This starts a new worker per request to keep the example short; use a pool in real services.)

Tested on Node.js 22: while /fib computed for about 4.4 seconds, a request to / was answered in about 30 ms, and /fib then returned fib(42) = 267914296.

docs.title: Streaming output from a child process
docs.text:
import { spawn } from "node:child_process";

const child = spawn("ffmpeg", ["-i", "input.mov", "-f", "mp4", "output.mp4"]);

child.stderr.on("data", (chunk) => process.stdout.write(chunk)); // ffmpeg logs to stderr
child.on("error", (error) => console.error("Failed to start:", error.message));
child.on("close", (code) => console.log(`ffmpeg exited with ${code}`));

docs.title: Running a command and capturing output
docs.text:
import { execFile } from "node:child_process";
import { promisify } from "node:util";

const execFileAsync = promisify(execFile);
const { stdout } = await execFileAsync("git", ["rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"]);
console.log(`Deployed commit: ${stdout.trim()}`);

docs.title: A cluster with automatic restarts
docs.text:
import cluster from "node:cluster";
import { availableParallelism } from "node:os";
import { createServer } from "node:http";

if (cluster.isPrimary) {
  const count = availableParallelism();
  console.log(`Primary ${process.pid} starting ${count} workers`);
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) cluster.fork();

  cluster.on("exit", (worker, code, signal) => {
    console.log(`Worker ${worker.process.pid} died (${signal ?? code}); restarting`);
    cluster.fork();
  });
} else {
  createServer((request, response) => {
    response.end(`Handled by worker ${process.pid}\n`);
  }).listen(3000);
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep the main thread for I/O and coordination; move CPU-heavy work to a worker pool sized near the number of cores.
  • Never pass untrusted input to exec; use execFile or spawn with an argument array.
  • Always handle error and exit events for workers and child processes.
  • Set limits on child processes: timeouts (timeout option or an AbortSignal) and output size.
  • Keep shared state (sessions, caches, counters) in an external store when running multiple processes.
  • In containers, prefer one process per container and scale horizontally.
  • For heavy work that does not need an immediate answer, use a job queue rather than doing it inside the request.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Memory blows up under load.
  • Symptom: RSS jumps with traffic to one endpoint, and the process is killed for running out of memory.
  • Detect: thread counts and memory rise together; each request creates a new Worker.
  • Cause: a worker per request: each one has its own V8 isolate and heap.
  • Fix: use a fixed-size pool (Piscina) sized near the number of cores, and queue the excess.
  • Users see each other's rate limits or sessions reset.
  • Symptom: logins appear to be "forgotten" on some requests, or rate limits allow far more traffic than configured.
  • Detect: the problem only appears with cluster, PM2 -i, or several containers; the process ID in logs differs between requests.
  • Cause: sessions, caches, or counters kept in process memory are not shared between processes.
  • Fix: move shared state to Redis or a database.
  • Command injection through a filename.
  • Symptom: unexpected commands appear in process listings or audit logs after an upload.
  • Detect: filenames with ;, &&, or backticks in request logs.
  • Cause: exec() with user input in the command string.
  • Fix: use execFile/spawn with an arguments array, and validate filenames.
  • A child process hangs or its output is cut off.
  • Symptom: requests that call an external tool never finish, or exec fails with ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER.
  • Detect: child processes pile up in ps, or the error names maxBuffer.
  • Cause: no timeout on the child, or output larger than exec's 1 MB default buffer.
  • Fix: set the timeout option or an AbortSignal, and use spawn to stream large output.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• CPU-bound: Work limited by processor speed rather than waiting.
  • Worker thread: An additional JavaScript thread with its own event loop inside the same process.
  • Structured clone: The algorithm used to copy messages between threads.
  • Transferable: An object (such as an ArrayBuffer) whose ownership can move between threads without copying.
  • Worker pool: A fixed set of reusable workers that process queued tasks.
  • Child process: A separate OS process started by your program.
  • IPC (inter-process communication): A channel for messages between processes, provided by fork.
  • Cluster: A primary process plus worker processes sharing a server port.
  • Horizontal scaling: Adding more instances rather than making one bigger.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Worker threads make I/O faster." I/O is already non-blocking; workers help with CPU work.
  • Creating a new worker for every request instead of using a pool.
  • Using exec with user input, enabling command injection.
  • Expecting cluster workers to share memory. Each is a separate process.
  • "Cluster is required to scale Node.js." Containers behind a load balancer are often the better choice.
  • Ignoring worker or child error events, which can crash the process or hide failures.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between I/O-bound and CPU-bound work, and why does it matter in Node.js?
  2. How do worker threads communicate, and what does transferring a buffer mean?
  3. Why is exec dangerous with user input, and what should you use instead?
  4. What does the cluster module do, and why can't workers share an in-memory cache?
  5. When would you scale with containers instead of the cluster module?
  6. Which tool would you choose to run ffmpeg, and why?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Node.js API: Worker threads
  • Node.js API: Child processes
  • Node.js API: Cluster
  • Node.js: Don't block the event loop (or the worker pool)
  • PM2 documentation: Cluster mode

docs.title: Databases
docs.text: This section explores how applications store, retrieve, organize, and optimize data using database concepts and selected database systems.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Understand core database concepts and the trade-offs behind data models.
  • Build familiarity with MongoDB and PostgreSQL.
  • Connect database choices and operations to application needs.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Database Fundamentals
  • MongoDB
  • PostgreSQL

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A database is an organized system for storing information so software can find and change it reliably. Applications use databases for user profiles, orders, messages, and product catalogs. The MongoDB learning path and PostgreSQL learning path show two approaches.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Keeping application data only in a program's memory loses it when the program stops and makes it hard to share. A database persists data, provides ways to search it, and coordinates simultaneous changes.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
The application sends a request using a database language or client library. The database locates or changes records, applies consistency rules, and returns a result. Relational databases organize values into tables; document databases store structured documents. Indexes speed up selected lookups at the cost of storage and write work.

Transactions group operations so they succeed or fail together. Backups and replication help with recovery and availability.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A shop might store customers, products, and orders. Staff can look up an order by number or total sales by date.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Choose a database based on data shape, query patterns, consistency needs, and operational constraints—not popularity alone. Define what each record means before optimizing. Use parameters, validate input, and keep credentials out of source code.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
This local-only SQL example illustrates a table and a read; it assumes a practice database and creates no external connection:

CREATE TABLE demo_notes (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO demo_notes (id, title) VALUES (1, 'Database basics');
SELECT title FROM demo_notes WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Schema: rules describing data structure.
  • Query: a request to read or change data.
  • Index: structure that helps locate records faster.
  • Transaction: a group of database operations treated as one unit.
  • Persistence: retaining data beyond a program's lifetime.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Databases make durable, shared, searchable data practical and can enforce constraints. They also add setup and maintenance. No one data model is best for every workload.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A database is not automatically a backup. Adding indexes to every field can slow writes and consume space. “NoSQL” does not mean “no structure”; document data still benefits from clear rules.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official PostgreSQL documentation — Getting Started: a guided introduction to relational database concepts and SQL.
  • Official MongoDB documentation — Documents: explains MongoDB's basic unit of stored data.

docs.title: MongoDB
docs.text: MongoDB stores BSON documents in collections. This module is a focused learning path through its data model, query language, development tools, performance, consistency, security, and operations. It is divided into short lessons so each subject can be studied on its own.

docs.title: Suggested learning path
docs.text:
1. Start with databases and collections, BSON documents and types, and ObjectIds.
  2. Practice query operators, projection and pagination, inserts, updates, upserts, and deletes.
  3. Learn data modeling, schema validation, index design, and query plans.
  4. Study aggregation pipelines, then work through the dedicated lessons on stages, expressions, joins, facets, and output.
  5. Use Atlas, Compass, mongosh, and driver connections to practice with a development deployment.
  6. Finish with consistency, transactions, replication, sharding, change streams, security, networking, backup, and operations.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text: Use the MongoDB questions and answers lesson to review the module and identify topics to revisit.

docs.title: Topics beyond the core path
docs.text:
The navigation also covers collation, geospatial queries, views, time-series collections, TTL indexes, capped collections, GridFS, MongoDB Search and Vector Search, storage engines, journaling, import/export, and migration.

Start with Database Fundamentals and compare this document model with PostgreSQL. Choose designs from workload and consistency needs; flexible schema still benefits from deliberate contracts and indexes.

docs.title: Official documentation
docs.text:
• MongoDB Manual
  • Atlas documentation
  • Compass documentation
  • mongosh documentation
  • MongoDB drivers

Use documentation for the server and tool versions you deploy because features and behavior evolve.

docs.title: Aggregation Expressions and Accumulators
docs.text:
Expressions compute values in stages such as $project, $set, and $group. A field path such as "$price" reads a field; $$ROOT refers to the current root document, while variables such as $$NOW expose server values in supported contexts.

Arithmetic operators include $add, $subtract, $multiply, and $divide. Conditional operators include $cond, $ifNull, and $switch. Comparison and boolean expressions can build derived flags. Array, string, date, and type operators support transformations without application-side loops.

Accumulators summarize a group or window: $sum, $avg, $min, $max, $first, $last, $push, and $addToSet. In $group, _id is the grouping key and each accumulator computes a value for that group. $first and $last depend on input order; sort explicitly if order matters.

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $set: { lineTotal: { $multiply: ["$quantity", "$unitPrice"] } } },
  { $group: {
      _id: "$customerId",
      revenue: { $sum: "$lineTotal" },
      average: { $avg: "$lineTotal" },
      products: { $addToSet: "$sku" }
  } }
])

Null, missing, and type conversions can produce subtle results. Use $ifNull, $convert, or explicit type checks where inputs vary, and test edge cases. See aggregation expressions and accumulators.

docs.title: Aggregation Joins, Facets, and Windows
docs.text:
$lookup performs a left outer join from the current collection to a foreign collection and places matching documents in an array. Equality joins use localField and foreignField; pipeline form supports more complex matching. Index the foreign join field and bound the result where possible.

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      localField: "customerId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "customer"
  } },
  { $unwind: { path: "$customer", preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true } }
])

$unwind turns array elements into separate pipeline documents. preserveNullAndEmptyArrays keeps documents with a missing or empty array. This option changes whether a join behaves like an inner or left join after unwind.

$facet runs multiple branches over a common input, often for a page plus facets or counts. $setWindowFields calculates over partitions and sort order, such as rankings or running totals, without collapsing every partition into one document. These stages can require substantial memory and sort work; inspect plans and pipeline limits. See lookup, unwind, and setWindowFields.

docs.title: Aggregation Output and Materialized Results
docs.text:
Most aggregation pipelines return a cursor. $merge and $out write pipeline output to a collection and must be the final stage. They are useful for batch summaries, precomputed reports, or materialized views.

$merge can insert new output and merge, replace, keep, or fail on matching target documents according to its options. Choose a stable on-field and unique index so reruns have predictable behavior. $out replaces a target collection with pipeline results and has restrictions on target namespace and deployment. Neither stage should be treated as a casual substitute for an application write.

Design refresh schedules and failure behavior: Is the result stale while recomputing? Can consumers read the old result until the new one is ready? What happens if the job stops midway? Restrict privileges on output collections and avoid targeting live collections unintentionally.

Use a non-production target while learning. Check server-version and sharded-cluster restrictions before deployment. See $merge and $out.

docs.title: Aggregation Patterns and Tuning
docs.text:
Aggregation is a staged transformation. A common reporting flow matches a bounded time range, unwinds line items, joins dimensions, computes values, groups results, sorts, and limits output. Stage order affects both meaning and cost.

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { state: "paid" } },
  { $unwind: "$items" },
  { $set: { lineTotal: { $multiply: ["$items.qty", "$items.price"] } } },
  { $group: {
      _id: "$customerId",
      spend: { $sum: "$lineTotal" },
      products: { $addToSet: "$items.sku" }
  } },
  { $sort: { spend: -1, _id: 1 } },
  { $limit: 20 }
])

Use $facet to run multiple branches over one input, such as a page and count summary. $bucket and $bucketAuto group values into ranges. $setWindowFields calculates over ordered partitions, for example a running total. $unionWith combines another collection's pipeline output. $replaceRoot and $replaceWith change the current document shape.

$merge writes results to a target collection and supports merge/replace strategies; $out writes pipeline output as a collection under its documented restrictions. Both are terminal write stages. Check deployed-version rules before using them.

Filter early where semantics allow, bound arrays before $unwind, and use indexes for initial matching and sorting. Large $group and sort stages can consume substantial memory. Inspect explain output and intermediate result sizes with representative data. See pipeline stages and pipeline limits.

docs.title: Aggregation Stages
docs.text:
A pipeline applies stages in sequence. Each stage receives the prior stage's documents, so placing a stage changes both output and cost.

  • $match filters by query predicates and can use an index when placed early.
  • $project selects or computes output fields; $set/$addFields adds or replaces fields.
  • $unwind emits one document per array element.
  • $group combines documents by a key and uses accumulators.
  • $sort orders output; $skip and $limit control result windows.
  • $lookup joins another collection into an array; $unionWith combines another pipeline's output.
  • $facet runs independent subpipelines over the same input.
  • $bucket and $bucketAuto group values into ranges; $setWindowFields computes over ordered partitions.
  • $replaceRoot/$replaceWith changes the current document shape.
  • $count returns a count of pipeline documents.

Use $match early to reduce work, but preserve semantics when moving stages. Put a limit before expensive work only when it does not change the intended result. See aggregation pipeline stages.

docs.title: Aggregation Pipelines
docs.text: An aggregation pipeline transforms documents through an ordered list of stages. Each stage receives the previous stage's output. Stages filter, reshape, split arrays, group, join, sort, paginate, or write results. Expressions compute values within stages.

docs.title: Example: category revenue
docs.text:
Assume each order has a status, date, and items array with productId, quantity, and unitPrice. Products contain a category.

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "paid", createdAt: { $gte: ISODate("2026-01-01") } } },
  { $unwind: "$items" },
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "products",
      localField: "items.productId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "product"
    }
  },
  { $unwind: "$product" },
  {
    $project: {
      category: "$product.category",
      lineTotal: { $multiply: ["$items.quantity", "$items.unitPrice"] }
    }
  },
  {
    $group: {
      _id: "$category",
      revenue: { $sum: "$lineTotal" },
      lineCount: { $sum: 1 },
      averageLine: { $avg: "$lineTotal" }
    }
  },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 }
])

The initial $match reduces input and may use an index. $unwind emits one pipeline document per array element. $lookup matches another collection and adds an array of results; the second $unwind turns each matched product into a document. $project keeps or computes fields, and $group groups by its _id expression.

docs.title: Common stages
docs.text:
• $match: keep documents matching a query predicate.
  • $project: include, exclude, rename, or compute fields.
  • $group: group documents and calculate accumulators.
  • $unwind: expand array elements into separate documents.
  • $lookup: join a foreign collection into an array field.
  • $sort, $skip, and $limit: order and paginate results. Large offsets with $skip require walking past skipped results; range pagination can scale better.
  • $facet: run multiple subpipelines over the same input, for example a result page and summary counts.
  • $merge: write pipeline output into a collection, merging with or replacing matching documents according to its options.
  • $out: write results to a collection by replacing it; it has restrictions, so check the server-version documentation before using it.

$merge and $out are terminal write stages and are useful for batch summaries or materialized views. Treat their target collections and rerun behavior as part of the job design.

docs.title: Expressions and accumulators
docs.text:
Expressions include field paths such as "$price"; arithmetic such as $add and $multiply; conditionals such as $cond and $ifNull; comparisons; and array, string, and date operations. For instance, { $cond: [{ $gte: ["$qty", 10] }, "bulk", "single"] } classifies a quantity.
