docs.title: Read Concern, Write Concern, and Read Preference
docs.text:
Read concern controls which data state a read may observe. Write concern controls the acknowledgment a write waits for. Read preference chooses which replica-set members can serve a read. These are distinct controls and should match the application's consistency and availability needs.

A majority write concern requests acknowledgment by a majority of voting members. A majority read concern returns data acknowledged by a majority. Local reads can observe data that may later roll back. Reading from secondaries can be stale even with a chosen read preference. Linearizable reads provide stronger real-time guarantees in supported contexts, with latency and availability costs.

db.orders.find({ state: "open" }).readConcern("majority")
db.orders.insertOne(
  { orderId: "o-42", state: "created" },
  { writeConcern: { w: "majority", wtimeout: 5000 } }
)

Driver APIs and shell helper syntax vary; use the driver documentation for application code. Transactions specify concerns at the transaction level. Avoid selecting strong settings by habit: write down the required guarantee, failure behavior, and latency budget. See read concern, write concern, and read preference.

docs.title: Replication and Replica Sets
docs.text:
A replica set is a group of mongod processes that maintain the same data set. The primary accepts writes and records them in its oplog; secondaries replicate oplog entries. If the primary becomes unavailable, eligible voting members can elect a replacement.

A majority of voting members is needed to elect and maintain a primary. Plan members across failure domains, and understand votes, priority, hidden members, delayed members, and maintenance procedures. Secondaries may serve reads, but their data can lag. Read preference chooses eligible nodes; it does not alone guarantee freshness.

Write concern controls the acknowledgment requested for writes. A majority write concern waits for acknowledgment from a majority of voting members, subject to configuration. Read concern controls visibility guarantees. These settings trade latency and availability for consistency and durability behavior; select them from the application's contract.

Monitor member health, elections, replication lag, and oplog window. Replication improves availability but is not a backup: accidental writes propagate. Maintain independent backups and test recovery. See replication and read and write concerns.

docs.title: Schema Validation and Evolution
docs.text:
MongoDB permits flexible document shapes, but collection validators can enforce required fields, BSON types, ranges, and allowed values. Validation is checked on inserts and updates. Invalid writes may be rejected or logged according to validationAction.

db.createCollection("products", {
  validator: {
    $jsonSchema: {
      bsonType: "object",
      required: ["sku", "price"],
      properties: {
        sku: { bsonType: "string" },
        price: { bsonType: ["int", "long", "double", "decimal"], minimum: 0 },
        status: { enum: ["draft", "active", "retired"] }
      }
    }
  },
  validationLevel: "strict",
  validationAction: "error"
})

strict checks every insert and update. moderate has different behavior for existing invalid records. error rejects invalid writes; warn records validation failures but allows the write. Understand these settings before changing production rules.

Evolve schemas compatibly: make readers tolerate old and new forms, introduce and backfill new fields, migrate writers, then tighten validation after old records and clients are handled. Use collMod to change a validator. Validation complements application and domain rules; it does not prove business correctness. See schema validation and JSON Schema query operator.

docs.title: MongoDB Search and Vector Search
docs.text:
MongoDB Search provides indexed full-text retrieval with analyzers, relevance scoring, facets, autocomplete, and other search operators. Search queries are expressed through aggregation stages and rely on a dedicated search index. It is distinct from ordinary B-tree indexes and the legacy $text operator.

Vector Search retrieves documents by similarity to an embedding. It supports approximate or exact nearest-neighbor modes depending on deployment and version. Hybrid retrieval combines lexical search, vector relevance, and metadata filters. Embeddings must be generated and versioned consistently with the model that produced them.

Design indexes for the fields and analyzers used by the search workload. Evaluate relevance with representative queries and data; do not assume vector similarity alone produces useful results. Search features, availability, and syntax vary between Atlas and self-managed releases, so check current deployment requirements.

See MongoDB Search and Vector Search.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Enable authentication and grant users only the roles their work requires.
  • Restrict network exposure; use TLS for connections and protect credentials in a secret manager.
  • Apply encryption for storage and backups according to the deployment's requirements.
  • Validate application input and construct filters from known fields and typed values. Do not pass untrusted objects directly as query documents.
  • Keep database credentials out of source control and client-side code. Rotate secrets and review access regularly.

Use the MongoDB security checklist for deployment-specific controls.

docs.title: Operational practices
docs.text:
Monitor query latency, slow operations, connection usage, disk space, memory pressure, replication lag, and storage growth. Use explain("executionStats") and representative workload measurements to investigate slow queries. Applications should reuse driver clients and their connection pools rather than opening a connection for each request.

Take backups and periodically test restoring them. Replication does not protect against logical mistakes or destructive writes. Plan upgrades against the deployed release's compatibility notes, and rehearse changes in a representative environment. Define alert thresholds and capacity plans before an incident.

See MongoDB's operations checklist and backup methods.

docs.title: Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
Authentication establishes who a user or service is. Authorization determines its permitted database actions. Atlas console users and database users are different identities: a person who can manage a project does not automatically need application data privileges.

Enable access control on self-managed deployments. Give applications the narrowest role and database scope that supports their work. Built-in roles cover common tasks; custom roles can grant a specific action set. Avoid application use of root or cluster-wide administrator roles.

Use strong, unique credentials or supported enterprise identity integrations. Rotate credentials, remove stale accounts, audit privilege changes, and keep secrets out of source control and client bundles. Authentication does not replace TLS, IP restrictions, or safe application query construction.

See authorization, built-in roles, and Atlas database users.

docs.title: Self-Managed Operations
docs.text:
Self-managed MongoDB requires ownership of installation, configuration, upgrades, storage, networking, security, monitoring, backups, recovery, and incident response. Follow official instructions for the operating system and exact server version.

Keep deployments on supported versions. Plan upgrades with server compatibility, feature compatibility version, drivers, and rollback constraints in mind. Test against representative data and workload, and automate consistent configuration across members. Protect configuration files and credentials.

Plan disk capacity for data, indexes, journal, oplog, temporary aggregation work, and backups. Monitor disk latency and free space as well as CPU and memory. Configure replica members across suitable failure domains. Document maintenance for index builds, certificate rotation, member replacement, and restore.

Restrict operating-system access and network paths. Prepare alerts and runbooks before incidents. Atlas shifts some infrastructure work to MongoDB but does not transfer responsibility for application access policy, schema, retention, query quality, and recovery objectives. See operations checklist and installation.

docs.title: Sessions and Causal Consistency
docs.text:
A session groups related operations and carries logical session metadata. Drivers use sessions for transactions, retryable writes, and causal consistency. Create sessions through the driver and pass them to operations that belong to the session.

Causal consistency lets a session observe its own causally prior writes and reads when used with the required concerns. This is useful when a user writes data and then reads it through a deployment that may route reads to different replica-set members. It does not make unrelated operations globally serializable.

Sessions have lifetimes and must be ended. Do not share one session concurrently across independent operations unless the driver explicitly supports that usage. Transactions run within a session and require sequential handling according to driver rules.

const session = client.startSession()
try {
  // pass { session } to related driver operations
} finally {
  await session.endSession()
}

Use the official driver API for the language in use; shell examples are not a substitute for application session handling. See sessions and causal consistency.

docs.title: Sharding
docs.text:
Sharding distributes collection data across multiple shards. A sharded deployment includes shards, mongos query routers, and config servers. Applications connect through mongos, which uses shard-key values and cluster metadata to target operations.

Shard-key choice strongly affects distribution and query efficiency. Evaluate cardinality, write patterns, range queries, common filters, and growth. A monotonically increasing key can concentrate new writes on one range. A hashed key can distribute writes but make range queries less targeted. Compound keys can balance access patterns when selected from measured workload.

Queries containing shard-key predicates can target a subset of shards. Queries without them may scatter across many shards. Balancing and chunk migration move data but do not fix a hot key or poor targeting. Unique indexes and shard-key rules constrain choices; plan carefully because changing a key can be costly.

Do not shard by default. First confirm that data modeling, indexes, and a replica set cannot meet measured capacity or throughput needs. Sharding adds operational complexity. See sharding and choose a shard key.

docs.title: Storage Engines and Journaling
docs.text:
A storage engine manages how MongoDB stores data in memory and on disk. WiredTiger is the default engine for current self-managed deployments. It provides document-level concurrency, compression, checkpoints, and journaling. Storage engine selection affects performance, durability, and operational behavior.

Journaling is write-ahead logging used to recover writes after an unexpected shutdown between checkpoints. Checkpoints create consistent on-disk snapshots; the journal records later operations needed for recovery. Current MongoDB versions enable journaling by default and remove older controls, so follow documentation for the deployed release.

Storage-engine concepts inform disk capacity, cache pressure, checkpoints, compression, and recovery time. Do not manually edit data files while mongod is running. Use supported backup and maintenance procedures. Atlas manages underlying storage configuration differently from self-managed deployments.

See storage engines and journaling.

docs.title: Time Series and TTL
docs.text:
Time-series collections are optimized for measurements recorded over time, such as telemetry and sensor readings. Choose a BSON Date timeField and a stable metaField that groups measurements by source or device. Set granularity based on event frequency and expected query windows. Time-series collections have feature and update limitations compared with regular collections, so check compatibility with the operations your application needs.

db.createCollection("readings", {
  timeseries: {
    timeField: "timestamp",
    metaField: "device",
    granularity: "minutes"
  }
})

A TTL index removes eligible documents after a configured duration. For example, an index on expiresAt with expireAfterSeconds set to zero expires documents at their stored timestamp. TTL cleanup is asynchronous, not an exact timer. Use BSON dates and do not rely on TTL for immediate deletion or precise scheduling.

Retention choices affect storage, compliance, and query history. Validate the actual behavior with the deployed server version. See time-series collections and TTL indexes.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A write to one document is atomic. Prefer a document model that keeps common invariants together. Use a multi-document transaction when a business operation must commit or roll back changes across multiple documents, such as transferring value between two accounts.

Transactions require a replica set or sharded cluster, not a standalone server. They add coordination and latency, so they should solve a real cross-document requirement rather than compensate for every modeling choice. Keep them short and avoid waiting on user input or unrelated external services inside a transaction.

In a driver, start a session and use the driver's transaction helper. It handles transaction labels and retry rules according to that driver. Operations in a transaction must use the session. Do not perform non-idempotent external side effects in a callback that may be retried. Use idempotency keys or an outbox pattern when a committed database change must trigger an external action.

Choose transaction read concern and write concern according to consistency requirements and deployment support. Test transient errors and uncertain commit results. See transactions and production considerations.

docs.title: Field Update Operators
docs.text:
Update operators change selected fields while preserving unspecified fields. updateOne() changes at most one match; updateMany() changes all matches. Always scope the filter deliberately and inspect matchedCount and modifiedCount.

db.inventory.updateOne(
  { sku: "p-100" },
  {
    $set: { price: 9.25, "details.color": "blue" },
    $unset: { legacyCode: "" },
    $inc: { stock: -1 },
    $currentDate: { updatedAt: true }
  }
)

$set creates or replaces fields, including dotted nested paths. $unset removes a field. $inc adds a numeric value, useful for counters when the update must be atomic. $min and $max only replace a value when the new value is lower or higher. $mul multiplies a numeric field; $rename changes a field name; $setOnInsert applies only when an upsert inserts.

Do not confuse update operators with aggregation pipeline stages that share names. In an update pipeline, $set computes an expression from the existing document. For array element updates, see array operators. See update operators.

docs.title: Update Operations and Operators
docs.text:
updateOne(filter, update) changes at most one matching document; updateMany() changes every match. A selective filter matters: an empty filter can update the entire collection. Inspect matchedCount and modifiedCount. Set upsert: true only when inserting a new document on no match is intended.

db.inventory.updateOne(
  { sku: "p-100" },
  { $set: { price: 9.25 }, $inc: { stock: -1 }, $currentDate: { updatedAt: true } }
)

Common update operators:

  • $set assigns fields, including dotted nested paths such as "profile.city".
  • $unset removes a field; its operand value is ignored.
  • $inc adds or subtracts a number.
  • $mul, $min, $max, and $rename update numeric values or field names.
  • $currentDate writes the current date or timestamp.
  • $setOnInsert runs only when an upsert inserts.
  • $push, $addToSet, $pull, $pullAll, and $pop modify arrays.

replaceOne() replaces the document, removing fields not in the replacement (subject to _id rules); it is not the same as $set. findOneAndUpdate() atomically updates and can return the before or after document. Array filters target matching embedded elements. Update pipelines can compute values from the old document; in a pipeline, $set and $unset are aggregation stages rather than update modifier operators.

See update methods and update operators.

docs.title: Upserts, Replacements, and Find-and-Modify
docs.text:
An upsert inserts a document when an update matches nothing. It is useful for idempotent synchronization when the filter identifies a stable business key and a unique index enforces that key.

db.settings.updateOne(
  { name: "theme" },
  { $set: { value: "dark" }, $setOnInsert: { createdAt: new Date() } },
  { upsert: true }
)

An upsert can construct inserted fields from equality predicates in the filter plus update operators. Design the filter carefully; a broad filter can create surprising records or duplicate logical entities. A unique index protects against concurrent duplicate upserts.

replaceOne() replaces the matched document contents, removing omitted fields while preserving _id constraints. Use it only when full replacement is intended. findOneAndUpdate() and findOneAndReplace() atomically modify one matching document and return a before or after image according to options. They are useful when the caller needs the changed record in the same round trip.

See upsert behavior and findOneAndUpdate.

docs.title: Views and On-Demand Materialized Views
docs.text:
A standard view is a read-only virtual collection defined by an aggregation pipeline. It does not store results; MongoDB runs the view pipeline when it is queried. Views can present a stable or restricted shape without duplicating source documents.

db.createView(
  "activeCustomers",
  "customers",
  [{ $match: { active: true } }, { $project: { name: 1, region: 1 } }]
)

Views are useful for reusable transformations and exposing only selected fields to a read role. They have restrictions on updates and pipeline stages; avoid assuming a view behaves like a writable collection.

An on-demand materialized view stores computed results in a collection, commonly using $merge or $out from an aggregation. It can make expensive reads faster but requires refresh, staleness, and failure policies. Index the stored results according to consumer queries.

See views and on-demand materialized views.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text: PostgreSQL is an open-source relational database. It stores data in tables with defined columns and supports SQL for querying and changing that data. Relationships and constraints help represent rules explicitly; PostgreSQL also supports additional data types and capabilities as application needs grow.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Describe tables, rows, columns, keys, and relationships.
  • Read a simple SQL query and understand its result.
  • Explain how constraints and indexes help protect and retrieve data.
  • Recognize the benefits and costs of a relational model.

docs.title: Learning path
docs.text: Start with Database Fundamentals, then follow the diagram from an application query to related PostgreSQL tables.

docs.title: Relevant resources
docs.text:
• Official PostgreSQL documentation — Tutorial: introduces PostgreSQL and fundamental SQL operations.
  • Official PostgreSQL documentation — Data Definition: explains creating tables, constraints, and related structures.
  • Official PostgreSQL documentation — Queries: covers retrieving and combining data.
  • Official PostgreSQL documentation — Indexes: describes index behavior and trade-offs.

Compare this relational model with MongoDB and review shared concepts in Database Fundamentals.

docs.title: Application Architecture
docs.text:
Application architecture is the set of decisions about how the parts of a system are divided, how they communicate, where data lives, and how the whole system keeps working as traffic, data, and teams grow. A single Express server and one database can serve an early product well; the same product at a hundred times the traffic needs caches, queues, replicas, and a clear structure that many developers can change safely.

Architecture is about trade-offs, not best answers. Every cache adds the risk of stale data, every queue adds eventual consistency, and every extra service adds a network call that can fail. This section teaches what each option buys, what it costs, and how to choose deliberately.

docs.title: What this section teaches
docs.text:
You will learn how to:

  • Structure an application: monoliths, modular monoliths, microservices, layered and clean architecture, design principles, and patterns.
  • Model a business domain with domain-driven design, and decouple parts of a system with events.
  • Make reads fast with caching, and choose the right caching strategy, invalidation approach, and eviction policy.
  • Use Redis for caching, sessions, rate limits, leaderboards, locks, pub/sub, and streams, and run it reliably.
  • Move work and communication onto message queues with RabbitMQ, Kafka, or cloud queues, with the right delivery guarantees.
  • Scale services and databases, reason about availability, consistency, and the CAP theorem, and plan capacity.
  • Design complete systems with a repeatable process, estimates, and case studies such as a URL shortener, chat application, and news feed.

docs.title: How architecture choices appear in one request
docs.text:
Follow a request for a user's news feed through a scaled system:

  1. A load balancer sends the request to one of many stateless application instances, so any instance can serve any user.
  2. The application checks a cache (often Redis) for the user's feed and returns it immediately on a hit.
  3. On a miss, it reads from a read replica of the database, accepting that the replica can lag slightly behind the primary (replication lag).
  4. When someone the user follows publishes a post, the write goes to the primary database, and an event is published to a message queue.
  5. Workers consume that event and update the feeds of the author's followers in the background, so the author's request returns quickly.
  6. Each part can be scaled, replaced, or fail independently, which is the goal and the cost of the design.

docs.title: Learning path
docs.text:
The navigation is organized into six subject groups:

  1. Software Architecture: how to structure code and services, and the principles and patterns behind good structure.
  2. Caching: making repeated reads fast without serving wrong data.
  3. Redis: the in-memory data store most backends use for caching and coordination.
  4. Message Queues: asynchronous communication between parts of a system.
  5. Scalability: growing capacity while staying available and consistent enough.
  6. System Design: combining all of the above to design complete systems.

A useful order is the order above. If you are preparing for system design interviews, read Scalability and the System Design process early, then return to the other subjects as the case studies need them.

Every lesson includes an explanation of how the concept works, practical examples, best practices, important terminology, common mistakes, revision questions, and official learning resources. Each subject ends with interview questions and answers.

docs.title: Related sections
docs.text:
• Backend Development for HTTP, APIs, authentication, rate limiting, background jobs, and real-time communication inside a single service.
  • Databases for data modeling, indexes, transactions, replication, and sharding.
  • Servers and Infrastructure for load balancers, reverse proxies, and CDNs.
  • DevOps and Deployment for containers, CI/CD, and monitoring.

docs.title: A first practical exercise
docs.text:
Take the task API from the Backend section and evolve it:

  1. Add a Redis cache in front of GET /tasks/:id using cache-aside, and measure the hit ratio.
  2. Invalidate the cached task when it is updated, and explain what a user could see if the delete happened before the database write.
  3. When a task is completed, publish an event to a queue and send the "task completed" email from a worker instead of the request handler.
  4. Run two instances of the API behind a load balancer and confirm nothing breaks because state lived in memory.

docs.title: Before moving on
docs.text:
• Why is every architectural choice a trade-off rather than an upgrade?
  • What does a cache, a queue, and a read replica each make faster, and what does each make harder?
  • Why must application instances be stateless before they can be scaled horizontally?
  • When is a single, well-structured service a better choice than microservices?

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Caching stores a copy of data somewhere faster or closer than its original source, so repeated requests can be answered without redoing the slow work. Browsers, CDNs, reverse proxies, application memory, Redis, and databases all cache. Used well, caching cuts latency and load dramatically; used carelessly, it serves stale or even wrong data.

docs.title: What caching provides
docs.text:
• Lower latency: reading from memory takes microseconds, while a database query or a call to another service can take milliseconds or more.
  • Less load on the source: a cache that answers 95% of reads leaves the database only 5% of the traffic.
  • Resilience: some caches can keep serving slightly stale data while the source is slow or unavailable.

Every cache also adds questions you must answer: how long data may be stale, how it is invalidated when the source changes, what is evicted when the cache is full, and what happens when the cache itself fails.

docs.title: How a typical application cache works
docs.text:
The most common pattern, cache-aside, works like this:

  1. The application receives a request for a product.
  2. It looks up the key product:42 in the cache.
  3. Cache hit: the value is returned immediately.
  4. Cache miss: the application reads the database, stores the result in the cache with a time to live (TTL), and returns it.
  5. When the product is updated, the application writes to the database and deletes product:42 from the cache, so the next read reloads fresh data.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
// Cache-aside with Redis (node-redis client).
async function getProduct(id) {
  const key = `product:${id}`;
  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached); // hit

  const product = await db.products.findById(id); // miss: go to the source
  if (product) {
    await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(product), { EX: 300 }); // 5-minute TTL
  }
  return product;
}

The TTL bounds how stale a cached product can be even if an invalidation is missed. (Recent node-redis versions mark the EX option as deprecated in favor of { expiration: { type: "EX", value: 300 } }; EX still works.)

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Measure before caching: find the slow, frequently repeated reads, then cache those. Decide how stale each kind of data may be, give every key a TTL, and monitor the hit ratio. Never cache one user's private data under a key another user can read.

  • A cache is not a database; data in it can disappear at any time and must be rebuildable from the source.
  • Caching does not fix a slow query for the first request or for cache misses.
  • Deleting a cache entry on update is usually safer than updating it in place.
  • A higher TTL is not always better; it trades freshness for hit ratio.

docs.title: Message Queues
docs.text: A message queue lets one part of a system send work or information to another part without waiting for it to be processed. The sender, called the producer, puts a message on a broker; one or more receivers, called consumers, take messages from the broker and process them at their own pace. This decouples services in time, in availability, and in load.

docs.title: What message queues provide
docs.text:
• Decoupling: producers do not need to know which consumers exist or whether they are running right now.
  • Load leveling: a burst of messages waits in the queue instead of overwhelming the consumers.
  • Resilience: if a consumer crashes, messages wait and are redelivered instead of being lost.
  • Scalability: more consumers can be added to process a queue faster.
  • Fan-out: one event can be delivered to many independent subscribers.

The costs are eventual consistency, duplicate deliveries that consumers must handle, harder debugging, and another piece of infrastructure to operate.

docs.title: How a message moves through a queue
docs.text:
1. The producer sends a message, such as {"type": "OrderPlaced", "orderId": "o_789"}, to the broker.
  2. The broker stores it durably in a queue (or topic partition).
  3. A consumer receives the message and processes it, for example by sending a confirmation email.
  4. The consumer acknowledges the message, and the broker removes it or advances the consumer's position.
  5. If the consumer fails before acknowledging, the broker redelivers the message, possibly to another consumer; after repeated failures it is moved to a dead-letter queue for inspection.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Without a queue                         With a queue
---------------                         ------------
POST /orders                            POST /orders
  save order          20 ms               save order              20 ms
  charge card        300 ms               publish OrderPlaced       5 ms
  send email         800 ms             -> 201 Created (25 ms)
  update analytics   200 ms
-> 201 Created (1.3 s)                  Workers, later and independently:
   (and fails if email is down)           email worker, analytics worker

The request returns quickly, and a slow or failing email provider no longer fails order creation.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Design consumers to be idempotent, because almost every broker delivers some messages more than once. Acknowledge only after processing succeeds, give every queue a dead-letter queue, and monitor queue depth and message age. Choose the broker by the problem: a task queue, a durable event log, or a managed cloud service.

  • A queue does not guarantee exactly-once processing on its own; idempotent consumers do the real work.
  • Asynchronous does not mean faster for the user who needs the result; it means the result arrives later.
  • Kafka and RabbitMQ are not interchangeable; one is a replayable log, the other a routing message broker.
  • A message queue is not a database; set retention and plan for messages that can never be processed.

docs.text: Build these to practice the architecture lessons on running systems. Several build on the Backend projects, TaskFlow API and ShopLite Checkout.

docs.title: Clean Architecture Refactor
docs.text: Restructure the TaskFlow API into ports and adapters so business rules no longer depend on Express or MongoDB. Swap the database for an in-memory store in tests, and write short decision records explaining each choice. Practices Software Architecture.

docs.title: Cache Lab
docs.text: Put Redis in front of a deliberately slow endpoint and learn caching by measuring it: latency and hit ratio under load, invalidation and the stale data it can cause, a cache stampede and its fix, and how LRU and LFU eviction behave on the same traffic. Practices Caching.

docs.title: LiveBoard
docs.text: A real-time game leaderboard with chat: rankings in a sorted set, chat shared across two server instances with Pub/Sub, game events processed with a stream consumer group, a daily reset job protected by a lock, and per-user rate limits. Practices Redis.

docs.title: OrderFlow Events
docs.text: Split ShopLite Checkout into order, inventory, payment, and notification services that communicate through a message broker. Add a transactional outbox, a saga that refunds when stock runs out, consumers that safely ignore duplicates, and a dead-letter queue you inspect and replay. Practices Message Queues and event-driven architecture.

docs.title: Scale It
docs.text: Run the TaskFlow API as several instances behind a load balancer, move sessions to Redis, and add a database replica set. Load-test it to find the bottleneck, watch replication lag, then stop an instance and a database node to see how the system recovers. Practices Scalability.

docs.title: Design-then-Build URL Shortener
docs.text: Write a short design document first, with requirements, estimates, API, and data model, then build the URL shortener from the case study with a cache and click analytics. Finish by load-testing it and comparing the results with your estimates. Practices System Design.

docs.title: Redis
docs.text: Redis is an in-memory data structure server. It stores keys whose values can be strings, lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams, and more, and it runs commands on them in well under a millisecond. Backends use Redis as a cache, a session store, a rate limiter, a leaderboard, a lock service, a lightweight message broker, and a queue backend.

docs.title: What Redis provides
docs.text:
• Speed: data lives in memory, and commands are executed one at a time on a main thread, so each command is atomic and very fast.
  • Data structures: instead of only storing blobs, Redis can increment counters, push to lists, rank members in sorted sets, and more on the server.
  • Expiration: any key can have a time to live, which makes caches and temporary data simple.
  • Messaging: Pub/Sub for fire-and-forget broadcasts and Streams for durable, consumer-group-based messaging.
  • Persistence and availability: optional snapshots and append-only files, replication, automatic failover with Sentinel, and sharding with Redis Cluster.

docs.title: How an application uses Redis
docs.text:
1. The application opens a long-lived connection to Redis through a client library.
  2. It sends commands such as GET, SET, INCR, or ZADD over that connection.
  3. Redis executes each command against data in memory and replies.
  4. Keys can expire automatically, and when memory is full Redis evicts keys according to its configured policy.
  5. Optionally, Redis persists data to disk and replicates it to replicas so it survives restarts and failures.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
$ redis-cli
127.0.0.1:6379> SET session:abc123 "user:42" EX 1800
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET session:abc123
"user:42"
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR page:home:views
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD leaderboard 1500 "alice" 1200 "bob"
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE leaderboard 0 1 REV WITHSCORES
1) "alice"
2) "1500"
3) "bob"
4) "1200"

A session with a 30-minute expiry, an atomic counter, and a ranked leaderboard each take one command.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Design key names deliberately (object:id:field), give temporary data a TTL, set a memory limit with an eviction policy that fits the use case, and avoid very large keys and slow commands such as KEYS * in production. Decide up front whether Redis holds data you can rebuild (a cache) or data you must not lose (sessions, queues), because that changes how you configure persistence.

  • Redis is not only a cache; its data structures solve many coordination problems.
  • "Single-threaded" refers to command execution; one slow command blocks all other clients.
  • Redis persistence exists, but Redis is not a drop-in replacement for a primary database.
  • Pub/Sub messages are not stored; a subscriber that is offline misses them.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text: Scalability is a system's ability to handle more load, such as more users, requests, or data, by adding resources, while keeping response times and error rates acceptable. A scalable system grows by adding capacity rather than by being rewritten, and it stays available and correct enough while it grows.

docs.title: What scalability involves
docs.text:
• Vertical scaling: giving one machine more CPU, memory, or faster disks. Simple, but limited and often a single point of failure.
  • Horizontal scaling: adding more machines or instances behind a load balancer. Nearly unlimited, but requires stateless services and shared state stores.
  • Data scaling: read replicas, connection pooling, partitioning, and sharding when one database can no longer keep up.
  • Availability: redundancy and failover so the system keeps serving when parts fail.
  • Consistency trade-offs: deciding where slightly stale data is acceptable in exchange for speed and availability.
  • Capacity planning: estimating future load and keeping enough headroom.

docs.title: How a system usually scales
docs.text:
1. Measure: load test and profile to find the real bottleneck.
  2. Optimize: fix slow queries, add indexes, and remove unnecessary work.
  3. Cache: serve repeated reads from memory or a CDN.
  4. Scale out the stateless tier: run more application instances behind a load balancer, with sessions and files moved out of instance memory.
  5. Offload work: move slow tasks to queues and background workers.
  6. Scale the data tier: add read replicas, then partition or shard when writes or data size outgrow one primary.

Each step adds complexity, so take the next one only when measurements show the current setup cannot meet the requirements.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Availability target    Allowed downtime per year    Allowed downtime per month
99%                    about 3.65 days              about 7.3 hours
99.9%                  about 8.77 hours             about 43.8 minutes
99.99%                 about 52.6 minutes           about 4.4 minutes
99.999%                about 5.26 minutes           about 26 seconds

Each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime by a factor of ten, and usually requires more redundancy, automation, and cost.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Design services to be stateless from the start, keep data access efficient, and measure with percentiles rather than averages. Scale the part that is actually the bottleneck, and remember that every added component is also something that can fail.

  • Scalability is not the same as performance: a fast system for one user can still collapse under load.
  • Adding servers does not help if the database or a shared lock is the bottleneck.
  • Microservices are not required for scalability; a stateless monolith scales horizontally too.
  • High availability is not achieved by one powerful machine; it comes from redundancy without single points of failure.

docs.title: Software Architecture
docs.text: Software architecture is the set of significant decisions about a system's structure: how it is split into parts, what each part is responsible for, how the parts depend on and talk to each other, and which qualities, such as availability, performance, or ease of change, the structure is optimized for. These are the decisions that are expensive to reverse later.

docs.title: What software architecture covers
docs.text:
• Structure: whether the system is one deployable application, a modular monolith, or many services, and where the boundaries between parts lie.
  • Dependencies: which parts may depend on which, for example business logic that does not depend on a web framework or database driver.
  • Communication: in-process function calls, synchronous HTTP or gRPC, or asynchronous events through a broker.
  • Quality attributes: the non-functional requirements, such as scalability, availability, security, and maintainability, that drive the choices above.
  • Principles and patterns: reusable solutions, such as repositories, dependency injection, sagas, and the outbox, that keep code and systems understandable.

docs.title: How architectural decisions are made
docs.text:
1. Identify the requirements, especially the quality attributes that matter most for this system and the constraints (team size, budget, deadlines).
  2. List the realistic options for the decision, such as one service or several.
  3. Compare the options against the quality attributes and name the trade-offs explicitly.
  4. Choose, and record the decision and its reasons in an architecture decision record (ADR) so future developers understand why.
  5. Revisit the decision when the requirements change; good architecture evolves.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
The same "place order" feature can be structured very differently:

Modular monolith                      Microservices
----------------                      -------------
OrdersModule.placeOrder()             Orders service  --HTTP-->  Inventory service
  -> InventoryModule.reserve()            |
  -> PaymentsModule.charge()              +--event "OrderPlaced"--> Payments service
  (one process, one database,             (separate deploys and databases,
   one transaction)                         network calls, eventual consistency)

The modular monolith can use one database transaction and is simple to deploy and debug. The microservices version lets teams deploy independently and scale parts separately, but must handle network failures and coordinate data with patterns such as sagas. Neither is better in general; the requirements decide.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions

Start simple and add structure when a real problem demands it. Keep business rules independent of frameworks and infrastructure so they can be tested and changed easily, and write down important decisions with their reasons.

  • Microservices are not an upgrade from a monolith. They buy strong module boundaries, independent deployment, and technology choice at the cost of distribution, eventual consistency, and operational complexity.
  • Architecture is not only diagrams; it is the decisions and the reasons behind them.
  • A design pattern is not automatically good; it adds indirection that must pay for itself.
  • Architecture is not decided once; it should evolve as requirements, scale, and teams change.

docs.title: System Design
docs.text: System design is the process of turning requirements into an architecture: the components, the data they store, the APIs between them, and the way they handle scale and failure. It combines everything in this section, from caching and queues to replication and consistency, into concrete decisions for a specific problem.

docs.title: What system design involves
docs.text:
• Requirements: what the system must do (functional) and how well it must do it (non-functional: latency, availability, consistency, scale, cost).
  • Estimation: rough numbers for requests per second, storage, and bandwidth that tell you which problems are real.
  • Interfaces and data: the API the system exposes and the data model behind it.
  • High-level design: the main components and how a read and a write flow through them.
  • Deep dives: the hardest parts, such as generating unique IDs, fanning out messages, or keeping caches consistent.
  • Trade-offs: what was chosen, what was rejected, and why.

docs.title: How a system design discussion flows
docs.text:
1. Clarify the requirements and agree on what is in and out of scope.
  2. Estimate the scale with back-of-the-envelope numbers.
  3. Define the core API endpoints.
  4. Sketch the data model and choose the storage.
  5. Draw the high-level design and walk through the main read and write paths.
  6. Deep-dive into the bottlenecks and failure modes.
  7. Summarize the trade-offs and how the design would evolve with more scale.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Requirement: "Shorten URLs; 100 million new links per month; reads are 100x writes."

Writes: 100,000,000 / (30 * 24 * 3600 s) ≈ 40 per second (peak ~ 80)
Reads:  40 * 100 ≈ 4,000 per second (peak ~ 8,000)
Storage: 100,000,000 links * 500 bytes ≈ 50 GB per month ≈ 600 GB per year

Conclusion: writes are modest; reads dominate, so cache hot links and serve
redirects from memory; one primary database is enough for writes at first.

Thirty seconds of arithmetic shows where the design effort should go.

  • Adding every component (Kafka, Redis, sharding) to every design is not thoroughness; each one must be justified.
  • Estimates do not need to be precise; they need the right order of magnitude.
  • A design is not finished at the happy path; failures, retries, and data growth are part of it.

docs.title: Cache Failure Modes
docs.text: Caches make systems faster, but they also create new ways to fail. Popular keys expiring at once can flood the database; requests for data that does not exist can bypass the cache entirely; one oversized or extremely hot key can overload a cache node; and a cache outage can take down the database behind it. This lesson names each failure mode and the standard defenses.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Once a system depends on a high hit ratio, the database is sized for the traffic that misses, not for all traffic. If the cache suddenly stops absorbing load, the database receives many times more queries than it can handle and the whole system can collapse. Most large caching incidents come from a handful of well-known patterns, so learning them is one of the highest-value topics in caching.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Facebook: leases against thundering herds. In the Scaling Memcache at Facebook paper, each memcached server hands out a lease token for a key at most once every 10 seconds by default. Other clients that miss within that window are told to wait briefly; by the time they retry, the lease holder has usually filled the cache within milliseconds.
  • Facebook: Gutter for cache server failures. The same paper describes Gutter, a small pool of machines (about 1% of the memcached servers in a cluster) that takes over for failed servers. Clients that get no response retry against Gutter, which keeps a failed cache server from turning into a flood of database queries.
  • Cloudflare: request collapsing. Cloudflare's default cache behavior includes a cache lock: only the first request for an uncached asset is forwarded to the origin from a given location, and the other requests wait for it, which is single-flight at the CDN.
  • Cloudflare: Tiered Cache. With Tiered Cache, lower-tier data centers ask an upper-tier data center before contacting the origin, reducing origin requests when many edge locations miss at once.

docs.title: Cache stampede (thundering herd)
docs.text:
When a popular key expires, every request that arrives before it is reloaded misses at the same time and runs the same expensive query.

Defenses:

Technique How it works Request coalescing (single-flight) Within one process, concurrent misses for the same key share one in-flight load Distributed lock Across instances, only the request that acquires a lock reloads; others wait briefly or serve stale data Stale-while-revalidate Keep serving the old value while one request refreshes it Probabilistic early expiration Each read has a small, rising chance of refreshing before expiry, so one request refreshes early Refresh-ahead A background job refreshes known hot keys before they expire

Probabilistic early expiration (called XFetch in the VLDB 2015 paper Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention) recomputes when:

now − delta × beta × ln(random()) ≥ expiry

delta  = how long the recomputation takes
beta   = tuning factor (1 by default; > 1 refreshes earlier)
random() returns (0, 1], so −ln(random()) is a positive, usually small number

As expiry approaches, the chance that some request decides to refresh grows, so one request usually refreshes the value before it actually expires and the others keep reading the cached copy.

docs.title: Cache penetration
docs.text:
Requests for keys that do not exist in the database are never cached (there is nothing to store), so every such request goes to the database. Attackers can exploit this by requesting random ids.

GET /products/999999991  -> cache miss -> DB: not found -> nothing cached
GET /products/999999992  -> cache miss -> DB: not found -> nothing cached
... every request reaches the database

Defenses:

  • Negative caching: cache "not found" results too, with a short TTL (for example 30–60 seconds), so repeated lookups are absorbed.
  • Bloom filter: a compact probabilistic set of all existing ids. If the filter says an id is absent, it is definitely absent and the database is skipped. It can occasionally say "maybe present" for a missing id (a false positive), but never "absent" for an existing one.
  • Input validation: reject malformed ids before any lookup.
  • Rate limiting per client for expensive lookups; see rate limiting and throttling.

docs.title: Cache avalanche
docs.text:
Many keys expire at the same moment, or the cache restarts empty, and the database receives a flood of misses for different keys.

Common causes: a bulk job sets thousands of keys with the same TTL, or a deploy flushes the cache.

Defenses:

  • TTL jitter: add a random spread, for example 300 s ± 10%, so expirations are spread out.
  • Warm-up: preload the most important keys before sending traffic to a new or restarted cache.
  • Gradual traffic shift to new cache nodes.
  • Load shedding and limits on the database path (see the fallback section below).

docs.title: Hot keys
docs.text:
A single key receives a huge share of traffic (a celebrity profile, a flash-sale product). In a clustered cache, one key lives on one node, so that node's CPU or network becomes the bottleneck while the others are idle.

Defenses:

  • A small in-process cache with a very short TTL (even 1–5 seconds) in front of the distributed cache absorbs most reads of the hot key.
  • Key replication: store copies under product:7#1 … product:7#8 (which hash to different nodes) and read a random copy; writes must update or delete all copies.
  • Read replicas of the cache node holding the hot key.
  • Detect them: redis-cli --hotkeys works when an LFU eviction policy is configured; client-side metrics per key prefix also help.

docs.title: Big keys
docs.text:
Very large values (multi-megabyte JSON documents, or collections with millions of members) cause trouble:

  • Redis executes commands one at a time, so reading, writing, or deleting a huge key blocks other clients.
  • Transferring large values uses network bandwidth and increases latency.
  • Uneven memory use across cluster nodes.

Defenses: keep values small, split large collections into several keys, cache only the fields needed, compress large blobs, use UNLINK (which frees memory in the background) instead of DEL for big keys, and find offenders with redis-cli --bigkeys or MEMORY USAGE key.

docs.title: Stale reads and inconsistency
docs.text: Cached data can disagree with the database because of races between reads and writes, missed invalidations, or replication lag in the cache itself. Symptoms are "I saved it but still see the old value" bugs. Defenses are covered in invalidation and expiration: correct write ordering, deleting instead of updating, versioning, short TTLs, and reading the database for decisions that must be correct.

docs.title: The cache as a single point of failure
docs.text:
If the cache is down or slow, a naive application either fails every request or sends all traffic to the database, which then collapses.

Normal:  1,000 req/s ── 95% hits ──> cache;   50 req/s ──> database
Outage:  1,000 req/s ──────────────────────────────────────> database (20× load)

Defenses:

  • Short timeouts on cache calls (a few milliseconds to tens of milliseconds). A slow cache must not slow every request.
  • Treat cache errors as misses, but limit concurrent database fallbacks (a semaphore or bulkhead), and shed load or serve degraded responses beyond that limit.
  • Circuit breaker: after repeated cache failures, skip the cache for a short period instead of waiting on timeouts. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.
  • High availability for the cache itself: replicas and automatic failover; see persistence and high availability.
  • Capacity planning that knows how much traffic the database can take without the cache.

docs.title: Cold starts and warming
docs.text: A new or flushed cache starts with a 0% hit ratio. Until it fills, every request misses. Warm it by preloading the top keys (from access logs or yesterday's most-read items), by shifting traffic gradually, or by replaying recent read traffic against it before going live.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Defense Use when Do not use when Single-flight (per process) Any cache with concurrent misses; cheap and always worth it Not a defense across instances on its own Distributed lock Expensive recomputation must run once across many instances You need a correctness guarantee (locks can expire mid-work) Stale-while-revalidate Slightly old data is acceptable during refresh Data must be current on every read Probabilistic early expiration Hot keys with predictable recomputation time Cold keys; it adds work without benefit Negative caching Lookups for missing ids are common or abusable "Not found" can change to "found" and must show immediately Bloom filter Huge id space with frequent probes for missing ids Small datasets, or ids created faster than the filter is rebuilt TTL jitter Many keys are written at the same time Never harmful; use it by default for bulk loads Local cache for hot keys One key dominates traffic The value must change everywhere instantly

docs.title: Single-flight request coalescing in Node.js
docs.text:
Cache the promise of an in-flight load so concurrent callers in the same process await the same database query.

// singleFlight.js
const inFlight = new Map(); // key -> Promise

export function singleFlight(key, load) {
  const existing = inFlight.get(key);
  if (existing) return existing;               // join the running load

  const promise = load().finally(() => inFlight.delete(key));
  inFlight.set(key, promise);
  return promise;
}

import { singleFlight } from "./singleFlight.js";

export async function getProduct(id) {
  const key = `product:${id}`;
  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached !== null) return JSON.parse(cached);

  // 500 concurrent misses in this process -> 1 database query
  return singleFlight(key, async () => {
    const product = await db.products.findById(id);
    const ttl = 300 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 60);  // TTL jitter
    await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(product ?? null), "EX", product ? ttl : 30);
    return product;
  });
}

This version also stores null for missing products with a 30-second TTL (negative caching). Callers must then treat a cached null as "not found" rather than as a miss.

docs.title: A distributed lock for recomputation across instances
docs.text:
Single-flight works per process. With many instances, a short Redis lock lets one instance recompute while others serve the stale copy.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const RELEASE = `
if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
end
return 0
`;

export async function refreshWithLock(key, load, ttlSeconds) {
  const lockKey = `lock:${key}`;
  const token = randomUUID();

  // NX: only if absent; PX: lock expires so a crash cannot hold it forever
  const acquired = await redis.set(lockKey, token, "PX", 5000, "NX");
  if (!acquired) return null; // someone else is refreshing; caller serves stale data

  try {
    const value = await load();
    await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(value), "EX", ttlSeconds);
    return value;
  } finally {
    // Delete the lock only if we still own it
    await redis.eval(RELEASE, 1, lockKey, token);
  }
}

A lock like this is fine for avoiding duplicate work. It is not a correctness guarantee for critical sections, because a lock can expire while its holder is still working.

docs.title: Database fallback with a concurrency limit
docs.text:
// Allow at most 20 concurrent database fallbacks per instance
let active = 0;
const MAX_FALLBACKS = 20;

export async function getWithFallback(key, load) {
  try {
    const cached = await withTimeout(redis.get(key), 25); // 25 ms budget
    if (cached !== null) return JSON.parse(cached);
  } catch {
    // cache down or slow: fall through to the limited fallback
  }

  if (active >= MAX_FALLBACKS) {
    const error = new Error("Service busy, please retry");
    error.status = 503;
    throw error;                     // shed load instead of overloading the DB
  }

  active += 1;
  try {
    return await load();
  } finally {
    active -= 1;
  }
}

function withTimeout(promise, ms) {
  return Promise.race([
    promise,
    new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error("timeout")), ms)),
  ]);
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Coalesce concurrent misses per process, and use stale-while-revalidate or locks for expensive hot keys.
  • Add jitter to TTLs, especially for bulk-loaded keys.
  • Cache negative results briefly and validate ids early.
  • Keep values small; split or trim big keys.
  • Give cache calls short timeouts and treat failures as misses, with a cap on database fallbacks.
  • Run the cache with replicas and automatic failover when the system depends on it.
  • Load-test the "cache down" and "cache cold" scenarios, not only the happy path.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Database CPU spikes on a regular rhythm. Detect: database load jumps every few minutes, matching a hot key's TTL, with many identical queries in the slow-query log. Cause: a cache stampede on expiry. Fix: single-flight per process, a lock or stale-while-revalidate across instances, and TTL jitter.
  • Database load rises while the hit ratio falls, with many 404s. Detect: access logs show requests for random or sequential ids that do not exist, often from a few clients. Cause: cache penetration. Fix: validate ids, cache "not found" briefly, rate-limit the clients, and add a Bloom filter for very large id spaces.
  • A flood of misses after a deploy or cache restart. Detect: misses for many different keys at once and a sharp database spike right after the cache restarted or a bulk job ran. Cause: an avalanche from identical TTLs or an empty cache. Fix: jitter TTLs, warm the cache, and shift traffic gradually.
  • One cache node at 100% CPU while the others idle. Detect: per-node metrics in the cluster are uneven, and redis-cli --hotkeys (which requires an LFU maxmemory-policy) or per-key client metrics point to one key. Cause: a hot key. Fix: a short-TTL local cache in front of it, or several replicated copies of the key.
  • Every request slows down when the cache is unhealthy. Detect: p99 latency equals the cache client's timeout; logs show cache timeouts. Cause: long default client timeouts and unlimited database fallbacks. Fix: short cache timeouts, a circuit breaker, and a cap on concurrent fallbacks.
  • Redis freezes briefly when cleaning up. Detect: latency spikes coincide with DEL of large keys in SLOWLOG. Cause: deleting a big key synchronously. Fix: use UNLINK, which reclaims memory in another thread, and split big keys.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Cache stampede / thundering herd: Many simultaneous misses for the same key overwhelming the source.
  • Request coalescing (single-flight): Sharing one in-flight load among concurrent requests for the same key.
  • Cache penetration: Requests for nonexistent data that always bypass the cache.
  • Negative caching: Caching "not found" results.
  • Bloom filter: A space-efficient probabilistic set with possible false positives and no false negatives.
  • Cache avalanche: Many keys expiring or disappearing at once.
  • TTL jitter: Randomizing TTLs to spread expirations.
  • Hot key / big key: A key with extreme traffic, or with an oversized value.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming the database can absorb the full load if the cache fails.
  • Setting identical TTLs on thousands of keys loaded together.
  • Not caching "not found", letting random-id requests hammer the database.
  • Waiting on a slow cache with the default (long) client timeout.
  • Using a cache lock as if it guaranteed mutual exclusion for critical business logic.
  • Deleting a multi-million-member key with DEL during peak traffic.
  • Forgetting that single-flight in one process does not coordinate other instances.

docs.title: Cache Fundamentals
docs.text: A cache is a fast, temporary copy of data kept closer to where it is needed, so later requests can skip slower work. Caches exist at every level of a system: inside the CPU, in the browser, at CDN edge servers, in application memory, in services such as Redis, and inside the database itself. This lesson explains why caching works, how to measure it, and how to decide what to cache.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Most applications read the same data far more often than they change it: product pages, user profiles, configuration, permission lists. Fetching that data from the original source every time wastes time and capacity. A well-placed cache can cut response times from tens of milliseconds to under one, and can reduce load on a database enough to postpone expensive scaling work. A badly designed cache, on the other hand, serves stale or even another user's data. Caching is therefore one of the most powerful and most error-prone tools in backend architecture.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Facebook (memcache). In Scaling Memcache at Facebook (NSDI 2013), Facebook engineers describe a memcached-based system that handles billions of requests per second and holds trillions of items. The paper explains that memcache is used as a "demand-filled look-aside cache" to lighten the read load on their databases: exactly the miss-then-fill pattern on this page.
  • Netflix (EVCache). Netflix's open-source EVCache is a memcached-based caching solution used mainly on AWS EC2 for caching frequently used data. Its name spells out the rules of any cache: ephemeral (data lives for its TTL), volatile (data can be evicted at any time), cache (an in-memory key-value store).
  • Amazon. The Amazon Builders' Library article Caching challenges and strategies describes how adding a cache cut latency and cost, until dependencies had reduced their fleet sizes and the database had been scaled down to match. From then on, the service depended on the cache to survive. That is why this page insists the system must keep working when the cache is lost.

Popular tools and providers: Redis, Memcached, Amazon ElastiCache, Caffeine (an in-process cache for the JVM), and the lru-cache npm package for in-process caching in Node.js.

docs.title: Why caching works: the latency gap
docs.text:
Different storage layers differ in speed by orders of magnitude. The numbers below are rough orders of magnitude for modern hardware, not precise measurements, but the ratios are what matter.

Operation Approximate time Read from CPU L1 cache ~1 ns Read from main memory (RAM) ~100 ns Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM a few µs Random read from an SSD tens to ~150 µs Network round trip inside one data center ~0.5 ms GET from Redis in the same data center well under 1 ms (mostly the round trip) Indexed database query ~1–10 ms Complex query or join over large tables 10 ms to seconds Round trip between continents ~100–150 ms

Reading a value from the application's own memory is thousands of times faster than a network round trip, and a network round trip to a cache is usually much cheaper than recomputing a query. Caching works because of locality: recently or frequently used data is likely to be used again soon.

docs.title: Hits, misses, and the hit ratio
docs.text:
• A hit means the requested key was found in the cache.
  • A miss means it was not, so the application must load it from the source (and usually store it in the cache).
  • The hit ratio is hits / (hits + misses).

The average (effective) latency of a cached lookup is:

effective latency = hit ratio × hit time + (1 − hit ratio) × miss time

where miss time = time to check the cache + time to load from the source

Example: a Redis lookup costs 1 ms and the database query costs 50 ms.

hit ratio 0.90:  0.90 × 1 + 0.10 × (1 + 50) = 0.90 + 5.10 = 6.0 ms
hit ratio 0.99:  0.99 × 1 + 0.01 × (1 + 50) = 0.99 + 0.51 = 1.5 ms
no cache:                                                  50.0 ms

Going from 90% to 99% hits makes the average four times faster, because misses dominate the cost. The same improvement cuts database load from 10% of requests to 1%.

docs.title: Cache layers
docs.text:
Layer Where it lives Shared by Typical contents Browser cache User's device One user Static assets, some API responses CDN Edge servers near users Everyone in a region Images, scripts, public pages, public API responses Reverse proxy In front of app servers (for example Nginx) All users Rendered pages, public responses In-process cache Inside each application process Requests to that instance Config, small lookup tables, memoized results Distributed cache Separate service (Redis, Memcached) All app instances Sessions, query results, computed objects Database buffer cache Database server memory All queries Recently used data and index pages

Each layer closer to the user saves more work but gives you less control over freshness. HTTP and CDN layers are covered in HTTP and CDN caching.

docs.title: Local compared with distributed caches
docs.text:
In-process (local) cache Distributed cache (Redis) Speed Fastest: no network Network round trip (sub-millisecond nearby) Consistency across instances Each instance has its own copy; they can disagree One shared copy Survives a restart or deploy No Yes (while the cache service is up) Memory Uses application memory; multiplied by instance count Separate memory you size independently Invalidation Hard: every instance must be told Delete the key once Good for Small, rarely changing data; very hot keys Shared data, sessions, larger datasets

Many systems use both: a tiny local cache with a short TTL in front of Redis, which in turn sits in front of the database.

docs.title: What to cache and what not to
docs.text:
Good candidates:

  • Data read much more often than it changes (catalogs, profiles, settings).
  • Expensive results: aggregations, rendered fragments, third-party API responses.
  • Data where slight staleness is acceptable for a known period.

Poor or dangerous candidates:

  • Highly personalized data with low reuse: each entry is used once, so the hit ratio is low and memory is wasted.
  • Sensitive data (tokens, health or payment details) unless it is scoped strictly per user, encrypted where required, and short-lived.
  • Rapidly changing data where staleness causes harm, such as account balances or stock counts used to accept orders.
  • Data that is cheap to compute or fetch: caching adds complexity for little gain.

docs.title: Designing cache keys
docs.text:
A key must uniquely identify the data and every input that changes it. Missing an input causes wrong data to be served.

Good:   product:42:v3                      (entity, id, schema version)
        user:17:orders:page=2:limit=20     (all query inputs)
        search:{sha256 of normalized query}
        tenant:acme:product:42             (tenant included in multi-tenant apps)

Bad:    orders:page=2      <- missing the user: one user's orders served to another
        product            <- not unique

Guidelines:

  • Use a consistent type:id:qualifier naming scheme with : separators.
  • Include the tenant, user, locale, currency, or permission scope when the value depends on it.
  • Normalize inputs (sort query parameters, lowercase where safe) so equivalent requests share a key.
  • Hash long inputs to keep keys short.
  • Add a version segment so a change in data format can use fresh keys.

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text: Distributed caches store bytes or strings, so objects must be serialized. JSON is the common choice: readable and portable, but Date objects come back as strings and undefined, Map, Set, and BigInt need special handling. Binary formats (MessagePack, Protocol Buffers) are smaller and faster but less convenient to inspect. Compress only large values, and keep values small; very large values are slow to transfer and can block the cache server (see cache failure modes).

docs.title: TTL basics
docs.text:
A time to live (TTL) limits how long an entry may be used. When it expires, the next read is a miss and loads fresh data. A TTL:

  • puts an upper bound on staleness,
  • lets unused entries disappear automatically, and
  • acts as a safety net when explicit invalidation fails.

Choosing TTLs and invalidating on writes is covered in invalidation and expiration.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Add a cache when:

  • Measurements show the same expensive reads repeating (high read/write ratio, many identical queries or API calls).
  • Slightly stale data is acceptable for a known period.
  • The source is slow, expensive, rate-limited, or far away.

Do not add a cache (or not yet) when:

  • A missing index or an N+1 query is the real problem; fix the query first.
  • Data must be exactly current for a decision (balances, stock checks, authorization).
  • Reads rarely repeat, so the hit ratio would be low.
  • The team cannot yet monitor hit ratio and handle invalidation.
Problem Better first step Cache it? One slow query, few repeats Index or rewrite the query No Same query repeated by many users Distributed cache (Redis) Yes Tiny, rarely changing lookup data on every request In-process cache with a short TTL Yes Many reads overloading the primary database Read replicas, then cache Often both Expensive aggregation shown on dashboards Precomputed table or materialized view Sometimes, in front of it Public static files and pages HTTP caching and a CDN Yes, at the edge

docs.title: Memoization with a bounded Map
docs.text:
Memoization caches the result of a function call by its arguments inside the process. An unbounded Map grows forever and eventually exhausts memory, so give it a maximum size and a TTL.

// memoize.js: in-process cache with TTL and a size limit
export function memoize(fn, { ttlMs = 60_000, maxEntries = 1_000 } = {}) {
  const cache = new Map(); // key -> { value, expiresAt }

  return async function memoized(...args) {
    const key = JSON.stringify(args);
    const entry = cache.get(key);

    if (entry && entry.expiresAt > Date.now()) {
      // Refresh position: Map keeps insertion order, newest at the end
      cache.delete(key);
      cache.set(key, entry);
      return entry.value;
    }

    const value = await fn(...args);
    // delete first: set() on an existing key keeps its old position in the Map
    cache.delete(key);
    cache.set(key, { value, expiresAt: Date.now() + ttlMs });

    // Evict the oldest entry (first in the Map) when over the limit
    if (cache.size > maxEntries) {
      cache.delete(cache.keys().next().value);
    }
    return value;
  };
}

import { memoize } from "./memoize.js";

async function loadExchangeRate(from, to) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://rates.example.com/${from}/${to}`);
  return (await res.json()).rate;
}

export const getExchangeRate = memoize(loadExchangeRate, { ttlMs: 5 * 60_000, maxEntries: 500 });

await getExchangeRate("USD", "EUR"); // miss: calls the API
await getExchangeRate("USD", "EUR"); // hit: returns from memory

This is a small LRU-style cache: entries used recently move to the end, and the oldest is evicted first. See eviction policies for proper LRU and LFU designs. Note that the cached value is the resolved result; caching the promise itself also merges concurrent calls, as shown in cache failure modes.

docs.title: Measuring the hit ratio
docs.text:
const stats = { hits: 0, misses: 0 };

export async function getCached(cache, key, load) {
  const cached = await cache.get(key);
  if (cached !== null) {
    stats.hits += 1;
    return JSON.parse(cached);
  }
  stats.misses += 1;
  const value = await load();
  await cache.set(key, JSON.stringify(value));
  return value;
}

export function hitRatio() {
  const total = stats.hits + stats.misses;
  return total === 0 ? 0 : stats.hits / total;
}

In production, export these counters as metrics; Redis also reports keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses in its INFO stats output.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Measure first: confirm the source is actually slow or overloaded and that reads repeat.
  • Treat the database as the source of truth; a cache is an optimization that can be lost at any time.
  • Include every input that affects the value in the key, especially the user or tenant.
  • Always set a TTL, even when you also invalidate explicitly.
  • Bound in-process caches by size and time.
  • Monitor hit ratio, latency, memory, and evictions.
  • Design the application to keep working (more slowly) if the cache is down.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Hit ratio collapses right after a deploy. Detect: keyspace_misses jumps in Redis INFO stats while database queries per second rise at the deploy time. Cause: the key format or version segment changed, so every key is new and the cache is cold. Fix: change key formats deliberately, warm the most-read keys before shifting traffic, and roll out gradually.
  • Memory grows until the process restarts. Detect: resident memory climbs steadily and out-of-memory restarts repeat, while heap snapshots show a large Map. Cause: an unbounded in-process cache. Fix: cap entries and add TTLs, or use a bounded LRU library.
  • A user sees someone else's data. Detect: a support report; logs show two users receiving the same cached response for a personalized endpoint. Cause: a cache key that omits the user or tenant. Fix: include every input in the key, flush the affected keys, and add a test that two users get different entries.
  • The database falls over when the cache restarts. Detect: database CPU and connection count spike to saturation right after a cache failover or flush. Cause: the database was sized only for cache misses, as Amazon's Builders' Library warns. Fix: capacity-plan for a cold cache, warm it before traffic, and limit concurrent database fallbacks.
  • Latency spikes on some requests only. Detect: Redis SLOWLOG or redis-cli --bigkeys shows multi-megabyte values. Cause: large serialized objects. Fix: cache only the fields needed, split large values, and compress big blobs.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Cache: A fast, temporary store holding copies of data.
  • Hit / miss: Whether a lookup found the key.
  • Hit ratio: The fraction of lookups that are hits.
  • Locality: The tendency of programs to reuse recently or frequently accessed data.
  • TTL (time to live): How long an entry may be used before it expires.
  • Stale data: A cached value that no longer matches the source.
  • Working set: The data actively used during a period of time.
  • Memoization: Caching a function's result by its arguments.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Caching before measuring, and adding complexity where none was needed.
  • Keys that omit the user or tenant, leaking one user's data to another.
  • Unbounded in-process caches that cause memory leaks.
  • Assuming a high hit ratio means the data is correct; it only means it was found.
  • Treating the cache as durable storage.
  • Caching everything, including data that is rarely reused, which evicts the data that matters.
  • Forgetting that every app instance has its own in-process cache.
