docs.title: Caching Strategies
docs.text: A caching strategy decides who reads from and writes to the cache, and when the cache and the source of truth are updated. The common patterns are cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind, write-around, and refresh-ahead. Each trades off freshness, write latency, complexity, and what happens when something fails.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: The same cache server can be used safely or dangerously depending on the strategy around it. One strategy keeps the database authoritative and tolerates cache loss; another makes the cache the first place writes land and risks losing data if it crashes. Knowing the patterns by name also helps in design discussions and interviews, where "we'll add a cache" is never a complete answer.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Amazon: inline versus side caches. The Amazon Builders' Library article Caching challenges and strategies separates inline caches (read-through/write-through, with cache management embedded in the data access path, such as DynamoDB Accelerator or an HTTP cache) from side caches (generic stores such as ElastiCache for Redis or Memcached, where application code manages the cache, which is cache-aside).
  • Facebook: delete on write. In the Scaling Memcache at Facebook paper, web servers read through memcache as a demand-filled look-aside (cache-aside) cache. On a write they update the database and then send a delete to memcache, and the paper explains: "We choose to delete cached data instead of updating it because deletes are idempotent."
  • Amazon ElastiCache guidance. The ElastiCache caching strategies guide presents lazy loading (cache-aside), write-through, and adding a TTL as the core strategies for populating and maintaining a cache.

docs.title: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
docs.text:
The application talks to both the cache and the database. On a read, it checks the cache first; on a miss, it loads from the database and stores the result. On a write, it updates the database and removes (or updates) the cached entry.

  • Only data that is actually requested gets cached.
  • If the cache is down, reads fall back to the database.
  • The first read after a miss or expiry is slow.
  • The application code owns the caching logic.

Cache-aside is the most common pattern and a good default.

docs.title: Read-through
docs.text:
The application asks only the cache (or a caching library). On a miss, the cache layer itself calls a loader to fetch from the database, stores the value, and returns it.

app ── get(key) ──> cache layer ── miss ──> loader ──> database
                         └── stores and returns the value

The behavior is like cache-aside, but loading logic is centralized in one component instead of repeated in every caller. Many in-process libraries and some managed caches support this with a "loader" function.

docs.title: Write-through
docs.text:
Every write goes to the cache and the database synchronously as part of the same operation (usually through a cache layer that writes to the database). The write succeeds only after both are updated.

app ── write ──> cache layer ──> database (commit)
                     └──> cache (store new value)
  • Cached data is fresh right after a write.
  • Writes are slower: they pay for both stores.
  • Data that is written but never read still occupies the cache (combine with a TTL).
  • If the database write succeeds and the cache write fails (or the reverse), the two disagree unless failures are handled carefully.

docs.title: Write-behind (write-back)
docs.text:
Writes go to the cache only and are acknowledged immediately. The cache layer flushes changes to the database later, often in batches.

app ── write ──> cache ── ack (fast)
                   └── queue ── batch ──> database (seconds later)
  • Very fast writes and fewer database operations (several updates to the same key can be merged).
  • Risk of data loss: if the cache crashes before flushing, acknowledged writes disappear unless the cache is durable.
  • The database is temporarily behind, so other systems reading it see old data.

Use it only where losing a few recent writes is acceptable (counters, view statistics, analytics) or where the cache layer provides durability.

docs.title: Write-around
docs.text:
Writes go directly to the database and skip the cache; the cached entry is invalidated. The cache is filled only by reads (as in cache-aside).

  • Avoids filling the cache with data written once and rarely read (logs, bulk imports).
  • The first read after a write is a miss.

In practice, "cache-aside with delete-on-write" is a write-around approach.

The three write strategies side by side:

docs.title: Refresh-ahead
docs.text:
Before a popular entry expires, the system reloads it in the background, so readers rarely see a miss.

  • Keeps latency low for hot keys.
  • Wasted work if the refreshed entry is not read again.
  • Needs care so only one refresh runs at a time (see cache failure modes).

docs.title: Trade-offs at a glance
docs.text: Strategy Who loads/writes the cache Read freshness Write latency If the cache fails Main risk Cache-aside Application Stale until TTL or invalidation Unchanged (DB + delete) Reads hit the DB Stale data after races; first-read latency Read-through Cache layer (loader) Same as cache-aside Unchanged Depends on the layer; often reads fail over Coupling to a cache library Write-through Cache layer on every write Fresh after writes Higher (two writes) Writes may fail or diverge Partial failures; caching unread data Write-behind Cache first, DB later Fresh in cache; DB lags Lowest Unflushed writes lost Data loss, DB temporarily behind Write-around DB only; cache filled by reads Fresh after the next miss Unchanged Reads hit the DB Misses right after writes Refresh-ahead Background refresher Usually fresh for hot keys Unchanged Falls back to normal misses Extra load from refreshing cold keys

docs.title: How to choose
docs.text:
1. Start with cache-aside plus a TTL and delete-on-write. It is simple, keeps the database authoritative, and survives cache outages.
  2. Use read-through when you want loading logic in one shared layer.
  3. Use write-through when data must be fresh immediately after a write and the extra write latency is acceptable.
  4. Use write-behind only for data where occasional loss is tolerable, or when the cache is durable and replicated.
  5. Use write-around for write-heavy data that is rarely read back.
  6. Add refresh-ahead for a small set of very hot keys whose misses are expensive.

Strategies combine: reads with cache-aside, writes with write-around, and refresh-ahead for the homepage data.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Cache-aside: use as the default for read-heavy data with an authoritative database. Avoid relying on it alone when a stale read right after a write is unacceptable.
  • Read-through: use when many callers load the same kinds of data and you want one loading path. Avoid it when it would tie your code to a cache product that may be unavailable.
  • Write-through: use when reads right after writes must hit fresh, cached data (settings, profiles shown immediately after saving). Avoid it for data written often but rarely read.
  • Write-behind: use only for loss-tolerant, high-frequency writes (counters, analytics) or with a durable cache layer. Never use it for orders, payments, or anything you must not lose.
  • Write-around: use for bulk or write-once data. Avoid it when the next read after a write is time-critical.
  • Refresh-ahead: use for a handful of very hot, expensive keys. Avoid it for large or cold key sets.
Need Cache-aside Read-through Write-through Write-behind Simplest correct default Best Good More work Risky Survives a cache outage Yes (reads go to the DB) Depends on the layer Writes may fail Unflushed writes lost Fresh data right after a write After the next miss After the next miss Yes Yes (in the cache) Write latency Normal Normal Higher Lowest Data-loss risk None None None Yes

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text: The examples use the ioredis client (npm install ioredis); the official redis package works the same way with slightly different method signatures.

docs.title: Cache-aside with delete-on-write
docs.text:
// productCache.js
import Redis from "ioredis";
import { db } from "./db.js";

const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL);
const TTL_SECONDS = 300;
const key = (id) => `product:${id}:v1`;

export async function getProduct(id) {
  // 1. Try the cache, but never let a cache error break the request
  try {
    const cached = await redis.get(key(id));
    if (cached !== null) return JSON.parse(cached);
  } catch (error) {
    console.warn("cache read failed", error.message);
  }

  // 2. Miss: load from the source of truth
  const product = await db.products.findById(id);
  if (!product) return null;

  // 3. Populate with a TTL; failures here are also non-fatal
  redis.set(key(id), JSON.stringify(product), "EX", TTL_SECONDS)
    .catch((error) => console.warn("cache write failed", error.message));

  return product;
}

export async function updateProduct(id, changes) {
  const product = await db.products.update(id, changes); // 1. write the DB first
  await redis.del(key(id));                              // 2. then invalidate
  return product;
}

Deleting rather than writing the new value avoids out-of-order updates when two writers race; the next read loads the latest committed row. The remaining race conditions are covered in invalidation and expiration.

docs.title: A read-through helper
docs.text:
// readThrough.js: callers provide a loader; the helper owns cache logic
export function createReadThroughCache(redis, { ttlSeconds, prefix }) {
  return async function get(id, loader) {
    const cacheKey = `${prefix}:${id}`;
    const cached = await redis.get(cacheKey);
    if (cached !== null) return JSON.parse(cached);

    const value = await loader(id);
    if (value !== null) {
      await redis.set(cacheKey, JSON.stringify(value), "EX", ttlSeconds);
    }
    return value;
  };
}

const userCache = createReadThroughCache(redis, { ttlSeconds: 600, prefix: "user:v1" });
const user = await userCache(42, (id) => db.users.findById(id));

docs.title: Write-through
docs.text:
export async function saveSettings(userId, settings) {
  // Commit to the database first; it is the source of truth
  const saved = await db.settings.upsert(userId, settings);
  // Then store the committed value; a TTL limits damage if this step fails
  await redis.set(`settings:${userId}`, JSON.stringify(saved), "EX", 3600);
  return saved;
}

Writing the database first means a crash between the two steps leaves the cache stale (bounded by the TTL) rather than leaving the cache holding data that was never saved.

docs.title: Write-behind for view counters
docs.text:
// Fast path: increment in Redis only
export async function recordView(articleId) {
  await redis.hincrby("views:pending", articleId, 1);
}

// Background job every 10 seconds: flush to the database in one batch
export async function flushViews() {
  // RENAME takes the pending hash atomically so new views go to a fresh one
  const exists = await redis.exists("views:pending");
  if (!exists) return;
  await redis.rename("views:pending", "views:flushing");

  const counts = await redis.hgetall("views:flushing");
  for (const [articleId, count] of Object.entries(counts)) {
    await db.articles.incrementViews(articleId, Number(count));
  }
  await redis.del("views:flushing");
}

If Redis restarts before a flush, those counts are lost, which is usually acceptable for view statistics but never for orders or payments. A production version would also run only one flusher at a time and handle a crash between RENAME and DEL.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Default to cache-aside with TTLs and delete-on-write.
  • Write to the database before touching the cache.
  • Prefer deleting cached entries to overwriting them on writes.
  • Treat cache errors as misses, not request failures, with short timeouts on cache calls.
  • Reserve write-behind for loss-tolerant data, and document that choice.
  • Keep caching logic in one module or helper rather than scattered across handlers.
  • Measure hit ratio and latency per strategy and adjust TTLs from data.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every request fails during a Redis failover. Detect: the API error rate spikes in step with Redis connection errors (ECONNREFUSED, timeouts) in logs. Cause: cache calls are not wrapped, so a cache error fails the request. Fix: treat cache errors as misses, set short cache timeouts, and cap the resulting database fallbacks.
  • Values appear that were never saved. Detect: the cache holds a value with no matching database row, usually after database errors or rollbacks. Cause: the cache was updated before the database write, and the write then failed. Fix: write the database first, then delete (or set) the cache entry.
  • View counts drop after a Redis restart. Detect: totals in the database lag the numbers users saw, with a gap matching the restart time. Cause: write-behind data not yet flushed when Redis lost it. Fix: accept and document the loss for counters, or enable persistence and flush more often; never use write-behind for critical data.
  • Write-through cache and database disagree. Detect: periodic comparisons find cached values different from the database. Cause: one of the two writes failed, or concurrent writers interleaved. Fix: give cached entries a TTL, prefer deleting over setting, and log and alert on cache write failures.
  • Refresh-ahead load with no benefit. Detect: background refresh jobs account for a large share of database queries, while many refreshed keys are never read before their next refresh. Cause: refreshing cold keys. Fix: refresh only keys with recent reads, or switch them back to plain TTL expiry.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Cache-aside (lazy loading): The application loads misses from the source and stores them in the cache.
  • Read-through: The cache layer loads misses itself through a loader.
  • Write-through: Writes update the cache and the source synchronously.
  • Write-behind (write-back): Writes update the cache and reach the source asynchronously later.
  • Write-around: Writes go to the source only; the cache is filled by reads.
  • Refresh-ahead: Hot entries are reloaded before they expire.
  • Source of truth: The system whose data is authoritative, usually the database.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Updating the cache before the database, so a failed database write leaves fake data in the cache.
  • Using write-behind for important data without durability.
  • Assuming write-through guarantees consistency; partial failures and concurrent writers can still cause divergence.
  • Letting a cache outage fail every request instead of falling back.
  • Caching with no TTL because "we invalidate on write"; one missed invalidation then lasts forever.
  • Refreshing every key ahead of time, wasting resources on cold data.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Describe the read and write paths of cache-aside.
  2. How does read-through differ from cache-aside?
  3. What are the risks of write-behind, and which data suits it?
  4. Why is deleting a cached entry on write often safer than updating it?
  5. When does write-around make sense?
  6. Which strategy would you choose for a product catalog, and why?

docs.title: Eviction Policies
docs.text: A cache has limited memory. When it is full and a new entry must be stored, an eviction policy decides which existing entry to remove. Common policies are LRU (least recently used), LFU (least frequently used), FIFO, random, and TTL-based eviction. Redis exposes these choices through its maxmemory-policy setting.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: The eviction policy decides which data stays in the cache, and therefore the hit ratio. The wrong policy can push out exactly the data that is reused most, or, in Redis, make writes fail with out-of-memory errors. Eviction is different from expiration: expiration removes entries whose TTL has passed; eviction removes entries early because memory ran out.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Redis recommends allkeys-lru as a starting point. The Redis key eviction guide calls allkeys-lru "a good default option" when a subset of keys is accessed far more often than the rest, and explains that Redis approximates LRU by sampling keys and keeping a pool of good eviction candidates.
  • Managed Redis can have a different default. Open-source Redis defaults to noeviction, but Amazon ElastiCache's parameter groups list volatile-lru as the default maxmemory-policy. Code that stores keys without TTLs behaves differently on the two.
  • Caffeine combines frequency and recency. The Java caching library Caffeine offers size-based eviction "based on frequency and recency", and its README points to the research behind its policy, including the TinyLFU admission policy paper.
  • Redis added an "LRM" policy. Since Redis 8.6, allkeys-lrm and volatile-lrm evict the least recently modified keys: only writes update the timestamp, so frequently read but rarely updated data can be told apart from data that is actively changing.

docs.title: Expiration compared with eviction
docs.text:
Expiration Eviction Trigger The entry's TTL passed Memory limit reached Chooses Exactly the expired entry A victim chosen by the policy Happens even with free memory Yes No Signal Normal; data aged out The cache may be too small

A healthy cache mostly expires entries. Constant eviction means the working set does not fit.

docs.title: LRU: least recently used
docs.text:
LRU removes the entry that has gone unused the longest, assuming recently used data will be used again soon (temporal locality). It is the most widely used general-purpose policy.

The classic O(1) implementation combines:

  • a hash map from key to node, for O(1) lookup, and
  • a doubly linked list ordered by recency, for O(1) moves and removal.

docs.title: LFU: least frequently used
docs.text:
LFU removes the entry with the lowest access count, assuming popular data stays popular. It protects long-term hot keys from being pushed out by a burst of one-time reads (for example a batch job scanning many keys once), which would flush an LRU cache.

Its weakness is history: an item that was popular last week can keep a high count forever. Practical LFU implementations therefore decay counts over time.

docs.title: FIFO, random, and TTL-based
docs.text:
• FIFO (first in, first out): evicts the oldest inserted entry regardless of use. Simple, but evicts hot entries just because they are old.
  • Random: evicts any entry. Surprisingly reasonable when access is roughly uniform, and very cheap.
  • TTL-based (shortest time to live first): evicts entries closest to expiring, since they would disappear soon anyway.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Policy Keeps Good for Weak when LRU Recently used General workloads, recency matters One-off scans flush hot data LFU Frequently used Stable popularity (top products, configs) Popularity shifts; needs decay FIFO Newest inserted Simple buffers Old entries are still hot Random Anything Uniform access; low overhead Skewed access patterns TTL-based Long-lived entries Data with meaningful TTLs TTLs not set or meaningless

docs.title: Approximated LRU and LFU in Redis
docs.text:
Keeping a perfect linked list over millions of keys costs memory and CPU. Redis instead approximates:

  • Each key stores a small access-time (LRU) or access-frequency (LFU) field.
  • When eviction is needed, Redis samples a few keys (the maxmemory-samples setting, default 5) and evicts the best candidate among them, keeping a small pool of good candidates between rounds.
  • Higher sample counts get closer to true LRU at more CPU cost.

Redis LFU uses a small logarithmic counter per key (a Morris-style counter) that grows more slowly as it gets larger, and decays over time so old popularity fades. lfu-log-factor controls how fast counters grow, and lfu-decay-time (in minutes) controls how fast they decay.

docs.title: Redis maxmemory and maxmemory-policy
docs.text:
# redis.conf
maxmemory 2gb
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

When memory use reaches maxmemory, Redis applies the policy. "All keys" policies consider every key; "volatile" policies consider only keys that have a TTL set.

Policy Evicts When to pick it noeviction (default) Nothing; write commands that need memory return an error Redis holds data that must not be silently dropped (queues, primary data) allkeys-lru Least recently used among all keys Pure cache with recency-based access; the usual choice allkeys-lfu Least frequently used among all keys Pure cache with a stable set of popular keys allkeys-random Random key Uniform access, or lowest overhead volatile-lru Least recently used among keys with a TTL Mixed use: cache keys have TTLs, persistent keys do not volatile-lfu Least frequently used among keys with a TTL Mixed use with stable popularity volatile-random Random key with a TTL Mixed use, uniform access volatile-ttl Key with the shortest remaining TTL TTLs reflect how long data is worth keeping allkeys-lrm (Redis 8.6+) Least recently modified among all keys Read-heavy data where recent writes signal value volatile-lrm (Redis 8.6+) Least recently modified among keys with a TTL Mixed use with the same idea

With any volatile-* policy, if no key has a TTL, Redis has nothing to evict and behaves like noeviction: writes start failing. Managed services can change the default policy (Amazon ElastiCache defaults to volatile-lru), so check the setting rather than assuming noeviction.

Warning

Mixing a cache and important data (job queues, sessions you cannot lose) in one Redis instance with an allkeys-* policy lets cache pressure evict the important data. Use separate instances or a volatile-* policy with TTLs only on cache keys.

docs.title: Sizing a cache
docs.text:
1. Estimate the working set: how many distinct keys are read in a typical TTL window, multiplied by the average value size plus per-key overhead.
  2. Look at the hit-ratio curve: hit ratio usually rises quickly and then flattens. Doubling memory past the flat part buys little.
  3. Leave headroom: Redis needs memory beyond the data for client buffers, replication buffers, and, during snapshot persistence, copy-on-write pages after forking.
  4. Monitor: watch used_memory, evicted_keys, expired_keys, keyspace_hits, and keyspace_misses from INFO.
Example estimate
  500,000 active products × (2 KB value + ~100 B key/overhead) ≈ 1.05 GB
  + 30% headroom                                               ≈ 1.4 GB
  -> start with maxmemory 1.5gb, then adjust from evicted_keys and hit ratio

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• LRU: use for general caches where recently used data is likely to be reused. Avoid it when large one-off scans or batch jobs read through the cache.
  • LFU: use when a stable set of keys stays popular for a long time. Avoid it when popularity shifts quickly and decay is not tuned.
  • Random: use when access is roughly uniform or eviction overhead must be minimal. Avoid it for skewed workloads.
  • TTL-based (volatile-ttl): use when TTLs genuinely express how long data is worth keeping. Avoid it when TTLs are arbitrary.
  • No eviction: use when the data must not be silently dropped (queues, primary data). Never use it for a pure cache that is allowed to fill.
Workload Recommended policy Why Pure cache, recency matters allkeys-lru Keeps recently used keys; a solid default Pure cache, stable popular set, periodic scans allkeys-lfu Scans do not push out long-term hot keys One instance for cache keys (with TTLs) and data you cannot lose volatile-lru / volatile-lfu Only TTL keys are candidates; better still, use two instances Queues, sessions you cannot lose, primary data noeviction + memory alerts Fail loudly instead of losing data Read-heavy data where writes mark value (Redis 8.6+) allkeys-lrm Evicts data that has not changed recently

docs.title: LRU cache with a hash map and a doubly linked list
docs.text:
class Node {
  constructor(key, value) {
    this.key = key;
    this.value = value;
    this.prev = null;
    this.next = null;
  }
}

export class LRUCache {
  constructor(capacity) {
    this.capacity = capacity;
    this.map = new Map();          // key -> Node
    this.head = new Node(null);    // sentinel: most recent side
    this.tail = new Node(null);    // sentinel: least recent side
    this.head.next = this.tail;
    this.tail.prev = this.head;
  }

  #remove(node) {
    node.prev.next = node.next;
    node.next.prev = node.prev;
  }

  #addToFront(node) {
    node.next = this.head.next;
    node.prev = this.head;
    this.head.next.prev = node;
    this.head.next = node;
  }

  get(key) {
    const node = this.map.get(key);
    if (!node) return undefined;   // miss
    this.#remove(node);            // hit: mark as most recently used
    this.#addToFront(node);
    return node.value;
  }

  set(key, value) {
    const existing = this.map.get(key);
    if (existing) {
      existing.value = value;
      this.#remove(existing);
      this.#addToFront(existing);
      return;
    }
    if (this.map.size === this.capacity) {
      const lru = this.tail.prev;  // least recently used
      this.#remove(lru);
      this.map.delete(lru.key);
    }
    const node = new Node(key, value);
    this.map.set(key, node);
    this.#addToFront(node);
  }
}

const cache = new LRUCache(2);
cache.set("a", 1);
cache.set("b", 2);
cache.get("a");        // 1  (a is now most recent)
cache.set("c", 3);     // evicts b, the least recently used
cache.get("b");        // undefined

Every operation is O(1). JavaScript's Map keeps insertion order, so a shorter LRU can delete and re-insert keys on access and evict map.keys().next().value; the explicit linked list shows the classic data structure used in other languages and interviews.

docs.title: LFU idea in brief
docs.text: An O(1) LFU keeps a map from key to { value, count } and a map from count to an ordered set of keys with that count, plus the current minimum count. On access, a key moves from bucket count to count + 1; on eviction, remove the oldest key in the minimum-count bucket.

docs.title: Configuring Redis as a cache
docs.text:
redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory 1gb
redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu
redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E "evicted_keys|keyspace_hits|keyspace_misses"
# evicted_keys:0
# keyspace_hits:982341
# keyspace_misses:41022

Settings changed with CONFIG SET are lost on restart unless also written to the configuration file (CONFIG REWRITE) or set by your managed service's parameter settings.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for a Redis instance that is purely a cache.
  • Keep noeviction for Redis instances holding data you cannot lose, and alert on memory before it fills.
  • Do not mix cache data and critical data under an allkeys-* policy.
  • Size from the working set, then tune from the hit ratio and eviction metrics.
  • Leave memory headroom for buffers and persistence.
  • Treat rising evicted_keys with a falling hit ratio as a capacity signal.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Writes start failing when the cache fills. Detect: application logs show Redis out-of-memory errors on SET, used_memory sits at maxmemory, and evicted_keys stays at 0. Cause: noeviction, or a volatile-* policy with keys that have no TTL. Fix: use an allkeys-* policy for a pure cache, or put TTLs on every cache key.
  • Users are logged out at random under load. Detect: evicted_keys rises during traffic peaks and session keys disappear before their TTL. Cause: sessions share an allkeys-* instance with cache data, so cache pressure evicts them. Fix: move sessions to a separate instance with noeviction, or use volatile-* with TTLs only on cache keys.
  • Hit ratio collapses every night. Detect: keyspace_misses and database load jump during a nightly batch job and stay high afterwards. Cause: the job reads many keys once and flushes the LRU cache. Fix: switch to allkeys-lfu, or let the job bypass the cache.
  • Behavior differs between local Redis and the managed service. Detect: keys without TTLs are never evicted locally but writes fail (or keys vanish) in the cloud. Cause: different default maxmemory-policy values, such as volatile-lru on ElastiCache. Fix: set the policy explicitly in every environment.
  • Latency spikes or the server is killed during snapshots. Detect: used_memory_rss approaches the machine's RAM during background saves, followed by swapping or an out-of-memory kill. Cause: maxmemory set too close to physical memory, with no room for copy-on-write pages and buffers. Fix: leave headroom; the Redis eviction guide also recommends leaving RAM free for buffers when using replication or persistence.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Eviction: Removing an entry early because the cache is full.
  • LRU: Evict the least recently used entry.
  • LFU: Evict the least frequently used entry.
  • FIFO: Evict the entry inserted first.
  • Approximated LRU/LFU: Choosing a victim from a random sample instead of tracking exact order.
  • maxmemory-policy: The Redis setting that selects the eviction policy.
  • Volatile key: In Redis, a key that has a TTL.
  • Working set: The data actively used over a period.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Leaving Redis on the default noeviction when using it as a cache, so writes fail with out-of-memory errors when it fills.
  • Choosing a volatile-* policy while setting no TTLs.
  • Confusing eviction with expiration.
  • Assuming LRU is always best; scans and batch jobs can flush it.
  • Setting maxmemory to the machine's full RAM, leaving no headroom.
  • Using an unbounded in-process cache, which has no eviction at all.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between eviction and expiration?
  2. Why does an O(1) LRU need both a hash map and a doubly linked list?
  3. When does LFU outperform LRU, and why does LFU need decay?
  4. Which Redis policy would you choose for a pure cache, and which for an instance that also stores job queues?
  5. What happens with volatile-lru when no keys have a TTL?
  6. Which metrics tell you a cache is too small?

docs.title: HTTP and CDN Caching
docs.text: HTTP has caching built into the protocol. Browsers, reverse proxies, and content delivery networks (CDNs) can store responses and reuse them without contacting your servers, guided by headers your application sends. This lesson looks at HTTP caching from an architecture point of view: where responses are cached, how caches decide what is "the same request", how to change cached content safely, and how to avoid leaking private data.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: The fastest request is the one that never reaches your servers. A CDN can serve static assets and public pages from an edge location a few milliseconds from the user, absorbing most traffic and traffic spikes. But HTTP caches are outside your application's direct control: once a response is stored in thousands of browsers or edge servers, you cannot easily take it back. One wrong header can make a fix invisible for days, or serve one user's account page to everyone.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Cloudflare caches by file extension, not content type. Cloudflare's default cache behavior page states that it caches based on file extension rather than MIME type and does not cache HTML or JSON by default. API responses and pages are therefore not cached at the edge unless you add rules.
  • Cloudflare documents web cache deception. Its Cache Deception Armor page describes a personalized page that the origin also serves at /newsfeed/foo.jpg: because the path ends in .jpg, the CDN caches it, and the attacker then receives the victim's cached content. Cloudflare offers a cache rule that protects against this.
  • Amazon CloudFront makes the cache key explicit. A CloudFront cache policy specifies which headers, cookies, and query strings are included in the cache key, which determines whether a request is a cache hit.
  • CDNs purge by tag. Fastly's Surrogate-Key header and Cloudflare's Cache-Tag header both let you purge every object with a given tag in one request.

Popular providers: Cloudflare, Amazon CloudFront, Fastly, Akamai, and Google Cloud CDN; reverse-proxy caches such as Nginx and Varnish.

docs.title: Private and shared caches
docs.text:
User A browser cache ─┐                                  ┌─> origin (your app)
(private: only A)     ├─> CDN edge cache ─> reverse proxy ┤
User B browser cache ─┘   (shared: all     (shared)       └─> database
(private: only B)          users nearby)
Cache Shared? Controlled by Can store personalized responses? Browser (private) cache No, one user Cache-Control from the origin Yes, if allowed (private) CDN edge cache Yes Cache-Control, s-maxage, CDN rules Only if the cache key separates users (usually avoid) Reverse proxy cache Yes Proxy configuration and headers Same as CDN

HTTP caching rules are defined in RFC 9111.

docs.title: Cache-Control recap
docs.text:
The Cache-Control response header tells caches whether and how long they may store a response. The directives are explained in detail in HTTP headers; the ones that matter most for architecture are:

Directive Effect max-age=N Fresh for N seconds in any cache s-maxage=N Overrides max-age for shared caches (CDN, proxy) only public Shared caches may store it, even in some cases they otherwise would not private Only the user's browser may store it no-cache May be stored, but must be revalidated with the origin before each use no-store Must not be stored anywhere immutable The content will never change while fresh; skip revalidation stale-while-revalidate=N May serve stale for N seconds while revalidating in the background stale-if-error=N May serve stale for N seconds if the origin errors

Some CDNs also honor CDN-Cache-Control (RFC 9213), which targets CDN caches separately from browsers.

docs.title: Freshness and validation
docs.text:
A cached response is fresh until its age exceeds max-age; fresh responses are served without contacting the origin. A stale response can be revalidated: the cache asks the origin whether its copy is still current.

First request:
  200 OK
  ETag: "v7-a1b2"
  Last-Modified: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:00:00 GMT
  Cache-Control: max-age=60

After 60 s (stale), the cache revalidates:
  GET /api/catalog
  If-None-Match: "v7-a1b2"
  If-Modified-Since: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:00:00 GMT

Origin, if unchanged:
  304 Not Modified          (no body; the cache reuses its copy for another 60 s)
Origin, if changed:
  200 OK + new body + new ETag
  • ETag is an identifier for a specific version of the content. Strong ETags mean byte-identical; weak ETags (W/"...") mean semantically equivalent.
  • Last-Modified is a timestamp; less precise (one-second resolution) but easy to produce.
  • A 304 still costs a round trip, but saves bandwidth and often origin work.

The same rules at a CDN edge, for a fresh hit, a miss, and a stale copy:

docs.title: CDN edge caching
docs.text:
A CDN runs servers in many locations (points of presence). DNS or anycast routing sends each user to a nearby edge, which serves cached responses or fetches from your origin on a miss. See CDN for how CDNs work as infrastructure.

User (Mumbai) ──> Mumbai edge ── hit ──> response in ~10 ms
                       │ miss
                       └──> (origin shield) ──> origin in another region (~150+ ms)

An origin shield (a mid-tier cache) makes edge misses go through one regional cache first, so a popular new object is fetched from the origin once rather than once per edge location.

docs.title: Cache keys
docs.text:
A shared cache decides whether two requests are "the same" by their cache key. By default this is usually the method, host, and full URL including the query string. CDNs let you customize it.

Key component Include it when Danger if mishandled Path Always — Query string It changes the response (?page=2) Including tracking parameters (utm_*) fragments the cache; excluding real ones serves wrong data Specific headers (Accept-Language) The response varies by it Including high-variety headers (User-Agent) destroys the hit ratio Cookies Almost never on shared caches Keying on session cookies means one entry per user; ignoring them on personalized pages leaks data Device class, country The content differs Too many variants

The Vary response header tells caches which request headers the response depends on, for example Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language. Caches then store one variant per value of those headers. Vary: Cookie or Vary: Authorization effectively makes a response uncacheable for shared caches in practice.

docs.title: Purging and invalidation
docs.text:
When content changes, you can:

Method How Notes Wait for expiry Short s-maxage Simple; staleness bounded by the TTL Purge by URL CDN API call for specific URLs Must know every affected URL and variant Purge by tag (surrogate key) Responses carry tags; purge all with a tag Ideal for "product 42 changed" across many pages; support varies by CDN and plan Purge everything Clear the whole cache Causes an origin load spike (an avalanche) Change the URL Versioned filenames No purge needed; best for assets

Purges propagate to edge locations quickly but not instantly, and they cannot reach browser caches. Anything a browser has cached with a long max-age stays there until it expires.

docs.title: Versioned assets and immutable
docs.text:
Build tools put a content hash in asset filenames. The file at a given URL never changes, so it can be cached for a year; a new deploy produces new URLs.

index.html                 Cache-Control: no-cache          (always revalidate)
  <script src="/assets/app.3f9a1c2b.js">
/assets/app.3f9a1c2b.js    Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
/assets/logo.8d21e0aa.svg  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

The HTML is revalidated on every visit so users pick up new asset URLs right after a deploy, while the large assets are served from cache.

docs.title: Caching API responses at the edge
docs.text:
Public, non-personalized API responses can also be cached at the edge:

GET /api/v1/products?category=books&page=1
Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, max-age=0, stale-while-revalidate=300
  • s-maxage=60: the CDN serves it for 60 seconds.
  • max-age=0: browsers revalidate each time, so the CDN controls freshness and purges take effect for users.
  • stale-while-revalidate=300: the CDN can answer instantly with a stale copy while refreshing.

Only GET and HEAD responses are normally cached. Never cache responses that depend on who the user is.

docs.title: The danger of caching private data
docs.text:
Shared caches that store personalized responses cause serious data leaks: user A's account page, cached at the edge, is served to user B.

Rules:

  • Responses for signed-in users: Cache-Control: private, no-store (or at least private) unless you have deliberately designed per-user caching.
  • Never let shared caches store responses carrying Set-Cookie.
  • Do not rely on the CDN "probably" not caching something; set explicit headers on every response.
  • Beware web cache deception: a request such as /account/profile.css that the app answers with the profile page, but the CDN caches because the path "looks static". Cache by explicit rules and content type, not file extension alone, and make the app return 404 for unexpected paths.
  • Beware cache poisoning: unkeyed inputs (for example an X-Forwarded-Host header used to build links) that change the response can let an attacker store a malicious version for everyone.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• CDN caching: use for static assets, public pages, and public, non-personalized API responses with many repeat readers. Do not use it for anything that depends on who the user is.
  • Browser caching: use long max-age only for versioned (hashed) URLs. Keep it short or no-cache for HTML and API responses you might need to change quickly.
  • no-store: use for sensitive data (account pages, tokens, financial or health records). Do not use it for public content; it throws away all caching benefits.
  • Purging: prefer versioned URLs for assets and tags for content shown on many pages. Avoid "purge everything" except in emergencies.
Response Cache-Control Where it is cached How changes reach users Hashed static asset public, max-age=31536000, immutable Browser and CDN New URL on deploy HTML entry page no-cache Stored, revalidated each time Revalidation (304/200) Public API list public, s-maxage=60, max-age=0, stale-while-revalidate=300 CDN Expiry or tag purge Signed-in user data private, no-store Nowhere Always fresh from the origin

docs.title: Setting cache headers in Express
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();

// Hashed build assets: cache for a year, never revalidate
app.use("/assets", express.static("dist/assets", {
  immutable: true,
  maxAge: "365d",
}));

// Public catalog API: CDN caches 60 s, browsers revalidate
app.get("/api/v1/products", async (req, res) => {
  const products = await listProducts(req.query);
  res.set("Cache-Control", "public, s-maxage=60, max-age=0, stale-while-revalidate=300");
  res.json(products); // Express adds a weak ETag and answers 304 when it matches
});

// Personalized data: never stored by shared caches
app.get("/api/v1/me", authenticate, async (req, res) => {
  res.set("Cache-Control", "private, no-store");
  res.json(await getProfile(req.user.id));
});

docs.title: Checking what a CDN did
docs.text:
curl -sI https://www.example.com/api/v1/products?page=1
# HTTP/2 200
# cache-control: public, s-maxage=60, max-age=0, stale-while-revalidate=300
# etag: W/"2f1-..."
# age: 37              <- seconds the response has been in a shared cache

The Age header shows the response came from a cache. Most CDNs also add a vendor-specific header reporting HIT or MISS.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Send an explicit Cache-Control header on every response.
  • Use hashed filenames with immutable for static assets, and no-cache for HTML entry points.
  • Use s-maxage for CDN freshness and keep browser max-age short for content you may need to purge.
  • Keep cache keys minimal but complete: drop tracking parameters, keep parameters that change the response.
  • Mark personalized responses private or no-store.
  • Prefer tag-based purging for content that appears on many URLs.
  • Use stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error to improve latency and resilience.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A fix is deployed, but users still see the bug. Detect: responses for the HTML or API carry a large Age and a long max-age, and a purge did not help for returning visitors. Cause: long browser caching of content that changes. Fix: no-cache for HTML, short max-age with s-maxage for APIs, and versioned asset URLs.
  • User A sees user B's account page. Detect: CDN logs show cache hits on personalized URLs; the response lacks private or no-store. Cause: a shared cache stored a personalized response, or web cache deception. Fix: mark personalized responses private, no-store, return 404 for unexpected paths, purge, and enable the CDN's deception protection.
  • The CDN hit ratio is low. Detect: CDN analytics show many distinct cache keys for the same page, differing only by utm_* or other tracking parameters. Cause: tracking parameters in the cache key. Fix: exclude them in the cache key policy and keep only parameters that change the response.
  • The origin is overloaded right after a purge. Detect: origin requests per second jump immediately after a "purge everything". Cause: every edge location misses at once. Fix: purge by URL or tag, and use an origin shield or tiered cache.
  • Conditional requests never return 304 in tests. Detect: a Node.js fetch() with If-None-Match always gets 200, while curl gets 304. Cause: fetch() adds Cache-Control: no-cache and Pragma: no-cache to such requests, and Express then treats the request as not fresh. Fix: test revalidation with curl or the http module, not as a sign that ETags are broken.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Private cache: A cache for one user, such as the browser cache.
  • Shared cache: A cache serving many users, such as a CDN or proxy.
  • Fresh / stale: Whether a cached response is within its allowed age.
  • Revalidation: Asking the origin whether a stale copy is still valid (If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since).
  • ETag: An identifier for a specific version of a representation.
  • Cache key: The request properties a cache uses to identify stored responses.
  • Purge: Explicitly removing content from a CDN.
  • Origin shield: A mid-tier cache between edge locations and the origin.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Setting a long max-age on HTML or API responses and being unable to roll out fixes.
  • Thinking a CDN purge also clears browsers; it does not.
  • Caching personalized responses at the edge.
  • Using no-cache when you mean no-store; no-cache still allows storage.
  • Including tracking query parameters in the cache key and getting a low hit ratio.
  • Adding Vary: User-Agent, which creates thousands of variants.
  • Purging everything after every deploy instead of versioning assets.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a private and a shared cache, and which directives target each?
  2. Walk through a revalidation with ETag and If-None-Match.
  3. Why do hashed asset filenames allow a one-year max-age?
  4. What should and should not be part of a CDN cache key?
  5. When would you use tag-based purging instead of URL purging?
  6. How can a CDN accidentally leak private data, and how do you prevent it?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: HTTP caching
  • MDN: Cache-Control
  • RFC 9111: HTTP Caching
  • RFC 9213: Targeted HTTP Cache Control
  • Amazon CloudFront: Optimizing caching and availability
  • Related: CDN, HTTP headers, invalidation and expiration.

docs.title: Caching Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review cache fundamentals, strategies, invalidation, eviction, failure modes, and HTTP/CDN caching. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is a cache, and why does caching improve performance?
docs.text: A cache is a fast, temporary store holding copies of data from a slower source. It improves performance because reading from memory or a nearby cache is much faster than repeating a database query, computation, or long network call, and because programs tend to reuse recently or frequently accessed data (locality).

docs.title: 2. What are a cache hit, a cache miss, and the hit ratio?
docs.text: A hit means the requested key was found in the cache; a miss means it was not and the data had to be loaded from the source. The hit ratio is hits / (hits + misses). It is the main measure of how much work a cache saves.

docs.title: 3. How do you calculate the effective latency of a cached lookup?
docs.text: hit ratio × hit time + (1 − hit ratio) × miss time, where the miss time includes checking the cache and loading from the source. With a 1 ms cache, a 50 ms source, and a 90% hit ratio, the average is about 6 ms; at 99% it is about 1.5 ms.

docs.title: 4. Where can caches exist in a typical web system?
docs.text: In the browser, at CDN edge servers, in a reverse proxy, inside each application process, in a distributed cache such as Redis, and inside the database's own memory (buffer cache). Each layer closer to the user saves more work but is harder to control.

docs.title: 5. When would you use an in-process cache instead of Redis?
docs.text: For small, rarely changing, very frequently read data where network round trips matter, such as configuration or lookup tables. Its downsides are that each instance has its own copy (they can disagree), memory is multiplied by the number of instances, and invalidation must reach every instance.

docs.title: 6. What data should you avoid caching?
docs.text: Data with low reuse (highly personalized responses), sensitive data unless strictly scoped and short-lived, data whose staleness causes harm (balances, stock used to accept orders), and data that is already cheap to fetch. Caching these adds risk or complexity without benefit.

docs.title: 7. What makes a good cache key?
docs.text: It uniquely identifies the value and includes every input that changes it: entity, id, query parameters, user or tenant, locale, and a version. Keys follow a consistent naming scheme (type:id:qualifier), and long inputs can be hashed. A key that omits the user can leak one user's data to another.

docs.title: 8. Why should cache entries have a TTL even if you invalidate on write?
docs.text: A TTL bounds how long a wrong value can survive when an invalidation is missed, fails, or loses a race. It also removes entries that are no longer used, freeing memory.

docs.title: 9. Explain the cache-aside pattern.
docs.text: The application checks the cache; on a miss, it loads from the database, stores the value with a TTL, and returns it. On writes, it updates the database and deletes the cached entry. It caches only requested data and survives cache outages, which makes it the common default.

docs.title: 10. How does read-through differ from cache-aside?
docs.text: In read-through, the cache layer itself loads missing data through a configured loader, so callers only talk to the cache. In cache-aside, the application code performs the load and the store. The data flow is similar; the difference is where the logic lives.

docs.title: 11. What is write-through caching, and what are its drawbacks?
docs.text: Each write updates both the cache and the database synchronously, so reads right after a write are fresh. Drawbacks are slower writes, caching data that may never be read, and divergence if one of the two writes fails.

docs.title: 12. What is write-behind (write-back) caching, and when is it appropriate?
docs.text: Writes go to the cache and are acknowledged immediately; they reach the database later, often batched. It gives very fast writes but risks losing acknowledged data if the cache fails before flushing. It suits loss-tolerant data such as view counters or analytics.

docs.title: 13. What is write-around?
docs.text: Writes go only to the database, and the cache is filled by later reads. It avoids filling the cache with data that is written but rarely read, at the cost of a miss on the first read after a write.

docs.title: 14. What is refresh-ahead?
docs.text: Hot entries are reloaded in the background shortly before they expire, so readers rarely see a miss. It lowers latency for popular keys but wastes work if refreshed entries are not read again.

docs.title: 15. On a write, should you update the cached value or delete it? Why?
docs.text: Usually delete it. If two writers update the cache, their cache writes can arrive in the wrong order and leave an older value cached. Deleting means the next read loads whatever the database committed last.

docs.title: 16. Should you write the database or the cache first?
docs.text: Write the database first, then delete the cache entry. Deleting first lets a concurrent reader repopulate the cache with the old value before the database write commits.

docs.title: 17. Why is cache invalidation considered hard?
docs.text: The cache and database cannot be updated in one transaction, many instances read and write concurrently, one record can feed many cached entries, and local caches exist on every instance. Any missed or mistimed invalidation leaves stale data.

docs.title: 18. What is the difference between absolute and sliding expiration?
docs.text: Absolute expiration removes an entry a fixed time after it was written, bounding staleness. Sliding expiration resets the timer on each access, keeping popular entries but possibly never refreshing them. Sliding expiration suits sessions; absolute expiration suits data copies.

docs.title: 19. Describe a race that leaves stale data even with write-then-delete.
docs.text: A reader misses and reads the old value from the database; then a writer updates the database and deletes the key; then the reader stores its old value in the cache. The cache now holds stale data until the TTL expires.

docs.title: 20. What is delayed double delete?
docs.text: Delete the cache entry, write the database, wait slightly longer than a typical read-and-populate, then delete again. The second delete removes stale values written by racing readers. It reduces the race window but does not eliminate it, so TTLs are still needed.

docs.title: 21. What is namespace bumping?
docs.text: Keys include a version number read from a counter, such as catalog:17:product:1. Incrementing the counter makes every key with the old version unreachable, invalidating a whole group with one command. The orphaned keys expire through their TTLs.

docs.title: 22. What is event-driven invalidation?
docs.text: A separate process watches the database's change log (MongoDB change streams or CDC tools such as Debezium) and deletes affected cache keys after each committed change. It catches writes from every service and avoids invalidation logic scattered through the code.

docs.title: 23. What is tag-based invalidation?
docs.text: Cache entries are associated with tags, such as product:42, stored as sets of keys. When the product changes, all keys in its tag set are deleted together. CDNs offer the same idea as surrogate keys or cache tags.

docs.title: 24. What does stale-while-revalidate mean?
docs.text: A stale value may be served immediately while one background request fetches a fresh one. Users get fast responses and the cache converges to fresh data. HTTP supports it as a Cache-Control directive.

docs.title: 25. How do you decide how stale data may be?
docs.text: Ask what harm a stale value causes and for how long that harm is acceptable. Descriptions can be minutes old; prices shown in a catalog can be seconds old but must be checked at checkout; permissions and balances need near-zero staleness or no caching.

docs.title: 26. What is the difference between eviction and expiration?
docs.text: Expiration removes an entry because its TTL passed, even if memory is free. Eviction removes an entry early because the cache is full, chosen by the eviction policy. Frequent eviction suggests the cache is too small.

docs.title: 27. How does LRU work, and how is it implemented in O(1)?
docs.text: LRU evicts the entry unused for the longest time. It combines a hash map for O(1) lookup with a doubly linked list ordered by recency; each access moves a node to the head, and eviction removes the tail.

docs.title: 28. When is LFU better than LRU?
docs.text: When popularity is stable over time. A one-time scan of many keys can flush an LRU cache, while LFU keeps frequently used keys. LFU needs count decay so formerly popular keys do not stay forever.

docs.title: 29. How does Redis implement LRU and LFU?
docs.text: Approximately. Redis samples a few keys (maxmemory-samples) and evicts the best candidate from a small pool, rather than keeping an exact list. Its LFU uses a small logarithmic counter per key that decays over time.

docs.title: 30. What does Redis's noeviction policy do?
docs.text: It never evicts. When memory reaches maxmemory, commands that need more memory return errors, while reads keep working. It is the default in open-source Redis (managed services can differ: Amazon ElastiCache defaults to volatile-lru) and suits Redis instances holding data that must not be silently dropped.

docs.title: 31. Which maxmemory-policy would you choose for a pure cache?
docs.text: allkeys-lru for recency-driven access, or allkeys-lfu when a stable set of keys is popular. Both consider every key for eviction.

docs.title: 32. What is the risk of a volatile-* policy?
docs.text: Only keys with a TTL can be evicted. If cache keys lack TTLs, Redis has nothing to evict and writes fail like noeviction. Conversely, these policies let you protect non-expiring keys in a mixed-use instance.

docs.title: 33. How do you size a cache?
docs.text: Estimate the working set (distinct keys used per TTL window times average entry size plus overhead), add headroom for buffers and persistence, then tune from the hit ratio, eviction count, and memory metrics. Hit ratio gains usually flatten after a point.

docs.title: 34. What is a cache stampede?
docs.text: When a popular key expires, many concurrent requests miss at once and all run the same expensive load, overwhelming the database. It is also called a thundering herd.

docs.title: 35. How do you prevent cache stampedes?
docs.text: Coalesce concurrent misses within a process (single-flight), use a distributed lock so one instance refreshes, serve stale data while revalidating, refresh hot keys ahead of expiry, or use probabilistic early expiration.

docs.title: 36. What is single-flight (request coalescing)?
docs.text: Concurrent requests for the same missing key share one in-flight load instead of each starting their own. In Node.js this is done by storing the pending promise in a map keyed by the cache key and removing it when it settles.

docs.title: 37. What is cache penetration, and how do you defend against it?
docs.text: Requests for data that does not exist always miss the cache and reach the database, which attackers can exploit with random ids. Defenses are caching "not found" results briefly, using a Bloom filter of existing ids, validating ids, and rate limiting.

docs.title: 38. Why is a Bloom filter useful here?
docs.text: It is a compact probabilistic set. If it says an id is absent, the id is definitely absent, so the database lookup is skipped. It may occasionally report a missing id as present (false positive), which only costs one database lookup.

docs.title: 39. What is a cache avalanche, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: Many keys expire or disappear at the same time (identical TTLs, a cache restart), flooding the database with misses for different keys. Prevent it with TTL jitter, warming the cache before traffic, gradual traffic shifts, and limits on database load.

docs.title: 40. How do you handle a hot key in a distributed cache?
docs.text: Add a small in-process cache with a short TTL in front of it, replicate the key under several names spread across nodes and read a random copy, or use replicas for the node holding it. Detect hot keys with metrics or Redis tools.

docs.title: 41. Why are big keys a problem in Redis?
docs.text: Redis executes commands one at a time, so reading, writing, or deleting a huge value blocks other clients and increases latency, and it uses network bandwidth and uneven memory. Split large values, store only what is needed, and delete big keys with UNLINK.

docs.title: 42. What should happen when the cache is down?
docs.text: Requests should continue by treating cache errors as misses, with short timeouts on cache calls. Database fallbacks must be limited (bulkheads, load shedding, circuit breakers), because the database is usually not sized to take all the traffic the cache was absorbing.

docs.title: 43. What is a cold cache, and how do you warm it?
docs.text: A new or flushed cache with no entries, so nearly every request misses. Warm it by preloading the most-read keys, shifting traffic gradually, or replaying recent read traffic before it goes live.

docs.title: 44. What is the difference between no-cache and no-store?
docs.text: no-cache allows storing the response but requires revalidation with the origin before each use. no-store forbids storing it at all. Sensitive responses need no-store.

docs.title: 45. What is the difference between max-age and s-maxage?
docs.text: max-age sets freshness for all caches, including browsers. s-maxage overrides it for shared caches such as CDNs and proxies, so you can let a CDN cache longer than browsers.

docs.title: 46. How does revalidation with ETags work?
docs.text: The origin sends an ETag identifying the version. When the cached copy is stale, the cache sends If-None-Match with that ETag; if the content has not changed, the origin replies 304 Not Modified without a body and the cache reuses its copy.

docs.title: 47. Why can hashed asset files be cached for a year?
docs.text: The hash is derived from the file's content, so a given URL always has the same content. A new deploy produces new filenames referenced from HTML that is revalidated on each visit, so users get updates without purging.

docs.title: 48. What is a CDN cache key, and what can go wrong with it?
docs.text: It is the set of request properties the CDN uses to identify a stored response, usually host, path, and query string, plus any configured headers or cookies. Including too much (tracking parameters, user agents) lowers the hit ratio; including too little can serve the wrong or another user's content.

docs.title: 49. How can HTTP caching leak private data?
docs.text: If a shared cache stores a personalized response, other users receive it. Prevent this with Cache-Control: private or no-store on user-specific responses, never caching responses that set cookies, and guarding against web cache deception and cache poisoning.

docs.title: 50. Does a CDN purge remove content from users' browsers?
docs.text: No. A purge clears CDN edge caches only. Responses already stored in browsers stay until their max-age expires, which is why browser max-age should be short for content you might need to change.

docs.title: 51. Right after a deploy, database CPU jumps from 30% to 95% and API latency doubles, but traffic is unchanged. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the cache hit ratio and Redis keyspace_misses before and after the deploy.

How to confirm: compare cache key names written before and after the deploy, and check whether database queries per second rose at the deploy time.

Likely causes and fixes: a changed key format or version segment (every key is new, so the cache is cold), or a code path that skips the cache. Warm the hot keys, roll out gradually, and change key formats deliberately. See cache fundamentals.

docs.title: 52. After editing their profile, users still see their old name for a few minutes. What is going on?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the write path deletes the profile's cache key, and in what order relative to the database write.

How to confirm: after an update, read the key's value and TTL in Redis and compare it with the database row.

Likely causes and fixes: no invalidation (only the TTL expires it), the cache deleted before the database write, or the read/write race. Write the database first, then delete the key; add versioned writes or a delayed second delete if the race persists. See invalidation and expiration.

docs.title: 53. Every five minutes the database shows a burst of identical queries for the homepage feed. How do you stop it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the TTL of the feed key and the timing of the bursts.

How to confirm: the slow-query log shows the same query many times in the same second, matching the key's expiry.

Likely causes and fixes: a cache stampede on a hot key. Add single-flight per process, a short lock or stale-while-revalidate across instances, probabilistic early refresh, and TTL jitter. See cache failure modes.

docs.title: 54. Redis memory is at maxmemory and SET commands fail with out-of-memory errors. Why isn't Redis evicting?
docs.text:
What to check first: CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy and how many keys have a TTL (INFO keyspace shows expires).

How to confirm: evicted_keys stays at 0 while used_memory sits at the limit.

Likely causes and fixes: the policy is noeviction, or a volatile-* policy with keys that have no TTL. Use allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for a pure cache, or set TTLs on every cache key. See eviction policies.

docs.title: 55. Users are logged out at random during traffic peaks. Sessions live in the same Redis as the cache. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: evicted_keys and the eviction policy during the peaks.

How to confirm: session keys disappear before their TTL, at the same times evictions rise.

Likely causes and fixes: an allkeys-* policy lets cache pressure evict sessions. Move sessions to a separate instance with noeviction, or use a volatile-* policy with TTLs only on cache keys. See eviction policies.

docs.title: 56. During a flash sale, one Redis Cluster node is at 100% CPU while the others sit at 10%. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: which keys that node serves and their request rates.

How to confirm: redis-cli --hotkeys (with an LFU policy) or per-key client metrics show one key dominating.

Likely causes and fixes: a hot key such as the sale product. Put a short-TTL in-process cache in front of it, or store several copies under keys that hash to different nodes and read a random copy. See cache failure modes.

docs.title: 57. Database load is rising and logs show thousands of lookups for product IDs that do not exist. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: the distribution of requested IDs and which clients send them.

How to confirm: the hit ratio for these lookups is zero and most return 404.

Likely causes and fixes: cache penetration, possibly an attack or scraping. Validate IDs, cache "not found" results briefly, rate-limit the clients, and use a Bloom filter for very large ID spaces. See cache failure modes.

docs.title: 58. Redis was down for two minutes and the whole site went down with it, although the database was healthy. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the application handles cache errors and the database load during the outage.

How to confirm: request latency matched the cache client timeout, and database connections hit their limit.

Likely causes and fixes: long cache timeouts and unlimited database fallbacks; the database was sized only for misses. Use short timeouts, treat errors as misses, cap concurrent fallbacks, add a circuit breaker, and run the cache with replicas. See cache failure modes.

docs.title: 59. A CSS fix was deployed an hour ago, but some users still see the old styling. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Cache-Control header on the CSS file and whether its URL changed with the deploy.

How to confirm: the old file is served with a long max-age from the browser cache or CDN (look at the Age header).

Likely causes and fixes: an unversioned file with long caching. Use content-hashed filenames with immutable, and serve HTML with no-cache so it picks up new asset URLs. See HTTP and CDN caching.

docs.title: 60. A customer reports seeing another customer's order history on the account page. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the response's Cache-Control header, CDN cache status for that URL, and the application cache key for the order list.

How to confirm: CDN logs show a cache hit for a personalized URL, or the cache key lacks the user ID.

Likely causes and fixes: a shared cache storing a personalized response, web cache deception, or a key missing the user. Mark personalized responses private, no-store, include the user in keys, purge the affected entries, and treat it as a security incident. See HTTP and CDN caching.

docs.title: 61. The CDN hit ratio is only 20% for a product page that should be highly cacheable. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the cache key configuration and the variety of query strings and headers on requests.

How to confirm: CDN logs show many distinct cache keys for the same page, differing by utm_* parameters or a header such as User-Agent.

Likely causes and fixes: tracking parameters or high-variety headers in the key, Vary: User-Agent, or a cache policy that prevents shared storage. Do not assume Set-Cookie alone makes a response uncacheable; inspect origin and CDN rules. Remove high-variety inputs from the key only when they do not change the response. See HTTP and CDN caching.

docs.title: 62. A price change shows on the product page, but category listings still show the old price. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: which cache entries include the price and which ones the write path invalidates.

How to confirm: the product key was deleted but list and search keys still hold the old value.

Likely causes and fixes: derived entries were not invalidated. Tag list and search entries with the product IDs they contain and delete by tag, or bump the namespace for listings. See invalidation and expiration.

docs.title: 63. After moving to a managed Redis service, keys without TTLs start disappearing (or writes start failing). Nothing changed in the code. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: maxmemory-policy in the new environment compared with the old one.

How to confirm: CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy returns a different value, for example volatile-lru, which is Amazon ElastiCache's default.

Likely causes and fixes: a different default eviction policy. Set the policy explicitly in every environment and give cache keys TTLs. See eviction policies.

docs.title: 64. After the nightly reporting job, the cache hit ratio drops from 95% to 60% and recovers slowly. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the job reads through the same cache and which eviction policy is used.

How to confirm: evicted_keys rises during the job and hot keys are missing the next morning.

Likely causes and fixes: the job's one-off reads pushed out hot keys under LRU. Switch to allkeys-lfu, let the job bypass the cache, or give it a separate cache. See eviction policies.
