docs.title: Cache Invalidation and Expiration
docs.text: Cache invalidation is the work of removing or replacing cached data once it no longer matches the source of truth. Expiration is the automatic version: an entry is discarded after a time limit. Together they decide how stale cached data can be, and they are the hardest part of caching to get right.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A cache that is never invalidated eventually serves wrong data: an old price, a deleted product, a revoked permission. A cache that is invalidated too aggressively has a poor hit ratio and stops helping. Concurrency makes it worse: a write and a read happening at the same moment can leave an old value in the cache even when the code "deletes the key on every update". Understanding these failure modes lets you choose how much staleness each kind of data can tolerate and design accordingly.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Facebook: leases against stale sets. The Scaling Memcache at Facebook paper introduces leases to solve "stale sets" (a client writing an out-of-date value back into the cache because concurrent updates were reordered). On a miss, memcached gives the client a 64-bit token bound to the key; the client must present it when setting the value, and a delete for that key invalidates the token, so the late write is rejected.
  • Facebook: invalidation from the commit log. The same paper describes invalidation daemons (mcsqueal) on every database that inspect the SQL statements the database commits, extract deletes, and broadcast them to memcache. That is event-driven invalidation driven by committed changes rather than by every code path.
  • Cloudflare cache tags. Cloudflare lets an origin add tags in a Cache-Tag response header and then purge every cached file with a given tag at once.
  • Fastly surrogate keys. Fastly's Surrogate-Key header "tags" content so that one key purge removes all related objects, the CDN version of tag-based invalidation.

Popular tools: MongoDB change streams, Debezium for change data capture from relational databases, and CDN tag or surrogate-key purging.

docs.title: Why invalidation is hard
docs.text:
• The cache and the database are separate systems with no shared transaction, so they can be updated in different orders or one update can fail.
  • Many app instances read and write at the same time.
  • One database row can feed many cache entries (a product appears in its own entry, in category lists, and in search results).
  • Local in-process caches exist on every instance, each needing its own invalidation.

docs.title: Time-based expiration (TTL)
docs.text:
Absolute TTL expires an entry a fixed time after it was written, regardless of use. It bounds staleness: data is never older than the TTL.

SET product:42 {...} EX 300      # expires 300 s after being set

Sliding TTL resets the timer every time the entry is read. Frequently used entries stay cached, but a constantly read entry may never expire and can become very stale. Sliding expiration suits sessions ("log out after 30 minutes of inactivity") better than data copies.

// Sliding expiration in Redis: read and reset the TTL in one round trip
const session = await redis.getex(`session:${id}`, "EX", 1800);

Choose TTLs per data type from how stale it may be, not one global value.

docs.title: Explicit invalidation on write
docs.text:
When the application changes data, it removes the cached copy so the next read loads fresh data.

Delete rather than update. Two writers updating the cache can finish in the wrong order:

Writer A: DB price=10 ............. cache SET price=10
Writer B:      DB price=12 ── cache SET price=12
Final: DB=12, cache=10  (A's cache write arrived last)

Deleting the key avoids this: whichever delete runs last, the next read loads the committed value from the database.

Order: write the database, then delete the cache. Deleting first opens a window in which a reader repopulates the cache with the old value before the database write commits:

Delete-then-write (wrong order):
Writer: DEL key
Reader:            miss -> read DB (old) -> SET key old
Writer:                                     UPDATE DB new
Result: cache holds old value until TTL

docs.title: The remaining race with write-then-delete
docs.text:
Even the correct order has a narrow race when a read miss overlaps a write:

It needs the reader's database read to start before the write and its cache write to land after the delete. It is rare but real at high traffic. Mitigations:

Mitigation Idea Short TTL Limits how long a stale value can survive Delayed double delete Delete, write the DB, wait a little (longer than a typical read), delete again Versioned values Store a version or updatedAt; never overwrite a newer cached version with an older one Leases The cache gives a token to the first reader after a miss; a delete invalidates the token so the late SET is rejected (used by large memcached deployments) Event-driven invalidation Delete after the database confirms the commit, via change events

docs.title: Delayed double delete
docs.text:
export async function updatePrice(productId, price) {
  await redis.del(`product:${productId}`);            // 1. first delete
  await db.products.update(productId, { price });     // 2. write the DB
  setTimeout(() => {                                  // 3. delete again later
    redis.del(`product:${productId}`).catch(() => {});
  }, 500);
}

The second delete removes any stale value a concurrent reader wrote during the window. The delay must be longer than a typical read-and-populate. It reduces, but does not fully eliminate, the race, and the timer is lost if the process crashes, which is why a TTL is still needed.

docs.title: Versioned keys and namespace bumping
docs.text:
Instead of deleting entries, change the key so old entries are simply never read again and expire on their own.

Per-entity version:
  user:42:profile:v{version}     version comes from the user row (updatedAt or a counter)

Namespace bumping (invalidate a whole group at once):
  catalog:ns            -> 17           (a counter in Redis)
  catalog:17:product:1
  catalog:17:category:books
  INCR catalog:ns       -> 18           (all catalog:17:* entries are now orphaned)

Namespace bumping invalidates thousands of keys with one command, without scanning. Orphaned entries waste memory until their TTL expires, so they must have one. A schema version in the key (:v2) also lets a deploy that changes the cached data format start with fresh keys.

docs.title: Event-driven invalidation
docs.text:
Instead of every code path remembering to delete keys, a separate process watches the database's change log and invalidates after each committed change.

  • MongoDB change streams deliver insert, update, and delete events; see change streams.
  • Change data capture (CDC) tools such as Debezium read the PostgreSQL write-ahead log or the MySQL binary log and publish changes to a message broker.

Benefits: invalidation happens only after commit, catches writes from every service and script, and keeps business code simpler. Costs: more moving parts and a small delay between commit and invalidation.

docs.title: Tag-based invalidation
docs.text:
One change often affects many cached entries. Tags group keys so they can be invalidated together.

Cache entries                         Tag sets (Redis SETs)
page:/books/42        ─┐              tag:product:42 = { page:/books/42,
list:category:books    ├── tagged       list:category:books, search:abc }
search:abc            ─┘

When product 42 changes, delete every key in tag:product:42, then the tag set itself. CDNs offer the same idea as surrogate keys or cache tags (see HTTP and CDN caching).

docs.title: Stale-while-revalidate
docs.text:
Serve the stale value immediately and refresh it in the background. Users get fast responses; the next reader gets fresh data.

fresh period  ┃ stale-but-usable period ┃ expired
0 ─────── 60 s ┃ 60 s ──────────── 300 s ┃ (must reload before answering)
   serve       ┃ serve stale + trigger   ┃
               ┃ one background refresh  ┃

HTTP supports it with Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=240. Applications implement it by storing a "fresh until" time inside the value and a longer TTL on the key.

docs.title: Choosing acceptable staleness
docs.text:
Data Acceptable staleness Approach Static assets with hashed filenames Forever (content never changes at that URL) Long TTL, immutable Blog post, product description Minutes TTL + delete on write Product list, search results Seconds to minutes Short TTL, namespace bumping Prices shown in a catalog Seconds; recheck at checkout Short TTL; checkout reads the DB Permissions, revoked sessions Near zero Event-driven invalidation or no caching Account balance, stock used to accept orders None Read the source of truth

Ask: "What harm does a stale value cause, and for how long is that acceptable?" Then pick the TTL and invalidation method that fits.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• TTL only: use when a known amount of staleness is fine and writes are frequent or come from systems you do not control. Avoid it when users must see their own changes immediately.
  • Delete on write: use when your own code performs the writes. Avoid relying on it alone when other services or scripts also write.
  • Versioned keys or namespace bumping: use to invalidate whole groups or to change the cached format on deploy. Avoid it without TTLs; orphaned keys then live forever.
  • Event-driven invalidation: use when many writers touch the same data or invalidation must follow commits. Avoid it for small systems where the extra moving parts cost more than occasional staleness.
  • Tags: use when one change affects many cached entries. Avoid huge tag sets that are themselves expensive to read and delete.
Approach Staleness Complexity Catches writes from other services Best for TTL only Up to the TTL Lowest Yes (eventually) Catalogs, public lists Delete on write Small race window Low No Entities your app owns Namespace bump Until the bump Low No Whole groups, deploys Event-driven (CDC) Commit + small lag High Yes Shared data, many writers Tags Small race window Medium Only if tagged writes run it Derived entries, CDN pages

docs.title: Never overwrite a newer cached version
docs.text:
// Store a version with the value; refuse to write an older one.
// Lua runs atomically inside Redis.
const SET_IF_NEWER = `
local current = redis.call("GET", KEYS[1])
if current then
  local decoded = cjson.decode(current)
  if decoded.version >= tonumber(ARGV[2]) then return 0 end
end
redis.call("SET", KEYS[1], ARGV[1], "EX", ARGV[3])
return 1
`;

export async function cacheProduct(product) {
  // product.version increments on every database update
  await redis.eval(SET_IF_NEWER, 1, `product:${product.id}`,
    JSON.stringify(product), product.version, 300);
}

docs.title: Event-driven invalidation with MongoDB change streams
docs.text:
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";
import Redis from "ioredis";

const mongo = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI);
const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL);
await mongo.connect();

const products = mongo.db("shop").collection("products");

// Change streams require a replica set or sharded cluster
for await (const change of products.watch([], { fullDocument: "updateLookup" })) {
  const id = change.documentKey._id.toString();
  const tagKey = `tag:product:${id}`;
  const keys = await redis.smembers(tagKey);  // every entry that used this product
  await redis.del(`product:${id}`, tagKey, ...keys);
}

A production invalidator also stores the stream's resume token so it can continue after a restart without missing changes.

docs.title: Tagging entries when caching them
docs.text:
export async function cacheWithTags(key, value, ttlSeconds, tags) {
  const tx = redis.multi();
  tx.set(key, JSON.stringify(value), "EX", ttlSeconds);
  for (const tag of tags) {
    tx.sadd(`tag:${tag}`, key);
    tx.expire(`tag:${tag}`, ttlSeconds * 2); // tag sets must not live forever
  }
  await tx.exec();
}

await cacheWithTags("list:category:books", books, 120, ["product:42", "product:43"]);

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Give every cache entry a TTL as a safety net.
  • Write the database first, then delete the cache entry.
  • Delete cached entries rather than overwriting them on writes.
  • Use namespace versions for groups of keys and schema versions for format changes.
  • Prefer event-driven invalidation when many services or scripts write the same data.
  • Set staleness budgets per data type and write them down.
  • Read the source of truth for decisions that must be correct (payments, stock, authorization).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• "I saved it, but I still see the old value." Detect: sampling shows cached values that differ from the database for recently updated rows, mostly under high traffic. Cause: the read/write race, or a delete that ran before the commit. Fix: write then delete, shorten the TTL, and add versioned writes or a delayed second delete.
  • A deleted product still shows in category pages. Detect: the product's own key is gone, but list and search entries still contain it. Cause: derived entries were not invalidated. Fix: tag derived entries with the record's ID, or bump the list's namespace.
  • Redis stalls while invalidating. Detect: latency spikes for all clients, and SLOWLOG GET shows KEYS commands. Cause: pattern-based deletion with KEYS on a large keyspace. Fix: use tags or namespaces, or iterate with SCAN.
  • Access still works after it was revoked. Detect: audit logs show requests allowed after a role change. Cause: permissions cached with a long TTL. Fix: invalidate on permission change through events, and keep authorization caches very short-lived.
  • Invalidations missed after the invalidator restarts. Detect: stale entries cluster around the invalidator's restart time. Cause: the change-stream consumer resumed from "now" instead of its last position. Fix: persist the resume token after each processed event and resume from it.
  • Memory keeps rising after namespace bumps. Detect: used_memory grows and many keys belong to old namespace versions. Cause: versioned keys without TTLs. Fix: always set TTLs on versioned keys.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Invalidation: Removing or replacing cached data that may be stale.
  • Absolute TTL: Expiry a fixed time after the entry was written.
  • Sliding TTL: Expiry that resets on each access.
  • Delayed double delete: Deleting a key before and shortly after a database write to remove values written by racing readers.
  • Namespace bumping: Changing a version number embedded in keys to orphan a whole group of entries.
  • Change data capture (CDC): Reading a database's change log to publish data changes as events.
  • Stale-while-revalidate: Serving a stale value while refreshing it in the background.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Deleting the cache before writing the database.
  • Updating cached values on write and suffering out-of-order overwrites.
  • Forgetting derived entries (lists, search results) when one record changes.
  • Using sliding TTLs for data copies, so hot entries never refresh.
  • Using KEYS pattern* to find entries to delete; it blocks Redis on large datasets. Use tags, namespaces, or SCAN.
  • Believing "delete on write" alone guarantees consistency.
  • Caching authorization decisions for a long time, so revoked access keeps working.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is "write the database, then delete the cache" better than the reverse order?
  2. Describe the race that can still leave a stale value after write-then-delete, and two ways to reduce it.
  3. When would you use a sliding TTL instead of an absolute one?
  4. How does namespace bumping invalidate many keys at once?
  5. What are the advantages of event-driven invalidation over invalidating in application code?
  6. How would you decide the staleness budget for product prices?

docs.title: Apache Kafka
docs.text: Apache Kafka is a distributed event-streaming platform built around a durable, append-only log. Producers append records to topics; consumers read them in order and keep track of their own position. Unlike a classic queue, Kafka does not delete a record when it is read: records stay for a configured retention period, so many independent consumers can read, and re-read, the same stream.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• High throughput: Kafka handles very large volumes of events by writing sequentially to disk, batching, and spreading partitions across brokers.
  • Many readers, one stream: analytics, search indexing, fraud detection, and notifications can all consume the same orders topic at their own pace without affecting each other.
  • Replay: a new service can start from the beginning of retained history; a buggy consumer can rewind and reprocess after a fix.
  • Ordering per key: all events for one customer or order can be processed in sequence.
  • It is the backbone for event-driven architectures, change data capture, and stream processing in many companies.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• LinkedIn. In a 2015 post, LinkedIn described Kafka as the circulatory system of its data: over 800 billion messages per day (more than 175 TB written and over 650 TB consumed daily), split into separate clusters for queuing, metrics, logs, and tracking data. Many consumers reading the same data is why Kafka's multi-consumer design mattered (LinkedIn Engineering).
  • Netflix Keystone. Netflix's Keystone platform combines a Kafka-based messaging service with routing and stream processing to collect, process, and move microservice events in near real time, at a scale of trillions of events per day (Netflix TechBlog).
  • Cloudflare. Cloudflare has used Kafka since 2014 to decouple microservices, announcing the creation, change, or deletion of resources in a common data format; it reported 14 clusters with roughly 330 nodes and over a trillion messages processed (Cloudflare blog).
  • Wikimedia. Wikimedia runs several Kafka clusters: "main" clusters for critical, lower-volume production services such as its event platform and change propagation, and a "jumbo" cluster carrying high-volume web-request and analytics data into Hadoop (Wikitech).
  • Shopify. Shopify rebuilt its change data capture on Kafka Connect and Debezium, turning database changes into an append-only stream of events in Kafka that feeds services such as merchant analytics (Shopify Engineering).

Popular tools and providers: Apache Kafka (self-managed), Confluent Cloud and Confluent Platform, Amazon MSK, Aiven for Apache Kafka, Kafka-compatible platforms such as Redpanda and Azure Event Hubs (Kafka endpoint), and ecosystem tools such as Kafka Connect, Debezium, Kafka Streams, and Apache Flink.

docs.title: The log model
docs.text:
A Kafka topic is a named stream of records. Each topic is split into partitions, and each partition is an ordered, immutable, append-only log. Every record in a partition gets a sequential offset.

Topic "orders" with 3 partitions

Partition 0: | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |      <- new records appended here
Partition 1: | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
Partition 2: | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
                         ^
             consumer group "email" has read partition 2 up to offset 2
  • Records are never modified; they are appended and later deleted by retention.
  • Offsets are per partition. "Offset 3" means nothing without a partition.
  • A record has a key, a value (bytes, often JSON, Avro, or Protobuf), headers, and a timestamp.

docs.title: Brokers and clusters
docs.text:
A broker is a Kafka server. A cluster is several brokers. Partitions are spread across brokers so that storage and load are shared, and a topic can be larger than any single machine.

Since Kafka 4.0, clusters run in KRaft mode: a quorum of controller nodes using a Raft-based protocol manages cluster metadata (topics, partitions, leaders). Earlier versions relied on a separate Apache ZooKeeper ensemble; ZooKeeper support was removed in 4.0.

docs.title: Replication: leaders, followers, and in-sync replicas
docs.text:
Each partition is copied to several brokers, set by the replication factor (3 is common in production).

  • One replica is the leader; producers write to it and it serves reads.
  • Followers fetch from the leader to stay up to date.
  • The in-sync replica set (ISR) is the leader plus the followers that are fully caught up.
  • If the leader's broker fails, a new leader is elected from the ISR.
  • min.insync.replicas sets how many replicas must have a write before it counts as committed when producers use acks=all. With replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, the cluster tolerates one broker failure without losing acknowledged data and keeps accepting writes.
  • Unclean leader election (choosing an out-of-sync replica as leader) can lose data; it is disabled by default.

docs.title: Producers
docs.text:
Choosing a partition:

  • A record with a key is assigned by hashing the key, so all records with the same key go to the same partition and stay in order.
  • A record without a key is spread across partitions (modern clients batch records to one partition at a time before moving on, for efficiency).
  • Adding partitions to a topic later changes the key-to-partition mapping for new records, so per-key ordering is broken across that change. Choose a partition count with growth in mind.

Durability with acks:

acks The producer considers a write successful when... Risk 0 It sent the record (no response awaited) Loss on any failure 1 The leader wrote it Loss if the leader dies before followers copy it all (-1) All in-sync replicas have it (at least min.insync.replicas) Highest durability; slightly higher latency

Idempotent producer: the producer gets an ID and numbers each record per partition. If a retry re-sends a record the broker already stored, the broker discards the duplicate. This removes duplicates caused by producer retries. Since Kafka 3.0, the Java producer enables idempotence and acks=all by default; check the defaults of the client you use.

Batching and compression: producers group records into batches (linger.ms, batch.size) and can compress them (gzip, snappy, lz4, zstd), trading a few milliseconds of latency for much higher throughput.

docs.title: Consumer groups
docs.text:
Consumers read by pulling records from brokers. Consumers that share a group.id form a consumer group and split the topic's partitions between them: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group at a time.

  • Within a group, partitions are the unit of parallelism. A group with more consumers than partitions leaves the extra consumers idle.
  • Different groups are independent: each gets every record and keeps its own offsets. That is how Kafka does publish/subscribe.

docs.title: Rebalancing
docs.text:
When a consumer joins, leaves, or is considered dead, the group rebalances: partitions are reassigned.

A consumer is considered dead when it stops sending heartbeats (session timeout) or does not call poll again within max.poll.interval.ms, which happens when processing one batch takes too long.

Rebalances pause consumption for the affected partitions, so frequent ones hurt. Mitigations:

  • Keep per-batch processing time well below max.poll.interval.ms.
  • Use cooperative (incremental) rebalancing, which moves only the partitions that must move instead of stopping everyone.
  • Use static membership (group.instance.id) so a quick restart of the same consumer does not trigger a rebalance.
  • Newer Kafka versions add a broker-driven consumer group protocol (KIP-848) designed to make rebalances faster and less disruptive.

docs.title: Offset commits
docs.text:
A consumer group records its progress by committing offsets to an internal topic (__consumer_offsets). The committed offset is the next offset to read. After a restart or rebalance, consumption resumes from it.

Strategy Effect Commit before processing At-most-once: a crash after the commit skips records Commit after processing At-least-once: a crash before the commit reprocesses records Auto-commit on a timer (enable.auto.commit) Convenient, but a crash can lose or duplicate work depending on timing Commit offsets inside a Kafka transaction Exactly-once for read-process-write within Kafka

auto.offset.reset decides where a group with no committed offset starts: earliest (beginning of retained data) or latest (only new records).

Consumer lag is the difference between the newest offset in a partition and the group's committed offset: how far behind the group is. It is the key health metric for Kafka consumers.

docs.title: Retention and log compaction
docs.text:
Kafka keeps records according to the topic's cleanup policy:

  • Delete (time or size retention): records older than retention.ms (the broker default is 7 days) or beyond retention.bytes are deleted, one log segment at a time, whether or not anyone has read them.
  • Compact: Kafka keeps at least the latest record for each key and removes older ones in the background. A record with a null value (a tombstone) marks the key for deletion. Compacted topics act as a durable "latest state per key" table: user profiles, configuration, changelogs for stream processing.
  • Both policies can be combined.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
• Order is guaranteed only within a partition.
  • To keep all events for an order in sequence, use the order ID (or customer ID) as the record key.
  • Idempotent producers preserve order even with several in-flight requests and retries.
  • Processing records from one partition concurrently (for example with a thread pool) gives up that order unless you serialize per key.

docs.title: Transactions and exactly-once semantics
docs.text:
A transactional producer (configured with a transactional.id) can write to several partitions and commit consumer offsets atomically: either all of it becomes visible or none of it does. Consumers set isolation.level=read_committed to see only committed data.

This gives exactly-once semantics for read-process-write pipelines that stay inside Kafka, such as a Kafka Streams application turning orders into order-totals. The moment a consumer writes to an external database or calls an API, you are back to at-least-once and need an idempotent consumer.

docs.title: The ecosystem
docs.text:
• Kafka Connect: a framework for moving data in and out of Kafka with reusable connectors (databases, object storage, search engines). Change data capture tools such as Debezium run on it.
  • Kafka Streams: a Java library for stateful stream processing (joins, aggregations, windowing) on top of Kafka.
  • Schema registries store Avro, Protobuf, or JSON Schema definitions so producers and consumers agree on record formats as they evolve.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use Kafka when:

  • Many services need to consume the same event streams independently (event-driven architecture).
  • You need retention and replay: new consumers reading history, or reprocessing after a bug fix.
  • Volumes are very high: activity tracking, clickstreams, metrics, logs.
  • You do change data capture from databases into search indexes, caches, and data warehouses.
  • You do stream processing and real-time analytics, or event sourcing where the log is the system of record.
  • You need strict ordering per key at scale.

Avoid it (or reconsider) when:

  • You need a simple task queue with per-message retries, delays, and priorities: RabbitMQ or SQS are simpler.
  • The system is small and cannot justify operating a cluster (managed services reduce, but do not remove, the cost).
  • You need request-reply interactions.
  • Messages are large (megabytes); store payloads elsewhere and send references.
Requirement Kafka RabbitMQ SQS Google Pub/Sub Replay history Yes, within retention Streams only No Seek within retention (with retained messages) Many independent consumers Consumer groups One queue per consumer SNS fan-out to queues One subscription per consumer Per-key ordering at scale Partitions Limited FIFO message groups Ordering keys Per-message retry, delay, priority Application-level Built in Visibility timeout, delay queues Retry policy, dead-letter topics Operational effort High (lower if managed) Medium None None

docs.title: Command-line basics
docs.text:
# Create a topic with 6 partitions, each replicated to 3 brokers
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --create --topic orders --partitions 6 --replication-factor 3

# Read everything retained in the topic
kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic orders --from-beginning

# Show each partition's committed offset and lag for a group
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --describe --group email-service

(Use a replication factor of 1 on a single-broker local setup.)

docs.title: Producer and consumer in Node.js with KafkaJS
docs.text:
These examples use KafkaJS (kafkajs), a pure-JavaScript client with a simple, well-documented API. KafkaJS has had no release since 2.2.4 in February 2023; for new production systems also evaluate Confluent's @confluentinc/kafka-javascript, which offers a KafkaJS-style API on top of the librdkafka C library.

// producer.js
import { Kafka } from "kafkajs";

const kafka = new Kafka({ clientId: "orders-api", brokers: ["localhost:9092"] });
const producer = kafka.producer();
await producer.connect();

export async function publishOrderPlaced(order) {
  await producer.send({
    topic: "orders",
    acks: -1, // wait for all in-sync replicas
    messages: [
      {
        key: order.id, // same order -> same partition -> ordered
        value: JSON.stringify({ type: "OrderPlaced", orderId: order.id, total: order.total }),
        headers: { "event-type": "OrderPlaced" },
      },
    ],
  });
}

// email-consumer.js
import { Kafka } from "kafkajs";

const kafka = new Kafka({ clientId: "email-service", brokers: ["localhost:9092"] });
const consumer = kafka.consumer({ groupId: "email-service" });

await consumer.connect();
await consumer.subscribe({ topics: ["orders"], fromBeginning: false });

await consumer.run({
  // Called once per record, in order within each partition
  eachMessage: async ({ partition, message }) => {
    const event = JSON.parse(message.value.toString("utf8"));
    if (event.type === "OrderPlaced") {
      await sendConfirmationEmail(event.orderId); // must be idempotent
    }
    // If this function throws, KafkaJS retries the record instead of moving on.
    // With the default auto-commit, the offset is committed only after records
    // are processed, so a crash leads to reprocessing (at-least-once).
  },
});

process.on("SIGTERM", async () => {
  await consumer.disconnect(); // leaves the group cleanly, triggering a rebalance
  process.exit(0);
});

async function sendConfirmationEmail(orderId) {
  console.log("email for", orderId);
}

A record that always throws will block its partition. Production consumers catch permanent failures and publish the record to a dead-letter topic (for example orders.email.dlt) so the partition can move on. See messaging patterns.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2, and acks=all for data you cannot lose.
  • Enable idempotent producers.
  • Key records by the entity whose order matters.
  • Choose partition counts for future parallelism; adding partitions later remaps keys.
  • Commit offsets after processing and make consumers idempotent.
  • Keep processing per poll short to avoid rebalances; use cooperative rebalancing and static membership.
  • Handle poison records with retry and dead-letter topics.
  • Monitor consumer lag, under-replicated partitions, and broker disk usage.
  • Manage schemas and evolve them compatibly.
  • Set retention deliberately; Kafka is not infinite storage unless you plan for it (tiered storage, compaction).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Consumer lag keeps growing. Detect: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe (or a lag exporter) shows lag rising on all partitions. Cause: consumers process more slowly than producers write, often because of a slow downstream database, or there are fewer consumers than needed. Fix: speed up processing (batch writes), add consumers up to the partition count, and plan more partitions for future parallelism.
  • Constant rebalancing. Detect: consumer logs repeatedly show partitions being revoked and reassigned; commits fail because the group has rebalanced; lag saw-tooths. Cause: processing one poll's batch takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, or frequent restarts. Fix: smaller batches or faster handlers, cooperative rebalancing, and static membership for rolling restarts.
  • Producers fail with "not enough replicas". Detect: producer errors such as NotEnoughReplicas; the under-replicated partitions metric is above zero. Cause: a broker is down or too slow to stay in the ISR, so fewer than min.insync.replicas copies are available. Fix: restore or replace the broker, check disk and network, and keep enough brokers for the replication factor.
  • Broker disks fill up. Detect: disk usage alerts on brokers; log segments accumulating. Cause: traffic grew, retention is longer than needed, or compaction is falling behind. Fix: set retention per topic, enable tiered storage where available, and add brokers before disks are full.
  • One partition is much hotter than the others. Detect: bytes-in and lag for one partition far exceed the rest. Cause: a skewed key, such as one very large tenant as the key. Fix: choose a key with better distribution, or split a hot key (for example key plus a bucket number) where strict ordering for that key is not required.
  • Data lost after a broker failure. Detect: gaps downstream after a leader change. Cause: acks=1, replication factor 1, or unclean leader election. Fix: replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all, and unclean leader election disabled.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Topic: a named stream of records.
  • Partition: an ordered, append-only log; the unit of parallelism and ordering.
  • Offset: a record's position within a partition.
  • Broker / cluster: a Kafka server / a group of them.
  • Replication factor: how many copies of each partition exist.
  • Leader / follower: the replica that handles writes / replicas that copy it.
  • ISR (in-sync replicas): replicas fully caught up with the leader.
  • Consumer group: consumers sharing a group ID that divide partitions between them.
  • Rebalance: reassigning partitions within a group.
  • Committed offset: the next offset a group will read.
  • Consumer lag: how far a group is behind the newest records.
  • Log compaction: keeping only the latest record per key.
  • Tombstone: a record with a null value that deletes a key in a compacted topic.
  • KRaft: Kafka's built-in Raft-based metadata management, replacing ZooKeeper.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Kafka is a queue." It is a log; records are not removed when read, and per-message ack, delay, and priority are not built in.
  • "Kafka guarantees global order." Only within a partition.
  • More consumers than partitions expecting more throughput; extra consumers sit idle.
  • Using acks=1 or replication factor 1 in production and losing data when a broker fails.
  • Long processing inside the poll loop, causing repeated rebalances and duplicate processing.
  • Assuming exactly-once covers external side effects.
  • Adding partitions to a keyed topic without considering ordering.
  • Letting one poison record stall a partition indefinitely.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain topics, partitions, and offsets. Why is an offset meaningless without a partition?
  2. How do replication factor, ISR, acks=all, and min.insync.replicas work together to prevent data loss?
  3. A topic has 4 partitions and a consumer group has 6 consumers. What happens, and why?
  4. What triggers a rebalance, and how can you reduce their impact?
  5. Compare delete retention and log compaction. Give a use case for each.
  6. What does Kafka's exactly-once semantics cover, and what does it not?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Apache Kafka: Documentation, especially the design and message delivery semantics sections.
  • Apache Kafka: Quickstart.
  • KafkaJS: Documentation.
  • Related: delivery guarantees, event-driven architecture, and MongoDB change streams.

docs.title: Cloud Queues: SQS and SNS
docs.text: Cloud providers offer fully managed messaging so you never install, patch, or scale a broker. On AWS, Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service) provides queues and Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) provides publish/subscribe topics; together they cover most messaging needs. Google Cloud Pub/Sub and Azure Service Bus offer similar building blocks.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• No servers to operate: capacity, replication, and durability are the provider's job. You pay per request.
  • Elastic scale: standard queues absorb huge bursts without capacity planning on your side.
  • Tight integration with the rest of the platform: serverless functions, IAM permissions, encryption keys, monitoring, and alarms.
  • The trade-off: fewer features than a self-hosted broker (limited routing, size limits, per-request pricing) and lock-in to one provider's API.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• AWS Lambda's asynchronous invocations. Lambda itself is built on queues: for an asynchronous invocation it places the event in a queue, returns success immediately, and a separate process reads the queue and runs the function. Invocation records can be sent on to a downstream service such as SQS or EventBridge (AWS Lambda documentation).
  • Shuffle-sharded queues inside Lambda. The AWS Builders' Library explains that polling a separate queue per Lambda customer would be too costly, while a single shared queue would let one customer's backlog affect everyone. Lambda instead provisions a fixed number of queues, hashes each customer to a few of them, and enqueues into the shortest one, so a busy customer's backlog stays mostly in its own queues (Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs).
  • Amazon S3 event notifications. S3 can publish events such as "object created" to SNS topics, SQS queues, Lambda functions, and EventBridge, a common way to start processing when files are uploaded (Amazon S3 documentation).
  • Spotify on Google Cloud Pub/Sub. When Spotify redesigned its event delivery system in 2016, it chose Cloud Pub/Sub as the transport for all events after struggling to make its Kafka 0.8 setup reliable at its event volumes (Spotify Engineering).

Popular tools and providers: Amazon SQS, SNS, EventBridge, and Kinesis Data Streams; Google Cloud Pub/Sub; Azure Service Bus, Azure Queue Storage, and Azure Event Grid; Kafka-compatible managed services (Amazon MSK, Confluent Cloud) when you need a log rather than a queue.

docs.title: Amazon SQS basics
docs.text:
A producer sends a message to a queue; consumers poll for messages, process them, and delete them. There is no push and no ack call: deleting the message is the acknowledgement.

Producer --SendMessage--> [ SQS queue ] <--ReceiveMessage-- Consumer
                                        <--DeleteMessage--- (after processing)

Every receive returns a receipt handle, a token for that specific delivery. You delete (or change visibility) with the receipt handle, not the message ID, and a new receive of the same message produces a new handle.

docs.title: Standard vs FIFO queues
docs.text:
Standard queue FIFO queue Delivery At least once; occasional duplicates Duplicates removed within a 5-minute deduplication interval Ordering Best effort; can arrive out of order Strict order within each message group Throughput Nearly unlimited Limited per queue (higher with batching and high-throughput mode) Name Any valid name Must end in .fifo Per-message delay Supported Not supported (queue-level delay only) Use when Order does not matter and consumers are idempotent Order per entity matters, or duplicate sends must be suppressed

FIFO concepts:

  • MessageGroupId: messages with the same group ID are delivered in order, one batch at a time; different groups are processed in parallel. Use an entity ID (an order or account) as the group, never a single constant, or you lose all parallelism.
  • MessageDeduplicationId: if a message with the same deduplication ID was sent within the last five minutes, the new one is accepted but not delivered again. Alternatively enable content-based deduplication, which uses a SHA-256 hash of the body.

Deduplication protects against duplicate sends (for example a producer retry). A consumer that crashes before deleting a message can still process it twice, so keep consumers idempotent.

docs.title: Visibility timeout
docs.text:
When a consumer receives a message, SQS hides it from other consumers for the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours). If the consumer deletes the message in time, it is gone. If not, the message becomes visible again and is redelivered.

  • Set the queue's timeout above your normal worst-case processing time.
  • For longer jobs, call ChangeMessageVisibility periodically to extend it.
  • Setting the visibility to 0 makes a message available immediately (a fast "nack").

See delivery guarantees for why this causes duplicates.

docs.title: Short polling vs long polling
docs.text:
• Short polling queries a subset of SQS's servers and returns at once, possibly empty even when messages exist. Many empty responses cost money.
  • Long polling (WaitTimeSeconds up to 20) waits until at least one message arrives or the wait time ends. It reduces empty responses, cost, and latency. Use it, either per request or as the queue default (ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds).

A single receive returns at most 10 messages (MaxNumberOfMessages). Sends and deletes can also be batched up to 10 per call, which cuts request costs.

docs.title: Dead-letter queues and the redrive policy
docs.text:
A queue's redrive policy names a dead-letter queue and a maxReceiveCount. Each receive increments the message's receive count; when it exceeds the maximum without being deleted, SQS moves the message to the DLQ.

{
  "deadLetterTargetArn": "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:123456789012:orders-dlq",
  "maxReceiveCount": "5"
}
  • The DLQ must be the same type as the source (FIFO with FIFO) and in the same account and region.
  • Set the DLQ's retention period longer than the source queue's. For standard queues, a message's expiry is based on its original enqueue time, so a short DLQ retention can delete it soon after it arrives.
  • After fixing the cause, redrive messages from the DLQ back to the source queue (from the console or with the StartMessageMoveTask API).
  • Alarm on the DLQ's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible being above zero.

docs.title: Retention, delays, and size
docs.text:
• Retention period: default 4 days, configurable from 60 seconds to 14 days. Unprocessed messages older than this are deleted.
  • Delay queues: DelaySeconds (up to 15 minutes) postpones delivery of new messages. Standard queues also accept a per-message delay (message timers).
  • Message size: the maximum is 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes), raised from 256 KiB in August 2025, so older articles quote 256 KiB. For larger payloads, store the data in S3 and send a reference (the claim-check pattern). The Amazon SQS Extended Client Libraries for Java and Python do this automatically, for payloads up to 2 GB. See messaging patterns.
  • Message attributes: typed key-value metadata (up to 10 per message), readable without parsing the body.

docs.title: Integration with AWS Lambda
docs.text: A Lambda function can be configured with an SQS event source mapping: Lambda polls the queue for you, invokes your function with a batch of messages, and deletes them when the function succeeds. If the function fails, the whole batch becomes visible again unless you enable partial batch responses and return only the IDs of the failed messages.

docs.title: Amazon SNS: topics and fan-out
docs.text:
SNS is push-based publish/subscribe. A publisher sends a message to a topic, and SNS delivers a copy to every subscription: SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP/HTTPS endpoints, email, SMS, mobile push, and Amazon Data Firehose.

The most common pattern is SNS to SQS fan-out:

Each queue buffers messages for its own consumers, so a slow analytics service never slows email. Adding a new consumer means adding a queue and a subscription; the publisher does not change.

Key features:

  • Subscription filter policies let a subscription receive only matching messages, based on message attributes or the message body:

    { "eventType": ["OrderPlaced", "OrderCancelled"], "total": [{ "numeric": [">=", 1000] }] }

  • Raw message delivery: by default SNS wraps the message in a JSON envelope with SNS metadata; enable raw delivery on SQS and HTTP subscriptions to receive the original body.

  • Retries and DLQs: SNS retries failed deliveries according to a policy that depends on the endpoint type, and a subscription can have its own dead-letter queue.
  • FIFO topics deliver to SQS FIFO queues with ordering and deduplication.
  • Permissions: an SQS queue must have a policy allowing the topic to send to it.

SNS does not store messages for later reading. If you need buffering and retries for a consumer, put an SQS queue between SNS and that consumer.

docs.title: Amazon EventBridge, briefly
docs.text:
EventBridge is an event bus. Producers put events on a bus; rules match events by content (event patterns on any field) and route them to targets such as Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, or external HTTP APIs. It also receives events from AWS services and SaaS partners, keeps an optional archive for replay, and includes a scheduler.

SNS EventBridge Model Topics and subscriptions Event buses and rules Filtering Filter policies per subscription Rich content-based patterns per rule Event sources Your publishers Your apps, AWS services, SaaS partners Strength Simple, high-throughput fan-out Routing many event types across many teams and services

docs.title: Google Cloud Pub/Sub, briefly
docs.text:
• Topics receive messages; subscriptions deliver them to consumers. Each subscription gets every message (publish/subscribe), and consumers on the same subscription share the work (competing consumers).
  • Delivery modes: pull, push to an HTTPS endpoint, and subscriptions that write straight to BigQuery or Cloud Storage.
  • Consumers acknowledge within the ack deadline (10 seconds by default, extendable); unacknowledged messages are redelivered.
  • Ordering keys give per-key ordering; dead-letter topics catch messages after a maximum number of delivery attempts; an optional exactly-once delivery mode exists for pull subscriptions.

docs.title: Azure Service Bus, briefly
docs.text:
• Queues for point-to-point and topics with subscriptions (with filter rules) for publish/subscribe, inside a namespace.
  • Peek-lock mode: a received message is locked while you process it, then you complete, abandon, or dead-letter it. Receive-and-delete mode is at-most-once.
  • A built-in dead-letter subqueue per queue and subscription, used after the maximum delivery count (10 by default) or by explicit dead-lettering.
  • Sessions give ordered, per-session processing; duplicate detection drops repeated message IDs within a time window; scheduled messages deliver at a future time; transactions span several operations.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Amazon SQS Amazon SNS Amazon EventBridge Google Pub/Sub Azure Service Bus Model Queue Pub/sub topic Event bus + rules Topic + subscriptions Queues, topics + subscriptions Delivery Pull Push Push to targets Pull or push Pull (peek-lock) Stores messages for consumers Yes (up to 14 days) No (retries only) Optional archive Yes Yes Ordering FIFO queues, per group FIFO topics No ordering guarantee Ordering keys Sessions Built-in DLQ Redrive policy Per subscription Per target Dead-letter topics Dead-letter subqueue Typical role Work queues, buffering Fan-out Cross-service event routing General messaging on GCP Enterprise messaging on Azure

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use managed cloud queues when:

  • You run on that cloud and want no broker to operate.
  • Traffic is bursty and you want capacity to follow it automatically.
  • You need simple, reliable work queues (SQS) or fan-out (SNS to SQS).
  • You want event routing across many services and AWS events (EventBridge).
  • Consumers are serverless functions that the platform polls for you.

Avoid them (or reconsider) when:

  • You need replay of past messages or long retention for many readers: use Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, or MSK.
  • You need rich broker routing, priorities, or protocols such as MQTT and AMQP: RabbitMQ or Amazon MQ.
  • You must stay portable across clouds or run on-premises.
  • Messages are large: use object storage with the claim-check pattern.
  • Throughput is enormous and per-request pricing would cost more than running your own cluster.
Need Amazon SQS Amazon SNS Amazon EventBridge Self-hosted RabbitMQ / Kafka Buffer work for a pool of workers Best No (no storage) No Yes Fan-out one event to many consumers With SNS Best Yes Yes Content-based routing across many teams and AWS services No Basic filter policies Best RabbitMQ topic/headers exchanges Replay No No Archive and replay Kafka Operations None None None You run it Portability AWS only AWS only AWS only Any environment

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text: These use the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3. The client reads the region and credentials from the environment or the instance role; never hard-code keys.

docs.title: Send messages (standard and FIFO)
docs.text:
import { SQSClient, SendMessageCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs";

const sqs = new SQSClient({});

// Standard queue
await sqs.send(new SendMessageCommand({
  QueueUrl: process.env.ORDERS_QUEUE_URL,
  MessageBody: JSON.stringify({ type: "OrderPlaced", orderId: "ord_901" }),
  MessageAttributes: {
    eventType: { DataType: "String", StringValue: "OrderPlaced" },
  },
}));

// FIFO queue: ordered per order, duplicates of the same event suppressed
await sqs.send(new SendMessageCommand({
  QueueUrl: process.env.ORDER_UPDATES_FIFO_URL, // name ends in .fifo
  MessageBody: JSON.stringify({ type: "OrderShipped", orderId: "ord_901" }),
  MessageGroupId: "ord_901",
  MessageDeduplicationId: "evt_5f2a", // the event's unique ID
}));

docs.title: A long-polling worker
docs.text:
import { SQSClient, ReceiveMessageCommand, DeleteMessageCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs";

const sqs = new SQSClient({});
const QueueUrl = process.env.ORDERS_QUEUE_URL;
let running = true;
process.on("SIGTERM", () => { running = false; }); // finish the current batch, then stop

while (running) {
  const { Messages = [] } = await sqs.send(new ReceiveMessageCommand({
    QueueUrl,
    MaxNumberOfMessages: 10, // up to 10 per call
    WaitTimeSeconds: 20, // long polling
  }));

  for (const message of Messages) {
    try {
      const event = JSON.parse(message.Body);
      await handleEvent(event); // must be idempotent
      await sqs.send(new DeleteMessageCommand({ QueueUrl, ReceiptHandle: message.ReceiptHandle }));
    } catch (err) {
      // Not deleted: it reappears after the visibility timeout and, after
      // maxReceiveCount attempts, moves to the dead-letter queue
      console.error("processing failed", { messageId: message.MessageId, err });
    }
  }
}

async function handleEvent(event) {
  console.log("handling", event.type);
}

docs.title: Publish to an SNS topic for fan-out
docs.text:
import { SNSClient, PublishCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sns";

const sns = new SNSClient({});

await sns.send(new PublishCommand({
  TopicArn: process.env.ORDER_EVENTS_TOPIC_ARN,
  Message: JSON.stringify({ type: "OrderPlaced", orderId: "ord_901", total: 4999 }),
  // Subscriptions can filter on these attributes
  MessageAttributes: {
    eventType: { DataType: "String", StringValue: "OrderPlaced" },
  },
}));

Each subscribed SQS queue receives its own copy; workers read it with the long-polling loop above.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use long polling and batch sends and deletes.
  • Delete only after successful processing, and make consumers idempotent.
  • Set the visibility timeout above worst-case processing time; extend it for long jobs.
  • Configure a DLQ with a sensible maxReceiveCount on every queue, with a longer retention than the source, and alarm on its size.
  • Prefer SNS to SQS fan-out over making one service call many others.
  • Choose FIFO only when you need ordering or send-side deduplication, and pick a group ID with enough distinct values for parallelism.
  • Keep messages small; use S3 references for large data.
  • Grant least-privilege IAM permissions per producer and consumer, and enable server-side encryption.
  • Watch ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage as well as queue depth: age tells you whether consumers keep up.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The SQS bill is high but traffic is low. Detect: the CloudWatch metric NumberOfEmptyReceives is very high. Cause: short polling in a tight loop. Fix: long polling (WaitTimeSeconds up to 20, or the queue's ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds), and batch receives and deletes.
  • Messages are processed twice. Detect: logs show the same MessageId handled twice; receive counts above 1 on messages that never failed. Cause: the visibility timeout is shorter than processing time (for Lambda consumers, shorter than the function's timeout). Fix: raise the visibility timeout above the worst-case processing time, extend it for long jobs, and keep consumers idempotent.
  • An SNS subscription receives nothing. Detect: SNS's NumberOfNotificationsFailed metric rises, or the queue stays empty while the topic publishes. Cause: the SQS queue policy does not allow the topic to send, or an encrypted queue's KMS key policy does not allow SNS to use the key. Fix: grant the topic permission in the queue policy and the key policy, then test with a published message.
  • A FIFO queue is slow while workers are idle. Detect: ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage keeps rising but consumers are mostly waiting. Cause: most messages share one MessageGroupId, so they are processed strictly one after another. Fix: use a group ID per entity (order, account) so groups run in parallel.
  • The dead-letter queue keeps growing. Detect: an alarm on the DLQ's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible above zero. Cause: a bug or a malformed message type exhausts maxReceiveCount. Fix: inspect sample messages, fix the consumer, then redrive them to the source queue (console or StartMessageMoveTask).
  • A whole Lambda batch is retried for one bad message. Detect: the same messages reappear repeatedly; successful messages are processed again. Cause: the function throws for one message, so the entire batch returns to the queue. Fix: enable partial batch responses and report only the failed message IDs.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• SQS standard queue: at-least-once, best-effort ordering, very high throughput.
  • SQS FIFO queue: ordered per message group, with deduplication.
  • Message group ID: the key within which FIFO order is guaranteed.
  • Deduplication ID: a token that suppresses duplicate sends within five minutes.
  • Receipt handle: the token identifying one receive of a message, used to delete it.
  • Visibility timeout: how long a received message stays hidden.
  • Long polling: waiting up to 20 seconds for messages to arrive.
  • Redrive policy: the rule that moves messages to a DLQ after maxReceiveCount receives.
  • SNS topic / subscription: a pub/sub channel / an endpoint receiving its messages.
  • Filter policy: a rule limiting which messages a subscription receives.
  • Fan-out: delivering one message to many independent consumers.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Short polling in a tight loop, paying for millions of empty responses.
  • Deleting a message before processing it, losing work on a crash.
  • Visibility timeout shorter than processing time, causing concurrent duplicate processing.
  • Using one constant MessageGroupId for a FIFO queue, which serializes everything.
  • "FIFO means no duplicates ever." Deduplication covers sends within five minutes, not consumer retries.
  • DLQ retention shorter than the source queue's, so failed messages expire before anyone looks.
  • Subscribing an SQS queue to SNS without a queue policy, so deliveries silently fail.
  • Expecting SNS to buffer for slow consumers. Put a queue in between.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. How does a consumer acknowledge a message in SQS, and why does it need the receipt handle?
  2. Compare standard and FIFO queues. What do MessageGroupId and MessageDeduplicationId each do?
  3. Why should you use long polling?
  4. Describe the redrive policy and what happens after maxReceiveCount is exceeded.
  5. Draw the SNS to SQS fan-out pattern and explain why each consumer gets its own queue.
  6. When would you choose EventBridge over SNS?
