docs.text:
• AWS: Amazon SQS Developer Guide, including FIFO queues and dead-letter queues.
  • AWS: Amazon SNS Developer Guide and fan-out to SQS queues.
  • AWS: Amazon EventBridge User Guide.
  • Google Cloud: Pub/Sub documentation.
  • Microsoft: Azure Service Bus messaging documentation.
  • Related: AWS overview.

docs.title: Delivery Guarantees and Ordering
docs.text: Every messaging system promises something about how often a message is delivered (never more than once? at least once?) and in what order. These promises decide whether your system can lose an order, charge a card twice, or apply updates in the wrong sequence. This page explains the guarantees, where they break, and how to build consumers that are correct anyway.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Networks and processes fail between any two steps. A consumer can finish its work and crash before acknowledging; a producer can send a message and lose the broker's confirmation. Each gap produces either a lost message or a duplicate.
  • Most production systems are at-least-once, so duplicates are normal, not exceptional. A consumer that is not idempotent will eventually double-ship, double-email, or double-charge.
  • Ordering is weaker than people assume. Parallel consumers and retries reorder messages even on a "FIFO" queue.
  • One malformed message can block or flood a system unless poison messages are detected and set aside.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe webhooks are at-least-once. Stripe's documentation warns that webhook endpoints might occasionally receive the same event more than once, and tells integrators to log the IDs of processed events and skip ones already seen. It also says not to use the event's created timestamp to decide order, but to track event IDs instead (Stripe webhooks).
  • Stripe idempotency keys. Stripe's API accepts an idempotency key so a client can safely retry after a connection error without creating a second object; for API v1 Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request made with a key and returns them for retries (Stripe API reference).
  • Shopify payments. Shopify's guide to resilient payment systems lists idempotency keys among its top practices: at Shopify's scale, a once-in-a-million failure during payment processing happens many times a day, and a retried payment must not charge a card twice (Shopify Engineering).
  • Slack avoids job loss with durable storage. Slack replaced its purely in-memory Redis job queue path with Kafka as durable storage, to buffer against memory exhaustion and job loss (Slack Engineering).
  • Amazon measures availability with DLQs. The AWS Builders' Library notes that a message which runs out of retries is dropped or put in a dead-letter queue, and that the rate of dropped or dead-lettered messages is a useful availability measurement, though it can detect problems late (Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs).

docs.title: The three delivery semantics
docs.text: Semantics Promise How it is achieved Risk At-most-once Delivered zero or one time Acknowledge (or commit) before processing; no retries Messages can be lost At-least-once Delivered one or more times Acknowledge after processing; redeliver if no ack Duplicates Exactly-once Delivered and processed exactly one time Only within a closed system (for example Kafka transactions), or approximated with deduplication Costly, limited in scope

docs.title: At-most-once
docs.text:
receive -> ACK -> process
                    X crash here: the message is gone forever

Acceptable for data where a loss is harmless and duplicates are worse: high-volume metrics, a live "user is typing" indicator.

docs.title: At-least-once
docs.text:
receive -> process -> ACK
                   X crash here: no ack, so the broker redelivers -> processed twice

The default choice for business data. You accept duplicates and make the consumer idempotent.

docs.title: Exactly-once and "effectively once"
docs.text:
True exactly-once delivery to an arbitrary consumer is not possible in general: the consumer's side effect (a database write, an email, a payment) and the acknowledgement to the broker are two separate actions in two separate systems, and a crash can always land between them.

What systems actually offer:

  • Exactly-once inside one system. Kafka transactions can atomically consume from a topic, produce to other topics, and commit offsets, so a read-process-write pipeline that stays inside Kafka produces each result once. See Apache Kafka.
  • Deduplication windows. SQS FIFO queues drop a message whose deduplication ID was already seen in the last five minutes. That prevents duplicate sends, not duplicate processing after a consumer crash.
  • Effectively once = at-least-once + idempotent processing. The broker may deliver twice, but the consumer recognizes the duplicate and the side effect happens once. This is the practical answer for almost every system.

docs.title: Where messages get lost or duplicated
docs.text:
Producer ---(1)---> Broker ---(2)---> Consumer ---(3)---> Side effect
Stage Loss happens when Duplicate happens when Protection (1) Publish The producer does not wait for the broker's confirmation, and the broker crashes before storing the message The broker stored the message, but the confirmation was lost, so the producer retries Publisher confirms / acks=all; idempotent producers or deduplication IDs Broker storage The message was not persisted, or stored on one node that died (rare) Durable queues, persistent messages, replication (2) Delivery and ack Auto-ack: the broker considers it done on delivery, then the consumer crashes The consumer processed it but the ack was lost or the consumer crashed before acking Manual ack after processing (3) Side effect The consumer acked, then failed to apply the effect Redelivery applies the effect again Ack after the effect; idempotent effect

Also note the dual-write problem on the producer side: saving to your database and publishing to the broker are two writes that can disagree. The transactional outbox pattern fixes it.

docs.title: Acknowledgements
docs.text:
• Automatic acknowledgement: the broker marks a message done as soon as it is delivered (RabbitMQ noAck: true) or the client commits positions on a timer (Kafka auto-commit). Simple and fast, but a crash mid-processing can lose work; with periodic commits it can also cause duplicates.
  • Manual acknowledgement: your code acknowledges after the work succeeds:
    • RabbitMQ: ack, or nack/reject to signal failure.
    • Amazon SQS: DeleteMessage with the receipt handle.
    • Kafka: commit the offset after processing.
    • Google Pub/Sub: ack before the acknowledgement deadline.

Always acknowledge after the side effect is durable. If processing fails, either negatively acknowledge (to retry or dead-letter) or simply do not ack and let the broker redeliver.

docs.title: Redelivery
docs.text:
What triggers a second delivery depends on the system:

  • RabbitMQ: unacknowledged messages are requeued when the consumer's channel or connection closes, or when the consumer nacks with requeue: true. Redelivered messages carry a redelivered flag.
  • Amazon SQS: a received message becomes invisible for the visibility timeout. If it is not deleted before the timeout ends, it becomes visible again and another consumer can receive it. The ApproximateReceiveCount attribute counts deliveries.
  • Kafka: there is no per-message redelivery. After a crash or rebalance, the consumer group resumes from the last committed offset, so everything after it is read again.
  • Google Pub/Sub: a message not acknowledged before its ack deadline is redelivered.

docs.title: Visibility timeouts
docs.text:
A visibility timeout (SQS) or acknowledgement deadline (Pub/Sub) is a lease: "this consumer has the message for N seconds".

t=0s    consumer A receives msg-1        msg-1 invisible to everyone else
t=0-30s A processes it
t=25s   A deletes msg-1                  done
---
t=0s    consumer A receives msg-2
t=30s   timeout expires, A still busy    msg-2 visible again
t=31s   consumer B receives msg-2        now processed twice in parallel

Rules:

  • Set the timeout longer than your worst-case processing time (SQS defaults to 30 seconds and allows up to 12 hours).
  • For long jobs, extend the lease while working (SQS ChangeMessageVisibility, Pub/Sub deadline extension), like a heartbeat.
  • Even with a good timeout, design for the parallel-duplicate case above.

docs.title: Ordering guarantees
docs.text:
System Ordering guarantee RabbitMQ queue FIFO into the queue; delivery order is preserved for a single consumer, but multiple consumers, prefetch, and requeues interleave and reorder processing Kafka Strict order within a partition; none across partitions. Messages with the same key go to the same partition SQS standard Best-effort ordering only; messages can arrive out of order SQS FIFO Strict order within a message group ID; groups are processed in parallel Google Pub/Sub Ordered per ordering key when message ordering is enabled Azure Service Bus Ordered per session when sessions are used

The common idea: global order does not scale. Systems give you order within a key (customer, order, account) and parallelism across keys. Pick the key so that messages that must stay in order share it.

What breaks ordering even on an ordered channel:

  • Competing consumers: message 1 goes to a slow worker and message 2 to a fast one, so 2 finishes first.
  • Retries: message 1 fails and is retried after message 2 succeeded.
  • Multiple producers: two services publishing about the same entity have no shared clock.

When order matters, combine a per-entity key with consumer-side checks such as version numbers ("apply only if event.version === current.version + 1"). See messaging patterns.

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text:
Sources of duplicate messages you should expect:

  • Producer retries after a lost confirmation.
  • Consumer crash after processing but before the ack.
  • Visibility timeout or ack deadline expiring during slow processing.
  • Kafka rebalances after offsets were processed but not committed.
  • Upstream systems (webhooks, other services) that themselves deliver at least once.
  • Operators replaying a dead-letter queue.

docs.title: Poison messages and dead-letter queues
docs.text:
A poison message fails every time it is processed: malformed JSON, a reference to a deleted record, a bug triggered by one specific input. With naive requeueing it loops forever, burning CPU and, on ordered channels, blocking everything behind it.

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is where such messages are moved after a limited number of attempts:

System How dead-lettering works RabbitMQ A queue's dead-letter exchange receives messages that are rejected without requeue, expire, overflow the queue, or exceed a quorum queue's delivery limit Amazon SQS A redrive policy moves a message to the DLQ after maxReceiveCount receives Kafka No built-in DLQ; applications publish failures to a retry or dead-letter topic Google Pub/Sub A dead-letter topic after a configured maximum number of delivery attempts Azure Service Bus A built-in dead-letter subqueue after the maximum delivery count

Also distinguish error types: permanent errors (validation failure, unknown message type) should go to the DLQ immediately; transient errors (timeouts, 503) deserve retries with backoff. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

docs.title: The idempotent consumer
docs.text:
An idempotent consumer produces the same result no matter how many times it sees a message. Three techniques, often combined:

  1. Natural idempotency. Write operations that are idempotent by nature: SET status = 'shipped' instead of "toggle", upserts keyed by a business ID, "add item X" as a set insert instead of a counter increment.
  2. Conditional updates. Apply a change only if the current state allows it: UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'pending'. A second delivery matches zero rows.
  3. Deduplication table (inbox). Record each processed message ID with a unique constraint, in the same database transaction as the business change. If the insert conflicts, the message is a duplicate and is skipped.

For external side effects that are not in your database (charging a card, calling a partner API), pass the message ID as the provider's idempotency key.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Choose the guarantee per kind of data:

  • At-most-once fits data where a loss is harmless and freshness matters more than completeness: high-volume metrics samples, presence ("user is typing"), live location pings that are replaced seconds later.
  • At-least-once with idempotent consumers fits almost all business data: orders, payments, emails, account changes. This should be your default.
  • Kafka exactly-once (transactions) fits read-process-write pipelines that stay entirely inside Kafka, such as stream aggregations.
  • Ordered channels (partitions, FIFO message groups, sessions) fit entities whose events must apply in sequence: balance changes, status transitions.

Do not use:

  • Exactly-once features as a substitute for idempotent side effects.
  • FIFO or single-partition ordering when order does not matter; it caps throughput and makes one slow message delay others.
  • Auto-ack or commit-before-processing for business data.
  • Infinite requeue as an error-handling strategy.
Data Semantics Ordering Typical mechanism Page-view metrics At-most-once acceptable None Fire-and-forget, auto-ack Order placed / payment captured At-least-once + idempotent consumer Per order Manual ack, inbox table, idempotency key to payment provider Account balance updates At-least-once + idempotent Strict per account Kafka key or FIFO group = account ID, version checks Stream aggregation inside Kafka Exactly-once Per partition Kafka transactions, read_committed Notifications At-least-once, duplicates tolerable but deduplicated None Dedup by message ID with a short TTL

docs.title: Idempotent consumer with PostgreSQL
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE processed_messages (
  message_id   text PRIMARY KEY,
  processed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

import pg from "pg";

const pool = new pg.Pool(); // connection settings from PG* environment variables

export async function handleDepositMessage(message) {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");

    // 1. Claim the message ID; a duplicate hits the primary key and inserts nothing
    const claim = await client.query(
      "INSERT INTO processed_messages (message_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING",
      [message.id],
    );
    if (claim.rowCount === 0) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");
      return; // already processed: safe to ack again
    }

    // 2. The business change, in the SAME transaction
    await client.query(
      "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2",
      [message.data.amount, message.data.accountId],
    );

    await client.query("COMMIT"); // both succeed or neither does
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw err; // do not ack: the broker will redeliver
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

The caller acknowledges the message only if handleDepositMessage resolves. A redelivery of the same message is now harmless. Clean old rows out of processed_messages after a period longer than any possible redelivery.

docs.title: Extending the lease during long work (SQS)
docs.text:
import { SQSClient, ChangeMessageVisibilityCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs";

const sqs = new SQSClient({});

// Every 20 s, push the visibility timeout out by another 60 s while we work
function keepInvisible(queueUrl, receiptHandle) {
  const timer = setInterval(() => {
    sqs.send(new ChangeMessageVisibilityCommand({
      QueueUrl: queueUrl,
      ReceiptHandle: receiptHandle,
      VisibilityTimeout: 60,
    })).catch((err) => console.error("extend visibility failed", err));
  }, 20_000);
  return () => clearInterval(timer); // call when processing ends
}

docs.title: Version check for ordering
docs.text:
async function applyStockEvent(event) {
  // Only apply if this is the next version; older or duplicate events match no rows
  const result = await db.query(
    "UPDATE stock SET quantity = $1, version = $2 WHERE sku = $3 AND version = $2 - 1",
    [event.data.quantity, event.version, event.data.sku],
  );
  if (result.rowCount === 0) {
    // Duplicate (already applied) or out of order (a gap): decide per business rule,
    // e.g. ignore stale events, or retry later if the expected version is missing
  }
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Default to at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers.
  • Confirm publishes (publisher confirms, acks=all) and use durable, replicated storage for important messages.
  • Acknowledge after the side effect is committed.
  • Store the dedup record and the business change in one transaction.
  • Set visibility timeouts above worst-case processing time and extend them for long jobs.
  • Partition by the entity whose order matters; never rely on global order.
  • Limit retries and configure a DLQ on every queue, with an alert when it is not empty.
  • Separate transient from permanent failures.
  • Use message IDs as idempotency keys for external APIs.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The same job runs twice, at the same time. Detect: two workers log the same message ID seconds apart; SQS ApproximateReceiveCount is 2 or more on messages that never failed. Cause: the visibility timeout (or ack deadline) is shorter than the slowest executions. Fix: raise the timeout above worst-case processing time and extend it with a heartbeat for long jobs; keep the consumer idempotent anyway.
  • Messages disappear during deploys. Detect: counts of processed messages are lower than published ones; work is missing after each release. Cause: auto-ack (or committing offsets before processing), so killed workers lose in-flight messages. Fix: acknowledge after processing and shut down gracefully (stop consuming, finish in-flight work, then exit).
  • One Kafka partition stops moving. Detect: consumer lag grows on a single partition while others stay near zero; logs repeat the same error for the same offset. Cause: a poison record that always throws, retried forever. Fix: after N attempts publish it to a retry or dead-letter topic and continue; alert on dead-letter volume.
  • CPU pegged by a hot retry loop. Detect: RabbitMQ shows a very high redelivery rate; the same message ID appears thousands of times in logs. Cause: nack with requeue: true on every error. Fix: cap attempts in the handler, then reject without requeue to a dead-letter exchange, and use delayed retry queues. Since RabbitMQ 4.3, a quorum queue's delivery limit does not count nack requeues, so it will not stop this loop.
  • Dead-lettered messages vanish before anyone looks. Detect: the DLQ count drops although nobody redrove it. Cause: DLQ retention shorter than needed (for SQS standard queues, expiry counts from the original enqueue time). Fix: give the DLQ a longer retention than the source and alarm as soon as it is not empty.
  • The deduplication table becomes slow. Detect: insert latency on processed_messages grows; the table has hundreds of millions of rows. Cause: IDs are never cleaned up. Fix: delete rows older than the longest possible redelivery window (or partition the table by date and drop old partitions).

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• At-most-once / at-least-once / exactly-once: the number of times a message may be delivered.
  • Effectively once: at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent processing.
  • Acknowledgement (ack) / negative acknowledgement (nack): success / failure signal from consumer to broker.
  • Redelivery: the broker delivering a message again because it was not acknowledged.
  • Visibility timeout / ack deadline: how long a received message stays hidden while a consumer works on it.
  • Offset commit: a Kafka consumer group recording how far it has read.
  • Message group / ordering key / partition key: the key within which order is guaranteed.
  • Poison message: a message that fails every time it is processed.
  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ): where failed messages go after limited attempts.
  • Idempotent consumer: a consumer for which duplicates have no extra effect.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Our broker guarantees exactly-once, so we don't need idempotency." Consumer crashes and producer retries still create duplicates in your side effects.
  • Acking on receipt (auto-ack) for important work, then losing messages on deploys and crashes.
  • Dedup check and business write in separate transactions, leaving a window where a crash marks a message processed but skips the work (or the reverse).
  • Visibility timeout shorter than processing time, so two workers process the same message concurrently.
  • Requeueing failures forever with no attempt limit or DLQ.
  • Assuming FIFO means globally ordered processing with many consumers.
  • Increasing partitions in Kafka without realizing that keys may move to different partitions, breaking per-key order across the change.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Where in the producer-broker-consumer chain can a message be duplicated, and where can it be lost?
  2. Why is exactly-once delivery to an arbitrary external side effect not achievable in general? What do systems offer instead?
  3. How does an SQS visibility timeout lead to duplicate processing, and how do you prevent it for long jobs?
  4. Kafka guarantees order within a partition. How do you make sure all events for one order are processed in order?
  5. What is a poison message, and how should transient and permanent errors be handled differently?
  6. Why must the deduplication record be written in the same transaction as the business change?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RabbitMQ: Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms.
  • Apache Kafka: Message delivery semantics.
  • AWS: Amazon SQS visibility timeout and dead-letter queues.
  • microservices.io: Idempotent Consumer pattern.
  • AWS Builders' Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs.

docs.title: Message Queues Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review messaging fundamentals, delivery guarantees, RabbitMQ, Apache Kafka, managed cloud queues, and the patterns that make asynchronous systems reliable. Each question is tagged Beginner, Intermediate, or Advanced; the final group contains scenario-based questions drawn from real production work.

docs.title: 1. What is a message queue, and why would you use one?
docs.text: A message queue is a buffer, managed by a broker, where producers put messages and consumers take them out to process later. It decouples services in time and space, levels out bursts of load, and lets consumers scale independently. It can retain work during consumer outages when the queue and messages are configured for durable storage, subject to retention limits.

docs.title: 2. What are a producer, a consumer, and a broker?
docs.text: The producer creates and sends messages. The broker (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS) receives, stores, routes, and delivers them. The consumer receives messages, processes them, and acknowledges them so the broker knows they are done.

docs.title: 3. What is the difference between a queue and a topic?
docs.text: In a queue, each message is processed by one consumer, even if several consumers read from it (point-to-point). With a topic, each message is delivered to every subscriber (publish/subscribe). Queues suit tasks and commands; topics suit events that several parts of the system care about.

docs.title: 4. What is the difference between a command and an event?
docs.text: A command asks a specific receiver to do something (SendInvoice) and usually has one consumer. An event records that something happened (OrderPlaced); the producer does not know or care who reacts, and there may be many consumers. Mixing them up couples producers to consumers.

docs.title: 5. What is the difference between push and pull consumers?
docs.text: With push, the broker sends messages to consumers as they arrive (RabbitMQ, SNS), so it needs flow control such as prefetch limits. With pull, consumers ask for messages when ready (Kafka, SQS), which gives natural backpressure; long polling keeps latency low without empty request storms.

docs.title: 6. When should you use asynchronous messaging instead of a synchronous HTTP call?
docs.text: Use messaging when the caller does not need the result to continue: sending emails, updating search indexes, notifying other services, slow or unreliable work. Use synchronous calls when the user needs the answer now, such as validating a coupon or reading data to display.

docs.title: 7. What should a message envelope contain?
docs.text: A unique message ID (for deduplication), a type, a timestamp, a schema version, a correlation ID (to trace a flow across services and logs), and the payload. Optional fields include a causation ID, reply-to address, and routing or partition key.

docs.title: 8. What is the difference between a message broker and an event-streaming platform?
docs.text: A broker such as RabbitMQ or SQS deletes messages once acknowledged and tracks per-message state, with rich routing and per-message retries. A streaming platform such as Kafka keeps an append-only log for a retention period; consumers track their own offsets and can replay history, and many independent groups can read the same data.

docs.title: 9. How does request-reply work over a message queue?
docs.text: The requester sends a message containing a reply-to address and a correlation ID, then waits with a timeout. The responder sends its answer to the reply-to address with the same correlation ID, which the requester uses to match the reply to the pending request.

docs.title: 10. Explain at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once delivery.
docs.text: At-most-once acknowledges before processing, so a crash can lose the message. At-least-once acknowledges after processing, so a crash can cause a duplicate. Exactly-once means each message affects the system exactly once; in practice it is achieved only inside a closed system or approximated with deduplication and idempotency.

docs.title: 11. Why is exactly-once delivery not achievable in general?
docs.text: The consumer's side effect (a database write or API call) and its acknowledgement to the broker are two separate actions in different systems. A crash between them either loses the ack (causing a duplicate) or loses the work (if acked first). No protocol can make two independent systems commit atomically without coordination.

docs.title: 12. What does "effectively once" mean?
docs.text: It means at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent processing. The broker may deliver a message more than once, but the consumer detects or tolerates duplicates so the business effect happens only once.

docs.title: 13. How do you make a consumer idempotent?
docs.text: Use naturally idempotent operations (set values, upserts), conditional updates that only apply in the expected state, or a deduplication (inbox) table keyed by message ID that is written in the same transaction as the business change. For external APIs, pass the message ID as an idempotency key.

docs.title: 14. Why should messages be acknowledged after processing rather than on receipt?
docs.text: Acknowledging on receipt marks the message done before the work happens; if the consumer then crashes, the message is lost. Acknowledging after the side effect is durable means a crash leads to redelivery instead, which idempotent consumers handle safely.

docs.title: 15. What is a visibility timeout, and what goes wrong if it is too short?
docs.text: In SQS, a received message is hidden from other consumers for the visibility timeout. If processing takes longer, the message reappears and a second consumer processes it concurrently. Set the timeout above worst-case processing time and extend it during long jobs.

docs.title: 16. What ordering guarantees do RabbitMQ, Kafka, and SQS provide?
docs.text: RabbitMQ queues are FIFO, but multiple consumers and requeues reorder processing. Kafka guarantees order only within a partition. SQS standard queues offer best-effort ordering; FIFO queues guarantee order within a message group.

docs.title: 17. How do you preserve order for related messages while keeping parallelism?
docs.text: Route related messages by a key (customer or order ID) to the same partition, message group, or session. Each key is processed in order, while different keys are processed in parallel. Version numbers in events let consumers detect gaps or stale events.

docs.title: 18. What is a poison message, and how do you handle it?
docs.text: A poison message fails every time it is processed, for example malformed data or a message that triggers a bug. Without limits it is retried forever or blocks an ordered channel. Cap the number of attempts and move it to a dead-letter queue for inspection.

docs.title: 19. What is a dead-letter queue?
docs.text: A DLQ holds messages that could not be processed after a configured number of attempts, or that were explicitly rejected or expired. It keeps failures from blocking or looping in the main queue and lets engineers inspect, fix, and replay them. A DLQ should always have an alert.

docs.title: 20. Describe RabbitMQ's routing model.
docs.text: Producers publish to an exchange with a routing key. Bindings connect exchanges to queues with rules, and the exchange copies each message into every queue whose binding matches. Consumers read from queues and acknowledge messages.

docs.title: 21. What exchange types does RabbitMQ have?
docs.text: Direct routes by exact routing key match. Topic routes by dot-separated patterns, where * matches one word and # matches zero or more. Fanout sends to all bound queues and ignores the key. Headers routes on message header values instead of the key.

docs.title: 22. What is needed for a RabbitMQ message to survive a broker restart?
docs.text: The queue must be durable and the message must be published as persistent. Quorum queues are always durable. For the producer to know the message was stored, it should also use publisher confirms.

docs.title: 23. What are publisher confirms?
docs.text: A channel mode in which the broker acknowledges each published message once it has taken responsibility for it (persisted and, for quorum queues, replicated), or nacks it if it could not. Without confirms, a producer cannot tell whether a message was lost on the way.

docs.title: 24. What does prefetch (basic.qos) do?
docs.text: It limits how many unacknowledged messages the broker pushes to a consumer. Without it, one consumer can receive thousands of messages, exhausting memory and starving other consumers. Low values give fair dispatch for slow tasks; higher values improve throughput for fast handlers.

docs.title: 25. When is a RabbitMQ message dead-lettered?
docs.text: When it is rejected or nacked without requeue, when its TTL expires, when the queue's length limit is exceeded, or when it exceeds a quorum queue's delivery limit. It then goes to the queue's dead-letter exchange, with an x-death header describing why.

docs.title: 26. What are quorum queues, and why use them?
docs.text: Quorum queues are replicated across nodes using the Raft consensus algorithm, so they keep data safe and available when a minority of nodes fail. They are the recommended queue type for durable, important data and support delivery limits for poison messages. They replaced the older mirrored classic queues.

docs.title: 27. How can you implement delayed retries in RabbitMQ?
docs.text: Send failed messages to a retry queue that has a message TTL and a dead-letter exchange pointing back to the work queue. When the TTL expires, the message is dead-lettered back for another attempt. Several retry queues with growing TTLs give exponential backoff; the delayed message exchange plugin is an alternative.

docs.title: 28. What are topics, partitions, and offsets in Kafka?
docs.text: A topic is a named stream of records. It is split into partitions, each an ordered, append-only log stored on brokers. Each record in a partition has a sequential offset, which consumers use to track their position.

docs.title: 29. How does Kafka decide which partition a record goes to?
docs.text: If the record has a key, the key is hashed, so records with the same key always go to the same partition and stay in order. Records without a key are spread across partitions. Adding partitions later changes the mapping for keys.

docs.title: 30. How do consumer groups work?
docs.text: Consumers with the same group ID share a topic's partitions; each partition is consumed by exactly one member at a time, so the group processes in parallel. Separate groups each receive all records independently, which is how Kafka provides publish/subscribe.

docs.title: 31. What happens if a consumer group has more consumers than partitions?
docs.text: The extra consumers receive no partitions and sit idle. Partitions are the unit of parallelism in a group, so to scale consumers you must have enough partitions.

docs.title: 32. What is a rebalance, and why can it be a problem?
docs.text: A rebalance reassigns partitions when consumers join, leave, crash, or exceed the maximum poll interval. Consumption of affected partitions pauses, and uncommitted work may be reprocessed. Cooperative rebalancing, static membership, and short processing per poll reduce the impact.

docs.title: 33. How do offset commits relate to delivery guarantees?
docs.text: Committing before processing gives at-most-once (a crash skips records); committing after processing gives at-least-once (a crash reprocesses). Committing offsets inside a Kafka transaction together with produced output gives exactly-once for pipelines that stay within Kafka.

docs.title: 34. What do acks, replication factor, and min.insync.replicas control?
docs.text: The replication factor is the number of copies of each partition. acks=all makes the producer wait until all in-sync replicas have the record. min.insync.replicas is the minimum number of replicas that must acknowledge for the write to succeed. Together (for example 3, all, and 2) they prevent data loss when one broker fails.

docs.title: 35. What is an idempotent producer?
docs.text: A producer that tags records with a producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers so the broker can discard duplicates caused by retries. It removes duplicates introduced by the producer's own retries and keeps ordering.

docs.title: 36. What is log compaction?
docs.text: A cleanup policy that keeps at least the latest record for each key and discards older ones. A record with a null value (a tombstone) deletes the key. Compacted topics store the current state per key, such as user settings or changelogs for stream processing.

docs.title: 37. What is consumer lag, and why monitor it?
docs.text: Consumer lag is the difference between the latest offset in a partition and the group's committed offset. Growing lag means consumers are falling behind, so data is processed later and may eventually be deleted by retention before it is read.

docs.title: 38. When would you choose Kafka over RabbitMQ, and the reverse?
docs.text: Choose Kafka for high-throughput event streams, many independent consumers, replay, retention, and stream processing. Choose RabbitMQ for task queues and commands that need flexible routing, per-message acknowledgements, retries, delays, and priorities.

docs.title: 39. What is the difference between SQS standard and FIFO queues?
docs.text: Standard queues offer very high throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering. FIFO queues guarantee order within each message group and suppress duplicate sends with a deduplication ID within a five-minute window, at lower throughput.

docs.title: 40. How do you acknowledge a message in SQS?
docs.text: By deleting it with the receipt handle returned by the receive call. If it is not deleted before the visibility timeout ends, it becomes visible again and is redelivered.

docs.title: 41. Why use long polling with SQS?
docs.text: Short polling returns immediately, often empty, wasting requests and money. Long polling waits up to 20 seconds for messages to arrive, reducing empty responses, cost, and the delay before a consumer sees a new message.

docs.title: 42. How does an SQS dead-letter queue work?
docs.text: A redrive policy on the source queue names the DLQ and a maxReceiveCount. When a message has been received more times than that without being deleted, SQS moves it to the DLQ. After fixing the cause, messages can be redriven back to the source queue.

docs.title: 43. What is the SNS to SQS fan-out pattern?
docs.text: A producer publishes to one SNS topic, and several SQS queues subscribe to it. Each queue receives its own copy and buffers it for its own consumers, so services process independently and a slow consumer cannot affect others. Filter policies let a queue receive only the events it needs.

docs.title: 44. What is the dual-write problem?
docs.text: When a service must update its database and publish a message, the two writes are not atomic. A crash between them leaves either a saved change with no event (lost event) or an event about a change that was never saved (phantom event).

docs.title: 45. How does the transactional outbox pattern work?
docs.text: The service writes the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change. A relay process (polling or change data capture) publishes outbox rows to the broker and marks them sent. The event is published if and only if the change committed, at least once.

docs.title: 46. What is the competing consumers pattern?
docs.text: Several identical consumers read from the same queue, and each message is delivered to only one of them. It scales throughput and tolerates worker failures, but gives up ordering across messages.

docs.title: 47. How should retries be designed in a messaging system?
docs.text: Classify failures: retry transient ones with exponential backoff and jitter through delay or retry queues, and send permanent ones to the DLQ at once. Cap the number of attempts, track the attempt count, and make consumers idempotent because retries cause repeats.

docs.title: 48. How do you handle a growing backlog in a queue?
docs.text: Find whether the cause is a traffic spike, slow consumers, or failing messages. Scale consumers based on backlog age or depth, within the capacity of downstream systems; fix or dead-letter failing messages; and apply backpressure or shed low-priority work if consumers cannot catch up.

docs.title: 49. What is the claim-check pattern?
docs.text: For large payloads, the producer stores the data in object storage and sends a small message with a reference to it. The consumer fetches the payload using the reference. It keeps messages under size limits and brokers fast.

docs.title: 50. What is a saga, and how does it relate to messaging?
docs.text: A saga implements a business process across services as a series of local transactions, each triggered by a message or event, with compensating actions that undo earlier steps if a later step fails. Messaging carries the events or commands between the steps, either by choreography or by an orchestrator.

docs.title: 51. Queue depth keeps growing every evening and messages are 20 minutes old by 9 p.m. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: compare the arrival rate with the processing rate over the evening, and look at the age of the oldest message rather than only depth. Check whether consumers are busy (CPU, in-flight messages) or idle.

How to confirm: if consumers are saturated, the handler or a downstream dependency is the limit; trace a few slow messages. If they are idle, something limits delivery (prefetch, a single FIFO group, too few partitions).

Likely causes and fixes: too few consumers for the evening peak (scale on message age, capped by downstream capacity); a slow database query in the handler (batch or index it); poison messages being retried repeatedly (dead-letter them). See messaging patterns.

docs.title: 52. Customers report receiving the same order confirmation email twice. How do you investigate?
docs.text:
What to check first: search logs for the message ID of an affected order and see whether two workers, or one worker twice, processed it.

How to confirm: look at the receive count or redelivered flag, worker crashes or deploys at that time, and processing durations compared with the visibility timeout.

Likely causes and fixes: at-least-once redelivery after a crash before the ack, or a visibility timeout shorter than processing time. Make the consumer idempotent (record sent emails by message ID in the same transaction), and fix the timeout. See delivery guarantees.

docs.title: 53. Orders exist in the database, but some downstream services never received their "OrderPlaced" events. Most cases coincide with deployments. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the service publishes: after the database commit, as a separate call?

How to confirm: compare order IDs in the database with published event IDs for the deployment window; check whether the process was killed between commit and publish (shutdown logs, missing publish logs).

Likely causes and fixes: the dual-write problem. A crash or SIGTERM between the commit and the publish loses the event. Adopt the transactional outbox with a relay, use publisher confirms, and add graceful shutdown. Run a reconciliation job to republish the missing events. See messaging patterns.

docs.title: 54. Kafka consumer lag grows on one partition while all the others stay near zero. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the consumer logs for that partition: is it repeatedly failing on the same offset?

How to confirm: check the bytes-in rate per partition (a hot key?) and whether the consumer assigned to that partition is healthy.

Likely causes and fixes: a poison record that throws on every attempt (publish it to a retry or dead-letter topic after N attempts and move on); a skewed key that sends one tenant's traffic to one partition (choose a better key or split the hot key); or a single slow consumer instance (replace it). See Apache Kafka.

docs.title: 55. A Kafka consumer group rebalances every few minutes and throughput collapses. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: consumer logs for partitions being revoked and assigned, and the time taken to process each poll's batch compared with max.poll.interval.ms.

How to confirm: correlate rebalances with long-running batches, pod restarts, or deployments.

Likely causes and fixes: processing a batch takes longer than the poll interval, so the broker considers the consumer dead (reduce the batch size or speed up handling); frequent restarts during rolling deploys (use static membership); eager rebalancing that stops all consumers (switch to cooperative rebalancing). Make processing idempotent, as rebalances cause reprocessing.

docs.title: 56. HTTP requests that publish to RabbitMQ suddenly hang and time out. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the RabbitMQ management UI or diagnostics for memory or disk alarms, and whether clients received connection.blocked.

How to confirm: look at queue depths: a large backlog usually explains the memory or disk pressure.

Likely causes and fixes: consumers stopped or slowed, so messages accumulated until the broker blocked publishers to protect itself. Restore or scale consumers, add queue length limits with an overflow policy, add disk, and alert on queue depth long before the alarm thresholds. Add a publish timeout so web requests fail fast. See RabbitMQ.

docs.title: 57. Two SQS workers process the same message at the same time. How?
docs.text:
What to check first: the queue's visibility timeout and the processing time of the affected messages.

How to confirm: the message's ApproximateReceiveCount is 2 or more, and the second receive happened just after the visibility timeout expired.

Likely causes and fixes: processing took longer than the visibility timeout, so the message became visible again. Raise the timeout above the worst-case processing time, extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility during long jobs, and keep the consumer idempotent. See SQS and SNS.

docs.title: 58. Right after a release, the dead-letter queue receives thousands of messages. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: sample several dead-lettered messages and their recorded error reasons.

How to confirm: check whether the failures started exactly at the deploy and whether they share a message type or schema version.

Likely causes and fixes: a consumer bug or an incompatible schema change (a renamed field). Roll back or fix forward, then redrive the DLQ to the source queue once the fix is live. Because consumers are idempotent, replaying is safe. Prevent recurrence with schema compatibility checks in CI. See messaging patterns.

docs.title: 59. A partner API was down for an hour. Minutes after it recovered, it went down again under a flood of requests from your workers. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the retry policy of the workers and the request rate to the partner when it recovered.

How to confirm: metrics show a spike far above normal traffic at the moment of recovery; retries had no delay or jitter.

Likely causes and fixes: a retry storm: every message that failed during the outage retried at once. Use exponential backoff with jitter, cap attempts, add a circuit breaker, and limit worker concurrency to the partner's rate limit. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

docs.title: 60. An SQS queue subscribed to an SNS topic never receives any messages. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the subscription status and the topic's NumberOfNotificationsFailed metric.

How to confirm: inspect the queue's access policy (does it allow this topic to send?) and, for encrypted queues, the KMS key policy; check any subscription filter policy against the message attributes.

Likely causes and fixes: a missing queue policy statement, a key policy that does not allow SNS, or a filter policy that matches nothing. Fix the policies, publish a test message, and alarm on delivery failures. See SQS and SNS.

docs.title: 61. Order status changes are sometimes applied out of order: orders show "shipped" and then flip back to "paid". How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether status events for the same order can be processed in parallel or retried after later events.

How to confirm: logs show the "paid" event processed after "shipped" for the same order ID, often after a retry.

Likely causes and fixes: competing consumers or retries on a channel with no per-order ordering. Route events by order ID (Kafka key, FIFO message group), and add version checks so a consumer only applies an event that moves the state forward. See delivery guarantees.

docs.title: 62. An SQS FIFO queue processes slowly even though workers are mostly idle. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how many distinct MessageGroupId values are in use.

How to confirm: sample messages; if most share one group ID, they must be processed strictly one after another.

Likely causes and fixes: a constant group ID (for example the queue name) serializes everything. Use a group ID per entity, such as an order or account ID, so different groups run in parallel while each stays ordered.

docs.title: 63. To clear a backlog, you scaled consumers from 5 to 50, and the whole system got slower. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the downstream database or API: connection counts, lock waits, and query latency when consumers scaled up.

How to confirm: the database hit its connection limit or CPU ceiling at the same moment; per-message processing time increased.

Likely causes and fixes: the bottleneck was downstream, not the number of consumers. Cap consumer count and concurrency to what the downstream system can absorb, batch writes, and drain the backlog more slowly. See messaging patterns.

docs.title: 64. Publishing fails for some messages with a size error, and broker memory spikes when large reports are sent. What do you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: message sizes for the failing type compared with the broker's or service's size limit.

How to confirm: the failing messages contain whole files or large report payloads.

Likely causes and fixes: payloads that do not belong in messages. Use the claim-check pattern: store the payload in object storage and publish a small message with its key, with a lifecycle rule that keeps objects longer than the queue and DLQ retention. See messaging patterns.

docs.title: Messaging Fundamentals
docs.text: Messaging lets one part of a system send information to another without both having to be available, fast, or even aware of each other at the same moment. A producer hands a message to a broker; the broker stores it; a consumer picks it up when it is ready. This page explains the core vocabulary and models that every queueing and streaming system builds on.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Synchronous HTTP calls chain services together: if the email service is slow, checkout is slow; if it is down, checkout fails. Asynchronous messaging breaks that chain.

  • Decoupling in time: the producer and consumer do not need to run at the same moment. The consumer can be down for maintenance while messages wait.
  • Decoupling in space: the producer does not need to know who consumes the message, how many consumers there are, or where they run.
  • Load leveling: a burst of 10,000 orders in a minute becomes a queue that workers drain at a steady, safe rate instead of overwhelming a database.
  • Resilience: a failed message can be retried later; a crashed consumer does not lose work, because the message stays in the broker until it is acknowledged.
  • Independent scaling: add more consumers to process faster without touching the producer.
  • Fan-out: one event ("order placed") can trigger email, analytics, inventory, and fraud checks, each owned by a different team.

The cost is complexity: eventual consistency, duplicate messages, ordering questions, and another piece of infrastructure to run and monitor.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Slack's job queue. Slack runs business logic that is too slow for a web request (message posts, push notifications, URL unfurls, billing calculations) through a job queue that was originally held in Redis. When a database slowdown made jobs execute slowly, Redis reached its memory limit, new jobs could not be enqueued, and every operation depending on the queue failed. Slack put Kafka in front of Redis as durable storage: a service called Kafkagate writes jobs to Kafka, and JQRelay relays them into Redis at a rate-limited pace (Scaling Slack's Job Queue).
  • Cloudflare's service communication. Cloudflare has run Kafka in production since 2014 and uses it to decouple microservices, announcing the creation, change, or deletion of resources in a common data format; its 14 clusters have processed over a trillion messages (Cloudflare blog).
  • AWS Lambda asynchronous invocation. When a function is invoked asynchronously, Lambda places the event in a queue and immediately returns success; a separate process reads events from the queue and runs the function (AWS Lambda documentation).
  • Mozilla Pulse. Mozilla runs Pulse, a managed RabbitMQ cluster, to give loose coupling between its automation and infrastructure tools and to replace polling: publishers send to topic exchanges and consumers bind their own queues (Mozilla wiki).

Popular tools and providers: RabbitMQ, Apache Kafka, Apache Pulsar, NATS, Redis Streams, and ActiveMQ (self-hosted); Amazon SQS, SNS, and EventBridge; Google Cloud Pub/Sub; Azure Service Bus; managed hosting such as Amazon MQ, Amazon MSK, Confluent Cloud, and CloudAMQP.

docs.title: Producer, broker, consumer
docs.text:
+----------+   publish    +-------------------+   deliver / poll   +----------+
| Producer | -----------> |      Broker       | -----------------> | Consumer |
| (orders  |              |  stores messages  |                    | (email   |
|  API)    |              |  until consumed   | <----------------- |  worker) |
+----------+              +-------------------+   acknowledge      +----------+
  • Producer (publisher): creates and sends messages. It only needs to know the broker and a destination name.
  • Broker: the middleware that receives, stores, routes, and delivers messages, such as RabbitMQ, Apache Kafka, or Amazon SQS.
  • Consumer (subscriber, worker): receives messages, processes them, and acknowledges them so the broker knows they are done.
  • Acknowledgement (ack): the consumer's signal that a message was handled. Until it arrives, the broker keeps the message and may deliver it again. See delivery guarantees.

docs.title: Message anatomy
docs.text:
A message is an envelope of metadata plus a body.

Part Purpose Example Message ID Unique identifier, used for deduplication and tracing "msg_01HF3K8..." Type What kind of message this is "OrderPlaced" Timestamp When it was created "2026-11-03T10:15:00Z" Headers / attributes Key-value metadata the broker or consumer can read without parsing the body content-type, schema-version, tenant Correlation ID Ties together all messages and logs belonging to one business flow or request The original HTTP request ID Causation ID The ID of the message that caused this one ID of the OrderPlaced message that triggered PaymentRequested Reply-to Where a response should be sent (request-reply) "orders.replies.instance-7" Routing key / partition key Used by the broker to route or partition "order.created", a customer ID Body (payload) The data itself, usually JSON, Avro, or Protobuf {"orderId": "ord_901", ...} 
{
  "id": "msg_01HF3K8Q2V",
  "type": "OrderPlaced",
  "schemaVersion": 2,
  "occurredAt": "2026-11-03T10:15:00Z",
  "correlationId": "req_7f3c9a2e",
  "data": {
    "orderId": "ord_901",
    "customerId": "cus_7",
    "total": { "amount": 4999, "currency": "USD" }
  }
}

Messages come in a few flavors:

  • Command: asks a specific receiver to do something (SendWelcomeEmail). Usually one consumer.
  • Event: states that something happened (OrderPlaced). The producer does not care who reacts; there may be many consumers.
  • Document / query result: carries data, for example the reply in a request-reply exchange.

Version your message schemas and make changes backward compatible (add fields, do not rename or remove them), exactly as with API design, because producers and consumers deploy at different times.

docs.title: Queues and topics
docs.text:
• A queue holds messages for one logical consumer. Each message is processed by exactly one of the consumers reading from that queue.
  • A topic broadcasts each message to every subscriber. Each subscriber gets its own copy (or its own position in the log).

docs.title: Point-to-point vs publish/subscribe
docs.text:
Point-to-point Publish/subscribe Recipients per message One All subscribers Typical message Command, task Event Scaling Add consumers to share the work (competing consumers) Add subscribers for new features Example "Resize this image" "User signed up"

The two combine: a topic fans out to several queues, and each queue has a pool of competing workers. See messaging patterns.

docs.title: Push vs pull consumers
docs.text:
Push Pull How it works The broker sends messages to a registered consumer as they arrive The consumer asks the broker for messages in a loop Flow control Broker must limit in-flight messages (for example RabbitMQ prefetch) Natural: the consumer only fetches what it can handle Latency Very low Low with long polling; higher with naive polling Examples RabbitMQ consumers, SNS to HTTP endpoints, Pub/Sub push subscriptions Kafka consumers, SQS ReceiveMessage, Pub/Sub pull subscriptions

Pull consumers should use long polling (wait up to N seconds for a message) rather than hammering the broker with empty requests.

docs.title: Synchronous request/response vs asynchronous messaging
docs.text:
Synchronous (HTTP, gRPC) Asynchronous (messages) Caller waits for the result Yes No (or only for "accepted") Both sides must be up Yes No; the broker buffers Failure of the callee Fails the caller unless handled Messages wait and are retried Latency of the overall task Immediate result Eventually done Consistency Easier to reason about Eventual consistency Debugging One request trace Flows spread across services and time Good for Reads, user needs the answer now Side effects, slow work, notifying many systems

Rule of thumb: use synchronous calls when the user needs the answer to continue ("is this coupon valid?"), and messages for everything that can happen after the response ("send the receipt", "update the search index").

docs.title: Request-reply over queues
docs.text:
Sometimes you want a response but still want the buffering of a broker. The requester includes a reply-to address and a correlation ID:

Requester                              Broker                         Responder
   |-- request ------------------------> [pricing.requests] ------------> |
   |   reply-to: replies.instance-7                                       |
   |   correlation-id: c-42                                               |
   |                                                                      | compute
   | <---------------------------------- [replies.instance-7] <-- reply --|
   |   correlation-id: c-42  (matches the pending request)                |

The requester keeps a map of pending correlation IDs and resolves the right one when a reply arrives, with a timeout for replies that never come. This works, but it reintroduces waiting; if you need it often, a plain HTTP or gRPC call may be simpler.

docs.title: Message brokers vs event-streaming platforms
docs.text:
There are two families of messaging systems with different mental models.

Message broker (queue) Event-streaming platform (log) Examples RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, Azure Service Bus Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Redis Streams, RabbitMQ Streams Storage model Messages are removed once acknowledged Append-only log; messages kept for a retention period Consumer position Broker tracks each message's state Each consumer group tracks its own offset Replay old messages No (once consumed, gone) Yes (rewind the offset) Routing Rich routing in the broker (exchanges, filters) Simple: topic and partition Per-message features Ack/reject, per-message retry, delays, priorities, TTL Ordered batches; retries handled by the application Ordering Per queue (weakened by competing consumers and retries) Strict within a partition Typical use Task queues, commands, work distribution Event streams, analytics, many independent readers, event sourcing, change data capture

Shorthand: a broker is a smart broker with simple consumers; a log is a simple broker with smart consumers.

docs.title: Overview of common systems
docs.text:
RabbitMQ Apache Kafka Amazon SQS Amazon SNS Category Message broker Distributed event log Managed queue Managed pub/sub Model Exchanges route to queues Topics split into partitions Queues (standard or FIFO) Topics with subscriptions Delivery Push with prefetch Pull by consumer groups Pull with long polling Push to subscribers Retention Until acknowledged (streams retain) Time/size based, replayable Up to 14 days Not stored (delivered and retried) Ordering Per queue Per partition Best effort (standard) or per message group (FIFO) FIFO topics only Operations You run it (or use a hosted service) You run a cluster (or use a managed service) Fully managed Fully managed Best for Flexible routing, task queues High-throughput streams, replay Simple, reliable queues on AWS Fan-out to queues, functions, HTTP

Details: RabbitMQ, Apache Kafka, SQS and SNS.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use asynchronous messaging when:

  • The work can finish after the response: receipts, notifications, search indexing, thumbnails, reports.
  • Traffic is bursty and a downstream system (a database, a partner API) must be protected from spikes.
  • Several services, often owned by different teams, need to react to the same event.
  • A dependency is slow or unreliable and work must survive its outages and be retried.
  • Work must be spread across many workers that scale independently.

Avoid it when:

  • The caller needs the result immediately to continue (a price check, a login).
  • The work is fast, local, and reliable, such as a single database write.
  • Several steps must be strongly consistent with each other at the moment of the request.
  • The team cannot yet operate and monitor another system; a database-backed job table may be enough at small scale (see background jobs).
  • You want a permanent record of data: a queue is a transport, not a database.
Need Synchronous HTTP/gRPC Database job table Message broker (RabbitMQ, SQS) Event log (Kafka) Caller needs the answer now Best No No No A few background jobs in a small app Overkill Best Fine Overkill Distribute tasks with retries, delays, DLQs No Possible, limited Best Possible, more work Many independent consumers of the same events Tight coupling No Fan-out with one queue per consumer Best Replay past events, rebuild state No No No (except RabbitMQ streams) Best Very high-throughput streams No No Good Best

docs.title: Before and after: sending a receipt
docs.text:
Synchronous: the user waits for the email provider, and checkout fails if it is down.

app.post("/api/orders", async (req, res) => {
  const order = await orders.create(req.body);
  await emailProvider.sendReceipt(order); // slow, and can fail checkout
  res.status(201).json(order);
});

Asynchronous: the order is saved, a message is published, and a worker sends the email later, with retries.

app.post("/api/orders", async (req, res) => {
  const order = await orders.create(req.body);
  await broker.publish("order-events", {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    type: "OrderPlaced",
    occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    correlationId: req.id,
    data: { orderId: order.id, customerId: order.customerId },
  });
  res.status(201).json(order); // returns immediately
});

// Separate process: the email worker
broker.consume("email-queue", async (message) => {
  if (message.type === "OrderPlaced") {
    await emailProvider.sendReceipt(message.data.orderId);
  }
  // returning without throwing = acknowledge; throwing = retry later
});

broker stands for any client library, and req.id is a request ID set by middleware such as pino-http (plain Express has none). Saving the order and publishing are two separate writes; the transactional outbox pattern makes them reliable together.

docs.title: A tiny in-memory queue to see the mechanics
docs.text:
// Demo only: messages live in memory and vanish on restart
class DemoQueue {
  #messages = [];
  #inFlight = new Map();

  publish(body) {
    this.#messages.push({ id: crypto.randomUUID(), body, attempts: 0 });
  }

  receive() {
    const msg = this.#messages.shift();
    if (!msg) return null;
    msg.attempts += 1;
    this.#inFlight.set(msg.id, msg); // invisible to others until acked
    return msg;
  }

  ack(id) {
    this.#inFlight.delete(id); // done: gone for good
  }

  nack(id) {
    const msg = this.#inFlight.get(id);
    this.#inFlight.delete(id);
    if (msg) this.#messages.push(msg); // back in line for another attempt
  }
}

const queue = new DemoQueue();
queue.publish({ type: "SendWelcomeEmail", userId: 42 });

const msg = queue.receive();
try {
  console.log("Processing", msg.body, "attempt", msg.attempts);
  queue.ack(msg.id);
} catch {
  queue.nack(msg.id);
}

Real brokers add durability, replication, routing, and many consumers, but the receive/ack/nack cycle is the same.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Publish events for facts, send commands for requests, and name them clearly (OrderPlaced vs SendReceipt).
  • Give every message a unique ID, a type, a timestamp, and a correlation ID.
  • Version message schemas and only make backward-compatible changes.
  • Assume duplicates and design idempotent consumers. See delivery guarantees.
  • Acknowledge after processing, not before.
  • Bound retries and use dead-letter queues for messages that keep failing.
  • Monitor queue depth, age of the oldest message, and consumer lag.
  • Keep messages small; store large payloads elsewhere and send a reference.
  • Do not use a queue as a database. It is a transport, not the source of truth.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Backlog grows at every daily peak. Detect: queue depth and "age of oldest message" climb in the evening and only drain overnight. Cause: too few consumers, or consumers slowed by a downstream database. Fix: scale consumers on message age (capped by what the database can take), speed up the handler, and check whether the work can be batched.
  • Customers receive the same email twice. Detect: logs show the same message ID handled by two workers, or support tickets about duplicates. Cause: at-least-once redelivery after a worker crash, a lost ack, or an expired visibility timeout. Fix: make the consumer idempotent (dedup by message ID) and size timeouts correctly; see delivery guarantees.
  • Events go missing after deployments. Detect: a reconciliation job finds orders with no matching "order placed" event downstream. Cause: the service committed to its database and was killed before publishing, or consumers used auto-ack. Fix: use the transactional outbox, manual acks after processing, and graceful shutdown.
  • Publishers suddenly block or time out. Detect: publish latency spikes; RabbitMQ reports a memory or disk alarm; Kafka brokers alert on disk usage. Cause: an unconsumed backlog filled the broker's memory or disk. Fix: restore consumers, bound queue lengths, tune retention, and alert on backlog long before the broker's limits.
  • A producer release breaks consumers. Detect: deserialization errors spike and the dead-letter queue fills right after a deploy. Cause: an incompatible schema change (renamed or removed field). Fix: version schemas, make only additive changes, and check compatibility in CI.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Producer / consumer: the sender / receiver of messages.
  • Broker: the system that stores and delivers messages.
  • Queue: a buffer where each message is processed by one consumer.
  • Topic: a named channel that delivers each message to all subscribers.
  • Point-to-point: one message, one receiver.
  • Publish/subscribe: one message, many receivers.
  • Acknowledgement: confirmation that a message was handled.
  • Correlation ID: an identifier linking related messages and logs.
  • Command / event: a request to do something / a record that something happened.
  • Long polling: a pull request that waits for messages instead of returning empty immediately.
  • Event-streaming platform: a system built on a durable, replayable, append-only log.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "A queue makes the system faster." It makes the response faster; the total work still takes as long, and consumers must keep up.
  • "Messages are delivered exactly once." Most systems deliver at least once; duplicates happen.
  • Treating an event as a command, so the producer starts depending on a specific consumer's behavior.
  • Putting huge payloads in messages instead of references.
  • No dead-letter queue, so one bad message is retried forever or silently dropped.
  • Ignoring queue depth until the backlog is hours old.
  • Using Kafka as a simple task queue (or a task queue for replayable event streams) without understanding the different models.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Give three benefits of asynchronous messaging over synchronous HTTP calls, and two costs.
  2. What is the difference between a queue and a topic, and between point-to-point and publish/subscribe?
  3. Which fields should every message envelope carry, and why is a correlation ID useful?
  4. Compare push and pull consumers. Which does Kafka use? Which does RabbitMQ use?
  5. How does request-reply work over queues, and when would you avoid it?
  6. Explain the difference between a message broker and an event-streaming platform.
