docs.title: Messaging Patterns
docs.text: Messaging systems give you queues, topics, and acknowledgements. Patterns are the proven ways to combine them into reliable designs: sharing work across workers, broadcasting events, retrying safely, publishing events without losing them, and keeping consumers healthy under load. This page covers the patterns you will use most often.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• The hard problems in messaging (lost events, duplicates, poison messages, backlogs, ordering) have well-known solutions. Reinventing them under production pressure usually goes badly.
  • Patterns give teams a shared vocabulary: "use an outbox and an idempotent consumer" says a lot in one sentence.
  • Many of these patterns appear in system design interviews and in every serious event-driven system.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Load leveling at Slack. After an outage in which its Redis-based job queue ran out of memory, Slack wrote jobs to Kafka first and added a relay (JQRelay) that moves them into Redis. When execution slows, Slack adjusts the relay's rate limits to match the dequeue rate, or pauses relaying, while the web app keeps enqueueing into durable Kafka (Slack Engineering).
  • Backpressure and load shedding at Discord. Discord's push notification pipeline handles bursts of over a million requests per minute. Each Pusher asks for only as many requests as its Firebase connection can handle (backpressure), and the collector in front of it buffers a bounded number of requests and sheds the rest in extreme bursts (Discord blog).
  • Log-based change capture at Shopify. Shopify moved its change data capture to Kafka Connect and Debezium, reading database changes from the log into Kafka; this log-based approach is the same mechanism used to relay a transactional outbox (Shopify Engineering).
  • Idempotent consumers for Stripe events. Stripe tells webhook consumers to record processed event IDs and skip duplicates, which is the inbox pattern (Stripe webhooks).
  • Isolating noisy neighbors in AWS Lambda. Lambda hashes each customer to a few of a fixed set of queues and enqueues into the shortest, so one customer's backlog does not delay everyone else (AWS Builders' Library).

Popular tools and providers: Debezium and Kafka Connect (change data capture and outbox relays), BullMQ (Node.js), Celery (Python), and Sidekiq (Ruby) for job queues with retries, Temporal for long-running workflows and sagas, and KEDA for autoscaling consumers on queue metrics in Kubernetes.

docs.title: 1. Work queue (competing consumers)
docs.text:
Several identical workers read from one queue; each message goes to exactly one of them.

               +--> worker 1
Producer --> [queue] --> worker 2
               +--> worker 3
  • Scale throughput by adding workers.
  • Resilience: if a worker dies, its unacknowledged messages go to the others.
  • Trade-off: processing order across messages is lost.

Use it for independent tasks: image processing, emails, report generation.

docs.title: 2. Fan-out (publish/subscribe)
docs.text:
One message is delivered to several independent consumers, each with its own queue (or its own consumer group).

                     +--> [email-queue]     --> email workers
Producer --> topic --+--> [search-queue]    --> search indexer
                     +--> [analytics-queue] --> analytics workers

Implementations: a RabbitMQ fanout or topic exchange bound to several queues, SNS subscribed by several SQS queues, or several Kafka consumer groups on one topic. Because each consumer has its own buffer, a slow or failing consumer never affects the others.

docs.title: 3. Request-reply
docs.text:
The requester sends a message with a replyTo address and a correlationId, then waits (with a timeout) for a reply carrying the same correlation ID. RabbitMQ offers a built-in "direct reply-to" feature (amq.rabbitmq.reply-to) that avoids declaring a reply queue per request.

Use sparingly: if the caller blocks waiting for the answer, an HTTP or gRPC call is usually simpler. See messaging fundamentals.

docs.title: 4. Retries with backoff and delay queues
docs.text:
Not every failure deserves the same treatment:

Failure type Examples Action Transient Timeout, 503, 429, connection reset, lock conflict Retry later with exponential backoff and jitter Permanent Invalid JSON, unknown message type, validation error, missing referenced record that will never exist Send to the DLQ immediately; retrying cannot help

Retrying in place (immediately requeueing) creates hot loops and hammers an already struggling dependency. Retry later instead:

                          fail (attempt 1)
work queue --> consumer ---------------------> retry-10s queue --(10 s)--> work queue
                          fail (attempt 2)
                       ----------------------> retry-1m queue  --(1 min)-> work queue
                          fail (attempt 3)
                       ----------------------> retry-10m queue --(10 min)-> work queue
                          fail (attempt 4)
                       ----------------------> DLQ (alert a human)

How each system delays a retry:

  • RabbitMQ: retry queues with a message TTL whose dead-letter exchange points back to the work queue, or the delayed message exchange plugin.
  • SQS: leave the message undeleted and set its visibility timeout to the backoff delay with ChangeMessageVisibility; the redrive policy caps the attempts.
  • Kafka: publish the failed record to retry topics (orders.retry.1m, orders.retry.10m) whose consumers wait until the record is due, then a dead-letter topic. The main partition keeps flowing.

Track the attempt count in a header, add jitter so retries from many messages do not synchronize, and cap the total number of attempts. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

docs.title: 5. Dead-letter queue handling and replay
docs.text:
A DLQ is only useful if someone looks at it.

  1. Alert when the DLQ is not empty (or grows quickly).
  2. Inspect: each dead message should carry why it failed: the error message, the stack or error code, the attempt count, the original queue, and timestamps (RabbitMQ adds an x-death header; add your own headers for the error).
  3. Fix the cause: deploy a bug fix, restore the missing data, or decide the message is invalid.
  4. Replay (redrive) the messages to the original queue, or discard them deliberately with a record of why.
  5. Make replay safe by keeping consumers idempotent; replayed messages may already have been partially processed.

Set DLQ retention long enough to investigate (days to weeks), and never let a DLQ become a silent graveyard.

docs.title: The dual-write problem
docs.text:
A service often needs to update its database and publish an event: save the order, then publish OrderPlaced. These are two writes to two systems, and there is no transaction spanning both.

Option A: write DB, then publish
  BEGIN; INSERT order; COMMIT;     ok
  publish("OrderPlaced")           X broker down / process crashes
  => order exists, but nobody hears about it (lost event)

Option B: publish, then write DB
  publish("OrderPlaced")           ok
  BEGIN; INSERT order; COMMIT;     X constraint violation / crash
  => consumers act on an order that does not exist (phantom event)

Retrying or reordering cannot close the gap; a crash can always land between the two writes.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
Write the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change. A separate relay process reads the outbox and publishes to the broker, marking rows as sent.

  • Polling publisher: the relay periodically selects unpublished rows, publishes them, and marks them published.
  • Change data capture (CDC): a tool such as Debezium reads the database's transaction log (the PostgreSQL WAL, the MySQL binlog, or MongoDB change streams) and publishes new outbox rows, with lower latency and no polling load. See MongoDB change streams.

The relay can publish a row and crash before marking it, so it publishes at least once. Consumers must be idempotent, which brings us to the inbox.

docs.title: 7. Inbox (idempotent consumer)
docs.text: The consumer records each processed message ID in an inbox table, in the same transaction as its business change. A redelivered message hits the unique constraint and is skipped. Outbox on the producer side plus inbox on the consumer side gives effectively-once processing end to end. The full code is in delivery guarantees.

docs.title: 8. Saga
docs.text: A business process spanning several services (reserve stock, charge the card, schedule shipping) cannot use one database transaction. A saga runs it as a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event or command that triggers the next, with compensating actions (release stock, refund) to undo earlier steps when a later one fails. Sagas are coordinated either by choreography (services react to each other's events) or orchestration (a coordinator tells each service what to do). See microservices patterns.

docs.title: 9. Backpressure and scaling consumers on queue depth
docs.text:
A queue absorbs bursts, but if producers are faster than consumers for long enough, the backlog grows without bound: latency rises, memory or storage fills, and messages may expire.

Measure:

  • Queue depth: messages waiting.
  • Age of the oldest message: how stale the work is. Often the better signal, because it maps directly to user-visible delay.
  • Consumer lag (Kafka): offsets behind the head of each partition.
  • Processing rate vs arrival rate.

Respond:

  • Autoscale consumers on backlog per consumer or on message age (for example with KEDA on Kubernetes, or target tracking on a custom metric). A useful target is "backlog per worker = acceptable delay x messages per second one worker processes".
  • Respect the limits of downstream systems: more workers can overload the database they write to. Cap concurrency where the bottleneck is.
  • Limit in-flight work per consumer (RabbitMQ prefetch, batch size).
  • Bound queues (for example RabbitMQ x-max-length with reject-publish) so producers get a clear signal instead of the broker running out of resources.
  • Shed or degrade low-priority work when overloaded.
  • In Kafka, consumers beyond the partition count add nothing; scale partitions first.

docs.title: 10. Ordering strategies
docs.text:
When order matters for some messages:

  • Partition by key: route all messages for one entity to the same partition, message group, or session (Kafka key, SQS FIFO MessageGroupId, Pub/Sub ordering key, Service Bus session).
  • Single active consumer per key or queue: RabbitMQ's single active consumer feature lets several consumers stand by while only one receives from the queue.
  • Version numbers or sequence numbers: consumers apply an event only if it is the next expected version, and park or ignore others.
  • Commutative design: make updates order-independent where possible (sets instead of lists, "set to value with timestamp" instead of increments).
  • Do not need order: often the cheapest fix is a consumer that re-reads the current state from the source of truth instead of trusting the sequence of events.

docs.title: 11. Priority queues
docs.text:
Some messages are more urgent: password-reset emails before marketing emails.

  • Separate queues per priority with more consumers (or weighted polling) on the high-priority queue. Works on every system, including SQS and Kafka, which have no per-message priority.
  • Broker priorities: RabbitMQ classic queues declared with x-max-priority, and quorum queues (strict priorities since RabbitMQ 4.3), deliver higher-priority messages first.
  • Watch for starvation: if high-priority traffic never stops, low priority never runs. Reserve some capacity for every level.

docs.title: 12. Claim check (large payloads)
docs.text:
Brokers are optimized for small messages and many cap message size. For a large payload (a PDF, an image, a big export):

The message is the "claim check" for the stored payload. Clean up stored objects with a lifecycle rule, and secure the storage as carefully as the queue. See file storage and uploads.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Pattern Use when Avoid when Competing consumers Independent tasks that can run in any order Strict order matters across messages Fan-out Several services react to the same event Only one consumer exists (just use a queue) Request-reply You need a response but also broker buffering, or replies over a bus The caller blocks waiting anyway: use HTTP or gRPC Delayed retries with backoff Transient failures of dependencies The error is permanent (send to the DLQ instead) Transactional outbox A database change must reliably produce an event There is no database write, or the event can be derived later by CDC on the main tables Inbox / idempotent consumer Any at-least-once consumer with side effects The operation is naturally idempotent already Saga A business process spans several services' data All the data lives in one database: use a local transaction Autoscaling on backlog Workload varies and downstream systems can absorb more workers The bottleneck is a downstream system with fixed capacity Priority queues Urgent work must not wait behind bulk work Everything ends up "high priority" Claim check Payloads are large or exceed size limits Messages are small; the extra fetch only adds latency

General guidance:

  • Start with the simplest combination (a queue, competing consumers, bounded retries, a DLQ, idempotent handlers) and add patterns when a concrete problem appears.
  • The outbox and inbox patterns are worth adopting early in any service that both writes to a database and publishes events.
  • Sagas and request-reply add the most complexity; reach for them only when simpler designs cannot meet the requirement.

docs.title: Transactional outbox with PostgreSQL
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  topic        text NOT NULL,
  payload      jsonb NOT NULL,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox (created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

import pg from "pg";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const pool = new pg.Pool();

// 1. The business change and the event, in ONE transaction
export async function placeOrder(order) {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");
    await client.query(
      "INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
      [order.id, order.customerId, order.total],
    );
    await client.query(
      "INSERT INTO outbox (id, topic, payload) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
      [randomUUID(), "order-events", { type: "OrderPlaced", orderId: order.id }],
    );
    await client.query("COMMIT");
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

// 2. The relay: publish unpublished rows, then mark them
export async function relayOutbox(broker) {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");
    // SKIP LOCKED lets several relay instances run without grabbing the same rows
    const { rows } = await client.query(
      `SELECT id, topic, payload FROM outbox
        WHERE published_at IS NULL
        ORDER BY created_at
        LIMIT 100
        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`,
    );
    for (const row of rows) {
      await broker.publish(row.topic, { id: row.id, ...row.payload }); // wait for the broker's confirm
      await client.query("UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = $1", [row.id]);
    }
    await client.query("COMMIT");
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK"); // rows stay unpublished and are retried next run
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

The outbox row's id becomes the message ID, so consumers can deduplicate the occasional re-publish. Delete or archive published rows periodically.

docs.title: Retry with backoff using SQS visibility
docs.text:
import { ChangeMessageVisibilityCommand, DeleteMessageCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs";

const BASE_SECONDS = 10;
const MAX_SECONDS = 15 * 60;

async function handleWithBackoff(sqs, queueUrl, message, receiveCount) {
  try {
    await processMessage(JSON.parse(message.Body));
    await sqs.send(new DeleteMessageCommand({ QueueUrl: queueUrl, ReceiptHandle: message.ReceiptHandle }));
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.permanent) throw err; // let the redrive policy (or explicit DLQ send) handle it
    // Exponential backoff with full jitter: 10 s, 20 s, 40 s ... capped
    const ceiling = Math.min(MAX_SECONDS, BASE_SECONDS * 2 ** (receiveCount - 1));
    const delay = Math.floor(Math.random() * ceiling);
    await sqs.send(new ChangeMessageVisibilityCommand({
      QueueUrl: queueUrl,
      ReceiptHandle: message.ReceiptHandle,
      VisibilityTimeout: delay, // reappears after the backoff delay
    }));
  }
}

receiveCount comes from the message's ApproximateReceiveCount attribute; the queue's redrive policy still moves the message to the DLQ after the maximum number of receives.

docs.title: Sizing consumers from the backlog
docs.text:
// How many workers do we need to clear the backlog within the target delay?
function desiredWorkers({ backlog, arrivalPerSec, perWorkerPerSec, targetDelaySec, maxWorkers }) {
  // Workers needed to keep up with new arrivals, plus drain the backlog in time
  const needed = (arrivalPerSec + backlog / targetDelaySec) / perWorkerPerSec;
  return Math.min(maxWorkers, Math.max(1, Math.ceil(needed)));
}

console.log(desiredWorkers({
  backlog: 12_000, arrivalPerSec: 50, perWorkerPerSec: 20, targetDelaySec: 300, maxWorkers: 40,
})); // (50 + 40) / 20 = 4.5 -> 5 workers

maxWorkers is where you encode the limit of the database or API the workers depend on.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Default to competing consumers for tasks and fan-out for events.
  • Use the transactional outbox whenever a database change must be followed by an event.
  • Make every consumer idempotent (inbox table, conditional updates, idempotency keys).
  • Classify errors: retry transient ones with backoff and jitter, dead-letter permanent ones at once.
  • Give every queue a DLQ, an alert, and a replay procedure.
  • Scale consumers on backlog age, capped by downstream capacity.
  • Get ordering from keys, not from global queues.
  • Keep messages small and use claim checks for big payloads.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Events arrive minutes late. Detect: the age of the oldest unpublished outbox row rises; relay logs show errors or the relay is not running. Cause: the relay crashed, cannot reach the broker, or its query scans the whole outbox table because the partial index is missing. Fix: monitor and alert on outbox age, run more than one relay with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, index unpublished rows, and archive published ones.
  • A dependency recovers and is knocked over again. Detect: when the dependency comes back, its request rate spikes far above normal and it returns 429 or 503 again. Cause: retries without backoff or jitter, so every failed message retries at the same moment. Fix: exponential backoff with jitter, a cap on attempts, and a circuit breaker in the consumer.
  • Autoscaling consumers takes the database down. Detect: database connections hit the maximum and query latency jumps right after the consumer count scales up. Cause: scaling on queue depth with no upper bound. Fix: cap the worker count and per-worker concurrency to what the database can handle; accept a slower drain.
  • The DLQ is a graveyard. Detect: the DLQ has held messages for weeks; nobody owns it. Cause: no alert, owner, or replay tooling. Fix: alert when it is not empty, assign an owning team, record the failure reason on each message, and build a documented redrive procedure.
  • Status changes apply out of order. Detect: logs show orders marked "shipped" before "paid", or version checks rejecting events. Cause: competing consumers or retries on a channel with no key-based ordering. Fix: partition by order ID (Kafka key, FIFO group) and enforce version checks in the consumer.
  • Claim-check payloads are missing. Detect: consumers fail with "not found" when fetching the stored payload, often on DLQ replays. Cause: a storage lifecycle rule deleted objects before slow or dead-lettered messages were processed. Fix: keep payloads longer than the queue's retention plus the DLQ's retention.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Competing consumers: several workers sharing one queue.
  • Fan-out: one message delivered to many consumers.
  • Backoff / jitter: increasing delays between retries / randomness added to those delays.
  • Delay queue / retry queue: a queue that holds messages until they are due for another attempt.
  • Redrive / replay: moving messages from a DLQ back for processing.
  • Dual-write problem: inconsistency from writing to two systems without a shared transaction.
  • Transactional outbox: storing outgoing events in the same transaction as the data change, and publishing them separately.
  • Change data capture (CDC): streaming changes from a database's transaction log.
  • Inbox: a record of processed message IDs used for deduplication.
  • Saga: a multi-step process of local transactions with compensations.
  • Backpressure: signals and limits that slow producers or bound work when consumers cannot keep up.
  • Claim check: sending a reference to a stored payload instead of the payload.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Publishing an event right after a database commit and assuming it always arrives.
  • Immediate requeue on every error, overloading a struggling dependency.
  • Retries without jitter, so thousands of messages retry at the same instant.
  • A DLQ nobody monitors.
  • Scaling consumers without limits and taking down the database.
  • Request-reply everywhere, rebuilding synchronous coupling on top of a queue.
  • Huge payloads in messages instead of claim checks.
  • Expecting sagas to behave like ACID transactions; other services can see intermediate states.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain the dual-write problem with a concrete failure scenario, and how the transactional outbox solves it.
  2. Why must consumers of an outbox relay be idempotent?
  3. Which errors should be retried and which sent straight to a DLQ? How would you implement delayed retries in RabbitMQ, SQS, and Kafka?
  4. What signals would you use to autoscale consumers, and what limits the number of consumers you should run?
  5. How would you guarantee that all events for one customer are processed in order while still processing different customers in parallel?
  6. When would you use the claim-check pattern?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• microservices.io: Transactional Outbox, Saga, and Idempotent Consumer.
  • RabbitMQ: Tutorials on work queues, publish/subscribe, and RPC.
  • AWS: Queue-based load leveling pattern.
  • AWS Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter.
  • Related: background jobs and scheduling.

docs.title: RabbitMQ
docs.text: RabbitMQ is a widely used open-source message broker. Producers publish messages to exchanges, which route them into queues according to bindings, and consumers receive messages from those queues and acknowledge them. Its strength is flexible routing and per-message control: acknowledgements, retries, dead-lettering, TTLs, and priorities.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• It is a natural fit for task queues and commands: "resize this image", "send this email", "generate this invoice".
  • Its routing model lets one published message reach exactly the queues that care about it, by exact key, by pattern, or to everyone.
  • Features such as manual acks, prefetch, dead-letter exchanges, and quorum queues give you the building blocks for reliable, at-least-once processing.
  • It speaks several protocols (AMQP 0-9-1, AMQP 1.0, MQTT, STOMP) and has client libraries for almost every language, including Node.js.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• OpenStack. OpenStack's services coordinate operations and status information through a message queue. OpenStack supports several message queue services, and its installation guide uses RabbitMQ because most distributions support it (OpenStack installation guide).
  • Mozilla Pulse. Mozilla runs Pulse, a managed RabbitMQ cluster, to loosely couple its automation and infrastructure tools and eliminate polling. Publishers own topic exchanges; consumers create and own queues bound to those exchanges, a direct use of the exchange-binding-queue model (Mozilla wiki).
  • Celery task queues. Celery, a widely used Python task queue, uses RabbitMQ as its default broker, so many Python web applications run their background jobs on RabbitMQ without writing AMQP code directly (Celery documentation).

Popular tools and providers: self-hosted RabbitMQ (packages, Docker images, or the RabbitMQ Cluster Kubernetes Operator); managed RabbitMQ from Amazon MQ and CloudAMQP; client libraries such as amqplib (Node.js), pika (Python), and the official Java and .NET clients.

docs.title: The AMQP 0-9-1 model
docs.text:
1. A producer publishes a message to an exchange with a routing key (a string such as order.created).
  2. The exchange looks at its bindings (rules connecting it to queues) and copies the message into every matching queue.
  3. Consumers consume from a queue. The broker pushes messages to them, limited by the prefetch count.
  4. Each consumer acknowledges a message when done; only then does the broker delete it.

Producers never write to queues directly. Even "send to queue X" goes through the default exchange, a nameless direct exchange to which every queue is automatically bound by its own name.

Other pieces of the model:

  • Connection: a long-lived TCP connection from your app to the broker.
  • Channel: a lightweight virtual connection inside a connection. Use one connection per process and separate channels for publishing and consuming.
  • Virtual host (vhost): an isolated namespace of exchanges, queues, and permissions inside one broker, like a database within a database server.

docs.title: Exchange types
docs.text:
Type Routing rule Example binding Typical use direct Routing key must equal the binding key Queue pdf-jobs bound with key pdf Route tasks by type topic Routing key matches a pattern of dot-separated words: * = exactly one word, # = zero or more words order.* matches order.created, not order.item.added; order.# matches both Route events by category fanout Ignores the key; every bound queue gets a copy Queues email, analytics, audit all bound Broadcast events headers Matches message header values instead of the key; x-match: all or any { "x-match": "all", "format": "pdf", "region": "eu" } Routing on several attributes

Topic examples with binding *.eu.#:

Routing key Matches? order.eu.created Yes payment.eu Yes (# can match zero words) order.us.created No eu.order No (* must match exactly one word before eu)

If no binding matches, the message is dropped unless the producer set the mandatory flag (the broker then returns it) or the exchange has an alternate exchange configured to catch unroutable messages.

docs.title: Queues and their properties
docs.text:
Property Meaning durable The queue definition survives a broker restart. (Messages also need to be persistent to survive.) exclusive Used by only one connection and deleted when that connection closes. Good for temporary reply queues autoDelete Deleted when its last consumer unsubscribes Arguments (x-...) Extra behavior: x-queue-type, x-dead-letter-exchange, x-message-ttl, x-max-length, x-overflow, and others

Queue types:

  • Classic queues: the original single-node queue type. Fine for temporary and non-critical queues.
  • Quorum queues: replicated across several nodes using the Raft consensus algorithm. They keep working if a minority of nodes fail and are the recommended choice for durable, important data. They also support a delivery limit that dead-letters poison messages. (Older "mirrored classic queues" were removed in RabbitMQ 4.0; quorum queues replace them.)
  • Streams: an append-only, replicated log inside RabbitMQ. Consumers read from an offset without removing messages, so many consumers can read and replay the same data, similar to Kafka.

docs.title: Persistent messages
docs.text: A message survives a broker restart only if both the queue is durable and the message is published as persistent (deliveryMode: 2, or persistent: true in amqplib). Quorum queues and streams always store messages durably. Persistence costs some throughput; use it for anything you cannot afford to lose.

docs.title: Publisher confirms
docs.text:
Publishing is asynchronous: without confirmation, the producer does not know whether the broker actually stored the message. With a confirm channel, the broker sends an ack for each message once it has taken responsibility for it (written to disk, replicated to a quorum for quorum queues), or a nack if it could not.

  • Wait for confirms before telling the user "done", or before deleting the row from an outbox table.
  • If a confirm never arrives (connection lost), republish. That can create a duplicate, so consumers must be idempotent.

docs.title: Consumer acknowledgements
docs.text: Action Effect ack Done; the broker deletes the message nack with requeue: true Failed; put it back in the queue for another attempt (risk of a tight retry loop) nack / reject with requeue: false Failed; dead-letter it if the queue has a DLX, otherwise discard it No ack, consumer disconnects All its unacked messages are requeued and marked redelivered noAck: true (automatic mode) The broker considers messages done on delivery: at-most-once

docs.title: Prefetch (QoS)
docs.text:
The prefetch count limits how many unacknowledged messages the broker pushes to a consumer at once.

  • Without a limit, the broker pushes as fast as possible: one consumer can hoard thousands of messages in memory while others sit idle, and a crash requeues all of them.
  • prefetch(1) gives fair dispatch (a worker gets the next message only after acking the current one) at the cost of throughput.
  • Values such as 10 to 100 are common for fast handlers; lower values for slow, heavy tasks. Measure.

With several consumers on one queue, RabbitMQ distributes messages round-robin among consumers that have spare prefetch capacity: the competing consumers pattern.

docs.title: Dead-letter exchanges (DLX)
docs.text:
A queue can name a dead-letter exchange (x-dead-letter-exchange) and optionally a routing key (x-dead-letter-routing-key). A message is dead-lettered when:

  • it is rejected or nacked with requeue: false;
  • its TTL expires;
  • the queue's length limit is exceeded (with the default overflow behavior);
  • it exceeds a quorum queue's delivery limit.

RabbitMQ adds an x-death header recording the reason, the original queue, and a count, so you can see why and how often a message died.

docs.title: Time-to-live (TTL)
docs.text:
• Per-queue message TTL (x-message-ttl, in milliseconds): messages older than this expire.
  • Per-message TTL (the expiration property): set on a single message.
  • Queue TTL (x-expires): delete an unused queue after a period.

Expired messages are dead-lettered if a DLX is set. Combining TTL and DLX gives a classic delayed retry pattern:

work queue --nack(requeue=false)--> DLX --> retry queue (x-message-ttl=30000,
                                                       x-dead-letter-exchange=work)
                                                 | after 30 s the message expires
work queue <--------------------------------------+ and is dead-lettered back

A community plugin (the delayed message exchange) offers per-message delays as an alternative.

docs.title: Other features worth knowing
docs.text:
• Priorities: classic queues can be declared with x-max-priority so higher-priority messages are delivered first. Since RabbitMQ 4.3, quorum queues always support strict priorities (levels 0 to 31) with no argument needed; x-max-priority applies only to classic queues.
  • Length limits: x-max-length / x-max-length-bytes with an overflow policy (drop-head, reject-publish, or reject-publish-dlx) protect the broker from unbounded backlogs.
  • Management UI and HTTP API: a web dashboard (port 15672 when the management plugin is enabled) shows queues, rates, consumers, and lets you inspect and move messages.
  • Clustering: several nodes share metadata; quorum queues and streams replicate data across them.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use RabbitMQ when:

  • You need task queues with per-message acknowledgement, retries, dead-lettering, TTLs, delays, or priorities.
  • Messages must be routed to different consumers by type or pattern (direct, topic, headers exchanges).
  • You need request-reply or RPC-style messaging between services.
  • Clients speak different protocols (AMQP, MQTT for devices, STOMP).
  • Throughput is high but not extreme, and messages are consumed soon after they are published.

Avoid it (or reconsider) when:

  • You need long retention and replay for many independent readers; Kafka (or RabbitMQ streams) fits better.
  • You need very high-throughput event streaming with strict per-key ordering across many consumer groups.
  • Backlogs are expected to grow to millions of messages for long periods.
  • You want zero operations; a managed queue such as SQS removes the broker entirely.
RabbitMQ Apache Kafka Amazon SQS Model Smart broker: exchanges route to queues Distributed log with partitions Managed queue Best at Routing, per-message control, task queues Throughput, retention, replay, many consumers Simple, elastic, zero-ops queues on AWS Replay Streams only Yes No Per-message retry, TTL, priority Yes Built by the application Retry via visibility timeout and DLQ; no priority Ordering Per queue (single consumer) Per partition FIFO queues, per message group Operations You run a cluster (or buy managed) You run a cluster (or buy managed) None

docs.title: Run RabbitMQ locally
docs.text:
docker run -d --name rabbitmq -p 5672:5672 -p 15672:15672 rabbitmq:management
# AMQP on localhost:5672, dashboard on http://localhost:15672 (guest/guest, local only)

docs.title: Topology: topic exchange, quorum queue, dead-letter queue
docs.text:
// topology.js
export async function setupTopology(channel) {
  // Main exchange for order events
  await channel.assertExchange("orders", "topic", { durable: true });

  // Dead-letter exchange and queue
  await channel.assertExchange("orders.dlx", "fanout", { durable: true });
  await channel.assertQueue("orders.email.dlq", { durable: true, arguments: { "x-queue-type": "quorum" } });
  await channel.bindQueue("orders.email.dlq", "orders.dlx", "");

  // Work queue for the email service
  await channel.assertQueue("orders.email", {
    durable: true,
    arguments: {
      "x-queue-type": "quorum",
      "x-dead-letter-exchange": "orders.dlx",
      "x-delivery-limit": 5, // quorum queues: dead-letter after repeated failed deliveries
    },
  });
  await channel.bindQueue("orders.email", "orders", "order.created");
}

docs.title: Publisher with confirms (amqplib)
docs.text:
// publisher.js
import amqp from "amqplib";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { setupTopology } from "./topology.js";

const connection = await amqp.connect(process.env.AMQP_URL ?? "amqp://localhost");
const channel = await connection.createConfirmChannel();
await setupTopology(channel);

export async function publishOrderCreated(order) {
  const body = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.id, total: order.total }));
  channel.publish("orders", "order.created", body, {
    persistent: true, // survive broker restarts
    contentType: "application/json",
    messageId: randomUUID(),
    type: "OrderCreated",
    timestamp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000),
  });
  await channel.waitForConfirms(); // throws if the broker nacked
}

waitForConfirms() waits for every outstanding publish on the channel. For high throughput, publish in batches and wait once per batch.

docs.title: Consumer with prefetch, manual ack, and dead-lettering
docs.text:
// email-worker.js
import amqp from "amqplib";
import { setupTopology } from "./topology.js";

const connection = await amqp.connect(process.env.AMQP_URL ?? "amqp://localhost");
const channel = await connection.createChannel();
await setupTopology(channel);
await channel.prefetch(10); // at most 10 unacked messages for this consumer

const { consumerTag } = await channel.consume("orders.email", async (msg) => {
  if (msg === null) return; // the broker cancelled this consumer

  try {
    const event = JSON.parse(msg.content.toString("utf8"));
    await sendOrderEmail(event.orderId); // must be idempotent
    channel.ack(msg);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error("email failed", { messageId: msg.properties.messageId, err });
    // Requeue once for a transient failure; otherwise dead-letter it
    const requeue = !msg.fields.redelivered;
    channel.nack(msg, false, requeue);
  }
}, { noAck: false });

// Graceful shutdown: stop taking new messages, then close
process.on("SIGTERM", async () => {
  await channel.cancel(consumerTag); // no new deliveries
  // A real worker would wait here for in-flight handlers to finish
  await channel.close(); // anything still unacked is requeued
  await connection.close();
});

async function sendOrderEmail(orderId) {
  console.log("sending email for", orderId);
}

On a quorum queue, x-delivery-limit (20 by default since RabbitMQ 4.0) counts failed deliveries. Since RabbitMQ 4.3, only genuine failures count: a consumer or channel crash, or basic.reject (amqplib's channel.reject(msg, true)). A basic.nack with requeue (channel.nack) no longer counts, so a handler that nacks and requeues forever is never dead-lettered by the limit. That is why this worker requeues only once and then nacks without requeue.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use quorum queues for important, durable work; classic queues for temporary data.
  • Declare topology idempotently at startup (assertExchange, assertQueue) or manage it as code.
  • Publish persistent messages with publisher confirms.
  • Ack manually after processing; never use auto-ack for business work.
  • Set a prefetch count; never leave it unlimited.
  • Configure a DLX on every work queue and alert when the DLQ grows.
  • Avoid tight requeue loops: cap attempts in the handler and use delayed retry queues; do not rely on the delivery limit to catch nack requeues.
  • One connection per process, separate channels for publishing and consuming; reconnect with backoff when the connection drops.
  • Bound queue length and monitor queue depth, consumer count, and unacked messages.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Publishers hang. Detect: publish calls stall; clients receive connection.blocked; the management UI or rabbitmq-diagnostics shows a memory or disk alarm. Cause: a backlog has filled the node's memory or pushed free disk below its limit, so the broker blocks publishers to protect itself. Fix: restore or scale consumers, set queue length limits with an overflow policy, add disk, and alert on queue depth well before the alarm thresholds.
  • One consumer holds thousands of unacked messages. Detect: the queue shows a large "unacked" count on one consumer while other consumers sit idle. Cause: no prefetch limit, or a very large one, with a slow handler. Fix: set a prefetch count that matches processing speed.
  • Broker CPU high with little traffic. Detect: management metrics show very high connection and channel creation and closure rates. Cause: the application opens a connection (or channel) per message or per HTTP request. Fix: use one long-lived connection per process and reuse channels.
  • Queue empty after a broker restart. Detect: messages that were waiting before a restart are gone. Cause: a non-durable classic queue or non-persistent messages. Fix: use quorum queues (always durable) or durable queues with persistent messages, plus publisher confirms.
  • Redelivery storm. Detect: the redelivered rate is far above the publish rate; logs (or the quorum queue's x-acquired-count header) show the same message failing over and over. Cause: handlers nack with requeue on permanent errors. Fix: cap attempts in the handler and dead-letter permanent failures (since RabbitMQ 4.3, nack requeues do not count towards x-delivery-limit), and use delayed retry queues for transient ones.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Exchange: the component that receives published messages and routes them to queues.
  • Binding: a rule linking an exchange to a queue, often with a binding key.
  • Routing key: the string a producer attaches to a message for routing.
  • Default exchange: a nameless direct exchange routing by queue name.
  • Channel: a lightweight virtual connection inside a TCP connection.
  • Virtual host: an isolated namespace inside a broker.
  • Durable queue / persistent message: survives a broker restart.
  • Publisher confirm: the broker's acknowledgement to a producer.
  • Prefetch (QoS): the limit on unacknowledged messages per consumer.
  • Dead-letter exchange (DLX): where rejected, expired, or over-limit messages are sent.
  • Quorum queue: a replicated, Raft-based queue type for data safety.
  • Stream: a replayable, append-only log queue type.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Durable queue but non-persistent messages (or the reverse), then losing messages on restart.
  • Publishing without confirms and assuming every message arrived.
  • Auto-ack for important work, losing messages whenever a worker crashes.
  • No prefetch limit, so one consumer hoards the queue and memory usage spikes.
  • nack with requeue on every error, creating an infinite hot loop on poison messages.
  • Opening a new connection per message; connections are expensive.
  • Expecting strict ordering with many consumers.
  • Using RabbitMQ as long-term storage; huge backlogs hurt performance. Streams or Kafka fit replay and retention needs better.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Trace a message from producer to consumer through an exchange, binding, and queue.
  2. Compare direct, topic, fanout, and headers exchanges. Which binding matches order.eu.created: order.*, order.#, or *.eu.*?
  3. What two settings must both be in place for a message to survive a broker restart?
  4. What does the prefetch count control, and what goes wrong without it?
  5. List the reasons a message can be dead-lettered.
  6. Why are quorum queues preferred over classic queues for important data?

docs.title: Common Redis Use Cases
docs.text: Beyond caching, Redis is the shared, fast memory that many backend features depend on: sessions, rate limits, leaderboards, counters, locks, job queues, unique-visitor counts, and location search. Each pattern below combines a data structure with a few atomic commands. The lesson shows how each works, gives Node.js code, and points out where the pattern has limits.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: These features all share three needs: several application instances must see the same state, updates must be safe when many requests arrive at once, and the operations must be fast. Implementing them in the primary database often adds load, contention, and complexity. Redis's atomic commands make them short and correct, as long as you understand each pattern's guarantees, especially for locks, where Redis is often trusted more than it should be.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Stripe rate-limits its API with the token bucket algorithm, with one bucket per user, and implements its rate limiters with Redis. A separate load shedder uses a Redis cluster to count in-flight requests by type so critical requests (such as creating charges) keep capacity. Stripe also stresses failing open: if Redis goes down, requests must still be served (Stripe: Scaling your API with rate limiters).
  • GitLab keeps sessions, rate-limiting state, and its Sidekiq job queue in Redis, and runs separate Redis instances for these jobs on GitLab.com (GitLab: Redis guidelines).
  • Slack built its original job queue on Redis: enqueue requests were routed to a Redis host by a hash of the job, workers polled Redis and moved jobs to an in-flight list, and failed jobs went to a retry queue (Slack engineering).

Popular tools: BullMQ for Node.js job queues, Sidekiq (used by GitLab and Mastodon) for Ruby, and session stores such as connect-redis for Express.

docs.title: Session store
docs.text:
When an app runs on several instances, in-memory sessions break: a user who logs in on instance A appears logged out on instance B. Storing sessions in Redis gives every instance the same view, and a TTL on each session key expires idle sessions automatically.

Browser --cookie: sid=abc--> any app instance --GET sess:abc--> Redis

With Express, express-session uses a Redis store such as connect-redis; the cookie holds only the session ID. Configuration and security options are covered in cookies and sessions in Express. Keep sessions on a Redis instance that does not evict them under memory pressure (noeviction). A volatile-* policy is not enough: session keys carry TTLs, so they are eviction candidates too.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
Rate limiting counts requests per client in a time window. The algorithms (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket) are explained in rate limiting and throttling; Redis is the usual place to keep the counters because all instances share them.

Fixed window with INCR and EXPIRE:

EXPIRE ... NX (Redis 7+) sets the TTL only when the key is new.

Run both commands in one MULTI/EXEC transaction (or a Lua script) so a crash between them cannot leave a counter without a TTL. Fixed windows allow bursts at window boundaries: a client can make the full limit at 12:00:59 and again at 12:01:00.

Sliding window log with a sorted set: store one member per request with the timestamp as its score, delete members older than the window, then count what remains.

This is accurate but uses memory per request; a sliding window counter or token bucket (often written as a Lua script) is cheaper at high volume.

docs.title: Leaderboards
docs.text:
A sorted set is a leaderboard: members are player IDs, scores are points.

Need Command Add points ZINCRBY board 50 player:7 Top 10 ZRANGE board 0 9 REV WITHSCORES A player's rank (1-based) ZREVRANK board player:7 + 1 A player's score ZSCORE board player:7 Players around me ZRANGE board (rank-2) (rank+2) REV

All of these are O(log N), so they stay fast with millions of players. Use separate keys for periods (board:2026-w45) with a TTL, and decide how to break ties: members with equal scores are ordered by their member string.

docs.title: Counters
docs.text: INCR, INCRBY, and HINCRBY are atomic, so counters stay exact under concurrency: page views, API usage per customer, "likes", or inventory reservations. Group related counters in a hash per day (stats:2026-11-07 with fields per page) and periodically copy totals to the primary database for long-term reporting.

docs.title: Distributed locks
docs.text:
Sometimes only one process across all instances may do something at a time: send a daily report, refresh a cache entry, or process one user's payment. A Redis lock is a key that only one client can create.

Acquire:

SET lock:report:2026-11-07 <random-token> NX PX 30000
  • NX creates the key only if it does not exist, so only one client wins.
  • PX 30000 makes the lock expire after 30 seconds, so a crashed holder cannot block everyone forever.
  • The random token identifies the owner.

Release safely: a holder must delete the lock only if it still owns it. Otherwise this can happen: client A's work takes longer than 30 seconds, the lock expires, client B acquires it, and then A finishes and deletes B's lock. Comparing the token and deleting must be atomic, so it is done in a Lua script:

if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end

The limits of Redis locks. An expiring lock cannot guarantee mutual exclusion on its own. If the holder pauses (a long garbage-collection pause, a slow network, a stopped VM) longer than the TTL, the lock expires and a second client acquires it while the first still believes it holds it. Also, with asynchronous replication, a lock written to a primary can be lost if the primary fails before the replica received it.

  • Redlock is an algorithm that acquires the lock on a majority of several independent Redis primaries to survive single-node failures. It has been criticized (notably by Martin Kleppmann) because its safety still depends on timing assumptions about clocks and pauses.
  • The robust fix for correctness is a fencing token: a number that increases each time the lock is granted and that the protected resource (for example the database) checks, rejecting writes with an older token.

Rule of thumb: use Redis locks for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work, where an occasional overlap is harmless). When overlap would corrupt data, rely on database constraints and transactions, or a coordination system designed for consensus (such as etcd or ZooKeeper), plus fencing. See concurrency and race conditions.

docs.title: Job queues
docs.text: Slow work (emails, image processing, reports) should leave the request path and run in background workers; see background jobs and scheduling. A raw Redis list with LPUSH/BRPOP works for simple cases but loses jobs when a worker crashes and has no retries. Libraries such as BullMQ build a full queue on Redis: retries with backoff, delayed jobs, scheduled (repeatable) jobs, priorities, concurrency limits, and progress, with third-party dashboards available. Because a queue must never silently lose jobs, BullMQ's documentation says its Redis must use the noeviction memory policy, and it needs appropriate persistence.

docs.title: Unique visitors with HyperLogLog
docs.text:
Counting unique visitors exactly needs memory for every visitor ID. A HyperLogLog estimates the count within about 1% using at most about 12 KB per key:

PFADD uv:2026-11-07 <visitorId>      on every page view
PFCOUNT uv:2026-11-07                daily uniques
PFMERGE uv:2026-w45 uv:2026-11-03 ... uv:2026-11-09   weekly uniques

Use it for dashboards and analytics where an estimate is acceptable, not for billing.

docs.title: Geo search
docs.text: Geospatial indexes answer "what is near this point?": nearby drivers, stores, or events. Drivers' apps send positions every few seconds (GEOADD drivers lon lat driver:7), and the dispatcher searches with GEOSEARCH drivers FROMLONLAT lon lat BYRADIUS 3 km ASC COUNT 10 WITHDIST. Remove offline drivers with ZREM (a geo index is a sorted set underneath).

docs.title: Other common patterns
docs.text: Pattern How Idempotency keys / deduplication SET idem:<key> <result> NX EX 86400; a second request with the same key is detected. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency Online presence SET presence:user:42 1 EX 60 refreshed by a heartbeat; the key expires when the user leaves Feature flags and runtime config Hash of flags read by every instance Real-time fan-out Pub/Sub or streams; see Pub/Sub and streams One-time codes and tokens SET otp:user:42 <code> EX 300, deleted after use

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use these Redis patterns when:

  • Many instances need the same short-lived coordination state: sessions, counters, rate limits, presence, one-time codes.
  • An occasional duplicate is harmless and the goal is efficiency (a lock that avoids running the same report twice).
  • An estimate is good enough (HyperLogLog uniques) or the data can be rebuilt (leaderboards recomputed from the database).

Use something else when:

  • Two holders of a lock would corrupt data: rely on database constraints and transactions, or a consensus system such as etcd or ZooKeeper, plus fencing tokens.
  • Messages must be retained for days, routed in complex ways, or survive disk-level failures: a broker such as RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, or Kafka.
  • Counts must be exact for billing or audits: the primary database.
Need Redis pattern Alternative Prefer the alternative when Mutual exclusion SET NX PX + token Database row lock, unique constraint, etcd/ZooKeeper Overlap would corrupt data Background jobs BullMQ on Redis RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, Kafka You need long retention or strong durability Rate limiting INCR + EXPIRE, sorted set, or a Lua token bucket API gateway or proxy limits Limits are simple and per IP at the edge Sessions Session hash or string with TTL Signed cookies or JWTs You want no server-side session store Unique visitors HyperLogLog Exact set or database count Exact numbers are required

docs.title: Fixed-window rate limiter middleware
docs.text:
import { redis } from "./redis.js"; // shared node-redis client

export function rateLimit({ limit, windowSeconds, keyPrefix }) {
  return async (req, res, next) => {
    const window = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000 / windowSeconds);
    const key = `rate:${keyPrefix}:${req.ip}:${window}`;

    const [count] = await redis
      .multi()
      .incr(key)
      .expire(key, windowSeconds, "NX") // TTL only on the first request
      .exec();

    res.set("RateLimit-Limit", String(limit));
    res.set("RateLimit-Remaining", String(Math.max(0, limit - count)));
    if (count > limit) {
      res.set("Retry-After", String(windowSeconds));
      return res.status(429).json({ error: "Too many requests" });
    }
    next();
  };
}

app.post("/auth/login", rateLimit({ limit: 10, windowSeconds: 900,
  keyPrefix: "login" }), loginHandler);

docs.title: Sliding-window log
docs.text:
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

export async function allowRequest(clientId, limit, windowMs) {
  const key = `rate:sliding:${clientId}`;
  const now = Date.now();
  const results = await redis
    .multi()
    .zRemRangeByScore(key, 0, now - windowMs)
    .zAdd(key, { score: now, value: `${now}:${randomUUID()}` })
    .zCard(key)
    .pExpire(key, windowMs)
    .exec();
  const count = results[2];
  return count <= limit;
}

docs.title: Leaderboard
docs.text:
export async function addPoints(playerId, points) {
  await redis.zIncrBy("board:2026-w45", points, `player:${playerId}`);
}

export async function topPlayers(n = 10) {
  return redis.zRangeWithScores("board:2026-w45", 0, n - 1, { REV: true });
}

export async function rankOf(playerId) {
  const rank = await redis.zRevRank("board:2026-w45", `player:${playerId}`);
  return rank === null ? null : rank + 1; // 1-based for display
}

127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE board:2026-w45 0 2 REV WITHSCORES
1) "player:7"
2) "980"
3) "player:3"
4) "955"
5) "player:12"
6) "940"

docs.title: Acquiring and releasing a lock
docs.text:
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const RELEASE_SCRIPT = `
if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end`;

export async function withLock(resource, ttlMs, work) {
  const key = `lock:${resource}`;
  const token = randomUUID();

  const acquired = await redis.set(key, token, { NX: true, PX: ttlMs });
  if (!acquired) return { ran: false }; // someone else holds it

  try {
    return { ran: true, result: await work() };
  } finally {
    // Delete only if the lock is still ours.
    await redis.eval(RELEASE_SCRIPT, { keys: [key], arguments: [token] });
  }
}

// Only one instance sends the daily report.
await withLock("report:2026-11-07", 60_000, () => sendDailyReport());

docs.title: A BullMQ queue and worker
docs.text:
By default BullMQ creates its own Redis connections with the ioredis client, so you pass connection settings rather than a node-redis client (recent versions also ship adapters for other clients, including node-redis).

import { Queue, Worker } from "bullmq";

const connection = {
  host: process.env.REDIS_HOST,
  port: Number(process.env.REDIS_PORT ?? 6379),
};

export const emailQueue = new Queue("emails", { connection });

// Producer: in the request handler
await emailQueue.add(
  "welcome",
  { userId: 42 },
  { attempts: 5, backoff: { type: "exponential", delay: 1000 },
    removeOnComplete: 1000 }
);

// Consumer: in a separate worker process
const worker = new Worker(
  "emails",
  async (job) => {
    await sendWelcomeEmail(job.data.userId); // throw to trigger a retry
  },
  { connection, concurrency: 10 }
);

worker.on("failed", (job, err) => {
  console.error(`job ${job?.id} failed: ${err.message}`);
});

docs.title: Unique visitors and nearby search
docs.text:
await redis.pfAdd(`uv:${today}`, visitorId);
const uniquesToday = await redis.pfCount(`uv:${today}`);

127.0.0.1:6379> GEOADD drivers -122.4194 37.7749 driver:7 -122.4089 37.7837 driver:9
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> GEOSEARCH drivers FROMLONLAT -122.4148 37.7790 BYRADIUS 2 km ASC COUNT 5 WITHDIST
1) 1) "driver:7"
   2) "0.6095"
2) 1) "driver:9"
   2) "0.7364"

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Combine related commands in MULTI or a Lua script so state is never half-updated.
  • Give every pattern's keys a TTL or an explicit cleanup path.
  • Keep durable patterns (sessions, queues) on Redis that does not evict them; keep caches separate.
  • Use random tokens and compare-and-delete for locks; never DEL blindly.
  • Treat Redis locks as best-effort; protect correctness with database constraints or fencing tokens.
  • Prefer proven libraries (BullMQ, rate-limit stores) over hand-written queue logic.
  • Partition keys by time period for leaderboards and analytics so old data expires.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
Clients stay rate-limited forever, or memory creeps up.

  • Detect: SCAN 0 MATCH rate:* COUNT 1000 finds counters, and TTL on them returns -1 (no expiry).
  • Cause: INCR and EXPIRE ran as separate calls and the process crashed in between, or EXPIRE was forgotten.
  • Fix: run them together in MULTI/EXEC or a Lua script, and use EXPIRE ... NX so only the first request sets the TTL.

A Redis outage blocks every request.

  • Detect: API error rates jump at the same time as Redis connection errors in the logs.
  • Cause: rate-limit or session middleware treats a Redis error as a hard failure.
  • Fix: decide per feature whether to fail open; Stripe's advice for rate limiters is to catch errors so a Redis failure does not affect requests (Stripe).

The same job runs twice.

  • Detect: logs show two workers processing the same lock key or job ID at overlapping times.
  • Cause: the work took longer than the lock's TTL (a slow call or a long pause), the lock expired, and a second worker took it.
  • Fix: make the work idempotent, size the TTL well above the worst-case duration, and use fencing tokens where overlap corrupts data.

The job backlog keeps growing.

  • Detect: BullMQ's queue.getJobCounts() shows waiting jobs rising; INFO memory shows Redis memory rising with it.
  • Cause: producers outpace workers, or workers are down. Slack's Redis job queue had an outage when the backlog filled Redis's memory and workers could no longer dequeue (Slack engineering).
  • Fix: alert on queue depth, scale workers, remove completed jobs (removeOnComplete), and keep queue Redis on noeviction with memory headroom.

Everyone is logged out after Redis restarts.

  • Detect: session cookies remain but GET sess:<id> returns nothing; INFO persistence shows persistence is off, or evicted_keys is rising.
  • Cause: sessions were kept on an instance without persistence, or one that evicts keys.
  • Fix: store sessions on their own instance with AOF persistence and noeviction (a volatile-* policy would not protect them, because sessions carry TTLs), or accept re-login as a deliberate trade-off.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Session store: Shared storage for server-side session data.
  • Fixed window / sliding window: Rate-limit windows aligned to the clock or moving with each request.
  • Distributed lock: A lock coordinated across processes or machines.
  • Lock token: A random value that identifies the lock owner.
  • Fencing token: An increasing number checked by the protected resource to reject stale lock holders.
  • Redlock: An algorithm for locks across several independent Redis primaries.
  • Idempotency key: A client-supplied key that makes a repeated request safe.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• INCR then EXPIRE as separate, unprotected calls. A crash in between leaves a counter that never expires.
  • Releasing a lock with plain DEL. It can delete another client's lock.
  • "A Redis lock guarantees only one holder." Pauses, expiry, and failover can produce two holders.
  • Using a plain list as a reliable queue. Jobs vanish when a worker crashes after popping.
  • Running a job queue on Redis with an eviction policy. Jobs can be evicted silently.
  • Using HyperLogLog for exact counts. It is an estimate.
  • Storing sessions in a cache instance with allkeys-lru. Users get logged out under memory pressure.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why must INCR and EXPIRE in a rate limiter be executed together?
  2. How does a sorted set implement a sliding-window rate limiter, and what does it cost?
  3. Why does a lock release need a token and an atomic compare-and-delete?
  4. Describe a scenario where two clients both believe they hold a Redis lock, and how fencing tokens help.
  5. What does BullMQ add on top of a Redis list?
  6. When is HyperLogLog appropriate, and when is it not?
