docs.title: Redis Data Structures
docs.text: Redis is called a data structure server because every value has a type, and each type comes with commands that run on the server. Instead of reading a whole value, changing it in the application, and writing it back, you ask Redis to "add 10 to this score" or "give me the top 10". This lesson covers each core type: what it is, when to use it, how fast its key commands are, and how to use it.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Choosing the right type is the most important Redis design decision. The right structure makes an operation a single atomic, fast command; the wrong one forces you to fetch large values, process them in the application, and deal with race conditions between clients. A leaderboard built on a sorted set needs one command to update and one to read; built on a JSON string it needs a read, a sort, and a write, and it breaks under concurrent updates.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Instagram needed to map about 300 million photo IDs to the user IDs that created them. Plain SET media:<id> <userId> keys took about 70 MB per million keys, so it bucketed IDs into hashes of 1,000 fields (HSET mediabucket:1155 1155315 939). Small hashes use a compact encoding, so the same million entries took about 16 MB and all 300 million fit in under 5 GB (Instagram Engineering).
  • Slack ran its job queue on Redis. Workers moved each job from a pending queue to an in-flight list, and the engineers later found that their choice of data structures made dequeuing cost proportional to the queue's length, so long queues became harder to drain (Slack engineering).
  • BullMQ, a popular Node.js job queue, keeps job state in Redis structures, such as a waiting list that every job enters and a set for prioritized jobs, and it changes states atomically with Lua scripts (BullMQ: Architecture).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Type Think of it as Typical uses String A single value (text, number, or bytes) Cached JSON, counters, flags, tokens List An ordered sequence; fast at both ends Simple queues, recent-activity feeds Hash A small object with fields User profiles, object attributes, per-field counters Set Unordered unique members Tags, followers, "who has seen this" Sorted set Unique members ordered by a score Leaderboards, priority queues, time-ordered indexes Stream An append-only log with IDs Event logs, durable message processing Bitmap A string treated as an array of bits Daily active flags per user ID HyperLogLog A probabilistic unique counter Unique visitors with tiny memory Geospatial index Members with coordinates "Find stores near me" JSON A nested JSON document Documents updated by path

Complexity notation: O(1) means constant time regardless of size; O(log N) grows slowly with the number of elements N; O(N) grows with the size of the data touched. Prefer O(1) and O(log N) commands on hot paths and be careful with O(N) commands on large values.

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
A string holds up to 512 MB of text or binary data. Redis also treats strings that look like integers or floats as numbers for INCR-style commands.

Command Purpose Complexity SET key value [EX s] [NX\|XX] [GET] [KEEPTTL] Set a value, optionally with expiry and conditions O(1) GET key Read a value O(1) INCR / INCRBY / DECR / INCRBYFLOAT Atomic arithmetic O(1) MGET / MSET Read or write several keys O(N) keys APPEND, STRLEN, GETRANGE Text operations O(1) / O(1) / O(N)

SET ... NX sets only if the key does not exist (the basis of locks and "first writer wins"); XX sets only if it does exist.

127.0.0.1:6379> SET page:home:views 0
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR page:home:views
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> INCRBY page:home:views 10
(integer) 11
127.0.0.1:6379> SET lock:invoice:7 "worker-a" NX EX 30
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> SET lock:invoice:7 "worker-b" NX EX 30
(nil)

INCR is atomic, so a thousand clients incrementing at once never lose an update, unlike "read, add one, write back" in application code.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
A list is an ordered sequence of strings. Pushing and popping at the ends is O(1); accessing the middle is O(N).

Command Purpose Complexity LPUSH / RPUSH key v... Add to the head / tail O(1) per element LPOP / RPOP key Remove from the head / tail O(1) LRANGE key start stop Read a range (0 -1 is everything) O(S+N) LLEN key Length O(1) LTRIM key start stop Keep only a range O(N) removed BLPOP / BRPOP key... timeout Pop, or wait until an element arrives O(N) keys LMOVE src dst LEFT RIGHT Atomically move an element between lists O(1) 
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH feed:42 "liked post 9" "followed ada"
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH feed:42 "commented on post 3"
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> LTRIM feed:42 0 99        # keep the newest 100 items
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE feed:42 0 1
1) "commented on post 3"
2) "followed ada"
127.0.0.1:6379> RPUSH jobs "email:1" "email:2"
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> BLPOP jobs 5              # wait up to 5 seconds
1) "jobs"
2) "email:1"

LPUSH plus BRPOP makes a simple work queue: producers push, workers block until a job is available. Because a popped job is gone, a worker that crashes loses it; LMOVE into a "processing" list, streams, or a library such as BullMQ solve that (see common use cases).

docs.title: Hashes
docs.text:
A hash maps field names to string values inside one key, like a small object. Small hashes are stored very compactly, so many small hashes are memory-efficient.

Command Purpose Complexity HSET key field value [field value ...] Set fields O(1) per field HGET key field / HMGET Read fields O(1) per field HGETALL key Read all fields O(N) HINCRBY key field n Atomic arithmetic on one field O(1) HDEL, HEXISTS, HLEN Delete, test, count O(1) 
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET user:42 name "Ada" plan "pro" logins 0
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> HINCRBY user:42 logins 1
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HGET user:42 plan
"pro"
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETALL user:42
1) "name"
2) "Ada"
3) "plan"
4) "pro"
5) "logins"
6) "1"

Use a hash instead of a JSON string when you update individual fields: HINCRBY changes one field atomically without rewriting the rest. TTLs apply to the whole key; Redis 7.4 and later can also expire individual hash fields with HEXPIRE.

docs.title: Sets
docs.text:
A set is an unordered collection of unique strings. Adding a member that is already present does nothing.

Command Purpose Complexity SADD key m... Add members O(1) per member SISMEMBER key m Membership test O(1) SREM key m... Remove members O(1) per member SCARD key Count O(1) SMEMBERS key All members O(N) SINTER Intersection O(N*M) worst case: N = smallest set, M = number of sets SUNION / SDIFF Union / difference O(N), N = total members of all sets SRANDMEMBER, SPOP Random member(s) O(1); O(N) with a count of N 
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD post:9:likes user:1 user:2 user:3
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD post:9:likes user:2
(integer) 0                     # already a member
127.0.0.1:6379> SISMEMBER post:9:likes user:2
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD user:1:follows ada sam lee
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD user:2:follows sam lee kim
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SINTER user:1:follows user:2:follows   # mutual follows
1) "sam"
2) "lee"                        # sets are unordered: order may differ

docs.title: Sorted sets
docs.text:
A sorted set stores unique members, each with a numeric score, and keeps them ordered by score. Internally it combines a skip list (for ordered ranges) with a hash table (for direct score lookups), which is why most operations are O(log N).

Command Purpose Complexity ZADD key score member... Add or update scores O(log N) per member ZINCRBY key n member Add to a member's score O(log N) ZSCORE key member Read a score O(1) ZRANK / ZREVRANK key member Position (0-based) O(log N) ZRANGE key start stop [REV] [WITHSCORES] Range by rank O(log N + M) ZRANGE key min max BYSCORE Range by score O(log N + M) ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key min max Delete by score range O(log N + M) ZCARD key Count O(1) 
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD leaderboard 120 ada 95 sam 140 lee
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> ZINCRBY leaderboard 30 sam
"125"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE leaderboard 0 2 REV WITHSCORES
1) "lee"
2) "140"
3) "sam"
4) "125"
5) "ada"
6) "120"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZREVRANK leaderboard ada
(integer) 2

Using a timestamp as the score turns a sorted set into a time index: ZRANGE events 1730000000 1730003600 BYSCORE returns everything in an hour, and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE deletes old entries. This is the basis of the sliding-window rate limiter in common use cases.

docs.title: Streams
docs.text:
A stream is an append-only log. Each entry has an ID (by default <milliseconds>-<sequence>, generated with *) and a set of field-value pairs. Unlike Pub/Sub, entries are stored, can be re-read, and can be processed by consumer groups with acknowledgments.

Command Purpose Complexity XADD key [MAXLEN ~ n] * field value... Append an entry O(1) XRANGE key start end [COUNT n] Read a range of entries O(N), N = entries returned XREAD [BLOCK ms] STREAMS key id Read new entries, optionally waiting O(M) returned XLEN key Number of entries O(1) 
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD orders * orderId 1001 total 49.90
"1730900000000-0"
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD orders * orderId 1002 total 15.00
"1730900000123-0"
127.0.0.1:6379> XRANGE orders - + COUNT 10
1) 1) "1730900000000-0"
   2) 1) "orderId"
      2) "1001"
      3) "total"
      4) "49.90"
2) 1) "1730900000123-0"
   2) 1) "orderId"
      2) "1002"
      3) "total"
      4) "15.00"

Consumer groups and trimming are covered in Pub/Sub and streams.

docs.title: Bitmaps
docs.text:
Bitmaps are not a separate type: they are strings manipulated bit by bit. A bit offset can represent a numeric user ID, so one key can record a yes/no fact for millions of users in a few megabytes.

Command Purpose Complexity SETBIT key offset 0\|1 Set one bit O(1) GETBIT key offset Read one bit O(1) BITCOUNT key Count bits set to 1 O(N) BITOP AND\|OR\|XOR dest keys... Combine bitmaps O(N) 
127.0.0.1:6379> SETBIT active:2026-11-07 42 1      # user 42 was active
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SETBIT active:2026-11-07 1001 1
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> BITCOUNT active:2026-11-07
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> GETBIT active:2026-11-07 7
(integer) 0

Bitmaps work best with dense, small integer IDs. Sparse or very large IDs (such as UUIDs) waste memory or do not fit.

docs.title: HyperLogLog
docs.text:
A HyperLogLog estimates how many unique items it has seen using at most about 12 KB per key, no matter how many items are added. The estimate has a standard error of about 0.81%, and you cannot list the members.

Command Purpose Complexity PFADD key element... Add elements O(1) per element PFCOUNT key... Estimated unique count O(1) for one key PFMERGE dest keys... Combine estimates O(N) keys 
127.0.0.1:6379> PFADD visitors:2026-11-07 ip:1 ip:2 ip:3 ip:2
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> PFCOUNT visitors:2026-11-07
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> PFMERGE visitors:week visitors:2026-11-06 visitors:2026-11-07
OK

A set would give an exact count but would store every visitor; for millions of daily uniques, HyperLogLog trades a tiny error for enormous memory savings.

docs.title: Geospatial indexes
docs.text:
Geospatial commands store members with longitude and latitude (internally in a sorted set, using a geohash as the score) and answer radius and box searches. Note the order: longitude first, then latitude.

Command Purpose Complexity GEOADD key lon lat member... Add locations O(log N) per item GEODIST key m1 m2 km Distance between two members O(1) GEOSEARCH key FROMLONLAT lon lat BYRADIUS r km [ASC] [COUNT n] [WITHDIST] Members within a radius or box O(N + log M) 
127.0.0.1:6379> GEOADD stores -73.9857 40.7484 midtown -74.0060 40.7128 downtown
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> GEODIST stores midtown downtown km
"4.3135"
127.0.0.1:6379> GEOSEARCH stores FROMLONLAT -73.99 40.73 BYRADIUS 5 km ASC WITHDIST
1) 1) "midtown"
   2) "2.0784"
2) 1) "downtown"
   2) "2.3407"

(Redis computes distances with the haversine formula, so the last digit can differ slightly between versions; ASC sorts nearest first.)

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
The JSON type stores a nested document and lets you read or update parts of it by JSONPath without rewriting the whole value. It is provided by the JSON module (part of Redis Stack) and is included in Redis 8 and later; it is not available on every Redis-compatible server, so check yours.

127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.SET cart:42 $ '{"items":[{"sku":"A1","qty":1}],"total":20}'
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.NUMINCRBY cart:42 $.total 5
"[25]"
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.GET cart:42 $.items[0].sku
"[\"A1\"]"

If JSON is not available, store a serialized string (whole-value updates) or a hash (flat fields).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a specialized Redis type when:

  • The operation you repeat is one of its commands: counting (INCR), ranking (ZINCRBY, ZRANGE ... REV), membership (SISMEMBER), capped feeds (LPUSH + LTRIM), approximate uniques (PFADD).
  • Many clients update the same value concurrently and must not lose updates.
  • The collection stays bounded (trimmed, expired, or split by time).

Use something else when:

  • You need to query records by arbitrary fields, sort by several columns, or join data: use a database (or a search index).
  • Values are large files or documents read as a whole: object storage or a document database is cheaper than RAM.
  • A collection would grow without limit and you cannot trim it.

Choosing how to store one object:

Option Read or update one field Atomic field increments Nested data Availability String with serialized JSON Read and rewrite the whole value No Yes Everywhere Hash HGET / HSET one field HINCRBY No (flat) Everywhere JSON type By JSONPath JSON.NUMINCRBY Yes Redis 8+ or the JSON module

Choosing a queue or feed:

Option Order Survives a worker crash Replay history Typical use List (LPUSH / BRPOP) Insertion No, unless moved to a processing list with LMOVE No Simple queues, capped feeds Sorted set By score (time, priority) Not by itself Yes, until removed Delayed jobs, time indexes Stream with consumer groups By entry ID Yes (pending entries, XACK) Yes, until trimmed Durable event processing

docs.title: Data structures from Node.js
docs.text:
import { createClient } from "redis";

const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
redis.on("error", (err) => console.error(err));
await redis.connect();

// String counter
await redis.incr("page:home:views");

// Hash: an object with fields
await redis.hSet("user:42", { name: "Ada", plan: "pro" });
await redis.hIncrBy("user:42", "logins", 1);
const user = await redis.hGetAll("user:42"); // { name: "Ada", plan: "pro", logins: "1" }

// Set: unique members
await redis.sAdd("post:9:likes", "user:1");
const liked = await redis.sIsMember("post:9:likes", "user:1"); // 1 (v4 returned true)

// Sorted set: leaderboard
await redis.zAdd("leaderboard", [
  { score: 120, value: "ada" },
  { score: 140, value: "lee" },
]);
await redis.zIncrBy("leaderboard", 30, "ada");
const top = await redis.zRangeWithScores("leaderboard", 0, 9, { REV: true });
// [ { value: "ada", score: 150 }, { value: "lee", score: 140 } ]

// List: recent activity capped at 100
await redis.lPush("feed:42", "logged in");
await redis.lTrim("feed:42", 0, 99);

// HyperLogLog: unique visitors
await redis.pfAdd("visitors:2026-11-07", ["ip:1", "ip:2"]);
const uniques = await redis.pfCount("visitors:2026-11-07");

Note that hash values come back as strings: Redis stores everything as strings or bytes, so convert numbers yourself.

docs.title: Choosing a structure
docs.text: Requirement Structure "Count page views" String + INCR "Store a user's profile and update one field" Hash "Has this user already voted?" Set + SISMEMBER "Top 10 players" Sorted set "Last 50 notifications" List + LPUSH + LTRIM "Process events reliably, with replay" Stream with consumer groups "Approximate unique visitors per day" HyperLogLog "Which users were active on each day" (integer IDs) Bitmap "Restaurants within 3 km" Geospatial index

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Pick the type from the operations you need, not from the data's shape alone.
  • Use atomic server-side commands (INCR, HINCRBY, ZINCRBY, SADD) instead of read-modify-write in the application.
  • Keep collections bounded: trim lists, cap streams, and expire keys.
  • Avoid O(N) commands (HGETALL, SMEMBERS, LRANGE 0 -1) on large values in hot paths; use HSCAN, SSCAN, or ZSCAN to iterate.
  • Split huge collections across several keys (for example by day or by ID range).
  • Remember that numbers come back as strings in most clients.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
Latency spikes caused by big keys.

  • Detect: redis-cli --bigkeys and redis-cli --memkeys scan the keyspace for the largest keys; MEMORY USAGE key measures one key; SLOWLOG GET shows HGETALL, SMEMBERS, LRANGE 0 -1, or DEL taking milliseconds.
  • Cause: a collection that grew without bounds, such as a per-user list that is never trimmed or one hash holding millions of fields.
  • Fix: cap collections (LTRIM, XADD ... MAXLEN ~), split them by time or ID range, iterate with HSCAN/SSCAN/ZSCAN, and delete with UNLINK.

Memory grows faster than the number of entries.

  • Detect: OBJECT ENCODING key changes from listpack to hashtable (or skiplist for sorted sets) once a collection grows; MEMORY USAGE per entry jumps.
  • Cause: small hashes, sets, and sorted sets use a compact encoding until they pass limits such as hash-max-listpack-entries; beyond that each entry costs more.
  • Fix: keep collections small where memory matters (Instagram's bucketing into hashes of 1,000 fields is the classic example), or plan capacity for the larger encoding.

WRONGTYPE errors after a deploy.

  • Detect: commands fail with a WRONGTYPE error; TYPE key shows the key holds a different type than the code expects.
  • Cause: two features use the same key name, or a new release changed a key from a string to a hash without changing its name.
  • Fix: prefix keys by feature and include a version (cache:v2:product:17) when the stored shape changes.

Streams and lists that never stop growing.

  • Detect: XLEN or LLEN rises steadily; XINFO GROUPS key shows consumer groups falling behind.
  • Cause: producers outpace consumers, or no trimming is configured.
  • Fix: trim with MAXLEN ~ or MINID, add consumers, and alert on queue length.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Score: The number that orders members of a sorted set.
  • Skip list: A layered linked structure that gives sorted sets O(log N) ordered access.
  • Stream entry ID: A milliseconds-sequence identifier for a stream entry.
  • Bitmap: A string addressed as individual bits.
  • HyperLogLog: A probabilistic algorithm that estimates distinct counts in fixed memory.
  • Geohash: An encoding of a location into a sortable number.
  • Big key: A single key holding a very large value or collection.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Storing everything as JSON strings. Updates require read-modify-write and race with other clients.
  • Using a list as a queue without handling crashes. A popped item is lost if the worker dies.
  • Unbounded lists, sets, and streams. They grow until memory runs out.
  • Swapping latitude and longitude in GEOADD. Longitude comes first.
  • Expecting exact counts from HyperLogLog. It returns an estimate.
  • Using bitmaps with UUIDs or sparse IDs. Offsets must be small integers to be efficient.
  • Assuming JSON commands exist everywhere. They require the JSON module or Redis 8+.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is INCR safer than reading a counter, adding one, and writing it back?
  2. When would you choose a hash over a JSON string?
  3. What makes sorted-set operations O(log N), and what problems do sorted sets solve well?
  4. What trade-off does HyperLogLog make compared with a set?
  5. How do streams differ from lists for message processing?
  6. Which structure would you use for "the latest 20 comments", and how do you keep it bounded?

docs.title: Redis Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review Redis fundamentals, data structures, caching, common patterns, messaging, atomic operations, persistence, and high availability.

docs.title: 1. What is Redis?
docs.text: Redis is an in-memory data structure server. Clients store values under keys and manipulate them with type-specific commands for strings, lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams, and more. It is used for caching, sessions, counters, rate limits, queues, leaderboards, and messaging.

docs.title: 2. Why is Redis so fast?
docs.text: Data lives in memory, commands are executed one at a time by a single main thread without locking, small values use compact encodings, and the protocol is cheap to parse. Optional I/O threads (since Redis 6) handle network reads and writes in parallel while command execution stays single-threaded.

docs.title: 3. If Redis is single-threaded, what is the main operational risk?
docs.text: A slow command blocks every other client until it finishes. KEYS * on a large dataset, DEL of a huge value, HGETALL on a giant hash, or a long Lua script can freeze the server. Use SCAN, UNLINK, bounded collections, and short scripts.

docs.title: 4. How does key expiration work?
docs.text: A key can have a TTL set with EXPIRE, SET ... EX, and related commands. Redis deletes expired keys lazily when they are accessed and actively through a background cycle that samples keys with TTLs. TTL returns -1 for no expiry and -2 for a missing key.

docs.title: 5. Which operations clear a key's TTL?
docs.text: Commands that replace the value, such as SET without KEEPTTL, clear the TTL. Commands that modify the value in place, such as INCR, LPUSH, or HSET, keep it. PERSIST removes a TTL explicitly.

docs.title: 6. Why should you use SCAN instead of KEYS?
docs.text: KEYS pattern walks the entire keyspace in one blocking call. SCAN returns keys in small batches with a cursor, so the server keeps serving other clients. SCAN may return a key more than once, so callers should deduplicate.

docs.title: 7. How does Redis compare with Memcached?
docs.text: Both are in-memory caches. Memcached stores only strings, is multi-threaded, and has no persistence or built-in replication. Redis offers rich data types, persistence, replication, failover, clustering, Pub/Sub, streams, transactions, and scripting.

docs.title: 8. What is Valkey?
docs.text: Valkey is a BSD-licensed fork of the last open-source Redis code (the 7.2 line), started under the Linux Foundation in March 2024 after Redis moved new versions to source-available licenses. It is command-compatible for shared features, and some managed services, such as Amazon ElastiCache, offer it.

docs.title: 9. What data types does Redis support?
docs.text: Strings, lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps (operations on strings), HyperLogLog, and geospatial indexes, plus JSON through the JSON module (included in Redis 8 and later). Each type has its own commands.

docs.title: 10. Why is INCR safer than reading and writing a counter in the application?
docs.text: INCR performs the read and update as one atomic command, so concurrent clients never overwrite each other's increments. A read-modify-write in the application can lose updates when two clients read the same value.

docs.title: 11. When would you use a hash instead of a JSON string?
docs.text: Use a hash when you read or update individual fields, such as incrementing a login counter with HINCRBY, because a JSON string must be read, changed, and rewritten as a whole. Small hashes are also stored compactly. JSON strings (or the JSON type) suit nested data that is read whole.

docs.title: 12. How is a sorted set implemented, and what is it good for?
docs.text: It combines a skip list, which keeps members ordered by score with O(log N) inserts and range queries, with a hash table for O(1) score lookups. It suits leaderboards, priority queues, time-ordered indexes, and sliding-window rate limiting.

docs.title: 13. How do lists and streams differ for queuing?
docs.text: A list pops an item and forgets it, so a worker crash loses the item and there are no acknowledgments. A stream stores entries with IDs, supports consumer groups, tracks unacknowledged entries, and allows replay and recovery.

docs.title: 14. What is HyperLogLog?
docs.text: A probabilistic structure that estimates the number of distinct elements using at most about 12 KB per key, with a standard error of about 0.81%. It cannot list its members. It is used for approximate unique visitors or searches.

docs.title: 15. What are bitmaps used for?
docs.text: Bitmaps treat a string as an array of bits addressed by offset. With integer user IDs as offsets, one key can record a yes/no fact, such as "was active today", for millions of users compactly, and BITCOUNT and BITOP compute totals and combinations.

docs.title: 16. How do geospatial commands work?
docs.text: GEOADD stores members with longitude and latitude in a sorted set, using a geohash as the score. GEOSEARCH finds members within a radius or box, and GEODIST measures distances. Longitude comes before latitude.

docs.title: 17. How does cache-aside work with Redis?
docs.text: The application checks Redis first. On a hit it returns the cached value; on a miss it loads from the database, stores the result in Redis with a TTL, and returns it. On writes, it updates the database and then deletes the cached key.

docs.title: 18. Why delete cache entries on write instead of updating them?
docs.text: Two concurrent writers that update the cache can finish in a different order than their database writes, leaving an old value cached. Deleting forces the next read to load the current value. A TTL bounds staleness if an invalidation is missed.

docs.title: 19. Why add jitter to TTLs?
docs.text: Keys created together with the same TTL expire together, sending a burst of misses to the database. Randomizing each TTL slightly spreads expirations out over time.

docs.title: 20. What eviction policies does Redis offer?
docs.text: noeviction rejects writes when memory is full. allkeys-lru and allkeys-lfu evict the least recently or least frequently used keys; volatile-lru, volatile-lfu, volatile-ttl, and volatile-random only evict keys with a TTL; allkeys-random evicts randomly. Current Redis documentation also lists allkeys-lrm and volatile-lrm (least recently modified). Caches usually use an allkeys policy.

docs.title: 21. What is a big key, and why is it a problem?
docs.text: A big key is a single value or collection that is very large. Reading, writing, or deleting it blocks the command thread, saturates the network, and concentrates memory on one cluster node. Find big keys with redis-cli --bigkeys or MEMORY USAGE and split or shrink them.

docs.title: 22. What is a cache stampede, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: When a popular key expires, many concurrent requests miss and all query the database at once. Prevent it with jittered TTLs, a short lock so only one request rebuilds the value, early background refresh of hot keys, and serving slightly stale data while rebuilding.

docs.title: 23. How do you measure cache effectiveness?
docs.text: Compute the hit rate from INFO stats: keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses). These counters are server-wide, so per-prefix metrics in the application are more precise. Also monitor evictions, memory, and latency.

docs.title: 24. Why store sessions in Redis?
docs.text: With several application instances, in-process sessions are not shared, so users appear logged out when routed elsewhere. Redis gives every instance the same session data with automatic expiry. Session data must not be evicted, so it belongs on an instance with noeviction; a volatile-* policy would not protect it, because session keys carry TTLs.

docs.title: 25. How do you implement a fixed-window rate limiter in Redis?
docs.text: Use a key per client and window, INCR it for each request, and set a TTL equal to the window when the key is created, inside one transaction or Lua script. Reject the request with 429 when the count exceeds the limit.

docs.title: 26. How does a sorted set implement a sliding-window rate limiter?
docs.text: Store each request as a member scored by its timestamp. For each new request, remove members older than the window with ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, add the new one, and count with ZCARD. It is accurate but stores one member per request.

docs.title: 27. How do you build a leaderboard?
docs.text: Use a sorted set with player IDs as members and points as scores. ZINCRBY adds points, ZRANGE ... REV WITHSCORES returns the top players, and ZREVRANK gives a player's rank, all in O(log N) time.

docs.title: 28. How do you acquire and release a Redis lock correctly?
docs.text: Acquire with SET lock:resource <random-token> NX PX <ttl> so only one client succeeds and the lock expires if the holder crashes. Release with a Lua script that deletes the key only if its value still equals your token, so you never delete a lock someone else acquired after yours expired.

docs.title: 29. What are the limitations of Redis locks and Redlock?
docs.text: An expiring lock can be held by two clients if the first pauses longer than the TTL, and asynchronous replication can lose a lock on failover. Redlock uses a majority of independent primaries, but its safety still depends on timing assumptions. Use Redis locks for efficiency, and fencing tokens or database constraints when correctness matters.

docs.title: 30. What is a fencing token?
docs.text: A number that increases every time a lock is granted. The protected resource remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects operations carrying an older one, so a client whose lock silently expired cannot overwrite newer work.

docs.title: 31. Why use BullMQ instead of a plain Redis list for jobs?
docs.text: A list loses jobs when a worker crashes after popping and has no retries. BullMQ adds retries with backoff, delayed jobs, scheduled (repeatable) jobs, priorities, concurrency control, and job events, and it moves each job between states atomically with Lua scripts. Its documentation requires the noeviction policy so jobs are never evicted.

docs.title: 32. What delivery guarantee does Redis Pub/Sub provide?
docs.text: At most once. Messages are delivered only to clients subscribed at that moment and are not stored, so disconnected or slow subscribers miss them. There are no acknowledgments or retries.

docs.title: 33. Why does a subscriber need its own connection?
docs.text: With the RESP2 protocol, a connection that has subscribed can only run subscription commands and PING. Applications therefore use one connection for subscriptions and another for normal commands.

docs.title: 34. How do consumer groups work in Redis Streams?
docs.text: A consumer group tracks the last entry delivered to the group. Each entry is given to one consumer in the group via XREADGROUP, recorded in the pending entries list until XACK, and can be claimed by another consumer with XAUTOCLAIM if the original consumer fails. Several groups can read the same stream independently.

docs.title: 35. What is the pending entries list?
docs.text: The list of entries delivered to consumers in a group but not yet acknowledged. It lets a restarted consumer reprocess its own unacknowledged entries and lets other consumers take over stale ones. It also records how many times each entry was delivered.

docs.title: 36. How do you stop a stream from growing forever?
docs.text: Trim it with MAXLEN (keep roughly N entries) or MINID (drop entries older than an ID), either on XADD or with XTRIM. The ~ modifier trims approximately and is much cheaper. Acknowledging entries does not delete them.

docs.title: 37. When would you choose Kafka or RabbitMQ over Redis Streams?
docs.text: When you need long retention or volumes larger than memory, partitioned scaling across many brokers, strong durability with disk-replicated acknowledgments, or rich routing features. Redis Streams fit moderate, short-lived workloads where Redis is already in use.

docs.title: 38. What does MULTI/EXEC guarantee?
docs.text: Queued commands run sequentially at EXEC with no other client's commands interleaved. If a command is rejected while queuing, nothing runs. It does not roll back: if a command fails during execution, the others still take effect.

docs.title: 39. What does WATCH do?
docs.text: WATCH marks keys so that the next EXEC on that connection aborts (returns nil) if any watched key changed in the meantime. It provides optimistic locking for read-decide-write logic, with the client retrying on conflict.

docs.title: 40. What is pipelining, and is it atomic?
docs.text: Pipelining sends many commands without waiting for each reply, saving round trips and system calls. It is not atomic: other clients' commands can run between pipelined commands. Combine it with MULTI/EXEC when atomicity is also needed.

docs.title: 41. Why use Lua scripts, and what are their risks?
docs.text: A script runs atomically on the server, so it can read, decide, and write in one step without races and in one round trip. Because nothing else runs during a script, long scripts block all clients and trigger BUSY errors. Scripts must receive all key names through KEYS.

docs.title: 42. Why must keys be passed in KEYS rather than built inside a script?
docs.text: Redis uses the declared keys to route the script to the right node in a cluster, to verify they share a hash slot, and to check access permissions. Keys built inside the script bypass these checks and break in clustered deployments.

docs.title: 43. What are Redis Functions?
docs.text: Introduced in Redis 7.0, Functions are named server-side functions grouped in libraries, loaded with FUNCTION LOAD and called with FCALL. Unlike scripts in the EVAL cache, they are persisted and replicated with the data, so they survive restarts and failovers.

docs.title: 44. Compare RDB and AOF persistence.
docs.text: RDB writes periodic point-in-time snapshots: compact and fast to load, but writes since the last snapshot are lost on a crash. AOF logs every write and replays it on restart; with appendfsync everysec at most about one second is lost. Many deployments use both.

docs.title: 45. Is Redis replication synchronous?
docs.text: No. The primary acknowledges writes before replicas receive them, so a failover can lose recent writes. WAIT can block until a number of replicas have the data, and min-replicas-to-write makes an isolated primary refuse writes, but neither makes Redis strongly consistent.

docs.title: 46. What does Redis Sentinel do?
docs.text: Sentinel processes monitor a primary and its replicas, agree by quorum that the primary has failed, promote a replica, reconfigure the others, and tell clients the new primary's address. At least three Sentinels on separate machines are recommended.

docs.title: 47. How does Redis Cluster distribute data?
docs.text: Keys map to one of 16,384 hash slots using CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each primary owns a range of slots, with replicas for failover. Hash tags ({...}) force related keys into the same slot. Clients follow MOVED and ASK redirects to reach the node that owns a slot.

docs.title: 48. What limitations does Redis Cluster place on applications?
docs.text: Multi-key commands, transactions, and scripts work only when all keys are in the same slot; otherwise Redis returns CROSSSLOT. Only database 0 is available, and clients must be cluster-aware.

docs.title: 49. When would you choose Sentinel versus Cluster?
docs.text: Choose Sentinel when the dataset and write load fit on one primary and you need automatic failover with no multi-key restrictions. Choose Cluster when data or write throughput exceeds one server and you can design keys with hash tags.

docs.title: 50. Is Redis persistence a backup strategy?
docs.text: No. Persistence and replicas reproduce mistakes such as FLUSHALL or a bad deploy. Take scheduled RDB backups, store them off the server, and test restores.

docs.title: 51. Redis latency spikes every few minutes and clients time out. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the spikes line up with something periodic: snapshots (save rules), AOF rewrites, key expiry bursts, or a cron job.

How to confirm: run SLOWLOG GET for slow commands; enable the latency monitor (CONFIG SET latency-monitor-threshold 100) and read LATENCY DOCTOR; compare latest_fork_usec in INFO stats with the spike times.

Likely causes and fixes: a slow command such as KEYS * or a DEL of a big key (use SCAN, UNLINK, split big keys); slow forks on a large dataset or with transparent huge pages (disable THP, smaller instances, schedule saves off-peak). See Redis fundamentals and persistence and high availability.

docs.title: 52. Writes start failing with out-of-memory errors while reads still work. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: INFO memory for used_memory versus maxmemory, and the maxmemory-policy.

How to confirm: the policy is noeviction (the default) and memory is at the limit; --bigkeys/--memkeys show which keys hold the memory.

Likely causes and fixes: keys without TTLs, big keys, or a growing backlog. Add TTLs, choose an eviction policy for cache instances, keep must-keep data on separate noeviction instances, and alert well before the limit. See using Redis as a cache.

docs.title: 53. Users are randomly logged out during busy hours. How do you investigate?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether sessions share a Redis instance with a cache that evicts keys.

How to confirm: evicted_keys in INFO stats rises during the busy hours; GET sess:<id> returns nothing for users who still hold a session cookie.

Likely causes and fixes: an allkeys-* policy evicts session keys, and a volatile-* policy would too, because sessions have TTLs. Move sessions to their own noeviction instance with persistence. See common use cases.

docs.title: 54. After you add a Redis cache, the database still gets a load spike every five minutes. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the hot keys share the same TTL (300 seconds) and expire together.

How to confirm: keyspace_misses and database queries per second jump at the same moments; TTL on the hot keys counts down in step.

Likely causes and fixes: synchronized expiry and a cache stampede on hot keys. Add TTL jitter, let one request rebuild with a short SET lock:<key> <token> NX PX lock, and refresh the hottest keys early. See using Redis as a cache.

docs.title: 55. A product's new price is in the database, but users still see the old one. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the code path that updated the price also deleted the cache key.

How to confirm: GET on the cache key returns the old JSON while the database has the new value; TTL shows how long it will survive.

Likely causes and fixes: a write path that skips invalidation, a cache update racing with another writer, or a key that omits an input such as the language. Delete keys after every write, keep TTLs as a safety net, and use versioned keys for bulk changes. See using Redis as a cache.

docs.title: 56. After a failover, a few orders marked "paid" in Redis are missing. How could that happen?
docs.text:
What to check first: the timeline of the failover against the missing writes.

How to confirm: the writes were acknowledged by the old primary just before it failed; the promoted replica's replication offset was behind.

Likely causes and fixes: replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes not yet sent to a replica are lost. Use WAIT for important writes, configure min-replicas-to-write and min-replicas-max-lag, and keep payment state in a database. See persistence and high availability.

docs.title: 57. After moving to Redis Cluster, some operations fail with CROSSSLOT. How do you fix them?
docs.text:
What to check first: which commands, transactions, or scripts touch more than one key.

How to confirm: CLUSTER KEYSLOT on each key shows different slots.

Likely causes and fixes: related keys hash to different slots. Give keys used together the same hash tag ({user:42}:cart, {user:42}:orders), pass every key in KEYS for scripts, and use pipelined single-key commands where keys cannot share a slot. See transactions, pipelining, and Lua.

docs.title: 58. EVALSHA calls start failing with NOSCRIPT right after a failover. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the script was loaded only on the old primary.

How to confirm: SCRIPT EXISTS <sha1> on the new primary returns 0.

Likely causes and fixes: the script cache is volatile and can be cleared on restart or failover. Fall back to EVAL on NOSCRIPT (most clients do), or load the logic as a Redis Function, which is persisted and replicated. See transactions, pipelining, and Lua.

docs.title: 59. Every client suddenly gets BUSY errors. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether a Lua script or Function is still running.

How to confirm: the Redis log reports a script running too long; the errors started when a script exceeded busy-reply-threshold.

Likely causes and fixes: a script looping over a large collection. Use SCRIPT KILL (or FUNCTION KILL) if it has not written anything; otherwise only SHUTDOWN NOSAVE is allowed. Rewrite it to touch a bounded number of keys. See transactions, pipelining, and Lua.

docs.title: 60. A stream's consumer group keeps falling behind and the pending list grows. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: XINFO GROUPS key for lag and pending.

How to confirm: the XPENDING key group summary shows old entries assigned to consumers that crashed or keep failing on the same entries.

Likely causes and fixes: crashed consumers, poison messages, or too few consumers. Run XAUTOCLAIM periodically, acknowledge only after success, dead-letter entries with high delivery counts, add consumers, and trim with MAXLEN ~ or MINID. See Pub/Sub and streams.

docs.title: 61. Users who reconnect to a chat miss messages sent while they were away. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether messages are delivered with Pub/Sub.

How to confirm: PUBLISH returned 0 or a lower count than expected while the user's server was reconnecting.

Likely causes and fixes: Pub/Sub is at-most-once and stores nothing. Load recent history from the database (or a stream) on reconnect, or carry must-deliver events in a stream with a consumer group. See Pub/Sub and streams.

docs.title: 62. One client stays rate-limited long after the window should have reset. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the TTL of that client's counter key.

How to confirm: TTL rate:<prefix>:<ip>:<window> returns -1, meaning the key never expires.

Likely causes and fixes: INCR and EXPIRE ran as separate calls and the process crashed in between, or EXPIRE was skipped. Run them together in MULTI/EXEC or a Lua script, use EXPIRE ... NX, and delete the stuck key. See common use cases.

docs.title: 63. A daily report was sent twice even though it is protected by a Redis lock. How?
docs.text:
What to check first: how long the job took compared with the lock's TTL.

How to confirm: logs show the first worker still running when the second acquired the lock; GC pauses or slow calls stretched the first run.

Likely causes and fixes: the lock expired while its holder was still working, so a second worker took it. Make the job idempotent, set the TTL well above the worst case, and use fencing tokens or a database constraint where duplicates cause harm. See common use cases.

docs.title: 64. After a traffic increase, new connections to Redis are refused. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: connected_clients versus maxclients (10,000 by default) in INFO clients.

How to confirm: rejected_connections in INFO stats is increasing; the connection count grows with request volume.

Likely causes and fixes: a client created per request, or connections never closed. Create one client per process, reuse it, close it on shutdown, and size maxclients and file-descriptor limits for the real number of processes. See Redis fundamentals.

docs.title: 65. A replica keeps re-copying the whole dataset from the primary. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: sync_full in INFO stats and the replica's master_link_status.

How to confirm: each reconnect triggers a full resynchronization instead of a partial one, and the logs show the replication link dropping during transfers.

Likely causes and fixes: the replication backlog (repl-backlog-size, 1 MB by default) is too small to cover the disconnect, or the client-output-buffer-limit replica setting cuts the link during large transfers. Raise both for big or busy datasets. See persistence and high availability.

docs.text:
• Redis overview
  • Redis documentation: Data types

docs.title: Persistence and High Availability
docs.text: Redis keeps data in memory, but it can also write that data to disk and copy it to other servers. Persistence (RDB snapshots and the AOF log) decides how much data survives a restart. Replication, Sentinel, and Redis Cluster decide whether Redis keeps serving when a server fails and how it grows beyond one machine. This lesson explains each mechanism, the trade-offs, and how managed services package them.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: If Redis is only a cache, losing it means a slow minute while the cache warms up. If it holds sessions, queues, rate limits, or the only copy of some data, losing it can log out every user or drop jobs. The right configuration depends on what the data is worth, so you need to know exactly what each option protects against and what it costs. Related theory is in availability and reliability and consistency and the CAP theorem.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Mastodon calls Redis a critical part of an instance: by default one Redis instance holds feeds and queues, so its failure takes the whole server down. Its scaling guide adds Redis Sentinel: the application is given the Sentinel addresses (REDIS_SENTINELS) and the primary's name (REDIS_SENTINEL_MASTER) and asks Sentinel for the current primary, so it follows failovers automatically (Mastodon: Scaling up your server).
  • GitLab runs separate Redis instances on GitLab.com and supports Redis Cluster for its cache workloads. Because Cluster spreads keys over slots, its developers must put hash tags in keys used together (project:{1}:set_a), and a validator checks this in development and tests (GitLab: Redis guidelines).
  • Slack learned that an in-memory queue is only as durable as Redis: after an outage, it put Kafka in front of its Redis job queue to provide "a buffer against memory exhaustion and job loss" (Slack engineering).

Popular providers: Amazon ElastiCache (Multi-AZ with automatic failover and replica promotion, plus scheduled backups), Amazon MemoryDB (a durable in-memory database with a Multi-AZ transactional log), and Google Cloud Memorystore for Redis.

docs.title: RDB snapshots
docs.text:
An RDB file is a compact, point-in-time snapshot of the whole dataset (dump.rdb by default).

Redis main process --fork()--> child process writes snapshot to temp file
       |                                   |
   keeps serving clients            rename temp -> dump.rdb when complete
  • Snapshots are taken automatically by save <seconds> <changes> rules (for example "after 300 seconds if at least 100 keys changed"), or manually with BGSAVE.
  • The child process shares memory with the parent using copy-on-write: pages are copied only when the parent modifies them. Under heavy writes, a snapshot can temporarily need much more memory, so leave headroom.
  • Restarting from an RDB file is fast.
  • Trade-off: everything written since the last snapshot is lost in a crash, often minutes of data.

docs.title: AOF (append-only file)
docs.text:
The AOF logs every write command. On restart, Redis replays the log to rebuild the dataset.

How often the log is flushed to disk with fsync is set by appendfsync:

Setting Durability Performance always Every write is on disk before the reply: minimal loss Slowest everysec (default when AOF is on) At most about one second of writes lost Good; the usual choice no The operating system decides when to flush (can be tens of seconds) Fastest

The log grows forever unless compacted. AOF rewrite (automatic, or BGREWRITEAOF) writes the minimal set of commands that recreates the current data. Since Redis 7, the AOF is stored as several files (a base file plus incremental files, tracked by a manifest) in a dedicated directory, and the base can be written in compact RDB format.

docs.title: Choosing persistence
docs.text:
Configuration What you lose in a crash Typical use No persistence Everything Pure cache that can be rebuilt RDB only Writes since the last snapshot Cache with faster warm-up; data where minutes of loss are acceptable AOF everysec (often plus RDB) About one second Sessions, queues, counters AOF always Almost nothing (at a large throughput cost) Rarely used; consider a database instead

When both are enabled, Redis loads the AOF on startup, because it is the more complete record. A common default for self-hosted Redis is RDB snapshots on and AOF off, so check your configuration rather than assuming.

Persistence protects against a process restart on the same disk. It does not protect against losing the machine or the disk; that needs replicas and backups.

docs.title: Replication
docs.text:
A replica keeps a copy of a primary's data:

            writes
clients ----------> PRIMARY ---- async replication stream ----> REPLICA 1
   \                                                    \-----> REPLICA 2
    \---- reads (optional, may be slightly stale) ---> replicas
  1. A replica connects with REPLICAOF host port.
  2. It receives a full snapshot, then a continuous stream of write commands.
  3. After a brief disconnect, it resumes from a replication backlog (partial resynchronization) instead of copying everything again.

Replication is asynchronous: the primary replies to the client before replicas confirm. If the primary dies, writes it acknowledged but had not yet sent are lost. Mitigations:

  • WAIT numreplicas timeout blocks until that many replicas have received the preceding writes. It reduces, but does not eliminate, the loss window.
  • min-replicas-to-write and min-replicas-max-lag make a primary refuse writes when it cannot reach enough replicas, limiting damage when it is cut off from the rest of the system.

Replicas are read-only by default and can serve read traffic, but reads may return slightly old data.

docs.title: Sentinel: automatic failover
docs.text:
Replication alone copies data; something must notice a failed primary and promote a replica. Redis Sentinel is a separate process (usually on port 26379) that does this:

  • Monitoring: Sentinels ping the primary and replicas.
  • Quorum: a configured number of Sentinels must agree the primary is unreachable before a failover starts, which avoids reacting to one Sentinel's network problem.
  • Automatic failover: a replica is promoted and the others are reconfigured.
  • Client discovery: applications connect to the Sentinels and ask for the current primary (for example with SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name mymaster), so they follow failovers.

Run at least three Sentinels on independent machines. Sentinel provides high availability for one primary's dataset; it does not shard data.

docs.title: Redis Cluster: sharding plus failover
docs.text:
When the dataset or write load is too big for one primary, Redis Cluster splits keys across several primaries, each with its own replicas.

  • The key space is divided into 16,384 hash slots. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each primary owns a range of slots.
  • Hash tags: if a key contains {...}, only the text inside the braces is hashed, so {user:42}:cart and {user:42}:orders share a slot.
  • Multi-key limits: commands, transactions, and Lua scripts that touch several keys work only if all keys are in the same slot; otherwise Redis returns a CROSSSLOT error. Only database 0 exists.
  • Redirects: if a client sends a command to the wrong node, the node replies MOVED <slot> <host:port> (the slot lives elsewhere; update your slot map) or, while a slot is being migrated, ASK <slot> <host:port> (try that node once, for this command only). Cluster-aware clients handle both.
  • Failover is built in: nodes gossip over a cluster bus, detect a failed primary, and promote one of its replicas; Sentinel is not used.
  • Resharding: slots can be moved between nodes while the cluster is running.

A common minimum is three primaries, each with at least one replica. See database scaling for sharding in general; MongoDB uses related ideas in replication and sharding.

docs.title: Sentinel or Cluster?
docs.text: Sentinel Cluster Purpose High availability for one dataset Sharding and high availability Write capacity One primary Several primaries Multi-key operations Unrestricted Same hash slot only Client requirements Sentinel-aware client Cluster-aware client Choose when Data fits on one server Data or writes exceed one server

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: Persistence and replicas do not protect against mistakes: a FLUSHALL or a bad deploy is replicated instantly. Back up RDB files on a schedule (the current dump.rdb can be copied safely, because Redis writes a temporary file and renames it only when complete), store copies off the server, and test restores. Managed services offer automatic snapshots. See backups.

docs.title: Managed services
docs.text:
Running replication, failover, patching, and backups yourself takes effort. Managed offerings handle them:

  • Amazon ElastiCache offers Valkey, Redis OSS, and Memcached engines, with replication groups, Multi-AZ automatic failover, cluster mode for sharding, and automatic backups. Amazon MemoryDB targets use as a durable primary database. See AWS.
  • Other clouds provide similar services, such as Google Cloud Memorystore and Azure Managed Redis (Microsoft is retiring Azure Cache for Redis in its favor), and Redis Ltd. offers its own cloud service.

Read the provider's documentation for exact failover times, durability guarantees, and supported commands; managed services restrict some administrative commands, so check the provider's list before relying on one.

docs.title: Memory limits and fragmentation
docs.text:
• Set maxmemory below the machine's RAM, leaving headroom for copy-on-write during snapshots and rewrites, replication buffers, and client buffers. Running out of RAM can get the process killed by the operating system.
  • Fragmentation: the allocator may hold more memory than the data needs. INFO memory reports mem_fragmentation_ratio (used_memory_rss divided by used_memory), but that ratio also includes other process overheads, so a high value only matters when mem_fragmentation_bytes is large; allocator_frag_ratio is the true fragmentation metric. Redis can defragment actively with activedefrag yes. A ratio below 1 (resident memory smaller than used memory) hints that memory was swapped out, which is very slow.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Choose each mechanism for what it protects against:

  • No persistence: a pure cache that can be rebuilt from the source.
  • RDB snapshots: faster restarts and simple backup files, when losing the writes since the last snapshot is acceptable.
  • AOF everysec (often with RDB): sessions, queues, and counters where losing about a second of writes is the most you can accept.
  • Replicas + Sentinel: keep one dataset available when a server fails.
  • Redis Cluster: the data or the write load no longer fits on one primary.

Do not rely on them when:

  • Losing even acknowledged writes is unacceptable (payments, ledgers): replication is asynchronous, so keep the record of truth in a database.
  • You need protection from mistakes such as FLUSHALL or bad deploys: persistence and replicas copy the mistake; only off-server backups help.
  • Your application needs many multi-key operations on unrelated keys: Cluster restricts them to one hash slot, so a single primary with Sentinel may be simpler.
RDB AOF everysec RDB + AOF Writes lost in a crash Everything since the last snapshot About one second About one second (AOF is loaded on startup) Restart speed with a big dataset Fastest Slower (replays the log) AOF used; a compact RDB-format base makes it faster File size Compact Usually bigger Both kept Extra disk I/O Periodic snapshots Continuous appends and fsyncs Both Good for Caches, backups Sessions, queues Must-keep state that also needs backup files

docs.title: Checking and changing persistence
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG GET save
1) "save"
2) "3600 1 300 100 60 10000"
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG GET appendonly
1) "appendonly"
2) "no"
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET appendonly yes
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> BGSAVE
Background saving started
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO persistence
# Persistence
rdb_last_bgsave_status:ok
aof_enabled:1
aof_last_bgrewrite_status:ok
...

The equivalent redis.conf settings:

save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec

docs.title: Replication status
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO replication
# Replication
role:master
connected_slaves:2
slave0:ip=10.0.1.12,port=6379,state=online,offset=884213,lag=0
slave1:ip=10.0.1.13,port=6379,state=online,offset=884213,lag=1
...
127.0.0.1:6379> SET order:1001 "paid"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> WAIT 1 100        # wait up to 100 ms for 1 replica
(integer) 2

(Redis output still uses the older words "master" and "slave" in some fields.)

docs.title: Hash slots and redirects
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:7000> CLUSTER KEYSLOT somekey
(integer) 11058
127.0.0.1:7000> CLUSTER KEYSLOT foo{hash_tag}
(integer) 2515
127.0.0.1:7000> CLUSTER KEYSLOT bar{hash_tag}
(integer) 2515                     # same tag, same slot

$ redis-cli -p 7000
127.0.0.1:7000> SET foo bar
(error) MOVED 12182 127.0.0.1:7002

$ redis-cli -c -p 7000              # -c follows redirects
127.0.0.1:7000> SET foo bar
-> Redirected to slot [12182] located at 127.0.0.1:7002
OK

127.0.0.1:7002> MSET user:1 a user:2 b
(error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot

docs.title: Connecting to Redis Cluster from Node.js
docs.text:
import { createCluster } from "redis";

const cluster = createCluster({
  rootNodes: process.env.REDIS_CLUSTER_URLS.split(",").map((url) => ({ url })),
});
cluster.on("error", (err) => console.error("Redis Cluster error", err));
await cluster.connect(); // discovers all nodes and the slot map

await cluster.set("user:42:name", "Ada");          // routed to the right node
await cluster.mGet(["{user:42}:cart", "{user:42}:orders"]); // same slot: allowed

For Sentinel-managed deployments, use a client with Sentinel support (check your client's documentation) and give it the Sentinel addresses and the primary's name instead of a fixed host.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Decide what losing Redis data would cost, then choose persistence to match.
  • Use AOF with everysec (often together with RDB) for sessions, queues, and other state you must keep.
  • Run replicas plus Sentinel, or Redis Cluster, when downtime matters; use at least three Sentinels on separate machines.
  • Remember that replication is asynchronous; never treat Redis as the only copy of critical financial or legal records.
  • Design keys with hash tags if you will use Cluster and need multi-key operations.
  • Take off-server backups and test restoring them.
  • Leave memory headroom for forks and buffers; monitor fragmentation and replication lag.
  • Use a managed service unless you have the operational capacity to run Redis yourself.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
Writes are suddenly refused after a background save fails.

  • Detect: INFO persistence shows rdb_last_bgsave_status:err; the Redis log shows the fork or the save failing; clients get errors on every write.
  • Cause: with stop-writes-on-bgsave-error yes (the default), Redis stops accepting writes after a failed snapshot. Common reasons are a full disk or fork() failing for lack of memory when the kernel's vm.overcommit_memory is 0.
  • Fix: free disk space, set vm.overcommit_memory = 1 as the Redis FAQ recommends, and leave memory headroom for copy-on-write.

Latency spikes every time a snapshot or AOF rewrite starts.

  • Detect: latest_fork_usec in INFO stats is large; LATENCY DOCTOR reports fork-related events; spikes line up with save rules.
  • Cause: the fork itself runs on the main thread and takes longer for large datasets; transparent huge pages make it worse.
  • Fix: disable transparent huge pages as the Redis latency guide says, keep each instance's dataset moderate, and schedule snapshots away from peaks.

Writes slow down while the disk is busy.

  • Detect: aof_delayed_fsync in INFO persistence keeps increasing.
  • Cause: the disk cannot keep up with AOF fsyncs, often while a snapshot or rewrite is also writing.
  • Fix: use faster local disks, keep appendfsync everysec, and consider no-appendfsync-on-rewrite yes if a small extra loss window during rewrites is acceptable.

Replicas keep re-copying the whole dataset.

  • Detect: sync_full keeps rising in INFO stats; the replica's master_link_status flips to down.
  • Cause: after a disconnect, the replica's position is no longer in the primary's replication backlog (repl-backlog-size, 1 MB by default), or the replica output buffer limit cuts the connection during the transfer.
  • Fix: raise repl-backlog-size and the client-output-buffer-limit replica setting for large or busy datasets.

Recent writes are missing after a failover.

  • Detect: data acknowledged just before the primary failed is absent on the promoted replica.
  • Cause: replication is asynchronous, so the replica never received those writes.
  • Fix: use WAIT for writes that matter, configure min-replicas-to-write and min-replicas-max-lag, and keep critical records in a database.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• RDB: A point-in-time snapshot file of the dataset.
  • AOF: The append-only file that logs write commands.
  • fsync: A system call that forces buffered data onto disk.
  • Copy-on-write: Sharing memory between processes until one modifies a page.
  • Replica: A server that holds a copy of a primary's data.
  • Failover: Promoting a replica when the primary fails.
  • Quorum: The number of Sentinels that must agree before acting.
  • Hash slot: One of 16,384 buckets that keys are assigned to in Redis Cluster.
  • MOVED / ASK: Redirect replies telling a client which node owns a slot.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Redis is in memory, so it cannot persist" or "it always persists." Persistence is configurable, and the defaults vary.
  • "Replicas mean zero data loss." Asynchronous replication can lose recently acknowledged writes during failover.
  • "Persistence is a backup." A deleted key is deleted in the AOF and replicas too.
  • Running one or two Sentinels. Too few to form a reliable majority.
  • Using multi-key commands across slots in Cluster. They fail with CROSSSLOT.
  • Setting maxmemory equal to the machine's RAM. Forks and buffers can push the process out of memory.
  • Hard-coding the primary's address with Sentinel. The application does not follow failovers.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Compare RDB snapshots and AOF in terms of data loss and performance.
  2. What does each appendfsync setting trade off?
  3. Why can a failover lose writes that clients saw as successful, and how does WAIT help?
  4. What jobs does Sentinel perform, and why does it need a quorum?
  5. How does Redis Cluster decide which node stores a key, and what are hash tags for?
  6. What is the difference between MOVED and ASK redirects?
