docs.title: Pub/Sub and Streams
docs.text: Redis offers two ways to move messages between parts of a system. Pub/Sub broadcasts a message instantly to whoever is listening and then forgets it. Streams append messages to a stored log that consumers read at their own pace, with acknowledgments and recovery. This lesson explains both, compares them, and shows when a dedicated broker such as Kafka or RabbitMQ is the better choice.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Backends constantly need to tell other processes that something happened: a chat message arrived, an order was placed, a cache entry is stale. Picking the wrong mechanism causes subtle bugs. Pub/Sub silently drops messages when a subscriber is offline, so it is wrong for "every order must be billed". Streams keep messages, but only within available memory. Knowing the delivery guarantees of each lets you choose deliberately; the general theory is in messaging fundamentals and delivery guarantees.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Mastodon backs its streaming API with Redis: its streaming servers receive updates through Redis Pub/Sub (they export a metric counting messages received from Redis pubsub) and stream them to connected clients (Mastodon: Scaling up your server).
  • GitLab uses Redis as the Pub/Sub backend for ActionCable, the Rails WebSocket framework behind its real-time features (GitLab: Redis guidelines).
  • Discourse's message_bus library, which pushes updates to Ruby processes and browsers, can use Redis as its storage backend (discourse/message_bus).
  • Slack ran its job queue on Redis, and after an outage caused by Redis running out of memory it put Kafka in front of Redis as a durable buffer "against memory exhaustion and job loss", keeping Redis for scheduling and execution (Slack engineering).

docs.title: Pub/Sub
docs.text:
Publishers send messages to a channel; every client currently subscribed to that channel receives a copy.

Command Purpose PUBLISH channel message Send a message; returns how many clients it was sent to (in Redis Cluster, only clients on the same node are counted) SUBSCRIBE channel... Listen on exact channel names PSUBSCRIBE pattern... Listen on glob patterns, such as chat:room:* UNSUBSCRIBE / PUNSUBSCRIBE Stop listening PUBSUB CHANNELS / PUBSUB NUMSUB Inspect active channels and subscriber counts

Key properties:

  • Fire-and-forget, at most once. Redis does not store messages. A subscriber that is disconnected, restarting, or not yet subscribed misses them forever. There are no acknowledgments or retries.
  • Fan-out. Every subscriber gets every message on its channels.
  • Subscribed connections are special. With the RESP2 protocol, a connection that has subscribed can only run subscription-related commands (and PING), so applications use a separate connection for subscribing.
  • Slow subscribers are disconnected. If a subscriber cannot keep up, messages pile up in its output buffer; once it exceeds the client-output-buffer-limit for Pub/Sub, Redis closes the connection.
  • Channels are independent of keys. Publishing to a channel has nothing to do with a key of the same name.

Sharded Pub/Sub (Redis 7.0+): in Redis Cluster, normal PUBLISH messages are broadcast to every node, which limits scaling. SPUBLISH and SSUBSCRIBE assign each channel to a hash slot, like a key, so messages stay within the shard that owns that slot.

Related feature: keyspace notifications (enabled with notify-keyspace-events) publish events such as "key expired" or "key deleted" on special channels. They inherit Pub/Sub's at-most-once delivery.

docs.title: Streams
docs.text:
A stream is an append-only log stored in a Redis key. Each entry has a unique, increasing ID and a set of fields.

stream "orders"
+------------------+------------------+------------------+
| 1730900000000-0  | 1730900000123-0  | 1730900000456-0  |  --> newer
| orderId=1001     | orderId=1002     | orderId=1003     |
+------------------+------------------+------------------+

Because entries are stored, a consumer can read history, stop, restart, and continue from where it left off.

Writing and reading:

Command Purpose XADD key [MAXLEN ~ n] * field value... Append an entry (* generates the ID) XRANGE key start end / XREVRANGE Read a range of IDs (- and + mean oldest and newest) XREAD [COUNT n] [BLOCK ms] STREAMS key id Read entries after an ID; $ means "only new entries from now" XLEN key Number of entries XTRIM key MAXLEN ~ n Delete old entries

docs.title: Consumer groups
docs.text:
With plain XREAD, every reader sees every entry (fan-out). To share the work among several workers, so each entry is processed by one of them, create a consumer group.

Command Purpose XGROUP CREATE key group $ [MKSTREAM] Create a group starting at new entries (0 to start from the beginning) XREADGROUP GROUP group consumer [COUNT n] [BLOCK ms] STREAMS key > Get entries never delivered to this group XACK key group id... Mark entries as processed XPENDING key group Show delivered-but-unacknowledged entries XAUTOCLAIM key group consumer min-idle-ms start [COUNT n] Take over entries another consumer left pending too long XCLAIM Claim specific pending entries

The pending entries list (PEL). When XREADGROUP delivers an entry, it is recorded as pending for that consumer until the consumer sends XACK. If the worker crashes before acknowledging:

  1. On restart, the same consumer can re-read its own pending entries with XREADGROUP ... STREAMS orders 0 (ID 0 instead of >).
  2. If it never comes back, another worker uses XAUTOCLAIM to take entries idle longer than a threshold.
  3. Each entry's delivery count is tracked; after too many attempts, move it to a "dead-letter" stream instead of retrying forever.

This gives at-least-once delivery: an entry can be processed twice (for example, the worker finishes but crashes before XACK), so handlers must be idempotent. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

Trimming. Acknowledging does not delete entries. Streams grow until trimmed, by MAXLEN (keep about N entries) or MINID (drop entries older than an ID, which is effectively a time). The ~ modifier trims approximately, which is much cheaper. Trim based on how far behind the slowest consumer group might fall.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Pub/Sub Streams List (LPUSH/BRPOP) Messages stored No Yes, until trimmed Yes, until popped Offline consumers Miss messages Catch up later Catch up later Fan-out to many readers Yes Yes (several groups, or plain XREAD) No: each item goes to one reader Work sharing No Yes (consumer groups) Yes Acknowledgments and recovery No Yes (PEL, XACK, XAUTOCLAIM) No (item lost if worker crashes) Replay history No Yes No Delivery guarantee At most once At least once At most once without extra work Typical use Live notifications, cache invalidation, WebSocket fan-out Event logs, background processing, activity feeds Simple queues

docs.title: When to use Kafka or RabbitMQ instead
docs.text:
Redis streams live in memory, on one primary per key, with asynchronous replication. Choose a dedicated broker (see message queues) when you need:

  • Long retention or very large volumes: days or months of events, more than fits comfortably in RAM. Kafka stores logs on disk and partitions them across many brokers. See Apache Kafka.
  • Rich routing and per-message features: exchanges, routing keys, per-message TTLs, priority queues, dead-lettering built into the broker. See RabbitMQ.
  • Strong durability: messages acknowledged only after being written to disk on several nodes.
  • An organization-wide event backbone shared by many teams, with schemas and connectors.

Redis is a good fit when you already run it, volumes are moderate, and messages are short-lived.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use Pub/Sub when a message is only useful right now and a receiver that misses it can recover another way: live notifications, cache invalidation, fan-out to WebSocket servers. Do not use it for work that must happen (billing, emails, orders).

Use Streams when consumers must not miss messages, need to catch up after a restart, share work through consumer groups, or replay recent history, and the retained volume fits in memory.

Use a dedicated broker when retention is long (days or more), volume is large, messages need rich routing, or acknowledged messages must survive the loss of a server's disk.

Requirement Pub/Sub Streams List queue Kafka RabbitMQ Receiver offline for a minute Misses messages Catches up Catches up Catches up Catches up Several independent readers of every message Yes Yes (groups) No Yes (consumer groups) Yes (one queue per reader) Work shared among workers with acks No Yes No acks Yes Yes Long retention and replay No Limited by RAM No Yes, on disk Not its focus Extra infrastructure None if Redis exists None if Redis exists None if Redis exists A cluster to run A broker to run

docs.title: Pub/Sub in redis-cli
docs.text:
Terminal 1:

127.0.0.1:6379> SUBSCRIBE chat:room:1
Reading messages... (press Ctrl-C to quit)
1) "subscribe"
2) "chat:room:1"
3) (integer) 1
1) "message"
2) "chat:room:1"
3) "hello everyone"

Terminal 2:

127.0.0.1:6379> PUBLISH chat:room:1 "hello everyone"
(integer) 1          # one subscriber received it
127.0.0.1:6379> PUBLISH chat:room:2 "anyone?"
(integer) 0          # nobody listening: the message is gone

docs.title: Pub/Sub in Node.js
docs.text:
import { createClient } from "redis";

const publisher = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
publisher.on("error", (err) => console.error(err));
await publisher.connect();

// Subscribing needs its own connection.
const subscriber = publisher.duplicate();
subscriber.on("error", (err) => console.error(err));
await subscriber.connect();

await subscriber.pSubscribe("chat:room:*", (message, channel) => {
  console.log(`${channel}: ${message}`);
});

await publisher.publish("chat:room:1", JSON.stringify({ user: "ada", text: "hi" }));

docs.title: WebSocket fan-out across app instances
docs.text:
Each user's WebSocket is connected to one app instance. When a user on instance A sends a chat message, users connected to instances B and C must receive it too. Redis Pub/Sub relays it between instances:

user1 --ws--> instance A --PUBLISH chat:room:1--> Redis
                                                    |
                    +-------------------------------+---------------+
                    v                               v               v
               instance A                      instance B      instance C
             (sends to its                   (sends to its   (sends to its
              local sockets)                  local sockets)  local sockets)

import { WebSocketServer } from "ws";
import { createClient } from "redis";

const pub = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
const sub = pub.duplicate();
await Promise.all([pub.connect(), sub.connect()]);

const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: Number(process.env.WS_PORT ?? 8080) });
const rooms = new Map(); // roomId -> Set of local sockets

wss.on("connection", (socket, req) => {
  const roomId = new URL(req.url, "http://localhost").searchParams.get("room");
  if (!rooms.has(roomId)) rooms.set(roomId, new Set());
  rooms.get(roomId).add(socket);

  socket.on("message", async (data) => {
    // Publish instead of sending directly: every instance will deliver it.
    await pub.publish(`chat:room:${roomId}`, data.toString());
  });
  socket.on("close", () => rooms.get(roomId)?.delete(socket));
});

await sub.pSubscribe("chat:room:*", (message, channel) => {
  const roomId = channel.slice("chat:room:".length);
  for (const socket of rooms.get(roomId) ?? []) {
    if (socket.readyState === socket.OPEN) socket.send(message);
  }
});

Because Pub/Sub does not store messages, a user who reconnects does not get what they missed; load recent history from the database (or a stream) on reconnect. Libraries such as Socket.IO provide a Redis adapter built on the same idea. See WebSockets and real-time communication.

docs.title: Streams with a consumer group in redis-cli
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> XGROUP CREATE orders billing $ MKSTREAM
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD orders MAXLEN ~ 100000 * orderId 1001 total 49.90
"1730900000000-0"
127.0.0.1:6379> XREADGROUP GROUP billing worker-1 COUNT 10 STREAMS orders >
1) 1) "orders"
   2) 1) 1) "1730900000000-0"
         2) 1) "orderId"
            2) "1001"
            3) "total"
            4) "49.90"
127.0.0.1:6379> XPENDING orders billing
1) (integer) 1                 # one entry delivered but not acknowledged
2) "1730900000000-0"
3) "1730900000000-0"
4) 1) 1) "worker-1"
      2) "1"
127.0.0.1:6379> XACK orders billing 1730900000000-0
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> XAUTOCLAIM orders billing worker-2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10
1) "0-0"
2) (empty array)               # nothing has been idle for 60 seconds
3) (empty array)

docs.title: A stream worker in Node.js
docs.text:
import { createClient } from "redis";

const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
await redis.connect();

const STREAM = "orders";
const GROUP = "billing";
const CONSUMER = `worker-${process.pid}`;

try {
  await redis.xGroupCreate(STREAM, GROUP, "0", { MKSTREAM: true });
} catch (err) {
  if (!String(err.message).includes("BUSYGROUP")) throw err; // group exists
}

// Blocking reads hold the connection, so use a dedicated one.
const reader = redis.duplicate();
await reader.connect();

let running = true;
process.on("SIGTERM", () => { running = false; });

while (running) {
  const response = await reader.xReadGroup(
    GROUP, CONSUMER,
    { key: STREAM, id: ">" },          // only new, undelivered entries
    { COUNT: 10, BLOCK: 5000 }          // wait up to 5 s for work
  );
  if (!response) continue;              // timed out with nothing new

  for (const { messages } of response) {
    for (const { id, message } of messages) {
      await chargeOrder(message.orderId); // must be idempotent
      await redis.xAck(STREAM, GROUP, id);
    }
  }
}
await Promise.all([reader.close(), redis.close()]); // close(): node-redis v5+

A production worker also runs a periodic XAUTOCLAIM to rescue entries left pending by crashed consumers, and moves entries with a high delivery count to a dead-letter stream.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use Pub/Sub only where losing a message is acceptable, or where the receiver can recover state another way.
  • Use a dedicated connection for subscriptions and for blocking reads.
  • Make stream handlers idempotent; delivery is at least once.
  • Acknowledge only after the work has fully succeeded.
  • Reclaim stuck entries with XAUTOCLAIM and dead-letter poison messages.
  • Always trim streams (MAXLEN ~ or MINID), sized for the slowest consumer group.
  • Monitor stream length, pending counts, and consumer lag.
  • Move to Kafka or RabbitMQ when retention, volume, or durability needs exceed what memory and asynchronous replication provide.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
Subscribers are disconnected under load.

  • Detect: subscriber clients log unexpected disconnects; INFO clients shows client_recent_max_output_buffer growing during bursts.
  • Cause: a slow subscriber cannot read fast enough, its output buffer passes the Pub/Sub client-output-buffer-limit, and Redis closes the connection (every message in between is lost).
  • Fix: keep subscriber handlers fast (hand work to a queue), scale the subscribers, or switch to Streams where consumers read at their own pace.

Messages "disappear" during deploys.

  • Detect: events published while a service restarted never reach it; PUBLISH returned 0 for those messages.
  • Cause: Pub/Sub delivers at most once and stores nothing.
  • Fix: move must-deliver events to a stream with a consumer group, or reload state from the database after reconnecting.

The pending entries list keeps growing.

  • Detect: the summary from XPENDING key group shows a rising count and very old smallest IDs; XINFO GROUPS key shows pending rising.
  • Cause: a consumer crashed before XACK, or a poison message fails on every attempt.
  • Fix: run XAUTOCLAIM periodically, acknowledge only after success, and move entries with a high delivery count to a dead-letter stream.

Consumers fall behind and memory grows.

  • Detect: lag in XINFO GROUPS key keeps increasing; XLEN and used_memory grow together.
  • Cause: producers outpace the group, or the stream is never trimmed.
  • Fix: add consumers, trim with MAXLEN ~ or MINID sized for the slowest group, and move to a log-based broker if the backlog must be kept for long.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Channel: A named Pub/Sub topic.
  • Fan-out: Delivering one message to many receivers.
  • At-most-once / at-least-once: A message is delivered zero or one times / one or more times.
  • Stream entry ID: A unique, increasing milliseconds-sequence ID.
  • Consumer group: A set of consumers that share a stream's entries, each entry going to one of them.
  • Pending entries list (PEL): Entries delivered to a consumer but not yet acknowledged.
  • Dead-letter stream: Where repeatedly failing entries are moved for inspection.
  • Sharded Pub/Sub: Pub/Sub in which channels belong to hash slots in a cluster.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using Pub/Sub for jobs that must not be lost. Offline subscribers never receive them.
  • Running normal commands on a subscribed connection. Use a separate connection.
  • "Acknowledging deletes the entry." XACK only clears it from the PEL; trimming deletes.
  • Never trimming streams. They consume memory without limit.
  • Ignoring the PEL. Entries from crashed workers sit pending forever.
  • Assuming exactly-once processing. Retries and crashes can deliver an entry twice.
  • "Streams replace Kafka." They overlap for moderate workloads but lack disk-based retention and partitioned scaling.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What happens to a Pub/Sub message published while a subscriber is disconnected?
  2. How does a consumer group divide work, and how does it differ from plain XREAD?
  3. What is the pending entries list, and how do XACK and XAUTOCLAIM use it?
  4. Why must stream consumers be idempotent?
  5. How does Redis Pub/Sub let several app instances deliver WebSocket messages to all users?
  6. Name three requirements that would push you from Redis streams to Kafka or RabbitMQ.

docs.title: Using Redis as a Cache
docs.text: Caching is one of the most common reasons teams add Redis. The application keeps the results of expensive work (database queries, API calls, rendered fragments) in Redis for a while, so later requests are answered from memory. This lesson shows how to implement cache-aside in Node.js and how to configure keys, expiry, memory limits, and monitoring so the cache stays fast and correct.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: An in-process cache (a Map in Node) disappears on restart and is not shared between instances, so each of ten servers warms its own copy and they disagree after updates. Redis gives every instance one shared cache that survives application deploys, with built-in expiry and eviction. Done badly, though, a cache serves stale data, fills memory, or collapses under a stampede of misses. The general theory is in cache fundamentals and caching strategies; this lesson covers the Redis specifics.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitLab uses Redis as the store behind its Rails cache (Rails.cache), alongside queues, sessions, and other state, and runs separate Redis instances on GitLab.com so each workload can be sized and tuned on its own (GitLab: Redis guidelines).
  • Mastodon uses Redis for volatile caching as well as for feeds and queues. Its scaling guide suggests a separate Redis just for the cache (CACHE_REDIS_URL), because the cache can be lost safely while the feeds and Sidekiq queues are data you would not want to lose (Mastodon: Scaling up your server).

Both follow the same rule this lesson repeats: a cache's eviction and persistence settings differ from those of must-keep data, so they live on different instances.

Popular tools and providers: managed Redis-compatible caches such as Amazon ElastiCache (Valkey, Memcached, or Redis OSS engines) and Google Cloud Memorystore for Redis.

docs.title: Cache-aside with Redis
docs.text:
In cache-aside (lazy loading), the application talks to both the cache and the database:

Writes go to the database first; the cached copy is then deleted (or updated), so the next read reloads fresh data. Redis never talks to the database itself: the application owns the logic.

docs.title: TTLs and jitter
docs.text:
Every cache entry should have a TTL, even when you also invalidate on writes. The TTL bounds how stale data can get if an invalidation is missed, and lets unused entries disappear.

If many keys are created at the same moment with the same TTL (for example after a deploy or a cache flush), they also expire together, and the database receives a burst of misses. Adding jitter (a small random amount) spreads expirations out: a base TTL of 300 seconds becomes 270–330.

Other TTL-related commands:

  • GETEX key EX 300 reads a value and resets its TTL (sliding expiry).
  • SET key value KEEPTTL replaces a value but keeps the existing TTL.

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
Redis stores strings or bytes, so objects must be serialized:

Format Pros Cons JSON Readable in redis-cli, works everywhere Larger; Date objects become strings MessagePack or similar binary formats Smaller, faster Not human-readable; both sides need the library Compressed JSON (gzip/Brotli) Much smaller for large values CPU cost; unreadable Hash fields Read or update single fields Flat structure only

Include a version in the key (cache:v2:...) so that changing the cached shape does not make new code read old-format values.

docs.title: Key design
docs.text:
A cache key must include every input that changes the result:

Cached result Key Product 17 cache:v1:product:17 Product 17 in French cache:v1:product:17:fr Search results cache:v1:search:<sha1 of normalized query and filters> A user's dashboard cache:v1:dashboard:user:42

If a key omits an input, such as the user's role or language, one user can receive another user's data. Normalize inputs (sort query parameters, lowercase) so equivalent requests share a key, and hash long inputs to keep keys short.

docs.title: Memory limits and eviction
docs.text:
maxmemory caps how much memory Redis uses for data. When the limit is reached, maxmemory-policy decides what happens on the next write:

Policy Behavior noeviction Reject writes with an out-of-memory error (common default) allkeys-lru Evict the least recently used keys allkeys-lfu Evict the least frequently used keys volatile-lru / volatile-lfu Same, but only keys that have a TTL volatile-ttl Evict keys with the shortest remaining TTL first allkeys-random / volatile-random Evict random keys allkeys-lrm / volatile-lrm Evict the least recently modified keys (listed in current Redis docs; check your server version)

For a dedicated cache, allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu is the usual choice. If the same Redis also stores data that must not disappear (sessions, queues), run separate Redis instances for cache and for durable state. A volatile-* policy only spares keys that have no TTL: sessions normally carry a TTL, so they would still be evicted, and queue libraries such as BullMQ require noeviction. Redis's LRU and LFU are approximations based on sampling, which is fast and close to exact in practice. The policies are explained in depth in eviction policies.

docs.title: Big keys
docs.text:
A big key is a single value or collection that is very large: a 50 MB string, or a hash with millions of fields. Big keys cause:

  • Latency spikes, because reading, writing, or deleting them blocks the single command thread.
  • Network saturation when the whole value is sent on each read.
  • Uneven memory in a cluster, because one key always lives on one node.

Find them with redis-cli --bigkeys or --memkeys (sampled scans that are safe to run) and MEMORY USAGE key. Fix them by caching smaller pieces, storing only the fields a page needs, splitting collections across keys, compressing, and deleting big values with UNLINK.

docs.title: Invalidation
docs.text:
The hard part of caching is keeping it correct after data changes. Common Redis approaches:

  • Delete on write: after updating the database, DEL (or UNLINK) the affected keys; the next read repopulates them.
  • TTL as a safety net: even if an invalidation is lost, data is fresh within one TTL.
  • Versioned keys: store a version number (product:17:version) and include it in cache keys; incrementing it makes all old entries unreachable, and their TTLs clean them up.
  • Broadcast for local caches: publish an invalidation message on Pub/Sub so every instance clears its in-process copy.

Delete rather than update the cache on writes: two concurrent writers that both update the cache can leave the older value there. See invalidation and expiration.

docs.title: Stampedes and outages
docs.text: When a popular key expires, hundreds of concurrent requests can miss at once and all hit the database (a cache stampede). Defenses include jittered TTLs, letting only one request rebuild the value (a short lock with SET lock:key token NX PX 5000), and refreshing hot keys before they expire. If Redis itself is down, the application should fall back to the database with timeouts and limits rather than crash, and must not overwhelm the database. These failure modes are covered in cache failure modes.

docs.title: Two-tier caching
docs.text:
For extremely hot data, add a small in-process cache in front of Redis:

The local tier removes network round trips for the hottest keys; its short TTL limits how long instances can disagree. Invalidation messages over Pub/Sub can clear local copies sooner.

docs.title: Measuring hit rate
docs.text:
A cache that misses most of the time adds latency and cost. Redis tracks reads that found a key (keyspace_hits) and reads that did not (keyspace_misses):

hit rate = keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses)

These counters are server-wide and include every read, not only cache lookups, so application-level metrics per key prefix give a more precise picture. Also watch evicted_keys (memory pressure) and expired_keys. See monitoring and logging.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a Redis cache when:

  • The same expensive result (a query, an API call, a rendered fragment) is read many times before it changes.
  • Several application instances should share one warm cache.
  • Serving data that is up to one TTL old is acceptable, or you can invalidate reliably on writes.

Skip it, or cache somewhere else, when:

  • Every read must see the latest committed write (account balances, inventory at checkout); read from the database.
  • Data is written more often than it is read, so entries are invalidated before they are reused.
  • The hit rate stays low because keys are too specific or values change constantly.
  • The data is small and per-process: an in-process LRU is faster and simpler.
Option Shared across instances Speed Invalidation Best for In-process LRU No Fastest (no network) Per instance; short TTLs The hottest few keys Redis cache-aside Yes Sub-millisecond on the server, plus a network round trip DEL/UNLINK on write, TTL as a backstop Shared query and API results HTTP cache or CDN Yes, at the edge Fastest for clients Cache-Control, purges Public, cacheable responses Database read replica Yes Database speed None needed; replication lag applies Fresh reads at lower cost than the primary

docs.title: Configuring memory and eviction
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy
1) "maxmemory-policy"
2) "noeviction"
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET maxmemory 2gb
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu
OK

CONFIG SET changes the running server only; put the same settings in redis.conf (or your managed service's parameter group) so they survive a restart:

maxmemory 2gb
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu

docs.title: A cache-aside helper in Node.js
docs.text:
import { createClient } from "redis";

export const redis = createClient({
  url: process.env.REDIS_URL,
  socket: { connectTimeout: 2000 },
  disableOfflineQueue: true, // fail fast instead of queueing while disconnected
});
redis.on("error", (err) => console.error("Redis error", err.message));
await redis.connect();

function withJitter(seconds, ratio = 0.1) {
  const spread = seconds * ratio;
  return Math.round(seconds - spread + Math.random() * spread * 2);
}

/**
 * Return a cached value, or load it, cache it, and return it.
 * A Redis failure falls back to the loader instead of failing the request.
 */
export async function getOrLoad(key, ttlSeconds, loader) {
  try {
    const cached = await redis.get(key);
    if (cached !== null) return JSON.parse(cached);
  } catch (err) {
    console.warn("cache read failed, using database", err.message);
    return loader();
  }

  const value = await loader();
  if (value !== undefined) {
    redis
      .set(key, JSON.stringify(value), { EX: withJitter(ttlSeconds) })
      .catch((err) => console.warn("cache write failed", err.message));
  }
  return value;
}

Using it in an Express route:

app.get("/products/:id", async (req, res) => {
  const id = req.params.id;
  const product = await getOrLoad(`cache:v1:product:${id}`, 300, () =>
    db.products.findById(id)
  );
  if (!product) return res.status(404).json({ error: "Product not found" });
  res.json(product);
});

loader returns null for a missing product, which is cached too. This is negative caching: it stops repeated requests for nonexistent IDs from hitting the database. Use a shorter TTL for negative entries if records can be created later.

docs.title: Invalidating on write
docs.text:
app.put("/products/:id", async (req, res) => {
  const updated = await db.products.update(req.params.id, req.body);
  // Delete after the database write succeeds; the next read reloads.
  await redis.unlink([`cache:v1:product:${req.params.id}`,
    `cache:v1:product:${req.params.id}:fr`]);
  res.json(updated);
});

docs.title: Preventing a stampede on one hot key
docs.text:
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

export async function getOrLoadOnce(key, ttlSeconds, loader) {
  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached !== null) return JSON.parse(cached);

  const token = randomUUID();
  const gotLock = await redis.set(`lock:${key}`, token, { NX: true, PX: 5000 });
  if (!gotLock) {
    // Someone else is rebuilding: wait briefly, then read again.
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
    const retry = await redis.get(key);
    if (retry !== null) return JSON.parse(retry);
    return loader(); // still nothing: load without caching
  }

  const value = await loader();
  if (value !== undefined) {
    await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(value), { EX: withJitter(ttlSeconds) });
  }
  return value; // lock expires on its own after 5 seconds
}

docs.title: Checking hit rate, evictions, and big keys
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO stats
# Stats
...
expired_keys:55310
evicted_keys:120
keyspace_hits:982341
keyspace_misses:41230
...
127.0.0.1:6379> MEMORY USAGE cache:v1:product:17
(integer) 1584

Here the hit rate is 982341 / (982341 + 41230) ≈ 96%.

$ redis-cli --bigkeys
# Scanning the entire keyspace to find biggest keys ...
...
-------- summary -------
Biggest string found "cache:v1:report:2026" has 18874368 bytes
Biggest hash found "user:42" has 12 fields

An 18 MB cached report is a big key worth splitting or compressing.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Give every cache key a TTL, with jitter.
  • Delete cache entries after database writes; do not update them in place from concurrent writers.
  • Put all result-affecting inputs and a format version in the key.
  • Set maxmemory and an allkeys-* eviction policy on cache instances.
  • Keep durable data (sessions, queues) on a separate instance from the cache; a volatile-* policy does not protect keys that carry TTLs.
  • Treat the cache as optional: time out quickly and fall back to the source.
  • Watch hit rate, evictions, memory, and latency; investigate big keys.
  • Cache what is expensive and read often, not everything.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
The database overloads when a hot key expires.

  • Detect: database queries per second spike at the same moment as keyspace_misses in INFO stats; the spike repeats on the key's TTL or right after a deploy or FLUSHALL.
  • Cause: a cache stampede: many requests miss together and all rebuild the same value, or many keys created together expire together.
  • Fix: jitter TTLs, let one request rebuild with a short SET lock:<key> <token> NX PX lock, and refresh the hottest keys before they expire.

Users are logged out or jobs disappear.

  • Detect: evicted_keys in INFO stats is above zero on an instance that also holds sessions or queues.
  • Cause: an allkeys-* eviction policy on a shared instance evicts must-keep keys along with cache entries.
  • Fix: move the cache to its own instance. A volatile-* policy is not a reliable fix: it still evicts sessions, which have TTLs.

Users see old data after an update.

  • Detect: the database holds the new value while GET on the cache key returns the old one; TTL key shows how long it will survive.
  • Cause: an invalidation was skipped (a code path that writes without deleting), or a slow reader re-filled the cache with data it read before the write.
  • Fix: delete after every write path, keep TTLs as a safety net, and use versioned keys for bulk changes.

A Redis outage makes the whole site slow.

  • Detect: request latency rises to the client's timeout and logs show Redis connection errors.
  • Cause: the application waits on Redis without a timeout, or queues commands while disconnected.
  • Fix: set socket.connectTimeout, use disableOfflineQueue to fail fast, and fall back to the source as getOrLoad does.

The cache costs memory but saves little.

  • Detect: hit rate computed from keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses (or better, per-prefix application metrics) stays low.
  • Cause: keys include inputs that rarely repeat, TTLs are too short, or evictions remove entries before reuse.
  • Fix: normalize keys, cache coarser results, and size maxmemory to the working set.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Cache-aside: The application reads the cache, loads from the source on a miss, and fills the cache.
  • Cache hit / miss: The requested key was / was not found.
  • TTL jitter: Randomizing expiry times to avoid synchronized expiry.
  • Negative caching: Caching "not found" results.
  • Eviction policy: The rule Redis uses to free memory at maxmemory.
  • Big key: A key whose value is large enough to cause latency or memory problems.
  • Cache stampede: Many concurrent misses for the same key overloading the source.
  • Two-tier cache: An in-process cache in front of a shared cache.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• No TTL "because we invalidate." A single missed invalidation leaves stale data forever.
  • noeviction on a cache. When memory fills, writes fail with out-of-memory errors instead of evicting old entries.
  • Mixing cache and must-keep data under allkeys-lru. Sessions or jobs get evicted.
  • Keys missing an input (language, role, tenant). Users see each other's data.
  • Letting a Redis outage crash the app. A cache should degrade gracefully.
  • Caching huge values. Big keys block Redis and saturate the network.
  • "A higher hit rate is always better." A high hit rate on stale or wrong data is still a bug; correctness comes first.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Walk through a cache-aside read and a write with invalidation.
  2. Why add jitter to TTLs?
  3. Which eviction policy suits a dedicated cache, and why should durable data live elsewhere?
  4. What problems do big keys cause, and how do you find them?
  5. How do you calculate the cache hit rate from Redis statistics, and what are its limitations?
  6. When is a two-tier (local + Redis) cache worth the extra complexity?

docs.text:
• Redis documentation: Key eviction

  • Redis command reference: MEMORY USAGE
  • Redis command reference: GETEX
  • node-redis on GitHub

docs.title: Redis Fundamentals
docs.text: Redis is an in-memory data structure server: a separate process that holds data in RAM and lets clients read and change it with simple commands over a network connection. Its values are not just strings but lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams, and more, each with commands designed for it. Backends use Redis for caching, sessions, counters, rate limits, queues, and real-time features.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A typical database query reads from disk, parses SQL or a query document, and may take several milliseconds. A Redis command usually completes in well under a millisecond on the server. When the same data is read thousands of times per second, or when several application instances need to share fast, temporary state, Redis removes load from the primary database and keeps response times low.

Redis is also easy to misuse: it is limited by memory, it is not durable by default in every configuration, and one slow command can stall every client. Understanding how it works is the basis for the other Redis lessons.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitLab uses Redis for many separate jobs at once. Its development guide lists caching, the Sidekiq job queue, shared application state, CI trace chunks, a Pub/Sub backend for ActionCable, rate-limiting state, and sessions, and notes that GitLab.com runs separate Redis instances rather than one shared server (GitLab: Redis guidelines). One fast, shared store serves many features; splitting instances keeps a busy cache from hurting queues and sessions.
  • Mastodon backs home feeds, list feeds, Sidekiq queues, and its streaming API with Redis, and also uses it for volatile caching. Its scaling guide recommends a separate Redis for the cache, because the other data is important to keep (Mastodon: Scaling up your server).
  • Stripe implements its API rate limiters with Redis and keeps a Redis cluster that counts in-flight requests for load shedding (Stripe: Scaling your API with rate limiters). Every API server needs the same counters at sub-millisecond speed, which a shared in-memory store provides.

Popular tools and providers:

  • Redis Open Source and Valkey, a BSD-licensed fork backed by the Linux Foundation.
  • Amazon ElastiCache, which runs Valkey, Memcached, and Redis OSS engines.
  • Google Cloud Memorystore for Redis and Azure Managed Redis (Microsoft is retiring Azure Cache for Redis in its favor).

docs.title: The client-server model
docs.text:
+--------------+       TCP (port 6379)        +--------------------+
| App instance |  --- SET user:42:name Ada -->|                    |
|  (Node.js)   |  <-------- OK --------------|   Redis server     |
+--------------+                              |                    |
+--------------+                              |  keys -> values    |
| App instance |  --- GET user:42:name ------>|  held in memory    |
|  (Node.js)   |  <-------- "Ada" -----------|                    |
+--------------+                              +--------------------+

Redis is a key-value store at its core. Every piece of data lives under a key (a string), and the value has a type: string, list, hash, set, sorted set, stream, and others covered in data structures. Each type has its own commands, and using the wrong command on a key returns a WRONGTYPE error.

docs.title: Why Redis is fast
docs.text:
1. Data lives in memory. Reads and writes do not wait for disk.
  2. Commands run one at a time. A single main thread executes commands sequentially. There are no locks between commands, and every individual command is atomic: no other command runs in the middle of it.
  3. I/O can use extra threads. Since Redis 6, optional I/O threads can read and write network data in parallel, while command execution stays on the main thread. Background threads also handle work such as freeing large values and syncing files to disk.
  4. Compact encodings. Small lists, hashes, sets, and sorted sets are stored in memory-efficient formats and switch to larger structures only when they grow.
  5. Simple protocol. The wire protocol is cheap to parse.

The flip side of single-threaded execution: a slow command blocks all clients. KEYS * on millions of keys, deleting a huge value with DEL, or a long Lua script freezes the server until it finishes. Prefer SCAN to KEYS, UNLINK (asynchronous delete) to DEL for big values, and keep scripts short.

docs.title: Keys and naming conventions
docs.text:
Keys are binary-safe strings (up to 512 MB, though they should be short). Redis has no tables or folders, so teams invent structure with a naming convention, usually segments separated by colons:

Key Meaning user:42 Hash with user 42's profile user:42:sessions Set of session IDs for user 42 session:9f3c... One session's data cache:v2:product:17 Cached product, cache format version 2 rate:login:203.0.113.5 Login attempt counter for one IP

Good keys are readable, predictable, include the object type and ID, and can include a version so a cache format change does not read old data.

Redis also has numbered logical databases (0–15 by default, chosen with SELECT), but Redis Cluster supports only database 0. Separate instances or key prefixes are the more common way to isolate data.

docs.title: Expiration (TTL)
docs.text:
Any key can have a time to live. When it expires, Redis deletes it.

Command Effect SET key value EX 60 Set a value that expires in 60 seconds (PX for milliseconds) EXPIRE key 60 Add or change a TTL on an existing key EXPIREAT key 1767225600 Expire at a Unix timestamp TTL key Seconds left: -1 means no expiry, -2 means the key does not exist PTTL key Milliseconds left PERSIST key Remove the TTL

Commands that replace a value (such as SET without KEEPTTL) clear the TTL. Commands that modify a value in place (such as INCR, LPUSH, or HSET) keep it.

Redis removes expired keys in two ways:

  • Lazy (passive) expiry: when a client accesses a key, Redis checks whether it has expired and deletes it before answering.
  • Active expiry: a background cycle repeatedly samples keys that have a TTL and deletes the expired ones, so keys nobody reads still disappear.

Because active expiry samples rather than scanning everything, an expired key may occupy memory briefly, but no client will ever read it.

docs.title: redis-cli basics
docs.text:
redis-cli is the command-line client. Run it with no arguments to connect to localhost:6379, or pass -h, -p, and -a/--user, or a URL with -u.

$ redis-cli
127.0.0.1:6379> PING
PONG
127.0.0.1:6379> SET greeting "hello" EX 60
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET greeting
"hello"
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL greeting
(integer) 57
127.0.0.1:6379> TYPE greeting
string
127.0.0.1:6379> EXISTS greeting missing
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> DEL greeting
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> GET greeting
(nil)

Useful commands while learning: SCAN 0 MATCH user:* COUNT 100 to list keys safely, INFO for server statistics, MONITOR to watch every command (only on a development server, because it slows Redis), and --latency to measure round-trip time.

docs.title: RESP, the wire protocol
docs.text:
Clients talk to Redis with RESP (REdis Serialization Protocol), a simple text-prefixed format. SET key value is sent as an array of bulk strings:

*3
$3
SET
$3
key
$5
value

and the reply +OK is a simple string. RESP3, introduced in Redis 6 and selected with the HELLO 3 command, adds richer types such as maps, doubles, and out-of-band push messages. Client libraries handle the protocol for you; knowing it exists explains why pipelining many commands is cheap.

docs.title: Running Redis locally
docs.text:
The quickest way is the official Docker image:

$ docker run -d --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis
$ docker exec -it redis redis-cli PING
PONG

See Docker. Never expose port 6379 to the internet: require authentication (passwords or ACL users), use TLS for connections across networks, and keep Redis on a private network.

docs.title: Connecting from Node.js
docs.text: The examples in these Redis lessons use the official node-redis client (redis on npm). Its methods mirror Redis commands in camelCase: GET is get, HSET is hSet, ZADD is zAdd. Option names occasionally change between major versions of the client, so check its documentation for the version you install.

docs.title: Redis compared with Memcached
docs.text:
Redis Memcached Values Many data types with server-side operations Strings (bytes) only Persistence Optional (RDB snapshots, AOF log) None Replication and failover Built in (replicas, Sentinel, Cluster) Not built in Threading Single-threaded command execution, optional I/O threads Multi-threaded Extra features Pub/Sub, streams, Lua scripts, transactions Minimal by design Typical use Cache plus shared state, counters, queues Simple, very large caches

Memcached remains a good, simple cache; Redis is chosen when you need data types, persistence, replication, or the other features.

docs.title: Redis, its license, and Valkey
docs.text: Redis was open source under the BSD license for most of its history. In 2024, Redis Ltd. moved new versions (starting with 7.4) to source-available licenses (RSALv2 and SSPLv1). In response, the Linux Foundation started Valkey, a BSD-licensed fork of the last open-source Redis code (the 7.2 line), which stays command-compatible with Redis for the features they share. Redis 8 (May 2025) later added the open-source AGPLv3 as a licensing option. For application code the commands in these lessons work on both; the choice matters mainly for companies that redistribute or host the server, and some managed services (for example Amazon ElastiCache) offer Valkey.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use Redis when:

  • Several application instances must share fast, temporary state: sessions, counters, rate limits, locks, or feature flags.
  • The same data is read far more often than it changes and can be rebuilt from a database (a cache).
  • An operation maps onto a server-side data structure command: a leaderboard, a capped feed, a set of unique visitors, a work queue.
  • The working data fits comfortably in RAM.

Avoid Redis, or use it only next to another store, when:

  • It would be the only copy of business-critical records that need joins, ad-hoc queries, or multi-table transactions; use a primary database.
  • The dataset is much larger than the memory you can afford.
  • You need months of replayable events at high volume; a log-based broker such as Kafka fits better (see Pub/Sub and streams).
  • One process could keep the data in memory itself, with no sharing needed.
Need In-process cache (Map) Memcached Redis Primary database Shared across instances No Yes Yes Yes Data types and server-side operations Any JS value, local only Strings only Many types, atomic commands Tables or documents, rich queries Survives a restart No No Optional (RDB/AOF) Yes Replication and failover No Not built in Built in Built in Typical role Hottest per-process data Simple shared cache Cache plus shared state System of record

docs.title: Connect, set, and read with node-redis
docs.text:
import { createClient } from "redis";

const client = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL }); // redis://host:6379
client.on("error", (err) => console.error("Redis client error", err));
await client.connect();

await client.set("greeting", "hello", { EX: 60 }); // SET greeting hello EX 60
console.log(await client.get("greeting"));           // "hello"
console.log(await client.ttl("greeting"));           // e.g. 60
console.log(await client.get("missing"));            // null

await client.close(); // waits for pending commands, then disconnects

close() is the node-redis v5+ name; older v4 code calls quit(), which still works but is deprecated. destroy() drops the connection immediately.

Always attach an error listener: without it, a connection error is an unhandled event that can crash the process. node-redis reconnects automatically after network failures.

docs.title: One shared client per process
docs.text:
// redis.js: create the client once and import it everywhere.
import { createClient } from "redis";

export const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
redis.on("error", (err) => console.error("Redis error", err));
await redis.connect();

Creating a client per request opens a new TCP connection each time and quickly exhausts the server's connection limit.

docs.title: Expiry in action
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET otp:42 "839201" EX 300
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL otp:42
(integer) 296
127.0.0.1:6379> PERSIST otp:42
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL otp:42
(integer) -1
127.0.0.1:6379> EXPIRE otp:42 5
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> GET otp:42      # six seconds later
(nil)

docs.title: Iterating keys safely with SCAN
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> SCAN 0 MATCH user:* COUNT 100
1) "1792"           <- cursor for the next call; "0" means finished
2) 1) "user:42"
   2) "user:7"

SCAN returns a page of keys and a cursor. Repeat with the returned cursor until it is 0. It may return a key more than once, so treat results as a set.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use a consistent key naming scheme with an object type, ID, and optional version.
  • Give temporary data a TTL; unbounded keys eventually fill memory.
  • Avoid KEYS, FLUSHALL, and other blocking or destructive commands in production; block them for application users with ACL rules (for example -@dangerous).
  • Keep values small; split very large hashes, lists, or sets.
  • Create one client per process and reuse it; handle error events.
  • Require authentication, use TLS across networks, and never expose Redis publicly.
  • Set maxmemory and an eviction policy appropriate to the workload (see using Redis as a cache).
  • Decide explicitly whether the data must survive restarts (see persistence and high availability).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
Latency spikes and client timeouts.

  • Detect: SLOWLOG GET 10 lists the slowest recent commands; enable the latency monitor with CONFIG SET latency-monitor-threshold 100 and read LATENCY LATEST or LATENCY DOCTOR.
  • Cause: one slow command blocks every client: KEYS *, DEL of a huge value, HGETALL or SMEMBERS on a collection with millions of members, or a long Lua script.
  • Fix: use SCAN and UNLINK, split big keys, fetch only the fields you need, and keep scripts short.

Writes fail or cached data vanishes when memory fills.

  • Detect: INFO memory shows used_memory reaching maxmemory; INFO stats shows evicted_keys rising. With noeviction, write commands start returning out-of-memory errors while reads still work.
  • Cause: keys without TTLs, big keys, or a backlog that grows faster than it drains. Slack's Redis job queue had an outage when Redis reached its memory limit and workers could no longer dequeue (Slack engineering).
  • Fix: add TTLs, choose an eviction policy that fits the data, alert on memory well before the limit, and keep caches and queues on separate instances.

New connections are refused.

  • Detect: INFO clients shows connected_clients near maxclients (10,000 by default); INFO stats shows rejected_connections increasing.
  • Cause: a client created per request, or connections that are never closed.
  • Fix: create one client per process and reuse it, and close it on shutdown.

The server becomes very slow or is killed by the operating system.

  • Detect: the Swap lines in /proc/<pid>/smaps for the Redis process are non-zero (the check the Redis latency guide recommends); used_memory_rss smaller than used_memory (a mem_fragmentation_ratio below 1) is another hint; system logs show the process was killed for memory.
  • Cause: maxmemory unset or set too close to the machine's RAM, with no headroom for snapshots, replication buffers, and client buffers.
  • Fix: set maxmemory well below physical RAM and monitor memory at the host level too.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• In-memory data store: A database that keeps its working data in RAM.
  • Key: The name under which a value is stored.
  • Data type: The structure of a value (string, hash, list, set, and so on).
  • TTL: Time to live: how long until a key expires.
  • Atomic command: A command that runs completely without other commands interleaving.
  • RESP: The Redis Serialization Protocol used between clients and server.
  • redis-cli: The official command-line client.
  • Valkey: A BSD-licensed, community fork of Redis maintained under the Linux Foundation.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Redis is only a cache." It is also used for sessions, queues, leaderboards, locks, and streams.
  • "In-memory means my data is never lost" or "always lost." Durability depends on persistence and replication settings.
  • "Single-threaded means slow." Sequential execution in memory is very fast; the risk is slow commands blocking others.
  • Using KEYS * in production. It scans every key and blocks the server.
  • Forgetting TTLs. Memory fills, and eviction or errors follow.
  • Overwriting a key and expecting the TTL to stay. SET clears it unless KEEPTTL is used.
  • Opening a connection per request. This wastes time and connections.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What makes Redis fast, and what is the main risk of its single-threaded command execution?

  3. Which commands keep a key's TTL and which clear it?
  4. Why is SCAN preferred over KEYS in production?
  5. How does Redis differ from Memcached?
  6. Why should an application create one Redis client per process?

docs.title: Transactions, Pipelining, and Lua
docs.text: Single Redis commands are atomic, but real features often need several commands: check a value, then change two keys. Redis gives you three tools for this. Transactions (MULTI/EXEC, optionally with WATCH) run a group of commands without interruption. Pipelining sends many commands in one round trip for speed. Lua scripts (and Redis Functions) run logic on the server atomically. This lesson explains what each guarantees and when to use which.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Many Redis bugs in production are race conditions or latency problems. Two clients that each read a seat count of 1 and both book the seat; a counter that is incremented but never gets its TTL because the process crashed between commands; a page that makes 200 sequential Redis calls and spends most of its time waiting on the network. Understanding atomicity and round trips fixes all three. Background on race conditions is in concurrency and race conditions.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• BullMQ implements every queue operation (adding a job, moving it to active, extending its lock) as a Lua script on its Redis backend, so each job state transition runs atomically even with many workers competing (BullMQ: Architecture).
  • GitLab asks developers to put hash tags in keys that are used together (project:{1}:set_a and project:{1}:set_b) so multi-key operations work on Redis Cluster. For multi-key reads across nodes it uses pipelining that splits commands per node, with a 1,000-command minimum batch for Rails.cache reads, and its guide notes that transactions cannot span slots (GitLab: Redis guidelines).

docs.title: Single-command atomicity
docs.text:
Redis executes commands one at a time, so each command completes without any other command running in the middle. INCR, SET ... NX, ZINCRBY, LMOVE, and HINCRBY are all atomic. Whenever one command can express the whole operation, use it: it is the simplest and fastest solution.

The problem starts when an operation needs several commands, especially "read, decide, then write".

docs.title: MULTI / EXEC transactions
docs.text:
client                         Redis
  | MULTI                        |
  |----------------------------->| OK
  | DECRBY account:1 50          |
  |----------------------------->| QUEUED     (not executed yet)
  | INCRBY account:2 50          |
  |----------------------------->| QUEUED
  | EXEC                         |
  |----------------------------->| 1) (integer) 50
  |                              | 2) (integer) 150   (both ran back to back)

What a transaction guarantees:

  • Isolation: queued commands run sequentially at EXEC, and no command from another client runs in between.
  • All or nothing for queuing errors: if a command is rejected while queuing (for example a wrong number of arguments), EXEC refuses to run any of them and returns an EXECABORT error.

What it does not guarantee:

  • No rollback. If a command fails while executing (for example INCR on a key holding text, or a WRONGTYPE error), that command returns an error, but the other commands still run and their effects remain.
  • No reading in the middle. Replies arrive only after EXEC, so you cannot use the result of one queued command to decide the next. For "read, then decide", you need WATCH or Lua.

DISCARD throws away the queued commands.

docs.title: WATCH: optimistic locking
docs.text:
WATCH tells Redis to abort the next EXEC if any watched key changes before it runs. This is optimistic concurrency: you do not lock anything, you detect conflicts and retry.

If nobody touches the watched key, EXEC returns the array of replies as usual.

Rules:

  • Call WATCH before MULTI, on the same connection.
  • EXEC, DISCARD, and UNWATCH clear all watches.
  • Under heavy contention, retries pile up; a Lua script is usually better.

Because watches belong to a connection, a client library that shares one connection among many concurrent requests needs a dedicated connection for WATCH.

docs.title: Pipelining
docs.text:
Every command normally costs one network round trip (RTT): send, wait for the reply, send the next. Pipelining sends many commands without waiting and reads all replies afterward.

Pipelining also reduces system calls on both sides, so Redis can serve more commands per second. It is purely a performance technique:

  • Commands in a pipeline are not atomic; other clients' commands can run between them.
  • You can combine both: send a MULTI ... EXEC block in one pipeline.

Batch large pipelines (for example 1,000 commands at a time) so replies do not consume too much memory. node-redis automatically pipelines commands issued in the same tick of the event loop, such as those inside one Promise.all.

Multi-key commands (MGET, MSET, HMGET) are often even better than a pipeline when they fit.

docs.title: Lua scripts
docs.text:
A Lua script runs on the server, and while it runs, no other command executes. This gives you atomic "read, decide, write" logic in one round trip.

EVAL "<lua source>" numkeys key1 key2 ... arg1 arg2 ...

Inside the script:

  • KEYS[1], KEYS[2], ... are the key names passed in.
  • ARGV[1], ARGV[2], ... are the other arguments.
  • redis.call("CMD", ...) runs a command and raises an error if it fails; redis.pcall returns the error instead.

KEYS vs ARGV matters. Every key the script touches must be passed in KEYS, never built inside the script from strings. Redis uses the declared keys to route the script in a cluster and to check access permissions. In Redis Cluster, all keys used by one script (or one MULTI transaction) must belong to the same hash slot; use hash tags to group them: only the part inside {} is hashed, so {user:42}:cart and {user:42}:orders land on the same slot. Otherwise Redis returns a CROSSSLOT error. See persistence and high availability for how slots work.

Caching scripts. Sending the full source every time wastes bandwidth. SCRIPT LOAD returns the script's SHA1, and EVALSHA sha1 ... runs it. The script cache can be emptied (for example by a restart or failover), so clients call EVALSHA and fall back to EVAL when they get a NOSCRIPT error. Most client libraries do this for you.

Keep scripts short. A running script blocks every other client. After a configurable threshold (5 seconds by default), Redis starts answering other clients with BUSY errors; a script that has not written anything can be stopped with SCRIPT KILL. Never loop over large collections in a script.

Type conversion gotcha: a Lua number returned to the client becomes an integer (decimals are truncated), so return non-integers as strings.

docs.title: Redis Functions
docs.text:
Redis 7.0 added Functions: named Lua functions grouped into libraries, loaded once with FUNCTION LOAD, and called with FCALL. Unlike the EVAL script cache, functions are part of the server's data: they are persisted and replicated, so they survive restarts and failovers, and applications call them by name instead of shipping source code.

FUNCTION LOAD "#!lua name=seats
redis.register_function('reserve_seat', function(keys, args)
  local left = tonumber(redis.call('GET', keys[1]) or '0')
  if left <= 0 then return 0 end
  redis.call('DECR', keys[1])
  redis.call('SADD', keys[2], args[1])
  return 1
end)"

FCALL reserve_seat 2 event:9:seats event:9:attendees user:42

docs.title: Choosing a tool
docs.text: Need Use One atomic operation A single command (INCR, SET NX, LMOVE) Several writes that must not interleave, no decisions in between MULTI / EXEC Read, decide, write with low contention WATCH + MULTI / EXEC with retries Read, decide, write with high contention, or complex logic Lua script or Function Many independent commands, fast Pipelining (or multi-key commands)

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use these tools when:

  • MULTI/EXEC: several writes must not interleave with other clients, and no decision depends on a value read in between.
  • WATCH: a read-decide-write operation sees little contention, so retries are rare.
  • Lua or Functions: the decision and the writes must happen in one atomic step under contention, or you want one round trip for a small piece of logic.
  • Pipelining: you send many independent commands and only need speed.

Avoid them when:

  • One built-in command already does the job (INCR, SET NX, LMOVE, ZINCRBY): it is simpler and just as atomic.
  • You need rollback or durable, multi-record integrity across your business data: use a database transaction.
  • A script would loop over large collections or run for long: it blocks every client.
  • Keys live in different hash slots in Redis Cluster and cannot share a hash tag: neither MULTI nor a script can span slots.
Need Redis tool Database transaction instead when Move money between two counters MULTI (no decision) or Lua (with a balance check) The balances are records of truth that must survive and roll back Book the last seat Lua script or Function The booking must commit together with other database rows Many reads per page Pipelining or MGET Not applicable: this is about round trips, not atomicity Retry-safe update with little contention WATCH + MULTI The data is primarily stored in the database

docs.title: A transaction in redis-cli, including a runtime error
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET name "Ada"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> MULTI
OK
127.0.0.1:6379(TX)> INCR name
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:6379(TX)> SET status "done"
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:6379(TX)> EXEC
1) (error) ERR value is not an integer or out of range
2) OK

The INCR failed, but SET status still ran: there is no rollback.

docs.title: WATCH conflict
docs.text:
# Client A                            # Client B
WATCH event:9:seats
GET event:9:seats      -> "1"
                                      DECR event:9:seats   -> 0
MULTI
DECR event:9:seats     -> QUEUED
EXEC                   -> (nil)       # aborted: the key changed; A retries

docs.title: MULTI in Node.js
docs.text:
// Fixed-window counter: increment and set TTL together.
const [count] = await redis
  .multi()
  .incr("rate:login:203.0.113.5")
  .expire("rate:login:203.0.113.5", 900, "NX")
  .exec(); // replies in order: [count, 1 or 0]

docs.title: WATCH with retries in Node.js
docs.text:
import { WatchError } from "redis";

export async function reserveSeat(conn, eventId, userId) {
  // conn: a dedicated connection (from redis.duplicate() or a pool),
  // because WATCH state belongs to the connection.
  const seatsKey = `event:${eventId}:seats`;
  const attendeesKey = `event:${eventId}:attendees`;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    await conn.watch(seatsKey);
    const left = Number(await conn.get(seatsKey) ?? 0);
    if (left <= 0) {
      await conn.unwatch();
      return false;
    }
    try {
      await conn.multi().decr(seatsKey).sAdd(attendeesKey, userId).exec();
      return true;
    } catch (err) {
      if (err instanceof WatchError) continue; // someone else changed it
      throw err;
    }
  }
  throw new Error("Too much contention, try again later");
}

docs.title: The same operation as a Lua script
docs.text:
const RESERVE_SEAT = `
local left = tonumber(redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) or "0")
if left <= 0 then
  return 0
end
redis.call("DECR", KEYS[1])
redis.call("SADD", KEYS[2], ARGV[1])
return 1`;

export async function reserveSeatAtomic(eventId, userId) {
  const result = await redis.eval(RESERVE_SEAT, {
    keys: [`event:${eventId}:seats`, `event:${eventId}:attendees`],
    arguments: [String(userId)],
  });
  return result === 1;
}

No retries and no dedicated connection: the check and both writes happen in one atomic step.

docs.title: EVALSHA with a NOSCRIPT fallback
docs.text:
const sha = await redis.scriptLoad(RESERVE_SEAT);

async function runReserve(keys, args) {
  try {
    return await redis.evalSha(sha, { keys, arguments: args });
  } catch (err) {
    if (!String(err.message).startsWith("NOSCRIPT")) throw err;
    return redis.eval(RESERVE_SEAT, { keys, arguments: args }); // reloads it
  }
}

docs.title: Pipelining in Node.js
docs.text:
// Issued in the same tick: node-redis sends them as one pipeline.
const ids = [17, 18, 19, 20];
const products = await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => redis.get(`product:${id}`)));

// Or with one multi-key command:
const sameResult = await redis.mGet(ids.map((id) => `product:${id}`));

// An explicit, non-atomic batch:
const replies = await redis
  .multi()
  .set("a", "1")
  .set("b", "2")
  .incr("visits")
  .execAsPipeline(); // pipelined without MULTI/EXEC wrapping

docs.title: Mass loading with redis-cli
docs.text:
$ cat data.txt
SET user:1 "Ada"
SET user:2 "Sam"
$ cat data.txt | redis-cli --pipe
All data transferred. Waiting for the last reply...
errors: 0, replies: 2

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Prefer a single atomic command whenever one exists.
  • Use Lua (or Functions) for read-decide-write logic under contention.
  • Declare every key in KEYS; use hash tags so cluster keys share a slot.
  • Keep scripts short and bounded; never iterate over large collections.
  • Do not rely on MULTI for rollback; validate inputs before queuing.
  • Use dedicated connections for WATCH, and cap retries.
  • Pipeline or use multi-key commands instead of many sequential calls.
  • Batch very large pipelines to limit memory use.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
Every client suddenly gets BUSY errors.

  • Detect: commands fail with a BUSY error; the Redis log reports a script running for too long; SLOWLOG GET shows EVAL, EVALSHA, or FCALL entries.
  • Cause: a script ran past busy-reply-threshold (5 seconds by default), usually because it loops over a large collection.
  • Fix: SCRIPT KILL (or FUNCTION KILL) stops it if it has not written anything; if it has written, only SHUTDOWN NOSAVE is allowed. Rewrite the script to touch a bounded number of keys.

NOSCRIPT errors after a restart or failover.

  • Detect: EVALSHA calls fail with NOSCRIPT No matching script.
  • Cause: the script cache is volatile: it is not persisted and can be cleared on restart, on failover when a replica becomes the primary, or by SCRIPT FLUSH.
  • Fix: fall back to EVAL on NOSCRIPT (as in the example above; most clients do it for you), or load the logic as a Redis Function, which is persisted and replicated.

CROSSSLOT errors after moving to Redis Cluster.

  • Detect: transactions, scripts, or multi-key commands fail with CROSSSLOT errors.
  • Cause: the keys involved hash to different slots.
  • Fix: give related keys the same hash tag ({user:42}:cart, {user:42}:orders), as GitLab's guidelines require for keys used together.

Throughput collapses under contention.

  • Detect: application metrics show many WatchError retries per successful update, and request latency climbs.
  • Cause: many clients WATCH the same hot key, so most EXEC calls abort and retry.
  • Fix: move the read-decide-write into a Lua script or Function, which never needs a retry.

Data is half-updated after a transaction.

  • Detect: the EXEC reply array contains an error for one command while the others succeeded.
  • Cause: a runtime error (such as WRONGTYPE or INCR on text) does not roll back the other commands.
  • Fix: check every element of the EXEC reply, validate types before queuing, and use a Lua script that checks conditions before writing.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Atomic: Executed as one indivisible step, with no interleaving.
  • Transaction: A group of commands executed together with MULTI/EXEC.
  • Optimistic locking: Detecting conflicting changes (with WATCH) and retrying instead of locking up front.
  • Round-trip time (RTT): The time for a request to reach the server and the reply to return.
  • Pipelining: Sending several commands before reading their replies.
  • Lua script: Server-side code executed atomically with EVAL.
  • Hash tag: The {...} part of a key that decides its cluster slot.
  • Redis Function: A named, persisted server-side function called with FCALL.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "MULTI rolls back on errors." Runtime errors leave other commands' effects in place.
  • "A pipeline is a transaction." Pipelined commands can interleave with other clients.
  • Reading inside MULTI to make a decision. Replies only come at EXEC.
  • Building key names inside Lua. It breaks cluster routing and ACL checks.
  • Long-running scripts. They block all clients and trigger BUSY errors.
  • Using WATCH on a shared connection. Another request's commands can clear or confuse the watch.
  • Many sequential awaits in a loop. Each costs a round trip; batch them.

docs.text:

  3. Why is pipelining faster, and why is it not atomic?
  4. Why must a Lua script receive its key names through KEYS?
  5. How do hash tags help scripts and transactions in Redis Cluster?
  6. How do Redis Functions differ from scripts run with EVAL?
