docs.title: Availability and Reliability
docs.text: Users judge a system first by whether it works when they need it. Availability measures how much of the time a service is usable, reliability measures how consistently it does the right thing, and durability measures whether data, once saved, stays saved. This page explains how these are measured, what makes systems fail, and the design techniques that keep them running through failures.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Downtime costs money and trust. An hour of checkout outage is lost revenue; repeated outages push customers to competitors.
  • Failures are constant at scale. Disks die, servers reboot, networks partition, deployments go wrong, and whole data centers lose power. A system with hundreds of machines sees some failure every day.
  • Every extra "nine" costs more. Going from 99.9% to 99.99% availability usually means more redundancy, more automation, and more engineering time, so the target must match the business need.
  • Reliability is a design property, not something added after launch. Single points of failure and missing timeouts are architectural decisions.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub's October 2018 incident. A 43-second loss of connectivity between GitHub's US East Coast network hub and its primary East Coast data center caused its Raft-based failover tool (Orchestrator) to move MySQL writes to the West Coast. The brief partition led to 24 hours and 11 minutes of degraded service, showing how automated cross-data-center failover can turn a short network fault into a long recovery (GitHub blog).
  • Netflix Chaos Monkey. Netflix built Chaos Monkey to randomly terminate instances in production so that engineers build services that tolerate instance failures (Chaos Monkey documentation).
  • Google's error budgets. Google SRE manages release velocity with error budgets: as long as a service meets its SLO, releases continue; when SLO violations use up the budget, releases are temporarily halted and effort shifts to reliability (Google SRE book).
  • AWS static stability. AWS runs many services as stateless fleets across three or more Availability Zones and overprovisions so that the remaining zones can carry the load if one is impaired: with three zones, it overprovisions by 50 percent (AWS Builders' Library).
  • Amazon S3's design targets. S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% durability and 99.99% availability of objects over a year, a clear example of durability and availability being separate goals (Amazon S3 documentation).

Popular tools and providers: chaos engineering with AWS Fault Injection Service, Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos, and Gremlin; resilience libraries such as resilience4j (Java), Polly (.NET), and opossum (Node.js circuit breaker); health checks and self-healing with Kubernetes probes and cloud load balancers; SLO tracking in Prometheus/Grafana, Datadog, and similar tools.

docs.title: Availability, reliability, and durability
docs.text:
Concept Question Typical measure Example Availability Is the service up and responding when called? Percentage of time (or of requests) served successfully 99.95% of requests succeed this month Reliability Does it perform correctly, without failure, over time? Error rate, mean time between failures Orders are never charged twice Durability Once data is stored, is it kept without loss? Probability of losing data per year Object storage designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability

They are related but different: a system can be available but unreliable (it responds quickly with wrong data), or durable but unavailable (your data is safe, but the service is down for an hour).

Availability is often measured in one of two ways:

  • Time-based: uptime / (uptime + downtime).
  • Request-based: successful requests / valid requests. This is more accurate for services that are partly degraded rather than fully up or down.

docs.title: The nines
docs.text:
Downtime allowed by an availability target (using a 365-day year and a 30-day month):

Availability Downtime per year Downtime per month (30 days) Common name 99% 3.65 days 7.2 hours "two nines" 99.5% 1.83 days 3.6 hours 99.9% 8.76 hours 43.2 minutes "three nines" 99.95% 4.38 hours 21.6 minutes 99.99% 52.6 minutes 4.32 minutes "four nines" 99.999% 5.26 minutes 25.9 seconds "five nines" 99.9999% 31.5 seconds 2.6 seconds "six nines"

At four nines, a single manual recovery that takes 10 minutes uses more than the whole month's budget. High targets require automatic detection and recovery.

docs.title: Availability of combined components
docs.text:
In series (a request needs every component), availabilities multiply:

Load balancer (99.99%) -> App (99.9%) -> Database (99.9%)
Total = 0.9999 x 0.999 x 0.999 = 0.9979  ->  about 99.8%

Each dependency on the critical path lowers the total. A service cannot be more available than the things it synchronously depends on.

In parallel (redundant copies, any one is enough), the system fails only if all copies fail:

Two independent app instances at 99% each:
Total = 1 - (1 - 0.99)^2 = 1 - 0.0001 = 99.99%

This assumes independent failures. Two instances in the same rack, on the same power supply, running the same buggy release, fail together. Real redundancy needs independence: different hosts, availability zones, and staggered deployments.

docs.title: SLI, SLO, and SLA
docs.text:
• SLI (service level indicator): a measured number, such as "proportion of requests answered successfully in under 300 ms".
  • SLO (service level objective): the target for an SLI over a window, such as "99.9% of requests succeed in under 300 ms over 30 days". An internal engineering goal.
  • SLA (service level agreement): a contract with customers that states consequences (credits, refunds) if a level is missed. SLAs are set looser than SLOs so the team has a margin.
  • Error budget: 100% minus the SLO. With a 99.9% SLO, 0.1% of requests may fail each month. While budget remains, teams can ship faster; when it runs out, they focus on reliability.

See logging and monitoring for how to measure them.

docs.title: MTBF, MTTR, and friends
docs.text:
Metric Meaning MTBF (mean time between failures) Average time a system runs before failing MTTD (mean time to detect) Average time until someone or something notices the failure MTTR (mean time to recovery/repair) Average time from failure to restored service 
Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)

MTBF = 30 days (43,200 min), MTTR = 60 min  ->  43,200 / 43,260 = 99.86%
Same MTBF, MTTR = 5 min                     ->  43,200 / 43,205 = 99.99%

Preventing every failure is impossible; shortening recovery (fast detection, automatic failover, quick rollbacks) often improves availability more cheaply than making failures rarer.

docs.title: Redundancy
docs.text:
Model How it works Failover time Cost Example Active-active All copies serve traffic; a load balancer spreads requests Near zero (others absorb the load) Each copy must handle extra load when one fails Stateless app servers behind a load balancer Active-passive (hot standby) A standby runs and stays in sync, but takes no traffic until promoted Seconds to minutes Standby capacity is idle Database primary with a synchronous replica Warm standby A scaled-down copy runs and can be scaled up Minutes Lower A small copy of the stack in another region Cold standby Infrastructure is defined but not running; restored from backups Hours Lowest Rebuild from infrastructure-as-code plus backups

N+1 means running one more instance than the load requires, so losing any one still leaves enough capacity. N+2 survives a failure during maintenance.

docs.title: Failover
docs.text:
Failover moves traffic or a role from a failed component to a healthy one.

  1. Detection: health checks, heartbeats, or a consensus protocol notice the failure.
  2. Decision: automatic (by the load balancer, a cluster manager, or a consensus election) or manual (an operator decides).
  3. Switch: route traffic to the healthy copy, or promote a replica to primary.
  4. Recovery: repair or replace the failed component and restore redundancy.

Pitfalls:

  • Split brain: two nodes both believe they are the primary and accept writes. Consensus-based elections and fencing (cutting off the old primary) prevent it.
  • False positives: an overloaded but healthy node is declared dead, failover adds load elsewhere, and failures cascade.
  • DNS caching slows failover based on DNS changes; clients keep using old addresses until the TTL expires. See DNS.
  • Untested failover often fails when needed. Practice it.

Databases are the hardest part; see MongoDB replication for how replica sets elect a new primary.

docs.title: Single points of failure
docs.text:
A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose failure takes the whole service down. Common ones:

  • One database primary with no replica or tested failover.
  • One load balancer, NAT gateway, or VPN tunnel.
  • Everything in one availability zone or one region.
  • One DNS provider or one certificate that expires unnoticed.
  • A shared configuration, authentication, or secrets service that every request depends on.
  • A cron job that runs on exactly one server.
  • One person who knows how to deploy or restore.

Walk through each request path and ask, "what happens if this disappears?"

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
Load balancers and orchestrators decide where to send traffic, and whether to restart instances, based on health checks.

Check Answers On failure Liveness Is the process alive and not stuck? Restart the instance Readiness Can it serve traffic right now (started, dependencies reachable, not shutting down)? Stop sending it traffic, but do not restart it Deep / dependency check Are the database, cache, and key APIs reachable? Alert or degrade, carefully

Keep liveness checks shallow. If liveness fails whenever the database is slow, every instance restarts at once during a database incident, turning a partial problem into a total outage. See load balancing.

docs.title: Availability zones and regions
docs.text:
• An availability zone (AZ) is one or more data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking, close enough to others in its region for low-latency replication.
  • Multi-AZ deployments (instances and database replicas spread across at least two or three AZs) survive a data center failure. This is the standard baseline for production on cloud platforms.
  • Multi-region deployments survive the loss of a whole region and can serve users from nearby regions. They are much harder: data must replicate across long distances, which forces trade-offs between consistency and latency (see consistency and the CAP theorem), and costs rise.
  • Static stability: provision enough capacity in each AZ so that losing one AZ does not require launching new resources in the middle of an incident, when control planes may themselves be struggling.

docs.title: Graceful degradation
docs.text:
When a dependency fails, serve a reduced experience instead of an error:

  • Show cached or slightly stale data if the source is down.
  • Hide non-essential features (recommendations, reviews) behind feature flags.
  • Switch to read-only mode if writes are impossible.
  • Return default values for optional parts of a page.
  • Shed load: reject low-priority work early (with 503 or 429) to keep critical paths fast, instead of letting everything slow down together.

Decide in advance which features are critical and which can be dropped.

docs.title: Bulkheads, circuit breakers, timeouts, and retries
docs.text:
• Timeouts stop a slow dependency from tying up your resources.
  • Retries with backoff and jitter handle brief glitches, but uncontrolled retries multiply load during an outage (retry storms).
  • Circuit breakers stop calling a dependency that keeps failing, fail fast, and probe periodically for recovery.
  • Bulkheads isolate resources (separate connection pools, thread pools, or instances per dependency or customer tier), so one failing part cannot exhaust everything.

These are explained in detail in timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

docs.title: Chaos engineering
docs.text:
Chaos engineering is the practice of deliberately injecting failures to verify that the system tolerates them, before real incidents do it for you.

  1. Define steady state with metrics (for example, checkout success rate).
  2. Form a hypothesis: "if one AZ's app instances are terminated, checkout success stays above 99.9%."
  3. Inject a realistic fault: kill instances, add latency, drop a dependency, fill a disk.
  4. Observe, and limit the blast radius (start in staging or with a small slice of traffic, with a stop button).
  5. Fix what broke and repeat.

Netflix popularized the practice with Chaos Monkey, which randomly terminates production instances. Simpler starting points are game days: planned exercises where the team simulates an outage and practices the response.

docs.title: Disaster recovery: RPO and RTO
docs.text:
Disaster recovery (DR) plans for large failures: region loss, data corruption, ransomware, an operator deleting a database.

  • RPO (recovery point objective): how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. An RPO of 5 minutes means backups or replication must be no more than 5 minutes behind.
  • RTO (recovery time objective): how long you can afford to be down before service is restored.
Strategy RPO / RTO Cost Backup and restore Hours / hours to a day Lowest Pilot light (core data replicated, minimal infrastructure ready) Minutes / tens of minutes to hours Low Warm standby (scaled-down full copy running) Seconds to minutes / minutes Medium Multi-site active-active Near zero / near zero Highest

Replication is not a backup: if a bug or attacker deletes data, the deletion replicates too. Keep point-in-time backups, store copies separately, and test restores regularly. See backups.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Match the investment to the cost of downtime:

Strategy Protects against Cost and complexity Use when Single instance + backups Data loss (with restore time) Lowest Development, internal tools, early prototypes Redundant instances in one zone Single server failure Low Small production services with modest SLOs Multi-AZ (redundancy across zones) Server and data center failure Moderate Default for production services Multi-region active-passive Region failure, with failover minutes to hours High Regulatory requirements, revenue-critical services Multi-region active-active Region failure with near-zero downtime; lower latency for global users Highest; hard data consistency problems Global products where minutes of downtime are very costly

Use high-availability techniques when:

  • Downtime directly costs revenue, safety, or trust (payments, healthcare, authentication, core APIs other teams depend on).
  • Other services depend on yours; your SLO caps theirs.
  • An SLA with penalties is promised to customers.

Do not over-invest when:

  • The service is internal, batch-oriented, or can be paused without harm.
  • A higher target would require multi-region data consistency the product cannot justify.
  • The team cannot operate the extra complexity; a well-run multi-AZ system usually beats a poorly run multi-region one.

docs.title: Liveness and readiness endpoints in Express
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
let shuttingDown = false;

// Liveness: the process is running and the event loop responds
app.get("/healthz", (req, res) => res.sendStatus(200));

// Readiness: can we serve traffic right now?
app.get("/readyz", async (req, res) => {
  if (shuttingDown) return res.status(503).json({ status: "draining" });
  try {
    await db.ping({ timeoutMs: 500 }); // a cheap, time-limited dependency check
    res.json({ status: "ready" });
  } catch {
    res.status(503).json({ status: "database unavailable" });
  }
});

const server = app.listen(3000);

// Graceful shutdown: fail readiness first so the load balancer stops sending
// traffic, then finish in-flight requests and exit
process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  shuttingDown = true;
  setTimeout(() => server.close(() => process.exit(0)), 10_000);
});

db.ping stands for your database client's health call. See running Express in production.

docs.title: Computing composite availability and error budgets
docs.text:
const series = (...parts) => parts.reduce((a, b) => a * b, 1);
const parallel = (a, copies) => 1 - (1 - a) ** copies;

const app = parallel(0.99, 3); // three instances at 99% each
const total = series(0.9999, app, 0.9995); // LB, app tier, managed database
console.log((total * 100).toFixed(3) + "%"); // ~99.940%

// Error budget for a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, request-based
const requestsPerMonth = 50_000_000;
// Round it: 1 - 0.999 is not exact in floating point (50000.000000000044 unrounded)
const budget = Math.round(requestsPerMonth * (1 - 0.999));
console.log(`${budget} failed requests allowed this month`); // 50000

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Set SLOs from user needs, measure SLIs, and manage error budgets.
  • Remove single points of failure on every critical path.
  • Run across multiple AZs with enough spare capacity to lose one.
  • Automate detection and failover, and test failover regularly.
  • Keep liveness checks shallow and readiness checks meaningful.
  • Use timeouts everywhere, bounded retries with jitter, circuit breakers, and bulkheads.
  • Design graceful degradation for non-critical features.
  • Define RPO and RTO, back up accordingly, and rehearse restores.
  • Reduce MTTR with good alerts, runbooks, fast rollbacks, and blameless post-incident reviews.
  • Practice failure with game days and controlled chaos experiments.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every instance restarts during a database blip. Detect: the orchestrator's events show liveness probe failures and restarts across all instances at the same moment the database is slow. Cause: the liveness check queries the database. Fix: keep liveness shallow (process responds) and put dependency checks in readiness, with short timeouts.
  • Failover works, but clients keep failing for minutes. Detect: errors continue long after the new database primary is up; some app instances recover and others do not. Cause: long DNS TTLs, connection pools holding connections to the old primary, or the primary address cached in application config. Fix: short TTLs on failover records, drivers that discover topology, connection validation, and retries on "not primary" errors.
  • A small outage becomes a big one through retries. Detect: request volume to a failing dependency multiplies during the incident, and errors continue after it recovers. Cause: retries at several layers (client, gateway, service) multiply each other, without backoff. Fix: retry at one layer, use backoff with jitter and retry budgets, and add circuit breakers.
  • Losing one zone overloads the others. Detect: CPU and p99 latency spike in the surviving zones; autoscaling cannot launch instances fast enough. Cause: capacity sized for normal load only. Fix: static stability: keep enough spare capacity in each zone to absorb a zone loss.
  • Backups exist, but the restore fails. Detect: a restore drill takes far longer than the RTO, or backups turn out corrupt or incomplete. Cause: backups were never tested. Fix: scheduled, automated restore tests with measured RPO and RTO.
  • Split brain after a partition. Detect: writes accepted in two data centers; replication errors or conflicting rows when the link returns. Cause: automatic failover promoted a second primary while the first was still reachable by some clients. Fix: consensus-based leader election, fencing of the old primary, and careful limits on automatic cross-region failover.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Availability: the fraction of time or requests a service works.
  • Reliability: the ability to perform correctly over time.
  • Durability: the likelihood that stored data is not lost.
  • SLI / SLO / SLA: measured indicator / internal target / external contract.
  • Error budget: the amount of unreliability an SLO allows.
  • MTBF / MTTR: mean time between failures / mean time to recovery.
  • Redundancy: extra copies so one failure does not stop the service.
  • Active-active / active-passive: all copies serve / a standby waits.
  • Failover: switching to a healthy copy after a failure.
  • Split brain: two nodes acting as primary at the same time.
  • Single point of failure: a component whose failure stops the system.
  • Graceful degradation: reduced functionality instead of total failure.
  • RPO / RTO: acceptable data loss / acceptable downtime in a disaster.
  • Chaos engineering: controlled fault injection to build confidence.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "We have replicas, so we have backups." Replication copies mistakes and deletions too.
  • Assuming redundancy is independent when copies share a zone, a power source, or the same faulty release.
  • Deep liveness checks that restart every instance during a database blip.
  • Chasing five nines for a product that needs three, at great cost.
  • Untested failover and restore procedures.
  • Retries without limits, turning a small outage into a retry storm.
  • Ignoring dependencies' availability: your SLO cannot exceed the product of your critical synchronous dependencies.
  • Counting only full outages, missing partial degradations that users feel.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Distinguish availability, reliability, and durability with an example of each.
  2. How much downtime per month does 99.95% allow? Per year?
  3. Three components in series each have 99.9% availability. What is the overall availability? How does adding a redundant copy of one change it?
  4. Why can reducing MTTR improve availability more cheaply than increasing MTBF?
  5. What is the difference between liveness and readiness checks, and why should liveness be shallow?
  6. Define RPO and RTO, and explain why replication alone does not satisfy them.

  • AWS Well-Architected: Reliability Pillar.

docs.title: Capacity Planning
docs.text: Capacity planning answers a simple question: will we have enough resources for the load we expect, with room to spare, at a sensible cost? It turns traffic forecasts and load-test results into numbers of servers, database size, storage, bandwidth, and budget, before users discover the limits for you.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Running out of capacity looks like an outage. Latency climbs, requests time out, queues back up, and errors cascade, usually at the busiest and most valuable moment (a launch, a sale, enrollment day).
  • Some capacity takes time to add. Autoscaling reacts in minutes, but a bigger database, more storage, a higher provider quota, or a new region can take days or weeks.
  • Over-provisioning wastes money. Servers idling at 5% utilization are a real cost, often one of the largest in a cloud bill.
  • Failures need spare capacity. If losing one availability zone leaves too little capacity for the remaining load, redundancy does not help.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google's Auxon. Google SRE built Auxon to automate capacity planning for services running in Google production. Instead of the traditional cycle of forecasting demand and hand-building allocation plans, service owners encode their requirements and dependencies (their intent), and the tool generates a new allocation plan whenever demand, supply, or requirements change (Google SRE book).
  • Shopify before Black Friday Cyber Monday. With over a million merchants relying on Shopify for BFCM, Shopify runs regular load tests (can the service withstand a known level of traffic?) and stress tests ahead of sales events, and anyone can start a large load test from Slack (Shopify Engineering).
  • Netflix's predictive autoscaling. Netflix built Scryer, a predictive autoscaling engine, because reactive autoscaling was not enough for its use cases: instance startup times ranged from 10 to 45 minutes, leaving existing servers exposed during rapid spikes, and outages could be followed by retry storms (Netflix TechBlog).
  • AWS plans for zone failure. AWS runs many services across three or more Availability Zones and overprovisions by 50 percent with three zones, so the remaining zones can carry the full load if one is impaired, without launching new capacity during the event (AWS Builders' Library).
  • Predictive scaling as a product. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling offers predictive scaling, which analyzes historical load to detect daily and weekly patterns and increases capacity ahead of the forecast load (AWS documentation).

Popular tools and providers: load testing with k6, Gatling, Apache JMeter, and Locust; scaling with cloud autoscaling groups (including scheduled and predictive policies), the Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, KEDA, and Karpenter; cost visibility with cloud cost explorers, budgets, and tools such as Kubecost.

docs.title: The capacity planning loop
docs.text:
1. Measure current demand and resource usage
2. Forecast future demand (growth, seasonality, events)
3. Measure capacity per unit (load test: what can one instance handle?)
4. Calculate required resources + headroom + failure margin
5. Provision (or configure autoscaling limits) and check cost
6. Monitor actual usage against the plan, and repeat regularly

docs.title: Forecasting load
docs.text:
Start from data, not guesses:

  • Baseline: current requests per second, active users, data growth per day, and resource utilization, per service and per endpoint.
  • Daily and weekly patterns: most services have a peak several times higher than their average. The peak-to-average ratio is often 2x to 5x; measure yours.
  • Growth trend: organic growth over months, from historical metrics.
  • Seasonality: holidays, end of month, back to school, tax season.
  • Planned events: launches, marketing campaigns, a big customer onboarding, a TV mention. Ask the business teams; they know before the metrics do.
  • Product changes: a new feature that polls every 10 seconds can multiply traffic overnight.

Plan for the peak, not the average, and add a margin for forecast error.

docs.title: Units of capacity
docs.text:
Every resource has a limit, and the first one you hit is the bottleneck:

Resource Example limits Compute CPU per instance, requests/s per instance, event loop saturation Memory Heap size, cache size, per-connection buffers Database Queries/s, connections (max_connections), IOPS, storage, replication lag, lock contention Storage Disk size and growth, IOPS and throughput limits Network Bandwidth per instance, load balancer limits, egress cost Queues Consumer throughput vs arrival rate, backlog size Third parties API rate limits and quotas (email, SMS, payments), account limits on the cloud provider

docs.title: Headroom and target utilization
docs.text:
Never plan to run resources at 100%. Plan a target utilization at peak that leaves headroom for:

  • Forecast error and sudden spikes.
  • Time for autoscaling to react.
  • Losing an instance or a whole availability zone.
  • Background work (deployments, backups, cache warming).

A common starting point is to keep CPU at peak around 50% to 70% of the measured maximum per instance, then adjust from experience.

Surviving a zone failure: with capacity spread evenly over Z zones, losing one leaves (Z - 1)/Z of it. To carry the full peak load after losing one of 3 zones, the remaining 2 zones must handle 100% of the traffic, so during normal operation each zone runs at most about two-thirds of what it could safely handle.

docs.title: Why latency explodes near full utilization
docs.text:
When requests arrive at random and a resource is busy, new requests wait in a queue. A classic queueing result (for a single server with random arrivals and service times, the M/M/1 model) shows how average response time grows with utilization ρ:

response time = service time / (1 - ρ)

Utilization (ρ) Response time as a multiple of service time 50% 2x 70% ~3.3x 80% 5x 90% 10x 95% 20x 99% 100x

Real systems are more complex, but the shape holds: latency rises slowly at first and then sharply as utilization approaches 100%. The point where the curve turns upward is the knee. Going from 60% to 90% utilization does not cost 50% more latency; it can cost several times more, and the tail gets worse faster than the average. That is why headroom is not waste.

docs.title: Load testing to find the limits
docs.text:
Capacity per instance must be measured, not guessed:

  • Ramp test: increase load step by step and record throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, and resource usage at each step. The maximum sustainable throughput is where latency stays within the SLO.
  • Find the bottleneck: note which resource saturates first (CPU, database connections, memory, a downstream service). Fixing it raises the ceiling until the next bottleneck appears.
  • Stress test: push past the limit to see how the system fails. Good systems shed load with 503s; bad ones collapse completely.
  • Soak test: hold expected load for hours to find memory leaks, connection leaks, and slow degradation.
  • Spike test: jump suddenly from low to high load to see whether autoscaling and caches cope.

Use production-like data volumes, a realistic mix of endpoints, and an environment that matches production. See performance testing and performance and latency.

docs.title: Autoscaling vs provisioned capacity
docs.text:
Autoscaling Provisioned (fixed) capacity How Add and remove instances based on metrics or schedules Run a planned, fixed number of resources Strengths Follows demand; saves money off-peak Predictable; instant capacity; no warm-up Weaknesses Reacts in minutes; new instances need warm-up (startup, caches, JIT); can fail if the provider is short of capacity Wasteful when demand is low Fits Stateless app tiers, workers on queues Databases, stateful systems, a known baseline

Practical combinations:

  • Provision a baseline (the minimum) for normal traffic, and autoscale above it.
  • Scheduled scaling before known peaks (9 a.m. on weekdays, a sale launch) so capacity is already there.
  • Set maximums that protect downstream systems: 200 app instances can exhaust a database's connections.
  • Remember that databases do not scale out instantly; plan their capacity ahead. See database scaling and stateless services and autoscaling.

docs.title: Cost awareness
docs.text:
Capacity is a cost decision as well as a technical one:

  • Track cost per unit of business value: per 1,000 requests, per active user, per order.
  • Right-size: instances consistently below 20% CPU can usually be smaller.
  • Commit for the baseline (reserved instances, savings plans, committed use discounts) and pay on demand for the variable part.
  • Use cheaper capacity for interruptible work: spot or preemptible instances for batch jobs and queue workers that can be retried.
  • Watch data transfer (egress): serving large responses across the internet or between regions can cost more than the servers.
  • Tier storage: move old data to cheaper storage classes; set retention and lifecycle rules for logs and backups.
  • Shut down idle environments (development and test outside working hours).
  • Balance against reliability: removing the spare zone's capacity saves money until the day a zone fails.

docs.title: Capacity for databases, storage, and bandwidth
docs.text:
Databases:

  • Queries per second for reads and writes, separately; writes usually limit the primary, and reads can move to replicas or caches.
  • Connections: instances x pool size per instance (plus workers and cron jobs) must stay below the database's connection limit. A connection pooler (such as PgBouncer) helps.
  • Working set in memory: performance drops sharply when frequently used data and indexes no longer fit in RAM.
  • Storage growth and IOPS, replication lag at peak, and time to back up and restore at the projected size.

Storage:

raw growth per day x retention period x replication factor
  + indexes and overhead + backups and snapshots

Bandwidth:

average response size x requests per second x 8 = bits per second

docs.title: Revisiting the plan
docs.text:
Capacity planning is continuous:

  • Review quarterly, and before every major launch.
  • Alert on saturation signals (CPU, memory, connections, disk, queue age) well before 100%.
  • Compare forecasts with reality and improve the model.
  • Record limits and assumptions so the next review starts from facts.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Invest in formal capacity planning when:

  • Traffic has predictable peaks or known events (sales, enrollment, launches).
  • Some resources are slow to scale: databases, storage, provider quotas, reserved hardware.
  • Downtime under load is costly, or an SLO must hold during peaks.
  • Cost is significant enough that over-provisioning matters.

Keep it lightweight when:

  • The product is early and traffic is small; a managed or serverless platform with sensible limits and alerts is enough.
  • Everything in the path scales automatically and quickly, and cost is minor.
Approach How it works Use when Weaknesses Provisioned capacity Fixed resources sized for peak plus headroom Databases, stateful systems, steady load Waste at low traffic Reactive autoscaling Add instances when metrics cross thresholds Stateless tiers with gradual changes Lags behind sudden spikes; warm-up time Scheduled scaling Scale at known times Daily or weekly patterns, planned events Does not handle surprises Predictive scaling Forecast from history and scale ahead Regular patterns with long instance startup Needs history; can mispredict unusual days Serverless / fully managed Provider scales per request Spiky or low traffic, small teams Concurrency limits, cold starts, cost at very high steady load

Most production systems combine them: provisioned databases, a baseline plus reactive and scheduled scaling for the app tier, and serverless for spiky side workloads.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
A service has 2 million daily active users, each making about 30 API requests per day.

1. Request rate

Daily requests  = 2,000,000 x 30          = 60,000,000
Average rate    = 60,000,000 / 86,400 s   ~ 694 requests/s
Peak (3x avg)   ~ 2,083 requests/s
Plan for growth (+40% next 12 months)     -> design peak ~ 3,000 requests/s

2. App instances

A load test shows one instance sustains 400 requests/s while p99 stays under the 300 ms SLO.

Normal operation at <= 60% of max (240 req/s per instance):
  3,000 / 240 = 12.5  -> 13 instances

Zone failure: 3 zones, survive losing 1, allowing up to 85% of max (340 req/s)
on the remaining instances during the incident:
  3,000 / 340 = 8.8 -> 9 instances needed in the 2 surviving zones
  -> 5 per zone (10 in 2 zones) -> 15 instances in total

Choose 15 (5 per zone). Normal utilization: 3,000 / 15 = 200 req/s = 50% of max.

3. Database

Each request makes ~2 queries      -> 6,000 queries/s at peak
80% reads, 20% writes              -> 4,800 reads/s, 1,200 writes/s
Cache absorbs 75% of reads         -> 1,200 reads/s reach the database
Primary: 1,200 writes/s; reads spread over 2 replicas (~600/s each)

Connections: 15 instances x pool of 10 = 150, + 20 for workers = 170
             (keep well below the database's connection limit)

4. Storage

New data per user per day ~ 5 KB
Raw growth   = 2,000,000 x 5 KB = 10 GB/day  -> ~3.65 TB/year
+ indexes and overhead (~30%)                -> ~4.7 TB/year
x 3 copies (primary + 2 replicas)            -> ~14 TB of disk per year
+ backups (separately, with retention)

5. Bandwidth

Average response 15 KB
Peak egress  = 3,000 x 15 KB = 45 MB/s ~ 360 Mbit/s
Monthly data = 694 req/s x 15 KB x 2,592,000 s (30 days) ~ 27 TB/month
-> compression and CDN caching matter for both speed and cost

For quick estimation techniques, see back-of-the-envelope estimation.

docs.title: A small capacity calculator
docs.text:
function planInstances({ peakRps, maxRpsPerInstance, targetUtilization, zones, failureUtilization }) {
  // Enough for peak at the target utilization
  const normal = Math.ceil(peakRps / (maxRpsPerInstance * targetUtilization));

  // Enough to carry peak with one zone lost, at a higher emergency utilization
  const neededInSurvivors = Math.ceil(peakRps / (maxRpsPerInstance * failureUtilization));
  const perZone = Math.ceil(neededInSurvivors / (zones - 1));
  const withZoneLoss = perZone * zones;

  const total = Math.max(normal, withZoneLoss);
  return { total, perZone: Math.ceil(total / zones), normalUtilization: peakRps / (total * maxRpsPerInstance) };
}

console.log(planInstances({
  peakRps: 3_000, maxRpsPerInstance: 400, targetUtilization: 0.6, zones: 3, failureUtilization: 0.85,
}));
// { total: 15, perZone: 5, normalUtilization: 0.5 }

docs.title: Utilization vs latency
docs.text:
// Average response time multiplier for a single queue (M/M/1 approximation)
for (const rho of [0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99]) {
  console.log(`${Math.round(rho * 100)}% busy -> ${(1 / (1 - rho)).toFixed(1)}x service time`);
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Plan for peak load plus growth plus failure, not the average.
  • Measure per-instance capacity with load tests and find the first bottleneck.
  • Keep headroom: target utilization well below 100% at peak.
  • Spread capacity across zones so losing one still fits the load.
  • Combine a provisioned baseline with autoscaling and scheduled scaling for known peaks.
  • Plan slow-to-scale resources early: databases, storage, quotas, and third-party limits.
  • Track cost per request or per user and right-size regularly.
  • Alert on saturation before limits are reached.
  • Write down assumptions and revisit the plan regularly.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Autoscaling cannot keep up with a spike. Detect: error rate and p99 rise for several minutes while the instance count climbs slowly behind demand. Cause: reactive scaling plus long startup and warm-up time. Fix: scheduled or predictive scaling before known peaks, a higher minimum capacity, and faster startup (smaller images, lazy initialization).
  • A limit nobody planned for. Detect: sudden throttling errors from a provider (429 from an email or SMS API, cloud API throttling errors), or "too many connections" from the database. Cause: quotas and connection limits were not part of the plan. Fix: keep an inventory of quotas and limits, request increases ahead of launches, and alert when usage reaches a set fraction of each limit.
  • A disk fills up. Detect: write failures with "No space left on device"; database or broker refusing writes. Cause: data or log growth faster than forecast, or retention never configured. Fix: forecast growth from metrics, alert at 70-80% usage, set retention and lifecycle rules, and enable storage autoscaling where the platform supports it.
  • Healthy averages, slow users. Detect: average CPU around 40%, but p99 latency is high and one database partition, one zone, or one instance is saturated. Cause: averages across a fleet hide a hot spot. Fix: monitor per-resource saturation and peak values (per minute, not per hour), and rebalance or fix the hot resource.
  • The cloud bill jumps. Detect: cost per request or per user rises month over month. Cause: over-provisioned instances, forgotten environments, cross-region or internet egress, or unbounded log storage. Fix: right-size from utilization data, tag resources by owner, set budgets and alerts, and add CDN caching or compression for egress-heavy traffic.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Capacity: the maximum load a system can handle while meeting its objectives.
  • Peak-to-average ratio: how much higher the busiest period is than the average.
  • Headroom: spare capacity kept for spikes, failures, and growth.
  • Target utilization: the planned busy fraction of a resource at peak.
  • Knee: the point where latency starts rising sharply with load.
  • Bottleneck: the resource that limits overall throughput.
  • Saturation: how close a resource is to its limit.
  • Right-sizing: matching resource sizes to actual needs.
  • N+1 capacity: one more unit than needed, so one failure still leaves enough.
  • Egress: data leaving a cloud network, usually billed.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Planning from average traffic and failing at the daily peak.
  • Assuming autoscaling solves everything: it is not instant, has limits, and does not scale your database.
  • Running at 90% utilization "to save money" and suffering huge latency and fragility.
  • Forgetting the failure case: enough capacity in total, but not after a zone goes down.
  • Ignoring connection limits: more app instances overload the database.
  • Load testing with unrealistic data or traffic mixes.
  • Forgetting third-party quotas, such as an email provider's daily limit.
  • Planning once and never revisiting.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why should capacity be planned for peak load rather than average load? How do you estimate the peak?
  2. Explain why response time rises sharply as utilization approaches 100%.
  3. With three availability zones, how much of each zone's capacity can you use normally if you must survive losing one zone?
  4. What does a ramp load test tell you, and what is the knee of the curve?
  5. When is provisioned capacity better than autoscaling?
  6. Estimate the peak request rate for 1 million daily users making 50 requests each, with a peak-to-average ratio of 4.
