  • AWS Well-Architected: Performance Efficiency Pillar and Reliability Pillar.
  • AWS Builders' Library: Using load shedding to avoid overload.
  • Related: back-of-the-envelope estimation and availability and reliability.

docs.title: Consistency and the CAP Theorem
docs.text: As soon as data is copied to more than one machine (for availability, for read scaling, or to be near users), the copies can disagree for a while. A consistency model describes what a reader may see while that happens. The CAP theorem explains a hard limit: when the network splits, a replicated system must choose between staying consistent and staying available. This page explains the models, the theorem, and how to choose per feature.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Replication lag causes real bugs: a user changes their name, refreshes, and sees the old one; a comment appears before the post it replies to.
  • Some data must never be inconsistent (a bank balance, the last seat on a flight, a unique username), while some can be slightly stale (a like count, a product's review summary). Using the strongest model everywhere wastes latency and availability; using the weakest everywhere causes correctness bugs.
  • Databases expose these choices as settings (read and write concerns, consistency levels, read preferences). You need the concepts to configure them correctly.
  • CAP is a staple of system design interviews and is often stated wrongly.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Amazon's always-writeable shopping cart. Amazon's CTO described Dynamo, the internal store behind services such as the shopping cart: customers must be able to view and add items to their cart even if disks fail, network routes flap, or data centers are destroyed, so the cart service must always be able to read and write. Dynamo sacrifices consistency under certain failure scenarios and uses object versioning with application-assisted conflict resolution (All Things Distributed).
  • DynamoDB's per-request choice. DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default; setting ConsistentRead returns the most up-to-date data for tables and local secondary indexes, while global secondary indexes and streams are always eventually consistent (DynamoDB documentation).
  • Amazon S3's strong consistency. S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUT and DELETE of objects in all AWS Regions, so a read after a successful write returns the new object (Amazon S3 documentation).
  • Google Spanner's external consistency. Spanner provides external consistency, which Google describes as stronger than linearizability: the system behaves as if all transactions ran one after another. Timestamps from its TrueTime clock service also allow consistent reads across a whole database, even across regions, without blocking writes (Spanner documentation).
  • Figma's multiplayer editing. Figma's real-time collaboration was informed by CRDTs. Its server defines the order of events, and when two people change the same property of the same object, the last value sent to the server wins, similar to a last-writer-wins register (Figma blog).

Popular tools and providers: strongly consistent distributed databases such as Google Spanner and CockroachDB; consensus stores such as etcd and ZooKeeper; tunable-consistency stores such as Apache Cassandra, Amazon DynamoDB, and MongoDB; CRDT libraries such as Automerge and Yjs for collaborative apps.

docs.title: Consistency models
docs.text:
From strongest to weakest:

Model Guarantee Example of what it rules out Cost Linearizable (strong) Every operation appears to happen at a single instant between its start and end; once a write completes, every later read sees it Reading an old value after someone else's write finished Coordination on every write and read; higher latency; unavailable during partitions Sequential All clients see all operations in the same order, consistent with each client's own order (but not necessarily real time) Two clients seeing two writes in different orders Coordination, slightly less than linearizable Causal Operations that are causally related (a reply after the message it answers) are seen in that order by everyone; unrelated ones may appear in any order Seeing a reply before the original message Tracking dependencies; can stay available during partitions Read-your-writes A client always sees its own previous writes A user not seeing the profile change they just saved Route the user's reads carefully Monotonic reads Once a client has seen a value, it never sees an older one later A refresh showing a newer comment list, then an older one Stick a client to one replica, or track versions Eventual If writes stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value Nothing in the short term; only guarantees convergence Cheapest, fastest, most available

Read-your-writes and monotonic reads are session guarantees: they are about what one client sees, and are often enough to make an eventually consistent system feel correct to users.

Two different C's

The "C" in ACID means a transaction keeps the database's rules and constraints valid. The "C" in CAP means linearizability across replicas. They are unrelated.

docs.title: Replication lag in practice
docs.text:
With a primary and asynchronous read replicas, writes reach replicas after a delay: usually milliseconds, sometimes seconds or minutes under load.

t=0 ms   user saves name "Ana Li"   -> primary: "Ana Li"
t=5 ms   user's page reloads         -> reads replica 2: still "Ana"   (read-your-writes broken)
t=40 ms  replica 2 catches up        -> "Ana Li"

Other anomalies:

  • Monotonic reads broken: the first refresh hits a caught-up replica (5 comments), the second hits a lagging one (3 comments).
  • Causality broken: a reply is replicated to a region before the question it answers.

Common fixes:

  • Read from the primary for a short time after a user writes (for example, mark the session for a few seconds), or always for the user's own data.
  • Pin a session to one replica (monotonic reads).
  • Track versions: the client remembers the version or timestamp of its last write, and the server reads from a replica that has caught up to it (or waits).
  • Causally consistent sessions, offered by some databases (MongoDB provides them with majority read and write concerns).

docs.title: The CAP theorem
docs.text:
The CAP theorem (conjectured by Eric Brewer in 2000, proved by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch in 2002) concerns a replicated data store and three properties:

  • C, consistency: linearizability; every read returns the most recent completed write.
  • A, availability: every request received by a non-failing node gets a non-error response.
  • P, partition tolerance: the system keeps operating even though the network drops or delays messages between nodes.

Stated precisely: when a network partition happens, a system must choose between consistency and availability.

Key points:

  • Partitions are not optional in a distributed system; networks fail. So the real choice is between CP (consistent, may refuse requests during partitions) and AP (available, may return stale or conflicting data during partitions).
  • "CA" is not a real option for a distributed system; it only describes a single node, which avoids partitions by not being distributed.
  • The choice applies only during a partition. When the network is healthy, a system can be both consistent and available.
  • Real systems are rarely purely one or the other: many are tunable per operation, and the CAP definitions are narrow (linearizability, and availability at every non-failing node).

Typical examples:

Leaning Behavior during a partition Examples CP The minority side stops accepting writes (and often reads) Consensus systems such as etcd and ZooKeeper; MongoDB replica sets (only a majority can elect a primary); databases using synchronous replication AP All sides keep serving; conflicts resolved later Dynamo-style stores such as Cassandra or Riak at low consistency levels; DNS; caches

docs.title: PACELC
docs.text:
CAP says nothing about normal operation. PACELC (proposed by Daniel Abadi) extends it:

if there is a Partition (P):
    choose Availability (A) or Consistency (C)
Else (E), in normal operation:
    choose lower Latency (L) or Consistency (C)

The "else" part is the everyday trade-off: waiting for replicas to confirm a write (or reading from several of them) gives consistency but adds latency, especially across regions. Dynamo-style stores lean PA/EL by default; systems built on synchronous replication and consensus lean PC/EC.

docs.title: Quorum reads and writes
docs.text:
Leaderless and quorum-based systems keep N copies of each item. A write waits for W replicas to acknowledge; a read queries R replicas and takes the newest value.

If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica,
so a read sees at least one copy of the latest successful write.
N W R R + W > N? Behavior 3 2 2 Yes (4 > 3) Balanced; tolerates one node down for both reads and writes 3 3 1 Yes (4 > 3) Fast reads; writes fail if any replica is down 3 1 3 Yes (4 > 3) Fast writes; reads fail if any replica is down 3 1 1 No (2 is not greater than 3) Fastest and most available; reads may be stale (eventual)

Cassandra exposes this as consistency levels per query, such as ONE, QUORUM (a majority of replicas), LOCAL_QUORUM (a majority within the local data center), and ALL.

Caveats: quorums do not by themselves give linearizability. Concurrent writes, writes that partly succeed and then fail, and "sloppy" quorums that accept writes on substitute nodes during failures can all still produce anomalies.

docs.title: Conflict resolution
docs.text:
When replicas accept writes independently (AP systems, multi-leader or offline-first setups), the same item can be changed in two places. The system must merge the versions:

  • Last-write-wins (LWW): keep the version with the latest timestamp. Simple, but clocks on different machines drift, and the "losing" write is silently discarded.
  • Version vectors / vector clocks: each replica tracks a counter per replica, which lets the system detect whether two versions are ordered or truly concurrent. Concurrent versions ("siblings") are kept and merged by the application or the user.
  • CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types): data structures such as counters, sets, and sequences designed so that concurrent updates always merge to the same result in any order. Used in collaborative editors and some databases.
  • Application-level merge: business rules decide, for example "union of shopping cart items" or "flag for manual review".

The best conflict is the one you avoid: route all writes for an item to one place (a single leader or a home region per user) when you can.

docs.title: Consensus
docs.text: Strong consistency across replicas relies on consensus algorithms such as Raft and Paxos. A majority of nodes must agree on each change, so a cluster of 2f + 1 nodes tolerates f failures (3 nodes tolerate 1, 5 tolerate 2). A minority partition cannot make progress, which is exactly the CP choice. etcd, ZooKeeper, Kafka's KRaft controllers, and RabbitMQ quorum queues use this approach.

docs.title: Choosing per feature
docs.text:
Feature Needs Why Account balance, payments, inventory decrements Strong (or serialized through one leader/transaction) A stale read allows overspending or overselling Unique usernames or emails Strong uniqueness check Two users must not claim the same name A user editing their own profile or settings Read-your-writes They must see their own change; others can lag Comments and chat Causal Replies must not appear before what they answer Social feeds, like and view counts Eventual Slight staleness is invisible and cheap Product catalog, search index Eventual (seconds to minutes) Updated in the background Analytics dashboards Eventual (minutes or more) Approximate and delayed is fine

One system often mixes models: strong consistency for the order and payment, eventual consistency for the "recently viewed" list on the same page.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Model Use when Avoid when Strong (linearizable, or one leader + transactions) Money, inventory, bookings, uniqueness, permissions changes that must apply immediately Data is read globally at high volume and slight staleness is harmless; cross-region writes make every request slow Session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads) Users editing their own data on top of replicas or caches Other users must also see the change immediately (needs strong) Causal Comments, chat, collaborative content where replies must follow what they answer Simple key-value data with no relationships between writes Eventual Feeds, counters, analytics, search indexes, caches, recommendations A stale read can cause loss, overselling, security problems, or duplicates

Strong consistency is not free: it adds latency (waiting for a majority or a leader), reduces availability during partitions, and makes multi-region writes slow. Eventual consistency is not free either: you must handle staleness in the UI and resolve conflicts. Choose per feature, and default to the weakest model that is still correct for the business.

docs.title: Read-your-writes with a replica router
docs.text:
// After a user writes, send their reads to the primary for a short window
const STICKY_MS = 5_000;
const lastWriteAt = new Map(); // userId -> timestamp (use Redis when running many instances)

export function recordWrite(userId) {
  lastWriteAt.set(userId, Date.now());
}

export function poolForRead(userId, { primary, replica }) {
  const wroteRecently = Date.now() - (lastWriteAt.get(userId) ?? 0) < STICKY_MS;
  return wroteRecently ? primary : replica;
}

// In a handler
app.patch("/api/me", async (req, res) => {
  const user = await pools.primary.query("UPDATE users SET name = $1 WHERE id = $2 RETURNING *",
    [req.body.name, req.user.id]);
  recordWrite(req.user.id);
  res.json(user.rows[0]);
});

app.get("/api/me", async (req, res) => {
  const pool = poolForRead(req.user.id, pools);
  const user = await pool.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", [req.user.id]);
  res.json(user.rows[0]);
});

docs.title: Tunable consistency in MongoDB
docs.text:
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";

const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI);
const orders = client.db("shop").collection("orders");

// Acknowledged only after a majority of replica set members have the write
await orders.insertOne({ _id: "ord_901", status: "paid" }, { writeConcern: { w: "majority" } });

// Read only data that a majority has acknowledged (it cannot be rolled back)
const doc = await orders.findOne({ _id: "ord_901" }, { readConcern: { level: "majority" } });

// Causally consistent session: this session's reads observe its own earlier writes,
// even when reading from secondaries
const session = client.startSession({ causalConsistency: true });
try {
  await orders.updateOne({ _id: "ord_901" }, { $set: { status: "shipped" } },
    { session, writeConcern: { w: "majority" } });
  const fresh = await orders.findOne({ _id: "ord_901" },
    { session, readConcern: { level: "majority" }, readPreference: "secondary" });
  console.log(fresh.status); // "shipped"
} finally {
  await session.endSession();
}

See MongoDB read and write concerns.

docs.title: Quorum check
docs.text:
function quorumInfo(n, w, r) {
  return {
    overlapping: r + w > n, // reads see the latest successful write
    writeToleratesDown: n - w, // replicas that can be down while writes succeed
    readToleratesDown: n - r,
  };
}

console.log(quorumInfo(3, 2, 2)); // { overlapping: true, writeToleratesDown: 1, readToleratesDown: 1 }
console.log(quorumInfo(5, 3, 3)); // tolerates 2 down for both

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Decide consistency per feature, starting from what a stale read would cost the business.
  • Give users read-your-writes on their own data even in eventually consistent systems.
  • Use strong consistency (or one leader and a transaction) for money, inventory, and uniqueness.
  • Prefer avoiding conflicts (single leader per item) over resolving them.
  • Measure replication lag and alert on it.
  • Use majority write concerns and quorums for data you cannot lose.
  • Be precise about CAP: it is a choice during partitions, not a menu of "pick two".
  • Document the guarantees your API provides, so clients do not assume more.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• "My change disappeared." Detect: support tickets right after edits; the replica-lag metric (seconds behind the primary) is above zero when they happen. Cause: reads routed to asynchronous replicas immediately after a write. Fix: read-your-writes routing (primary for a window after writes, or version tracking) or causally consistent sessions.
  • Replica lag spikes during batch jobs. Detect: lag alerts every night at the same time; stale data in the morning. Cause: a large bulk update or long transaction that replicas must replay. Fix: chunk and throttle batch jobs, and avoid routing latency-sensitive reads to lagging replicas.
  • Updates silently revert. Detect: users report values jumping back; NTP clock-offset alerts on some hosts. Cause: last-write-wins with skewed clocks, so an older write with a later timestamp wins. Fix: conditional updates with versions (compare-and-set), or a single writer per item.
  • Writes fail during a network incident. Detect: errors such as "not writable primary" from MongoDB, or timeouts waiting for w: "majority". Cause: the primary lost contact with the majority, so the system chose consistency. Fix: expected CP behavior; spread replicas across three zones so a single failure keeps a majority, and use retryable writes.
  • Duplicate usernames appear. Detect: a reconciliation query finds two accounts with the same name. Cause: "check, then insert" against a replica or without a constraint. Fix: a unique index enforced on the primary, and handle the duplicate-key error.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Consistency model: the rules about what values reads may return.
  • Linearizability: operations appear to take effect instantly, in real-time order; the strongest single-object model.
  • Causal consistency: causally related operations are seen in order by everyone.
  • Read-your-writes / monotonic reads: session guarantees about a client's own view.
  • Eventual consistency: replicas converge if writes stop.
  • Replication lag: the delay before a replica reflects a write.
  • Network partition: nodes cannot communicate with each other.
  • CAP theorem: during a partition, choose consistency or availability.
  • PACELC: without a partition, choose latency or consistency.
  • Quorum: the number of replicas that must take part in a read or write.
  • Last-write-wins: keep the version with the latest timestamp.
  • Vector clock: per-replica counters for detecting concurrent updates.
  • CRDT: a data type whose concurrent updates always merge consistently.
  • Consensus: agreement among a majority of nodes (Raft, Paxos).

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Pick any two of C, A, and P." Partitions are a fact; the choice is C or A during them.
  • Calling a single-node database "CA" as if it solved the distributed problem.
  • Confusing ACID consistency with CAP consistency.
  • "Eventual consistency means data might be wrong forever." It converges; the question is how fast and what users see meanwhile.
  • Reading from replicas right after writing and treating the stale result as a bug in the database.
  • Trusting last-write-wins with unsynchronized clocks, silently dropping writes.
  • Assuming R + W > N gives full linearizability in all failure cases.
  • Using one consistency level for everything.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Order these from strongest to weakest: eventual, linearizable, causal, read-your-writes. Give an anomaly that each stronger model prevents.
  2. State the CAP theorem precisely. Why is "CA" not a meaningful choice for a distributed database?
  3. What does PACELC add to CAP?
  4. With N = 5, which values of W and R guarantee overlapping quorums while tolerating two failed replicas for both reads and writes?
  5. A user updates their profile and the page shows the old data. Explain the cause and two ways to fix it.
  6. Which consistency level would you choose for a wallet balance, a like counter, and a chat thread, and why?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Jepsen: Consistency models, a map of models and their relationships.
  • Amazon: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, the paper behind quorum-based, eventually consistent stores.
  • MongoDB: Read concern and causal consistency.
  • AWS: DynamoDB read consistency.
  • Related: database scaling and MongoDB replication.

docs.title: Database Scaling
docs.text: Application servers are easy to scale because they are stateless; the database is hard to scale because it is the state. Database scaling covers the techniques for handling more queries and more data: tuning, caching, connection pooling, read replicas, bigger machines, partitioning, sharding, denormalization, and separate read models. The order in which you apply them matters as much as the techniques themselves.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: In most growing systems the database becomes the first serious bottleneck. Adding app instances multiplies the queries and connections the database receives. Some scaling steps (an index, a cache) take an afternoon; others (sharding) change the data model, the queries, and operations forever. Knowing the cheap steps lets you postpone the expensive ones, and knowing the expensive ones lets you design so they remain possible.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub: replicas first, then split by domain. In 2019 GitHub's main MySQL cluster, mysql1, answered about 950,000 queries/s, of which 900,000 went to replicas and only 50,000 to the primary: read replicas were carrying the read load. To go further, GitHub grouped tables into "schema domains", used SQL linters to block queries and transactions that crossed domains, then moved domains (130 of its busiest tables in one cutover) onto separate clusters. By 2021 those tables served 1.2 million queries/s, and the average load on each host had halved. (GitHub Blog, 2021)
  • Notion: application-level sharding with logical shards. When Postgres VACUUM began to stall and transaction ID wraparound became a risk, Notion sharded by workspace ID. It chose 480 logical shards (one Postgres schema each, 15 per database) on 32 physical databases, sized to stay under 500 GB per table and 10 TB per physical database. That is the "many logical shards" pattern in the shard-routing example. (Notion blog, 2021)
  • Figma: vertical partitioning, then horizontal sharding. Moving groups of tables to their own databases was "a relatively easy and very impactful scaling lever". When single tables reached several terabytes and billions of rows, and vacuums began to hurt reliability, Figma looked at CockroachDB, TiDB, Spanner, and Vitess, then chose to build horizontal sharding on its existing RDS Postgres to avoid a risky data migration. (Figma blog, 2024)
  • Shopify: shards isolated into pods. Shopify sharded in 2015, when "it was no longer possible to continue buying a larger database server". It then grouped shards into pods, each with fully isolated datastores and no cross-pod requests, so one failing shard cannot take down the platform. (Shopify Engineering)

docs.title: Popular tools and providers
docs.text: Need Common choices Connection pooling PgBouncer, Amazon RDS Proxy, the driver's built-in pool Managed replicas and failover Amazon RDS and Aurora, Google Cloud SQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL, MongoDB Atlas Partitioning PostgreSQL declarative partitioning, MySQL partitioning Sharding MongoDB sharded clusters, Vitess (MySQL), Citus (PostgreSQL), application-level routing Distributed SQL (sharding built in) Google Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB Read models and change feeds Debezium or MongoDB change streams into Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Redis, or a reporting database

docs.title: The usual order of steps
docs.text:
1. Tune queries and indexes          cheapest; one missing index can be the whole problem
2. Cache hot reads                   removes repeated reads
3. Pool and limit connections        protects the database from app scale-out
4. Add read replicas                 scales reads
5. Scale up (bigger machine)         scales everything, simply, up to a limit
6. Partition tables                  smaller indexes, easier maintenance
7. Shard across machines             scales writes and data size; highest complexity

Steps 4 and 5 are often swapped; a larger machine is frequently the simplest next step. Sharding comes last because it is hard to undo.

docs.title: Step 1: queries and indexes
docs.text:
Most "the database is slow" problems are a missing index, an unbounded query, or an N+1 query pattern (one query per item in a list).

  • Look at the slowest and most frequent queries (slow-query logs, EXPLAIN, database monitoring).
  • Add indexes that match filters and sort order; see MongoDB indexes and performance.
  • Fetch only needed fields and paginate.
  • Batch N+1 queries into one query with IN (...) or $in.

docs.title: Step 2: caching
docs.text: Caching hot, rarely changing reads (profiles, catalogs, configuration) can remove most read traffic. See cache fundamentals and caching strategies.

docs.title: Step 3: connection pooling and connection limits
docs.text:
Opening a database connection is expensive (network handshake, TLS, authentication, server memory per connection), so drivers keep a pool of open connections that requests borrow and return.

The trap appears when you scale out the application:

Each app instance pool size: 20
Instances: 4   -> 80 connections     fine
Instances: 30  -> 600 connections    database may refuse connections
                                     or slow down from memory and context switching

Databases have connection limits (PostgreSQL's default max_connections is typically 100, for example), and many connections can hurt performance even below the limit.

Remedies:

  • Size pools so instances × pool size stays within what the database handles well, and keep autoscaling maximums consistent with that.
  • Use a connection pooler / proxy between apps and the database, such as PgBouncer for PostgreSQL or a managed proxy (for example Amazon RDS Proxy), which multiplexes many client connections onto fewer database connections.
  • In serverless functions, create the client outside the handler so warm invocations reuse it, and prefer a proxy.

docs.title: Step 4: read replicas
docs.text:
A replica is a copy of the database that continuously applies changes from the primary. Reads can go to replicas; writes go to the primary.

Replication is usually asynchronous, so replicas lag behind by milliseconds to seconds (more under heavy load). That causes the classic bug:

1. User updates their display name   -> write to primary
2. Page reloads and reads the profile -> read from a lagging replica
3. User sees the OLD name and thinks the save failed

Guaranteeing read-your-writes consistency:

Technique How Read from the primary after a write For a short window (for example 5–10 s) after a user writes, route that user's reads to the primary Read the primary for the user's own data Profile and settings pages read the primary; public lists use replicas Track replication position Remember the write's log position and read from a replica that has applied it (or wait) Causal consistency sessions Some databases offer sessions that track causality. In MongoDB, a causally consistent session guarantees read-your-writes (and three related guarantees) in all situations only when reads use "majority" read concern and writes use "majority" write concern; see read and write concerns

Replicas also provide failover: if the primary fails, a replica can be promoted. See MongoDB replication.

docs.title: Primary-replica compared with multi-primary
docs.text:
Primary-replica (single leader) Multi-primary (multi-leader) Writes accepted by One primary Several nodes Conflicts None (one writer) Concurrent writes to the same row on different nodes conflict Write scaling Limited to one node Spread across nodes Typical use Most applications Multi-region writes, offline-capable clients Complexity Low High: conflict detection and resolution (last-write-wins, merges, CRDTs)

Most systems should stay single-primary and scale writes with partitioning or sharding when needed.

docs.title: Step 5: scale up
docs.text: A larger instance (more CPU, RAM to hold the working set in memory, faster storage with more IOPS) improves everything without code changes. Managed databases make this a configuration change with a brief failover. Its limits are cost and the largest available machine, and it does not remove the single primary as a point of failure.

docs.title: Step 6: partitioning
docs.text:
Partitioning splits one large table into smaller pieces, often still on the same server.

  • Horizontal partitioning splits rows: orders from 2025 in one partition, 2026 in another.
  • Vertical partitioning splits columns or tables: rarely used, large columns (descriptions, blobs) move to a separate table, or unrelated features move to separate databases.

Common partitioning schemes:

Scheme Rows assigned by Good for Watch out for Range Ranges of a key (dates, ids) Time-series data; dropping old data by partition Recent ranges get all new writes (hot partition) Hash Hash of a key modulo N Even distribution Range queries touch every partition List Explicit values (region = "EU") Data grouped by category or region Uneven sizes

PostgreSQL supports declarative range, list, and hash partitioning. Benefits include smaller indexes, faster maintenance, and cheap deletion of old data by dropping a partition. Queries that filter on the partition key skip irrelevant partitions (partition pruning).

docs.title: Step 7: sharding
docs.text:
Sharding is horizontal partitioning across multiple database servers. Each shard holds a subset of the data and handles reads and writes for it, so total write capacity and storage grow with the number of shards.

Choosing a shard key is the most important decision:

Property Why it matters High cardinality Many distinct values allow spreading data across many shards Even frequency One very common value (one giant customer) creates a hot shard Not monotonically increasing for range sharding Timestamps or auto-increment ids send all new writes to the last shard Matches main queries Queries that include the shard key go to one shard; others must ask all shards

Problems sharding introduces:

  • Hot shards: uneven load from a skewed key or a celebrity tenant.
  • Cross-shard queries: queries without the shard key become scatter-gather (ask every shard, merge results), which is slower and harder to paginate.
  • Cross-shard transactions: atomic updates across shards need distributed transactions or careful design to avoid them.
  • Resharding: adding shards means moving data. Designs reduce the pain with consistent hashing or by creating many small logical shards up front and moving whole logical shards between servers.
  • Operations: backups, schema changes, and monitoring multiply by the number of shards.

Some databases shard natively (MongoDB sharded clusters; see MongoDB sharding); others use extensions or middleware (for example Citus for PostgreSQL, Vitess for MySQL), or application-level routing.

docs.title: Denormalization
docs.text: A normalized schema stores each fact once and joins at read time. Denormalization stores redundant copies (an order stores the customer's name; a post stores its comment count) so reads avoid joins or aggregations. It speeds up reads at the cost of extra writes and the risk of copies disagreeing. Update copies in the same transaction where possible, or asynchronously through events when slight lag is acceptable. See data modeling and validation.

docs.title: CQRS read models
docs.text:
Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) separates the model that handles writes from models optimized for reads. Writes go to the primary database; change events update one or more read models shaped for specific queries (a search index, a precomputed dashboard table, a feed per user).

commands ──> write model (normalized DB) ──events──> projector ──> read model(s)
queries  <────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                         (search index, cache, reporting DB)

Read models scale independently and make complex queries cheap, but they are eventually consistent with the write model and add infrastructure. Use CQRS for parts of a system with very different read and write needs, not as a default. See event-driven architecture.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Always start with steps 1 to 3 (queries and indexes, caching, connection budgets). They are cheap and often make later steps unnecessary.
  • Add read replicas when reads dominate and most of them can tolerate a little staleness. Do not add them to fix slow writes or a missing index.
  • Scale up when the working set no longer fits in memory or CPU is saturated and a larger instance is available at an acceptable cost.
  • Partition a table (on one server) when it is huge and queries or retention follow a natural key, usually time.
  • Shard only when write volume, data size, or maintenance on a single primary cannot be fixed by the steps above. It changes queries, transactions, and operations for good.
  • Do not use multi-primary just for write scaling; use it for multi-region writes or offline clients, and only if you can resolve conflicts.
Read replicas Partitioning (one server) Sharding (many servers) Scales Reads Maintenance, index size, deletion of old data Writes, storage, and reads Write capacity Unchanged (one primary) Unchanged (one server) Grows with the number of shards Application changes Route reads; handle replica lag Usually none; queries should filter on the partition key Every query needs the shard key; cross-shard work is redesigned Consistency Replicas lag the primary Same as before Cross-shard transactions are hard Operational cost Low to medium Low High: per-shard backups, migrations, rebalancing Reversible? Yes, remove replicas Mostly Very hard Typical trigger Read-heavy load, many lag-tolerant reads Huge time-series or log tables; slow VACUUM Largest instance not enough; write or storage limits

docs.title: Routing reads and writes in Node.js
docs.text:
import pg from "pg";

// Pools sized per instance: instances × max must fit the database's limits
const primary = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DB_PRIMARY_URL, max: 10 });
const replica = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DB_REPLICA_URL, max: 10 });

const RECENT_WRITE_MS = 10_000;
const lastWriteAt = new Map(); // userId -> timestamp (use Redis with many instances)

export async function updateDisplayName(userId, name) {
  await primary.query("UPDATE users SET display_name = $1 WHERE id = $2", [name, userId]);
  lastWriteAt.set(userId, Date.now());
}

export async function getProfile(userId) {
  // Read-your-writes: recent writers read from the primary
  const recentlyWrote = Date.now() - (lastWriteAt.get(userId) ?? 0) < RECENT_WRITE_MS;
  const pool = recentlyWrote ? primary : replica;
  const { rows } = await pool.query("SELECT id, display_name FROM users WHERE id = $1", [userId]);
  return rows[0] ?? null;
}

docs.title: Range partitioning in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          bigint      NOT NULL,
  customer_id bigint      NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  total_cents integer     NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)          -- the partition key must be in the primary key
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

CREATE TABLE orders_2026 PARTITION OF orders
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2027-01-01');

CREATE TABLE orders_2027 PARTITION OF orders
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2027-01-01') TO ('2028-01-01');

-- Only orders_2026 is scanned (partition pruning)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-01' AND created_at < '2026-12-01';

docs.title: Application-level shard routing
docs.text:
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

// Many logical shards mapped onto fewer physical databases.
// Moving a logical shard later only changes this map, not the hash.
const LOGICAL_SHARDS = 256;
const shardMap = buildShardMap(); // your code: logical shard number -> connection pool

function logicalShardFor(customerId) {
  const hash = createHash("sha256").update(String(customerId)).digest();
  return hash.readUInt32BE(0) % LOGICAL_SHARDS;
}

export function poolForCustomer(customerId) {
  return shardMap.get(logicalShardFor(customerId));
}

// Every query for a customer's data includes the shard key
const pool = poolForCustomer(customerId);
await pool.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1", [customerId]);

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Exhaust query tuning, indexing, and caching before adding infrastructure.
  • Budget database connections across all instances and use a pooler when instance counts grow.
  • Send reads to replicas only when they tolerate lag; read the primary for read-your-writes cases.
  • Prefer a single primary; avoid multi-primary unless you need multi-region writes and can handle conflicts.
  • Partition large, time-based tables early; it is cheap and simplifies retention.
  • Choose shard keys from your main access patterns, with high cardinality and even distribution.
  • Design for many logical shards from the start if sharding is likely.
  • Denormalize or build read models only for proven slow reads.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
"Too many connections" after a scale-out

  • Symptom: new app instances fail health checks, or requests fail with connection errors (PostgreSQL error 53300, too_many_connections).
  • Detect: count connections (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity) against max_connections; alert at around 80% of the limit.
  • Cause: every instance opens its own pool: 30 instances × 20 connections is 600, against a default limit that is typically 100.
  • Fix: budget connections (max instances × pool size below the limit), put PgBouncer or RDS Proxy in front, and set the autoscaler's maximum from that budget.

Users say "my change didn't save"

  • Symptom: a user edits a record, the page reloads, and the old value appears; refreshing again "fixes" it.
  • Detect: replica lag. On PostgreSQL, replay_lag in pg_stat_replication on the primary; on MongoDB, rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo(). Correlate lag spikes with the complaints.
  • Cause: the read after the write went to an asynchronous replica that had not applied it yet.
  • Fix: read-your-writes routing (the example above), alerts on lag, and taking replicas out of the read pool when they fall too far behind.

One shard is overloaded

  • Symptom: one shard's CPU or storage is far above the others; slow queries for one set of customers.
  • Detect: per-shard metrics (queries/s, CPU, size) and the busiest shard-key values.
  • Cause: a skewed or monotonically increasing shard key, or one very large tenant sharing a shard.
  • Fix: move logical shards between physical databases, give the large tenant its own shard, or reshard with a better key (hashed, or a compound key).

VACUUM cannot keep up on a huge table

  • Symptom: disk keeps growing after deletes, queries slow down, and autovacuum runs for hours.
  • Detect: n_dead_tup and last_autovacuum in pg_stat_user_tables; table and index sizes trending up.
  • Cause: one very large, busy table; Notion and Figma both hit this before sharding.
  • Fix: tune autovacuum for that table and partition it. Each partition is a smaller table to vacuum, and dropping or detaching an old partition "entirely avoid[s] the VACUUM overhead caused by a bulk DELETE" (PostgreSQL docs). Archive cold data; shard if the primary is still too busy.

A shard-key-less query slows every shard

  • Symptom: one admin search or report makes all shards slower at once.
  • Detect: query logs or EXPLAIN show the query running on every shard.
  • Cause: the query does not include the shard key, so it becomes scatter-gather.
  • Fix: add the shard key to the query, keep a lookup table from the searched field to the shard key, or serve the query from a read model (search index, reporting database).

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Connection pool: A set of reusable open database connections.
  • Read replica: A copy of the database that serves reads and follows the primary.
  • Replication lag: How far a replica is behind the primary.
  • Read-your-writes consistency: A guarantee that users see their own recent writes.
  • Partitioning: Splitting a table into smaller pieces by a key.
  • Sharding: Partitioning data across multiple database servers.
  • Shard key: The field that determines which shard holds a record.
  • Hot shard: A shard receiving disproportionate load.
  • Scatter-gather query: A query sent to every shard with results merged.
  • Denormalization: Storing redundant data to speed up reads.
  • CQRS: Separating write models from read-optimized models.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Sharding before fixing slow queries and missing indexes.
  • Scaling app instances without considering total database connections.
  • Sending every read to replicas and confusing users with stale data after their own updates.
  • Choosing a timestamp or auto-increment id as a range shard key, so all writes hit one shard.
  • Assuming replicas increase write capacity; they only scale reads.
  • Thinking partitioning and sharding are the same; partitions can live on one server.
  • Adopting CQRS everywhere and paying for eventual consistency where it was not needed.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. In what order would you apply database scaling techniques, and why is sharding last?
  2. Why can scaling out the application overload the database, and how do you prevent it?
  3. What is replication lag, and how can you provide read-your-writes consistency?
  4. Compare range, hash, and list partitioning.
  5. What makes a good shard key, and what is a hot shard?
  6. What problem does CQRS solve, and what does it cost?
  7. GitHub's main cluster sent about 95% of its queries to replicas. What does that tell you about its workload, and why did it still need to partition?
  8. Why did Notion create 480 logical shards for only 32 physical databases?

docs.title: Scalability Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review scalability fundamentals, stateless services and autoscaling, database scaling, availability and reliability, consistency and the CAP theorem, performance and latency, and capacity planning. Each question is tagged Beginner, Intermediate, or Advanced; the final group contains scenario-based questions drawn from real production work.

docs.title: 1. What is scalability?
docs.text: Scalability is a system's ability to handle more load (users, requests, data) by adding resources, while still meeting its goals for latency, errors, and cost. A scalable system's capacity grows roughly in proportion to the resources added, without a redesign.

docs.title: 2. What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
docs.text: Vertical scaling (scaling up) gives one machine more CPU, memory, or disk. It is simple but has a hard ceiling, gets expensive, and leaves a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more machines and spreads the load; it scales further and adds redundancy, but needs load balancing and stateless design.

docs.title: 3. What is the difference between scalability and performance?
docs.text: Performance is how fast the system handles a given load (latency for one request). Scalability is how well it keeps that performance as load grows. A system can be fast for one user and collapse at a thousand, or be slow per request but scale linearly.

docs.title: 4. What is a bottleneck, and how do you find it?
docs.text: A bottleneck is the resource that limits overall throughput, such as database CPU, connection pools, or a slow downstream service. Find it by measuring: load test while watching utilization, saturation, and latency for each component, and use tracing to see where time goes. Scaling anything other than the bottleneck does not help.

docs.title: 5. What is the scale cube?
docs.text: The AKF scale cube describes three ways to scale. The X axis clones the application behind a load balancer (horizontal duplication). The Y axis splits the system by function or service (functional decomposition). The Z axis splits data, for example by customer or key range (partitioning or sharding). Real systems usually combine them.

docs.title: 6. Why can adding servers fail to improve throughput?
docs.text: Because the bottleneck is elsewhere: a single database, a shared lock, a rate-limited third party, or a cache. More app servers may even make things worse by opening more database connections. Amdahl's law also limits gains when part of the work is serialized.

docs.title: 7. What is a stateless service, and why does it scale well?
docs.text: A stateless service keeps no client-specific data in its own memory between requests; any state lives in a database, cache, or token. Any instance can serve any request, so you can add or remove instances freely, and losing one loses nothing but in-flight requests.

docs.title: 8. How do you remove session state from application servers?
docs.text: Store sessions in a shared store such as Redis or a database, keyed by a session ID in a cookie, or use self-contained signed tokens (such as JWTs) that the client sends with each request. Uploaded files go to object storage and background work to queues, not to local disk or memory.

docs.title: 9. What are sticky sessions, and what are their drawbacks?
docs.text: Sticky sessions make a load balancer send all of a user's requests to the same instance, usually with a cookie. They let in-memory state work, but load spreads unevenly, losing an instance loses its users' sessions, and scaling in or deploying disrupts users. They are best avoided for typical web APIs.

docs.title: 10. What signals can drive autoscaling?
docs.text: CPU utilization, request rate per instance, latency, number of in-flight requests, queue depth or age of the oldest message for workers, and custom business metrics. Schedules handle predictable peaks, and some platforms offer predictive scaling based on history.

docs.title: 11. What are common autoscaling pitfalls?
docs.text: Scaling too slowly for sudden spikes (new instances need minutes to start and warm up), flapping up and down without cooldown periods, scaling on a metric that does not reflect the bottleneck, missing minimum or maximum limits, and scaling the app tier into a database that cannot take the extra connections.

docs.title: 12. How should a service shut down gracefully during scale-in or deployment?
docs.text: It should stop accepting new work (fail readiness checks so the load balancer drains it), finish in-flight requests within a timeout, stop consumers from taking new messages, close database connections cleanly, and then exit.

docs.title: 13. How do read replicas help scale a database?
docs.text: Replicas copy data from the primary and serve read queries, spreading read load across several machines. Writes still go to the primary. They suit read-heavy workloads and also provide failover candidates.

docs.title: 14. What is replication lag, and what problems does it cause?
docs.text: Replication lag is the delay before a write on the primary appears on a replica. Reads from a lagging replica return stale data, such as a user not seeing a change they just made. Fixes include reading from the primary after writes, session stickiness, and causal consistency features.

docs.title: 15. Why do you need connection pooling?
docs.text: Opening a database connection is expensive, and databases support a limited number of connections. A pool keeps a set of open connections that requests borrow and return. With many app instances, an external pooler such as PgBouncer keeps the total under the database's limit.

docs.title: 16. What is the difference between partitioning and sharding?
docs.text: Partitioning splits a table into pieces, often within one database server (for example, by date range). Sharding distributes data across multiple database servers, each holding a subset, so that storage and write load scale horizontally. Sharding is partitioning across machines.

docs.title: 17. How do you choose a shard key?
docs.text: Pick a key with high cardinality and even distribution that matches the most common queries, so most queries hit one shard. Avoid keys that create hot spots, such as a timestamp that sends all new writes to one shard or a celebrity user who dominates traffic. Changing the key later is very expensive.

docs.title: 18. What are the drawbacks of sharding?
docs.text: Cross-shard queries and joins become slow or impossible, transactions across shards are hard, rebalancing data when adding shards is complex, and operations (backups, schema changes) multiply. It should come after indexing, caching, replicas, and vertical scaling.

docs.title: 19. What can you try before sharding a database?
docs.text: Optimize queries and add indexes, cache hot reads, use read replicas, scale the server vertically, archive or tier old data, move some workloads to specialized stores (search, analytics), and split data by function into separate databases.

docs.title: 20. What is the difference between availability, reliability, and durability?
docs.text: Availability is the fraction of time or requests the service works. Reliability is how consistently it behaves correctly over time. Durability is the likelihood that stored data is never lost. A service can be available yet return wrong results, or have durable data while being down.

docs.title: 21. How much downtime does 99.9% availability allow?
docs.text: About 8.76 hours per year, or about 43 minutes per 30-day month. 99.99% allows about 52.6 minutes per year (about 4.3 minutes per month), and 99.999% about 5.3 minutes per year.

docs.title: 22. How do you calculate the availability of components in series and in parallel?
docs.text: In series (all are required), multiply the availabilities: two 99.9% components give about 99.8%. In parallel (any one suffices), the system fails only if all fail: two independent 99% copies give 1 - 0.01^2 = 99.99%. This assumes failures are independent.

docs.title: 23. What are SLI, SLO, SLA, and an error budget?
docs.text: An SLI is a measured indicator such as the success rate. An SLO is the internal target for it, such as 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is a customer contract with penalties, usually looser than the SLO. The error budget (100% minus the SLO) is the unreliability the team may spend on releases and experiments.

docs.title: 24. What is the relationship between MTBF, MTTR, and availability?
docs.text: Availability is approximately MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). Because failures cannot be eliminated, reducing mean time to recovery (fast detection, automatic failover, quick rollback) often improves availability more than reducing failure frequency.

docs.title: 25. What is the difference between active-active and active-passive redundancy?
docs.text: In active-active, all copies serve traffic and absorb a failed copy's load. In active-passive, a standby stays in sync but takes traffic only after failover. Active-active uses capacity better and fails over faster; active-passive is simpler for stateful systems such as databases.

docs.title: 26. What is a single point of failure, and how do you find them?
docs.text: A component whose failure stops the whole system, such as one database, one load balancer, one zone, or one person who knows the deployment. Find them by tracing every request path and dependency and asking what happens if each part disappears.

docs.title: 27. What is the difference between liveness and readiness checks?
docs.text: A liveness check asks whether the process is alive; failing it triggers a restart. A readiness check asks whether the instance can serve traffic now; failing it removes the instance from the load balancer without a restart. Liveness checks should be shallow so a slow dependency does not restart every instance.

docs.title: 28. What are RPO and RTO?
docs.text: RPO (recovery point objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time. RTO (recovery time objective) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service. They drive the disaster recovery strategy, from backup and restore to active-active multi-region.

docs.title: 29. What is graceful degradation?
docs.text: Serving a reduced but useful experience when a dependency fails instead of failing completely: showing cached data, hiding non-essential features, switching to read-only mode, or shedding low-priority traffic to protect critical paths.

docs.title: 30. What is chaos engineering?
docs.text: The practice of deliberately injecting failures (killing instances, adding latency, cutting dependencies) in a controlled way to verify that the system tolerates them. You define a steady state, form a hypothesis, inject the fault with a limited blast radius, observe, and fix weaknesses.

docs.title: 31. State the CAP theorem.
docs.text: For a replicated data store, when a network partition occurs, the system must choose between consistency (every read returns the latest write, i.e. linearizability) and availability (every non-failing node returns a non-error response). Without a partition, both can be provided.

docs.title: 32. Why is "CA" not a real choice for distributed systems?
docs.text: Network partitions cannot be ruled out in a distributed system, so partition tolerance is not optional. A system that gives up partition tolerance is effectively a single node. The meaningful choice is CP or AP behavior during partitions.

docs.title: 33. What is PACELC?
docs.text: An extension of CAP: if there is a partition (P), choose availability (A) or consistency (C); else (E), in normal operation, choose lower latency (L) or consistency (C). It captures the everyday trade-off of waiting for replicas.

docs.title: 34. Explain strong consistency versus eventual consistency.
docs.text: With strong (linearizable) consistency, once a write completes every subsequent read sees it. With eventual consistency, replicas may temporarily return older values but converge if writes stop. Strong consistency costs latency and availability; eventual consistency is faster and more available but can show stale data.

docs.title: 35. What are read-your-writes and monotonic reads?
docs.text: Read-your-writes guarantees that a client always sees its own earlier writes. Monotonic reads guarantees that once a client has seen a value, it never sees an older one later. They are session guarantees that make eventually consistent systems feel correct to users.

docs.title: 36. How do quorum reads and writes work?
docs.text: With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read queries R replicas. If R + W > N, every read overlaps the latest successful write in at least one replica. For example, N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 tolerates one replica failure for both reads and writes.

docs.title: 37. How are conflicts resolved in eventually consistent systems?
docs.text: With last-write-wins (simple, but loses data and depends on clocks), version vectors that detect concurrent updates for the application to merge, CRDTs that merge automatically and deterministically, or application rules such as merging shopping cart items. Avoiding conflicts with a single writer per item is often best.

docs.title: 38. Which consistency level would you choose for a bank balance and for a like counter?
docs.text: A bank balance needs strong consistency, or all updates serialized through one leader in a transaction, to prevent overspending. A like counter can be eventually consistent: a few seconds of staleness is invisible and the cheaper, more available option scales better.

docs.title: 39. What is the difference between latency and throughput?
docs.text: Latency is the time one operation takes; throughput is how many operations complete per unit of time. They are related through concurrency (Little's law) but distinct: batching can raise throughput while increasing per-item latency.

docs.title: 40. Why use percentiles instead of averages for latency?
docs.text: Averages hide the slow tail: a few very slow requests barely move the mean while badly affecting real users. Percentiles such as p95 and p99 describe actual user experiences. Percentiles must be computed from histograms and never averaged across servers.

docs.title: 41. What is tail latency amplification?
docs.text: When one request fans out to many backends and waits for all of them, the chance that at least one is slow grows quickly. If each of 100 backends is slow 1% of the time, about 63% of fan-out requests hit at least one slow call, so the parts' p99 becomes the whole request's typical latency.

docs.title: 42. What is Little's law, and how is it used?
docs.text: L = λ x W: the average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there. It sizes concurrency, connection pools, and workers: 200 requests/s at 0.25 s each means about 50 in flight.

docs.title: 43. What is the N+1 query problem?
docs.text: Loading a list with one query and then running one extra query per item, so 50 items cost 51 round trips. Fix it with a join, a single batched IN query, eager loading in an ORM, or DataLoader-style batching in GraphQL.

docs.title: 44. Name techniques to reduce API latency.
docs.text: Caching, avoiding N+1 queries, adding indexes, parallelizing independent calls, connection pooling and keep-alive, moving slow work to background jobs, pagination and smaller payloads, compression, CDNs and servers close to users, and precomputing expensive results.

docs.title: 45. Roughly how do memory, SSD, and network latencies compare?
docs.text: A main memory reference is around 100 nanoseconds, a random SSD read is tens to roughly a hundred microseconds, a round trip within a data center is about half a millisecond, and a round trip between continents is on the order of 100 milliseconds. Avoiding network round trips usually matters most.

docs.title: 46. What is capacity planning?
docs.text: The process of forecasting demand and making sure enough resources (compute, database, storage, bandwidth, quotas) exist to meet it with headroom and at a reasonable cost. It combines traffic forecasts, measured per-instance capacity, failure margins, and regular review.

docs.title: 47. Why should systems not run near 100% utilization?
docs.text: Queueing makes response time grow sharply as utilization approaches 100%: in a simple model, response time is service time / (1 - utilization), so 90% busy means about 10 times the service time. Headroom also absorbs spikes, failures, and autoscaling delays.

docs.title: 48. How do you determine how many instances you need?
docs.text: Forecast peak requests per second (including growth), load test to find the maximum sustainable throughput per instance within the latency SLO, divide peak load by a target utilization of that maximum, then add capacity so that losing one zone or instance still carries the peak.

docs.title: 49. When would you use provisioned capacity instead of autoscaling?
docs.text: For a predictable baseline, for stateful systems such as databases that cannot scale out instantly, when warm-up time is long, and for known events where capacity must be in place before traffic arrives. Autoscaling then covers the variable part above the baseline.

docs.title: 50. Estimate the peak request rate for 10 million daily users making 20 requests each.
docs.text: That is 200 million requests per day, or about 200,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 2,300 requests per second on average. With a peak-to-average ratio of 3, plan for roughly 7,000 requests per second, plus growth and failure headroom.

docs.title: 51. Checkout p99 latency doubled after traffic grew 30%, but p50 barely moved and average CPU is only 55%. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: latency histograms per dependency of the checkout request, and saturation of shared resources (database connection pool wait time, lock waits, one hot partition or replica).

How to confirm: trace slow requests and compare them with fast ones; check whether slow requests all wait on the same resource.

Likely causes and fixes: a resource near saturation causes queueing that first shows in the tail (pool exhaustion, lock contention, a hot shard). Increase or fix the constrained resource, reduce time held per request, and add headroom. Averages hide this; see performance and latency and capacity planning.

docs.title: 52. Users update their profile, refresh, and see the old value for a few seconds. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: where profile reads are routed: to asynchronous read replicas or a cache?

How to confirm: compare the replica-lag metric at the time of the complaints, and check whether the cache is invalidated on update.

Likely causes and fixes: replication lag (or a stale cache) breaks read-your-writes. Route a user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, track versions, use causally consistent sessions, or invalidate the cache on write. See consistency and the CAP theorem.

docs.title: 53. During an availability-zone outage, latency and errors spiked in the surviving zones even though autoscaling started adding instances. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how much spare capacity each zone had before the outage, and how long new instances took to become ready.

How to confirm: CPU and connection metrics in surviving zones hit their limits immediately, while new instances arrived many minutes later.

Likely causes and fixes: the system relied on reacting to the failure instead of being statically stable. Keep enough capacity in each zone to carry the load if one zone fails (for example, overprovision by 50% with three zones), and treat autoscaling as a supplement. See availability and reliability.

docs.title: 54. A short database slowdown caused every application instance to restart at the same time, turning it into a full outage. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the liveness and readiness probe definitions.

How to confirm: orchestrator events show liveness probe failures across all instances during the database slowdown.

Likely causes and fixes: the liveness probe checks the database, so a dependency problem triggered mass restarts. Make liveness shallow (the process responds), move dependency checks into readiness with short timeouts, and degrade gracefully when the database is slow. See availability and reliability.

docs.title: 55. After scaling the API from 10 to 40 instances, the database reports "too many connections". How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: pool size per instance multiplied by instance count (plus workers and cron jobs) compared with the database's connection limit.

How to confirm: connection count on the database rises in step with the instance count.

Likely causes and fixes: each instance opens its own pool, so total connections grew fourfold. Reduce per-instance pool sizes based on Little's law, put a connection pooler such as PgBouncer in front of the database, and set autoscaling maximums that respect the limit. See database scaling.

docs.title: 56. Marketing plans a flash sale in two weeks expecting five times normal peak traffic. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the current peak per service and which components are slowest to scale (database, third-party quotas, caches).

How to confirm: run load tests at and above the expected peak with a realistic traffic mix and data size; find the first bottleneck and the knee of the latency curve.

Likely causes and fixes: pre-provision or schedule scaling before the sale, scale the database ahead (bigger instance, replicas, caching for hot products), request quota increases, add load shedding and queueing for non-critical work, and prepare a runbook and dashboards. See capacity planning.

docs.title: 57. Several times an hour, every endpoint in a Node.js service slows down at the same moment. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the event-loop delay metric and CPU profiles around the slow periods.

How to confirm: event-loop delay spikes coincide with the slowdowns, and a CPU profile shows one synchronous function dominating (large JSON.parse, sync crypto, a heavy regex, a big report).

Likely causes and fixes: synchronous CPU work blocking the event loop, so all requests wait. Move it to worker threads or a background job, or stream the data. See the event loop and performance and latency.

docs.title: 58. Every night, read replica lag rises to several minutes, and morning reports show stale numbers. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: which jobs write to the database at night and how large their transactions are.

How to confirm: lag spikes line up with a nightly batch or migration; replicas are replaying a few very large transactions.

Likely causes and fixes: large bulk writes that replicas apply slowly. Chunk and throttle the batch, avoid one giant transaction, schedule reports after replicas catch up (or read them from the primary or a dedicated analytics replica), and alert on lag. See database scaling.

docs.title: 59. Database load spikes every 10 minutes like clockwork. What is the likely cause?
docs.text:
What to check first: cache TTLs and scheduled jobs with a 10-minute period.

How to confirm: cache miss rate spikes at the same moments; many requests miss the same keys at once.

Likely causes and fixes: a cache stampede when many hot keys expire together. Add random jitter to TTLs, coalesce concurrent misses for the same key, or refresh hot keys in the background before they expire. See caching.

docs.title: 60. After a database failover, half the app instances kept failing for 15 minutes while the others recovered immediately. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how instances find the primary: DNS name and TTL, cached addresses, connection pool behavior.

How to confirm: the failing instances still had open connections or a cached address pointing at the old primary; errors such as "not primary".

Likely causes and fixes: long DNS TTLs or pools that keep stale connections. Use short TTLs for failover endpoints, drivers that discover the replica-set topology, connection validation, and retries on "not primary" errors. Test failover regularly. See availability and reliability.

docs.title: 61. The product team wants 99.99% availability for a service that synchronously calls three internal services, each at 99.9%. Is it possible?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the three calls are on the critical path and synchronous.

How to confirm: in series, availability multiplies: 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 ≈ 99.7%, before counting the service's own failures.

Likely causes and fixes: not as designed. Options are raising the dependencies' availability, removing them from the critical path (caching, asynchronous processing, fallbacks and graceful degradation), or agreeing on a realistic SLO. See availability and reliability.

docs.title: 62. Average CPU across the fleet is 40%, yet users complain about slowness at peak times. How can both be true?
docs.text:
What to check first: per-instance and per-resource saturation at peak, using per-minute maximums rather than hourly averages.

How to confirm: one zone, one instance group, one database partition, or one dependency is saturated while the rest are idle; or short peaks are averaged away.

Likely causes and fixes: uneven load (a hot key, sticky sessions, an unbalanced zone) or averaged metrics. Monitor percentiles and peaks per resource, rebalance load, and fix the hot spot. See capacity planning.

docs.title: 63. Two customers both bought the last unit in stock. How do you prevent overselling?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the stock check and decrement are implemented, and whether the check reads from a replica or cache.

How to confirm: logs show two concurrent "check stock, then decrement" sequences both seeing quantity 1.

Likely causes and fixes: a race condition with a check-then-act pattern and possibly a stale read. Use an atomic conditional update on the primary (UPDATE ... SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = $1 AND qty > 0), a transaction with row locking, or a reservation step. See concurrency and race conditions.

docs.title: 64. A downstream service recovered from an outage and was immediately overwhelmed again by your service. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: retry configuration at every layer (client, gateway, service) and the request rate at the moment of recovery.

How to confirm: traffic to the dependency spiked far above normal right when it came back; retries had no backoff or jitter.

Likely causes and fixes: a retry storm amplified by retries at several layers. Retry at one layer with exponential backoff and jitter, use retry budgets and circuit breakers, and shed low-priority work. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.
