docs.text:
• Scalability overview
  • Availability and reliability, consistency and the CAP theorem, performance and latency, and capacity planning
  • Google SRE book
  • AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar

docs.title: Performance and Latency
docs.text: Performance is how quickly a system responds and how much work it can do. Users feel latency directly: a page that takes three seconds feels broken, and a checkout that occasionally takes ten seconds loses sales. This page explains how to measure performance correctly, where time actually goes, and the techniques that make backends fast.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Speed affects behavior and revenue. Slow pages are abandoned; slow APIs make every client that uses them slow.
  • Averages hide pain. A service with a 100 ms average can still make one user in a hundred wait three seconds, and at scale that is thousands of people.
  • Latency and capacity are linked. Slow requests hold connections, memory, and workers longer, so the same hardware serves fewer users.
  • Guessing wastes effort. Most "optimizations" made without measurement speed up code that was never the bottleneck.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Discord measures the tail. When Discord moved its message storage from Cassandra to ScyllaDB, it reported results as p99 latencies: fetching historical messages went from a p99 of 40-125 ms to 15 ms, and inserts from 5-70 ms to a steady 5 ms. Its data services also use request coalescing: if many users request the same row at the same time, the database is queried once, and consistent-hash routing by channel ID sends related requests to the same service instance so coalescing works better (Discord blog).
  • Google SRE monitors latency distributions. Google's SRE book recommends collecting request counts bucketed by latency (a histogram) rather than only averages, to tell a slow average from a slow tail, and lists latency as one of the four golden signals (Google SRE book).
  • Shopify lowers its timeouts. Shopify's advice for resilient payment systems starts with lowering timeouts, pointing out that Ruby's built-in Net::HTTP client defaults to 60 seconds for each of connecting, writing, and reading, far longer than an online user will wait (Shopify Engineering).

Popular tools and providers: tracing and metrics with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Grafana, Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Datadog, and New Relic; profiling with node --cpu-prof, Chrome DevTools, and flame graph tools; load testing with k6, Gatling, Apache JMeter, and Locust; CDNs such as Cloudflare, Amazon CloudFront, Fastly, and Akamai.

docs.title: Latency, throughput, and bandwidth
docs.text:
Term Meaning Unit Analogy (a highway) Latency Time for one operation to complete ms, µs How long one car takes to drive from A to B Throughput Operations completed per unit of time requests/s, messages/s How many cars arrive per hour Bandwidth Maximum data rate a link can carry Mbit/s, Gbit/s How many lanes the highway has

They are related but independent: adding lanes (bandwidth) raises throughput without making any single car faster. A satellite link can have high bandwidth and terrible latency.

Two more terms:

  • Response time is what the client experiences: queueing time + service time (+ network). Under load, queueing often dominates.
  • Utilization is the fraction of time a resource is busy. As it approaches 100%, queueing time grows sharply. See capacity planning.

docs.title: Percentiles and tail latency
docs.text:
A percentile tells you the latency that a given share of requests stays under:

  • p50 (median): half the requests are faster than this.
  • p95: 95% are faster; 1 in 20 is slower.
  • p99: 99% are faster; 1 in 100 is slower.
  • p99.9: 1 in 1,000 is slower.

The slow end of the distribution is the tail.

Why averages mislead:

100 requests: 98 take 50 ms, 2 take 5,000 ms

Average = (98 x 50 + 2 x 5,000) / 100 = 149 ms   <- looks fine
p50     = 50 ms
p99     = 5,000 ms                                <- 1 in 50 users waits 5 s

The average describes no real user. Percentiles describe actual experiences.

Tail latency matters even more than it seems:

  • Heavy users hit the tail most. A user loading a page that makes 50 API calls almost certainly experiences at least one p99 request.
  • Fan-out amplifies the tail. If one request waits for 100 backend calls in parallel, and each call is slow 1% of the time, the chance that at least one is slow is 1 - 0.99^100, about 63%. The p99 of the parts becomes the typical experience of the whole.

Measurement rules:

  • Record latencies in histograms and compute percentiles from them. Never average percentiles across servers or time windows; the result is meaningless.
  • Measure at the client or load balancer, not only inside the handler, so queueing and network time are included.
  • Track percentiles per endpoint; a fast health check averaged with a slow search hides both.

docs.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know
docs.text:
Orders of magnitude matter more than exact values, which vary with hardware. These approximate figures are adapted from the well-known list popularized by Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig:

Operation Approximate time Order of magnitude L1 cache reference ~1 ns nanoseconds Branch mispredict ~3 ns nanoseconds L2 cache reference ~4 ns nanoseconds Main memory reference ~100 ns nanoseconds Compress 1 KB with a fast compressor ~2 µs microseconds Send 1 KB over a 1 Gbit/s network ~10 µs microseconds Random 4 KB read from an SSD tens to ~150 µs microseconds Read 1 MB sequentially from memory tens to hundreds of µs microseconds Round trip within one data center ~500 µs sub-millisecond Read 1 MB sequentially from an SSD hundreds of µs to ~2 ms ~milliseconds Hard disk seek ~2 to 10 ms milliseconds Read 1 MB sequentially from a hard disk several ms milliseconds Round trip across a continent tens of ms tens of milliseconds Round trip between continents (e.g. US to Europe) ~80 to 150 ms ~100 milliseconds

Typical application-level costs (very rough, same region):

Operation Typical latency In-process cache or memory lookup microseconds or less Redis GET over the network well under 1 ms Indexed database query returning a few rows ~1 to 10 ms Unindexed scan of a large table hundreds of ms to seconds Call to another internal service a few ms to tens of ms Call to an external third-party API tens to hundreds of ms

Lessons:

  • Memory is roughly a thousand times faster than an SSD read and far faster than a network round trip. Avoid unnecessary round trips above all.
  • A request that makes 30 sequential database calls at 2 ms each spends 60 ms just waiting on the network, before any query work.
  • Physics sets a floor: light in fiber takes tens of milliseconds to cross a continent. Put data and servers near users (CDNs, regional deployments) when that matters.

docs.title: Little's law
docs.text:
For a stable system:

L = λ x W

L = average number of requests in the system (concurrency)
λ = average arrival rate (throughput)
W = average time each request spends in the system (latency)

Uses:

  • Concurrency needed: 200 requests/s x 0.25 s = 50 requests in flight on average. That tells you how many connections, workers, or threads you need.
  • Throughput limit: a database pool of 20 connections with queries of 10 ms can support at most 20 / 0.01 = 2,000 queries/s.
  • Why latency hurts capacity: if latency doubles at the same arrival rate, concurrency doubles; you hit pool and memory limits sooner.

And for queues: if arrivals exceed the processing rate for long, the queue grows without bound; Little's law then tells you the wait grows with it.

docs.title: Where time goes in a request
docs.text:
Phase Typical causes of slowness DNS, TCP, TLS setup New connections for each request, distant servers Network transfer Large payloads, no compression, long distances Load balancer and proxy Queueing under load, extra hops Waiting for a worker All workers or the event loop busy (queueing) Application CPU Heavy JSON serialization, synchronous work blocking the Node.js event loop, inefficient algorithms Database Missing indexes, N+1 queries, lock contention, large result sets Cache Low hit rate, cache stampedes Downstream services Slow dependencies, sequential calls that could be parallel, no timeouts Garbage collection Large heaps, many short-lived objects

See the request lifecycle and the Node.js event loop.

docs.title: Techniques for lower latency and higher throughput
docs.text: Technique How it helps Watch out for Caching Serves repeated reads from memory instead of recomputing or querying Staleness, invalidation, stampedes; see caching Batching One round trip for many items (bulk inserts, IN queries, batched API calls) Larger single requests; partial failures Connection pooling and keep-alive Skips TCP/TLS setup and database authentication on every call Pool sizes vs database connection limits Parallelizing independent calls Total time becomes the slowest call, not the sum Load on dependencies; error handling Asynchronous processing Moves slow work (emails, reports) out of the request path Eventual consistency; see message queues Compression Smaller responses transfer faster CPU cost; skip tiny or already-compressed data Pagination and field selection Smaller queries and payloads Clients needing more requests Indexing Turns full scans into fast lookups Slower writes, storage; index what you query CDN and edge caching Serves static and cacheable content near users Cache rules for personalized data; see CDN Precomputation and denormalization Store results ready to read (counters, feeds, summaries) Keeping copies in sync Doing less Remove unnecessary work, fields, and calls Requires measuring to find it

docs.title: The N+1 query problem
docs.text:
The most common backend performance bug: one query to load a list, then one more query per item.

// N+1: 1 query for orders + 1 query per order for its customer
const orders = await db.query("SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50");
for (const order of orders.rows) {
  const customer = await db.query("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = $1", [order.customer_id]);
  order.customer = customer.rows[0]; // 50 extra round trips
}

Fixes: a join, or one batched query.

const orders = (await db.query("SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50")).rows;
const ids = [...new Set(orders.map((o) => o.customer_id))];
const customers = (await db.query("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = ANY($1)", [ids])).rows;
const byId = new Map(customers.map((c) => [c.id, c]));
for (const order of orders) order.customer = byId.get(order.customer_id); // 2 queries total

ORMs hide N+1 behind lazy-loaded relations, and GraphQL resolvers create it naturally (DataLoader fixes it there). Detect it by logging the number of queries per request.

docs.title: Profiling and measuring
docs.text:
1. Define the goal: "p99 of GET /api/feed under 300 ms at 500 requests/s".
  2. Measure in production-like conditions: metrics per endpoint (rate, errors, duration percentiles), distributed tracing to see time per span, and slow query logs.
  3. Find the biggest contributor with traces and profilers: CPU profiles (node --cpu-prof, flame graphs), database EXPLAIN plans, event loop delay, garbage collection metrics.
  4. Change one thing and measure again under the same load.
  5. Load test before launches and after big changes. See performance testing.

Benchmarking pitfalls: measuring without warm-up (cold caches, JIT not optimized), testing on a laptop with different hardware and data size, load generators that wait for slow responses before sending the next request (which hides queueing and understates tail latency), and testing with tiny datasets where every query is fast.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Optimize when:

  • A measured SLO is missed (for example p99 above target) or is trending towards it as traffic grows.
  • Latency is costing users or money: abandoned checkouts, timeouts in clients, too many servers for the load.
  • A profile or trace shows a clear hotspot.

Do not optimize when:

  • There is no measurement showing a problem; clarity beats speculative speed.
  • The code is not on a hot path (an admin page used twice a day).
  • The change trades correctness or consistency for speed without a business decision (for example caching data that must be fresh).
Technique Use when Avoid when Caching Reads repeat and slightly stale data is acceptable Data must be fresh on every read, or the hit rate would be low Batching Many small operations of the same kind Each operation needs an immediate individual result Parallel calls Independent calls on the critical path Calls depend on each other, or parallelism overloads a dependency Asynchronous processing Work is not needed for the response The user needs the result now Denormalization / precomputation Expensive reads dominate and writes are rarer Data changes constantly and keeping copies in sync is costly CDN Static or public cacheable content, global users Personalized or sensitive responses More hardware The bottleneck is resource saturation and the code is reasonable The bottleneck is an N+1 pattern, lock contention, or a missing index

docs.title: Timing middleware with percentiles
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
const samples = new Map(); // route -> recent durations (ms); use a real metrics library in production

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const start = process.hrtime.bigint();
  res.on("finish", () => {
    const ms = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / 1e6;
    const key = `${req.method} ${req.route?.path ?? req.path}`;
    const list = samples.get(key) ?? [];
    list.push(ms);
    if (list.length > 10_000) list.shift(); // keep a bounded window
    samples.set(key, list);
  });
  next();
});

function percentile(values, p) {
  const sorted = [...values].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const index = Math.min(sorted.length - 1, Math.ceil((p / 100) * sorted.length) - 1);
  return sorted[Math.max(0, index)];
}

app.get("/internal/latency", (req, res) => {
  const report = {};
  for (const [route, values] of samples) {
    report[route] = {
      count: values.length,
      p50: percentile(values, 50).toFixed(1),
      p95: percentile(values, 95).toFixed(1),
      p99: percentile(values, 99).toFixed(1),
    };
  }
  res.json(report);
});

Production systems export histograms to a metrics system (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry) instead; see logging and monitoring.

docs.title: Parallel instead of sequential
docs.text:
// Sequential: ~120 ms + ~80 ms + ~60 ms = ~260 ms
async function loadDashboardSequential(id) {
  const user = await getUser(id);
  const orders = await getOrders(id);
  const recommendations = await getRecommendations(id);
  return { user, orders, recommendations };
}

// Parallel: ~120 ms (the slowest call), because the calls are independent
async function loadDashboard(id) {
  const [user, orders, recommendations] = await Promise.all([
    getUser(id),
    getOrders(id),
    getRecommendations(id),
  ]);
  return { user, orders, recommendations };
}

Use Promise.allSettled when a failed optional call (recommendations) should not fail the whole response.

docs.title: Exposing timings with Server-Timing
docs.text:
app.get("/api/feed", async (req, res) => {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  const posts = await loadPosts(req.user.id);
  const t1 = performance.now();
  const enriched = await attachAuthors(posts);
  const t2 = performance.now();

  // Shows up in the browser DevTools Network panel under "Timing"
  res.set("Server-Timing", `db;dur=${(t1 - t0).toFixed(1)}, enrich;dur=${(t2 - t1).toFixed(1)}`);
  res.json(enriched);
});

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Set latency targets as percentiles per endpoint (p95, p99), not averages.
  • Measure before optimizing, and re-measure after each change.
  • Eliminate round trips first: N+1 queries, sequential calls, unnecessary hops.
  • Index for your actual queries and check EXPLAIN plans.
  • Pool and reuse connections.
  • Move slow work off the request path.
  • Cache deliberately, with clear invalidation.
  • Keep payloads small with pagination, field selection, and compression.
  • Never block the Node.js event loop with heavy synchronous work.
  • Set timeouts so slow dependencies cannot drag every request down.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• p99 spikes while p50 stays flat. Detect: latency histograms per endpoint show the tail moving and the median not. Cause: something that affects a minority of requests: garbage collection pauses, lock contention, one slow replica or dependency, large outlier payloads. Fix: use traces to find what slow requests have in common, add timeouts, and fix the specific dependency or query.
  • Every endpoint slows down at once. Detect: the Node.js event-loop delay metric (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay) jumps together with latency on unrelated routes. Cause: synchronous CPU work (huge JSON.parse, sync crypto, a pathological regex) blocking the event loop. Fix: move heavy work to worker threads or background jobs, stream large payloads; see worker threads and cluster.
  • Database load doubles after a release with flat traffic. Detect: queries-per-request (or total database QPS) rises sharply right after a deploy. Cause: a new N+1 query pattern, often a lazy-loaded relation in an ORM. Fix: batch or join, and add a test or metric that fails when query counts per request jump.
  • Latency jumps under load with idle CPUs. Detect: errors such as "timeout acquiring connection" from the pool; time spent waiting for a connection rises. Cause: a pool too small for throughput x query time (Little's law), slow queries holding connections, or connections not released in an error path. Fix: size pools from measured numbers, fix slow queries, and release connections in finally blocks.
  • Periodic database spikes. Detect: database load spikes at regular intervals that match a cache TTL. Cause: many hot keys expiring at once (cache stampede). Fix: add jitter to TTLs and coalesce concurrent misses for the same key; see caching.
  • Latency spikes after every deployment. Detect: p99 rises for a few minutes after each rollout. Cause: cold caches, JIT warm-up, and new connection pools on fresh instances. Fix: warm up instances before they receive full traffic (readiness checks, gradual rollout), and pre-fill critical caches.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Latency: time to complete one operation.
  • Throughput: operations completed per unit of time.
  • Bandwidth: maximum data rate of a link.
  • Response time: latency as experienced by the client, including queueing.
  • Percentile (p50, p95, p99): the latency below which that share of requests falls.
  • Tail latency: the slowest requests in the distribution.
  • Little's law: concurrency = throughput x latency.
  • N+1 queries: one query for a list plus one per item.
  • Profiling: measuring where a program spends time or memory.
  • Flame graph: a visualization of CPU time by call stack.
  • Histogram: counts of values in ranges, used to compute percentiles.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Reporting average latency and missing the users stuck in the tail.
  • Averaging percentiles from several servers.
  • Optimizing code when the time is spent waiting on the database or the network.
  • Measuring only inside the handler, missing queueing and network time.
  • "More bandwidth fixes latency." Round trips and distance often dominate.
  • Benchmarks on tiny datasets or cold caches that do not resemble production.
  • Fixing N+1 with a cache instead of fixing the query pattern.
  • Running CPU-heavy work on the event loop, slowing every request in the process.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Define latency, throughput, and bandwidth, and give an example where bandwidth is high but latency is poor.
  2. Why are percentiles better than averages? Why must you not average them?
  3. A request fans out to 50 services, each slow 1% of the time. Roughly how often is the whole request slow?
  4. Using Little's law, how many concurrent requests does a service handle at 400 requests/s with 150 ms average latency?
  5. Explain the N+1 query problem and two ways to fix it.
  6. Which latencies differ by roughly a factor of a thousand: memory access, SSD read, or same-data-center round trip?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Google SRE book: Monitoring Distributed Systems, including why to monitor latency distributions.
  • AWS Builders' Library: Using load shedding to avoid overload.
  • AWS Well-Architected: Performance Efficiency Pillar.
  • Node.js: Performance measurement APIs (perf_hooks).
  • MDN: Server-Timing header.
  • Related: capacity planning and performance testing.

docs.title: Scalability Fundamentals
docs.text: Scalability is a system's ability to handle more work (more users, more requests, more data) while still meeting its performance goals, by adding resources in a reasonable, cost-effective way. A scalable system is not one that is fast today; it is one with a clear, affordable path to handling ten or a hundred times today's load.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A design that works for a demo with ten users can fail completely at ten thousand: responses slow down, databases run out of connections, and queues back up. On the other hand, building for massive scale too early wastes money and adds complexity a small product does not need. Knowing how to describe load, find bottlenecks, and choose between scaling approaches lets you scale the right part of the system at the right time.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
Large companies usually follow the same path: scale up as far as is sensible, then split by function, then split the data.

  • Shopify: scale up, then shard, then isolate (the Z axis). "In 2015, it was no longer possible to continue buying a larger database server", so Shopify sharded its database. When one shard failing could still break platform-wide actions, it introduced pods: groups of shops on fully isolated datastores, with no action allowed to reach across pods, so adding a pod adds capacity without interfering with the others. (Shopify Engineering)
  • GitHub: bigger machines until they were not enough (the Y axis for data). GitHub.com was built around one main MySQL cluster, mysql1, and kept "moving to newer and bigger machines to scale up". From 2019 it grouped tables into schema domains, enforced the boundaries with SQL linters, then moved those domains to separate clusters. By 2021 the same tables served 1.2 million queries/s across several clusters, and the average load on each host had halved. (GitHub Blog, 2021)
  • Notion: why not just keep scaling vertically? Notion's answer was that "playing Cookie Clicker with the RDS 'Resize Instance' button is not a viable long-term strategy": maintenance such as Postgres VACUUM began to stall well before the hardware limit. It sharded by workspace ID into 480 logical shards on 32 physical databases. (Notion blog, 2021)
  • Figma: the incremental route. Figma's database stack grew almost 100x from 2020. Moving groups of tables onto their own databases ("vertical partitioning") was "a relatively easy and very impactful scaling lever" that bought time to build horizontal sharding on its existing RDS Postgres. (Figma blog, 2024)
  • AKF Partners: the scale cube. The X/Y/Z model used below comes from The Art of Scalability by Martin L. Abbott and Michael T. Fisher. (AKF Partners)

docs.title: Popular tools and providers
docs.text: Need Common choices Spreading traffic (X axis) Cloud load balancers (AWS ALB/NLB, Google Cloud Load Balancing, Azure Load Balancer), NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy Adding instances automatically Kubernetes HPA, KEDA, cloud autoscaling groups Taking load off the database Redis or Valkey caches, CDNs (CloudFront, Cloudflare, Fastly), read replicas Splitting data (Z axis) Application-level sharding, Vitess (MySQL), Citus (PostgreSQL), MongoDB sharding, managed distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB) Finding the bottleneck Load-testing tools (k6, Gatling, JMeter, Locust), APM and tracing (OpenTelemetry)

docs.title: Describing load: load parameters
docs.text:
You cannot discuss scaling without saying what is growing. Load parameters are the numbers that describe the workload:

Load parameter Example Requests per second 2,000 API requests/s at peak Read/write ratio 95% reads, 5% writes Concurrent users or connections 50,000 open WebSocket connections Data volume and growth 2 TB, growing 100 GB/month Payload sizes Average response 4 KB; uploads up to 50 MB Fan-out One post delivered to 1,000 followers' feeds Peak-to-average ratio Traffic 5× higher at 9 a.m. or during a sale

Two systems with the same requests per second can need very different designs if one is read-heavy and the other write-heavy, or if one has huge fan-out.

docs.title: Throughput and latency
docs.text:
• Throughput is how much work is completed per unit of time (requests per second, messages per second).
  • Latency is how long one operation takes (milliseconds per request).

They are related but different. A system can have high throughput and poor latency (a batch pipeline), or low latency and limited throughput. As load approaches a component's capacity, queues form and latency rises sharply:

latency
  │                                   ╱
  │                                 ╱
  │                              ╱
  │                         _ ─ ╯       <- queueing: latency explodes
  │ ___________________ ─ ─              near saturation
  └──────────────────────────────────── utilization
  0%                       ~70–80%   100%

The simplest queueing model (one server, random arrivals, the M/M/1 queue) shows why. Average response time is the service time divided by (1 − utilization):

utilization   50%   80%   90%   95%
response time  2×    5×   10×   20×   the time one request takes alone

Real systems differ in detail, but the shape is the same: the last 10–20% of capacity costs a lot of latency. This is why teams keep headroom instead of running servers at 100%. Latency is usually described with percentiles (p50, p95, p99) rather than averages; see performance and latency.

docs.title: Vertical and horizontal scaling
docs.text:
Vertical scaling (scale up) gives one machine more CPU, memory, or faster disks. Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds more machines or instances and spreads work across them.

Vertical (scale up) Horizontal (scale out) How Bigger machine More machines Code changes Usually none Application must be stateless or partitioned Upper limit The largest machine available Very high, in principle Cost Sized for peak and paid for around the clock; each step up is a big jump Pay per instance; capacity can follow load up and down Failure impact One machine is a single point of failure Losing one instance removes only part of capacity Downtime to scale Often a restart or failover Add instances without downtime Complexity Low Load balancing, shared state, coordination Good for Databases early on, quick wins Stateless web and API tiers, workers

Most real systems use both: horizontally scaled stateless application servers in front of a database that is first scaled vertically and later scaled with replicas and partitioning (see database scaling).

docs.title: Common bottlenecks
docs.text:
Resource Symptoms Typical fixes CPU High CPU, latency grows with load Optimize code, scale out, move CPU-heavy work to workers Memory Swapping, out-of-memory restarts, GC pauses Fix leaks, reduce per-request memory, bigger instances Disk I/O High I/O wait, slow queries Indexes, caching, faster storage Database Slow queries, connection limits, lock waits Query and index tuning, caching, replicas, partitioning Network Bandwidth limits, high transfer costs Compression, CDN, smaller payloads Locks and contention Throughput stops rising, many waiting threads Reduce shared mutable state, finer-grained locks, partition work External services Timeouts, rate-limit errors Caching, queues, retries with backoff, quotas

In Node.js, a common bottleneck is synchronous CPU work blocking the event loop; see the event loop.

docs.title: Amdahl's law: why adding machines has limits
docs.text:
If part of a job cannot be parallelized, that part limits the maximum speed-up no matter how many machines you add.

speed-up(N) = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / N)

p = fraction of the work that can run in parallel
N = number of workers

p = 0.95:  N = 10  -> 6.9×    N = 100 -> 16.8×    N = ∞ -> 20×
p = 0.50:  N = 10  -> 1.8×    N = ∞   -> 2×

In systems terms: if every request must pass through one shared component (a single database primary, a global lock, one queue consumer), that component caps total throughput. In practice coordination costs can even make throughput fall as more nodes are added, which is why scalable designs minimize shared state and cross-node coordination.

docs.title: The scale cube
docs.text:
The AKF Scale Cube, from AKF Partners' book The Art of Scalability by Martin L. Abbott and Michael T. Fisher, names three independent ways to scale:

Axis Technique Example Trade-off X Run identical copies (of services or data) 10 instances of the API behind a load balancer; database read replicas Simple; every copy still needs all the data Y Decompose by function Separate checkout, catalog, and search services, each with its own data Independent scaling and teams; distributed-system complexity Z Partition by customer or data key Customers A–M on shard 1, N–Z on shard 2 Scales data and writes; cross-partition queries are hard

Most systems start with the X axis, add Y as teams and features grow, and use Z when data or write volume outgrows one database. See monolith, modular monolith, and microservices.

docs.title: Shared-nothing architecture
docs.text: In a shared-nothing design, each node has its own CPU, memory, and storage and does not share them with others. Nodes coordinate only over the network. Stateless web servers are shared-nothing: any request can go to any server. Partitioned databases are shared-nothing at the data level: each shard owns its slice. Shared-nothing systems scale out well because adding a node adds capacity without adding contention on a shared resource.

docs.title: Measure before scaling
docs.text:
Scaling the wrong component wastes money and can move the bottleneck somewhere worse (for example, more app servers overwhelming the database).

  1. Define goals: for example, "p99 under 300 ms at 3,000 requests/s".
  2. Measure current behavior with metrics and tracing.
  3. Load-test to find where latency or errors rise; see performance testing.
  4. Fix or scale the bottleneck, then measure again.
  5. Repeat; the bottleneck moves after each fix.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Scale up first when one machine is clearly enough for the next year of growth. It is the cheapest change in engineering time, and databases in particular benefit.
  • Scale out stateless tiers (web, API, workers) from the start: run at least two instances for availability, and add more as load grows.
  • Split by function (Y axis) when parts of the system have very different load or are owned by different teams, not just to "do microservices".
  • Partition data (Z axis) only when the data or write volume, or maintenance on huge tables, outgrows the largest sensible machine. It is the most expensive axis to adopt and to undo.
  • Do not scale ahead of evidence: measure first. Designing for millions of users before you have thousands mostly buys complexity.
Question Vertical (scale up) Horizontal (scale out) Load fits on one machine with headroom for 6–12 months? Yes: simplest option Not needed yet, except two instances for availability Stateless component (API, worker)? Works, but leaves a single point of failure Preferred: add or remove instances freely Stateful single-writer component (database primary)? Usually the first step Needs replicas, partitioning, or sharding; much more work Need to survive the loss of a machine or zone? No: one machine is one failure Yes: spread instances across zones Load swings a lot during the day? Pays for peak all day Autoscaling follows the load Already on the largest sensible instance, or maintenance is slowing down? No more room Time to partition (see database scaling)

docs.title: Estimating whether to scale out
docs.text:
Current: 4 API instances, each handles ~300 req/s at 70% CPU (the safe limit)
Capacity: 4 × 300 = 1,200 req/s
Expected peak next quarter: 2,000 req/s, plus 30% headroom = 2,600 req/s
Instances needed: 2,600 / 300 = 8.67, so 9 instances
Plus one spare (N+1) so losing an instance keeps full capacity: 10 instances

Check the next bottleneck: 2,600 req/s × 2 queries per request = 5,200 queries/s
Can the database handle 5,200 queries/s? If not, add caching or replicas first.

Capacity estimates like this are covered in capacity planning.

docs.title: Making a Node.js service horizontally scalable
docs.text:
// Not horizontally scalable: state lives in one process's memory
const sessions = new Map();          // lost on restart, invisible to other instances
const uploadsDir = "./uploads";      // files exist on one machine only

// Horizontally scalable: state moved to shared services
import { Redis } from "ioredis";
const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL);      // sessions and cache in Redis
const bucket = process.env.UPLOADS_BUCKET;           // files in object storage

Once no request depends on which instance served the previous one, you can add instances behind a load balancer. See stateless services and autoscaling.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Describe load with concrete load parameters before discussing solutions.
  • Set goals in percentiles (p95, p99), not averages.
  • Measure and load-test to find the real bottleneck before scaling.
  • Keep application servers stateless so they can scale horizontally.
  • Scale the database deliberately: tune, cache, replicate, then partition.
  • Keep headroom (often 20–40%) for spikes and failures.
  • Prefer the simplest design that meets the next order of magnitude of growth.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
p99 latency spikes at peak while average CPU looks fine

  • Symptom: p99 jumps from 150 ms to 2 s at peak, but the fleet's average CPU is 55%.
  • Detect: chart utilization per component (each instance, the database, each queue) against latency; averages hide the one saturated piece.
  • Cause: one resource is close to 100% (a hot instance, the database CPU, a connection pool), and latency explodes near saturation.
  • Fix: add headroom at that component (scale it, or spread load more evenly), and set alerts on saturation, not just averages.

Adding app instances made things slower

  • Symptom: after scaling the API from 10 to 30 instances, errors and latency go up.
  • Detect: database connections, lock waits, and CPU rise in step with the instance count.
  • Cause: the bottleneck was the shared database; more instances means more connections and more contention (Amdahl's serial part).
  • Fix: scale the database side: tune queries and indexes, cache, add read replicas, put a pooler in front, and cap the app's instance count to what the database can serve.

Throughput stops rising as instances are added

  • Symptom: doubling the instances adds only a few percent of throughput.
  • Detect: load tests at several instance counts; per-instance throughput falls as N grows.
  • Cause: a serial step (one queue consumer, a global lock, a single writer, a counter row everyone updates).
  • Fix: partition the serial step (per-key queues, sharded counters, per-tenant locks) so it can run in parallel.

One customer or shard is far busier than the rest

  • Symptom: one shard or partition is at 90% while others idle; incidents affect one group of customers.
  • Detect: per-shard and per-tenant metrics (queries/s, CPU, storage).
  • Cause: a skewed partition key, or one very large tenant.
  • Fix: choose a key with more even distribution, split or move the hot tenant, or isolate large tenants (Shopify's pods isolate groups of shops).

The database is already on the biggest instance

  • Symptom: each resize gives less benefit; maintenance (Postgres VACUUM, index builds, backups) takes longer every month.
  • Detect: instance size at the top of the family, CPU or IOPS near the limit, maintenance duration trending up.
  • Cause: vertical scaling has reached its ceiling; Notion and GitHub both hit this.
  • Fix: plan partitioning months before the ceiling: split by function first (often simpler), then shard.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Scalability: The ability to handle growing load by adding resources while meeting performance goals.
  • Load parameters: Numbers describing the workload, such as requests per second or read/write ratio.
  • Throughput: Work completed per unit of time.
  • Latency: Time taken for one operation.
  • Vertical scaling: Adding resources to one machine.
  • Horizontal scaling: Adding machines or instances.
  • Bottleneck: The component that limits overall capacity.
  • Shared-nothing architecture: Nodes that do not share memory or storage and coordinate over the network.
  • Scale cube: The X (clone), Y (function), and Z (data partition) axes of scaling.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming more servers always mean faster responses; they add throughput, and only help latency if the bottleneck was capacity.
  • Scaling the web tier while the database is the bottleneck.
  • Designing for "millions of users" before having thousands.
  • Keeping state in process memory and then being unable to add instances.
  • Using average latency, which hides slow outliers users notice.
  • Running components near 100% utilization, where latency explodes.
  • Treating scalability and performance as the same thing: a fast system can still be impossible to scale.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which load parameters would you collect for a social media feed service?
  2. Explain the difference between throughput and latency, and why latency rises near full utilization.
  3. Compare vertical and horizontal scaling in terms of limits, cost, and failure impact.
  4. Using Amdahl's law, what is the maximum speed-up if 10% of the work is serial?
  5. Describe the three axes of the scale cube with an example of each.
  6. Why should you measure before scaling, and what can go wrong if you do not?
  7. In a simple queue, how many times slower is a request at 90% utilization than on an idle server?
  8. Shopify, GitHub, and Notion all scaled vertically first. What made each of them move on?

docs.title: Stateless Services and Autoscaling
docs.text: A stateless service keeps no client-specific data in its own memory or disk between requests, so any instance can handle any request. That property is what makes horizontal scaling and autoscaling, adding and removing instances automatically as load changes, safe and simple. This lesson explains how to make services stateless and how autoscaling decides when to act.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Traffic is rarely flat: it rises during the day, spikes during sales, and drops at night. Running enough servers for the peak all the time wastes money; running too few causes slow responses and errors at peak. Autoscaling solves this, but only if instances are interchangeable, start quickly, and can be removed without dropping requests. Hidden state in one instance (a session in memory, a file on local disk) breaks all of that.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix: predictive plus reactive autoscaling. Netflix built Scryer to forecast traffic and add capacity before it is needed, because reactive scaling alone fell short: instance start-up took 10 to 45 minutes, and outages were sometimes followed by retry storms that hit a fleet the autoscaler had just shrunk. Scryer runs "in tandem" with the reactive Amazon Auto Scaling, which still catches surprises. (Netflix Tech Blog, 2013)
  • Kubernetes: the HPA algorithm in the open. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler documents its exact rule (ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetric / desiredMetric)), a 10% tolerance, a 300-second scale-down stabilization window and immediate scale-up by default; the HPA section below uses them. (Kubernetes docs)
  • AWS Application Load Balancer: stickiness, slow start, draining. ALB can pin clients with a load-balancer cookie (AWSALB) or your application's cookie; can ramp traffic to new targets gradually (slow start); and stops sending new requests to a deregistering target while waiting up to 300 seconds (the default) for in-flight requests to finish. (AWS docs)
  • Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: "Avoid instance stickiness". Its scale-out design principle warns that stickiness "limits the application's ability to scale out", for example because a high-volume user's traffic is not spread across instances. (Microsoft Learn)
  • The Twelve-Factor App: stateless processes. "Twelve-factor processes are stateless and share-nothing", and "sticky sessions are a violation of twelve-factor and should never be used or relied upon". (12factor.net)

docs.title: Popular tools and providers
docs.text: Need Common choices Autoscaling containers Kubernetes HPA; KEDA for event-driven scaling (queue length, Kafka lag, Redis lists) and scale-to-zero Autoscaling VMs Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, Google Cloud managed instance groups, Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets Autoscaling managed containers Amazon ECS service auto scaling, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps Shared session storage Redis or Valkey (connect-redis), a database-backed store, or signed tokens Load balancing AWS ALB, Google Cloud Load Balancing, Azure Load Balancer / Application Gateway, NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy

docs.title: Stateless and stateful services
docs.text:
Stateless service Stateful service Keeps per-client data between requests No Yes Any instance can serve any request Yes No: the client must reach "its" instance Losing an instance Requests retry elsewhere; nothing lost Data or sessions on it are lost or must fail over Scaling Add or remove instances freely Needs partitioning, replication, or rebalancing Examples REST API servers, rendering services Databases, caches, WebSocket gateways, game servers

Stateless does not mean the system has no state; it means state lives in dedicated services built to manage it (databases, caches, object storage), not in the application instances.

docs.title: Moving state out of the application
docs.text: State Where it often starts (problem) Where it should live User sessions Process memory (express-session default MemoryStore) Redis or a database session store, or signed tokens Uploaded files Local disk Object storage (S3 or similar); see file storage and uploads Cached data Per-process Map Redis (or keep a small local cache that is safe to lose) Background jobs setTimeout or in-memory arrays A job queue; see background jobs and scheduling Scheduled tasks Cron inside every instance (runs N times) One scheduler, or a lock so only one instance runs each job WebSocket subscriptions Connections in one instance Pub/sub (Redis, a broker) to fan messages out to all instances Rate-limit counters In-memory counters per instance Redis, so limits apply across instances Configuration Files edited on a server Environment variables or a config service

docs.title: Sticky sessions and their trade-offs
docs.text:
A load balancer can use sticky sessions (session affinity), routing each client to the same instance, usually with a cookie. This lets a stateful app run on several instances without moving its state.

Benefit Cost Works with in-memory sessions or caches Uneven load: heavy users pile onto some instances Can improve local cache hit rates When an instance dies or is scaled in, its users lose their state Required by some protocols during a connection New instances receive traffic only from new clients, so scaling out helps slowly Deployments and rebalancing become harder

Treat stickiness as an optimization or a temporary workaround, not a correctness requirement. Long-lived connections (WebSockets) are naturally pinned to one instance for their lifetime, which is fine as long as reconnecting to another instance works.

docs.title: Horizontal scaling behind a load balancer
docs.text:
┌─> instance 1 ─┐
clients ─> load ────┼─> instance 2 ─┼─> shared data services
          balancer  └─> instance 3 ─┘
              │ health checks every few seconds; unhealthy instances get no traffic

The load balancer spreads requests, checks health, and stops sending traffic to failed instances. Algorithms and setup are covered in load balancing.

docs.title: Autoscaling signals
docs.text:
An autoscaler watches a metric and adjusts the instance count.

Signal Good for Caveats CPU utilization CPU-bound services Misleading for I/O-bound Node.js services that wait on databases Request rate per instance Web and API tiers Needs a known per-instance capacity Latency (p95/p99) User-facing goals Reacts late; latency can rise from downstream causes that more instances will not fix Queue depth / backlog per worker Background workers Best signal for consumers: scale by "messages waiting per worker" Concurrent connections WebSocket gateways Connections are long-lived; scaling in disconnects users Memory Rarely a good scaling signal Usually indicates leaks or sizing, not load Schedule Predictable daily or weekly peaks Combine with a reactive policy for surprises

docs.title: Scaling policies
docs.text:
• Target tracking: keep a metric near a target, such as "average CPU at 60%" or "1,000 requests per instance". The autoscaler computes how many instances are needed. This is the usual default.
  • Step scaling: add or remove a set number of instances when a metric crosses thresholds ("+2 if CPU > 70%, +4 if > 85%").
  • Scheduled scaling: set capacity for known times ("20 instances at 08:45 on weekdays").
  • Predictive scaling: some cloud providers forecast load from history and scale ahead of it.

Always set a minimum (enough for availability, usually at least two instances in different zones) and a maximum (to cap cost and protect downstream systems such as the database).

One full turn of the loop, using target tracking:

docs.title: Cooldowns and stabilization
docs.text:
New instances take time to start and to affect metrics. Without a pause, an autoscaler can overreact, adding far too many instances or flapping up and down.

  • Cooldown / warm-up period: after a scaling action, wait before acting again or before counting new instances' metrics.
  • Stabilization window: use the highest recommendation over recent minutes before scaling in, so a brief dip does not remove capacity.
  • Scale out quickly and in slowly: under-capacity hurts users; over-capacity only costs money for a few minutes.

docs.title: Scale-in protection
docs.text: Removing an instance can interrupt work. Protect instances that are running long jobs, holding many connections, or acting as a leader. Cloud autoscaling groups offer instance-level scale-in protection, and Kubernetes lets you control scale-down behavior and disruption budgets. Workers should finish or hand back their current job when asked to stop.

docs.title: Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
docs.text:
In Kubernetes, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) adjusts the number of pod replicas of a Deployment from metrics. Its basic rule is:

desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / targetMetricValue)

Example: 4 pods at 90% average CPU, target 60%
         ceil(4 × 90 / 60) = ceil(6) = 6 pods

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60   # percent of each pod's CPU request
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300  # the default, shown explicitly

Details that decide how the HPA behaves:

  • Tolerance. If currentMetric / desiredMetric is within 0.1 of 1.0 (10%, the default), the HPA does nothing. 63% CPU against a 60% target is a ratio of 1.05, so no pods are added.
  • Default behaviour. Scale-down waits a 300-second stabilization window and uses the highest recommendation in that window. Scale-up has no window: it acts at once, adding at most 4 pods or 100% of the current replicas (whichever is more) every 15 seconds.
  • Resource requests. CPU utilization is measured against each container's CPU request. If a pod's containers have no request set, utilization is undefined and the HPA takes no action for that metric.
  • Metrics sources. CPU and memory come from the metrics.k8s.io API, usually provided by Metrics Server, which is installed separately. Custom and external metrics (requests per second, queue length) need an adapter for custom.metrics.k8s.io or external.metrics.k8s.io.

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
When an instance is removed, it should finish in-flight work instead of dropping it:

1. Orchestrator sends SIGTERM. At the same time it starts removing the
   instance from load balancing, which takes a moment to reach every proxy
2. Instance fails its readiness check but keeps serving for a short drain
   delay (a few seconds), so late-routed requests are not refused
3. Instance stops accepting new connections and closes idle keep-alive ones
4. In-flight requests finish (with a time limit)
5. Close database pools, flush logs, release locks
6. Exit; the orchestrator force-kills after its grace period
   (Kubernetes default: 30 seconds)

docs.title: Readiness, liveness, and warm-up
docs.text:
• Readiness check: "Can this instance take traffic now?" It fails while starting up (connecting to the database, loading config) and while shutting down. Load balancers and Kubernetes route only to ready instances.
  • Liveness check: "Is this instance stuck and in need of a restart?" Keep it simple; it should not depend on the database, or a database outage will restart every instance.
  • Warm-up: new instances may be slow at first (cold connection pools, empty local caches, just-in-time compilation). Some load balancers can ramp traffic to new targets gradually ("slow start").

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
• Make web and API tiers stateless almost always. It is what lets you deploy, scale, and replace instances without logging users out.
  • Keep state where it belongs: databases, caches, queues, and object storage are the stateful parts. Scale them with replication and partitioning, not with a CPU-based autoscaler.
  • Autoscale when load varies (daily cycles, campaigns, batch backlogs) and new instances start in seconds to a few minutes.
  • Prefer scheduled or predictive capacity when start-up is slow or peaks are predictable, and keep a reactive policy for surprises.
  • Do not autoscale a service whose real limit is downstream (a saturated database, a rate-limited third-party API): more instances just add pressure there.
  • Fixed capacity is fine for small, steady internal services, where two instances for availability are all you need.
Approach Use when Avoid when Scaling impact Sticky sessions A legacy app keeps sessions in memory and cannot change yet; a protocol needs several requests to reach one instance You need even load, fast scale-in, or painless deploys New instances only get new clients; losing an instance loses its users' sessions Shared session store (Redis, database) Server-side sessions (revocable logins, carts) across many instances Adding one more stateful dependency is not justified for a tiny app Any instance serves any request; the store must be highly available Signed tokens (JWT, signed cookies) Short-lived, read-mostly identity data; many services verify the user You need instant revocation or large session data No shared lookup per request; revocation needs short expiry or a deny-list

docs.title: Moving Express sessions into Redis
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import session from "express-session";
import { RedisStore } from "connect-redis";
import { createClient } from "redis";

const redisClient = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
redisClient.on("error", (err) => console.error("Redis client error", err)); // without a listener, an error crashes the process
await redisClient.connect();

const app = express();
app.set("trust proxy", 1); // behind a load balancer that terminates HTTPS

app.use(session({
  store: new RedisStore({ client: redisClient, prefix: "sess:" }),
  secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET,
  resave: false,
  saveUninitialized: false,
  cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax", maxAge: 8 * 60 * 60 * 1000 },
}));

Any instance can now read any user's session, so sticky sessions are no longer needed. The import style above matches recent connect-redis versions; older versions export the store differently, so check the package documentation for the version you install.

docs.title: Health endpoints and graceful shutdown in Node.js
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
let shuttingDown = false;

app.get("/health/live", (req, res) => res.sendStatus(200));     // process is running
app.get("/health/ready", (req, res) => {
  res.sendStatus(shuttingDown ? 503 : 200);                     // stop new traffic during shutdown
});

const server = app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

const DRAIN_DELAY_MS = 5_000; // time for load balancers to stop routing here

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  shuttingDown = true;                          // readiness now returns 503
  setTimeout(() => {                            // keep serving while routing updates spread
    server.close(async () => {                  // stop accepting; wait for in-flight requests
      await db.close();                         // release connections
      process.exit(0);
    });
    server.closeIdleConnections();              // drop idle keep-alive sockets so close() can finish
  }, DRAIN_DELAY_MS);
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 25_000).unref(); // hard stop before the grace period ends
});

Here db stands for your database client or pool. The order matters:

  1. Readiness flips to 503 at once, but the server keeps accepting requests for DRAIN_DELAY_MS. Load balancers take a moment to notice, and closing the port immediately would refuse the requests they still send.
  2. server.close() then stops new connections and waits for in-flight requests. Since Node.js 19 it also closes idle keep-alive connections itself; the explicit closeIdleConnections() (added in 18.2) covers Node 18.
  3. The 25-second timer is a safety net inside Kubernetes' default 30-second grace period, after which the process is killed anyway.

In Kubernetes you can put the drain delay in a preStop hook instead; it runs before the container gets SIGTERM and counts against the same grace period. See running Express in production for keep-alive connections and timeouts during shutdown.

docs.title: Scaling workers by queue backlog
docs.text:
Target: 100 waiting messages per worker
Backlog: 2,400 messages  ->  2,400 / 100 = 24 workers (capped at max 30)
Backlog: 150 messages    ->  2 workers (min)

Backlog per worker reacts to the actual amount of pending work, unlike CPU, which may stay low while workers wait on slow downstream APIs.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep application instances stateless; move sessions, files, and jobs to shared services.
  • Avoid relying on sticky sessions for correctness.
  • Choose a scaling metric that reflects real load for that service (queue backlog for workers, requests or CPU for APIs).
  • Set minimums for availability and maximums to protect cost and downstream systems.
  • Scale out quickly and in slowly, with cooldowns or stabilization windows.
  • Implement readiness checks, liveness checks, and graceful shutdown.
  • Load-test scaling behavior: how long does it take for new capacity to help?

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
Users are logged out after a deploy or a scale-in

  • Symptom: bursts of 401 responses or "please sign in again" right after instances are replaced or removed.
  • Detect: overlay 401 counts on deploy and scaling events; log when a request carries a session cookie that the server cannot find.
  • Cause: sessions live in process memory (the express-session default MemoryStore), or sticky sessions pin users to instances that were just removed.
  • Fix: move sessions to a shared store (Redis) or signed tokens, then drop the dependency on stickiness.

502 or connection-refused errors during every rollout

  • Symptom: a short spike of 502/503 at the load balancer each time pods or instances are stopped.
  • Detect: load-balancer 5xx metrics (for ALB, HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count and HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count) lining up with termination events.
  • Cause: the app closes its port on SIGTERM before the load balancer has stopped routing to it; or the app closes idle keep-alive connections sooner than the load balancer does, so it reuses a socket the app just closed.
  • Fix: fail readiness, wait a drain delay, then close (the example above). Set the app's keep-alive timeout above the load balancer's idle timeout, as AWS recommends (ALB default: 60 seconds; Node's server.keepAliveTimeout is documented as 5 seconds by default).

Replica count flaps up and down

  • Symptom: instances are added and removed every few minutes; cold caches and connection churn make latency worse.
  • Detect: a sawtooth in the replica graph; frequent scaling events in kubectl describe hpa or the cloud's activity history.
  • Cause: a noisy metric, a target set too tightly, or a scale-down window shortened far below the default.
  • Fix: keep or lengthen the scale-down stabilization window, add scale-down policies (for example "at most 10% per minute"), and pick a steadier metric.

Latency climbs but the autoscaler does nothing

  • Symptom: p95 latency and queue time rise while the replica count stays flat.
  • Detect: kubectl get hpa shows CPU far below target, or kubectl describe hpa reports that it cannot compute the metric.
  • Cause: an I/O-bound Node.js service waits on the database, so CPU stays low; or containers have no CPU request, so utilization cannot be computed.
  • Fix: set resource requests; scale on requests per pod, concurrency, or backlog through a metrics adapter or KEDA; check whether the real bottleneck is downstream.

Scale-out takes the database down

  • Symptom: during a spike, new instances fail to start or requests fail with "too many connections" (PostgreSQL error 53300, too_many_connections).
  • Detect: database connection count at its limit while the replica count rises.
  • Cause: every instance opens its own pool. 20 replicas × a pool of 20 is 400 connections, against PostgreSQL's typical default max_connections of 100.
  • Fix: cap maxReplicas from the database budget, shrink pools, or put a connection pooler (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy) in front; see database scaling.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Stateless service: A service that keeps no per-client data between requests in its instances.
  • Sticky session (session affinity): Routing a client's requests to the same instance.
  • Autoscaling: Automatically changing the number of instances based on metrics or schedules.
  • Target tracking: A policy that keeps a metric near a target value.
  • Cooldown / stabilization window: A delay that prevents rapid, repeated scaling actions.
  • Scale-in protection: Preventing specific instances from being removed.
  • Readiness / liveness probe: Checks for "can receive traffic" and "needs restarting".
  • Graceful shutdown: Finishing in-flight work before an instance exits.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using in-memory sessions and wondering why users are logged out after scaling or deploys.
  • Running cron jobs inside every instance, so they execute many times.
  • Scaling an I/O-bound Node.js API on CPU, which stays low while latency climbs.
  • Setting no maximum, so a traffic spike scales the app until the database collapses.
  • Liveness checks that query the database, causing mass restarts during a database outage.
  • Exiting immediately on SIGTERM and dropping in-flight requests.
  • Assuming autoscaling reacts instantly; new instances take minutes to start and warm up.

docs.text:
1. What does "stateless" mean for a service, and where does the state go?
  2. What are the drawbacks of sticky sessions?
  3. Which autoscaling signal would you use for a queue worker, and why?
  4. Calculate the HPA's desired replicas for 5 pods at 80% CPU with a 50% target.
  5. Why should scale-in be slower than scale-out?
  6. What is the difference between readiness and liveness checks?
  7. Why does the shutdown example wait a few seconds before calling server.close(), and what happens if it closes immediately?
  8. The HPA target is 60% CPU and pods average 64%. Does it scale? Why?

docs.title: Architecture Fundamentals
docs.text: Software architecture is the set of significant decisions about how a system is structured: its main parts, their responsibilities, how they communicate, and the constraints they follow. A useful working definition is "the decisions that are expensive to change later." This page explains what architecture covers, how quality goals drive it, and how teams record and communicate architectural decisions.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Code-level choices—a variable name, a loop—are cheap to change. Architectural choices—one deployable or twenty, which database, synchronous calls or events—shape every later feature and are costly to reverse. Good architecture lets a system meet its goals for speed, reliability, security, and cost, and lets the team keep changing it safely. Poor architecture shows up as slow delivery, fragile releases, and outages that are hard to diagnose.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Spotify — recording decisions as ADRs. Spotify's engineering blog describes teams, such as its Creator team, that document significant decisions as architecture decision records, capturing the context and the consequences of each one (Spotify Engineering).
  • UK Government Digital Service — ADRs as a standard. The GDS Way tells government teams to record decisions that affect a service's architecture, and defines an ADR lifecycle of Proposed, Accepted, and Superseded (The GDS Way).
  • Amazon — shaping teams to fit the architecture. Amazon explains that changing its technology was not enough: it also restructured teams into small "two-pizza teams" to take advantage of a microservices architecture, which is Conway's law applied on purpose (AWS Executive Insights).

Popular tools:

  • Structurizr: "models as code" for C4 diagrams.
  • adr-tools: command-line tools for creating and superseding ADRs.
  • dependency-cruiser: validates JavaScript and TypeScript dependency rules in CI, a ready-made fitness function.
  • Review frameworks: the AWS Well-Architected Framework and the Azure Architecture Center.

docs.title: What counts as architecture
docs.text:
Architecture is less about drawing boxes than about deciding:

  • Structure: which components exist and what each is responsible for.
  • Communication: how components talk (in-process calls, HTTP, gRPC, messages) and what contracts they share.
  • Data ownership: which component owns which data, and how others read it.
  • Deployment: what runs where, and what can be released independently.
  • Constraints and principles: rules everyone follows, such as "services never share database tables" or "all external calls have timeouts."

A decision is architectural when it is significant (it affects quality attributes or many parts of the system) and hard to change.

docs.title: Quality attributes
docs.text:
Functional requirements describe what the system does ("users can place orders"). Quality attributes, also called non-functional requirements, describe how well it does it. Architecture is mostly driven by quality attributes, because many different structures can deliver the same features.

Attribute Question it answers How it is measured Performance How fast does it respond? Latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99), throughput (requests per second) Scalability Can it handle more load by adding resources? Throughput and latency as load and instances grow Availability Is it up when users need it? Uptime percentage (for example, 99.9% ≈ 8.8 hours of downtime per year) Reliability Does it work correctly and recover from faults? Error rate, mean time between failures, mean time to recovery (MTTR) Security Is it protected against misuse? Vulnerabilities found, time to patch, audit results, access reviews Maintainability How easily can it be changed? Lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to onboard a developer Testability How easily can behavior be verified? Test speed, ability to test parts in isolation, coverage of critical paths Observability Can we understand what it is doing in production? Time to detect and diagnose incidents; quality of logs, metrics, and traces Cost What does it cost to build and run? Infrastructure cost per month or per request, engineering effort

Vague goals such as "it must be fast" are not useful. Turn them into measurable statements, often called quality attribute scenarios:

 Under normal load (500 requests/s), 99% of "place order" requests
 complete within 300 ms, measured at the load balancer.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
Quality attributes compete. Every architectural decision improves some attributes at the expense of others:

Decision Gains Costs Split into microservices Independent deploys and scaling, team autonomy Network failures, distributed data, operational complexity Add a cache Performance, lower database load Stale data, invalidation complexity, another system to run Replicate across regions Availability, lower latency for distant users Cost, consistency challenges Strong consistency everywhere Simpler reasoning about data Latency and availability during failures Add abstraction layers Testability, swappable infrastructure More code and indirection

The architect's job is to choose the trade-offs that best fit the current goals and constraints, and to make them explicit. There is no universally "best" architecture.

docs.title: Architecture styles at a glance
docs.text:
Style Core idea Fits when Layered (n-tier) Code organized in horizontal layers: presentation, business logic, data access Most business applications; a clear default Modular monolith One deployable split into strongly separated modules Small to medium teams wanting clear boundaries without distributed complexity Microservices Many small, independently deployable services, each owning its data Large organizations with many teams and well-understood domains Event-driven Components communicate by publishing and reacting to events Workflows with many independent reactions, integration between systems Serverless Functions run on demand by a cloud platform Spiky or event-triggered workloads, small teams avoiding server management Hexagonal / clean Business logic at the center, infrastructure behind interfaces Complex domains that need testability and replaceable infrastructure Pipes and filters Data flows through a chain of independent processing steps Data processing, ETL, media pipelines

Styles combine: a modular monolith can use hexagonal architecture inside each module and publish events to other systems. The following pages cover them in depth: monoliths and microservices, layered, hexagonal, and clean architecture, event-driven architecture, and serverless architecture.

docs.title: Conway's law
docs.text:
"Organizations which design systems … are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations." — Melvin Conway

In practice, system boundaries tend to mirror team boundaries. Conway's own example: eight people were to build a COBOL and an ALGOL compiler; five were assigned to COBOL and three to ALGOL, and the COBOL compiler ran in five phases while the ALGOL compiler ran in three. If two teams must coordinate on every change to a shared module, that module becomes a bottleneck.

Teams use this deliberately with the inverse Conway maneuver: shape teams around the architecture you want. If you want independent services for payments and catalog, give each one a team that owns it end to end.

docs.title: Architecture decision records (ADRs)
docs.text:
Decisions are easily forgotten, and new team members repeat old debates. An architecture decision record is a short document, stored with the code, that captures one significant decision and why it was made.

# ADR 007: Use PostgreSQL for the orders service

## Status
Accepted (2026-03-14). Supersedes ADR 002.

## Context
Orders need multi-row transactions (order + items + payment intent) and
reporting queries with joins. The team already runs PostgreSQL for billing.
Write volume is ~200 orders/minute at peak.

## Decision
Store orders in PostgreSQL 16 using a managed service, with one schema
owned by the orders service.

## Consequences
+ ACID transactions across order tables; mature tooling; team familiarity.
- Schema migrations must be planned; no flexible per-document schema.
- Other services must use the orders API, not the tables directly.

Key properties of good ADRs:

  • One decision per record, numbered and never deleted.
  • Record the context and the alternatives considered, not just the outcome.
  • When a decision changes, write a new ADR that supersedes the old one.
  • Keep them in the repository (for example, docs/adr/) so they are reviewed like code.

docs.title: Evolutionary architecture and fitness functions
docs.text:
Requirements change, so architecture must evolve. Evolutionary architecture means designing for incremental, guided change rather than a big up-front plan. A fitness function is an automated check that protects an architectural characteristic as the code changes, for example:

  • A test that fails if a module imports another module's internal files.
  • A CI performance test that fails if p95 latency exceeds a budget.
  • A dependency check that blocks packages with known critical vulnerabilities.

Fitness functions turn architectural rules from documents people forget into checks that run on every change.

docs.title: Communicating architecture: the C4 model
docs.text:
Architecture diagrams often fail because they mix levels of detail. The C4 model defines four zoom levels:

Level Shows Audience 1. System context Your system as one box, its users, and the external systems it talks to Everyone, including non-technical people 2. Container The deployable/runnable parts: web app, API, database, queue, mobile app Technical people inside and outside the team 3. Component The main components inside one container and their responsibilities Developers and architects 4. Code Classes or modules for one component Developers (usually generated, rarely drawn)

Label every arrow with what flows and how (protocol, sync or async). A diagram without labels hides the decisions that matter.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
The practices on this page cost time, so match their weight to the stakes.

Use them fully when:

  • Several teams change the same system, so decisions must be shared and remembered.
  • A decision is expensive to reverse: a database, a deployment model, a public API, a split into services.
  • Quality targets are explicit (an SLA, a latency budget, a compliance rule) and must be designed for rather than hoped for.
  • Newcomers keep asking "why is it built this way?"

Keep them light when:

  • You are building a prototype or a short-lived internal tool.
  • The decision is easy to undo, such as a library choice behind an adapter.
  • One small team owns everything and talks daily; a short README note may be enough.
Practice Worth it when Keep it light or skip when Quality attribute scenarios Performance, availability, or cost targets exist No real load or users yet ADRs Decisions are significant and debated The choice is trivial or easily reversed C4 diagrams People outside the team must understand the system A diagram would only restate one file C4 level 3 and 4 A container is complex and changes slowly Code changes quickly; generate instead of drawing Fitness functions A rule has been broken before, or matters a lot The rule is still being discovered

docs.title: Turning goals into decisions
docs.text:
Suppose a course platform has these requirements:

  • 20,000 students, peaks of 300 requests per second during exams.
  • Quiz submissions must never be lost.
  • A team of six developers.
  • Monthly infrastructure budget is limited.

Reasonable decisions and their rationale:

Decision Driven by Modular monolith with modules for accounts, courses, quizzes, and progress Six developers; clear boundaries without microservice operations Two or more stateless app instances behind a load balancer Availability and peak load Quiz submissions written to the database in a transaction before responding "Never lost" reliability requirement Cache course catalog pages Read-heavy traffic at exam peaks Background queue for certificate PDF generation Keep request latency low; slow CPU work off the request path Structured logs, metrics, and alerts from day one Observability to meet the availability target

Each decision is recorded as an ADR with its context and trade-offs.

docs.title: A fitness function in a test
docs.text:
// test/architecture.test.js — run with: node --test
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { readFile, readdir } from "node:fs/promises";
import path from "node:path";

const MODULES_DIR = path.resolve("src/modules");

test("modules import each other only through their public index.js", async () => {
  for (const moduleName of await readdir(MODULES_DIR)) {
    const files = await readdir(path.join(MODULES_DIR, moduleName), { recursive: true });
    for (const file of files.filter((f) => f.endsWith(".js"))) {
      const source = await readFile(path.join(MODULES_DIR, moduleName, file), "utf8");
      // Simplified: assumes each module's files sit at its root folder.
      // Forbid deep imports such as "../billing/internal/tax.js"
      const deepImport = source.match(/from "\.\.\/(?!\.)([\w-]+)\/(?!index\.js")/);
      assert.equal(deepImport, null, `${moduleName}/${file} reaches into another module`);
    }
  }
});

Dedicated tools (dependency-cruiser, ESLint import rules) do this more thoroughly, but the idea is the same: architecture rules enforced in CI.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start from measurable quality attribute scenarios, not technology preferences.
  • Prefer the simplest architecture that meets current goals; keep options open for likely changes.
  • Make trade-offs explicit and record significant decisions as ADRs.
  • Align team boundaries with system boundaries.
  • Enforce important rules with automated fitness functions.
  • Draw diagrams at one C4 level at a time and label every relationship.
  • Revisit decisions when constraints change; architecture is never "done."

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Decision amnesia. Symptom: the same debate returns every few months, or a decision is reversed and then reinstated. Detect: review threads that ask "why do we do it this way?" with no answer. Cause: the reasoning lived in someone's head or a chat thread. Fix: write ADRs for current decisions, including the ones made long ago.
  • Architecture drift. Symptom: modules import each other's internals and every change touches many folders. Detect: a dependency graph (for example from dependency-cruiser) shows cycles and cross-module edges that grow release by release. Cause: the rules were documented but not enforced. Fix: turn the rules into fitness functions that fail CI.
  • A quality target missed at peak. Symptom: p99 latency or error rate breaks during a busy period that nobody load-tested. Detect: latency percentiles and saturation on dashboards. Cause: "fast enough" was never written as a measurable scenario. Fix: write the scenario, load-test against it, and design for it.
  • Team and system boundaries do not match. Symptom: small features need several teams and coordinated releases. Detect: lead time grows and many pull requests span repositories owned by different teams. Cause: Conway's law working against you. Fix: realign ownership so each team owns a whole capability, or move the boundary.
  • Stale diagrams during an incident. Symptom: on-call engineers find the diagram shows components that no longer exist. Detect: the diagram disagrees with what is deployed. Cause: hand-drawn diagrams nobody updates. Fix: keep levels 1 and 2 small, store diagrams as code next to the system, and review them with the changes that affect them.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Software architecture: The significant, hard-to-change decisions about a system's structure and behavior.
  • Quality attribute (non-functional requirement): A measurable property such as availability, latency, or maintainability.
  • Trade-off: Gaining one property at the expense of another.
  • Architecture style: A named, reusable way of structuring systems, such as layered or microservices.
  • Conway's law: Systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them.
  • ADR (architecture decision record): A short document recording one decision, its context, and its consequences.
  • Fitness function: An automated check that protects an architectural characteristic.
  • C4 model: A set of four diagram levels—context, container, component, code—for describing architecture.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Architecture is the diagram." Diagrams communicate decisions; the decisions and their reasons are the architecture.
  • Choosing a style because large companies use it. Their constraints are not yours.
  • Ignoring non-functional requirements until production load reveals them.
  • Designing everything up front instead of deferring decisions that can wait.
  • Not recording why a decision was made, so it is later reversed for the wrong reasons.
  • "There is a best architecture." There are only trade-offs that fit or do not fit your situation.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What makes a decision "architectural"?
  2. Name six quality attributes and how you would measure each.
  3. Give an example of a trade-off between two quality attributes.
  4. What is Conway's law, and how can a company use it deliberately?
  5. What sections does an ADR contain, and why keep ADRs in the repository?
  6. What are the four levels of the C4 model, and who is each for?
