docs.title: Design Patterns for Backends
docs.text: A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a problem that keeps appearing in software design. Patterns give teams a shared vocabulary—"put a repository in front of that collection," "wrap the client in an adapter"—and proven structures to start from. This page covers the patterns that appear most often in backend code, each with the problem it solves, a JavaScript example, and when not to use it.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Backends face the same problems repeatedly: isolating database code, swapping implementations for tests, talking to third-party APIs with awkward interfaces, adding cross-cutting behavior such as logging and retries, and reacting to events. Recognizing which pattern fits saves design time and produces code other developers understand quickly. Recognizing when a pattern does not fit prevents needless complexity. The principles behind these patterns are covered in design principles.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix — repository plus adapter. When Netflix's Studio Workflows team had to read one entity from a new service, it "created a GraphQL data source that implemented the repository interface," and a one-line change switched the app to it (Netflix TechBlog).
  • Passport.js — strategy. Passport authenticates requests through interchangeable strategies, each implementing one authentication mechanism such as username and password or OAuth (Passport documentation).
  • Express — wrapping requests in middleware. Express describes an application as "essentially a series of middleware function calls," each able to add behavior and pass control on with next(), the same idea as the decorator pattern (Express guide).
  • NestJS — dependency injection as the core. NestJS states that it is built around the dependency injection design pattern and resolves dependencies by their type (NestJS documentation).
  • Node.js — observer in the core API. Much of Node.js is built on emitters that call listener functions, and an EventEmitter calls its listeners synchronously in the order they were registered (Node.js documentation).

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Problem: business logic is littered with database queries, so it is tied to one database and hard to test.

Solution: a repository presents a collection-like interface for one type of domain object (findById, save, findByCustomer) and hides how objects are stored.

export function makeUserRepository(db) {
  const users = db.collection("users");
  return {
    findById: (id) => users.findOne({ _id: id }),
    findByEmail: (email) => users.findOne({ email: email.toLowerCase() }),
    async save(user) {
      // Store emails in the same normalized form that findByEmail searches for
      const doc = { ...user, email: user.email.toLowerCase() };
      await users.replaceOne({ _id: user._id }, doc, { upsert: true });
    },
  };
}

Services call userRepository.findByEmail(...) and never see query syntax. Tests pass an in-memory repository.

Avoid when: the repository just mirrors every ORM method one-to-one (find, findOne, update…), adding a layer with no meaning; or for reporting queries, which are clearer as dedicated query functions.

docs.title: Service layer
docs.text:
Problem: route handlers grow business logic, and the same logic is needed from HTTP, queue consumers, and scheduled jobs.

Solution: a service layer defines the application's operations (use cases) in one place. Entry points stay thin and call services.

export function makeAccountService({ users, mailer, hasher }) {
  return {
    async register({ email, password }) {
      if (await users.findByEmail(email)) throw new ConflictError("Email in use");
      const user = { _id: crypto.randomUUID(), email, passwordHash: await hasher.hash(password) };
      await users.save(user);
      await mailer.sendWelcome(email);
      return { id: user._id, email };
    },
  };
}

Avoid when: services become "anemic pass-throughs" that only call one repository method each, or "god services" with hundreds of unrelated methods. Group operations by business capability.

docs.title: Unit of work
docs.text:
Problem: one business operation changes several records, and they must be saved together or not at all.

Solution: a unit of work tracks changes during an operation and commits them in one transaction. In Node.js this usually means a database transaction or session passed to each repository call:

await mongoClient.withSession(async (session) => {
  await session.withTransaction(async () => {
    await orders.insertOne(order, { session });
    await inventory.updateOne({ sku }, { $inc: { stock: -1 } }, { session });
  });
});

ORMs often implement unit of work internally. See MongoDB transactions.

Avoid when: a single document or row update is enough; transactions add latency and contention.

docs.title: Dependency injection
docs.text:
Problem: a module creates its own dependencies (new Database(), import stripe), so it cannot be configured or tested in isolation.

Solution: pass dependencies in from outside. The most common form is constructor (or factory) injection:

// The service receives what it needs
export function makeOrderService({ orderRepository, paymentGateway, logger }) {
  return {
    async pay(orderId) {
      const order = await orderRepository.findById(orderId);
      await paymentGateway.charge(order.totalCents, order.currency);
      logger.info({ orderId }, "order paid");
    },
  };
}

// Composition root wires real implementations
const orderService = makeOrderService({
  orderRepository: makeMongoOrderRepository(db),
  paymentGateway: makeStripeGateway(process.env.STRIPE_KEY),
  logger,
});

// Tests wire fakes
const testService = makeOrderService({
  orderRepository: makeInMemoryOrderRepository(),
  paymentGateway: { charge: async () => {} },
  logger: { info() {} },
});

DI containers (such as InversifyJS, Awilix, or the one built into NestJS) automate wiring by registering and resolving dependencies by name or type. They help in large applications; manual wiring in one composition root is enough for most Node.js services.

Avoid when: injecting things that never vary (a pure utility function like slugify)—just import them.

docs.title: Factory
docs.text:
Problem: creating an object requires logic—choosing a type based on configuration, applying defaults, validating inputs—and that logic is repeated at every new.

Solution: a factory function centralizes creation.

export function createStorage(config) {
  switch (config.STORAGE_DRIVER) {
    case "s3":
      return makeS3Storage({ bucket: config.S3_BUCKET, region: config.AWS_REGION });
    case "local":
      return makeLocalStorage({ root: config.UPLOAD_DIR });
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unknown storage driver: ${config.STORAGE_DRIVER}`);
  }
}

Factory functions are idiomatic in JavaScript and also give you encapsulation through closures (the make… functions on this page are factories).

Avoid when: creation is a plain object literal with no logic.

docs.title: Strategy
docs.text:
Problem: an algorithm varies (pricing rules, shipping calculators, authentication methods), and if/else chains grow with every variant.

Solution: define a family of interchangeable functions or objects with the same interface, and pick one at runtime.

const shippingStrategies = {
  standard: (order) => (order.totalCents >= 10_000 ? 0 : 499),
  express: (order) => 1499,
  pickup: () => 0,
};

export function shippingCost(order, method) {
  const strategy = shippingStrategies[method];
  if (!strategy) throw new ValidationError(`Unknown shipping method: ${method}`);
  return strategy(order);
}

This is the main tool for the open/closed principle. Passport.js authentication strategies are a well-known example.

Avoid when: there are only two stable variants; a simple condition is clearer.

docs.title: Adapter
docs.text:
Problem: a third-party library or legacy API has an interface that does not match what your code expects, or you want to be able to replace the provider.

Solution: an adapter wraps the external API and exposes your own interface.

// Your interface: send({ to, subject, html })
export function makeSendGridMailer(client) {
  return {
    async send({ to, subject, html }) {
      await client.send({
        to,
        from: "no-reply@example.com",
        subject,
        html,
      }); // translate to the provider's shape
    },
  };
}

export function makeSesMailer(sesClient, SendEmailCommand) {
  return {
    async send({ to, subject, html }) {
      await sesClient.send(new SendEmailCommand({
        Destination: { ToAddresses: [to] },
        Message: { Subject: { Data: subject }, Body: { Html: { Data: html } } },
        Source: "no-reply@example.com",
      }));
    },
  };
}

Switching email providers now touches one adapter, not every caller. Adapters are the "adapters" in ports and adapters.

Avoid when: the library is stable, used in one place, and its interface is already fine.

docs.title: Facade
docs.text:
Problem: a task requires coordinating several subsystems with complex APIs, and every caller repeats that coordination.

Solution: a facade offers one simple entry point over the complexity.

export function makeReportFacade({ queryRunner, csvWriter, storage, mailer }) {
  return {
    async emailMonthlyReport(month, recipient) {
      const rows = await queryRunner.monthlySales(month);
      const csv = csvWriter.write(rows);
      const url = await storage.uploadTemporary(`reports/${month}.csv`, csv);
      await mailer.send({ to: recipient, subject: `Sales ${month}`, html: `<a href="${url}">Download</a>` });
    },
  };
}

Avoid when: the facade starts accumulating unrelated operations and becomes a "god object."

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text:
Problem: you need to add behavior—logging, caching, retries, metrics, authorization—to an object or function without changing it, and in combinations.

Solution: wrap the original with an object or function that has the same interface, adds behavior, and delegates.

export function withCache(repository, cache, ttlSeconds = 60) {
  return {
    ...repository,
    async findById(id) {
      const key = `product:${id}`;
      const cached = await cache.get(key);
      if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);
      const product = await repository.findById(id);
      if (product) await cache.set(key, JSON.stringify(product), { EX: ttlSeconds });
      return product;
    },
  };
}

const products = withCache(makeProductRepository(db), redis);

Express middleware is closely related: each middleware wraps the request handling with extra behavior (logging, authentication, parsing) and passes control on with next(). Higher-order functions such as withRetry(fn) are decorators for functions.

Avoid when: the stack of wrappers becomes so deep that it is hard to see what actually runs; keep decoration explicit and close to the composition root.

docs.title: Observer and publish/subscribe
docs.text:
Problem: when something happens (an order is placed), several unrelated parts need to react (email, analytics, stock), and the source should not know about all of them.

Solution: the observer pattern lets listeners subscribe to a subject and be notified of events. Publish/subscribe adds an intermediary—an event bus or message broker—so publishers and subscribers do not know each other at all.

import { EventEmitter } from "node:events";

export const domainEvents = new EventEmitter();

// subscribers: registered once at startup, before any event is emitted
domainEvents.on("order.placed", (event) => sendConfirmation(event).catch(logError));
domainEvents.on("order.placed", (event) => trackAnalytics(event).catch(logError));

// publisher: later, when an order is placed (emit runs listeners synchronously)
domainEvents.emit("order.placed", { orderId, customerId });

In-process events are lost if the process crashes and are invisible to other instances. For reliable or cross-service reactions, use a message broker (see messaging patterns and event-driven architecture).

Avoid when: the flow must be easy to follow step by step; heavy use of events makes control flow implicit and harder to debug.

docs.title: Singleton (and Node.js module caching)
docs.text:
Problem: exactly one instance of something should exist, such as a database connection pool or a configuration object.

Solution in Node.js: modules are cached after their first load, so a module that exports an instance is effectively a singleton:

// db.js — every importer shares this pool
import pg from "pg";
export const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

Pitfalls:

  • Hidden global state: any code can import and mutate it, which makes tests interfere with each other.
  • Hard to replace in tests: callers import the real instance directly. Prefer creating the instance once in the composition root and injecting it.
  • Not truly single: the cache is per process and per resolved file path. Two copies of a package in node_modules, or several cluster workers, produce several "singletons."
  • Import-time side effects: connecting to a database just because a file was imported makes startup order fragile.

Avoid when: you can create the object once and pass it where needed.

docs.title: Builder
docs.text:
Problem: constructing an object or query needs many optional parts, and constructors with long argument lists are error-prone.

Solution: a builder assembles the object step by step and produces it at the end.

export function queryBuilder(collection) {
  const filter = {};
  let sort = {};
  let limit = 50;

  return {
    whereStatus(status) { filter.status = status; return this; },
    createdAfter(date) { filter.createdAt = { $gt: date }; return this; },
    sortBy(field, direction = -1) { sort = { [field]: direction }; return this; },
    take(n) { limit = Math.min(n, 100); return this; }, // enforce a maximum
    run() { return collection.find(filter).sort(sort).limit(limit).toArray(); },
  };
}

const recent = await queryBuilder(db.collection("orders"))
  .whereStatus("PAID")
  .createdAfter(new Date("2026-01-01"))
  .sortBy("createdAt")
  .take(20)
  .run();

Query builders (Knex, MongoDB's fluent cursor) and HTTP request builders are common examples.

Avoid when: an options object with defaults is enough—in JavaScript it usually is: createReport({ month, format = "csv", includeTax = true }).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a pattern when:

  • You can name the problem it solves in your code today (see "Choosing a pattern" below).
  • The same structure appears in several places and a shared vocabulary helps reviewers.
  • You need a seam for tests or for a likely change of provider.

Skip it when:

  • A plain function, an options object, or one if statement is clearer.
  • The pattern would wrap a single call with no added meaning.
  • It hides control flow that people need to follow while debugging.
Need Simpler option Pattern Pick the pattern when Data access Query functions in one module Repository Business logic must not know the database Wiring dependencies One composition root, by hand DI container Hundreds of components, or a framework that expects it Varying algorithm if / switch Strategy New variants keep arriving Cross-cutting behavior Edit the function Decorator or middleware The same behavior wraps many functions Reacting to events Direct function calls Observer, or a message broker Reactions are independent; use a broker if they must survive crashes One shared instance Module-level export Injected instance Tests need to replace it Complex construction Options object Builder Construction has rules and many steps

docs.title: Patterns working together
docs.text:
HTTP route (thin)
   └─► OrderService (service layer, receives dependencies via DI)
         ├─► OrderRepository (repository) ──wrapped by──► withCache (decorator)
         ├─► PaymentGateway (port) ◄── StripeAdapter (adapter)
         ├─► shippingStrategies[method] (strategy)
         └─► domainEvents.emit("order.placed") (observer / pub-sub)
 All created in main.js (composition root) using createStorage(...) (factory)

docs.title: Choosing a pattern
docs.text: Symptom Consider Queries spread through business logic Repository Logic duplicated across HTTP, jobs, and consumers Service layer Several writes must succeed together Unit of work / transaction Hard to test because of hard-coded dependencies Dependency injection Growing if/else on a type or method Strategy Third-party API leaks into your code Adapter Callers repeat multi-step coordination Facade Need logging/caching/retries without editing code Decorator Many reactions to one occurrence Observer / pub-sub Complex optional construction Builder (or an options object)

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Reach for a pattern to solve a problem you have, not to demonstrate the pattern.
  • Prefer JavaScript idioms—factory functions, closures, plain objects, higher-order functions—over class-heavy translations from Java.
  • Keep creation and wiring in one composition root.
  • Name things after the pattern when it helps readers (OrderRepository, StripeAdapter), not mechanically.
  • Combine patterns deliberately and keep the call path easy to follow.
  • Revisit patterns when they stop paying for their indirection.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Users cannot log in with a capitalized email. Symptom: login fails for some users only. Detect: failures cluster on addresses with uppercase letters. Cause: a repository normalizes the value it searches for but stores the raw value. Fix: normalize on write and on read, as the repository above now does, and add a unique index on the normalized field.
  • Stale reads after an update. Symptom: a product page shows the old price for minutes after an edit. Detect: the cached value and the database disagree. Cause: a caching decorator such as withCache caches reads but never invalidates on save. Fix: delete or refresh the key when writing, and keep TTLs short for data that changes.
  • In-process events vanish. Symptom: some orders never get a confirmation email. Detect: the missing emails line up with deploys or crashes. Cause: EventEmitter events live only in memory. Fix: publish through a durable broker, with the transactional outbox for reliability.
  • One failing listener crashes the process. Symptom: restarts with an unhandled promise rejection. Detect: crash logs point at an async event listener. Cause: a listener's promise rejected with no .catch. Fix: catch and log inside every async listener, as in the observer example above.
  • Too many database connections. Symptom: "too many connections" errors after scaling out. Detect: the database's connection count is pool size × processes × instances. Cause: the module-level "singleton" pool exists once per process, not once per system. Fix: size pools per process and plan for the total, or put a connection pooler in front of the database.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Design pattern: A named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem.
  • Repository: A collection-like abstraction over persistence for one type of object.
  • Service layer: A layer defining the application's operations.
  • Unit of work: Tracking changes and committing them together.
  • Dependency injection: Supplying dependencies from outside a component.
  • Factory: A function or object that encapsulates creation logic.
  • Strategy: Interchangeable algorithms selected at runtime.
  • Adapter: A wrapper that converts one interface into another.
  • Facade: A simplified interface over a complex subsystem.
  • Decorator: A wrapper that adds behavior while keeping the same interface.
  • Observer / publish–subscribe: Notifying interested listeners of events without coupling them to the source.
  • Singleton: A single shared instance.
  • Builder: Step-by-step construction of a complex object.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Pattern-driven design: adding patterns because they are "best practice," producing layers without purpose.
  • Generic repositories that expose the whole ORM and hide nothing.
  • Singletons as global variables, making tests order-dependent.
  • Event-driven spaghetti: so many in-process events that nobody can trace what happens after an action.
  • "Patterns are only for object-oriented languages." Most have simpler functional forms in JavaScript.
  • Decorators that change behavior unexpectedly, such as a caching decorator that returns stale data for writes.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What problem does the repository pattern solve, and when is it a useless layer?
  2. How does dependency injection improve testability? Show a factory-injection example.
  3. Compare the adapter and facade patterns.
  4. How is Express middleware related to the decorator pattern?
  5. Why is Node.js module caching a weak form of singleton?
  6. What is the difference between observer and publish/subscribe?

docs.text:
• Martin Fowler: Repository (Catalog of Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture)
  • Martin Fowler: Service layer
  • Martin Fowler: Unit of work
  • Martin Fowler: Inversion of control containers and the dependency injection pattern
  • Node.js API: Modules — caching
  • Domain-driven design

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text: Design principles are guidelines for structuring code so it stays easy to understand, test, and change. They are not laws: each one addresses a particular kind of pain, and applying one blindly can create a different pain. This page explains the principles backend developers rely on most, with JavaScript examples, and when each one stops helping.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Most of a backend's cost comes after the first release, when features are added and bugs fixed. Code that mixes concerns, depends on everything, or hides surprises makes every change slow and risky. These principles are the vocabulary teams use in code reviews and design discussions—"this function has two reasons to change," "this module is too coupled to the database"—and they underpin architecture styles such as hexagonal and clean architecture.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google — YAGNI and KISS in code review. Google's published code review guide asks reviewers to be "especially vigilant about over-engineering" and to encourage developers to solve the problem they know needs solving now, not one they speculate might arrive later (Google engineering practices).
  • Shopify — low coupling enforced by a tool. Shopify's Packwerk checks two kinds of boundaries in its Rails codebase: dependency boundaries (an intentional, ideally small list of dependencies) and privacy boundaries (other code may use only a package's public API) (Shopify Engineering).
  • Netflix — dependency inversion around data sources. Netflix's Studio Workflows team kept persistence details out of its business logic behind interfaces, which let it switch one data source from a JSON API to GraphQL within 2 hours (Netflix TechBlog).

Popular tools: linters with complexity rules (ESLint), dependency checkers such as dependency-cruiser, and TypeScript interfaces for narrow, explicit dependencies.

docs.title: Separation of concerns
docs.text:
A concern is one aspect of the program: HTTP handling, validation, business rules, persistence, logging. Separation of concerns means each part of the code deals with one concern, so changing one aspect does not require touching unrelated code.

// Mixed concerns: HTTP, validation, business rules, and SQL in one place
app.post("/orders", async (req, res) => {
  if (!req.body.items?.length) return res.status(400).send("No items");
  const total = req.body.items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0);
  const discount = total > 100 ? total * 0.1 : 0;
  await db.query("INSERT INTO orders ...", [total - discount]);
  res.status(201).json({ total: total - discount });
});

// Separated: each piece has one concern
app.post("/orders", validate(orderSchema), async (req, res) => {
  const order = await orderService.place(req.body);   // business rules
  res.status(201).json(order);                         // HTTP only
});

docs.title: Cohesion and coupling
docs.text:
• Cohesion measures how closely the contents of a module belong together. High cohesion: an invoice module containing invoice calculation, numbering, and formatting. Low cohesion: a utils.js with date helpers, email sending, and tax rules.
  • Coupling measures how much one module depends on another. Low coupling: modules talk through small, stable interfaces. High coupling: one module reads another's internal data or database tables.

The goal is high cohesion, low coupling: related things together, unrelated things apart, connected through narrow interfaces.

Kind of coupling (from worse to better) Example Shared mutable state / shared tables Two modules write the same orders table Depending on internals Importing another module's private helper Depending on a concrete implementation new MongoOrderRepository() inside a service Depending on an interface or message Receiving a repository with save and findById

docs.title: SOLID
docs.text: SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles collected by Robert C. Martin. They apply equally to modules and functions in JavaScript.

docs.title: S — Single responsibility principle
docs.text:
Each software module should have one and only one reason to change. — Robert C. Martin

"Reason to change" means one source of change—often one group of people. Invoice calculation changes when finance changes tax rules; PDF layout changes when marketing changes branding. Keep them apart.

// Two reasons to change in one class
class InvoiceService {
  calculateTotal(invoice) { /* tax rules: finance */ }
  renderPdf(invoice) { /* layout and fonts: design */ }
  emailToCustomer(invoice) { /* SMTP details: operations */ }
}

// One reason each
export const invoiceCalculator = { calculateTotal(invoice) { /* ... */ } };
export const invoicePdfRenderer = { render(invoice) { /* ... */ } };
export const invoiceMailer = { send(invoice, pdf) { /* ... */ } };

docs.title: O — Open/closed principle
docs.text:
Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.

You should be able to add behavior without editing existing, tested code.

// Every new payment method edits this function
function charge(order, method) {
  if (method === "card") { /* ... */ }
  else if (method === "paypal") { /* ... */ }
  else if (method === "upi") { /* ... */ } // and so on
}

// Extended by registering, not by modifying
const paymentHandlers = new Map([
  ["card", chargeCard],
  ["paypal", chargePaypal],
]);

export function registerPaymentMethod(name, handler) {
  paymentHandlers.set(name, handler);
}

export function charge(order, method) {
  const handler = paymentHandlers.get(method);
  if (!handler) throw new Error(`Unsupported payment method: ${method}`);
  return handler(order);
}

This is the strategy pattern. Apply open/closed where variation is expected; don't build extension points for variation that never comes.

docs.title: L — Liskov substitution principle
docs.text:
Objects of a subtype must be usable wherever the base type is expected, without breaking correctness.

A subclass must honor the base type's contract: accept the same inputs, not throw new kinds of errors for valid calls, and keep its promises.

class FileStorage {
  async read(key) { /* ... */ }
  async write(key, data) { /* ... */ }
}

// Violation: callers that write through FileStorage now fail unexpectedly
class ReadOnlyArchiveStorage extends FileStorage {
  async write() {
    throw new Error("Archive is read-only");
  }
}

The fix is a different abstraction: a ReadableStorage contract with only read, and a WritableStorage with write, so read-only storage never claims it can write.

docs.title: I — Interface segregation principle
docs.text:
Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use.

In JavaScript, apply it by asking for the narrowest dependency a function needs:

// Depends on a huge "userService" just to read an email address
async function sendReceipt(userService, order) {
  const user = await userService.getById(order.userId);
  // ...
}

// Depends only on what it uses: easier to test and reuse
async function sendReceipt({ findEmailByUserId }, order) {
  const email = await findEmailByUserId(order.userId);
  // ...
}

docs.title: D — Dependency inversion principle
docs.text:
High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.

Business logic (high level) should not import database drivers or SDKs (low level) directly. It declares what it needs, and the concrete implementation is supplied from outside—dependency injection.

// High-level code tied to a low-level detail
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";
export async function registerUser(data) {
  const db = (await MongoClient.connect(process.env.MONGODB_URI)).db();
  await db.collection("users").insertOne(data);
}

// Depends on an abstraction supplied by the caller
export function makeRegisterUser({ userRepository, passwordHasher }) {
  return async function registerUser({ email, password }) {
    const passwordHash = await passwordHasher.hash(password);
    return userRepository.create({ email, passwordHash });
  };
}

Dependency inversion is the principle behind ports and adapters.

docs.title: DRY — Don't repeat yourself
docs.text:
Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. — The Pragmatic Programmer

DRY is about knowledge, not identical-looking lines. If the rule "orders over $100 ship free" exists in three places, one will eventually be updated and the others forgotten. Put it in one place.

But two pieces of code that look the same may represent different knowledge that will change for different reasons. Merging them creates a shared function that both callers keep modifying with flags and special cases—the wrong abstraction. As Sandi Metz put it, "duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction."

A practical guideline is the rule of three: tolerate a second copy, and extract an abstraction when a third appears and you understand what really varies.

docs.title: KISS — Keep it simple
docs.text: Choose the simplest design that solves the actual problem. A plain function beats a class hierarchy; a single database beats a database plus a cache plus a queue if the load does not require them. Complexity must justify itself with a concrete benefit.

docs.title: YAGNI — You aren't gonna need it
docs.text: Do not build features, configuration options, or abstraction layers for requirements you merely imagine. Speculative generality costs effort now, adds code to maintain, and is often wrong when the real requirement arrives. YAGNI applies to features; it does not excuse skipping tests or refactoring that keeps code easy to change.

docs.title: Composition over inheritance
docs.text:
Inheritance creates rigid "is-a" hierarchies where a change to a base class affects every subclass. Composition builds behavior from small parts that are combined.

// Inheritance: deep, rigid hierarchy
class Notifier { send() {} }
class EmailNotifier extends Notifier {}
class RetryingEmailNotifier extends EmailNotifier {}
class LoggingRetryingEmailNotifier extends RetryingEmailNotifier {} // explosion

// Composition: wrap behaviors around any notifier
const withRetry = (notifier, attempts = 3) => ({
  async send(message) {
    for (let i = 1; ; i++) {
      try { return await notifier.send(message); }
      catch (error) { if (i === attempts) throw error; }
    }
  },
});

const withLogging = (notifier, logger) => ({
  async send(message) {
    logger.info({ to: message.to }, "sending notification");
    return notifier.send(message);
  },
});

const notifier = withLogging(withRetry(emailNotifier), logger);

docs.title: Law of Demeter (principle of least knowledge)
docs.text:
A function should talk to its immediate collaborators, not reach through them into their internals ("don't talk to strangers").

// Knows the whole object graph; breaks if any link changes or is null
const city = order.customer.profile.address.city;

// Ask the object that owns the knowledge
const city = order.shippingCity();

Long chains (a.b().c().d) are a signal of high coupling. Fluent builders and plain data objects are reasonable exceptions.

docs.title: Principle of least astonishment
docs.text:
Code and APIs should behave the way their names and conventions suggest.

  • A function named getUser should not create a user when none exists.
  • A GET endpoint should not change data.
  • sort() mutating the array surprises people; document or avoid such side effects.
  • Consistent naming and error formats across an API reduce surprises.

docs.title: Fail fast
docs.text:
Detect problems as early as possible and stop with a clear error, instead of continuing in a broken state and failing later in a confusing place.

// Fail fast at startup if configuration is missing
if (!process.env.DATABASE_URL) {
  throw new Error("DATABASE_URL is required");
}

// Fail fast on invalid input at the boundary
export function createMoney(amountCents, currency) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(amountCents)) throw new TypeError("amountCents must be an integer");
  if (!/^[A-Z]{3}$/.test(currency)) throw new TypeError("currency must be an ISO code");
  return Object.freeze({ amountCents, currency });
}

Failing fast is different from crashing on every error: operational errors such as a timeout are still handled gracefully. It means not hiding invalid state.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Lean on these principles when:

  • Code is long-lived, changed by several people, and covered by reviews.
  • A change in one place keeps forcing changes elsewhere.
  • Tests are slow or impossible because logic is tied to infrastructure.

Hold back when:

  • The code is a short script, a spike, or a prototype you will discard.
  • Adding an interface or class would serve a future you cannot name.
  • Two pieces of code only look alike and change for different reasons.
Principle Apply when Stop when Single responsibility One module changes for unrelated reasons Splitting creates files that always change together Open/closed Variants are added regularly Only one or two stable variants exist Dependency inversion Logic touches databases, SDKs, or networks The dependency is a pure, stable utility Interface segregation Callers use a small part of a big object The object is already small DRY The same business rule lives in several places The code is similar but means different things Composition over inheritance Behaviors must combine freely A shallow, stable hierarchy is clearer YAGNI A feature is only imagined The work makes code easier to change (refactoring, tests)

docs.title: Refactoring a function with several principles
docs.text:
Before:

export async function checkout(req, res) {
  const user = await db.collection("users").findOne({ _id: req.user.id });
  let total = 0;
  for (const item of req.body.items) total += item.price * item.qty;
  if (user.tier === "gold") total *= 0.9;
  else if (user.tier === "silver") total *= 0.95;
  await stripe.charges.create({ amount: Math.round(total * 100), currency: "usd" });
  await db.collection("orders").insertOne({ userId: user._id, total });
  res.json({ total });
}

Problems: HTTP, pricing rules, payment, and persistence mixed (separation of concerns, SRP); discount tiers edited inline (open/closed); direct dependencies on the database and Stripe (dependency inversion); floating-point money.

After:

// pricing.js — pure business rules, one reason to change
const tierDiscounts = { gold: 0.1, silver: 0.05 };

export function priceOrder(items, tier) {
  const subtotalCents = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.unitPriceCents * i.qty, 0);
  const discount = tierDiscounts[tier] ?? 0;
  return Math.round(subtotalCents * (1 - discount));
}

// checkout.js — use case with injected dependencies
export function makeCheckout({ users, orders, payments }) {
  return async function checkout({ userId, items }) {
    const user = await users.findById(userId);
    const totalCents = priceOrder(items, user.tier);
    await payments.charge({ amountCents: totalCents, currency: "USD" });
    return orders.create({ userId, totalCents });
  };
}

// route — HTTP only
app.post("/checkout", async (req, res) => {
  const order = await checkout({ userId: req.user.id, items: req.body.items });
  res.status(201).json(order);
});

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Optimize for code that is easy to change, not code that anticipates every change.
  • Aim for high cohesion and low coupling at every level: functions, modules, services.
  • Depend on narrow abstractions at boundaries with infrastructure.
  • Remove duplicated knowledge; tolerate duplicated code until the right abstraction is clear.
  • Prefer composition and small functions over deep inheritance.
  • Name things so their behavior is unsurprising; avoid hidden side effects.
  • Validate early and fail with clear messages.
  • Treat principles as tools for discussing trade-offs, not rules to apply mechanically.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The same rule, three answers. Symptom: checkout, invoice, and email show different totals for one order. Detect: support tickets and reconciliation reports; searching the code finds the discount rule in several places. Cause: duplicated knowledge (a DRY violation). Fix: move the rule into one pricing module that everything calls.
  • The wrong abstraction bites. Symptom: a fix for one feature breaks another that shares a helper. Detect: the shared function has grown boolean flags and if (caller === ...) branches. Cause: code merged because it looked alike, not because it meant the same thing. Fix: inline the helper back into its callers, then extract only what is truly shared.
  • A GET request changes data. Symptom: records are deleted or emails sent when nobody pressed anything. Detect: the changes line up with crawler, link-preview, or prefetch user agents in access logs. Cause: a surprising side effect behind a safe method. Fix: make changes only through POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE.
  • Long property chains crash. Symptom: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined for some customers only. Detect: error tracking groups the crashes on one deep chain. Cause: code reaches through objects (a Law of Demeter violation) and one link is missing. Fix: ask the object that owns the data, and handle the missing case there.
  • Money off by a cent. Symptom: totals differ from the payment provider by small amounts. Detect: daily reconciliation mismatches. Cause: floating-point arithmetic on currency. Fix: integer minor units (cents) and one rounding rule, as in the refactored example above.
  • Bad configuration found at 3 a.m. Symptom: a service starts fine but fails on the first request that needs a missing setting. Detect: errors appear only on one code path, long after deploy. Cause: configuration was read lazily. Fix: validate configuration at startup and refuse to start.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Separation of concerns: Dividing code so each part handles one aspect of the program.
  • Cohesion: How strongly the contents of a module belong together.
  • Coupling: How much one module depends on another.
  • SOLID: Single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion.
  • Dependency injection: Supplying a component's dependencies from outside instead of creating them inside.
  • DRY: Each piece of knowledge has one authoritative representation.
  • Wrong abstraction: A shared abstraction that does not match how its callers actually vary.
  • YAGNI: Don't build for requirements you don't have.
  • Law of Demeter: Talk only to immediate collaborators.
  • Fail fast: Detect and report invalid state immediately.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "DRY means no two lines may look alike." It concerns knowledge; premature merging creates the wrong abstraction.
  • Applying SOLID by adding interfaces and classes everywhere, making simple code hard to follow.
  • Using YAGNI to justify skipping tests or refactoring.
  • "Single responsibility means one function per file" or "do one thing." It means one reason to change.
  • Deep inheritance hierarchies for code reuse.
  • Catching and ignoring errors in the name of robustness, which hides failures instead of failing fast.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain cohesion and coupling with one good and one bad example each.
  2. What does "one reason to change" mean in the single responsibility principle?
  3. Show how the open/closed principle and the strategy pattern relate.
  4. Why is the wrong abstraction more costly than duplication?
  5. How does dependency inversion make code easier to test?
  6. Give an example of a Law of Demeter violation and how to fix it.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Martin Fowler: Yagni
  • Martin Fowler: Beck design rules
  • Martin Fowler: Tell, don't ask
  • Sandi Metz: The wrong abstraction
  • Robert C. Martin: The clean architecture
  • Design patterns for backends

docs.title: Domain-Driven Design
docs.text: Domain-driven design (DDD), introduced by Eric Evans, is an approach to building software for complex business domains. It puts the business domain and its language at the center of the design, divides large systems into bounded contexts with clear boundaries, and offers building blocks—entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events—for modeling business rules in code.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: The hardest part of many backends is not the technology but the business rules: when an order can be cancelled, how a refund interacts with a discount, what "active customer" means in billing versus marketing. When code does not reflect how the business thinks, every change requires translation and creates bugs. DDD gives teams a way to discover the domain with experts, express it directly in code, and draw service or module boundaries that match the business—the boundaries that matter most when choosing between a modular monolith and microservices.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Shopify — boundaries from business concepts. When modularizing its monolith, Shopify reorganized code from software concepts (models, views, controllers) to real-world concepts "like orders, shipping, inventory, and billing," drawing up the list with input from stakeholders across the company (Shopify Engineering).
  • Uber — domains over microservices. Uber's Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture groups services into domains behind gateways and says it "draws heavily" from domain-driven design and clean architecture (Uber Engineering).
  • Microsoft — tactical DDD in a reference application. Microsoft's eShopOnContainers sample implements its Ordering microservice with DDD layers and aggregates whose rules run through a single aggregate root (Microsoft Learn).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
DDD has two halves:

  • Strategic design: understanding the domain, dividing it into parts, and defining boundaries and relationships between them.
  • Tactical design: patterns for modeling one part in code.

Strategic design is the more valuable half; tactical patterns are useful only inside well-chosen boundaries.

docs.title: Domain and subdomains
docs.text:
The domain is the area of business the software serves, such as online retail. It divides into subdomains:

Subdomain type Description Retail example Investment Core What gives the business its competitive advantage Pricing and personalized recommendations Best developers, custom code, careful modeling Supporting Necessary and specific to the business, but not a differentiator Order fulfillment workflow Custom but simpler code Generic Solved problems common to many businesses Authentication, payments, email Buy or use existing services

This classification tells you where to spend design effort: deep DDD modeling for the core, off-the-shelf solutions for generic subdomains.

docs.title: Ubiquitous language
docs.text:
A ubiquitous language is a shared vocabulary that developers and domain experts use in conversations, documents, and the code itself. If warehouse staff say "pick list" and "short-ship," the code has PickList and shortShip(), not TaskBatch and partialProcess().

  • Terms are precise: "order placed" and "order confirmed" are different events if the business treats them differently.
  • When a conversation reveals that a term is ambiguous, the model and code change.
  • The language is valid within one bounded context; another context may use the same word with a different meaning.

docs.title: Bounded contexts
docs.text:
A bounded context is an explicit boundary within which one model and its language apply consistently. Large domains cannot share one model: "Product" means different things to different parts of a business.

 ┌──────── Catalog context ────────┐   ┌──────── Inventory context ───────┐
 │ Product: name, description,     │   │ Product: SKU, quantity on hand,  │
 │ images, categories, price       │   │ warehouse location, reorder level│
 └─────────────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────────────┘
 ┌──────── Sales context ──────────┐   ┌──────── Shipping context ────────┐
 │ Product: SKU, price at time of  │   │ Product: weight, dimensions,     │
 │ order, tax category             │   │ hazardous-goods flag             │
 └─────────────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────────────┘

Each context has its own model, owned by one team, usually with its own data. Bounded contexts are the natural candidates for modules in a modular monolith or for microservices.

docs.title: Context maps
docs.text:
A context map documents how bounded contexts relate. Common relationships:

Relationship Meaning Partnership Two teams coordinate closely and succeed or fail together. Shared kernel Two contexts share a small, jointly owned part of the model (for example, a Money type). Changes need agreement from both. Customer–supplier The upstream (supplier) context provides what the downstream (customer) needs; the downstream's needs influence the upstream's plans. Conformist The downstream simply adopts the upstream's model, with no influence over it. Anticorruption layer (ACL) The downstream translates the upstream's model into its own, protecting its model from foreign concepts. Open host service The upstream offers a well-defined protocol or API for many consumers. Published language A documented shared format for exchanging information, such as an event schema.

The anticorruption layer is especially important when integrating with legacy systems or third-party APIs:

// Shipping context's ACL over a legacy ERP API
export function makeErpProductTranslator(erpClient) {
  return {
    async getShippingProfile(sku) {
      const raw = await erpClient.fetchItem(sku); // { ITEM_WT_LBS, DIM_STR: "10x4x2", HAZ: "Y" }
      const [length, width, height] = raw.DIM_STR.split("x").map(Number);
      return {
        sku,
        weightKg: raw.ITEM_WT_LBS * 0.4536,
        dimensionsCm: { length: length * 2.54, width: width * 2.54, height: height * 2.54 },
        hazardous: raw.HAZ === "Y",
      };
    },
  };
}

The rest of the shipping code works with weightKg and hazardous, never with the ERP's field names.

docs.title: Entities and value objects
docs.text:
Entities have an identity that continues over time even as their attributes change. Two customers with the same name are different customers; an order is the same order after its status changes.

Value objects have no identity; they are defined entirely by their values and are immutable. Two Money objects of 10.00 USD are interchangeable. Examples: money, an address, a date range, an email address.

// Value object: immutable, compared by value, validates itself
export function money(amountCents, currency) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(amountCents)) throw new TypeError("amountCents must be an integer");
  if (!/^[A-Z]{3}$/.test(currency)) throw new TypeError("Invalid currency");
  return Object.freeze({ amountCents, currency });
}

export function addMoney(a, b) {
  if (a.currency !== b.currency) throw new Error("Currency mismatch");
  return money(a.amountCents + b.amountCents, a.currency);
}

export const moneyEquals = (a, b) =>
  a.amountCents === b.amountCents && a.currency === b.currency;

Using value objects instead of raw numbers and strings ("primitive obsession") puts validation and behavior in one place and makes invalid values impossible to construct.

docs.title: Aggregates, aggregate roots, and invariants
docs.text:
An invariant is a business rule that must always be true, such as "an order's total equals the sum of its lines" or "a submitted order cannot be changed."

An aggregate is a cluster of entities and value objects treated as one unit for changes, so its invariants can be enforced together. One entity is the aggregate root: the only object outside code may hold a reference to or call. All changes go through the root.

Rules for designing aggregates:

  • Protect invariants inside the boundary; that is the aggregate's purpose.
  • Keep aggregates small. Large aggregates cause contention and slow loads.
  • Reference other aggregates by ID, not by object (an order stores customerId, not a Customer object).
  • One aggregate per transaction. Changes to other aggregates happen through domain events and are eventually consistent.
  • Load and save whole aggregates through a repository.

docs.title: Domain events
docs.text:
A domain event records something meaningful that happened in the domain, named in the past tense with the ubiquitous language: OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed, ItemShipped. Other parts of the system react to them— sending emails, reserving stock, updating read models—without the aggregate knowing who listens.

Domain events also connect aggregates and bounded contexts while respecting the "one aggregate per transaction" rule. Publishing them reliably across services uses the transactional outbox pattern; see also event-driven architecture.

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text: In DDD, a repository provides access to aggregates as if they were an in-memory collection: orderRepository.findById(id), orderRepository.save(order). There is one repository per aggregate root, not per table or entity; you never fetch an OrderLine on its own.

docs.title: Domain services and application services
docs.text:
• Domain services hold domain logic that does not naturally belong to one entity or value object, often because it involves several aggregates or a domain policy—for example, a PricingService that applies promotions across a cart. They speak the ubiquitous language and contain no infrastructure code.
  • Application services coordinate a use case: load aggregates through repositories, call domain methods, save, and publish events. They handle transactions and security but contain no business rules.
 HTTP controller → Application service (use case: PlaceOrder)
                     ├─ loads Customer, Cart via repositories
                     ├─ calls PricingService (domain service)
                     ├─ calls Order.place(...) (aggregate enforces invariants)
                     ├─ saves Order via repository
                     └─ publishes OrderPlaced (domain event)

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use DDD when:

  • The business rules are the hard part, and experts are available to explain them.
  • Several teams or modules use the same words with different meanings.
  • You are drawing module or service boundaries and want them to follow the business.

Use less of it when:

  • An area is simple CRUD with few rules; a plain data model is clearer.
  • The subdomain is generic (authentication, email, payments); buy or reuse instead of modeling.
  • Nobody with domain knowledge is available; you cannot build a ubiquitous language alone.
Situation Simple CRUD model Strategic DDD only Strategic + tactical DDD Admin screens over reference data Good fit Not needed Overkill Many teams, one tangled "Customer" model Breaks down Good fit Add where rules are rich Core subdomain with complex rules Rules scatter Helps boundaries Best fit Integrating a legacy system Leaks its model ACL and context map Same, plus rich model inside Generic subdomain Use a product Mark it generic Not worth it

docs.title: A worked order aggregate
docs.text:
// domain/order.js
import { money, addMoney } from "./money.js";

export class Order {
  #lines = [];
  #status = "DRAFT";
  #events = [];

  constructor({ id, customerId, currency }) {
    this.id = id;
    this.customerId = customerId; // reference another aggregate by ID
    this.currency = currency;
  }

  addLine(productId, quantity, unitPrice) {
    if (this.#status !== "DRAFT") throw new Error("Only draft orders can change");
    const existing = this.#lines.find((l) => l.productId === productId);
    const newQuantity = (existing?.quantity ?? 0) + quantity; // check the merged line
    if (!Number.isInteger(quantity) || quantity < 1 || newQuantity > 100) {
      throw new Error("Quantity must be between 1 and 100");
    }
    if (unitPrice.currency !== this.currency) throw new Error("Currency mismatch");

    if (existing) existing.quantity = newQuantity;
    else this.#lines.push({ productId, quantity, unitPrice });
  }

  get total() {
    return this.#lines.reduce(
      (sum, l) => addMoney(sum, money(l.unitPrice.amountCents * l.quantity, this.currency)),
      money(0, this.currency),
    );
  }

  place(now) {
    if (this.#status !== "DRAFT") throw new Error("Order already placed");
    if (this.#lines.length === 0) throw new Error("Cannot place an empty order");
    this.#status = "PLACED";
    this.#events.push({
      type: "OrderPlaced",
      orderId: this.id,
      customerId: this.customerId,
      total: this.total,
      occurredAt: now.toISOString(),
    });
  }

  get status() { return this.#status; }
  get lines() { return this.#lines.map((l) => ({ ...l })); } // copies: no outside mutation

  pullEvents() {
    const events = this.#events;
    this.#events = [];
    return events;
  }
}

docs.title: The application service
docs.text:
// application/place-order.js
export function makePlaceOrder({ orderRepository, eventPublisher, clock }) {
  return async function placeOrder(orderId) {
    const order = await orderRepository.findById(orderId);
    if (!order) throw new NotFoundError("Order");

    order.place(clock.now());               // business rules live in the aggregate
    await orderRepository.save(order);      // one aggregate per transaction
    await eventPublisher.publishAll(order.pullEvents());
    return { id: order.id, status: order.status, total: order.total };
  };
}

The aggregate guarantees that no code path can place an empty order, change a placed order, or mix currencies. Other contexts—inventory, email, analytics—react to OrderPlaced.

docs.title: Strategic versus tactical DDD
docs.text:
Strategic DDD Tactical DDD Subdomains (core, supporting, generic) Entities and value objects Ubiquitous language Aggregates and invariants Bounded contexts Domain events Context maps and integration patterns Repositories Team and service boundaries Domain and application services

Teams can benefit from strategic DDD even when they write simple code inside each context. Applying tactical patterns without strategic boundaries usually produces elaborate code in the wrong places.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Work with domain experts; listen for terms, rules, and edge cases, and reflect them in the code.
  • Invest modeling effort in the core subdomain; buy or reuse generic ones.
  • Make bounded contexts explicit and give each an owner.
  • Use anticorruption layers when integrating with legacy or external models.
  • Prefer value objects over primitives for domain concepts.
  • Keep aggregates small, reference others by ID, and change one per transaction.
  • Keep business rules in entities, value objects, and domain services—not in controllers or application services.
  • Don't apply DDD to simple CRUD areas where there are few rules.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Write conflicts on a hot aggregate. Symptom: saves fail with version conflicts or time out under load. Detect: the conflict or lock-wait rate is concentrated on one aggregate type. Cause: the aggregate is too large (for example, a Store holding every order). Fix: split it into smaller aggregates that reference each other by ID.
  • An invariant that only some paths enforce. Symptom: data that breaks a rule, such as a line with 120 items when the limit is 100. Detect: data-quality queries or reports find impossible values. Cause: one code path (a merge, an admin script, a direct database update) skips the root's checks. Fix: route every change through the aggregate root and add database constraints as a backstop.
  • Events lost between save and publish. Symptom: inventory or email never reacts to some placed orders. Detect: orders exist with no matching downstream record. Cause: the process crashed after saving the aggregate but before publishing its events. Fix: write events in the same transaction with a transactional outbox.
  • One context's change breaks another. Symptom: a field rename in Catalog breaks Shipping. Detect: incidents that cross team boundaries after unrelated releases. Cause: contexts share a model instead of translating. Fix: an anticorruption layer or a versioned published language between them.
  • The language drifts. Symptom: features built from a ticket do the wrong thing because "active customer" meant something else. Detect: recurring misunderstandings in reviews and support. Cause: code names no longer match how the business talks. Fix: keep a glossary per context and rename code when the language changes.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Domain: The business area the software serves.
  • Subdomain: A part of the domain: core, supporting, or generic.
  • Ubiquitous language: Shared vocabulary used by experts and in code within a context.
  • Bounded context: A boundary in which one model applies consistently.
  • Context map: A description of relationships between bounded contexts.
  • Anticorruption layer: A translation layer protecting a model from another model.
  • Entity: An object with identity that persists over time.
  • Value object: An immutable object defined by its values.
  • Aggregate / aggregate root: A consistency boundary and its single entry point.
  • Invariant: A rule that must always hold.
  • Domain event: A record of something meaningful that happened in the domain.
  • Domain service / application service: Domain logic across objects / coordination of a use case.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "DDD means using entities, repositories, and aggregates." The strategic part—language and boundaries—matters most.
  • One giant model for the whole company, where "Customer" has hundreds of fields used differently everywhere.
  • Anemic domain models: entities that are just data bags, with all rules in services.
  • Huge aggregates that load half the database and conflict on every write.
  • Holding object references across aggregates and changing several in one transaction.
  • Using DDD for simple CRUD, adding ceremony without benefit.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What are core, supporting, and generic subdomains, and how should investment differ between them?
  2. What is a bounded context, and why can "Product" mean different things in different contexts?
  3. When would you use an anticorruption layer?
  4. Explain the difference between entities and value objects with examples.
  5. What is an aggregate, and why should one transaction change only one?
  6. What belongs in an application service versus a domain service?

docs.title: Event-Driven Architecture
docs.text: In an event-driven architecture, components communicate by producing and reacting to events—records that something happened, such as OrderPlaced or PaymentFailed. Producers publish events without knowing who will react; consumers subscribe to the events they care about. Related patterns—event sourcing and CQRS—use events as the system's source of truth and separate how data is written from how it is read.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Event-driven designs decouple parts of a system: adding a new reaction (send an SMS when an order ships) means adding a consumer, not changing the producer. They absorb load spikes through queues, let slow work happen asynchronously, and integrate many systems cleanly. They also introduce eventual consistency, harder debugging, and schema evolution problems. Knowing both sides lets you use events where they help and avoid them where a simple function call is better.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The New York Times — a log as the source of truth. The Times appends all published content to a Kafka topic in chronological order and makes that log the source of truth; consumers such as search and personalization read it and reprocess content when their schemas or algorithms change (NYT Open).
  • Segment — queues between ingestion and delivery. Segment's data infrastructure ingests hundreds of thousands of events per second; its API forwarded events to a distributed message queue from which they were delivered to more than a hundred types of destinations (Segment blog).
  • Zalando — an in-house event bus. Zalando built Nakadi, a distributed event bus broker with a RESTful API on top of Kafka-like queues; the project is now archived because its use was internal to Zalando (Nakadi on GitHub).

Popular tools and providers: Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, Amazon SNS/SQS and EventBridge, Azure Service Bus and Event Grid; Debezium for change data capture; the CloudEvents specification for event envelopes.

docs.title: Events, commands, and queries
docs.text:
Message Meaning Naming Receivers Can be rejected? Command A request to do something Imperative: PlaceOrder, ChargeCard Exactly one handler Yes Event A fact that something happened Past tense: OrderPlaced, CardCharged Zero or more subscribers No—it already happened Query A request for information GetOrderStatus One handler Returns data, changes nothing

A command expresses intent and expects someone to act on it. An event announces a fact; the producer does not care who listens or whether anyone does.

docs.title: Event notification versus event-carried state transfer
docs.text:
Events can carry very different amounts of data:

  • Event notification: the event says that something changed and includes minimal data, often just IDs.
{ "type": "CustomerAddressChanged", "customerId": "c-42" }

Consumers that need details call the producer's API. Events stay small and the producer remains the source of truth, but consumers depend on the producer being available, and a burst of events can produce a burst of API calls.

  • Event-carried state transfer: the event includes the data consumers need.
{
  "type": "CustomerAddressChanged",
  "customerId": "c-42",
  "address": { "line1": "12 High St", "city": "Pune", "postalCode": "411001" }
}

Consumers keep a local copy and never need to call back, which improves resilience and latency. The cost is larger events, duplicated data, and consumers that may briefly hold stale copies.

docs.title: Publish/subscribe through a broker
docs.text:
Events usually travel through a message broker such as RabbitMQ, Apache Kafka, or a cloud service (Amazon SNS/SQS, EventBridge). The broker stores events durably and delivers them to each subscriber, so producers and consumers do not need to be online at the same time.

                         ┌──► [ Email service ]      sends confirmation
 [ Orders service ] ─────┤
   publishes             ├──► [ Inventory service ]  reserves stock
   OrderPlaced  ──► (broker / topic)
                         ├──► [ Analytics ]          updates dashboards
                         └──► [ Loyalty service ]    adds points (added later,
                                                     no change to Orders)

Delivery is usually at least once, so consumers must be idempotent and tolerate duplicates and out-of-order events. Broker details, delivery guarantees, and consumer patterns are covered in messaging fundamentals, delivery guarantees, and messaging patterns.

docs.title: Choreography versus orchestration
docs.text:
A business process that spans several services can be coordinated in two ways.

Choreography: each service reacts to events and publishes its own; no one is in charge.

Orchestration: a central orchestrator tells each service what to do (with commands) and tracks the state of the process.

Choreography Orchestration Coupling Very loose; services only know events Orchestrator knows every step Visibility of the flow Spread across services; hard to see the whole process In one place; easy to read and monitor Adding a step Add a subscriber Change the orchestrator Risk Cyclic dependencies, "who handles failure?" Orchestrator becomes a bottleneck or god service Good for Simple flows, independent reactions Complex multi-step processes with compensations

Both are used to implement sagas; see microservices patterns.

docs.title: Eventual consistency
docs.text:
When a service reacts to an event asynchronously, its data catches up a little later than the producer's. For a short time, different parts of the system disagree—the order exists but the loyalty points have not appeared yet. This is eventual consistency: if no new updates occur, all copies eventually converge.

Designing for it means:

  • Showing users accurate states such as "payment processing" instead of pretending everything happened instantly.
  • Making operations idempotent so retries and duplicates are safe.
  • Handling events that arrive out of order (for example, using version numbers or timestamps per entity).
  • Accepting that cross-service queries may see slightly stale data.

See consistency and the CAP theorem.

docs.title: Event schemas and versioning
docs.text:
Events are a contract between teams that may deploy at different times. A common shape is an envelope with metadata plus a payload:

{
  "id": "6f1c2a9e-4b1d-4d3e-9a51-2f8f0c1e7b20",
  "type": "order.placed",
  "version": 2,
  "source": "orders-service",
  "occurredAt": "2026-11-07T10:15:30Z",
  "data": {
    "orderId": "o-981",
    "customerId": "c-42",
    "totalCents": 4599,
    "currency": "INR"
  }
}
  • The id lets consumers deduplicate.
  • The type and version let consumers interpret the payload.
  • The CloudEvents specification standardizes envelope fields like these.

Evolving schemas safely:

  • Backward-compatible changes are fine: adding an optional field.
  • Breaking changes—renaming or removing fields, changing types or meaning—need a new version (order.placed v3), and producers often publish both versions until all consumers migrate.
  • Consumers should ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader).
  • Teams often use a schema registry (with JSON Schema, Avro, or Protobuf) to validate events and check compatibility automatically.

docs.title: Event sourcing
docs.text:
In most systems the database stores current state: the account balance is 70. With event sourcing, the system stores the sequence of events that led to the state, and the current state is derived by replaying them.

 Event store (append-only, per account)
   1. AccountOpened      { accountId: "a-1" }
   2. MoneyDeposited     { amount: 100 }
   3. MoneyWithdrawn     { amount: 50 }
   4. MoneyDeposited     { amount: 20 }
 Current state = replay(1..4) → balance 70

Key ideas:

  • Append-only: events are never updated or deleted; corrections are new events (DepositReversed).
  • Replay: rebuild state at any point in time, or rebuild a read model after fixing a bug.
  • Snapshots: for long streams, periodically store the computed state (for example, every 100 events) and replay only the events after it.
  • Projections: consumers turn events into query-friendly read models (an account_balances table, a search index).
  • Optimistic concurrency: appending checks the expected stream version, so two concurrent writers cannot both succeed.

Benefits: a complete audit trail, the ability to answer "what was the state on March 3?", and easy creation of new read models. Costs: a different programming model, event schema evolution forever, more complex queries, and handling personal data deletion in an immutable log.

docs.title: CQRS
docs.text:
Command Query Responsibility Segregation separates the model used to change data (commands) from the model used to read it (queries).

  • The write side enforces business rules on a normalized model or aggregates.
  • The read side serves precomputed, denormalized views—fast and simple to query.
  • Read models are updated from events, so they are eventually consistent.

CQRS is often combined with event sourcing but does not require it; a simple form is reading from a replica or a separate reporting table. Use it when read and write needs differ greatly (complex domain rules but simple, high-volume reads), not by default.

docs.title: Change data capture
docs.text: Events can also be produced from database changes. Change data capture (CDC) reads the database's change log and publishes changes as events. MongoDB exposes this through change streams; tools such as Debezium do it for relational databases. CDC is a practical way to emit events from a system that was not built for them.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use events when:

  • Several independent reactions follow one occurrence, and more will be added later.
  • Work can finish after the user gets a response (emails, analytics, search indexing).
  • You need to absorb spikes with a queue, or integrate systems owned by different teams.
  • Event sourcing: you need a full audit trail, "what was true on date X?", or new read models built from history.

Do not use them for:

  • Simple request/response needs: if the caller needs the answer now ("is this coupon valid?"), make a direct call.
  • Strong consistency requirements across steps that must happen atomically.
  • Small systems and teams where the added infrastructure, tracing, and debugging cost outweigh decoupling benefits.
  • Event sourcing for CRUD-style data with no audit or temporal needs. Martin Fowler warns that for most systems CQRS "adds risky complexity."
Need Direct call Events through a broker Event sourcing + CQRS Answer needed immediately Best fit Poor fit Poor fit Many independent reactions Caller knows everyone Best fit Possible Survive a slow or down consumer Caller fails too Queue absorbs it Queue absorbs it Audit trail and history Extra work Partial (if events are kept) Built in Reads very different from writes One model One model plus copies Best fit Team new to messaging Simplest Moderate cost Highest cost

docs.title: Publishing and consuming an event (idempotent consumer)
docs.text:
// orders service — publish after the order is saved
await orderRepository.save(order);
await broker.publish("order.placed", {
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  type: "order.placed",
  version: 1,
  occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  data: { orderId: order.id, customerId: order.customerId, totalCents: order.totalCents },
});

Publishing right after saving can lose the event if the process crashes in between; production systems use the transactional outbox.

// loyalty service — consume, skipping duplicates
broker.subscribe("order.placed", async (event) => {
  const firstTime = await processedEvents.insertIfAbsent(event.id); // unique index on id
  if (!firstTime) return; // duplicate delivery: already handled

  const points = Math.floor(event.data.totalCents / 100);
  await loyaltyAccounts.addPoints(event.data.customerId, points);
});

docs.title: A tiny event-sourced aggregate
docs.text:
function applyEvent(state, event) {
  switch (event.type) {
    case "AccountOpened":  return { id: event.accountId, balance: 0, version: 1 };
    case "MoneyDeposited": return { ...state, balance: state.balance + event.amount, version: state.version + 1 };
    case "MoneyWithdrawn": return { ...state, balance: state.balance - event.amount, version: state.version + 1 };
    default: return state;
  }
}

export async function withdraw(eventStore, accountId, amount) {
  const events = await eventStore.readStream(accountId);
  const account = events.reduce(applyEvent, null); // rebuild current state
  if (!account) throw new Error("Account not found"); // empty stream

  if (account.balance < amount) throw new Error("Insufficient funds"); // invariant

  // Append only if nobody else wrote since we read (optimistic concurrency)
  await eventStore.append(accountId, [{ type: "MoneyWithdrawn", amount }], {
    expectedVersion: account.version,
  });
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Name events in the past tense using the business language; keep commands and events distinct.
  • Choose deliberately between notification and state-transfer events.
  • Include an event ID, type, version, and timestamp in every event.
  • Make every consumer idempotent and tolerant of reordering.
  • Evolve schemas compatibly; version breaking changes and support both during migration.
  • Use orchestration for complex, multi-step processes with compensation; choreography for simple, independent reactions.
  • Invest in observability: correlation IDs carried through events and distributed tracing.
  • Adopt event sourcing and CQRS only where their benefits are needed.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Consumer lag. Symptom: read models, search results, or dashboards fall minutes or hours behind. Detect: consumer lag (unprocessed messages or offset distance) grows steadily. Cause: consumers too slow or too few for the event rate. Fix: scale consumers or partitions, batch work, and alert on lag before users notice.
  • A poison message blocks the queue. Symptom: processing stalls, and one message is retried over and over. Detect: the same message ID appears repeatedly in error logs. Cause: a message that can never be processed, such as malformed data. Fix: cap retries and move failures to a dead-letter queue for inspection.
  • Duplicate side effects. Symptom: customers get two emails or double points. Detect: duplicate records with the same event ID. Cause: at-least-once delivery with a non-idempotent consumer. Fix: record processed event IDs, as the loyalty consumer above does.
  • Old events overwrite new data. Symptom: a customer's address flips back to an old value. Detect: the stored version is older than one already seen. Cause: events for one entity arrived out of order. Fix: carry a version or sequence number per entity and ignore older events.
  • A schema change breaks consumers. Symptom: consumers crash after a producer deploys. Detect: deserialization or validation errors spike right after the release. Cause: a renamed or removed field without a new version. Fix: additive changes only, versioned events for breaking changes, and a schema registry check in CI.
  • Rebuilding a projection takes too long. Symptom: replaying events to fix a read model takes hours. Detect: replay throughput is far below the stream size. Cause: long streams with no snapshots. Fix: snapshots, and rebuild into a new table before switching reads to it.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Event: An immutable record that something happened.
  • Command: A request for a specific action, handled by one receiver.
  • Event notification: A minimal event that tells consumers to fetch details.
  • Event-carried state transfer: An event that carries the data consumers need.
  • Choreography: Decentralized coordination through events.
  • Orchestration: Central coordination by an orchestrator.
  • Eventual consistency: Copies of data converge over time rather than instantly.
  • Event sourcing: Storing state as an append-only sequence of events.
  • Projection (read model): A view of data built from events.
  • Snapshot: Stored computed state used to speed up replay.
  • CQRS: Separating the write model from the read model.
  • Change data capture: Producing events from database change logs.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating events as commands in disguise (SendEmailRequested aimed at one service), recreating tight coupling.
  • Assuming exactly-once delivery and writing non-idempotent consumers.
  • Publishing an event outside the database transaction and losing it on a crash, or publishing it for a change that was rolled back.
  • Breaking event schemas without versioning.
  • "Event-driven means real time." It means asynchronous; latency depends on the broker and consumers.
  • Adopting event sourcing everywhere, including simple CRUD data.
