docs.title: Software Architecture Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review architecture fundamentals, monoliths and microservices, code organization styles, design principles and patterns, domain-driven design, event-driven systems, microservices patterns, and serverless. Try to answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is software architecture?
docs.text: Software architecture is the set of significant, hard-to-change decisions about a system: its main components and responsibilities, how they communicate, who owns which data, how it is deployed, and the constraints it follows. It is driven mostly by quality attributes rather than features.

docs.title: 2. What are quality attributes, and why do they drive architecture?
docs.text: Quality attributes (non-functional requirements) describe how well a system works: performance, scalability, availability, reliability, security, maintainability, testability, observability, and cost. Many structures can deliver the same features, so these attributes decide which structure fits. They should be stated as measurable scenarios.

docs.title: 3. Give an example of an architectural trade-off.
docs.text: Adding a cache improves read latency and reduces database load, but introduces stale data, invalidation logic, and another system to operate. Splitting into microservices enables independent deploys but adds network failures and distributed data problems.

docs.title: 4. What is Conway's law?
docs.text: Conway's law states that systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them. Teams use it deliberately with the inverse Conway maneuver: organizing teams around the boundaries they want the architecture to have.

docs.title: 5. What is an architecture decision record?
docs.text: An ADR is a short document stored with the code that records one significant decision: its status, context, the decision, alternatives, and consequences. ADRs preserve the reasoning behind decisions and are superseded, not deleted, when decisions change.

docs.title: 6. What is the C4 model?
docs.text: C4 is a way of drawing architecture at four zoom levels: system context (the system and its users and external systems), containers (deployable units such as apps and databases), components (inside one container), and code. Each level targets a different audience.

docs.title: 7. What are the advantages of a monolith?
docs.text: A monolith is simple to develop, test, debug, deploy, and operate; calls between features are fast and cannot fail over the network; and database transactions can span features. It can scale horizontally by running several stateless instances.

docs.title: 8. What is a modular monolith?
docs.text: A single deployable application divided into modules with enforced boundaries: each module exposes a small public API, owns its own tables, and never reaches into another module's internals. It provides clear boundaries without the operational cost of microservices and eases later extraction.

docs.title: 9. What are microservices?
docs.text: Small services organized around business capabilities that are deployed independently, own their data, communicate over the network, and are owned by a single team. They enable independent releases and scaling for large organizations.

docs.title: 10. What are the main costs of microservices?
docs.text: Network calls that can fail or be slow, no cross-service transactions and eventual consistency, many pipelines and deployments to operate, the need for distributed tracing and centralized logging, harder integration testing, added latency, and API versioning across teams.

docs.title: 11. What is a distributed monolith?
docs.text: A set of services that are deployed separately but remain tightly coupled: they must be released together, share a database, or depend on long chains of synchronous calls. It has the costs of microservices without their benefits.

docs.title: 12. How do you decide between a monolith and microservices?
docs.text: Consider team size and the need for independent releases, how well the domain boundaries are understood, differing scaling needs, operational maturity, and consistency requirements. A common recommendation is to start with a modular monolith and extract services when a concrete need appears.

docs.title: 13. What is the strangler fig pattern?
docs.text: An incremental migration approach: place a routing layer in front of a legacy system, build one capability at a time as a new component, route its traffic to the new component, and retire the old system when nothing routes to it. It avoids risky big-bang rewrites.

docs.title: 14. What is layered architecture, and what is its main weakness?
docs.text: Code is organized into layers—presentation, business, data access—with dependencies pointing down. Its weakness is that business logic depends on the data access layer, tying business rules to the database technology and making them harder to test in isolation.

docs.title: 15. Explain ports and adapters.
docs.text: In hexagonal architecture, the application core defines ports: interfaces for the use cases it offers (inbound) and the services it needs (outbound). Adapters implement them for specific technologies—HTTP controllers drive the core, while database repositories and API clients are driven by it.

docs.title: 16. What is the dependency rule in clean architecture?
docs.text: Source code dependencies must point inward, toward entities and use cases. Inner circles never reference frameworks, databases, or UI. When the core needs infrastructure, it defines an interface that an outer layer implements.

docs.title: 17. What is a composition root?
docs.text: The single place, usually at application startup, where concrete implementations are created and wired into the components that depend on them. It keeps knowledge of infrastructure choices out of the business code.

docs.title: 18. When is hexagonal or clean architecture over-engineering?
docs.text: For thin CRUD applications with few business rules, a single entry point, and stable infrastructure. The extra interfaces, adapters, and mappers add indirection without much benefit; simple layering is usually enough.

docs.title: 19. What are cohesion and coupling?
docs.text: Cohesion is how closely the contents of a module belong together; coupling is how much a module depends on others. Good designs have high cohesion and low coupling, connecting modules through small, stable interfaces.

docs.title: 20. Explain the single responsibility principle.
docs.text: A module should have one reason to change—one source of change such as a particular business rule or stakeholder. Mixing tax calculation, PDF rendering, and email delivery in one class gives it several reasons to change.

docs.title: 21. Explain the open/closed principle with an example.
docs.text: Code should be open for extension but closed for modification. Instead of editing a growing if/else for each payment method, register payment handlers in a map (strategy pattern) so new methods are added without changing existing code.

docs.title: 22. What is the Liskov substitution principle?
docs.text: A subtype must be usable anywhere its base type is expected without breaking correctness. A read-only storage class that inherits a write method and throws when it is called violates it; the abstraction should be split instead.

docs.title: 23. What is dependency inversion, and how does it help testing?
docs.text: High-level business logic should depend on abstractions, not on low-level details such as database drivers. Dependencies are injected from outside, so tests can supply in-memory fakes and run without real infrastructure.

docs.title: 24. What is the difference between DRY and avoiding the wrong abstraction?
docs.text: DRY means each piece of knowledge has one authoritative representation. Code that merely looks similar may represent different knowledge; merging it creates a wrong abstraction that grows flags and special cases. Duplicate code is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

docs.title: 25. What do YAGNI and KISS mean?
docs.text: YAGNI ("you aren't gonna need it") means not building features or abstractions for imagined future requirements. KISS ("keep it simple") means choosing the simplest design that solves the actual problem.

docs.title: 26. What is the repository pattern?
docs.text: A repository provides a collection-like interface for one type of domain object—findById, save—and hides how and where objects are stored. Business code stays free of query syntax and can be tested with in-memory repositories.

docs.title: 27. What is dependency injection?
docs.text: Supplying a component's dependencies from outside instead of having it create them. In Node.js, factory functions that receive dependencies as parameters, wired in a composition root, are a simple and common form.

docs.title: 28. Compare the adapter, facade, and decorator patterns.
docs.text: An adapter converts one interface into another your code expects. A facade provides a simple interface over a complex subsystem. A decorator wraps an object with the same interface to add behavior such as caching or logging.

docs.title: 29. Why is a Node.js module-level singleton risky?
docs.text: It is hidden global state that tests can interfere with, it is hard to replace with a fake, it is only single per process and resolved file path, and creating it may cause side effects at import time. Creating the instance once and injecting it is safer.

docs.title: 30. What is a bounded context?
docs.text: An explicit boundary within which one domain model and its language apply consistently. The same word, such as "product," can have different meanings and data in different contexts, such as catalog and shipping.

docs.title: 31. What is the ubiquitous language?
docs.text: A shared vocabulary used by developers and domain experts in conversation, documentation, and code within a bounded context. It reduces translation errors between business requirements and implementation.

docs.title: 32. What is the difference between an entity and a value object?
docs.text: An entity has an identity that persists as its attributes change, such as an order or customer. A value object has no identity, is immutable, and is defined by its values, such as money or an address.

docs.title: 33. What is an aggregate?
docs.text: A cluster of entities and value objects treated as one unit for changes, with a single aggregate root that outside code interacts with. The aggregate enforces its invariants; aggregates should be small, reference each other by ID, and change one per transaction.

docs.title: 34. What is an anticorruption layer?
docs.text: A translation layer that converts another system's model into your bounded context's model, so foreign concepts and naming do not leak into your domain. It is common when integrating with legacy systems or third-party APIs.

docs.title: 35. What are core, supporting, and generic subdomains?
docs.text: The core subdomain gives the business its competitive advantage and deserves the most design effort. Supporting subdomains are necessary but not differentiating. Generic subdomains are common problems, such as authentication, best bought or reused.

docs.title: 36. What is the difference between an event and a command?
docs.text: A command is a request for a specific action, handled by one receiver, and can be rejected. An event is a fact that something already happened, named in the past tense, and can have zero or many subscribers.

docs.title: 37. What is the difference between choreography and orchestration?
docs.text: In choreography, services react to each other's events with no central coordinator. In orchestration, a central orchestrator sends commands to services and tracks the process state. Orchestration is easier to monitor for complex flows; choreography is looser for simple reactions.

docs.title: 38. What is eventual consistency?
docs.text: A model in which different copies of data may temporarily disagree after an update but converge if no new updates occur. Systems using asynchronous events must design for it with clear intermediate states, idempotency, and handling of out-of-order events.

docs.title: 39. What is event sourcing?
docs.text: Storing an entity's state as an append-only sequence of events and deriving current state by replaying them. It provides a full audit trail and the ability to rebuild views, at the cost of a more complex programming model and long-term event schema management. Snapshots speed up replay.

docs.title: 40. What is CQRS?
docs.text: Command Query Responsibility Segregation uses separate models for writing data (enforcing business rules) and reading data (denormalized views optimized for queries). Read models are often updated from events and are eventually consistent.

docs.title: 41. How do you evolve event schemas safely?
docs.text: Include a type and version in each event, make only backward-compatible changes such as adding optional fields, have consumers ignore unknown fields, introduce a new version for breaking changes, publish both versions during migration, and validate compatibility with a schema registry.

docs.title: 42. What does an API gateway do?
docs.text: It is the single entry point for clients: routing requests to services, authenticating, rate limiting, terminating TLS, aggregating responses, and handling cross-cutting concerns. It should not contain business logic.

docs.title: 43. What is the backend-for-frontend pattern?
docs.text: Each client type, such as mobile and web, gets its own backend layer that aggregates and shapes data for that client's needs. It does not inherently improve security; authorization and validation still belong in the relevant layers. Business rules should not be duplicated across BFFs.

docs.title: 44. What is a saga?
docs.text: A way to implement a business transaction across services as a sequence of local transactions, with compensating transactions that semantically undo completed steps if a later step fails. Sagas are coordinated by choreography or orchestration and must be idempotent.

docs.title: 45. What is the transactional outbox pattern?
docs.text: A service writes its state change and the outgoing event to an outbox table in the same local transaction. A relay process later publishes outbox rows to the broker. This prevents lost or phantom events, with at-least-once delivery handled by idempotent consumers.

docs.title: 46. What is a circuit breaker?
docs.text: A wrapper around calls to a dependency that opens after too many failures, failing fast for a cool-down period, then allows trial calls in a half-open state before closing again. It prevents cascading failures and wasted resources.

docs.title: 47. What is a service mesh?
docs.text: A layer of proxy sidecars deployed next to every service and managed by a control plane. It provides mutual TLS, retries, timeouts, traffic management, and telemetry for service-to-service traffic without changing application code, at the cost of operational complexity.

docs.title: 48. Why is distributed tracing important in microservices?
docs.text: A request crosses many services, so per-service logs cannot show the full picture. Tracing propagates a trace ID across calls and messages and records timed spans, letting you see the whole request path and find slow or failing steps.

docs.title: 49. What is a cold start, and how do you reduce it?
docs.text: The added latency when a serverless platform must create a new execution environment and initialize your code. Reduce it with small packages, lazy or once-per-environment initialization, more memory, provisioned concurrency for latency-critical paths, or by accepting it for asynchronous work.

docs.title: 50. When is serverless a poor choice?
docs.text: For long-running or CPU-heavy jobs beyond time limits, latency-critical APIs that cannot tolerate cold starts, steady high-volume traffic where always-on compute is cheaper, workloads needing persistent in-process connections or special hardware, and teams that must avoid provider lock-in.

docs.title: Scenario-based questions
docs.text: These describe a symptom in a running system. A good answer moves from what to look at first, to how to prove the cause, to the fix.

docs.title: 51. After splitting into microservices, every deploy needs five teams to coordinate — what went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: Whether the services share a database, call each other in long synchronous chains, or share a library or contract whose change forces everyone to release together.

How to confirm: Recent features each touched several repositories, and the call graph shows long sync chains or tables used by several services.

Likely causes and fixes: The boundaries follow technical layers or entities, not business capabilities, giving a distributed monolith. Redraw them around bounded contexts, give each service its own data, make API changes backward compatible (expand, then contract), and use events instead of sync chains. Merge services that always change together. See Monoliths, modular monoliths, and microservices and Domain-driven design.

docs.title: 52. Customers get the same order-confirmation email two or three times — where do you look?
docs.text:
What to check first: Most queues deliver at least once, so check whether the email consumer is idempotent and whether it marks a message done before or after the send succeeds.

How to confirm: The same message ID is processed more than once in the logs, often after a crash or a run longer than the visibility timeout.

Likely causes and fixes: At-least-once delivery with no deduplication, or a handler slower than the visibility timeout, so the message reappears while still in progress. Record processed message IDs under a unique key and skip repeats, pass an idempotency key to the email provider if it supports one, and set the timeout above the worst-case run time. See Event-driven architecture and the SQS handler in Serverless architecture.

docs.title: 53. Orders are saved, but the warehouse service sometimes never hears about them — why?
docs.text:
What to check first: How the event is published. Committing to the database and then publishing to the broker as a separate step is a dual write: a crash, deploy or broker error in between loses the event.

How to confirm: Compare order rows with published OrderPlaced events for a time window, and match the missing IDs with broker errors or restarts.

Likely causes and fixes: The dual write. Use a transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the order, and let a relay publish it. Change data capture (for example Debezium) on the database's log is the alternative. Either can publish twice, so consumers must handle duplicates. See Microservices patterns.

docs.title: 54. The outbox table keeps growing and events reach consumers minutes late — what do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: The age of the oldest unpublished row, and whether the relay is running at all or stuck retrying one bad row.

How to confirm: Query the count and oldest created_at of unpublished rows, read the relay logs for one row failing repeatedly, and check the query plan of the relay's "fetch next batch" query.

Likely causes and fixes: The relay is down, a poison row blocks every batch, the "unpublished" column has no index, or several relay copies fight over the same rows. Alert on outbox lag, index the column, claim batches with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, move rows that keep failing aside, and delete published rows on a schedule. See Microservices patterns.

docs.title: 55. A booking saga leaves some bookings stuck in "pending" forever — how do you debug it?
docs.text:
What to check first: The saga's stored state: the last step that completed, and whether it waits on a reply that never came or on a failed compensation.

How to confirm: Follow the booking's correlation ID through each participant's logs and traces, and count sagas not updated for longer than the slowest step should take.

Likely causes and fixes: A lost reply (the participant has no outbox), a waiting step with no timeout, a compensation that failed and was never retried, or a non-idempotent step that rejected its own retry. Give each step a deadline and a retry, make steps and compensations idempotent, run a sweeper that times out or resumes stale sagas, and alert on the stuck count. See Microservices patterns.

docs.title: 56. One slow downstream service makes the whole site time out, and retries make it worse — what went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: The timeout and retry settings on every outbound call along the path: HTTP client, SDK, gateway and service code.

How to confirm: Traces show requests waiting on that one dependency, pools sit at their limit, and the dependency gets far more requests than users send.

Likely causes and fixes: Calls without timeouts pile up and exhaust shared pools, and retries at several layers multiply: three layers trying three times each send up to 27 requests per user action. Give each hop a shorter timeout than its caller, retry in one layer only (idempotent calls, with exponential backoff and jitter), add a circuit breaker with a fallback, and give each dependency its own pool (a bulkhead). See Microservices patterns.

docs.title: 57. The p99 latency of a Lambda-backed API spikes after quiet periods and after each deploy — why?
docs.text:
What to check first: Whether the slow requests are cold starts. Lambda's REPORT log line includes Init Duration only when a new execution environment was initialized for that request.

How to confirm: Filter the logs for Init Duration and match those request IDs with the slow ones. Measure the bundle size, and time the code that runs at module load (SDK clients, config fetches, large imports).

Likely causes and fixes: New environments are created after idle periods, after deploys and during scale-out, and a heavy package or slow initialization makes each one expensive. Trim and bundle dependencies, lazy-load what the hot path does not need, and try more memory, which also adds CPU. Use provisioned concurrency for latency-critical endpoints. See Serverless architecture.

docs.title: 58. During a traffic spike the database hits its connection limit and Lambda invocations start failing — what is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: Open database connections against the maximum, next to the function's concurrent executions at the same moment.

How to confirm: Open connections roughly equal concurrent executions times the connections each environment opens. Check whether the client is created inside the handler, which connects on every invocation.

Likely causes and fixes: Every execution environment holds its own connections, so scaling out to hundreds of environments multiplies them. Create the client once outside the handler and reuse it, keep each environment's pool to one or two connections, put a pooler such as RDS Proxy in front of the database, and cap the function with reserved concurrency. See Serverless architecture.

docs.title: 59. Users still see their old profile details for minutes after saving changes — where do you look?
docs.text:
What to check first: Whether reads come from a cache, a read replica or a read model built from events, rather than from the record just written.

How to confirm: For one user, compare the value in the primary database, the cache and the API response. Check the cache TTL, whether the write path clears the key, and the replica or projection lag.

Likely causes and fixes: A cache never invalidated on write, a long TTL, replica lag, or an eventually consistent read model (CQRS) still catching up. Delete or refresh the cache key after the write commits, shorten the TTL, read a user's own recent writes from the primary or write model, and show the saved value from the write response in the UI. See Design patterns for backends and Event-driven architecture.

docs.title: 60. Some users cannot log in, though their accounts clearly exist — what do you suspect?
docs.text:
What to check first: How the identifier is stored compared with how it is looked up. A classic cause is email case: User@Example.com is saved but user@example.com is searched.

How to confirm: Search the users case-insensitively for the failing address, and check every path that creates users (sign-up, invites, imports).

Likely causes and fixes: Some paths normalize the value and others do not, so stored values differ in case or whitespace. Normalize in one place (the repository or an Email value object), add a unique index on the normalized value, and migrate existing rows, checking for accounts that clash once normalized. See Design patterns for backends and value objects in Domain-driven design.

docs.title: 61. The API returns 500 when a client sends an order with no lines — what is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: How errors thrown by the domain reach the HTTP response. If the error middleware turns every exception into a 500, a broken business rule looks like a server bug.

How to confirm: Reproduce with an empty lines array and read the logged stack trace. The domain's "An order needs at least one line" check throws, and nothing between it and Express maps it to a client error.

Likely causes and fixes: Business-rule violations and real bugs share one error type and one status code. Throw a dedicated DomainError from the domain and translate it to 400 or 422 in the HTTP adapter. Keep 500 for unexpected errors, and alert only on 5xx, so on-call is not paged for bad input. See Layered, hexagonal, and clean architecture.

docs.title: 62. A producer team changed an event and two consumer services broke in production — how do you prevent it next time?
docs.text:
What to check first: Exactly what changed (a field added, renamed, removed or retyped) and how consumers parse events: strict validation may reject unknown fields.

How to confirm: Consumer errors or dead-letter messages start at the producer's deploy time. Diff event payloads from before and after it.

Likely causes and fixes: A breaking change shipped without a new version, or consumers that reject anything unexpected. Make only additive changes to an existing event and have consumers ignore unknown fields (a tolerant reader). For a breaking change, publish a new version alongside the old one until every consumer moves, and check compatibility in CI with a schema registry or contract tests. See Event-driven architecture.

docs.title: 63. Loading one page triggers 40 calls between services and takes two seconds — what do you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: A distributed trace of the page request: how many spans, which run one after another, and whether a call repeats per item.

How to confirm: The trace shows a long waterfall, often an N+1 pattern across the network: one call for the list, then one call per item.

Likely causes and fixes: Services cut too fine (one per entity), so one use case needs many of them. Add batch endpoints, run independent calls in parallel, compose the response in a backend for frontend or gateway, or keep a local copy of data a service reads often, updated by events. Merge services that are always called and changed together. See Monoliths, modular monoliths, and microservices and Microservices patterns.

docs.title: 64. In a modular monolith, changes in billing keep breaking shipping — how do you stop the modules eroding?
docs.text:
What to check first: Whether shipping imports billing's internal files or reads billing's tables instead of using billing's public interface.

How to confirm: A dependency checker (dependency-cruiser for Node.js, Packwerk for Rails) lists the imports that cross module boundaries.

Likely causes and fixes: Nothing enforces the boundaries, so shortcuts pile up under deadline pressure. Give each module a small public API, make the allowed dependencies a rule that fails the build (a fitness function), and let exactly one module own each table. Record today's violations as a baseline, block new ones, and fix the rest step by step. See Architecture fundamentals, Design principles and Monoliths, modular monoliths, and microservices.

docs.title: 65. Adding each new payment provider means editing the same switch in five files — what is broken?
docs.text:
What to check first: Whether every place that charges, refunds or reports branches on provider, scattering knowledge of the providers.

How to confirm: The last provider change touched many files, and bugs appear where one switch was missed (refunds work, reports do not).

Likely causes and fixes: The code is not open for extension (the open/closed principle), and one decision is repeated everywhere, which breaks DRY in its real sense: duplicated knowledge. Define one PaymentProvider interface (charge, refund, report), implement it once per provider (the strategy pattern), and pick the implementation in one place, such as a factory. A new provider then means one new module. See Design principles and Design patterns for backends.

docs.title: Layered, Hexagonal, and Clean Architecture
docs.text: These three styles describe how to organize code inside one application or service. Layered architecture stacks code in horizontal layers. Hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters) puts business logic at the center and connects the outside world through interfaces. Onion and clean architecture refine the same idea with one strict rule: dependencies point inward, toward the business logic.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: In many backends, business rules end up scattered across route handlers, database queries, and framework callbacks. Changing the database, testing a rule without a running server, or reusing logic from a queue consumer then becomes painful. These styles keep the most valuable and longest-lived code—the business rules—independent of frameworks and infrastructure, which change more often. They also make fast, reliable unit tests possible.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix — swapping a data source in hours. Netflix's Studio Workflows team built a new app with hexagonal architecture because its data would move from a monolith to new microservices. When the monolith hit a read limit, the team moved one entity's reads from a JSON API to a GraphQL data source within 2 hours, crediting the hexagonal design for keeping persistence details out of the business logic (Netflix TechBlog).
  • Uber — layering rules across services. Uber's Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture applies the layered idea at the scale of services: "Layers only depend on the layers under them," which Uber uses to reason about blast radius and dependencies (Uber Engineering).

Popular tools: dependency-cruiser to fail CI when a layer imports the wrong way, and frameworks with built-in dependency injection (such as NestJS) that make adapters easy to swap.

docs.title: Layered architecture
docs.text:
The classic structure divides an application into layers, each with one kind of responsibility:

 ┌──────────────────────────────┐
 │ Presentation / API layer     │  HTTP routes, controllers, request/response
 ├──────────────────────────────┤
 │ Business (service) layer     │  use cases, business rules, workflows
 ├──────────────────────────────┤
 │ Data access layer            │  repositories, queries, ORM models
 ├──────────────────────────────┤
 │ Database                     │
 └──────────────────────────────┘
        dependencies point DOWN

Rules:

  • A layer may call only the layer directly below it (in a strict layering) or any layer below (in a relaxed layering).
  • Lower layers know nothing about higher ones: a repository never builds an HTTP response.

This is the structure most Express projects use (routes → controllers → services → repositories); see structuring an Express project.

Strengths: simple, familiar, and a big improvement over putting everything in route handlers.

Weakness: the business layer still depends on the data access layer. Its code imports a Mongo or SQL repository directly, so business rules are tied to the database technology and hard to test without one.

docs.title: Hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)
docs.text:
Alistair Cockburn's hexagonal architecture removes that dependency. The application core (business logic) sits in the middle and defines ports: interfaces describing what it needs and what it offers. Adapters outside the core implement those ports for specific technologies.

  • Inbound (driving) ports are the use cases the application offers, such as placeOrder. Driving adapters translate external input into calls on them: an HTTP controller, a CLI, a message consumer, a test.
  • Outbound (driven) ports are interfaces the core needs, such as OrderRepository or PaymentGateway. Driven adapters implement them: a MongoDB repository, a Stripe client, an in-memory fake.

The core depends only on its own port definitions, never on Express, MongoDB, or Stripe. Swapping MongoDB for PostgreSQL means writing a new adapter; the core does not change.

docs.title: Onion and clean architecture
docs.text:
Jeffrey Palermo's onion architecture and Robert C. Martin's clean architecture express the same idea as concentric circles:

Circle Contains Depends on Entities Core business objects and rules that would exist even without software (an order must have at least one line) Nothing Use cases Application-specific workflows that orchestrate entities (place an order: validate, price, save, notify) Entities, and port interfaces it defines Interface adapters Convert data between use cases and the outside: controllers, repository implementations, mappers Use cases, entities Frameworks and drivers Express, database drivers, external SDKs, configuration Everything inside

The dependency rule: code in an inner circle must not mention anything in an outer circle—no imports, no types, no framework objects. When an inner circle needs something from outside (saving data), it defines an interface (a port) and an outer circle implements it. This is the dependency inversion principle applied to architecture (see design principles).

docs.title: How the three relate
docs.text:
Style Core idea Dependency direction Layered Horizontal layers by responsibility Down toward the database Hexagonal Core with ports; adapters on all sides Adapters → core Onion / clean Concentric rings; entities in the center Outer rings → inner rings

Hexagonal, onion, and clean architecture are variations of one idea; the names and number of rings differ, the dependency rule does not.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Ports, adapters, and mappers add files and indirection. They pay off when:

  • Business rules are substantial and change often.
  • Several entry points (HTTP, queue consumers, scheduled jobs) share the same use cases.
  • Infrastructure is likely to change, or you need fast tests of complex logic.

They are overkill for a thin CRUD API that mostly moves data between HTTP and a database with few rules. A sensible approach is to start with simple layering and introduce ports where a real need appears—for example, around an external payment provider you want to fake in tests.

Situation Logic in route handlers Layered Hexagonal / clean Prototype or tiny CRUD API Acceptable Good fit Overkill Typical business app Becomes a tangle Good default Good fit Complex, changing rules Poor fit Rules tied to the database Best fit Many entry points (HTTP, queue, cron) Duplicated logic Workable Best fit Database or provider likely to change Painful Painful Write one new adapter Fast tests without infrastructure Hard Hard Easy with in-memory adapters

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text: The example below implements "place an order" with ports and adapters in an Express application.

docs.title: Folder layout
docs.text:
src/
├── domain/
│   └── order.js                 ← entity and business rules (no imports from outside)
├── application/
│   ├── ports.js                 ← port definitions (documentation of the contracts)
│   └── place-order.js           ← use case
├── adapters/
│   ├── http/orders.routes.js    ← driving adapter (Express)
│   ├── persistence/
│   │   ├── mongo-order-repository.js      ← driven adapter
│   │   └── in-memory-order-repository.js  ← driven adapter for tests
└── main.js                      ← composition root: wires adapters to the core

docs.title: Domain entity
docs.text:
// src/domain/order.js — pure business rules, no framework or database code
export class DomainError extends Error {} // a broken business rule, not a bug

export function createOrder({ id, customerId, lines, createdAt }) {
  if (lines.length === 0) {
    throw new DomainError("An order needs at least one line");
  }
  for (const line of lines) {
    if (!Number.isInteger(line.quantity) || line.quantity <= 0) {
      throw new DomainError("Quantity must be a positive integer");
    }
  }
  const totalCents = lines.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.unitPriceCents * l.quantity, 0);
  return { id, customerId, lines, totalCents, status: "PLACED", createdAt };
}

docs.title: The port
docs.text:
JavaScript has no interface keyword, so a port is a documented contract. JSDoc (or TypeScript) makes it explicit:

// src/application/ports.js
/**
 * Outbound port: how the application stores orders.
 * @typedef {object} OrderRepository
 * @property {(order: object) => Promise<void>} save
 * @property {(id: string) => Promise<object | null>} findById
 */
export {};

docs.title: The use case
docs.text:
// src/application/place-order.js
import { createOrder } from "../domain/order.js";

// Dependencies arrive as parameters: the use case never imports an adapter.
export function makePlaceOrder({ orderRepository, generateId, now }) {
  return async function placeOrder({ customerId, lines }) {
    const order = createOrder({ id: generateId(), customerId, lines, createdAt: now() });
    await orderRepository.save(order);
    return order;
  };
}

docs.title: Two driven adapters for the same port
docs.text:
// src/adapters/persistence/mongo-order-repository.js
export function makeMongoOrderRepository(db) {
  const collection = db.collection("orders");
  return {
    async save(order) {
      const { id, ...rest } = order;
      await collection.replaceOne({ _id: id }, rest, { upsert: true });
    },
    async findById(id) {
      const doc = await collection.findOne({ _id: id });
      if (!doc) return null;
      const { _id, ...rest } = doc;
      return { id: _id, ...rest }; // map database shape back to the domain shape
    },
  };
}

// src/adapters/persistence/in-memory-order-repository.js
export function makeInMemoryOrderRepository() {
  const orders = new Map();
  return {
    async save(order) {
      orders.set(order.id, structuredClone(order));
    },
    async findById(id) {
      return orders.has(id) ? structuredClone(orders.get(id)) : null;
    },
  };
}

docs.title: The driving adapter (Express)
docs.text:
// src/adapters/http/orders.routes.js
import { Router } from "express";
import { DomainError } from "../../domain/order.js";

export function makeOrdersRouter({ placeOrder }) {
  const router = Router();

  router.post("/orders", async (req, res) => {
    // Translate HTTP → use case input, and use case output → HTTP.
    try {
      const order = await placeOrder({ customerId: req.user.id, lines: req.body?.lines ?? [] });
      res.status(201).location(`/orders/${order.id}`).json(order);
    } catch (error) {
      if (error instanceof DomainError) {
        return res.status(400).json({ error: error.message }); // rule broken: client's fault
      }
      throw error; // anything else is a bug: the error handler answers 500
    }
  });

  return router;
}

docs.title: The composition root
docs.text:
// src/main.js — the only place that knows about every concrete adapter
import express from "express";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";
import { makePlaceOrder } from "./application/place-order.js";
import { makeMongoOrderRepository } from "./adapters/persistence/mongo-order-repository.js";
import { makeOrdersRouter } from "./adapters/http/orders.routes.js";

const client = await MongoClient.connect(process.env.MONGODB_URI);
const orderRepository = makeMongoOrderRepository(client.db());

const placeOrder = makePlaceOrder({
  orderRepository,
  generateId: randomUUID,
  now: () => new Date(),
});

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.use(makeOrdersRouter({ placeOrder }));
app.listen(3000);

docs.title: Testing the core without a database or server
docs.text:
// test/place-order.test.js — run with: node --test
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { makePlaceOrder } from "../src/application/place-order.js";
import { makeInMemoryOrderRepository } from "../src/adapters/persistence/in-memory-order-repository.js";

test("places an order and stores it", async () => {
  const orderRepository = makeInMemoryOrderRepository();
  const placeOrder = makePlaceOrder({
    orderRepository,
    generateId: () => "order-1",
    now: () => new Date("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"),
  });

  const order = await placeOrder({
    customerId: "c-7",
    lines: [{ productId: "p-1", quantity: 2, unitPriceCents: 1500 }],
  });

  assert.equal(order.totalCents, 3000);
  assert.deepEqual(await orderRepository.findById("order-1"), order);
});

test("rejects an empty order", async () => {
  const placeOrder = makePlaceOrder({
    orderRepository: makeInMemoryOrderRepository(),
    generateId: () => "x",
    now: () => new Date(),
  });
  await assert.rejects(placeOrder({ customerId: "c-7", lines: [] }), /at least one line/);
});

These tests run in milliseconds, need no database, and stay valid even if the persistence technology changes.

docs.title: Testing benefits
docs.text:
Test type Uses Speed Confidence in Entity unit tests Pure functions Fastest Business rules Use case tests In-memory adapters Fast Workflows Adapter integration tests Real database/SDK in a test environment Slower That each adapter honors its port End-to-end tests Whole app Slowest Wiring and configuration

Most tests can be fast use case and entity tests; fewer, focused tests cover each adapter.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep business rules free of framework, HTTP, and database objects.
  • Let inner code define the interfaces it needs; implement them outside.
  • Wire concrete implementations in one composition root.
  • Map between persistence models and domain objects at the adapter boundary.
  • Write most tests against the core with in-memory adapters, and a few integration tests per adapter.
  • Match the amount of structure to the complexity of the domain.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Business-rule failures reported as server errors. Symptom: 5xx alerts fire when clients send invalid orders. Detect: error logs show domain messages such as "An order needs at least one line" with status
  • Cause: the driving adapter never translates domain errors. Fix: throw a typed DomainError from the core and map it to 400 in the adapter, as the Express adapter above does.
  • Persistence leaking into the API. Symptom: responses contain _id, ORM metadata, or columns clients should not see. Detect: contract tests or API diffs show database field names. Cause: use cases return database documents. Fix: map to domain objects at the repository adapter and to response shapes at the HTTP adapter.
  • The fake adapter lies. Symptom: tests pass, but production fails, for example a save that does not overwrite or a lookup that returns the wrong shape. Detect: failures appear only in staging or production. Cause: the in-memory adapter behaves differently from the real one. Fix: run the same port contract tests against both adapters.
  • The dependency rule quietly breaks. Symptom: the domain imports a framework, logger, or SDK, and unit tests start needing real infrastructure. Detect: a dependency check shows edges from domain/ to adapters/ or node_modules. Cause: a convenient direct import under deadline pressure. Fix: inject what the core needs and enforce the rule in CI.
  • Ceremony without benefit. Symptom: adding one field to a simple CRUD endpoint touches five files. Detect: lead time for trivial changes grows. Cause: full ports and adapters around code with no real rules. Fix: collapse layers for thin CRUD and keep ports where they pay off.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Layer: A horizontal grouping of code with one kind of responsibility.
  • Port: An interface that defines how the application core interacts with the outside.
  • Adapter: An implementation that connects a port to a specific technology.
  • Driving (primary) adapter: An adapter that calls into the application, such as an HTTP controller.
  • Driven (secondary) adapter: An adapter the application calls, such as a repository.
  • Dependency rule: Source code dependencies must point toward the core.
  • Entity: A core business object with identity and rules.
  • Use case: An application-specific workflow.
  • Composition root: The single place where concrete dependencies are created and connected.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Passing req and res into services, tying business logic to Express.
  • Returning database documents or ORM models from use cases, leaking persistence details everywhere.
  • Creating interfaces for everything in a simple CRUD app.
  • "Clean architecture means many folders." It means correct dependency direction; folders are secondary.
  • Letting the domain import a logger, config, or SDK directly instead of receiving what it needs.
  • Thinking hexagonal architecture requires microservices. It organizes code within any deployable.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What weakness of layered architecture does hexagonal architecture fix?
  2. Explain ports, driving adapters, and driven adapters with an example of each.
  3. State the dependency rule and how dependency inversion makes it possible.
  4. Why do these styles make business logic easier to test?
  5. What is a composition root, and why should there be only one?
  6. When would ports and adapters be over-engineering?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Alistair Cockburn: Hexagonal architecture
  • Robert C. Martin: The clean architecture
  • Martin Fowler: Presentation domain data layering
  • Azure Architecture Center: N-tier architecture style
  • Design patterns for backends

docs.title: Microservices Patterns
docs.text: Splitting a system into microservices creates problems a monolith never had: how clients find and call many services, how a business transaction spans several databases, how to publish events reliably, and how to debug a request that crosses ten processes. Over time the industry settled on a set of named patterns for these problems. This page explains the essential ones and how they fit together.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Most microservice failures come from ignoring these patterns: services that call each other in long synchronous chains and fail together, orders charged but never shipped because a step failed halfway, events lost when a process crashed, and outages nobody can trace. Knowing the patterns—and their costs—is what makes a microservice architecture workable. If you have not yet decided whether to use microservices, read monoliths, modular monoliths, and microservices first.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix — a gateway at the edge. Netflix's open-source Zuul is a gateway service that provides dynamic routing, monitoring, resiliency, and security in front of backend services (Netflix/zuul on GitHub).
  • Netflix — circuit breakers against cascading failure. Netflix built Hystrix, a latency and fault-tolerance library that isolates calls to remote systems to "stop cascading failure." It is now in maintenance mode: stable enough for Netflix's existing applications, while Netflix's focus shifted to more adaptive approaches (Netflix/Hystrix on GitHub).
  • Uber — gateways per domain. In Uber's Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture, each domain exposes a gateway as "a single point of entry" into its collection of services, so callers depend on one interface instead of many services (Uber Engineering).

Popular tools: API gateways (Kong, Nginx, cloud API gateways); Envoy, an L7 proxy designed to run alongside every application server (the sidecar model); service meshes such as Istio and Linkerd; workflow engines such as Temporal and AWS Step Functions for sagas; Debezium's outbox event router; and OpenTelemetry for tracing.

docs.title: API gateway
docs.text:
Without a gateway, clients must know the address of every service, call several of them per screen, and handle authentication and protocols for each. An API gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of the services.

                        ┌─► [ catalog service ]
 [ web / mobile ] ──► [ API gateway ] ─┼─► [ orders service ]
                        └─► [ users service ]

Typical responsibilities:

  • Routing requests to the right service (/orders/* → orders).
  • Authentication and token validation at the edge.
  • Rate limiting, TLS termination, request size limits.
  • Aggregation: combining several service responses into one.
  • Protocol translation (for example, HTTP/JSON outside, gRPC inside).
  • Cross-cutting concerns: CORS, caching, request IDs, logging.

Costs: another component to run and scale, a possible bottleneck and single point of failure (run several instances), and a temptation to put business logic in it—keep it thin. Managed gateways, Nginx, Envoy, and Kong are common implementations; see also reverse proxy and rate limiting.

docs.title: Backend for frontend (BFF)
docs.text:
Different clients need different data: a mobile app wants small payloads and few round trips; a web dashboard wants rich data. A single general-purpose gateway becomes a compromise for everyone. The BFF pattern gives each client type its own backend layer, owned by the team building that client.

Each BFF aggregates and reshapes data for its screens. The risk is duplicated logic between BFFs; shared business rules belong in the services, not the BFFs.

docs.title: Service discovery
docs.text:
In dynamic environments, service instances start, stop, and move, so their IP addresses change constantly. Service discovery lets callers find healthy instances.

  • Server-side discovery: the caller sends requests to a stable address (a load balancer or a DNS name), which forwards to a healthy instance. Kubernetes Services work this way: http://orders resolves to a virtual IP that balances across pods.
  • Client-side discovery: the caller asks a service registry (such as Consul or Eureka) for the list of instances and chooses one itself.
 Server-side:  caller ──► [ load balancer / DNS ] ──► instance A | B | C
 Client-side:  caller ──query──► [ registry ] ; caller ──► chosen instance

Instances register on startup (or are registered by the platform) and are removed when health checks fail. Most teams today use the server-side discovery their platform provides.

docs.title: Synchronous versus asynchronous communication
docs.text:
Synchronous (REST, gRPC) Asynchronous (messaging) Caller waits for a response Yes No Availability coupling Caller fails or slows if the callee does Producer works even if consumers are down Latency Adds up along call chains Work completes later Consistency Immediate answer Eventual Complexity Familiar, simple to trace Broker, idempotency, ordering, retries Good for Queries, operations needing an immediate answer Notifications, workflows, integration, load leveling

A dangerous anti-pattern is a long synchronous chain: A calls B calls C calls D. If each is 99.9% available, the chain is about 99.6% available, and latencies add up. Prefer asynchronous events for work that does not need an immediate answer, and keep synchronous chains short. See REST and other API styles and messaging fundamentals.

docs.title: Saga
docs.text:
With a database per service, there is no transaction spanning orders, payments, and inventory. A saga implements a business transaction as a sequence of local transactions, one per service. If a step fails, the saga runs compensating transactions to undo the effects of the earlier steps.

Key points:

  • Compensations are semantic undos, not database rollbacks. You cannot "un-send" an email; you send a correction. A refund compensates a charge.
  • Sagas lack isolation: other requests can see intermediate states. Use explicit states such as PENDING (a "semantic lock") so others know the order is not final.
  • Each step and compensation must be idempotent because messages can be redelivered.
  • Steps that cannot be compensated (shipping a parcel) should come last, after the steps that can fail.

Sagas are coordinated by choreography (services react to each other's events) or orchestration (a saga orchestrator sends commands and tracks state). Orchestration is easier to understand and monitor for processes with more than a few steps. See event-driven architecture for the comparison.

docs.title: Transactional outbox
docs.text:
A service often needs to update its database and publish an event. Doing them separately is unsafe:

  • Save, then publish: the process crashes in between → the event is lost.
  • Publish, then save: the save fails → consumers react to something that never happened.

You cannot put the database and the broker in one transaction. The transactional outbox solves this: write the event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the business change. A separate relay process reads the outbox and publishes to the broker, marking rows as sent.

The relay can poll the table or use change data capture (such as MongoDB change streams or Debezium). Because the relay may publish a row twice (for example, it crashes after publishing but before marking it sent), delivery is at least once, and consumers must deduplicate.

docs.title: Idempotent consumer
docs.text:
Brokers deliver messages at least once, so a consumer can receive the same message twice. An idempotent consumer records the IDs of messages it has processed and skips duplicates, ideally in the same transaction as its own state change:

 receive message (id = m-123)
   BEGIN
     INSERT INTO processed_messages (id) VALUES ('m-123')   ← unique key
       → if it already exists: duplicate, ROLLBACK, acknowledge, stop
     apply the business change
   COMMIT
   acknowledge the message

See timeouts, retries, and idempotency and delivery guarantees.

docs.title: Circuit breaker
docs.text:
When a downstream service is failing or very slow, callers that keep retrying waste resources, pile up waiting requests, and can bring themselves down—a cascading failure. A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and, after too many failures, "opens" to fail fast for a while, then lets a few trial calls through to check recovery.

 CLOSED ──(failures exceed threshold)──► OPEN ──(cool-down elapsed)──► HALF-OPEN
   ▲                                                                    │
   └──────────────(trial calls succeed)─────────────────────────────────┘
                   (trial call fails) ──► back to OPEN

Combine circuit breakers with timeouts, limited retries with backoff, and fallbacks (cached data, a degraded response). Implementation details are in timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

docs.title: Strangler fig
docs.text: The strangler fig pattern migrates from a monolith to services incrementally: put a routing layer in front of the monolith and move one capability at a time to a new service, routing its traffic there, until the monolith can be retired. See monoliths, modular monoliths, and microservices.

docs.title: Sidecar and service mesh
docs.text:
Every service needs the same networking features: mutual TLS, retries, timeouts, load balancing, metrics, and tracing. Implementing them in every service and language is repetitive.

  • A sidecar is a helper process deployed alongside each service instance (in Kubernetes, a second container in the same pod). It shares the service's network and lifecycle and handles a cross-cutting concern, such as proxying traffic or shipping logs.
  • A service mesh (such as Istio or Linkerd) places a proxy sidecar next to every service and manages them centrally. All service-to-service traffic flows through the proxies, which provide mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting for canary releases, and uniform telemetry—without changing application code.
 [ orders app ]⇄[ proxy ] ════ mTLS ════ [ proxy ]⇄[ payments app ]
                    ▲                        ▲
                    └──── control plane: policies, certificates, config

A mesh adds operational complexity and some latency; it pays off with many services and strict security or traffic-management needs.

docs.title: Database per service
docs.text: Each service owns its data and exposes it only through its API or events. This enables independent deployment and scaling, but cross-service queries need API composition (call several services and join in memory) or a read model built from events (CQRS). See monoliths, modular monoliths, and microservices and event-driven architecture.

docs.title: Distributed tracing
docs.text:
A single user request may pass through a gateway and many services. Logs in each service do not show the whole story unless they are connected. Distributed tracing assigns each request a trace ID that is passed along on every call and message. Each unit of work records a span with its timing and parent span, and a tracing backend assembles them into one timeline.

 Trace 4f2a…  POST /checkout                                  [==========] 820 ms
   ├─ gateway: auth                                           [=]           20 ms
   ├─ orders: create order                                     [===]       150 ms
   │    └─ postgres: INSERT                                     [=]         40 ms
   ├─ payments: charge                                             [=====] 600 ms  ← slow
   └─ publish order.placed                                              [=] 10 ms

OpenTelemetry is the standard for producing traces, metrics, and logs. Always include the trace or correlation ID in logs. See logging and monitoring.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
These patterns solve problems that only exist once you have several services. In a monolith, most of them are unnecessary.

Pattern Use when Skip or postpone when API gateway External clients call more than a few services One service, or internal-only traffic BFF Mobile and web need very different data shapes One client type, or a gateway already fits Saga (orchestration) Many steps, compensations, monitoring needs Two simple steps, or one database transaction is possible Saga (choreography) Few, independent reactions The flow is long and must be visible in one place Transactional outbox A state change must publish an event reliably Losing an occasional notification is acceptable Idempotent consumer Messages are delivered at least once (almost always) The handler is naturally idempotent Circuit breaker Synchronous calls to dependencies that can fail or slow down Calls are asynchronous through a queue Service mesh Many services, strict mTLS and traffic policies A handful of services; libraries are simpler

Use these patterns when:

  • You already run several independently deployed services, or are extracting them.
  • Failures in one service must not take down others.
  • Business processes span services that each own their data.

Do not adopt them speculatively: a gateway, mesh, and saga engine in front of two services add moving parts without solving a problem you have.

docs.title: Transactional outbox with PostgreSQL
docs.text:
import pg from "pg";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

// 1. Business change and event in ONE local transaction
export async function placeOrder(order) {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");
    await client.query(
      "INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total_cents, status) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, 'PENDING')",
      [order.id, order.customerId, order.totalCents],
    );
    await client.query(
      "INSERT INTO outbox (id, topic, payload) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
      [crypto.randomUUID(), "order.placed", JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.id })],
    );
    await client.query("COMMIT");
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw error;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

// 2. Relay: publish unsent rows. SKIP LOCKED lets several relays run safely.
export async function relayOutbox(broker) {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");
    const { rows } = await client.query(
      `SELECT id, topic, payload FROM outbox
       WHERE published_at IS NULL
       ORDER BY created_at
       LIMIT 100
       FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`,
    );
    for (const row of rows) {
      await broker.publish(row.topic, row.payload, { messageId: row.id }); // id lets consumers dedupe
      await client.query("UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = $1", [row.id]);
    }
    await client.query("COMMIT");
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw error;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

docs.title: A minimal saga orchestrator
docs.text:
export async function runCheckoutSaga({ orderId, items, payment }, services) {
  const completed = [];
  try {
    await services.inventory.reserve(orderId, items);
    completed.push(() => services.inventory.release(orderId));

    await services.payments.charge(orderId, payment);
    completed.push(() => services.payments.refund(orderId));

    await services.orders.confirm(orderId);
  } catch (error) {
    // Compensate completed steps in reverse order
    for (const compensate of completed.reverse()) {
      await compensate(); // must be idempotent; production code retries and records progress
    }
    await services.orders.cancel(orderId, { reason: error.message });
    throw error;
  }
}

A production orchestrator persists the saga's state after each step (so it can resume after a crash), retries compensations, and usually communicates with services through messages. Workflow engines such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions provide this durability.

docs.title: How the patterns fit together
docs.text:
client ─► API gateway / BFF ─► orders service ─(outbox)─► broker ─► inventory, payments
                │                    │                       (idempotent consumers)
           auth, routing,       saga orchestrator coordinates checkout,
           rate limiting        circuit breakers on sync calls,
                                trace IDs propagated everywhere,
                                database per service

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep the gateway thin: routing and cross-cutting concerns, no business logic.
  • Prefer asynchronous messaging for work that does not need an immediate answer; keep synchronous call chains short.
  • Put timeouts, bounded retries, and circuit breakers on every remote call.
  • Use the transactional outbox whenever a state change must publish an event.
  • Make every consumer, saga step, and compensation idempotent.
  • Prefer saga orchestration for multi-step processes; persist saga state.
  • Propagate trace IDs everywhere and log them.
  • Adopt a service mesh only when the number of services and security needs justify it.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Outbox relay lag. Symptom: consumers react to orders minutes late. Detect: the age of the oldest unpublished outbox row keeps growing. Cause: the relay is down, too slow, or blocked; or the published_at query has no index. Fix: alert on that age, run several relays (SKIP LOCKED allows it), index unsent rows, and delete published rows on a schedule so the table stays small.
  • Stuck sagas. Symptom: orders stay PENDING forever. Detect: a count of sagas in a non-final state older than a few minutes. Cause: the orchestrator crashed without persisted progress, or a compensation keeps failing. Fix: persist saga state after every step, retry compensations, alert on stuck sagas, and keep a runbook for manual repair.
  • Retry storms. Symptom: a recovering service is flattened by traffic again. Detect: request rate to the dependency jumps to several times normal right after an incident. Cause: every caller retries immediately, at every layer. Fix: exponential backoff with jitter, retry budgets, and circuit breakers that open quickly.
  • Cascading timeouts. Symptom: one slow service makes the whole checkout slow or failing. Detect: traces show requests waiting on one span, and thread or connection pools saturate. Cause: synchronous chains without timeouts. Fix: timeouts on every call, circuit breakers, and asynchronous messaging where possible.
  • Traces that stop at the queue. Symptom: the trace for a request ends when it publishes an event, hiding what happened next. Detect: traces missing consumer spans. Cause: trace context not copied into message headers. Fix: propagate trace context through messages with OpenTelemetry instrumentation.
  • The gateway becomes the bottleneck. Symptom: every request is slow, even simple ones. Detect: gateway CPU and p99 latency rise with traffic. Cause: business logic or heavy aggregation in the gateway, or too few instances. Fix: move logic into services or BFFs and scale the gateway horizontally.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• API gateway: A single entry point that routes and secures requests to services.
  • BFF (backend for frontend): A client-specific backend layer.
  • Service discovery / registry: Finding healthy service instances.
  • Saga: A sequence of local transactions with compensations for failure.
  • Compensating transaction: An action that semantically undoes an earlier step.
  • Transactional outbox: Storing outgoing events in the same transaction as the state change.
  • Relay: The process that publishes outbox rows to the broker.
  • Idempotent consumer: A consumer that safely ignores duplicate messages.
  • Circuit breaker: A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency for a while.
  • Sidecar: A helper process deployed next to each service instance.
  • Service mesh: A network of sidecar proxies managed by a control plane.
  • Distributed trace / span: The end-to-end record of a request / one timed unit of work within it.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Business logic in the API gateway, turning it into a shared monolith.
  • Long chains of synchronous calls, multiplying latency and failure probability.
  • Publishing events outside the transaction and losing or inventing events.
  • Assuming a saga is like a database transaction, ignoring visible intermediate states.
  • Retrying without idempotency, causing double charges.
  • Retries without circuit breakers or backoff, creating retry storms.
  • No trace IDs, making cross-service debugging nearly impossible.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What responsibilities belong in an API gateway, and what should stay out?
