docs.title: Monoliths, Modular Monoliths, and Microservices
docs.text: One of the first architectural decisions is how many deployable units a system has. A monolith is one application deployed as a single unit. A modular monolith is still one deployable but is divided into strongly separated modules. Microservices split the system into many small services that are deployed and scaled independently and own their own data.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: This choice affects nearly everything: how teams work together, how releases happen, how data stays consistent, how failures spread, and how much operational work is needed. Many teams have adopted microservices too early and spent their time on infrastructure instead of features; others have let a monolith decay into a tangle no one can change safely. Understanding the real costs of each option lets you pick the one that fits your team and domain today, and evolve later.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Shopify — a modular monolith instead of microservices. Shopify describes one of the largest Ruby on Rails codebases, worked on by more than a thousand developers. Rather than split it into services, it chose to keep one codebase and enforce boundaries between components (Shopify Engineering). It later built Packwerk, a tool that statically checks references between components (Shopify Engineering).
  • Segment — from microservices back to a monolith. Segment's per-destination microservices grew to over 140 services. Its velocity dropped, defects rose, and three full-time engineers spent most of their time keeping the system alive, so it consolidated the services into a single service (Segment blog).
  • Netflix — from a monolith to hundreds of microservices. After a major database corruption in 2008 stopped DVD shipments for three days, Netflix rebuilt its technology for the cloud, migrating "from a monolithic app to hundreds of micro-services," and finished the migration in early 2016 (Netflix).
  • Uber — grouping microservices into domains. With around 2,200 critical microservices, Uber felt the complexity first hand and introduced Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture, classifying the services into 70 domains with a single entry point each (Uber Engineering).

Popular tools:

  • Boundary checking inside one codebase: Packwerk (Ruby) and dependency-cruiser (JavaScript and TypeScript).
  • Running many services: containers with an orchestrator such as Kubernetes, plus centralized logs, metrics, and distributed tracing.

docs.title: The monolith
docs.text:
A monolith contains all features—users, catalog, orders, payments—in one codebase that builds into one deployable artifact and usually uses one database.

 ┌─────────────────────── one process / one deploy ───────────────────────┐
 │  users   catalog   orders   payments   notifications   (function calls)│
 └─────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   ▼
                           [ one database ]

Advantages:

  • Simple to develop, test, and debug: one repository, one process, one debugger session, stack traces that cover the whole request.
  • Simple to deploy and operate: one build, one pipeline, one set of dashboards.
  • Fast in-process calls with no network failures between features.
  • Easy transactions: one database transaction can update orders and inventory together.
  • Easy refactoring across feature boundaries.

Disadvantages as it grows:

  • Without discipline, boundaries erode into a "big ball of mud" where everything depends on everything.
  • Every change requires redeploying the whole application; a bug in one feature can take everything down.
  • Build and test times grow; many teams coordinating on one codebase slow each other down.
  • Scaling is all-or-nothing: you scale the whole app even if only search is busy.
  • Technology choices are shared; upgrading a framework affects everyone.

A monolith is not inherently bad or unscalable. Run several stateless instances behind a load balancer and it scales horizontally; many large products run on well-structured monoliths.

docs.title: The modular monolith
docs.text:
A modular monolith keeps the single deployable but divides the code into modules with enforced boundaries, usually aligned with business capabilities (see domain-driven design):

 ┌──────────────────────────── one deploy ─────────────────────────────┐
 │ ┌─────────┐  public API   ┌─────────┐  public API   ┌──────────┐    │
 │ │ catalog │◄──────────────│ orders  │──────────────►│ payments │    │
 │ │ internal│               │ internal│               │ internal │    │
 │ └────┬────┘               └────┬────┘               └────┬─────┘    │
 └──────┼─────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼──────────┘
        ▼                         ▼                         ▼
   catalog tables            orders tables            payments tables
   (same database, separate schemas; no cross-module table access)

Rules that make it work:

  • Each module exposes a small public interface (functions or events); everything else is internal.
  • Modules never read or write another module's tables; they call its public API.
  • Dependencies between modules are explicit and checked automatically (for example, lint rules or architecture tests).
  • Modules communicate with in-process calls or in-process events.

You keep the operational simplicity of a monolith while gaining most of the design benefits of services. If one module later needs independent scaling or deployment, it already has a clean boundary to extract.

docs.title: Microservices
docs.text:
Microservices split the system into services that:

  • Are independently deployable: each has its own pipeline and release schedule.
  • Are organized around business capabilities (orders, payments, shipping), not technical layers.
  • Own their data: each service has its own database or schema that no other service accesses directly.
  • Communicate over the network with HTTP/gRPC calls or messages.
  • Are usually owned end to end by one team.
              [ API gateway ]
       ┌───────────┼─────────────┐
       ▼           ▼             ▼
  [ catalog ]  [ orders ] ──event──► [ queue ] ──► [ shipping ]
       │           │                                   │
   catalog DB   orders DB                          shipping DB

Benefits:

  • Teams deploy independently, without coordinating releases.
  • Services scale independently according to their own load.
  • A failure can be contained to one service if callers handle it well.
  • Each service can choose the technology that fits it.
  • Smaller codebases are easier for one team to understand.

docs.title: The real costs of microservices
docs.text:
These costs are often underestimated:

Cost What it means in practice Network failures Every call can time out, fail, or be slow. You need timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and idempotency (see timeouts, retries, and idempotency). Distributed data No transactions across services. Consistency becomes eventual and requires patterns such as sagas and the outbox (see microservices patterns). Reports that join data across services need extra work. Operational overhead Many pipelines, deployments, configurations, secrets, and runtime versions to maintain; usually containers and an orchestrator. Observability One user request crosses many services; you need centralized logs, metrics, and distributed tracing to debug it. Testing Integration tests across services are harder; contract testing becomes necessary. Latency Network hops add milliseconds that in-process calls do not. Versioning Changing a service's API requires backward compatibility for its callers.

Martin Fowler calls this the microservice premium: microservices bring complexity of their own, which adds to a project's cost and risk. His guideline is not to consider microservices unless a system is too complex to manage as a monolith.

A distributed monolith is the worst case: services that must be deployed together, share a database, or call each other synchronously in long chains. It has all the costs of microservices and none of the benefits.

docs.title: Database per service
docs.text:
Giving each service its own data store is what makes services independent:

  • Schema changes stay inside one service.
  • A slow query in one service cannot lock another's tables.
  • Each service can use the store that fits (relational, document, search index).

The cost: queries that span services need API composition (call several services and combine), a read model built from events, or a data warehouse. Services must never "just read" another service's tables—doing so silently couples them again.

docs.title: How to choose
docs.text:
Factor Points toward a (modular) monolith Points toward microservices Team size One or a few teams Many teams that need to release independently Domain understanding New product, boundaries still changing Stable, well-understood domain boundaries Scaling needs Uniform load, or scaling the whole app is affordable Parts with very different load or resource profiles Operational maturity Limited DevOps capacity Mature CI/CD, containers, monitoring, and on-call Consistency needs Many operations need strong, multi-entity transactions Boundaries where eventual consistency is acceptable

A widely recommended path is monolith first: start with a well-modularized monolith, learn where the real boundaries are, and extract services only when a concrete need appears (team scaling, independent scaling, isolation). Drawing service boundaries in a domain you don't yet understand usually produces the wrong boundaries, which are expensive to move across a network.

docs.title: Migrating with the strangler fig pattern
docs.text:
The strangler fig pattern (named after a vine that gradually grows around a tree) replaces a legacy system incrementally instead of rewriting it all at once:

Each step is small, reversible, and delivers value. Big-bang rewrites, by contrast, often take far longer than planned while the old system keeps changing.

When extracting a service, migrate its data too: the new service must become the owner, often with a period of synchronization from the old database.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a monolith or modular monolith when:

  • One team, or a few teams that talk daily, build the product.
  • The domain is new and its boundaries are still moving.
  • Many operations need transactions across several entities.
  • You lack mature CI/CD, monitoring, and on-call practices for many services.

Use microservices when:

  • Many teams need to release independently without coordinating.
  • Parts of the system have very different load, scaling, or technology needs.
  • Domain boundaries are stable and well understood.
  • You can afford the platform work: pipelines, tracing, service discovery, and contract testing.

Avoid microservices when the main goal is "cleaner code"; a modular monolith gives you that without the network. Avoid a plain, unstructured monolith when more than one team works in it; add enforced modules first.

Situation Monolith Modular monolith Microservices New product, one small team Good fit Good fit Too early Several teams in one codebase Boundaries erode Good fit Possible, costly Many teams needing independent releases Poor fit Strained Good fit One part needs 10× the compute of the rest Scale everything Scale everything Scale just that service Strong cross-entity transactions Easy Easy Needs sagas Limited DevOps capacity Good fit Good fit Poor fit

docs.title: A module's public interface in a modular monolith
docs.text:
src/modules/
├── catalog/
│   ├── index.js            ← public API: the only file other modules import
│   ├── catalog.service.js
│   └── catalog.repository.js
└── orders/
    ├── index.js
    ├── orders.service.js
    └── orders.repository.js

// src/modules/catalog/index.js — the module's contract
import { catalogService } from "./catalog.service.js";

export async function getProductPrice(productId) {
  const product = await catalogService.findById(productId);
  return product ? { productId, price: product.price, currency: product.currency } : null;
}

// src/modules/orders/orders.service.js
import { getProductPrice } from "../catalog/index.js"; // allowed: public API
// import { catalogRepository } from "../catalog/catalog.repository.js"; ← forbidden

export async function addItem(order, productId, quantity) {
  const price = await getProductPrice(productId);
  if (!price) throw new Error("Unknown product");
  order.items.push({ productId, quantity, unitPrice: price.price });
}

If catalog later becomes a separate service, only catalog/index.js changes: its functions call the catalog service over HTTP instead of in-process.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Aspect Monolith Modular monolith Microservices Deployables 1 1 Many Boundaries Often informal Enforced modules Network + separate data Communication Function calls Function calls via public APIs, in-process events HTTP/gRPC, messaging Data Shared database One database, schema per module Database per service Transactions Easy Easy within a module; possible across Local only; sagas across services Independent deploys No No Yes Independent scaling No (scale whole app) No (scale whole app) Yes Operational complexity Low Low High Debugging Easy Easy Needs distributed tracing Best for Small apps, prototypes Most products and teams Large organizations, clear domains

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start with a modular monolith unless you have a clear, present reason for microservices.
  • Draw boundaries around business capabilities, not technical layers.
  • Enforce module boundaries automatically; informal boundaries erode.
  • Never share database tables between modules or services.
  • Before extracting a service, ensure you have CI/CD, centralized logging, metrics, tracing, and on-call practices.
  • Migrate incrementally with the strangler fig pattern; avoid big-bang rewrites.
  • Watch for distributed-monolith symptoms: lock-step deploys, shared databases, long synchronous call chains.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Distributed monolith. Symptom: a change to one service needs coordinated releases of several others. Detect: release notes and deploy logs show services always shipping together; contract changes break callers. Cause: boundaries cut across a business capability, or services share tables. Fix: merge services that always change together, give each its own data, and make API changes backward compatible.
  • Chatty services and slow pages. Symptom: p99 latency climbs as features are added. Detect: distributed traces show one request fanning out into dozens of sequential calls. Cause: fine-grained services, or a loop that calls another service per item. Fix: batch endpoints, move data closer to where it is used, or merge the services.
  • Cascading failure. Symptom: one slow dependency takes down unrelated features. Detect: thread or connection pools saturate and error rates rise across many services at once. Cause: synchronous calls without timeouts or circuit breakers. Fix: timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and asynchronous messaging where an immediate answer is not needed.
  • A shared database couples everything again. Symptom: a schema change in one service breaks another. Detect: database logs show several services' credentials querying the same tables. Cause: reading another service's tables as a shortcut. Fix: give each table one owning service; others use its API or events.
  • Module boundaries erode in the monolith. Symptom: "small" changes touch many modules and tests get slow. Detect: boundary checks (for example Packwerk or dependency-cruiser) report a growing number of violations. Cause: boundaries were a convention, not a rule. Fix: make violations fail CI and pay down the existing list.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Monolith: An application built and deployed as a single unit.
  • Modular monolith: A single deployable divided into modules with enforced boundaries.
  • Microservice: A small, independently deployable service that owns its data and a business capability.
  • Business capability: Something the business does, such as billing or shipping, used to draw boundaries.
  • Database per service: Each service owns its data store exclusively.
  • Distributed monolith: Services that are separately deployed but tightly coupled, combining the downsides of both styles.
  • Strangler fig pattern: Incrementally replacing a system by routing features to new components.
  • Microservice premium: The extra cost and risk that microservices' own complexity adds; worth paying only for systems too complex to manage as a monolith.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Monoliths don't scale." Stateless monolith instances scale horizontally well; the limits are usually organizational.
  • "Microservices are more modern, so better." They solve organizational scaling problems at a high technical cost.
  • Splitting by technical layer (a "database service," a "validation service"), creating chatty, coupled services.
  • Sharing a database between services, which recreates the coupling microservices were meant to remove.
  • Making services too small ("nanoservices"), so every feature touches many services.
  • Big-bang rewrites of a working monolith.

docs.title: Serverless Architecture
docs.text: Serverless architecture builds applications from managed cloud services and short-lived functions that the provider runs on demand. You write a function, connect it to a trigger—an HTTP request, a file upload, a queue message—and the platform starts, scales, and stops the compute for you. You pay for what runs rather than for idle servers. There are still servers; you just do not manage them.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Serverless can remove most infrastructure work: no operating systems to patch, no capacity planning, automatic scaling from zero to thousands of concurrent executions, and very low cost for spiky or low-traffic workloads. It also brings constraints that change how you design: cold starts, execution time limits, statelessness, connection management, and dependence on one cloud provider. Understanding them lets you decide where serverless fits and where containers or servers are a better choice.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• BBC — rendering its website with Lambda. When the BBC rebuilt its website for the cloud, around half of the site came to be rendered serverlessly with AWS Lambda, because managing virtual machines or containers securely and reliably was expensive (BBC Product & Technology).
  • CreditorWatch — lessons from 2 billion executions. The Australian credit bureau's engineering blog reports that, at that scale, records were processed out of order and a failed batch was retried as a whole, which made idempotency essential (CreditorWatch on Medium).
  • Superbet — sports modelling on Lambda. Superbet's engineering team wrote that it had used AWS Lambda for sports modelling for over three years and expected to extend that use (Superbet Engineering).

Popular providers: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Run functions, and Cloudflare Workers; managed building blocks such as API gateways, queues, object storage, and serverless databases; Amazon RDS Proxy or PgBouncer for connection pooling.

docs.title: Two meanings of "serverless"
docs.text:
• Functions as a service (FaaS): you deploy individual functions that run in response to events. Examples: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Run functions, Cloudflare Workers.
  • Serverless managed services (backend as a service, BaaS): databases, queues, storage, and authentication that scale automatically and bill by usage, such as Amazon DynamoDB, S3, SQS, Cognito, or Firebase.

A serverless architecture typically combines both: functions glue managed services together.

docs.title: The FaaS execution model
docs.text:
Using AWS Lambda as the reference example:

  • An execution environment is an isolated micro-VM or sandbox running your function's runtime (for example, Node.js).
  • With Lambda's default compute type, each environment processes one request at a time. If ten requests arrive at once, Lambda runs ten environments in parallel—this is how it scales. (Lambda Managed Instances, a newer option that runs on EC2 instances, lets one environment handle several invocations at once, so code there must be safe for concurrency.)
  • Code outside the handler (module scope) runs once per environment during initialization and is reused by later invocations in that environment. Code inside the handler runs on every invocation.
  • Idle environments are eventually shut down. You cannot control when.

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text:
Functions are invoked by events from many sources:

Trigger Example use HTTP (API Gateway, function URLs) REST or webhook endpoints Object storage events (S3) Create thumbnails when an image is uploaded Queues (SQS) Process orders or emails in batches Pub/sub notifications (SNS, EventBridge) React to domain events Schedules (EventBridge Scheduler/cron) Nightly reports and cleanup Database streams (DynamoDB Streams) Update search indexes on data changes

Invocations can be synchronous (the caller waits, as with HTTP) or asynchronous (the event is queued and the platform retries failures). Because asynchronous and queue-based invocations can be retried, handlers must be idempotent.

docs.title: Cold starts
docs.text:
A cold start is the extra latency when no warm environment is available and the platform must create one: allocate the sandbox, load your code, start the runtime, and run initialization code. It ranges from tens of milliseconds to seconds, depending on runtime, package size, memory, and what your initialization does (for example, connecting to a database).

Cold starts happen on first traffic, after idle periods, and whenever traffic rises faster than existing environments can absorb. Ways to reduce their impact:

  • Keep deployment packages small; bundle and tree-shake dependencies.
  • Do expensive setup lazily or once in module scope, not on every request.
  • Allocate more memory (Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory, which also speeds initialization).
  • Use provisioned concurrency (pre-initialized environments, billed even when idle) for latency-sensitive endpoints.
  • Accept them for asynchronous work, where an extra second rarely matters.

docs.title: Statelessness
docs.text: You cannot rely on anything staying in memory or on local disk between invocations: the next request may run in a different environment, and any environment may disappear. Keep state in external services—databases, caches, object storage. In-memory data may be reused as an optimization (a warm cache of configuration), never as the source of truth.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Every platform imposes limits. For AWS Lambda, important ones include:

Limit AWS Lambda (check current quotas) Design impact Maximum execution time 15 minutes (900 seconds) Long jobs must be split, chunked, or moved to containers or workflow services Memory 128 MB to 10,240 MB (CPU scales with memory; about one vCPU at 1,769 MB) Choose memory for both RAM and CPU needs Synchronous request/response payload 6 MB each way (streamed responses can be larger) Upload large files directly to object storage with presigned URLs Concurrency An account-level regional quota (default 1,000, can be raised) One noisy function can starve others; set reserved concurrency Temporary disk (/tmp) 512 MB by default, configurable up to 10,240 MB Not durable; cleared when the environment ends

Quotas change over time, so verify them in the provider's documentation before designing around a number.

docs.title: Pricing model
docs.text:
FaaS is usually billed by:

  • Number of invocations, and
  • Duration × memory (for Lambda, GB-seconds, billed in 1 ms increments).

There is no charge while nothing runs. This is very cheap for spiky or low-volume workloads and for event processing. For steady, high-throughput traffic, an always-on container or server can be cheaper, because you pay a premium per unit of compute for on-demand elasticity. Also count the cost of managed services around the functions (API gateway requests, queues, logs).

docs.title: Database connections
docs.text:
Traditional databases expect a modest number of long-lived connections. With serverless, hundreds of concurrent environments may each open their own connections and exhaust the database's limit.

Mitigations:

  • Create clients outside the handler so warm invocations reuse connections.
  • Keep per-environment pools tiny (often one connection).
  • Use a connection proxy or pooler, such as Amazon RDS Proxy or PgBouncer, which multiplexes many client connections onto few database connections.
  • Use HTTP-based or serverless-friendly data stores (DynamoDB, Data APIs, serverless database offerings) designed for this access pattern.
  • Limit function concurrency to protect the database.

docs.title: Vendor lock-in
docs.text: Serverless applications depend heavily on provider-specific triggers, services, permissions, and deployment tooling. Moving to another cloud often means rewriting integration code and infrastructure definitions. Reduce the impact by keeping business logic in plain modules separate from the handler (see hexagonal architecture) and by using infrastructure-as-code. Accept some lock-in consciously when the productivity gain is worth it.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Good fits:

  • Event processing: file uploads, queue consumers, webhooks, stream processing.
  • Spiky or unpredictable traffic, and workloads that are idle most of the time.
  • Scheduled jobs and automation.
  • APIs for new products where traffic is unknown and the team is small.
  • Glue code between managed services.

Poor fits:

  • Long-running or CPU-heavy jobs exceeding time limits.
  • Latency-critical APIs that cannot tolerate cold starts (unless you pay for provisioned concurrency).
  • Steady, high-volume traffic where always-on compute is cheaper.
  • Applications needing persistent connections in the same process, such as a WebSocket server holding sockets (managed WebSocket gateways exist, but the model differs).
  • Workloads that need special hardware, OS access, or full control of the runtime.

docs.title: Containers versus serverless functions
docs.text:
Aspect Containers (ECS, Kubernetes, Cloud Run) Serverless functions (Lambda) Unit of deployment Container image with a long-running server Function code and handler Scaling Autoscaling rules; scale to zero only on some platforms Automatic per request, scales to zero Startup Seconds to start new containers; warm instances serve many requests Cold starts per new environment Execution time Unlimited Limited (15 minutes on Lambda) Concurrency per instance Many requests per process One request per environment (Lambda default compute type) Billing Provisioned capacity (or per-request on serverless container platforms) Per invocation and duration Operations Images, orchestration, scaling configuration Minimal infrastructure, more cloud configuration Portability High (standard images) Lower (provider-specific triggers and services) Local development Run the same image locally Emulators or deploy-to-test

Serverless container platforms blur the line by running containers with request-based scaling and billing.

docs.title: An HTTP handler on AWS Lambda (Node.js)
docs.text:
// handler.js — invoked through an API Gateway HTTP API
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";

// Module scope: runs once per execution environment and is reused while warm.
const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI, { maxPoolSize: 1 });
const clientReady = client.connect();

export const handler = async (event) => {
  const id = event.pathParameters?.id;
  if (!id) {
    return { statusCode: 400, body: JSON.stringify({ error: "id is required" }) };
  }

  await clientReady; // reuse the connection on warm invocations
  const product = await client.db().collection("products").findOne({ _id: id });

  if (!product) {
    return { statusCode: 404, body: JSON.stringify({ error: "Not found" }) };
  }
  return {
    statusCode: 200,
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(product),
  };
};

docs.title: Processing a queue batch idempotently
docs.text:
// Invoked by SQS with a batch of messages; reports which ones failed
export const handler = async (event) => {
  const batchItemFailures = [];

  for (const record of event.Records) {
    try {
      const message = JSON.parse(record.body);
      if (await processedMessages.has(message.id)) continue; // duplicate: already done
      await sendReceiptEmail(message);
      await processedMessages.add(message.id); // mark done only after the work succeeded
    } catch (error) {
      console.error("Failed to process message", record.messageId, error);
      batchItemFailures.push({ itemIdentifier: record.messageId }); // retry only this one
    }
  }

  return { batchItemFailures }; // requires partial batch responses to be enabled
};

docs.title: A serverless image pipeline
docs.text:
client ──presigned URL──► [ S3 uploads bucket ]
                                 │ ObjectCreated event
                                 ▼
                         [ resize function ] ──► [ S3 thumbnails bucket ] ──► CDN
                                 │
                                 └──► [ DynamoDB: image metadata ]

No servers to run, nothing billed while no images are uploaded, and the pipeline scales automatically with upload volume.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep handlers thin; put business logic in plain modules you can test without the cloud.
  • Initialize clients and configuration in module scope; reuse them across warm invocations.
  • Make every handler idempotent; assume retries and duplicate events.
  • Set timeouts on downstream calls shorter than the function's own timeout.
  • Protect databases with connection proxies, tiny pools, and concurrency limits.
  • Keep deployment packages small to reduce cold starts.
  • Use dead-letter queues or failure destinations for events that keep failing.
  • Monitor cost, duration, errors, throttles, and cold starts; set budgets and alerts.
  • Define all infrastructure as code.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Cold-start latency spikes. Symptom: p99 latency jumps after deploys, idle periods, or sudden traffic. Detect: the Init Duration field in Lambda's REPORT log lines appears on the slow requests. Cause: new environments loading a large bundle or doing heavy initialization. Fix: smaller bundles, lighter init, more memory, or provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive endpoints.
  • Throttling. Symptom: requests fail with throttling errors during a spike. Detect: the Throttles metric rises while concurrency sits at a limit. Cause: the account or function concurrency limit is reached, or another function used it up. Fix: reserved concurrency for critical functions, a quota increase, and a queue in front of bursty work.
  • Database connections exhausted. Symptom: "too many connections" errors as traffic grows. Detect: database connections track function concurrency. Cause: every environment opens its own connections. Fix: clients in module scope, a pool size of one, a connection proxy, and a concurrency limit.
  • A failed batch retried as a whole. Symptom: duplicate side effects and repeated errors for the same queue messages. Detect: the same message IDs processed several times. Cause: one bad record fails the whole batch. Fix: partial batch responses, idempotent processing, and a dead-letter queue for messages that never succeed.
  • Lost work from early "done" marks. Symptom: some customers never get an email after a provider outage. Detect: messages marked processed with no matching email sent. Cause: recording a message as processed before the side effect succeeded, so retries skip it. Fix: mark it done only after the work succeeds, as the queue handler above does.
  • Runaway recursion and cost. Symptom: invocations and the bill climb with no matching user traffic. Detect: a function's invocations grow exponentially, often a function writing to the same queue or bucket that triggers it. Fix: separate input and output locations, and rely on Lambda's recursive loop detection only as a backstop: it stops a chain after about 16 invocations, and only for supported services.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Serverless: Running applications on managed infrastructure you do not provision or operate.
  • FaaS (functions as a service): Running individual functions on demand in response to events.
  • BaaS (backend as a service): Managed backend services such as databases and authentication.
  • Trigger: The event source that invokes a function.
  • Execution environment: The isolated sandbox that runs a function instance.
  • Cold start / warm start: Invocation that must create a new environment / reuses an existing one.
  • Provisioned concurrency: Pre-initialized environments kept ready to avoid cold starts.
  • Reserved concurrency: A cap (and guarantee) on concurrent executions for one function.
  • Connection proxy: A service that pools database connections for many short-lived clients.
  • Vendor lock-in: Dependence on one provider's proprietary services.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Serverless means no servers." It means no servers that you manage.
  • "Serverless is always cheaper." It is cheap for spiky or low traffic and can be expensive for steady, high throughput.
  • Opening a new database connection in every invocation, exhausting the database.
  • Storing state in memory or /tmp and expecting it to persist.
  • Non-idempotent handlers that double-process retried events.
  • Huge deployment packages that make cold starts slow.
  • Functions calling functions synchronously in chains, multiplying cost, latency, and failure points.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between FaaS and BaaS?
  2. Explain the lifecycle of a Lambda execution environment and what runs at initialization versus per invocation.
  3. What causes cold starts, and how can you reduce them?
  4. Why can serverless functions overwhelm a relational database, and what are three mitigations?
  5. Name three workloads that suit serverless and three that do not.
  6. Compare containers and serverless functions on scaling, time limits, and cost.

docs.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
docs.text: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is quick, rough arithmetic that tells you the order of magnitude of a system's load: requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth, memory for caching, and number of servers. The answers are not precise, and they do not need to be — the difference between 50 requests per second and 50,000 decides the design, while the difference between 50,000 and 60,000 usually does not.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Without numbers, design decisions are guesses. Estimation answers questions like:

  • Will one database handle the write rate, or do we need sharding?
  • Does the hot data fit in memory, so a cache is cheap and effective?
  • How much will storage cost in three years?
  • Can this run on a handful of servers, or does it need hundreds?

It also exposes requirements nobody stated: a "small" feature that stores every event forever may need petabytes. In interviews, estimation shows you can reason about scale; at work, it prevents both over- and under-building.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google SRE turns reliability into numbers: services set availability targets and manage unreliability through error budgets (Embracing Risk); the SRE book includes an availability table translating nines into allowed downtime.
  • Google's Auxon is "a powerful tool developed within SRE to automate capacity planning"; teams moved to intent-based capacity planning — "specify the requirements, not the implementation" (Software Engineering in SRE).
  • Amazon validates capacity assumptions with tests: "At Amazon we spend a great deal of time load testing our services," including past the point where they break (Using load shedding to avoid overload).
  • Discord hit a size threshold that estimation predicts: message volume grew from 40 million to over 120 million per day within months, and at 100 million stored messages "the data and the index could no longer fit in RAM," making latencies unpredictable (How Discord Stores Billions of Messages).

docs.title: Powers of two and storage units
docs.text:
Power Exact value Approximate Unit 2^10 1,024 1 thousand (10^3) 1 KB 2^20 1,048,576 1 million (10^6) 1 MB 2^30 1,073,741,824 1 billion (10^9) 1 GB 2^40 ~1.1 × 10^12 1 trillion (10^12) 1 TB 2^50 ~1.13 × 10^15 1 quadrillion (10^15) 1 PB

For estimates, treat 1 KB as 1,000 bytes and so on. (Strictly, the binary units are KiB, MiB, GiB; the difference is under 13% even at the petabyte level and rarely matters for an estimate.)

docs.title: Typical data sizes
docs.text:
Item Approximate size ASCII character 1 byte (UTF-8 non-ASCII characters: 2–4 bytes) 32-bit / 64-bit integer 4 / 8 bytes Timestamp 8 bytes UUID 16 bytes binary, 36 characters as text A short text post with metadata ~0.5–1 KB A JSON API response (list page) ~5–50 KB A compressed photo from a phone ~0.5–3 MB One minute of compressed HD video ~10–100 MB (depends on bitrate)

Remember overhead: indexes, replication, and storage engine overhead can easily double or triple raw data size.

docs.title: Approximate latency numbers
docs.text:
These are rough orders of magnitude; real values depend on hardware, network, and load.

Operation Approximate time CPU L1 cache reference ~1 ns Main memory reference ~100 ns Read 1 MB sequentially from memory ~50–100 µs Random 4 KB read from an SSD ~0.1 ms Read 1 MB sequentially from an NVMe SSD ~0.3–1 ms Network round trip within a data center ~0.5 ms Round trip between availability zones in one region Single-digit ms Hard disk seek ~5–10 ms Read 1 MB sequentially from a hard disk ~5–10 ms Round trip between continents ~70–150 ms

AWS, for example, describes its availability zones as close enough for synchronous replication "with single-digit millisecond latency" (AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries).

What to take away:

  • Memory is roughly 1,000× faster than SSD random access, which is why caches work.
  • Network round trips dominate: ten sequential calls inside a data center cost ~5 ms before any work is done; one cross-continent call costs more than an entire well-built request.
  • Avoid cross-region calls in the request path; batch and parallelize calls.

docs.title: Availability nines
docs.text:
Availability Downtime per year Downtime per 30-day month 99% ("two nines") ~3.65 days ~7.2 hours 99.9% ~8.76 hours ~43 minutes 99.95% ~4.4 hours ~22 minutes 99.99% ~53 minutes ~4.3 minutes 99.999% ~5.3 minutes ~26 seconds

Composing components:

  • In series (the request needs all of them): multiply availabilities. An app at 99.9% that depends on a database at 99.9% is at most 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.8%.
  • In parallel (any one of N redundant copies is enough): 1 − (1 − a)^N. Two independent 99% replicas give 1 − 0.01² = 99.99% — if their failures really are independent.

docs.title: Time conversions
docs.text:
Period Seconds Rounded 1 day 86,400 ~10^5 (100,000) 1 month (30 days) 2,592,000 ~2.5 × 10^6 1 year 31,536,000 ~3 × 10^7

Using 10^5 for a day underestimates per-second rates by about 14%; that is acceptable for an estimate, and you can say so.

docs.title: Requests per second from daily active users
docs.text:
average QPS = daily active users × actions per user per day ÷ 86,400
peak QPS    = average QPS × peak factor (commonly 2–3×; more for spiky events)

Estimate reads and writes separately; their ratio (for example, 100:1 for a URL shortener, 1:1 for chat) shapes the design. Traffic is rarely flat — daily cycles, time zones, and events like sales or sports finals create peaks.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
storage per day = new records per day × size per record
storage total   = storage per day × retention days × replication factor
                  (+ overhead for indexes, typically ×1.2–2)

Separate small structured data (rows in a database) from large blobs (images, video in object storage) — they are stored, priced, and scaled differently.

docs.title: Bandwidth
docs.text:
egress (out) = read QPS × average response size
ingress (in) = write QPS × average request size

Convert bytes per second to bits per second (× 8) when comparing with network link speeds. Large media egress is usually served from a CDN, so the origin carries only a fraction.

docs.title: Cache memory sizing (80/20 rule)
docs.text:
Access is usually skewed: a small fraction of items receives most requests. A common rule of thumb is that about 20% of items serve about 80% of reads, so caching the hottest 20% of a day's read set captures most of the benefit.

cache memory ≈ 0.2 × (unique items read per day) × size per item

If you only know requests per day, using requests in place of unique items gives an upper bound (many requests repeat the same items). Compare the result with the memory of one cache node to decide how many nodes you need.

docs.title: Estimating server count
docs.text:
servers = peak QPS ÷ (QPS one server handles at acceptable latency × target utilization)
  • Get per-server capacity from load tests, not guesses — it varies by orders of magnitude between a cached lookup and a heavy report.
  • Target utilization of ~50–70% leaves headroom for spikes and garbage collection.
  • Add redundancy: if you spread across three availability zones and must survive losing one, the remaining two must carry the full peak.

Order-of-magnitude reference points (measure your own): a single Redis instance can serve on the order of 100,000 simple operations per second; a well-indexed relational database on one server typically handles thousands to tens of thousands of simple queries per second; an application instance handles hundreds to a few thousand typical API requests per second.

docs.title: Rounding rules
docs.text:
• Round inputs to one or two significant figures (86,400 → 100,000; 3.65 → 4).
  • Work in powers of ten: 2 × 10^8 ÷ 10^5 = 2 × 10^3.
  • Keep units on every number and convert explicitly (bytes ↔ bits, seconds ↔ days).
  • State each assumption out loud so others can correct it.
  • Sanity-check results against things you know ("20 TB per day is a lot of disks — does that match a photo app with 10 million uploads?").

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use estimation when:

  • Choosing between architectures before any code exists.
  • Deciding whether a component (cache, shard, queue, CDN) is needed at all.
  • Planning capacity and cost for a launch or the next year.
  • Sanity-checking a vendor's claims or a teammate's proposal.
  • In interviews, to justify each design decision.

Do not rely on estimates when:

  • Real measurements exist — production metrics beat assumptions.
  • You need final capacity numbers — confirm with load tests.
  • Tuning latency-critical paths — profile and measure instead.
  • Calculating exact bills or contractual commitments — use real usage data.
Question Estimate or measure? "Will one database handle next year's writes?" Estimate first, then track real growth "How many instances do we need at launch?" Estimate, then load test "What is the p99 latency of this endpoint?" Measure "Does the working set fit in cache memory?" Estimate, then check hit rate in production "What will storage cost in 3 years?" Estimate early; revise from actual growth

docs.title: Example 1: Social posts — QPS, storage, and bandwidth
docs.text:
Assumptions: 100 million daily active users (DAU). Each user posts 2 times per day and loads their feed 20 times per day. A post is 300 bytes of text plus 200 bytes of metadata. A feed page returns 20 posts. Peak is 3× average. 10% of posts include a 500 KB image.

Write QPS:

posts/day  = 100 M × 2         = 200 M = 2 × 10^8
avg writes = 2 × 10^8 ÷ 10^5   = 2,000 /s     (exact: ~2,300 /s)
peak       = 2,000 × 3         ≈ 6,000 /s

Read QPS:

feed loads/day = 100 M × 20        = 2 × 10^9
avg reads      = 2 × 10^9 ÷ 10^5   = 20,000 /s   (exact: ~23,000 /s)
peak           = 20,000 × 3        ≈ 60,000 /s
read:write ratio ≈ 10:1

Text storage:

per day   = 2 × 10^8 posts × 500 B = 10^11 B = 100 GB/day
per year  = 100 GB × 365          ≈ 36.5 TB/year
with 3 replicas                    ≈ 110 TB/year

Image storage:

images/day = 10% × 200 M = 20 M
per day    = 20 M × 500 KB = 10 TB/day
per year   = 10 TB × 365   ≈ 3.65 PB/year  → object storage + CDN

Feed bandwidth (text only, average):

response = 20 posts × 500 B = 10 KB
egress   = 20,000 /s × 10 KB = 200 MB/s ≈ 1.6 Gbit/s

Conclusions: text data grows modestly but reads are heavy — feeds should be cached or precomputed. Images dominate storage and must live in object storage behind a CDN. Writes at ~6,000/s peak are within reach of a sharded database or a write-optimized store.

docs.title: Example 2: URL shortener — cache sizing
docs.text:
Assumptions: 100 million new short URLs per month; 100 redirects per URL created (read:write = 100:1); each mapping record is ~500 bytes; keep records for 5 years.

writes/s  = 10^8 ÷ (2.5 × 10^6 s/month)    ≈ 40 /s
reads/s   = 40 × 100                       ≈ 4,000 /s   (peak ×3 ≈ 12,000 /s)

storage   = 10^8 × 500 B = 50 GB/month → 600 GB/year → 3 TB over 5 years

Cache:

reads/day     = 4,000 /s × 86,400 s ≈ 3.5 × 10^8
cache (80/20) = 0.2 × 3.5 × 10^8 × 500 B ≈ 35 GB  (upper bound)

Conclusions: 35 GB fits comfortably in a small cache cluster (or one large node with a replica). Total storage of a few terabytes over five years is modest; the challenge is read throughput and low latency, which caching solves. See the URL shortener case study.

docs.title: Example 3: How many application servers?
docs.text:
Assumptions: peak of 60,000 requests per second (from example 1). A load test shows one instance serves 1,500 requests per second within the latency target. We run at 60% target utilization, across 3 availability zones, and must survive losing one zone.

usable capacity per instance = 1,500 × 0.6 = 900 req/s
instances for peak            = 60,000 ÷ 900 ≈ 67 → round to 70

survive one zone of three: the other two zones must carry 100% of peak
total instances = 70 ÷ (2/3) = 105 → 35 per zone

Conclusions: about 105 instances at peak; autoscaling can run fewer at night. The estimate is only as good as the per-instance figure — that number must come from a load test (see performance testing).

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• State every assumption explicitly and keep it adjustable.
  • Estimate reads and writes separately; note the ratio.
  • Always compute peak as well as average.
  • Separate structured data from blobs; include replication and index overhead.
  • Keep units on every number; convert bytes and bits carefully.
  • Round aggressively; aim for the right order of magnitude.
  • Sanity-check results against known systems or hardware limits.
  • Replace estimates with measurements (load tests, production metrics) as soon as they exist.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Capacity runs out early. Symptom: latency climbs and requests are throttled months before the planned upgrade. Detect: utilization and saturation dashboards with alerts at ~70%. Cause: the peak factor or growth rate was underestimated. Fix: forecast from real metrics, keep headroom, and autoscale where possible.
  • The cache does not help. Symptom: database load stays high after adding a cache. Detect: low cache hit-rate metric. Cause: the working set is larger than estimated, or access is less skewed than the 80/20 assumption. Fix: size from the measured working set; cache only hot data.
  • Storage fills faster than planned. Symptom: disk-space alerts or a storage bill spike. Detect: storage growth trend per day. Cause: replication, indexes, logs, and backups were left out of the estimate. Fix: include overhead factors; set retention and lifecycle policies.
  • Network saturation. Symptom: packet drops and timeouts during peaks. Detect: network throughput metrics near link limits. Cause: a bits versus bytes mistake (8×) or media served from the origin. Fix: recompute in consistent units; move media to a CDN.
  • Load test numbers do not match production. Symptom: production saturates at half the tested throughput. Detect: compare per-instance throughput in production with test results. Cause: the test used a warm cache, a tiny dataset, or an unrealistic request mix. Fix: test with production-like data volumes and traffic mixes.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Order of magnitude: a factor of ten; estimation aims to get this right.
  • DAU / MAU: daily / monthly active users.
  • QPS / RPS: queries / requests per second.
  • Peak factor: the ratio of peak load to average load.
  • Read:write ratio: how many reads occur per write.
  • Replication factor: the number of copies of each piece of data.
  • Egress / ingress: data leaving / entering the system.
  • Working set: the data actively accessed in a period.
  • 80/20 rule (Pareto principle): a small share of items receives most of the accesses.
  • Headroom: spare capacity kept for spikes and failures.
  • Nines: shorthand for availability percentages (99.9% = three nines).

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Spending minutes on precise arithmetic. Precision is not the goal.
  • Forgetting peak traffic, sizing for the average.
  • Mixing bits and bytes, which is an 8× error.
  • Forgetting replication and indexes in storage estimates.
  • Treating blobs and metadata together, which hides where storage goes.
  • Guessing per-server capacity and then trusting the server count.
  • Assuming redundant components fail independently, when they share a power supply, region, or software bug.
  • Not stating assumptions, so nobody can correct them.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Convert 10 million requests per day to average requests per second, and estimate the peak with a 3× factor.
  2. How much downtime per month does 99.95% availability allow?
  3. Two services, each 99.9% available, are called in series. What is the best combined availability?
  4. Estimate yearly storage for 50 million 2 KB records per day with 3 replicas.
  5. Explain the 80/20 rule for cache sizing and why using total requests gives an upper bound.
  6. Why should per-server capacity come from a load test rather than a guess?

docs.title: System Design Building Blocks
docs.text: Most large systems are assembled from the same set of components: DNS, CDNs, load balancers, gateways, stateless application servers, caches, databases, object storage, queues, search indexes, rate limiters, ID generators, and partitioning schemes such as consistent hashing. Knowing what each block does, what problem it solves, and what it costs lets you assemble a design from requirements instead of from habit.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: In a design discussion, every box on the diagram must earn its place. A cache added "for performance" without a read-heavy workload only adds staleness and a failure mode. A queue added "for scalability" without a slow or bursty task only adds latency. Understanding each block's purpose and trade-offs lets you justify it — or leave it out.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Twitter's Snowflake generated unique IDs without coordination because Twitter needed to "keep our ids under 64bits": 41 bits of time with a custom epoch (69 years), a 10-bit machine ID (up to 1,024 machines), and a 12-bit sequence that rolls over every 4,096 IDs per machine (Snowflake README).
  • Amazon's Dynamo partitions data with consistent hashing and, instead of one point per node, assigns each node "multiple points in the ring" using virtual nodes (Amazon's Dynamo).
  • Netflix Open Connect is Netflix's program for delivering its content efficiently: Netflix partners with over a thousand ISPs, embedding Open Connect Appliances in their networks to localize traffic — a CDN pushed as close to viewers as possible (Netflix Open Connect).
  • Slack maps each channel to a stateful, in-memory Channel Server using consistent hashing; at peak, about 16 million channels are served per host (Real-time Messaging).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: The typical request path through the blocks looks like this:

docs.title: DNS
docs.text: DNS translates names like api.example.com into IP addresses. Managed DNS can also route users to the nearest or healthiest region (latency-based, geolocation, weighted, and failover routing). Answers are cached for their TTL, so changes are not instant — keep TTLs short on records you may need to fail over. See DNS and domains and DNS configuration.

docs.title: CDN
docs.text: A content delivery network caches content at edge locations close to users: static assets, images, video, and cacheable public API responses. It cuts latency, terminates TLS near the user, reduces origin load and egress cost, and absorbs spikes. Behavior is controlled with headers such as Cache-Control. See CDN and HTTP and CDN caching.

docs.title: Load balancer
docs.text:
A load balancer spreads requests across servers, runs health checks, and stops sending traffic to unhealthy instances.

  • Layer 4 (transport): balances TCP/UDP connections by IP and port; very fast; does not inspect HTTP.
  • Layer 7 (application): understands HTTP; routes by path, host, or header, terminates TLS, adds headers like X-Forwarded-For.
  • Algorithms: round robin, least connections, weighted, hash-based (for affinity).

Load balancers are themselves made redundant. See load balancing.

docs.title: Reverse proxy and API gateway
docs.text:
A reverse proxy sits in front of application servers and forwards requests to them, commonly handling TLS termination, compression, static files, request buffering, caching, and basic rate limiting (Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy). A layer 7 load balancer is a reverse proxy that also balances. See reverse proxy.

An API gateway is a specialized entry point for APIs with many backend services: routing to services, token validation, per-key rate limits and quotas, request transformation, versioning, and usage analytics. Use it when several services or external developers need one consistent front door; for a single application, a load balancer plus middleware may be enough.

docs.title: Stateless application servers
docs.text: Application servers run the business logic. Keeping them stateless — no sessions or uploaded files in local memory or disk — means any instance can serve any request, so instances can be added, removed, and replaced freely. State goes to shared stores. See stateless services and autoscaling.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text: A cache keeps copies of frequently read data in fast storage (usually memory) to cut latency and database load. Use it for read-heavy data that tolerates some staleness. Key decisions: what to cache, the strategy (cache-aside, read-through, write-through), invalidation, and behavior when the cache fails. See cache fundamentals, caching strategies, and cache failure modes.

docs.title: Databases: SQL and NoSQL
docs.text:
Relational (SQL) NoSQL (document, key-value, wide-column, graph) Data model Tables with fixed schema and relationships Flexible documents, key-value pairs, column families, or graphs Queries Rich SQL, joins, aggregations Optimized for specific access patterns; joins limited Transactions Strong ACID transactions across rows and tables Varies; many support single-item atomicity, some multi-item transactions Scaling Vertical first; read replicas; sharding is harder Many designed for horizontal partitioning from the start Good for Related business data, payments, inventory Huge-scale key lookups, flexible schemas, event data

Choose from access patterns and consistency needs; many systems use both. See database fundamentals and database scaling.

docs.title: Object storage
docs.text: Object storage (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and S3-compatible services) stores large binary objects — images, video, backups, exports — durably and cheaply, addressed by bucket and key. Keep the bytes there and metadata in a database; deliver through a CDN and use presigned URLs for direct uploads and private downloads. See file storage and uploads.

docs.title: Message queue
docs.text: A message queue (or log) decouples producers from consumers: the producer writes a message and continues; consumers process it at their own pace. Use it for slow or unreliable work, to absorb bursts, to fan events out to several consumers, and to connect services loosely (RabbitMQ, Kafka, Amazon SQS/SNS). Design for at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers. See messaging fundamentals and delivery guarantees.

docs.title: Search index
docs.text:
Databases are poor at full-text search with typo tolerance and relevance ranking. A search engine builds an inverted index: a map from each term to the documents containing it.

Documents:  1: "fresh coffee beans"   2: "coffee shop downtown"   3: "fresh bread"

Inverted index:
  beans → [1]    bread → [3]       coffee → [1, 2]
  fresh → [1, 3] downtown → [2]    shop → [2]

Query "fresh coffee" → score [1, 3] and [1, 2] → document 1 ranks first

Analyzers tokenize and normalize text (lowercase, stemming); results are ranked by relevance (for example, BM25). Elasticsearch and OpenSearch are common choices. The database stays the source of truth; the index is updated asynchronously, so search can lag slightly behind writes.

docs.title: Rate limiter
docs.text: A rate limiter caps how many requests a client can make in a time window, protecting against abuse, brute force, and overload. It usually sits at the API gateway or in middleware, with counters in a shared store such as Redis. See rate limiting and throttling and the distributed rate limiter case study.

docs.title: Unique ID generation
docs.text:
Distributed systems need IDs that are unique across many servers, without a single database sequence becoming a bottleneck.

Approach Size Sortable by time Coordination Notes Database auto-increment 64-bit Yes Single sequence (bottleneck, SPOF) Simple; reveals counts; hard across shards UUID v4 128-bit No None 122 random bits; random inserts fragment B-tree indexes UUID v7 128-bit Yes (millisecond) None Unix-time prefix + random bits (RFC 9562); index-friendly Snowflake-style 64-bit Yes (roughly) Unique worker IDs Compact; fits in a BIGINT ID ranges from a service 64-bit Roughly Allocate blocks (e.g. 1,000 at a time) Simple; used for counters like URL codes

Snowflake-style IDs (introduced at Twitter) pack a timestamp, a machine ID, and a sequence number into 64 bits:

They sort by creation time and are generated locally once each machine has a unique ID. Watch for the clock moving backwards (refuse or wait) and for sequence exhaustion within one millisecond (wait for the next). Time-ordered IDs keep index inserts near the end of the index, but they reveal creation time — never rely on IDs being unguessable for access control.

docs.title: Consistent hashing
docs.text:
To spread keys across N cache or database nodes, the naive approach is node = hash(key) % N. When N changes, most keys map to a different node (going from N to N + 1 nodes moves about N/(N + 1) of them — 75% for 3 → 4) — a massive reshuffle that empties caches and moves most data.

Consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on a hash ring (for example, 0 to 2^32 − 1). A key belongs to the first node found moving clockwise from the key's position.

On average, adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.

Virtual nodes fix two problems with one point per node: uneven distribution (some nodes get large arcs) and heterogeneous capacity. Each physical node is placed at many points (for example, 100–200). Load evens out, a removed node's keys spread across many nodes instead of one neighbor, and bigger machines can be given more virtual nodes.

Consistent hashing is used in distributed caches, Dynamo-style key-value stores, Cassandra, and load balancers that need affinity. Redis Cluster uses a related idea: 16,384 fixed hash slots assigned to nodes. See database scaling.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a block when its problem is real: a CDN when many users fetch the same content; a cache when reads dominate and staleness is acceptable; a queue when work is slow, bursty, or unreliable; a search index when users need full-text search; sharding or consistent hashing when one node cannot hold the data or load.

Leave it out when: the load fits on simpler infrastructure (one database with replicas handles a lot); the data must always be fresh (no cache); the caller needs the result immediately (no queue); simple LIKE or prefix queries are enough (no search cluster yet); you have no operational capacity to run it.

Choice Prefer the first when… Prefer the second when… Queue vs direct call The caller does not need the result now; work is slow, bursty, or retried; several consumers react The caller needs the answer to respond; latency matters; the work is fast and reliable SQL vs NoSQL Related data, transactions, ad hoc queries, moderate scale Simple key-based access at very large scale, flexible schema, horizontal partitioning from day one CDN vs origin only Static or media content, global users, cacheable public responses Personalized or private responses that cannot be cached, a single-region internal tool Cache vs no cache High read:write ratio, tolerable staleness, measured database pressure Data must be exactly current, low traffic, or poor hit rate expected API gateway vs load balancer only Many services or external developers, per-key quotas One application with its own auth middleware Snowflake/UUID v7 vs auto-increment Many writers across shards or regions One database, simplicity matters, IDs not exposed

docs.title: A Snowflake-style ID generator
docs.text:
// 41-bit timestamp | 10-bit worker ID | 12-bit sequence, as a BigInt
const EPOCH = 1735689600000n; // 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z, a custom epoch

export function createIdGenerator(workerId) {
  let lastMs = -1n;
  let sequence = 0n;

  return function nextId() {
    let now = BigInt(Date.now());
    if (now < lastMs) throw new Error("Clock moved backwards; refusing to generate IDs");

    if (now === lastMs) {
      sequence = (sequence + 1n) & 4095n; // 12 bits
      if (sequence === 0n) {
        // Sequence exhausted for this millisecond: wait for the next one
        while (now <= lastMs) now = BigInt(Date.now());
      }
    } else {
      sequence = 0n;
    }
    lastMs = now;

    return ((now - EPOCH) << 22n) | (BigInt(workerId) << 12n) | sequence;
  };
}

const nextId = createIdGenerator(7); // workerId must be unique, 0–1023
console.log(nextId().toString());    // a large integer, printed as a string

Send such IDs to JavaScript clients as strings — they exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 − 1), so as JSON numbers many of them lose precision and change value.

docs.title: A consistent hash ring with virtual nodes
docs.text:
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

const hash32 = (value) => createHash("md5").update(value).digest().readUInt32BE(0);

// Place each physical node at many virtual positions, sorted around the ring
export function buildRing(nodes, virtualNodes = 150) {
  return nodes
    .flatMap((node) =>
      Array.from({ length: virtualNodes }, (_, i) => ({ position: hash32(`${node}#${i}`), node }))
    )
    .sort((a, b) => a.position - b.position);
}

// A key belongs to the first virtual node clockwise (use binary search at scale)
export function getNode(ring, key) {
  const position = hash32(key);
  return (ring.find((entry) => entry.position >= position) ?? ring[0]).node;
}

const ring = buildRing(["cache-a", "cache-b", "cache-c"]);
console.log(getNode(ring, "user:42")); // "cache-a" (MD5 is deterministic, so always the same node)

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Add a block only when a requirement or estimate justifies it.
  • Keep application servers stateless; put state in shared, replicated stores.
  • Remove single points of failure: redundancy across availability zones.
  • Put a CDN in front of static and media content.
  • Treat caches and search indexes as derived data, not the source of truth.
  • Use queues for slow, unreliable, or bursty work; make consumers idempotent.
  • Prefer time-ordered IDs (UUID v7, Snowflake-style) for keys at scale.
  • Use consistent hashing (with virtual nodes) or hash slots when nodes change.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Cache stampede. Symptom: database CPU spikes after a deploy or at regular intervals. Detect: cache hit rate drops while database load jumps. Cause: a cold cache or many keys expiring at once. Fix: jittered TTLs, request coalescing, and cache warm-up (see cache failure modes).
  • Hot shard. Symptom: one database or cache node is saturated while others idle. Detect: per-node CPU and request metrics. Cause: a skewed key (a celebrity, a viral item, a timestamp shard key). Fix: a better partition key, splitting hot keys, local caching, more virtual nodes.
  • Queue backlog. Symptom: jobs finish later and later. Detect: queue depth and age-of-oldest-message alarms. Cause: consumers slower than producers, or a poison message retried forever. Fix: scale consumers, cap retries, send failures to a dead-letter queue.
  • Slow DNS failover. Symptom: traffic keeps reaching a failed region for many minutes. Detect: synthetic checks per region. Cause: long DNS TTLs and clients caching answers. Fix: shorter TTLs on failover records, health-checked routing, and load balancer–level failover.
  • Health checks that lie. Symptom: errors from instances the load balancer still considers healthy — or all instances removed at once. Detect: 5xx rates at the load balancer versus instance health. Cause: a check that ignores the app's real state, or one that fails when a shared dependency blips. Fix: separate liveness and readiness checks.
  • ID generator clock problems. Symptom: ID generation errors or duplicate-key failures. Detect: error logs from the generator. Cause: the clock stepped backwards, or two workers share an ID. Fix: time sync that slews rather than steps, refusing to issue IDs while the clock is behind, and enforced unique worker IDs.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Layer 4 / layer 7 load balancing: balancing by connection (IP, port) / by HTTP content (path, host, headers).
  • Stateless service: a service that keeps no client state locally.
  • Inverted index: a map from terms to the documents that contain them.
  • Snowflake ID: a 64-bit, time-ordered ID combining timestamp, machine ID, and sequence.
  • UUID v4 / v7: random / time-ordered 128-bit unique identifiers.
  • Consistent hashing: partitioning where adding or removing a node moves only a small share of keys.
  • Virtual node: one of many ring positions assigned to a physical node.
  • Hash slot: one of a fixed number of key partitions assigned to nodes.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Adding every block to every design. Each adds cost, latency, and failure modes.
  • Storing sessions or files on app servers, blocking horizontal scaling.
  • Using hash(key) % N for nodes that change, causing massive reshuffles.
  • Random UUID v4 primary keys on huge tables without considering index fragmentation.
  • Sending 64-bit IDs as JSON numbers to JavaScript clients.
  • Forgetting that load balancers and gateways need redundancy too.
  • "NoSQL scales, SQL doesn't." Both scale with the right design; choose by access patterns and consistency needs.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a load balancer, a reverse proxy, and an API gateway?
  2. Why should application servers be stateless?
  3. How does an inverted index answer a full-text query?
  4. Compare auto-increment IDs, UUID v4, UUID v7, and Snowflake-style IDs.
  5. Why does hash(key) % N cause problems when N changes, and how does consistent hashing fix it?
  6. What two problems do virtual nodes solve?
