docs.title: Case Study: Chat Application
docs.text: A chat application delivers messages between people in near real time, in one-to-one and group conversations, across phones and browsers that go online and offline constantly. The design challenges are holding millions of long-lived connections, routing each message to whichever server holds the recipient's connection, keeping messages ordered and never lost, and handling receipts, presence, offline users, and media.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• One-to-one (direct) chats and group chats (up to 500 members).
  • Send and receive text messages in real time.
  • Send images and files.
  • Message history, available on every device of a user.
  • Delivery and read receipts (sent → delivered → read).
  • Online presence and "last seen."
  • Offline users receive messages when they reconnect, plus a push notification.
  • Conversation list with the latest message and unread count.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• Scale: 50 million daily active users; 10 million concurrent connections at peak.
  • Latency: message delivered to an online recipient in the same region in under ~300 ms at p99.
  • Ordering: messages appear in the same order for every member of a conversation.
  • Durability: once the sender sees "sent," the message is never lost.
  • No duplicates: retries must not create duplicate messages.
  • Availability: 99.99%; a connection server failure only forces its clients to reconnect.
  • Security: TLS for all traffic; access only for conversation members.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assumptions: 50 M DAU; 40 messages sent per user per day; average 2 recipients per message (mostly direct chats); 200 bytes per stored message (text + metadata); 5% of messages carry media averaging 300 KB; peak = 3×; 20% of DAU connected at peak; one connection server holds 100,000 connections comfortably.

Messages sent:   50 M × 40           = 2 × 10^9 /day
                 2 × 10^9 ÷ 10^5     ≈ 20,000 /s   peak ≈ 60,000 /s
Deliveries:      × 2 recipients      ≈ 40,000 /s   peak ≈ 120,000 /s

Message storage: 2 × 10^9 × 200 B    = 400 GB/day ≈ 146 TB/year
                 × 3 replicas        ≈ 440 TB/year

Media:           5% × 2 × 10^9 × 300 KB = 30 TB/day → object storage + CDN

Connections:     20% × 50 M          = 10 M concurrent
Connection servers: 10 M ÷ 100,000   = 100 (+ headroom → ~150)

Presence: refresh every 60 s per connection → 10 M ÷ 60 ≈ 170,000 writes/s
          (in-memory store with TTLs, sharded)

Conclusions: message storage needs a horizontally scalable store partitioned by conversation; connections need a dedicated, stateful tier; media goes to object storage; presence needs an in-memory store and careful fan-out.

docs.title: API design
docs.text:
Real-time traffic uses a WebSocket connection; history, conversation management, and uploads use REST. See real-time communication.

Connect

GET wss://chat.example.com/ws?ticket=<one-time ticket from an authenticated REST call>
→ 101 Switching Protocols

WebSocket messages (JSON frames)

client → server  { "type": "send", "clientMsgId": "c-7f3a", "conversationId": "cv_91",
                   "body": "On my way!" }
server → client  { "type": "ack", "clientMsgId": "c-7f3a", "messageId": "1290481234567892992",
                   "seq": 1048, "createdAt": "2026-11-07T14:32:10.512Z" }
server → client  { "type": "message", "conversationId": "cv_91", "messageId": "1290481234567892992",
                   "seq": 1048, "senderId": "u_42", "body": "On my way!", "createdAt": "..." }
client → server  { "type": "receipt", "conversationId": "cv_91", "kind": "read", "upToSeq": 1048 }
server → client  { "type": "receipt", "conversationId": "cv_91", "userId": "u_77",
                   "kind": "read", "upToSeq": 1048 }
server → client  { "type": "presence", "userId": "u_77", "status": "online" }

REST

GET  /v1/conversations?cursor=...&limit=20       conversation list with unread counts
POST /v1/conversations                           { "type": "group", "memberIds": [...], "name": "..." }
GET  /v1/conversations/{id}/messages?beforeSeq=1048&limit=50   older history
GET  /v1/conversations/{id}/messages?afterSeq=990               catch up after reconnect
POST /v1/media/uploads                           { "contentType": "image/jpeg", "size": 284113 }
                                                 → { "uploadUrl": "...", "mediaKey": "..." }

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
conversations — id (PK), type (direct | group), name, createdAt, lastSeq, lastMessageAt. For direct chats, a unique pairKey = sorted userA:userB ensures one conversation per pair.

conversation_members — PK (conversationId, userId); role, joinedAt, lastDeliveredSeq, lastReadSeq. A secondary access path (userId, lastMessageAt DESC) powers the conversation list.

messages — the large table, in a wide-column store (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, DynamoDB) designed for "messages of a conversation in order":

Field Notes conversationId + bucket Partition key; bucket (for example, the month) keeps partitions bounded for long-lived chats seq Clustering key, descending: per-conversation order messageId Globally unique, time-ordered (Snowflake-style) senderId, clientMsgId (conversationId, senderId, clientMsgId) deduplicates retries type, body, mediaKey, mediaMeta Text or media reference createdAt Server time

The message is stored once per conversation, not once per member.

devices — (userId, deviceId) → platform, push token, last active.

In Redis (ephemeral):

sessions:{userId}   → hash deviceId → connectionServerId      (who is connected where)
presence:{userId}   → "online", TTL 90 s                      (refreshed by heartbeats)
lastseen:{userId}   → timestamp (also persisted periodically)
recent:{convId}     → list of the last 100 messages          (hot history cache)

docs.title: High-level design
docs.text:
Connection servers are the WebSocket gateways in the diagram. History, group management, and upload requests use REST through a stateless API service that reads the same messages DB; media goes to object storage and is served through the CDN (deep dive 6).

Send path (user A → conversation with user B):

  1. A's device sends send with a clientMsgId over its WebSocket.
  2. The connection server forwards it to the chat service.
  3. The chat service checks membership, deduplicates by clientMsgId, assigns the next seq for the conversation, generates messageId, and persists the message.
  4. It replies to A with ack (A's UI shows "sent").
  5. It looks up the members' sessions in the registry and publishes the message to each relevant connection server's channel.
  6. B's connection server pushes message to B's devices. B's device replies with a delivered receipt.
  7. Members with no active session get a push notification via the queue.

Read path (opening a conversation / reconnecting):

  1. The client knows the last seq it has for each conversation.
  2. On reconnect it calls GET .../messages?afterSeq=<last> for conversations with newer lastSeq values (from the conversation list), filling gaps.
  3. Scrolling up calls ?beforeSeq=...&limit=50, served from the recent-list cache or the messages DB.

docs.title: 1. Connection servers and routing messages between them
docs.text:
Each connection server holds tens of thousands of open WebSockets. It is stateful (the socket lives in its memory), while everything else stays stateless.

  • On connect, the server authenticates the ticket and registers sessions:{userId}[deviceId] = serverId in Redis; on disconnect, it removes the entry.
  • To deliver, the chat service reads the recipients' sessions and publishes to each target server's channel (deliver:{serverId}), batching all recipients on the same server into one publish.
  • Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget: if a connection server misses a publish (restarting), the message is still safe in the database, and the client recovers it through afterSeq sync on reconnect. The database is the source of truth; pub/sub is only a fast path. (A durable log such as Kafka is an alternative when you need replay on the delivery path.)
  • Heartbeats (ping/pong every ~30 s) detect dead connections behind NATs and mobile networks.
  • Deploys and failures: draining a server closes its connections; clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter to avoid a thundering herd onto the remaining servers. The load balancer must support WebSocket upgrades and long idle timeouts. See WebSockets and load balancing.

docs.title: 2. Message IDs, ordering, storage, and history
docs.text:
Two identifiers serve different purposes:

  • messageId — globally unique and roughly time-ordered (Snowflake-style; see building blocks). Used for references (replies, reactions) across the system.
  • seq — a per-conversation sequence number (1, 2, 3 …) that defines the authoritative order and lets clients detect gaps ("I have 1040, server says lastSeq is 1048 → fetch 1041–1048").

Client timestamps are never used for ordering — device clocks are wrong. Ordering is guaranteed per conversation only; there is no global order, and none is needed.

Assigning seq must be atomic per conversation:

  • Atomic increment of lastSeq on the conversation (database conditional update, or Redis INCR conv:{id}:seq persisted with the message), or
  • Route all writes for a conversation to one owner (partition the chat service work by conversationId, for example with Kafka partitions), so a single writer assigns sequence numbers in order.

Idempotency: the client generates clientMsgId and reuses it on retries; the chat service records (conversationId, senderId, clientMsgId) and returns the original ack for duplicates. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency.

Storage and pagination: the partition (conversationId, month) with clustering by seq DESC makes "latest 50 messages" and "50 before seq X" a single sequential read:

SELECT * FROM messages
WHERE conversation_id = ? AND bucket = ? AND seq < ?
ORDER BY seq DESC LIMIT 50;      -- continue into the previous bucket if needed

Cursor pagination by seq stays fast and stable as new messages arrive. The last 100 messages of active conversations are cached in a Redis list.

docs.title: 3. Delivery and read receipts, offline users, and push
docs.text:
Message states from the sender's view:

sending (on device) ─► sent (server persisted, ack received)
                    ─► delivered (a recipient device received it)
                    ─► read (a recipient opened the conversation)

Instead of a row per message per recipient, store watermarks per member: lastDeliveredSeq and lastReadSeq. "Read up to 1048" marks everything at or below 1048 as read with one update. Unread count = conversation.lastSeq − member.lastReadSeq. For groups, "read by 12 of 40" is computed from members' watermarks. Clients batch receipts (for example, send one read receipt when the user stops scrolling), which cuts receipt traffic dramatically.

Offline recipients: if a member has no sessions, the chat service enqueues a push job. The notification service sends via APNs (Apple) or FCM (Google) with minimal content (or just "New message" for privacy), using collapse identifiers (APNs apns-collapse-id, an Android notification tag with FCM) so ten messages do not create ten alerts. See the notification system case study.

When the app opens, it connects and syncs every conversation whose lastSeq exceeds the device's own cursor. Each device keeps its own cursor, so a phone and a laptop both catch up independently (multi-device sync).

docs.title: 4. Group chat fan-out
docs.text:
For a group of up to 500 members, the message is stored once and fanned out on delivery:

  1. Load the member list (cached; invalidated on membership changes).
  2. Look up sessions for all members in one batched Redis call.
  3. Group online recipients by connection server; publish one batch per server.
  4. Enqueue pushes for offline members (respecting their mute settings).

Costs grow with group size × message rate; an active 500-member group is the expensive case. Mitigations: cap group size, rate-limit senders, skip real-time delivery for members who have the conversation muted and backgrounded, and for very large broadcast channels (thousands of members), push only a lightweight "conversation updated" signal and let clients fetch messages when they open the channel.

docs.title: 5. Presence
docs.text:
• The connection server sets presence:{userId} = online with a TTL (for example, 90 s) on connect and refreshes it with heartbeats; if the server dies, the key expires and the user appears offline automatically.
  • On graceful disconnect, it records lastseen:{userId}.
  • Debounce flapping: mobile clients drop and reconnect often; wait a few seconds before broadcasting "offline."
  • Fan-out is the real cost. Broadcasting every status change to every contact is (users × contacts × changes). Instead, clients subscribe to presence only for conversations currently on screen, and the conversation list fetches presence in bulk when opened.
  • Presence is best-effort and eventually consistent — perfectly fine for a green dot.

docs.title: 6. Media messages
docs.text:
1. The client requests an upload URL (POST /v1/media/uploads); the API authorizes it and returns a short-lived presigned URL and mediaKey.
  2. The client uploads directly to object storage, then sends a normal message with mediaKey and metadata (type, size, dimensions).
  3. A background job creates thumbnails and scans the file.
  4. Recipients download through the CDN using signed URLs, checked against conversation membership.

Media never flows through connection servers. See file storage and uploads.

docs.title: Bottlenecks and trade-offs
docs.text:
• What fails first: connection servers (memory and file descriptors) and the session/presence Redis at peak. Scale connection servers horizontally; shard Redis; keep per-connection memory small.
  • Hot conversations: very active large groups concentrate writes on one partition and one seq counter. Single-writer-per-conversation ordering handles thousands of messages per second per conversation; beyond that, product limits (slow mode, size caps) are the practical answer.
  • Partition growth: time buckets keep message partitions bounded; old buckets can move to cheaper storage.
  • Pub/sub reliability vs simplicity: Redis Pub/Sub can drop messages during failures; this is acceptable because clients sync by seq from the database. Kafka would add durability and replay at higher latency and operational cost.
  • Storage per conversation vs per-user inboxes: storing each message once per conversation saves space and keeps ordering simple. The alternative — writing a copy into every recipient's inbox (fan-out on write) — makes "sync my device" a single-partition read but multiplies writes by group size. This design chooses per-conversation storage plus watermarks.
  • Multi-region: users are connected to their nearest region; each conversation has a home region that assigns sequence numbers, and messages are replicated to other regions asynchronously — cross-region members see slightly higher latency.
  • End-to-end encryption (where only devices hold keys) is a strong privacy choice, but it moves search, moderation, and multi-device key management to the clients and complicates server-side features.
  • Alternatives considered: long polling instead of WebSockets (rejected: higher latency and overhead at this scale); client timestamps for ordering (rejected: unreliable clocks).

docs.title: Real-world references
docs.text:
• Slack splits real-time messaging into stateful services: Channel Servers are "stateful and in-memory," each mapped to a subset of channels by consistent hashing (about 16 million channels per host at peak), while Gateway Servers hold users' WebSocket subscriptions and are deployed across multiple geographic regions so clients connect to the nearest one (Real-time Messaging).
  • Discord describes its real-time layer as mostly pub/sub: each user's WebSocket has a session process, and anything published in a server ("guild") "is fanned out to every session connected to it" (How Discord Scaled Elixir to 5,000,000 Concurrent Users).
  • Discord's message storage moved from MongoDB to Cassandra once the data and index no longer fit in RAM. Messages are partitioned by channel and a time bucket (about 10 days of messages, keeping partitions under 100 MB) and ordered by a Snowflake message_id (How Discord Stores Billions of Messages). Later, hot partitions in busy channels hurt latency across the cluster; Discord moved from 177 Cassandra nodes to 72 ScyllaDB nodes and added Rust "data services" that coalesce identical concurrent requests, routed by channel ID with consistent hashing (How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Reconnect storm after a deploy. Symptom: connection attempts and authentication load spike; some users cannot connect. Detect: connections-per-second and auth error metrics. Cause: thousands of clients reconnecting at the same instant. Fix: drain servers gradually; clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter.
  • A busy conversation slows everyone. Symptom: message history loads slowly across the app. Detect: per-partition read latency and request counts in the database. Cause: a hot partition from a very active channel. Fix: cache recent messages, coalesce identical reads, bound partitions with time buckets.
  • Missing messages. Symptom: users report gaps that appear after a refresh. Detect: client telemetry for sequence gaps. Cause: pub/sub deliveries lost during a connection server restart. Fix: clients detect gaps by seq and fetch from the database on reconnect.
  • Ghost presence. Symptom: users appear online long after leaving. Detect: presence keys without recent heartbeats. Cause: a crashed connection server never published "offline." Fix: presence keys with TTLs refreshed by heartbeats.
  • Connection server memory creep. Symptom: memory per server rises until restarts. Detect: memory per open connection over time. Cause: listeners or buffers not released on disconnect. Fix: clean up on every close path; load-test long-lived connections.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why are connection servers stateful while the chat service is stateless, and how does a message reach the server holding the recipient's socket?
  2. Why does the design use both a global messageId and a per-conversation seq?
  3. How do clients recover messages missed while offline or during a connection server crash?
  4. Why store read receipts as per-member watermarks instead of per-message rows?
  5. How does group fan-out work, and what changes for very large channels?
  6. Why is presence fan-out expensive, and how do subscriptions reduce it?

docs.text:

  • Firebase Cloud Messaging documentation

docs.title: Case Study: News Feed
docs.text: A news feed shows each user a stream of recent posts from the accounts they follow, like the home timeline of a social network. The central problem is that a single post must appear in many feeds, and a single feed draws from many authors. Deciding when to do that work — when a post is written, when a feed is read, or a mix — shapes the whole design, especially for accounts with millions of followers.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• Users create posts with text and optional images.
  • Users follow and unfollow other users.
  • The home feed shows posts from followed accounts, newest or ranked first.
  • Infinite scroll: load more posts as the user scrolls.
  • Each post shows its author, media, and like/comment counts.
  • New posts appear in followers' feeds within seconds.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• Scale: 300 million monthly users, 100 million daily active users.
  • Latency: feed load under ~300 ms at p99.
  • Availability: feed reads 99.99%; posting 99.9%.
  • Consistency: eventual — a few seconds before a post reaches followers is fine; authors must see their own post immediately.
  • Skewed graph: most users have hundreds of followers; some have tens of millions.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assumptions: 100 M DAU; 10 feed loads per user per day; 10% of DAU post once per day; average 200 followers per poster; 1 KB per post record; 30% of posts include a 1 MB image; peak = 3×; ~70 bytes per feed entry in a Redis sorted set (ID + score + overhead).

Posts:          100 M × 10%          = 10 M /day   → ~100 /s   peak ~300 /s
Feed reads:     100 M × 10           = 1 B /day    → ~10,000 /s  peak ~30,000 /s

Fan-out on write (average):
                10 M posts × 200 followers = 2 B feed inserts/day
                                            → ~20,000 /s  peak ~60,000 /s
One celebrity post with 50 M followers      → 50 M inserts for one post (!)

Post storage:   10 M × 1 KB          = 10 GB/day   ≈ 3.65 TB/year
Media:          3 M images × 1 MB    = 3 TB/day    → object storage + CDN

Feed cache (active users only, 200 entries each):
                100 M × 200 × 70 B   ≈ 1.4 TB      → sharded Redis cluster
Follow graph:   300 M × 200 follows  = 6 × 10^10 edges, stored in both
                directions (followers and following)

Conclusions: reads outnumber posts ~100:1, which favors precomputing feeds at write time — except for very high-follower accounts, whose fan-out would be enormous. Feeds should store post IDs, not post bodies.

docs.title: API design
docs.text:
POST /v1/posts
{ "text": "Sunset over the bay", "mediaKeys": ["m_8f3a"] }
→ 201 { "id": "1290481234567892992", "createdAt": "2026-11-07T18:02:11Z" }

GET /v1/feed?limit=20
GET /v1/feed?limit=20&cursor=eyJiZWZvcmUiOiIxMjkwNDgxMjM0NTY3ODkyOTkyIn0
→ 200
{ "items": [
    { "postId": "1290481234567892992",
      "author": { "id": "u_42", "handle": "maya", "avatarUrl": "https://cdn..." },
      "text": "Sunset over the bay",
      "media": [ { "url": "https://cdn.example.com/m_8f3a_1080.webp", "width": 1080, "height": 720 } ],
      "likeCount": 31, "commentCount": 4,
      "createdAt": "2026-11-07T18:02:11Z" } ],
  "nextCursor": "eyJiZWZvcmUiOiIxMjkwNDgxMTk5ODc2NTQzMjEwIn0" }

POST   /v1/users/{id}/follow     → 204
DELETE /v1/users/{id}/follow     → 204
GET    /v1/users/{id}/posts?cursor=...   → author's own timeline

Post IDs are returned as strings because 64-bit IDs exceed JavaScript's safe integer range. The cursor is opaque to clients. See API design best practices.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
users — id (PK), handle (unique), name, avatarKey, followerCount, followingCount.

posts — postId (PK; Snowflake-style, time-ordered), authorId, text, mediaKeys, createdAt, deletedAt. Index (authorId, postId DESC) serves each author's timeline — used by fan-out on read.

Follow graph — stored twice, one table per access direction:

Table Partition key Sort key Used for followers followeeId followerId Fan-out on write: "who should receive this post?" following followerId followeeId Fan-out on read: "whose posts do I pull?"

A wide-column or key-value store handles billions of edges partitioned this way; a graph database is not required for one-hop lookups.

Home feeds (precomputed) — Redis sorted set per user:

feed:{userId}  → members: postId, score: createdAt in milliseconds
                 trimmed to the newest ~200–500 entries

The score is the creation time, not the 64-bit post ID itself: sorted-set scores are double-precision floats, which represent integers exactly only up to 2^53, so large Snowflake IDs would lose precision and misorder.

Post cache — post:{postId} → serialized post, for fast batched hydration. Counters (likes, comments) are kept in a separate counter service/cache and merged in at read time.

docs.title: High-level design
docs.text:
Write path: the post service stores the post and returns immediately; the PostCreated event lets fan-out workers asynchronously add the post ID to each follower's precomputed feed. The author's own feed is updated synchronously so they see their post at once.

Read path: the feed service reads post IDs from the user's precomputed feed, merges recent posts from any high-follower accounts the user follows, ranks the candidates, hydrates the top ones in batch, filters out deleted or blocked content, and returns a page with a cursor.

docs.title: 1. Fan-out on write, fan-out on read, and the hybrid
docs.text:
Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull) When work happens When a post is created: insert its ID into every follower's feed When a feed is read: fetch recent posts from every followed account and merge Read cost Very low (one sorted-set read) High (N author timelines per read, merge, sort) Write cost Proportional to follower count Minimal Freshness Seconds of fan-out delay Always current Problem case Celebrities: 50 M inserts per post; wasted work for inactive followers Users following thousands of accounts; heavy reads at 30,000/s

Hybrid (chosen):

  • Normal accounts (below a threshold, for example 100,000 followers): fan out on write.
  • High-follower accounts (above the threshold): do not fan out. At read time, the feed service pulls their recent posts (from the cached author timeline) for users who follow them and merges them in. Each celebrity's recent posts are read by millions of users, so their timelines stay hot in cache.
  • Inactive users (no visit in, say, 30 days) are skipped during fan-out. When they return, their feed is rebuilt on demand by pulling, then kept warm by push again.

This bounds the write amplification while keeping reads cheap for the common case.

docs.title: 2. The feed cache
docs.text:
• Store post IDs only (with a score), not post bodies. A post edit or like count change then never requires updating millions of feed entries; hydration fetches current data.
  • Trim each feed to the newest ~200–500 entries (ZADD then ZREMRANGEBYRANK); older history is served by pulling if anyone scrolls that far.
  • Hydration fetches posts with one batched read (MGET on the post cache, falling back to the posts DB for misses), plus authors and counters, in parallel.
  • Cache miss (evicted or new user): rebuild by pulling from followed authors' timelines — expensive, so rate-limit rebuilds and keep feeds for active users in memory. Persisting feeds to a wide-column store is an option if rebuilds become too costly.
  • Sizing: ~1.4 TB for active users, sharded by userId across a Redis cluster with replicas. See Redis as a cache and cache failure modes.

docs.title: 3. Ranking basics
docs.text:
A chronological feed sorts by time. A ranked feed tries to show the most relevant posts first, in stages:

  1. Candidate generation: IDs from the precomputed feed + celebrity pulls (a few hundred candidates).
  2. Feature lookup: recency, the user's affinity with the author (past interactions), engagement so far (likes, comments, shares), content type, whether the user has already seen it.
  3. Scoring: a weighted formula or a machine-learning model predicting engagement. A simple illustrative formula combines engagement, affinity, and time decay:
score = (1 + likes + 2 × comments) × affinity(user, author) / (ageHours + 2)^1.5
  1. Re-ranking: diversity rules (avoid five posts in a row from one author), boosting fresh posts, removing already-seen ones.

Ranking must fit the latency budget: keep candidate sets small, precompute features, and cache affinity scores.

docs.title: 4. Cursor pagination
docs.text:
Offset pagination (?page=3) breaks when new posts arrive at the top: items shift down, so the user sees duplicates or misses posts.

  • Chronological feeds: the cursor holds the score (timestamp) and post ID of the last item seen. The next page is "the 20 newest entries at or below that timestamp," skipping entries already returned that share the same millisecond:
ZRANGE feed:{userId} 1793815331000 -inf BYSCORE REV LIMIT 0 21
→ drop items up to and including the cursor's post ID, return 20

(ZRANGE ... BYSCORE REV needs Redis 6.2+; older versions use ZREVRANGEBYSCORE.)

  • Ranked feeds: rankings change between requests, so a cursor on score is unstable. Rank once when the user opens the feed, store the ordered list of IDs as a short-lived feed session (for example, in Redis for 30 minutes), and page through that snapshot. Newer posts surface through a "New posts" prompt that starts a fresh session.

Cursors are encoded (for example, base64 JSON) so clients treat them as opaque and the server can change their contents.

docs.title: 5. Media and the CDN
docs.text: Images are uploaded directly to object storage with presigned URLs, then a background job creates resized variants (thumbnail, 480 px, 1080 px) in modern formats. Feed responses contain CDN URLs, never bytes. Variant URLs are immutable (a new upload gets a new key), so the CDN can cache them for a long time. Clients request the size that fits the screen. See CDN and file storage and uploads.

docs.title: 6. Consistency expectations
docs.text:
• Eventual consistency is acceptable: followers may see a post a few seconds after it is created; counts may lag slightly.
  • Read-your-writes for authors: write to the author's own feed synchronously (or merge their latest posts on read) so they never wonder whether posting worked.
  • Deletes: mark the post deleted in the posts DB and cache; hydration drops deleted posts. Removing the ID from millions of feeds happens lazily or not at all — it simply never renders.
  • Unfollow: filter the unfollowed author at read time immediately; clean their entries out of the feed asynchronously.
  • Follow: asynchronously backfill the new followee's recent posts into the follower's feed.
  • Privacy changes and blocks are enforced at read time (filtering), because cached feeds may contain stale entries.

See consistency and the CAP theorem.

docs.title: Bottlenecks and trade-offs
docs.text:
• What fails first: fan-out workers during spikes (a burst of posts from popular-but-below-threshold accounts) — the queue backs up and feeds lag. Scale workers on queue depth; tune the celebrity threshold; prioritize fan-out to recently active users first.
  • Redis memory: feed caches dominate memory; keep only active users and short feeds, store IDs only.
  • Hot posts: a viral post's cache key is read by millions; use local in-process caches on feed servers and cache replicas.
  • Ranking latency: model scoring is the most expensive step; bound the candidate count and precompute features.
  • Alternatives considered: pure pull (simple writes, but too expensive at 30,000 feed reads per second for users following hundreds of accounts); pure push (celebrity posts cause tens of millions of writes); storing full posts in feeds (fast reads, but edits, deletes, and counts become massive update fan-outs).
  • Trade-off accepted: feeds are eventually consistent and slightly stale in exchange for fast, cheap reads.

docs.title: Real-world references
docs.text: • Facebook's Multifeed assembles News Feed when it is requested. Aggregators are the "query engine that accepts user queries and retrieves News Feed info from backend storage," doing aggregation, ranking, and filtering; leaf servers form a distributed storage layer that indexes the most recent News Feed actions in memory (about 20 leaves make one full replica); tailers feed user actions into the leaves. Separating aggregators (CPU-heavy) from leaves (memory-heavy) let each scale independently and gave a reported 40% efficiency improvement (Serving Facebook Multifeed). This is a fan-out-on-read design, made fast by keeping recent activity in memory — the opposite end of the trade-off from precomputed feeds.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Followers see posts late. Symptom: new posts take minutes to appear. Detect: fan-out lag metric (time from post to fan-out complete) and queue depth. Cause: a burst from popular accounts just under the celebrity threshold. Fix: autoscale fan-out workers on queue depth, lower the threshold, fan out to recently active users first.
  • Feed cache evictions. Symptom: slow feeds and expensive rebuilds. Detect: Redis memory usage and evicted-keys metrics, rebuild rate. Cause: feeds for too many users or too many entries per feed. Fix: trim feeds, cache only active users, add shards.
  • Viral post overloads one shard. Symptom: one cache node saturated. Detect: per-node CPU and top-key reports. Cause: millions of hydrations of the same post. Fix: in-process caching of hot posts and cache replicas.
  • Ranking blows the latency budget. Symptom: feed p99 above target. Detect: distributed traces showing time per stage. Cause: too many candidates or slow feature lookups. Fix: cap candidates, precompute and cache features.
  • Deleted posts still visible. Symptom: reports of removed content in feeds. Detect: user reports, audit of deleted IDs served. Cause: stale post cache entries. Fix: invalidate the post cache on delete and check deletion status during hydration.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Compare fan-out on write and fan-out on read. Which would you use for an account with 50 million followers, and why?
  2. How does the hybrid approach combine both, and what decides the threshold?
  3. Why should the feed cache store post IDs rather than full posts?
  4. Why does offset pagination fail for feeds, and how do cursors and feed sessions fix it?
  5. How does the design give authors read-your-writes consistency while followers see eventual consistency?
  6. How are deletes and unfollows handled without rewriting millions of feeds?

docs.title: Case Study: Notification System
docs.text: A notification system lets every other service in a company say "tell this user that X happened" without knowing how. It decides which channels to use — mobile push, SMS, email, in-app — according to the user's preferences, renders the right template, sends through third-party providers, retries failures, avoids duplicates and spam, and tracks what was delivered. Its challenges are reliability across unreliable providers, respecting user choices and regulations, and handling huge campaign bursts without delaying urgent messages.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• Internal services send a notification for one user or a list of users, with a category (security, order updates, marketing) and template data.
  • Channels: mobile push (APNs for iOS, FCM for Android), SMS, email, and in-app (a notification center plus a live badge).
  • Templates per channel and language, with variables.
  • User preferences: per category and channel, global unsubscribe, quiet hours; mandatory categories (security alerts) cannot be disabled.
  • Scheduling: send at a specific time, including "9 AM in the user's time zone."
  • Delivery tracking: queued, sent, delivered, opened/read, failed, bounced.
  • No duplicates when callers or queues retry; rate limits so users are not spammed.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• Scale: 50 million users; ~60 million notifications per day; campaigns of 50 million messages within an hour.
  • Latency by priority: high-priority messages (sign-in codes, security alerts) delivered to the provider within seconds, even during campaigns; bulk marketing can take hours.
  • Reliability: no accepted notification is lost (at-least-once processing, deduplicated).
  • Isolation: an outage at one channel's provider must not delay others.
  • Compliance: honor opt-outs and consent (email unsubscribe, SMS STOP).

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assumptions: per day — 20 M push, 2 M SMS, 10 M email, 30 M in-app notifications; 1 KB of stored metadata per delivery; 90-day retention for delivery logs; a marketing campaign to 50 M users in one hour.

Daily total:      ~62 M /day   → ~620 /s average  (62 × 10^6 ÷ 10^5)
Campaign peak:    50 M ÷ 3,600 s ≈ 14,000 /s on top of normal traffic

Delivery log:     62 M × 1 KB   = 62 GB/day
90-day retention: 62 GB × 90    ≈ 5.6 TB  (× replicas)

SMS:              2 M /day ≈ 20 /s average — limited mainly by provider
                  and sender-number throughput, not by our servers

Conclusions: average load is modest; the design is driven by bursts, priorities, provider limits, and reliability. Queues absorb campaign spikes; priority separation keeps urgent messages fast.

docs.title: API design
docs.text:
Send (internal, called by other services):

POST /v1/notifications
Idempotency-Key: order-812-shipped
{ "userIds": ["u_42"],
  "category": "order_updates",
  "templateId": "order_shipped",
  "data": { "orderId": "812", "eta": "2026-11-09" },
  "priority": "normal",                 ("high" | "normal" | "bulk")
  "channels": ["push", "email", "in_app"],  (optional; default from category)
  "sendAt": "2026-11-08T09:00:00",      (optional; local time when "timeZone": "user")
  "expiresAt": "2026-11-10T00:00:00Z" } (optional; drop if not sent by then)

202 Accepted
{ "notificationId": "n_7f3a9c", "status": "accepted" }

GET /v1/notifications/n_7f3a9c
→ { "id": "n_7f3a9c", "deliveries": [
      { "channel": "push",  "status": "sent" },
      { "channel": "email", "status": "delivered" },
      { "channel": "in_app","status": "read" } ] }

User-facing:

GET  /v1/me/notifications?cursor=...         in-app notification center
POST /v1/me/notifications/{id}/read
GET  /v1/me/notification-preferences
PUT  /v1/me/notification-preferences         { "marketing": { "email": false, "push": true }, ... }
POST /v1/me/devices                          { "platform": "ios", "pushToken": "..." }

Provider callbacks (webhooks): delivery, bounce, and complaint events from email and SMS providers, verified by signature. See webhooks.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
Table / collection Key Contents templates (templateId, channel, locale, version) Subject, body with placeholders, status (draft/approved) preferences (userId) Per category × channel switches, quiet hours, time zone, global unsubscribe consents (userId, channel, purpose) When and how consent/opt-out was recorded (audit) devices (userId, deviceId) Platform, push token, active, last seen suppressions (channel, address) Hard-bounced emails, complaint addresses, numbers that sent STOP notifications notificationId; unique (sourceService, idempotencyKey) Category, template, data, priority, sendAt, expiresAt deliveries (notificationId, channel, target) Status, provider, providerMessageId, attempts, last error, timestamps; index on providerMessageId for webhooks inbox (userId, createdAt DESC) In-app items: title, body, deep link, readAt

Delivery logs are high volume and time-based; store them in a partitioned table or a store with TTL so old rows expire automatically.

docs.title: High-level design
docs.text:
Each queue also has a dead-letter queue with alerting; the worker-side retry and failover logic is shown in deep dive 2.

Send path:

  1. A service calls the API with an idempotency key. The API validates the request, stores the notification (or returns the existing one for a repeated key), and responds 202.
  2. Future sendAt values go to the scheduler; others go straight to the orchestrator queue.
  3. The orchestrator applies preferences, consent, suppressions, quiet hours, and rate limits; renders each channel's content; creates deliveries rows in queued state; and enqueues one job per channel and target into that channel's high-priority or bulk queue.
  4. Channel workers send to providers, record the result, and retry or dead-letter failures.
  5. Provider webhooks update delivery status (delivered, bounced). In-app workers write to the inbox and push a live badge update to connected clients.

Read path (in-app center): the client lists inbox for the user with cursor pagination; unread count is cached per user.

docs.title: 1. Preferences, opt-outs, and compliance
docs.text:
For each notification and channel, the orchestrator asks:

Is the category mandatory (security, legal, transactional)?  → send (respect only hard limits)
Otherwise:
  global unsubscribe for this channel?        → skip
  category × channel disabled by the user?    → skip
  address suppressed (bounce, complaint, STOP)? → skip
  consent required and missing (e.g. marketing SMS)? → skip
  within quiet hours and not urgent?          → delay until quiet hours end
  • Email: include List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post headers for one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058), required by major mailbox providers for bulk senders; honor unsubscribes promptly; suppress hard bounces and spam complaints to protect sender reputation.
  • SMS: honor STOP keywords and record consent; marketing SMS needs prior opt-in in many jurisdictions. Respect local sending hours.
  • Push: the operating system also lets users disable notifications; an invalid or unregistered token response means deactivate that device.
  • Templates: render per locale, escape variables in HTML email, and respect channel limits — SMS segments (160 GSM-7 characters, or 70 when non-GSM characters such as emoji force UCS-2), and push payloads of about 4 KB for APNs and FCM.

Record every consent and opt-out change with a timestamp and source — this is the audit trail regulators ask for.

docs.title: 2. A queue per channel, priorities, retries, and dead letters
docs.text:
Separate queues per channel give isolation and independent scaling: an email provider outage fills the email queue while push keeps flowing, and SMS workers can be throttled to the provider's throughput without affecting anyone else.

Priority lanes within each channel (high and bulk) ensure a sign-in code never waits behind 50 million campaign emails. Workers always drain the high lane first, or dedicated workers serve it.

Retries:

Error Example Action Transient Timeout, provider 5xx, 429 Retry with exponential backoff and jitter; honor Retry-After Permanent (recipient) Invalid or unregistered push token, hard bounce, invalid phone number Do not retry; deactivate device or add to suppressions Permanent (content) Template rendering error, payload too large Do not retry; alert the sending team Expired expiresAt passed (an OTP after 5 minutes) Drop and mark expired

After the maximum attempts, jobs go to a dead-letter queue with the error; alerts fire when DLQs grow; operators can replay after fixing the cause. See timeouts, retries, and idempotency and messaging patterns.

docs.title: 3. Deduplication and idempotency
docs.text:
Duplicates can enter at three points:

  1. The caller retries the API request → the unique (sourceService, idempotencyKey) returns the existing notification instead of creating another.
  2. The queue redelivers a job (at-least-once delivery) → before sending, the worker atomically moves the delivery row from queued to sending with a conditional update; if the update matches no row, another worker already took it, so skip.
  3. The worker crashes after the provider accepted the message but before recording sent → a retry may send again. True exactly-once across a third-party provider is impossible; keep this window tiny, and use provider idempotency keys where available.

Push also supports collapsing, useful for "order status" updates. With APNs, notifications that share an apns-collapse-id are shown as a single notification. With FCM, an Android notification tag makes a new notification replace one already shown in the notification drawer, while collapse_key lets a newer message replace an older one that has not been delivered yet (for example, while the device is offline). See delivery guarantees.

docs.title: 4. Rate limiting, batching, and scheduling
docs.text:
• Per-user limits: for example, at most 3 marketing pushes per day and 1 per hour; transactional messages are exempt or have separate limits. Implemented with token buckets in Redis (see the rate limiter case study).
  • Digests: instead of "Alex liked your photo" ten times, hold low-priority events for a short window and send one "Alex and 9 others liked your photo."
  • Per-provider limits: SMS throughput depends on the sender number type; APNs and FCM enforce limits too. Workers use a token bucket per provider account to stay under them.
  • Campaign pacing: large campaigns are enqueued gradually (or consumed at a capped rate) so they never saturate providers or downstream systems such as the app servers that users open after tapping a notification.
  • Scheduling: sendAt is stored with an index on (status, sendAt); the scheduler moves due notifications to the orchestrator queue (or uses delayed jobs). "9 AM local time" is computed per user from their time zone, so a global campaign runs over about 24 hours. Before sending, workers re-check that the notification was not cancelled. See background jobs and scheduling.

docs.title: 5. Delivery tracking and provider failover
docs.text:
Tracking: each deliveries row moves through queued → sending → sent → delivered → opened/read, or to failed, bounced, suppressed, expired. Sources of truth differ by channel:

  • Email and SMS: providers send webhooks (delivered, bounced, complained, undelivered) referencing providerMessageId.
  • Push: APNs and FCM confirm they accepted the message, not that the device displayed it; "opened" comes from the app reporting a tap.
  • Email opens via tracking pixels are unreliable (some mail clients prefetch images); clicks are a better signal.
  • In-app: the client reports reads.

Aggregate these into analytics per template and campaign.

Provider failover: wrap each channel's providers behind one interface. For SMS and email, configure a primary and a secondary provider; a circuit breaker watches error rates and latency and switches traffic to the secondary when the primary degrades.

  • Email failover requires both providers to be authenticated for your sending domain (SPF, DKIM, DMARC alignment), and sudden volume shifts can hurt deliverability — keep the secondary warm with a small share of traffic.
  • Push has no alternative path: only APNs delivers to iOS devices and FCM to most Android devices, so outages are handled by queuing and retrying.

docs.title: Bottlenecks and trade-offs
docs.text:
• What fails first: third-party providers (rate limits, outages) — not our servers. Queues, per-provider throttling, retries, and failover handle it.
  • Campaign bursts vs urgent messages: solved with priority lanes and campaign pacing; without them, OTPs would arrive late during sales events.
  • Preference lookups at 14,000 messages/s: cache preferences and suppressions in Redis or in-process with short TTLs; invalidate on change.
  • At-least-once vs duplicates: accepted rare duplicates in exchange for never losing messages; minimized with idempotency keys, conditional status updates, and collapse IDs.
  • One orchestrator vs per-service sending: centralizing gives consistent preferences, compliance, and tracking, at the cost of a shared dependency — so the API and queues are run with high availability.
  • Alternatives considered: one queue for all channels (rejected: one slow provider blocks everything); synchronous sending in the API (rejected: provider latency and outages would propagate to callers); storing rendered content for every notification forever (rejected: storage cost; keep template ID, version, and data instead).

docs.title: Real-world references
docs.text:
• Netflix's RENO (Rapid Event Notification System) sends server-initiated updates to member devices. Because a phone is almost always reachable but a smart TV is online only while in use, Netflix "chose a hybrid Push AND Pull communication model": the server pushes to devices immediately, and devices also call home at stages of the app lifecycle. Events are routed to priority-based Amazon SQS queues with matching processing clusters, so each priority can be tuned and scaled independently, and a Cassandra store keeps each device's notifications so devices can poll at their own cadence; online devices are reached over Zuul Push persistent connections (Rapid Event Notification System at Netflix).
  • Slack found that answering whether a notification was sent, where it was sent, whether it was viewed, and whether it was opened took several days and expertise across the whole stack, so it built end-to-end tracing of the notification flow across its backend (Tracing Notifications). Delivery tracking is a first-class requirement, not an afterthought.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Campaigns delay one-time codes. Symptom: sign-in codes arrive minutes late during a marketing send. Detect: age of the oldest message per queue and priority. Cause: urgent and bulk messages share a queue or workers. Fix: separate priority lanes with dedicated capacity; pace campaigns.
  • A provider outage. Symptom: SMS or email error rate jumps. Detect: per-provider error-rate and latency alerts. Cause: the provider is degraded. Fix: circuit breaker failover to the secondary provider; queue and retry for push, which has no alternative path.
  • Duplicate notifications. Symptom: users receive the same message twice after a deploy. Detect: duplicate-send metrics by idempotency key, user reports. Cause: queue redelivery after workers restarted mid-send. Fix: conditional queued → sending status updates, provider idempotency keys, push collapse IDs.
  • Many invalid push tokens. Symptom: a rising share of push sends fail. Detect: invalid/unregistered token error rate. Cause: uninstalled apps and rotated tokens. Fix: deactivate tokens on those responses; refresh tokens when the app starts.
  • Email lands in spam. Symptom: open and click rates fall. Detect: bounce and complaint rates from provider webhooks. Cause: sending to stale addresses or ignoring complaints. Fix: suppression lists, domain authentication, gradual volume changes.
  • Messages at 3 AM. Symptom: complaints about night-time alerts. Detect: send-time histogram in users' local time. Cause: schedules computed in server time. Fix: store user time zones; enforce quiet hours at send time.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the system use a separate queue per channel and separate priority lanes?
  2. Which errors should be retried, which should not, and what happens after the last retry?
  3. Identify three places duplicates can arise and how each is prevented.
  4. How do user preferences, suppressions, consent, and quiet hours combine to decide whether to send?
  5. Why can't push notifications fail over to another provider, while SMS and email can?
  6. How would you send a campaign at 9 AM local time to users worldwide without overloading providers?

docs.title: Case Study: Distributed Rate Limiter
docs.text: A rate limiter decides, for every incoming request, whether the client is still within its allowance — for example, 1,000 requests per minute for a paid API key, or 5 sign-in attempts per 15 minutes per account. In a distributed system with dozens of gateway or service instances, the hard parts are keeping counts accurate across instances, adding almost no latency, and staying safe when the limiter's own storage fails.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• Limit requests per client key: API key, user ID, or IP address.
  • Support multiple rules per request: per plan tier (free, pro, enterprise), per endpoint (stricter limits on POST /login or /v1/exports), and global per-client limits.
  • Allow short bursts while enforcing an average rate.
  • Reject over-limit requests with 429 Too Many Requests, Retry-After, and rate-limit headers; tell allowed requests how much quota remains.
  • Change rules and per-customer overrides without a redeploy.
  • A shadow (dry-run) mode to test new rules by logging would-be rejections.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• Low latency: adds under ~2 ms at p99 to each request.
  • Accurate enough: consistent counts across all instances; small over-admission during failures is tolerable, systematic multiplication of limits is not.
  • Highly available: a limiter failure must not take the API down.
  • Scalable: handle the platform's peak request rate.
  • Observable: metrics on allowed and rejected requests per rule and client.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assumptions: 1 million requests per second at peak across the API platform; on average 2 rules evaluated per request; 50 million distinct client keys per day; ~100 bytes of state per (rule, client) key in Redis, including overhead.

Checks per second   = 1,000,000 req/s × 2 rules  = 2,000,000 rule checks/s
With one Lua call per request (rules colocated, see deep dive 4)
                    → ~1,000,000 Redis script calls/s

Redis throughput: a script call costs more than a plain GET; assume a
conservative ~50,000–100,000 script calls/s per shard (measure!)
                    → ~10–20 primary shards, each with a replica

Memory = 50 M clients × 2 rules × 100 B = 10 GB  (+ replicas)

Latency budget: same-zone Redis round trip ≈ 0.3–0.5 ms → fits in 2 ms

Conclusions: memory is small; throughput and latency drive the design. The counter store must be sharded, and each request should need one round trip.

docs.title: API design
docs.text:
The limiter runs inside the API gateway (or as a shared middleware library); there is no extra network hop to a separate service. Its internal interface:

check(request) → { allowed: boolean,
                   rule: "pro-api-default",
                   limit: 1000, remaining: 412,
                   resetSeconds: 23, retryAfterSeconds: 0 }

Rule management API (internal, admin-only):

PUT /v1/rate-limit-rules/pro-api-default
{ "match": { "pathPrefix": "/v1/", "plan": "pro" },
  "key": "apiKey",
  "algorithm": "token_bucket",
  "capacity": 200,            (burst size)
  "refillPerSecond": 16.67,   (≈ 1,000 per minute)
  "mode": "enforce" }         ("shadow" logs only)

200 OK { "id": "pro-api-default", "version": 7 }

What clients see:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
RateLimit-Policy: "default";q=1000;w=60
RateLimit: "default";r=412;t=23

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 4
RateLimit-Policy: "default";q=1000;w=60
RateLimit: "default";r=0;t=4
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{ "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/rate-limited",
  "title": "Too many requests", "status": 429,
  "detail": "Limit of 1000 requests per minute exceeded for this API key.",
  "retryAfterSeconds": 4 }

RateLimit-Policy and RateLimit follow the IETF rate-limit header fields draft; the exact syntax has changed between drafts, so many APIs still also send the older X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset. Retry-After is standard (RFC 9110). See HTTP headers.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
Rules (source of truth in a database or config repository; cached in every gateway's memory):

Field Example Notes id pro-api-default Unique match path prefix, method, plan tier Most specific rule wins key apiKey, userId, ip, ip+email What is counted algorithm token_bucket, sliding_window capacity / refillPerSecond 200 / 16.67 Token bucket parameters limit / windowSeconds 5 / 900 Window algorithm parameters mode enforce, shadow Shadow logs instead of blocking failMode open, closed Behavior when Redis is unavailable version 7 Gateways reload on change

Per-client overrides: (clientKey, ruleId) → custom limits for negotiated enterprise contracts.

Counter state (Redis):

key:   rl:{api_key_8f3c}:pro-api-default        (hash)
value: { tokens: "187.4", ts: "1793812345123" } (tokens left, last refill ms)
TTL:   time to refill the bucket completely (state disappears when idle)

The {api_key_8f3c} part is a Redis Cluster hash tag: only the text in braces is hashed, so all of one client's rule keys land in the same slot and can be updated by one script.

docs.title: High-level design
docs.text:
Request path:

  1. The gateway authenticates the request and determines the client key — API key or user ID from the verified credentials; for anonymous traffic, the client IP, correctly derived behind proxies (see rate limiting and throttling).
  2. It matches the request against cached rules (path, method, plan).
  3. It runs one atomic Lua script in Redis covering all matching rules.
  4. If any enforced rule denies, it returns 429 with headers. Otherwise it forwards the request with the remaining-quota headers.
  5. It records metrics; shadow-mode denials are logged but not enforced.

Rule update path: an admin updates a rule → the rules DB increments the version → a change event (pub/sub) tells gateways to reload; gateways also poll periodically as a fallback.

docs.title: 1. Choosing the algorithm
docs.text:
Rule type Algorithm Why General API limits per key Token bucket Allows bursts, enforces average, cheap state (2 numbers) Simple per-minute/hour quotas Sliding window counter Smooths boundary bursts with two counters Sign-in / OTP attempts Sliding window log or small fixed window Exactness matters more than memory at low limits Monthly plan quotas Usage counters aggregated asynchronously Billing-style accuracy, not per-request blocking

Algorithm details (fixed window, sliding log, sliding counter, token bucket, leaky bucket) are explained in rate limiting and throttling. This design uses the token bucket for most rules.

docs.title: 2. Atomicity with Redis and Lua
docs.text:
A naive implementation reads the count, decides in the gateway, and writes back. Two gateway instances handling the same client at the same moment both read tokens = 1, both allow, both write 0 — the limit is exceeded.

Gateway A: GET → 1 token ─┐
Gateway B: GET → 1 token ─┤  both see 1
Gateway A: allow, SET 0  ─┤
Gateway B: allow, SET 0  ─┘  two requests allowed with one token

Redis executes a Lua script atomically — no other command runs in between — so read, compute, and write happen as one step. The script also uses Redis's own clock (TIME), avoiding clock differences between gateway machines.

-- KEYS[1]: bucket key   ARGV: capacity, refill tokens/second, cost
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate     = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local cost     = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local t   = redis.call("TIME")                       -- { seconds, microseconds }
local now = tonumber(t[1]) * 1000 + math.floor(tonumber(t[2]) / 1000)

local state  = redis.call("HMGET", KEYS[1], "tokens", "ts")
local tokens = tonumber(state[1]) or capacity
local last   = tonumber(state[2]) or now

-- refill for the time elapsed since the last request, up to capacity
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + math.max(0, now - last) * rate / 1000)

local allowed, retryAfterMs = 0, 0
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
else
  retryAfterMs = math.ceil((cost - tokens) / rate * 1000)
end

redis.call("HSET", KEYS[1], "tokens", tokens, "ts", now)
redis.call("PEXPIRE", KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity / rate * 1000) + 1000)

return { allowed, math.floor(tokens), retryAfterMs }

Calling it from Node.js with ioredis:

import Redis from "ioredis";
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

const redis = new Redis.Cluster([{ host: process.env.REDIS_HOST, port: 6379 }]);

// Registers the script once; ioredis uses EVALSHA and reloads it if needed
redis.defineCommand("tokenBucket", {
  numberOfKeys: 1,
  lua: readFileSync(new URL("./token-bucket.lua", import.meta.url), "utf8"),
});

export async function checkTokenBucket(clientKey, rule) {
  const key = `rl:{${clientKey}}:${rule.id}`;
  const [allowed, remaining, retryAfterMs] = await redis.tokenBucket(
    key, rule.capacity, rule.refillPerSecond, 1
  );
  return { allowed: allowed === 1, remaining, retryAfterMs };
}

The script is shown for a single rule to keep it readable. The production version takes several keys (one per matching rule, all sharing the client's hash tag), checks every bucket first, and only deducts tokens if all of them allow the request.

docs.title: 3. Placement: gateway, service, or sidecar
docs.text:
Placement Pros Cons Edge (CDN / WAF) Stops volumetric attacks before your network Coarse rules; little business context API gateway One place for all services; per-key and per-plan limits; consistent headers Gateway must know identities and plans Service middleware Business context (per action, per tenant, cost-based limits) Each service must integrate; risk of inconsistency Sidecar / central service (e.g. Envoy global rate limit service) Language-agnostic; central policy Extra hop or extra component to run

Choice: volumetric protection at the edge; per-key and per-plan limits at the API gateway using the shared Redis cluster; action-specific limits (sign-in attempts, SMS sends, exports) in the owning service, using the same library and Redis so behavior is consistent.

docs.title: 4. Multiple rules, races, and accuracy
docs.text:
• One round trip for all rules: using the hash tag, all keys for a client are in one slot, so a single script can check every matching rule and only consume tokens if all allow — avoiding wasted tokens when one rule passes and another fails.
  • Rule keys for different clients spread across shards evenly.
  • Huge single tenants (a hot key doing 100,000 requests/s) overload one shard. Split such a bucket into N sub-buckets (rl:{key:0} … rl:{key:7}), each with 1/N of the rate, and pick one at random per request; accuracy drops slightly, throughput scales.
  • Local pre-allocation for very high volumes: each gateway takes a small batch of tokens from Redis and spends them locally, returning to Redis only when its batch runs out. This cuts Redis calls dramatically at the cost of brief over- or under-admission.
  • Precision is "good enough" by design: rate limiting protects capacity and fairness; it is not a billing ledger.

docs.title: 5. Multi-region
docs.text:
A single global counter would add a cross-region round trip (70–150 ms) to every request — unacceptable. Options:

Approach Behavior Trade-off Independent per-region limits Each region enforces the full limit A client spreading traffic across regions can get N× the limit Split the limit across regions Each region enforces limit ÷ N (or weighted by traffic) Clients concentrated in one region are limited early Local enforcement + async sync Each region counts locally and periodically shares usage with others Near-global accuracy with small overshoot; more complexity

Choice: enforce locally in each region against a regional Redis cluster, with limits weighted by each client's usual traffic split; aggregate usage asynchronously for long-window quotas (daily, monthly), where a few seconds of delay do not matter. Most clients are served from one region, so overshoot is rare and small.

docs.title: 6. Fail-open versus fail-closed
docs.text:
If Redis is slow or unavailable, the gateway must still decide.

  • Call Redis with a tight timeout (for example, 5–10 ms) and wrap it in a circuit breaker so a sick Redis does not add latency to every request.
  • Fail open (allow) for general API limits: availability of the product matters more than strict limiting for a few minutes. Fall back to a coarse in-memory limit per gateway instance (limit ÷ number of instances) so a total limiter outage is not unlimited.
  • Fail closed (deny) for security- and cost-sensitive rules — sign-in, OTP verification, SMS sending — where unlimited attempts would enable brute force or run up bills.
  • Alert immediately on fallback mode; record it in metrics.

The per-rule failMode field captures this decision.

docs.title: Bottlenecks and trade-offs
docs.text:
• What fails first: Redis throughput or a hot shard as traffic grows. Mitigations: more shards, hash-tag colocation (one call per request), sub-bucket splitting for giant tenants, local token pre-allocation.
  • Latency: every request pays one Redis round trip; keep Redis in the same zone or region and pipelines short.
  • Accuracy versus cost: exact global counting is expensive; this design accepts small overshoot in failures and across regions.
  • Availability: fail-open with local fallback protects uptime; fail-closed protects sensitive actions.
  • Alternatives considered: in-memory counters per instance (rejected: limits multiply with instance count and change during autoscaling); sticky routing of each client to one gateway (rejected: fragile during scaling and failures); a managed gateway's built-in throttling (good for simple per-key limits, but less flexible for custom rules and shared use inside services).
  • Operational risk: a bad rule can block legitimate traffic — mitigated by shadow mode, rule versioning, and quick rollback.

docs.title: Real-world references
docs.text:
• Stripe describes four kinds of limiters: a request rate limiter, a concurrent requests limiter ("you can only have 20 API requests in progress at the same time"), a fleet usage load shedder that reserves part of the fleet for critical requests (using a Redis cluster to count requests of each type), and a worker utilization load shedder. Stripe uses the token bucket algorithm, added the ability to briefly burst above limits for events like flash sales, and recommends dark-launching each limiter to watch what it would block before enforcing it (Scaling your API with rate limiters).
  • Cloudflare built rate limiting for millions of domains under a constraint: its counters lived in memcached, which offered only GET, SET, and INCR. It used a sliding window approximation based on the previous and current counters, created an isolated counting system inside each point of presence to cut latency, and reported that on 400 million requests from 270,000 sources only 0.003% were wrongly allowed or limited (How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains).
  • GitHub documents its limits publicly: personal requests count toward a primary limit of 5,000 requests per hour, every response carries x-ratelimit-limit, x-ratelimit-remaining, x-ratelimit-used, and x-ratelimit-reset headers, and secondary rate limits — including no more than 100 concurrent requests — exist "to prevent abuse and keep the API available for all users" (Rate limits for the REST API).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Limits multiply after scaling out. Symptom: clients exceed their quota by a factor that tracks the instance count. Detect: per-client request totals above configured limits. Cause: counters kept in each instance's memory. Fix: move counters to the shared Redis store.
  • Everyone limited at once. Symptom: a sudden wave of 429s for unrelated customers. Detect: 429 metrics grouped by key show one key (the load balancer's IP). Cause: the client IP is read wrongly behind proxies. Fix: configure trusted proxies correctly; key authenticated traffic by API key or user.
  • Redis latency slows every request. Symptom: gateway p99 latency rises in step with Redis latency. Detect: Redis latency and slow-log metrics, gateway traces. Cause: an overloaded shard or a slow script. Fix: tight timeouts, a circuit breaker with local fallback limits, more shards.
  • One tenant overloads a shard. Symptom: one Redis node near 100% CPU. Detect: per-node CPU and top keys. Cause: a giant customer's single bucket key. Fix: split the bucket into sub-keys or use local token pre-allocation.
  • A bad rule blocks real users. Symptom: 429 spike right after a configuration change. Detect: 429 rate per rule with deploy markers. Cause: a rule matched more traffic than intended. Fix: shadow mode first, versioned rules, instant rollback.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why does a read-then-write implementation of a rate limiter over-admit requests, and how does a Lua script fix it?
  2. Why does the script use Redis's TIME instead of the gateway's clock?
  3. How do Redis Cluster hash tags let one script check several rules for the same client?
  4. Compare enforcing limits at the edge, the API gateway, and inside services.
  5. What are the options for rate limiting across regions, and what does each sacrifice?
  6. Which rules should fail open and which should fail closed when Redis is unavailable? Why?

docs.text:

  • Redis Cluster specification: hash tags
