docs.title: Case Study: URL Shortener
docs.text: A URL shortener turns a long URL into a short one, such as https://sho.rt/aZ3kP9q, and redirects visitors to the original. It looks trivial, but at scale it exercises many core design skills: unique ID generation, read-heavy caching, choosing redirect semantics, analytics without slowing the hot path, and abuse prevention.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• Create a short link for a long URL; return the short code and URL.
  • Visiting a short link redirects to the original URL.
  • Optional custom alias (sho.rt/spring-sale).
  • Optional expiration date; expired links stop redirecting.
  • Owners can see click analytics (total clicks, clicks per day, referrers, countries).
  • Owners can disable or delete their links.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• Scale: 100 million new links per month; 100 redirects per link created (read:write ≈ 100:1).
  • Latency: redirect handled in under ~50 ms at p99 on the server side.
  • Availability: redirects 99.99%; link creation 99.9% is acceptable.
  • Durability: a created link must never be lost or point somewhere else.
  • Uniqueness: two links must never share a code.
  • Analytics may lag by a few minutes (eventual consistency).
  • Safety: prevent the service from being used to spread phishing or malware; codes should not be trivially enumerable.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assumptions: 100 M links/month, 100:1 read:write, peak = 3× average, 500 bytes per link record, 5-year retention, 200 bytes per click event.

Writes:   10^8 / (2.5 × 10^6 s per month)  ≈ 40 /s     peak ≈ 120 /s
Reads:    40 × 100                          ≈ 4,000 /s  peak ≈ 12,000 /s

Links over 5 years: 100 M × 12 × 5          = 6 × 10^9 links
Link storage:       6 × 10^9 × 500 B        = 3 TB  (× 3 replicas ≈ 9 TB)

Code space (base62):
  6 characters: 62^6 ≈ 5.7 × 10^10   (enough, but ~10% full after 5 years)
  7 characters: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 × 10^12   (very roomy) → use 7

Cache (80/20 of a day's reads):
  4,000 /s × 86,400 ≈ 3.5 × 10^8 reads/day
  0.2 × 3.5 × 10^8 × 500 B ≈ 35 GB (upper bound)

Click events: 4,000 /s × 200 B = 800 KB/s ≈ 70 GB/day raw

Conclusions: modest write rate and total size; the challenges are read throughput, low redirect latency, high availability, and collision-free code generation. Raw analytics data grows fastest and should be aggregated.

docs.title: API design
docs.text:
All management endpoints require authentication (API key or session) and are rate limited. See REST APIs.

Create a link

POST /v1/links
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: 5d1c...           (optional; safe retries)
Content-Type: application/json

{ "longUrl": "https://example.com/blog/2026/11/very-long-article?utm_source=x",
  "customAlias": "spring-sale",     (optional)
  "expiresAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" }  (optional)

201 Created
Location: /v1/links/spring-sale
{ "code": "spring-sale",
  "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/spring-sale",
  "longUrl": "https://example.com/blog/2026/11/very-long-article?utm_source=x",
  "expiresAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" }

400 Bad Request   invalid or unsafe URL, invalid alias format
409 Conflict      alias already taken
429 Too Many Requests

Redirect

GET /aZ3kP9q

302 Found
Location: https://example.com/blog/2026/11/very-long-article?utm_source=x
Cache-Control: private, max-age=60

404 Not Found   unknown code
410 Gone        expired or disabled link

Analytics

GET /v1/links/aZ3kP9q/stats?from=2026-11-01&to=2026-11-07

200 OK
{ "code": "aZ3kP9q", "totalClicks": 18234,
  "byDay": [ { "date": "2026-11-01", "clicks": 2410 }, ... ],
  "topReferrers": [ { "referrer": "news.example", "clicks": 5120 } ],
  "topCountries": [ { "country": "US", "clicks": 9012 } ] }

Disable / delete

DELETE /v1/links/aZ3kP9q   → 204 No Content

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
links — the hot, key-value table. Every redirect is a lookup by code.

Field Type Notes code string (≤ 32) Primary / partition key longUrl string (≤ ~2,048) Destination ownerId string Creator createdAt timestamp expiresAt timestamp, nullable Checked on every redirect status enum active, disabled isCustom boolean Custom alias or generated

Indexes:

  • Primary key on code (unique; enforces no collisions).
  • Secondary index on (ownerId, createdAt) for "list my links."

Storage choice: the access pattern is a single-key lookup at high volume, which suits a horizontally partitioned key-value or wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) partitioned by code. A relational database with read replicas would also handle these numbers comfortably, especially behind a cache; the key-value store is chosen for simple horizontal scaling and built-in TTL support.

id_blocks — the ID range allocator's state (one row, or a coordination service): { name: "links", nextStart: 1203000000 }.

Analytics:

  • click_events — an append-only stream (Kafka topic): code, timestamp, referrer, country (derived from IP, then discard the IP), user agent class.
  • link_stats_daily — aggregated per (code, date): clicks, top referrers, countries, approximate unique visitors. Stored in an analytics or columnar store, queried by the stats endpoint.

docs.title: High-level design
docs.text:
The redirect service and the link API are separate deployments: the redirect path is the critical, high-volume one and is scaled and protected independently.

Write path (create link):

  1. Authenticate, rate limit, and validate the URL (scheme http/https only, length limit, not pointing to the shortener itself).
  2. Check the URL against malware and phishing lists.
  3. If a custom alias is given, validate its format and reserved words; otherwise generate a code (see deep dive 1).
  4. Conditional insert (put if not exists on code). On conflict: return 409 for an alias, or generate another code.
  5. Return 201 with the short URL.

Read path (redirect):

  1. Look up code in a small in-process LRU cache, then Redis, then the links store.
  2. If missing → 404 (and cache the miss briefly). If expired or disabled → 410.
  3. Populate caches on a miss, with a TTL no later than expiresAt.
  4. Respond 302 with Location.
  5. Emit a click event to a local buffer that is flushed to Kafka asynchronously — the redirect never waits for analytics.

docs.title: 1. Generating short codes
docs.text:
Codes use base62 (0–9, a–z, A–Z): URL-safe without escaping and dense (7 characters ≈ 3.5 trillion values).

const ALPHABET = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";

// Encode a non-negative BigInt as base62, left-padded to a fixed length
export function toBase62(value, length = 7) {
  let result = "";
  let n = value;
  do {
    result = ALPHABET[Number(n % 62n)] + result;
    n /= 62n;
  } while (n > 0n);
  return result.padStart(length, "0");
}

toBase62(125n);           // "0000021"
toBase62(3521614606207n); // "ZZZZZZZ" (62^7 − 1, the largest 7-character code)

Three ways to choose the number to encode:

a) Hash the long URL. Take SHA-256 (or MD5) of the URL, use the first 41 bits (62^7 ≈ 2^41.7, so 41 bits always fit in 7 characters), and encode them.

  • The same URL always produces the same code (built-in deduplication — but two users shortening the same URL then share analytics and settings, which is usually undesirable; add the owner ID to the hash input).
  • Collisions are possible when truncating a hash: different URLs can produce the same prefix. You must check, and on collision append a salt or counter and rehash — extra reads on the write path.

b) Counter with ID-range allocation. A global counter guarantees uniqueness without collision checks, but a single counter incremented on every write is a bottleneck and single point of failure. Instead, each API server leases a block of IDs (for example, 10,000 at a time) from the allocator by atomically advancing nextStart, then hands them out from memory.

  • No collisions, no extra lookups; the allocator is contacted once per 10,000 links.
  • If a server crashes, the rest of its block is skipped — gaps are harmless.
  • Sequential IDs produce guessable codes (...aZ3kP9q, ...aZ3kP9r), letting anyone enumerate links. Scramble the ID with a reversible (bijective) transform before encoding — for example, multiply by a large constant that has no common factor with 62^7, modulo 62^7, or apply a small Feistel cipher. This is obfuscation, not security: links are public capabilities, so private content must not rely on code secrecy.

c) Random codes. Pick 7 random base62 characters and conditionally insert; retry on conflict. With 6 billion codes in a space of 3.5 trillion, a new random code collides with probability ≈ 6 × 10^9 / 3.5 × 10^12 ≈ 0.17%, so retries are rare and cheap. Codes are naturally unguessable.

Choice: ID-range allocation with scrambling for predictable, collision-free generation (option b), or random codes with conditional insert (option c) if simplicity is preferred. Either way, the conditional insert on the primary key is the final guarantee of uniqueness — it also protects against a generated code matching an existing custom alias.

docs.title: 2. 301 versus 302 and analytics
docs.text:
301 Moved Permanently 302 Found (or 307) Browser behavior Cacheable by default (RFC 9110 calls 301 "heuristically cacheable"), and browsers often keep it for a long time; later clicks may skip the server Not cached unless Cache-Control or Expires allows it, so clicks reach the server unless you set a max-age Analytics Undercounts repeat visits Every click is seen, apart from repeats within any max-age you allow Changing or disabling a link Visitors with a cached 301 keep going to the old target Takes effect immediately Server load Lower Higher (mitigated by caching)

Because analytics, disabling abusive links, and editable destinations are requirements, this design uses 302 with a short Cache-Control max-age. (301/308 suit links that are truly permanent and where analytics do not matter.) If a CDN caches redirects at the edge, analytics must come from CDN logs instead.

Analytics never block the redirect: the handler appends an event to an in-memory buffer flushed to Kafka every few hundred milliseconds. A stream processor aggregates per code and day; unique visitors can be approximated with HyperLogLog. If Kafka is down, events are buffered briefly and then dropped — losing some analytics is acceptable; failing redirects is not.

docs.title: 3. Read-heavy caching
docs.text:
• Cache-aside in Redis: link:{code} → { longUrl, expiresAt, status } with a TTL (for example, 24 hours, never beyond expiresAt); ~35 GB fits a small cluster. See caching strategies.
  • In-process LRU of a few thousand entries per redirect server absorbs viral links (hot keys) without hitting Redis at all.
  • Negative caching: cache "not found" for 30–60 seconds so bots scanning random codes do not hammer the database.
  • Invalidation: on disable or delete, delete the Redis key; the short in-process TTL bounds staleness elsewhere. See invalidation and expiration.
  • Stampede protection: when a hot key expires, let one request reload it (request coalescing) while others wait briefly. See cache failure modes.
  • If Redis fails, redirect servers fall back to the links store, which must be provisioned for the extra load (or shed load gracefully).

docs.title: 4. Custom aliases and expiration
docs.text:
Aliases: validate length (for example, 4–32), characters ([A-Za-z0-9-_]), and a reserved list (api, admin, login, help, offensive terms). Insert with the same conditional write; conflicts return 409. Aliases and generated codes share one namespace, which the primary key protects.

Expiration:

  • Check expiresAt on every redirect; return 410 Gone once expired.
  • Never cache a link past its expiry.
  • Remove expired rows with the store's TTL feature (DynamoDB TTL, MongoDB TTL indexes) or a nightly batch job.
  • Do not recycle expired codes for new links: old copies of the short URL remain in emails and documents and would silently point to someone else's content.

docs.title: 5. Abuse prevention
docs.text:
• Rate limit creation per account, API key, and IP; require sign-up or a CAPTCHA for anonymous creation. See rate limiting.
  • Check destinations against malware and phishing lists (such as Google Safe Browsing) at creation and re-check periodically, since a domain can turn malicious later.
  • Allow only http and https (no javascript: or data: URLs); block redirects to the shortener's own domain and to other shorteners to prevent loops and chains.
  • Disable reported or flagged links quickly (status → disabled, cache invalidated); optionally show a warning interstitial page.
  • Non-enumerable codes (deep dive 1) stop easy scraping of all links.
  • Provide an abuse reporting endpoint and audit trail.

docs.title: Bottlenecks and trade-offs
docs.text:
• What fails first: the links store under read load if the cache is cold or down. Mitigation: layered caches, provisioning for cache-miss load, and load shedding.
  • Hot keys: a viral link concentrates traffic on one cache shard and one partition; in-process caching and short CDN caching spread it.
  • Availability of redirects: the redirect path depends only on its own servers, the cache, and the links store (replicated across zones). Analytics, the ID allocator, and URL checking are off the redirect path.
  • ID allocator: an outage only stops creation after servers use up their leased blocks; run it on a replicated store.
  • Multi-region: replicate the links store to each region (global tables or read replicas) so redirects are served locally; creation can write to one home region, with region-prefixed ID ranges if multiple regions write. New links may take a moment to appear in other regions — acceptable here.
  • Alternatives considered: hashing (rejected: collision handling and shared-code semantics); 301 redirects (rejected: lose analytics and control); a single relational database (viable at this size, but sharding later is harder than with a partitioned key-value store).
  • Trade-off accepted: 302 increases server traffic compared with 301, in exchange for accurate analytics and the ability to disable links.

docs.title: Real-world references
docs.text:
• Google's goo.gl shows why link permanence is a core requirement. In 2018 Google stopped new link creation for most users but promised that "all existing links will continue to redirect to the intended destination" (Transitioning Google URL Shortener to Firebase Dynamic Links). In 2024 it announced that goo.gl links would stop working after August 25, 2025, first showing an interstitial warning page on a growing share of links; in August 2025 it revised the plan to preserve actively used links, noting they "are embedded in countless documents, videos, posts and more" (Google URL Shortener links will no longer be available). Lesson: short links outlive products, so plan for long-term redirect availability and never recycle codes.
  • Twitter's Snowflake is a well-known example of the ID-generation side of this design: unique 64-bit, roughly time-ordered IDs generated without central coordination, from a timestamp, a machine ID, and a sequence (Snowflake README). Encoding such IDs in base62 is one way to produce short codes.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A viral link slows redirects. Symptom: p99 redirect latency jumps while one code dominates traffic. Detect: per-key request counts, one Redis shard's CPU rising. Cause: a hot key concentrated on one cache shard and one database partition. Fix: in-process LRU caches on redirect servers and short CDN caching of the redirect.
  • Bots scanning codes. Symptom: database read load rises with a surge of 404 responses. Detect: 404 rate per client and overall. Cause: scanners guessing codes, each a cache miss. Fix: negative caching, per-IP rate limits, non-sequential codes.
  • The domain gets flagged for phishing. Symptom: browsers or email providers warn about or block all your short links. Detect: abuse reports, safe-browsing status checks, sudden drops in click-through. Cause: attackers using the service to hide malicious destinations. Fix: scan destinations at creation and periodically, disable links fast, rate-limit anonymous creation.
  • Link creation fails. Symptom: 5xx on create while redirects work. Detect: error rate on the create endpoint, allocator errors. Cause: the ID allocator is unavailable and servers have used up their leased blocks. Fix: larger blocks, a replicated allocator store, alerts on low remaining block capacity.
  • Stale analytics. Symptom: owners see click counts hours behind. Detect: Kafka consumer lag. Cause: the aggregator cannot keep up with click events. Fix: scale consumers; redirects remain unaffected because analytics are off the hot path.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why are 7 base62 characters enough for this system, and how did you calculate it?
  2. Compare hashing, counter ranges, and random codes for generating short codes. How is uniqueness ultimately guaranteed?
  3. Why does this design use 302 instead of 301, and what does it cost?
  4. How do in-process caching, Redis, and negative caching each protect the database?
  5. Why should expired codes not be reused?
  6. Which components are on the redirect path, and why were analytics kept off it?

docs.title: System Design Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review the system design process, estimation, the standard building blocks, and the recurring themes of the case studies. Each question is tagged Beginner (definitions, basic usage), Intermediate (how it works, trade-offs), or Advanced (scale, failure modes, design decisions). Answer each one aloud, with a reason for every choice, before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What are the main steps of a system design discussion?
docs.text: Clarify functional and non-functional requirements, agree the scope, estimate scale, define the API, define the data model, draw the high-level design with read and write paths, deep dive into the hardest parts, discuss bottlenecks and trade-offs, and wrap up. You loop back when new information changes an earlier decision.

docs.title: 2. Why start with requirements instead of components?
docs.text: Components only make sense relative to requirements. Read-heavy versus write-heavy, strict versus eventual consistency, and 100 versus 100,000 requests per second lead to completely different designs. Starting with technologies risks solving the wrong problem or over-engineering.

docs.title: 3. What are non-functional requirements? Give examples.
docs.text: Quality targets and constraints rather than features: latency (p99 under 200 ms), availability (99.99%), durability (never lose a payment), consistency (read-your-writes), scale (10 M daily users), security, privacy, and cost. They drive most architectural decisions.

docs.title: 4. How would you spend 45 minutes in a system design interview?
docs.text: Roughly 5–8 minutes on requirements and scope, 3–5 on estimates, 5–7 on API and data model, 10–12 on the high-level design, 10–15 on deep dives, and 3–5 on bottlenecks and wrap-up. The most common failure is running out of time before the deep dives.

docs.title: 5. How do you communicate a trade-off well?
docs.text: State the options, the criteria from the requirements, your choice, and what you give up: "Fan-out on write makes reads cheap because reads outnumber writes 100:1; the cost is heavy writes for celebrities, which I handle by pulling their posts at read time."

docs.title: 6. What should a real-world design document contain?
docs.text: Context and goals, non-goals, requirements, the proposed design (APIs, data model, components, flows), alternatives considered and why they were rejected, rollout and migration plan, monitoring, security and privacy considerations, risks, and open questions.

docs.title: 7. How do you convert daily active users into requests per second?
docs.text: Multiply DAU by actions per user per day and divide by 86,400 seconds (round to 10^5). For 10 M users making 20 requests each: 2 × 10^8 ÷ 10^5 = 2,000 requests per second on average. Then multiply by a peak factor such as 2–3×.

docs.title: 8. Why estimate peak and not just average load?
docs.text: Average load alone can understate capacity needs when traffic has peaks or bursts. Estimate representative peak and burst rates, identify the bottleneck, then choose headroom and autoscaling limits from the service objective.

docs.title: 9. How much downtime does 99.99% availability allow?
docs.text: About 52.6 minutes per year, or about 4.3 minutes per 30-day month. Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by a factor of ten, and usually increases cost and complexity substantially.

docs.title: 10. How do you estimate storage?
docs.text: Records per day × size per record × retention period × replication factor, plus overhead for indexes. Estimate large blobs (images, video) separately from structured data, since they belong in object storage.

docs.title: 11. How do you size a cache?
docs.text: There is no universal 80/20 cache size. Measure the workload's hot-key working set over the relevant TTL and target hit ratio, account for object sizes and cache overhead, and validate with hit, eviction, latency, and origin-load metrics.

docs.title: 12. Name some latency numbers every engineer should know.
docs.text: Main memory access ~100 ns; SSD random read ~0.1 ms; round trip inside a data center ~0.5 ms; hard disk seek ~5–10 ms; round trip between continents ~70–150 ms. Memory is far faster than disk, and network round trips often dominate request latency.

docs.title: 13. What does a load balancer do, and what is the difference between layer 4 and layer 7?
docs.text: It distributes traffic across healthy servers and removes unhealthy ones via health checks. Layer 4 balances TCP/UDP connections without reading HTTP; layer 7 understands HTTP, so it can route by path or host, terminate TLS, and add headers.

docs.title: 14. What is the difference between a reverse proxy and an API gateway?
docs.text: A reverse proxy forwards client requests to backend servers and handles concerns like TLS termination, compression, and caching. An API gateway is a specialized entry point for APIs that adds routing to many services, authentication, per-key rate limits and quotas, versioning, and analytics.

docs.title: 15. When should you use a CDN?
docs.text: Use a CDN when content is cacheable and users benefit from geographic proximity or origin offload. Static assets and media are common examples; public API responses need explicit cache semantics and a suitable cache key. A CDN can cut latency by serving from nearby edge locations, reduce origin load and egress cost, and absorb traffic spikes.

docs.title: 16. Why should application servers be stateless?
docs.text: So any instance can handle any request. That enables horizontal scaling, autoscaling, and replacing failed instances without losing data. Sessions, uploads, and other state live in shared stores such as Redis, databases, and object storage.

docs.title: 17. When would you add a cache, and what are the risks?
docs.text: When data is read far more often than it changes and some staleness is acceptable, or when the database cannot handle the read load. Risks include stale data, invalidation bugs, cache stampedes when hot keys expire, and the database being overwhelmed if the cache fails.

docs.title: 18. How do you choose between SQL and NoSQL databases?
docs.text: By access patterns, consistency needs, and scale. Relational databases suit related data with transactions and flexible queries. Key-value, document, and wide-column stores suit massive volumes of simple access patterns and horizontal partitioning. Many systems use both.

docs.title: 19. Why use a message queue?
docs.text: To decouple producers from consumers, absorb bursts, move slow or unreliable work off the request path, retry failures, and fan events out to several consumers. Consumers must be idempotent because most queues deliver at least once.

docs.title: 20. What is an inverted index?
docs.text: A map from each term to the documents containing it. Search engines such as Elasticsearch and OpenSearch use it to answer full-text queries quickly and rank results by relevance. It is derived data, updated asynchronously from the source of truth.

docs.title: 21. Compare UUID v4, UUID v7, and Snowflake-style IDs.
docs.text: UUID v4 is 128 bits of mostly random data — no coordination, but random inserts fragment B-tree indexes. UUID v7 starts with a millisecond timestamp, so it is time-ordered and index-friendly. Snowflake IDs pack a timestamp, machine ID, and sequence into 64 bits: compact and time-ordered, but each generator needs a unique machine ID.

docs.title: 22. What problem does consistent hashing solve?
docs.text: With hash(key) % N, changing N remaps most keys (about 75% going from 3 to 4 nodes), emptying caches and moving most data. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.

docs.title: 23. Why use virtual nodes in consistent hashing?
docs.text: With one position per node, arcs on the ring are uneven, so load is unbalanced, and a failed node's whole load moves to one neighbor. Many virtual positions per node even out the load, spread a failed node's keys across many nodes, and let bigger machines take more virtual nodes.

docs.title: 24. What is a single point of failure, and how do you remove it?
docs.text: A component whose failure stops the whole system, such as one database server or one load balancer. Remove it with redundancy (replicas, multiple instances across availability zones), automatic failover, and by keeping critical paths independent of non-critical components.

docs.title: 25. What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
docs.text: Vertical scaling uses a bigger machine — simple but limited and often a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds more machines — needs stateless services, load balancing, and data partitioning, but scales much further and improves availability.

docs.title: 26. What are read replicas, and what problem do they introduce?
docs.text: Copies of the primary database that serve reads, increasing read capacity. Replication is usually asynchronous, so replicas may lag: a user may not see their own write immediately. Solutions include reading your own writes from the primary or tracking replication position.

docs.title: 27. What is sharding, and how do you choose a shard key?
docs.text: Splitting data across multiple databases by a key so each holds a part. Choose a key that spreads data and load evenly, matches the main access pattern (queries should hit one shard), and avoids hot spots — for example, userId or conversationId, not a timestamp or a celebrity's ID.

docs.title: 28. What does the CAP theorem say?
docs.text: During a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a response). Without partitions, systems still trade consistency against latency. Design per feature: payments need consistency; feeds and likes can be eventually consistent.

docs.title: 29. What is eventual consistency? Give an example where it is acceptable.
docs.text: If no new writes occur, all replicas eventually converge to the same value, but reads may briefly be stale. It is acceptable for social feeds, like counts, presence indicators, and analytics — users tolerate a few seconds of delay there.

docs.title: 30. What is a hot spot, and how do you mitigate one?
docs.text: A key, partition, or server receiving disproportionate traffic, such as a viral post or a celebrity account. Mitigations include caching with local in-process caches, replicating hot data, splitting hot keys into sub-keys, and special handling (for example, pulling celebrity posts instead of pushing them).

docs.title: 31. How would you generate short codes?
docs.text: Base62-encode a number. Options: hash the URL (needs collision handling), use a counter with pre-allocated ID ranges per server (no collisions, scramble to avoid enumeration), or pick random codes and insert-if-absent. A conditional insert on the primary key is the final uniqueness guarantee.

docs.title: 32. How long should the code be?
docs.text: Enough for the total links over the system's life. 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion, so 7 characters comfortably hold billions of links; 6 characters (≈ 57 billion) works for smaller systems but fills faster, raising collision rates for random codes.

docs.title: 33. Should redirects use 301 or 302?
docs.text: 301 is permanent and cacheable by default, so browsers often keep it for a long time: that reduces load but hides repeat clicks from analytics and prevents changing or disabling the link. 302 (or 307) is temporary and is not cached unless cache headers allow it, so clicks reach the server (apart from any short max-age you set), enabling accurate analytics and control. Choose based on whether analytics and control matter.

docs.title: 34. How do you keep redirects fast and available?
docs.text: Keep the redirect path minimal — server, cache, key-value store — with analytics sent asynchronously. Use layered caching (in-process LRU, Redis), negative caching for unknown codes, replicated storage across zones, and regional replicas for global users.

docs.title: 35. Which rate limiting algorithm would you choose for an API, and why?
docs.text: Usually the token bucket: it allows bursts up to a capacity while enforcing an average rate and needs only two values of state per client. Sliding window counters are a good alternative for simple quotas; strict sign-in limits may use a sliding window log.

docs.title: 36. How do you prevent race conditions in a distributed rate limiter?
docs.text: Perform read, compute, and write atomically in the shared store — for example, a Redis Lua script — instead of reading the count in the application and writing it back. Using Redis's own clock in the script also avoids clock differences between gateway instances.

docs.title: 37. Should a rate limiter fail open or fail closed?
docs.text: It depends on the rule. General API limits usually fail open (with a coarse local fallback) to protect availability. Security- and cost-sensitive limits — sign-in attempts, OTP verification, SMS sending — fail closed to prevent brute force and runaway costs.

docs.title: 38. Why use WebSockets for chat, and what makes them hard to scale?
docs.text: They give a persistent, bidirectional, low-latency connection for pushing messages. They are stateful: each server holds open connections, so you need a session registry, routing between servers, heartbeats, reconnection with backoff and jitter, and load balancers that support long-lived connections.

docs.title: 39. How does a message reach a recipient connected to a different server?
docs.text: The chat service persists the message, looks up the recipient's connection server in a session registry (for example, Redis), and publishes the message to that server's channel via pub/sub. The server pushes it down the recipient's WebSocket. If the publish is lost, the client recovers the message from the database on reconnect.

docs.title: 40. How do you keep chat messages in order?
docs.text: Assign a per-conversation sequence number on the server — via an atomic counter or a single writer per conversation — and order by it. Never rely on client timestamps. Global ordering across conversations is unnecessary.

docs.title: 41. How do you implement read receipts efficiently?
docs.text: Store per-member watermarks (lastDeliveredSeq, lastReadSeq) instead of one row per message per recipient. A single update marks everything up to a sequence number as read, unread counts are simple subtraction, and clients batch receipt updates.

docs.title: 42. Compare fan-out on write and fan-out on read.
docs.text: Fan-out on write pushes each new post ID into every follower's precomputed feed: reads are cheap, writes scale with follower count. Fan-out on read assembles the feed at read time from followed authors: writes are cheap, reads are expensive. A hybrid pushes for normal accounts and pulls for high-follower accounts.

docs.title: 43. Why store post IDs rather than full posts in feed caches?
docs.text: Posts change: edits, deletions, and like counts would otherwise require updating millions of feed copies. Storing IDs keeps feeds small and lets the read path hydrate current post data in one batched lookup.

docs.title: 44. How do you paginate a feed that changes constantly?
docs.text: Use cursor pagination instead of offsets: pass the position of the last item seen (for example, its timestamp and ID) and fetch items after it. For ranked feeds, rank once into a short-lived feed session and page through that snapshot so items do not shift between pages.

docs.title: 45. Why use a separate queue per notification channel?
docs.text: Isolation and independent scaling: an email provider outage or slow SMS throughput only backs up that channel's queue, while push and in-app keep flowing. Each channel can be throttled to its provider's limits, with priority lanes so urgent messages bypass bulk campaigns.

docs.title: 46. How do you avoid sending duplicate notifications?
docs.text: Require idempotency keys on the send API, make queue consumers check and update delivery status atomically before sending (conditional queued → sending transition), use provider idempotency features and push collapse IDs, and accept that a tiny window for duplicates remains with external providers.

docs.title: 47. How do you respect user preferences and regulations?
docs.text: Check each notification against category and channel preferences, global unsubscribes, suppression lists (hard bounces, complaints, SMS STOP), consent records, and quiet hours before sending. Mandatory categories like security alerts bypass optional preferences. Email bulk messages include one-click unsubscribe headers.

docs.title: 48. Your URL shortener's redirect latency spikes whenever a link goes viral — what is happening and how do you fix it?
docs.text: What to check first: whether the spike is limited to one code and one cache shard, or affects every redirect. How to confirm: per-key request counts, per-node Redis CPU, and cache hit rate during the spike; check whether the hot key recently expired. Likely causes and fixes: a hot key concentrating traffic on one Redis shard and one database partition, sometimes made worse by a stampede when its entry expires. Add an in-process LRU cache on redirect servers, cache the redirect briefly at the CDN, and use request coalescing so only one request reloads an expired key. See the URL shortener case study and cache failure modes.

docs.title: 49. You added a Redis cache, but database load barely dropped. Why?
docs.text: What to check first: the cache hit rate, and which queries still reach the database. How to confirm: hit/miss metrics per key pattern, TTL distribution, and the database's top queries before and after. Likely causes and fixes: TTLs far shorter than the data's real change rate; keys that include volatile parameters, so identical data is cached under many keys; a working set larger than the cache (evictions); or the heavy queries were never cached. Normalize keys, lengthen TTLs where staleness is acceptable, size the cache from the measured working set (see back-of-the-envelope estimation), and cache the expensive queries. See cache fundamentals.

docs.title: 50. Every hour, on the hour, database CPU spikes for a few minutes. What do you investigate?
docs.text: What to check first: what else happens on the hour — cache TTLs set to round numbers, scheduled jobs, batch imports. How to confirm: line up cache hit rate, scheduled job runs, and the database's top queries on the same timeline. Likely causes and fixes: many cache entries created together with the same TTL expire together (a stampede), or every instance runs the same cron job at once. Add random jitter to TTLs, coalesce reloads, run scheduled jobs once through a queue or lock, and spread batch work over time. See cache failure modes and background jobs and scheduling.

docs.title: 51. After scaling the API gateway from 3 to 12 instances, customers exceed their rate limits by about 4×. Why?
docs.text: What to check first: where the rate limiter keeps its counters. How to confirm: compare a customer's actual request count per minute with their configured limit; check whether the overshoot matches the ratio of new to old instance counts (12 ÷ 3 = 4). Likely causes and fixes: counters held in each instance's memory, with each instance's limit set to the quota divided by the original 3 instances. Each of the 12 instances now grants a third of the quota, so a client whose requests are spread across all of them gets 12 × ⅓ = 4× its limit (with a full quota per instance it would be up to 12×). Move counters to a shared store such as Redis and update them atomically with a Lua script; keep a coarse local limit only as a fallback when Redis is unavailable. See the distributed rate limiter case study.

docs.title: 52. After moving behind a new load balancer, all anonymous users suddenly get 429 errors. What happened?
docs.text: What to check first: which key the limiter is counting for anonymous traffic. How to confirm: group 429 responses by limiter key; if almost all share one IP, it is the load balancer's address. Likely causes and fixes: the app reads the TCP peer address (the load balancer) instead of the client IP from forwarding headers. Configure the trusted proxy hop count precisely — never trust X-Forwarded-For from everyone, which allows spoofing. See rate limiting and throttling.

docs.title: 53. Chat users report missing messages that reappear after they refresh. What is going on?
docs.text: What to check first: whether the gaps coincide with connection server restarts or deploys. How to confirm: client telemetry for sequence-number gaps; pub/sub and connection-server logs at those times. Likely causes and fixes: real-time deliveries over pub/sub were lost while a connection server restarted; the messages are safely stored, which is why a refresh shows them. Make clients compare their last seq with the conversation's lastSeq on reconnect and fetch the gap; consider a durable log if real-time delivery itself must not drop. See the chat application case study.

docs.title: 54. Every chat deploy causes a wave of failed connections and the authentication service falls over. How do you fix it?
docs.text: What to check first: connection attempts per second and their timing during deploys. How to confirm: a sharp spike of reconnects within seconds of each server shutting down, followed by auth errors. Likely causes and fixes: all clients of a drained server reconnect at the same instant, and each reconnect re-authenticates — a thundering herd. Drain servers gradually, make clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, use short-lived reconnect tickets that are cheap to verify, and scale or rate-limit the auth path. See the chat application case study.

docs.title: 55. When a popular creator posts, followers see it minutes late and the fan-out queue backs up. What do you change?
docs.text: What to check first: the creator's follower count versus the celebrity threshold, and fan-out queue depth over time. How to confirm: fan-out lag metrics (post time to fan-out complete) spiking with posts from specific accounts. Likely causes and fixes: the account is just below the threshold, so each post triggers millions of feed inserts. Lower the threshold so such accounts are pulled at read time, fan out to recently active followers first, skip inactive users, and autoscale workers on queue depth. See the news feed case study.

docs.title: 56. Users scrolling their feed see duplicate posts or miss some. Why?
docs.text: What to check first: how the feed endpoint paginates. How to confirm: reproduce by loading page 1, creating new posts, then loading page 2 — items shift between pages. Likely causes and fixes: offset pagination over a list that changes as new posts arrive at the top. Switch to cursor pagination on (timestamp, ID) for chronological feeds, or rank once into a feed session snapshot for ranked feeds. See the news feed case study and API design best practices.

docs.title: 57. During a marketing campaign, sign-in codes arrive several minutes late. What is wrong with the design?
docs.text: What to check first: whether one-time codes share queues or workers with bulk campaign messages. How to confirm: age of the oldest message per queue and priority during the campaign; OTP send latency against campaign start time. Likely causes and fixes: urgent and bulk messages compete for the same capacity and provider throughput. Add priority lanes with dedicated workers, pace campaigns, reserve provider capacity for transactional messages, and give OTPs a short expiry so stale codes are dropped. See the notification system case study.

docs.title: 58. After a worker deploy, some users received the same push notification twice. How do you prevent it?
docs.text: What to check first: whether the duplicates have the same notification and delivery IDs. How to confirm: delivery records showing two sends for one delivery row, around the time workers restarted. Likely causes and fixes: the queue redelivered jobs whose workers were killed mid-send (at-least-once delivery). Atomically move the delivery from queued to sending before calling the provider, shut workers down gracefully, use push collapse IDs, and accept that a tiny window remains with external providers. See the notification system case study and delivery guarantees.

docs.title: 59. One database shard runs at 95% CPU while the others sit at 20%. What do you do?
docs.text: What to check first: which keys and queries dominate that shard. How to confirm: per-shard request counts and top keys; check whether one tenant, user, or time range owns most of the traffic. Likely causes and fixes: a skewed shard key (a timestamp, a huge tenant, a celebrity). Cache the hot data, split hot keys, choose a key that spreads writes and reads (such as a hashed user ID), and rebalance with more partitions or virtual nodes. See building blocks and database scaling.

docs.title: 60. Your estimate said 10 instances would handle launch traffic, but production saturates at half that load. Why?
docs.text: What to check first: how the per-instance capacity figure was obtained. How to confirm: compare production per-instance throughput, CPU, and latency with the load test; compare data sizes, cache hit rates, and request mix. Likely causes and fixes: the load test used a warm cache, a tiny dataset, or only cheap endpoints, so capacity was overstated; or peak traffic was underestimated. Re-test with production-like data and traffic mixes, add headroom, and autoscale. See back-of-the-envelope estimation and performance testing.

docs.title: 61. A region failed, and users kept hitting it for 15 minutes despite DNS failover. Why, and how do you shorten that?
docs.text: What to check first: the TTL on the failover DNS records and how fast health checks marked the region unhealthy. How to confirm: synthetic checks from several locations, DNS query logs, and client errors over time after the failure. Likely causes and fixes: long TTLs and resolvers or clients caching answers, plus slow health checks. Use short TTLs on failover records, faster health checks, and failover at the load balancer or global traffic-routing layer where possible; make clients retry against alternative endpoints. See building blocks and DNS.

docs.title: The System Design Process
docs.text: System design turns a vague goal — "build a URL shortener," "add notifications" — into a concrete plan: which components exist, how data flows between them, how they store data, and how the system behaves under load and failure. A repeatable process keeps the design grounded in requirements instead of favorite technologies, and it works the same way for a real project at work and for a 45-minute interview.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Most expensive design mistakes come from skipping steps, not from choosing the wrong database:

  • Building for millions of users when the product has hundreds, adding queues, caches, and services that only add failure modes.
  • Building for hundreds when the product will have millions, and discovering the bottleneck in production.
  • Designing a strongly consistent system when users would accept a few seconds of delay — or the reverse, for payments.
  • Agreeing on components before anyone agreed on what the system must do.

A structured process makes requirements, assumptions, and trade-offs explicit, so teammates (or interviewers) can challenge them early, when changes are cheap.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Amazon Web Services publishes the Well-Architected Framework, which it describes as helping you "understand the pros and cons of decisions you make while building systems on AWS" — a structured set of review questions for designing reliable, secure, efficient, cost-effective, and sustainable systems.
  • Google SRE created a dedicated team of "Launch Coordination Engineers" and curated a "launch checklist" of common questions to ask about a launch, to enable a rapid pace of change without compromising stability (Reliable Product Launches at Scale).
  • Microsoft offers the Azure Well-Architected Framework: "quality-driven tenets, architectural decision points, and review tools," including an assessment tool teams run against their workloads.
  • Discord, before replacing its message database, first analyzed its read/write patterns — reads were "extremely random" and the read/write ratio was about 50/50 — and chose Cassandra to fit those requirements (How Discord Stores Billions of Messages).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: The process has nine steps. In practice you loop back — a capacity estimate may change the data model — but working through them in order keeps the discussion organized.

docs.title: Step 1: Clarify requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements describe what users and systems can do:

  • "Users can create a short link for a long URL."
  • "Visiting the short link redirects to the original URL."
  • "Users can see click counts for their links."

Non-functional requirements describe how well the system must do it:

Quality Example question Example answer Scale How many users, requests, records? 100 M new links/month, 10:1 read/write Latency How fast must key operations be? Redirect p99 under 50 ms Availability How much downtime is acceptable? 99.99% for redirects Consistency Can readers see stale data? A new link may take a second to work everywhere Durability Can we ever lose data? Never lose a created link Security / privacy Who can see what? Regulations? Only owners see analytics Cost Budget constraints? Minimize storage costs

Ask questions instead of assuming. "Is this read-heavy or write-heavy?", "Global users or one region?", "Do we need real-time updates?" The answers change the design.

docs.title: Step 2: Agree scope
docs.text: You cannot design everything in detail. Agree on the core use cases to focus on and list what is out of scope (for example, "authentication and billing are handled by existing services"). Writing the scope down prevents spending half the time on a side feature.

docs.title: Step 3: Estimate scale
docs.text:
Rough numbers decide whether you need one database or a sharded cluster, a cache or not, one region or several. Estimate:

  • Requests per second (average and peak) for reads and writes.
  • Storage per day and over the retention period.
  • Bandwidth in and out.
  • Memory needed for caching hot data.

Round aggressively; the goal is the right order of magnitude. See back-of-the-envelope estimation.

docs.title: Step 4: Define the API
docs.text:
Write the main endpoints or operations with inputs and outputs. This pins down exactly what the system does and exposes edge cases (pagination, idempotency, errors).

POST /v1/links          { "url": "...", "alias"?: "...", "expiresAt"?: "..." }
                        → 201 { "code": "aZ3kP9q", "shortUrl": "..." }
GET  /{code}            → 302 Location: <original url>
GET  /v1/links/{code}/stats → 200 { "clicks": 1234, ... }

Use REST conventions unless there is a reason not to; mention API design practices such as cursor pagination and idempotency keys where they matter.

docs.title: Step 5: Define the data model
docs.text: List the main entities, their key fields, how they are accessed, and which indexes support those accesses. Access patterns drive the choice of database: key-value lookups at huge scale suit a NoSQL store; relational data with transactions suits SQL. Note the partition (shard) key early if you expect to shard.

docs.title: Step 6: High-level design
docs.text:
Draw the main components and the paths a request takes: clients, DNS, CDN, load balancer, application services, caches, databases, queues, object storage. Walk through the main write path and the main read path end to end. Keep it simple first — a design that clearly works at the required scale beats an impressive diagram.

The standard components are described in building blocks.

docs.title: Step 7: Deep dives
docs.text: Pick the three to five hardest parts and go deep: how short codes are generated without collisions, how messages are routed between WebSocket servers, how a feed is built for a user who follows celebrities. These are where the real design decisions are, and where interviewers look for depth.

docs.title: Step 8: Bottlenecks and trade-offs
docs.text:
Ask "what breaks first?" as load grows 10× and when each component fails:

  • Single points of failure: one database, one region, one queue.
  • Hot spots: a celebrity's post, a viral link, a hot shard key.
  • Consistency trade-offs: caching and replication introduce staleness.
  • Cost: storing every event forever, over-provisioned capacity.

For each decision, state the alternative and why you chose this one. "I chose fan-out on write because reads outnumber writes 100:1, at the cost of slower posting for accounts with millions of followers, which I handle with a hybrid approach."

docs.title: Step 9: Wrap up
docs.text: Summarize the design in a few sentences, restate how it meets the requirements, and list what you would do next: monitoring and alerting, load testing, security review, features deferred from scope.

docs.title: Time allocation in a 45-minute interview
docs.text:
Phase Minutes Output Requirements and scope 5–8 Functional and non-functional list, out-of-scope list Estimation 3–5 QPS, storage, bandwidth, cache size API and data model 5–7 Main endpoints, entities, keys High-level design 10–12 Diagram, read and write paths Deep dives 10–15 Two or three hard problems solved in detail Bottlenecks, trade-offs, wrap-up 3–5 Failure modes, scaling plan, summary

Watch the clock: running out of time before the deep dives is the most common interview failure. In a real project, these phases become documents — a requirements doc, a design doc with alternatives, and review meetings.

docs.title: Communicating trade-offs
docs.text:
Good system design communication sounds like this:

  • State assumptions: "I'll assume 10 million daily active users, mostly in one region. If it's global, I'd add regional read replicas."
  • Offer options: "We could generate codes by hashing or with a counter. Hashing needs collision checks; a counter needs coordination. I'll use pre-allocated ID ranges because..."
  • Tie decisions to requirements: "Because redirects need 99.99% availability, the redirect path only depends on the cache and a replicated key-value store, not the analytics pipeline."
  • Admit uncertainty: "I'm not sure of the exact write throughput of that database; I'd load test it before committing."
  • Think aloud and check in: "Does this level of detail work, or should I go deeper on storage?"

docs.title: Design documents in real projects
docs.text: At work, the same steps produce a design document, typically with: context and goals, non-goals, requirements, proposed design, alternatives considered (and why rejected), data model and APIs, rollout and migration plan, monitoring, security and privacy review, and open questions. Reviews catch problems while they are still cheap to fix.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use the full process when:

  • Building a new system or service, or redesigning an existing one.
  • Making decisions that are hard to reverse: the data model, the storage engine, a public API, a large data migration.
  • The work spans several teams or services.
  • The stakes are high: payments, personal data, availability commitments.
  • Preparing for or sitting a system design interview.

Use a lighter version, or skip it, when:

  • The change is small and reversible (a bug fix, a feature behind a flag in an existing service).
  • You are building a throwaway prototype to learn — still write down the assumptions you are testing.
  • You are repeating a well-understood pattern your team already documented — reuse the existing design.
Situation Appropriate depth Bug fix or small feature in an existing service Code review only New endpoint that stores new data Short design note: API, data model, risks New service, new datastore, or major refactor Full design document and review Irreversible or high-risk change (migration, payments, public API) Full document, alternatives, rollout and rollback plan, load test Interview Full process, time-boxed to the session

docs.title: Mini example: "Design a pastebin" in outline
docs.text:
1. Requirements. Users paste text and get a link; anyone with the link can read it; optional expiry. Non-functional: 1 million new pastes/day, reads 10× writes, pastes up to 1 MB, available and fast to read, durable until expiry.

2. Scope. In: create, read, expiry. Out: accounts, editing, search.

3. Estimates.

writes: 1,000,000 / 86,400 s ≈ 12/s average, ~25/s peak (×2)
reads:  ×10 → ~120/s average, ~250/s peak
storage: average paste 10 KB × 1 M/day = 10 GB/day ≈ 3.6 TB/year

4. API.

POST /v1/pastes { "content": "...", "expiresIn": "7d" } → 201 { "id": "x7Kp2Qa" }
GET  /v1/pastes/{id}                                    → 200 { "content": "..." }

5. Data model. Metadata table: id (primary key), storageKey, createdAt, expiresAt, size. Content stored in object storage because pastes can be large and metadata stays small.

6. High-level design.

Client ─► Load balancer ─► Paste service ─┬─► Metadata DB (id → key, expiry)
                                          ├─► Object storage (content)
                                          └─► Cache (hot pastes)

Write path: generate ID, upload content, insert metadata, return ID. Read path: check cache, else read metadata and content, cache it, return.

7. Deep dives. ID generation (random base62 with collision check vs counter ranges); serving popular pastes via a CDN; deleting expired pastes with a scheduled job plus storage lifecycle rules.

8. Trade-offs. Object storage adds a second read but keeps the database small; cache misses on rarely read pastes are acceptable. The single metadata database is fine at 250 reads/s; add replicas before sharding.

9. Wrap-up. Summarize, then mention monitoring (read latency, cache hit rate) and abuse prevention (rate limits, malware/phishing checks).

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Spend real time on requirements; ask about scale, latency, consistency, and failure tolerance.
  • Write scope and assumptions down so they can be challenged.
  • Estimate before choosing components; let numbers justify complexity.
  • Define the API and data model before drawing boxes.
  • Walk through read and write paths end to end, including failures.
  • Go deep on the hardest problems rather than shallow on everything.
  • Name alternatives and explain each trade-off in terms of requirements.
  • Start simple and show how the design evolves at 10× and 100× load.
  • Include observability, security, and operations, not just the happy path.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
Process gaps show up later as production problems:

  • Launch-day overload. Symptom: latency and errors climb as traffic arrives. Detect: latency, error-rate, and saturation alerts. Cause: capacity sized for average load, no load test. Fix: estimate peaks, load test to the breaking point, roll out gradually behind a flag.
  • A missed non-functional requirement. Symptom: users see stale data right after saving, or a report times out. Detect: support tickets and bug reports rather than alerts. Cause: consistency or latency expectations were never written down. Fix: make non-functional requirements an explicit, reviewed section of every design.
  • A hidden single point of failure. Symptom: one component's outage takes everything down. Detect: an incident and its postmortem. Cause: the review only covered the happy path. Fix: add a "what if X fails?" pass for every component; rehearse with failure drills.
  • Cost surprise. Symptom: the cloud bill jumps months after launch. Detect: budget alerts and cost dashboards. Cause: storage, egress, or retention never estimated. Fix: include cost in estimates; set retention and lifecycle rules from day one.
  • Design drift. Symptom: the design doc no longer matches the system, and new engineers make wrong assumptions. Detect: confusion during onboarding and incidents. Fix: record later decisions as short architecture decision records and keep the main doc current.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Functional requirement: behavior the system must provide.
  • Non-functional requirement: a quality target or constraint (latency, availability, consistency, cost).
  • Scope: the agreed set of features the design covers.
  • Access pattern: how data is read and written (by key, by range, by search).
  • Read path / write path: the sequence of components a read or write passes through.
  • Single point of failure (SPOF): a component whose failure stops the system.
  • Hot spot: a key, shard, or server receiving disproportionate load.
  • Trade-off: choosing one quality at the cost of another.
  • Design document: a written proposal describing the design and its alternatives.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Jumping straight to components ("Kafka, Redis, Kubernetes") before requirements.
  • Treating system design as picking fashionable tools. It is about meeting requirements with the simplest workable design.
  • Over-engineering for scale nobody asked for.
  • Ignoring non-functional requirements, which drive most decisions.
  • No numbers, so nothing justifies caching or sharding.
  • Only the happy path, with no discussion of failures or hot spots.
  • Silent thinking in interviews; the interviewer cannot evaluate what they cannot hear.
  • Running out of time before the deep dives.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between functional and non-functional requirements? Give three examples of each for a chat app.
  2. Why should estimation come before the high-level design?
  3. Why define the API and data model before drawing the architecture?
  4. How would you divide a 45-minute interview across the nine steps?
  5. What does a good trade-off statement contain?
  6. What sections belong in a design document for a real project?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• AWS Well-Architected Framework
  • Azure Architecture Center
  • Google SRE book
  • Martin Fowler: Software Architecture Guide
  • Related notes: Back-of-the-envelope estimation, Building blocks, System design overview

docs.title: Servers and Infrastructure
docs.text: This section introduces the infrastructure that makes applications reachable and available in production, including domains, servers, and delivery services.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Understand how domains and DNS configuration connect users to services.
  • Learn the roles of servers, Nginx, reverse proxies, and load balancers.
  • Become familiar with cloud infrastructure and content delivery networks.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Domains and DNS Configuration
  • Servers
  • Nginx
  • Reverse Proxy
  • Load Balancing
  • AWS
  • CDN

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Amazon Web Services (AWS) is a cloud platform offering computing, storage, databases, and networking. Instead of maintaining physical machines, a team can rent resources and manage them through a console, command-line tools, or APIs.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Organizations need infrastructure that can be provisioned and resized quickly. Cloud services let teams start small and pay for measured usage, but do not remove the need to secure and monitor infrastructure.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: AWS divides its infrastructure into geographic Regions and Availability Zones. Amazon EC2 provides virtual servers, S3 stores objects, and Route 53 offers DNS. Teams combine services and configure access permissions. Costs depend on service and usage.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A small web application might run its API on EC2, save images in S3, and use Route 53 for its domain. More instances can later sit behind a load balancer. This is only one possible design.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Developers should understand service dependencies, data location, and who can access resources. Keep configuration repeatable, use least-privilege permissions, and review costs and backups. See servers, load balancing, and CDNs.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Before deploying, list application, storage, and DNS needs. Choose services, set a spending alert, and test a small deployment. Never place credentials in source code.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Cloud computing: on-demand access to computing resources over a network.
  • Region: a geographic AWS area.
  • Availability Zone: an isolated location within a Region.
  • EC2 instance: a virtual server.
  • IAM: AWS identity and access management.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: AWS offers broad choices and global infrastructure. Its breadth can make selection difficult, and unmonitored usage can create unexpected bills. Cloud hosting does not automatically make an application reliable.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: Cloud resources are not free or maintenance-free. AWS manages underlying facilities, but customers remain responsible for application behavior, data protection, access rules, and many configuration choices.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official AWS documentation: What is Amazon EC2? introduces virtual server concepts and EC2 terminology.
  • Official AWS documentation: What is Amazon S3? explains object storage and buckets.
  • Third-party explainer: Cloudflare: What is cloud computing? gives a vendor-neutral introduction to cloud concepts.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A content delivery network (CDN) is a distributed group of servers that delivers content closer to users. CDNs commonly cache public assets such as images, stylesheets, and scripts.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: When every request travels to one distant server, network delay and origin workload can rise. A CDN can serve cached content from a nearby point of presence, reducing repeated trips to the origin.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A site's configuration sends requests through the CDN. On a cache hit, it returns the stored response; on a miss, it fetches from the origin and may cache the response. Cache headers, time-to-live settings, and invalidation control freshness.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A user opening a product page may download the same images as other visitors. A CDN can return cached images without asking the web server each time. Personalized account details should not be cached publicly.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Decide which paths are safe to cache and for how long. Version static filenames, such as app.a81f.js, or arrange invalidation. Test cache hits and misses. Related: DNS and reverse proxies.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For /images/logo.svg, configure a suitable cache lifetime. A new versioned filename lets browsers and CDN edges retain the old image safely.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Origin: the source server or storage for content.
  • Edge/point of presence: a CDN location serving nearby users.
  • Cache hit/miss: whether the requested response was already cached.
  • TTL: how long a cached item may remain fresh.
  • Purge/invalidation: removing cached content before expiry.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: CDNs can reduce latency and origin traffic. They add configuration complexity; stale content and extra costs are possible. Dynamic or private responses may not benefit.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A CDN does not automatically speed every page: cacheability and origin response time matter. It does not replace secure application code.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Cloudflare documentation: What is a CDN? explains CDN locations, caching, and delivery.
  • Official AWS documentation: What is Amazon CloudFront? describes AWS CDN distributions, origins, and caching.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A domain name, such as example.com, is a human-readable name used to reach internet services. The Domain Name System (DNS) lets software look up records associated with a domain, such as addresses or mail servers.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Names are easier to remember than numeric IP addresses. DNS lets an organization change hosting addresses without changing the domain name. Cached answers mean updates may take time to appear.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A registrar manages a domain's registration. Its delegation points resolvers to authoritative nameservers, which publish records. A recursive resolver looks up an answer and may cache it for its time to live. Common records include A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), and TXT (verification or policy text).

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: For www.example.com, an A record can point to a web server's IPv4 address, or a CNAME can point a subdomain to a provider hostname. Email uses MX records.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Resolvers cache DNS answers, so changes may not be immediate. Confirm the record type, hostname, destination, and TTL before changing production DNS. DNS directs clients to a service; the service decides its response. See servers, CDN, and SSL certificates.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: To direct api.example.com, get the exact target and record type from the hosting provider. Add it in the DNS control panel and verify with a DNS lookup tool.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Registrar: company through which a domain is registered.
  • Authoritative nameserver: source of published DNS records.
  • Resolver: service that looks up DNS on a client's behalf.
  • TTL: time a DNS answer can be cached.
  • Propagation: informal term for caches updating after a change.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: Buying a domain does not create a website or mailbox. DNS helps clients find a service; it does not store a web page. Lowering a TTL does not instantly clear existing caches.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Internet standard: RFC 1034: Domain Names—Concepts and Facilities describes DNS architecture and concepts.
  • Official Cloudflare learning resource: What is DNS? provides a beginner-friendly lookup walkthrough and record overview.
  • Official AWS documentation: What is Amazon Route 53? explains hosted zones, records, and AWS DNS routing.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Load balancing distributes requests across backend servers or application instances. A load balancer sits between clients and backends and chooses where requests go.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: A single server can become overloaded or unavailable. Sharing work across healthy instances increases capacity and reduces the effect of one failure. Other parts of the system must also be designed for failure.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Clients connect to the balancer, which selects a backend using a policy such as round robin or least connections. Health checks help it avoid unresponsive instances. Some balancers understand HTTP hostnames and paths. Session affinity keeps a client on one backend but may limit flexibility.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: An online store has three web instances. The balancer sends requests to available instances and avoids one that fails its health check.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Applications should avoid relying on local memory or disk for shared user state. Store durable data in a shared service and make health checks reflect readiness. Understand forwarded headers, TLS termination, and timeouts. Related: servers, Nginx, and reverse proxies.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Start with two instances and a /health endpoint. Route traffic only to healthy instances, then stop one in a test environment and confirm requests still succeed.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Backend/target: a server receiving forwarded requests.
  • Health check: a test used to decide whether a target is usable.
  • Algorithm: rule for choosing a target.
  • Failover: directing traffic away from an unavailable component.
  • Session affinity: repeatedly choosing the same backend for a client.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Load balancing spreads load and can help with maintenance or failure recovery. It adds a component to monitor and does not fix slow code or an overloaded database.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: Adding instances does not always make an application scale: shared dependencies may still limit it. A passing health check does not prove every feature works.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Nginx documentation: HTTP load balancing explains upstream servers and balancing methods.
  • Official AWS documentation: Elastic Load Balancing describes load balancers, targets, and health checks.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Nginx (pronounced “engine-x”) is web-server software used to serve files and handle HTTP traffic. It can also act as a reverse proxy, TLS endpoint, or load balancer.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Web applications need to accept requests, serve static content, and route requests to application processes. Nginx can sit in front of an application server, separating public traffic entry from application execution.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Nginx reads configuration blocks describing listeners, hostnames, and actions. A server block can match a hostname; a location block serves a file or proxies to an upstream application. Configuration changes should be syntax-tested before reload.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A Node.js app listens on a private port while Nginx listens on port 443. Nginx serves /assets/ and forwards /api/ to the app.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Included files can affect the effective configuration. Restrict public access to upstream applications when appropriate, preserve needed headers, and configure timeouts. Related: reverse proxies and load balancing.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Configure a development host to proxy an API path to a local service. Run nginx -t before reloading. If it fails, inspect the error log and confirm the upstream is listening.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Directive: a configuration instruction.
  • Server block: virtual host configuration for a listener and host.
  • Location: rule matching a request URI.
  • Upstream: one or more proxy backend servers.
  • TLS termination: decrypting HTTPS at a front-end component.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Nginx is flexible, widely deployed, and can efficiently serve static files or proxy traffic. Its configuration language has details that take time to learn; mistakes in headers, paths, or access rules can cause outages or expose unintended content.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: Nginx is not a programming language or a replacement for an application's business logic. It can be a web server and proxy at once, but those roles are distinct and independently configured.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Nginx documentation: Beginner’s Guide introduces configuration structure and common tasks.
  • Official Nginx documentation: Reverse proxy module documents proxy directives and behavior.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A reverse proxy accepts client requests and forwards them to backend services. To a visitor, it appears to be the site's server, though the application may run elsewhere.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: A reverse proxy provides a front door for application servers. It can route by hostname or path, terminate HTTPS, serve static files, and distribute traffic. With suitable network rules, it can keep backends off the public network.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: The proxy evaluates routing rules, forwards a request to an upstream, then returns its response. It may add headers such as X-Forwarded-For. Applications should trust these only from known proxies; a client could otherwise forge them.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: Route example.com/api/ to an API and example.com/ to a frontend. Both can stay private while the proxy exposes intended routes.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: When debugging, identify whether a response came from the proxy or application. Check path rewriting, forwarded headers, TLS settings, and timeouts. See Nginx and load balancing.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Configure a development proxy to forward /api/ to a local API. Compare proxied and direct requests to identify routing problems.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Client: program or user making the request.
  • Upstream/backend: service receiving a forwarded request.
  • Forwarded header: metadata about the original client or connection.
  • TLS termination: ending the encrypted connection at the proxy.
  • Path rewriting: changing a URI before forwarding it.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: A reverse proxy centralizes routing and can simplify TLS and traffic management. It adds a network hop and can become a bottleneck or single point of failure.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A reverse proxy is not automatically a firewall or authentication system. Backends still need access controls and secure application logic.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Nginx documentation: Reverse proxy module explains proxying requests and related directives.
  • Official Cloudflare learning resource: What is a reverse proxy? gives a visual overview and compares proxy roles.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A server is a computer or software process that provides a service to clients. A web server receives HTTP requests and returns pages or data. “Server” describes a role, not necessarily hardware.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Applications need a place to run and respond to requests. A server can provide a website, API, or database. It may be physical hardware, a virtual machine, or a managed platform.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A server process listens on an address and port. A client connects and sends a request using an agreed protocol; the server returns a response. Operating systems, networking rules, and software affect whether it works. Public servers need updates and access control.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: When a browser requests https://example.com, DNS helps find the service address and web software handles the request. The server may return a file or call an application and database.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Know what listens on each port, how to view logs, and how services restart. Keep private services private and apply updates. Applications must handle timeouts and unavailable dependencies. Related: DNS, Nginx, and AWS.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Run a local development server and open its address in a browser. If it fails, check the process, port, and firewall or container mapping. Do not expose development servers publicly without understanding their protections.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Client: requester of a service.
  • Host: a network-connected computer.
  • Port: number identifying a service endpoint on a host.
  • Process: running program managed by an operating system.
  • Virtual machine: software-defined computer with its own operating environment.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Servers give teams control over software and runtime settings. They require planning, patching, backups, and monitoring. Managed hosting reduces some work but not application responsibilities.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A server need not be a large physical computer. One host can run several services, and one service can span hosts. “Always on” does not mean “always available.”

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official AWS documentation: Amazon EC2 concepts introduces virtual servers and their lifecycle.
  • Third-party tutorial: DigitalOcean: What Is a Server? explains the client-server model in plain language.

docs.title: DevOps and Deployment
docs.text: This section covers the practices and tools used to build, test, deploy, and maintain applications throughout their lifecycle.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Understand source control and automated build-and-release workflows.
  • Learn the purpose of containers and environment-specific configuration.
  • Explore certificates, operational visibility, and data backups.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Git and GitHub
  • Docker
  • CI/CD
  • Environment Variables
  • SSL Certificates
  • Monitoring and Logging
  • Backups

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A backup is a recoverable copy of data or configuration. It protects against accidental deletion, bugs, device failure, and some security incidents. It is useful only if it can be restored in time.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Production data can be lost or corrupted. Replication may keep a service running but also copy accidental deletion. A backup provides a point-in-time recovery option.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A backup process copies selected data to another location on a schedule or continuously. A retention policy defines how long copies are kept. Protect copies and test that they can be restored.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A shop keeps a month's worth of nightly database backups. If a migration corrupts records, the team can restore a clean copy.

docs.title: Developer perspective
