docs.title: AI and Machine Learning Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions cover AI foundations, application patterns, model customization, and production engineering. Model capabilities and provider interfaces change, so verify version-specific details against current documentation.

docs.title: 1. What is the difference between AI, machine learning, and deep learning?
docs.text: AI is the broad field of systems performing tasks associated with intelligent behavior. Machine learning is a group of methods that learn patterns from data. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning based on multi-layer neural networks.

docs.title: 2. What is the difference between training and inference?
docs.text: Training adjusts model parameters using data and an objective. Inference uses an already trained model to produce an output for an input. Calling a hosted model API normally performs inference, not training.

docs.title: 3. What is a large language model?
docs.text: An LLM is a language model with a large learned parameter set, commonly trained on large text corpora and adapted for tasks such as instruction following. "Large" does not guarantee correctness, safety, or suitability for a specific task.

docs.title: 4. What is a transformer?
docs.text: A transformer is a neural-network architecture that uses attention to process relationships among input elements. Transformer variants are used for text, images, audio, and multimodal tasks.

docs.title: 5. What is attention in a transformer?
docs.text: Attention computes how representations at different positions should influence one another. It is a model operation; it is not proof of human-like understanding or a source citation.

docs.title: 6. What is a token?
docs.text: A token is a model-specific unit of input or output. It may represent a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or another piece of data. Token counts affect context and often cost.

docs.title: 7. What is a context window?
docs.text: The context window is the amount of tokenized input and generated output a model can process for a request. System instructions, history, tools, and retrieved documents all consume context.

docs.title: 8. What is an embedding?
docs.text: An embedding is a numeric vector generated from content. Vector search compares these vectors to retrieve semantically related items. Similarity does not prove correctness or authorization.

docs.title: 9. What is a hallucination?
docs.text: A hallucination is plausible-looking generated content that is unsupported or incorrect. Retrieval, validation, and review can reduce specific risks, but no prompt guarantees truth.

docs.title: 10. How should a browser application call a hosted model?
docs.text: Usually through the application's backend. The backend protects credentials, authenticates and authorizes the user, validates input, applies quotas, calls the provider, checks the output, and handles errors. A secret key embedded in frontend code is exposed to users.

docs.title: 11. How would you build a chat feature?
docs.text: Define authentication and conversation ownership, bound the history sent to the model, set input and output limits, handle streaming and disconnects, and validate responses. Store conversation state only according to the product's privacy and retention policy.

docs.title: 12. How would you use AI to summarize personal notes?
docs.text: Authorize access to the notes, send only relevant content, request a structured summary, validate the result, and preserve links to source sections. Provide correction and deletion workflows.

docs.title: 13. What is structured output?
docs.text: Structured output asks a model to return data in a defined shape, often using a schema-constrained provider feature. The application must still parse and validate the result and enforce business rules.

docs.title: 14. What is CORS, and does it protect an AI API?
docs.text: CORS is a browser-enforced policy controlling whether frontend JavaScript can read a cross-origin response. It is not authentication or authorization; the API must protect itself for every client.

docs.title: 15. Why should API keys not be placed in frontend code?
docs.text: Frontend code is delivered to the user's device and can be inspected. Exposed keys can be copied and used to incur charges or access data. Keep secrets in a protected backend environment and rotate exposed keys.

docs.title: 16. How do you handle provider rate limits and outages?
docs.text: Use timeouts, respect documented retry guidance, apply bounded backoff with jitter, limit concurrency, and present a clear fallback or unavailable state. Retries should not duplicate side effects or silently turn failures into empty success responses.

docs.title: 17. What is RAG?
docs.text: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant external information and provides it as context to a model for a response. It can ground answers in current or private sources, but does not guarantee the response follows those sources.

docs.title: 18. What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning?
docs.text: RAG supplies information at inference time without changing model weights. Fine-tuning updates a pretrained model using examples to change behavior. Use retrieval for changing facts and citations; consider fine-tuning for repeatable behavior after evaluating simpler approaches.

docs.title: 19. How do you evaluate a RAG system?
docs.text: Measure retrieval quality separately from answer quality. Check whether expected authorized passages are retrieved, whether answers are supported, whether citations resolve to real sources, and whether access controls prevent cross-user leakage.

docs.title: 20. Why is chunking important in RAG?
docs.text: Chunks determine the text units embedded, retrieved, and placed in model context. Chunks that are too small lose context; chunks that are too large can reduce relevance and consume more context. Tune them using known question-source examples.

docs.title: 21. What is fine-tuning?
docs.text: Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on a task-specific dataset to change its behavior. It needs high-quality examples and held-out evaluation, and may cause regressions in other behaviors.

docs.title: 22. When would you train a model from scratch?
docs.text: Usually only for research or a compelling unique-data or strategic requirement. Foundation-model training needs substantial data governance, compute, expertise, evaluation, and operations. Most product teams should start with an existing model.

docs.title: 23. Can fine-tuning make a model know current company documents?
docs.text: It is not a dependable document lookup or permission mechanism. Documents change and need traceable retrieval, so RAG or direct application queries are usually more suitable for current private information.

docs.title: 24. How can you run a model without a paid hosted API?
docs.text: Run a model with available weights locally or on self-managed hardware using a compatible runtime. This avoids provider per-request charges but still uses hardware, electricity, disk, setup, and maintenance. Check model licenses and protect the local endpoint.

docs.title: 25. What is tool calling?
docs.text: The model returns a structured request for an application-defined tool. The backend must validate the tool and arguments, authorize the action, execute it, and decide what result to return. The model's request is not itself permission.

docs.title: 26. What is an AI agent?
docs.text: An agent is commonly a model-driven loop that selects actions, observes results, and continues toward a goal. The term is broad. Bound its steps, time, cost, and permissions, and prefer deterministic workflows when possible.

docs.title: 27. What is prompt injection?
docs.text: Prompt injection is untrusted content that attempts to alter model behavior or override instructions. Treat user input and retrieved documents as untrusted; keep authorization and tool permissions in application code.

docs.title: 28. Why is a system prompt not a security boundary?
docs.text: The model may follow conflicting or malicious content despite the instruction. Security-sensitive rules must be enforced by trusted code, permissions, and data boundaries.

docs.title: 29. How do you prevent a model from accessing another user's documents?
docs.text: Authenticate the user and filter retrieval using server-derived ownership or tenant permissions before results reach the model. Test cross-user isolation, cache keys, logs, citations, and deletion flows.

docs.title: 30. How do you evaluate generated responses?
docs.text: Use task-specific representative examples and criteria for factual support, task completion, formatting, safety, and uncertainty. Combine automated checks with human review, especially for consequential outcomes.

docs.title: 31. What metrics should be monitored in production?
docs.text: Track latency percentiles, errors, timeouts, rate limits, output validation failures, token usage, cost per completed task, retrieval coverage, refusals, and user corrections or escalations. Minimize sensitive content in logs.

docs.title: 32. Why is a successful HTTP response not proof of a good AI answer?
docs.text: HTTP success means the API returned according to its protocol. It does not mean generated content is true, relevant, safe, or useful. Application quality needs separate evaluation.

docs.title: 33. How would you reduce model latency?
docs.text: Measure the full request first. Then consider reducing unnecessary context, using a smaller adequate model, improving retrieval, streaming when appropriate, or moving long work to background jobs. Test quality and total cost for each change.

docs.title: 34. How would you reduce AI feature cost?
docs.text: Limit input and output, avoid sending irrelevant history, use a suitable lower-cost model for simple tasks, cache only when safe, prevent duplicate calls, and track cost per completed task. Do not trade away required quality or privacy without approval.

docs.title: 35. What should happen before a model can send an email or make a
docs.text:
purchase?

The backend should validate arguments and user permissions, show the exact action and consequences, require confirmation where appropriate, and execute through a narrow audited operation. The model should not perform irreversible actions merely because it generated a tool request.

docs.title: 36. How do local and hosted models differ?
docs.text: Hosted models offload serving infrastructure to a provider but introduce network dependency, provider terms, quotas, and usage costs. Local models offer more control over where inference runs but require hardware, operations, and compatible model licenses. Compare both on the actual task.

docs.title: 37. What is model drift?
docs.text: Drift describes changes in incoming data or in the relationship between inputs and desired outcomes that can reduce deployed performance. Monitor quality and re-evaluate when data, product behavior, or model versions change.

docs.title: 38. When should a human review an AI result?
docs.text: Use human review when mistakes could materially affect people, money, rights, safety, or irreversible actions, and when the model cannot be validated reliably. Reviewers need sufficient context and authority to correct the output.

docs.title: 39. How do you choose between a model and deterministic code?
docs.text: Use deterministic code when rules are explicit, exactness matters, and the input space is manageable. Use a model when flexible interpretation or generation adds measurable value. Many products combine both.

docs.title: 40. How should an AI feature respond when it does not know?
docs.text: Design an explicit no-answer or clarification path. For grounded tasks, check whether usable sources were retrieved; for other tasks, constrain claims and offer escalation. Do not present an invented answer as success.

docs.title: 41. What is the difference between a language model and an AI product?
docs.text: A language model predicts or generates from model input. An AI product also includes the user experience, application data, access control, retrieval, tools, validation, monitoring, and support workflow. Product reliability cannot be inferred from model capability alone.

docs.title: 42. What does temperature change?
docs.text: Temperature rescales next-token scores before sampling in supported decoding methods. Lower values tend to make selection more concentrated; higher values can increase variation. It does not update model weights, provide new facts, or verify correctness.

docs.title: 43. How does a diffusion image model generate an image?
docs.text: A diffusion model is trained to estimate or remove noise from corrupted examples. Generation begins from noise and applies learned denoising steps, often conditioned on text or another input. The output is a generated sample, not evidence that a depicted event occurred.

docs.title: 44. What is multimodal AI?
docs.text: Multimodal AI processes or generates more than one data modality, such as text, images, audio, or video. A product may use one multimodal model or a pipeline of specialist models. Verify the selected model's exact supported inputs, outputs, limits, and evaluation needs.

docs.title: 45. What is the difference between vector search and a reranker?
docs.text: Vector search retrieves candidates by comparing embeddings. A reranker scores a smaller candidate set against the query to improve ordering. A reranker cannot find a relevant source that retrieval omitted and adds latency and cost.

docs.title: 46. What does LoRA do?
docs.text: Low-Rank Adaptation adds small trainable low-rank matrices to selected layers while most base weights remain fixed. It can reduce training resource and artifact requirements for some setups, but still needs compatible models, data, and held-out evaluation.

docs.title: 47. What is quantization?
docs.text: Quantization represents model values at reduced numeric precision to lower memory or improve inference efficiency in supported runtimes. It can affect quality and speed differently across models and hardware, so test the quantized version on the real task.

docs.title: 48. What is Model Context Protocol?
docs.text: MCP is an open protocol that lets an AI host connect through clients to servers exposing tools, resources, or prompts. It standardizes integration interfaces; the host and application still need to authenticate, authorize, validate, and audit operations.

docs.title: 49. What is data leakage in machine learning?
docs.text: Data leakage occurs when training or evaluation uses information that would not legitimately be available at prediction time, or when evaluation data influences model selection in a way that makes the final estimate misleading. It can produce impressive offline metrics that fail in production.

docs.title: 50. What is MLOps?
docs.text: MLOps covers repeatable data and training pipelines, experiment and model versioning, evaluation gates, deployment, monitoring, and retirement. Generative AI applications also need versions for prompts, tools, embedding models, retrieval indexes, and safety policies.

docs.title: 51. How would you scale self-hosted inference?
docs.text: Measure request arrival, queue time, time to first token, generation throughput, accelerator memory, and tail latency. Then select appropriate batching, worker capacity, model size, and scaling behavior. Bound queues and concurrency; model-loading time and accelerator supply make autoscaling different from scaling a small stateless API.

docs.title: 52. How do you evaluate an AI system that handles images or audio?
docs.text: Create representative samples and criteria for the actual task, such as transcription accuracy, timestamp alignment, visual grounding, schema validity, and safety. Include varying conditions such as noise, accents, lighting, and file quality, and use human review for ambiguous or consequential cases.

docs.title: 53. Why does an AI application need to decode media before inference?
docs.text: Image, audio, and video files are encoded representations, not necessarily the tensors or media tokens a model consumes. The application or provider must decode and preprocess them, while respecting format, dimensions, duration, timestamps, and size limits.

docs.title: 54. How can an AI feature safely use terminal commands?
docs.text: The model should propose a narrowly defined operation; application code must validate it, enforce user permissions, and execute only within a bounded environment. Avoid passing model-generated strings directly to a shell, and use least privilege, timeouts, resource limits, and audit logs.

docs.title: 55. What is the difference between MCP stdio and Streamable HTTP?
docs.text: With stdio, the host launches a local server process and exchanges protocol messages over standard input and output. Streamable HTTP connects to a remote HTTP endpoint and requires appropriate authentication and transport security. Both need capability validation and host-side authorization.

docs.title: 56. Does connecting an MCP server authorize every tool it exposes?
docs.text: No. A connection and capability discovery do not grant the model or user permission to perform every operation. The host should expose only needed capabilities, validate each request, enforce authorization, and require confirmation for sensitive actions.

docs.title: 57. How do image classification, object detection, and segmentation differ?
docs.text: Classification assigns one or more labels to an image. Detection predicts labels with bounding boxes around objects. Segmentation predicts pixel-level regions, either by class or by individual object. Choose the task based on the output the application needs.

docs.title: 58. How do CNNs and vision transformers process images differently?
docs.text: CNNs apply learned filters over local image regions and combine features through layers. Vision transformers commonly divide an image into patches and process patch representations with transformer layers. They have different architectural biases and trade-offs; neither is best for every dataset, task, or hardware target.

docs.title: 59. What is transfer learning in computer vision?
docs.text: Transfer learning starts from a model whose weights were learned on another dataset. Feature extraction keeps much of that model fixed and trains a task-specific head; fine-tuning updates some or more of the pretrained model. It can reduce data and compute needs compared with training from scratch, but still requires compatible preprocessing, permitted data, and held-out evaluation.

docs.title: 60. Why should image datasets sometimes be split by subject or source?
docs.text: Related images can be near-duplicates. If images of the same subject, scene, or video appear in both training and test sets, the test score may overstate generalization. Split by the source or group that best represents how genuinely new production examples will differ.

docs.title: 61. What does a small-scale model-training exercise teach, and what does it not teach?
docs.text: It teaches data splitting, fitting, held-out evaluation, metrics, and inference on a manageable dataset. A small classical classifier does not reproduce the training of a deep vision model or an LLM, and its score does not prove performance on a different real-world image distribution.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A language model assigns likelihoods to sequences of tokens and can generate a continuation from a context. A large language model (LLM) is a language model with a large number of learned parameters and broad training. "Large" is relative; it does not specify a particular capability or quality level.

docs.title: How next-token generation works
docs.text:
1. The input text is tokenized into token identifiers.
  2. The model processes the token sequence and returns scores for possible next tokens.
  3. A decoding strategy selects a token, such as the highest-scoring option or a sampled option.
  4. The selected token is appended to the context, and generation repeats.
  5. Generation stops at a configured limit or model stop condition.

This next-token objective can support many downstream behaviors after training and instruction tuning, but the model is still generating based on learned patterns and current context. It does not inherently verify a claim against the world.

docs.title: Tokens and context windows
docs.text:
A token is a model-specific unit: it can represent a word, part of a word, punctuation, or other text. Tokenization differs by model. A context window is the limit on the combined input and generated content the model can process in one request. It is usually measured in tokens, not pages or characters.

The total input may include system instructions, conversation history, retrieved passages, tool definitions, and the user's message. Output tokens also consume budget. Long contexts can increase cost and latency, and relevant material can still be overlooked.

docs.title: Sampling controls
docs.text:
• Temperature: changes how concentrated or varied token selection is for supported sampling methods. Lower is generally more predictable, not automatically more correct.
  • Top-p: restricts sampling to a probability mass chosen by the parameter, where supported.
  • Maximum output tokens: bounds generation length; it is not a guarantee that an answer will be complete.
  • Stop sequence: stops output at configured tokens or strings when the interface supports them.

Provider parameters differ. Start with documented defaults and evaluate changes on representative prompts rather than assuming a setting has a universal effect.

docs.title: Why hallucinations happen
docs.text: Language models are trained to produce likely continuations under an objective. A question may be ambiguous, outside the model's useful knowledge, or missing context. The model can still produce fluent text. Retrieval, constrained output, tool use, calibrated refusal behavior, and human review can reduce specific error types, but none guarantees truth.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A note-taking assistant may summarize a meeting transcript. The transcript is part of the context, but the model can omit a detail or invent a connection. A reliable feature links summary bullets back to source segments and lets the user correct them.

docs.title: Full-stack developer perspective
docs.text: Count the full request, not just the visible user message, when estimating cost and context size. Stream output for user experience when supported, but do not treat partial streamed text as a completed or validated answer. Record model and prompt versions for debugging while avoiding sensitive content in logs.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Tokenizer: converts input text to tokens and generated tokens back to text.
  • Context window: maximum input and output context a model can handle for one generation.
  • Logit: unnormalized score the model assigns to a possible token.
  • Decoding: method for choosing tokens from model output scores.
  • Instruction tuning: additional training intended to make a pretrained model follow instructions more usefully.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A token is not always a whole word.
  • A larger context window does not guarantee that all included details will be used correctly.
  • Lower temperature does not make an answer factually verified.
  • An LLM does not have a database-style, guaranteed lookup of every fact in its training data.

docs.text:

  • OpenAI: Tokens and tokenization

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Local inference runs a model on your own computer or on infrastructure you control instead of sending each request to a hosted model API. It can be useful for learning, offline experiments, privacy-sensitive workflows, or reducing dependence on a particular hosted service.

"Free" usually means no provider charge per request. It does not mean zero cost: hardware, electricity, disk space, setup, speed, and maintenance still matter. Some model weights also have licenses or usage terms.

docs.title: Common ways to run a model
docs.text:
Approach What it provides Useful when Desktop model application UI for downloading and chatting with local models Learning and manual experiments Local model runner with an HTTP endpoint A local service an application can call Prototyping an integration on one machine Python inference libraries Code-level model loading and inference Experiments, model evaluation, and ML development Self-hosted inference server Model endpoint on your own machine or cloud GPU A team needs controlled hosting or a private deployment

Examples include Ollama and LM Studio for local experimentation, llama.cpp for efficient inference across supported hardware, and Hugging Face Transformers for programmatic model workflows. These tools are not interchangeable; check supported hardware, model formats, licenses, and security settings.

docs.title: Local application flow
docs.text:
1. Select a model whose license permits your intended use.
  2. Download its weights from a trusted source and verify the source and published checksums where available.
  3. Load it with a compatible runtime and hardware configuration.
  4. Send prompts to the local process or its loopback HTTP endpoint.
  5. Measure latency, memory use, output quality, and failure behavior.

For an application running on the same computer, bind development services to loopback where possible. Do not expose a local model server to a network without authentication and access controls.

docs.title: Hardware and model size
docs.text:
Inference requires model weights and working memory for intermediate calculations and the context. Quantization stores weights with fewer bits than the original representation and can reduce memory needs, usually with some quality or numerical trade-off. GPU support can increase throughput, but model format and available memory determine what fits.

A smaller quantized model may be more practical on a laptop than a larger model, but task quality varies. Use a small test set for your task rather than choosing only by model size or a benchmark score from another workload.

docs.title: Privacy and offline use
docs.text:
Local inference can keep prompts on a machine you control, but it does not automatically guarantee privacy. The application may still log prompts, synchronize files, expose a local network port, or load untrusted model artifacts. Review telemetry, storage, permissions, and network behavior.

Offline operation is possible only if the runtime, weights, and application dependencies are already available and the chosen features do not require an external service.

docs.title: Local versus hosted inference
docs.text:
Consideration Local Hosted API Per-request provider billing None for local-only inference Usually usage-based or subscription-based Upfront resources Local/server hardware and operations Provider manages inference infrastructure Data path Can remain on controlled hardware Input is transmitted to the provider under its terms Scaling You provision and operate capacity Provider may scale within quotas and service limits Model access Depends on available weights and license Depends on provider's available models Maintenance Runtime, drivers, model updates, monitoring Provider API and model lifecycle management

There is no universal winner. Hybrid systems may route sensitive or offline tasks locally and other tasks to an approved hosted service.

docs.title: Full-stack development
docs.text: The browser should call your backend, and the backend should call the local model server. Do not make a local inference endpoint public merely to let the browser reach it. In production, use an authenticated service boundary, resource limits, monitoring, and a queue if generation is too slow for request-response work.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Local models do not require a paid API key, but still consume hardware and operational resources.
  • A model downloaded locally is not necessarily open source or unrestricted.
  • Quantization can help a model fit; it does not guarantee unchanged quality.
  • Running locally does not make outputs accurate or safe by itself.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Machine learning includes methods that learn patterns from data. Deep learning is a branch of machine learning based on neural networks with multiple learned layers. Modern language, image, speech, and multimodal models often use deep learning, but many valuable prediction tasks use simpler methods.

docs.title: Why are there different methods?
docs.text: Different tasks have different data sizes, shapes, risks, and latency requirements. A small decision tree can be easier to inspect for a structured business rule. A neural network can learn useful representations from large amounts of text or images. The most complex model is not automatically the best system.

docs.title: A practical comparison
docs.text:
Method family Typical inputs Example task Strengths and limits Rules and heuristics Explicit conditions Reject an expired session Predictable and easy to explain; brittle when cases multiply Linear models Structured numeric or encoded features Estimate churn probability Fast and often interpretable; limited nonlinear relationships Decision trees and ensembles Structured tabular features Rank applications for manual review Strong on tabular data; care is needed with bias and explanations Clustering Feature vectors without labels Group similar products Finds structure; groups may not match useful business categories Neural networks Text, images, audio, and other representations Transcribe speech or classify an image Learns rich patterns; needs suitable data, compute, and evaluation Foundation models Broad pretraining across large datasets Generate text, images, or code Reusable across tasks; can be expensive, opaque, or unreliable for a specific task

These descriptions are indicative, not rules. A neural network can also work with structured data, and a foundation model is itself a trained model family, not a guarantee of general intelligence.

For regression, a model predicts a numeric value such as delivery time. For classification, it predicts a label or class score such as ticket category. Clustering groups examples without known labels. A recommendation or ranking system orders candidate items for a user or context. A simple rule or linear model can be the right starting point when its behavior is easier to validate than a more complex model.

docs.title: Training, validation, and test data
docs.text:
To estimate generalization, teams commonly separate examples into:

  • Training set: data used to fit model parameters.
  • Validation set: data used to compare configurations and tune decisions.
  • Test set: held-back data used for a final estimate after choices are made.

The split must reflect how the model will be used. For time-dependent events, a chronological split may be more realistic than random shuffling. For user-level data, keep the same user's records from leaking across training and test sets when that would make evaluation misleading.

Overfitting happens when a model fits accidental details in its training data and performs poorly on new examples. Underfitting happens when the model is too limited or insufficiently trained to capture useful patterns. Evaluation data, regularization, and appropriate model capacity help identify these problems.

docs.title: Metrics depend on the task
docs.text:
Accuracy alone can be misleading. If only 1 in 1,000 transactions is fraudulent, a model that always predicts "not fraud" has 99.9% accuracy but detects none of the fraud cases.

Metric What it summarizes Example use Precision Of predicted positives, how many were positive? Reduce false alerts Recall Of actual positives, how many were found? Catch more cases needing review F1 score Harmonic balance of precision and recall Compare a selected classification threshold Mean absolute error Average absolute numeric prediction error Demand or delivery-time estimate Calibration Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies Risk scores used for prioritization

Choose metrics with stakeholders and examine errors by relevant groups and conditions. The cost of a false positive and a false negative may be very different.

For a binary classifier, a true positive is a positive case correctly found; a false positive is an incorrect alert; a true negative is a correctly rejected case; and a false negative is a missed positive. Changing a score threshold trades precision against recall. In a banking fraud-review workflow, the model can prioritize cases for a person to inspect; it should not be treated as an infallible decision or as a substitute for an appeal and compliance process.

docs.title: How model parameters are learned
docs.text: During training, a model produces predictions in a forward pass. A loss function compares those predictions with targets. Backpropagation computes gradients describing how parameters contributed to that loss, and an optimizer such as stochastic gradient descent uses those gradients to update parameters. Learning rate, batch size, model capacity, data quality, and objective all affect the result. A lower training loss alone does not prove that a model generalizes.

docs.title: Data leakage and drift
docs.text:
Data leakage occurs when evaluation or training accidentally includes information that would not be available at prediction time, or when evaluation examples indirectly reveal their labels. It can make offline scores look excellent while production performance is poor.

Data drift means the distribution of incoming inputs changes. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the desired outcome changes. A deployed model needs monitoring and a plan for re-evaluation; it does not stay correct merely because its code has not changed.

docs.title: Full-stack example
docs.text: Suppose a support application predicts a ticket category. The API validates the submitted text, sends safe features to the model service, stores the prediction and model version, and routes low-confidence cases to a person. The user interface should explain the suggestion and support correction. The model should not be given private account data it does not need.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Start with a baseline such as a rule or simple model and define a measurable target. Keep training and serving data pipelines explicit and versioned. Evaluate failure cases rather than only reporting one average score.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Deep learning is not always more accurate than simpler methods for every dataset.
  • A model score is not a certainty or an explanation.
  • Randomly splitting data is not always a valid evaluation design.
  • A high metric can result from data leakage or an unsuitable test set.

docs.text:

  • Google Machine Learning: Generalization

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: You do not need advanced mathematics to call a model API. A practical understanding of vectors, probability, loss, and gradients helps explain what models learn, how embeddings are compared, and why training changes parameters.

docs.title: Scalars, vectors, and matrices
docs.text:
• A scalar is one value, such as a learning rate.
  • A vector is an ordered list of values, such as an embedding or a row of numeric features.
  • A matrix is a grid of values. A dataset with rows for examples and columns for features can be represented as a matrix.
  • A tensor generalizes arrays to more dimensions, such as a batch of images with height, width, and color channels.

Dimensions are part of the meaning. If a batch has 32 examples and each has 10 features, its shape is commonly written (32, 10). Matrix operations require compatible dimensions; shape errors often reveal a mistaken assumption about the data.

docs.title: Dot product and cosine similarity
docs.text:
For vectors (a) and (b), the dot product multiplies corresponding entries and sums the results:

[ a \cdot b = \sum_i a_i b_i ]

Cosine similarity divides the dot product by the vector lengths:

[ \operatorname{cosine}(a,b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{|a||b|} ]

It emphasizes direction rather than raw magnitude. Embedding models and indexes may use cosine similarity, dot product, or another distance; use the metric expected by the specific embedding and index.

from math import sqrt

def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    norm_a = sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    norm_b = sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    if norm_a == 0 or norm_b == 0:
        raise ValueError("cosine similarity is undefined for a zero vector")
    return dot / (norm_a * norm_b)

print(round(cosine([1, 0], [0.8, 0.2]), 3))  # 0.970

High similarity means the representation is close under the chosen metric. It does not mean that a passage is correct, authorized, or actually answers a question.

docs.title: Probability, logits, and softmax
docs.text:
A model classifier may return logits, real-valued scores that are not probabilities. The softmax function converts a vector of logits into positive values that sum to one:

[ \operatorname{softmax}(z_i) = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} ]

In practice, subtract the largest logit before exponentiation to reduce overflow:

from math import exp

def softmax(logits):
    peak = max(logits)
    values = [exp(value - peak) for value in logits]
    total = sum(values)
    return [value / total for value in values]

print([round(p, 3) for p in softmax([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])])
# [0.659, 0.242, 0.099]

The resulting values sum to one for this candidate set, but a value such as 0.659 is not automatically a calibrated 65.9% chance of correctness. Calibration must be measured against outcomes.

docs.title: Loss and cross-entropy
docs.text:
A loss function assigns a numeric penalty to model predictions during training. For a classification task with a correct class (y) and predicted probabilities (p), cross-entropy loss is:

[ L = -\log(p_y) ]

Assigning higher probability to the correct class reduces this loss. Training usually averages or otherwise aggregates losses across examples. The training objective is a useful signal, not a complete measure of product quality, truthfulness, or safety.

docs.title: Gradients and gradient descent
docs.text:
A gradient describes how a small change in parameters would change a loss. Gradient descent updates parameters in the direction that reduces loss:

[ \theta_{\text{new}} = \theta_{\text{old}} - \eta \nabla_\theta L ]

Here, (\theta) represents model parameters and (\eta) is the learning rate. If the learning rate is too large, optimization can overshoot; if too small, learning can be slow. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to calculate gradients through a neural network.

For a tiny linear regression example, use the model (y = wx + b). The following pseudocode-like Python sketch shows the repeated update:

for x, target in examples:
    prediction = weight * x + bias
    error = prediction - target
    weight_gradient += 2 * error * x / len(examples)
    bias_gradient += 2 * error / len(examples)

weight -= learning_rate * weight_gradient
bias -= learning_rate * bias_gradient

This sketch omits initialization and the outer training loop; it illustrates the update only. In deep networks, automatic differentiation libraries calculate these gradients over many tensor operations.

docs.title: Batches, epochs, and generalization
docs.text:
• A batch is a subset of training examples used for one parameter update.
  • An epoch is one pass through a training dataset.
  • A learning rate schedule changes the update size during training.
  • Regularization discourages some forms of overly complex fitting.
  • A validation set helps compare choices; a test set should remain held out for a final estimate.

Training well on examples is not enough. A model must generalize to cases that represent its actual use. See Machine Learning and Deep Learning for data splits, metrics, and leakage.

docs.title: Full-stack developer perspective
docs.text: For application work, these ideas explain why embeddings have dimensions, why similarity is only a ranking signal, why classifiers need thresholds, and why training loss is not a user-facing success metric. You usually use a library or API for the calculations, but you should still understand what its scores and metrics do—and do not—mean.

docs.text:

  • Google Machine Learning: Gradient descent
  • Google Machine Learning: Classification metrics

docs.title: Model Context Protocol and Agent Integrations
Introduction
docs.text: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol for connecting AI applications to external tools and context sources through a common client-server model. An MCP server can expose capabilities such as tools, resources, or prompts. MCP standardizes parts of the connection; it does not make a server trustworthy or decide whether a user may perform an action.

docs.title: Main concepts
docs.text:
• Host: the AI application that manages the user's session and model interaction.
  • Client: the protocol component in the host that connects to a particular server.
  • Server: a process or service that advertises capabilities.
  • Tools: operations the model may request through the host.
  • Resources: data the host may retrieve through the protocol.
  • Prompts: reusable prompt templates or workflows provided by a server.

The exact protocol version, transports, and capability details evolve. Consult the current MCP specification when implementing a client or server.

docs.title: What can an MCP server provide?
docs.text:
The server advertises capabilities; the host decides which ones to expose to the model or user.

Capability Direction and purpose Example Tools The model may request an operation through the host Search an issue tracker or create a draft Resources The host can read data exposed by a server A document, record, or application context Prompts The server can provide a reusable prompt template A guided code-review or research prompt

Depending on protocol version and negotiated capabilities, client-side features can include roots, sampling, elicitation, and tasks. A capability is not automatically available just because the other side implements MCP; the client and server negotiate supported protocol features.

docs.title: How an MCP connection is established
docs.text:
1. A user or administrator configures a trusted server for an MCP-capable host.
  2. The host creates an MCP client and selects a compatible transport.
  3. Client and server exchange protocol/version and capability information.
  4. The client discovers server capabilities and presents only approved tools, resources, or prompts to the model.
  5. When the model proposes a tool call, the host applies policy and confirmation before invoking the server.
  6. Results return through the client, are treated as untrusted data, and may be added to the model's context.

The protocol connection is between host/client and server. The model typically does not open an MCP socket or directly execute a server tool.

docs.title: Standard transports and deployment choices
docs.text:
The current MCP specification defines two standard transports:

Transport How it connects Typical use Main security considerations stdio The host launches a local server process and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages over standard input/output Local tools and developer integrations The configured command runs as a process with the host user's permissions; review its executable, arguments, working directory, and environment Streamable HTTP A client sends JSON-RPC messages to one HTTP endpoint; responses may be JSON or a request-scoped server-sent-event stream Remote or shared servers Authenticate and authorize requests, protect transport, validate origin/host behavior, and isolate tenants

Streamable HTTP replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport in protocol 2025-03-26. Older clients may still support HTTP+SSE for compatibility; new integrations should follow the current specification and verify the client/server versions. Transport and capability details can change, so check compatibility rather than assuming every host supports every mode.

docs.title: Illustrative host configuration
docs.text:
Some desktop hosts use a JSON configuration shaped like this for a local stdio server:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "project-search": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["server.py"],
      "env": {}
    }
  }
}

Remote-server configuration may instead specify a URL and authentication settings. Configuration schemas and file locations are host-specific; mcpServers is an example convention, not a field required by the MCP protocol. Do not copy tokens or secrets into a checked-in config file.

Conceptually, a remote client connects to a configured MCP endpoint:

MCP client -> HTTPS endpoint -> authenticated MCP server

The host may start the stdio process itself, or a platform may manage that process. For remote services, follow the server's authentication and deployment guidance. MCP authorization supports OAuth-based patterns for HTTP transports; stdio normally relies on local process configuration and OS permissions instead of HTTP OAuth.

docs.title: Tool use through a host
docs.text:
1. The host connects to a configured server and discovers supported capabilities.
  2. The application decides which capabilities are appropriate for the current user and task.
  3. The model may propose a tool call with structured arguments.
  4. The host validates the request, checks authorization, and obtains any required user confirmation.
  5. The host invokes the tool and returns a bounded result to the model.
  6. The application validates and presents the final answer or action.

docs.title: MCP and custom tool calling
docs.text:
Choice Advantages Considerations Provider-specific function calling Direct integration with one model API Tied to that provider's tool format Application-defined tools Full control over exposed operations Each integration needs custom schemas and maintenance MCP Common protocol for capability discovery and integrations Requires client/server lifecycle, version, security, and compatibility management

MCP can improve interoperability; it does not replace application authorization, business rules, audit logging, or user confirmation.

docs.title: What MCP servers and integrations are available?
docs.text:
The ecosystem includes local or remote servers for categories such as files and project search, source-control and issue trackers, databases, documentation, communications, and other business systems. Implementations may be first-party, community-maintained, or vendor-provided. Availability, maintenance, and trustworthiness are not implied by being listed in a catalog or appearing in a host's UI.

Before connecting one, verify its publisher and source code where appropriate, supported protocol version, requested permissions, data handling, update process, and whether it transmits information to another service. Prefer the narrowest server and access scope that satisfies the task. A database server should expose task-specific operations rather than unrestricted credentials or query execution when a narrower interface is possible.

docs.title: Security checklist
docs.text:
• Trust only reviewed, explicitly configured servers.
  • Authenticate remote connections and protect transport credentials.
  • Use least privilege for each server and tool.
  • Validate all arguments and outputs against schemas and business rules.
  • Treat resource contents and tool results as untrusted input.
  • Require confirmation for destructive, financial, or external actions.
  • Record useful audit events without retaining unnecessary sensitive data.
  • Set network, time, size, and call-count limits.
  • Review dependencies and update protocol implementations.

docs.title: Agent design
docs.text: An agent is a model-directed control loop that can select tools, inspect results, and continue. Keep the loop bounded by allowed tools, step count, time, token budget, and user permissions. Prefer a deterministic workflow when the task has a known sequence. Make state, retries, and side effects explicit and idempotent.

docs.title: Images, Audio, and Video Formats for AI
Introduction
docs.text: An image, audio recording, or video file is encoded data—not a model input format by itself. An application must decode a file, interpret its dimensions, color or timing, apply any required preprocessing, and send a representation the selected model accepts.

docs.title: Raster and vector images
docs.text:
Raster images store a grid of pixels. Each pixel has color samples, often represented by red, green, and blue channels (RGB), and may include an alpha channel for transparency. Resolution is the number of pixels; a larger image can carry detail but use more memory and model context.

Vector graphics describe shapes and paths mathematically, often with text and style rules. They can scale cleanly for diagrams and icons, but they must be rendered to pixels for many computer-vision models.

Format Kind and typical properties Useful fit and caveat PNG Raster; lossless compression; transparency supported Screenshots, diagrams, and sharp edges; can be large for photographs JPEG / JPG Raster; lossy photographic compression Photos; repeated re-encoding can add artifacts and it does not support alpha WebP Raster; lossy and lossless options, transparency and animation supported Web delivery; confirm target tool and model accept it AVIF Raster image format based on AV1 image coding Efficient web images in supported pipelines; decoding support varies GIF Palette-based raster; animation supported Simple short animations; limited color compared with modern formats SVG XML-based vector description Logos, icons, and diagrams; sanitize untrusted SVG before serving or rendering

PNG was developed by the PNG Development Group and is now specified by standards organizations including W3C. JPEG is specified through the Joint Photographic Experts Group standards process (including ISO/IEC and ITU-T publications). SVG is maintained by the W3C SVG Working Group. Google introduced WebP as a web image format. AVIF builds on the AV1 image coding work from the Alliance for Open Media. These names describe standards or organizations rather than one individual inventor.

docs.title: What an image model receives
docs.text:
A vision pipeline commonly decodes an image into pixel values, applies orientation and color handling, resizes or crops it, and converts it into numeric tensors. Some vision transformer systems split an image into patches. Multimodal systems may encode patches or crops into representations that are combined with text tokens. Exact pipelines vary by model.

The model may resize a large image, sample several crops, or impose a resolution limit. A small chart can become unreadable if the application resizes it too aggressively. Strip unnecessary metadata and enforce upload limits, but preserve task-relevant resolution.

docs.title: A small image-inspection example
docs.text:
Using Pillow in a Python environment, inspect dimensions and color mode before deciding on preprocessing:

from PIL import Image

with Image.open("diagram.png") as image:
    print(image.format, image.size, image.mode)
    rgb_image = image.convert("RGB")

This reads and converts pixels; it does not call an AI model. The Pillow decoder must support the input format, and uploaded data should be validated and size-limited before decoding.

docs.title: Video: container, codec, frames, and timestamps
docs.text:
A container such as MP4 or WebM packages streams and metadata. A codec such as H.264, VP9, AV1, or H.265 compresses video frames; audio may use codecs such as AAC or Opus. A filename extension alone does not guarantee that the content uses a particular codec.

Video models may consume a video file, sampled frames, audio, or a mixture. For frame sampling, the application chooses times or a rate; sparse sampling can miss short events, while dense sampling costs more. Retain timestamps so an answer can link to the relevant moment. Audio may be transcribed separately or processed by an audio-capable model.

# Inspect a local file's streams and codecs when FFmpeg is installed.
ffprobe -hide_banner -show_streams -show_format .\meeting.mp4

Review the command output before passing media to an external provider. FFmpeg tools are optional; model providers may accept different containers, codecs, durations, and sizes.

docs.title: Audio representation
docs.text:
Digital audio is a sequence of samples. Sample rate describes samples per second; bit depth describes the precision of each sample; channels describe separate streams such as left and right stereo. Compression may be lossless (for example FLAC) or lossy (for example MP3, AAC, or Opus). A container such as WAV can store uncompressed PCM, while other containers can carry compressed streams.

Speech models may require a particular encoding, sample rate, channel layout, and duration. Resampling and channel mixing must be deliberate; they can change speech quality. Preserve timestamps and speaker segments when the application needs a transcript users can verify.

docs.title: Web delivery versus model input
docs.text: The best browser asset is not necessarily the best model input. WebP or AVIF may reduce download size, while a provider endpoint may accept only a different set of formats. A browser can display SVG while a vision model expects raster pixels. Keep the delivery format and inference preprocessing as separate decisions.

docs.title: Security and privacy
docs.text: Validate actual file content, not only its extension or client-supplied MIME type. Bound size, pixel dimensions, duration, and decompression work. Treat metadata, embedded text, subtitles, and OCR output as untrusted. Images and recordings can contain faces, locations, voices, or other sensitive data; minimize processing and apply the product's consent, retention, and access policies.

docs.text:

  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • MDN: Web video codec guide

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: MLOps applies software delivery and operations practices to machine learning systems. It covers reproducible data and training pipelines, model and prompt versioning, evaluation gates, deployment, monitoring, and retirement. For a full-stack AI feature, the lifecycle also includes retrieval indexes, tool definitions, policy configuration, and application code.

docs.title: Lifecycle components
docs.text:
1. Data pipeline: ingest, validate, transform, and version inputs.
  2. Experiment tracking: record code, configuration, data, model parameters, metrics, and artifacts.
  3. Evaluation gate: compare a candidate with a baseline on a held-out suite; test safety, latency, and cost constraints as well as quality.
  4. Model registry: store approved artifacts and metadata with reproducible identifiers.
  5. Deployment: release through staged environments, shadow testing, canary traffic, or a rollback plan.
  6. Monitoring: track system health and quality signals, investigate drift, and re-evaluate when data or model behavior changes.
  7. Retirement: remove unsupported versions and clean up dependent indexes, endpoints, and credentials.

docs.title: Version more than model weights
docs.text:
A reproducible AI feature may depend on:

  • model provider, model identifier, and version;
  • prompt and tool schemas;
  • retrieval index and embedding-model version;
  • data transformations and chunking configuration;
  • safety policy and output validator;
  • application code and evaluation set.

If one of these changes, compare system behavior before and after the change. A provider alias that silently points to a new model can alter quality, latency, or cost.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Track service availability, latency percentiles, timeouts, rate limits, queue depth, resource use, and cost. Where appropriate and privacy-safe, track task completion, user corrections, citation validity, refusal and escalation rates, and evaluation results. Log identifiers and aggregate signals rather than sensitive prompts by default.

Model quality is harder to monitor than CPU or HTTP status. Add sampled human review, user feedback, offline regression suites, and privacy-aware incident investigation. A change in model output may come from input distribution, retrieval, prompt, provider version, or code.

docs.title: Rollback and incidents
docs.text: Keep a known-good version and a safe fallback. Define how to disable a feature, revoke a key, rebuild an index, or route a task to human review. Do not use a previous model blindly if its license, safety status, or data dependencies differ.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Google Cloud MLOps continuous delivery and automation
  • MLflow documentation
  • NIST AI Risk Management Framework

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Model serving exposes a trained model through an interface that an application can call. A serving system loads model weights, accepts requests, runs inference on available hardware, and returns results. It may be a hosted provider, a managed cloud endpoint, or infrastructure operated by your team.

docs.title: Serving choices
docs.text:
Option Team operates Trade-offs Hosted provider API Application integration and policy controls Fastest setup; provider terms, quotas, latency, and price apply Managed cloud endpoint Model selection, application integration, and configuration Less infrastructure work than self-hosting; availability and hardware choices vary Self-hosted inference server Model runtime, hardware, scaling, upgrades, security, and observability More control; high operational and capacity-planning burden On-device runtime Packaging, supported hardware, updates, and local UX Can work offline and keep inference local; device capability and model size constrain quality and speed

Choose by measured quality, data policy, availability, latency, throughput, operational capability, and total cost. "Open weights" does not remove license obligations or operational work.

docs.title: What happens inside a serving system?
docs.text:
1. A gateway checks authentication, quotas, request size, and model access.
  2. A scheduler queues requests and may combine compatible work into a batch.
  3. The runtime tokenizes or otherwise prepares the input, loads model weights, and uses CPU, GPU, or another accelerator.
  4. The model produces output; a decoder or task-specific postprocessor formats it.
  5. A response layer streams or returns the result and emits operational metrics.

docs.title: Performance techniques and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Quantization: represents weights or activations with lower precision to reduce memory or improve throughput. Quality changes must be evaluated; support varies by model and hardware.
  • Batching: executes multiple requests together to use accelerators efficiently. Waiting to form a batch can add latency.
  • Continuous batching: adds and removes sequences while a batch is running, improving utilization in some generation workloads.
  • KV caching: retains attention state for active generation, reducing repeated computation while consuming memory.
  • Model parallelism: splits a large model across devices, adding communication and operational complexity.
  • Autoscaling: adds capacity when demand rises, but model loading, accelerator availability, and warm-up time make scaling slower than ordinary stateless web workers.

Optimize only after measuring queue time, time to first token, generation speed, tail latency, memory, throughput, and cost per completed task.

docs.title: Reliability and security
docs.text: Limit request and output size, protect model endpoints, isolate tenants, patch the runtime, and monitor GPU or accelerator health. Use deadlines, bounded queues, cancellation, and explicit overload responses. Do not allow an internal inference endpoint to become publicly reachable without authentication and rate controls.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Most full-stack developers should begin with a hosted API or managed endpoint. Self-host when privacy, latency, control, economics at measured scale, or product requirements justify the operational cost.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Hugging Face Text Generation Inference
  • vLLM documentation
  • NVIDIA Triton Inference Server

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: "AI model" describes many systems with different input and output types. Before selecting a provider or architecture, describe the task: what information goes in, what should come out, how errors are handled, and whether a person must review the result.

docs.title: Common model categories
docs.text:
Model category Typical input Typical output Example use Chat and language generation Text and conversation context Text, structured fields, or tool-call requests Assistant, drafting, Q&A Reasoning-oriented language model Text or structured task Multi-step answer or plan Complex analysis with verification; cost and latency may be higher Code model Source code, tests, instructions Code completion, explanation, or patch suggestion Developer assistance; generated code still needs review and tests Embedding model Text, image, or other supported content Numeric vector Semantic search, clustering, retrieval Classifier Example and candidate labels Category or score Routing support tickets or detecting content categories Image generation model Text prompt, sometimes reference images Generated or edited image Concept art, assets, design exploration Speech model Audio or text Transcription, translation, or generated speech Voice interface, captions, audio summaries Video model Text, images, or video, depending on model Video, summary, or extracted description Creative generation, scene search, summarization Multimodal model Multiple modalities such as text and images Text or other supported outputs Ask questions about a chart or image Recommendation/ranking model User, item, and context features Ranking or recommendation scores Product or media discovery OCR / document understanding Page image or document file Extracted text, fields, or layout Invoice review and searchable scans Anomaly detector Events or measurements Unusualness score or flag Operations review and equipment monitoring

Categories overlap. A multimodal model might accept images and audio; a single product can combine several specialized models in one workflow. Capabilities and limits vary by model version and deployment.

docs.title: Generative and predictive models
docs.text:
Generative models produce content such as text, an image, or audio. Discriminative models estimate labels, scores, or distinctions for inputs. These are broad modeling categories; real model designs can blur the line.

Choose deterministic code or a conventional model when it is easier to validate than free-form generation. For example, calculate a tax total with application code rather than asking a chatbot to perform arithmetic that must be exact.

docs.title: Open weights, source, and hosted access
docs.text:
• Hosted model/API: a provider runs the model and exposes an interface. The model's weights may not be available to the customer.
  • Open-weight model: weights are available under a license for permitted use, but training data, code, or full reproducibility may not be available.
  • Open-source AI system: the term can mean different things; inspect the license, weights, data and documentation available, and usage restrictions instead of assuming every component is open.
  • Commercial product: may combine models, tools, safety systems, retrieval, and proprietary infrastructure.

Model access and license terms change. Confirm the current license, allowed use, retention behavior, and deployment terms for the exact model and version.

docs.title: Public examples
docs.text:
Examples of public AI products and model platforms include OpenAI's ChatGPT/API offerings, Google's Gemini products and APIs, Anthropic's Claude products and API, GitHub Copilot for coding assistance, Adobe Firefly for creative workflows, and Meta's Llama model family. These are examples of different product and provider categories, not an endorsement, a complete market list, or a claim that every product uses one model for every feature.

Public product names and capabilities evolve. Prefer current official documentation when selecting a model for a project.

docs.title: How a full-stack application may combine models
docs.text:
A study-notes app could use:

  1. A speech-to-text model to transcribe a lecture.
  2. A language model to draft a summary.
  3. An embedding model to index notes for semantic search.
  4. A language model with retrieved passages to answer a question with citations.
  5. Application code to enforce access permissions and store the user's notes.

A shopping application might instead use a ranking model to sort eligible items, an image model to describe product photos, and ordinary business rules to filter unavailable items. Eligibility and price calculations should remain deterministic backend operations.

Each step has a distinct contract and should be evaluated separately.

docs.title: Model routing: selecting a model for a task
docs.text:
Model routing is the application-level decision about which model or processing path should handle a request. A system may route an image question to a vision-capable model, a semantic-search query to an embedding model, or a simple deterministic calculation to ordinary code.

Routing can be implemented with:

  • Explicit application rules: choose a model from a known feature, input type, account setting, or user selection. This is predictable and easy to inspect.
  • A lightweight classifier: classify the task into a small set of allowed routes. The backend still validates the route and permissions.
  • A model-based router: ask a model to select from a bounded set of tools or model choices. This can handle less structured requests, but adds another model call and can choose incorrectly.

An example policy might send ordinary note questions to a lower-cost text model, image questions only to a model that supports images, and questions requiring current private information through an authorized retrieval workflow. A request to calculate a total should normally use application code rather than a language model.

Keep the router separate from authorization. A route is a technical choice, not permission to read a user's data or perform an action. Define allowed routes on the server, validate the selected model's actual input and output capabilities, and provide a safe fallback when no route fits. Compare the routed result with a fixed baseline for task quality, latency, and cost; otherwise routing can add complexity without improving the experience.

Do not route solely by a model's name, size, or marketing category. Provider capabilities, limits, and model versions change, so keep model configuration replaceable and verify the current provider documentation.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Choose based on task quality, latency, cost, availability, data policy, language or modality coverage, output constraints, and operational requirements. Use task-specific tests instead of comparing model names or parameter counts alone.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A chatbot, a model, and an AI product are not the same thing.
  • "Open weight" does not automatically mean unrestricted commercial use.
  • A coding model can generate plausible but insecure or incorrect code.
  • Image, audio, video, and text models have different input, output, and evaluation requirements.
  • A model router does not grant access to data or tools; authorization remains an application responsibility.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• OpenAI API documentation
  • Google Gemini API documentation
  • Anthropic documentation
  • GitHub Copilot documentation
  • Adobe Firefly
  • Meta Llama

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A neural network is a mathematical model made of connected operations with parameters adjusted during training. A transformer is a neural network architecture that uses attention to process relationships among items in a sequence or other structured input. Transformers underpin many modern language models and are also used for images, audio, video, and multimodal tasks.

docs.title: Neural-network basics
docs.text:
A network receives numeric inputs, applies parameterized operations and nonlinear transformations through layers, then produces outputs. During training, an objective (loss) measures how far predictions are from training targets. An optimization algorithm calculates how to adjust parameters to reduce that loss.

  • Forward pass: compute a model output from an input.
  • Loss: numeric training objective measuring some prediction error.
  • Backpropagation: calculate how the loss changes with model parameters.
  • Optimizer: update parameters using those calculated gradients.
  • Epoch: one pass through the training dataset, in training setups that use epochs.

Inference uses the learned parameters to produce outputs; it usually does not update them.

docs.title: Attention and the transformer idea
docs.text:
Attention lets a model compute which parts of an input are relevant to processing another part. In a language sequence, the representation for a token can incorporate information from other tokens. Self-attention computes these relationships within the same sequence.

The transformer architecture commonly combines attention with feed-forward layers, residual connections, normalization, and positional information. Details differ across model architectures. The key idea is that attention helps model long-range relationships and can be parallelized during training more readily than recurrent sequence processing.

In a simplified self-attention operation, each input representation is projected into a query (Q), key (K), and value (V). Similarity between a query and keys determines weights over the values. Multiple attention heads learn different relationships in parallel and their results are combined. This helps the model contextualize tokens, but the weights are not a human-readable explanation of why an answer is true.

docs.title: Encoder, decoder, and encoder-decoder patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Broad behavior Common use Encoder-style Build contextual representations of the input Classification, search embeddings, extraction Decoder-style Generate an output sequence one token at a time Chat, completion, code generation Encoder-decoder Encode an input and generate a related output Translation, summarization, speech or text transformations

These are useful architectural families, not a complete list of current designs. Some systems combine components or use other architectures.

Vision transformers commonly split an image into patches and process them as a sequence of representations. Audio models may use frames, learned tokens, or other encodings. Their inputs and training objectives are specialized; a text-only decoder cannot automatically process raw media.

docs.title: From text to model input
docs.text:
Text is split into tokens, which are converted to numeric identifiers and then to learned embeddings (vectors). The model processes these representations and produces output scores. A decoder-style language model selects or samples a next token, appends it to the context, and repeats until a stopping condition is met.

The output is generated token by token. This is why a long response takes time, why context limits matter, and why the model can produce a plausible continuation that is not factually grounded.

docs.title: Why use transformers?
docs.text: Attention gives models a flexible way to relate different positions in an input, and large-scale training can produce representations useful across many tasks. Trade-offs include substantial compute and memory requirements, quadratic attention cost in some common designs with sequence length, latency for autoregressive generation, and difficult-to-predict behavior. Modern systems use optimizations and architectures that change these costs; do not assume one cost profile fits every model.

docs.title: Full-stack developer perspective
docs.text: You generally call an inference endpoint rather than implement backpropagation or attention yourself. Knowing the high-level flow helps explain prompt length, context windows, streaming responses, embeddings, and latency. For a production feature, treat the model version and its input format as dependencies that can change.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Attention is a model operation, not human attention or an explicit source citation.
  • A transformer is an architecture, not a single model or product.
  • An embedding is a learned numeric representation, not a guaranteed definition of meaning.
  • Neural networks do not retrieve exact training examples on command like a database query.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
