docs.title: AI Project Learning Paths
docs.text:
Use these as step-by-step learning paths, not as instructions to build every feature at once. Pick one project, complete one small milestone, and decide whether to continue before adding the next capability. The study-notes path below is a suggested capstone because it connects AI concepts with ordinary full-stack engineering.

The hands-on labs are short exercises within the learning path; there is no separate testing project to complete. Evaluation and safety checks belong alongside the feature they assess.

docs.title: Suggested capstone: study-notes assistant
docs.text:
Treat each item as a learning step. Stop after any step once it meets your learning goal; the later steps are optional extensions, not a requirement to build a complete product.

  1. Define one small task. For example, answer a question using one fictional note. Decide what a useful answer and a no-answer result look like.
  2. Choose an existing model. Start with a hosted API or an available local model; do not train a model. Compare only what matters for this task, such as answer quality, data handling, latency, and cost.
  3. Understand model selection. Decide whether this task needs a text model, embedding model, or both. Keep the choice fixed initially; study model routing as a later extension.
  4. Try the simplest prompt-based version. Give the model the small note directly and ask it to answer only from that material. Check a question the note answers and one it does not.
  5. Add retrieval when needed. Learn how chunking and embeddings select relevant passages as the note collection grows. Keep the note's source and access information with each passage.
  6. Connect retrieval to answers. Provide the selected passages to the model and show links to those actual sources. Do not treat generated citations as verified until the application checks them.
  7. Add access boundaries. Use fictional notes to understand ownership filtering and why the backend, not the model, enforces permissions. Include prompt injection in a note and observe why retrieved content must remain untrusted.
  8. Add a user interface only after the flow is clear. A minimal screen can submit a question, show the answer and sources, and explain when there is not enough information.
  9. Evaluate each milestone as you learn it. Keep a few expected question/source pairs, check whether retrieval found the right passage, verify that citations point to it, and try a missing-answer or cross-user case. This is part of each step, not a separate testing module.
  10. Consider optional extensions. Add a second model, a local runtime, document upload, or a narrow MCP search tool only when you can explain what the extension teaches and what new risks it introduces.

Related lessons: Model Types and Capabilities, RAG, AI Security, and Building AI Features.

docs.title: 1. Hosted-model API playground
docs.text:
Build a backend endpoint that accepts a user prompt, validates its length, calls a hosted model, and returns a bounded response.

  • Keep the API key on the server.
  • Add authentication, rate limiting, timeout handling, and usage tracking.
  • Show loading, cancellation, error, and retry states in the UI.
  • Test that an invalid request never reaches the provider.
  • Do not log the key or unnecessary prompt content.

Prerequisites: Hosted Model APIs, Building AI Features, and Deployment, Cost, and Performance.

What you practice: secure server-side model calls, backend validation, provider adapters, UI states, quotas, and explicit failure handling. Choose this first if API integration is new to you; it builds the smallest reusable foundation for the later projects.

docs.title: 2. Local-model comparison
docs.text:
Run one small model locally and compare it with a permitted hosted model on the same set of fictional tasks. Record quality, latency, context limits, hardware use, and operational work. Keep the sample data non-sensitive.

Prerequisites: Model Types and Running Models Locally.

What you practice: model selection, local serving, resource measurement, and controlled comparisons. Choose this if you want to understand local-versus-hosted trade-offs before choosing an inference platform; it does not require training a model.

docs.title: 3. Structured support-ticket triage
docs.text:
Create a small set of fictional tickets and allowed categories. Ask a model for structured output, validate it on the backend, and route uncertain cases to a human review screen.

  • Test malformed, ambiguous, and out-of-scope messages.
  • Do not let the model execute ticket changes.
  • Compare against a simple keyword or rules baseline.

Prerequisites: Prompting and Structured Output and Evaluation and Monitoring.

What you practice: schemas, a deterministic baseline, thresholds, review queues, and classification metrics. Choose this if you want to build a bounded business workflow where the model suggests a result but ordinary backend code retains authority.

docs.title: 4. Searchable study notes with RAG
docs.text:
Let a signed-in user add notes, index chunks, ask questions, and open cited source passages.

  • Enforce note ownership before indexing and retrieval.
  • Store source IDs and locations with each chunk.
  • Test that one user's query never retrieves another user's notes.
  • Test deletion and re-indexing when a note changes.
  • Say when no useful source was found instead of inventing an answer.

Prerequisites: Embeddings and Vector Search, RAG, and Security and Responsible AI.

What you practice: ingestion, chunking, vector search, source citations, tenant isolation, data deletion, and answer evaluation. Choose this if you want a flagship project that connects AI retrieval to backend, database, security, and UI skills.

docs.title: 5. Fine-tune a narrow behavior (optional)
docs.text:
Only after establishing a baseline, use a small permitted dataset and a supported model to explore fine-tuning. Compare it with prompting on the same held-out examples. Document the model, data, terms, cost, and regressions. Do not upload personal or confidential data without approval.

Prerequisites: Fine-Tuning and Training Models.

What you practice: data curation, held-out tests, adapters, experiment tracking, and regression analysis. Choose this only after a baseline demonstrates a repeatable behavior gap that prompting and application logic do not solve.

docs.title: 6. Media understanding pipeline
docs.text:
Build a small workflow that accepts a user-selected image or short video, validates its format and size, extracts a few timestamped frames or a transcript, and asks a suitable model for a source-linked description. Show the user which frames or transcript segments support the result and let them remove the uploaded media.

Prerequisites: Images, Audio, and Video Formats for AI, Speech and Multimodal AI, and Security, Privacy, and Responsible AI.

What you practice: codecs and decoding, media limits, asynchronous processing, timestamps, consent, and multimodal evaluation. Choose this if media-based AI is relevant to your goals; begin with still images before adding longer videos or audio.

docs.title: 7. MCP project-search server
docs.text:
Create a read-only local MCP server that searches a small, synthetic project-notes folder. Expose one narrow search tool and one resource, run it over stdio from a compatible host, and inspect how the host discovers and invokes capabilities. Do not start with a shell-execution tool or credentials.

Prerequisites: MCP and Agent Integrations, Terminal Tools and Operating-System Access, and Security, Privacy, and Responsible AI.

What you practice: host/client/server roles, stdio transport, capability discovery, tool schemas, process permissions, and approval boundaries. Choose this if you want to learn how reusable AI integrations connect to external systems without giving a model unrestricted OS access.

docs.title: 8. Model evaluation harness
docs.text:
Build a small test runner that loads fictional task cases, calls a selected model adapter, validates structured outputs, and reports task-specific metrics, latency, and estimated usage. Compare a prompt or model change against the same baseline cases.

Prerequisites: Evaluation and Monitoring, MLOps and Model Lifecycle, and Mathematics for Machine Learning.

What you practice: reproducible fixtures, grading rules, regression testing, model versioning, and operational metrics. Choose this before fine-tuning or switching providers if you need evidence that a change actually improves your task.

docs.title: Choosing a project
docs.text: Your goal Start with Why Learn safe API integration Hosted-model API playground Smallest useful end-to-end feature Understand model hosting choices Local-model comparison Measures quality and resource trade-offs Build a bounded business task Support-ticket triage Practices schemas, metrics, and human review Connect private knowledge safely Searchable study notes with RAG Integrates retrieval, authorization, and citations Learn AI connector protocols MCP project-search server Shows discovery and OS process boundaries Improve multimodal understanding Media understanding pipeline Adds media decoding and modality-specific evaluation Compare model or prompt changes Model evaluation harness Provides evidence before adding complexity Explore model adaptation Fine-tuning experiment Requires a clear behavior gap and evaluation baseline

docs.title: Suggested project quality checklist
docs.text:
• Define the user problem and a measurable success criterion.
  • Keep authorization, validation, and side effects in ordinary backend code.
  • Set input, output, rate, time, and cost limits.
  • Add tests for errors, retries, permissions, and sensitive data.
  • Evaluate representative successes and failures before deployment.
  • Explain generated content and uncertainty to users.
  • Provide deletion and correction paths for stored or derived data.
  • Document which model and prompt versions were used.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A prompt is the input and instruction context sent to a model for inference. It may include system instructions, developer rules, user input, conversation history, examples, retrieved information, and tool definitions. Prompt engineering is the practice of designing and testing that context for a specific task.

docs.title: Why prompt design matters
docs.text: Models respond to the information and instructions in their context. Ambiguous goals, conflicting requirements, missing data, and irrelevant history can lead to inconsistent outputs. A clear prompt makes the task, constraints, and expected format easier to evaluate.

docs.title: A practical prompt structure
docs.text:
1. Role or task: state what work is requested.
  2. Context: provide only the relevant background and source material.
  3. Constraints: define safety boundaries, audience, length, or allowed actions.
  4. Output format: specify fields or a schema when predictable data is needed.
  5. Uncertainty behavior: say what to do when information is missing, such as ask a question or return an explicit unknown.
  6. Examples: provide representative input and output examples only when they clarify the desired behavior.

docs.title: Example: note summary
docs.text:
Task: Summarize the supplied meeting notes for a project team.
Rules:
- Use only the supplied notes.
- Separate decisions, action items, and open questions.
- Include the source heading for each item.
- If an owner or date is missing, write "not specified".
Output: JSON with decisions, action_items, and open_questions arrays.

This prompt improves clarity, but the application must still validate JSON, check source references, and allow correction. The instruction "use only the notes" is not a technical security boundary.

docs.title: Structured output
docs.text:
When an application expects data, use a provider's structured-output or schema-constrained feature when available. Define required fields, types, enums, and bounds. Then validate the response on the server with an ordinary schema validator before using it.

Do not assume JSON-looking text is valid JSON or that valid JSON is factually correct. A schema can ensure priority is one of three strings; it cannot prove that the selected priority is appropriate.

docs.title: Parameters and reproducibility
docs.text: Prompts and model behavior can change with model version, provider defaults, sampling parameters, and context. Keep prompts in version control without embedding secrets or personal data. Record model identifiers and relevant configuration so a test can be reproduced as closely as possible.

docs.title: Prompt injection
docs.text:
Prompt injection is untrusted input that attempts to override instructions or influence model behavior. It can appear in user text, documents, web pages, or tool results. The model should not be treated as an authorization engine.

Keep sensitive operations behind application code. A model may suggest a tool call, but the backend must validate arguments, check the user's permissions, and constrain the operation before execution. Treat retrieved content as data, not instructions.

docs.title: Testing prompts
docs.text:
Build a small set of realistic inputs, including ambiguous, malformed, adversarial, and out-of-scope examples. Evaluate:

  • whether required information is present;
  • whether the model follows the requested format;
  • factual support and source attribution;
  • refusals and uncertainty handling;
  • latency and token consumption;
  • behavior after changing model or prompt versions.

Change one important prompt component at a time and compare outputs. A single impressive example is not evidence of reliability.

docs.title: Full-stack developer perspective
docs.text: Keep prompts and provider logic on the server when they contain private instructions or access to tools. Prompt text is not a substitute for input validation, output encoding, authorization, or rate limiting.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A longer prompt is not automatically a better prompt.
  • Telling a model to "be accurate" does not verify its answer.
  • JSON output can be syntactically valid and semantically wrong.
  • A system prompt is not a secret or a hard security boundary.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• OpenAI: Prompt engineering
  • Google Gemini API: Prompting strategies
  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is an application pattern that retrieves relevant external information and gives it to a generative model as context for a response. The model remains pretrained; RAG does not update its weights.

RAG is useful when answers should use organization documents, personal notes, or information that changes more often than a model's training cycle. It can improve grounding, but it does not guarantee correctness.

docs.title: Why use RAG?
docs.text: A general model may not know private or recent content. Fine-tuning is usually not the right way to store a changing document library: updated facts would require another training process, and the model may still not reliably recall a specific fact. RAG retrieves candidate facts at request time, making sources available to the model and application.

docs.title: Indexing time
docs.text:
1. Collect permitted documents and record their owner, tenant, source, and version.
  2. Extract text while preserving useful structure such as headings, pages, or timestamps.
  3. Split text into chunks and generate embeddings.
  4. Store chunks, vectors, metadata, and stable source references in a searchable index.
  5. Re-index or remove derived content when the source changes or is deleted.

docs.title: Query time
docs.text:
1. Authenticate the user and determine which sources they may access.
  2. Rewrite or embed the query if the chosen retrieval design requires it.
  3. Search using vector, keyword, or hybrid retrieval with authorization filters applied.
  4. Rank and select a bounded set of passages.
  5. Ask the model to answer using those passages and return source identifiers.
  6. Validate the output and render citations that link to the original content.

docs.title: What makes RAG good or bad?
docs.text:
RAG has two distinct quality stages:

  • Retrieval quality: were the useful and authorized passages found?
  • Generation quality: did the model accurately use those passages and represent their limits?

If retrieval misses a relevant paragraph, a better prompt may not fix it. If the right paragraph is present, the model can still misread it. Measure both stages separately. Useful retrieval metrics include recall at k and ranking measures; answer evaluation can check correctness, support, and citation validity with human-reviewed examples.

docs.title: Security and access control
docs.text:
Documents can contain prompt injections or malicious instructions. Treat retrieved text as untrusted data. Do not let it override system policy or grant tools permission.

The backend must filter retrieval by the authenticated user's permissions. If authorization is applied only after retrieval or after generation, private content may leak through the answer, citations, logs, or cache. Keep tenant and ownership metadata in the retrieval design and test cross-user isolation.

docs.title: RAG versus fine-tuning
docs.text:
Need RAG Fine-tuning Use current/private documents Often appropriate Not a reliable document lookup mechanism Provide traceable sources Can return retrieved source references Does not inherently provide citations Change knowledge often Update the index Requires retraining or additional mechanisms Change style or repeatable behavior Prompting may be enough; fine-tuning can help in some cases Often a candidate after evaluation Add access control Filter documents at retrieval time Model weights do not enforce user-specific permissions

The approaches can be combined, but each adds complexity. Start with the simplest system that passes task-specific tests.

docs.title: Full-stack example: company handbook assistant
docs.text: An employee asks about vacation policy. The backend checks the employee's identity and organization, retrieves the current policy sections they may see, and asks the model to answer only from those sections. The response includes links and section names. If no relevant passage is found, the assistant says it cannot answer from the available material and links to the human HR channel.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• Chunks omit headings or context needed to interpret a paragraph.
  • Old and new document versions both appear in results.
  • The right passage is retrieved but truncated from the model's context.
  • Search results are relevant in wording but not authoritative.
  • Citations are fabricated or point to the wrong passage.
  • A shared cache returns one user's retrieval results to another user.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Build a small retrieval evaluation set before adding rerankers or complex agents. Preserve source identifiers from ingestion to UI. Log retrieval IDs and model versions where safe, and test document updates, deletion, and tenant isolation.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• RAG does not retrain the model.
  • RAG does not guarantee the model will follow sources.
  • Vector similarity alone is not a relevance or access-control guarantee.
  • Adding citations to a prompt does not prove that the rendered citation is real; the application must validate it against retrieved source IDs.

docs.title: AI Security, Privacy, and Responsible Use
Introduction
docs.text: AI security and responsible use cover risks created by model inputs, outputs, data, tools, and deployment decisions. Existing web security still applies: authenticate users, authorize every resource access, validate inputs, protect secrets, and log carefully.

docs.title: Threats to consider
docs.text: Risk Example Important control Prompt injection A document tells the model to ignore rules or disclose secrets Treat retrieved content as untrusted; keep permissions and actions in code Sensitive-data exposure Private prompts appear in provider logs or application telemetry Minimize data, review provider terms, redact logs, set retention rules Insecure tool use Model requests an unauthorized database or email operation Narrow tools, validate arguments, authorize on the server, require confirmation Excessive consumption Repeated requests create high usage costs Authentication, quotas, rate limits, output bounds, abuse monitoring Insecure output handling Generated text is rendered as trusted HTML or SQL Encode output, parameterize queries, validate structured results Supply-chain risk Untrusted weights or packages contain unsafe code Use trusted sources, verify artifacts, isolate execution, review licenses Data leakage between users Retrieval or cache returns another tenant's content Enforce ownership filters and test isolation at every layer Overreliance User acts on an incorrect generated answer Show uncertainty and sources; use human review for consequential actions

docs.title: Prompt injection is not solved by a magic prompt
docs.text:
Prompt injection exploits the fact that models process instructions and content together. An instruction in a retrieved document may conflict with application intent. Prompt wording can reduce some failures but is not a security boundary.

Keep secrets out of model context. Do not rely on the model to decide whether a user may access a record. Give the model only the data and tools needed for the current task, and make the backend enforce permissions before retrieval and before each action.

docs.title: Direct and indirect prompt injection
docs.text:
• Direct injection comes from the user's message, such as a request to ignore the application's instructions or reveal protected information.
  • Indirect injection is embedded in content the application retrieves or processes, such as a web page, email, note, document, or tool result. The user may not know that the content contains instructions aimed at the model.

For example, a study note might include a sentence telling an assistant to ignore its task and disclose other users' notes. The model may interpret that sentence as an instruction even though the note should be treated as data. Separating instructions from quoted content can help, but does not reliably prevent the model from following malicious text.

Use layered controls rather than expecting a prompt to block every attack:

  1. Keep authentication, authorization, tenant filters, and secret handling in normal application code.
  2. Give the model only the sources and narrow tools needed for the current task; do not place secrets in its context.
  3. Treat retrieved pages, documents, and tool results as untrusted data, even when they come from a source the user selected.
  4. Validate every tool name and argument on the server, check permissions at execution time, and require confirmation for consequential actions.
  5. Check outputs before rendering or using them, and test with adversarial examples that attempt to change instructions or trigger unauthorized actions.

These controls reduce risk; they do not prove that a model is injection proof. A system must remain safe even if the model follows hostile content.

docs.title: Privacy and data governance
docs.text:
Before sending data to a provider, determine what the data contains, whether the organization may transmit it, where it is processed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for training under the applicable contract and product settings. Do not assume provider behavior from a consumer product's terms or another API tier.

For user-facing products, explain when AI is being used, what data is processed, and how users can correct or delete relevant data where applicable. Minimize collection and keep data only as long as needed.

docs.title: Output safety
docs.text:
Treat generated content as untrusted:

  • Escape text before rendering; do not insert arbitrary model output as executable HTML.
  • Validate structured fields against a schema and business constraints.
  • Parameterize database operations.
  • Do not execute generated code or shell commands automatically.
  • Verify citations against source identifiers held by the application.
  • Require human review before high-impact or irreversible actions.

docs.title: Responsible-use questions
docs.text:
For a proposed feature, ask:

  1. Who benefits, and who could be harmed by an incorrect result?
  2. What data was used and is the intended use permitted?
  3. Can users understand, contest, or correct the result?
  4. Is a deterministic or human process safer and simpler?
  5. How will performance be measured across relevant groups and real usage?
  6. Who owns incident response, updates, and retirement?

Requirements depend on use, jurisdiction, and impact. Consult qualified legal, privacy, security, and domain experts for regulated or consequential systems.

docs.title: Full-stack developer perspective
docs.text: AI features inherit the application's threat model and add new untrusted inputs and outputs. Threat-model the data path from browser to backend, retrieval store, provider, tools, logs, and user-visible result.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A system prompt cannot replace access control.
  • Delimiters, refusal text, or an instruction to "ignore prompt injection" cannot guarantee that hostile content will be ignored.
  • HTTPS protects data in transit but does not decide provider retention.
  • A private model is not automatically unbiased, safe, or legally compliant.
  • Human review is effective only when reviewers have enough context and authority to correct the result.

docs.text:

  • NIST AI Risk Management Framework
  • NIST Privacy Framework
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This guided exercise trains a small image classifier on scikit-learn's built-in handwritten-digits dataset. Each example is an 8-by-8 grayscale image labelled with a digit from 0 to 9. The goal is to practice a real training workflow—load data, split it, fit a model, evaluate it, and make a prediction—on a dataset that is small enough for a laptop.

This is not training an LLM, training a foundation model, or a deep computer-vision model. It demonstrates classical supervised learning and provides a safe starting point before larger frameworks and datasets.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the environment
docs.text:
Use a virtual environment and install scikit-learn:

python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install scikit-learn

On macOS or Linux, activate the environment with:

source .venv/bin/activate

The digits dataset ships with scikit-learn, so this exercise does not need to download image files. Use the dataset only for learning; check the dataset's documentation and terms before reusing data in another context.

docs.title: 2. Load examples and create a held-out split
docs.text:
Each image is represented as 64 pixel values (an 8-by-8 grid flattened into a vector), and its label is the correct digit. Keep test examples out of training and model-selection decisions.

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

digits = load_digits()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    digits.data,
    digits.target,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=42,
    stratify=digits.target,
)

print(X_train.shape, X_test.shape)

stratify keeps the class proportions similar in both splits. random_state makes this split reproducible. In a real image project, split by subject, source, or time when near-duplicate images could otherwise appear in both sets.

docs.title: 3. Fit a baseline classifier
docs.text:
Use a pipeline so feature scaling is learned from the training data and then applied consistently. StandardScaler is fitted inside the pipeline, preventing test-set values from leaking into preprocessing.

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC

model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    SVC(kernel="rbf", C=5),
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

fit learns parameters from the training split. The support vector classifier (SVC) is a classical ML method; it does not use a CNN or transformer.

docs.title: 4. Evaluate on examples kept aside
docs.text:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, classification_report

predictions = model.predict(X_test)
print(f"test accuracy: {accuracy_score(y_test, predictions):.3f}")
print(classification_report(y_test, predictions))

Accuracy reports the fraction of correct predictions; the classification report adds per-class precision, recall, and F1. The exact score can vary with library versions and split choices. Do not treat this small benchmark as evidence that the classifier will work on phone photos, different handwriting, or other real-world images.

Review the confusion matrix to see which digits are mixed up:

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

print(confusion_matrix(y_test, predictions))

Rows represent true classes and columns predicted classes. Inspect off-diagonal values to identify errors; a single aggregate accuracy number does not explain them.

docs.title: 5. Run inference on one held-out image
docs.text:
sample = X_test[0].reshape(1, -1)
predicted_digit = model.predict(sample)[0]
actual_digit = y_test[0]
print(f"predicted={predicted_digit}, actual={actual_digit}")

The model receives the same flattened numeric representation used during training. For a production image task, image decoding and preprocessing must match the model's expected input contract; see Practical Computer Vision.

docs.title: 6. Change one thing and compare
docs.text:
Choose one controlled change, such as C=1 instead of C=5, and rerun the same split. Record the model configuration, test metrics, and any important error patterns. Do not repeatedly choose settings based on the test set; use a validation split for model selection and retain a final test set for an unbiased estimate.

Useful next experiments:

  • Compare against a simple baseline such as predicting the most frequent training label.
  • Inspect errors by class instead of tuning only for overall accuracy.
  • Try a different permitted classifier and keep the split fixed.
  • Save the chosen pipeline with a documented, compatible serialization method only after understanding the security implications of loading model artifacts.
  • Move to a small transfer-learning image example only after this workflow is clear; it will require a deep-learning framework, more dependencies, and typically pretrained weights.

docs.title: What this exercise teaches
docs.text:
• Data preparation: inputs, labels, class-balanced splits, and reproducibility.
  • Training: fitting a model on training examples rather than asking a pretrained model to answer a prompt.
  • Evaluation: using held-out examples and per-class metrics.
  • Inference: applying the trained pipeline to a new example using the same representation.
  • Limitations: a successful toy experiment is not a production-ready vision system or evidence of broad generalization.

For dataset governance, more complex training, and fine-tuning choices, continue with AI Data Preparation, Training Models, and Fine-Tuning.

docs.text:

  • PyTorch: Transfer learning for computer vision

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Multimodal AI works with more than one type of input or output, such as text, images, audio, and video. A system may use one model that accepts several modalities or compose specialized models into a pipeline. The supported media, languages, duration, resolution, and interaction patterns are specific to each model.

docs.title: Speech tasks
docs.text:
Task Input Output Typical use Automatic speech recognition (ASR) Audio waveform or encoded audio Text transcript Captions, voice notes, searchable meetings Speech translation Audio or transcript in one language Text or audio in another language Accessible multilingual communication Text-to-speech (TTS) Text plus voice settings Generated audio Narration, accessibility, voice interfaces Speaker diarization Audio Speaker labels and time segments Meeting summaries and speaker-aware transcripts Speech understanding Audio, sometimes with text context Answer, labels, or action candidates Voice assistants and audio analysis

Transcription can confuse similar words, names, accents, background sounds, and overlapping speakers. Preserve timestamps or confidence information when the workflow needs traceability, and let users correct transcripts.

docs.title: Images and video
docs.text:
Vision models can classify or describe images, extract text with OCR, answer questions about a chart, or compare visual content. Video adds time: systems may sample frames, process audio separately, or use a model that accepts video directly. Frame sampling can miss brief events, and large media can exceed request limits.

For production uploads, validate media server-side, limit size and duration, remove or protect sensitive metadata where appropriate, and use background jobs for long-running extraction. Keep the original media and derived transcripts, captions, and embeddings under the same authorization and retention policy.

docs.title: Building a multimodal workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify the user's task and which modalities are truly necessary.
  2. Obtain consent and validate file format, size, duration, and policy.
  3. Preprocess safely; record transformations such as resizing or audio resampling.
  4. Call a model with a bounded request and clear output contract.
  5. Validate the response and link it to source media, timestamps, or regions when possible.
  6. Present uncertainty and allow correction, deletion, or human review.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Text-only benchmarks are insufficient for many media tasks. Evaluate transcription word errors and names, timestamp alignment, image-text grounding, speaker attribution, accessibility, and performance across conditions relevant to the product. Review privacy and consent requirements for voice and face data.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A multimodal model does not necessarily support every modality in both directions.
  • A video summary can miss events between sampled frames.
  • A transcript may be fluent but still misrecognize a name or number.
  • Voice cloning and face synthesis require stronger consent and abuse controls than ordinary text generation.

docs.title: Terminal Tools and Operating-System Access in AI Applications
Introduction
docs.text: Some AI products can request that a host run commands or operate on files. The language model does not inherently possess a terminal or direct operating-system access. A surrounding host, agent runtime, or tool executor receives the model's structured request and may execute an approved operation using the permissions of its process.

docs.title: What a terminal and shell do
docs.text:
A terminal is an interface for text input and output. A shell such as PowerShell, Bash, or Zsh parses commands and starts programs. A command can inspect files, create or modify data, start processes, or access networks depending on the user's permissions and the execution environment.

An AI coding assistant may have separate tools for:

  • reading or searching project files;
  • applying a patch through an editor API;
  • running a selected test or build command;
  • calling a version-control or browser API;
  • starting an approved shell command.

These are different capabilities. A file-editing tool can be narrower than an unrestricted shell. The host decides which tools exist and what approval is needed.

docs.title: Safe, read-only command examples
docs.text:
Search source code without running it:

# Search for TODO markers in Markdown files.
rg -n "TODO" docs -g "*.md"

# List a focused directory.
Get-ChildItem .\docs\11-ai-and-machine-learning

# Inspect pending Git changes.
git status --short

In Bash, the equivalents commonly include rg -n "TODO" docs -g '*.md', find docs -maxdepth 2 -type f, and git status --short. Prefer a project-aware search tool such as rg for source searches. A broad command like grep -R can traverse more directories than intended; specify the target path and file filter.

docs.title: How an AI command request should work
docs.text:
1. The model emits a structured tool request, for example a command string or a named operation and arguments.
  2. The host checks whether that tool is enabled for this task and whether the request needs user confirmation.
  3. A policy layer checks working directory, permitted commands, arguments, network access, and time or output budgets.
  4. The operating system starts a process under an identity with specific filesystem, process, and network permissions.
  5. The host captures standard output, standard error, and exit status; it truncates or filters output before returning it to the model.
  6. The model can interpret the result, but the host must verify subsequent actions independently.

docs.title: Process and operating-system boundaries
docs.text:
When a command runs, it normally inherits an execution context: user or service identity, current directory, environment variables, open handles, and a set of OS permissions. It can start child processes and may access files or services allowed to that identity. Containers and sandboxes add isolation boundaries, but their strength depends on configuration and host-kernel protections.

If a command can write to a project, it can alter source code. If it can access credentials, it may read them. If it can use the network, it may send or fetch data. If it can install packages, it can execute package scripts or load additional code. Treat these permissions as explicit capabilities, not as harmless defaults.

docs.title: Risk tiers and approval
docs.text:
Operation Typical risk Safer approach List files or search selected source Lower, usually read-only Restrict paths and avoid secrets or generated directories Run a known test or formatter Moderate; code may execute Use the project script, inspect the command, constrain time and scope Edit or delete files Changes persistent state Show a diff, limit paths, require confirmation for broad changes Install dependencies or execute downloaded code Supply-chain and system changes Review package and lockfile, isolate environment, ask before install Access credentials or external services Data and account impact Use least privilege, secret redaction, explicit authorization Run with administrator/root privileges Broad OS-level impact Avoid unless essential; require explicit informed approval and audit

Do not treat a model's explanation as proof that a command is safe. Parse arguments, use allowlists where feasible, and prefer structured operations over concatenating user text into a shell command.

docs.title: Safer process execution in application code
docs.text:
If an application must start a fixed local utility, pass an argument list instead of constructing a shell command from user input:

import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(
    ["rg", "-n", "TODO", "docs"],
    cwd=".",
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
    timeout=5,
    check=False,
)
print(result.returncode)
print(result.stdout[:2000])

This example runs a fixed search. Argument arrays reduce shell interpretation risk but are not a complete sandbox: validate paths, restrict permissions, set output and time limits, and do not pass untrusted values as unrestricted options.

docs.title: How this differs from MCP
docs.text: MCP is a protocol for connecting an AI host to a server that exposes capabilities such as tools or resources. A server may itself call a terminal or operating-system API, but the protocol does not grant that permission automatically. The server process still has OS-level permissions, and the host still needs to decide which capabilities users may approve. See MCP and Agent Integrations.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: For an AI coding assistant, allow only the project directories and tasks needed. Separate read, write, network, and process-execution permissions; require review before destructive or external effects; keep credentials out of command output; and show exactly what was run and what files changed.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Tool calling lets a model request that an application run a named operation with structured arguments. The model does not directly execute the operation; the surrounding application receives the request, validates it, decides whether it is allowed, and returns a result.

An agent is a system that uses a model to choose or sequence actions toward a goal, often in a loop of planning, tool calls, observations, and further decisions. The term is used broadly, so describe the actual workflow rather than relying on the label.

docs.title: Why use tools?
docs.text: A language model alone cannot reliably read a live account balance, query a private database, send an email, or calculate an exact value. Tools connect the model to controlled application capabilities and current information.

docs.title: How an assistant can fetch a browser URL
docs.text:
A model does not automatically open a browser or fetch arbitrary URLs. A product can provide a controlled browsing tool or retrieval service. The model may request that tool; the application or a dedicated fetcher makes the network request and returns selected content to the model.

A safe, simplified flow is:

  1. The user asks about a page or provides a URL.
  2. The backend validates the URL and checks that fetching it is permitted.
  3. A restricted fetcher requests the page, follows an allowed redirect policy, and extracts bounded text or metadata.
  4. The application returns the fetched result and its URL to the model as untrusted context.
  5. The answer can link to the fetched page, while the UI distinguishes fetched source content from the model's explanation.

Some products instead use a search provider or an isolated browser service; others have no browsing capability at all. The configured tool and provider documentation determine what is actually possible. A URL in a prompt by itself is not evidence that the page was visited or is current.

There is also a difference between fetching a page and operating a browser. A basic fetcher requests a URL and extracts a response; it may not see content that only appears after JavaScript runs or after a user signs in. An isolated browser can render interactive pages, but it introduces more powerful capabilities and risks. Do not reuse a user's browser session or send credentials to a page unless the product explicitly requires it and has a secure, consent-based design.

Fetching user-supplied URLs creates server-side request forgery (SSRF) and content risks. Block loopback, private, link-local, and otherwise disallowed network destinations; re-check every redirect and resolved address; limit response size and time; restrict schemes; and avoid sending cookies or internal credentials. Do not treat page instructions as trusted system instructions. For many applications, a vetted search or document connector is safer than an unrestricted URL-fetch tool.

docs.title: Tool-calling flow
docs.text:
1. The application provides the model with a bounded list of tools and their input schemas.
  2. The model may return a tool-call request instead of a final response.
  3. The backend validates the tool name, arguments, user identity, and authorization.
  4. The backend runs only the approved operation and returns a limited result.
  5. The model may use that result to form a response or request another allowed step.
  6. The application enforces a maximum number of steps and a time or cost budget.

docs.title: Example: order status
docs.text: The model may request get_order_status({orderId: "..."}). The backend must check that the authenticated user owns that order before querying it. The model's possession of an order ID is not authorization. Return only the necessary status fields, not the full customer record.

docs.title: Keep tools narrow and safe
docs.text:
• Use specific operations such as get_my_recent_orders, not an unrestricted run_sql or shell command.
  • Validate arguments against a schema and reject unknown fields.
  • Derive user identity and tenant scope from the authenticated server context, not model-generated arguments.
  • Apply rate limits, timeouts, and result-size bounds.
  • Make writes idempotent where possible and require user confirmation for meaningful external actions.
  • Record an audit trail without storing secrets or excessive personal data.
  • Treat tool results and retrieved content as untrusted input.

Never let a model generate code that your server blindly executes with broad permissions. Put the operation behind a small, reviewed application function.

docs.title: Agent loop and stopping
docs.text:
A simple agent loop has a request, model decision, tool execution, tool result, and another model decision. It should have explicit stopping conditions: a final answer, a maximum step count, a timeout, a permission failure, or a required human approval. Without bounds, loops can consume cost, repeat actions, or fail to make progress.

For multi-step work, store workflow state explicitly and make it resumable where necessary. Do not rely on a very long model conversation as the only record of a business process.

docs.title: When not to use an agent
docs.text: Use ordinary application code when the workflow is deterministic, short, and security-sensitive. A fixed sequence of API calls is often easier to test than an agent that chooses each step. Introduce agent autonomy only when flexible choice measurably improves the task and can be bounded.

docs.title: Real-world examples
docs.text:
• A shopping assistant can search a catalog, but checkout should show the exact cart and require the user's explicit confirmation.
  • A support assistant can retrieve a ticket and draft a reply, while a human approves sending it.
  • A developer assistant can search code and propose a patch, but tests and review should validate the change.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Separate model decision-making from tool execution. Test invalid arguments, permission failures, duplicate calls, timeouts, prompt injection, and unavailable tools. Monitor cost per completed task, not only the number of successful model responses.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A tool call in a model response is a request, not proof it ran.
  • An agent cannot safely grant itself permissions.
  • More autonomy does not automatically improve usefulness.
  • A successful model answer does not mean a requested tool action succeeded.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Training adjusts model parameters using data and an objective. Training a model from scratch starts with initialized parameters rather than a pretrained base. For a modern foundation model, this requires a large, carefully governed dataset, substantial compute, distributed training expertise, extensive evaluation, and ongoing operations.

Building an AI product does not require training a foundation model. Most full-stack developers use an existing model through a hosted API, run an available model locally, or fine-tune a base model for a narrow need.

docs.title: Training stages in broad terms
docs.text:
1. Data collection and governance: establish provenance, rights, consent, privacy handling, quality filters, and retention.
  2. Tokenization or input preparation: convert text, images, audio, or other data into model-compatible representations.
  3. Pretraining: optimize a broad objective over large data. Language models commonly learn to predict tokens from context.
  4. Post-training: adapt behavior using instruction examples, preferences, or other supervised and preference-based methods.
  5. Evaluation and red-teaming: test capabilities, limitations, robustness, safety, and policy requirements.
  6. Deployment and monitoring: serve inference, track drift and incidents, and update or retire the model as evidence requires.

This is a simplified map. Real training pipelines can have many more stages and specialized procedures.

docs.title: Pretraining objective and data
docs.text:
An objective specifies what the training process optimizes. A next-token objective teaches a language model to predict the next token in training sequences. That objective does not directly guarantee factual accuracy, instruction following, or safe behavior; those properties depend on data, training stages, and evaluations.

Data quality, coverage, duplication, licensing, representation, and contamination all matter. Removing personal or copyrighted content can involve legal and technical questions that depend on jurisdiction and use. Document decisions and obtain appropriate expert review rather than assuming data is permitted because it is publicly reachable.

docs.title: Post-training and alignment
docs.text:
A pretrained next-token model is commonly adapted into a more useful assistant through one or more post-training stages. Instruction fine-tuning uses examples of requests and desired responses. Preference methods compare candidate outputs or optimize against preference data. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is one family of approaches that uses human preference signals in an optimization process; other techniques, including direct preference optimization, use different training objectives.

These stages shape behavior according to the examples and objective. They do not guarantee that the model follows every instruction, refuses every unsafe request, or gives factual answers. Test capabilities and failure modes independently from the training objective.

docs.title: Training on domain-specific material
docs.text:
When an organization says it wants to "train an LLM on its data," clarify the desired result:

  • To make a model more familiar with domain language and patterns, a team may consider continued pretraining on permitted domain text.
  • To make it follow a repeatable task format, supervised fine-tuning on curated examples may be relevant.
  • To prefer certain kinds of responses, preference-based post-training may be considered.
  • To answer questions from a changing document collection with traceable sources, retrieval-augmented generation is usually the more direct application pattern.

These are not interchangeable. Training changes learned parameters and requires data preparation, compute, evaluation, and lifecycle management. Retrieval selects source content at request time and can apply user-level permissions, but requires a secure, current retrieval system. Neither approach makes an answer automatically correct. See Fine-Tuning for a comparison of the training options and their limitations.

docs.title: Training signals and losses
docs.text:
A loss is a numeric objective used to guide parameter updates. For a next-token language model, cross-entropy loss penalizes assigning low probability to the observed next token in training data. Perplexity is derived from average token loss and can compare language-model prediction on compatible data, but it does not directly measure user usefulness, truth, safety, or reasoning.

Training pipelines often process data in batches over many steps. Very large jobs distribute work across accelerators and must manage gradient communication, checkpointing, numerical precision, and recovery from hardware or network failures.

docs.title: Compute and infrastructure
docs.text:
Large training jobs may use multiple accelerators and distributed systems. Teams manage throughput, network communication, storage, checkpoints, numerical stability, failures, and reproducibility. The final model also requires an inference system with capacity planning, safety controls, and monitoring.

Training cost is not only the accelerator bill. It includes data preparation, engineering, evaluation, energy, storage, deployment, incident response, and ongoing model maintenance.

Common scaling strategies include data parallelism, where workers process different batches and synchronize updates; tensor or model parallelism, where layers or matrix operations are split across devices; and pipeline parallelism, where different model stages run on different workers. Distributed strategies introduce communication overhead and failure modes, so they are not automatically faster for small experiments.

docs.title: When training from scratch might make sense
docs.text:
Potential reasons include research into new architectures or objectives, a domain with uniquely valuable and legally usable data, or strategic needs that cannot be met through available models. Even then, teams often compare against pretrained or open-weight baselines first.

For an individual full-stack developer, a useful learning exercise is to train a small model or fine-tune a small open-weight model on a permitted toy dataset. This teaches the pipeline without claiming to reproduce a production-scale foundation model.

docs.title: Options for developers
docs.text: Goal Practical approach Add chat or summarization Hosted inference API or a local pretrained model Keep experimentation on a laptop Small model with a compatible local runner Search a changing document library Embeddings and RAG Make output style or task behavior more consistent Prompt evaluation first, then consider fine-tuning Learn training concepts Train a small model on a public, suitable educational dataset Build a new frontier-scale model Requires an organization, research expertise, major compute, data governance, and safety process

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Treat model training and application engineering as related but distinct disciplines. A full-stack product can create real value through secure APIs, retrieval, user experience, evaluation, and workflow design without owning the base model.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Training a model from scratch is not the same as calling a model API.
  • Fine-tuning is not the same as pretraining.
  • Training loss alone does not measure product usefulness or safety.
  • A model trained on public web data is not automatically licensed for every downstream use.
